Once upon a time, there was a shy animal. This animal was very scared of people and would always hide whenever someone came near. One day, the animal saw a big puddle of water and decided to take a drink. As it was drinking, a little girl came by and said hello. The animal was scared at first, but the girl was very nice and didn't try to hurt the animal. Instead, she splashed in the puddle with the animal and they had a lot of fun together. From that day on, the animal wasn't so shy anymore and would come out to play with the little girl whenever she came by.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the yard. One day, Lily's mom gave her a rag to clean her toys.

Lily looked at the rag and said, "This rag is dull. I don't like it."

Her mom replied, "It may be dull, but it will clean your toys well."

Lily went outside to play and discovered a shiny rock. She picked it up and ran to her mom, saying, "Look what I found! It's shiny!"

Her mom smiled and said, "That's great, Lily. You can use that rock to polish your toys and make them shiny too."

Lily remembered what her mom said about the dull rag and realized that even though something may seem dull, it can still be useful. From then on, Lily used the rag to clean her toys and the shiny rock to make them sparkle.

name_of_work: The Song of the Wreck by Charles Dickens
content: The wind blew high, the waters raved, A ship drove on the land, A hundred human creatures saved Kneel'd down upon the sand. Three-score were drown'd, three-score were thrown Upon the black rocks wild, And thus among them, left alone, They found one helpless child. A seaman rough, to shipwreck bred, Stood out from all the rest, And gently laid the lonely head Upon his honest breast. And travelling o'er the desert wide It was a solemn joy, To see them, ever side by side, The sailor and the boy. In famine, sickness, hunger, thirst, The two were still but one, Until the strong man droop'd the first And felt his labours done. Then to a trusty friend he spake, "Across the desert wide, O take this poor boy for my sake!" And kiss'd the child and died. Toiling along in weary plight Through heavy jungle, mire, These two came later every night To warm them at the fire. Until the captain said one day, "O seaman good and kind, To save thyself now come away, And leave the boy behind!" The child was slumbering near the blaze: "O captain, let him rest Until it sinks, when God's own ways Shall teach us what is best!" They watch'd the whiten'd ashy heap, They touch'd the child in vain; They did not leave him there asleep, He never woke again.

Chaucer, 'The Pardoner's Prologue' The walk home from school got longer those first weeks of September, listening to the mini bus diminish through the hedges and trees, then slipping the straps of my bag over each shoulder to free up both hands for the picking of blackberries. Another lesson perhaps, this choice of how to take them. One by one, tracing their variety on my tongue, from the bitterness of an unripe red tightly packed as a nervous heart, to the rain-bloated looseness of those older, cobwebbed and dusty as a Claret laid down for years in a cellar. Or to hoard them? Piling in the palm until I cupped a coiled black pearl necklace, a hedgerow caviar, the bubbles of just poured wine stilled in my fingers which I'd take together, each an eye of one great berry, a sudden symphony. Or as I did just once, strolling towards the low house growing at the lane's end, not to eat them at all, but slowly close my palm into a fist instead, dissolving their mouthfeel over my skin and emerging from the hedge and tree tunnel, my knuckles scratched and my hand blue-black red, as bloodied as a butcher's or a farmer's at lambing, or that of a boy who's discovered for the very first time, just how dark he runs inside.

Once upon a time there was a little girl name Abbie. She was so happy and grateful for a special basket her Grandma had given her.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who lived on a farm with her mommy and daddy. She loved playing with the friendly sheep in the fields. Lily was sad because she couldn't play with her sheep friends. She went to her mommy and daddy, and they tried to unlock the gate, but the key was missing. They searched and searched, but they couldn't find it anywhere. 

Lily didn't give up. She decided to look for the key herself. She searched high and low, and finally found the key under a rock. She ran back to the gate, unlocked it, and was reunited with her friendly sheep friends. From then on, she made sure to keep the key in a safe place so that she could always play with her sheep.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Tim. Tim had an unusual belt. This belt was not like other belts. It could reveal things that were hidden. Tim liked to play with his belt and find new things.

One day, Tim was playing with his belt in the park. He saw a big tree and thought, "I will use my belt to reveal what is under the tree." He put the belt around the tree and pulled. Suddenly, a big hole opened up under the tree. Tim was very excited and wanted to see what was inside the hole.

Tim climbed down into the hole, but it was very dark. He could not see anything. He tried to use his belt to help him see, but it did not work. Tim was very scared and cried for help. But no one could hear him. Tim was stuck in the hole forever. The moral of the story is to be careful with unusual things and not to use them without knowing what they can do.

Once upon a time, there was a yummy strawberry. It was so tasty, that everyone wanted to have a bite. A little boy lived close to the strawberry and he wanted to have some. He wanted it all for himself, so he thought of a plan.

One day, he took a knife and he split the big, juicy strawberry into two pieces. It was so sweet that a little bee flew by and wanted some too. The little boy shared a tiny piece with the bee. But then he saw something very scary - a lot of gas coming from the ground.

The little boy was very scared. He knew that something awful was going to happen if he didn't run away fast. But he was too busy eating the yummy strawberry, so he didn't move away soon enough. An explosion happened and sadly, the little boy was hurt and hurt badly. The tasty strawberry was no more.

Once upon a time, there was a jolly little boy. His mommy had a special surprise for him - a lovely gift!

The little boy was so excited. He asked his mom, "What is it?" 

His mom smiled and told him, "Let me show you!" 

She opened the package and inside was a toy hammer. The little boy was delighted. He ran around and waved the hammer around asking "What can I do with it?" 

His mom said, "Let's build something together". So they put some blocks together and built a castle. Then the little boy hit it with his hammer and said, "I made it!" 

The mommy gave him a big hug and said, "I'm so proud of you." They had a jolly time together and the little boy thanked his mom for the special gift.

Once upon a time, there was a big, friendly dog named Max. Max loved to play fetch and go for walks with his owner, Emily. One day, Max and Emily went to the park to play. Max chased after the ball and brought it back to Emily.

Suddenly, a boy came over and said that he didn't like dogs. Emily asked him why and he said it was just his opinion. Max didn't like that and began to bark and yell at the boy. Emily told Max to calm down and that everyone has their own opinion.

After playing for a while longer, Emily and Max went home. Emily told Max that he was a brilliant dog and gave him a treat. Max wagged his tail happily and went to sleep, dreaming of playing fetch again the next day.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the bright sunshine. One day, she saw a butterfly fluttering by and she wondered where it was going. She followed it for a while, but then she had to pause and catch her breath. 

As she sat on a rock, she noticed a big tree with a swing hanging from its branches. She wondered if she could swing as high as the birds in the sky. She ran over to the swing and started to pump her legs back and forth. Soon, she was soaring high into the air, feeling the wind rush past her face. 

Suddenly, she heard her mom calling her for lunch, so she had to pause her swinging and run back home. As she sat at the table, she wondered what delicious food her mom had made for her. She was so happy and full of wonder about the world around her.

Once there was a stubborn girl named Sara. She wanted to take a taxi but her mom wanted her to walk. Sara refused and said no with a firm voice. Mom and Sara argued for a long time until Mom said, "Ok, you can take a taxi, but you'll have to examine it first."

So Sara went to take a look at the taxi. To her surprise, the taxi was old and dirty. Still, she found it interesting. She examined the taxi all around and felt its bumpers. She even knocked on the door to see if it was strong. In the end, she decided it was safe to ride in.

Sara enjoyed her ride. She waved to the people she saw on the street and sang songs to herself. When the taxi reached Sara's house, Mom was waiting with a smile. Finally, Sara had to admit her mom was right- it was a great experience. From then on she was more willing to try things.

Once upon a time, there was a wise man. He loved to create things. One day, he put together some special ingredients. He mixed them together and made something delicious. It was called chocolate!

The man enjoyed the chocolate so much that he decided to share it with everyone. He created more and more chocolate, in all sorts of shapes and sizes. He shared it with near and far.

The people loved the chocolate and thanked the wise man for his generosity. From then on, the man was known throughout the land as the chocolate-maker. He created chocolate for everyone and the people were forever grateful.

Once upon a time, there was a dependable truck. It had big, round tires, a shiny radiator and a loud horn. Every day, the truck drove along the highway as people watched.

One day, the truck got stuck. The driver tried to get it moving, but the engine would not start. He tried and tried and tried, but it was no use. He asked the people watching what he should do.

They said, "You should call a tow truck to help you."

So the driver made a call. But the tow truck said it was too busy, and it would not come right away. The driver had to delay.

Finally, after two hours, the tow truck showed up. The driver was so glad to see the tow truck and thanked it for coming. The tow truck hooked up the truck and towed it away.

The driver was thankful for the dependable tow truck. He thanked it again and gave it a friendly honk from his truck's horn!

name_of_work: Such Simple Love by Thomas McGrath
content: All night long I hear the sleepers toss Between the darkened window and the wall. The madman's whimper and the lover's voice, The worker's whisper and the sick child's call-- Knowing them all I'd walk a mile, maybe, hearing some cat Crying its guts out, to throttle it by hand, Such simple love I had. I wished I might-- Or God might--answer each call in person and Each poor demand. Well, I'd have been better off sleeping myself. These fancies had some sentimental charm, But love without direction is a cheap blanket And even if it did no one any harm, No one is warm.

The older kids laughed at him and Jack became very upset. He started to cry and ran away from the playground. He wanted to find his mommy to accept him no matter what.

Jack found his mommy, who gave him a big hug. His mommy told him that it was okay to accept motion no matter how hard it was. She said she was proud of him for trying.

Jack wiped away his tears and felt much better. He still wasn't very good at the motion the older kids were doing, but he was no longer upset. He was now happy and knew he was accepted no matter what.

Jack was a builder. He loved to build all kinds of things. He had hammers and nails and wood and all kinds of tools. 

One day, he found a big scale. It was so shiny and new! He was excited to build something with it. 

But when he looked closer, he saw that the scale was dirty. Jack knew he had to clean it first before he could build anything. 

So Jack grabbed a bucket and filled it with water. He washed the scale until it was very clean. Then he dried it off and put it back on the ground. 

Finally, Jack was ready to start building. He used the scale to make the most beautiful castle! Everyone in the village was amazed. 

Jack was proud of his work. He had built something special using the shiny, clean scale.

Once upon a time, there was a gray bird. He wanted to teach everyone how to tie a knot. 

He searched high and low but couldn't find anyone to teach. One day, he saw a small rabbit. He thought that the rabbit might be able to learn.

The bird flew right next to the rabbit and said, "Hello, rabbit! I have something special to teach you. I am going to show you how to tie a knot!" 

The rabbit was so excited. He watched very carefully as the bird showed him how to tie a knot. The bird slowly moved his beak in a round motion to make the knot. 

The rabbit tried to do it too. After a few tries, the rabbit was able to tie the knot all by himself. The bird was so proud of the little rabbit. 

From then on, the rabbit knew how to tie a knot and the bird went on to teach others how to tie knots. The End.

name_of_work: On My First Daughter by Ben Jonson
content: Here lies, to each her parents' ruth, Mary, the daughter of their youth; Yet all heaven's gifts being heaven's due, It makes the father less to rue. At six months' end she parted hence With safety of her innocence; Whose soul heaven's queen, whose name she bears, In comfort of her mother's tears, Hath placed amongst her virgin-train: Where, while that severed doth remain, This grave partakes the fleshly birth; Which cover lightly, gentle earth!

Once upon a time there was a great gem. The gem was so sparkly and bright! Everyone wanted to see it. 

One day a little girl named Hannah saw the gem. She smiled and reached out to touch it. But the gem was too high for her to reach.  

Hannah cried and cried, but the gem didn't come down. Suddenly a magical fairy came out of nowhere and said "I can help you!" 

The fairy waved her wand and the great gem floated down to where Hannah could touch it. She was so happy, she couldn't stop smiling. 

The fairy said, "Take the gem and remember, when you need help, I can always be there". 

Hannah thanked the fairy and with the gem in her hand, she ran off to show her friends.

name_of_work: At The Border, 1979 by Choman Hardi
content: 'It is your last check-in point in this country!' We grabbed a drink - soon everything would taste different. The land under our feet continued divided by a thick iron chain. My sister put her leg across it. 'Look over here,' she said to us, 'my right leg is in this country and my left leg in the other.' The border guards told her off. My mother informed me: We are going home. She said that the roads are much cleaner the landscape is more beautiful and people are much kinder. Dozens of families waited in the rain. 'I can inhale home,' somebody said. Now our mothers were crying. I was five years old standing by the check-in point comparing both sides of the border. The autumn soil continued on the other side with the same colour, the same texture. It rained on both sides of the chain. We waited while our papers were checked, our faces thoroughly inspected. Then the chain was removed to let us through. A man bent down and kissed his muddy homeland. The same chain of mountains encompassed all of us.

name_of_work: To the Mercy Killers by Dudley Randall
content: If ever mercy move you murder me, I pray you, kindly killers, let me live. Never conspire with death to set me free, but let me know such life as pain can give.. Even though I be a clot, an aching clench, a stub, a stump, a butt, a scab, a knob, a screaming pain, a putrefying stench, still let me live, so long as life shall throb. Even though I turn such traitor to myself as beg to die, do not accomplice me. Even though I seem no human, mute shelf of glucose, bottled blood, machinery to swell the lung and pump the heart-even so, do not put out my life. Let me still glow.

name_of_work: The Drowned Children by Louise Gluck
content: You see, they have no judgment. So it is natural that they should drown, first the ice taking them in and then, all winter, their wool scarves floating behind them as they sink until at last they are quiet. And the pond lifts them in its manifold dark arms. But death must come to them differently, so close to the beginning. As though they had always been blind and weightless. Therefore the rest is dreamed, the lamp, the good white cloth that covered the table, their bodies. And yet they hear the names they used like lures slipping over the pond: What are you waiting for come home, come home, lost in the waters, blue and permanent.

Once there was a little girl called Lola. She was only three years old, but she had a big adventure coming up. Lola was going on a plane to a faraway country and the most exciting thing of all was that she was going to get to visit the beach!

Before Lola left, her daddy gave her a passport. It was yellow with her name on it and Lola was so excited to have her own passport.

On the day of the trip, Lola was so excited she was jiggling in her seat. As they got off the plane and went through customs, Lola was confused when the woman asked her dad for a passport.

Lola quickly realized that she had left her passport at the check-in desk. She had scattered it with her other things, and forgotten to put it back in her bag. 

The woman allowed them through, but Lola and her dad had to use a fake passport â€” the one he'd made at home. 

Lola had a wonderful holiday, but she promised herself that she would never forget her passport again!

name_of_work: Flying Inside Your Own Body by Margaret Atwood
content: Your lungs fill & spread themselves, wings of pink blood, and your bones empty themselves and become hollow. When you breathe in you'll lift like a balloon and your heart is light too & huge, beating with pure joy, pure helium. The sun's white winds blow through you, there's nothing above you, you see the earth now as an oval jewel, radiant & seablue with love. It's only in dreams you can do this. Waking, your heart is a shaken fist, a fine dust clogs the air you breathe in; the sun's a hot copper weight pressing straight down on the think pink rind of your skull. It's always the moment just before gunshot. You try & try to rise but you cannot.

One day, a lazy cat named Tom was lying in the sun. He liked to sleep all day and not do much. Tom had a big bowl of food that was on a tip of a table. The table was near a tree.

A little bird saw the food on the tip of the table. The bird wanted to eat some of the cat's food. The bird flew down and started to eat the food. Tom woke up and saw the bird eating his food.

Tom jumped up to catch the bird, but something funny happened. The table shook and the food bowl fell off the tip. The food went all over the ground. The bird flew away and Tom was sad. From that day, Tom was not lazy anymore and he kept his food safe.

Once upon a time, there was a gray mouse who lived in a quiet house. He was very lonely, but one day he found something specialâ€”a special new friend.

His new friend was a beautiful blue butterfly and he called her Daisy. Daisy and the mouse became very close friends. They did everything together and were always happy.

One day, Daisy told the mouse that she had to take a trip and would not be around for a while. The mouse was very sad. Then, Daisy promised the mouse she would bring a special surprise back with her.

When Daisy arrived back home, she gave the mouse the surpriseâ€”it was a brand new red heart! The mouse was so happy to have a new replacement for Daisy's friendship, and he was even happier that it was a heartâ€”a special reminder of Daisy's love. 

The mouse and his new heart were very happy together, and they never felt lonely again! From then on, their house was filled with laughter and joy, in the quiet gray house.

Bob and Sarah are good friends. They both love to go to the park to play. Today, Bob and Sarah went to the park to enjoy the sunny day. 

First, they saw the swing. Bob and Sarah ran over to the swing and hopped on. They both enjoyed the wind on their faces as they flew back and forth. 

After a while, Bob and Sarah got scared of how high they were going. Bob slowly slowed down the swing until they both stopped. They were happy to have the swing all to themselves.

Bob and Sarah enjoyed their time on the swings. They had so much fun that they decided to come back to the park again soon.

Our Mothers, lovely women pitiful; Our Sisters, gracious in their life and death; To us each unforgotten memory saith: "Learn as we learned in life's sufficient school, Work as we worked in patience of our rule, Walk as we walked, much less by sight than faith, Hope as we hoped, despite our slips and scathe, Fearful in joy and confident in dule." I know not if they see us or can see; But if they see us in our painful day, How looking back to earth from Paradise Do tears not gather in those loving eyes?-- Ah, happy eyes! whose tears are wiped away Whether or not you bear to look on me.

Once upon a time there was a man who was very ignorant. One day he saw a window and wanted it for himself. He went up to the window and said, "I want to give you this window!"

The window didn't answer him. Instead, a small voice said, "Please don't take my window!" 
The man looked down and saw a little girl in a pink dress. She had big eyes with tears spilling down her cheeks. 

The man felt bad and said, "I'm sorry! I didn't know this window was yours. I won't take it." He smiled kindly and gave the little girl a hug. 

The girl smiled back and said, "Thank you! Can I give you something?" She reached behind her and brought out a small box. 

The man opened the box and saw a beautiful keychain. He thanked the little girl and accepted her gift. Then he went on his way, feeling glad that he was no longer so ignorant.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She had a pot that she loved to play with. One day, she saw her friend Sarah playing with a pot too, but it was different from hers. 

Lily said, "Sarah, your pot is different from mine. Can I see it?" 

Sarah said, "Sure, you can squeeze it too. It's fun!" 

Lily squeezed Sarah's pot and giggled. Then, Sarah asked, "Do you want to trade pots for a little while?" 

Lily thought about it and said, "Yes, let's trade pots!" They played with each other's pots and had fun. 

After a while, they traded back and Lily said, "Thank you for letting me play with your different pot, Sarah. It was so much fun!" 

Sarah replied, "You're welcome, Lily. I'm glad we could play together."

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Beth. Beth was very clever, and liked to admire things. One day, Beth went upstairs to her bedroom to admire the flowers outside her window.

As Beth looked out of her bedroom window at the pretty flowers, her mum came in and asked her what she was looking at. Beth smiled and said, "I'm admiring the flowers. They're so colourful and happy!â€

Mum smiled and said, "Yes, they are very pretty. You are so clever to appreciate them." Beth was very happy to hear this, and ran out of her bedroom to play. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a lamp in her room that shone bright and clear. Every night, Lily's mommy would turn on the lamp and read her a story. Lily loved listening to the stories and would always applaud when her mommy finished. 

One day, Lily went to a show with her mommy and daddy. There were dancers and singers on the stage. When the show ended, everyone in the audience started to applaud. Lily clapped her hands too, and she felt very happy. 

After the show, Lily and her family went to a restaurant. There was a big fish tank in the middle of the room. Lily saw a fish that was stuck in some plants. She pointed it out to her mommy, who told the waiter. The waiter came and cleared the plants so the fish could swim freely again. Lily was happy that the fish was okay.

Once upon a time, there was a big park with a long line to get on the swings. A little girl named Lily wanted to play on the swings, but the line was too long. She stood at the back of the line and waited patiently.

Suddenly, an unusual sound came from the trees. "What was that?" Lily asked the boy in front of her. "I don't know," he replied. "Maybe it's a bird?"

The sound grew louder and louder until a big, friendly dog came running out of the trees. The dog ran straight to Lily and stood next to her. "Wow, what an unusual dog!" Lily exclaimed.

The boy in front of her smiled and said, "Looks like you have a new friend to play with on the swings!" And sure enough, Lily and the dog played on the swings together until it was time to go home. From that day on, Lily and her new friend stood in line together every time they visited the park.

Sara and Tom are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big dog. The dog has brown fur and a long tail. He looks friendly.

"Hello, dog. What is your name?" Sara asks.

The dog wags his tail and barks. He likes Sara and Tom.

"His name is Max. He is my dog. Do you want to play with him?" A boy comes out of a house. He has a leash in his hand.

"Yes, please. We like dogs. We have a cat at home. Her name is Luna. She is white and soft." Tom says.

"OK, then. Let's go to the park. Max loves to run and fetch. Are you ready?" The boy says.

Sara and Tom nod. They are ready. They follow the boy and Max to the park. They have a lot of fun. They make a new friend. They are happy.

Once upon a time, there was a normal glove. It belonged to a girl, who liked to play with it in the garden. 

One day, the girl put the glove on and waved her hand around. Suddenly, she felt something move inside the glove, and when she looked inside she saw something small and furry!

It was a little mouse! The girl took the glove off carefully, so that she wouldn't hurt the mouse.

The girl ran to find her dad and soon the two were in the garden, looking at the mouse. Her dad smiled and fetched a box from inside. He carefully put the glove in the box and the mouse came out.

The mouse quickly ran away into the garden. The little girl and her dad watched it until it was out of sight.

The girl smiled and hugged her glove. Dad said it was ok to put it back on and go play. And so the girl put it back on, and began to play again in the garden.

The adventure had ended, but it was a happy ending - just like a normal day should be.

Once upon a time, there was a girl who had a very special case. Inside was something that was very important to her. Every night, she would open her case and take out a special book. She would spend hours signing in the book.

One night, when the girl was signing in her book, her brother walked into the room. He saw what she was doing and started to laugh. The girl was embarrassed and quickly shut her case. 

From then on, the girl was too embarrassed to take her case out again. She was afraid her brother would make fun of her.

But one day, her brother told her he was sorry for embarrassing her. He said he was proud of her for spending so much time signing in her special book. 

From then on, the girl was no longer embarrassed. She was glad she had a brother who encouraged her to do what she loved. And the girl was very happy to keep signing in her special case. The end.

Once there was a great dog called Max. He loved to run and play all day. One day, when Max was playing, he found a strange bottle with something inside. He was curious and started to sniff it. Suddenly, the lid came off and out flew a little creature with wings!
 It was an ink fairy! Max barked in surprise.

The little fairy smiled at Max and said, â€œHello, Iâ€™m Ink! I guess you found my bottle â€“ thank you for releasing me. Iâ€™ve been trying to get out for days!â€ Max was so happy that he barked and wagged his tail.

Ink explained that she was a magical fairy who could make anything happen with her special ink. â€œI can grant any wish you want!â€ she said. Max was so excited, he started to jump around in circles.

Ink asked Max what his wish was. Max thought for a minute, then said, â€œHow about a doggy treat? I love doggy treats!â€ Suddenly, a big doggy treat appeared! Max barked and ran around with excitement.

Ink said, â€œThat was a great wish, Max. You deserve lots of doggy treats!â€ 
Max thanked Ink and said goodbye before running off to eat his special treat. Max and Ink were happy to have found each other, and they both had a great

Tom and Sam are brothers. They like to play with their toy cars. They have many cars of different colors and sizes. They drive them on the floor, on the sofa, on the table. They make sounds like vroom, beep, honk.

One day, their mom gives them a big envelope. She says it is a surprise for them. She tells them to open it together. Tom and Sam are very excited. They wonder what is inside the envelope. They think maybe it is a new car, or a book, or a puzzle.

They run to their room and tear the envelope open. They see a picture of a real car. It is red and shiny. It has four doors and a big trunk. It looks very fast and cool. They also see a note from their dad. He writes that he loves them very much and that he has a big gift for them. He says he will come home soon and drive them in his new car.

Tom and Sam are very happy. They hug the picture and the note. They thank their mom and tell her they love her too. They can't wait to see their dad and his new car. They imagine how fun it will be to drive with him. They feel calm and safe. They put the picture and the note on their wall. They play with their toy cars until it is time for bed.

Silent night! Holy night! All are sleeping, alone and awake Only the intimate holy pair, Lovely boy with curly hair, Sleep in heavenly peace! Sleep in heavenly peace! Silent night! Holy night! John was persistent in finding a way to restore the old refrigerator. He looked for help from all his family members, but nobody could do it. He was disappointed and didn't know what to do.

But one day, John remembered a story that his grandma told him. She said that if you think hard and use your imagination, you can do anything.

So, John closed his eyes and concentrated very hard. And suddenly, he knew exactly how to fix the refrigerator. He grabbed the tools he needed, and began working on the refrigerator. It was tricky, but with a lot of patience, John was able to fix it!

John was so happy to see the refrigerator restored back to its original condition. He had done it all by himself, and was proud of his accomplishment.

name_of_work: See It Through by Edgar Albert Guest
content: When you're up against a trouble, Meet it squarely, face to face; Lift your chin and set your shoulders, Plant your feet and take a brace. When it's vain to try to dodge it, Do the best that you can do; You may fail, but you may conquer, See it through! Black may be the clouds about you And your future may seem grim, But don't let your nerve desert you; Keep yourself in fighting trim. If the worst is bound to happen, Spite of all that you can do, Running from it will not save you, See it through! Even hope may seem but futile, When with troubles you're beset, But remember you are facing Just what other men have met. You may fail, but fall still fighting; Don't give up, whate'er you do; Eyes front, head high to the finish. See it through!

One day, a little girl named Lucy went to the zoo with her mom. They saw many animals, like a big elephant, a funny monkey, and a tall giraffe. But Lucy's favorite animal was the panda. She loved how the panda looked with its black and white fur.

In the panda area, Lucy saw a mysterious box. She asked her mom, "What is in that box?" Her mom said, "I don't know, but it seems important." Lucy thought about the box while they walked around the zoo.

At the end of the day, they went back to the panda area. The zookeeper opened the mysterious box. Inside was a baby panda! Lucy was so happy to see the baby panda. The zookeeper said, "This baby panda was a surprise for everyone today!" Lucy knew the box was important, and she was glad she got to see the baby panda.

Anna and Ben were playing in the garden. They liked to dig in the dirt and look for bugs. Anna found a big worm and showed it to Ben.

"Look, Ben, a worm! It is long and slimy. Do you want to touch it?" Anna asked.

Ben was afraid of worms. He thought they were gross and scary. He shook his head and backed away.

"No, Anna, I don't want to touch it. It is yucky and icky. It might be poison. Throw it away!" Ben said.

Anna was angry. She thought Ben was silly and rude. She wanted to make him embarrassed. She had a naughty idea. She ran after Ben with the worm in her hand.

"Ben, Ben, look at the worm! It wants to be your friend. It wants to give you a kiss!" Anna shouted.

Ben screamed and ran away. He tripped over a bucket and fell on the grass. The worm flew out of Anna's hand and landed on his face. Ben cried and wiped the worm off. He was very embarrassed. He felt something wet on his cheek. He looked and saw blood. He had cut himself on the bucket.

Anna saw Ben's blood and felt sorry. She realized she had been mean and hurtful. She ran to Ben and hugged him.

"Ben, Ben, I'm sorry. I didn't mean to make you embarrassed. I didn't mean to hurt you. Are you okay?" Anna said.

Ben was still crying. He was angry and sad. He pushed Anna away.

"Go away, Anna. You are a bad friend. You are not nice. You are not tidy. You made me bleed. I don't want to play with you anymore!" Ben said.

Anna felt sad and ashamed. She wished she had not played with the worm. She wished she had been kind and gentle. She learned a lesson. She learned that making fun of someone is not funny. She learned that playing with poison is not smart. She learned that being tidy is not only about things, but also about words and actions. She hoped Ben would forgive her. She hoped they could be friends again.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Megan. She loved to play and explore. She especially loved finding new things. One day, Megan was walking in the park when she spotted something shiny on the ground. It was a key! She picked it up and was excited to show it to her friends. 

Megan showed the key to her friends, who all said it was very cool. Then, the group had a fun idea. They decided to display the key in the garden. So they dug a small hole and put the key in. 

Meanwhile, some funny animals had watched the whole thing. They decided to join in the fun. They helped to bury the key and stepped back to admire their work. 

The next day, Megan returned to the park and was amazed by what she saw - the key was proudly displayed for all of the world to enjoy! She showed it to her friends and smiled. Megan was very proud of her work. 

The End.

Once upon a time there was a little girl. She was very upset because she had a bad nightmare. It made her feel scared and sad.

So one night she asked her parents to help her feel better. They comforted her and made her feel better. Then they told her to stand up and take a deep breath. 

She listened to her parents and slowly got out of bed. She slowly took a deep breath in and out. Then she felt her bad nightmare going away. 

Soon she was feeling much better and the nightmare was gone. She thanked her parents for helping her feel better and hugged them tight. She was so happy to feel better again! 

And that is why it is important to talk to your parents when you are upset. They can always help you feel better and make the bad nightmares go away.

Once upon a time there was a pen. It was a special pen because this pen could come alive.

One day, it decided to go on an adventure. It came out of the house and started walking down the street. Suddenly, it saw a little girl sitting by herself. She was looking sad.

The pen came closer and asked her what the matter was. The girl said she was too ashamed to tell anyone.

The pen was kind and said, "It's ok. You can tell me, I won't tell anyone."

So the girl told the pen her secret. It turned out that she had lost her mother's pen and was too scared to tell her.

The pen was very happy! It had been looking for a purpose and this was it. "I'll help you!", it exclaimed.

The pen and the girl went looking for the missing pen. After a few hours of searching, they found it!

The girl was so happy and she hugged the pen tightly. She thanked it for being so kind and helping her.

The pen smiled and was happy it had come alive and gone on an adventure. From then on, it always tried to help others in need.

Once upon a time, there was a little fish named Nemo. Nemo was swimming in the ocean and saw a yellow shark. Nemo was scared and swam away as fast as he could. 

Nemo met his friend, a crab named Crabby, and told him what he saw. "I saw a yellow shark!" Nemo said. "Oh no, that's not good," said Crabby. "Sharks can be dangerous."

Nemo was worried and didn't want to swim anymore. But Crabby told him, "Don't be afraid. Just spread your fins and swim away fast if you see the shark again." 

Nemo listened to Crabby and felt better. He realized that he didn't have to be scared if he knew what to do. The moral of the story is that even if something scares you, you can still be brave and smart.

name_of_work: Anne Hathaway by Carol Ann Duffy
content: 'Item I gyve unto my wief my second best bed...' (from Shakespeare's will) The bed we loved in was a spinning world of forests, castles, torchlight, cliff-tops, seas where he would dive for pearls. My lover's words were shooting stars which fell to earth as kisses on these lips; my body now a softer rhyme to his, now echo, assonance; his touch a verb dancing in the centre of a noun. Some nights I dreamed he'd written me, the bed a page beneath his writer's hands. Romance and drama played by touch, by scent, by taste. In the other bed, the best, our guests dozed on, dribbling their prose. My living laughing love - I hold him in the casket of my widow's head as he held me upon that next best bed.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Jack. He loved puzzles. His mom gave him a smelly puzzle. He said it made his nose scrunch! He tried to put it together but he had a hard time. So his mom said, "Let's eat and then you can try again."

Jack was so excited. He went and got his bowl and spoon. He filled it with cereal and milk. Then he started eating. He ate and ate until he finished it all.

After he was done, he went back to the puzzle. He worked on it for a while and then he put it together! It was amazing! Jack was so happy that he solved the smelly puzzle. From that day on, he always loved puzzles.

One sunny day, a little girl named Lily went to the park with her mom. They sat down on a bench and shared some grapes. "Mommy, can we drive to the store and get more grapes?" asked Lily. "Sure, we can go for a drive and get some more grapes," replied her mom.

So, they got into their car and drove to the store. They found some really juicy grapes that were rich in flavor. "These grapes are so yummy!" said Lily. "Yes, they are very delicious," agreed her mom.

On the way back home, they saw a big truck driving on the road. "Look, Mommy! That truck is so big!" exclaimed Lily. "Yes, it is a very big truck," said her mom. When they got home, they enjoyed their grapes and talked about their fun drive to the store.

John was so excited for his first day of school. He put on his special shirt, tied his shoelaces, and was ready to go. His mom drove him to school and mentioned the exam he'd have in a few weeks. John was a bit nervous at first, but then his mom said that if he studied hard he could have a delicious reward after the exam. 

John felt better and set off to school with a smile on his face. Every day he got better and better at school, and made lots of new friends. 

When the day of the exam arrived, John was a bit nervous but also excited. He was sure that he'd pass if he just tried his best. After the exam, sure enough, he passed with flying colors. When he got home, his mom had a surprise: the most tasty chocolate cake he had ever seen! He was very excited and thanked his mom for the reward. 

John had enjoyed the exam and the reward so much that he couldn't wait for the next one. He was sure that that one would be even more fun.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy who loved to go on journeys. He was always eager to explore new places and see new things. One day, Timmy decided to go on a journey to find a treasure. He got his backpack and started walking.

As he walked, Timmy saw many things he had never seen before. He saw big trees, little animals, and a river with fish swimming in it. He was so excited to keep going and see what else he could find.

After a while, Timmy got tired and sat down to rest. He looked in his backpack and saw that he had forgotten to bring a snack. He was hungry and sad, but he knew he had to keep going to find the treasure. So, he got up and continued on his journey, hoping to find something to eat along the way.

Once upon a time, there was a group of animals. They were all friends but they lived far apart from each other. One day, they decided to unite and live together in a big forest.

As they were walking together, they saw an arrow on the ground. They didn't know where it came from or who shot it. It was unknown to them.

But they didn't let the unknown arrow scare them. They continued to walk together and explore their new home in the big forest. They were happy to be united and living together as friends.

name_of_work: Introduction to Poetry by Billy Collins
content: I ask them to take a poem and hold it up to the light like a color slide or press an ear against its hive. I say drop a mouse into a poem and watch him probe his way out, or walk inside the poem's room and feel the walls for a light switch. I want them to waterski across the surface of a poem waving at the author's name on the shore. But all they want to do is tie the poem to a chair with rope and torture a confession out of it. They begin beating it with a hose to find out what it really means.

Once upon a time, there was a little dog named Max. Max had an owner named Tim. Tim loved Max very much and always made sure he had food to eat.

One day, Max was feeling very hungry. He barked and barked until Tim gave him some food to eat. After eating, Max felt better and decided to play outside.

Max saw a big tree and wanted to climb it. He tried and tried, but he couldn't climb very high. Tim saw Max struggling and helped him climb to the top of the tree. Max was so happy and wagged his tail. From then on, Max knew he could always count on Tim to help him when he needed it.

Ink runs from the corners of my mouth. There is no happiness like mine. I have been eating poetry. The librarian does not believe what she sees. Her eyes are sad and she walks with her hands in her dress. The poems are gone. The light is dim. The dogs are on the basement stairs and coming up. Their eyeballs roll, their blond legs burn like brush. The poor librarian begins to stamp her feet and weep. She does not understand. When I get on my knees and lick her hand, she screams. I am a new man. I snarl at her and bark. I romp with joy in the bookish dark.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the mud. One day, Lily was playing in the mud when her friend Max came over.

"Hi Lily, what are you doing?" Max asked.

"I'm playing in the mud. Do you want to play with me?" Lily asked.

Max thought about it for a moment and said, "I don't want to get my clothes dirty."

"It's okay, Max. We can wash them later. Let's unite and have fun together!" Lily said.

Max decided to join Lily and they both played in the mud together. They made mud pies and splashed in the mud puddles. When they were finished, they both had to take a fine shower to clean themselves up. They had so much fun playing together in the mud that they couldn't wait to do it again.

Once upon a time, there was a poor little girl named Lily. She lived in a small house with her mommy and daddy. They didn't have a lot of toys or money, but they had each other and that made them happy.

One day, Lily went to the park to play. She saw a big spirit flying in the sky. It was so pretty! Lily wanted to catch it, but she couldn't reach it. She felt sad and started to cry.

Then, a boy came up to her and told her a joke. It was so funny that Lily stopped crying and started to laugh. The boy made her feel better and they became friends. Even though Lily was poor, she knew that having friends was the most important thing in the world.

Once upon a time, there were two best friends, Tom and Harry. Tom liked to go to the market, while Harry liked to stay at home.

One day, Tom excitedly asked Harry if he wanted to come to the market. "Yes!" said Harry, excitedly. 

The two happily walked to the market, and they looked all around. Tom saw all of the different treats that he could order. He wanted them all! 

Harry saw something that looked different than the other treats. He pointed it out to Tom, and asked what it was. Tom grinned, and told Harry that it was his favorite treat - ice cream! 

Tom quickly ordered two scoops, and the two happily enjoyed the treat together.  It was the best market trip ever!

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. He loved to play by the river with his toy raft. Tim was very independent and liked to play alone.

One day, Tim went to the river and stared at the water. He put his raft in the water and watched it float away. The raft went far, far away. Tim wanted to get his raft back, so he walked along the river.

As Tim followed the raft, it got dark and he became lost. He was scared and didn't know what to do. Tim called for help, but no one could hear him. He sat down and cried, wishing he hadn't been so independent.

Once upon a time there was a volcano. It was big and strong and it was very enthusiastic. Every day it would smoke and puff, and sometimes a big bubble would appear and pop.

One day the volcano begged for help. "Please someone help me," it said. Everyone was a bit scared of the volcano, so nobody answered. 

But then, a brave little girl heard it and said, "I will help." She was very enthusiastic and wanted to do something nice. 

So she put her hands in the volcano and pushed. There was a lot of smoke and dirt, but soon it was gone. All the people around cheered and thanked the brave little girl. 

"Thank you for helping us," said the volcano. All the animals and people were very happy and said, "Thank you!" 

The brave little girl was so proud. She knew she had made the volcano and everyone very happy.

Lily and Tom are friends. They like to play outside. But today the weather is bad. It is cold and wet and windy. Lily and Tom are sad.

They look out the window and see the gray sky. They see the rain and the leaves. They see the cars and the people with umbrellas. They want to go out and have fun.

Lily has an idea. She runs to her room and gets her crayons and paper. She comes back and gives some to Tom. She says, "Let's draw what we want to do outside. Maybe the weather will get better soon."

Tom likes the idea. He takes a crayon and starts to draw. He draws a big sun and a blue sky. He draws a green park and a slide. He draws himself and Lily smiling and holding hands.

Lily draws too. She draws a rainbow and some clouds. She draws a lake and a boat. She draws herself and Tom wearing hats and sunglasses.

They show each other their drawings and laugh. They feel happy. They put their drawings on the wall. They say, "These drawings remind us of the good weather. We hope it comes back soon. But we can still have fun inside."

One day, Jackie was playing in her house and she saw something strange. She noticed that there was a big wall blocking her from getting outside. Jackie had never seen a wall before and she was very upset.

Jackie decided to talk to a grown-up. She found her mom and said, â€œMom, why is there a wall? I want to go outside.â€ 

Her mom smiled at her and said, â€œThat wall is there to keep you safe. You donâ€™t need to be upset.â€  

Jackie nodded and smiled. She was happy that the wall was there to keep her safe. She gave the wall a big hug and started counting again, looking forward to the adventures she would have outside.

name_of_work: One's-Self I Sing by Walt Whitman
content: One's-Self I sing, a simple separate person, Yet utter the word Democratic, the word En-Masse. Of physiology from top to toe I sing, Not physiognomy alone nor brain alone is worthy for the Muse, I say the Form complete is worthier far, The Female equally with the Male I sing. Of Life immense in passion, pulse, and power, Cheerful, for freest action form'd under the laws divine, The Modern Man I sing.

Once upon a time, a little girl named Lily went to the park. She saw a squirrel on a tree and said, "Hello, squirrel!" The squirrel looked at Lily and ran away. Lily said, "I guess the squirrel is shy."

Lily then saw her friend Timmy eating a yummy snack. She asked him, "What are you eating, Timmy?" Timmy said, "I'm eating a yummy apple." Lily said, "Can I have a bite?" Timmy said, "Sure!" and gave her a piece of the yummy apple.

As they were eating, they saw the squirrel again. It was looking for some nuts to eat. Lily said, "Look, Timmy! The squirrel is hungry. Let's give it some nuts." They gave the squirrel some nuts and it was very happy. They all became friends and had a fun day at the park. The end.

Once upon a time there was a little girl. She was very sad because she had worry. She was worry about her Daddy who sometimes said harsh words to her.

So one day she told her Mummy about her worry. She said, "Mummy I worry about Daddy, he is so harsh sometimes".

Her Mummy hugged her, and said, "I know you worry about Daddy, but he still loves you very much."

So little girl decided to try and be brave, and not worry anymore. She smiled, and decided to give Daddy a big hug the next time he said something harsh.

And it worked - when she hugged her Daddy, he stopped saying harsh words and he smiled at her. Little girl was so happy, she stopped worrying and was happy ever after.

name_of_work: Hide and Seek by Vernon Scannell
content: Call out. Call loud: 'I'm ready! Come and find me!' The sacks in the toolshed smell like the seaside. They'll never find you in this salty dark, But be careful that your feet aren't sticking out. Wiser not to risk another shout. The floor is cold. They'll probably be searching The bushes near the swing. Whatever happens You mustn't sneeze when they come prowling in. And here they are, whispering at the door; You've never heard them sound so hushed before. Don't breathe. Don't move. Stay dumb. Hide in your blindness. They're moving closer, someone stumbles, mutters; Their words and laughter scuffle, and they're gone. But don't come out just yet; they'll try the lane And then the greenhouse and back here again. They must be thinking that you're very clever, Getting more puzzled as they search all over. It seems a long time since they went away. Your legs are stiff, the cold bites through your coat; The dark damp smell of sand moves in your throat. It's time to let them know that you're the winner. Push off the sacks. Uncurl and stretch. That's better! Out of the shed and call to them: 'I've won! Here I am! Come and own up I've caught you!' The darkening garden watches. Nothing stirs. The bushes hold their breath; the sun is gone. Yes, here you are. But where are they who sought you?

Once upon a time there was a boy named John. He was three years old and liked to have fun.

One day, John decided to stand in an orderly line with some of his friends. He got in a line that was very long. He was excited to have so many friends around him.

They all stood quietly and the line started to move. John and his friends all took a few steps forward.

John waited patiently until it was his turn. The line was very long and it took a long time for John to get to the front. But finally, he reached the front of the line and it was his turn to pick something.

John decided to pick a toy. He was so happy! He thanked everyone in the line for waiting so patiently and went back to his place.

John and his friends were very happy to be standing together in the orderly line. They had lots of fun and the line was a long one.

The End.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside in his backyard. One day, he saw something strange happen. He saw a bird fly into his backyard and land on the ground.

"Hello, little birdie," said Timmy. "What are you doing here?"

"I'm thirsty," said the bird. "I need water."

Timmy knew just what to do. He took the bird to the oasis in his backyard. The oasis was a small pond with regular water. The bird drank some water and felt better.

"Thank you, Timmy," said the bird. "You saved my life."

"You're welcome," said Timmy. "I'm happy to help."

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He loved to eat cookies, especially the ones his mom made. One day, he was walking in the park and saw a beautiful light shining in the sky. It was so pretty that he wanted to touch it. But he couldn't reach it.

He saw a bird flying and asked, "Birdie, can you help me reach the light?" The bird replied, "I can't, but I can show you where to find more delicious cookies." Timmy was happy and followed the bird.

They walked and walked until they found a bakery. Timmy saw a big cookie jar and wanted to take one, but it was too high. He struggled to reach it, but the jar was too far. The baker saw him and said, "Do you need help?" Timmy replied, "Yes, please. Can you give me a cookie?" The baker smiled and gave him a delicious cookie. Timmy was happy and thanked the baker and the bird. They all enjoyed the cookies together.

name_of_work: Wild With All Regrets by Wilfred Owen
content: To Siegfried Sassoon My arms have mutinied against me--brutes! My fingers fidget like ten idle brats, My back's been stiff for hours, damned hours. Death never gives his squad a Stand-at-ease. I can't read. There: it's no use. Take you book. A short life and a merry one, my buck! We said we'd hate to grow dead old. But now, Not to live old seems awful: not to renew My boyhood with my boys, and teach 'em hitting, Shooting and hunting,--all the arts of hurting! --Well, that's what I learnt. That, and making money. your fifty years in store seem none too many; But I've five minutes. God! For just two years To help myself to this good air of yours! One Spring! Is one too hard to spare? Too long? Spring air would find its own way to my lung, And grow me legs as quick as lilac-shoots. Yes, there's the orderly. He'll change the sheets When I'm lugged out, oh, couldn't I do that? Here in this coffin of a bed, I've though I'd like to kneel and sweep his floors for ever,-- And ask no nights off when the bustle's over, For I'd enjoy the dirt; who's prejudiced Against a grimed hand when his own's quite dust,-- Less live than specks that in the sun-shafts turn? Dear dust,--in rooms, on roads, on faces' tan! I'd love to be a sweep's boy, black as Town; Yes, or a muckman. Must I be his load? A flea would do. If one chap wasn't bloody, Or went stone-cold, I'd find another body. Which I shan't manage now. Unless it's yours. I shall stay in you, friend, for some few hours. You'll feel my heavy spirit chill your chest, And climb your throat on sobs, until it's chased On sighs, and wiped from off your lips by wind. I think on your rich breathing, brother, I'll be weaned To do without what blood remained me from my wound.

Love bade me welcome. Yet my soul drew back Guilty of dust and sin. But quick-eyed Love, observing me grow slack From my first entrance in, Drew nearer to me, sweetly questioning, If I lacked any thing. A guest, I answered, worthy to be here: Love said, You shall be he. I the unkind, ungrateful? Ah my dear, I cannot look on thee. Love took my hand, and smiling did reply, Who made the eyes but I? Truth Lord, but I have marred them: let my shame Go where it doth deserve. And know you not, says Love, who bore the blame? My dear, then I will serve. You must sit down, says Love, and taste my meat: So I did sit and eat.

Jack and Emma hugged and cheered. They knew that their prayer had been answered. Jack and Emma continued to eat their toast and enjoyed breakfast together.

name_of_work: He Wishes His Beloved Were Dead by William Butler Yeats
content: Were you but lying cold and dead, And lights were paling out of the West, You would come hither, and bend your head, And I would lay my head on your breast; And you would murmur tender words, Forgiving me, because you were dead: Nor would you rise and hasten away, Though you have the will of wild birds, But know your hair was bound and wound About the stars and moon and sun: O would, beloved, that you lay Under the dock-leaves in the ground, While lights were paling one by one.

Tho' Grief and Fondness in my Breast rebel, When injur'd Thales bids the Town farewell, Yet still my calmer Thoughts his Choice commend, I praise the Hermit, but regret the Friend, Resolved at length, from Vice and London far, To breathe in distant Fields a purer Air, And, fix'd on Cambria's solitary shore, Give to St. David one true Briton more. For who would leave, unbrib'd, Hibernia's Land, Or change the Rocks of Scotland for the Strand? There none are swept by sudden Fate away, But all whom Hunger spares, with Age decay: Here Malice, Rapine, Accident, conspire, And now a Rabble Rages, now a Fire; Their Ambush here relentless Ruffians lay, And here the fell Attorney prowls for Prey; Here falling Houses thunder on your Head, And here a female Atheist talks you dead. While Thales waits the Wherry that contains Of dissipated Wealth the small Remains, On Thames's Banks, in silent Thought we stood, Where Greenwich smiles upon the silver Flood: Struck with the Seat that gave Eliza Birth, We kneel, and kiss the consecrated Earth; In pleasing Dreams the blissful Age renew, And call Britannia's Glories back to view; Behold her Cross triumphant on the Main, The Guard of Commerce, and the Dread of Spain, Ere Masquerades debauch'd, Excise oppress'd, Or English Honour grew a standing Jest. A transient Calm the happy Scenes bestow, And for a Moment lull the Sense of Woe. At length awaking, with contemptuous Frown, Indignant Thales eyes the neighb'ring Town. Since Worth, he cries, in these degen'rate Days, Wants ev'n the cheap Reward of empty Praise; In those curst Walls, devote to Vice and Gain, Since unrewarded Science toils in vain; Since Hope but sooths to double my Distress, And ev'ry Moment leaves my Little less; While yet my steady Steps no Staff sustains, And Life still vig'rous revels in my Veins; Grant me, kind Heaven, to find some happier Place, Where Honesty and Sense are no Disgrace; Some pleasing Bank where verdant Osiers play, Some peaceful Vale with Nature's Paintings gay; Where once the harass'd Briton found Repose, And safe in Poverty defy'd his Foes; Some secret Cell, ye Pow'rs, indulgent give. Let ---- live here, for ---- has learn'd to live. Here let those reign, whom Pensions can incite To vote a Patriot black, a Courtier white; Explain their Country's dear-bought Rights away, And plead for Pirates in the Face of Day; With slavish Tenets taint our poison'd Youth, And lend a Lye the confidence of Truth. Let such raise Palaces, and Manors buy, Collect a Tax, or farm a Lottery, With warbling Eunuchs fill a licens'd Stage, And lull to Servitude a thoughtless Age. Heroes, proceed! What Bounds your Pride shall hold? What Check restrain your Thirst of Pow'r and Gold? Behold rebellious Virtue quite o'erthrown, Behold our Fame, our Wealth, our Lives your own. To such, a groaning Nation's Spoils are giv'n, When publick Crimes inflame the Wrath of Heav'n: But what, my Friend, what Hope remains for me, Who start at Theft, and blush at Perjury? Who scarce forbear, tho' Britain's Court he sing, To pluck a titled Poet's borrow'd Wing; A Statesman's Logic, unconvinc'd can hear, And dare to slumber o'er the Gazetteer; Despise a Fool in half his Pension drest, And strive in vain to laugh at H--y's jest. Others with softer Smiles, and subtler Art, Can sap the Principles, or taint the Heart; With more Address a Lover's Note convey, Or bribe a Virgin's Innocence away. Well may they rise, while I, whose Rustic Tongue Ne'er knew to puzzle Right, or varnish Wrong, Spurn'd as a Beggar, dreaded as a Spy, Live unregarded, unlamented die. For what but social Guilt the Friend endears? Who shares Orgilio's Crimes, his Fortune shares. But thou, should tempting Villainy present All Marlb'rough hoarded, or all Villiers spent; Turn from the glitt'ring Bribe thy scornful Eye, Nor sell for Gold, what Gold could never buy, The peaceful Slumber, self-approving Day, Unsullied Fame, and Conscience ever gay. The cheated Nation's happy Fav'rites, see! Mark whom the Great caress, who frown on me! London! the needy Villain's gen'ral Home, The Common Shore of Paris and of Rome; With eager Thirst, by Folly or by Fate, Sucks in the Dregs of each corrupted State. Forgive my Transports on a Theme like this, I cannot bear a French metropolis. Illustrious Edward! from the Realms of Day, The Land of Heroes and of Saints survey; Nor hope the British Lineaments to trace, The rustic Grandeur, or the surly Grace; But lost in thoughtless Ease, and empty Show, Behold the Warriour dwindled to a Beau; Sense, Freedom, Piety, refin'd away, Of France the Mimic, and of Spain the Prey. All that at home no more can beg or steal, Or like a Gibbet better than a Wheel; Hiss'd from the Stage, or hooted from the Court, Their Air, their Dress, their Politicks import; Obsequious, artful, voluble and gay, On Britain's fond Credulity they prey. No gainful Trade their Industry can 'scape, They sing, they dance, clean Shoes, or cure a Clap; All Sciences a fasting Monsieur knows, And bid him go to Hell, to Hell he goes. Ah! what avails it, that, from Slav'ry far, I drew the Breath of Life in English Air; Was early taught a Briton's Right to prize, And lisp the Tale of Henry's Victories; If the gull'd Conqueror receives the Chain, And what their Armies lost, their Cringes gain? Studious to please, and ready to submit, The supple Gaul was born a Parasite: Still to his Int'rest true, where'er he goes, Wit, Brav'ry, Worth, his lavish Tongue bestows; In ev'ry Face a Thousand Graces shine, From ev'ry Tongue flows Harmony divine. These Arts in vain our rugged Natives try, Strain out with fault'ring Diffidence a Lye, And get a Kick for awkward Flattery. Besides, with Justice, this discerning Age Admires their wond'rous Talents for the Stage: Well may they venture on the Mimic's art, Who play from Morn to Night a borrow'd Part; Practis'd their Master's Notions to embrace, Repeat his Maxims, and reflect his Face; With ev'ry wild Absurdity comply, And view each Object with another's Eye; To shake with Laughter ere the Jest they hear, To pour at Will the counterfeited Tear; And as their Patron hints the Cold or Heat, To shake in Dog-days, in December sweat. How, when Competitors like these contend, Can surly Virtue hope to fix a Friend? Slaves that with serious Impudence beguile, And lye without a Blush, without a Smile; Exalt each Trifle, ev'ry Vice adore, Your Taste in Snuff, your Judgment in a Whore; Can Balbo's Eloquence applaud, and swear He gropes his Breeches with a Monarch's Air. For Arts like these preferr'd, admir'd, carest, They first invade your Table, then your Breast; Explore your Secrets with insidious Art, Watch the weak Hour, and ransack all the Heart; Then soon your ill-plac'd Confidence repay, Commence your Lords, and govern or betray. By Numbers here from Shame or Censure free, All Crimes are safe, but hated Poverty. This, only this, the rigid Law persues, This, only this, provokes the snarling Muse; The sober Trader at a tatter'd Cloak, Wakes from his Dream, and labours for a Joke; With brisker Air the silken Courtiers gaze, And turn the varied Taunt a thousand Ways. Of all the Griefs that harrass the Distrest, Sure the most bitter is a scornful Jest; Fate never wounds more deep the gen'rous Heart, Than when a Blockhead's Insult points the Dart. Has Heaven reserv'd, in Pity to the Poor, No pathless Waste, or undiscover'd Shore? No secret Island in the boundless Main? No peaceful Desart yet unclaim'd by SPAIN? Quick let us rise, the happy Seats explore, And bear Oppression's Insolence no more. This mournful Truth is ev'ry where confest, Slow rises worth, by poverty deprest: But here more slow, where all are Slaves to Gold, Where Looks are Merchandise, and Smiles are sold, Where won by Bribes, by Flatteries implor'd, The Groom retails the Favours of his Lord. But hark! th' affrighted Crowd's tumultuous Cries Roll thro' the Streets, and thunder to the Skies; Rais'd from some pleasing Dream of Wealth and Pow'r, Some pompous Palace, or some blissful Bow'r, Aghast you start, and scarce with aking Sight, Sustain th' approaching Fire's tremendous Light; Swift from pursuing Horrors take your Way, And Leave your little All to Flames a Prey; Then thro' the World a wretched Vagrant roam, For where can starving Merit find a Home? In vain your mournful Narrative disclose, While all neglect, and most insult your Woes. Should Heaven's just Bolts Orgilio's Wealth confound, And spread his flaming Palace on the Ground, Swift o'er the Land the dismal Rumour flies, And publick Mournings pacify the Skies; The Laureat Tribe in servile Verse relate, How Virtue wars with persecuting Fate; With well-feign'd Gratitude the pension's Band Refund the Plunder of the begger'd Land. See! while he builds, the gaudy Vassals come, And crowd with sudden Wealth the rising Dome; The Price of Boroughs and of Souls restore, And raise his Treasures higher than before. Now bless'd with all the Baubles of the Great, The polish'd Marble, and the shining Plate, Orgilio sees the golden Pile aspire, And hopes from angry Heav'n another Fire. Could'st thou resign the Park and Play content, For the fair Banks of Severn or of Trent; There might'st thou find some elegant Retreat, Some hireling Senator's deserted Seat; And stretch thy Prospects o'er the smiling Land, For less than rent the Dungeons of the Strand; There prune thy Walks, support thy drooping Flow'rs, Direct thy Rivulets, and twine thy Bow'rs; And, while thy Beds a cheap Repast afford, Despise the Dainties of a venal Lord: There ev'ry Bush with Nature's Music rings, There ev'ry Breeze bears Health upon its Wings; On all thy Hours Security shall smile, And bless thine Evening Walk and Morning Toil. Prepare for Death, if here at Night you roam, And sign your Will before you sup from Home. Some fiery Fop, with new Commission vain, Who sleeps on Brambles till he kills his Man; Some frolick Drunkard, reeling from a Feast, Provokes a Broil, and stabs you for a Jest. Yet ev'n these Heroes, mischievously gay, Lords of the Street, and Terrors of the Way; Flush'd as they are with Folly, Youth and Wine, Their prudent Insults to the Poor confine; Afar they mark the Flambeau's bright Approach, And shun the shining Train, and golden Coach. In vain, these Dangers past, your Doors you close, And hope the balmy Blessings of Repose: Cruel with Guilt, and daring with Despair, The midnight Murd'rer bursts the faithless Bar; Invades the sacred Hour of silent Rest, And plants, unseen, a Dagger in your Breast. Scarce can our Fields, such Crowds at Tyburn die, With Hemp the Gallows and the Fleet supply. Propose your Schemes, ye Senatorian Band, Whose Ways and Means support the sinking Land; Lest Ropes be wanting in the tempting Spring, To rig another Convoy for the K--g. A single Jail, in Alfred's golden Reign, Could half the Nation's Criminals contain; Fair Justice then, without Constraint ador'd, Sustain'd the Ballance, but resign'd the Sword; No Spies were paid, no Special Juries known, Blest Age! But ah! how diff'rent from our own! Much could I add, ---- but see the Boat at hand, The Tide retiring, calls me from the Land: Farewel! ---- When Youth, and Health, and Fortune spent, Thou fly'st for Refuge to the Wilds of Kent; And tir'd like me with Follies and with Crimes, In angry Numbers warn'st succeeding Times; Then shall thy Friend, nor thou refuse his Aid, Still Foe to Vice forsake his Cambrian Shade; In Virtue's Cause once more exert his Rage, Thy Satire point, and animate thy Page.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Tim. Tim loved to run very fast. He was the fastest boy in his town. One day, he met a girl named Sue. Sue was also very fast. They decided to have a race to see who was the fastest.

Tim and Sue started the race. They ran as fast as they could. Tim was in front, but Sue was right behind him. They did not quit. They wanted to win the race. They passed a big tree, a small house, and a little dog. The dog barked at them as they ran by.

As Tim and Sue got closer to the finish line, they saw a man with a trade. The man was selling ice cream. Tim and Sue both wanted ice cream, so they stopped running. They decided to quit the race and have ice cream instead. They traded their fast running for a cold, sweet treat. Tim and Sue became good friends and enjoyed their ice cream together.

name_of_work: A Hymn to the Evening by Phillis Wheatley
content: Soon as the sun forsook the eastern main The pealing thunder shook the heav'nly plain; Majestic grandeur! From the zephyr's wing, Exhales the incense of the blooming spring. Soft purl the streams, the birds renew their notes, And through the air their mingled music floats. Through all the heav'ns what beauteous dies are spread! But the west glories in the deepest red: So may our breasts with ev'ry virtue glow, The living temples of our God below! Fill'd with the praise of him who gives the light, And draws the sable curtains of the night, Let placid slumbers sooth each weary mind, At morn to wake more heav'nly, more refin'd; So shall the labours of the day begin More pure, more guarded from the snares of sin. Night's leaden sceptre seals my drowsy eyes, Then cease, my song, till fair Aurora rise.

Once upon a time, there was a person named Tim. Tim liked to fly kites on sunny days. One day, Tim went to the park to fly his kite. But, when he got there, he saw that his kite was broken. Tim was upset because he couldn't fly his kite. 

Suddenly, Tim saw a butterfly flying in the sky. He watched the butterfly flutter up and down, and it made him feel happy. Tim realized that he didn't need a kite to fly, he could just watch the butterfly. So, he sat down on the grass and watched the butterfly fly up and down. 

After a while, Tim saw a bird flying high in the sky. He thought it was amazing how the bird could fly so high. Tim wanted to fly like the bird, but he knew he couldn't. Instead, he decided to go home and draw a picture of the bird flying. Tim was no longer upset about his broken kite, he was happy just watching things fly.

Say this city has ten million souls, Some are living in mansions, some are living in holes: Yet there's no place for us, my dear, yet there's no place for us. Once we had a country and we thought it fair, Look in the atlas and you'll find it there: We cannot go there now, my dear, we cannot go there now. In the village churchyard there grows an old yew, Every spring it blossoms anew: Old passports can't do that, my dear, old passports can't do that. The consul banged the table and said, "If you've got no passport you're officially dead": But we are still alive, my dear, but we are still alive. Went to a committee; they offered me a chair; Asked me politely to return next year: But where shall we go to-day, my dear, but where shall we go to-day? Came to a public meeting; the speaker got up and said; "If we let them in, they will steal our daily bread": He was talking of you and me, my dear, he was talking of you and me. Thought I heard the thunder rumbling in the sky; It was Hitler over Europe, saying, "They must die": O we were in his mind, my dear, O we were in his mind. Saw a poodle in a jacket fastened with a pin, Saw a door opened and a cat let in: But they weren't German Jews, my dear, but they weren't German Jews. Went down the harbour and stood upon the quay, Saw the fish swimming as if they were free: Only ten feet away, my dear, only ten feet away. Walked through a wood, saw the birds in the trees; They had no politicians and sang at their ease: They weren't the human race, my dear, they weren't the human race. Dreamed I saw a building with a thousand floors, A thousand windows and a thousand doors: Not one of them was ours, my dear, not one of them was ours. Stood on a great plain in the falling snow; Ten thousand soldiers marched to and fro: Looking for you and me, my dear, looking for you and me.

Once upon a time there was a little boy called Ben. He was three years old.

One day, Ben went to school for the very first time. He felt a bit nervous but he was very excited.

When he got to the classroom he saw lots of things. He could see coloured pencils on the tables. Ben smiled and ran over to get one. He picked up a yellow pencil and started to draw.

Suddenly his teacher shut the door. All the children in the room jumped and Ben felt a bit scared. He dropped his pencil on the ground and started to cry.

But his teacher smiled and gave him a hug. She said everything was going to be ok. Ben felt better and he was no longer so nervous. As Ben picked up his pencil, he knew that he was going to love school.

Tom and Lily were friends who liked to play outside. One day, it was raining hard and they could not go out. They were sad and bored in their houses.

Tom had an idea. He called Lily on the phone and said, "Lily, I have a surprise for you. Look out of your window in five minutes."

Lily was curious and waited for five minutes. Then she saw Tom's dad driving his car to her house. He got out and knocked on the door. He had a big box in his hands.

Lily opened the door and said, "Hello, Mr. Smith. What is in the box?"

Mr. Smith smiled and said, "This is a gift from Tom. He wanted to send you something to cheer you up. Open it and see."

Lily opened the box and found a beautiful umbrella inside. It was pink and purple and had flowers and butterflies on it. She was so happy and said, "Wow, this is the best umbrella ever! Thank you, Tom. Thank you, Mr. Smith."

Mr. Smith said, "You're welcome, Lily. Tom said he hopes you like it and he can't wait to play with you again when the rain stops."

Lily ran to the phone and called Tom. She said, "Tom, I love the umbrella you sent me. It is so pretty and fun. You are a very good friend. Thank you so much."

Tom said, "You're welcome, Lily. I'm glad you like it. I saw it in the store and I thought of you. You are a very good friend too. I hope the rain stops soon so we can play together."

They both smiled and said goodbye. They felt happy and warm in their hearts.

The moral of the story is: Sending a gift to a friend can make them happy and show them you care.

Suddenly, a boy and a girl were standing at the base of the tree. The little boy looked up at the bird and said, â€œMust be nice to be so wild and free!â€
