Once upon a time, there was a little train. It loved to care for its friends. One day, the train went to the station. It was a high station, up on a hill. The train liked to help its friends get to the top.

At the station, the train met a small car. The car was sad because it could not climb the high hill. The train wanted to care for the car. So, it thought of a plan to help the car reach the station.

The train tied a rope to the car. Then, it pulled the car up the high hill. The car was so happy! It thanked the train for caring and helping it reach the station. They became best friends, and the train kept on caring for all its friends at the high station.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Tom. Tom was a very restless boy. He never stayed still and was always looking for something to fix.

One day, while Tom was exploring, he noticed a volcano. He decided he needed to fix the volcano and make it better. So, Tom worked on it all day and night, until he finally got it fixed.

With much joy, Tom went to sleep. The next day he woke up and went back to the volcano. But something strange had happened. It was no longer a volcano, but instead, a big mountain. 

Tom was very excited! He had fixed the volcano and it was now a mountain! He was so proud of his work and was now even more restless to explore and find something else to fix.

name_of_work: A Child's Garden by Rudyard Kipling
content: Now there is nothing wrong with me Except--I think it's called T.B. And that is why I have to lay Out in the garden all the day. Our garden is not very wide, And cars go by on either side, And make an angry-hooty noise That rather startles little boys. But worst of all is when they take Me out in cars that growl and shake, With charabancs so dreadful-near I have to shut my eyes for fear. But when I'm on my back again, I watch the Croydon aeroplane That flies across to France, and sings Like hitting thick piano-strings. When I am strong enough to do The things I'm truly wishful to, I'll never use a car or train But always have an aeroplane; And just go zooming round and round, And frighten Nursey with the sound, And see the angel-side of clouds, And spit on all those motor-crowds!

Once upon a time, there was a little bunny named Bun Bun. Bun Bun loved to eat dessert, especially carrot cake. One day, Bun Bun saw his friend, a little squirrel named Nutty, eating a big slice of carrot cake. Bun Bun felt envious and wanted some too. 

Bun Bun asked Nutty if he could have a piece of cake, but Nutty said no. Bun Bun felt sad and walked away. As he was walking, he saw a big carrot on the ground. Bun Bun tried to bite it, but it was too hard. So, he used his strong teeth to snap the carrot into smaller pieces. 

Bun Bun was happy he had a snack and forgot all about the carrot cake. From then on, Bun Bun learned that it's okay to want things, but it's important to be happy with what you have.

Once there was a little boy named Ryan. He was three years old. Ryan liked to put on his new sock in the morning. It was smooth and comfortable. His mom had bought it for his birthday.

One day, he was playing with his new sock when he saw a bunny in the garden. They looked at each other and smiled. 

"Hi, bunny!" said Ryan.

The bunny hopped closer to Ryan and said, "Hi! What are you doing?"

Ryan showed the bunny his smooth sock and said, "See this? It's my new sock!"

The bunny smiled and said, "It looks very nice!"

Ryan nodded and said, "Yes, it is! I really like it!"

The bunny hopped away, still smiling. Ryan watched it go, still feeling happy with his new sock.

name_of_work: All that is gold does not glitter by J.R.R. Tolkien
content: All that is gold does not glitter, Not all those who wander are lost; The old that is strong does not wither, Deep roots are not reached by the frost. From the ashes a fire shall be woken, A light from the shadows shall spring; Renewed shall be blade that was broken, The crownless again shall be king.

It was first marching, hardly we had settled yet To think of England, or escaped body pain - (Cotswold or music -- or poetry, the pack to forget) Flat country going leaves but small chance, small hope for The mind to escape to any resort but its vain Own circling grayness and stain; First halt, second halt, and then to spoiled country again. There were unknown kilometres to march, one must settle To play chess, or talk home talk, or think as might happen After three weeks of February frost, few were in fettle, Barely frost bite the most of us Gloucesters had escaped. To move, then, to go onward, at least to be moved - Myself had revived and then dulled down. It was I Who stared for body-ease on the gray sky And watched in grind of pain the monotony Of grit, road metal, slide underneath by dull down by To get there being the one thought under, to get marching done. Suddenly, a road's turn brought the sweet unexpected Pleasure. Snowdrops bloomed in a ruined garden neglected: Roman the road; as of Birdlip we were on the verge, And this West Country thing so from chaos to emerge (Surely Witcombe with dim water lay under March's morning-falter?) One gracious touch the whole wilderness corrected. But words are only words and the snowdrops were such Then, as some Bach fugue wonder -- or some Winter Tale touch.

Once upon a time, in a lovely big forest, there lived a rhinoceros. The rhinoceros had many friends. They would play and laugh together every day. The sun was always shining, and everyone was happy.

One day, a big storm came to the forest. The wind blew hard, and the rain fell down. The rhinoceros and his friends were scared. They did not know what to do. They could not play and laugh like before. They wanted the storm to go away.

The rhinoceros had an idea. He told his friends to come together and help each other. They all worked hard to make the forest lovely again. They picked up the fallen branches and leaves. They helped the little animals find their homes.

At last, the storm went away. The sun came out, and the forest was lovely again. The rhinoceros and his friends could play and laugh once more. They were very happy. They knew that they could face any problem if they stayed together. And they lived happily ever after.

I What shall we add now? He is dead. And I who praise and you who blame, With wash of words across his name, Find suddenly declared instead-- "On Sunday, third of August, dead.' II Which stops the whole we talked to-day. I quickened to a plausive glance At his large general tolerance By common people's narrow way, Stopped short in praising. Dead, they say. III And you, who had just put in a sort Of cold deduction--"rather, large Through weakness of the continent marge, Than greatness of the thing contained'-- Broke off. Dead!--there, you stood restrained. IV As if we had talked in following one Up some long gallery. "Would you choose An air like that? The gait is loose-- Or noble.' Sudden in the sun An oubliette winks. Where is he? Gone. V Dead. Man's "I was' by God's "I am'-- All hero-worship comes to that. High heart, high thought, high fame, as flat As a gravestone. Bring your Jacet jam-- The epitaph's an epigram. VI Dead. There's an answer to arrest All carping. Dust's his natural place? He'll let the flies buzz round his face And, though you slander, not protest? --From such an one, exact the Best? VII Opinions gold or brass are null. We chuck our flattery or abuse, Called Caesar's due, as Charon's dues, I' the teeth of some dead sage or fool, To mend the grinning of a skull. VIII Be abstinent in praise and blame. The man's still mortal, who stands first, And mortal only, if last and worst. Then slowly lift so frail a fame, Or softly drop so poor a shame.

Once there was a small bird who wanted to fly. One day, he saw a vase high in the sky and he said to himself, "I will soar to the top!" He was so excited, he quickly took off, flapping his wings as fast as he could.

The bird got closer and closer, but he was getting tired. He started to slow down, but then he saw something shining in the sky - it was the top of the vase! He put on a burst of speed and soon he was there. He rested on the vase for a moment and looked down. It was so beautiful.

Just then, he heard a voice from somewhere below. "Be careful bird! You don't want to fall!" He looked down to see an old man waving at him from the ground. He knew he had to be careful and he slowly flew back down. When he landed, the old man smiled and said, "You should be proud. You soared to the vase and back again." The bird smiled back and knew his journey was very special.

name_of_work: Tears Fall in My Heart by Paul Verlaine
content: Tears fall in my heart Rain falls on the town; what is this numb hurt that enters my heart? Ah,the soft sound of rain on roofs, on the ground! To a dulled heart they came, ah, the song of the rain! Tears without reason in the disheartened heart. What? no trace of treason? This grief's without reason. It's far the worst pain to never know why without love or disdain my heart has such pain!

Once upon a time there were two friends, Joe and Sari. They were both so excited to go on an adventure. So they put on their shoes and began to walk. They walked for a long time, until they eventually got to a big, twisty tree. Joe and Sari loved the tree so much that they stopped to take a look. They were amazed by it's gnarled branches and ancient, twisted trunk.

Then something strange happened. Sari put her hand on the trunk and something magical happened. The tree began to change! It started to open up and it warped back in time. Joe and Sari were filled with wonder and amazement.

They soon realized that the twisty tree was taking them back in time. They kept going, farther and farther back in history. Soon, they were surrounded by distant memories and ancient secrets. They marveled at this hidden history as they continued their journey.

Eventually they arrived at the beginning of time, or at least they felt they had. Joe and Sari were so filled with awe and astonishment. It felt like they had really gone back in time!

The two friends eventually climbed back up the twisty tree and returned back to the present. Though their travels in time had been short, Joe and Sari will never forget the distant history they had discovered.

Once upon a time, there was a big dragon. He was very kind and compassionate. He loved to fly around and play with his friends. One day, he decided to go to the park. 

At the park, he saw other animals playing and having fun. He wanted to join in, but they were scared of him because he was a dragon. So, he decided to show them his compassionate side. He helped a little bird who had fallen out of its nest and gave some food to a squirrel who was hungry. 

The other animals saw how kind he was and they started to play with him. They ran around and had so much fun together. From that day on, the dragon visited the park often and made many new friends. And everyone knew that he was not scary, but a kind and compassionate dragon. The end.

Once upon a time, a little boy named Tom wanted to find something special. He went to the forest and he kneeled down so he could look for something exciting. Suddenly, something sparkled in front of him. It was fiery, shiny, and fancy! Tom was so excited to discover it was a golden firefly. He said hello to the firefly and asked if he could take it home.

The firefly said he could only stay with Tom if he could help him find his way back to his family. So, Tom and the firefly started their journey together. On the way they saw roses and butterflies, and they even stopped to eat some delicious apples.

Finally, they arrived at a big tree. Tom kneeled down again and he could spot a group of fireflies in the distance. He said goodbye to his special friend and hugged him tight. The firefly flew back to his family and Tom waved goodbye as he walked home with a smile on his face.

One day, Tom and Lily went to the park with their dad. They saw a big field with many holes and flags. Dad said, "This is a golf course. People hit a small ball with a stick and try to make it go in the holes."

Tom and Lily wanted to try. Dad gave them each a stick and a ball. He showed them how to hold the stick and swing it. Tom and Lily tried to hit the ball, but it was hard. Sometimes the ball went too far, sometimes too near, sometimes to the side.

They walked around the field, looking for their balls. They saw other people playing golf too. Some were good, some were not. They also saw a man with a white beard and a hat. He was sitting on a bench, watching the players. He smiled at Tom and Lily.

"Hello, little ones," he said. "Do you like golf?"

Tom and Lily nodded. They asked him, "Are you a golf player?"

The man laughed. He said, "I used to be, a long time ago. Now I just enjoy watching. I like to see how people learn and improve. Golf is a game of skill and patience. You have to practice a lot and listen to good advice."

Tom and Lily wanted to learn more. They asked him, "Can you give us some good advice?"

The man nodded. He said, "Of course. Come here, I'll show you some tips." He took their sticks and balls and walked with them to a hole. He taught them how to stand, how to grip, how to aim, and how to swing. He was very kind and wise. He made golf fun and easy.

Tom and Lily thanked him. They said, "You are a great teacher. We learned a lot from you. Can we play with you again?"

The man smiled. He said, "Sure, anytime. I'm always here. My name is Bob. What are yours?"

Tom and Lily told him their names. They said, "We are happy to meet you, Bob. You are our new friend."

They hugged him and said goodbye. They ran back to their dad, who was waiting for them. They told him about Bob and what they learned. Dad was proud of them. He said, "You are very lucky to find such a wise golf teacher. He must really like you. Maybe next time we can all play together."

name_of_work: Meeting the British by Paul Muldoon
content: We met the British in the dead of winter. The sky was lavender and the snow lavender-blue. I could hear, far below, the sound of two streams coming together (both were frozen over) and, no less strange, myself calling out in French across that forest- clearing. Neither General Jeffrey Amherst nor Colonel Henry Bouquet could stomach our willow-tobacco. As for the unusual scent when the Colonel shook out his hand- kerchief: C'est la lavande, une fleur mauve comme le ciel. They gave us six fishhooks and two blankets embroidered with smallpox.

name_of_work: Sabbath Morning at Sea by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: I The ship went on with solemn face; To meet the darkness on the deep, The solemn ship went onward: I bowed down weary in the place, For parting tears and present sleep Had weighed mine eyelids downward. II Thick sleep which shut all dreams from me, And kept my inner self apart And quiet from emotion, Then brake away and left me free, Made conscious of a human heart Betwixt the heaven and ocean. III The new sight, the new wondrous sight! The waters round me, turbulent, The skies impassive o'er me, Calm in a moonless, sunless light, Half glorified by that intent Of holding the day-glory! IV Two pale thin clouds did stand upon The meeting line of sea and sky, With aspect still and mystic: I think they did foresee the sun, And rested on their prophecy In quietude majestic, V Then flushed to radiance where they stood, Like statues by the open tomb Of shining saints half risen. The sun! -- he came up to be viewed, And sky and sea made mighty room To inaugurate the vision. VI I oft had seen the dawnlight run As red wine through the hills, and break Through many a mist's inurning; But, here, no earth profaned the sun: Heaven, ocean, did alone partake The sacrament of morning. VII Away with thoughts fantastical! I would be humble to my worth, Self-guarded as self-doubted: Though here no earthly shadows fall, I, joying, grieving without earth, May desecrate without it. VIII God's sabbath morning sweeps the waves; I would not praise the pageant high Yet miss the dedicature: I, carried toward the sunless graves By force of natural things, -- should I Exult in only Nature? IX And could I bear to sit alone 'Mid Nature's fixed benignities, While my warm pulse was moving? Too dark thou art, O glittering sun, Too strait ye are, capacious seas, To satisfy the loving! X It seems a better lot than so, To sit with friends beneath the beech, And feel them dear and dearer; Or follow children as they go In pretty pairs, with softened speech, As the church-bells ring nearer. XI Love me, sweet friends, this sabbath day! The sea sings round me while ye roll Afar the hymn unaltered, And kneel, where once I knelt to pray, And bless me deeper in the soul, Because the voice has faltered. XII And though this sabbath comes to me Without the stoled minister Or chanting congregation, God's Spirit brings communion, H E Who brooded soft on waters drear, Creator on creation. XIII Himself, I think, shall draw me higher Where keep the saints with harp and song An endless sabbath morning, And on that sea commixed with fire Oft drop their eyelids, raised too long To the full Godhead's burning.

Once upon a time, there was a fancy mineral. It was very special, because it had magical powers.

Many people were curious about the mineral and wanted to see it, but the mineral wouldn't permit. It said only special people were allowed to come closer.

So, the people decided to find someone special who could prove that she was trustworthy. After much searching, they found a little girl. She was only three years old, but she seemed to be the perfect person for the job.

The mineral allowed the little girl to come closer, and when she did, it sparkled with the most beautiful light. Everyone was amazed and the girl was so happy!

The little girl played with the mineral every day and it changed her life forever. And they all lived happily ever after.

Sweet day, so cool, so calm, so bright, The bridal of the earth and sky; The dew shall weep thy fall to-night, For thou must die. Sweet rose, whose hue angry and brave Bids the rash gazer wipe his eye; Thy root is ever in its grave, And thou must die. Sweet spring, full of sweet days and roses, A box where sweets compacted lie; My music shows ye have your closes, And all must die. Only a sweet and virtuous soul, Like season'd timber, never gives; But though the whole world turn to coal, Then chiefly lives.

name_of_work: The Best Cigarette by Billy Collins
content: There are many that I miss having sent my last one out a car window sparking along the road one night, years ago. The heralded one, of course: after sex, the two glowing tips now the lights of a single ship; at the end of a long dinner with more wine to come and a smoke ring coasting into the chandelier; or on a white beach, holding one with fingers still wet from a swim. How bittersweet these punctuations of flame and gesture; but the best were on those mornings when I would have a little something going in the typewriter, the sun bright in the windows, maybe some Berlioz on in the background. I would go into the kitchen for coffee and on the way back to the page, curled in its roller, I would light one up and feel its dry rush mix with the dark taste of coffee. Then I would be my own locomotive, trailing behind me as I returned to work little puffs of smoke, indicators of progress, signs of industry and thought, the signal that told the nineteenth century it was moving forward. That was the best cigarette, when I would steam into the study full of vaporous hope and stand there, the big headlamp of my face pointed down at all the words in parallel lines.

Once upon a time, there was a little hedgehog named Spike. Spike had very tight quills all over his body that kept him safe from danger. One day, Spike met a curious rabbit named Benny. Benny dared Spike to come out and play with him. Spike was scared at first, but then he realized that Benny was friendly. So, Spike came out and they played together in the field. They had so much fun that they became best friends forever!

There are just not enough straight lines. That is the problem. Nothing is flat or parallel. Beams balance crookedly on supports thrust off the vertical. Nails clutch at open seams. The whole structure leans dangerously towards the miraculous. Into this rough frame, someone has squeezed a living space and even dared to place these eggs in a wire basket, fragile curves of white hung out over the dark edge of a slanted universe, gathering the light into themselves, as if they were the bright, thin walls of faith.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy had a red jacket that he loved to wear. One day, Timmy's mom said it was too small and didn't fit him anymore. Timmy was sad because he loved his jacket.

Timmy's mom took him to the store to get a new jacket. Timmy tried on many jackets, but none of them fit him right. Finally, Timmy found a blue jacket that fit him perfectly! He was so happy that he nodded his head and smiled.

From that day on, Timmy wore his new blue jacket everywhere he went. He even wore it to bed because he loved it so much. Timmy was grateful for his mom helping him find a new jacket that fit him just right.

name_of_work: When Death Comes by Mary Oliver
content: When death comes like the hungry bear in autumn; when death comes and takes all the bright coins from his purse to buy me, and snaps the purse shut; when death comes like the measle-pox when death comes like an iceberg between the shoulder blades, I want to step through the door full of curiosity, wondering: what is it going to be like, that cottage of darkness? And therefore I look upon everything as a brotherhood and a sisterhood, and I look upon time as no more than an idea, and I consider eternity as another possibility, and I think of each life as a flower, as common as a field daisy, and as singular, and each name a comfortable music in the mouth, tending, as all music does, toward silence, and each body a lion of courage, and something precious to the earth. When it's over, I want to say all my life I was a bride married to amazement. I was the bridegroom, taking the world into my arms. When it's over, I don't want to wonder if I have made of my life something particular, and real. I don't want to find myself sighing and frightened, or full of argument. I don't want to end up simply having visited this world

All others talked as if talk were a dance. Clodhopper I, with clumsy feet would break the gliding ring. Early I learned to hunch myself close by the door: then when the talk began I'd wipe my mouth and wend unnoticed back to the barn to be with the warm beasts, dumb among body sounds of the simple ones. I'd see by a twist of lit rush the motes of gold moving from shadow to shadow slow in the wake of deep untroubled sighs. The cows munched or stirred or were still. I was at home and lonely, both in good measure. Until the sudden angel affrighted me--light effacing my feeble beam, a forest of torches, feathers of flame, sparks upflying: but the cows as before were calm, and nothing was burning, nothing but I, as that hand of fire touched my lips and scorched my tongue and pulled my voice into the ring of the dance.

Ben liked to jog with his dad in the park. They wore boots to keep their feet dry and warm. They saw many things in the park: trees, birds, dogs, and people. Ben was happy and smiled a lot.

One day, they saw a big bear in the park. The bear was hungry and angry. It roared and ran towards them. Ben and his dad were frightened. They tried to jog away, but the bear was faster. The bear caught up with them and bit them. It hurt a lot.

Ben and his dad fell to the ground. They could not move or talk. They were very sad and scared. The bear ate them and left. No one helped them. The end.

name_of_work: Imagining Their Own Hymns by Brigit Pegeen Kelly
content: What fools they are to believe the angels in this window are in ecstasy. They do not smile. Their eyes are rolled back in annoyance not in bliss, as my mother's eyes roll back when she finds us in the dirt with the cider-- flies and juice blackening our faces and hands. When the sun comes up behind the angels then even in their dun robes they are beautiful, with their girlish hair and their mean lit faces, but they do not love the light. As I do not love it when I am made clean for the ladies who bring my family money. They stroke my face and smooth my hair. So sweet, they say, so good, but I am not sweet or good. I would take one of the possums we kill in the dump by the woods where the rats slide like dark boats into the dark stream and leave it on the heavy woman's porch just to think of her on her knees scrubbing and scrubbing at a stain that will never come out. And these angels that the women turn to are not good either. They are sick of Jesus, who never stops dying, hanging there white and large, his shadow blue as pitch, and blue the bruise on his chest, with spread petals, like the hydrangea blooms I tear from Mrs. Macht's bush and smash on the sidewalk. One night they will get out of here. One night when the weather is turning cold and a few candles burn, they will leave St. Blase standing under his canopy of glass lettuce and together, as in a wedding march, their pockets full of money from the boxes for the sick poor, they will walk down the aisle, imagining their own hymns, past the pews and the water fonts in which small things float, down the streets of our narrow town, while the bells ring and the birds fly up in the fields beyond--and they will never come back.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy. He was playing outside with a bucket of water. He scooped the bucket up and splashed it so he could make waves. When the waves got too big, the bucket started to feel heavy. But the boy kept on playing and kept on splashing.

Suddenly, from the water appeared a magical fish. It swam up to the boy and said a word to him. He was so scared, he almost dropped his heavy bucket!

But the magical fish just opened its mouth and said the same word again: "Friends."

The boy smiled, and so did the fish. They both knew that they were going to be friends for a long time. They kept splashing and playing together until the sun went down.

name_of_work: To John Donne by Michael Symmons Roberts
content: Unlike an area of land, when you patent a gene, you are enclosing a part of me, the shared landscape. Sir John Sulston Now, as your mistress strips for bed, her body is already mapped, its ancient names a cracked code. That new found land is paced out, sized up, written down as hope or prophecy, probability or doubt. Her charts are held on laptops, mastered by medics, laid bare. Her peaks and gorges, fell slopes, oceans, woodlands, stars, this atlas of hers is no mystic book, it is a textbook of disease. The sun turns dust to smoke, and picks out, as it sets, a path your hands might take - your roving hands - she lets them roam, though she's no landowner. By law, her breast's curve has a patent, so you know that bankers - tired of gold - have bought a piece of her and you. You call her your America - too right. Her wilderness, those prairies have been carved up into real estate, ranches ringed with barbed wire, lights and guns. KEEP OUT OUR DOGS EAT TRESPASSERS. Do you care? Does she? What can it matter at this fleet May dusk, as you seek each other out, and her body's secret name is much like yours, and yours is so close to the crab apple and silver birch which interweave with collar doves and greenfinches, akin to grass which drapes in blossom as the light dies. Let your hands, and hers, lead us in love's mass trespass, let your lips, the co-ordinates of bodies: TTA, GAG, TGT, CCC, TGT (this is, yes, a litany) CTG, GAG, TTG . . .

name_of_work: The Last Time by Rachel Mckibbens
content: I did it alone, without leaving. The welt on my face still hot, I crept downstairs, pried open the toolbox and grabbed the hammer with his initials burned deep into the handle. Upstairs, my brother slept in his room, a glass box of reptiles watching over him. I turned the knob slowly, and stood over my father's body, his chest heaving, then sinking, when his tongue rattled, then stopped, and the whites of his eyes rolled over, and he stared only at the weapon in my hand and I looked at him and said, If you ever touch us again, I will kill you. And then he saw me. Okay, he said. Okay.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside and explore the world around him. One day, Timmy went to the beach with his family. He saw a big boat with a giant anchor. The anchor was so big, it looked like it could hold the whole world!

Timmy's mom told him to be careful and not go too far into the water. But Timmy didn't listen and went too deep. Suddenly, a big wave came and Timmy got scared. He couldn't swim back to shore. Luckily, a lifeguard saw him and swam out to save him.

After that day, Timmy learned an important lesson. He should always listen to what his mom tells him and be careful around the water. He was lucky the lifeguard was there to help him. From then on, Timmy always remembered to be safe and listen to his parents.

One day, Jenny was looking for a new friend. She saw a yawning cat hiding in the bushes. Jenny approached the cat, who meowed at her. Jenny was very happy and decided to take her new friend home.

On the way, the cat kept yawning. Jenny was worried that her new friend was tired so she asked the cat if he wanted a nap. The cat nodded and soon he was fast asleep.

When they got home, Jenny took her new friend up to her bedroom. She made the cat a warm bed and tucked him in. He was so tired that he fell asleep quickly.

The following morning, Jenny heard some strange noises coming from her bedroom. She opened the door to find the cat playing in the sun! He had woken up and was ready to explore and have fun! 

Jenny and the cat have been friends ever since. They love to go exploring and even hide together. Every time Jenny sees her cat sleeping or yawning, she is reminded of their special friendship.

Once upon a time, a little boy named Timmy went on a trip with his family. They got on a big jet plane that could fly in the sky. Timmy was nervous because he had never been on a plane before.

As they were flying, Timmy's dad let him sit on his lap and drive the plane for a little bit. Timmy was so excited and happy to drive the jet, even though it was just for a short time.

"Wow, Timmy! You're such a good pilot!" said Timmy's dad.

"Thanks, Dad! I love driving the jet!" Timmy replied.

After a while, Timmy fell asleep and dreamt about flying his own jet one day. When they landed, Timmy woke up and said, "That was the best trip ever! I can't wait to drive a jet again!"

Molly's mom smiled, "Yes, Molly, the sun is shining".

Molly spun around and twirled in the sunshine. Then she shouted, "Oh, look what I found! It's mine!". Molly had found a pretty shiny stone in the garden. She held it tight in her hands and smiled.

Molly's mom came over and said, "That's so beautiful. You can keep it. It's yours".

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Emma. She was always asking her parents what she needed for her birthday. One day, her aunt came to visit the family. She was very old, but she was very kind.

As Emma was talking to her aunt, she noticed that her aunt kept saying that she needed help. Emma asked her parents what she could do to help her aunt. They told Emma that she could help by doing household chores.

So Emma started helping her aunt by doing chores every day. She swept, cleaned, did the washing and helped her aunt with anything she needed.

The next day, Emma noticed something special. Her aunt had a big smile on her face. She said that because of Emma's help, she felt less alone.

The moral of the story is that we should always help out those who need us, especially when they are elderly. Helping others is a reward in itself.

name_of_work: O What Is That Sound by W.H. Auden
content: O what is that sound which so thrills the ear Down in the valley, drumming, drumming? Only the scarlet soldiers, dear, The soldiers coming. O what is that light I see flashing so clear Over the distance brightly, brightly? Only the sun on their weapons, dear, As they step lightly. O what are they doing with all that gear, What are they doing this morning, this morning? Only their usual manoeuvres, dear, Or perhaps a warning. O why have they left the road down there? Why are they suddenly wheeling, wheeling? Perhaps a change in their orders, dear, Why are you kneeling? O haven't they stopped for the doctor's care, Haven't they reined their horses, their horse? Why, they are none of then wounded, dear. None of these forces. O is it the parson they want, with white hair, Is it the parson, is it, is it? No, they are passing his gateway, dear, Without a visit. O it must be the farmer who lives so near. It must be the farmer, so cunning, so cunning? They have passed the farmyard already, dear, And now they are running. O where are you going? Stay with me here! Were the vows you swore deceiving, deceiving? No, I promised to love you, dear, But I must be leaving. O it's broken the lock and splintered the door, O it's the gate where they're turning, turning; Their boots are heavy on the floor And their eyes are burning

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside and explore the world around her. One day, she went on a walk with her mom and found a shiny rock on the ground. 

"Mommy, look what I found!" Lily exclaimed with excitement.

"That's an impressive rock, Lily. Do you want to name it?" her mom asked.

Lily thought for a moment and then said, "I want to name it Sparkle because it's so shiny!"

As they continued their walk, they came across a friendly dog. Lily asked the dog's owner, "What's your dog's name?"

name_of_work: Sonnet: I Thank You by Henry Timrod
content: I thank you, kind and best beloved friend, With the same thanks one murmurs to a sister, When, for some gentle favor, he hath kissed her, Less for the gifts than for the love you send, Less for the flowers, than what the flowers convey; If I, indeed, divine their meaning truly, And not unto myself ascribe, unduly, Things which you neither meant nor wished to say, Oh! tell me, is the hope then all misplaced? And am I flattered by my own affection? But in your beauteous gift, methought I traced Something above a short-lived predilection, And which, for that I know no dearer name, I designate as love, without love's flame.

Tom and Jen are friends. They like to play with cars and trucks. They have a big box of toys in the yard. One day, they find a new toy in the box. It is a red fire truck with a ladder and a hose.

"Wow, look at this!" Tom says. "It is a fire truck. We can be firefighters and save people."

"Yes, let's play!" Jen says. "But we need fuel for the fire truck. Where can we get fuel?"

Tom thinks for a moment. He sees a bottle of water on the table. He has an idea. He runs to the table and grabs the bottle. He pours some water into the fire truck's tank.

"Here, I have fuel!" he says. "Now we can drive the fire truck and put out fires."

Jen smiles. She gets in the fire truck with Tom. They turn on the siren and the lights. They drive around the yard, looking for fires. They see a pile of leaves. They pretend it is a fire.

"Oh no, there is a fire!" Tom says. "We have to put it out. Jen, you use the hose. I will use the ladder."

"OK, Tom!" Jen says. She rubs the hose and sprays water on the leaves. Tom climbs the ladder and pretends to rescue a cat.

"Meow, meow!" he says. He holds the cat and comes down the ladder. He gives the cat to Jen.

"Good job, Jen!" he says. "We put out the fire and saved the cat. We are brave firefighters."

"Good job, Tom!" Jen says. She hugs the cat and rubs its fur. The cat purrs and licks her face. It is a calm and happy cat.

They put the cat in the fire truck and drive back to the box. They park the fire truck and put the bottle back on the table. They are tired but proud. They sit on the grass and play with the cat.

"We had fun today," Tom says.

"Yes, we did," Jen says. "We are good friends."

They smile and hug each other. They love to play with cars and trucks. They love their new toy. It is a red fire truck with a ladder and a hose.

Once upon a time, there was a very angry mommy. She was so mad that she went outside and ordered the landscape to change. She was very cross and said that it had to be redone. The landscape had a big hill and a pond and she wanted that gone. 

So she ordered the workers to come and make changes. They worked hard to do what she said. They dug and moved things around, making the landscape look different. 

Mommy looked at it and was still angry. She wanted more flowers and trees and more birds. So the workers used yellow and green and the landscape looked like a fairytale. 

Mommy was happy now. She smiled and hugged the workers and thanked them for their hard work. And they all lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time, in a big forest, there lived a black bunny named Bob. Bob was very strong because he had big muscles. He loved to hop and play with his friends.

One sunny day, Bob and his friend, a bird named Billy, were playing hide and seek. Billy closed his eyes and counted, "One, two, three!" When he opened his eyes, Bob had vanished! Billy looked up and down, left and right, but he could not find Bob.

"Where are you, Bob?" Billy called out. "I am here, Billy!" Bob said, hopping out from behind a big tree. "You hid so well, I could not see you!" Billy laughed. They played all day long, and when the sun went down, they went home, tired but very happy.

One day, her mom suggested that they go out to pick some olives from the tree in the garden. Molly was very excited! She put on her hat, shoes and coat and the two went outside.

Molly's mom asked her to be very quiet so that she wouldn't scare the birds away. Molly listened carefully and carefully looked around for the olives on the tree. She eventually found some and picked them for her mom.

Once she finished, Molly and her mom had a picnic dinner in the garden. Molly really enjoyed because it was so quiet and peaceful there.

Not mine own fears, nor the prophetic soul Of the wide world dreaming on things to come, Can yet the lease of my true love control, Suppos'd as forfeit to a confin'd doom. The mortal moon hath her eclipse endur'd And the sad augurs mock their own presage; Incertainties now crown themselves assur'd And peace proclaims olives of endless age. Now with the drops of this most balmy time My love looks fresh, and Death to me subscribes, Since, spite of him, I'll live in this poor rhyme, While he insults o'er dull and speechless tribes; And thou in this shalt find thy monument, When tyrants' crests and tombs of brass are spent.

I visited the place where we last met. Nothing was changed, the gardens were well-tended, The fountains sprayed their usual steady jet; There was no sign that anything had ended And nothing to instruct me to forget. The thoughtless birds that shook out of the trees, Singing an ecstasy I could not share, Played cunning in my thoughts. Surely in these Pleasures there could not be a pain to bear Or any discord shake the level breeze. It was because the place was just the same That made your absence seem a savage force, For under all the gentleness there came An earthquake tremor: Fountain, birds and grass Were shaken by my thinking of your name.

Tommy was at the store and wanted to buy some candy. As he was looking around, he slipped and fell on the floor. He was scared and started crying. 

Mommy came to help him. "It's ok Tommy," she said. "Let's go home". 

But Tommy was not ready to go home. "No! I want candy!" Tommy shouted.

Mommy saw how scared Tommy was and decided to buy him a lollipop. "Here you go," She said. "Everything is going to be alright". 

Tommy's tears dried up and he smiled. He took the lollipop and they left the store.

Once there was a lively family who lived in a big house. Mummy and Daddy lived together with their three year old child, Mia. She was a very happy and curious little girl who loved exploring every corner of their house.

Each night Mia liked to explore the upstairs. There was something special up there that she really liked - a big star! Every night Mia was so excited to find her star and so she asked her mum, â€œMummy, please can I go upstairs and find my star?â€

Mummy said, â€œYes, of course Mia! Just be sure to get back to bed soon because you need some rest.â€

Mia was so excited and so she hurried up the stairs to find her star. She ran around the landing, looking all around for the big star. She was getting tired and soon found it - right outside her bedroom window! When Mia saw the star, she clapped her hands in delight.

But then Mia realised, she had been away too long. She had to get back to bed before Mummy and Daddy missed her. So she quickly climbed back down the stairs and back into her bed.

Mia had had a lovely time looking for her star and promised herself, â€œIâ€™ll come back tomorrow night and look for it again.â€ And she did. Mia loved exploring the upstairs and the big star made it even more lively and fun.

Once upon a time, there was a nice little girl. She was so excited for her birthday present. A special present that was going to change her life! 

On the morning of her birthday, the girl was so excited. She ran into the garden and saw a phone! It was different than any other phone she had ever seen before.

The girl picked up the phone and noticed that when she pressed the button, it began to ring. She ran inside to ask her dad what this special phone was.

He told her that it was a special phone connected to the nature. He told her that it would help her explore the world and see things she'd never seen before. 

The girl was so excited! She began to explore right away. But soon she noticed that not everything was as it seems. Many of the things she saw on her phone were fake. She realized that her dad had given her something special, a way for her to learn about the real world and experience nature in a different way. 

That special phone helped her explore and learn more about nature. She was so happy and ever since then her special phone has opened up an entire world of nature exploration to her.

Anna and Ben are playing in the kitchen. They want to make a cake with flour, sugar, eggs and milk. Anna is bossy. She tells Ben what to do.

"Ben, bring me the flour from the cupboard," Anna says.

"OK, Anna," Ben says. He opens the cupboard and looks for the flour. He sees a big bag of flour on the top shelf. He tries to reach it, but it is too high.

"Anna, I can't get the flour. It is too high," Ben says.

"Use a chair, Ben. Hurry up," Anna says.

Ben finds a chair and puts it in front of the cupboard. He climbs on the chair and grabs the bag of flour. But the bag is too heavy. Ben loses his balance and falls off the chair. The bag of flour falls with him and bursts open. Flour goes everywhere.

"Ben, look what you did! You made a mess!" Anna shouts.

"Sorry, Anna. It was an accident," Ben says.

"No, it was not. You are clumsy and silly. You can't help me make a cake. Go away," Anna says.

Ben feels sad and angry. He doesn't want to play with Anna anymore. He picks up his teddy bear and leaves the kitchen. Anna is left alone with the flour. She tries to make a cake by herself, but she doesn't know how. She wishes she had Ben to help her. She realizes she was too bossy and mean to him. She feels sorry and lonely. She wants to say sorry to Ben and ask him to come back. But she doesn't know where he is. She starts to cry.

One day, a little boy named Tim went into the woods. He liked to play and imagine he was an amazing hero. Tim was not scared of anything, not even a big, bad wolf.

As Tim played, he heard a voice. "Hello, little boy," said the voice. Tim looked and saw a wolf. The wolf was big, but Tim was not scared. "Hello, Mr. Wolf," said Tim. "I am an amazing hero, and I can imagine anything."

The wolf laughed. "That's nice, little boy. But can you imagine what I will do next?" Tim thought for a moment. He imagined the wolf would be his friend. But the wolf had other ideas. The wolf was hungry and wanted to eat Tim.

In the end, Tim could not imagine a way to escape the big, bad wolf. The wolf ate Tim, and it was a bad ending for our little hero. Remember, not all stories have happy endings, and it's important to be careful in the woods.

name_of_work: Where I'm From by Melanie Poonai
content: I am from a life filled with colour, From the chocolate brown that is my skin. I am from the sunshine yellow of my mother's laugh, From the red and white of my brother's favourite football shirt. I am from the crisp new white pages of a book, From the miserable grey of the street I live on. I am from green, pink and yellow; My garden in summer filled with flowers, From the terrifying black of the nightmares that haunt me. I am from the ginger orange of my buried cat, From the blue and gold of my ever-short school tie. I am from the dark oak of my grandmother's coffin, From the golden "Aum" pendant around my neck.. I am from every pink scar etched into my body, From the red, orange and brown of a hot curry. I am from every identical colour of the twins I love, From the blue and green of a hospital ward. I am from all that has happened, And all that will be.

name_of_work: A Prayer in Spring by Robert Frost
content: Oh, give us pleasure in the flowers to-day; And give us not to think so far away As the uncertain harvest; keep us here All simply in the springing of the year. Oh, give us pleasure in the orchard white, Like nothing else by day, like ghosts by night; And make us happy in the happy bees, The swarm dilating round the perfect trees. And make us happy in the darting bird That suddenly above the bees is heard, The meteor that thrusts in with needle bill, And off a blossom in mid air stands still. For this is love and nothing else is love, The which it is reserved for God above To sanctify to what far ends He will, But which it only needs that we fulfil.

Sara and Tom are friends. They like to play in the park. They run, slide, swing and laugh. They are popular. Many children want to play with them.

One day, they see a big bin in the park. It is full of old things. Sara and Tom are curious. They want to see what is inside. They climb on the bin and look.

"Wow, look at this!" Sara says. She finds a teddy bear. It is brown and soft. It has a red bow. "It is so cute! Can I keep it?"

"Sure, why not?" Tom says. He finds a book. It has many pictures. It has a blue cover. "This looks fun! Can I keep it?"

They are happy. They jump off the bin and hug their new things. They sit on a bench and read the book. They share the teddy bear. They are tired. They sleep on the bench.

A lady walks by. She sees Sara and Tom. She smiles. She knows them. They are her children. She was looking for them. She is glad they are safe. She wakes them up.

"Hello, my darlings!" she says. "What are you doing here? Where did you get these things?"

"We found them in the bin, mommy!" Sara and Tom say. "They are ours! Can we keep them?"

The lady looks at the bin. She sees the old things. She understands. She is not angry. She is proud. Sara and Tom are kind. They love old things. They are popular.

"Of course, you can keep them, my darlings!" she says. "But we have to go home now. It is late. You need to sleep in your bed."

Sara and Tom nod. They are sleepy. They hold their things. They hold their mommy's hand. They walk home. They are happy. They sleep in their bed.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the sunshine, but sometimes it would rain. When it rained, she would get sad and angry because she couldn't play outside.

One day, Lily made a wish that it would never rain again. But then she thought about all the plants and flowers that needed the rain to grow. She realized that her wish was not very nice and she felt bad.

Lily learned that sometimes things happen that we don't like, but they are important for other things to grow and be happy. So, she decided to be happy even when it rained and she found fun things to do inside. And she was never angry again. The end.

One day, Maisy looked for something to do. She saw her Mommy polishing a black velvet pillow. She asked her Mommy what she was doing.

Mommy said: "I am polishing this pillow so it looks nice and shiny."

Maisy was very curious. She asked: "Can I help you polish it?"

Mommy smiled and said: "Yes, sure! Grab the rag and move it back and forth in circular motions to make the pillow look shiny."

Maisy grabbed the rag and moved it back and forth just like her Mommy said. Soon enough,the black velvet pillow was looking shiny and nice.

Maisy was so proud she helped her Mommy with the polishing! She felt very happy and hugged the pillow with a big smile on her face.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to eat spicy food. One day, she went to her grandma's house for dinner. Her grandma made a spicy soup, and Lily ate it all up. But after dinner, Lily started to complain that her mouth was too hot.

"Grandma, my mouth is too hot," Lily said.

"It's because of the spicy soup," said her grandma.

Lily put her paw on her mouth and said, "I don't like spicy food anymore."

"It's okay, Lily. Next time, I'll make something less spicy for you," said her grandma.

From then on, Lily always asked her grandma to make less spicy food. And she never complained about her mouth being too hot again.

name_of_work: After Prayers, Lie Cold by C.S. Lewis
content: Arise my body, my small body, we have striven Enough, and He is merciful; we are forgiven. Arise small body, puppet-like and pale, and go, White as the bed-clothes into bed, and cold as snow, Undress with small, cold fingers and put out the light, And be alone, hush'd mortal, in the sacred night, -A meadow whipt flat with the rain, a cup Emptied and clean, a garment washed and folded up, Faded in colour, thinned almost to raggedness By dirt and by the washing of that dirtiness. Be not too quickly warm again. Lie cold; consent To weariness' and pardon's watery element. Drink up the bitter water, breathe the chilly death; Soon enough comes the riot of our blood and breath.

Sara and Sam were twins. They liked to play in the park with their dog, Spot. Spot was a big, brown dog who could run very fast and catch a ball. Sara and Sam could whistle, and they taught Spot to come when they whistled.

One day, they went to the park with their mom. The park was very busy. There were many kids and dogs and bikes and kites. Sara and Sam wanted to play with Spot, but they had to be careful not to lose him. They put a red collar on him, so they could see him better.

"Spot, stay close to us," Sara said. "We don't want you to get lost."

"Whistle if you can't find him," Sam said. "He will hear you and come back."

They threw the ball for Spot, and he ran after it. He was very happy. He liked to play with Sara and Sam. They whistled and he came back. They did this many times.

But then, something bad happened. A big, black dog ran into the park. He saw Spot and wanted to play with him. He barked and chased Spot. Spot was scared. He ran away from the big, black dog. He ran so far that he could not see Sara and Sam anymore.

"Sara, where is Spot?" Sam asked. He looked around, but he could not see him.

"I don't know, Sam. He was here a minute ago," Sara said. She was worried. She looked around, but she could not see him either.

They started to whistle. They whistled very loud. They hoped that Spot would hear them and come back. But Spot did not come back. He was lost.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to help her mommy in the kitchen. One day, Lily's mommy was cooking on the stove, but she had to go to the store. She told Lily to be careful and not touch the stove.

Lily promised to be safe and not touch the stove. But then, she saw a shiny spoon on the stove and wanted to play with it. She reached for the spoon and accidentally touched the hot stove! It hurt a lot.

Lily's mommy came back and saw what happened. She told Lily to surrender the spoon and put her hand under cool water. Lily learned that the stove can be dangerous, but it's always safe to ask for help.

Once upon a time, there was a musician who wanted to play. He was ready with his guitar, ready to make music.

The musician looked around. He saw three year old Jimmy, who was playing with his toys.

The musician went over to Jimmy and said, "Hello Jimmy! Would you like to play with me?"

Jimmy looked up and smiled. He said, "Yes!"

The musician took his guitar and began to play a song. Jimmy clapped along and tried to make music too.

The musician smiled at Jimmy and said, "I think you are a very good musician! You are ready to play some music!"

Jimmy laughed and nodded. He said, "Let's play!" 

The musician and Jimmy made music together. They sang and played until the sun went down. At the end, they hugged each other and said goodbye. It was the best day ever!

name_of_work: Dulce et Decorum Est by Wilfred Owen
content: Bent double, like old beggars under sacks, Knock-kneed, coughing like hags, we cursed through sludge, Till on the haunting flares we turned our backs, And towards our distant rest began to trudge. Men marched asleep. Many had lost their boots, But limped on, blood-shod. All went lame; all blind; Drunk with fatigue; deaf even to the hoots Of gas-shells dropping softly behind. Gas! GAS! Quick, boys!--An ecstasy of fumbling Fitting the clumsy helmets just in time, But someone still was yelling out and stumbling And flound'ring like a man in fire or lime.-- Dim through the misty panes and thick green light, As under a green sea, I saw him drowning. In all my dreams before my helpless sight, He plunges at me, guttering, choking, drowning. If in some smothering dreams, you too could pace Behind the wagon that we flung him in, And watch the white eyes writhing in his face, His hanging face, like a devil's sick of sin; If you could hear, at every jolt, the blood Come gargling from the froth-corrupted lungs, Obscene as cancer, bitter as the cud Of vile, incurable sores on innocent tongues,-- My friend, you would not tell with such high zest To children ardent for some desperate glory, The old Lie: Dulce et decorum est Pro patria mori.

Anna and Ben love to play with their toys. They have cars, dolls, blocks and a big elephant. The elephant is soft and gray and has a long nose. Anna and Ben like to hug the elephant and make it talk.

One day, Mom says it is time to go to the park. Anna and Ben are happy. They want to see the swings, the slide and the ducks. But Mom says they have to tidy their room first. She says they have to put their toys in the box and make their bed.

Anna and Ben do not want to tidy their room. They want to go to the park. They think Mom will not see their toys if they hide them under the bed. They rush to the bed and push their toys under it. All the toys except the elephant. The elephant is too big to fit under the bed.

Mom comes to check their room. She sees the bed is not made and the toys are under it. She is not happy. She says Anna and Ben have to tidy their room properly. She says they have to take out their toys and put them in the box. She says they have to make their bed and fluff their pillows. She says they have to say sorry to the elephant for leaving it out.

Anna and Ben feel bad. They love their elephant. They do not want to make it sad. They take out their toys and put them in the box. They make their bed and fluff their pillows. They hug the elephant and say sorry. They say they will not hide their toys again. They say they will be tidy.

Mom sees their room is tidy. She smiles. She says Anna and Ben are good children. She says they can go to the park now. She says they can take the elephant with them. Anna and Ben are happy. They take the elephant and go to the park. They have fun with the swings, the slide and the ducks. They share the elephant with their friends. The elephant is happy too.

name_of_work: A Description of the Morning by Jonathan Swift
content: Now hardly here and there a hackney-coach Appearing, show'd the ruddy morn's approach. Now Betty from her master's bed had flown, And softly stole to discompose her own. The slip-shod 'prentice from his master's door Had par'd the dirt, and sprinkled round the floor. Now Moll had whirl'd her mop with dext'rous airs, Prepar'd to scrub the entry and the stairs. The youth with broomy stumps began to trace The kennel-edge, where wheels had worn the place. The small-coal man was heard with cadence deep; Till drown'd in shriller notes of "chimney-sweep." Duns at his lordship's gate began to meet; And brickdust Moll had scream'd through half a street. The turnkey now his flock returning sees, Duly let out a-nights to steal for fees. The watchful bailiffs take their silent stands; And schoolboys lag with satchels in their hands.

Once upon a time, there was an elderly pony. He lived on a peaceful farm in the countryside. One day, an adventurous little girl decide to go for a ride on the pony. She went up to him and asked, â€œCan I ride on you?â€ 

The elderly pony slowly nodded his head. The girl hopped onto his back and they started to go for a ride. The little girl was very happy as the pony trotted along.

Suddenly, the pony tripped over a stone and threw the girl off his back. The girl fell to the ground and hurt her leg. She started to cry and the pony felt very sad.

The elderly pony looked around, but he couldnâ€™t find the girl. He had to go back to the farm alone. When the girl got back home, her parents were very worried. 

The little girl was never able to ride the pony again.

name_of_work: Boat Stealing: The Prelude (Extract) by William Wordsworth
content: I went alone into a Shepherd's boat, A skiff, that to a willow-tree was tied Within a rocky cave, its usual home. The moon was up, the lake was shining clear Among the hoary mountains; from the shore I pushed, and struck the oars, and struck again In cadence, and my little boat moved on Just like a man who walks with stately step Though bent on speed. It was an act of stealth And troubled pleasure. Not without the voice Of mountain echoes did my boat move on, Leaving behind her still on either side Small circles glittering idly in the moon, Until they melted all into one track Of sparkling light. A rocky steep uprose Above the cavern of the willow-tree, And now, as suited one who proudly rowed With his best skill, I fixed a steady view Upon the top of that same craggy ridge, The bound of the horizon--for behind Was nothing but the stars and the grey sky. She was an elfin pinnace; twenty times I dipped my oars into the silent lake, And as I rose upon the stroke my boat Went heaving through the water like a swan - When from behind that rocky steep, till then The bound of the horizon, a huge cliff, As if voluntary power instinct, Upreared its head. I struck, and struck again, And, growing still in stature, the huge cliff Rose up between me and the stars, and still, With measured motion, like a living thing Strode after me. With trembling hands I turned, And through the silent water stole my way Back to the cavern of the willow tree. There in her mooring-place I left my bark, And through the meadows homeward went with grave And serious thoughts; and after I had seen That spectacle, for many days my brain Worked with a dim and undetermined sense Of unknown modes of being. In my thoughts There was a darkness - call it solitude, Or blank desertion - no familiar shapes Of hourly objects, images of trees, Of sea or sky, no colours of green fields, But huge and mighty forms that do not live Like living men moved slowly through my mind By day, and were the trouble of my dreams.

Once upon a time, there was a small girl called Daisy. Daisy was only three years old and was very curious. She and her mommy went outside to play one day. When they looked up, they saw a big, thick cloud in the sky.

"Mommy, what's that?", asked Daisy, pointing to the cloud.

"That's a cloud, sweetheart," said her mommy, "it's made of water."

Daisy was so excited.

"Can I introduce myself to the cloud?" she asked.

"Of course you can!" said her mommy.

So, Daisy closed her eyes and shouted up to the thick cloud: "Hello, cloud! My name is Daisy!"

For a few moments, nothing happened. Then, suddenly, the cloud started to move and it floated down towards Daisy and her mommy. Daisy smiled, giggled and said, "Hi cloud! It's nice to meet you!"

The cloud floated away to a faraway place, but ever since that day, every time Daisy and her mommy look up at the sky, Daisy remembers the day she introduced herself to the cloud.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside and explore the world around her. One day, she saw a mysterious shadow under a tree. She got scared and ran away.

The next day, Lily saw the shadow again. This time, she decided to be brave and go closer. She realized that the shadow was just from a bird flying above the tree. She felt silly for being scared.

Lily learned that sometimes things can seem scary, but if you get closer and take a closer look, you might find out that there's nothing to be afraid of. It's important to not let fear stop you from exploring and discovering new things.

Once upon a time, there was a big, wild lion. The lion lived in a big jungle with lots of trees and animals. One day, the lion went to a museum with his friends. They saw lots of old things like bones and paintings. The lion liked the paintings with bright colors. After the museum, they went to a party. The lion got a present and he helped his friend wrap it with pretty paper. They had lots of fun together!

One day, a boy named Tim went on a trip with his mom and dad. They had big luggage with them. Tim was very happy to go on the trip. The sun was shining, and the sky was blue.

On the way, Tim saw a big ice cream shop. He gazed at the yummy ice cream cones in the window. "Mom, can we get some ice cream?" Tim asked. Mom said, "Maybe later, we need to get to our hotel first."

When they got to the hotel, Tim saw a big surprise. There was a yummy ice cream party! Tim looked at his mom and said, "You knew about the ice cream party!" Mom smiled and said, "Yes, I did. Now, let's have some fun and enjoy the yummy ice cream!"

Once there was a little girl. She wanted to help her mom and dad. So the little girl decided to serve them dinner. She was so excited!

She put the food on the plates, but it didn't look very nice. She was a bit ashamed. But when her mom and dad tasted the food, they said it tasted very good!

The little girl was so happy! Her mom and dad thanked her for serving them dinner. She was proud of herself and smiled.

Sometimes the little girl still helps her mom and dad. She always serves them dinner really well. She never gets ashamed of her work now - because she knows she is doing a good job!

Tim and Sue were friends who liked to play ball. They had a big red ball that they would kick and catch in the park. One day, they saw a new boy sitting on a bench. He had a small blue ball that he hugged to his chest.

"Hi, what is your name?" Sue asked the new boy.

"Tom," he said in a low voice. He looked shy and sad.

"Do you want to play with us?" Tim asked. He was a kind and modest boy who liked to share.

"No, thank you," Tom said. He did not look at them.

Tim and Sue shrugged and went back to their game. They kicked the big red ball high in the air and laughed. Tom watched them from the bench. He felt lonely and angry. He wanted the big red ball. He thought it was better than his small blue ball.

He waited until Tim and Sue were not looking. Then he ran to their ball and kicked it hard. The ball flew away and hit a tree. It bounced back and hit Tom in the face. He fell to the ground and cried. His lip was bleeding and his nose was sore.

Tim and Sue heard the noise and ran to see what happened. They saw Tom on the ground and their ball next to him.

"What did you do?" Sue asked. She was angry and scared.

"I'm sorry, I'm sorry," Tom sobbed. He tried to get up, but he was dizzy.

Tim and Sue did not help him. They picked up their ball and walked away. They did not want to play with Tom anymore. They thought he was mean and selfish.

Tom was left alone on the bench. He hugged his small blue ball and wished he had been nicer. He learned a hard lesson that day. He should not have kicked the big red ball.

name_of_work: In Memory of My Mother by Patrick Kavanagh
content: I do not think of you lying in the wet clay Of a Monaghan graveyard; I see You walking down a lane among the poplars On your way to the station, or happily Going to second Mass on a summer Sunday - You meet me and you say: 'Don't forget to see about the cattle - ' Among your earthiest words the angels stray. And I think of you walking along a headland Of green oats in June, So full of repose, so rich with life - And I see us meeting at the end of a town On a fair day by accident, after The bargains are all made and we can walk Together through the shops and stalls and markets Free in the oriental streets of thought. O you are not lying in the wet clay, For it is a harvest evening now and we Are piling up the ricks against the moonlight And you smile up at us - eternally.

Once upon a time there was a princess. She liked to play outside in the rain. One day it started to rain. She wanted to keep playing, so she ran and ran until she was soaking wet. All of a sudden, the rain stopped and it got very cold. She shivered and wished it was warm again. 

The princess heard a noise in the sky. She looked up and saw a big cloud in the sky. The princess was scared and ran home until she was safe inside. 

The next morning, the princess woke up and looked outside. Everything was covered in white. The snow had frozen the ground like a sheet of ice. The princess was amazed and went outside to play in the snow. She laughed and made snowballs. She was so excited!

But then, she heard a noise in the sky. She looked up and saw the big cloud again. It was cold, snow began to fall and it was very dark. The princess ran to her home and quickly ran inside. 

Outside, the snow kept falling and the temperature became colder and colder. Suddenly, everything froze! The garden trees, flowers, everything had frozen solid. The princess was so happy the next morning when the sun melted the ice. She enjoyed playing in the warm sun and rain again.

name_of_work: Requiem for the Croppies by Seamus Heaney
content: The pockets of our greatcoats full of barley... No kitchens on the run, no striking camp... We moved quick and sudden in our own country. The priest lay behind ditches with the tramp. A people hardly marching... on the hike... We found new tactics happening each day: We'd cut through reins and rider with the pike And stampede cattle into infantry, Then retreat through hedges where cavalry must be thrown. Until... on Vinegar Hill... the final conclave. Terraced thousands died, shaking scythes at cannon. The hillside blushed, soaked in our broken wave. They buried us without shroud or coffin And in August... the barley grew up out of our grave.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lucy. She loved to explore the big, green park near her house. One day, Lucy was running through the park when she suddenly fell. Her knee hurt and she started to cry.

A friendly dog nearby saw her sad face and came over. His name was Spot.

"Why are you crying?" Spot asked. Lucy sniffled.

"I fell and it hurts!" she replied.

Spot said in a kind voice, "It's ok. Let's get you back up." Spot helped Lucy stand up again and she stopped crying. Suddenly, they heard a loud, harsh noise coming from the sky.

It was a thunderstorm. Spot and Lucy started to run back to Lucy's house together. It was a race against the rain. They made it to Lucy's house just in time and the storm was far away. 

Lucy thanked Spot and said goodbye. She was so happy that Spot helped her get home safely. "Thanks Spot!" she said with a smile.

Once upon a time, there was a little squirrel named Sammy. Sammy loved to play in the forest with his friends. One day, he found a smooth acorn on the ground. He picked it up and showed it to his friends. They all thought it was very pretty.

Sammy decided to keep the acorn and take it home. He wanted to show it to his family. When he got to his tree, he climbed up and entered his little home. He showed the acorn to his mom and dad, and they thought it was very nice too.

From that day on, Sammy kept the acorn in his home. He loved to look at it and remember the fun day he found it with his friends. And every time he entered his home, he would see the smooth acorn and smile.

Millie was a 3-year old who loved animals. One day, her mom mentioned that there was a cow on the farm. Millie was so excited! She put on her shoes and ran outside to see the cow.

The cow was big and white. Millie wanted to give it a hug but the cow looked shy. Instead, Millie talked softly to the cow. She told the cow her name and asked the cow what its name was.

Suddenly, something spicy hit Millie's nose. It was coming from the cow! Millie thought it was funny and kept talking to the cow. After a while, the cow started to feel more comfortable and even let Millie pet its back. Millie was so happy! She ran off to tell her mom what happened.

No ancient mariner I, Hawker of public crosses, Snaring the passersby With my necklace of albatrosses. I blink no glittering eye Between tufts of gray sea mosses Nor in the high road ply My trade of guilts and glosses. But a dark and inward sky Tracks the flotsam of my losses. No more becalmed to lie, The skeleton ship tosses.

WHILE on my lonely couch I lie, I seldom feel myself alone, For fancy fills my dreaming eye With scenes and pleasures of its own. Then I may cherish at my breast An infant's form beloved and fair, May smile and soothe it into rest With all a Mother's fondest care. How sweet to feel its helpless form Depending thus on me alone! And while I hold it safe and warm What bliss to think it is my own! And glances then may meet my eyes That daylight never showed to me; What raptures in my bosom rise, Those earnest looks of love to see, To feel my hand so kindly prest, To know myself beloved at last, To think my heart has found a rest, My life of solitude is past! But then to wake and find it flown, The dream of happiness destroyed, To find myself unloved, alone, What tongue can speak the dreary void?

Ben and Lily were playing in the park. They liked to slide, swing and run. They saw a big pile of leaves. They wanted to jump in it.

"Let's go, Ben!" Lily said. "It looks fun!"

They ran to the pile of leaves and jumped in. They laughed and threw leaves in the air. They felt something hard under the leaves. They moved the leaves and saw a skeleton.

"Ah!" Ben screamed. "It's a scary skeleton!"

Lily was not scared. She looked at the skeleton. It was brown and had no eyes, nose or hair. It had a big smile.

"It's not scary, Ben," Lily said. "It's just a skeleton. It can't hurt us. Maybe it was a nice person before."

Ben was still scared. He wanted to run away. He did not like the skeleton.

"No, Lily, it's scary!" Ben said. "Let's go away!"

Lily did not want to go. She wanted to hug the skeleton. She thought it was lonely and needed a friend.

"Please, Ben, don't go," Lily said. "Let's hug the skeleton. Maybe it will be happy."

Ben did not want to hug the skeleton. He thought it was cold and creepy. He did not want to make it happy.

"No, Lily, don't hug it!" Ben said. "It might bite you!"

Lily did not listen to Ben. She hugged the skeleton. It did not bite her. It did not move. It just smiled.

"See, Ben, it's not scary," Lily said. "It's nice. You can hug it too."

Ben looked at Lily and the skeleton. He saw that Lily was happy. He saw that the skeleton was not scary. He felt sorry for the skeleton. He decided to hug it too.

He hugged the skeleton. It did not bite him. It did not move. It just smiled.

"See, Lily, you were right," Ben said. "It's nice. I'm sorry I was scared."

Lily and Ben hugged the skeleton. They felt happy. They made a new friend. They played with the skeleton and the leaves. They had fun.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Emma. Emma was three years old. On Tuesdays, Emma believed that the world was dark. She would go outside and look into the sky and think that the night time had come early. Emma had been told that nighttime was dark, and she was convinced that every Tuesday had become dark.

But her friends told her that the sky was still light, and that it was just her imagination! She didn't believe them at first, but then she went back outside and saw that the sky was still bright. She was so happy to know that it wasn't dark like she thought.

Emma smiled and realized that Tuesdays weren't always dark after all. She knew that the next one would be bright and happy again!

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Polly. Polly was three years old and she loved to go outside and explore the big world around her. One day while she was out walking, she came to a street.

Polly carefully balanced her way down the street, welcoming each new challenge as she stepped from one foot to the other. Suddenly, a loud car startled her, and she stumbled.

"Oh no!" shouted Polly, as she fell onto the street. A kind man walked over to help her. 

"Are you alright?" he asked in a gentle, patient voice.

"Yes," said Polly. She was a bit scared, but the man's kind demeanor made her feel better.

The man offered to help Polly get back on her feet and Polly said yes. She held on to him as he balanced her back to safety. 

Unfortunately, the man was not as kind as he seemed. As soon as they reached the other side of the street, he grabbed Polly and ran away. 

Polly cried and screamed but no one was around to save her. She was never seen again.

Jen wanted to go to the park but her mom said they had to wait. Jen was sad. She didn't understand why they had to delay the fun. Mom said it was because it wouldn't be dependable.

The wind was blowing, and Jen saw a stand with lots of flowers. Mom stopped and bought a few to brighten up the house. Jen was happy and forgot that they were going to the park.

On the way home, they saw the park. Mom told Jen that if it wasn't dependable they wouldn't have to wait forever to go. Jen smiled and jumped in the car. 

They went home and Jen put the flowers in the stand. She looked outside and saw the park in the distance and knew that one day they'd be able to go together.

Sara and Tom liked each other very much. They played together every day at the park. They shared their toys and snacks. They said they wanted to marry when they grew up.

One day, Sara and Tom went to the ice cream shop. They each got a cone with their favorite flavor. Sara had chocolate and Tom had vanilla. They were very happy.

But then, a big boy came and took Sara's cone. He said it was his and he liked chocolate. Sara was very sad and cried. Tom tried to get the cone back, but the big boy pushed him and ran away.

Sara and Tom had no ice cream left. They were very angry and hurt. They blamed each other for losing their cones. They said mean things and stopped being friends.

They never played together again. They never married. They never had original cones. They were very lonely. The end.

Once there was a little girl named Daisy. One day Daisy got very wet playing in the rain. She had forgotten to bring a raincoat, but that was okay. She had a dry shirt in her bag. 

Daisy changed out of her wet clothes and put on her dry shirt. Unfortunately, Daisy had forgotten her pants. She quickly looked around and asked her mom for help. 

Mommy went into Daisy's room and found a pair of dry pants for her. Daisy was so happy to have something dry to wear. She put on the pants and then smiled. 

After that, Daisy went outside to play again. This time she remembered to take a raincoat so she didn't forget again.

Once upon a time, there was a big, huge bear. He lived in the woods and loved to drink cocoa. Every day he would go out and get his favorite treat. 

One day, he noticed something different. There were huge trees blocking the way to the cocoa shop. He tried to push the trees away, but they were too big. He started to feel sad and he sighed. 

Suddenly, he heard a tiny voice. "Don't worry!", said the small voice. He looked around and saw a small bird in a tree. It was the bird who had spoken. She said, "I know a secret way." 

The bear was happy. He followed the bird through the secret way to the cocoa shop. As he sipped his cocoa, he couldn't help but sigh with joy.

Once upon a time, a little girl named Lola saw an animal in the park. It was a harmless bunny. She wanted to get closer and say "Hi", but she was scared it might not be too friendly.

Just then, her mommy let her take a closer look. When Lola got closer, she noticed the bunny was standing next to a swing. She got an idea.

Lola asked her mommy to let her swing, and mommy said yes. As Lola swung, the bunny watched. After a few swings, Lola noticed the bunny hopped on the swing, too!

From then on, Lola and the bunny had lots of fun together, going for swings in the park. Lola never had to worry about the bunny, for it was harmless. They even became friends. The bunny became an important part of the park, and everyone was happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily and her mom went to the park to play. The sky was blue and the sun was shining. Lily saw a bird in the sky and said, "Look, Mommy! The bird is flying so high!" 

Suddenly, Lily felt very tired and said, "Mommy, I want to take a nap." Her mom said, "Okay, let's find a nice spot for you to rest." They found a soft patch of grass under a tree and Lily lay down. 

As she closed her eyes, Lily saw something incredible in her dream. She dreamt that she was flying in the sky with the bird she saw earlier. She felt so happy and free. When she woke up, she said to her mom, "Mommy, I had an incredible dream. I was flying in the sky like a bird!" Her mom smiled and said, "That sounds like a wonderful dream, Lily."

Once upon a time there was a big, old tree. Every day it softly joined the birds in singing a nice song. Lucy, a 3 year old girl, loved it so much. She would always take a few minutes and stop to listen. 

One day, as Lucy was passing by the tree, she spotted a new and shiny file on the ground. When she picked it up, it felt really light and smooth. She opened it up, and was amazed by what she saw inside. 

"Wow," she said. "What is this?"

"It's an amazing file," said the tree. "It holds all the secrets of the earth. Keep it safe, and listen carefully to the things it tells you."

Lucy was excited, and felt proud to be trusted with something as special as this. She made sure to keep the file close to her and listen to the stories it had to tell. 

Later, when Lucy listened closely to the file, she began to understand some of the secrets of the world. She felt proud of herself and amazed at what she'd learned.
