Once upon a time there was a powerful wizard. He had a special power that allowed him to freeze things. One day he wanted to show everyone his power. So he went outside and waved his magic wand. Suddenly, everything around him stopped moving. Everything was frozen. The birds were suspended in mid-air and the trees were still. Everyone was amazed by the wizard's powerful magic. Even the sun stopped in the sky and time seemed to stand still. 

The wizard was proud of his power and he enjoyed showing it off. He finally unfroze everything but now he knew he had an amazing and powerful power that nobody else had. From that day on he was known as the wizard with the power to freeze.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Susie. She had a big red scarf that she loved very much. She always wore it, especially when she went out with her mum and dad.

One day, Susie and her parents went to a restaurant selling spicy food. The smells were very exciting and made Susie curious. She wanted to try some of the spicy food, but she was a little bit scared. 

So, dad said: â€œSusie, you need to trust us. We will take care of you and keep you safe.â€

Susie felt much better, and she tied her scarf around her neck. She felt so brave! With her parents watching over her, she tried all of the spicy food and enjoyed every bite!

At the end of the day, Susie knew that she could trust her parents. With their help, she was always safe and nothing ever bad happened to her.

name_of_work: Keeping Things Whole by Mark Strand
content: In a field I am the absence of field. This is always the case. Wherever I am I am what is missing. When I walk I part the air and always the air moves in to fill the spaces where my body's been. We all have reasons for moving. I move to keep things whole.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Jane. She liked to wear her favourite dress which was a pretty pink one.

One evening, when Jane went outside to play, she saw a big angry dog. She was scared and very quickly ran back into her house.

When Jane's mum saw her she asked, "Why are you so scared, darling?"

Jane said, "I saw an angry dog outside".

Mum said, "It's ok, sweetheart. Next time, wear your shoes. That way, if you see a scary dog, you can run away quickly".

Jane nodded and from then on, she always made sure to wear her shoes whenever she went outside.

name_of_work: The Ballad of William Sycamore by Stephen Vincent Benet
content: My father, he was a mountaineer, His fist was a knotty hammer; He was quick on his feet as a running deer, And he spoke with a Yankee stammer. My mother, she was merry and brave, And so she came to her labor, With a tall green fir for her doctor grave And a stream for her comforting neighbor. And some are wrapped in the linen fine, And some like a godling's scion; But I was cradled on twigs of pine And the skin of a mountain lion. And some remember a white, starched lap And a ewer with silver handles; But I remember a coonskin cap And the smell of bayberry candles. The cabin logs, with the bark still rough, And my mother who laughed at trifles, And the tall, lank visitors, brown as snuff, With their long, straight squirrel-rifles. I can hear them dance, like a foggy song, Through the deepest one of my slumbers, The fiddle squeaking the boots along And my father calling the numbers. The quick feet shaking the puncheon-floor, And the fiddle squealing and squealing, Till the dried herbs rattled above the door And the dust went up to the ceiling. There are children lucky from dawn till dusk, But never a child so lucky! For I cut my teeth on "Money Musk" In the Bloody Ground of Kentucky! When I grew tall as the Indian corn, My father had little to lend me, But he gave me his great, old powder-horn And his woodsman's skill to befriend me. With a leather shirt to cover my back, And a redskin nose to unravel Each forest sign, I carried my pack As far as a scout could travel. Till I lost my boyhood and found my wife, A girl like a Salem clipper! A woman straight as a hunting-knife With as eyes as bright as the Dipper! We cleared our camp where the buffalo feed, Unheard-of streams were our flagons; And I sowed my sons like the apple-seed On the trail of the Western wagons. They were right, tight boys, never sulky or slow, A fruitful, a goodly muster. The eldest died at the Alamo. The youngest fell with Custer. The letter that told it burned my hand. Yet we smiled and said, "So be it!" But I could not live when they fenced the land, For it broke my heart to see it. I saddled a red, unbroken colt And rode him into the day there; And he threw me down like a thunderbolt And rolled on me as I lay there. The hunter's whistle hummed in my ear As the city-men tried to move me, And I died in my boots like a pioneer With the whole wide sky above me. Now I lie in the heart of the fat, black soil, Like the seed of a prairie-thistle; It has washed my bones with honey and oil And picked them clean as a whistle. And my youth returns, like the rains of Spring, And my sons, like the wild-geese flying; And I lie and hear the meadow-lark sing And have much content in my dying. Go play with the towns you have built of blocks, The towns where you would have bound me! I sleep in my earth like a tired fox, And my buffalo have found me.

Jack and his mother were playing a silly game. Jack pretended he was a dog. He crawled around on the floor and barked. His mother laughed and pretended she was a cat. She meowed and swatted at him playfully. Then Jack pretended to be a bird and started flapping his arms like wings. His mother tried to catch him, but he flew out of her reach. She said "You can fly away, but you have to come back to me!" Jack smiled and kept flying around the room. The game kept going until Jack got tired. Then his mother hugged him and said "That was a very silly game, wasn't it?". Jack nodded and giggled. He had a lot of fun pretending with his mother!

Once upon a time, there was a little dog. The dog had an owner. The owner loved the dog. One day, the owner and the dog went for a walk. They went to a big park. The park had many trees and flowers. The owner saw a hidden spot behind a big tree. The owner wanted to sit there.

The owner said to the dog, "Sit here with me." The owner sat down with the dog. The owner did not attach the dog to a leash. The dog saw a squirrel. The squirrel was running and playing. The dog wanted to play too. The dog ran after the squirrel. The owner called the dog, but the dog did not come back.

The owner looked for the dog. The owner called the dog's name. The dog did not hear the owner. The dog was lost. The owner was sad. The dog was sad too. They could not find each other. The owner went home without the dog. The dog stayed in the park. The dog and the owner did not have a happy ending.

name_of_work: The Heat of Autumn by Jane Hirshfield
content: The heat of autumn is different from the heat of summer. One ripens apples, the other turns them to cider. One is a dock you walk out on, the other the spine of a thin swimming horse and the river each day a full measure colder. A man with cancer leaves his wife for his lover. Before he goes she straightens his belts in the closet, rearranges the socks and sweaters inside the dresser by color. That's autumn heat: her hand placing silver buckles with silver, gold buckles with gold, setting each on the hook it belongs on in a closet soon to be empty, and calling it pleasure.

One day, a little boy named Tim found a newspaper on the floor. He picked it up and looked at the big words and impressive pictures. He did not know what the words said, but he liked the pictures a lot.

Tim ran to his mom and showed her the newspaper. He said, "Mom, look at this! What are these words?" His mom smiled and said, "This is a newspaper, Tim. It has stories and pictures about things that happen in the world."

Tim looked at the newspaper again and started to wonder. He asked his mom, "Can I make my own newspaper with my own stories and pictures?" His mom thought it was a great idea. She said, "Yes, Tim! That would be very impressive. Let's get some paper and colors to make your own newspaper."

Together, they made a newspaper with Tim's stories and pictures. Tim was very happy and proud of his impressive newspaper.

One day there was a bird who lived in a cage. The bird was very sad because it wanted to fly free in the sky, not be stuck in a cage. The bird tried to explain to the person taking care of it why it wanted to be free.

"Let me fly!" said the bird. 
But the person was very ignorant and just said, "No, you are too small and delicate."

The bird was so sad and decided to find another way to fill its cage with something else. So, it thought very hard and found a way to fill its cage with sunshine.

The bird flew to the top of the cage and sang to the sun. The sun was very happy and shined its light into the cage. The bird felt so warm, and eventually it was filled with the sunshine. 

The bird was so happy and sang a song of joy for being free. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a big house. It had a porch that was very special. Inside the porch was something fragile.

Every morning the family would go out to the porch and work together. They would be very careful not to break the fragile thing.

The family worked hard, and one day they finished what they were doing. Everyone was very happy. They had finished making the special thing!

At the end of the day, they stepped back to admire what they had made. It was a beautiful thing.

The family was so proud of their work. They smiled and hugged each other.

They knew that something very special had been made on their porch.

name_of_work: Time Is by Henry van Dyke
content: Time is too slow for those who wait, too swift for those who fear, too long for those who grieve, too short for those who rejoice, but for those who love, time is eternity.

Lily and Max are friends. They like to play at the park. They run, slide, and swing. Swing is fun. They go up and down, fast and slow.

One day, they see a new thing at the park. It is a big box with many colors. It says "Art". Lily and Max are curious. They go to the box and look inside. They see paper, crayons, glue, scissors, and many other things. They also see a lady with a smile.

"Hello, children. Do you want to make some art?" the lady asks.

"Yes, please!" Lily and Max say.

The lady gives them paper and crayons. She tells them to draw whatever they want. Lily draws a flower. Max draws a car. They are happy.

Then, the lady shows them something else. It is a big bag with many pieces of fabric. They have different colors, shapes, and textures. Texture is how something feels. Some are soft, some are rough, some are smooth, some are fuzzy.

"Do you want to try some textures?" the lady asks.

"Yes, please!" Lily and Max say.

The lady gives them glue and scissors. She tells them to cut the fabric and stick it on their paper. Lily and Max have fun. They touch the fabric and choose their favorites. They make their flower and car more colorful and more textured.

They are proud of their art. They show it to the lady and to each other.

"Wow, you are very creative!" the lady says.

"Thank you!" Lily and Max say.

They want to take their art home. But first, they want to play some more. They put their art in the box and run to the swing. They swing and laugh.

They are hungry. They smell something yummy. It is a cart with ice cream. They see their moms. Their moms have ice cream for them.

"Hi, Lily and Max. Did you have fun at the park?" their moms ask.

"Yes, we did!" Lily and Max say.

They tell their moms about the art and the textures. They show their moms their paper and fabric. Their moms are impressed.

"That's very nice!" their moms say.

They give them a hug and a kiss. They give them ice cream. Ice cream is yummy. Lily and Max are happy.

They eat their ice cream and share their art. They are friends. They like to play at the park. They run, slide, and swing. Swing is fun. They go up and down, fast and slow.

name_of_work: Epic Simile by A. E. Stallings
content: Right shoulder aching with day-long butchery, Left shoulder numb with dints clanged on the shield, The hero is fouled with blood, his own and others', First slick, then sticky, then caked, starting to mat His beard--the armor deadweight all around him; His teeth grit and rattle with every jolt Of bronze-rimmed wheels behind the shit-flecked horses. But when he glimpses the mountains, the distant snow, A blankness swoons upon him, and he hears Nothing but the white vowels of the wind Brushing through stands of spears like conifers While a banner slips its staff and hangs in the blue Like a kestrel or a contrail. The hero's death, The prize, elusive quarry of his life, Stands stock-still in her cloven tracks in snow And turns, one ear tuned to the creek's far bank, One dished towards him. Her unstartled gaze Beads on him like a sniper's sights, until At the clean report of a cracking poplar branch, She leaps away like luck, over rapid water, And snowfall scrims the scene like a mist of tears, Like a migraine, like sweat or blood streaming into your eyes.

One day, a little boy named Bobo was playing in the park. He was running around, feeling very cool. Suddenly, he tripped and dropped his lunch. His stomach growled, feeling sad and empty.

Bobo then noticed the park's snack stand and he got an idea. He ran towards the snack stand and asked for something to eat. The lady in the stand told him he had to pay for the food, but he didn't have any money.

The lady refused to give him anything, so Bobo started to cry. She still refused to help him. Bobo was very disappointed, so he left the park feeling very sad and hungry.

The bad ending was that Bobo had to go home without any food. He was very upset, but he held back his tears. His stomach was still empty, but he was too cool to let anyone know.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside with her friends. One day, Lily saw a small plant in her garden. She thought it was very important to take care of the plant, so it could grow big and strong.

Lily watered the plant every day. She talked to it and even sang songs to make it happy. The plant grew bigger and bigger. One day, there was a contest in the town to see who had the biggest plant. Lily knew her plant was big, so she decided to join the contest.

On the day of the contest, many people came to see the big plants. Lily's plant was the biggest of them all! Everyone clapped and cheered for Lily. She was so happy and proud. At the end of the contest, Lily won a prize for having the biggest plant. She knew that taking care of her important plant had helped her win.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy. He loved to play with drums. One day, he went to the park with his parents to show off his drumming skills. His parents were very proud and excited to watch. 

The little boy played the drum brilliantly. Everyone was amazed and started clapping, including his parents. 

After the drumming performance, his parents asked him, "Wasn't that tune successful?"

The little boy replied, "Yes, it was very successful! I even embarrassed my dad with my drumming!"

Everyone laughed and his parents gave him a hug. They were all very proud of him and his successful drumming.

I see the countless Christmas trees around the world below With tiny lights, like Heaven's stars, reflecting on the snow The sight is so spectacular, please wipe away the tear For I am spending Christmas with Jesus Christ this year. I hear the many Christmas songs that people hold so dear But the sounds of music can't compare with the Christmas choir up here. I have no words to tell you, the joy their voices bring, For it is beyond description, to hear the angels sing. I know how much you miss me, I see the pain inside your heart. But I am not so far away, We really aren't apart. So be happy for me, dear ones, You know I hold you dear. And be glad I'm spending Christmas with Jesus Christ this year. I sent you each a special gift, from my heavenly home above. I sent you each a memory of my undying love. After all, love is a gift more precious than pure gold. It was always most important in the stories Jesus told. Please love and keep each other, as my Father said to do. For I can't count the blessing or love He has for each of you. So have a Merry Christmas and wipe away that tear. Remember, I am spending Christmas with Jesus Christ this year.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She loved to draw with her pastel colors. One day, Lily's mom took her to an art show. Lily saw many impressive paintings and sculptures. She was amazed!

As they were walking around, Lily saw a bell. She asked her mom, "Can I ring the bell?" Her mom said, "Sure, go ahead." So, Lily rang the bell and it made a loud noise.

Later that day, Lily and her mom went to a bakery. Lily saw a cake with a bell on top. She said, "Mom, can we get that cake with the bell?" Her mom said, "Sure, let's get it." When they got home, Lily's mom cut the cake and the bell rang again. Lily was so happy and said, "I love ringing bells!"

Mia and Ben were bored. They had played with all their toys and read all their books. They wanted to do something fun.

"Can we watch a film?" Mia asked her mom.

"Sorry, sweetie, the film is not for little kids. It is scary and loud. You will not like it." Mom said.

"Can we go outside?" Ben asked.

"Sorry, honey, it is too cold and wet. You will catch a cold. You need to stay inside." Mom said.

Mia and Ben sighed. They did not know what to do.

"Hey, I have an idea!" Mom said. "Why don't you take a nap? You will feel better and have more energy later."

"A nap?" Mia and Ben said. They did not want to nap. They wanted to have fun.

"Yes, a nap. Come on, I will tuck you in. You can cuddle with your teddy bears and listen to some music." Mom said.

She led them to their bedroom and helped them get into their beds. She gave them each a kiss and turned on the music.

"Sleep well, my loves. I will wake you up when the film is over." She said.

Mia and Ben closed their eyes. They tried to stay awake, but the music was soft and soothing. They felt warm and cozy. They drifted off to sleep.

They had a nice dream. They dreamed that they were in a film. They were the stars. They had adventures and made friends. They laughed and sang. They were not bored at all.

When they woke up, they saw Mom smiling at them. She looked pale. She had dark circles under her eyes.

"Did you enjoy the film?" Mia asked.

"Not really. It was scary and loud. I did not like it." Mom said.

"Can we watch it?" Ben asked.

"No, you can't. It is not for little kids. Trust me, you would not like it." Mom said.

"Can we go outside?" Mia asked.

"Yes, you can. It is sunny and dry. You can play in the garden. Come on, let's go." Mom said.

Mia and Ben jumped out of their beds. They grabbed their coats and shoes. They ran to the door.

"Thank you for the nap, Mom. It was fun." They said.

"You're welcome, my loves. I'm glad you had fun." Mom said.

She followed them outside. She felt tired and sore. She wished she had taken a nap too.

name_of_work: every single day by John Straley
content: Suppose I said the word "springtime" and I wrote the words "king salmon" on a piece of paper and mailed it to you. When you opened it would you remember that afternoon we spent together in the yellow boat when the early whales were feeding and we caught our first fish of the year? Or would you remember that time off Cape Flattery when you were a little girl: your father smoking, telling stories as he ran the boat, then the tug and zing of that very first fish spooling off into the gray-green world; you laughing and brushing back your hair before setting the hook? I know I am hard to understand sometimes particularly when you are standing at the post office with only a piece of paper saying "king salmon" on it but just think of it as a promissary note and that electric tug, that thrill pulling your mind into deep water is how I feel about you every, single day.

Once upon a time, there was a small park. In the park, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim liked to play with his ball in the park every day. One day, Tim met a girl named Amy. Amy was sad because she could not play with the ball well.

Tim said, "I can help you improve!" So, they played together and Amy got better at playing with the ball. They were happy and had fun in the park.

One day, a big dog came to the park. The dog saw the ball and wanted it. The dog took the ball and ran away. Tim and Amy were very sad. They learned that it is important to be careful with their toys and not to let them out of their sight.

name_of_work: Among School Children by William Butler Yeats
content: I walk through the long schoolroom questioning; A kind old nun in a white hood replies; The children learn to cipher and to sing, To study reading-books and history, To cut and sew, be neat in everything In the best modern way--the children's eyes In momentary wonder stare upon A sixty-year-old smiling public man. I dream of a Ledaean body, bent Above a sinking fire, a tale that she Told of a harsh reproof, or trivial event That changed some childish day to tragedy-- Told, and it seemed that our two natures blent Into a sphere from youthful sympathy, Or else, to alter Plato's parable, Into the yolk and white of the one shell. And thinking of that fit of grief or rage I look upon one child or t'other there And wonder if she stood so at that age-- For even daughters of the swan can share Something of every paddler's heritage-- And had that colour upon cheek or hair, And thereupon my heart is driven wild: She stands before me as a living child. Her present image floats into the mind-- Did Quattrocento finger fashion it Hollow of cheek as though it drank the wind And took a mess of shadows for its meat? And I though never of Ledaean kind Had pretty plumage once--enough of that, Better to smile on all that smile, and show There is a comfortable kind of old scarecrow. What youthful mother, a shape upon her lap Honey of generation had betrayed, And that must sleep, shriek, struggle to escape As recollection or the drug decide, Would think her son, did she but see that shape With sixty or more winters on its head, A compensation for the pang of his birth, Or the uncertainty of his setting forth? Plato thought nature but a spume that plays Upon a ghostly paradigm of things; Solider Aristotle played the taws Upon the bottom of a king of kings; World-famous golden-thighed Pythagoras Fingered upon a fiddle-stick or strings What a star sang and careless Muses heard: Old clothes upon old sticks to scare a bird. Both nuns and mothers worship images, But those the candles light are not as those That animate a mother's reveries, But keep a marble or a bronze repose. And yet they too break hearts--O Presences That passion, piety or affection knows, And that all heavenly glory symbolise-- O self-born mockers of man's enterprise; Labour is blossoming or dancing where The body is not bruised to pleasure soul, Nor beauty born out of its own despair, Nor blear-eyed wisdom out of midnight oil. O chestnut tree, great rooted blossomer, Are you the leaf, the blossom or the bole? O body swayed to music, O brightening glance, How can we know the dancer from the dance?

John stared at the big stage. He had dreamed of performing on it someday. He knew it would be fun, but he also knew it might not be easy. 

John had never been on a stage before, but today was his first day. His mom was there to give him a big hug and wish him luck. John smiled and took a deep breath.

When it was his turn, John stepped onto the stage. He looked out at the audience nervously and smiled. He was so excited! He remembered to take his time and not rush his performance. 

He performed his song perfectly, and when it was over the audience cheered and clapped. John smiled and thanked them. He was so proud of himself!

John waved goodbye and stepped off the stage. He looked back one more time, still in awe of the big stage. He knew he wanted to come back and perform again soon.

name_of_work: The Country of the Blind by C.S. Lewis
content: Hard light bathed them-a whole nation of eyeless men, Dark bipeds not aware how they were maimed. A long Process, clearly, a slow curse, Drained through centuries, left them thus. At some transitional stage, then, a luckless few, No doubt, must have had eyes after the up-to-date, Normal type had achieved snug Darkness, safe from the guns of heavn; Whose blind mouths would abuse words that belonged to their Great-grandsires, unabashed, talking of light in some Eunuch'd, etiolated, Fungoid sense, as a symbol of Abstract thoughts. If a man, one that had eyes, a poor Misfit, spoke of the grey dawn or the stars or green- Sloped sea waves, or admired how Warm tints change in a lady's cheek, None complained he had used words from an alien tongue, None question'd. It was worse. All would agree 'Of course,' Came their answer. "We've all felt Just like that." They were wrong. And he Knew too much to be clear, could not explain. The words -- Sold, raped flung to the dogs -- now could avail no more; Hence silence. But the mouldwarps, With glib confidence, easily Showed how tricks of the phrase, sheer metaphors could set Fools concocting a myth, taking the worlds for things. Do you think this a far-fetched Picture? Go then about among Men now famous; attempt speech on the truths that once, Opaque, carved in divine forms, irremovable, Dear but dear as a mountain- Mass, stood plain to the inward eye.

Anna was a healthy girl who liked to play with her friends. She liked to run, jump, and swing on the playground. She also liked to eat fruits and vegetables that made her strong and happy.

One day, Anna saw a new boy sitting on a bench. He looked sad and lonely. He was very big and had a lot of weight. Anna wanted to be nice and make a new friend. She walked up to him and said, "Hi, I am Anna. What is your name?"

The boy looked up and smiled a little. He said, "I am Ben. I just moved here with my family. I don't know anyone here."

Anna said, "Don't be sad, Ben. I can introduce you to my friends. They are very fun and kind. Do you want to play with us?"

Ben nodded and said, "Yes, please. I like to play. Thank you, Anna."

Anna took Ben by the hand and led him to the playground. She introduced him to her friends, who welcomed him and invited him to join their games. Ben had a lot of fun and laughed a lot. He felt happy and grateful to Anna.

Anna and Ben became good friends. They played together every day. They also helped each other to be healthy. Anna taught Ben how to eat fruits and vegetables that made him strong and happy. Ben taught Anna how to do puzzles and read books that made her smart and curious. They both learned new things and had fun. They were happy and healthy.

Once there was a friendly little boy who loved playing outside. He was walking around when he saw something shining on the ground. He kneeled down to get a closer look and discovered it was a piece of cardboard! He smiled and picked it up.

He decided to take the cardboard home and make something special with it. He walked back home and asked his mom if he could have some scissors and markers, so he could decorate the cardboard. His mom said yes and gave them to him.

The little boy carefully cut the cardboard into the shape of a boat. He then used the markers and bright colours to turn his boat into something really special. He was so proud of his boat!

On the next sunny day, he took the boat out and to the park to play with. He asked his mom if his mom and dad could come with him, and they said yes. When they got to the park, the little boy kneeled down in the grass and began playing with his boat. Everyone in the park was smiling and being friendly to the little boy.

Once upon a time, there was a serious problem. Everywhere, people were in a rush and could not take time to enjoy life. 

One day, a big helicopter came from nowhere. It was a very big surprise for everyone because none of them expected it!

The helicopter hovered over the town centre, and then lowered some rope. Everyone could see that there was something important in the helicopter, but no one knew what. 

Suddenly, the helicopter lifted up again and disappeared into the sky! Everyone was very sad that it had gone, but then they noticed that time had stopped. 

No one had to hurry any more, the helicopter had delayed the time! Everyone was so happy, that they decided to take time to appreciate and enjoy life from then on. 

The end.

Oh when I think of my long-suffering race, For weary centuries despised, oppressed, Enslaved and lynched, denied a human place In the great life line of the Christian West; And in the Black Land disinherited, Robbed in the ancient country of its birth, My heart grows sick with hate, becomes as lead, For this my race that has no home on earth. Then from the dark depths of my soul I cry To the avenging angel to consume The white man's world of wonders utterly: Let it be swallowed up in earth's vast womb, Or upward roll as sacrificial smoke To liberate my people from its yoke!

Jimmy was a 3-year-old who loved to explore the beach. On this particular day, he had packed a bag with his shovel, bucket, and net and headed off to the shore.

When he arrived, he couldn't believe his eyes! Just a little ways ahead was a cute, gentle seal playing in the waves. Jimmy was mesmerized.

He slowly approached, wanting to get a better view. The seal stopped and looked at him, and Jimmy paused in surprise. The seal slowly moved closer, and Jimmy couldn't help but giggle.

The seal spoke to him, saying, "Hello Jimmy! I recommend you go this way today. It's a beautiful spot and I think you'll love it."

Jimmy was so excited! He thanked the seal and headed off, his heart filled with joy. After exploring the spot all morning, Jimmy returned to the beach, hoping the seal was still around. He was luckyâ€”there was the seal, playing in the waves.

Jimmy ran over, feeling so happy he'd made a new friend. He thanked the seal again and gave him a big hug before returning home. From that day forth, the seal was a part of Jimmyâ€™s adventures.

One day, a little girl and her daddy went to the park. The girl was so excited! She liked to run and swing, but most of all she liked to slide. While they were at the park, her daddy brought a big dictionary. The girl wondered why he brought it.

Her daddy said, "Look at all the big words in the dictionary. Maybe one day you can learn them." The girl thought it sounded like fun.

Daddy brought healthy snacks for their picnic. They ate apples and carrots and drank water. The girl was so happy to be outside in the sunshine and to be spending the day with her daddy. 

After snack time, the girl asked to play more. Daddy said, "Let's play tag. That's a healthy game." So the girl ran and laughed and played tag with her daddy until it was time to go home. 

The girl was so tired from their adventure at the park that she fell asleep as soon as her head hit the pillow. She was glad that she had a fun and healthy day at the park with her daddy!

Tom and Jen are twins. They like to play with their toys in their room. But sometimes they fight over the toys. One day, they find a box of matches in their dad's drawer. They think the matches are fun and shiny.

"Let me have a match!" Tom says. He grabs a match from the box.

"No, it's mine!" Jen says. She pulls the match from Tom's hand.

They tug and pull the match until it breaks in two. They both cry.

"Look what you did!" Tom says. He throws his half of the match on the floor.

"Your fault!" Jen says. She rubs her half of the match on the wall.

The match makes a spark and a flame. The flame is fierce and hot. It burns the wall and the curtain.

"Fire! Fire!" Tom and Jen scream. They run out of the room.

Their mom and dad hear them and smell the smoke. They rush to the room and see the fire. They use water and a blanket to put out the fire.

They are angry and scared. They hug Tom and Jen and tell them to never play with matches again.

"Matches are not toys. Matches are dangerous. Matches can hurt you and the house," their mom says.

"We're sorry, mom. We're sorry, dad. We didn't know. We won't do it again," Tom and Jen say.

They are sorry and sad. They learn a lesson. They promise to share their toys and not fight. They also promise to not touch matches ever again.

Once upon a time, there was a team made up of a bunch of friends. They decided to spread around and visit the neighbourhood to see what they could do to help.

The first place they visited was an old lady's house. She was very happy to see them but didn't need any help. She thanked them for asking and said how nice it was to have such a kind and helpful team.

The group travelled around for a few more hours, but didn't find anywhere else that needed them. They were about to give up when they heard a loud sob coming from a nearby park.

When they arrived, they saw a little girl crying. She had scraped her knee and no one was around to help. The team quickly got to work. They gave the little girl a bandage and made sure she was okay. She thanked them and said they were the most helpful team ever!

The girl's smile filled the team with joy. They decided to keep spreading and helping people who needed it. From that day on, they were known as the Helpful Team!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a desert with lots of cactuses. One day, she saw a big cactus with lots of thorns. She wanted to touch it, but her mom said no because it would hurt her. Lily tried to resist touching it, but it looked so interesting. 

Suddenly, a helpful rabbit came along and told her that cactuses have sharp thorns that can hurt her. Lily was happy that the rabbit was helpful and listened to him. She didn't touch the cactus and thanked the rabbit. 

From that day on, Lily learned to resist touching things that could hurt her and always looked for helpful animals like the rabbit. She loved living in the desert with all the cactuses, but knew to be careful around them.

Once there was a man named Rob who had a young daughter. She was always very helpful and loved to joke around. One day, the daughter asked Rob for something very special. She wanted to go to the beach to swim in the ocean. Rob said no, but she kept trying to get him to say yes.

Rob was unfazed by her persistence, however. He said that it was too dangerous to go to the beach. He didn't want his daughter in deep water without an adult watching. His daughter was very disappointed and stopped trying to get what she wanted.

Rob had a good reason for saying no, and his daughter soon understood that. Even though it was difficult, she realized that her dad had only said no because he loves her and wants to keep her safe. This showed that love doesn't always mean getting what you want, but it can mean being helpful and understanding why certain things are not allowed.

Lily and Ben were playing in the backyard. They saw a big wire on the ground. It was long and shiny and had many colors.

"What is this?" Lily asked.

"I don't know. Maybe it is a snake," Ben said.

They touched the wire. It was cold and smooth. They pulled the wire. It made a funny noise.

"Beep beep boop boop," the wire said.

Lily and Ben were surprised. They looked at each other.

"Did the wire talk?" Lily asked.

"I think so. It is a mysterious wire," Ben said.

They wanted to hear more. They pulled the wire again.

"Hello, hello, I am a robot. I love to sing and dance," the wire said.

Lily and Ben laughed. They liked the wire. It was a friendly wire.

"Can you sing and dance with us?" Lily asked.

"Of course, of course, I love to have fun," the wire said.

The wire moved and twisted. It made a song with its beeps and boops. Lily and Ben sang and danced with the wire. They had a lot of fun. They made a new friend. They loved the mysterious wire.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Mary who liked to play near the sea. Every day, Mary spent hours playing in the sand and crystal blue water. One day, Mary was playing a game with her friends when a kind old man approached. He smiled and asked, "Are you honest?" Mary nodded, feeling unsure. 

The old man said, "I need help washing my boat. It can be a lot of work for one person. Would you like to help me?" Mary smiled and agreed.

 Mary worked hard and had a lot of fun helping the old man. When they were finished, the boat shone brightly in the sun. The old man thanked Mary and said, "Thank you, sweetheart, for your honesty and hard work. You did a really good job washing my boat." Mary beamed with pride. 

They both said goodbye and Mary skipped off, happy and tired. She watched the old man sail away in his sparkling clean boat and waved goodbye.

Once upon a Sunday morning, a little girl named Anna went outside to play in the garden. She saw an old man with a big bag filled with sand. Anna was curious and asked him what he was doing. The old man smiled and shrugged.

He then took some sand out of the bag and filled his hands. He spread the sand on the ground around him. Anna asked him why he was doing this. He smiled again, and shrugged.

Then he brought out a little stick from his bag and started to draw shapes in the sand. Anna watched him carefully and asked, "What are you making?". The old man shrugged and started to sing a little song. 

It was lots of fun watching the old man play in the sand. He made beautiful shapes and sang happy songs in the sun. Anna clapped her hands in joy and smiled. The old man smiled back and shrugged.

Once upon a time, there was a small boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to climb. One day, he saw a small ladder and he wanted to stand on it. He climbed up the ladder and stood on the top rung. He felt very tall! Suddenly, the ladder started to shake and Timmy fell down. He was okay, but he learned that it's important to be careful when you stand on a ladder.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and go on adventures. One day, Lily's mommy took her to the harbor to see the boats. Lily was so happy to see the big boats and the water.

As they walked around, they saw a man who was trying to call his friend on the phone. But his phone wasn't working. Lily's mommy offered to let him use her phone. The man was very grateful and said, "Thank you so much! You are very kind."

Lily and her mommy continued to walk around the harbor and saw many different boats. Lily pointed to one boat and said, "That one looks happy!" Her mommy laughed and said, "Boats can't be happy, silly. But I'm glad you're having fun." They spent the whole day at the harbor and had a great time together.

Romance, who loves to nod and sing, With drowsy head and folded wing, Among the green leaves as they shake Far down within some shadowy lake, To me a painted paroquet Hath been--a most familiar bird-- Taught me my alphabet to say-- To lisp my very earliest word While in the wild wood I did lie, A child--with a most knowing eye. Of late, eternal Condor years So shake the very Heaven on high With tumult as they thunder by, I have no time for idle cares Through gazing on the unquiet sky. And when an hour with calmer wings Its down upon my spirit flings-- That little time with lyre and rhyme To while away--forbidden things! My heart would feel to be a crime Unless it trembled with the strings.

Once upon a time, there was a delicate gorilla. He loved to play outside in the spring. He would jump and swing from tree to tree until he was too tired and had to rest.

One day, while he was out, he heard a funny noise. He looked around to see where it was coming from and spotted a bright yellow bird. She had a beautiful yellow beak that was singing a song. He smiled and listened to it chirping in the spring sun.

The gorilla slowly walked closer to take a better look. Suddenly, the bird flew up into the sky! The gorilla watched as it flew higher and higher until it disappeared into the clouds. He waved goodbye and smiled.

Then, it was time to go home. As he walked through the forest, the sun began to set, lighting up the sky with delicate colors. He watched as the sky turned pink and orange, before turning a deep purple. He smiled, happy to be part of such beauty.

He arrived home feeling content and refreshed. The delicate gorilla was ready to take on the next adventure.

name_of_work: Diary of a Church Mouse by John Betjeman
content: Here among long-discarded cassocks, Damp stools, and half-split open hassocks, Here where the vicar never looks I nibble through old service books. Lean and alone I spend my days Behind this Church of England baize. I share my dark forgotten room With two oil-lamps and half a broom. The cleaner never bothers me, So here I eat my frugal tea. My bread is sawdust mixed with straw; My jam is polish for the floor. Christmas and Easter may be feasts For congregations and for priests, And so may Whitsun. All the same, They do not fill my meagre frame. For me the only feast at all Is Autumn's Harvest Festival, When I can satisfy my want With ears of corn around the font. I climb the eagle's brazen head To burrow through a loaf of bread. I scramble up the pulpit stair And gnaw the marrows hanging there. It is enjoyable to taste These items ere they go to waste, But how annoying when one finds That other mice with pagan minds Come into church my food to share Who have no proper business there. Two field mice who have no desire To be baptized, invade the choir. A large and most unfriendly rat Comes in to see what we are at. He says he thinks there is no God And yet he comes ... it's rather odd. This year he stole a sheaf of wheat (It screened our special preacher's seat), And prosperous mice from fields away Come in to hear our organ play, And under cover of its notes Ate through the altar's sheaf of oats. A Low Church mouse, who thinks that I Am too papistical, and High, Yet somehow doesn't think it wrong To munch through Harvest Evensong, While I, who starve the whole year through, Must share my food with rodents who Except at this time of the year Not once inside the church appear. Within the human world I know Such goings-on could not be so, For human beings only do What their religion tells them to. They read the Bible every day And always, night and morning, pray, And just like me, the good church mouse, Worship each week in God's own house, But all the same it's strange to me How very full the church can be With people I don't see at all Except at Harvest Festival.

One day, a little girl named Sarah wanted to go on an exciting adventure. She took out her calendar and saw that tomorrow would be the perfect day for a sail.

The next day, Sarah was up bright and early. She gathered some supplies like food, drinks, and her trusty telescope. Then she went to the beach.

At the beach, Sarah saw a helpful captain who was getting ready to sail. She asked him if he could take her out on a boat ride. The captain said yes, so Sarah hopped on board.

The captain and Sarah sailed out into the ocean. They saw dolphins jumping in the water and Sarah even saw a seagull fly overhead. After an hour, they were back at the dock.

Sarah thanked the captain for his help. He smiled and said, "My pleasure! Come back anytime." She knew she would be visiting the beach again soon.

Life has loveliness to sell, All beautiful and splendid things, Blue waves whitened on a cliff, Soaring fire that sways and sings, And children's faces looking up Holding wonder like a cup. Life has loveliness to sell, Music like a curve of gold, Scent of pine trees in the rain, Eyes that love you, arms that hold, And for your spirit's still delight, Holy thoughts that star the night. Spend all you have for loveliness, Buy it and never count the cost; For one white singing hour of peace Count many a year of strife well lost, And for a breath of ecstasy Give all you have been, or could be.

name_of_work: Of Mere Being by Wallace Stevens
content: The palm at the end of the mind, Beyond the last thought, rises In the bronze decor, A gold-feathered bird Sings in the palm, without human meaning, Without human feeling, a foreign song. You know then that it is not the reason That makes us happy or unhappy. The bird sings. Its feathers shine. The palm stands on the edge of space. The wind moves slowly in the branches. The bird's fire-fangled feathers dangle down.

Anna and Ben like to play with their toys. They have a lot of toys, but their favorite is the big van. The van is red and shiny, and it has four wheels and a horn. Anna and Ben can make the van go fast or slow, and they can make it beep.

But sometimes, Anna is bossy. She wants to have the van all the time, and she does not let Ben play with it. She says, "I am the driver, and you are the passenger. You have to do what I say, or you can't play with the van." Ben does not like that. He wants to be the driver sometimes, too.

One day, Ben has an idea. He says to Anna, "Do you know what is in the back of the van?" Anna says, "No, what is it?" Ben says, "It is a surprise. You have to close your eyes and follow me." Anna is curious. She closes her eyes and holds Ben's hand. Ben leads her to the back of the van and opens the door.

But there is nothing in the back of the van. Ben quickly jumps in the front seat and closes the door. He says, "Ha ha, I tricked you. Now I am the driver, and you are the passenger. You have to do what I say, or you can't play with the van." Anna is angry. She says, "That is not fair. Give me the van back. You are mean." Ben says, "No, I am not mean. You are bossy. You have to share the van with me. We can take turns being the driver and the passenger. That is more fun."

Anna thinks for a moment. She knows that Ben is right. She says, "Okay, I am sorry. I will share the van with you. We can take turns being the driver and the passenger. That is more fun." Ben says, "Thank you. I am sorry, too. I will not trick you again. We can be friends." Anna and Ben smile and hug. They play with the van happily. They make it go fast and slow, and they make it beep. They have fun.

Once there was a little girl who loved to play baseball. Every day she would go out to the backyard and practice her pitching. She would throw the ball over and over again until she got it just right.

One day the little girl was out in the backyard throwing the baseball, when she noticed something pale in the grass. It was a big, white worm! She bent down to get a closer look and saw it was wriggling away.

The little girl was scared and she began to hate the worm. She decided she would never play baseball with it. She thought it was too gross!

So instead of playing baseball with the worm, the little girl just sat back and watched it wiggle away. She thought it was so silly and she couldn't help but laugh. 

After a few minutes, the worm finally disappeared, and the little girl went back to practicing her pitches. She was relieved to be rid of the pale worm and she vowed never to hate baseball again!

name_of_work: Out to Tender by Jean Bleakney
content: Ceasefire, 1994 All along the motorway they're resurfacing and bridge-strengthening and seeding the central reservation with wild flowers. But only an hour or so ahead there is fierce growth in the ditches and the road diminishes to unmendable potholes. And there are places where the light suddenly drops; where the branches, out of reach of the hedgecutter, are irrevocably pleached. The whole talk these days is about words; the glitzy newly-honed nouns --like peace and process and permanence. But there are other things to be said with reference to particular definitions and in deference to the vernacular. There are townlands where parameters invariably decline to perimeters; where you can't be middle-of-the-road when you're the whole road. Here come the cowboy landscapers with their quick-fix Castlewellan Golds. As an old Fermanagh woman would've said, The same boys can do feats and shite wonders.

Bee had a hive. It was full of friends! Every day they gathered together to help support each other. But one day, wasp flew in. He wanted to be part of the hive too. But Bee was jealous! He didn't want to share his friends. So, he made a plan. He told the other bees to ignore Wasp. Then the other bees started to get jealous too. They thought that Wasp was trying to take over the hive. So, together, they chased Wasp away. They were happy that they had their hive all to themselves again. From then on, they made sure that they always supported each other!

name_of_work: Love and a Question by Robert Frost
content: A Stranger came to the door at eve, And he spoke the bridegroom fair. He bore a green-white stick in his hand, And, for all burden, care. He asked with the eyes more than the lips For a shelter for the night, And he turned and looked at the road afar Without a window light. The bridegroom came forth into the porch With, 'Let us look at the sky, And question what of the night to be, Stranger, you and I.' The woodbine leaves littered the yard, The woodbine berries were blue, Autumn, yes, winter was in the wind; 'Stranger, I wish I knew.' Within, the bride in the dusk alone Bent over the open fire, Her face rose-red with the glowing coal And the thought of the heart's desire. The bridegroom looked at the weary road, Yet saw but her within, And wished her heart in a case of gold And pinned with a silver pin. The bridegroom thought it little to give A dole of bread, a purse, A heartfelt prayer for the poor of God, Or for the rich a curse; But whether or not a man was asked To mar the love of two By harboring woe in the bridal house, The bridegroom wished he knew.

Tim and Lily are friends. They like to play in the park. They like to swing, slide and run. They are very happy.

One day, Tim has a new toy. It is a robot. It can talk and move. Tim thinks it is very intelligent. He brings it to the park to show Lily.

"Look, Lily, this is my robot. It can tell me things. It is smarter than you," Tim says.

Lily feels sad. She does not like Tim's robot. She does not like Tim's words. She says, "I don't want to play with you. You are mean. Your robot is not intelligent. It is just a toy."

Tim gets angry. He does not like Lily's words. He says, "You are wrong. My robot is intelligent. It is better than you. You are just a girl."

They start to fight. They push and pull. They yell and cry. They do not see the big dog. The big dog sees the robot. The big dog likes to chew toys. It runs to the robot. It bites the robot. It breaks the robot.

Tim sees the dog. He sees his robot. He is very sad. He screams. He runs to the dog. He tries to get his robot. The dog does not like Tim. It growls. It snaps. It bites Tim.

Lily sees the dog. She sees Tim. She is very scared. She calls for help. She runs to Tim. She tries to help him. The dog does not like Lily. It growls. It snaps. It bites Lily.

They are both hurt. They are both bleeding. They are both crying. They are not happy. They are not friends. They are sorry. But it is too late. The end.

Bella the squirrel was very sleepy. She had been playing all day with her friends in the forest. She wanted to go to her nest and take a nap, but she had one more thing to do. She had to find an acorn for her mom.

She looked around the trees and the ground, but she could not see any acorns. She yawned and rubbed her eyes. She was too tired to keep looking. She saw a big oak tree with a hole in it. Maybe there was an acorn inside, she thought.

She climbed up the tree and peeked into the hole. She saw a shiny brown acorn. She reached in and grabbed it. She was about to leave when she heard a voice.

"Hey, that's my acorn!" It was Sammy the chipmunk. He lived in the hole with his family. He looked angry and sad.

Bella felt guilty. She knew she had done something bad. She did not want to make Sammy cry. She said, "I'm sorry, Sammy. I did not know it was your acorn. I was looking for one for my mom. I'm very sleepy and I wanted to go home."

Sammy looked at Bella. He saw that she was sorry and sleepy. He said, "It's okay, Bella. I have more acorns in my hole. You can have this one for your mom. But next time, please ask before you take something that is not yours."

Bella smiled and thanked Sammy. She said, "You are very kind, Sammy. I will ask next time. I hope you have a good nap." She took the acorn and climbed down the tree. She ran to her nest and gave the acorn to her mom. Her mom hugged her and said, "You are a good squirrel, Bella. I'm proud of you." Bella snuggled with her mom and fell asleep. She dreamed of acorns and friends.

name_of_work: Autumn Song by Dante Gabriel Rossetti
content: Know'st thou not at the fall of the leaf How the heart feels a languid grief Laid on it for a covering, And how sleep seems a goodly thing In Autumn at the fall of the leaf? And how the swift beat of the brain Falters because it is in vain, In Autumn at the fall of the leaf Knowest thou not? and how the chief Of joys seems--not to suffer pain? Know'st thou not at the fall of the leaf How the soul feels like a dried sheaf Bound up at length for harvesting, And how death seems a comely thing In Autumn at the fall of the leaf?

name_of_work: Life's Scars by Ella Wheeler Wilcox
content: They say the world is round, and yet I often think it square, So many little hurts we get From corners here and there. But one great truth in life I've found, While journeying to the West -- The only folks who really wound Are those we love the best. The man you thoroughly despise Can rouse your wrath, tis true; Annoyance in your heart will rise At things mere strangers do; But those are only passing ills; This rule all lives will prove; The ranking wound which aches and thrills Is dealt by hands we love. The choicest garb, the sweetest grace, Are oft to strangers shown; The careless mien, the frowning face, Are given to our own. We flatter those we scarcely know, We please the fleeting guest, And deal many a thoughtless blow To those we love the best. Love does not grow on every tree, Nor true hearts yearly bloom. Alas for those who only see This cut across the tomb! But soon or late, the fact grows plain To all through sorrow's test: The only folks who give us pain Are those we love the best.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went to her friend's house to play. Her friend had a big jar of cookies, but Lily didn't have any treats.

Lily said, "Can I have some cookies, please?"

Her friend replied, "Sure, but you have to lend me your toy for a little while."

Lily thought about it and agreed to lend her toy. She got some cookies and they played together. But then, Lily accidentally spilled her juice on the floor and it became wet.

Her friend said, "Don't worry, we can clean it up together."

So, they got some towels and cleaned up the wet mess. They had a lot of fun playing and sharing things with each other. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a teddy bear named Brownie that she loved to hug every night before going to sleep. One day, Lily went to the park to play with her friends. They played hide and seek, and Lily found a new friend named Timmy. 

Timmy had a puzzle with him, and he asked Lily if she wanted to help him match the pieces. Lily was happy to help, and they worked together to complete the puzzle. After they finished, Timmy gave Lily a big hug to say thank you. 

Lily felt happy inside and smiled. She liked Timmy's hug because it was mild and friendly. They continued to play together and had a lot of fun. At the end of the day, Lily hugged Brownie tightly and went to bed, dreaming about the fun day she had with her new friend Timmy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went to the store with her mommy. They picked out some yummy snacks and went to the cashier. The cashier said, "That will be five dollars, please." 

Lily's mommy gave the cashier some money, and the cashier gave them their snacks. Lily looked up at her mommy and said, "Mommy, can I pay next time?" 

Her mommy smiled and said, "Of course, sweetie." Lily was so grateful that her mommy said yes. 

As they walked out of the store, Lily held her mommy's hand and said, "Thank you for letting me pay next time, mommy. I love you." Her mommy gave her a big hug and said, "I love you too, Lily."

One day, a family went on a picnic. Dad packed their lunch and little Sally, who was three years old, had her new yellow rubber ducky. After they finished their lunch, Sally wanted to take a bath in the nearby river. Dad said "Yes" and put down a towel for Sally to sit on. 

Dad filled up a bucket with water from the river and put it down next to Sally. Little Sally was so excited to get into the river! She wanted to bathe. She put her rubber ducky in the water and splashed around. 

Suddenly, Dad shouted "Be careful Sally, don't get too close to the gas!" Dad quickly explained that the gas was dry and if Sally touched it, she would be in trouble. Little Sally listened and kept her distance from the gas. She kept playing and bathing safely in the river. 

When it was time to leave, Dad wrapped Sally in her towel and they all drove home. Sally was so happy to finish her bath in the river that she kept talking about it all the way home.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside and explore the world around him. One day, he found a funny-looking skull in the woods. It had big teeth and made him feel a bit scared.

Later that day, Timmy's mom noticed he was feeling sad. She asked him what was wrong, and he told her about the skull he found. His mom knew just how to comfort him. She told him that sometimes things can look scary, but they're really not. 

That night, Timmy had a dream about the skull. In the dream, it turned into a friendly monster who played games with him. When he woke up, he felt happy and not scared anymore. From that day on, Timmy knew that things aren't always what they seem, and that his mom was always there to comfort him when he needed it.

One day, Mom and Dad took Mark to the store. Mark was excited. They said they were going to buy him a tank. When they got to the store, Mark saw all the different tanks. He saw big tanks and small tanks. He saw red tanks and blue Tanks. Then, he saw a smooth green tank. It was just the right size. Mom and Dad said they would buy it for him.

After they paid for the tank, they took it to the car. On the way home, Mark looked at the tank. It was so smooth and beautiful. He couldn't wait to get home and put it in his room. 

When they finally arrived home, Mark ran straight for his room. Mom and Dad brought the smooth green tank and put it in his room. Mark was so excited! He ran his hand over the tank and smiled. Now he had the perfect tank!

name_of_work: The Trouble with Snowmen by Roger McGough
content: The trouble with snowmen,' Said my father one year 'They are no sooner made than they just disappear. I'll build you a snowman And I'll build it to last Add sand and cement And then have it cast. And so every winter,' He went on to explain 'You shall have a snowman Be it sunshine or rain.' And that snowman still stands Though my father is gone Out there in the garden Like an unmarked gravestone. Staring up at the house Gross and misshapen As if waiting for something Bad to happen. For as the years pass And I grow older When summers seem short And winters colder. The snowmen I envy As I watch children play Are the ones that are made And then fade away.

Tim and Sam were best friends. They liked to play in the park with their toys. One day, they saw a big truck in the park. It had a lot of ropes on it. They wondered what it was for.

"Let's go see!" Tim said.

"OK!" Sam said.

They ran to the truck and saw a man with a hat and a coat. He was holding a rope. He smiled at them.

"Hello, boys. Do you know who I am?" he asked.

Tim and Sam looked at him. They did not know him.

"No, sir. Who are you?" Tim asked.

"I am a famous magician. I can do amazing tricks with ropes. Do you want to see?" he said.

Tim and Sam nodded. They liked magic.

"OK, watch this. I will make this rope disappear!" he said.

He waved his hand and the rope was gone. Tim and Sam gasped.

"Wow! How did you do that?" Sam asked.

"It's a secret. But I will tell you something. If you want to be a magician, you have to practice a lot and recognize patterns. Patterns are things that repeat or look the same. Like this rope. It has stripes. Can you see them?" he said.

He showed them another rope with stripes.

"Yes, we can see them!" Tim and Sam said.

"Good. Now, can you find another thing in the park that has stripes?" he asked.

Tim and Sam looked around. They saw a zebra in the zoo. They saw a flag on a pole. They saw a shirt on a boy.

"There! There! There!" they pointed.

"Very good! You are very smart. You can recognize patterns. Maybe you can be magicians too. But remember, magic is also about fun and surprise. So, here is a surprise for you. Look at the rope again!" he said.

He waved his hand and the rope came back. But it was not the same rope. It was a snake!

Tim and Sam screamed and ran away.

The magician laughed and said, "Don't worry, boys. It's not a real snake. It's a toy. Come back and I will show you more tricks!"

But Tim and Sam did not come back. They were too scared. They decided to play with their toys instead. They did not like ropes anymore.

name_of_work: Forrest Fenn's Treasure Poem Deciphered - Update: Treasure has been FOUND
content: As I have gone alone in there And with my treasures bold, I can keep my secret where, And hint of riches new and old. Begin it where warm waters halt And take it in the canyon down, Not far, but too far to walk. Put in below the home of Brown. From there it's no place for the meek, The end is drawing ever nigh; There'll be no paddle up your creek, Just heavy loads and water high. If you've been wise and found the blaze, Look quickly down, your quest to cease, But tarry scant with marvel gaze, Just take the chest and go in peace. So why is it that I must go And leave my trove for all to seek? The answer I already know I've done it tired, and now I'm weak. So hear me all and listen good, Your effort will be worth the cold. If you are brave and in the wood I give you title to the gold.

Once upon a time there was a girl who wasn't scared of anything. She was as brave as could be, and nothing could ever make her scared.

One day when the girl was out walking in the park, she noticed a funny shimmer in the sky, far away. She looked all around to see what it was, and pointed her finger in the sky.

"What is that?" she asked.

No one was around who could answer her question, so she decided to find out herself. She walked and walked until she came to a grand old building. Inside, a kind old man sat at a desk.

The girl asked the old man about the sparkle in the sky. The old man smiled and said, "That, my dear, is the universe."

The girl was so curious. She asked the old man many questions about the universe, and he explained it all to her. By the end, she was no longer scared of anything. The old man told her that the universe could be explored through courage. She said thank you, and left the old building feeling brave.

The girl continued her journey and eventually found the shimmer in the sky - it was the starry universe!

She was no longer scared because she had gained knowledge and courage from the old man. She continued to explore the universe and its wonders, never feeling scared again.

One day, a little boy named Tim went to the park to play. He saw a big, hairy dog. The dog was playing with a ball. Tim was a bit scared of the hairy dog.

Tim's friend, Sue, came to the park too. Sue said, "Don't be scared, Tim. The hairy dog is nice. He just wants to play with his ball." Tim watched the dog play and started to feel less scared.

Then, the hairy dog came over to Tim and Sue with his ball. Tim was scared, but he remembered what Sue said. Tim threw the ball, and the dog ran to get it. They all played together and had fun. Tim was not scared of the hairy dog anymore. He learned that sometimes things that look scary can be fun to play with.

Life is short, though I keep this from my children. Life is short, and I've shortened mine in a thousand delicious, ill-advised ways, a thousand deliciously ill-advised ways I'll keep from my children. The world is at least fifty percent terrible, and that's a conservative estimate, though I keep this from my children. For every bird there is a stone thrown at a bird. For every loved child, a child broken, bagged, sunk in a lake. Life is short and the world is at least half terrible, and for every kind stranger, there is one who would break you, though I keep this from my children. I am trying to sell them the world. Any decent realtor, walking you through a real shithole, chirps on about good bones: This place could be beautiful, right? You could make this place beautiful.

Once upon a time, there was a hunter who went outside to the pond. He wanted to take a dive. The hunter was brave and went to the edge of the pond. But then he saw something bad. It was a big, scary frog! The hunter was scared and ran away.

He tried again to take a dive. But again, something bad was there - a big, scurrying mouse! The hunter was too scared to stay and ran away.

The hunter tried again to take a dive. This time, it was safe. He splashed into the pond and swam around. He was so happy to finally be able to dive! He had lots of fun and stayed in the pond for a long time. 

The hunter had learnt his lesson. He now knew that the pond was only safe if he looked out for bad things first.

Rain, midnight rain, nothing but the wild rain On this bleak hut, and solitude, and me Remembering again that I shall die And neither hear the rain nor give it thanks For washing me cleaner than I have been Since I was born into this solitude. Blessed are the dead that the rain rains upon: But here I pray that none whom once I loved Is dying tonight or lying still awake Solitary, listening to the rain, Either in pain or thus in sympathy Helpless among the living and the dead, Like a cold water among broken reeds, Myriads of broken reeds all still and stiff, Like me who have no love which this wild rain Has not dissolved except the love of death, If love it be towards what is perfect and Cannot, the tempest tells me, disappoint.

Grandma had a special armchair. Her grandkids always loved to sit in it and be with her. Grandma always gave them lots of hugs and told them wonderful stories.

One day, the grandkids came to visit. Grandma had bought a new, beautiful armchair and wanted to show it to them. She looked so proud!

Grandma said, "This is my special armchair. I want you to sit here and be comfortable. I want to protect you when you are in this chair."

The grandkids were very excited and hugged Grandma tight. They each took turns sitting in the armchair and feeling protected. They felt safe in Grandma's special armchair and with Grandma there watching over them, they knew they were loved.

Lily liked bananas very much. She ate one every day after lunch. But today, she saw a big bunch of bananas on the table. She wanted to eat more than one. She asked her mom, "Can I have two bananas, please?"

Her mom said, "No, Lily, one banana is enough for you. Too many bananas will make your tummy hurt. You can have another fruit if you want."

Lily was sad. She really wanted two bananas. She looked at the bunch of bananas. They looked so yellow and sweet. She had an idea. She waited until her mom was busy in the kitchen. Then she climbed on a chair and reached for the bananas.

But the bananas were too high for her. She stretched her arm as far as she could, but she could not grab them. She tried to pull the bunch of bananas down, but they were too heavy for her. She was not strong enough. She lost her balance and fell off the chair. She bumped her head on the floor. She started to cry.

Her mom heard her cry and ran to her. She saw Lily on the floor and the chair tipped over. She saw the bananas on the table. She understood what happened. She hugged Lily and said, "Oh, Lily, are you okay? You should not try to take the bananas by yourself. You could have asked me for help. I would have allowed you to have one more banana if you really wanted it. But you have to be careful and listen to me. Bananas are good for you, but too many are not. Do you understand?"

Lily nodded. She was sorry for being naughty. She said, "I'm sorry, mom. I just wanted two bananas. They looked so yummy. But I hurt my head and I could not get them. They were too high and too heavy. I'm not strong enough."

Her mom said, "It's okay, Lily. I forgive you. You are still a little girl. You will grow stronger and taller as you get older. But you have to eat healthy and follow the rules. Now, let me put some ice on your head. And then you can have one more banana if you still want it. But only one, okay?"

Lily smiled. She said, "Okay, mom. Thank you. I love you. And I love bananas."

Summer is fading: The leaves fall in ones and twos From trees bordering The new recreation ground. In the hollows of afternoons Young mothers assemble At swing and sandpit Setting free their children. Behind them, at intervals, Stand husbands in skilled trades, An estateful of washing, And the albums, lettered Our Wedding, lying Near the television: Before them, the wind Is ruining their courting-places That are still courting-places (But the lovers are all in school), And their children, so intent on Finding more unripe acorns, Expect to be taken home. Their beauty has thickened. Something is pushing them To the side of their own lives.

name_of_work: Mad Girl's Love Song by Sylvia Plath
content: I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead; I lift my lids and all is born again. (I think I made you up inside my head.) The stars go waltzing out in blue and red, And arbitrary blackness gallops in: I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead. I dreamed that you bewitched me into bed And sung me moon-struck, kissed me quite insane. (I think I made you up inside my head.) God topples from the sky, hell's fires fade: Exit seraphim and Satan's men: I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead. I fancied you'd return the way you said, But I grow old and I forget your name. (I think I made you up inside my head.) I should have loved a thunderbird instead; At least when spring comes they roar back again. I shut my eyes and all the world drops dead. (I think I made you up inside my head.)

One day, a little boy named Tim went to the park with his mom. Tim saw an ancient tree. The tree was very big and old. Tim wanted to find something that could match the tree.

Tim walked around the park and found a big can of tuna. He said, "Mom, look! I found a can of tuna. Can it match the old tree?" His mom smiled and said, "No, Tim. The tuna is not as old as the tree. But it is a good try."

Tim kept looking for something to match the ancient tree. He saw a big rock, a tall slide, and a small pond. But nothing could match the old tree. Tim said, "Mom, I cannot find anything to match the tree." His mom hugged him and said, "That's okay, Tim. The tree is very special and old. It is hard to find something to match it." Tim smiled and knew he had a fun day at the park.

From fairest creatures we desire increase, That thereby beauty's rose might never die, But as the riper should by time decease, His tender heir might bear his memory; But thou, contracted to thine own bright eyes, Feed'st thy light's flame with self-substantial fuel, Making a famine where abundance lies, Thyself thy foe, to thy sweet self too cruel. Thou that art now the world's fresh ornament And only herald to the gaudy spring, Within thine own bud buriest thy content, And, tender churl, mak'st waste in niggarding. Pity the world, or else this glutton be, To eat the world's due, by the grave and thee.

Max and his mom were walking in the park. Everywhere Max looked he saw noise and animals. He heard birds tweeting and dogs barking. He was so excited!

He saw a deer in the distance. It was so beautiful! Max and his mom stepped closer to take a better look. The deer was very quiet, but the birds were still making a lot of noise.

Suddenly, Max saw a rabbit! It was hopping around and making lots of noise. Max stepped closer to get a better look. The rabbit was so cute!

Max and his mom stepped back and watched the animals for a few more minutes, then it was time to go home. Max smiled, feeling happy to have seen a deer and a noisy rabbit.
