This is for the Pullman Porters who organized when people said they couldn't. And carried the Pittsburgh Courier and the Chicago Defender to the Black Americans in the South so they would know they were not alone. This is for the Pullman Porters who helped Thurgood Marshall go south and come back north to fight the fight that resulted in Brown v. Board of Education because even though Kansas is west and even though Topeka is the birth- place of Gwendolyn Brooks, who wrote the powerful "The Chicago Defender Sends a Man to Little Rock," it was the Pullman Porters who whispered to the traveling men both the Blues Men and the "Race" Men so that they both would know what was going on. This is for the Pullman Porters who smiled as if they were happy and laughed like they were tickled when some folks were around and who silently rejoiced in 1954 when the Supreme Court announced its 9--0 decision that "sepa- rate is inherently unequal." This is for the Pullman Porters who smiled and welcomed a fourteen-year-old boy onto their train in 1955. They noticed his slight limp that he tried to disguise with a doo-wop walk; they noticed his stutter and probably understood why his mother wanted him out of Chicago during the summer when school was out. Fourteen-year-old Black boys with limps and stutters are apt to try to prove themselves in dangerous ways when mothers aren't around to look after them. So this is for the Pullman Porters who looked over that fourteen-year-old while the train rolled the reverse of the Blues Highway from Chicago to St. Louis to Memphis to Mississippi. This is for the men who kept him safe; and if Emmett Till had been able to stay on a train all summer he would have maybe grown a bit of a paunch, certainly lost his hair, probably have worn bifocals and bounced his grand- children on his knee telling them about his summer riding the rails. But he had to get off the train. And ended up in Money, Mississippi. And was horribly, brutally, inexcusably, and unac- ceptably murdered. This is for the Pullman Porters who, when the sheriff was trying to get the body secretly buried, got Emmett's body on the northbound train, got his body home to Chicago, where his mother said: I want the world to see what they did to my boy. And this is for all the mothers who cried. And this is for all the people who said Never Again. And this is about Rosa Parks whose feet were not so tired, it had been, after all, an ordi- nary day, until the bus driver gave her the opportunity to make history. This is about Mrs. Rosa Parks from Tuskegee, Alabama, who was also the field secretary of the NAACP. This is about the moment Rosa Parks shouldered her cross, put her worldly goods aside, was willing to sacrifice her life, so that that young man in Money, Mississippi, who had been so well protected by the Pullman Porters, would not have died in vain. When Mrs. Parks said "NO" a passionate movement was begun. No longer would there be a reliance on the law; there was a higher law. When Mrs. Parks brought that light of hers to expose the evil of the system, the sun came and rested on her shoulders bringing the heat and the light of truth. Others would follow Mrs. Parks. Four young men in Greensboro, North Carolina, would also say No. Great voices would be raised singing the praises of God and exhorting us "to forgive those who trespass against us." But it was the Pullman Porters who safely got Emmett to his granduncle and it was Mrs. Rosa Parks who could not stand that death. And in not being able to stand it. She sat back down.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Sally. Sally liked exploring outside and she always looked up at the sky. She loved when the sky was clear, so she could see the sunshine. One day she was walking outside when she saw something special. It was the sun, so big and yellow! She danced around with joy.

Sally wanted to do something to improve the sky. She pointed up to the sun and shouted "shine brighter!". Suddenly, the sky started to get brighter and the sun was shining more than ever!

Sally clapped and cheered. The sun was making the sky so clear and warm. She was so happy that she had improved the sky.

From then on Sally always went outside to enjoy the sunshine. She danced and sang, happy to have improved the sky.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Ruth. She had a mop and she wanted to hang it up so it could dry out. 

Ruth asked her daddy, 'Can you help me hang my mop up, please?' 

Daddy smiled and said, 'Yes, I can help you hang up your mop.'

Daddy took Ruth over to the wall, where a hook was hanging. He said, 'This hook is the perfect size for hanging your mop.' 

Ruth placed her little mop on the hook, and then she jumped for joy. 'Daddy, thank you for helping me hang up my mop!' 

Daddy patted Ruth on the head and said, 'You're welcome sweetheart. Now you can use your mop whenever you need to!'

name_of_work: A Dream Lies Dead by Dorothy Parker
content: A dream lies dead here. May you softly go Before this place, and turn away your eyes, Nor seek to know the look of that which dies Importuning Life for life. Walk not in woe, But, for a little, let your step be slow. And, of your mercy, be not sweetly wise With words of hope and Spring and tenderer skies. A dream lies dead; and this all mourners know: Whenever one drifted petal leaves the tree- Though white of bloom as it had been before And proudly waitful of fecundity- One little loveliness can be no more; And so must Beauty bow her imperfect head Because a dream has joined the wistful dead!

Billy was a nice little boy who loved running around outside. One day, he found an old shirt in the grass. It had a bright yellow color and looked really pretty. Even though it was kind of big for him, he really wanted to keep it. So he picked it up and put it on.

Billy kept his new shirt with him all day and he was so happy and excited. He ran and ran and ran around, playing all kinds of games. Everywhere he went, the bright yellow shirt seemed to shine in the sunshine.

But then while he was swinging on the swings, his shirt suddenly dropped off his body and fell in the mud. Billy was so sad, he started to cry. But then he remembered he pocket full of sweet treats his Mom had given him.

He quickly ran home and grabbed the candy. He then washed his shirt in the sink and lay it out to dry in the sun. After it dried out, Billy was so happy to see that the old shirt was still really pretty and still had its bright yellow color! He put it on again and was always sure to hold onto it from then on.

Once upon a time, there was an ocean and in it lived a fish. Her name was Molly and she liked to swim around in the water.

One day, Molly wanted to explore past the edge of the ocean. She swam and swam until she reached the edge. She could see something in the distance and she wondered what it was.

Molly decided to dive in and find out. As she swam closer and closer to the object, she could see that it was a boat! Molly was friends with the boat and she started to move around it in a circle.

The boat started to move too! The motion was fast and fierce! Molly was scared and swam away quickly.

"Don't be afraid, little fish," called the boat. "I'm just trying to say hello!"

Molly was relieved and she said Hi back. She was so glad the boat was friendly! After that, Molly and the boat became the best of friends. They would often dive together and explore all kinds of new places.

Noah's flood is coming nearer! The city is sinking little...by little Birds flee And water rises On the steps of houses Shops The post office Banks Statues (of our immortal ancestors) Temples Wheat sacks Maternity hospitals The prison gate The State House The corridors of fortified barracks. Birds are leaving Slowly... Slowly... Geese on the water float Furniture floats... And a child's toy... And a gasp of a sad mother Young women on the roofs waver! Noah's flood is coming nearer Here are "the wise men" fleeing to the ship The singers, the prince's horseman, the usurers, the judge of judges (And his Mamlouk...), The sword bearer, the temple dancer (She rejoiced when she picked up her wig...) Tax collectors, weapons importers, The princess's lover in his radiant effeminate manner Noah's flood is coming nearer. Here are the cowards fleeing to the ship While I was... The city's youth were Bridling the unruly horse of the water Carrying water on both shoulders. And racing time They were building stone dams for themselves Hoping to save the bosom of youth and civilization Hoping to save...the homeland! ...the master of the Ark shouted at me--before the advent Of quietude: "Escape from a country...where the spirit is no longer!" I said: Blessed are those who ate its bread... In days of prosperity And turned their back on it In times of adversity! Glory to us, we who have stood (God has obliterated our names!) to defy destruction... And seek refuge in a mountain that doesn't die (They call it 'the people'!) We refuse to flee... And we refuse to wander! My heart, knit with injuries Cursed by commentaries Is resting, now, on the city's remains A blossom bland Still... After it said "No" to the ship ... and loved the homeland

This evening I unzipped my skin And carefully unscrewed my head, Exactly as I always do When I prepare myself for bed. And while I slept a coo-coo came As naked as could be And put on the skin And screwed on the head That once belonged to me. Now wearing my feet He runs through the street In a most disgraceful way. Doin' things and sayin' things I'd never do or say, Ticklin' the children And kickin' the men And Dancin' the ladies away. So if he makes your bright eyes cry Or makes your poor head spin, That scoundrel you see Is not really me He's the coo-coo Who's wearing my skin.

One day, Susan saw a beautiful sunflower in the park. She wanted to take a closer look so she slowly walked up to it and sat down in the grass.

"Hello, sunflower!" Susan said. The sunflower didn't answer back, but Susan knew it was important to say hello.

Suddenly, Susan heard a voice.

"Hello, Susan!" It was coming from a little bird sitting on a nearby tree branch.

"How did you know my name?" Susan asked.

"I can see you all the way from my nest!" the bird replied, "you are very important!"

Susan smiled and thanked the bird. Then, she looked back at the sunflower and said, "right now, I want to sit here with you and enjoy the sunshine."

From then on, Susan and the sunflower were best friends. Susan would always come to the park to sit with the sunflower and enjoy the warm sunshine.

Ben and Mia like to play in the park. They like to swing, slide and run. One day, they see something new in the grass. It is long and thin and has no legs. It moves like a worm, but faster.

"What is that?" Ben asks.

"I don't know," Mia says. "Let's go and see."

They walk closer to the thing in the grass. It has a head with two eyes and a mouth. It looks at them and makes a hiss sound.

"It is a snake!" Ben says. "I saw one in a book. They can bite and hurt you."

Mia is scared. She wants to run away. But Ben is curious. He wants to touch the snake. He thinks it is cool.

"Ben, don't!" Mia says. "It is dangerous. Come back!"

But Ben does not listen. He reaches out his hand to the snake. The snake does not like that. It opens its mouth and shows its teeth. It bites Ben's finger.

"Ow!" Ben cries. "It bit me! It bit me!"

Mia runs to Ben and hugs him. She is sorry for him. She is also angry at the snake. She thinks it is mean and stupid.

"Bad snake!" she shouts. "Go away! Leave us alone!"

The snake hisses again and slithers away. It does not want to play with them. It wants to be alone.

Ben and Mia run to their mom. She sees Ben's finger and puts a band-aid on it. She tells them to be careful and not to touch snakes. They can be dangerous and hurt you.

Ben and Mia nod. They learned their lesson. They do not want to touch snakes again. They wonder why snakes are so mean and stupid. They prefer to play with nice and fun things. Like swings, slides and balls.

Once upon a time, there was a bossy tiger. He loved to boss around all of the animals in the jungle. One day, he decided to start a new game. He asked all the animals if they wanted to play. Everyone said yes!

The tiger started the game by saying that they had to all chase each other around the jungle. He made sure to boss them around even more. He said that whoever crossed the finish line first would be the winner of the game.

So, all the animals started running around the jungle. There were monkeys, lions, gazelles, and even a zebra running around. They all ran as fast as they could. But, when they all crossed the finish line, the bossy tiger was first! He was so proud.

The other animals cheered. They all agreed that the tiger was the winner of the game. Everyone had so much fun playing the game with the bossy tiger.

Once upon a time there was a girl called Sally. She had a blue doll.

One day Sally took her blue doll outside. She spun round and round until she was dizzy. Her blue doll spun round and round too.

Sally laughed and laughed as she and her blue doll spun together. It was so much fun!

When they stopped spinning, Sally hugged her blue doll tight and took it back inside. She smiled, happy that she and her blue doll had spun together.

One morning, there was a big boy who was feeling sad. He started to cry. His mom asked him what was wrong, but the boy just kept crying. She gave him a big hug and said, "Let's get you some cereal. That will make you feel better." 

The boy still looked sad, so his mom said, "Just try it. It's really yummy." The boy slowly walked to the kitchen and sat down at the table. He was still sniffling a bit, but he picked up the spoon and started to eat the cereal. 

And then, something happened. As the boy ate more and more of the cereal, he started to smile. Soon, there were big smiles on his face and he was laughing. He said to his mom, "This cereal is really yummy! Thank you for making me feel better.â€ 

The mom smiled and said, "Anytime. You can always count on me and cereal."

name_of_work: This Is Not a Small Voice by Sonia Sanchez
content: This is not a small voice you hear this is a large voice coming out of these cities. This is the voice of LaTanya. Kadesha. Shaniqua. This is the voice of Antoine. Darryl. Shaquille. Running over waters navigating the hallways of our schools spilling out on the corners of our cities and no epitaphs spill out of their river mouths. This is not a small love you hear this is a large love, a passion for kissing learning on its face. This is a love that crowns the feet with hands that nourishes, conceives, feels the water sails mends the children, folds them inside our history where they toast more than the flesh where they suck the bones of the alphabet and spit out closed vowels. This is a love colored with iron and lace. This is a love initialed Black Genius. This is not a small voice you hear.

Once upon a time, a leopard named Lyra was enjoying a walk in the forest. Suddenly she stopped and pointed with her paw. "Look, animals!" She said in an enthusiastic voice.

Lyra was pointing to a group of colorful birds. She watched them, then pointed to a tree with a swing, and finally she pointed to a pond.

She was so excited that she decided to take a closer look. She walked to the pond and saw a frog swimming. Lyra was so enthusiastic that she jumped and shouted, "Hi frog!"

The frog looked startled and hopped away. Lyra clapped her paws and laughed. She ran back to the swing and started to swing.

The sun was setting and it was time for Lyra to go home. With one last look, she pointed with her paw and said goodbye to the forest.

Tom and Lily wanted to play outside, but it was very cold. Their mom said they had to wear coats and hats and gloves. Tom and Lily did not like that. They wanted to wear their costumes and pretend to be superheroes.

"No, no, no!" they said. "We are not cold. We are strong and brave. We can resist the cold."

Their mom shook her head. "You are silly. You will get sick if you go out like that. Come on, let me help you get dressed."

Tom and Lily ran away from their mom. They ran to the door and tried to open it. But it was locked. Their mom had locked it to keep them safe.

"Let us out, let us out!" they shouted. "We want to play outside. We want to be superheroes."

Their mom came to the door. She had a smile on her face. She had a surprise for them.

"Okay, okay," she said. "You can play outside. But first, look what I have for you."

She opened the door and showed them two big boxes. Inside the boxes were costumes. But not any costumes. Superhero costumes. Coats and hats and gloves that looked like capes and masks and boots.

Tom and Lily gasped. They were so happy. They forgot about the cold. They put on their costumes and thanked their mom.

"Wow, mom, you are the best!" they said. "You are a superhero too."

Their mom hugged them and said, "You are welcome, my little heroes. Now go and have fun. But remember, don't stay out too long. It is still cold outside."

Tom and Lily nodded. They ran outside and played. They pretended to fly and fight and save the world. They had so much fun. They did not feel the cold. They felt warm and happy. They felt like superheroes.

Tom and Sam are friends. They like to swim in the lake. One day, they see a big gray fish in the water. They want to catch it.

"Look, Sam, a big fish!" Tom says.

"Let's catch it, Tom!" Sam says.

They swim after the fish. The fish is fast. It swims away from them. Tom and Sam do not give up. They swim faster and faster.

They do not see the bottle in the water. It is a glass bottle. It is sharp. Tom swims into the bottle. He cuts his arm. He cries.

"Ow, ow, ow! It hurts!" Tom says.

Sam hears Tom. He swims to him. He sees the blood. He is scared.

"Tom, are you okay?" Sam says.

"No, Sam, it hurts a lot. Help me!" Tom says.

Sam helps Tom. He wraps his shirt around Tom's arm. He swims with Tom to the shore. He calls for help.

A man comes. He is a doctor. He sees Tom's arm. He takes him to the hospital. He fixes his arm.

Tom is sad. He says sorry to Sam.

"Sam, I'm sorry. I was silly. I wanted to catch the fish. I did not see the bottle. I was not careful." Tom says.

Sam hugs Tom. He says it is okay.

"Tom, it is okay. I'm sorry too. I wanted to catch the fish too. I did not see the bottle either. I was not careful too." Sam says.

They learn a lesson. They learn to be careful in the water. They learn to not chase things that are not theirs. They learn to be good friends. They are happy.

One day, a little boy named Tim went to the park with his dad. They saw a peaceful lake with ducks swimming in it. Tim wanted to play golf with his dad by the lake. His dad said, "Okay, let's play!"

Tim found a small stick and his dad found a big one. They used the sticks to hit a small ball. "I love golf!" Tim said, laughing. They played and played until the sun went down.

When they got home, Tim's mom asked, "Did you have fun?" Tim said, "Yes, we played golf by the peaceful lake!" His mom smiled and said, "Now, let's polish our shoes before bedtime." So, Tim and his dad cleaned their shoes together. They all had a very happy day.

Once upon a time, there was a very smart monster. He loved to play, but most of all he loved fishing. He had a special fish hook made of gold that he could use to catch the biggest and most delicious fish. 

Every morning he would get up early, grab his trusty hook, and head down to the river. He was so excited and happy to be able to go fishing. But one day he realized he had left his hook at home. 

He was so sad to realize he didn't have his hook. He missed it, and he missed fishing. He missed being able to catch the big fish and bring it home for dinner. 

But the smart monster knew that all he had to do was go home and get his hook. So he turned around and went home to get it. 

When the monster arrived, he was so happy to find his special golden hook. He grabbed it and ran back to the river. He was so excited to be able to go fishing again. 

From then on, the monster made sure to never forget his hook. And he continued to have a very happy and successful fishing life!

Tom liked to play with his ball. He liked to kick it and throw it and catch it. He liked to play with his ball in the park, where there was a lot of grass and trees and flowers. He did not like to play with his ball in the street, where there were cars and buses and noises.

One day, Tom saw a large gray cat in the park. He wanted to play with the cat. He thought the cat would like his ball. He ran after the cat with his ball. The cat did not like the ball. The cat did not like Tom. The cat ran away from Tom. Tom ran after the cat.

Tom did not see the street. He did not see the car. He did not hear the horn. He only saw the cat. He threw his ball at the cat. The ball missed the cat. The ball hit the car. The car stopped. The driver got out. The driver was angry. The driver took Tom's ball. The driver drove away.

Tom was sad. He lost his ball. He lost his cat. He wanted his ball back. He wanted his cat back. He regretted throwing his ball at the cat. He regretted running after the cat. He regretted not seeing the street. He regretted not hearing the car. He regretted not playing in the park. He regretted not listening to his mom. He regretted not being careful. He regretted a lot of things. He cried.

name_of_work: Crows in a Strong Wind by Cornelius Eady
content: Off go the crows from the roof. The crows can't hold on. They might as well Be perched on an oil slick. Such an awkward dance, These gentlemen In their spottled-black coats. Such a tipsy dance, As if they didn't know where they were. Such a humorous dance, As they try to set things right, As the wind reduces them. Such a sorrowful dance. How embarrassing is love When it goes wrong In front of everyone.

Once upon a time, there was a friendly bear called Big Ted. Big Ted lived in a huge forest surrounded by tall trees. Every Tuesday, Big Ted would wake up feeling calm. He would stretch his arms and lay down on the grass for a snooze. He would take a deep breath and watch the clouds roll by. After his snooze, he often explored the forest and made new friends with animals. He especially liked to go on long walks and search for special treats. Big Ted was always very calm and loved Tuesdays!

We alone can devalue gold by not caring if it falls or rises in the marketplace. Wherever there is gold there is a chain, you know, and if your chain is gold so much the worse for you. Feathers, shells and sea-shaped stones are all as rare. This could be our revolution: to love what is plentiful as much as what's scarce.

name_of_work: A Walk After Dark by W.H. Auden
content: A cloudless night like this Can set the spirit soaring: After a tiring day The clockwork spectacle is Impressive in a slightly boring Eighteenth-century way. It soothed adolescence a lot To meet so shameless a stare; The things I did could not Be so shocking as they said If that would still be there After the shocked were dead Now, unready to die Bur already at the stage When one starts to resent the young, I am glad those points in the sky May also be counted among The creatures of middle-age. It's cosier thinking of night As more an Old People's Home Than a shed for a faultless machine, That the red pre-Cambrian light Is gone like Imperial Rome Or myself at seventeen. Yet however much we may like The stoic manner in which The classical authors wrote, Only the young and rich Have the nerve or the figure to strike The lacrimae rerum note. For the present stalks abroad Like the past and its wronged again Whimper and are ignored, And the truth cannot be hid; Somebody chose their pain, What needn't have happened did. Occurring this very night By no established rule, Some event may already have hurled Its first little No at the right Of the laws we accept to school Our post-diluvian world: But the stars burn on overhead, Unconscious of final ends, As I walk home to bed, Asking what judgment waits My person, all my friends, And these United States.

Once upon a time there was a princess. She was very healthy and strong. Every morning the princess got up early to eat a big breakfast. She loved to pour fresh orange juice into a cup and eat fresh fruit for a snack.

Then the princess would go for a walk in the woods. She loved to hear the birds singing and smell all the wonderful smells in the forest.

When the princess got hungry, she would pour herself some yummy soup. She added lots of healthy vegetables and a sprinkle of salt.

At the end of the day, the princess would relax and enjoy the sun setting over the horizon. She felt so fortunate to be healthy and strong!

Once there was a little girl called Jane. She was three years old and often felt pain in her body.

One day, she was walking with her family in the woods. Suddenly, she saw something unknown in the leaves up ahead. Jane's family stopped to look. It was a small, light brown animal. 

"What is it?" asked Jane.

"It's a baby squirrel," said her mom.

Jane was very happy. She asked if she could keep it. Her mom said she could, but only if she was gentle.

Jane was gentle and held the baby squirrel close. Then, she released it back into the woods. As she watched it go, she felt a wonderful feeling in her heart. It was like the pain had gone away and been replaced with something else. 

"What happened?" asked Jane.

"You released the pain," said her mom.

Jane smiled and said a quiet thank you to the baby squirrel. She had discovered something unknown and it had helped her feel better.

name_of_work: Far over the misty mountains cold by J.R.R. Tolkien
content: Far over the misty mountains cold To dungeons deep and caverns old We must away ere break of day To seek the pale enchanted gold. The dwarves of yore made mighty spells, While hammers fell like ringing bells In places deep, where dark things sleep, In hollow halls beneath the fells. For ancient king and elvish lord There many a gleaming golden hoard They shaped and wrought, and light they caught To hide in gems on hilt of sword. On silver necklaces they strung The flowering stars, on crowns they hung The dragon-fire, in twisted wire They meshed the light of moon and sun. Far over the misty mountains cold To dungeons deep and caverns old We must away, ere break of day, To claim our long-forgotten gold. Goblets they carved there for themselves And harps of gold; where no man delves There lay they long, and many a song Was sung unheard by men or elves. The pines were roaring on the height, The winds were moaning in the night. The fire was red, it flaming spread; The trees like torches blazed with light. The bells were ringing in the dale And men looked up with faces pale; Then dragon's ire more fierce than fire Laid low their towers and houses frail. The mountain smoked beneath the moon; The dwarves, they heard the tramp of doom. They fled their hall, to dying fall Beneath his feet, beneath the moon. Far over the misty mountains grim To dungeons deep and caverns dim We must away, ere break of day, To win our harps and gold from him!

Once upon a time, there was a boy called John. John had a magic hat. He was so excited to try it on and he gathered it up from his room. Then, he put it on his head.

Suddenly, he felt an anxious feeling in his chest. He didn't know why. He took his hat off and looked outside. Everything was very foggy and a mist was gathering in the air.

John felt scared and he said to himself, "What is happening?" Suddenly, a friendly voice answered, "Don't worry John, the mist is just a magical fog that usually only appears around this time of the year."

John was still a bit anxious, but he knew he was safe. He and the friendly voice talked until the mist cleared. John gathered up his hat and went off to play, feeling happy and safe.

Once upon a time there was a nosy squirrel named Sandy. Sandy would always stick her nose in everything. One day, Sandy discovered some clay and carefully took it back to her home. She was going to use the clay to make something special.

As Sandy was making her project, some of her friends came to visit. They were so curious about what Sandy was doing. They asked her what she was making.

Sandy replied, "I'm making something special out of clay! I want to surprise everyone with it!"

Her friends smiled and told her to be sure to let them know when she was done. They waved goodbye and left.

Sandy worked hard and before long, her clay masterpiece was finished. All of her friends had gathered around and they were amazed by the clay sculpture Sandy had made. Every squirrel smiled and clapped their paws as Sandy proudly remained proud of her accomplishment.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her rag doll every day. One day, Lily heard a loud noise that made her fearful. She looked around and saw her mom's phone ringing. Lily picked up the phone and gave it to her mom. 

Lily's mom said thank you and hugged her tightly. She told Lily that there was nothing to be afraid of and that the phone ringing was just a sound. Lily felt better and continued to play with her rag doll. From that day on, whenever she heard the phone ringing, she remembered her mom's words and didn't feel scared anymore.

Once upon a time, there was a big box. A little girl wanted the box to be opened. She tried to open it, but it wouldn't budge. The girl started to feel helpless.

Suddenly, she saw a wire lying on the ground. She picked it up and tought about what she could do with it. She stuck the wire into the box and opened it. Inside, the girl found a toy she had been wanting for ages! She was so happy!

The girl thanked the wire for helping her open the box. She kept playing with the toy for the rest of the day.

The End.

name_of_work: That girl who laughed and had black eyes by Stephen Spender
content: That girl who laughed and had black eyes Spoke here ten days ago. She smiles Still in my thought; the lip still promises The body lives, and the quick eye beguiles. Now that she's dead, I feel the living flame Move across walls and twist across my sight: Through tilting, smothering waters of Death's name, Through the transparent grave, I see her bright. She lives beneath our common objects, dust And chairs, and her few poems about the room. Although death play its tricks, and the earth's crust Swallow her up in the enormous tomb, I meet her every turn; the muffled part The stilled applause, the pageant to appal, Startle her shade to take birth in my heart: I see her dancing through the solid wall!

Once upon a time, there was a little fox. The fox was very anxious. He wanted to find his friend, the bear. The fox walked and walked, looking for the bear.

The fox saw a bird in a tree. The bird said, "Why are you so anxious, little fox?" The fox said, "I can't find my friend, the bear. Can you help me?" The bird said, "Yes, I can help you. I saw the bear go that way." The bird used his wing to point to the right.

The fox was happy and said, "Thank you, bird!" The fox followed the bird's point and found the bear. The bear and the fox played all day. They were very happy. And the anxious little fox was not anxious anymore.

Jill and Tom were twins. They liked to play in the kitchen. One day, they saw a big cake on the table. It was for Mom's birthday.

"Let's have some cake," Jill said.

"No, we can't. Mom will be mad," Tom said.

But Jill did not listen. She took a knife and cut a slice of cake. She gave some to Tom and some to herself. They ate the cake. It was sweet and soft.

"Yum, yum, yum," Jill said.

"Rub, rub, rub," Tom said. He rubbed his tummy. He felt sick.

"Me too," Jill said. She rubbed her tummy. She felt sick.

They heard Mom coming. They hid under the table. They hoped Mom would not see them.

But Mom saw the cake. She saw the knife. She saw the crumbs. She saw the twins.

"Jill, Tom, what did you do?" Mom said. She was angry.

"We ate some cake," Jill said. She was sorry.

"We ate some cake," Tom said. He was sorry.

Mom was very mad. She took the cake away. She took the twins to their room. She did not give them a hug. She did not give them a kiss. She did not say happy birthday.

Jill and Tom cried. They wished they had not eaten the cake. They wished they had been gentle. They wished they had listened to Tom. They wished Mom would love them.

Once there was a little girl named Sophie. She was walking down a long, lonely hall. She felt so lonely as she walked and the hall was so long. But suddenly she heard a noise coming from the other end of the hall. It sounded like something was poking around the corner. She was curious to find out what it was.

Sophie carefully crept towards the corner and peeked around it. To her surprise there was a kitten poking around the corner. It had soft, white fur and bright pink eyes. The kitten looked up as Sophie peered around the corner. 

Sophie felt so happy and excited. She slowly reached out and gently poked the kitten's fur. The kitten purred and snuggled against Sophie. 

Sophie smiled and reached out again to give the kitten a hug. The little kitten felt so warm and the lonely hall suddenly felt much less lonely with the kitten around. 
 
From then on Sophie and the little kitten were best friends. They spent their days playing and exploring the long, lonely hall.

Tommy was playing with his toy cars in his room. He liked to make them zoom and crash on the floor. He did not hear his mom call him for bath time. She came to his room and saw the mess.

"Tommy, it's time for your bath. Put away your cars and come with me," she said.

"But I don't want a bath. I want to play more," Tommy said. He held his cars tight and did not move.

Mom was not happy. She took his cars and put them on the shelf. She urged Tommy to get up and follow her. She said, "You need a bath to be clean and fresh. You can play with your cars again tomorrow. Now, let's go."

Tommy was sad and angry. He did not like to leave his cars. He did not like to be wet and soapy. He walked slowly behind his mom. He hoped she would change her mind.

But she did not. She filled the bathtub with warm water and bubbles. She put Tommy in the water and gave him a washcloth and a rubber duck. She said, "Look, you have a duck to play with. And the bubbles are fun. You can make shapes and pop them. Try it."

Tommy looked at the duck and the bubbles. He did not want to admit it, but they looked a little fun. He took the duck and squeezed it. It made a quack sound. He smiled. He dipped the washcloth in the water and made it wet. He threw it in the air and watched it fall. He laughed.

Mom smiled too. She said, "See, bath time is not so bad. You can have fun and be clean at the same time. Now, let me wash your hair and then you can play some more."

Tommy nodded. He let mom wash his hair and rinse it. He did not cry or fuss. He felt the water and the bubbles on his skin. He felt good. He said, "Thank you, mom. I like bath time."

Mom hugged him and said, "You're welcome, Tommy. I'm proud of you. You're a good boy. Now, let's get you dry and put on your pajamas. Then we can read a story before bed."

Tommy agreed. He got out of the bathtub and wrapped himself in a towel. He felt warm and cozy. He followed mom to his room. He saw his cars on the shelf. He did not miss them so much. He was ready for bed. He said, "Mom, can you read me the story about the big red car?"

Mom said, "Of course, Tommy. I love that story. Let's go to your bed and I'll read it to you."

They went to his bed and mom opened the book. She read the story about the big red car and its adventures. Tommy listened and imagined. He felt happy and sleepy. He closed his eyes and drifted to sleep. Mom kissed him and said, "Good night, Tommy. I love you."

Tommy murmured, "I love you too, mom. Good night."

name_of_work: The Paradoxical Commandments by Kent M. Keith
content: People are illogical, unreasonable, and self-centered. Love them anyway. If you do good, people will accuse you of selfish ulterior motives. Do good anyway. If you are successful, you will win false friends and true enemies. Succeed anyway. The good you do today will be forgotten tomorrow. Do good anyway. Honesty and frankness make you vulnerable. Be honest and frank anyway. The biggest men and women with the biggest ideas can be shot down by the smallest men and women with the smallest minds. Think big anyway. People favor underdogs but follow only top dogs. Fight for a few underdogs anyway. What you spend years building may be destroyed overnight. Build anyway. People really need help but may attack you if you do help them. Help people anyway. Give the world the best you have and you'll get kicked in the teeth. Give the world the best you have anyway.

name_of_work: Waking from Sleep by Robert Bly
content: Inside the veins there are navies setting forth, Tiny explosions at the waterlines, And seagulls weaving in the wind of the salty blood. It is the morning. The country has slept the whole winter. Window seats were covered with fur skins, the yard was full Of stiff dogs, and hands that clumsily held heavy books. Now we wake, and rise from bed, and eat breakfast! Shouts rise from the harbor of the blood, Mist, and masts rising, the knock of wooden tackle in the sunlight. Now we sing, and do tiny dances on the kitchen floor. Our whole body is like a harbor at dawn; We know that our master has left us for the day.

Mummy was so troubled. She was worried about the leaf that had fallen from the tree. She didn't know which way the leaf had flown and she wanted to know it was safe. She asked her three year old daughter, Kim, if she knew where the leaf had gone.

Kim pointed up to the sky and said, "Look mummy! There it is, way up on that big cloud".

Mummy sighed. She was still worried about the leaf, so she said, "It's too high for me to reach".

Kim looked at her and smiled. She said, "Don't worry mummy. I can get it for you".

Mummy was amazed. She said, "How will you do that?"

Kim said, "I'll jump up and grab it".

Mummy was still a bit worried, but she smiled and said, "Do you think you can jump that high?!"

Kim nodded and said, "Yes, I can do it!" She jumped up and grabbed the leaf and brought it back to mummy.

Mummy was so relieved! She hugged Kim and thanked her for bringing the leaf safely back to her. Kim was happy that she'd been able to help her mummy and make her worries go away.

Anna loves to read books. She has many books in her room. She likes to read about animals, stars, and princesses. Sometimes she reads to her teddy bear. He listens very well.

One day, Anna feels sick. Her stomach hurts. She feels hot. She does not want to play or eat. She only wants to lie in bed. Her mom comes to see her. She puts a hand on her forehead.

"Anna, you have a fever. You need to rest and drink water. I will bring you some soup later. Do you want me to read you a story?" her mom asks.

Anna nods. She loves when her mom reads to her. Her mom picks a book from the shelf. It is a book about a brave lion. Anna likes lions. They are big and strong.

Her mom sits on the bed and opens the book. She reads in a soft voice. Anna listens and looks at the pictures. She forgets about her stomach and her fever. She feels warm and cozy. She smiles and hugs her teddy bear. She is happy. Reading makes her feel better.

Once upon a time, there was a wealthy man. He was kind and generous and always gave back to his community. One day, he decided to take a rest and enjoy the beautiful season.

He found a spot in the woods and laid down and closed his eyes to relax. Before he knew it, he fell into a deep sleep. Hours later, he awoke to find that all of his belongings had been taken.

The wealthy man was sad and scared and knew he had made a mistake. He realized he should have been more careful, but it was too late. He slowly made his way back home and vowed to never go off alone again.

The moral of the story is this: always be aware of your surroundings, even when taking a rest. Even the wealthiest people can be vulnerable to danger.

Molly was playing in the park. She saw a tree with a big shade. Molly thought it looked nice. She wanted to go and sit under the shade.

So Molly walked over to the tree. She spread out her blanket and sat down in the shade. She felt the nice cool breeze and chirping of the birds. She closed her eyes and imagined she was in a magical garden.

Molly thought it was so nice and peaceful. She wanted to stay forever! So she decided to tell her mom and dad she was going to stay in the shade, so they would not worry.

But then it started to get dark and the sky began to turn red. So Molly got up and went back home. She looked back and said, â€œI'll come back tomorrow and sit under the nice shade againâ€.

Once upon a time there was a girl who had a special note. Whenever she felt sad or mad she would take the note out of her pocket and read it. It always made her happy and feel better. 

One day she decided to share her note with others, so she began to increase the number of copies of the note. She said to each person, "Read this when you need help feeling happy!"

At first, everyone seemed excited and happy, but then something sour happened. One of the copies of the note was stolen! 

The girl was very sad and had to start over. But she decided to try again and increase the number of copies of the note one more time. This time she kept a better watch over them, and everyone was very happy that the note was still safe.

The girl was so proud of herself for not giving up, and she was glad that more people could get help from her special note.

One day, Max was walking down the street. He saw something strange! There was a man painting on the street! Max thought it was weird.

Max went to the man and asked what he was doing. The man said he was painting a picture of a big bear. Max thought it was cool!

Max wanted to paint too, so they painted a rainbow together. They used lots of colors to make it look beautiful.

When they were done, Max was really happy! He had never seen a picture as pretty as the one they made. The street looked weird but fun with all the colors.

Max smiled and waved goodbye to the man. He was really happy with the painting they made together.

Lila and Ben were playing with their toys in the living room. They had a lot of fun making noises and pretending to be animals. But their mom was working in the kitchen and she needed some quiet.

"Please, kids, can you play a little quieter?" she asked. "I have to make a phone call and I can't hear anything."

Lila and Ben nodded, but they soon forgot and started to play loud again. They had a big urge to make more noises and have more fun. They did not want to stop.

Their mom came back to the living room and saw them. She was not happy. She had a stern look on her face.

"That's enough, kids. You have to shut your mouths and play nice. Or you will have to go to your rooms and take a nap. Do you understand?" she said.

Lila and Ben did not like that. They did not want to shut their mouths or take a nap. They wanted to play. They looked at each other and made a plan.

They ran to their mom and gave her a big hug. They said they were sorry and they loved her. They said they would play quiet and nice. They said they would help her with the phone call.

Their mom was surprised. She smiled and hugged them back. She said they were sweet and she loved them too. She said they could help her with the phone call if they wanted.

Lila and Ben were happy. They had a new game to play. They followed their mom to the kitchen and picked up the phone. They said hello to the old lady on the other end. They said they were Lila and Ben and they were mom's helpers. They said they wanted to talk to her and make her happy.

The old lady was happy too. She said she was grandma and she missed them. She said she wanted to talk to them and hear their stories. She said they were smart and kind.

Lila and Ben talked to grandma for a long time. They told her about their toys and their animals and their dreams. They listened to her stories and her jokes and her advice. They laughed and learned and loved.

Their mom watched them and smiled. She was proud and glad. She did not mind the noise anymore. She joined the conversation and thanked grandma for calling. She said they would call again soon.

They all said goodbye and hung up the phone. They hugged each other and said they had a lot of fun. They said they loved each other and grandma. They said they would play quiet and nice.

And they did.

Once there was a little girl. She was 3 years old. She loved to explore.

One day, she found a button on the floor. It was a very special button. It made lights in the room. She was so excited!

But then something else happened. Her mom and dad encouraged her to keep exploring. They were so proud of her!

The little girl wanted to make the button do something else. She wanted it to make noise. But it didn't. It stayed silent.

The little girl was sad. But then her mom reminded her that her grandfather was deaf. He also loved lights.

So the little girl figured out a way to make the button into a special toy for her grandfather. She used it to make lights for him, when he visited.

He was so happy, he smiled and hugged her. The little girl was so proud. She was so happy that she was able to make her grandfather smile.

The little girl had learned that sometimes exploring can help encourage others.

Once there was a little girl named Lily who loved to sing. Every Sunday she would go to church. Lily felt very comfortable at church. She loved warm feeling it gave her.

When she was at church, Lily would stand up and sing out loud. Everyone in the church would be so proud of how she sang with all her heart.

One day the church was extra special because Lily was going to sing a solo. Everyone gathered around her and she sang her song so sweetly.  Everyone in the church smiled and clapped for her when she was done.

Lily looked out at all the faces in the church, feeling so comfortable and happy. Her beautiful singing made everyone so proud of her.  She loved that feeling and knew it would stay with her always.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She was very thirsty and wanted a drink. Her mommy offered her a bottle of water. Lily took the bottle and drank all the water. It was yummy and made her feel better. 

Lily said, "Thank you, mommy. The water was yummy." 

Mommy smiled and said, "You're welcome, Lily. I'm happy to offer you a drink when you're thirsty." 

Lily hugged her mommy and said, "You're the best mommy ever!"

Billy and his mommy were in the park. Billy looked around and soon saw a white bird on the tree. He pointed to the bird and exclaimed, "Look mommy, birds!"

Mommy smiled and nodded. "Yes, Billy, those are birds. I can teach you to perform like those birds." She held out her hands with the palms facing up to imitate the bird.

But Billy shook his head. "No, mommy, I don't wanna perform."

Mommy gave a gentle smile and said, "I think you will enjoy it, Billy. Watching the white birds perform is very nice."

Billy shook his head again. "No, mommy, I don't wanna!"

Mommy sat down next to Billy and put her arm around him. "It's okay, sweetie. You don't have to perform if you don't want to. We can watch the white birds together here in the park."

Billy smiled and hugged his mommy. He waved at the white birds and said, "Bye birds!" Then the mommy and her son walked away, hand in hand.

name_of_work: A Bag of Tools by R. L. Sharpe
content: Isn't it strange That princes and kings, And clowns that caper In sawdust rings, And common people Like you and me Are builders for eternity? Each is given a bag of tools, A shapeless mass, A book of rules; And each must make- Ere life is flown- A stumbling block Or a stepping stone.

I had a dream, which was not all a dream. The bright sun was extinguish'd, and the stars Did wander darkling in the eternal space, Rayless, and pathless, and the icy earth Swung blind and blackening in the moonless air; Morn came and went--and came, and brought no day, And men forgot their passions in the dread Of this their desolation; and all hearts Were chill'd into a selfish prayer for light: And they did live by watchfires--and the thrones, The palaces of crowned kings--the huts, The habitations of all things which dwell, Were burnt for beacons; cities were consum'd, And men were gather'd round their blazing homes To look once more into each other's face; Happy were those who dwelt within the eye Of the volcanos, and their mountain-torch: A fearful hope was all the world contain'd; Forests were set on fire--but hour by hour They fell and faded--and the crackling trunks Extinguish'd with a crash--and all was black. The brows of men by the despairing light Wore an unearthly aspect, as by fits The flashes fell upon them; some lay down And hid their eyes and wept; and some did rest Their chins upon their clenched hands, and smil'd; And others hurried to and fro, and fed Their funeral piles with fuel, and look'd up With mad disquietude on the dull sky, The pall of a past world; and then again With curses cast them down upon the dust, And gnash'd their teeth and howl'd: the wild birds shriek'd And, terrified, did flutter on the ground, And flap their useless wings; the wildest brutes Came tame and tremulous; and vipers crawl'd And twin'd themselves among the multitude, Hissing, but stingless--they were slain for food. And War, which for a moment was no more, Did glut himself again: a meal was bought With blood, and each sate sullenly apart Gorging himself in gloom: no love was left; All earth was but one thought--and that was death Immediate and inglorious; and the pang Of famine fed upon all entrails--men Died, and their bones were tombless as their flesh; The meagre by the meagre were devour'd, Even dogs assail'd their masters, all save one, And he was faithful to a corse, and kept The birds and beasts and famish'd men at bay, Till hunger clung them, or the dropping dead Lur'd their lank jaws; himself sought out no food, But with a piteous and perpetual moan, And a quick desolate cry, licking the hand Which answer'd not with a caress--he died. The crowd was famish'd by degrees; but two Of an enormous city did survive, And they were enemies: they met beside The dying embers of an altar-place Where had been heap'd a mass of holy things For an unholy usage; they rak'd up, And shivering scrap'd with their cold skeleton hands The feeble ashes, and their feeble breath Blew for a little life, and made a flame Which was a mockery; then they lifted up Their eyes as it grew lighter, and beheld Each other's aspects--saw, and shriek'd, and died-- Even of their mutual hideousness they died, Unknowing who he was upon whose brow Famine had written Fiend. The world was void, The populous and the powerful was a lump, Seasonless, herbless, treeless, manless, lifeless-- A lump of death--a chaos of hard clay. The rivers, lakes and ocean all stood still, And nothing stirr'd within their silent depths; Ships sailorless lay rotting on the sea, And their masts fell down piecemeal: as they dropp'd They slept on the abyss without a surge-- The waves were dead; the tides were in their grave, The moon, their mistress, had expir'd before; The winds were wither'd in the stagnant air, And the clouds perish'd; Darkness had no need Of aid from them--She was the Universe.

Once upon a time there was a Prince and his loving wife. Every day the Prince would tell his wife all of his exciting plans and she would get so enthusiastic. He wanted to explore his kingdom and see the world.

One day, the Prince decided to finally go out and explore his kingdom. He was sad to leave, but his wife said she would be okay. She smiled, even though her eyes were glistening with tears. 

The Prince set out and as he traveled, he found many wonderful things. Everywhere he went, people would tell him stories. 

One evening, he happened to stumble upon a mysterious castle. He heard an old storyteller in the courtyard telling a tale. As the Prince listened, he heard some shocking news. This castle belonged to a wicked witch and his wife was inside! 

The Prince was scared, but he hurried home. He told his wife what he had heard and they knew what they had to do.

The next day, the Prince and his wife set off to the castle. They were so brave and enthusiastic. When they arrived, they were able to battle the wicked witch and free his wife. In the end, they were able to defeat the witch and save their kingdom. 

The Prince and his wife were so happy and they returned home together. From that day on, the Prince was always telling his wife stories of his adventures and she was always delighted.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who loved to read books. She read all day and all night. But she was sad because she had never seen a bridge before.

One day she went for a walk, and suddenly she saw a bridge up ahead. She was so excited! She ran as fast as she could and as soon as she came to the bridge she read all the signs that were on it.

She learned so much about bridges. She read about how bridges help people get to the other side of the river and she read about how bridges are built.

When she was done reading she was not so sad anymore. She felt happy to have finally seen a bridge. She crossed the bridge and continued on her way. She never forgot what she had read that day.

One day, a man was feeling uncomfortable. He was in a rush and had an important meeting, but he realized he had forgotten to shave. He grabbed his razor and started to pinch his face with it. 

Suddenly,he heard a voice. "What are you doing?" The man turned and saw a 3 year old boy staring at him, wide-eyed. The man put the razor down and smiled. "I am just trying to look nice for my meeting," he explained. 

The boy looked surprised. "You have to pinch yourself to make yourself look nice?" The man laughed and said, "No, no. It's ok. I was just using the razor to shave my face." 

The man smiled at the little boy and said, "See, all done". The man was relieved to have finished before his meeting and the boy was relieved too - he was glad that the man wasn't pinching himself anymore!

Lily and Tom are friends. They like to play with toys. Today, they have a big box of toys. They want to make a zoo with the toys.

Lily picks a gray elephant. She puts it on the floor. She says, "This is my elephant. He is big and friendly. He likes to eat leaves."

Tom picks a gray mouse. He puts it next to the elephant. He says, "This is my mouse. He is small and friendly. He likes to eat cheese."

Lily and Tom look at the toys. They see a gray cat, a gray dog, a gray rabbit, and a gray bird. They say, "Wow, we have many gray animals. They are all friendly. They can be friends in our zoo."

They put the gray cat, the gray dog, the gray rabbit, and the gray bird on the floor. They make a fence with some blocks. They say, "This is our zoo. We have a gray elephant, a gray mouse, a gray cat, a gray dog, a gray rabbit, and a gray bird. They are happy and friendly. We love our zoo."

Once upon a time there was a poor little kitten named Mittens who was stuck on the side of a tall building. She mewed sadly and didn't know what to do.

Just then, a nice man named Jacob saw the scared kitten. He ran over to help her. He said: "Mittens, don't worry. I'll rescue you!"

Jacob carefully grabbed the kitten and carried her away from the edge of the tall building. Mittens was so happy and meowed with joy.

Jacob looked around for something for Mittens to eat. He saw a bakery and ran inside. He grabbed a fruit pastry and handed it to Mittens. She licked it up hungrily and thanked Jacob.

Mittens couldn't stop purring and was happy to be safe and have a yummy snack. Jacob knew he had found a friend and they both went on an adventure together.

Once upon a time, a little boy named Tim found a mysterious box. The box was open. Inside the box, there were many colorful balls. Tim was very happy.

Tim decided to play with the balls. He would throw them high into the air and catch them. Sometimes, the balls would bounce and roll away. Tim would laugh and chase after them.

One day, while Tim was playing, a small bird came to him. The bird liked the balls too. Tim and the bird became friends. They would throw the balls and play together every day. And they lived happily ever after.

name_of_work: As I Ebb'd with the Ocean of Life by Walt Whitman
content: As I ebb'd with the ocean of life, As I wended the shores I know, As I walk'd where the ripples continually wash you Paumanok, Where they rustle up hoarse and sibilant, Where the fierce old mother endlessly cries for her castaways, I musing late in the autumn day, gazing off southward, Held by this electric self out of the pride of which I utter poems, Was seiz'd by the spirit that trails in the lines underfoot, The rim, the sediment that stands for all the water and all the land of the globe. Fascinated, my eyes reverting from the south, dropt, to follow those slender windrows, Chaff, straw, splinters of wood, weeds, and the sea-gluten, Scum, scales from shining rocks, leaves of salt-lettuce, left by the tide, Miles walking, the sound of breaking waves the other side of me, Paumanok there and then as I thought the old thought of likenesses, These you presented to me you fish-shaped island, As I wended the shores I know, As I walk'd with that electric self seeking types. As I wend to the shores I know not, As I list to the dirge, the voices of men and women wreck'd, As I inhale the impalpable breezes that set in upon me, As the ocean so mysterious rolls toward me closer and closer, I too but signify at the utmost a little wash'd-up drift, A few sands and dead leaves to gather, Gather, and merge myself as part of the sands and drift. O baffled, balk'd, bent to the very earth, Oppress'd with myself that I have dared to open my mouth, Aware now that amid all that blab whose echoes recoil upon me I have not once had the least idea who or what I am, But that before all my arrogant poems the real Me stands yet untouch'd, untold, altogether unreach'd, Withdrawn far, mocking me with mock-congratulatory signs and bows, With peals of distant ironical laughter at every word I have written, Pointing in silence to these songs, and then to the sand beneath. I perceive I have not really understood any thing, not a single object, and that no man ever can, Nature here in sight of the sea taking advantage of me to dart upon me and sting me, Because I have dared to open my mouth to sing at all. You oceans both, I close with you, We murmur alike reproachfully rolling sands and drift, knowing not why, These little shreds indeed standing for you and me and all. You friable shore with trails of debris, You fish-shaped island, I take what is underfoot, What is yours is mine my father. I too Paumanok, I too have bubbled up, floated the measureless float, and been wash'd on your shores, I too am but a trail of drift and debris, I too leave little wrecks upon you, you fish-shaped island. I throw myself upon your breast my father, I cling to you so that you cannot unloose me, I hold you so firm till you answer me something. Kiss me my father, Touch me with your lips as I touch those I love, Breathe to me while I hold you close the secret of the murmuring I envy. Ebb, ocean of life, (the flow will return,) Cease not your moaning you fierce old mother, Endlessly cry for your castaways, but fear not, deny not me, Rustle not up so hoarse and angry against my feet as I touch you or gather from you. I mean tenderly by you and all, I gather for myself and for this phantom looking down where we lead, and following me and mine. Me and mine, loose windrows, little corpses, Froth, snowy white, and bubbles, (See, from my dead lips the ooze exuding at last, See, the prismatic colors glistening and rolling,) Tufts of straw, sands, fragments, Buoy'd hither from many moods, one contradicting another, From the storm, the long calm, the darkness, the swell, Musing, pondering, a breath, a briny tear, a dab of liquid or soil, Up just as much out of fathomless workings fermented and thrown, A limp blossom or two, torn, just as much over waves floating, drifted at random, Just as much for us that sobbing dirge of Nature, Just as much whence we come that blare of the cloud-trumpets, We, capricious, brought hither we know not whence, spread out before you, You up there walking or sitting, Whoever you are, we too lie in drifts at your feet.

Lila and Ben were playing with their toys in the living room. They liked to pretend they were firefighters and put out fires with their water guns. They had a cheap red hat and a cheap yellow coat that they shared.

"Look, there is a flame on the candle!" Ben said, pointing to the table. "We have to work fast and save the day!"

Lila grabbed the water gun and ran to the table. She aimed at the flame and squeezed the trigger. But nothing came out. The water gun was empty.

"Oh no, what do we do now?" Lila asked, worried.

Ben thought for a moment. He had an idea. He ran to the kitchen and came back with a cup of water. He handed it to Lila.

"Here, use this!" he said. "But be careful, don't spill it on the table or the floor."

Lila nodded. She took the cup and poured some water on the flame. The flame went out with a hiss. Lila and Ben cheered.

"We did it, we put out the fire!" Lila said, happy.

They high-fived each other and hugged. They were proud of their work. They were the best firefighters ever.

name_of_work: When You Come by Maya Angelou
content: When you come to me, unbidden, Beckoning me To long-ago rooms, Where memories lie. Offering me, as to a child, an attic, Gatherings of days too few. Baubles of stolen kisses. Trinkets of borrowed loves. Trunks of secret words, I CRY.

Jack was a gifted three year old, and he was eager to learn something new every day. One day, his grandma came to visit. Grandma wanted to show Jack something special.

â€œLetâ€™s do numbers," said Grandma. "It will be fun!â€

Jack was excited. He wanted to know how to do numbers! Grandma showed him the numbers 1, 2 and 3.

â€œCan you count to three?â€ asked Grandma.

Jack smiled and counted, â€œOne, two, three!â€

Grandma was proud of Jack. â€œVery good!" she said. "Now, let's do more numbers. We can go higher than three!"

Jack was happy to learn more. He counted all the way to ten! Grandma was proud to see how quickly Jack had learned.

â€œWell done, Jack! You are a gifted learner!â€ said Grandma.

Jack grinned and hugged Grandma. He had learned something new and he was very proud of himself.

Sam was brave. Every day he would play with his friends in the park. He loved the park, it was full of fun and adventure. He felt so lucky.

One day, his friends were all talking about a special parade. They said it was the biggest parade in town and everyone wanted to win it! Sam wanted to join the parade too.

Sam went home and asked his mum if he could join the parade. His mum was so proud of him and said yes. 

The next day, Sam put on his special outfit and set off to join the parade. He was so excited! 

When it was time for the parade to start, Sam was one of the bravest of them all. He marched in the parade with all his friends and held his head up high.

At the end of the parade, the judges announced that Sam had won! Everyone cheered and clapped for Sam. He was so happy he had won and now his friends would be even more proud of him.

Sam held his chin up and enjoyed the parade as he shouted "Yay! I won!"

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play in the water, but he did not have a raft. One day, Timmy's dad made him an incredible raft out of some wood and ropes. Timmy was so happy and he thanked his dad a lot. 

Timmy took the raft to the lake and started to paddle. He saw many fish in the water and he was so excited. As he paddled, he saw a little plant growing on the shore. The plant was so small, but Timmy knew it would grow bigger and bigger. 

After a while, Timmy got tired and decided to go back home. He hugged his dad and told him about his day. He was so happy to have his incredible raft and he knew that the little plant would grow bigger and bigger just like him.
