I have a fairy by my side Which says I must not sleep, When once in pain I loudly cried It said "You must not weep" If, full of mirth, I smile and grin, It says "You must not laugh" When once I wished to drink some gin It said "You must not quaff". When once a meal I wished to taste It said "You must not bite" When to the wars I went in haste It said "You must not fight". "What may I do?" at length I cried, Tired of the painful task. The fairy quietly replied, And said "You must not ask". Moral: "You mustn't."

The glory of the beauty of the morning, - The cuckoo crying over the untouched dew; The blackbird that has found it, and the dove That tempts me on to something sweeter than love; White clouds ranged even and fair as new-mown hay; The heat, the stir, the sublime vacancy Of sky and meadow and forest and my own heart: - The glory invites me, yet it leaves me scorning All I can ever do, all I can be, Beside the lovely of motion, shape, and hue, The happiness I fancy fit to dwell In beauty's presence. Shall I now this day Begin to seek as far as heaven, as hell, Wisdom or strength to match this beauty, start And tread the pale dust pitted with small dark drops, In hope to find whatever it is I seek, Hearkening to short-lived happy-seeming things That we know naught of, in the hazel copse? Or must I be content with discontent As larks and swallows are perhaps with wings? And shall I ask at the day's end once more What beauty is, and what I can have meant By happiness? And shall I let all go, Glad, weary, or both? Or shall I perhaps know That I was happy oft and oft before, Awhile forgetting how I am fast pent, How dreary-swift, with naught to travel to, Is Time? I cannot bite the day to the core.

Once there was a little girl who liked to write. She used to write every day. One day, she wrote on a big piece of paper. It was so wide that it covered her desk!

The girl wrote a beautiful story on the paper. When she was done, she looked at it. It was so beautiful! She was very proud of what she had written.

However, there was one problem. The girl didn't know what to do with it. Then she had an idea. She would put the story on the left side of the paper. Then she could hang it up on her wall!

She got to work right away. She glued the paper to the wall. She was so excited to show everyone! The wide paper looked beautiful on the wall. Everyone was amazed at how she wrote such a wonderful story.

The girl was so proud of what she wrote. She showed it to her friends and family. They all praised her for her writing skills! From then on, she wrote lots of stories. She was glad to have left her mark on the wall with her wide paper story!

name_of_work: Foxes Among the Lambs by Ernest G. Moll
content: EACH morning there were lambs with bloody mouth, Their tongues cut out by foxes; behind trees, Where they had sheltered from the rainy South, They'd rise to run, but fall on wobbly knees. And knowing, though my very heart was sick, That only death could cure them of their ills, I'd smash their heads in with a handy stick And curse the red marauders from the hills. Each afternoon, safe in a sheltered nook Behind the smithy, I'd prepare the bait; And I remember how my fingers shook With the half-frightened eagerness of hate Placing the strychnine in the hidden rift Made with the knife-point in the piece of liver; And I would pray some fox would take my gift And eat and feel the pinch and curse the giver. Each night I'd lie abed sleepless until, Above the steady patter of the rain, I'd hear the first sharp yelp below the hill And listen breathless till it rang again, Nearer this time; then silence for a minute While something in me waited for the leap Of a wild cry with death and terror in it; And then -- it strikes me strange now -- I could sleep!

Once upon a time, there was a round open thing. It was soft and white and it floated in the sky. All the animals wanted to touch it and feel it.

A bird flew up to the round thing and tried to peck it. But instead of pecking it, he made a hole in it. Then air started to come out.

The little bird was very afraid, but then he thought of a plan. He flew to a pond, and sprayed some water on the round thing. The water filled up the hole and the round thing floated up in the sky again. Everyone was very happy!

Ben and Mia are playing with their toy guns in the garden. They like to pretend they are cowboys and robbers. Ben wears a hat and a badge. Mia wears a mask and a scarf.

"Stop, robber! You are naughty!" Ben shouts. He points his toy gun at Mia.

"No, you stop, cowboy! You are silly!" Mia shouts back. She points her toy gun at Ben.

They run around the garden, shooting and dodging. They laugh and have fun.

But then, they hear a loud bark. It is Rex, the big dog from next door. He has jumped over the fence and is running towards them. He looks angry and hungry.

"Help, help!" Ben and Mia scream. They drop their toy guns and run to the house. Rex chases them, barking and growling.

They reach the door and slam it shut. Rex scratches and bites at the door, but he can't get in.

"Are you okay, kids?" Mom asks. She hears the noise and comes to see what is wrong.

"Yes, Mom, we are okay. But Rex is outside. He is scary and mean!" Ben says.

"Rex is outside? Oh no, he must have escaped from his yard. I'll call his owner and tell him to come and get him. Don't worry, he won't hurt you." Mom says.

She picks up the phone and dials a number. Ben and Mia hug each other and watch Rex through the window.

"Mom, can we have a treat?" Mia asks. "We were brave and we ran away from Rex."

"Yes, you can have a treat. You were very brave and smart. How about some cookies and milk?" Mom says.

"Yay, cookies and milk!" Ben and Mia say. They smile and forget about Rex.

They go to the kitchen and enjoy their treat. They decide to play something else later. Maybe they will be pirates and mermaids. Or astronauts and aliens. Or doctors and patients. They have many ideas and they love to play.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside and explore the world around her. One day, she saw a big, scary tornado in the sky. She ran to her mommy and said, "Mommy, look! Tornado!" 

Her mommy picked her up and they went inside to watch the tornado from a safe place. Lily asked, "Mommy, why is the tornado so big and scary?" Her mommy replied, "I'm not sure, Lily. Let's examine it and find out." 

They watched the tornado for a while and noticed that it was moving very fast and making loud noises. But then, something kind happened. The tornado started to slow down and eventually disappeared. Lily said, "Mommy, the tornado is gone! That was kind of it to leave us alone." 

Her mommy smiled and said, "Yes, Lily. Sometimes even scary things can be kind in their own way." And with that, they hugged each other and went back to playing outside, grateful for the kind tornado that had come and gone.

name_of_work: I Sit and Think by J.R.R. Tolkien
content: I sit beside the fire and think of all that I have seen, of meadow-flowers and butterflies in summers that have been; Of yellow leaves and gossamer in autumns that there were, with morning mist and silver sun and wind upon my hair. I sit beside the fire and think of how the world will be when winter comes without a spring that I shall never see. For still there are so many things that I have never seen: in every wood in every spring there is a different green. I sit beside the fire and think of people long ago, and people who will see a world that I shall never know. But all the while I sit and think of times there were before, I listen for returning feet and voices at the door.

Ben likes to stretch his arms and legs when he wakes up. He feels big and strong. He jumps out of his bed and runs to the kitchen. He smells something good. Mom is making breakfast.

"Good morning, Ben!" Mom says. "Do you want some fish and eggs?"

"Yes, please!" Ben says. He loves fish and eggs. They are tasty and make him grow. He sits at the table and waits for his plate.

Mom gives him a big piece of fish and some eggs. She also gives him some bread and milk. "Eat well, Ben. You have a busy day ahead."

Ben takes a big bite of his fish. It is tough and chewy. He likes it. He makes a funny face and says, "Mom, this fish is tough. Where did you get it?"

Mom smiles and says, "I got it from the market. It is a special fish. It is called a shark."

Ben's eyes widen. He is surprised and excited. He says, "A shark? Wow! Sharks are cool. They are big and strong and scary. They live in the water and have sharp teeth."

Mom nods and says, "That's right. Sharks are amazing animals. But they are also very hard to catch. You have to be brave and smart to catch a shark."

Ben feels proud and curious. He says, "Did you catch the shark, Mom?"

Mom laughs and says, "No, Ben. I didn't catch the shark. I bought it from a fisherman. He caught the shark. He is brave and smart. He told me a story about how he caught the shark. Do you want to hear it?"

Ben nods eagerly. He says, "Yes, please! Tell me the story, Mom!"

Mom says, "Okay. But first, finish your breakfast. You need to eat well to be brave and smart like the fisherman."

Ben agrees. He eats his fish and eggs and bread and milk. He listens to Mom's story about the fisherman and the shark. He imagines he is the fisherman. He feels big and strong and happy. He likes fish and eggs and stories. He loves Mom.

Halfway through an afternoon of coca cola bottles sweating rings on veneered tabletops and the steel drone of window fans above the silence in each darkened room, I open a stiff drawer and find the old hot combs, black with grease, the teeth still pungent as burning hair. One is small, fine toothed as if for a child. Holding it, I think of my mother's slender wrist, the curve of her neck as she leaned over the stove, her eyes shut as she pulled the wooden handle and laid flat the wisps at her temples. The heat in our kitchen made her glow that morning I watched her wincing, the hot comb singeing her brow, sweat glistening above her lips, her face made strangely beautiful as only suffering can do.

Tom and Mia are friends. They like to play in the park. They see a big slide. They want to go on the slide.

Tom says, "I go first. You wait." He runs to the slide. He climbs up the ladder. He sits on the slide. He slides down. He laughs.

Mia says, "My turn. You wait." She runs to the slide. She climbs up the ladder. She sits on the slide. She slides down. She smiles.

They do it again and again. They have fun.

But then, a big child comes. He is mean. He says, "This is my slide. You go away." He pushes Tom and Mia. They fall down. They are sad.

Tom and Mia say, "No, this is our slide. You are bad. You go away." They stand up. They push the big child. He falls down. He is mad.

Tom and Mia run to the slide. They climb up the ladder. They sit on the slide. They slide down. They are happy.

They see a clear sky. They see the sun. They see the birds. They say, "We are friends. We share the slide. We are good." They hug. They play.

name_of_work: Life's Tragedy by Paul Laurence Dunbar
content: t may be misery not to sing at all And to go silent through the brimming day. It may be sorrow never to be loved, But deeper griefs than these beset the way. To have come near to sing the perfect song And only by a half-tone lost the key, There is the potent sorrow, there the grief, The pale, sad staring of life's tragedy. To have just missed the perfect love, Not the hot passion of untempered youth, But that which lays aside its vanity And gives thee, for thy trusting worship, truth-- This, this it is to be accursed indeed; For if we mortals love, or if we sing, We count our joys not by the things we have, But by what kept us from the perfect thing.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to explore and discover new things. One day, Timmy found a funny-looking thing called a microscope. He looked through it and saw tiny things that he never saw before! Timmy was so happy that he found this new thing.

As Timmy looked through the microscope, he saw a tiny piece of candy. He took a lick of it and it tasted bitter. Timmy then decided to change the candy to a sweeter one. He went to his mom and asked for a different candy. His mom gave him a sweet candy, and Timmy was happy again.

From that day on, Timmy loved to use his microscope to look at tiny things, and he always made sure to have a sweet candy with him. The end.

Once there was a little girl named Evelina. Every day she loved to go and play in the big hedge. Her favorite games to play were hide-and-seek and tag.

One day, as Evelina was playing in the hedge, she heard a loud noise. It was coming from the other side. She was scared so she hid. But then she heard two very angry voices. It sounded like two grown ups were arguing.

Evelina slowly came out of her hiding place and peered around the bush. On the other side of the bush were two people. One of them was her mum. She was saying "Why do you keep coming here? I don't love you anymore!"

Evelina had never seen her mum so angry before. Even though Evelina was scared she knew what she had to do. She ran up to her mum, hugged her and said "I do love you, mummy!"

They hugged for a long time and cried. The person her mum had been arguing with walked away. Evelina's mum smiled and said "Let's forget about this and go play in the hedge again."

Evelina said "Yes, let's go!" and they both ran back to the hedge, where their games and fun could renew.

name_of_work: Sonnet 19 - (On His Blindness) When I Consider How My Light Is Spent by John Milton
content: When I consider how my light is spent, Ere half my days, in this dark world and wide, And that one Talent which is death to hide Lodged with me useless, though my Soul more bent To serve therewith my Maker, and present My true account, lest he returning chide; "Doth God exact day-labour, light denied?" I fondly ask. But patience, to prevent That murmur, soon replies, "God doth not need Either man's work or his own gifts; who best Bear his mild yoke, they serve him best. His state Is Kingly. Thousands at his bidding speed And post o'er Land and Ocean without rest: They also serve who only stand and wait."

Once upon a time, there was an old couch. It was a nice couch, but it was also very difficult to use. One day a little boy walked up to the couch and said, "Can I use it?" 

The couch, being very old, replied, "No, my cushions are far too stiff to sit on." 

The little boy was sad, but then he had an idea. He said, "Couch, I will bring you some pillows and then you will be nice and soft."

The old couch said, "Yes, that would be nice. I'm sure I'll be much easier to use then."

The little boy went off and found two soft pillows. He brought them back and put them on the couch. Now the old couch was much softer. Everyone who used the couch was happy because it was now much more comfortable.

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the park with her friends. One day, while playing, she found a shiny copper penny on the ground. It was so clean and sparkly, she was very happy.

As she was walking home, she saw a big dog appear out of nowhere. It was a scary dog and it started to chase her. Lily tried to run away, but she tripped and fell. The dog caught up to her and took the copper penny from her hand. Lily was sad and scared.

She went home and told her mom what happened. Her mom hugged her and told her it was okay. But Lily was still sad because she lost her special penny. She learned that sometimes things can appear to be good, but they can turn out bad.

Tom and Lily are twins. They like to watch cartoons on TV. Every morning, they wake up early and rush to the living room. They turn on the TV and look for their favorite cartoon. They laugh and clap when they see the funny animals and the silly jokes.

One day, their mom says, "Tom and Lily, today is a special day. We are going to the zoo. You can see real animals, not just cartoons. Get ready and eat your breakfast."

Tom and Lily are excited. They want to see the zoo. But they also want to watch their cartoon. They say, "Mom, can we watch our cartoon first? It is almost over. Please, please, please."

Mom smiles and says, "OK, you can watch your cartoon for five more minutes. But then you have to turn off the TV and eat your breakfast. We have to leave soon. The zoo is far away."

Tom and Lily say, "Thank you, mom. You are the best." They watch their cartoon until the end. Then they turn off the TV and go to the kitchen. Mom has made them yummy pancakes with syrup and butter. They eat their pancakes and drink their milk. They say, "Mom, this is yummy. You are a good cook."

Mom says, "Thank you, Tom and Lily. You are good eaters. Now, put on your shoes and jackets. We are going to the zoo. Are you ready?"

Tom and Lily say, "Yes, mom. We are ready. We want to see the animals. Let's go, let's go, let's go."

They grab their backpacks and follow mom to the car. They buckle their seat belts and wave goodbye to the TV. They say, "Bye, bye, cartoons. We will see you later. Now we are going to see real animals. We are going to have fun."

Tom and Sue are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big tunnel in the hill. They want to find out what is inside.

"Let's go in the tunnel!" Tom says. "Maybe we can find something fun!"

"OK, but be careful!" Sue says. "It might be dark and scary!"

They hold hands and walk into the tunnel. It is dark and cold. They hear strange noises. They see bats and spiders. They are afraid.

"Tom, I don't like this tunnel!" Sue says. "It is crazy! Let's go back!"

But Tom is curious. He sees a light at the end of the tunnel. He wants to find out what it is.

"Come on, Sue!" Tom says. "Let's find the light! Maybe it is something good!"

He pulls Sue along. They reach the end of the tunnel. They see a big rainbow. It is bright and colorful. They are happy.

"Wow, look at the rainbow!" Tom says. "It is so pretty! We found something good!"

"Yes, we did!" Sue says. "But I still think this tunnel is crazy!"

They laugh and hug. They enjoy the rainbow. Then they go back to the park. They tell their friends about their adventure. They are brave and proud.

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. They see a big dog. The dog is brown and furry. The dog runs to them and wags his tail.

"Hello, dog!" Lily says. She wants to pet the dog. She holds out her hand. The dog licks her hand. Lily giggles.

"Can I pet him too?" Ben asks. He is a little scared of the dog. He holds Lily's hand.

"Sure, he is nice," Lily says. She shows Ben how to be gentle. She strokes the dog's head and ears. The dog closes his eyes and makes a happy sound.

Ben tries to be gentle too. He touches the dog's back and tail. The dog wags his tail more. Ben smiles.

"You are a good friend, dog," Ben says. He hugs the dog. The dog hugs him back.

Lily and Ben are happy. They have a new friend. They hold each other's hand and the dog's paw. They play in the park.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily who loved playing with her toys. One day, Lily's friend Jack came over to play with her. They both wanted to play with the same toy, but there was only one. Jack said, "I want to play with it, Lily!" Lily said, "No, I want to play with it!" They started to argue and push each other.

Suddenly, Lily's mom came in and saw what was happening. She said, "Stop pushing each other! That's not nice. You both can play with the toy together." Jack and Lily stopped pushing and played together. They had so much fun that they both felt like they won the victory.

After they finished playing, Lily's mom said, "Remember, sharing is modern. When you share, you both win." Jack and Lily smiled and hugged each other. From that day on, they always shared their toys and never fought again.

Tom and Anna are brother and sister. They like to play hide and seek in the house. One day, they decide to play in the living room, where there is a big TV.

"Anna, you count to ten and I will hide," Tom says. He runs to find a good spot.

Anna covers her eyes and counts. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten! Ready or not, here I come!" She opens her eyes and looks around.

She sees the TV. It is blue and shiny. She likes to watch cartoons on it. But she does not see Tom. She walks to the TV and looks behind it. She sees a pair of feet sticking out.

"Found you, Tom!" she shouts. She pulls Tom out from behind the TV. He is laughing.

"You are a bad hider, Tom. I saw your feet," Anna says.

"OK, OK, you win. You are a good finder, Anna. Now it is my turn to count and your turn to hide," Tom says.

They switch roles and play again. They have fun hiding and finding each other in the living room. They do not break the TV or make a mess. They are good kids.

name_of_work: The Beauty of Union by George the Poet
content: There's an indescribable beauty in union In two beings forming one new being Entering each other's world Surrendering each other's selves Accepting the invitation to be everything to someone else There's an unparallelled bravery in union In telling the one you love: "The only way that we can truly win Is if I think of you in everything I do And honour every decision you faithfully include me in." Love gives union true meaning It illuminates the path It wants us to compromise, communicate and laugh It wants us to elevate, appreciate without pride Love is oblivious to the outside Even with an audience of millions Even when that love bears immortal significance All of this is met with cordial indifference By the two people at the heart of it Two individuals when they started it Becoming two halves of one partnership Such is the beauty of union Such is the beauty of union

name_of_work: The Rights of Women by Anna Laetitia Barbauld
content: Yes, injured Woman! rise, assert thy right! Woman! too long degraded, scorned, opprest; O born to rule in partial Law's despite, Resume thy native empire o'er the breast! Go forth arrayed in panoply divine; That angel pureness which admits no stain; Go, bid proud Man his boasted rule resign, And kiss the golden sceptre of thy reign. Go, gird thyself with grace; collect thy store Of bright artillery glancing from afar; Soft melting tones thy thundering cannon's roar, Blushes and fears thy magazine of war. Thy rights are empire: urge no meaner claim,-- Felt, not defined, and if debated, lost; Like sacred mysteries, which withheld from fame, Shunning discussion, are revered the most. Try all that wit and art suggest to bend Of thy imperial foe the stubborn knee; Make treacherous Man thy subject, not thy friend; Thou mayst command, but never canst be free. Awe the licentious, and restrain the rude; Soften the sullen, clear the cloudy brow: Be, more than princes' gifts, thy favours sued;-- She hazards all, who will the least allow. But hope not, courted idol of mankind, On this proud eminence secure to stay; Subduing and subdued, thou soon shalt find Thy coldness soften, and thy pride give way. Then, then, abandon each ambitious thought, Conquest or rule thy heart shall feebly move, In Nature's school, by her soft maxims taught, That separate rights are lost in mutual love.

Anna was sick. She had a sore throat and a cough. Mommy said she had to take medicine to feel better. But Anna did not like medicine. It was spicy and bitter and made her face twist.

"No, Mommy, no medicine!" Anna cried. She hid under the blanket and shook her head.

"Anna, please, you need the medicine. It will help you heal and stop the germs. It's only a little spoon. I'll give you some water and a hug after. Come on, be a brave girl." Mommy said. She lifted the blanket and smiled gently.

Anna looked at Mommy's face. She saw love and worry in her eyes. She remembered how Mommy took care of her when she was sick. She gave her soup and stories and kisses. Anna loved Mommy very much. She did not want to make her sad.

"Okay, Mommy, I'll take the medicine." Anna said. She opened her mouth and swallowed the spoon. It was spicy and bitter and made her face twist. But she did not cry. She drank some water and hugged Mommy.

"Good girl, Anna. I'm so proud of you. You are very brave and strong. The medicine will make you feel better soon. I love you very much." Mommy said. She kissed Anna's forehead and tucked her in.

Anna smiled and closed her eyes. She felt warm and safe. She knew Mommy was right. The medicine was good for her. She learned that sometimes she had to do things she did not like for her own good. She was happy to have Mommy by her side.

Bobby Shafto's gone to sea, With silver buckles at his knee; He'll come back and marry me,- Pretty Bobby Shafto! Bobby Shafto's fat and fair, Combing out his yellow hair, He's my love for evermore,- Pretty Bobby Shafto!

Timmy was walking down the street and was becoming very thirsty. His pockets were empty and he had no money to buy a drink. He looked around and saw a lemonade stand with a friendly lady behind it. Timmy shuffled over to the stand and politely said "Please may I have some lemonade?"

The lady smiled warmly and said "Of course you can dear! Would you like a small or large cup?" Timmy's eyes lit up and he said "A large one please" as he reached into his pocket and pulled out some coins. The lady handed him a cup and said "That will be two coins" and Timmy handed over the coins.

The lady smiled as she said "Thank you very much, here is your lemonade". Timmy was so pleased, he took a sip and said "It is delicious! I would like some more please". The lady poured some more into his cup and said "Have some more, it's on the house".

Timmy was so thankful and his smile increase with every sip. He thanked the lady for being so polite and for the lemonade. He finished his drink, smiled and said goodbye before walking off with a happy heart and full belly.

------The sky is overcast With a continuous cloud of texture close, Heavy and wan, all whitened by the Moon, Which through that veil is indistinctly seen, A dull, contracted circle, yielding light So feebly spread, that not a shadow falls, Chequering the ground--from rock, plant, tree, or tower. At length a pleasant instantaneous gleam Startles the pensive traveller while he treads His lonesome path, with unobserving eye Bent earthwards; he looks up--the clouds are split Asunder,--and above his head he sees The clear Moon, and the glory of the heavens. There, in a black-blue vault she sails along, Followed by multitudes of stars, that, small And sharp, and bright, along the dark abyss Drive as she drives: how fast they wheel away, Yet vanish not!--the wind is in the tree, But they are silent;--still they roll along Immeasurably distant; and the vault, Built round by those white clouds, enormous clouds, Still deepens its unfathomable depth. At length the Vision closes; and the mind, Not undisturbed by the delight it feels, Which slowly settles into peaceful calm, Is left to muse upon the solemn scene.

Hog Butcher for the World, Tool Maker, Stacker of Wheat, Player with Railroads and the Nation's Freight Handler; Stormy, husky, brawling, City of the Big Shoulders: They tell me you are wicked and I believe them, for I have seen your painted women under the gas lamps luring the farm boys. And they tell me you are crooked and I answer: Yes, it is true I have seen the gunman kill and go free to kill again. And they tell me you are brutal and my reply is: On the faces of women and children I have seen the marks of wanton hunger. And having answered so I turn once more to those who sneer at this my city, and I give them back the sneer and say to them: Come and show me another city with lifted head singing so proud to be alive and coarse and strong and cunning. Flinging magnetic curses amid the toil of piling job on job, here is a tall bold slugger set vivid against the little soft cities; Fierce as a dog with tongue lapping for action, cunning as a savage pitted against the wilderness, Bareheaded, Shoveling, Wrecking, Planning, Building, breaking, rebuilding, Under the smoke, dust all over his mouth, laughing with white teeth, Under the terrible burden of destiny laughing as a young man laughs, Laughing even as an ignorant fighter laughs who has never lost a battle, Bragging and laughing that under his wrist is the pulse, and under his ribs the heart of the people, Laughing! Laughing the stormy, husky, brawling laughter of Youth, half-naked, sweating, proud to be Hog Butcher, Tool Maker, Stacker of Wheat, Player with Railroads and Freight Handler to the Nation.

Once upon a time, there was a boy who really wanted to play a game with his mom and dad. So, he asked his mom, "Can we play a game together?" Mom said, "Yes, let's do it!" So they all laughed and had lots of fun.

They started playing the game and the boy was winning. He was so happy and kept saying, "Yay!" But then he had to stop because he was too tired. 
He said, "I'm sorry I have to stop, but I'm so tired."

His mom and dad said, "That's okay, you can keep playing tomorrow." But the boy wasn't sure. He was still a bit tired, so he said, "I'm not sure yet. Maybe in a few days I'll be ready to play again."

His mom and dad thought this was really funny. Even though they wanted to keep playing with him, they were happy that he wanted to be careful and take his time. So they all smiled and hugged each other and said, "Good night!" 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a curious little girl named Lily. One day, Lily's mom took her to the doctor's office to get an x-ray of her arm. Lily was scared because she didn't know what an x-ray was. 

"What's an x-ray, Mommy?" asked Lily.

"It's a special picture that shows what's inside your arm," replied her mom.

Lily watched as the x-ray machine took a picture of her arm. When the doctor came in, he said that Lily's arm was broken and needed a cast. 

"Oh no, when will it end?" cried Lily.

"Don't worry, sweetie. The cast will help your arm heal and it will end in a few weeks," said her mom.

Lily felt better knowing that her arm would get better soon. She left the doctor's office feeling a little bit braver than before.

Once there was a boy. His name was Dan. One day he had a magazine. He thought it was really stupid. He was so mad that he threw it away.

When he threw it away, it hit a man. He was really mad and came over to Dan. He yelled at him and said he was very bad. Dan was scared and started to cry.

The man was so mad that he took Dan away. He took him to a place where he would be all alone. It was a very dark place and Dan was alone. He was very scared and cried all night.

The next morning, the man came back with a police officer. The officer said Dan was going to be in trouble. He said he was stupid and that he should go to school instead of playing with a magazine.

Dan was so sad and scared. He was sent away and never seen again. The end.

Once there was a boy named Paul who was only three years old. One day, Paul was playing in the backyard when he spotted a big mound of icy snow. 

"Can I play with it?" Paul asked his dad.

"Sure," said his dad. Paul was so excited. He rolled around the icy snow, laughing and feeling so free.

But then, suddenly, there was a loud crash. His dad hadn't seen the old wall that Paul was playing near and he crashed into it with the tractor. The wall was left with a big crack in it.

"Oh no," gasped Paul's dad. He went over to the wall and tried to restore it. But no matter what he did, the crack still remained.

Paul felt so bad and he wanted to help. He slowly walked over to the wall and carefully placed the icy snow all around it.

His dad beamed at him and smiled. With the snow in place, the wall was restored. The score was 1 for Paul and 0 for the wall.

Paul and his dad hugged and Paul smiled with pride. He had saved the day.

One day, a little boy went to the beach with his parents. When he got there, he was so happy that he started running along the shore. Then he saw a big surprise. A big wave was coming in! He was so excited and he ran to the edge of the water. The wave was so high and he was full of joy. He jumped up and down and clapped his hands.

But then, the wave crashed down on him and he fell down. It was very bad. He was so scared, but his parents were with him. They helped him to his feet and showed him the beauty of the wave.

The little boy was so amazed and happy that he couldn't believe it. He had seen something so incredible and he wanted to do it again. He ran to the edge of the water and waited for another wave. Eventually, another big wave came and he ran with it. He laughed and clapped his hands as he rode the wave until it ended. He had so much fun.

The little boy had such a great day at the beach. He learned a lot about waves and he had a lot of surprises. He will remember his day at the beach forever.

Tom and Lily were playing with their toys in the living room. They had cars, dolls, blocks and books. They made a lot of noise and mess. Mom was in the kitchen, making lunch. She heard them and came to see.

"Tom, Lily, what are you doing?" she asked. "Look at this mess! You need to clean up before lunch. Put your toys back in the box."

Tom and Lily did not want to clean up. They liked their mess. They wanted to keep playing.

"But Mom, we are having fun!" Tom said. "We are making a city with our toys. See, this is the tower, and this is the bridge, and this is the park."

"And this is the spot!" Lily said. She pointed to a big stain on the carpet. She had spilled some juice there. "It is a lake for the ducks. Quack, quack!"

Mom frowned. She did not like the spot. It was dirty and sticky. She got a cloth and a spray bottle. She sprayed some liquid on the spot. It smelled nice.

"This is not a lake, Lily. This is a spot. And it needs to go away. Watch me. I will clean it with this. It is very powerful. It can make the spot disappear." Mom said.

She rubbed the cloth on the spot. She rubbed hard and fast. The spot started to fade. Tom and Lily watched. They were curious.

"Wow, Mom, you are right. It is powerful. It is magic!" Tom said.

"It is not magic, Tom. It is science. It is a special liquid that can break down the dirt and make it go away. It is called cleaner." Mom said.

"Cleaner. I like that word. Can I try it, Mom?" Lily asked.

"Sure, Lily. But be careful. Do not spray it on your eyes or mouth. It can hurt you. Only spray it on the spot." Mom said.

She gave Lily the spray bottle and the cloth. Lily sprayed some cleaner on the spot. She rubbed the cloth on it. The spot was gone. The carpet was clean.

"Yay, I did it! I cleaned the spot!" Lily said.

"Good job, Lily. You are a great helper. And so are you, Tom. Thank you for cleaning up your toys. Now you can have lunch. And after lunch, you can play some more. But please, no more spots, OK?" Mom said.

"OK, Mom. We love you. And we love cleaner. It is powerful and nice." Tom and Lily said.

They hugged Mom and went to the kitchen. They were hungry and happy. They had learned a new word and a new skill. They had cleaned the spot.

One day, a little girl named Lucy saw a patch of green grass. It looked very fair, and she wanted to go explore it. So she ran out to the patch. Once she got there, she saw that the patch was shaking! She was so surprised that her eyes opened wide. She started to giggle and clap her hands together. Then she ran over to the patch and started to jump up and down with it, shaking even more! Before she knew it, Lucy was laughing and shaking the whole patch up and down. She had so much fun bouncing around with the patch that she didn't want to stop. It was the best time she ever had!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys, but one day she got bored. She went to her mommy and said, "Mommy, what can I do? I'm bored." Her mommy said, "Why don't you help me with something?" 

Lily followed her mommy to the fireplace. Her mommy said, "We need to spread the wood out so we can make a fire." Lily asked, "What's a fire?" Her mommy said, "It's something that keeps us warm." 

Lily helped her mommy spread the wood out, but she accidentally knocked over a candle. The fire spread quickly and Lily was scared. Her mommy said, "Don't worry, we'll be okay. But remember, we need to be careful around the fireplace." 

The moral of the story is to always be careful around fireplaces. It's important to listen to our parents and follow their instructions to stay safe.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Sam. He was packing his things into a bag. He was going on a tour.

Sam put in all his favourite things. He put on his hat and his socks. He even packed a snack.

When Sam was ready to go, he went outside. It was an unknown place. It was exciting!

Sam jumped on the bus and it drove him to the unknown place. There, he saw lots of new things. He explored and had lots of fun.

At the end of the day, Sam packed up his things and got back on the bus. He was so happy he went on the tour!

Once upon a time there was a boy named Jack. He was a happy boy, who loved to play outside.

One day, Jack was feeling a little sad. He sat outside and started to cry. His friend, Teddy, saw him and came over to check on him.

Teddy said, â€œWhatâ€™s wrong?â€

Jack sniffled and said, â€œI want a hug.â€

But Teddy did not want to give him a hug. He said, â€œNo, hugs make me feel yucky.â€

Jack looked so sad and Teddy felt bad. He thought of a way to make Jack feel better. He said, â€œI can give you a soft pat on the back instead.â€

Jack thought about it for a moment and then smiled. He said, â€œYes! That would make me feel better.â€

Teddy smiled back and gave Jack a soft pat on the back. Jack felt much better after that and went back to playing outside.

Once upon a time there was a cabin. It had a big door that was always shut. Every morning the animals around the cabin would try to open it, but they never could. They all wanted to see what was inside, but it was too hard to open.

One day a successful, brave little squirrel came along. She sniffed the door and climbed right up to the top. Then she used all her determination and she pushed the door open. Everyone was very excited!

Then the animals all went inside and they saw a beautiful room. It was filled with toys, popcorn, and even candy! They all laughed and played until it was time to go home. Then the squirrel shut the door and everyone promised to come back soon. Everyone had a lot of fun and were very successful in opening the door.

name_of_work: Brown Penny by William Butler Yeats
content: I whispered, 'I am too young,' And then, 'I am old enough'; Wherefore I threw a penny To find out if I might love. 'Go and love, go and love, young man, If the lady be young and fair.' Ah, penny, brown penny, brown penny, I am looped in the loops of her hair. O love is the crooked thing, There is nobody wise enough To find out all that is in it, For he would be thinking of love Till the stars had run away And the shadows eaten the moon. Ah, penny, brown penny, brown penny, One cannot begin it too soon.

Ah broken is the golden bowl! the spirit flown forever! Let the bell toll!--a saintly soul floats on the Stygian river; And, Guy De Vere, hast thou no tear?--weep now or never more! See! on yon drear and rigid bier low lies thy love, Lenore! Come! let the burial rite be read--the funeral song be sung!-- An anthem for the queenliest dead that ever died so young-- A dirge for her the doubly dead in that she died so young. "Wretches! ye loved her for her wealth and hated her for her pride, "And when she fell in feeble health, ye blessed her--that she died! "How shall the ritual, then, be read?--the requiem how be sung "By you--by yours, the evil eye,--by yours, the slanderous tongue "That did to death the innocent that died, and died so young?" Peccavimus; but rave not thus! and let a Sabbath song Go up to God so solemnly the dead may feel so wrong! The sweet Lenore hath "gone before," with Hope, that flew beside Leaving thee wild for the dear child that should have been thy bride-- For her, the fair and debonair, that now so lowly lies, The life upon her yellow hair but not within her eyes-- The life still there, upon her hair--the death upon her eyes. "Avaunt! to-night my heart is light. No dirge will I upraise, "But waft the angel on her flight with a Paean of old days! "Let no bell toll!--lest her sweet soul, amid its hallowed mirth, "Should catch the note, as it doth float up from the damned Earth. "To friends above, from fiends below, the indignant ghost is riven-- "From Hell unto a high estate far up within the Heaven-- "From grief and groan, to a golden throne, beside the King of Heaven."

Once upon a time, there was a cool wardrobe in a house. One day, a little monster came to stay with the family who lived there. The monster wanted to play with the familyâ€™s stuff. 

The little monster loved to pull the things out of the wardrobe and shower the familyâ€™s stuff with hugs and kisses.

The dad put a big lock on the wardrobe to protect their stuff. The family felt safe and happy. The little monster was sad, but soon found other cool things to play with. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there lived an old man called Jack. He sold delicious spicy food from his cart to the people of the village.

One day, a young man carrying a backpack knocked on Jack's door. 

"Do you sell youth?" asked the young man.

Jack shook his head. "No, I'm afraid not," he said.

The young man thanked Jack, and continued his journey.

Days passed, and Jack noticed the same young man had returned to the village. He carried the same backpack, but it felt lighter this time.

Curious, Jack asked the young man what he had in his magical backpack. 

"Youth," the young man replied, with a big smile.

Jack was surprised, but he thought about his own age and he knew he would need youth soon. So, he asked the man if he could buy some. 

The young man agreed and said, "Yes, I sell the most spicy youth you will ever taste!"

Jack was excited and from that day on, he bought all the spicy youth from the young man, so that he could stay young forever.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Primrose. She was only three years old. One day, Primrose wanted to have a party. She asked her mummy and daddy if it was ok, and they said yes!

Primrose was very excited. She worked very hard to get everything ready. She sang and danced while she spring around the house, picking up all the things she needed for her party.

On the day of the party, everything was ready. Primrose welcomed all her friends when they arrived. They ate lots of yummy food, but the best part was when they danced and swayed around the room.

At the end of the day, Primrose felt exhausted. She realised that preparing for a party can be tiring, but also very useful. She thought to herself that when you put in lots of effort and hard work, you can make something magical!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. Lily loved to read the newspaper with her mommy every morning. One day, Lily's mommy brought home a smelly fish from the market. Lily didn't like the smell, but promised her mommy she would help cook it for dinner. 

As they cooked, Lily's mommy read the newspaper aloud. Lily was excited to hear about all the animals in the zoo. She promised her mommy she would be good and they could go visit the zoo soon. 

After dinner, Lily helped clean up and promised to take out the trash. As she walked outside, she saw her neighbor's cat playing with a ball of yarn. Lily promised to play with the cat tomorrow and went back inside to cuddle with her mommy.

The sun shone brightly as Jack and his mommy went for a walk.

"Let's play a game," said Jack's mommy. "I'll hide, and you have to find me!"

Jack put his hands over his eyes and started to count to ten. When he finished counting, he opened his eyes and started looking for his mommy.

"Where are you?" he called out.

Suddenly, he heard a loud cry. He followed the sound and found a zebra in the meadow. Its eyes were filled with tears.

Jack couldn't understand why the zebra was crying and looked at his mommy for answers.

"The zebra is sad because it lost its mommy," she explained gently. "Its mommy is dead."

Jack was very sad to hear this and hugged his mommy. His mommy hugged him back and the zebra smiled.

Tom and Jen are friends. They like to play with blocks and cars. One day, they have a race with their cars. Tom has a red car and Jen has a blue car. They say, "Ready, set, go!" and push their cars on the floor.

Tom's car is very fast. It zooms past Jen's car. Tom is happy. He thinks he will win the race. He looks at Jen and smiles. He says, "I am the best!"

Jen's car is not so fast. It goes slow and steady. Jen is sad. She thinks she will lose the race. She looks at Tom and frowns. She says, "You are not fair!"

Tom does not care. He is too busy watching his car. He does not see the big book on the floor. His car hits the book and flips over. Tom is shocked. He says, "Oh no!"

Jen sees the book and the car. She is smart. She steers her car around the book. Her car crosses the finish line. Jen is happy. She says, "I win!"

Tom is angry. He says, "That is not fair! You cheated!" He throws his car on the floor. He stomps his feet. He cries.

Jen does not cheat. She plays by the rules. She does not like Tom's tantrum. She shrugs. She says, "You are a sore loser!" She picks up her car and her victory. She leaves Tom alone. She finds a new friend.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the sunshine. One day, she went to the park with her mom. 

Lily saw a big green tree and she wanted to climb it. Her mom said it was too high, so Lily had to choose another game to play. 

She saw some other kids playing with a ball, so she decided to join them. They played until it was time to go home. 

On the way back, Lily saw many trees of different colors. She liked the green ones the most. When they got home, she told her mom that she wanted to plant a green tree in their garden. Her mom said it was a great idea and they went to the store to choose a tree. They picked a little green tree and took it home to plant it. Lily was very happy to have a green tree in her garden.

Once upon a time, there was a sad little house. It was so miserable. Once, it was high and mighty. Now, it looked very lonely.

One day, a big and strong crew came to the house. They had large sacks on their backs. With their hands, they picked up the house and put it in the sack.

The house was so scared. They had never been carried away before.

But, once the house was inside the sack, something wonderful happened. A kind and gentle voice said, "Don't worry little house - you are safe now."

The house was excited to hear the voice and realised that the big and strong crew was here to help. So, they stayed inside the sack and allowed themselves to be taken away to a much happier place. 

The house never felt so happy, safe and loved before.

Once upon a time, there was a little boat named Billy. Billy loved to sail in the big blue sea. One day, Billy saw a big storm coming. He knew he needed to find a safe place to stay.

Billy saw a harbor in the distance. He sailed towards it as fast as he could. When he got there, he saw a big ship named Sally. Sally was very lonely because no one wanted to be her friend. Billy decided to behave kindly and be Sally's friend.

The storm came and Billy and Sally were safe in the harbor. They had each other to keep company and they were no longer lonely. From that day on, Billy and Sally were the best of friends and they sailed the big blue sea together.

Once upon a time there was a healthy girl who had a special bow. She wanted to reach high in the sky with her bow so she stood at the edge of a hill. The girl stretched her arms up with the bow in her hands. She twirled and spun, stretching her arms even higher. All of a sudden, she felt herself reach the clouds. She was so happy. She spun around and around until she touched the stars in the sky. Then she came back down to the hill, feeling very proud of herself for reaching so high. She hugged her bow tightly, happy that she had done something special. She smiled, knowing she had reached something amazing.

Poppy was a little girl who loved to slide. She had a big slide in her backyard that she played on every day. She liked to go fast and feel the wind in her hair. She also liked to make funny noises when she slid down.

One day, Poppy saw a new boy in the house next door. He was playing with a ball and a bat. Poppy wanted to make a new friend, so she ran over to him and said hello. The boy looked at her and said, "Go away, you are ignorant. You don't know how to play ball. You only know how to slide."

Poppy felt sad and angry. She did not like the boy's words. She thought he was mean and rude. She said, "I am not ignorant. I know many things. I know how to slide, and how to sing, and how to count, and how to draw. You are ignorant. You don't know how to be nice."

The boy got mad and threw his ball at Poppy. Poppy dodged the ball and ran back to her slide. She slid down as fast as she could and shouted, "You are a bad boy. I don't want to be your friend. I have a better friend. My slide is my friend. It is fun and kind and makes me happy."

Poppy smiled and slid down again and again. She did not care about the boy anymore. She had her slide, and that was enough.

Once upon a time, there was a girl called Sarah. She was only three and loved to do things. One day, when she was out in the garden, she saw something shiny. It was a coin! It was different to any other coin Sarah had seen before. She picked it up and looked at it. What could she do with it? Suddenly, Sarah got an idea. She ran to her mum and showed her the coin. She asked her mum if they could go to the shop and buy some sweets with it. Her mum said yes, and they set off together. 

When they arrived at the shop, Sarah put the coin in the red machine. The machine made a noise and then gave her some sweets. Sarah was so excited and couldn't wait to eat them. On their way home, Sarah and her mum talked about all the different things you can do with a coin. 

Sarah was so happy to have found such a nice coin. She thanked her mum for taking her to the shop. From that day on, Sarah was always on the lookout for different coins!

"Let's go to the park!" said Ted. He and his best friend Joey hopped into the jeep and drove off.

When they arrived it was very peaceful and quiet. Ted and Joey wandered around for a while, looking at all the different things. They were having a great time.

Suddenly Ted saw something that made him panic. He shouted to Joey, "Look! It's a bear!" Sure enough, there was a big, furry bear pacing around. Ted and Joey quickly tried to get away, but the bear came after them!

Joey ran as fast as his little legs could take him and soon he was far away from the bear. Ted, however, was stuck. He panicked and tried to run, but it was too late. The bear grabbed him and dragged him away.

Joey was never able to see Ted again. He was so overwhelmed with sadness that he couldn't think straight. Joey returned home without his best friend, feeling defeated and scared.

Tom and Anna like to play with cars. They have many cars of different colors and sizes. They pretend to drive them on the floor and make noises. Vroom, vroom, beep, beep!

One day, Tom finds a card in his dad's wallet. It has his dad's name and picture on it. Tom thinks it is a license to drive cars. He shows it to Anna and says, "Look, I have a license. I can drive real cars now. Do you want to come with me?"

Anna is not sure. She says, "But Tom, we are too small to drive real cars. And we need to ask dad first. He will be angry if you take his card."

Tom does not listen. He says, "No, we don't need to ask. We can go outside and find a car. It will be fun. Come on, Anna, don't be scared."

Tom and Anna sneak out of the house and go to the street. It is dark outside and there are many cars. Tom sees a red car that is parked. He tries to open the door with the card, but it does not work. He tries another car, and another, but none of them open. He gets frustrated and angry.

Anna says, "Tom, this is a bad idea. We should go back home. It is dark and cold and we can't drive any cars. And dad will be worried about us."

Tom says, "No, Anna, I want to drive a car. I have a license. I will find a car that works. You can go back if you want, but I will stay here."

Anna is scared and sad. She does not want to leave Tom alone, but she also does not want to stay. She says, "Tom, please, let's go back. This is not a game. This is dangerous. You can play with your cars at home. Please, Tom, please."

But Tom does not hear her. He is too busy trying to open cars with the card. He does not see the police car that is coming. He does not hear the siren that is loud. He does not feel the hand that grabs him. He only sees the flash of the light that is bright.

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a regular crown. Every day it would go on number adventures. One day the crown went to the park. It counted the number of birds in the sky. It counted the number of trees in the park. It was having a lot of fun!

The next day, the crown went to the beach. It counted the number of shells on the sand. It counted the number of waves in the sea. It was having a great time!

The next day, the crown went to the woods. It counted the number of animals in the woods. It counted the number of leaves on the trees. It was having a wonderful time!

Finally, the regular crown came back home. It was tired but happy after its number adventures.

Pile the bodies high at Austerlitz and Waterloo. Shovel them under and let me work-- I am the grass; I cover all. And pile them high at Gettysburg And pile them high at Ypres and Verdun. Shovel them under and let me work. Two years, ten years, and passengers ask the conductor: What place is this? Where are we now? I am the grass. Let me work.

Once there was a cute lion cub. Every day he would roar and run around, making everything so much fun. He could often be found climbing on his big brother's shoulder, who was a big lion. His big brother didn't mind because he loved the cub very much.

One day, the cub decided that he wanted to go explore the world by himself. He was so excited and he ran off, roaring with joy. His big brother followed close behind, just to make sure he was safe. The cub lead the way, running and jumping and roaring at anything that he found interesting.

When the cub tired, he scrambled up onto his brother's shoulder for a rest. His brother gave him a hug and kept walking. Eventually, they reached the cub's home, the jungle. The cub's nose twitched, filling up with all the new smells. He hopped down off his big brother's shoulder and went to explore his new home. He was so excited and he roared with joy!

Danny was an ordinary three year old. Every day he loved to paint, using different colors for different things. His parents were very impressed with the picture he painted of their house, it was even hung up in the living room. 

One day something special happened. Danny's parents had a special quiz for him. They asked him to paint a picture of a rainbow, and he was so excited. He worked hard and eventually finished it with all the different colors in the correct order.

When Danny's parents saw it, they were so proud of him. They hugged him and told him that his rainbow painting was so special, it was hung up in the living room with the other picture he painted. Danny was so proud to have two of his pictures hanging up in his house!

name_of_work: I am the Reaper by William Ernest Henley
content: I am the Reaper. All things with heedful hook Silent I gather. Pale roses touched with the spring, Tall corn in summer, Fruits rich with autumn, and frail winter blossoms-- Reaping, still reaping-- All things with heedful hook Timely I gather. I am the Sower. All the unbodied life Runs through my seed-sheet. Atom with atom wed, Each quickening the other, Fall through my hands, ever changing, still changeless. Ceaselessly sowing, Life, incorruptible life, Flows from my seed-sheet. Maker and breaker, I am the ebb and the flood, Here and Hereafter, Sped through the tangle and coil Of infinite nature, Viewless and soundless I fashion all being. Taker and giver, I am the womb and the grave, The Now and the Ever

name_of_work: Washington's Monument, February, 1885 by Walt Whitman
content: Ah, not this marble, dead and cold: Far from its base and shaft expanding--the round zones circling, comprehending, Thou, Washington, art all the world's, the continents' entire--not yours alone, America, Europe's as well, in every part, castle of lord or laborer's cot, Or frozen North, or sultry South--the African's--the Arab's in his tent, Old Asia's there with venerable smile, seated amid her ruins; (Greets the antique the hero new? 'tis but the same--the heir legitimate, continued ever, The indomitable heart and arm--proofs of the never-broken line, Courage, alertness, patience, faith, the same--e'en in defeat defeated not, the same:) Wherever sails a ship, or house is built on land, or day or night, Through teeming cities' streets, indoors or out, factories or farms, Now, or to come, or past--where patriot wills existed or exist, Wherever Freedom, pois'd by Toleration, sway'd by Law, Stands or is rising thy true monument.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play dress-up and wear pretty clothes. Lily's mom always let her pick out her own fashion. One day, Lily wanted to wear her favorite yellow dress, but it was dirty. She asked her mom to wash it, but her mom said no because they didn't have time.

Lily was frustrated and started to cry. "I want to wear my yellow dress!" she said. But her mom said, "No, we have to go now." They went to the park, but Lily didn't want to play. She just sat on a bench and cried.

Suddenly, it started to rain. Lily's mom tried to cover her with an umbrella, but Lily was still sad. She said, "I wish I could wear my yellow dress. It would make me happy." But it was too late. They had to go home and Lily was still sad. The end.

Lily was a little girl who liked to play with her toys. She had many toys, but her favorite was a black cat. She named him Shadow and took him everywhere. She hugged him, brushed him, and talked to him.

One day, Lily went to the park with her mom and Shadow. She saw a big pond with water and ducks. She wanted to feed the ducks, so she asked her mom for some bread. Her mom gave her some bread and told her to be careful with Shadow.

Lily threw some bread to the ducks and watched them eat. She was happy and smiled. But then, she saw a big dog running towards her. The dog barked and jumped on her. Lily was scared and dropped Shadow. The dog grabbed Shadow and ran away.

Lily cried and screamed. She wanted her Shadow back. Her mom hugged her and tried to calm her down. She told her they would look for the dog and Shadow. They walked around the park and asked people if they saw the dog. But no one knew where the dog went.

Lily was very sad and sighed. She missed her Shadow. She wished she had held him tighter. She learned that she should be more careful with her things and not let them go. She hoped that Shadow was safe and happy. She prayed that she would see him again.

Once upon a time, there was a young boy named Sam. He was very selfish, and only thought of himself and not others. Sam was going on an adventure and was excited to ride his bike. He was planning to go very fast, but his mom reminded him that he first needed to attach his helmet. Sam didn't want to wear the helmet because it was too itchy and he thought it would ruin the adventure.

But his mom explained that the helmet was necessary if he didn't want to get hurt. So Sam reluctantly attached the helmet. Even with the helmet on, Sam loved the ride. He felt so brave zooming through the streets with the wind in his face.

As Sam enjoyed his ride, he started to forget about the uncomfortable helmet. Suddenly, Sam made a wrong move and crashed his bike. He was very scared, but when he looked down, he saw the helmet he had attached was still intact. He had been saved from a possible injury. Sam was so glad he had attached the helmet. He realized his mom was right - it was worth it in the end. From that day forward, Sam never forgot to attach his helmet before riding his bike.

name_of_work: God's Grandeur by Gerard Manley Hopkins
content: The world is charged with the grandeur of God. It will flame out, like shining from shook foil; It gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil Crushed. Why do men then now not reck his rod? Generations have trod, have trod, have trod; And all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil; And wears man's smudge and shares man's smell: the soil Is bare now, nor can foot feel, being shod. And for all this, nature is never spent; There lives the dearest freshness deep down things; And though the last lights off the black West went Oh, morning, at the brown brink eastward, springs -- Because the Holy Ghost over the bent World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.

name_of_work: On the Morning of Christ's Nativity by John Milton
content: This is the month, and this the happy morn, Wherein the Son of Heav'n's eternal King, Of wedded Maid, and Virgin Mother born, Our great redemption from above did bring; For so the holy sages once did sing, That he our deadly forfeit should release, And with his Father work us a perpetual peace. That glorious Form, that Light unsufferable, And that far-beaming blaze of Majesty, Wherewith he wont at Heav'n's high council-table, To sit the midst of Trinal Unity, He laid aside, and here with us to be, Forsook the courts of everlasting day, And chose with us a darksome house of mortal clay. Say Heav'nly Muse, shall not thy sacred vein Afford a present to the Infant God? Hast thou no verse, no hymn, or solemn strain, To welcome him to this his new abode, Now while the heav'n, by the Sun's team untrod, Hath took no print of the approaching light, And all the spangled host keep watch in squadrons bright? See how from far upon the eastern road The star-led wizards haste with odours sweet: O run, prevent them with thy humble ode, And lay it lowly at his blessed feet; Have thou the honour first thy Lord to greet, And join thy voice unto the angel quire, From out his secret altar touch'd with hallow'd fire. It was the winter wild, While the Heav'n-born child, All meanly wrapt in the rude manger lies; Nature in awe to him Had doff'd her gaudy trim, With her great Master so to sympathize: It was no season then for her To wanton with the Sun, her lusty paramour. Only with speeches fair She woos the gentle air To hide her guilty front with innocent snow, And on her naked shame, Pollute with sinful blame, The saintly veil of maiden white to throw, Confounded, that her Maker's eyes Should look so near upon her foul deformities. But he, her fears to cease, Sent down the meek-ey'd Peace: She, crown'd with olive green, came softly sliding Down through the turning sphere, His ready harbinger, With turtle wing the amorous clouds dividing; And waving wide her myrtle wand, She strikes a universal peace through sea and land. No war or battle's sound Was heard the world around; The idle spear and shield were high uphung; The hooked chariot stood Unstain'd with hostile blood; The trumpet spake not to the armed throng; And kings sate still with awful eye, As if they surely knew their sovran Lord was by. But peaceful was the night Wherein the Prince of Light His reign of peace upon the earth began: The winds with wonder whist, Smoothly the waters kist, Whispering new joys to the mild Ocean, Who now hath quite forgot to rave, While birds of calm sit brooding on the charmed wave. The Stars with deep amaze Stand fix'd in steadfast gaze, Bending one way their precious influence; And will not take their flight, For all the morning light, Or Lucifer that often warn'd them thence, But in their glimmering orbs did glow, Until their Lord himself bespake, and bid them go. And though the shady gloom Had given day her room, The Sun himself withheld his wonted speed, And hid his head for shame, As his inferior flame The new-enlighten'd world no more should need: He saw a greater Sun appear Than his bright throne or burning axle-tree could bear. The shepherds on the lawn, Or ere the point of dawn, Sate simply chatting in a rustic row; Full little thought they than That the mighty Pan Was kindly come to live with them below: Perhaps their loves, or else their sheep, Was all that did their silly thoughts so busy keep; When such music sweet Their hearts and ears did greet, As never was by mortal finger strook, Divinely warbled voice Answering the stringed noise, As all their souls in blissful rapture took: The air such pleasure loth to lose, With thousand echoes still prolongs each heav'nly close. Nature, that heard such sound Beneath the hollow round Of Cynthia's seat, the Airy region thrilling, Now was almost won To think her part was done, And that her reign had here its last fulfilling: She knew such harmony alone Could hold all heav'n and earth in happier union. At last surrounds their sight A globe of circular light, That with long beams the shame-fac'd Night array'd; The helmed Cherubim And sworded Seraphim Are seen in glittering ranks with wings display'd, Harping in loud and solemn quire, With unexpressive notes to Heav'n's new-born Heir. Such music (as 'tis said) Before was never made, But when of old the sons of morning sung, While the Creator great His constellations set, And the well-balanc'd world on hinges hung, And cast the dark foundations deep, And bid the welt'ring waves their oozy channel keep. Ring out ye crystal spheres! Once bless our human ears (If ye have power to touch our senses so) And let your silver chime Move in melodious time, And let the bass of Heav'n's deep organ blow; And with your ninefold harmony Make up full consort to th'angelic symphony. For if such holy song Enwrap our fancy long, Time will run back and fetch the age of gold, And speckl'd Vanity Will sicken soon and die, And leprous Sin will melt from earthly mould; And Hell itself will pass away, And leave her dolorous mansions to the peering Day. Yea, Truth and Justice then Will down return to men, Orb'd in a rainbow; and, like glories wearing, Mercy will sit between, Thron'd in celestial sheen, With radiant feet the tissu'd clouds down steering; And Heav'n, as at some festival, Will open wide the gates of her high palace hall. But wisest Fate says no: This must not yet be so; The Babe lies yet in smiling infancy, That on the bitter cross Must redeem our loss, So both himself and us to glorify: Yet first to those ychain'd in sleep, The wakeful trump of doom must thunder through the deep, With such a horrid clang As on Mount Sinai rang While the red fire and smould'ring clouds outbrake: The aged Earth, aghast With terror of that blast, Shall from the surface to the centre shake, When at the world's last session, The dreadful Judge in middle air shall spread his throne. And then at last our bliss Full and perfect is, But now begins; for from this happy day Th'old Dragon under ground, In straiter limits bound, Not half so far casts his usurped sway, And, wrath to see his kingdom fail, Swinges the scaly horror of his folded tail. The Oracles are dumb; No voice or hideous hum Runs through the arched roof in words deceiving. Apollo from his shrine Can no more divine, With hollow shriek the steep of Delphos leaving. No nightly trance or breathed spell Inspires the pale-ey'd priest from the prophetic cell. The lonely mountains o'er, And the resounding shore, A voice of weeping heard and loud lament; From haunted spring, and dale Edg'd with poplar pale, The parting Genius is with sighing sent; With flow'r-inwoven tresses torn The Nymphs in twilight shade of tangled thickets mourn. In consecrated earth, And on the holy hearth, The Lars and Lemures moan with midnight plaint; In urns and altars round, A drear and dying sound Affrights the flamens at their service quaint; And the chill marble seems to sweat, While each peculiar power forgoes his wonted seat. Peor and Ba{:a}lim Forsake their temples dim, With that twice-batter'd god of Palestine; And mooned Ashtaroth, Heav'n's queen and mother both, Now sits not girt with tapers' holy shine; The Libyc Hammon shrinks his horn; In vain the Tyrian maids their wounded Thammuz mourn. And sullen Moloch, fled, Hath left in shadows dread His burning idol all of blackest hue: In vain with cymbals' ring They call the grisly king, In dismal dance about the furnace blue. The brutish gods of Nile as fast, Isis and Orus, and the dog Anubis, haste. Nor is Osiris seen In Memphian grove or green, Trampling the unshower'd grass with lowings loud; Nor can he be at rest Within his sacred chest, Naught but profoundest Hell can be his shroud: In vain with timbrel'd anthems dark The sable-stoled sorcerers bear his worshipp'd ark. He feels from Juda's land The dreaded Infant's hand, The rays of Bethlehem blind his dusky eyn; Nor all the gods beside Longer dare abide, Not Typhon huge ending in snaky twine: Our Babe, to show his Godhead true, Can in his swaddling bands control the damned crew. So when the Sun in bed, Curtain'd with cloudy red, Pillows his chin upon an orient wave, The flocking shadows pale Troop to th'infernal jail, Each fetter'd ghost slips to his several grave, And the yellow-skirted fays Fly after the night-steeds, leaving their moon-lov'd maze. But see, the Virgin blest Hath laid her Babe to rest: Time is our tedious song should here have ending. Heav'n's youngest-teemed star, Hath fix'd her polish'd car, Her sleeping Lord with handmaid lamp attending; And all about the courtly stable, Bright-harness'd Angels sit in order serviceable.

Tim and Kim are twins. They like to play with their toys. They have many toys, but their favorite is the big red vehicle. The vehicle can make noises and move fast. Tim and Kim can sit inside and pretend to drive.

One day, they want to play with the vehicle outside. They ask their mom if they can go. Mom says yes, but they need to wear their hats and coats. It is cold outside. Tim and Kim are eager to go. They put on their hats and coats and run to the door.

"Wait, wait!" Mom says. "You need to take something else."

"What do we need, Mom?" Tim and Kim ask.

"You need to take this," Mom says. She gives them a basket with some bread and cheese. "This is for Mr. Lee. He lives next door. He is sick and can't go out. He needs some food. Can you be kind and give this to him?"

Tim and Kim nod. They like Mr. Lee. He is nice and tells them stories. They take the basket and put it in the vehicle. They say bye to Mom and go outside.

They drive the vehicle to Mr. Lee's house. They knock on the door. Mr. Lee opens it. He looks pale and tired. He smiles when he sees Tim and Kim.

"Hello, Tim and Kim. What a surprise. What are you doing here?" he asks.

"Hi, Mr. Lee. We are here to give you this," Tim says. He hands him the basket. "Mom says you are sick and need some food. We hope you feel better soon."

Mr. Lee takes the basket and thanks them. He invites them in, but they say they have to go back. They have to play with their vehicle. They say bye to Mr. Lee and drive away.

Mr. Lee watches them go. He feels happy and grateful. He opens the basket and sees the bread and cheese. He thinks Tim and Kim are very sweet and thoughtful. He eats some of the food and feels a little better. He thinks maybe he will tell them another story when he sees them again.

Once upon a time, there was a kid named Timmy. Timmy was very tired and wanted to go to bed. He put on his warm pajamas and climbed into bed. Timmy's mom read him a story and soon he started to yawn. 

As Timmy closed his eyes, he heard a noise. It was his cat, Mittens. Mittens was also tired and wanted to sleep on Timmy's bed. Timmy let Mittens snuggle up next to him and they both fell asleep. 

In the morning, Timmy woke up feeling refreshed and ready to play. Mittens was still asleep and looked very cozy. Timmy smiled and whispered, "Good morning, Mittens," but Mittens just yawned and went back to sleep.

name_of_work: Small Towns and The River by Mamang Dai
content: Small towns always remind me of death. My hometown lies calmly amidst the trees, it is always the same, in summer or winter, with the dust flying, or the wind howling down the gorge. Just the other day someone died. In the dreadful silence we wept looking at the sad wreath of tuberoses. Life and death, life and death, only the rituals are permanent. The river has a soul. In the summer it cuts through the land like a torrent of grief. Sometimes, sometimes, I think it holds its breath seeking a land of fish and stars The river has a soul. It knows, stretching past the town, from the first drop of rain to dry earth and mist on the mountaintops, the river knows the immortality of water. A shrine of happy pictures marks the days of childhood. Small towns grow with anxiety for the future. The dead are placed pointing west. When the soul rises it will walk into the golden east, into the house of the sun. In the cool bamboo, restored in sunlight, life matters, like this. In small towns by the river we all want to walk with the gods.

Once upon a time there was a wise kangaroo. He was hopping around in the forest one day when he stopped to look around. Suddenly he noticed a little bird sitting on a branch. The bird said "hello Kangaroo, are you looking for something?".

The kangaroo smiled and said "Hello little bird, I was just trying to figure out what I should do today". The bird replied "Well, did you mention going to visit your friends?". 

The kangaroo thought for a second, then remembered he had an important playdate later on. He leapt up and said "Oh, that's right! I had almost forgotten! Thanks for reminding me, little bird". 

The kangaroo said goodbye, and hopped away to meet his friends. He was so excited to see what fun adventures they would have today!

Her mom said, â€œLetâ€™s go to the store and see what we can find.â€ Lucy was excited! 

When they got to the store, Lucy spotted a deep blue toy with lots of wires. She wanted it so badly! Her mom said, â€œThat looks like fun! You really need it?â€ Lucy smiled and nodded. 

They bought the toy and went home. Lucy had so much fun playing with it. She twisted the wires and made different shapes. She saw how deep the blue color was.
