name_of_work: In the Bleak Midwinter by Christina Rossetti
content: In the bleak midwinter, frosty wind made moan, Earth stood hard as iron, water like a stone; Snow had fallen, snow on snow, snow on snow, In the bleak midwinter, long ago. Our God, Heaven cannot hold Him, nor earth sustain; Heaven and earth shall flee away when He comes to reign. In the bleak midwinter a stable place sufficed The Lord God Almighty, Jesus Christ. Enough for Him, whom cherubim, worship night and day, Breastful of milk, and a mangerful of hay; Enough for Him, whom angels fall before, The ox and ass and camel which adore. Angels and archangels may have gathered there, Cherubim and seraphim thronged the air; But His mother only, in her maiden bliss, Worshipped the beloved with a kiss. What can I give Him, poor as I am? If I were a shepherd, I would bring a lamb; If I were a Wise Man, I would do my part; Yet what I can I give Him: give my heart.

name_of_work: Poppies on Ludlow Castle by Willa Cather
content: THROUGH halls of vanished pleasure, And hold of vanished power, And crypt of faith forgotten, A came to Ludlow tower. A-top of arch and stairway, Of crypt and donjan cell, Of council hall, and chamber, Of wall, and ditch, and well, High over grated turrets Where clinging ivies run, A thousand scarlet poppies Enticed the rising sun, Upon the topmost turret, With death and damp below,-- Three hundred years of spoilage,-- The crimson poppies grow. This hall it was that bred him, These hills that knew him brave, The gentlest English singer That fills an English grave. How have they heart to blossom So cruel and gay and red, When beauty so hath perished And valour so hath sped? When knights so fair are rotten, And captains true asleep, And singing lips are dust-stopped Six English earth-feet deep? When ages old remind me How much hath gone for naught, What wretched ghost remaineth Of all that flesh hath wrought; Of love and song and warring, Of adventure and play, Of art and comely building, Of faith and form and fray-- I'll mind the flowers of pleasure, Of short-lived youth and sleep, That drunk the sunny weather A-top of Ludlow keep.

But the mosquito was not a nice friend. It bit Tim on his arm. Tim cried and went to his mom. His mom said, "Oh no, Tim! The mosquito was not a good friend. We need to be careful of mosquitoes." The amazing big red ball was left all alone, and Tim never played with the mosquito again.

name_of_work: Our Deepest Fear by Marianne Williamson
content: Our deepest fear is not that we are inadequate. Our deepest fear is that we are powerful beyond measure. It is our light, not our darkness that most frightens us. We ask ourselves, "Who am I to be brilliant, gorgeous, talented, fabulous?" Actually, who are you not to be? You are a child of God. Your playing small does not serve the world. There's nothing enlightened about shrinking so that other people won't feel insecure around you. We are all meant to shine, as children do. We were born to make manifest the glory of God that is within us. It's not just in some of us; it's in everyone. And as we let our own light shine, we unconsciously give other people permission to do the same. As we're liberated from our own fear, our presence automatically liberates others.

Once upon a time there was a very yummy milk. It was a mild milk and it was kept in a big cool box. When you tasted it, it was like nothing else. It was so good that all the children wanted to drink it all the time.

Every day, the milk was kept cool in the box. The children would come over and slowly sip it until it was gone. 

But one day, the milk ran out. So the children had to keep looking for more. They searched high and low but they couldn't find any milk as mild and tasty as the one they had. 

But then, one day, someone rather magical happened along. She gave the children a cool box of mild, tasty milk. All the children cheered and drank it until it was gone. 

And from then on, the children kept looking for that same mild, tasty milk. They never found it again, but it was a taste theyâ€™d never forget.

The sun was shining brightly in the sky. Mary was very excited, for she had a new blouse given by her mum. Mary's friends were all envious of the new blouse. But just as she was about to show her friends her blouse, it started to rain. Mary was very disappointed, her new blouse was getting wet. She hoped it will dry soon.

But the rain didn't stop. As the rain got harder and harder, Mary quickly ran home. When she reached home, she saw her blouse was all wet. She sadly hung it on the wall to dry.

The next day, Mary was excited to wear her new blouse again. But to her surprise, it was all stained. The rain ruined her blouse and it was no longer shine when she looked at it.

Mary was so sad, she wished the rain did not come. She wanted her new blouse to shine again. Unfortunately, that did not happen, and her blouse never shone again.

Once there was a family who had a reliable cactus. Each day, the family would act happy around the cactus. They would talk to it and even water it.

One day, the family decided to take the cactus on an outing. They loaded it into the car and drove to the park. The family acted very careful with the cactus, making sure it didn't get too much sun.

At the park, they unloaded the cactus and put it under a tree. Then, they all went to play together. They ran around, played tag, and had a picnic. The family acted like they were having a great time!

When it was time to go home, the family packed up the cactus and loaded it in the car. When they got home, they placed the cactus back in its spot in the family room.

The family was very happy with their reliable cactus. They would act like friends with it each day, and take good care of it.

Tom was a boy who liked to play with his toys. He had a big box of toys in his room. He had cars, trains, dolls, blocks, and books. He also had a feather that he found in the park. He liked to tickle his nose with the feather and make funny noises.

One day, Tom was playing with his feather in his room. He heard a knock on the door. He thought it was his mom or dad. He said, "Come in!" But it was not his mom or dad. It was a big, scary monster. The monster had sharp teeth, long claws, and red eyes. The monster saw Tom and his feather. The monster wanted the feather. The monster said, "Give me the feather, or I will eat you!"

Tom was very scared. He did not want to give the monster his feather. He liked his feather. He said, "No, this is my feather. Go away!" He tried to run to the door, but the monster was faster. The monster grabbed Tom and his feather. The monster said, "Too bad, this is my feather now. And you are my snack!" The monster opened his mouth and bit Tom. Tom screamed, but no one heard him. The monster ate Tom and his feather. The monster was happy. Tom was gone. The end.

A broken ALTAR, Lord, thy servant rears, Made of a heart and cemented with tears: Whose parts are as thy hand did frame; No workman's tool hath touch'd the same. A HEART alone Is such a stone, As nothing but Thy pow'r doth cut. Wherefore each part Of my hard heart Meets in this frame, To praise thy name: That if I chance to hold my peace, These stones to praise thee may not cease. Oh, let thy blessed SACRIFICE be mine, And sanctify this ALTAR to be thine.

Once upon a time, there was a small bird who loved to soar. He could fly high above the trees and look out at the world around him. One day, the bird wanted to fly even higher. So, he spread his wings and took off.

The bird soared away from the trees and over the fields. He flew over the meadows and beyond the mountains. After a while, he found a gray road far below. The bird decided to descend and landed on the road.

Suddenly, he saw a car coming his way. The bird tried to move away but he was too slow. The car stopped right in front of him.

The driver was a kind old man. He opened his car door and said, "Hi little bird. How about a ride?". The bird was scared but he was curious. He looked at the old man, and then at the gray road. Seeing no other way out, he decided to accept the offer.

The old man gently picked up the bird. He put him inside the car, and drove away. The bird was still scared but he was happy. For the first time, he was soaring on the ground. He could see the world from an entirely different perspective. The bird was so excited he almost forgot to be scared.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her dolls and wear her mommy's perfume. One day, Lily's friend Emily came over to play. 

"Hi Lily, can I borrow your doll?" asked Emily. 

Lily thought about it for a moment and said, "Sure, but you have to give it back to me later. You can lend it for a little while." 

Emily was happy and played with the doll. But then, she accidentally broke it. "I'm sorry Lily, I broke your doll," said Emily. 

"It's okay," said Lily. "It was a rare doll anyways. I have lots of other dolls to play with. But please be careful next time." 

Emily felt bad, but Lily forgave her. They continued playing and putting on perfume, making their dolls smell nice. They had a fun day together, even with the little accident.

Now that I, tying thy glass mask tightly, May gaze thro' these faint smokes curling whitely, As thou pliest thy trade in this devil's-smithy-- Which is the poison to poison her, prithee? He is with her, and they know that I know Where they are, what they do: they believe my tears flow While they laugh, laugh at me, at me fled to the drear Empty church, to pray God in, for them!--I am here. Grind away, moisten and mash up thy paste, Pound at thy powder,--I am not in haste! Better sit thus and observe thy strange things, Than go where men wait me and dance at the King's. That in the mortar--you call it a gum? Ah, the brave tree whence such gold oozings come! And yonder soft phial, the exquisite blue, Sure to taste sweetly,--is that poison too? Had I but all of them, thee and thy treasures, What a wild crowd of invisible pleasures! To carry pure death in an earring, a casket, A signet, a fan-mount, a filigree basket! Soon, at the King's, a mere lozenge to give And Pauline should have just thirty minutes to live! But to light a pastile, and Elise, with her head And her breast and her arms and her hands, should drop dead! Quick--is it finished? The colour's too grim! Why not soft like the phial's, enticing and dim? Let it brighten her drink, let her turn it and stir, And try it and taste, ere she fix and prefer! What a drop! She's not little, no minion like me-- That's why she ensnared him: this never will free The soul from those masculine eyes,--say, "no!" To that pulse's magnificent come-and-go. For only last night, as they whispered, I brought My own eyes to bear on her so, that I thought Could I keep them one half minute fixed, she would fall, Shrivelled; she fell not; yet this does it all! Not that I bid you spare her the pain! Let death be felt and the proof remain; Brand, burn up, bite into its grace-- He is sure to remember her dying face! Is it done? Take my mask off! Nay, be not morose; It kills her, and this prevents seeing it close: The delicate droplet, my whole fortune's fee-- If it hurts her, beside, can it ever hurt me? Now, take all my jewels, gorge gold to your fill, You may kiss me, old man, on my mouth if you will! But brush this dust off me, lest horror it brings Ere I know it--next moment I dance at the King's!

Once upon a time there was a little boy called John. He loved playing make-believe with his original shield. One day, he was playing when he heard a loud voice. This voice demanded that John come closer.

John was scared. He grabbed his shield and ran. He was so small that he was able to hide behind it.

John peeked around the edge of his shield and saw a great big dragon. The dragon made the same demand again. He said, â€œI must have your shield. Give it to me now!â€

John was very brave. He stood up tall and shouted, â€œNo! This is my shield and I will keep it. You cannot have it!â€

The dragon was surprised. He had never met such a brave little boy before. After a few moments, the dragon smiled and said, â€œYou have courage little one. You can keep your shield.â€

John smiled and hugged his original shield. He was so glad that he had been brave enough to stand up to the dragon.

Once upon a time, there was a big, green frog. The frog loved to eat bugs. He was very healthy. One day, the frog saw a big bug near the pond. The bug was sitting on a leaf. The frog was hungry and wanted to eat the bug.

The frog jumped and tried to snap the bug with his long tongue. But the bug was too fast. The frog tried again and again, but he could not catch the bug. The frog was sad.

Then, the frog saw some oil on the ground. He had an idea. The frog put the oil on the leaf where the bug was sitting. The bug slipped on the oil and could not move fast. The frog jumped and snapped the bug with his long tongue. The frog was happy and full.

Once upon a time, there was a clever dog named Spot. Spot liked to help people. One day, Spot went to a big hotel. The hotel was full of people who needed help.

Spot saw a lady who was sad. She lost her bag. Spot said, "Please, let me help you find your bag." The lady said, "Thank you, Spot!" They looked and looked, and they found the bag. The lady was so happy!

Spot saw a boy who was lost. The boy said, "I can't find my mom!" Spot said, "Please, let me help you find your mom." They looked and looked, and they found the boy's mom. The boy and his mom were so happy! Everyone at the hotel said, "Spot is a very clever dog!"

Once upon a time, there was a modest little town. In the town, there was a long rail. The rail was for the train to go on. All the people in the town loved to watch the train go by.

One day, a girl named Amy found a big box. She wanted to give the box to her friend, Tom. So, she decided to wrap the box with pretty paper. Amy was so excited to give the box to Tom.

Amy carried the wrapped box to Tom's house. On her way, she had to cross the rail. As she was crossing, she saw the train coming. Amy was scared and said, "Oh no! The train is coming! I must hurry!"

Tom heard Amy and came running to help her. Together, they crossed the rail just in time. Amy gave the wrapped box to Tom and said, "I found this for you, Tom!"

Tom opened the box and found a toy train inside. He was so happy and said, "Thank you, Amy! This is the best gift ever!" They played with the toy train all day, and they were the best of friends.

Sara likes to write. She writes with crayons on paper. She writes her name, and the names of her friends. She writes big and small, and in many colors.

One day, Sara goes to the zoo with her mom. She sees many animals. She sees lions, and monkeys, and elephants. She likes the animals. She wants to write about them.

She asks her mom for a paper and a crayon. Her mom gives her a paper and a blue crayon. Sara writes "ZOO" on the paper. Then she draws a lion, and a monkey, and an elephant.

She sees a cell near the lion. She asks her mom, "What is that?"

Her mom says, "That is a cell. It is where the lion sleeps. It is like his home."

Sara says, "But it is so small. And it has bars. The lion cannot run, or play, or see his friends. He must be sad."

Her mom says, "Yes, it is sad. The lion needs more space, and more freedom. He needs a compassionate zookeeper, who cares about him, and helps him."

Sara says, "I want to be a compassionate zookeeper. I want to help the lion, and the other animals. I want to make them happy."

She writes "I LOVE LION" on the paper. She shows it to the lion. The lion looks at her, and roars softly. Sara smiles. She thinks the lion likes her writing. She hopes he feels a little better.

Once upon a time, there were two friends: Peter and Sarah. They both loved to play together. One day, they decided to play dress up.

Peter found a beautiful pin in his drawer and was eager to wear it. But Sarah was envious and didn't want him to wear it. She grabbed it before he could and spread it all around the room.

"Give it back!" Peter yelled.

"No!" Sarah said with a smirk.

Peter looked around the room and desperately tried to find the pin. He searched high and low until he saw a sparkle under the sofa. He quickly ran over and grabbed the pin.

"See! I found it!" he said with a proud smile.

Sarah was unhappy and envious. But Peter and Sarah continued to play dress up and had lots of fun until it was time to go home.

The young girl was feeling bored. She looked around the room, looking for something to do. Suddenly, she had an idea. She decided to perform a show.

The girl started by gathering her clothes. She quickly searched the house for her favorite items. She found a yellow dress with a matching scarf. She chose a pair of blue shorts and a pink shirt. She was ready!

The girl put on her clothes. She marched around the room, pretending to be a soldier. She gathered some chairs and placed them together in a neat row. Then, she called out to the audience. At that moment, a great thunder clap shook the room.

The girl was worried. It had started to rain outside. She had promised a show, but there was no way it could go ahead in the rain. She sat down and thought carefully. Then, she realized what she could do- she would perform a dry show!

The girl quickly gathered all of the chairs and placed them close to the window so they would not get wet. Then, she took in her show. She told stories, did silly dances and even sang a few songs. In the end, everyone was laughing and clapping. She had done it! She had performed a dry show.

Once upon a time there was a dog named Rover. Rover liked to go for long walks but one day it was raining. He couldn't take a walk so he had to store himself inside the house. He found a shower and thought it was interesting. He smelled the shower and it smelled really nice. Rover took off his wet coat and hopped in the shower. He felt much better after his shower. He dried off and curled up in his cozy bed. It was a very interesting day for Rover!

name_of_work: When green buds hang in the elm by A. E. Housman
content: When green buds hang in the elm like dust And sprinkle the lime like rain, Forth I wander, forth I must, And drink of life again. Forth I must by hedgerow bowers To look at the leaves uncurled, And stand in the fields where cuckoo-flowers Are lying about the world.

Once there was a fish who lived in a deep blue ocean. He loved swimming around with his friends.

One day he had a great idea to catch his dinner with a net. He swam to a temple and asked the fish there if he could borrow a net. They refused because it was not theirs to give.

The fish was sad but he had an even better idea! He found a big leaf at the bottom of the ocean and decided to use it to catch his dinner.

He waved the leaf around and the fish jumped right into it. He was so happy!

With his dinner safely in the leaf, the fish made his happy journey home.

Dear love, what thing of all the things that be Is ever worth one thought from you or me, Save only Love, Save only Love? The days so short, the nights so quick to flee, The world so wide, so deep and dark the sea, So dark the sea; So far the suns and every listless star, Beyond their light--Ah! dear, who knows how far, Who knows how far? One thing of all dim things I know is true, The heart within me knows, and tells it you, And tells it you. So blind is life, so long at last is sleep, And none but Love to bid us laugh or weep, And none but Love, And none but Love.

One day, there was a sweet little girl named Lily. Lily had long, brown hair and big, blue eyes. She was very adorable!

Everyday, Lily would go outside and hope to find something new and exciting in her backyard. Today was special, because she found something very unusual - a big patch of green plants! They were very tall and Lily was very surprised.

Lily decided to carefully pick one of the plants to take home with her. Carefully, she grabbed the plant and headed home. She was so excited! Once she got home, she planted the plant in her garden and hoped it would grow.

Everyday, Lily would water the plant and talk to it. She hoped that it would grow and be healthy. Over time, the plant grew bigger and bigger and more beautiful. Lily was so happy!

Lily now has a very special and adorable garden full of all kinds of green plants, and she loves it! She hopes that she can add more plants in the future and continue to watch them grow.

Tom and Sam are brothers. They like to play with cars and blocks. But they do not like to share. Sometimes they fight over their toys.

One day, they are playing in their room. Tom has a big red car. Sam has a small blue car. Tom wants to play with both cars. He says to Sam, "Give me your car. It is nice. Mine is nice too. I want two nice cars."

Sam says, "No, Tom. This is my car. You have your car. We can play together. Do not take my car."

Tom does not listen. He grabs Sam's car and runs away. Sam is angry. He runs after Tom and tries to get his car back. They push and pull and yell.

Mom hears them. She comes to their room. She sees them fighting. She is not happy. She says, "Stop, Tom and Sam. You are being bad. You are hurting each other and your toys. You need to rest. Go to your beds and rest for zero minutes. Then you can play again. But you have to share and be nice."

Tom and Sam are sad. They do not want to rest. They want to play. But they know Mom is right. They are being bad. They go to their beds and rest for zero minutes. Zero minutes is not long. It is like no minutes.

After zero minutes, Mom comes back. She says, "Are you ready to play again? Do you want to share and be nice?"

Tom and Sam nod. They say, "Yes, Mom. We are sorry. We want to share and be nice."

Mom smiles. She says, "Good. I am glad. You can play again. But remember, be nice to each other and your toys."

Tom and Sam hug Mom. They say, "Thank you, Mom. We love you."

They go back to their room. They play with their cars and blocks. They share and be nice. They have fun. They are happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Laura. She had a hurt foot and her mommy was so worried about her. "We need to hurry," she said.

So, they got in the car and drove to the hospital. When they arrived, they saw that the hospital was very poor. There were no toys and not many nurses.

But Laura did not care. She was happy to go to the hospital to get help for her foot.

When they arrived at the hospital, the nurse said, "You can come inside now."

So, Laura and her mommy followed the nurse inside. The nurse looked closely at Laura's foot and smiled.

"We can make it better," said the nurse. Then she gave Laura some medicine and a bandage.

Laura was very happy when she got better. She thanked the nurse and said goodbye.

Then they all waved goodbye as Laura and her mommy went back home.

name_of_work: The Road Goes Ever On by J.R.R. Tolkien
content: Roads go ever ever on, Over rock and under tree, By caves where never sun has shone, By streams that never find the sea; Over snow by winter sown, And through the merry flowers of June, Over grass and over stone, And under mountains in the moon. Roads go ever ever on Under cloud and under star, Yet feet that wandering have gone Turn at last to home afar. Eyes that fire and sword have seen And horror in the halls of stone Look at last on meadows green And trees and hills they long have known.[2]

One gloomy day, a little boy was walking through the park. He looked around and saw a big tree. He pointed at it with his eye. He saw something special on the tree. It was just peeking out from behind the leaves.

The little boy ran up to the tree and climbed up it. He looked at the thing he had seen and it was a little bird. The bird had a yellow beak and colourful feathers. It stared back at the little boy and blinked its eye. 

The little boy was so happy - he was so pleased to see the bird that he pointed at it and waved. The bird chirped in response and flew away into the sky. 

The little boy watched the bird until it was out of sight. He smiled and gently touched the tree trunk, remembering his meeting with the bird. He walked away feeling very excited - after all, it was a very special day!

name_of_work: Resolution and Independence by William Wordsworth
content: There was a roaring in the wind all night; The rain came heavily and fell in floods; But now the sun is rising calm and bright; The birds are singing in the distant woods; Over his own sweet voice the Stock-dove broods; The Jay makes answer as the Magpie chatters; And all the air is filled with pleasant noise of waters. All things that love the sun are out of doors; The sky rejoices in the morning's birth; The grass is bright with rain-drops;--on the moors The hare is running races in her mirth; And with her feet she from the plashy earth Raises a mist, that, glittering in the sun, Runs with her all the way, wherever she doth run. I was a Traveller then upon the moor; I saw the hare that raced about with joy; I heard the woods and distant waters roar; Or heard them not, as happy as a boy: The pleasant season did my heart employ: My old remembrances went from me wholly; And all the ways of men, so vain and melancholy. But, as it sometimes chanceth, from the might Of joys in minds that can no further go, As high as we have mounted in delight In our dejection do we sink as low; To me that morning did it happen so; And fears and fancies thick upon me came; Dim sadness--and blind thoughts, I knew not, nor could name. I heard the sky-lark warbling in the sky; And I bethought me of the playful hare: Even such a happy Child of earth am I; Even as these blissful creatures do I fare; Far from the world I walk, and from all care; But there may come another day to me-- Solitude, pain of heart, distress, and poverty. My whole life I have lived in pleasant thought, As if life's business were a summer mood; As if all needful things would come unsought To genial faith, still rich in genial good; But how can He expect that others should Build for him, sow for him, and at his call Love him, who for himself will take no heed at all? I thought of Chatterton, the marvellous Boy, The sleepless Soul that perished in his pride; Of Him who walked in glory and in joy Following his plough, along the mountain-side: By our own spirits are we deified: We Poets in our youth begin in gladness; But thereof come in the end despondency and madness. Now, whether it were by peculiar grace, A leading from above, a something given, Yet it befell that, in this lonely place, When I with these untoward thoughts had striven, Beside a pool bare to the eye of heaven I saw a Man before me unawares: The oldest man he seemed that ever wore grey hairs. As a huge stone is sometimes seen to lie Couched on the bald top of an eminence; Wonder to all who do the same espy, By what means it could thither come, and whence; So that it seems a thing endued with sense: Like a sea-beast crawled forth, that on a shelf Of rock or sand reposeth, there to sun itself; Such seemed this Man, not all alive nor dead, Nor all asleep--in his extreme old age: His body was bent double, feet and head Coming together in life's pilgrimage; As if some dire constraint of pain, or rage Of sickness felt by him in times long past, A more than human weight upon his frame had cast. Himself he propped, limbs, body, and pale face, Upon a long grey staff of shaven wood: And, still as I drew near with gentle pace, Upon the margin of that moorish flood Motionless as a cloud the old Man stood, That heareth not the loud winds when they call, And moveth all together, if it move at all. At length, himself unsettling, he the pond Stirred with his staff, and fixedly did look Upon the muddy water, which he conned, As if he had been reading in a book: And now a stranger's privilege I took; And, drawing to his side, to him did say, "This morning gives us promise of a glorious day." A gentle answer did the old Man make, In courteous speech which forth he slowly drew: And him with further words I thus bespake, "What occupation do you there pursue? This is a lonesome place for one like you." Ere he replied, a flash of mild surprise Broke from the sable orbs of his yet-vivid eyes. His words came feebly, from a feeble chest, But each in solemn order followed each, With something of a lofty utterance drest-- Choice word and measured phrase, above the reach Of ordinary men; a stately speech; Such as grave Livers do in Scotland use, Religious men, who give to God and man their dues. He told, that to these waters he had come To gather leeches, being old and poor: Employment hazardous and wearisome! And he had many hardships to endure: From pond to pond he roamed, from moor to moor; Housing, with God's good help, by choice or chance; And in this way he gained an honest maintenance. The old Man still stood talking by my side; But now his voice to me was like a stream Scarce heard; nor word from word could I divide; And the whole body of the Man did seem Like one whom I had met with in a dream; Or like a man from some far region sent, To give me human strength, by apt admonishment. My former thoughts returned: the fear that kills; And hope that is unwilling to be fed; Cold, pain, and labour, and all fleshly ills; And mighty Poets in their misery dead. --Perplexed, and longing to be comforted, My question eagerly did I renew, "How is it that you live, and what is it you do?" He with a smile did then his words repeat; And said that, gathering leeches, far and wide He travelled; stirring thus about his feet The waters of the pools where they abide. "Once I could meet with them on every side; But they have dwindled long by slow decay; Yet still I persevere, and find them where I may." While he was talking thus, the lonely place, The old Man's shape, and speech--all troubled me: In my mind's eye I seemed to see him pace About the weary moors continually, Wandering about alone and silently. While I these thoughts within myself pursued, He, having made a pause, the same discourse renewed. And soon with this he other matter blended, Cheerfully uttered, with demeanour kind, But stately in the main; and, when he ended, I could have laughed myself to scorn to find In that decrepit Man so firm a mind. "God," said I, "be my help and stay secure; I'll think of the Leech-gatherer on the lonely moor!"

Once upon a time, there was a thin boy named Timmy. Timmy loved playing in his backyard, but one day he found a treasure map! He ran to his mom and said, "Mommy, I found a treasure map! Can we bury treasure in our backyard?"

His mom smiled and said, "Of course, Timmy! You can be the hero who finds the treasure!" They went outside and dug a hole. Timmy carefully placed the treasure in the hole and covered it up with dirt. He was so happy to be a hero!

As they walked back inside, Timmy's mom asked, "What do you think is in the treasure?" Timmy replied, "Maybe it's gold or jewels or toys!" They both laughed and Timmy went to bed dreaming of all the adventures he would have as a hero.

name_of_work: Sad and Alone by Maurice Manning
content: Well, this is nothing new, nothing to rattle the rafters in the noggin, this moment of remembering and its kissing cousin the waking dream. I wonder if I'll remember it? I've had a vision of a woman reclining underneath a tree: she's about half naked and little by little I'm sprinkling her burial mounds with grass. This is the kind of work I like. It lets me remember, and so I do. I remember the time I laid my homemade banjo in the fire and let it burn. There was nothing else to burn and the house was cold; the cigar box curled inside the flames. But the burst of heat was over soon, and once the little roar was done, I could hear the raindrops plopping up the buckets and kettles, scattered out like little ponds around the room. It was night and I was a boy, alone and left to listen to that old music. I liked it. I've liked it ever since. I loved the helpless people I loved. That's what a little boy will do, but a grown man will turn it all to sadness and let it soak his heart until he wrings it out and dreams about another kind of love, some afternoon beneath a tree. Burial mounds--that's hilarious.

Anna and Ben were playing in the park with their ball. They liked to kick the ball to each other and run after it. They were having fun until a big dog came out of nowhere and chased them. The dog was barking loudly and had sharp teeth.

Anna and Ben were scared and ran away from the dog. They tried to find their mom, who was sitting on a bench nearby. But the dog was faster and caught up with them. The dog bit Ben's leg and made him fall down. Ben cried out in pain and felt blood on his skin.

"Help, help!" Anna shouted. She wanted to help her brother, but she was afraid of the dog. She trembled and hugged her ball. She hoped the dog would go away.

Their mom heard their cries and ran to them. She saw the dog and yelled at it. "Go away, you bad dog! Leave my children alone!" She threw her bag at the dog and scared it away. She hugged Anna and Ben and checked their wounds.

"Are you okay, my darlings?" she asked. She saw that Ben's leg was bleeding and Anna's face was pale. She felt sorry for them and kissed them. "Don't worry, I'm here. We'll go to the doctor and he'll make you feel better. You're very brave, both of you."

Anna and Ben felt safer in their mom's arms. They still felt pain and fear, but they knew their mom loved them and would protect them. They thanked their mom and told her they loved her too. They learned that some dogs can be harsh and dangerous, and they should always stay close to their mom in the park.

Once upon a time, there was a powerful and magical mineral. Everywhere it went, it served a wonderful purpose.

It was so magical that it could make even the rockiest of hills into a smooth path. People came from all around to marvel at it.

One day, a young boy and girl were playing in the woods. They found the mineral and it glowed brightly!

The two friends took it home and thought of all the fun things they could do with it. From making gardens to building structures, they each had so many ideas for its use.

Finally, they decided to serve the mineral to their families that evening. When everyone tasted it, it was full of flavour and sweetness. Everyone was so thankful for the powerful and wonderful mineral. 

The families celebrated with joy. They added the mineral to their daily meals and never forgot the magical moment when they found it. 

And from that day forward, the powerful mineral served its purpose in everyone's lives.

name_of_work: Oh, oh, you will be sorry for that word! by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: Oh, oh, you will be sorry for that word! Give back my book and take my kiss instead. Was it my enemy or my friend I heard, "What a big book for such a little head!" Come, I will show you now my newest hat, And you may watch me purse my mouth and prink! Oh, I shall love you still, and all of that. I never again shall tell you what I think. I shall be sweet and crafty, soft and sly; You will not catch me reading any more: I shall be called a wife to pattern by; And some day when you knock and push the door, Some sane day, not too bright and not too stormy, I shall be gone, and you may whistle for me.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to dance and twirl around. One day, she went to a party and saw a big plate of toast. She was so happy and ate a lot of it. 

After a while, Lily started to feel upset in her tummy. She went to her mom and said, "My tummy hurts." Her mom said, "Maybe you ate too much toast, sweetie." 

Lily learned that it's important to listen to your body and not eat too much of something even if it's yummy. From then on, she made sure to only have a little bit of toast and continued to dance and twirl around happily.

Once upon a time, there was a lovely little girl named Lucy. She loved to bake pies with her mommy. One day, they decided to make a big, yummy pie together.

Lucy said, "Mommy, can I squeeze the fruit for the pie?" Mommy said, "Yes, Lucy, you can. Be careful, and don't make a mess." So, Lucy squeezed the fruit very hard to get all the juice out. She was so happy to help her mommy.

They put the pie in the oven and waited for it to cook. While they waited, Lucy played with her toys. But then, she smelled something bad. "Mommy, what's that smell?" she asked. Mommy looked at the oven and saw smoke coming out.

"Oh no, Lucy! The pie is burned!" Mommy said. They opened the oven and saw the black, yucky pie. Lucy was sad, and so was her mommy. They didn't get to eat the lovely pie they made together.

The evening passes fast away, 'Tis almost time to rest; What thoughts has left the vanished day, What feelings, in thy breast? "The vanished day? It leaves a sense Of labour hardly done; Of little, gained with vast expense, -- A sense of grief alone! "Time stands before the door of Death, Upbraiding bitterly; And Conscience, with exhaustless breath, Pours black reproach on me: "And though I've said that Conscience lies, And Time should Fate condemn; Still, sad Repentance clouds my eyes, And makes me yield to them! "Then art thou glad to seek repose? Art glad to leave the sea, And anchor all thy weary woes In calm Eternity? "Nothing regrets to see thee go -- Not one voice sobs "farewell," And where thy heart has suffered so, Canst thou desire to dwell?" "Alas! The countless links are strong That bind us to our clay; The loving spirit lingers long, And would not pass away! "And rest is sweet, when laurelled fame Will crown the soldier's crest; But, a brave heart, with a tarnished name, Would rather fight than rest." "Well, thou hast fought for many a year, Hast fought thy whole life through, Hast humbled Falsehood, trampled Fear; What is there left to do?" "'Tis true, this arm has hotly striven, Has dared what few would dare; Much have I done, and freely given, But little learnt to bear!" "Look on the grave, where thou must sleep, Thy last, and strongest foe; It is endurance not to weep, If that repose seem woe. "The long war closing in defeat, Defeat serenely borne, Thy midnight rest may still be sweet, And break in glorious morn!"

Tom and Sam are brothers. They like to play in the woods. One day, they find a big axe. Tom wants to keep it. Sam wants to share it.

"Give me the axe!" Tom says. He pulls the axe.

"No, it is mine!" Sam says. He pulls the axe too.

They tug and tug. The axe is heavy. They fall down. The axe flies away. It lands on a tree. It is stuck.

"Oh no!" Tom and Sam say. They run to the tree. They try to get the axe. But it is too high. They cannot reach it.

They are sad. They want the axe. They look at each other. They are angry.

"What do we do?" Tom asks.

"I don't know," Sam says.

They think and think. They need to solve the problem.

Then, they see a big rock. It is near the tree. They have an idea.

"Maybe we can use the rock," Tom says.

"How?" Sam asks.

"Like this," Tom says. He picks up the rock. He throws it at the axe. The rock hits the axe. The axe falls down.

"Wow, you are smart!" Sam says.

"Thank you," Tom says. He smiles.

They run to the axe. They are happy. They hug each other.

"Let's share the axe," Tom says.

"OK, let's share it," Sam says.

They play with the axe. They take turns. They have fun. They are friends.

Ben and Mia like to play with snow. They make snowballs and snowmen and snow forts. They have fun in the cold.

One day, they find a big wire in the snow. It is shiny and hard. They wonder what it is.

"Maybe it is a snake," Ben says.

"No, it is not a snake. Snakes are soft and have eyes and a mouth. This is just a wire," Mia says.

"Maybe it is a toy," Ben says.

"Let's see if it can do something," Mia says.

They pull and twist and bend the wire. They make shapes and letters and numbers. They have fun with the wire.

But then, the sun comes out. It is warm and bright. The snow starts to melt. The wire gets hot.

"Ow, ow, ow!" Ben says. He drops the wire. It burns his hand.

"Are you okay?" Mia says. She is worried.

"It hurts, it hurts!" Ben says. He cries.

Mia hugs him. She says, "I'm sorry, Ben. The wire is not a good toy. It is dangerous. We should leave it alone."

They run back to their house. They tell their mom what happened. She puts some ice on Ben's hand. She says, "You are brave, Ben. The wire is not a snake or a toy. It is a power line. It carries electricity. It can melt the snow and hurt you. You should never touch it. Do you understand?"

Ben and Mia nod. They say, "Yes, mom. We understand. We are sorry. We will not touch the wire again."

Mom smiles. She says, "It's okay. You are curious and creative. But you have to be careful and safe. There are many other things you can play with in the snow. How about we make some hot chocolate and cookies?"

Ben and Mia smile. They say, "Yes, mom. We love hot chocolate and cookies. Thank you, mom."

They hug their mom. They are happy and warm. They learn a lesson. They are good kids.

Once upon a time there was a family who needed some decorations for their home. They had a special picture of their family that they wanted to hang on the wall. But when they tried to hang the picture, they realized that it didn't look very nice. The frame was ugly and didnâ€™t match the other decorations. 

So the family decided to make a new frame for the picture. They bought supplies for the frame and then worked together to create one. They each had special jobs to do. Dad painted the frame and Mom glued on some colorful decorations. Then they all helped to hang it up. 

When they were done, the picture looked so much better. It was framed in bright colors and sparkled in the light. The family was very proud of their work. Now they could see their special family picture every day.

Tom and Sam are friends. They like to play with a ball in the park. One day, they see a big man with a lot of beef in his bag. The big man is rich. He has a shiny car and a gold watch.

"Wow, look at all that beef!" Tom says. "I wish we had some. We only have bread and cheese for lunch."

"Me too," Sam says. "Maybe we can ask him to share some with us. He has so much."

They run to the big man and say hello. They ask him if he can give them some beef. The big man is angry. He does not like to share. He says no and tells them to go away.

"But we are hungry," Tom says. "Please, just a little bit."

The big man kicks the ball away. He says they are rude and annoying. He says he worked hard for his beef and they are lazy and poor.

Tom and Sam are sad and scared. They run after the ball. They do not want to lose it. It is their favorite toy.

They find the ball near a fence. They see a dog on the other side. The dog is thin and hungry. It smells the beef in the big man's bag. It jumps over the fence and runs to the big man. It barks and bites his leg.

The big man screams and drops his bag. The beef falls out. The dog grabs a piece and runs away. Tom and Sam grab another piece and run away too. They are happy and full. They share their beef with the dog. The dog is happy and full too. It licks their faces and wags its tail.

The big man is angry and hurt. He has no beef left. He has no friends. He gets in his shiny car and drives away. He is rich, but he is not happy.

When I was young and there were five of us, all running riot to my mother's quiet despair, our old enamel tub, age-stained and pocked upon its griffin claws, was never full. Such plenty was too dear in our expanse of drought where dams leaked dry and windmills stalled. Like Mommy's smile. Her lips stretched back and anchored down, in anger at some fault - of mine, I thought - not knowing then it was a clasp to keep us all from chaos. She saw it always, snapping locks and straps, the spilling: sums and worries, shopping lists for aspirin, porridge, petrol, bread. Even the toilet paper counted, and each month was weeks too long. Her mouth a lid clamped hard on this. We thought her mean. Skipped chores, swiped biscuits - best of all when she was out of earshot stole another precious inch up to our chests, such lovely sin, lolling luxuriant in secret warmth disgorged from fat brass taps, our old compliant co-conspirators. Now bubbles lap my chin. I am a sybarite. The shower's a hot cascade and water's plentiful, to excess, almost, here. I leave the heating on. And miss my scattered sisters, all those bathroom squabbles and, at last, my mother's smile, loosed from the bonds of lean, dry times and our long childhood.

This is the beginning. Almost anything can happen. This is where you find the creation of light, a fish wriggling onto land, the first word of Paradise Lost on an empty page. Think of an egg, the letter A, a woman ironing on a bare stage as the heavy curtain rises. This is the very beginning. The first-person narrator introduces himself, tells us about his lineage. The mezzo-soprano stands in the wings. Here the climbers are studying a map or pulling on their long woolen socks. This is early on, years before the Ark, dawn. The profile of an animal is being smeared on the wall of a cave, and you have not yet learned to crawl. This is the opening, the gambit, a pawn moving forward an inch. This is your first night with her, your first night without her. This is the first part where the wheels begin to turn, where the elevator begins its ascent, before the doors lurch apart. This is the middle. Things have had time to get complicated, messy, really. Nothing is simple anymore. Cities have sprouted up along the rivers teeming with people at cross-purposes-- a million schemes, a million wild looks. Disappointment unshoulders his knapsack here and pitches his ragged tent. This is the sticky part where the plot congeals, where the action suddenly reverses or swerves off in an outrageous direction. Here the narrator devotes a long paragraph to why Miriam does not want Edward's child. Someone hides a letter under a pillow. Here the aria rises to a pitch, a song of betrayal, salted with revenge. And the climbing party is stuck on a ledge halfway up the mountain. This is the bridge, the painful modulation. This is the thick of things. So much is crowded into the middle-- the guitars of Spain, piles of ripe avocados, Russian uniforms, noisy parties, lakeside kisses, arguments heard through a wall-- too much to name, too much to think about. And this is the end, the car running out of road, the river losing its name in an ocean, the long nose of the photographed horse touching the white electronic line. This is the colophon, the last elephant in the parade, the empty wheelchair, and pigeons floating down in the evening. Here the stage is littered with bodies, the narrator leads the characters to their cells, and the climbers are in their graves. It is me hitting the period and you closing the book. It is Sylvia Plath in the kitchen and St. Clement with an anchor around his neck. This is the final bit thinning away to nothing. This is the end, according to Aristotle, what we have all been waiting for, what everything comes down to, the destination we cannot help imagining, a streak of light in the sky, a hat on a peg, and outside the cabin, falling leaves.

Lily and Tom were playing in the park. They liked to slide on the big slide. It was fun and fast. Lily went first. She sat on the slide and said, "Ready, set, go!" Then she slid down and laughed.

Tom wanted to slide too. He climbed up the ladder and sat on the slide. He said, "Ready, set, go!" But he did not slide. He slipped. He slipped off the slide and fell on the grass. He cried.

Lily ran to him. She said, "Are you okay, Tom?" She helped him stand up. She looked at his knee. It was red and had a small cut. She said, "You have a boo-boo. It will be better in a minute. Do you want a hug?"

Tom nodded. He hugged Lily. He said, "Thank you, Lily. You are a good friend. You are very attractive." He smiled.

Lily smiled too. She said, "You are welcome, Tom. You are a good friend too. You are very attractive." They hugged again. Then they went to play on the swings. They were happy.

Once upon a time, there was a big, hairy kid named Max. Max had a pet dog named Spot. One day, Max and Spot went for a walk in the park. 

Max saw a group of kids playing and he wanted to join them. He asked, "Can I play with you guys?" 

One of the kids said, "Sure! Do you want to lead the game?" 

Max was happy and said, "Yes, I want to lead!" 

So, Max led the game and they all had fun playing together. Spot even joined in the game and the kids laughed at how silly he looked. After the game, Max said goodbye to his new friends and went home with Spot. 

From that day on, Max would often go to the park and play with his new friends. He was no longer a lonely kid and he was happy to have people to play with.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Johnny. Johnny wanted to go outside and play with his friends, but his mom wouldn't permit it. 

Johnny became very angry and he started to yell. He stomped his feet and said, "Mom, why can't I go outside and play?" His mom calmly replied, "Johnny, it's not safe, so I can't permit it." 

Johnny replied angrily, "I want to go outside, I'm sick of staying in!" His mom said, "Please don't be angry, Johnny. I'll get you some jelly, okay?" 

Johnny smiled, and said, "Okay, mom. I can wait." His mom smiled back, and gave Johnny a big bowl of jelly. "There you go, Johnny. Now, why don't you have some fun right here with me?" 

Johnny smiled and nodded. He enjoyed spending time with his mom, even if he couldn't go outside. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a bossy cat named Mittens. Mittens liked to tell everyone what to do. She meowed loudly and always wanted things her way. One day, Mittens saw a little mouse scurrying by. She thought to herself, "I want to catch that mouse!"

Mittens waited patiently for the mouse to come closer. She pounced, but the mouse was too quick and ran away. Mittens was disappointed. She tried again and again, but the mouse always got away.

One day, Mittens saw the mouse again. This time, she didn't try to catch it. Instead, she meowed softly and said, "Hello little mouse. Do you want to be friends?" The mouse was surprised but happy to have a new friend. Mittens learned that being bossy doesn't always work, and sometimes it's better to be kind.

Once upon a time, there was a funny cat named Tom. Tom loved to play with his friend, a little girl named Sue. Yesterday, they played with a big red ball in the yard.

"Do you remember when we played with the ball yesterday?" Tom asked Sue. "Yes, I remember!" Sue said with a big smile. They laughed and remembered how much fun they had together.

Today, Tom and Sue played with a toy car. They pushed it back and forth, having so much fun. They knew they would remember this day too, just like yesterday. And they lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time, there was an octopus who wanted to play a game. He asked his fish friends, "Who wants to play a game with me?" An eager fish agreed to play, and the octopus said, "Let's play a game of twist!"

The octopus and the fish began trying to twist. The fish quickly managed to twist his body into a tight knot, and the octopus couldn't help but laugh. He said to his friend, "You managed to twist yourself so quickly, it's fair!"

The octopus tried his best to twist and twist, but he just couldn't do it. He soon realized that it was too difficult for him to twist. He sighed and said, "I don't think I am able to twist like you do." 

The fish said, "That's OK. Let's go and explore instead. Maybe we'll find something else fun to do!" 

The octopus smiled and the two went off on an adventure. They had lots of fun exploring the underwater world and found many exciting things to do. 

In the end, even though the octopus couldn't twist like his fish friend, he still had a fair share of fun.

Once upon a time, there was a powerful man named Bob. He liked to sell apples. One day, he went to the market with a big bag of apples.

At the market, he met a little girl named Sue. Sue said, "Hi, Bob! Can I have an apple, please?" Bob said, "Yes, you can have one apple, but you have to give me one coin." Sue gave Bob one coin and took an apple.

Bob was not a nice man. He wanted more coins. So, he took the apple back from Sue and said, "No, you need to give me two more coins." Sue was sad and gave him two more coins. She took the apple and went home.

But, the apple was bad. It made Sue feel sick. Her mom and dad were angry at Bob. They went to the market and told everyone that Bob's apples were bad. No one wanted to buy apples from Bob anymore.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He loved to play and run around in his backyard. One day, he saw a butterfly and wanted to catch it. He ran after it and chased it all around the yard. But the butterfly was too fast and Timmy struggled to catch it.

Later that day, Timmy's mom asked him to go upstairs to get his pajamas. But Timmy didn't want to go upstairs because he was scared of the dark. He struggled to find the courage to go up the stairs. Finally, he took a deep breath and went upstairs.

That night, Timmy had a lively dream about catching the butterfly. He felt so happy and proud of himself. The next day, he woke up feeling brave and ready to face his fears. He went outside and saw the butterfly again. This time, he didn't struggle to catch it. He caught it and set it free, feeling proud of himself once again.

name_of_work: Man Listening to Disc by Billy Collins
content: This is not bad -- ambling along 44th Street with Sonny Rollins for company, his music flowing through the soft calipers of these earphones, as if he were right beside me on this clear day in March, the pavement sparkling with sunlight, pigeons fluttering off the curb, nodding over a profusion of bread crumbs. In fact, I would say my delight at being suffused with phrases from his saxophone -- some like honey, some like vinegar -- is surpassed only by my gratitude to Tommy Potter for taking the time to join us on this breezy afternoon with his most unwieldy bass and to the esteemed Arthur Taylor who is somehow managing to navigate this crowd with his cumbersome drums. And I bow deeply to Thelonious Monk for figuring out a way to motorize -- or whatever -- his huge piano so he could be with us today. This music is loud yet so confidential. I cannot help feeling even more like the center of the universe than usual as I walk along to a rapid little version of "The Way You Look Tonight," and all I can say to my fellow pedestrians, to the woman in the white sweater, the man in the tan raincoat and the heavy glasses, who mistake themselves for the center of the universe -- all I can say is watch your step, because the five of us, instruments and all, are about to angle over to the south side of the street and then, in our own tightly knit way, turn the corner at Sixth Avenue. And if any of you are curious about where this aggregation, this whole battery-powered crew, is headed, let us just say that the real center of the universe, the only true point of view, is full of hope that he, the hub of the cosmos with his hair blown sideways, will eventually make it all the way downtown.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved going to the beach with her family. One day, Lily saw a big wave coming towards her. She got scared and ran to her mommy. 

Mommy hugged her and said, "Don't worry, Lily. The wave is far away. Look at the pink sky, it's so pretty!" 

Lily looked up and saw the sky turning pink. She smiled and felt happy. When it was time to go home, Lily helped her daddy close the car door. She was a big helper!

name_of_work: A Word to Husbands by Ogden Nash
content: To keep your marriage brimming With love in the loving cup, Whenever you're wrong, admit it; Whenever you're right, shut up.

Lily and Tom were friends. They liked to play in the woods. They had a hut made of sticks and leaves. They had fun in the hut.

One day, a big boy came to the woods. He saw the hut. He wanted the hut. He said, "This is my hut now. Go away!"

Lily and Tom were sad and angry. They said, "No, this is our hut. We made it. You go away!"

The big boy laughed. He said, "You can't stop me. Your hut is dirty and weak. I will break it and make a better hut."

He kicked the hut. The sticks and leaves fell down. Lily and Tom cried. They ran away.

But the big boy did not know. The hut had a secret. The hut had a bee nest inside. The bees were angry. They came out of the nest. They buzzed and stung the big boy. He screamed and ran away.

Lily and Tom came back. They saw the big boy running. They saw the bees flying. They saw the hut broken. They smiled. They said, "The hut was not dirty and weak. The hut was smart and strong. The hut had a surprise for the big boy. The hut saved us."

They hugged the hut. They fixed the hut. They played in the hut. They were happy.

One day, a big boat was near the beach. The boat had a big anchor. A little fish saw the anchor and was scared. The fish swam away fast.

The fish found a crab and said, "I saw a big thing that scared me!" The crab said, "Let's go see it together." So, the fish and the crab went to see the anchor.

When they saw the anchor, the crab said, "Don't be scared. It's just an anchor. It helps the boat stay in one place." The fish felt guilty for being scared. The fish and the crab swam away and played together, happy and not scared anymore.

Once upon a time, there was a small girl called Lucy. Every day she admired the beautiful sunsets from her bedroom window. One night, she realised that she was very hungry and asked her mom for dinner. 

Her mom smiled and said "Yes, I've made you something special". Lucy followed her mom to the kitchen and saw a small dinner on the table. It was macaroni and cheese, with some fruit. As soon as Lucy saw it, she admired the meal.

She asked her mom if she could have the dinner, so her mom made her a plate. And even though the dinner was small, it was enough to satisfy Lucy's hunger. She thanked her mom and ate the dinner right away. 

Afterwards, Lucy was full and snuggled up in bed for a long nap. The small dinner was just enough to make her feel content.

Once upon a time, there was a big storm. The wind was very strong and it made a mighty tornado. The tornado spun around and around, knocking down trees and houses. The people were scared and they ran to hide in their basements. 

After the storm was over, the people came out to see the damage. The houses were destroyed, and the trees were all knocked down. The people were sad because they lost their homes. 

But there was one person who was happy. He was a printer, and he had printed lots of flyers about fixing the houses. He thought he would make lots of money from the people who needed help. But the people were too sad and didn't have any money to pay him. So, the printer didn't make any money, and he was sad too.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy had a big sack that he liked to carry around with him. It was his favorite thing in the world. He would put all sorts of things in it like toys and snacks.

One day, Timmy met a man who said he would take care of his sack for him. The man seemed nice and reliable, so Timmy gave him his sack. But then the man ran away with Timmy's sack and Timmy never saw it again.

Timmy was very sad and cried a lot. His mom asked him what was wrong and he told her about the man who took his sack. His mom hugged him and said, "I'm sorry Timmy, but sometimes bad things happen and we can't always get our things back." The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little fish named Nemo. Nemo lived in a big ocean with his friends. One day, Nemo's friend, Dory, asked him if he wanted to dive with her to find some treasure. Nemo was nervous, but he wanted to be brave and said yes.

As they were swimming, they saw a big bubble of gas coming up from the bottom of the ocean. They followed it and found a sunken ship with a treasure chest inside. Dory and Nemo were so excited!

But then, they saw a big shark coming towards them. Nemo wanted to swim away, but Dory said, "Don't be scared, let's just share the treasure with the shark." And so, they shared the treasure with the shark and all became friends.

The moral of the story is that even when you're nervous, you can still be brave and make new friends by sharing.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Joe. Joe was three years old and he loved to explore his neighbourhood.

One day, he decided to explore further than ever before. He walked and walked until he came across something big and interesting - a tank! Joe was really proud of himself for finding it.

When Joe got closer, he noticed someone inside the tank. It was a soldier! Joe was a little scared, so he stayed a few steps back.

Joe shouted out: "Hello?". 

The soldier smiled and said "Hello! I'm glad you found me! I'm looking for someone to help me repair this tank. Do you think you can help me?". 

Joe was very proud. He smiled and said "Yes, I can help!"

The tank was fixed in no time. The soldier thanked Joe, and they both went off on their way.

Joe was happy and proud. He had helped a soldier and he had found something special.

Once upon a time there was a scared little boy. He had on his favourite sunglasses and was walking along in the park. Suddenly, he heard a loud noise and was frightened. He quickly ran away and tried to count to ten to feel better. 

He started counting but felt too scared to keep going. He knew he needed help. Then, out of nowhere, a nice lady appeared. The lady put her arm around him and said, "Don't be afraid. I'm here to help and I will count with you." 

The boy smiled and the lady began to count. As they counted together, the boy stopped feeling so scared and began to relax. When they reached ten, the lady smiled. "See," she said, "you're not so scared anymore. Now you can go back to exploring the park with your sunglasses." 

The boy thanked the lady and waved goodbye. He put his sunglasses back on, feeling less frightened. He continued exploring the park, never forgetting the kind lady who helped him count to ten.

Written on the banks of the Arun, Oct. 1785. WHEN latest Autumn spreads her evening veil, And the grey mists from these dim waves arise, I love to listen to the hollow sighs, Through the half-leafless wood that breathes the gale: For at such hours the shadowy phantom, pale, Oft seems to fleet before the poet's eyes; Strange sounds are heard, and mournful melodies, As of night wanderers, who their woes bewail Here, by his native stream, at such an hour, Pity's own Otway I methinks could meet, And hear his deep sighs swell the sadden'd wind! O Melancholy!--such thy magic power, That to the soul these dreams are often sweet, And sooth the pensive visionary mind!

Since Christmas they have lived with us, Guileless and clear, Oval soul-animals, Taking up half the space, Moving and rubbing on the silk Invisible air drifts, Giving a shriek and pop When attacked, then scooting to rest, barely trembling. Yellow cathead, blue fish-------- Such queer moons we live with Instead of dead furniture! Straw mats, white walls And these traveling Globes of thin air, red, green, Delighting The heart like wishes or free Peacocks blessing Old ground with a feather Beaten in starry metals. Your small Brother is making His balloon squeak like a cat. Seeming to see A funny pink world he might eat on the other side of it, He bites, Then sits Back, fat jug Contemplating a world clear as water. A red Shred in his little fist. 5 February 1963

Once upon a time, there was a bossy cat named Tom. Tom liked to tell everyone what to do. One day, he met a little dog named Max. Max was playing with his toy car. The car could go fast and reverse.

"Max, let me play with your car!" Tom said in a bossy way. Max did not like how Tom talked to him, but he shared his toy car.

"Look, Max! I can make the car go fast and reverse!" Tom said as he played with the car. Max watched Tom play and said, "You have to be nice to play with my car."

Tom thought about what Max said. He did not want to be bossy anymore. He gave the car back to Max and said, "I'm sorry for being bossy. Can we play together?"

Max smiled and said, "Yes, we can play together!" They played with the toy car, taking turns to make it go fast and reverse. They laughed and had fun. From that day on, Tom was not bossy anymore, and they became good friends.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Daisy. Daisy wanted to go on an adventure. So she set off to discover something new.

On her journey, Daisy saw a tall building. She saw a sign outside the building that said 'The Hospital'. Daisy was curious, so she decided to go inside.

When she entered the hospital, Daisy saw a kind nurse. She went up to the nurse and asked, "What is this place?". The nurse replied, "This is where the doctors and nurses help people who are ill or hurt".

She wanted a new haircut. But it was still winter.

Lily and Max were playing with their toys in the living room. Lily had a big doll and Max had a small car. Lily liked to be the boss and tell Max what to do.

"Max, you have to make your car go fast and crash into the wall. That's fun!" Lily said.

Max did not like that. He liked to make his car go slow and careful. He did not want to break his car.

"No, Lily. I don't want to do that. I want to play my way." Max said.

Lily frowned. She did not like it when Max said no to her. She tried to grab his car from his hand.

"Give me your car, Max. You are playing wrong. I will show you how to play right." Lily said.

Max held on to his car. He did not want to give it to Lily. He was angry.

"Let go of my car, Lily. It's mine. You are being bossy. I don't like you." Max said.

Lily and Max pulled and tugged on the car. They both wanted to have it. They did not see that their mom was watching them from the kitchen.

"Hey, kids. What are you doing?" Mom asked.

Lily and Max stopped pulling. They looked at mom. They did not know what to say.

Mom came to the living room. She saw the car in their hands. She saw the doll on the floor. She saw the spot on the wall where the car had hit it.

"Kids, you are making a mess. And you are not sharing. That's not nice. Why are you fighting over the car?" Mom asked.

Lily and Max shrugged. They did not have a good answer. They felt bad.

Mom smiled. She had an idea.

"Why don't you trade toys for a while? Lily, you can play with the car. Max, you can play with the doll. Maybe you will find a new way to have fun. And maybe you will learn to be kind to each other." Mom said.

Lily and Max looked at each other. They looked at the toys. They were not sure.

"Can we try?" Lily asked.

"Sure, you can try. But you have to be gentle and respectful. And you have to say please and thank you." Mom said.

Lily and Max nodded. They gave each other their toys. They said please and thank you. They started to play with the new toys. They were curious and careful. They did not fight. They did not be bossy. They had fun.

Mom was happy. She watched them play. She was proud of them. She gave them a hug and a kiss. She said she loved them. Lily and Max smiled. They said they loved her too. They were happy.

Sara and Tom went to the park with Mom. They saw many birds near the pond. Sara liked the ducks. Tom liked the geese. He wanted to feed them some bread.

"Look, Mom, a big goose!" Tom said. He ran to the pond with a piece of bread in his hand.

name_of_work: Song of Autumn by Mary Oliver
content: Don't you imagine the leaves dream now how comfortable it will be to touch the earth instead of the nothingness of the air and the endless freshets of wind? And don't you think the trees, especially those with mossy hollows, are beginning to look for the fires that will come--six, a dozen--to sleep inside their bodies? And don't you hear the goldenrod whispering goodbye, the everlasting being crowned with the first tuffets of snow? The pond stiffens and the white field over which the fox runs so quickly brings out its long blue shadows. The wind wags its many tails. And in the evening the piled firewood shifts a little, longing to be on its way

These are outsiders, always. These stars-- these iron inklings of an Irish January, whose light happened thousands of years before our pain did; they are, they have always been outside history. They keep their distance. Under them remains a place where you found you were human, and a landscape in which you know you are mortal. And a time to choose between them. I have chosen: out of myth in history I move to be part of that ordeal who darkness is only now reaching me from those fields, those rivers, those roads clotted as firmaments with the dead. How slowly they die as we kneel beside them, whisper in their ear. And we are too late. We are always too late.

You might forget the exact sound of her voice Or how her face looked when sleeping. You might forget the sound of her quiet weeping Curled into the shape of a half moon, When smaller than her self, she seemed already to be leaving Before she left, when the blossom was on the trees And the sun was out, and all seemed good in the world. I held her hand and sang a song from when I was a girl - Heil Ya Ho Boys, Let her go Boys And when I stopped singing she had slipped away, Already a slip of a girl again, skipping off, Her heart light, her face almost smiling. And what I didn't know, or couldn't see then, Was that she hadn't really gone. The dead don't go till you do, loved ones. The dead are still here holding our hands.

All night the sound had come back again, and again falls this quiet, persistent rain. What am I to myself that must be remembered, insisted upon so often? Is it that never the ease, even the hardness, of rain falling will have for me something other than this, something not so insistent-- am I to be locked in this final uneasiness. Love, if you love me, lie next to me. Be for me, like rain, the getting out of the tiredness, the fatuousness, the semi- lust of intentional indifference. Be wet with a decent happiness.

There is a silence where hath been no sound, There is a silence where no sound may be, In the cold grave--under the deep deep sea, Or in the wide desert where no life is found, Which hath been mute, and still must sleep profound; No voice is hush'd--no life treads silently, But clouds and cloudy shadows wander free, That never spoke, over the idle ground: But in green ruins, in the desolate walls Of antique palaces, where Man hath been, Though the dun fox, or wild hyena, calls, And owls, that flit continually between, Shriek to the echo, and the low winds moan, There the true Silence is, self-conscious and alone.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with yarn. She had a big ball of yarn that she would roll around and around. One day, Lily's mom noticed that the yarn was all gone. "Lily, where did all the yarn go?" her mom asked. "I used it to make a blanket for my doll," Lily replied. 

Her mom smiled and said, "That's so creative of you, Lily. But you need to ask me before using all the yarn." Lily nodded and promised to ask next time. 

The next day, Lily was playing outside when it started to rain. She ran inside and noticed that her clothes were all wet. "Mom, my clothes are wet!" she exclaimed. Her mom replied, "Don't worry, we'll hang them up to dry." 

Lily watched as her mom hung up her clothes on a clothesline. She noticed that the sun was coming out and soon her clothes would be dry. "Look, Mom! My clothes are dry now!" Lily said happily. Her mom smiled and replied, "Yes, they are. Now let's go make some more things with yarn."

"Once upon a time, there was a loyal cat named Samson. He lived in a small house near the ocean. Every day, Samson would watch the sailors pass by on their big boats.

One day, Samson noticed that one of the boats was having an emergency. The sailor on the boat was shooting a rope from the ship to the beach. Samson understood that he had to help the sailor, so he sprinted to the beach and grabbed the rope. 

The sailor was able to tie the rope to an anchor at the shore. The sailor was so grateful to Samson that he rewarded the cat with a large fish. Samson was happy to have helped the sailor, and he looked forward to helping more sailors in the future.

The next day, Samson noticed a powerful storm brewing in the sky. He knew the boats were in danger and, without hesitating, he ran to the beach. Once he got there, he saw many boats with ropes in danger of being washed away by the stormy winds.

Samson quickly grabbed all of the ropes and used them to anchor the boats. He worked quickly and used all of his strength to help secure the boats. Soon, the boats were secure and the sailors were safe.

Samson's loyalty and courage had saved the day. From that day onward, he became known as the hero of the waters."

Nautilus Island's hermit heiress still lives through winter in her Spartan cottage; her sheep still graze above the sea. Her son's a bishop. Her farmer is first selectman in our village; she's in her dotage. Thirsting for the hierarchic privacy of Queen Victoria's century, she buys up all the eyesores facing her shore, and lets them fall. The only legend I have ever loved is the story of a daughter lost in hell. And found and rescued there. Love and blackmail are the gist of it. Ceres and Persephone the names. And the best thing about the legend is I can enter it anywhere. And have. As a child in exile in a city of fogs and strange consonants, I read it first and at first I was an exiled child in the crackling dusk of the underworld, the stars blighted. Later I walked out in a summer twilight searching for my daughter at bed-time. When she came running I was ready to make any bargain to keep her. I carried her back past whitebeams and wasps and honey-scented buddleias. But I was Ceres then and I knew winter was in store for every leaf on every tree on that road. Was inescapable for each one we passed. And for me. It is winter and the stars are hidden. I climb the stairs and stand where I can see my child asleep beside her teen magazines, her can of Coke, her plate of uncut fruit. The pomegranate! How did I forget it? She could have come home and been safe and ended the story and all our heart-broken searching but she reached out a hand and plucked a pomegranate. She put out her hand and pulled down the French sound for apple and the noise of stone and the proof that even in the place of death, at the heart of legend, in the midst of rocks full of unshed tears ready to be diamonds by the time the story was told, a child can be hungry. I could warn her. There is still a chance. The rain is cold. The road is flint-coloured. The suburb has cars and cable television. The veiled stars are above ground. It is another world. But what else can a mother give her daughter but such beautiful rifts in time? If I defer the grief I will diminish the gift. The legend will be hers as well as mine. She will enter it. As I have. She will wake up. She will hold the papery flushed skin in her hand. And to her lips. I will say nothing.

It's ripe, the melon by our sink. Yellow, bee-bitten, soft, it perfumes the house too sweetly. At five I wake, the air mournful in its quiet. My wife's eyes swim calmly under their lids, her mouth and jaw relaxed, different. What is happening in the silence of this house? Curtains hang heavily from their rods. Ficus leaves tremble at my footsteps. Yet the colors outside are perfect-- orange geranium, blue lobelia. I wander from room to room like a man in a museum: wife, children, books, flowers, melon. Such still air. Soon the mid-morning breeze will float in like tepid water, then hot. How do I start this day, I who am unsure of how my life has happened or how to proceed amid this warm and steady sweetness?

name_of_work: On Another's Sorrow by William Blake
content: Can I see another's woe, And not be in sorrow too? Can I see another's grief, And not seek for kind relief? Can I see a falling tear, And not feel my sorrow's share? Can a father see his child Weep, nor be with sorrow filled? Can a mother sit and hear An infant groan, an infant fear? No, no! never can it be! Never, never can it be! And can He who smiles on all Hear the wren with sorrows small, Hear the small bird's grief and care, Hear the woes that infants bear - And not sit beside the nest, Pouring pity in their breast, And not sit the cradle near, Weeping tear on infant's tear? And not sit both night and day, Wiping all our tears away? O no! never can it be! Never, never can it be! He doth give His joy to all: He becomes an infant small, He becomes a man of woe, He doth feel the sorrow too. Think not thou canst sigh a sigh, And thy Maker is not by: Think not thou canst weep a tear, And thy Maker is not near. O He gives to us His joy, That our grief He may destroy: Till our grief is fled and gone He doth sit by us and moan. Can I see another's woe, And not be in sorrow too? I'll tell you why. To survive the onslaught of religion. To outlive the ghosts of martyrs. To recover from the world's longest war since WWII. To live beyond the hatreds of patriotism. To see the kinder face of humanity. To think free of the Faith's manacles. To believe without the obligation of forming belief. To discover the basic joys of being. The price? I'll tell you. Evaporation. Marginalised to the point of disappearance. Barred for nothing more profound than a shade of skin, a tone of speech, a taste of lifestyle. Alienated beyond the word. Ignored by the mighty. Detested by the commoner. Worth it? Doubtless. To finally grasp humanity's fraudulent truth. To dream the sweetness of equality. To see past the facade of brotherhood. To be touched you might say, by the rays of a luminous discovery. To abandon all faith, and come to cherish the immense solitude of non-believing. To desire. To know the power of desire. To wait joyfully amid unpalatable sadness. Recommend it? Only to loathsome enemies and to my dearest friends.

Once upon a time, there was a little bunny named Benny. He loved to hop around and play with his friends. One day, Benny found a shiny piece of jewelry on the ground. He thought it was pretty and decided to wear it around his neck.

Benny's friend, a wise old owl, saw the jewelry and told Benny it might be uncomfortable to wear. But Benny didn't listen and kept wearing it anyway.

One day, while Benny was hopping through the forest, a sneaky fox saw the shiny jewelry and decided to steal it. Benny tried to hop away, but the fox was too fast. Benny was very sad that he lost his pretty jewelry.

Benny went to his wise old friend and told him what happened. The owl said, "I told you it might be uncomfortable to wear. Now you have learned a lesson to be careful with shiny things." Benny nodded his head sadly and went home, feeling sad that he lost his jewelry.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to eat tuna sandwiches for lunch. Her mom made her a great sandwich every day.

One day, Lily went to the park with her mom. She played on the swings and the slide. But then it started to rain. Lily and her mom ran to a nearby tree to stay dry.

Lily was sad and cried. She asked her mom, "Why did this happen?" Her mom said, "I don't know, but we still have each other." They hugged each other and tried to stay positive, even though they were wet and had no place to go.
