Sara was restless. She did not want to nap. She wanted to play. She got out of her bed and went to the door. She opened it and saw the hall. She saw the kitchen. She saw Mom.

Sara moved to the kitchen. She wanted to see what Mom was doing. Mom was making a cake. Sara liked cake. She wanted to help. She climbed on a chair and reached for a bowl. Mom saw her and said, "No, Sara, that is hot. You can get hurt. Go back to your room and nap."

Sara was sad. She did not want to nap. She wanted to help. She moved the bowl anyway. The bowl was hot. It burned her hand. She dropped the bowl. The bowl broke. The cake mix spilled. Sara cried. Mom came and hugged her. She said, "I'm sorry, Sara, you are hurt. Let me see your hand. It is red. I will put some ice on it. It will feel better soon."

Mom took Sara to the couch. She put some ice on her hand. She gave her a kiss. She said, "Sara, I know you are restless. But you have to listen to me. I am trying to keep you safe. You can help me later. But now you need to rest. Do you want to read a book with me?" Sara nodded. She liked books. She snuggled with Mom and read a book. She felt sleepy. She closed her eyes. She napped.

Lily wanted to make her friend feel happy too, so she tried to come up with an original joke of her own. She thought and thought, but nothing seemed funny enough. One day, Sam was out in the sea with his dad. They had a reliable boat and were looking for a reef. Suddenly, Sam spotted something colourful and bright on the reef and he shouted "Reverse!"

Her mom was very surprised when she saw her daughter cooking by herself. She watched over her daughter, giving her tips to make it better.

Ben and Lily were best friends. They liked to play in the park every day. One day, they saw a big, hairy dog. The dog was friendly and wagged its tail. Ben and Lily wanted to pet the dog, but they were a little scared.

"Can we touch the dog?" Ben asked Lily.

"I don't know. Maybe we should ask the owner first," Lily said.

They looked around and saw a man sitting on a bench. He was reading a book and did not notice the dog or the children.

"Excuse me, sir. Is this your dog?" Lily called out.

The man looked up and smiled. "Yes, this is Max. He is very nice and loves to play. Do you want to pet him?"

"Yes, please!" Ben and Lily said.

They ran to the dog and started to stroke his fur. Max licked their faces and wagged his tail harder. Ben and Lily laughed and hugged the dog.

"Thank you for letting us pet your dog. He is very soft and warm," Lily said.

"You're welcome. I'm glad you like him. He is a good dog, but he needs a lot of care. He needs to eat, drink, walk, and brush every day. Do you know how to care for a dog?" the man asked.

Ben and Lily nodded. They had learned about animals at school. They knew that dogs were like people. They needed love and attention.

"We know how to care for a dog. We would give him food and water, take him for walks, and brush his fur. We would also play with him and cuddle him. We would be good friends," Ben said.

"That's wonderful. You sound like very kind and responsible children. Do you have a dog of your own?" the man asked.

Ben and Lily shook their heads. They did not have a dog. They lived in a small apartment with their parents. They did not have enough space or money for a dog.

"We wish we had a dog. We love dogs. But we can't have one. Maybe when we grow up," Lily said.

The man looked at them with a twinkle in his eye. He had an idea. He closed his book and stood up.

"Well, I have a surprise for you. I am moving to another city next week. I can't take Max with me. He is too big and hairy for the plane. I have been looking for a new home for him. Do you think your parents would let you have him?" he asked.

Ben and Lily gasped. They could not believe their ears. They looked at each other and then at the dog. They wanted to say yes, but they were not sure.

"We don't know. We have to ask them first. They might say no. We don't have a lot of room or money," Ben said.

The man nodded. He understood. He did not want to pressure them. He wanted them to be happy.

"I see. Well, why don't you go home and talk to them? Here is my phone number. You can call me tomorrow and let me know what they say. If they say yes, you can have Max. He is yours. If they say no, I will find another home for him. But I hope they say yes. You are the best friends he could have," he said.

He handed them a piece of paper with his number. He also gave them a leash and a collar for Max. He hugged them and kissed the dog.

"Goodbye, Max. I love you. Be good to your new friends. They will take good care of you," he said.

He walked away, waving and smiling. Ben and Lily waved back, holding the leash and the collar. They looked at Max. He looked at them. They felt a warm feeling in their hearts. They hoped their parents would say yes. They wanted to care for Max. They wanted to be his family. They ran home, excited and nervous. They had a big question to ask. They had a big, hairy dog to love.

Sam and Lily liked to play music. They had a band with their toys. Sam played the drum and Lily played the flute. They made loud and happy sounds.

One day, they wanted to fill their room with music. They played and played for a long time. They sang and danced with their toys. They had a lot of fun.

But soon, they started to feel tired. Their arms and legs were sore. Their mouths were dry. Their ears were ringing. They stopped playing and looked at each other.

"Are you tired, Sam?" Lily asked.

"Yes, I am tired, Lily. Are you tired, too?" Sam answered.

"Yes, I am very tired. Let's take a break," Lily said.

They put down their instruments and toys. They drank some water and ate some cookies. They lay down on their bed and cuddled. They closed their eyes and listened to the quiet.

They felt happy and sleepy. They filled their room with music and love. They fell asleep and dreamed of more songs.

Once there was a man who did lots of bad things. He did not listen to other people or be kind. One day, he did something so very wrong that he had to go to jail. The jail was very high and he could not get out.

The man stayed in the high jail for a long time. He was sad and he wanted to be with his family. But he still had to stay in jail and the guards did not let him out.

The man promised himself that when he got out of jail, he would do better things. He would be kind to other people and listen to what they said.

Finally, after a long time, the man was allowed to leave the high jail. He was so happy! He said goodbye to the guards and promised them he would never do bad things again. 

The man kept his promise and he was never sent to jail again. He did nice things and he was very happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He loved to play outside and climb trees. One day, he saw a very tall tree with tough bark. 

Timmy: "Wow, that tree looks tough! Can I climb it?"

Tree: "Yes, you can climb me, but be careful!"

Timmy started to climb the tree, but suddenly something happened. A strong wind blew and Timmy lost his balance. He fell down and hurt his arm.

Timmy: "Ouch! What happened?"

Tree: "The wind happened. I'm sorry you got hurt. Let me give you a hug."

The tree wrapped its branches around Timmy and he felt better. From that day on, Timmy and the tree became good friends and Timmy never forgot to be careful when climbing tough trees.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. Lily liked to go to the park and play with her friends. One day, her mommy told her that she had to go to a special talk called a "lecture." Lily did not know what a lecture was, but she wanted to be a good girl and listen.

At the lecture, there was a man talking about being "flexible." Lily thought that being flexible was like when she could touch her toes. The man said, "Being flexible is good. It helps us do many things." Lily liked the idea of being flexible.

After the lecture, Lily went home and told her mommy about it. She said, "Mommy, I want to be flexible like the man said. Then I can play more games with my friends." Her mommy smiled and said, "That's a great idea, Lily. Being flexible will help you a lot in life." And from that day on, Lily tried her best to be flexible in everything she did.

Once upon a time, there was a purple bulb who loved to scatter. He would jump high into the air and then throw his petals every which way. The petals from the purple bulb twirled and danced, filling the air with color. Everyone who saw him was filled with joy.

One day, the purple bulb felt a strong wind. He held on tight and the wind scattered him even further! He flew over farms and streets, until the wind finally stopped. 

When the purple bulb landed, he was in a big, green garden. He was excited to discover he was surrounded by so many different colored bulbs - yellow, pink and blue. 

The purple bulb was so happy to be in such a beautiful place. He scattered his petals with even more enthusiasm and joy. From that day on, the purple bulb and his friends scattered together, filling the garden with life and love.

Once upon a time, there was a loyal swan. It sailed across a sunny sky. Everywhere it went, it saw happy faces.

The swan sailed on a lake. It was so calm and quiet. It swam around, feeling so peaceful.

Suddenly, a big, bright rainbow appeared! It shone like a million diamonds. The swan sailed closer to the rainbow and then sat down. It was so beautiful.

The swan stayed there, at the foot of the rainbow, until the sun went down. It was so happy and loyal.

The end.

A young spring-tender girl combed her joyous hair 'You are very ugly' said the mirror. But, on her lips hung a smile of dove-secret loveliness, for only that morning had not the blind boy said, 'You are beautiful'?

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to play in the park. One day, they saw a big slide that looked very fun. They ran to the slide and waited for their turn. Tom went first and slid down very fast. He laughed and shouted, "This is so fun!"

Lily wanted to try too, but she was a little scared. She climbed up the ladder slowly and looked down. The slide was very high and shiny. She held on to the sides and pushed herself forward. But she did not slide very well. She slipped and bumped her head on the slide. She cried and felt pain.

Tom heard Lily cry and ran to her. He hugged her and said, "Are you okay, Lily?" Lily nodded and wiped her tears. She said, "I'm okay, Tom. But I don't like the slide. It's too slippery and hard."

Tom said, "I'm sorry, Lily. I didn't know you would slip. Do you want to play something else?" Lily said, "Yes, please. Let's play on the swings. They are more fun and soft."

Tom and Lily went to the swings and pushed each other. They smiled and forgot about the slide. They had a good time and made a happy memory. They did not know that the slide was very expensive and new. They only knew that they liked to play together.

Jill and Ben are playing with blocks. They like to make towers and houses and cars. They have many blocks of different colors and shapes. They try to make a pattern with the blocks. A pattern is when you put the same things in a row or a circle or a square.

"Look, Jill, I made a pattern with the red and blue blocks. Red, blue, red, blue, red, blue. Do you like it?" Ben says.

"Yes, Ben, I like it. It is very pretty. Can I make a pattern with the yellow and green blocks?" Jill says.

"Sure, Jill, you can make a pattern with the yellow and green blocks. Yellow, green, yellow, green, yellow, green. Let's see who can make the longest pattern." Ben says.

They start to make their patterns on the floor. They are having fun. They do not hear the door open. They do not see the big dog come in. The big dog is hungry. He sees the blocks. He thinks they are food. He runs to the blocks. He starts to bite them and chew them and throw them. He makes a big mess.

Jill and Ben are fearful. They do not like the big dog. They do not want him to eat their blocks. They do not want him to hurt them. They scream. They scream very loud.

"Help! Help! Go away, big dog! Leave our blocks alone!" Jill and Ben scream.

Mom hears them scream. She runs to the room. She sees the big dog. She sees the blocks. She sees Jill and Ben. She is angry. She is scared. She grabs a broom. She chases the big dog away. She hugs Jill and Ben. She calms them down.

"I'm sorry, Jill and Ben. I did not know the big dog was here. He is a bad dog. He should not come in our house. He should not eat your blocks. He should not make you scream. Are you okay?" Mom says.

"Yes, Mom, we are okay. Thank you for saving us. Thank you for chasing the big dog away. We do not like the big dog. We like our blocks. We like our patterns. Can we play with them again?" Jill and Ben say.

"Of course, Jill and Ben. You can play with your blocks again. But first, let's clean up the mess. Let's put the blocks back in the box. Let's find the blocks that the big dog did not eat. Let's make new patterns. And let's close the door. We do not want the big dog to come back." Mom says.

Jill and Ben nod. They help Mom clean up the mess. They put the blocks back in the box. They find the blocks that the big dog did not eat. They make new patterns. They close the door. They are happy. They are safe. They do not scream. They smile.

The Farrand Chapelette was gathering dust in the shadowy porch of Marsden Church. And was due to be bundled off to the skip. Or was mine, for a song, if I wanted it. Sunlight, through stained glass, which day to day could beatify saints and raise the dead, had aged the harmonium's softwood case and yellowed the fingernails of its keys. And one of its notes had lost its tongue, and holes were worn in both the treadles where the organist's feet, in grey, woollen socks and leather-soled shoes, had pedalled and pedalled. But its hummed harmonics still struck a chord: for a hundred years that organ had stood by the choristers' stalls, where father and son, each in their time, had opened their throats and gilded finches - like high notes - had streamed out. Through his own blue cloud of tobacco smog, with smoker's fingers and dottled thumbs, he comes to help me cart it away. And we carry it flat, laid on its back. And he, being him, can't help but say that the next box I'll shoulder through this nave will bear the freight of his own dead weight. And I, being me, then mouth in reply some shallow or sorry phrase or word too starved of breath to make itself heard.

Louder than gulls the little children scream Whom fathers haul into the jovial foam; But others fearlessly rush in, breast high, Laughing the salty water from their mouthes-- Heroes of the nursery. The horny boatman, who has seen whales And flying fishes, who has sailed as far As Demerara and the Ivory Coast, Will warn them, when they crowd to hear his tales, That every ocean smells of tar.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her mommy's sewing kit. One day, she found a long thread on the floor. She picked it up and held it in her hand. It was a pretty blue thread.

Lily decided to lean over and put the thread through the eye of the needle. But the needle was hot! She quickly dropped it and learned a lesson. From then on, she always checked if the needle was hot before touching it. 

Lily was proud of herself for being careful and learned that it's important to be safe when playing with mommy's sewing kit.

name_of_work: A Quoi Bon Dire by Charlotte Mew
content: Seventeen years ago you said Something that sounded like Good-bye; And everybody thinks that you are dead, But I. So I, as I grow stiff and cold To this and that say Good-bye too; And everybody sees that I am old But you. And one fine morning in a sunny lane Some boy and girl will meet and kiss and swear That nobody can love their way again While over there You will have smiled, I shall have tossed your hair.

Once upon a time, there was a wise old man who lived in a small village. He provided lots of help to all the people who lived there. 

He would listen to their worries and solve their problems. He wasn't just great at giving advice, he was also very generous. He was always willing to provide food and warm clothing to those who needed it. 

The old man showed the villagers the value of kindness and love. He used positive words and acted wisely to everyone he met. His thoughtfulness made everyone in the village so happy and grateful. 

The old man gave everyone an important lesson about life; that it is much more rewarding to help others than to do something for yourself. He showed that the most valuable thing you can give someone is your kindness.

Brave comrade, answer! When you joined the war, What left you? "Wife and children, wealth and friends, A storied home whose ancient roof-tree bends Above such thoughts as love tells o'er and o'er." Had you no pang or struggle? "Yes; I bore Such pain on parting as at hell's gate rends The entering soul, when from its grasp ascends The last faint virtue which on earth it wore." You loved your home, your kindred, children, wife; You loathed yet plunged into war's bloody whirl!-- What urged you? "Duty! Something more than life. That which made Abraham bare the priestly knife, And Isaac kneel, or that young Hebrew girl Who sought her father coming from the strife."

name_of_work: For Some Executors of Gay Writers by Dan Vera
content: For the manuscript you kept locked up in a wall safe, For the diaries you made sure would not be discovered, For the letters from lovers you burned in the furnace, For the measures you took to tear out their tongues, For all of the ways you straightened the record, For the zeal with which you smothered all knowledge, For condemning the lovers to eternal silence, May you see their faces in each mirror you gaze in. May the names of their loved ones ring in your ears. May you wake in the night to the sound of their fucking, and be forced to lose sleep to all of their groans. May the pages you hide catch fire from their smoldering, till the wall safe explodes and consumes your house whole. May you escape to find your charmed life in ruins. May you call out in grief but hear nothing but silence.

Suddenly as the riot squad moved in it was raining exclamation marks, Nuts, bolts, nails, car-keys. A fount of broken type. And the explosion Itself - an asterisk on the map. This hyphenated line, a burst of rapid fire . . . I was trying to complete a sentence in my head, but it kept stuttering, All the alleyways and side-streets blocked with stops and colons. I know this labyrinth so well - Balaklava, Raglan, Inkerman, Odessa Street - Why can't I escape? Every move is punctuated. Crimea Street. Dead end again. A Saracen, Kremlin-2 mesh. Makrolon fae-shield. Walkie-talkies. What is My name? Where am I coming from? Where am I going? A fusillade of question-marks.

Once there was a little boy who liked to wander. He had a mighty Daddy who always knew what to do. One day Daddy told the little boy to wander off for a little while, so thatâ€™s what he did.

The little boy wandered around his house, looking at the fuzzy carpet and bright walls. He opened the door to the backyard and smiled when he saw the sunshine and the trees. He liked to wander around outside.

He wandered up to the big tree and touched its mighty trunk. Daddy had told him that it was the biggest tree in the neighborhood! The little boy smiled, thinking about how big and strong Daddy was.

After a while, the little boy wandered back inside and up the stairs. He went into Daddyâ€™s bedroom and saw his big bed. He climbed in and said, â€œI love you, Daddy.â€

Daddy smiled. He was mighty and the little boy was very proud. They laughed and hugged and cuddled until it was time for the little boy to go to bed.

The little boy went off to bed, but he knew that his mighty Daddy was always right there.

Teddy saw a phone. He liked it so much! He picked it up and he felt a light touch. The phone made a funny sound and Teddy smiled. 

Then, suddenly, the phone started to ring. Teddy became worried and he didn't like the loud noise. He quickly put the phone down and said, "I hate this!" 

Teddy's mom saw this and quickly hugged him. She said, "It's okay, Teddy. Don't be scared. It's just a phone." Teddy felt more relaxed and smiled. 

Then, Teddy's mom asked Teddy, "Would you like a light?" Teddy smiled and said, "Yes, please!" His mom then put a light above his bed and Teddy was happy. 

Teddy waved goodbye to the phone as it lay there quietly. He was now happy and he had a light to sleep by.

Once, there was an elderly man. He had an automobile. Every day, he would take the automobile for a drive. He used to love to seat in the driver's seat and feel the wind in his hair.

One day, the wind was extra strong and the man could hardly seat in the car. But he persevered and finally got to his destination. When he parked the car, he found the seat was broken!

The man was very disappointed. He knew he had to get his seat fixed. He looked around and found a repair shop. He drove his automobile to the repair shop and they fixed the seat.

When the man got back into the car, he was so happy. He could seat properly in the driver's seat now and take his car for a spin again. He was very relieved. The elderlyman was so thankful that he was able to drive his automobile again!

Summer dust settled over the garden in bloom and full of bees, their hives full of such marketable honey, you bought a jar. Then, amid the light blue and white of the ground floor, there was the lemon-yellow room and the room in two pale blues with a Hiroshige carp and a falcon, its talons folded under because the hands were difficult, though worked on over some days, and the neck difficult, the edges of the object fleeing toward the horizon, fleeing the unity of flesh and (that word again!) spirit; so, perhaps it was easier to leave the eyes out altogether, as in the small Cezanne upstairs, where the face is wide and slightly empty. The features caught in the shadow of an overhang. Outside the leaves fell from bamboo in the Japanese water garden, leaves that gathered light gray stripes upon light green stripes and the stream that ran between pinioned banks, as if we had opened a desk marked by all who had used it, who had slept in its dust, who had slept in the dew in the summer.

Once upon a time, there was a little bug. The bug was very small and loved to crawl. It had a fine, shiny back and six little legs. It lived in a big green garden with many flowers and leaves.

One day, the little bug found a square. The square was a bright red color, and it was hard. The bug was very curious, so it crawled all around the square. It crawled up and down, and side to side, exploring every part of the square.

After a long day of crawling and exploring, the little bug was tired. It crawled back to its cozy home under a big leaf. The bug felt happy and safe. It closed its tiny eyes and went to sleep, dreaming of more adventures to come.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went to the airport with her mommy and daddy. They were going on a trip to visit her grandma. 

While they were waiting for their jet to take off, Lily got very tired. She started to yawn and rub her eyes. Her mommy asked her if she wanted to take a nap. 

Lily said, "Yes, please. But can we sit in a regular seat instead of a bumpy one?" Her daddy laughed and said, "Of course, we'll find a nice regular seat for you to sleep in." 

Soon, they found a seat for Lily and she fell asleep. When she woke up, they were in the sky! She looked out the window and saw the clouds. She was very excited to see her grandma soon.

Once upon a time, there lived a nation of people who all loved each other very much. They cared for each other in the most adorable ways. Every morning they would do very kind things, like bringing each other breakfast in bed.

They also liked to do fun activities together, like playing with balloons and doing races around the park. Everyone had fun and made lots of memories that would last forever.

At the end of each day, they all held hands and danced in a big circle. It was such a happy time! Everyone smiled and laughed with joy. 

The people in this nation were very lucky to have each other. They showed love in every adorable way and were a family like no other.

Quarterly, is it, money reproaches me: 'Why do you let me lie here wastefully? I am all you never had of goods and sex. You could get them still by writing a few cheques.' So I look at others, what they do with theirs: They certainly don't keep it upstairs. By now they've a second house and car and wife: Clearly money has something to do with life --In fact, they've a lot in common, if you enquire: You can't put off being young until you retire, And however you bank your screw, the money you save Won't in the end buy you more than a shave. I listen to money singing. It's like looking down From long french windows at a provincial town, The slums, the canal, the churches ornate and mad In the evening sun. It is intensely sad.

Once upon a time, there was a big fierce lion. He lived in a jungle with his friends, the monkeys and the birds. One day, the lion felt a tickle in his nose and he sneezed so hard that he fell into a barrel. 

The monkeys and the birds saw what happened and they all laughed. "Are you okay, Mr. Lion?" asked the monkeys. "Yes, I'm fine," said the lion. "I just sneezed and fell into this barrel."

The monkeys and the birds helped the lion out of the barrel and they all continued to play together. From that day on, whenever the lion felt a sneeze coming on, he made sure to move away from any barrels.

Bob was walking in the park. It was a beautiful day and he could hear the birds singing. Suddenly, he saw a beautiful view of the mountains. He was so happy to see it.

Suddenly, he heard a noise. He became worried and looked around. He couldn't find anything. He was so scared.

Suddenly, he heard a voice calling his name. It was his friend Jen. She said to him, "What are you worried about?". Bob told Jen about the noise he heard. 

Jen smiled and said, "It's just the wind. Don't be worried."

Bob was so relieved. He smiled and looked around. He could see the beautiful view of the mountains again.

Once upon a time, there was a young girl named Lucy. She was very obedient and enjoyed playing with her friends.

One day, Lucy was given a special bracelet by her mother. It was very pretty! Lucy wanted to learn more about it. She asked her mom to show her how to wear it.

Mom told Lucy that she needed to be very careful when wearing it. She showed Lucy how to put it on properly and promised that she would never take it off.

Lucy was so excited to wear her new bracelet. She showed it to her friends and she learned how to take care of it. She was so happy that she had something so special.

From then on, Lucy was always obedient and she took good care of her bracelet. She always remembered to keep it clean and she was never too rough with it.

The bracelet was a reminder of how important it was to be a good person and be kind to everyone. Lucy was very proud of her bracelet and she loved wearing it!

name_of_work: Song: How sweet I roam'd from field to field by William Blake
content: How sweet I roam'd from field to field, And tasted all the summer's pride, 'Till I the prince of love beheld, Who in the sunny beams did glide! He shew'd me lilies for my hair, And blushing roses for my brow; He led me through his gardens fair, Where all his golden pleasures grow. With sweet May dews my wings were wet, And Phoebus fir'd my vocal rage; He caught me in his silken net, And shut me in his golden cage. He loves to sit and hear me sing, Then, laughing, sports and plays with me; Then stretches out my golden wing, And mocks my loss of liberty.

Once upon a time, there was a mommy and a baby bear. They were walking through the forest when the baby bear got very messy. He made mommy very mad. 

Mommy said, "Uh oh! We need to clean you up!" But the baby bear kept getting messier and messier. 

The mommy sighed and said, "Let's go find some help." 

The mommy and baby bear looked around, but there was no one to help them. Suddenly, they saw a bunny hopping by.

Mommy asked, "Bunny, can you help us clean up the baby bear?" The bunny nodded, then hopped over and began to lick the baby bear. 

Mommy smiled, and both mommy and baby bear sighed happily as the bunny made the baby bear all clean and neat again.

Once upon a time there was a prince. He was very troubled. He wanted to prove that he was brave and noble. One day he set off on a journey. He needed a sword to protect himself from the bad things he might find on his journey.

He searched for days, but he could not find a sword. Finally he met a kind old man. The man said he could help the prince. He gave him a beautiful golden sword.

The prince thanked the old man and set off once more on his journey. When he ran into danger, he pulled out the sword and felt very brave and strong. 

He made it safely home and the prince was no longer troubled. He had the sword he needed.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Mia who liked to sail. Every day, she would take the big boat out and go on long adventures, with the wind blowing in her hair.

But one day, something terrible happened. As Mia was sailing far away, she hit something and the boat started to leak. She looked around and saw a little needle sticking out of the boat. Mia was very upset.

Mia thought and thought, until she came up with an idea. She needed a patch to fix the boat, so she decided to look for one. She quickly found a patch, and put it on the boat where the needle was stuck.

Mia was happy again, and the boat no longer leaked. She hugged the patch and said "Thank you for helping me, little patch. I won't let anything like this happen again."

And so, Mia happily sailed on, never again experiencing such an upsetting moment.

Tom and Lily were playing with their blocks in the living room. They liked to build towers and bridges and houses with the blocks. They had many blocks of different colors and shapes.

But their baby brother Ben did not like the blocks. He liked to crawl and grab and throw things. He saw the blocks and wanted to play with them too. He crawled to the living room and disturbed Tom and Lily's game.

"Hey, stop that!" Tom shouted. He was angry because Ben knocked down his tower. "You are ruining our game!"

"No, no, no!" Lily cried. She was sad because Ben threw her bridge. "You are breaking our blocks!"

Ben did not understand. He thought they were playing with him. He laughed and clapped his hands. He saw a large block with a zero on it. He liked the zero. He grabbed the block and put it in his mouth.

"Yuck, don't do that!" Tom said. He ran to Ben and took the block from him. "That is not food, that is a block!"

"Give it back, give it back!" Ben whined. He reached for the block and pulled Tom's hair. "That is mine, that is mine!"

Tom and Lily started to cry. They did not like Ben. They wanted him to go away. They called their mom.

"Mom, mom, help!" they said. "Ben is disturbing us! He is taking our blocks and putting them in his mouth!"

Mom heard their cries and came to the living room. She saw the mess and the tears. She felt sorry for Tom and Lily and angry with Ben.

"Ben, what are you doing?" she asked. She took Ben from the floor and held him in her arms. "You are not being nice. You are disturbing your brother and sister. You have to share and play gently with the blocks. Say sorry to Tom and Lily."

Ben looked at Mom and then at Tom and Lily. He saw their sad faces. He felt a little sorry. He said in a small voice, "Sorry, sorry."

Mom smiled and kissed Ben. She said, "That's good, Ben. Now, let's clean up the blocks and play together nicely. OK?"

Tom and Lily nodded. They wiped their tears and smiled too. They said, "OK, OK."

They helped Mom to pick up the blocks and put them in a box. Then they took some blocks and gave them to Ben. They showed him how to stack them and make shapes with them. Ben liked that. He smiled and clapped his hands. He said, "Thank you, thank you."

They played together nicely with the blocks. They did not disturb each other. They had fun. Mom was happy. She said, "Good job, kids. I love you all."

name_of_work: Ragged Island by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: There, there where those black spruces crowd To the edge of the precipitous cliff, Above your boat, under the eastern wall of the island; And no wave breaks; as if All had been done, and long ago, that needed Doing; and the cold tide, unimpeded By shoal or shelving ledge, moves up and down, Instead of in and out; And there is no driftwood there, because there is no beach; Clean cliff going down as deep as clear water can reach; No driftwood, such as abounds on the roaring shingle, To be hefted home, for fires in the kitchen stove; Barrels, banged ashore about the boiling outer harbor; Lobster-buoys, on the eel-grass of the sheltered cove: There, thought unbraids itself, and the mind becomes single. There you row with tranquil oars, and the ocean Shows no scar from the cutting of your placid keel; Care becomes senseless there; pride and promotion Remote; you only look; you scarcely feel. Even adventure, with its vital uses, Is aimless ardour now; and thrift is waste. Oh, to be there, under the silent spruces, Where the wide, quiet evening darkens without haste Over a sea with death acquainted, yet forever chaste.

Lila and Tom were playing in the garden. They liked to pretend they were knights and dragons. Lila was a knight and Tom was a dragon. They had a wooden sword and a cardboard shield.

Tom roared and breathed fire. He tried to burn Lila's shield. Lila swung her sword and hit Tom's tail. Tom cried out and ran away. He hid behind a big plant.

Lila followed him and found him. She said, "Surrender, dragon! You are no match for me!"

Tom peeked out from the plant. He said, "No, I will not surrender! I am a fierce dragon!"

Lila smiled and said, "But you are also my brother. And I love you. You are loyal to me, right?"

Tom nodded and said, "Yes, I am loyal to you. And you are loyal to me, right?"

Lila nodded and said, "Yes, I am loyal to you. We are a team. How about we share the plant? It has pretty flowers."

Tom agreed and said, "OK, we can share the plant. And we can play again later. Maybe we can be pirates and mermaids."

Lila and Tom hugged and picked some flowers. They were happy and had fun. They were loyal to each other.

Once upon a time, there was a poor little girl who lived with her mom. Every day the girl asked her mom if she could play outside, but her mom always said no.

One day, the girl was feeling brave and asked her mom if she could go outside again. This time, the mom hesitated and said maybe. The girl got so excited that she ran outside without waiting for a yes or no from her mom.

When the mom saw that the girl was outside, she was very angry. She ran outside and grabbed the girl's arm. She took her inside and put her in the closet. The mom insisted that the girl stay in the closet until she calmed down.

The little girl stayed in the closet for a while. Finally, her mom opened the door and said she could go play. The girl learned her lesson that day and never asked to go outside without permission again.

Once upon a time, there was a kind rabbit named Benny. Benny liked to hop around and eat carrots. One day, Benny found a lost letter on the ground. The letter had an address on it, so Benny knew he had to deliver it to the right house. Benny hopped and hopped until he found the house.

When Benny arrived, he saw a little girl with a sad face. She had lost her favorite earrings. Benny had an idea! He remembered he had found a pair of earrings while hopping around earlier. Benny gave the earrings to the little girl and her face lit up with joy. She was so grateful to Benny for being so thoughtful.

From that day on, the little girl and Benny became friends. They played together and Benny would often bring her carrots as a gift. Benny was happy to have made a new friend and the little girl was happy to have found her lost earrings.

Once upon a time, there was a small boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with clay. He would often make small animals and put them on the windowsill.

One day, Timmy's friend Billy came over to play. Billy saw the clay and asked, "Can I play too?" Timmy said, "Yes, you can! Let's make a small house together."

Billy and Timmy worked on the clay, putting it together and shaping it into a small house. When they were finished, they both looked at it and said, "Wow! It's so pretty!" They were both happy and proud of what they had made.

Once upon a time, there was a little dog named Spot. Spot had a fancy sack. He would carry it with him everywhere he went. Inside the sack, he kept his toys and treats.

One day, Spot went to the park with his friends. They all wanted to perform a fun dance. Spot said, "Let's dance!" His friends said, "Yes, let's dance!" So, they all danced together in a circle. They were very happy.

After the dance, Spot opened his fancy sack. He shared his toys and treats with his friends. They played and ate together. At the end of the day, they all said, "Thank you, Spot!" Spot smiled and said, "You're welcome!" They all went home, excited to play and dance together again soon.

name_of_work: Rain on a Grave by Thomas Hardy
content: Clouds spout upon her Their waters amain In ruthless disdain, - Her who but lately Had shivered with pain As at touch of dishonour If there had lit on her So coldly, so straightly Such arrows of rain: One who to shelter Her delicate head Would quicken and quicken Each tentative tread If drops chanced to pelt her That summertime spills In dust-paven rills When thunder-clouds thicken And birds close their bills. Would that I lay there And she were housed here! Or better, together Were folded away there Exposed to one weather We both, - who would stray there When sunny the day there, Or evening was clear At the prime of the year. Soon will be growing Green blades from her mound, And daisies be showing Like stars on the ground, Till she form part of them - Ay - the sweet heart of them, Loved beyond measure With a child's pleasure All her life's round.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Jo. Jo was only three years old, but she was already so smart. One day, she decided to go for a walk in the garden.

Suddenly, she noticed something orange in the sky. She looked up and saw a beautiful fairy flying in the sky, waving silently at her. Jo was stunned and decided to raise her hand in an attempt to say hello.

The fairy smiled and waved back. Jo then turned her hand into a fist and closed her eyes. To her surprise, the fairy sprinkled Jo with a magical dust and flew away.

Jo opened her eyes again and she was shocked to find a bright orange tree growing next to her. She was so thrilled that she raised her hands in joy.

When Jo asked her parents why the fairy had done this, the replied: â€œThe kind fairy wanted to teach you an important lesson: whatever actions you do, good or bad, will eventually come back to you.â€

So, no matter what, itâ€™s important to always choose to do good things!

"Mommy, what's in the box?" asked John, a 3 year old boy.

"It's a surprise, John!" replied his mom.

John was very curious, he wanted to open the box and find out what was inside.

"It's hidden, you have to share it with your sister," said his mom.

John and his sister eagerly opened the box and were delighted to find it filled with colourful toys. They both jumped up and down, they couldn't believe their eyes!

John smiled at his mom. He was so happy to be able to share the box of toys with his sister.

One day, Joe and his mom went to the farmers market. Joe was so excited to see all the different veggies! He wanted to try them all. 

His mom smiled and said, "Let's go pick out some onion." Joe was confused but he followed his mom. When they got to the onions the farmer said, "Would you like to buy my onions? They're really fresh." Joe's mom smiled and said yes. 

Joe asked the farmer, "Can I try one?" The farmer nodded and said. "Sure, go ahead." Joe took one and slowly bit into it. He did not like the taste and said, "Ew, it's yucky!" 

His mom chuckled and said, "It's an acquired taste, Joe." But Joe was still confused. He looked at the farmer and asked, "What do you mean?" 

The farmer smiled and offered Joe a piece of candy. Joe was so excited and he quickly took it. He unwrapped it and put it in his mouth. But suddenly Joe started coughing. The farmer had offered him a onion instead of a candy! 

Joe was horrified. He never wanted to try onion again!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved flowers and her favorite was the bright red poppy. One day, her mom took her to a big garden where there were many poppies. Lily was so happy to see them all. 

As they were walking, Lily saw a butterfly flying around the poppies. She tried to catch it, but it flew away. Suddenly, her dad arrived and he was wearing his new suit. Lily thought he looked very fit in his suit. 

They all had a picnic in the garden and Lily's mom gave her a poppy to smell. It smelled so good! Lily was so happy and couldn't wait to come back to the garden to see more flowers. The end.

name_of_work: A Crowned Poet by Anne Reeve Aldrich
content: In thy coach of state Pass, O King, along: He no envy feels To whom God giveth song. Starving, still I smile, Laugh at want and wrong: He is fed and crowned To whom God giveth song. Better than all pomps That to rank belong,-- One such dream as his To whom God giveth song. Let us greet, O King, As we pass along: He, too, is a king To whom God giveth song.

name_of_work: Abolition of Slavery in the District of Columbia, 1862 by John Greenleaf Whittier
content: WHEN first I saw our banner wave Above the nation's council-hall, I heard beneath its marble wall The clanking fetters of the slave! In the foul market-place I stood, And saw the Christian mother sold, And childhood with its locks of gold, Blue-eyed and fair with Saxon blood. I shut my eyes, I held my breath, And, smothering down the wrath and shame That set my Northern blood aflame, Stood silent, -- where to speak was death. Beside me gloomed the prison-cell Where wasted one in slow decline For uttering simple words of mine, And loving freedom all too well. The flag that floated from the dome Flapped menace in the morning air; I stood a perilled stranger where The human broker made his home. For crime was virtue: Gown and Sword And Law their threefold sanction gave, And to the quarry of the slave Went hawking with our symbol-bird.On the oppressor's side was power; And yet I knew that every wrong, However old, however strong, But waited God's avenging hour. I knew that truth would crush the lie, -- Somehow, some time, the end would be; Yet scarcely dared I hope to see The triumph with my mortal eye. But now I see it! In the sun A free flag floats from yonder dome, And at the nation's hearth and home The justice long delayed is done. Not as we hoped, in calm of prayer, The message of deliverance comes, But heralded by roll of drums On waves of battle-troubled air! Midst sounds that madden and appall, The song that Bethlehem's shepherds knew ! The harp of David melting through The demon-agonies of Saul! Not as we hoped; but what are we? Above our broken dreams and plans God lays, with wiser hand than man's, The corner-stones of liberty. I cavil not with Him: the voice That freedom's blessed gospel tells Is sweet to me as silver bells, Rejoicing! yea, I will rejoice!Dear friends still toiling in the sun; Ye dearer ones who, gone before, Are watching from the eternal shore The slow work by your hands begun, Rejoice with me! The chastening rod Blossoms with love; the furnace heat Grows cool beneath His blessed feet Whose form is as the Son of God! Rejoice! Our Marah's bitter springs Are sweetened; on our ground of grief Rise day by day in strong relief The prophecies of better things. Rejoice in hope! The day and night Are one with God, and one with them Who see by faith the cloudy hem Of Judgment fringed with Mercy's light!

Once there was a little boy called Sam. He was three years old, and very curious. One day he wanted to find out the truth about something. He asked his mom if he could fix it. 

But his mom said no. She said, "That's too hard for you to fix right now, Sam. You'll need to wait until you're a bit older." 

Sam was sad. His mom was usually very compassionate, but this time she was just not listening. So Sam decided to try and fix it by himself. 

He worked hard all day long but, in the end, he could not fix it. When his mom found out what he had done, she was very angry. She told him he should have listened to her earlier. 

Sam learned a valuable lesson, that sometimes it's best to wait and seek help instead of trying to fix something on your own.

Once upon a time, there were two little girls. One day, they went on an adventure. They wanted to find something special and unique.

The first girl said to the second, "Let's look for it!" They both smiled, and then started to explore in the woods.

After walking for a bit, they saw a shiny bottle. They picked it up and held it tight. It was a unique bottle and it had something inside.

The second girl asked, "What is it?" The first girl said, "I'm not sure, it smells weird!"

At that moment, the first girl noticed something written on the bottle. It said, "Danger! Poison!" The girls knew they had to be careful, so the first one closed the bottle tight and put it away.

The second girl said, "That was a close one! Let's keep exploring. We might find something even more special and unique!"

The two girls smiled and kept walking together. They were sure that their next adventure would be something even more special!

Once upon a time there were two friends - Sam and Mia. They liked to do lots of things together, like playing games and dancing to music. One day, Sam wanted to play a game where Mia had to listen to music and resist the urge to dance. 
Sam said to Mia, "I know you like to dance to the music, but can you resist the urge this time?" Mia said "I'll try!"

So, Mia listened to the music but it was so catchy she couldnâ€™t help but to dance. Sam saw her and said, â€œI told you that you wouldnâ€™t be able to resist, didn't I?â€ 
Mia said "I'm sorry, I couldn't help it!" Sam smiled and said, "It's ok, it's kind of me to keep trying."

Moral of the story: Even if something seems like it's impossible, it's kind to keep trying. People appreciate it when we show kindness, even if we don't succeed.

Little Jack was having so much fun at the festival. He ran and laughed around the colorful tents and games. His parents watched him with a smile, happy that he was having a good time.

Suddenly, Jack heard a loud rumble. He trembled in fear, unsure of what was going on. He looked up at his father, who was watching the sky.

"What's that noise Dad?" Jack asked, trembling.

His dad knelt down and said with a calm voice,"It's okay, Jack. It's only thunder. It's funny to hear sometimes, but it's OK."

Little Jack smiled and calmed down, understanding that the thunder was nothing to worry about. He went back to running around and enjoying the festival.

Once there were two children named Lily and Jack. They both wanted to win something special. They went to the mall to look around. Suddenly, Lily saw a really big teddy bear. She got so excited, she wanted to win it!

Jack and Lily started to race around the mall. They went so fast it made them feel dizzy. After running up and down the hallways and around the store displays, it was time to find out who had won the teddy bear.

At first it looked like Lily had won. But Jack was very fast and raced ahead to the finish line. In the end, Jack won the teddy bear!

Lily was sad at first. But Jack was happy to give her a big hug. Lily smiled and said, "You are the best win-ner ever!"

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved playing with his toy cars and trucks. One day, Timmy's favorite truck got stuck under the couch. He tried to get it out, but it was too far away.

Timmy's mom came to help him. She used a long stick to reach the truck. But the stick was sharp and it scratched the wall. Timmy's mom got upset and Timmy felt bad.

Later that day, Timmy saw a big space in the park where he could play with his trucks. But there were other kids already playing there. Timmy thought their toys were more attractive than his. He felt sad and didn't know what to do.

Once there was a little boy called David who was very sad. He was sad because he had lost his toy car at the beach. He had gone to the beach with his family and had been playing with the car in the sand, but when it was time to go home he couldn't find it anywhere. 

David's mummy and daddy tried to comfort him, but he still felt sad. Then David's daddy said, "I know what might make you feel better.Let's go an look for oysters at the beach."

They went to the beach and searched until they found an oyster. Daddy opened it and inside was the toy car. David was so happy. Daddy said the car was dry now and they should keep it safe. David hugged his toy car and never let it out of his sight.

name_of_work: Love is Enough by William Morris
content: Love is enough: though the World be a-waning, And the woods have no voice but the voice of complaining, Though the sky be too dark for dim eyes to discover The gold-cups and daisies fair blooming thereunder, Though the hills be held shadows, and the sea a dark wonder And this day draw a veil over all deeds pass'd over, Yet their hands shall not tremble, their feet shall not falter; The void shall not weary, the fear shall not alter These lips and these eyes of the loved and the lover.

Once upon a time, there was a small town. In this town, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim loved fireworks. One day, Tim found a firework in his house.

Tim's mom said, "Tim, I warn you, do not play with the firework. It is not safe." But Tim did not listen to his mom. He wanted to see the firework go up in the sky and make a big boom.

Tim went outside with the firework. He put it on the ground and lit it with a match. The firework went up in the sky and made a big boom, just like Tim wanted. But, the firework also started a fire.

The fire grew bigger and bigger. The people in the town were scared. They tried to put out the fire, but it was too big. The fire burned down many houses.

In the end, the town was very sad. Tim learned that he should have listened to his mom's warning.

Once upon a time, there was a rabbit that lived in the country. The rabbit wanted to have a perfect day, but was scared of what might happen. 

So the rabbit asked her friend, a frog, for help. The frog answered, "Don't worry, it'll be perfect. Just believe in yourself."

The rabbit felt better and decided to wander around the country. She wasn't scared this time. 

The rabbit had a lovely time visiting the meadows and forests and she thought that the country was so beautiful. 

But then, on her way back home, she saw a dark and scary shape in the distance. She was scared again!

But with some courage, and with the help of her friend, the rabbit got closer and realized that it was only a big bush. She had nothing to fear!

And so the rabbit felt happy and sure that everything would be perfect. She ran home with a smile, glad the scary thing was not real.

name_of_work: Nightstand with Roses by Jody Zorgdrager
content: They weren't red nor was I angry, but with something five shades lighter than passion, I plucked the roses bald. Anyway, they were sorry things. Their nodding heads on such long stems reminded me how tiring it is, always trying to forgive. And besides, I did it gently, pulling petals the way one tugs off an insect's wings, by twos. What my thumb and fingertips began to hear--yes, they listened for it-- was the shaggy center's thick dribble, the tiny rip of dismemberment, and, in between, the moment of small panic that comes before--as just before withdrawing a mouth from another mouth there comes that in-suck, that sudden taking back although you've already given it up, given up to it--the letting go. I couldn't stop until I had the whole drawer full of floating pink on pink.

Lily loved to skip. She skipped in the park, she skipped in the school, she skipped at home. She liked to skip with her family, too. Her mom, her dad, and her baby brother. They skipped and laughed and had fun.

One day, Lily saw a big dog in the park. The dog was bad. It barked and growled and chased people. Lily was scared. She ran to her mom and dad and held their hands. The dog came near them and tried to bite.

"Go away, bad dog!" Lily's dad shouted. He picked up a stick and threw it at the dog. The dog ran after the stick and left them alone.

"Are you okay, Lily?" Lily's mom asked. She hugged Lily and kissed her cheek.

"I'm okay, mom," Lily said. "But I don't like the bad dog."

"Me neither, Lily," Lily's mom said. "But don't worry, the bad dog is gone now. We are safe."

Lily smiled and nodded. She felt better. She looked at her family and said, "Can we skip again?"

"Of course, Lily," Lily's dad said. "We love to skip with you."

They skipped and laughed and had fun. Lily was happy. She loved her family and they loved her.

Lily liked to write poems. She wrote them on paper with her crayons. She wrote about her toys, her family, and her dreams. She was very proud of her poems and showed them to everyone.

One day, Lily found a big book of poems in the library. She wanted to read them and learn new words. She opened the book and saw many words she did not know. She tried to sound them out, but they were too hard. She felt sad and confused.

She decided to copy some of the poems from the book and pretend they were hers. She thought that would make her happy and smart. She wrote them on paper with her crayons and showed them to everyone.

But everyone knew that the poems were not hers. They were too long and too fancy for a three year old. They did not sound like Lily at all. They did not like her poems and they did not like her lying. They were angry and disappointed.

Lily felt ashamed and lonely. She wished she had not copied the poems. She wished she had written her own poems with her own words. She wished she had been regular and honest. She learned that copying was wrong and that poems were not just words, but feelings. She cried and cried and threw away the book. She did not write poems anymore.

The wind blows east, the wind blows west, And the frost falls and the rain: A weary heart went thankful to rest, And must rise to toil again, 'gain, And must rise to toil again. The wind blows east, the wind blows west, And there comes good luck and bad; The thriftiest man is the cheerfulest; 'Tis a thriftless thing to be sad, sad, 'Tis a thriftless thing to be sad. The wind blows east, the wind blows west; Ye shall know a tree by its fruit: This world, they say, is worst to the best;-- But a dastard has evil to boot, boot, But a dastard has evil to boot. The wind blows east, the wind blows west; What skills it to mourn or to talk? A journey I have, and far ere I rest; I must bundle my wallets and walk, walk, I must bundle my wallets and walk. The wind does blow as it lists alway; Canst thou change this world to thy mind? The world will wander its own wise way; I also will wander mine, mine, I also will wander mine.
Bravery runs in my family.

Once upon a time, there was a big blanket. It was so large that it covered everything in the room. A little girl named Lily loved to play hide and seek under the blanket. But one day, Lily's little brother, Jack, wanted to play too.

Lily didn't want to share the blanket with Jack. She thought it was too large for both of them to fit under. So, she tried to separate the blanket into two pieces. But the blanket was too big and too heavy for her to do it alone.

Jack started to cry because he wanted to play too. Lily felt bad for making him sad, so she decided to share the blanket with him. They both crawled under the large blanket and played together. They had so much fun that they forgot all about their fight. From that day on, they always shared the blanket when they played hide and seek.

The gingham dog and the calico cat Side by side on the table sat; 'T was half-past twelve, and (what do you think!) Nor one nor t' other had slept a wink! The old Dutch clock and the Chinese plate Appeared to know as sure as fate There was going to be a terrible spat. (I was n't there; I simply state What was told to me by the Chinese plate!) The gingham dog went "Bow-wow-wow!" And the calico cat replied "Mee-ow!" The air was littered, an hour or so, With bits of gingham and calico, While the old Dutch clock in the chimney-place Up with its hands before its face, For it always dreaded a family row! (Now mind: I'm only telling you What the old Dutch clock declares is true!) The Chinese plate looked very blue, And wailed, "Oh, dear! what shall we do!" But the gingham dog and the calico cat Wallowed this way and tumbled that, Employing every tooth and claw In the awfullest way you ever saw-- And, oh! how the gingham and calico flew! (Don't fancy I exaggerate-- I got my news from the Chinese plate!) Next morning, where the two had sat They found no trace of dog or cat; And some folks think unto this day That burglars stole that pair away! But the truth about the cat and pup Is this: they ate each other up! Now what do you really think of that! (The old Dutch clock it told me so, And that is how I came to know.)

Abortions will not let you forget. You remember the children you got that you did not get, The damp small pulps with a little or with no hair, The singers and workers that never handled the air. You will never neglect or beat Them, or silence or buy with a sweet. You will never wind up the sucking-thumb Or scuttle off ghosts that come. You will never leave them, controlling your luscious sigh, Return for a snack of them, with gobbling mother-eye. I have heard in the voices of the wind the voices of my dim killed children. I have contracted. I have eased My dim dears at the breasts they could never suck. I have said, Sweets, if I sinned, if I seized Your luck And your lives from your unfinished reach, If I stole your births and your names, Your straight baby tears and your games, Your stilted or lovely loves, your tumults, your marriages, aches, and your deaths, If I poisoned the beginnings of your breaths, Believe that even in my deliberateness I was not deliberate. Though why should I whine, Whine that the crime was other than mine?-- Since anyhow you are dead. Or rather, or instead, You were never made. But that too, I am afraid, Is faulty: oh, what shall I say, how is the truth to be said? You were born, you had body, you died. It is just that you never giggled or planned or cried. Believe me, I loved you all. Believe me, I knew you, though faintly, and I loved, I loved you All.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved going to the zoo to see all the animals. One day, she saw a big, fluffy panda. The panda was eating bamboo and looked very happy.

Lily wanted to play with the panda, so she tried to catch it. But the panda was too fast and ran away. Lily was sad, but she didn't give up. She tried again and again, but the panda was always too quick.

One day, Lily had a perfect idea. She brought some bamboo with her and offered it to the panda. The panda was so happy that it stayed with Lily and they played together all day. From that day on, Lily and the panda were best friends and caught bamboo together every day.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a wide smile and loved to follow her mom around the house. One day, while they were in the kitchen, Lily looked up and saw a funny bug on the ceiling.

"Look, Mom! Bug on ceiling!" Lily said, pointing up. Her mom looked up and saw the bug too. "Oh, it's just a little bug, Lily. It won't hurt us," her mom said with a smile.

Lily watched the bug as it walked across the ceiling. She followed it with her eyes, and it seemed to be going to her room. "Mom, I want to follow the bug!" Lily said. So, they went to her room and saw the bug crawl out the window. Lily and her mom laughed, and they went back to the kitchen to make a yummy snack together.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside in his backyard. One day, he found a pit in the ground. It was big and deep, so he decided to store his toys in it.

Timmy was so lucky to have found the pit because now he had a secret hiding spot for all his favorite toys. He played with them every day and put them back in the pit when he was done.

One day, Timmy's little sister came to play with him. She saw the pit and wanted to play too. Timmy warned her not to go in, but she didn't listen. She fell in and got hurt.

Timmy felt very sad and guilty. He realized he should have covered the pit or told his parents about it. From that day on, he always made sure to put safety first.

Once upon a time there was a thin dog named Fluffy. Fluffy lived on a farm with lots of other animals. One day, Fluffy saw a farmer trying to save a pig from a muddy hole. Fluffy ran over and told the farmer his opinion.

"What do you think, Fluffy?" asked the farmer.

"I think we should try to save the pig," said Fluffy.

The farmer smiled and thought it was a good idea. So they carefully pulled the pig from the muddy hole and Fluffy barked in excitement.

The farmer and Fluffy each gave the pig a big hug and congratulated each other on a job well done. Fluffy was so proud of himself for being able to help save the pig!

From then on, the farmer asked Fluffy for his opinion whenever he needed help. Fluffy was always happy to help him out and make sure the animals were safe and happy.

Tom and Lily were friends. They liked to play in the park with their toys. One day, they saw some big men with guns and tanks. They were very loud and scary. They said they were fighting a war.

Tom and Lily were afraid. They ran to their mom and dad. They hugged them tight. They asked them what was happening. Mom and dad said they had to go away from the park. They had to find a safe place. They said they loved them very much.

Tom and Lily took their toys. They followed mom and dad. They saw many people running and crying. They saw smoke and fire. They saw things broken and smashed. They felt sad and angry. They did not like the war.

They walked for a long time. They were tired and hungry. They carried their toys. They were heavy. They wished they could play in the park again. They wished the war would stop. They wished the big men with guns and tanks would go away.

They found a small house. It was not their home, but it was warm and cozy. Mom and dad said they could stay there for a while. They said they would try to make them happy. They said they would hope for peace.

Tom and Lily put their toys on the floor. They cuddled with mom and dad. They felt safe and loved. They still did not like the war, but they did not cry. They smiled and said thank you. They said they were friends. They said they were brave.

Sam ran outside and saw the snow. He was so excited! He was going to write in the snow. He grabbed the stick and started writing the alphabet. He was so happy to see what he wrote in the snow. 

His mom saw him and said, "Sam, be careful when you write in the snow. Remember to stay safe!" 
Sam nodded and said, "Yes mom!"

He wrote slowly and carefully to make sure the letters looked nice. He was so proud of himself! When he finished, he looked at what he wrote and smiled. 

Sam's mom came back outside and smiled. She said, "Wow, look at what you wrote! It looks amazing, Sam!" 
Sam grinned and said, "Thanks mom!" 

Sam and his mom watched the snow and Sam smiled. He was so happy he wrote in the snow and stayed safe!

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy who loved to play in the river. He had a red kayak that he liked to paddle around in. One day, Timmy saw a big storm cloud in the sky.

He asked his friend, a smart duck, "What should we do?"

The duck said, "We should go back to shore before the storm comes."

Timmy quickly zipped up his life jacket and paddled back to shore. Just as they got out of the water, the storm hit. Timmy was safe and dry because he listened to his smart friend.

John wanted to go to the lake, because he thought it would be fun. He asked his mom if they could go. She said yes, and packed a big picnic lunch.
John was very excited, but his older brother Mark teased him. Mark said John was too little to go. John said he was not too little, and he would show Mark. 

John and his family went to the lake. Everyone got in the raft and paddled around. John wanted to help paddle the raft, but Mom said he was too little. He frowned, but tried to make the best of it. 

Mark was bossy and told John what to do. He said to look out for trees, and to watch for other boats on the lake. John did what Mark said, and he had some fun. It was not as much fun as he thought it would be, since Mark was so bossy. But John was happy to show Mark he could go to the lake with his family.

Tom and Mia are friends. They like to play together. One day, they go to Mia's house for breakfast. Mia's mom makes toast for them. She puts butter and jam on the toast.

"Can I have some toast, please?" Tom asks.

"Sure, here you go," Mia's mom says. She gives Tom a plate with toast.

"Thank you," Tom says. He takes a bite of the toast. He makes a funny face. "This toast is funny," he says.

"What do you mean?" Mia asks. She looks at her toast. It looks normal to her.

"It tastes funny," Tom says. He shows Mia his tongue. It is purple.

Mia laughs. She sees the jam on Tom's toast. It is grape jam. "That's not funny, that's grape," she says. "Do you like grape?"

Tom thinks for a moment. He takes another bite of the toast. He smiles. "I do like grape," he says. "It is sweet and yummy."

Mia is happy. She likes grape too. She shares her toast with Tom. They eat all the toast. They say thank you to Mia's mom. They go to play with Mia's toys. They have a lot of fun. They are good friends.

Sara and Ben are twins. They like to play outside in the sun. One day, they see a big hive on a tree. The hive is full of bees. Sara and Ben want to see the bees up close.

"Let's dress like bees," Sara says. "Then they will think we are bees too."

They go to their room and find yellow and black clothes. They put on the clothes and make wings out of paper. They also find a hat with a net to cover their face.

"Now we are bees," Ben says. "Let's go to the hive."

They run to the tree and climb on a branch. They try to buzz like bees. But the bees do not like them. The bees see that they are not bees. The bees are angry. They fly out of the hive and sting Sara and Ben.

"Ow, ow, ow!" Sara and Ben cry. They jump off the branch and run to their mom. Their mom sees them and gasps. Their faces are red and swollen. Their clothes are torn and dirty. Their wings are broken.

"What happened to you?" their mom asks.

"We dressed like bees," Sara says.

"We wanted to see the hive," Ben says.

"But the bees did not like us," Sara says.

"They stung us," Ben says.

Their mom hugs them and takes them inside. She puts ice on their stings and gives them juice. She tells them not to dress like bees again. She tells them to be careful of the hive.

Sara and Ben nod. They are sorry. They are also pale and tired. They lie on the couch and watch TV. They do not want to play outside anymore. They do not like bees anymore.

Once upon a time, there was a cheerful boy named Tim. He had a big machine in his backyard. The machine was colorful and could make fun toys for Tim to play with.

One day, Tim's friend, Sue, came over to play. Tim said, "Sue, do you want to see my machine?" Sue said, "Yes, Tim! Show me!" So, they went to the backyard.

Tim started the machine with a push of a button. The machine made a loud noise and out came a ball. Tim and Sue played with the ball all day long. They were very happy and had lots of fun.

name_of_work: The Heart of a Woman by Georgia Douglas Johnson
content: The heart of a woman goes forth with the dawn, As a lone bird, soft winging, so restlessly on, Afar o'er life's turrets and vales does it roam In the wake of those echoes the heart calls home. The heart of a woman falls back with the night, And enters some alien cage in its plight, And tries to forget it has dreamed of the stars While it breaks, breaks, breaks on the sheltering bars.

name_of_work: I Sing the Body Electric by Walt Whitman
content: I sing the body electric, The armies of those I love engirth me and I engirth them, They will not let me off till I go with them, respond to them, And discorrupt them, and charge them full with the charge of the soul. Was it doubted that those who corrupt their own bodies conceal themselves? And if those who defile the living are as bad as they who defile the dead? And if the body does not do fully as much as the soul? And if the body were not the soul, what is the soul? The love of the body of man or woman balks account, the body itself balks account, That of the male is perfect, and that of the female is perfect. The expression of the face balks account, But the expression of a well-made man appears not only in his face, It is in his limbs and joints also, it is curiously in the joints of his hips and wrists, It is in his walk, the carriage of his neck, the flex of his waist and knees, dress does not hide him, The strong sweet quality he has strikes through the cotton and broadcloth, To see him pass conveys as much as the best poem, perhaps more, You linger to see his back, and the back of his neck and shoulder-side. The sprawl and fulness of babes, the bosoms and heads of women, the folds of their dress, their style as we pass in the street, the contour of their shape downwards, The swimmer naked in the swimming-bath, seen as he swims through the transparent green-shine, or lies with his face up and rolls silently to and fro in the heave of the water, The bending forward and backward of rowers in row-boats, the horseman in his saddle, Girls, mothers, house-keepers, in all their performances, The group of laborers seated at noon-time with their open dinner-kettles, and their wives waiting, The female soothing a child, the farmer's daughter in the garden or cow-yard, The young fellow hoeing corn, the sleigh-driver driving his six horses through the crowd, The wrestle of wrestlers, two apprentice-boys, quite grown, lusty, good-natured, native-born, out on the vacant lot at sun-down after work, The coats and caps thrown down, the embrace of love and resistance, The upper-hold and under-hold, the hair rumpled over and blinding the eyes; The march of firemen in their own costumes, the play of masculine muscle through clean-setting trowsers and waist-straps, The slow return from the fire, the pause when the bell strikes suddenly again, and the listening on the alert, The natural, perfect, varied attitudes, the bent head, the curv'd neck and the counting; Such-like I love--I loosen myself, pass freely, am at the mother's breast with the little child, Swim with the swimmers, wrestle with wrestlers, march in line with the firemen, and pause, listen, count. I knew a man, a common farmer, the father of five sons, And in them the fathers of sons, and in them the fathers of sons. This man was of wonderful vigor, calmness, beauty of person, The shape of his head, the pale yellow and white of his hair and beard, the immeasurable meaning of his black eyes, the richness and breadth of his manners, These I used to go and visit him to see, he was wise also, He was six feet tall, he was over eighty years old, his sons were massive, clean, bearded, tan-faced, handsome, They and his daughters loved him, all who saw him loved him, They did not love him by allowance, they loved him with personal love, He drank water only, the blood show'd like scarlet through the clear-brown skin of his face, He was a frequent gunner and fisher, he sail'd his boat himself, he had a fine one presented to him by a ship-joiner, he had fowling-pieces presented to him by men that loved him, When he went with his five sons and many grand-sons to hunt or fish, you would pick him out as the most beautiful and vigorous of the gang, You would wish long and long to be with him, you would wish to sit by him in the boat that you and he might touch each other. I have perceiv'd that to be with those I like is enough, To stop in company with the rest at evening is enough, To be surrounded by beautiful, curious, breathing, laughing flesh is enough, To pass among them or touch any one, or rest my arm ever so lightly round his or her neck for a moment, what is this then? I do not ask any more delight, I swim in it as in a sea. There is something in staying close to men and women and looking on them, and in the contact and odor of them, that pleases the soul well, All things please the soul, but these please the soul well. This is the female form, A divine nimbus exhales from it from head to foot, It attracts with fierce undeniable attraction, I am drawn by its breath as if I were no more than a helpless vapor, all falls aside but myself and it, Books, art, religion, time, the visible and solid earth, and what was expected of heaven or fear'd of hell, are now consumed, Mad filaments, ungovernable shoots play out of it, the response likewise ungovernable, Hair, bosom, hips, bend of legs, negligent falling hands all diffused, mine too diffused, Ebb stung by the flow and flow stung by the ebb, love-flesh swelling and deliciously aching, Limitless limpid jets of love hot and enormous, quivering jelly of love, white-blow and delirious juice, Bridegroom night of love working surely and softly into the prostrate dawn, Undulating into the willing and yielding day, Lost in the cleave of the clasping and sweet-flesh'd day. This the nucleus--after the child is born of woman, man is born of woman, This the bath of birth, this the merge of small and large, and the outlet again. Be not ashamed women, your privilege encloses the rest, and is the exit of the rest, You are the gates of the body, and you are the gates of the soul. The female contains all qualities and tempers them, She is in her place and moves with perfect balance, She is all things duly veil'd, she is both passive and active, She is to conceive daughters as well as sons, and sons as well as daughters. As I see my soul reflected in Nature, As I see through a mist, One with inexpressible completeness, sanity, beauty, See the bent head and arms folded over the breast, the Female I see. The male is not less the soul nor more, he too is in his place, He too is all qualities, he is action and power, The flush of the known universe is in him, Scorn becomes him well, and appetite and defiance become him well, The wildest largest passions, bliss that is utmost, sorrow that is utmost become him well, pride is for him, The full-spread pride of man is calming and excellent to the soul, Knowledge becomes him, he likes it always, he brings every thing to the test of himself, Whatever the survey, whatever the sea and the sail he strikes soundings at last only here, (Where else does he strike soundings except here?) The man's body is sacred and the woman's body is sacred, No matter who it is, it is sacred--is it the meanest one in the laborers' gang? Is it one of the dull-faced immigrants just landed on the wharf? Each belongs here or anywhere just as much as the well-off, just as much as you, Each has his or her place in the procession. (All is a procession, The universe is a procession with measured and perfect motion.) Do you know so much yourself that you call the meanest ignorant? Do you suppose you have a right to a good sight, and he or she has no right to a sight? Do you think matter has cohered together from its diffuse float, and the soil is on the surface, and water runs and vegetation sprouts, For you only, and not for him and her? A man's body at auction, (For before the war I often go to the slave-mart and watch the sale,) I help the auctioneer, the sloven does not half know his business. Gentlemen look on this wonder, Whatever the bids of the bidders they cannot be high enough for it, For it the globe lay preparing quintillions of years without one animal or plant, For it the revolving cycles truly and steadily roll'd. In this head the all-baffling brain, In it and below it the makings of heroes. Examine these limbs, red, black, or white, they are cunning in tendon and nerve, They shall be stript that you may see them. Exquisite senses, life-lit eyes, pluck, volition, Flakes of breast-muscle, pliant backbone and neck, flesh not flabby, good-sized arms and legs, And wonders within there yet. Within there runs blood, The same old blood! the same red-running blood! There swells and jets a heart, there all passions, desires, reachings, aspirations, (Do you think they are not there because they are not express'd in parlors and lecture-rooms?) This is not only one man, this the father of those who shall be fathers in their turns, In him the start of populous states and rich republics, Of him countless immortal lives with countless embodiments and enjoyments. How do you know who shall come from the offspring of his offspring through the centuries? (Who might you find you have come from yourself, if you could trace back through the centuries?) A woman's body at auction, She too is not only herself, she is the teeming mother of mothers, She is the bearer of them that shall grow and be mates to the mothers. Have you ever loved the body of a woman? Have you ever loved the body of a man? Do you not see that these are exactly the same to all in all nations and times all over the earth? If any thing is sacred the human body is sacred, And the glory and sweet of a man is the token of manhood untainted, And in man or woman a clean, strong, firm-fibred body, is more beautiful than the most beautiful face. Have you seen the fool that corrupted his own live body? or the fool that corrupted her own live body? For they do not conceal themselves, and cannot conceal themselves. O my body!
