I dare not desert the likes of you in other men and women, nor the likes of the parts of you, I believe the likes of you are to stand or fall with the likes of the soul, (and that they are the soul,) I believe the likes of you shall stand or fall with my poems, and that they are my poems, Man's, woman's, child's, youth's, wife's, husband's, mother's, father's, young man's, young woman's poems, Head, neck, hair, ears, drop and tympan of the ears, Eyes, eye-fringes, iris of the eye, eyebrows, and the waking or sleeping of the lids, Mouth, tongue, lips, teeth, roof of the mouth, jaws, and the jaw-hinges, Nose, nostrils of the nose, and the partition, Cheeks, temples, forehead, chin, throat, back of the neck, neck-slue, Strong shoulders, manly beard, scapula, hind-shoulders, and the ample side-round of the chest, Upper-arm, armpit, elbow-socket, lower-arm, arm-sinews, arm-bones, Wrist and wrist-joints, hand, palm, knuckles, thumb, forefinger, finger-joints, finger-nails, Broad breast-front, curling hair of the breast, breast-bone, breast-side, Ribs, belly, backbone, joints of the backbone, Hips, hip-sockets, hip-strength, inward and outward round, man-balls, man-root, Strong set of thighs, well carrying the trunk above, Leg fibres, knee, knee-pan, upper-leg, under-leg, Ankles, instep, foot-ball, toes, toe-joints, the heel; All attitudes, all the shapeliness, all the belongings of my or your body or of any one's body, male or female, The lung-sponges, the stomach-sac, the bowels sweet and clean, The brain in its folds inside the skull-frame, Sympathies, heart-valves, palate-valves, sexuality, maternity, Womanhood, and all that is a woman, and the man that comes from woman, The womb, the teats, nipples, breast-milk, tears, laughter, weeping, love-looks, love-perturbations and risings, The voice, articulation, language, whispering, shouting aloud, Food, drink, pulse, digestion, sweat, sleep, walking, swimming, Poise on the hips, leaping, reclining, embracing, arm-curving and tightening, The continual changes of the flex of the mouth, and around the eyes, The skin, the sunburnt shade, freckles, hair, The curious sympathy one feels when feeling with the hand the naked meat of the body, The circling rivers the breath, and breathing it in and out, The beauty of the waist, and thence of the hips, and thence downward toward the knees, The thin red jellies within you or within me, the bones and the marrow in the bones, The exquisite realization of health; O I say these are not the parts and poems of the body only, but of the soul, O I say now these are the soul!

Lily and Sam are brother and sister. They like to play with their toys in the living room. One day, they find a big scale in the closet. It is a thing that tells you how heavy you are.

"Let's play with the scale!" Lily says. "I want to see how much I weigh."

"Okay," Sam says. "You go first."

Lily steps on the scale. The scale shows a number. Lily does not know what the number means, but she thinks it is big.

"Wow, you are so heavy!" Sam says. "You weigh more than the sofa!"

Lily feels sad. She does not like being heavy. She thinks Sam is mean.

"No, I don't!" Lily says. "You are just being weird. You weigh more than the fridge!"

Sam laughs. He does not believe Lily. He thinks she is silly.

"No, I don't!" Sam says. "You are just being funny. Let me see how much I weigh."

Sam steps on the scale. The scale shows a different number. Sam does not know what the number means, but he thinks it is small.

"Ha, ha, ha!" Lily says. "You are so light! You weigh less than the cat!"

Sam feels mad. He does not like being light. He thinks Lily is rude.

"No, I don't!" Sam says. "You are just being weird. You weigh less than the feather!"

Lily and Sam start to argue. They call each other weird and funny and mean and rude. They forget to have fun.

Mom hears them from the kitchen. She comes to the living room. She sees them on the scale.

"What are you doing?" Mom asks. "Why are you fighting?"

Lily and Sam stop arguing. They look at Mom. They feel ashamed.

"We are playing with the scale," Lily says. "But we don't know how much we weigh."

"We are trying to guess," Sam says. "But we don't agree."

Mom smiles. She hugs them.

"The scale is not a toy," Mom says. "It is not important how much you weigh. It is important how much you love each other. You are both wonderful and special and beautiful. You are my brother and sister."

Lily and Sam feel happy. They love Mom. They love each other.

"Sorry, Lily," Sam says. "You are not heavy. You are strong."

"Sorry, Sam," Lily says. "You are not light. You are fast."

They hug Mom. They hug each other. They put the scale back in the closet. They play with their toys. They have fun.

Lily and Tom are friends. They like to play with stickers. They have many stickers of animals, stars, flowers and cars. They stick them on their books, bags and toys.

One day, Lily and Tom find a big box of stickers in the park. They are very happy. They open the box and see many shiny stickers. They are gold and silver and glittery. They are very pretty.

"Wow, look at these stickers!" Lily says. "They are so shiny! Can we have some?"

"Yes, let's share them!" Tom says. "We can make labels with them. We can write our names and stick them on our things."

Lily and Tom take some shiny stickers and a marker. They write their names on the stickers. Lily writes L-I-L-Y and Tom writes T-O-M. They stick them on their books, bags and toys. They also stick some shiny stickers on their clothes and faces. They look very funny.

"Look at us!" Lily says. "We are shiny too! We are like stars!"

"Yes, we are!" Tom says. "We are shiny and happy!"

Lily and Tom laugh and hug. They are happy with their shiny stickers and labels. They are happy with their friendship.

name_of_work: Never Shall I Forget by Elie Wiesel
content: Never shall I forget that night, the first night in camp, that turned my life into one long night seven times sealed. Never shall I forget that smoke. Never shall I forget the small faces of the children whose bodies I saw transformed into smoke under a silent sky. Never shall I forget those flames that consumed my faith for ever. Never shall I forget the nocturnal silence that deprived me for all eternity of the desire to live. Never shall I forget those moments that murdered my God and my soul and turned my dreams to ashes. Never shall I forget those things, even were I condemned to live as long as God Himself. Never

Once upon a time, there was a mighty dog named Max. Max loved to play with his ball and take videos with his best friend, a little boy named Tim. They would run, jump, and laugh all day long.

One sunny day, Max and Tim went to the park. They saw a big tree and decided to take a video of their fun day. Tim said, "Max, let's take a video by the tree!" Max barked happily and wagged his tail.

As they took the video, a friendly squirrel came down from the tree. The squirrel wanted to play too! Max, Tim, and the squirrel played together, and they took a video of their new friend. They all had a mighty fun day at the park.

name_of_work: Description of Spring by Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey
content: The soote season, that bud and bloom forth brings, With green hath clad the hill and eke the vale: The nightingale with feathers new she sings; The turtle to her make hath told her tale. Summer is come, for every spray now springs: The hart hath hung his old head on the pale; The buck in brake his winter coat he flings; The fishes flete with new repaired scale. The adder all her slough away she slings; The swift swallow pursueth the flies smale; The busy bee her honey now she mings; Winter is worn that was the flowers' bale. And thus I see among these pleasant things Each care decays, and yet my sorrow springs.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play sports with his friends. They would play soccer, basketball, and baseball. Timmy thought it was so much fun to run, jump, and kick the ball.

One day, Timmy's friends wanted to try a different sport. They wanted to play tennis. Timmy had never played tennis before, but he wanted to try it too. At first, he was not very good, but he practiced every day. Soon, he was able to manage the tennis ball and hit it over the net.

Timmy was so happy that he learned a new sport. He realized that trying something different can be a lot of fun. He continued to play tennis with his friends and they all had a great time together.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toys and stuff them in his toy box. One day, Timmy saw a black cat outside his window. He wanted to pet the cat, so he rushed outside to see it. 

When he got outside, the cat was gone. Timmy looked around for the cat, but he couldn't find it. He felt sad because he really wanted to pet the black cat. 

The next day, Timmy saw the black cat again. This time, he didn't rush outside. Instead, he slowly walked towards the cat and softly said, "Here kitty, kitty." The black cat came to Timmy and he was so happy. He petted the cat gently and it purred loudly. From that day on, Timmy and the black cat were the best of friends.

name_of_work: Bartow Black by Timothy Thomas Fortune
content: 'Twas when the Proclamation came,-- Far in the sixties back,-- He left his lord, and changed his name To "Mister Bartow Black." He learned to think himself a man, And privileged, you know, To adopt a new and different plan,-- To lay aside the hoe. He took the lead in politics, And handled all the "notes,"-- For he was up to all the tricks That gather in the votes; For when the war came to a close And negroes "took a stand," Young Bartow with the current rose, The foremost in command. His voice upon the "stump" was heard; He "Yankeedom" did prate; The "carpet-bagger" he revered; The Southerner did hate. He now was greater than the lord Who used to call him slave, For he was on the "County Board," With every right to rave. But this amazing run of luck Was far too good to stand; And soon the chivalrous "Ku-Klux" Rose in the Southern land. Then Bartow got a little note,-- 'Twas very queerly signed,-- It simply told him not to vote, Or be to death resigned. Young Bartow thought this little game Was very fine and nice To bring his courage rare to shame And knowledge of justice. "What right have they to think I fear?" He to himself did say. "Dare they presume that I do care How loudly they do bray? "This is my home, and here I die, Contending for my right! Then let them come! My colors fly! I'm ready now to fight! "Let those who think that Bartow Black,-- An office-holder, too!-- Will to the cowards show his back, Their vain presumption rue!" Bartow pursued his office game, And made the money, too, But home at nights he wisely came And played the husband true. When they had got their subject tame, And well-matured their plan, They at the hour of midnight came, And armed was every man! They numbered fifty Southern sons, And masked was every face; And Winfield rifles were their guns,-- You could that plainly trace. One Southern brave did have a key, An entrance quick to make; They entered all; but meek, you see, Their victim not to wake! They reached his room! He was in bed,-- His wife was by his side! They struck a match above his head,-- His eyes he opened wide! Poor Bartow could not reach his gun, Though quick his arm did stretch, For twenty bullets through him spun, That stiffly laid the wretch. And then they rolled his carcass o'er, And filled both sides with lead; And then they turned it on the floor, And shot away his head! Ere Black his bloody end did meet His wife had swooned away; The Southern braves did now retreat,-- There was no need to stay!

name_of_work: A Tiger in the Zoo by Leslie Norris
content: He stalks in his vivid stripes The few steps of his cage, On pads of velvet quiet, In his quiet rage. He should be lurking in shadow, Sliding through long grass Near the water hole Where plump deer pass. He should be snarling around houses At the jungle's edge, Baring his white fangs, his claws, Terrorising the village! But he's locked in a concrete cell, His strength behind bars, Stalking the length of his cage, Ignoring visitors. He hears the last voice at night, The patrolling cars, And stares with his brilliant eyes At the brilliant stars.

name_of_work: The Bangle Sellers by Sarojini Naidu
content: Bangle sellers are we who bear Our shining loads to the temple fair... Who will buy these delicate, bright Rainbow-tinted circles of light? Lustrous tokens of radiant lives, For happy daughters and happy wives. Some are meet for a maiden's wrist, Silver and blue as the mountain mist, Some are flushed like the buds that dream On the tranquil brow of a woodland stream, Some are aglow wth the bloom that cleaves To the limpid glory of new born leaves Some are like fields of sunlit corn, Meet for a bride on her bridal morn, Some, like the flame of her marriage fire, Or, rich with the hue of her heart's desire, Tinkling, luminous, tender, and clear, Like her bridal laughter and bridal tear. Some are purple and gold flecked grey For she who has journeyed through life midway, Whose hands have cherished, whose love has blest, And cradled fair sons on her faithful breast, And serves her household in fruitful pride, And worships the gods at her husband's side.

name_of_work: Song of the Builders by Mary Oliver
content: On a summer morning I sat down on a hillside to think about God - a worthy pastime. Near me, I saw a single cricket; it was moving the grains of the hillside this way and that way. How great was its energy, how humble its effort. Let us hope it will always be like this, each of us going on in our inexplicable ways building the universe.

Once upon a time, a little girl named Sally was playing in her backyard. She saw a fierce figure passing by. She wondered what it was and asked her mom, "Mommy, what was that figure?"

Her mom replied, "That was a wolf, Sally. He's very fierce and he lives in the forest."

Sally thought of a plan and said, "I can go pass him and show him I'm brave!"

Her mom shook her head and said, "No, that would be very dangerous! Wolves can be very fierce and you would not be safe if you passed him."

Sally was sad, but her mom gave her a hug and said, "We'll find some other way to show off your bravery."

So, Sally and her mom thought of a plan and they decided to go on a hike and explore the forest. Sally was very brave, and she was able to explore the forest without getting hurt. She learned all about the fierce figures passing by and she was proud of herself for being so brave.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside with his friends. They would run and jump and laugh all day long. Timmy had a red coat that he always wore when he played outside. It kept him warm when it was cold.

One day, Timmy and his friends decided to have a race. They all lined up at the starting line, ready to run. Timmy was feeling very competitive. He wanted to win the race more than anything. He ran as fast as he could, but he tripped and fell. He scraped his knee and his coat got dirty.

Timmy was very sad. He couldn't run anymore because his knee hurt. His friends saw that he was hurt and they all stopped to rest with him. They helped him up and walked him back home. Timmy's mom cleaned his knee and washed his coat. Timmy learned that it was okay to be competitive, but it was more important to have friends who cared about him.

Once upon a time, there was a red car named Max. Max loved to drive fast and do loops around the track. One day, Max met a lion named Leo. Leo liked to roar very loudly. 

"Hi Leo," said Max. "Why do you like to roar so much?"

"I roar to show everyone that I am big and strong," replied Leo.

Max thought for a moment and then said, "I like to do loops to show everyone that I am fast and brave."

Leo smiled and said, "We are both very good at something. Let's be friends and show everyone what we can do together!"

Max and Leo became best friends and would often do loops and roar together. They were very happy and everyone could see that they were the best of friends.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who felt very lonely. No one wanted to play with her, so she just sat alone by herself. She wished she could find someone to talk to. 

One day, she decided to take a walk. As she was walking, she came to a big tree and she saw a bird perched on one of its branches. The little girl said "hello". 

The bird looked at her and chirped. She was excited that the bird had answered her. They started to talk and became friends. The bird told the little girl that it liked to snack on nuts and berries. 

The little girl was so happy to have a new friend that she went to the store and bought the bird some snacks. The bird was so thankful and they kept talking until the sun began to set. From then on, the little girl knew she was never alone.

Lily and Ben were best friends. They liked to play in the park and share their toys. One day, Lily found a shiny stone in the grass. It was blue and sparkly, like the sky. She put it in her pocket and showed it to Ben.

"Wow, what a pretty stone!" Ben said. "Can I see it?"

Lily nodded and gave him the stone. Ben held it in his hand and admired it. He liked it very much. He wanted to keep it for himself.

"Can I have it?" he asked Lily. "Please?"

Lily shook her head. "No, Ben. It is mine. I found it. It is rare and I care for it."

Ben frowned. He did not like Lily's answer. He wanted the stone more than anything. He thought of a plan. He pretended to give the stone back to Lily, but he dropped it on the ground instead. Then he said, "Oops, I'm sorry. I dropped it. Let me help you find it."

Lily bent down and looked for the stone. She could not see it in the grass. She was worried. She loved her stone. She hoped it was not lost.

Ben saw the stone behind a flower. He quickly picked it up and put it in his pocket. He smiled. He had the stone now. He was happy.

He said to Lily, "I can't find it, Lily. Maybe it rolled away. I'm sorry. Let's go play something else."

Lily was sad. She did not want to play. She wanted her stone. She felt something was wrong. She looked at Ben. She saw a bulge in his pocket. She realized what he had done.

She said to Ben, "Ben, you took my stone. You lied to me. You are not my friend. Give it back to me. Now!"

Ben was scared. He knew he had been caught. He knew he had been bad. He did not want to lose Lily's friendship. He felt sorry.

He said to Lily, "Lily, I'm sorry. I was wrong. I was greedy. I should not have taken your stone. Here, take it back. It is yours. Please forgive me."

Lily took the stone from Ben. She held it in her hand and felt happy. She still liked the stone, but she liked Ben more. She knew he had made a mistake, but he had said sorry. She decided to forgive him.

She said to Ben, "Ben, thank you for giving me back my stone. I forgive you. You are still my friend. But don't do that again. OK?"

Ben nodded. He felt relieved. He hugged Lily and said, "Lily, thank you for forgiving me. You are a good friend. I won't do that again. I promise."

Lily and Ben smiled. They put the stone in Lily's pocket and went to play. They learned a lesson. They learned to be honest and to share. They learned to care for each other. They were happy.

It's like living in a light bulb, with the leaves Like filaments and the sky a shell of thin, transparent glass Enclosing the late heaven of a summer day, a canopy Of incandescent blue above the dappled sunlight golden on the grass. I took the train back from Poughkeepsie to New York And in the Port Authority, there at the Suburban Transit window, She asked, "Is this the bus to Princeton?"--which it was. "Do you know Geoffrey Love?" I said I did. She had the blondest hair, Which fell across her shoulders, and a dress of almost phosphorescent blue. She liked Ayn Rand. We went down to the Village for a drink, Where I contrived to miss the last bus to New Jersey, and at 3 a.m. we Walked around and found a cheap hotel I hadn't enough money for And fooled around on its dilapidated couch. An early morning bus (She'd come to see her brother), dinner plans and missed connections And a message on his door about the Jersey shore. Next day A summer dormitory room, my roommates gone: "Are you," she asked, "A hedonist?" I guessed so. Then she had to catch her plane. Sally--Sally Roche. She called that night from Florida, And then I never heard from her again. I wonder where she is now, Who she is now. That was thirty-seven years ago. And I'm too old to be surprised again. The days are open, Life conceals no depths, no mysteries, the sky is everywhere, The leaves are all ablaze with light, the blond light Of a summer afternoon that made me think again of Sally's hair.

name_of_work: Rubaiyat XII: A Book of Verses underneath the Bough by Omar Khayyam
content: A Book of Verses underneath the Bough, A Jug of Wine, A Loaf of Bread--and Thou Beside me singing in the Wilderness-- Oh, Wilderness were Paradise enow!

Bob was a big kid. He could carry lots of things. His nose was always sniffing for something new.

One day, Bob went to the park with his dad. He saw a great big kite in the sky. "Hey Dad," said Bob, "Can I carry the kite?"

His dad smiled. "Sure," he said. He gave Bob the string and said, "Carry this and don't let go!"

Bob held the string with his two hands. He ran and skipped around the park, feeling the kite bounce behind him. As his nose guided the way, the kite flew high in the sky.

Bob laughed and shouted, "This is a great adventure!"

Anna and Ben like to cook with Mom. They help her make soup and bread. They put carrots, potatoes and chicken in a big pot. They mix flour, water and yeast in a bowl. Mom says they are good helpers.

But sometimes they are messy too. They spill water on the floor. They drop flour on the table. They splash soup on their clothes. Mom says they need to be careful. She gives them a cloth to clean up.

When the soup and bread are ready, they put them on a tray. They want to surprise Dad, who is working in his room. They walk slowly and quietly to the door. They say, "Shh, don't make noise."

But then, Ben trips on a toy. He falls down and the tray flies in the air. The soup and bread land on the floor, on the wall, on the door. They make a big mess. Dad opens the door and sees them. He says, "Oh no, what happened?"

Anna and Ben start to cry. They say, "We are sorry, Dad. We wanted to cook for you. But we made a mess. We are bad cooks."

Dad hugs them and says, "Don't cry, my loves. You are not bad cooks. You are sweet and kind. You tried to make me happy. I appreciate your effort. But next time, please be more careful. And use a pass to carry the tray. It is safer and easier."

Mom comes and sees the mess too. She says, "Oh dear, what a disaster. But don't worry, we can clean it up. And we can cook again. We have more food in the fridge. And we have each other. That is what matters most."

They all smile and hug. They say, "We love you, Mom. We love you, Dad. We love to cook with you."

Clustering atop a leggy stem ten elf green bodices tapered down to blown about yellow pinafores. Near the ground a mob of blotched leaves, belching and gulping, stiff with liquor, watched constellations kink and bend and languages drift from grammar to grammar. Sister Mary's favourite flower cast a light on all the gougers that she coaxed, effing and blinding, to various degrees of joined-up writing. One great arching cadence glosses the world as a double spiral speaks to itself with epochs for clauses root shoot and flower stitching together the heavens and the earth

Once upon a time, there was a tidy garden. It was full of flowers and butterflies. One day, a little girl named Kate came to visit. She looked around and saw how neat and tidy the garden was.

Kate said to the garden, "Thank you for being so tidy."

The garden said, "You're welcome. I always make sure to keep everything neat and clean."

Kate looked around and noticed a little red plant in a corner. "What's that?" she asked.

The garden said, "It's a surprise. You'll see when it blooms."

Throughout the spring, Kate watched the little red plant. One day, it finally bloomed into a beautiful flower! Kate gasped in amazement.

The garden said, "That's what you get when you keep a garden tidy. Surprises blossoming all around you!"

name_of_work: The Lammas Hireling by Ian Duhig
content: After the fair, I'd still a light heart and a heavy purse, he struck so cheap. And cattle doted on him: in his time mine only dropped heifers, fat as cream. Yields doubled. I grew fond of company that knew when to shut up. Then one night, disturbed from dreams of my dear late wife, I hunted down her torn voice to his pale form. Stock-still in the light from the dark lantern, stark-naked but for one bloody boot of fox-trap, I knew him a warlock, a cow with leather horns. To go into the hare gets you muckle sorrow, the wisdom runs, muckle care. I levelled and blew the small hour through his heart. The moon came out. By its yellow witness I saw him fur over like a stone mossing. His lovely head thinned. His top lip gathered. His eyes rose like bread. I carried him in a sack that grew lighter at every step and dropped him from a bridge. There was no splash. Now my herd's elf-shot. I don't dream but spend my nights casting ball from half-crowns and my days here. Bless me Father for I have sinned. It has been an hour since my last confession.

Mommy was in the kitchen making dinner and heard three year old Hannah playing in the living room.

"Mom!" shouted Hannah, "Can you come play with me?"

Mommy smiled and said, "What are you playing?"

"I'm playing match," said Hannah, "I want you to stay and play with me!"

Mommy saw how eager Hannah was, so she decided to stay and play with her.

Hannah carefully put all the pieces of the match puzzle on the table. Mommy smiled and started picking them up one by one and put them in the right places. Hannah was very eager to help Mommy, so she grabbed every piece she could find and helped.

After a while, Mommy and Hannah had built the puzzle together.

"We did it!" cried Hannah, jumping up and down with joy.

Mommy hugged her tight and said, "That was fun, wasn't it? Let's do it again soon!"

Lila and Tom were playing in the big house. They liked to find new rooms and hide from each other. One day, they saw a door that they had never seen before. It was in the hall, next to the stairs. It had a sign that said "Do not enter".

"What is in there?" Lila asked.

"I don't know. Let's see." Tom said. He opened the door and looked inside. He saw a big chamber with many things. There were books, toys, paintings, and statues. Some of them looked very old and some of them looked very new.

"Wow, this is cool!" Tom said. He walked into the chamber and picked up a toy car. "Look, Lila, this car can move by itself!"

Lila followed him and looked around. She saw a doll that looked like a princess. She reached for it, but then she noticed something. The doll had a button on its back. She pressed it and the doll started to talk.

"Hello, I am a fake princess. I am not real. I am here to trick you. If you stay in this chamber, you will be trapped forever. Ha ha ha!"

Lila was scared. She dropped the doll and ran to Tom. "Tom, we have to go! This is a bad place! The things here are fake and they want to hurt us!"

Tom heard the doll's voice and saw Lila's face. He dropped the car and ran to the door. But the door was locked. They tried to open it, but they could not. They banged on it and shouted for help, but no one heard them.

They were stuck in the chamber with the fake things. They hugged each other and cried. They wished they had never entered the door.

Max was a 3 year old boy. One day he was playing outside in the garden when he saw something in the grass. It was an ordinary cloth. He walked over and picked it up. Max shook it and watched it spring back into shape. 

He used the cloth to make a pretend cape and flew around the garden. Max used the cloth to make a hat and put it on his head. He even put a rock inside the cloth and pretended it was a bag of stones. 

Max had so much fun with the ordinary cloth! He used it to play all kinds of pretend games. Max shook the cloth and held it up high. He used it to play imaginary games. 

Max had a wonderful time playing with the ordinary cloth. It was such a great way to keep him entertained while playing in the garden.

name_of_work: Go, Lovely Rose by Edmund Waller
content: Go, lovely rose! Tell her that wastes her time and me, That now she knows, When I resemble her to thee, How sweet and fair she seems to be. Tell her that's young, And shuns to have her graces spied, That hadst thou sprung In deserts, where no men abide, Thou must have uncommended died. Small is the worth Of beauty from the light retired; Bid her come forth, Suffer herself to be desired, And not blush so to be admired. Then die! that she The common fate of all things rare May read in thee; How small a part of time they share That are so wondrous sweet and fair!

name_of_work: I Saw From the Beach by Thomas Moore
content: I saw from the beach, when the morning was shining, A bark o'er the waters move gloriously on; I came when the sun o'er that beach was declining, The bark was still there, but the waters were gone. And such is the fate of our life's early promise, So passing the spring-tide of joy we have known; Each wave that we danced on at morning ebbs from us, And leaves us, at eve, on the bleak shore alone. Oh, who would not welcome that moment's returning When passion first waked a new life through his frame, And his soul, like the wood that grows precious in burning, Gave out all its sweets to love's exquisite flame.

Once there was a small girl. She was only three years old. She had a microphone and she loved to poke it and make noise. One day, she poked the microphone too hard and it hurt her. She started to cry. Her mom saw what had happened and came to help. She gave the little girl a hug and said she was sorry it hurt. Then she took the little girl and the microphone outside to play. They sang and danced and even used the microphone to talk to each other! The little girl was so happy that the microphone didn't hurt anymore.

Sara loves ponies. She likes to visit the farm and feed them carrots and apples. She has a favorite pony, Brownie, who has a soft brown coat and a long mane. Sara likes to brush Brownie and give him hugs.

One day, Sara goes to the farm with her mom and dad. She brings a big bag of carrots and apples for Brownie. She runs to the fence and calls his name. But Brownie does not come. Sara sees another girl with a pink dress and a bow in her hair. The girl is feeding Brownie carrots and apples from her hand. Brownie is eating them and nuzzling her.

Sara feels sad and angry. She wants to feed Brownie, not the girl. She says, "Hey, that's my pony! Go away!"

The girl looks at Sara and says, "No, he's my pony! I'm his friend. You go away!"

Sara and the girl start to argue. They pull Brownie's mane and try to push each other away. Brownie does not like this. He neighs and shakes his head. He does not want to be fed by anyone. He wants to be left alone.

The farmer hears the noise and comes to see what is wrong. He sees Sara and the girl fighting over Brownie. He says, "Stop it, both of you! You are scaring Brownie. He is not your pony. He is a farm pony. He belongs to everyone. You have to share him and be nice to him. If you want to feed him, you have to take turns and be gentle. Do you understand?"

Sara and the girl nod. They feel sorry for making Brownie unhappy. They say sorry to each other and to Brownie. They decide to be friends and feed Brownie together. They give him carrots and apples and stroke his coat. Brownie feels happy again. He licks their hands and lets them ride on his back. Sara and the girl smile and laugh. They have fun with Brownie. They learn to share and be kind.

name_of_work: The Fair Singer by Andrew Marvell
content: To make a final conquest of all me, Love did compose so sweet an enemy, In whom both beauties to my death agree, Joining themselves in fatal harmony; That while she with her eyes my heart does bind, She with her voice might captivate my mind. I could have fled from one but singly fair, My disentangled soul itself might save, Breaking the curled trammels of her hair. But how should I avoid to be her slave, Whose subtle art invisibly can wreath My fetters of the very air I breathe? It had been easy fighting in some plain, Where victory might hang in equal choice, But all resistance against her is vain, Who has th'advantage both of eyes and voice, And all my forces needs must be undone, She having gained both the wind and sun.

There were two friends yesterday. One was a bossy girl and the other was a little boy. The bossy girl wanted to own all the toys in their room so she yelled at the little boy. "You can't play with my toys, they all belong to me!"

But the little boy was very clever and came up with an idea. "We can take turns," he said, "If you own them one day, then I can own them for the next."

The bossy girl thought about this for a moment and then slowly smiled. She agreed and from then on they shared the toys. They had lots of fun playing together yesterday.

Soldiers are citizens of death's grey land, Drawing no dividend from time's to-morrows. In the great hour of destiny they stand, Each with his feuds, and jealousies, and sorrows. Soldiers are sworn to action; they must win Some flaming, fatal climax with their lives. Soldiers are dreamers; when the guns begin They think of firelit homes, clean beds and wives. I see them in foul dug-outs, gnawed by rats, And in the ruined trenches, lashed with rain, Dreaming of things they did with balls and bats, And mocked by hopeless longing to regain Bank-holidays, and picture shows, and spats, And going to the office in the train.

Sara and Ben were playing in the park. They liked to slide, swing and run. They saw a big tent with a zipper. It was green and yellow. It looked mysterious.

"Who lives in the tent?" Sara asked.

"I don't know. Maybe a clown or a magician," Ben said.

"Can we go inside and see?" Sara said.

Ben was not sure. He looked around. He did not see anyone near the tent.

"OK, but we have to be quiet and careful," he said.

They walked to the tent. They pulled the zipper. It made a loud noise. They opened the tent. They saw a lot of toys and books. They also saw a big dog. It was brown and white. It had a red collar. It barked at them.

"Wow, look at all the stuff!" Sara said.

"Shh, the dog might bite us!" Ben said.

They heard a voice. It was a woman. She sounded angry.

"Hey, what are you doing in my tent? Get out of here!" she said.

She came out of the tent. She had long hair and a hat. She looked like a hippie.

"Sorry, we were just curious," Sara said.

"Yeah, we didn't mean to bother you," Ben said.

They ran out of the tent. They ran back to their mom. She was sitting on a bench. She had a book and a sandwich.

"Mom, we saw a mysterious tent and a big dog and a hippie lady!" Sara said.

"Really? That sounds exciting. But you shouldn't go into other people's tents without permission. That's rude and dangerous," mom said.

She hugged them and gave them a bite of her sandwich.

"We know, mom. We're sorry. We won't do it again," Ben said.

Mom smiled and kissed them.

"I love you, my little adventurers. You remind me of myself when I was young," she said.

name_of_work: Artist's Life by Ella Wheeler Wilcox
content: Of all the waltzes the great Strauss wrote, Mad with melody, rhythm--rife From the very first to the final note, Give me his "Artist's Life"! It stirs my blood to my finger ends, Thrills me and fills me with vague unrest, And all that is sweetest and saddest blends Together within my breast. It brings back that night in the dim arcade, In love's sweet morning and life's best prime, When the great brass orchestra played and played, And set our thoughts to rhyme. It brings back that Winter of mad delights, Of leaping pulses and tripping feet, And those languid moon-washed Summer nights When we heard the band in the street. It brings back rapture and glee and glow, It brings back passion and pain and strife, And so of all the waltzes I know, Give me the "Artist's Life." For it is so full of the dear old time-- So full of the dear friends I knew. And under its rhythm, and lilt, and rhyme, I am always finding--you.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to listen to the radio. One day, he asked his mommy for a new radio for his birthday. 

On his birthday, Timmy's mommy gifted him a brand new radio. Timmy was so happy and hugged his mommy tightly. "Thank you mommy, you're so gifted!" Timmy exclaimed.

As Timmy was listening to his new radio, he noticed that the lights on it would blink on and off. "Mommy, why does the radio blink?" Timmy asked. "That's just how it works, sweetie," his mommy replied. 

From that day on, Timmy would always listen to his radio and watch the lights blink. He loved his new gifted radio and was grateful to have such a wonderful mommy.

name_of_work: Portrait of Girl with Comic Book by Phyllis McGinley
content: Thirteen's no age at all. Thirteen is nothing. It is not wit, or powder on the face, Or Wednesday matinees, or misses' clothing, Or intellect, or grace, Twelve has its tribal customs. But thirteen Is neither boys in battered cars nor dolls, Not Sara Crewe or movie magazine, Or pennants on the walls. Thirteen keeps diaries and tropical fish (A month, at most); scorns jump-ropes in the spring; Could not, would fortune grant it, name its wish; Wants nothing, everything; Has secrets from itself, friends it despises; Admits none of the terrors it feels; Owns half a hundred masks but no disguises; And walks upon its heels. Thirteen's anomalous - not that, not this: Not folded bud, or wave that laps a shore, Or moth proverbial from the chrysalis. Is the one age defeats the metaphor. Is not a town, like childhood, strongly walled But easily surrounded; is no city. Nor, quitted once, can it be quite recalled - Not even with pity.

name_of_work: The Black Lace Fan My Mother Gave Me by Eavan Boland
content: It was the first gift he ever gave her, buying it for five francs in the Galeries in pre-war Paris. It was stifling. A starless drought made the nights stormy. They stayed in the city for the summer. They met in cafes. She was always early. He was late. That evening he was later. They wrapped the fan. He looked at his watch. She looked down the Boulevard des Capucines. She ordered more coffee. She stood up. The streets were emptying. The heat was killing. She thought the distance smelled of rain and lightning. These are wild roses, appliqued on silk by hand, darkly picked, stitched boldly, quickly. The rest is tortoiseshell and has the reticent, clear patience of its element. It is a worn-out, underwater bullion and it keeps, even now, an inference of its violation. The lace is overcast as if the weather it opened for and offset had entered it. The past is an empty cafe terrace. An airless dusk before thunder. A man running. And no way to know what happened then -- none at all -- unless, of course, you improvise: The blackbird on this first sultry morning, in summer, finding buds, worms, fruit, feels the heat. Suddenly she puts out her wing -- the whole, full, flirtatious span of it.

name_of_work: Naming of Parts by Henry Reed
content: Today we have naming of parts. Yesterday, We had daily cleaning. And tomorrow morning, We shall have what to do after firing. But today, Today we have naming of parts. Japonica Glistens likecoral in all the neighboring gardens, And today we have naming of parts. This is the lower sling swivel. And this Is the upper sling swivel, whose use you will see, When you are given your slings. And this is the piling swivel, Which in your case you have not got. The branches Hold in the gardens their silent, eloquent gestures, Which in our case we have not got. This is the safety-catch, which is always released With an easy flick of the thumb. And please do not let me See anyone using his finger. You can do it quite easy If you have any strength in your thumb. The blossoms Are fragile and motionless, never letting anyone see Any of them using their finger. And this you can see is the bolt. The purpose of this Is to open the breech, as you see. We can slide it Rapidly backwards and forwards: we call this Easing the spring. And rapidly backwards and forwards The early bees are assaulting and fumbling the flowers: They call it easing the Spring. They call it easing the Spring: it is perfectly easy If you have any strength in your thumb: like the bolt, And the breech, the cocking-piece, and the point of balance, Which in our case we have not got; and the almond blossom Silent in all of the gardens and the bees going backwards and forwards, For today we have the naming of parts.

name_of_work: Author Never Dies by Riyas Qurana
content: That there is no bird in the in the text written on a bird You need not feel amazed. For our need For our urgency We cannot compel the bird to come at once It may be having some important chores Or the texts might surface as suits their whims and fancies There are no rules that dictate that we should place the bird inside the text and read it. It is not proper to have it caged inside the text. If it likes your way of reading sometimes the possibility of it getting into the text willingly comes to be. Seeing some bird flying high please don't conclude that it should be the one to stay within the text. That one which hovers so closely going round the text- even that needn't be the bird for the text. Not just of the bird inside the text I wrote causing it to exit too. True, away from anyone's hear Wandering in silence shrilling silently wanders the bird of the text.

name_of_work: Morning on the Sinnecock by Olivia Ward Bush-Bank
content: The rising sun had crowned the hills, And added beauty to the plain; O grand and wondrous spectacle! That only nature could explain. I stood within a leafy grove, And gazed around in blissful awe; The sky appeared one mass of blue, That seemed to spread from sea to shore. Far as the human eye could see, Were stretched the fields of waving corn. Soft on my ear the warbling birds Were heralding the birth of morn. While here and there a cottage quaint Seemed to repose in quiet ease Amid the trees, whose leaflets waved And fluttered in the passing breeze. O morning hour! so dear thy joy, And how I longed for thee to last; But e'en thy fading into day Brought me an echo of the past. 'Twas this,--how fair my life began; How pleasant was its hour of dawn; But, merging into sorrow's day, Then beauty faded with the morn.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who lived in a house with her mommy and daddy. One day, Lily's mommy asked her to go upstairs and tidy her room. Lily was very lazy, and didn't want to do it. 

"I don't want to go upstairs," Lily said. 

"But you need to tidy your room," her mommy replied. 

Lily felt ashamed because she had made a mess, so she went upstairs to clean. While she was cleaning, she found an old toy that she used to play with. She admired how pretty it was and decided to keep it. 

When Lily's mommy came to check on her, she saw that Lily had cleaned her room and found her old toy. 

"I'm so proud of you, Lily!" her mommy said. 

Lily felt happy that her mommy was proud of her and promised to always keep her room clean.

Lily and Ben were camping with their mom and dad in the woods. They had a big tent where they slept at night. They liked to explore the trees and the flowers and the animals during the day.

One day, they saw a small bird with a broken wing on the ground. It looked sad and scared. Lily and Ben wanted to help the bird. They ran to their mom and dad and told them what they saw.

"Mom, dad, there is a bird that is suffering. It has a bad wing and it cannot fly. Can we help it?" Lily asked.

"Let's go and see, but we have to be very gentle and careful. The bird might be afraid of us," dad said.

They followed Lily and Ben to where the bird was. Mom took a soft cloth and wrapped it around the bird. She lifted it up and held it close to her chest. The bird made a quiet sound.

"Shh, it's okay, little bird. We are not going to hurt you. We are going to take you to our tent and make you feel better," mom said.

Lily and Ben smiled. They walked with mom and dad to their tent. They made a cozy nest for the bird with some leaves and grass. They gave it some water and seeds. The bird ate and drank and looked more calm.

"Thank you for helping the bird, mom and dad. You are very kind," Lily said.

"Yes, thank you. Maybe the bird will get better soon and fly again," Ben said.

They watched the bird for a while. Then they cuddled with mom and dad in their sleeping bags. They fell asleep, dreaming of the bird and the woods.

Nina was so excited! It was her first time riding a bike. Her sister had shown her how to do it. She said Nina couldn't be afraid and had to be gentle with the bike. 

Nina tried it. She pushed the pedals and the bike began to zoom. She zoomed around and around the garden, laughing with joy. She could feel the wind in her face.

Nina's sister cheered, "super Nina! You can do it!"

Nina was so happy, she zoomed even faster! She kept going around in circles until she suddenly went too fast and fell off.

Nina's sister ran to her. She was gentle and said, "Are you okay, Nina? It's okay if you fall."

Nina nodded and smiled. Her sister helped her back on the bike and said, "Try to be gentle and you'll be able to zoom around like a pro!"

So, Nina tried again and soon she was able to zoom around like a pro! She was so proud of herself. 

The End.

name_of_work: On the Beach at Night Alone by Walt Whitman
content: On the beach at night alone, As the old mother sways her to and fro singing her husky song, As I watch the bright stars shining, I think a thought of the clef of the universes and of the future. A vast similitude interlocks all, All spheres, grown, ungrown, small, large, suns, moons, planets, All distances of place however wide, All distances of time, all inanimate forms, All souls, all living bodies though they be ever so different, or in different worlds, All gaseous, watery, vegetable, mineral processes, the fishes, the brutes, All nations, colors, barbarisms, civilizations, languages, All identities that have existed or may exist on this globe, or any globe, All lives and deaths, all of the past, present, future, This vast similitude spans them, and always has spann'd, And shall forever span them and compactly hold and enclose them.

Once upon a time, there was a little bird named Bob. Bob liked to fly in the calm sky. One day, Bob's friend, Cat, had a message for him. Cat said, "Bob, I need help. Will you allow me to come with you?"

Bob said, "Yes, Cat. I will allow you to come with me." So, Bob and Cat went to find the message. They flew and walked until they found a big tree.

In the tree, they found the message. It was a happy message from their friend, Dog. Dog said, "Hi, Bob and Cat! Let's play together!" Bob and Cat were very happy. They went to play with Dog, and they all had a fun day.

name_of_work: The Blessed Damozel by Dante Gabriel Rossetti
content: THE blessed Damozel lean'd out From the gold bar of Heaven: Her blue grave eyes were deeper much Than a deep water, even. She had three lilies in her hand, And the stars in her hair were seven. Her robe, ungirt from clasp to hem, No wrought flowers did adorn, But a white rose of Mary's gift On the neck meetly worn; And her hair, lying down her back, Was yellow like ripe corn. Herseem'd she scarce had been a day One of God's choristers; The wonder was not yet quite gone From that still look of hers; Albeit, to them she left, her day Had counted as ten years. (To one it is ten years of years: ...Yet now, here in this place, Surely she lean'd o'er me,--her hair Fell all about my face.... Nothing: the Autumn-fall of leaves. The whole year sets apace.) It was the terrace of God's house That she was standing on,-- By God built over the sheer depth In which Space is begun; So high, that looking downward thence, She scarce could see the sun. It lies from Heaven across the flood Of ether, as a bridge. Beneath, the tides of day and night With flame and darkness ridge The void, as low as where this earth Spins like a fretful midge. But in those tracts, with her, it was The peace of utter light And silence. For no breeze may stir Along the steady flight Of seraphim; no echo there, Beyond all depth or height. Heard hardly, some of her new friends, Playing at holy games, Spake gentle-mouth'd, among themselves, Their virginal chaste names; And the souls, mounting up to God, Went by her like thin flames. And still she bow'd herself, and stoop'd Into the vast waste calm; Till her bosom's pressure must have made The bar she lean'd on warm, And the lilies lay as if asleep Along her bended arm. From the fixt lull of Heaven, she saw Time, like a pulse, shake fierce Through all the worlds. Her gaze still strove, In that steep gulf, to pierce The swarm; and then she spoke, as when The stars sang in their spheres. 'I wish that he were come to me, For he will come,' she said. 'Have I not pray'd in solemn Heaven? On earth, has he not pray'd? Are not two prayers a perfect strength? And shall I feel afraid? 'When round his head the aureole clings, And he is clothed in white, I'll take his hand, and go with him To the deep wells of light, And we will step down as to a stream And bathe there in God's sight. 'We two will stand beside that shrine, Occult, withheld, untrod, Whose lamps tremble continually With prayer sent up to God; And where each need, reveal'd, expects Its patient period. 'We two will lie i' the shadow of That living mystic tree Within whose secret growth the Dove Sometimes is felt to be, While every leaf that His plumes touch Saith His name audibly. 'And I myself will teach to him,-- I myself, lying so,-- The songs I sing here; which his mouth Shall pause in, hush'd and slow, Finding some knowledge at each pause, And some new thing to know.' (Alas! to her wise simple mind These things were all but known Before: they trembled on her sense,-- Her voice had caught their tone. Alas for lonely Heaven! Alas For life wrung out alone! Alas, and though the end were reach'd?... Was thy part understood Or borne in trust? And for her sake Shall this too be found good?-- May the close lips that knew not prayer Praise ever, though they would?) 'We two,' she said, 'will seek the groves Where the lady Mary is, With her five handmaidens, whose names Are five sweet symphonies:-- Cecily, Gertrude, Magdalen, Margaret and Rosalys. 'Circle-wise sit they, with bound locks And bosoms covered; Into the fine cloth, white like flame, Weaving the golden thread, To fashion the birth-robes for them Who are just born, being dead. 'He shall fear, haply, and be dumb. Then I will lay my cheek To his, and tell about our love, Not once abash'd or weak: And the dear Mother will approve My pride, and let me speak. 'Herself shall bring us, hand in hand, To Him round whom all souls Kneel--the unnumber'd solemn heads Bow'd with their aureoles: And Angels, meeting us, shall sing To their citherns and citoles. 'There will I ask of Christ the Lord Thus much for him and me:-- To have more blessing than on earth In nowise; but to be As then we were,--being as then At peace. Yea, verily. 'Yea, verily; when he is come We will do thus and thus: Till this my vigil seem quite strange And almost fabulous; We two will live at once, one life; And peace shall be with us.' She gazed, and listen'd, and then said, Less sad of speech than mild,-- 'All this is when he comes.' She ceased: The light thrill'd past her, fill'd With Angels, in strong level lapse. Her eyes pray'd, and she smiled. (I saw her smile.) But soon their flight Was vague 'mid the poised spheres. And then she cast her arms along The golden barriers, And laid her face between her hands, And wept. (I heard her tears.)

name_of_work: Give All to Love by Ralph Waldo Emerson
content: Give all to love; Obey thy heart; Friends, kindred, days, Estate, good-fame, Plans, credit and the Muse,-- Nothing refuse. 'T is a brave master; Let it have scope: Follow it utterly, Hope beyond hope: High and more high It dives into noon, With wing unspent, Untold intent: But it is a god, Knows its own path And the outlets of the sky. It was never for the mean; It requireth courage stout. Souls above doubt, Valor unbending, It will reward,-- They shall return More than they were, And ever ascending. Leave all for love; Yet, hear me, yet, One word more thy heart behoved, One pulse more of firm endeavor,-- Keep thee to-day, To-morrow, forever, Free as an Arab Of thy beloved. Cling with life to the maid; But when the surprise, First vague shadow of surmise Flits across her bosom young, Of a joy apart from thee, Free be she, fancy-free; Nor thou detain her vesture's hem, Nor the palest rose she flung From her summer diadem. Though thou loved her as thyself, As a self of purer clay, Though her parting dims the day, Stealing grace from all alive; Heartily know, When half-gods go, The gods arrive.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to walk outside and feel the cold air on her face. One day, she went for a walk with her mommy and they came across a big step. Lily's mommy helped her climb up the step and they looked out at the beautiful view. Lily admired the pretty trees and the blue sky. She felt happy and warm inside, even though it was cold outside. After a little while, they climbed back down the step and continued their walk. Lily couldn't stop thinking about how much she admired the view from the step. She knew she wanted to come back and see it again someday.

name_of_work: Waiting at the Window by A. A. Milne
content: These are my two drops of rain Waiting on the window-pane. I am waiting here to see Which the winning one will be. Both of them have different names. One is John and one is James. All the best and all the worst Comes from which of them is first. James has just begun to ooze. He's the one I want to lose. John is waiting to begin. He's the one I want to win. James is going slowly on. Something sort of sticks to John. John is moving off at last. James is going pretty fast. John is rushing down the pane. James is going slow again. James has met a sort of smear. John is getting very near. Is he going fast enough? (James has found a piece of fluff.) John has quickly hurried by. (James was talking to a fly.) John is there, and John has won! Look! I told you! Here's the sun!

name_of_work: If You Forget Me by Pablo Neruda
content: I want you to know one thing. You know how this is: if I look at the crystal moon, at the red branch of the slow autumn at my window, if I touch near the fire the impalpable ash or the wrinkled body of the log, everything carries me to you, as if everything that exists, aromas, light, metals, were little boats that sail toward those isles of yours that wait for me. Well, now, if little by little you stop loving me I shall stop loving you little by little. If suddenly you forget me do not look for me, for I shall already have forgotten you. If you think it long and mad, the wind of banners that passes through my life, and you decide to leave me at the shore of the heart where I have roots, remember that on that day, at that hour, I shall lift my arms and my roots will set off to seek another land. But if each day, each hour, you feel that you are destined for me with implacable sweetness, if each day a flower climbs up to your lips to seek me, ah my love, ah my own, in me all that fire is repeated, in me nothing is extinguished or forgotten, my love feeds on your love, beloved, and as long as you live it will be in your arms without leaving mine.

Once upon a time, there was a little cat named Mittens. Mittens had a long tail that she would often play with. One day, Mittens went on an adventure in the forest. She saw many animals, like birds, squirrels, and rabbits. 

As she was walking, she saw a mysterious creature hiding behind a tree. It was a big, brown bear! Mittens was scared at first, but then she realized that the bear was friendly. They became friends and played together.

Mittens admired the bear's big size and strong muscles. She also loved how the bear's tail was fluffy and brown, just like a teddy bear. Mittens and the bear went on many adventures together, always exploring the forest and having fun. The end.

Yes. I remember Adlestrop-- The name, because one afternoon Of heat the express-train drew up there Unwontedly. It was late June. The steam hissed. Someone cleared his throat. No one left and no one came On the bare platform. What I saw Was Adlestrop--only the name And willows, willow-herb, and grass, And meadowsweet, and haycocks dry, No whit less still and lonely fair Than the high cloudlets in the sky. And for that minute a blackbird sang Close by, and round him, mistier, Farther and farther, all the birds Of Oxfordshire and Gloucestershire.

name_of_work: A Satirical Elegy on the Death of a Late Famous General by Jonathon Swift
content: His Grace! impossible! what dead! Of old age too, and in his bed! And could that mighty warrior fall? And so inglorious, after all! Well, since he's gone, no matter how, The last loud trump must wake him now: And, trust me, as the noise grows stronger, He'd wish to sleep a little longer. And could he be indeed so old As by the newspapers we're told? Threescore, I think, is pretty high; 'Twas time in conscience he should die This world he cumbered long enough; He burnt his candle to the snuff; And that's the reason, some folks think, He left behind so great a stink. Behold his funeral appears, Nor widow's sighs, nor orphan's tears, Wont at such times each heart to pierce, Attend the progress of his hearse. But what of that, his friends may say, He had those honours in his day. True to his profit and his pride, He made them weep before he died. Come hither, all ye empty things, Ye bubbles raised by breath of kings; Who float upon the tide of state, Come hither, and behold your fate. Let pride be taught by this rebuke, How very mean a thing's a Duke; From all his ill-got honours flung, Turned to that dirt from whence he sprung.

I left you in the morning, And in the morning glow, You walked a way beside me To make me sad to go. Do you know me in the gloaming, Gaunt and dusty grey with roaming? Are you dumb because you know me not, Or dumb because you know? All for me? And not a question For the faded flowers gay That could take me from beside you For the ages of a day? They are yours, and be the measure Of their worth for you to treasure, The measure of the little while That I've been long away.

Ben and Sam were brothers who liked to play in the park. One day, they saw a big box under a tree. They ran to the box and opened it. Inside, they found many toys and books and clothes. They were very happy and started to take what they wanted.

But they did not see a sign on the box that said: "These are donations for the poor children. Please do not touch." They were ignorant and did not know what donations or poor meant. They thought the box was a gift for them.

A lady came to the park and saw the boys with the box. She was angry and said: "What are you doing? These are not your things. You are stealing from the poor children. How can you be so selfish and greedy?"

The boys were scared and dropped the things. They tried to run away, but the lady caught them. She looked at their faces and saw that they were dirty and hungry. She felt sorry for them and said: "Are you poor too? Do you have a home and a family?"

The boys nodded and said: "Yes, we have a home and a family, but they are far away. We came here to search for a better life, but we have no money and no friends. We are sorry for taking the things. We did not know they were for the poor children. We thought they were for us."

The lady understood and said: "I see. You are not bad, just ignorant. You need to learn more about the world and how to help others. Come with me, I will take you to a place where you can get some food and clothes and education. Maybe you can also make some friends there."

The boys agreed and followed the lady. They learned that the box was part of a charity project that helped poor children in different countries. They felt ashamed and sorry for what they did. They also learned how to read and write and share and care. They made some friends who were also poor but kind. They realized that they were lucky to have a home and a family, and that they should be grateful and generous. They decided to give back some of the things they took and to help the charity project in any way they could. They became happier and smarter and better. They thanked the lady for teaching them and helping them. They never forgot the lesson they learned from the box.

Sara and Ben were playing in the garden. They liked to look for bugs and put them in a jar. They had a big jar with holes in the lid. They found a cute ladybug with red spots and a green caterpillar with tiny legs. They put them in the jar and watched them crawl.

"Look, they are friends!" Sara said. "They are sharing the leaf."

"No, they are not friends. They are enemies!" Ben said. "The caterpillar wants to eat the leaf and the ladybug wants to stop him. They are fighting!"

Sara and Ben argued. They both wanted the jar. They pulled and pushed. The jar fell on the ground and broke. The ladybug and the caterpillar escaped.

"Oh no!" Sara and Ben cried. "We lost our bugs!"

They felt sad and sorry. They looked at each other. They hugged and said sorry.

"Let's find more bugs," Sara said. "But this time, we will not put them in a jar. We will let them go."

"OK," Ben said. "But we have to be careful. We don't want to hurt them."

They smiled and ran to look for more bugs. They learned to be kind and share. They did not want to fight or surrender. They wanted to play and have fun.

Tom and Lily were playing in the kitchen. They saw a big bag of potatoes on the floor. Tom had an idea.

"Let's make potato people!" he said. "We can use eyes, noses, mouths and hair from the fridge."

Lily liked the idea. She nodded and smiled. They took some potatoes and some food from the fridge. They started to make potato people.

They made a potato with grapes for eyes, a carrot for a nose, a banana for a mouth and cheese for hair. They made another potato with olives for eyes, a pickle for a nose, a tomato for a mouth and lettuce for hair. They made many more potato people. They had fun.

But then Mom came into the kitchen. She saw the mess. She saw the potato people. She was not happy.

"What are you doing?" she asked. "You are wasting food. You are making a mess. You are crazy!"

Tom and Lily looked at Mom. They looked at the potato people. They felt bad.

"We are sorry, Mom," they said. "We were just playing. We wanted to make potato people."

Mom sighed. She was not very angry. She knew they were just kids. She hugged them and said, "I love you, but you have to clean up. And no more potato people, OK?"

Tom and Lily nodded. They said, "OK, Mom. We love you too."

They helped Mom clean up the kitchen. They threw away the potato people. They said goodbye to them. They learned a lesson. They never made potato people again.

Once upon a time, there were two friends called Peter and Sammy. They both wanted to find something exciting to do on the weekend.

Sammy said to Peter: "I've heard about a network that is lots of fun! I recommend we go there this Saturday."

Peter was very excited and said, "Yes let's go!"

So on Saturday, they both got dressed and headed to the network. It was a huge, clumsy place, but they both had fun exploring it. They went on swings, climbed trees, and jumped on trampolines.

At the end of the day, they both agreed it had been a great adventure and they already wanted to go back the next weekend. 

The End.

Once upon a time there was a brave sailor. He had a black hat and black gloves. One day he saw something in the sky. It was a huge black puzzle. The sailor wanted to solve it, so he climbed up a nearby tree to take a closer look.

Suddenly, a voice from the sky said, "Can you solve this puzzle sailor?" The sailor replied, "Yes, I can!"

He thought and thought about the puzzle, and finally he solved it. The sailor was so happy and in return the sky gave him a treasure. He opened the box and found lots and lots of shiny gold coins. 

The sailor smiled and sailed away with his treasure.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim had a big red ball. He played with his ball every day. One day, Tim saw a sack near a tree. Tim was scared, but he wanted to see what was in the sack.

Tim went to the sack and opened it. Inside the sack, he found a wheel. Tim was happy. He took the wheel and played with it. He rolled the wheel and chased it. Tim and the wheel had lots of fun.

Tim was not scared anymore. He played with his ball and the wheel every day. Tim learned that new things can be fun. He was a brave little boy. Tim and his new wheel were the best of friends.

A ball will bounce; but less and less. It's not A light-hearted thing, resents its own resilience. Falling is what it loves, and the earth falls So in our hearts from brilliance, Settles and is forgot. It takes a sky-blue juggler with five red balls To shake our gravity up. Whee, in the air The balls roll around, wheel on his wheeling hands, Learning the ways of lightness, alter to spheres Grazing his finger ends, Cling to their courses there, Swinging a small heaven about his ears. But a heaven is easier made of nothing at all Than the earth regained, and still and sole within The spin of worlds, with a gesture sure and noble He reels that heaven in, Landing it ball by ball, And trades it all for a broom, a plate, a table. Oh, on his toe the table is turning, the broom's Balancing up on his nose, and the plate whirls On the tip of the broom! Damn, what a show, we cry: The boys stamp, and the girls Shriek, and the drum booms And all come down, and he bows and says good-bye. If the juggler is tired now, if the broom stands In the dust again, if the table starts to drop Through the daily dark again, and though the plate Lies flat on the table top, For him we batter our hands Who has won for once over the world's weight.

Once upon a time, there was a generous bird named Blue. Blue lived in a big tree with many vines. Blue liked to help other animals in the forest.

One day, Blue saw a small fire in the forest. The fire began to burn the vines on the trees. Blue knew the fire was bad and the animals needed help. Blue called all of his friends to stop the fire. The animals worked together to put out the fire and save the vines.

After the fire was gone, the animals were happy and thankful for Blue's help. They learned that working together is important. Blue and his friends were safe, and the vines grew back. The forest was beautiful again. The moral of this story is that being generous and helping others can make a big difference.

Once upon a time, there was a big red barn. In the barn, there were many animals. There was a cow, a pig, a horse, and a duck. They all lived happily in the barn.

One sunny day, the animals were talking. The enthusiastic duck said, "Let's play a game outside!" The cow agreed, but the pig and the horse disagreed. The pig said, "I want to stay inside and eat." The horse said, "I want to rest."

So the duck and the cow went outside to play. They had a lot of fun. They played in the sun and splashed in the water. The pig and the horse stayed in the barn. The pig ate and the horse rested.

At the end of the day, the duck and the cow came back to the barn. They told the pig and the horse about their fun day. The pig and the horse felt sad that they missed out. The next day, all the animals agreed to play outside together. They all had a great time and lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time, there was a big boat in the sea. The boat was very blue, like the sky. It was a navy boat. The boat was perfect, with no scratches or bumps.

The boat had a very big job to do. It had to carry lots of things from one place to another. One day, the boat had to carry some big boxes. The boxes were very heavy, and the boat had to be very careful not to split them.

But, as the boat was sailing, a big wave hit it. The wave was so strong that it made the boat split in two! Oh no! The boxes fell into the sea. The boat was not perfect anymore. But, the good news was that everyone was safe.

Lily and Tom are friends. They like to play with cars and trucks. One day, they find a big box in the garage. Inside the box, there are many shiny things. Lily sees a shiny thing that looks like a star. She says, "Look, Tom, a diamond!"

Tom says, "Wow, it is so pretty! Can I hold it?" Lily says, "Yes, but be careful. It is cold and hard." Tom holds the diamond and feels how cold and hard it is. He says, "It is like ice. I wonder where it came from."

Lily says, "Maybe it came from a faraway place. Maybe someone drove a long way to bring it here. Maybe they drove through snow and ice." Tom says, "That sounds fun. I wish we could drive through snow and ice." Lily says, "Me too. Let's pretend we are driving through snow and ice."

They put the diamond in a small car and push it around the garage. They make noises like a car engine and a horn. They pretend they see snowflakes and icicles. They have a lot of fun driving with the diamond. They forget about the other shiny things in the box. They only care about the diamond and their car. They are happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who wanted to fly. She told her mom about it and her mom decided to explain the science behind why she couldn't fly. She took her daughter to the doctor's office to show her an x-ray. 

"See this?" Mom said as she pointed at the x-ray. "Humans can't fly because of all of these bones. We can't make our wings like a bird can."

The little girl's face lit up. "You mean if I had wings like a bird then I could fly?"

Mom smiled. "Yes. But it's very difficult to do. We just have to be happy that birds can fly and people can't."

The little girl thought about it for a few moments. Then she smiled and said, "It's ok. I'm happy that birds can fly. That makes me feel better!"

Mom hugged her daughter and said, "That's a great attitude to have! Remember, it's ok if things are difficult. We just have to keep trying and stay positive."

The little girl nodded and went back to playing, content with her newfound knowledge. 

The moral of the story is that it's ok for things to be difficult, but it's important to stay positive and keep trying.

The little girl was hungry. She saw a bowl of rice on the table and clapped her hands. Her mommy smiled and put the rice on her plate. She clapped her hands again with joy.

The little girl took a spoon and started eating the rice. It was so yummy. She ate and ate until she was full.

After eating all the rice, the little girl clapped her hands one more time. She said â€œYay! I am not hungry anymoreâ€. She was so happy that she had a full stomach. 

Her mommy was very happy too. She took her in her arms and gave her a big hug. They were both happy that the little girl was no longer hungry.

name_of_work: The Buck in the Snow by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: White sky, over the hemlocks bowed with snow, Saw you not at the beginning of evening the antlered buck and his doe Standing in the apple-orchard? I saw them. I saw them suddenly go, Tails up, with long leaps lovely and slow, Over the stone-wall into the wood of hemlocks bowed with snow. Now lies he here, his wild blood scalding the snow. How strange a thing is death, bringing to his knees, bringing to his antlers The buck in the snow. How strange a thing,--a mile away by now, it may be, Under the heavy hemlocks that as the moments pass Shift their loads a little, letting fall a feather of snow-- Life, looking out attentive from the eyes of the doe.

Lily was a little girl who liked to eat celery. She thought celery was crunchy and tasty and good for her. She always asked her mom for celery when she was hungry or bored.

One day, Lily saw a big bunch of celery at the market. She wanted it very much. She asked her mom to buy it for her, but her mom said no. She said they had enough celery at home and they needed to buy other things. Lily was sad and angry. She did not listen to her mom. She sneaked the celery into her bag when her mom was not looking.

When they got home, Lily ran to her room with the celery. She wanted to eat it all by herself. She did not share it with anyone. She did not say thank you to her mom. She did not think about how her mom worked hard to buy food for her.

But Lily did not know that the celery was not fresh. It was old and rotten and had bugs in it. When she bit into it, she felt something slimy and bitter in her mouth. She spit it out and saw a worm on the floor. She screamed and cried. She felt sick and scared. She wished she had listened to her mom.

Her mom heard her scream and came to her room. She saw the celery and the worm and understood what happened. She was not happy with Lily. She scolded her for stealing and being greedy and ungrateful. She took away the celery and threw it in the trash. She told Lily to go to bed without dinner. She said she hoped Lily learned her lesson.

The moral of the story is: Do not take what is not yours. Be happy with what you have. Listen to your mom. She knows what is best for you. Celery is not always charming.

Once, there was a little girl named Sam. She wanted to go to the beach. But she didn't know how. 

So Sam thought and thought. Then she had an idea. She decided to plan. She wanted to make sand on the beach. 

Sam ran to the beach. She scooped up the sand and made a big pile. Then she found some shells and stones and started to decorate the sand. 

It was the most beautiful sand pile ever! Just then, Sam spotted an old lady walking by. The lady looked so sad. 

Sam asked the lady why she was so sad. The lady said that she was very lonely and life had been spoiled. 

Sam smiled and invited her to play in the sand pile. So the two of them played for hours and had the best time! 

At the end of the day, the old lady said goodbye to Sam and told her it was the best day she'd had in a long time. 

Sam was so happy she could help someone. And she was also happy she could plan to make the beach so much more fun!

name_of_work: My Lost Youth by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
content: Often I think of the beautiful town That is seated by the sea; Often in thought go up and down The pleasant streets of that dear old town, And my youth comes back to me. And a verse of a Lapland song Is haunting my memory still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." I can see the shadowy lines of its trees, And catch, in sudden gleams, The sheen of the far-surrounding seas, And islands that were the Hesperides Of all my boyish dreams. And the burden of that old song, It murmurs and whispers still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." I remember the black wharves and the slips, And the sea-tides tossing free; And Spanish sailors with bearded lips, And the beauty and mystery of the ships, And the magic of the sea. And the voice of that wayward song Is singing and saying still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." I remember the bulwarks by the shore, And the fort upon the hill; The sunrise gun, with its hollow roar, The drum-beat repeated o'er and o'er, And the bugle wild and shrill. And the music of that old song Throbs in my memory still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." I remember the sea-fight far away, How it thundered o'er the tide! And the dead captains, as they lay In their graves, o'erlooking the tranquil bay, Where they in battle died. And the sound of that mournful song Goes through me with a thrill: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." I can see the breezy dome of groves, The shadows of Deering's Woods; And the friendships old and the early loves Come back with a Sabbath sound, as of doves In quiet neighborhoods. And the verse of that sweet old song, It flutters and murmurs still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." I remember the gleams and glooms that dart Across the school-boy's brain; The song and the silence in the heart, That in part are prophecies, and in part Are longings wild and vain. And the voice of that fitful song Sings on, and is never still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." There are things of which I may not speak; There are dreams that cannot die; There are thoughts that make the strong heart weak, And bring a pallor into the cheek, And a mist before the eye. And the words of that fatal song Come over me like a chill: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." Strange to me now are the forms I meet When I visit the dear old town; But the native air is pure and sweet, And the trees that o'ershadow each well-known street, As they balance up and down, Are singing the beautiful song, Are sighing and whispering still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts." And Deering's Woods are fresh and fair, And with joy that is almost pain My heart goes back to wander there, And among the dreams of the days that were, I find my lost youth again. And the strange and beautiful song, The groves are repeating it still: "A boy's will is the wind's will, And the thoughts of youth are long, long thoughts."

Once there was a little girl who was very curious. She wanted to explore and discover new things. One day while she was out exploring, she found something very interesting. It was a delicate pattern on a leaf. She wanted to touch it and see what it felt like. So she carefully poked it with her finger. 

The pattern started to move and become bigger! The little girl was so excited to see how far it would expand when she poked it again. Sure enough, every time she poked it, it grew bigger and bigger. She kept on poking and poking until it got so big that she couldn't reach it anymore. 

The little girl was amazed at what she had discovered. She couldn't believe she had found something so delicate, yet so strong with her poking. She went back to look for it every day to see if it was still there. It never got any bigger, but she still enjoyed poking the pattern and watching it move.

name_of_work: Taking Off My Clothes by Carolyn Forche
content: I take off my shirt, I show you. I shaved the hair out under my arms. I roll up my pants, I scraped off the hair on my legs with a knife, getting white. My hair is the color of chopped maples. My eyes dark as beans cooked in the south. (Coal fields in the moon on torn-up hills) Skin polished as a Ming bowl showing its blood cracks, its age, I have hundreds of names for the snow, for this, all of them quiet.
