In the night I come to you and it seems a shame to waste my deepest shudders on a wall of a man. You recognize strangers, think you lived through destruction. You can't explain this night, my face, your memory. You want to know what I know? Your own hands are lying.

Once upon a time, there was a driver named Bob. Bob loved to drive his big red car all around the town. One day, Bob was driving his car when he saw a little girl named Lily. 

Lily was crying because her cup was empty. Bob asked, "What's wrong, little girl?" Lily said, "My cup is empty, and I'm thirsty." Bob said, "Don't worry, I can help you." 

Bob stopped his car and got out. He went to a store and bought Lily a drink. He opened the drink and filled her cup. Lily was so happy and said, "Thank you, Mr. Driver!" Bob smiled and said, "You're welcome, little girl. Now, you can enjoy your drink." 

From that day on, Bob and Lily became good friends. They would often see each other while Bob was driving his car around the town. And every time they met, Lily would always remember how Bob helped her when she was thirsty.

Lily and Ben were playing doctors and nurses with their toys. Lily had a big spoon and Ben had a bandage. They pretended to do an operation on their teddy bear.

"Teddy has a bad tummy," Lily said. "We need to stir his food and make him feel better."

Ben nodded and wrapped the bandage around Teddy's paw. "He also has a sore paw," he said. "We need to be very gentle and careful."

They stirred some cereal in a bowl and fed it to Teddy with the spoon. They also gave him some water and a hug. Teddy looked happy and sleepy.

"Good job, doctors," Mommy said, coming into the room. "You are very kind and helpful."

Lily and Ben smiled and thanked Mommy. They were proud of their operation.

But then they saw that they had made a big mess on the floor. There was cereal and water and bandage everywhere.

"Oh no," Lily said. "We are sorry, Mommy. We did not mean to make a mess."

Mommy sighed and shook her head. "It's okay, sweeties," she said. "I know you were having fun. But next time, please use a smaller spoon and a smaller bowl. And put a towel under your toys."

Lily and Ben nodded and said sorry again. They helped Mommy clean up the mess. Then they cuddled with Teddy and read a story. They were happy and tired.

Once upon a time, there was a big boat. The boat had a big sail that helped it move. One day, the boat went on a trip to find a treasure. The treasure was a shiny coin that was very special. The boat was very helpful because it took the people to the treasure. They found the coin and were very happy. They sailed back home with the coin and the boat's helpful sail. The end.

name_of_work: Stony Grey Soil by Patrick Kavanagh
content: O stony grey soil of Monaghan The laugh from my love you thieved; You took the gay child of my passion And gave me your clod-conceived. You clogged the feet of my boyhood And I believed that my stumble Had the poise and stride of Apollo And his voice my thick tongued mumble. You told me the plough was immortal! O green-life conquering plough! The mandril stained, your coulter blunted In the smooth lea-field of my brow. You sang on steaming dunghills A song of cowards' brood, You perfumed my clothes with weasel itch, You fed me on swinish food You flung a ditch on my vision Of beauty, love and truth. O stony grey soil of Monaghan You burgled my bank of youth! Lost the long hours of pleasure All the women that love young men. O can I stilll stroke the monster's back Or write with unpoisoned pen. His name in these lonely verses Or mention the dark fields where The first gay flight of my lyric Got caught in a peasant's prayer. Mullahinsa, Drummeril, Black Shanco- Wherever I turn I see In the stony grey soil of Monaghan Dead loves that were born for me.

name_of_work: A Poem about Baseballs by Denis Johnson
content: for years the scenes bustled through him as he dreamed he was alive. then he felt real, and slammed awake in the wet sheets screaming too fast, everything moves too fast, and the edges of things are gone. four blocks away a baseball was a dot against the sky, and he thought, my glove is too big, i will drop the ball and it will be a home run. the snow falls too fast from the clouds, and night is dropped and snatched back like a huge joke. is that the ball, or is it just a bird, and the ball is somewhere else, and i will miss it? and the edges are gone, my hands melt into the walls, my hands do not end where the wall begins. should i move forward, or back, or will the ball come right to me? i know i will miss, because i always miss when it takes so long. the wall has no surface, no edge, the wall fades into the air and the air is my hand, and i am the wall. my arm is the syringe and thus i become the nurse, i am you, nurse. if he gets around the bases before the ball comes down, is it a home run, even if i catch it? if we could slow down, and stop, we would be one fused mass careening at too great a speed through the emptiness. if i catch the ball, our side will be up, and i will have to bat, and i might strike out.

Timing's everything. The vapor rises high in the sky, tossing to and fro, then freezes, suddenly, and crystalizes into a perfect flake of miraculous snow. For countless miles, drifting east above the world, whirling about in a swirling free- for-all, appearing aimless, just like love, but sensing, seeking out, its destiny. Falling to where the two young skaters stand, hand in hand, then flips and dips and whips itself about to ever-so-gently land, a miracle, across her unkissed lips: as he blocks the wind raging from the south, leaning forward to kiss her lovely mouth.

Once upon a time there was a mom, dad and their three year old. One day their little one wanted to dress up in a costume for a party. So the parents discussed how much the costume would cost.

After much discussing, the mom and dad found a costume that was just right. The little one was so happy! They went to the party and the little one played with the other kids. All the kids had different costumes and the little one's costume was really special.

At the party, the kids started a costume competition. They showed off their costumes and the little one's costume was voted the best! Everyone cheered and clapped and the little one won the competition.

With a big smile, the three year old proudly showed off the winning costume. The little one had found the perfect costume and was the winner of the competition!

name_of_work: Archaic Torso of Apollo by Rainer Maria Rilke
content: We cannot know his legendary head with eyes like ripening fruit. And yet his torso is still suffused with brilliance from inside, like a lamp, in which his gaze, now turned to low, gleams in all its power. Otherwise the curved breast could not dazzle you so, nor could a smile run through the placid hips and thighs to that dark center where procreation flared. Otherwise this stone would seem defaced beneath the translucent cascade of the shoulders and would not glisten like a wild beast's fur: would not, from all the borders of itself, burst like a star: for here there is no place that does not see you. You must change your life.

name_of_work: Above the Dock by Thomas Ernest Hulme
content: Above the quiet dock in midnight, Tangled in the tall mast's corded height, Hangs the moon. What seemed so far away Is but a child's balloon, forgotten after play.

Once upon a time, there was a crab who loved spending time with his friends. He was a very happy crab. But one day, he got very sick and everything changed. He was so sick that he couldn't even move or play. 

The crab's friends wanted to help. They took him to many different places, hoping that he would get well. But nothing changed. It was very sad.

The crab's friends made a plan. They decided to take him to the beach and spend some time there. They thought the crab might get better if he could enjoy the sun and sand.

The crab was happy and he told his friends he felt better already. But when they got to the beach, the water was bitter and salty. It made the crab feel sicker. He stayed with his friends, but he couldn't enjoy the day. 

The crab's friends were very sad. They had tried their best to help him, but in the end they couldn't save him. The crab eventually died.

name_of_work: An Army Corps on the March by Walt Whitman
content: With its cloud of skirmishers in advance, With now the sound of a single shot snapping like a whip, and now an irregular volley, The swarming ranks press on and on, the dense brigades press on, Glittering dimly, toiling under the sun--the dust-cover'd men, In columns rise and fall to the undulations of the ground, With artillery interspers'd--the wheels rumble, the horses sweat, As the army corps advances.

One day, there was a tired girl. She was tired from playing all day. She wanted something to make her feel better. 

So she asked her mom for some powder. Her mom said yes and gave her a small, round container.

The girl opened the container and saw a white powder inside. She carefully sprinkled a small amount of powder into her hand. Then, she blew it away.

Suddenly, she felt much better. All her tiredness disappeared! She thanked her mom and went back outside to play.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside with her friends. One day, they decided to climb a big tree. Lily was scared, but she didn't want to look like a baby in front of her friends.

As she climbed, she saw a knot in the tree. She thought it would be a good place to mark her spot. She was proud of herself for finding it. When she reached the top, she looked down and saw how high she was. She started to feel scared again.

Suddenly, she heard a loud crack and the branch she was standing on broke. She fell to the ground, but luckily she wasn't hurt. Her friends rushed over to make sure she was okay. Lily realized that she should have listened to her fear and not climbed so high. From then on, she was proud of herself for being safe and smart.

When I was happy alone, too young for love Or to be loved in any but a way Cloudless and gentle, I would find the day Long as I wished its length or web to weave. I did not know or could not know enough To fret at thought or even try to whittle A pattern from the shapeless stony stuff That now confuses since I've grown too subtle. I used the senses, did not seek to find Something they could not touch, made numb with fear; I felt the glittering landscape in the mind And O was happy not to have it clear.

Ali was anxious to bake his first cake. He asked mummy if he could put it in the oven. Mummy allowed him to do it. He was so excited and happy he could bake his own cake.

He got the ingredients from the pantry and mixed them together. He carefully put the mixture in the oven and waited for it to cook. Ali was so excited about his cake that he kept looking in to see how it was doing.

Mummy watched him anxiously as Ali waited for the cake to be ready. The timer rang and it was time to take it out of the oven! Ali opened the oven and smiled as he saw his cake. He thanked mummy and they both enjoyed the cake together.

Tim and Mia were playing in the park. They liked to slide, swing and run. They saw a big tent with a sign that said "Spooky Show". They wanted to see what was inside.

They paid one coin each and entered the tent. It was dark and scary. They heard strange noises and saw shadows. They held hands and walked slowly.

"Look, there is a skeleton!" Mia said, pointing to a white thing that hung from the ceiling. "It has no skin or hair. It is just bones."

Tim felt afraid. He did not like the skeleton. He thought it was ugly and mean. He wanted to leave.

"I hate the skeleton!" he said. "It is scary and bad. Let's go, Mia!"

But Mia was curious. She wanted to see more. She liked the skeleton. She thought it was funny and cool. She wanted to touch it.

"I like the skeleton!" she said. "It is not scary or bad. It is just a toy. Come, Tim, let's touch it!"

She pulled Tim towards the skeleton. Tim tried to resist. He did not want to touch it. He screamed and cried.

"Help! Help! The skeleton will get me!"

The noise attracted the man who ran the show. He came out of a corner and saw the children. He was not happy. He had a frown and a loud voice.

"What are you doing here?" he said. "You are not supposed to touch anything. You are ruining my show. Go away, now!"

He grabbed the skeleton and shook it. It made a rattling sound. Tim and Mia were scared. They ran out of the tent. They did not want to see the spooky show anymore.

They hugged each other and said sorry. They learned their lesson. They decided to play something else. They looked for something fun and nice. They found a balloon seller. He had a smile and a soft voice.

"Hello, children," he said. "Do you want a balloon? They are colorful and happy. You can choose any one you like."

Tim and Mia liked the balloons. They each picked one. Tim chose a blue one and Mia chose a pink one. They thanked the balloon seller. He was patient and kind.

They played with their balloons. They felt happy and safe. They forgot about the skeleton. They did not hate anything. They liked each other. They were friends.

name_of_work: Photograph of Haymaker, 1890 by Molly Holden
content: It is not so much the image of the man that's moving -- he pausing from his work to whet his scythe, trousers tied below the knee, white shirt lit by another summer's sun, another century's -- as the sight of the grasses beyond his last laid swathe, so living yet upon the moment previous to death; for as the man stooping straightened up and bent again they died before his blade. Sweet hay and gone some seventy years ago and yet they stand before me in the sun, stems damp still where their neighbours' fall uncovered them, succulent and straight, immediate with moon-daisies

name_of_work: First Day At School by Roger McGough
content: A millionbillionwillion miles from home Waiting for the bell to go. (To go where?) Why are they all so big, other children? So noisy? So much at home they Must have been born in uniform Lived all their lives in playgrounds Spent the years inventing games That don't let me in. Games That are rough, that swallow you up. And the railings. All around, the railings. Are they to keep out wolves and monsters? Things that carry off and eat children? Things you don't take sweets from? Perhaps they're to stop us getting out Running away from the lessins. Lessin. What does a lessin look like? Sounds small and slimy. They keep them in the glassrooms. Whole rooms made out of glass. Imagine. I wish I could remember my name Mummy said it would come in useful. Like wellies. When there's puddles. Yellowwellies. I wish she was here. I think my name is sewn on somewhere Perhaps the teacher will read it for me. Tea-cher. The one who makes the tea.

Once upon a time, there was a big bookcase. It was very quiet, and nobody ever bothered it. But one day, a little boy came along. He was only three, but he loved to tease. He teased the bookcase, making funny noises and silly faces at it. The bookcase stayed quiet, and didn't do anything back.

The little boy came back each day, teasing the bookcase. He would yell and laugh, and even do little dances in front of it. All the while, the bookcase stayed quiet. It didn't like being teased, but it didn't know what to do.

One day, the little boy wasn't there. Nobody had seen him at all that day. The bookcase felt a little sad, missing the boy's teasing. It waited, but the boy never came back.

The bookcase has been quiet ever since.

name_of_work: Prologue of the Earthly Paradise by William Morris
content: Of Heaven or Hell I have no power to sing, I cannot ease the burden of your fears, Or make quick-coming death a little thing, Or bring again the pleasure of past years, Nor for my words shall ye forget your tears, Or hope again for aught that I can say, The idle singer of an empty day. But rather, when aweary of your mirth, From full hearts still unsatisfied ye sigh, And, feeling kindly unto all the earth, Grudge every minute as it passes by, Made the more mindful that the sweet days die-- --Remember me a little then I pray, The idle singer of an empty day. The heavy trouble, the bewildering care That weighs us down who live and earn our bread, These idle verses have no power to bear; So let me sing of names remembered, Because they, living not, can ne'er be dead, Or long time take their memory quite away From us poor singers of an empty day. Dreamer of dreams, born out of my due time, Why should I strive to set the crooked straight? Let it suffice me that my murmuring rhyme Beats with light wing against the ivory gate, Telling a tale not too importunate To those who in the sleepy region stay, Lulled by the singer of an empty day. Folk say, a wizard to a northern king At Christmas-tide such wondrous things did show, That through one window men beheld the spring, And through another saw the summer glow, And through a third the fruited vines a-row, While still, unheard, but in its wonted way, Piped the drear wind of that December day. So with this Earthly Paradise it is, If ye will read aright, and pardon me, Who strive to build a shadowy isle of bliss Midmost the beating of the steely sea, Where tossed about all hearts of men must be; Whose ravening monsters mighty men shall slay, Not the poor singer of an empty day.

Once upon a time there was a planet. It was all alone in space. The planet was very lonely and uncomfortable. But then it saw another planet in the far away sky. It waved to the other planet with its big cloudy hands.

The other planet saw the wave. It smiled and waved back to the lonely planet. The lonely planet was very happy.

Suddenly, a bright shooting star flew by. It flew back and forth between the two planets. The planets laughed and waved to each other. They were not so lonely and uncomfortable anymore.

The stars kept twinkling, the planets kept waving and they were best friends forever. The end.

Tom and Lily were best friends. They liked to play in the park with their toys. One day, they found a big box under a tree. It was a wrap with red and green paper and a bow.

"Wow, what is this?" Tom asked.

"Maybe it is a gift for us!" Lily said.

They opened the wrap and looked inside. But the box was empty. There was nothing in it.

"Oh, no. Who left this here?" Tom said.

"Maybe someone forgot it. Or maybe it is a trick," Lily said.

They felt sad and angry. They wanted to find something fun in the box. They threw the wrap and the box away.

Then they saw a man and a woman walking to the tree. They had smiles on their faces. They picked up the wrap and the box.

"Look, honey. Someone found our surprise!" the man said.

"What surprise?" the woman asked.

The man opened the box and showed her. Inside was a ring with a shiny stone. He put it on her finger and said, "Will you marry me?"

The woman gasped and nodded. She hugged him and said, "Yes, yes, yes!"

Then they kissed each other. They were very happy.

Tom and Lily watched them. They felt confused and curious.

"What are they doing?" Tom asked.

"They are kissing. It means they love each other," Lily said.

"Do you love me?" Tom asked.

"Yes, you are my best friend," Lily said.

"Can I kiss you?" Tom asked.

Lily giggled and nodded. They kissed each other on the cheek. They felt warm and fuzzy.

They smiled and said, "We are happy, too!"

It started as a pilgrimage Exalting minds and making all The burdens light, The second stage Explored but did not test the call. The sun beat down to match our rage. 5 We stood it very well, I thought , Observed and put down copious notes On things the peasants sold and bought The way of serpents and of goats. Three cities where a sage had taught 10 But when the differences arose On how to cross a desert patch, We lost a friend whose stylish prose Was quite the best of all our batch. A shadow falls on us and grows . 15 Another phase was reached when we Were twice attacked, and lost our way. A section claimed its liberty To leave the group. I tried to pray . Our leader said he smelt the sea 20 We noticed nothing as we went, A straggling crowd of little hope, Ignoring what the thunder meant , Deprived of common needs like soap. Some were broken, some merely bent. 25 When, finally, we reached the place , We hardly know why we were there. The trip had darkened every face, Our deeds were neither great nor rare. Home is where we have to gather grace.

One day, a boy named Pete was wandering in the woods. He was searching for something sweet. He saw a tree full of sugar and he couldn't believe his eyes.

His stomach grumbled, but something made him hesitate. He heard a strange noise coming from the tree. He took a step closer and then he realized that it was a little creature. He could not believe it and he was a bit scared.

The creature was deaf and it was chomping on the sugar. Pete tried to communicate with it, but the creature could not hear him. Pete was frustrated and not sure what to do. He wanted the sugar and he was about to take it.

Pete suddenly felt a bit guilty and couldn't take the sugar away from the creature. He decided to go home without it. As he was walking away, he could still hear the chomping of the sugar from the deaf creature.

Once upon a time, there was a humble tower in a small village. One day, a little boy came to the village and he saw the tower.

"Wow! What a beautiful tower!" said the boy.

He was so excited and he wanted to go nearer to the tower. He began to squeeze himself between the people who were around the tower. He was so small so he could squeeze himself through.

When he got closer to the tower, he saw a farmer standing next to it.

"What's that?" asked the boy, pointing at the tower.

The farmer smiled, "That's the humble tower. Many people have been living here for a long time."

The little boy smiled. He was happy to have found out about the tower. From then on, the little boy visited the tower every day. He would squeeze through the crowd and admire the beautiful, humble tower.

Once upon a time, a gentle little girl had a problem: her toys were always messy and unorganized. She wanted to fix it and make order in her room. So, she decided to organize all her toys. But she had a problem: she was only little, and it was hard for her.

She asked her mom for help. Her mom gave her a fork and said "you can use this to pick up all the toys and organize them neatly in the boxes." The little girl was excited!

She started to organize her toys with the fork. But soon she realized it was hard to be gentle with a fork. Her toys were all over the floor, and she was getting frustrated.

So the little girl put down the fork and thought of something else. She came up with an idea. She used her hands to very gently pick up the toys and carefully put them in the boxes.

Finally, her room was organized. She was happy and proud of herself. "I did it!" she said.

Jake ate his breakfast and was ready to go outside. He was excited to visit the ranch with his family. While they walked, he looked up at the hot sun and smiled.

When they arrived at the ranch, Jake saw all the animals. He wanted to pet them, so he ran over to the cow. His mom warned him not to go too close, but he didn't listen. Suddenly, the cow kicked him and he fell down. He was covered in mud!

His mom rushed over, worried. She carefully wiped the mud off him and hugged him. They said goodbye to the ranch and decided not to come back. Jake was sad but he knew he had been naughty. 

His mom promised that they could visit somewhere else soon, but Jake wasn't sure if he believed her. He was worried the bad ending would happen again.

name_of_work: Camping Out by Gina Marie Lauchner
content: Sticks and sleeping bags and ants Dirty hands and grass-stained pants Gathering wood and piling up leaves Carrying toilet paper and finding a tree Sitting by a fire and dodging the sparks There's nothing greater than The great outdoors after dark.

Once upon a time there was a princess. She was very happy. She went out to gather what she needed for a very special sleepover. 

She gathered some blankets, a pillow, and a comfy mattress. The mattress was very comfortable. She put all of the things in a nice pile. 

Then she invited her friends to come and join her. When they arrived, they were so excited to make a nice bed for their sleepover. They put the mattress on the floor, covered it with the blankets, and put the pillow on top. 

They all snuggled together in the comfy bed and told stories until the early morning. 

Everyone had a wonderful time at their special sleepover because they had such a comfortable mattress to snuggle in.

Once upon a time, there was a little bug. The bug had wide wings. It lived in a big green tree. The bug liked to fly and play with its friends.

One day, the bug saw a bright red flower. It wanted to go there. The bug did not look around. It did not see a big cat. The bug started to rush to the flower.

The big cat saw the bug. The cat wanted to catch the bug. The cat jumped and caught the bug. The bug was not fast enough. The cat ate the bug. The bug was gone. The end.

name_of_work: Hiram Powers' Greek Slave by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: They say Ideal beauty cannot enter The house of anguish. On the threshold stands An alien Image with enshackled hands, Called the Greek Slave! as if the artist meant her (That passionless perfection which he lent her, Shadowed not darkened where the sill expands) To so confront man's crimes in different lands With man's ideal sense. Pierce to the centre, Art's fiery finger! and break up ere long The serfdom of this world. Appeal, fair stone, From God's pure heights of beauty against man's Wrong! Catch up in thy divine face, not alone East griefs but West, and strike and shame the strong, By thunders of white silence, overthrown.

Barbara was tall and loved to play outside. One day, while she was playing near her house, she heard a van coming down the street. Barbara was curious, so she came closer to see the van.

Suddenly, the van stopped right in front of Barbara. Suddenly, the door of the van opened and out walked a man. The man looked very angry and started talking loudly.

"Who are you?" he shouted. "Can you tell me who lives in this house?"

Barbara was very scared and shook her head. "I don't know," she said in a quiet voice.

The man frowned and said, "I don't think anyone lives here. I just needed to make sure I didn't disturb anyone." Then he got back in his van and drove away.

Barbara was relieved that the man had gone and she went back to playing outside. She was glad that the tall man had not disturbed her day.

name_of_work: Piazza Piece by John Crowe Ransom
content: --I am a gentleman in a dustcoat trying To make you hear. Your ears are soft and small And listen to an old man not at all, They want the young men's whispering and sighing. But see the roses on your trellis dying And hear the spectral singing of the moon; For I must have my lovely lady soon, I am a gentleman in a dustcoat trying. --I am a lady young in beauty waiting Until my truelove comes, and then we kiss. But what grey man among the vines is this Whose words are dry and faint as in a dream? Back from my trellis, Sir, before I scream! I am a lady young in beauty waiting.

Mama and her little boy were walking through the park. The sun was shining and it was so quiet.

"What do you see, sweetheart?" asked Mama.

The boy stopped and pointed at something on the ground. "I see a bug, Mama!" he said.

Mama looked down and smiled. "Oh! I know that bug, the Ladybird! Do you know why the Ladybird is so special?" she asked.

The little boy shook his head and smiled.

Mama said "Well, if you're quiet and listen, you might find out!"

They both stayed very quiet and waited. Suddenly, the little boy heard something buzzing and he looked up. He saw a swarm of red and black bugs in the sky!

Mama said "Those bugs, the Ladybirds, all fly together to keep warm and find food. Isn't that amazing? See, now you know why the Ladybird is so special!"

The little boy smiled and felt proud that he had learnt something new. He squealed with delight and ran off to tell everyone his new discovery!

Timmy and Lila were playing on the beach. They liked to dig in the sand and look for shells and crabs. Sometimes they found shrimp, too. Shrimp were small and pink and had many legs. Timmy and Lila liked to eat shrimp. They thought shrimp were delicious.

One day, they found a big shrimp in a hole. It was bigger than their hands. They were very happy. They wanted to take it home and cook it for dinner. They put it in a bucket and filled it with water. They carried the bucket to their car.

"Look, Mommy, look!" Timmy said. "We found a big shrimp!"

"Wow, that's amazing!" Mommy said. "Where did you find it?"

"On the beach, in a hole!" Lila said. "Can we eat it for dinner?"

"Sure, why not?" Mommy said. "But first, we have to go to the store and buy some things. You can leave the bucket in the car. Don't worry, the shrimp will be fine."

Timmy and Lila nodded. They followed Mommy to the store. They were excited to eat the big shrimp.

But when they came back to the car, the bucket was empty. The shrimp was gone. It had disappeared.

"Where is our shrimp?" Timmy cried.

"Someone stole it!" Lila said.

They looked around. They saw a man running away with a big bag. He had a big smile on his face.

"Hey, that's our shrimp!" Timmy shouted.

"Stop, thief!" Lila yelled.

But it was too late. The man was gone. He had taken their shrimp.

Timmy and Lila were very sad. They had lost their big shrimp. They had nothing to eat for dinner. They wished they had never found the shrimp. They wished they had eaten it right away. They learned a hard lesson. Sometimes, things disappear.

Once there was a baby bear. He was very small and liked to explore. One day he was walking through the woods when something dangerous caught his eye. He looked closer and he saw that it was a large increase in the size of his stomach.

The baby bear was very scared and he didn't know what to do. He looked around, but he couldn't see any other animals. The stomach was still growing larger and he knew it was dangerous. He was afraid and he wished he had someone to help him.

Suddenly he saw a rabbit hopping by. The baby bear called out to the rabbit, but he was scared and his voice was soft. The rabbit came running over and asked the bear what was wrong.

The baby bear explained his situation and the rabbit listened carefully. The rabbit said that he could help, and the two made a plan. Together, they got to work and found a way to make the stomach smaller.

When it was all over, the baby bear thanked the rabbit. He was so happy to be safe again. The rabbit said goodbye and they both went their separate ways. The baby bear learned a valuable lesson that day: never underestimate the power of friendship.

Lay your sleeping head, my love, Human on my faithless arm; Time and fevers burn away Individual beauty from Thoughtful children, and the grave Proves the child ephemeral: But in my arms till break of day Let the living creature lie, Mortal, guilty, but to me The entirely beautiful. Soul and body have no bounds: To lovers as they lie upon Her tolerant enchanted slope In their ordinary swoon, Grave the vision Venus sends Of supernatural sympathy, Universal love and hope; While an abstract insight wakes Among the glaciers and the rocks The hermit's carnal ecstasy. Certainty, fidelity On the stroke of midnight pass Like vibrations of a bell, And fashionable madmen raise Their pedantic boring cry: Every farthing of the cost, All the dreaded cards foretell, Shall be paid, but from this night Not a whisper, not a thought, Not a kiss nor look be lost. Beauty, midnight, vision dies: Let the winds of dawn that blow Softly round your dreaming head Such a day of welcome show Eye and knocking heart may bless, Find the mortal world enough; Noons of dryness find you fed By the involuntary powers, Nights of insult let you pass Watched by every human love.

They throw in Drummer Hodge, to rest Uncoffined--just as found: His landmark is a kopje-crest That breaks the veldt around; And foreign constellations west Each night above his mound. Young Hodge the Drummer never knew-- Fresh from his Wessex home-- The meaning of the broad Karoo, The Bush, the dusty loam, And why uprose to nightly view Strange stars amid the gloam. Yet portion of that unknown plain Will Hodge for ever be; His homely Northern breast and brain Grow up a Southern tree, And strange-eyed constellations reign His stars eternally.

Once upon a time, there was a bunny named Benny. Benny was a poor bunny because he didn't have any carrots to eat. One day, Benny saw a hoop on the ground. He decided to hop through the hoop to cheer himself up. 

As he was hopping through the hoop, he saw a carrot patch on the other side. Benny was so happy! He hopped and hopped until he reached the carrot patch. Benny ate as many carrots as he could and felt much better. 

From that day on, Benny would hop through the hoop every time he felt sad. He knew that on the other side of the hoop, there might be something that would make him feel better. Benny was no longer a poor bunny, he was a happy bunny who loved to hop through hoops.

Sara loved her doll very much. She hugged her doll every night and played with her every day. She named her doll Lily and gave her a pink dress and a bow.

One day, Sara went to the park with her mom and Lily. She saw a girl on the swing who had a doll too. The girl's doll had a blue dress and a hat. Sara thought the girl's doll was pretty and wanted to see it.

"Hi, can I play with your doll?" Sara asked the girl.

"No, this is my doll. You can't touch her," the girl said.

"Please, just for a little bit. I'll let you play with my doll too," Sara said.

"No, go away. Your doll is ugly and old," the girl said.

Sara felt sad and angry. She wanted to take the girl's doll by force. She reached out her hand and tried to grab it. The girl screamed and pulled her doll back. They both started to fight over the doll.

"Stop it, both of you!" Sara's mom said. She ran over and separated them. She took Sara's doll and the girl's doll and held them in her arms.

"Look what you did. You ripped the doll's dress and hat. How do you think the girl feels?" Sara's mom said.

Sara looked at the girl's doll and saw that it was torn and dirty. She felt sorry and ashamed. She looked at the girl and saw that she was crying and scared.

"I'm sorry, I didn't mean to hurt your doll. I just wanted to play with her," Sara said.

"I'm sorry too, I shouldn't have been mean to you and your doll. I was afraid you would take her away from me," the girl said.

Sara's mom smiled and gave them back their dolls. She hugged Sara and said, "It's good that you apologized. Sometimes, it's better to surrender and share than to fight and hurt. You can make new friends and have more fun that way."

Sara nodded and smiled. She gave her doll to the girl and said, "Do you want to play with Lily? She's very nice and soft."

The girl smiled and gave her doll to Sara and said, "Do you want to play with Daisy? She's very pretty and smart."

They both took each other's dolls and went to the slide. They played together and had a lot of fun. They forgot about their fight and became friends.

The end.

Lily and Tom were playing in the park with their ball. They saw an elderly lady sitting on a bench. She looked sad and lonely. Lily and Tom wanted to make her happy, so they ran to her and offered her their ball.

The elderly lady smiled and thanked them. She said she liked their ball very much. She asked them if they wanted to hear a story. Lily and Tom nodded. They liked stories.

The elderly lady told them a story about a word that could make anything happen. She said the word was very powerful and secret. She said she would tell them the word if they promised to keep it to themselves. Lily and Tom promised. They were curious and excited.

The elderly lady whispered the word in their ears. It was a strange and scary word. Lily and Tom felt a shiver down their spines. They repeated the word after her. Suddenly, the sky turned dark and stormy. The wind howled and the thunder roared. The park was filled with shadows and monsters. Lily and Tom screamed and dropped their ball. They wanted to run away, but they couldn't move. They were stuck to the bench.

The elderly lady laughed wickedly. She said she had tricked them. She said the word was a curse that made their worst fears come true. She said she was a witch who liked to make children suffer. She said she would keep their ball and their souls. She said they would never see their parents or their home again. Lily and Tom cried and begged for mercy, but the elderly lady ignored them. She took their ball and flew away on her broomstick, leaving them alone in the dark and the horror.

name_of_work: For Heidi With Blue Hair by Fleur Adcock
content: When you dyed your hair blue (or, at least ultramarine for the clipped sides, with a crest of jet-black spikes on top) you were sent home from school because, as the headmistress put it, although dyed hair was not specifically forbidden, yours was, apart from anything else, not done in the school colours. Tears in the kitchen, telephone-calls to school from your freedom-loving father: 'She's not a punk in her behaviour; it's just a style.' (You wiped your eyes, also not in a school colour.) 'She discussed it with me first - we checked the rules.' 'And anyway, Dad, it cost twenty-five dollars. Tell them it won't wash out - not even if I wanted to try. It would have been unfair to mention your mother's death, but that shimmered behind the arguments. The school had nothing else against you; the teachers twittered and gave in. Next day your black friend had hers done in grey, white and flaxen yellow - the school colours precisely: an act of solidarity, a witty tease. The battle was already won

Once upon a time, there was a little bug who loved to crawl. The bug lived in a big house with a kind girl named Lilly. Lilly liked to wear her soft bathrobe and play with her toys. The bug liked to watch Lilly play and wished he could join her.

One day, the bug found a bitter fruit on the floor. He didn't like the taste, but he knew Lilly loved fruits. So, he decided to push the fruit to Lilly as a gift. It was hard work, but the bug wanted to make Lilly happy.

When Lilly saw the fruit, she was so happy! She knew the bug had brought it to her. She picked up the bug and gave him a big hug. From that day on, they became best friends. The moral of the story is that even small acts of kindness can bring happiness to others and create strong friendships.

Lily and Tom are playing in the garden. They have a small tent that they pretend is their house. They like to make up stories and act them out.

One day, they decide to play that they are animals. Lily wants to be a cat and Tom wants to be a dog. They crawl into the tent and make noises.

"Meow, meow, I am a cat. I like to sleep and catch mice," Lily says.

"Woof, woof, I am a dog. I like to run and fetch sticks," Tom says.

They have fun playing for a while, but then they hear a loud noise. They peek out of the tent and see a big truck. The truck is carrying a lot of wood and nails. It stops in front of their house.

"What is that?" Lily asks.

"I don't know. Let's go and see," Tom says.

They get out of the tent and run to the truck. They see a man get out of the truck. He is wearing a hat and a tool belt. He smiles at them.

"Hello, kids. I am here to fix your roof. It has a hole and it leaks when it rains," he says.

"Our roof? What is a roof?" Lily asks.

"A roof is the top part of your house. It keeps you warm and dry. But sometimes it gets old and broken and needs to be fixed," he says.

"Oh, I see. But we don't live in that house. We live in this tent. It is our house," Tom says.

The man laughs. He thinks they are very cute and funny.

"That is a nice tent, but it is not a real house. It is a fake house. You can play in it, but you can't sleep in it. It is too cold and wet and small," he says.

Lily and Tom look at each other. They think about their tent and their house. They think the man is right. They like their tent, but they also like their house. They decide to go back to their tent and pack their things.

"Thank you for fixing our roof, mister. We are going to our real house now. But we will come back and play in our fake house later," Lily says.

"You're welcome, kids. Have fun and be careful," the man says.

Lily and Tom wave goodbye to the man and run to their house. They are happy to have a roof that does not leak. They are also happy to have a tent that they can pretend is their house. They think they have the best of both worlds.

Once there was a fierce wolf. He loved to run and jump through the forest. He had long, strong legs and loved to chase after the birds and bugs. One day, he came across a big, wooden door. He didn't know what it was and he wanted to explore. He stepped closer and closer to the door, but each time he got close, the door would shut. He banged and howled, but no matter how fierce he was, the door just kept shutting. He tried and tried, but the door wouldn't open. Eventually, he gave up and walked away. He was very disappointed, but happy to be able to feel the sunshine, as he left the deep shadows of the big wooden door.

Once upon a time, in a small town, there was a unique toy shop. In the shop, there was a dark room. The room was always closed. One day, a little girl named Lily went into the shop with her mom.

Lily saw the dark room and asked her mom, "Mom, what's in that room?" Her mom said, "I don't know, Lily. But we should not go in there." Lily felt curious but did not open the door.

One day, the shop owner decided to restore the dark room. He opened the door and found a big, beautiful toy. It was a special toy that could talk and play with kids. The owner showed the toy to everyone in the town.

Lily and her mom came back to the shop. Lily saw the toy and said, "Wow! That's the best toy ever!" The toy smiled and said, "Hi, Lily! Let's be friends!" Lily and the toy played together and had lots of fun.

From that day on, the dark room was not dark anymore. The toy made the room bright and happy. The unique toy made everyone in the town happy, too. And Lily and the toy became best friends forever.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Beth. Beth was so excited to go play outside on a sunny day.

She was running and playing when suddenly, she tripped and fell. She started to feel sleepy, so she decided to take a nap. She found the softest patch of grass and lay down.

Beth had the best nap ever. But when she woke up there was something that no one had ever seen before! It was a big black lump of coal!

Beth got up and walked over to it. She was so excited that she called out to her mom. "Mom! Look what I found!"

Her mom came over and said, "Oh wow Beth! That must have been put there by a lazy coal miner!" Beth laughed and smiled. 

From that day on, Beth always remembered the special nap she had and the fun adventure she had gone on!

One day, a little girl named Lucy went to the park. She saw a big tree with many branches. She had a creative idea to build a tree house with her friends.

Lucy and her friends found wood and started to build the tree house. They used a rub to make the wood smooth. They worked together and had a lot of fun.

A little bird flew near and stared at Lucy and her friends. The bird liked their tree house too. When they finished, they all played in the tree house together. The bird stayed and became their new friend.

Once upon a time, there was a girl called Mia. Mia's mommy taught her to be kind and generous.

One day, Mia's mommy said: "It's your birthday soon, Mia, and guess what? I'm going to teach you a special birthday dance!" 

Mia was so excited she could not be still. She jumped up and down and said "Yes, Yes!" 

Mia hopped around the house and practiced her moves every day. On her birthday, Mia showed her mommy the dance she had learned. Her mommy clapped and cheered.

Mia was happy. She felt so proud of herself. With her restless energy, she had learned the birthday dance!

Once upon a time, there was a little dog named Spot. Spot loved to try new things. One day, he saw a firework in the sky. It was big and bright. Spot wanted to see it up close.

Spot ran and ran to find the firework. He ran so far that he became tired. But he did not give up. He kept trying to find the firework. Spot knew that if he tried hard enough, he would find it.

Finally, Spot found the firework. It was on the ground, all done making pretty lights. Spot was very happy that he tried so hard to find it. He knew that trying his best was important. Spot went home, still tired but very proud of himself.

September rain falls on the house. In the failing light, the old grandmother sits in the kitchen with the child beside the Little Marvel Stove, reading the jokes from the almanac, laughing and talking to hide her tears. She thinks that her equinoctial tears and the rain that beats on the roof of the house were both foretold by the almanac, but only known to a grandmother. The iron kettle sings on the stove. She cuts some bread and says to the child, It's time for tea now; but the child is watching the teakettle's small hard tears dance like mad on the hot black stove, the way the rain must dance on the house. Tidying up, the old grandmother hangs up the clever almanac on its string. Birdlike, the almanac hovers half open above the child, hovers above the old grandmother and her teacup full of dark brown tears. She shivers and says she thinks the house feels chilly, and puts more wood in the stove. It was to be, says the Marvel Stove. I know what I know, says the almanac. With crayons the child draws a rigid house and a winding pathway. Then the child puts in a man with buttons like tears and shows it proudly to the grandmother. But secretly, while the grandmother busies herself about the stove, the little moons fall down like tears from between the pages of the almanac into the flower bed the child has carefully placed in the front of the house. Time to plant tears, says the almanac. The grandmother sings to the marvelous stove and the child draws another inscrutable house.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Sally. She was happy and nice. Every day she went to school and tried her best. 

One day the teacher said it was time for a test. The test was hard and Sally was worried. But she tried not to show it. 

Her teacher knew that tests can be hard, so she told Sally to take a deep breath and hold her pencil tight. She said, "Take your time and do your best. Don't worry, I'm here to help you." Sally nodded and smiled. 

With a deep breath, Sally held her pencil tightly and started the test. She got some questions right and some questions wrong but she tried her best. 

When Sally was done, the teacher smiled and said, "Well done, Sally! You did a great job." Sally was so happy and felt nice inside.

name_of_work: A Song for St. Cecilia's Day by John Dryden
content: Stanza 1 From harmony, from Heav'nly harmony This universal frame began. When Nature underneath a heap Of jarring atoms lay, And could not heave her head, The tuneful voice was heard from high, Arise ye more than dead. Then cold, and hot, and moist, and dry, In order to their stations leap, And music's pow'r obey. From harmony, from Heav'nly harmony This universal frame began: From harmony to harmony Through all the compass of the notes it ran, The diapason closing full in man. Stanza 2 What passion cannot music raise and quell! When Jubal struck the corded shell, His list'ning brethren stood around And wond'ring, on their faces fell To worship that celestial sound: Less than a god they thought there could not dwell Within the hollow of that shell That spoke so sweetly and so well. What passion cannot music raise and quell! Stanza 3 The trumpet's loud clangor Excites us to arms With shrill notes of anger And mortal alarms. The double double double beat Of the thund'ring drum Cries, hark the foes come; Charge, charge, 'tis too late to retreat. Stanza 4 The soft complaining flute In dying notes discovers The woes of hopeless lovers, Whose dirge is whisper'd by the warbling lute. Stanza 5 Sharp violins proclaim Their jealous pangs, and desperation, Fury, frantic indignation, Depth of pains and height of passion, For the fair, disdainful dame. Stanza 6 But oh! what art can teach What human voice can reach The sacred organ's praise? Notes inspiring holy love, Notes that wing their Heav'nly ways To mend the choirs above. Stanza 7 Orpheus could lead the savage race; And trees unrooted left their place; Sequacious of the lyre: But bright Cecilia rais'd the wonder high'r; When to her organ, vocal breath was giv'n, An angel heard, and straight appear'd Mistaking earth for Heav'n. GRAND CHORUS As from the pow'r of sacred lays The spheres began to move, And sung the great Creator's praise To all the bless'd above; So when the last and dreadful hour This crumbling pageant shall devour, The trumpet shall be heard on high, The dead shall live, the living die, And music shall untune the sky.

Lily and Ben were playing in the park. They liked to swing, slide and run. They also liked to eat snacks. They had a bag of snacks with them. Some snacks were sweet, some were salty and some were sour.

"Can I have a snack?" Ben asked Lily.

"Sure, you can have one. But only one, okay?" Lily said. She opened the bag and gave Ben a snack. It was a sour snack. It was a lemon candy.

Ben put the candy in his mouth. He made a funny face. He did not like the sour snack. It was too sour for him. He spit it out.

"Yuck! This snack is bad! I don't want it!" Ben said. He threw the candy on the ground.

Lily was angry. She did not like that Ben wasted the snack. She did not like that Ben littered the park. She did not like that Ben was rude.

"That was not nice, Ben. You should not waste food. You should not throw trash on the ground. You should say thank you when someone gives you something. You should try new things. Maybe you would like them if you tried them." Lily said.

Ben felt sorry. He knew that Lily was right. He picked up the candy from the ground. He put it in the trash can. He said sorry to Lily.

"I'm sorry, Lily. You are right. I should not waste food. I should not throw trash on the ground. I should say thank you when someone gives me something. I should try new things. Maybe I would like them if I tried them." Ben said.

Lily smiled. She forgave Ben. She gave him another snack. It was a sweet snack. It was a chocolate cookie.

"Here, Ben. Try this snack. It is sweet. I think you will like it." Lily said.

Ben took the cookie. He bit it. He liked the sweet snack. It was yummy. He said thank you to Lily.

"Thank you, Lily. This snack is good. I like it." Ben said.

Lily and Ben hugged. They were happy. They learned to be grateful, respectful and adventurous. They heard a ring. It was their mom. She came to pick them up. They went home with their mom. They told her about their day. They told her about their snacks. They told her what they learned. Their mom was proud of them. She gave them a hug and a kiss. She said she loved them. They said they loved her too. They had a good day.

Jill was a girl who liked to eat. She ate a lot of food every day. She ate more food than her brother Jack and her sister Jane. She ate more food than her mom and dad. She ate more food than her dog Spot.

One day, Jill saw a big plate of cookies on the table. She wanted to eat all the cookies. She did not want to share with anyone. She did not listen to her mom, who said, "Jill, leave some cookies for the others. Too many cookies are bad for you."

Jill took the plate of cookies and ran to her room. She locked the door and ate all the cookies. She ate them very fast. She did not enjoy them. She only wanted to have them all.

Soon, Jill felt sick. Her tummy hurt. She felt hot and cold. She felt dizzy and tired. She wanted to throw up. She hoped she would feel better soon. But she did not.

Her mom knocked on the door and asked, "Jill, are you okay?" Jill did not answer. She was too sick. Her mom opened the door with a key and saw Jill on the bed. She saw the empty plate of cookies. She saw Jill's pale face. She was very worried.

She called the doctor and said, "Please come quickly. My daughter ate too many cookies and now she is very sick." The doctor came and checked Jill. He said, "She has a fever and a stomach ache. She needs to go to the hospital. She may have to stay there for a long time."

Jill was scared. She did not want to go to the hospital. She did not want to leave her mom and dad and her brother and sister and her dog Spot. She wished she had not eaten all the cookies. She wished she had shared with the others. She wished she had listened to her mom. She learned a hard lesson. She learned that being greedy is bad and being kind is good. She learned that too much of anything is not good for you. She learned that she should hope for the right things and not the wrong things.

Sara and Ben are twins. They like to play outside at night. They have a flashlight and a sign. The sign says "Sara and Ben's Club". They put the sign on a tree and turn on the flashlight. The sign glows in the dark.

One night, they hear a noise. It is a big dog. The dog is barking and running towards them. Sara and Ben are scared. They are alert. They grab the flashlight and the sign and run to their house. The dog follows them.

They reach their door and knock. Their mom opens the door. She sees the dog and the sign. She is surprised. She lets Sara and Ben in and closes the door. The dog stops barking and goes away.

Sara and Ben hug their mom. They tell her about their club and the dog. Their mom smiles and hugs them back. She says they are brave and clever. She says they can keep the sign and the flashlight, but they have to play outside only when it is light. Sara and Ben agree. They are happy. They put the sign and the flashlight in their room. The sign still glows a little. They go to sleep.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He loved to march around the house with his toy drum. Timmy had a friend named Sally who liked to play with dolls. One day, Sally came over to Timmy's house to play. They were having fun until Timmy's big brother came in and took Timmy's drum away. Timmy was sad and didn't know what to do.

Sally was a thoughtful friend and wanted to help Timmy. She told him to speak to his brother and tell him how he felt. Timmy was scared, but he knew Sally was right. He went to his brother and tried to speak, but his brother just laughed and walked away.

Timmy felt even sadder now. He didn't want to play with Sally anymore and just wanted to be alone. The bad ending was that Timmy didn't have fun with his friend and was left feeling sad.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Amy. She lived in a small house near the big woods. One day, Amy went for a walk in the woods and saw a black bird. The bird was sad because it was lost. Amy wanted to help the bird find its way home.

Amy asked the bird, "Do you feel sad?" The bird said, "Yes, I feel sad. I miss my home." So, they walked together to find the bird's home. They saw a big tree with a hole in it. Inside the hole was some ash from a fire.

Amy said, "Is this your home?" The bird looked at the ash and said, "Yes, this is my home! Thank you for helping me find it." The bird felt happy again, and Amy felt happy too. They became good friends and played together in the woods every day.

Once upon a time there was a giant who lived in the forest. He loved to play games, but he was very lonely. One day he made a huge pedal boat and paddled off to sea looking for adventure. But before he could go too far, the boat suddenly got stuck in the mud!

The giant was about to give up when his friend the bird flew into the sky and spotted help. The bird flew quickly to the nearest village and asked everyone for help. The villagers came straight away and rescued the giant from the mud with huge muscles and long ropes.

But the giant still felt sad. He was embarrassed and wanted to continue his journey. Then everyone had an idea. A small girl who lived in the village said she could help him. She brought the biggest wheel she could find, and the giant connected it to the pedal boat. 

The villagers cheered and the huge wheel spun the pedal boat free. The giant was relieved and could now continue his journey. Everyone in the village waved and cheered him on as he sailed away into the sunset.

name_of_work: The Youngest Daughter by Cathy Song
content: The sky has been dark for many years. My skin has become as damp and pale as rice paper and feels the way mother's used to before the drying sun parched it out there in the fields. Lately, when I touch my eyelids, my hands react as if I had just touched something hot enough to burn. My skin, aspirin colored, tingles with migraine. Mother has been massaging the left side of my face especially in the evenings when the pain flares up. This morning her breathing was graveled, her voice gruff with affection when I wheeled her into the bath. She was in a good humor, making jokes about her great breasts, floating in the milky water like two walruses, flaccid and whiskered around the nipples. I scrubbed them with a sour taste in my mouth, thinking: six children and an old man have sucked from these brown nipples. I was almost tender when I came to the blue bruises that freckle her body, places where she has been injecting insulin for thirty years. I soaped her slowly, she sighed deeply, her eyes closed. It seems it has always been like this: the two of us in this sunless room, the splashing of the bathwater. In the afternoons when she has rested, she prepares our ritual of tea and rice, garnished with a shred of gingered fish, a slice of pickled turnip, a token for my white body. We eat in the familiar silence. She knows I am not to be trusted, even now planning my escape. As I toast to her health with the tea she has poured, a thousand cranes curtain the window, fly up in a sudden breeze.

Once upon a time, there was a blueberry. It was round and looked yummy. One day, it saw a little boy and wanted him to eat it. So, it hopped into his hands. The boy was so happy! 

He decided to take the blueberry home with him. When he got there, he washed the blueberry. It was so filthy! But after a good scrub, it was nice and clean.

He was all ready to eat the blueberry. He put it in his mouth and took one big bite. It tasted so sweet! He gobbled the blueberry up in no time at all. 

The boy was very happy. He had enjoyed his blueberry treat.

I'm not yet comfortable with the word, its short clean woosh that sounds like life. At dinner last night my single girls said in admonition, "It's not wife-approved" about a friend's upcoming trip. Their eyes rolled up and over and out their pretty young heads. Wife, why does it sound like a job? "I need a wife" the famous feminist wrote, "a wife that will keep my clothes clean, ironed, mended, replaced if need be." A word that could be made easily into maid. A wife that does, fixes soothes, honors, obeys, Housewife, fishwife, bad wife, good wife, what's the word for someone who stares long into the morning, unable to even fix tea some days, the kettle steaming over loud like a train whistle, she who cries in the mornings, she who tears a hole in the earth and cannot stop grieving, the one who wants to love you, but often isn't good at even that, the one who doesn't want to be diminished by how much she wants to be yours.

Once upon a time, there was a fierce branch. It kept sprouting leaves and spreading around the forest. Every day, it would get bigger and bigger.

One day, a little lamb wanted to explore the forest. She saw the big fierce branch and decided to take a closer look. She got to the branch and tried to grab it, but the branch kept sprouting leaves and wouldn't let her touch it!

The little lamb decided to defeat the fierce branch. She took out a spray bottle and sprayed the branch. The branch started shrinking, and soon it was back to its original size.

The little lamb was happy. She patted the branch and smiled at it. From that day on, the fierce branch stayed small, and the little lamb could explore the forest without worrying.

Once upon a time, there was a bunny called Ben. Ben was very polite and loved to hop. One day, he hopped through a field and saw an apple on the ground. Ben was very polite so he asked the apple if it was okay for him to take it. The apple replied happily and Ben took it and hopped off. 

Ben hopped for miles until he found a nice, quiet spot and ate the apple. He crunched it with joy, and soon he had finished it all. After, Ben said thank you and hopped away. 

Ben the bunny kept hopping and hopping, until at last he came home. He hopped into the garden and hopped around all the flowers and plants. He was happy and polite, and he knew he'd have a big sleep later. 

The End.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Lucy. She was three years old and loved playing with friends. 

One day Lucy went to the park with her friends. She wanted to swing on the swings but her friends wanted to play tag. Lucy felt sad and started to complain. 

"No, I wanna swing!", Lucy said. 

Her friends laughed and said, "No Lucy, let's play tag!"

Lucy started to get more upset, so her friends decided to make a deal. 

"Let's make a bet," they said to Lucy. "If you try to play tag, we will give you a prize!"

Lucy reluctantly agreed. She got up and started to run with her friends, even though she was a bit worried. 

In the end, Lucy had so much fun playing tag that she forgot all about swinging. Her friends gave her a prize for playing and she was so happy. 

The moral of the story is: it's important to try something new even if you are worried or uncomfortable. You just might have lots of fun!

One day, a little boy wanted to try something new. He saw a deep porch near his house. He wanted to find out how deep the porch was. So, he stepped onto it and he tried to see how deep it was. The porch was deep but he couldn't see the bottom. So he just tried to take a few steps. He walked around and around the porch's edge. He finally got back to the front of the porch and he was very happy. He had tried something new and it was really fun!

name_of_work: The Black Man's Burden by H. T. Johnson
content: Pile on the Black Man's Burden. 'Tis nearest at your door; Why heed long bleeding Cuba, or dark Hawaii's shore? Hail ye your fearless armies, Which menace feeble folks Who fight with clubs and arrows and brook your rifle's smoke. Pile on the Black Man's Burden His wail with laughter drown You've sealed the Red Man's problem, And will take up the Brown, In vain ye seek to end it, With bullets, blood or death Better by far defend it With honor's holy breath.

Once upon a time there were two friends, Joey and Sally. They were very different, but they were both very special. One day they decided to play.

Joey said, "Let's play fight!"

Sally said, "Okay!"

So they grabbed some newspapers and made funny shapes with them. They moved around with their pretend swords and laughed.

Joey shouted, "I'm an incredible fighter!"

Sally cheered and said, "Me too!"

They kept playing until they were too tired to fight. They sat together and watched the sun go down.

Joey said, "That was so much fun!"

Sally smiled and said, "It was incredible!"

name_of_work: In This Place (An American Lyric) by Amanda Gorman
content: There's a poem in this place-- in the footfalls in the halls in the quiet beat of the seats. It is here, at the curtain of day, where America writes a lyric you must whisper to say. There's a poem in this place-- in the heavy grace, the lined face of this noble building, collections burned and reborn twice. There's a poem in Boston's Copley Square where protest chants tear through the air like sheets of rain, where love of the many swallows hatred of the few. There's a poem in Charlottesville where tiki torches string a ring of flame tight round the wrist of night where men so white they gleam blue-- seem like statues where men heap that long wax burning ever higher where Heather Heyer blooms forever in a meadow of resistance. There's a poem in the great sleeping giant of Lake Michigan, defiantly raising its big blue head to Milwaukee and Chicago-- a poem begun long ago, blazed into frozen soil, strutting upward and aglow. There's a poem in Florida, in East Texas where streets swell into a nexus of rivers, cows afloat like mottled buoys in the brown, where courage is now so common that 23-year-old Jesus Contreras rescues people from floodwaters. There's a poem in Los Angeles yawning wide as the Pacific tide where a single mother swelters in a windowless classroom, teaching black and brown students in Watts to spell out their thoughts so her daughter might write this poem for you. There's a lyric in California where thousands of students march for blocks, undocumented and unafraid; where my friend Rosa finds the power to blossom in deadlock, her spirit the bedrock of her community. She knows hope is like a stubborn ship gripping a dock, a truth: that you can't stop a dreamer or knock down a dream. How could this not be her city su nacion our country our America, our American lyric to write-- a poem by the people, the poor, the Protestant, the Muslim, the Jew, the native, the immigrant, the black, the brown, the blind, the brave, the undocumented and undeterred, the woman, the man, the nonbinary, the white, the trans, the ally to all of the above and more? Tyrants fear the poet. Now that we know it we can't blow it. We owe it to show it not slow it although it hurts to sew it when the world skirts below it. Hope-- we must bestow it like a wick in the poet so it can grow, lit, bringing with it stories to rewrite-- the story of a Texas city depleted but not defeated a history written that need not be repeated a nation composed but not yet completed. There's a poem in this place-- a poem in America a poet in every American who rewrites this nation, who tells a story worthy of being told on this minnow of an earth to breathe hope into a palimpsest of time-- a poet in every American who sees that our poem penned doesn't mean our poem's end. There's a place where this poem dwells-- it is here, it is now, in the yellow song of dawn's bell where we write an American lyric we are just beginning to tell.

Once upon a time, there was a big mountain. The mountain was very tall and had snow on the top. One day, the sun came up and it was a beautiful sunrise. The sun made the snow on the mountain shine and it was very pretty. 

A little boy named Timmy was walking on the mountain with his mom. Timmy saw a big rock and wanted to climb it. But the rock was too big and heavy for him to move. 

Timmy's mom had an idea. She found a stick and used it to separate the rock into two pieces. Now the rock was smaller and Timmy could climb it. The stick was very useful! 

Timmy was very happy and climbed to the top of the rock. He could see the sunrise and it was very beautiful. Timmy and his mom sat on the rock and watched the sunrise together. It was a very happy day.

One day, there was a little girl. She loved to play outside in the sunshine. She had bright, blue eyes and soft, brown hair. She wore a white dress, and she looked very pretty.

She played with her toys and had lots of fun. Her friends came to play too and they all laughed and behaved brilliantly. The little girl ran and skipped and raced around, feeling so happy and alive.

They played until the sun went down, then the little girl and her friends said goodbye. As she went inside, her mum smiled. She said "You were very well behaved today." And the little girl smiled and nodded. She knew that behaving brilliantly was the right thing to do!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a big house with her mommy and daddy. They had a garden with lots of trees, including a prune tree. 

One night, Lily went to sleep and had a wonderful dream. In her dream, she was a princess who lived in a castle made of candy. The castle was so big and rich with candy walls and floors. 

When she woke up, she told her mommy and daddy about her dream. They were happy to hear about it and gave her a big prune to eat for breakfast. It was so yummy and juicy! 

From that day on, Lily loved to dream and imagine new things. She would always remember her dream of being a princess in a rich candy castle and how it all started with a simple prune.

Jack and his mom were walking in the park. Jack spotted a bench and wanted to sit but his mom said: "No, we have to rush. We have to get home before it gets dark". Jack felt sad.

Then a deaf old man came by. He saw Jack and stopped by the bench. He lightly waved and smiled at Jack.

Jack was happy. He and his mom went over to the bench and sat down. The old man showed Jack a funny trick with a stick. Jack and his mom laughed together.

They stayed at the bench and watched the old man until it got dark. The man waved his goodbye to Jack and his mom and walked away.

Jack and his mom talked together while they walked home. Jack was happy, as it had been a lovely time at the bench.

name_of_work: To have without holding by Marge Piercy
content: Learning to love differently is hard, love with the hands wide open, love with the doors banging on their hinges, the cupboard unlocked, the wind roaring and whimpering in the rooms rustling the sheets and snapping the blinds that thwack like rubber bands in an open palm. It hurts to love wide open stretching the muscles that feel as if they are made of wet plaster, then of blunt knives, then of sharp knives. It hurts to thwart the reflexes of grab, of clutch ; to love and let go again and again. It pesters to remember the lover who is not in the bed, to hold back what is owed to the work that gutters like a candle in a cave without air, to love consciously, conscientiously, concretely, constructively. I can't do it, you say it's killing me, but you thrive, you glow on the street like a neon raspberry, You float and sail, a helium balloon bright bachelor's button blue and bobbing on the cold and hot winds of our breath, as we make and unmake in passionate diastole and systole the rhythm of our unbound bonding, to have and not to hold, to love with minimized malice, hunger and anger moment by moment balanced.

Tim and Mia are playing with blocks. They like to make towers and houses and cars. Tim has a lot of red blocks and Mia has a lot of blue blocks. They share some yellow blocks.

"Look, Mia, I made a triangle!" Tim says, holding up a block with three sides. "It is red and yellow and red."

"Wow, Tim, that is a nice triangle!" Mia says. "Can I see it?"

Tim gives Mia the triangle block. Mia looks at it and smiles. She puts it on top of her tower.

"Thank you, Tim. Now my tower is taller and prettier!" Mia says.

Tim nods. He looks at his own tower. It is shorter and has only red blocks. He feels a little sad.

"Can I have a blue block, Mia?" Tim asks. "I want to make my tower different."

Mia shakes her head. She likes her blue blocks. She does not want to give them to Tim.

"No, Tim, these are my blue blocks. You have your red blocks. Go make your own tower." Mia says.

Tim frowns. He thinks Mia is not nice. He does not want to play with her anymore. He looks around and sees a fat cat. The cat is sleeping on the sofa. Tim has an idea.

"Okay, Mia, I will make my own tower. But I need one more block." Tim says.

He walks to the sofa and picks up the fat cat. The cat meows and scratches Tim. Tim does not care. He runs back to his tower and puts the cat on top of it.

"Look, Mia, I made a better tower!" Tim says. "It has a red block, a yellow block, a red block, and a fat cat!"

Mia gasps. She sees Tim's tower and the cat. She thinks Tim is silly and mean. She does not like his tower. She does not like his cat. She does not like him.

"Tim, that is not a tower! That is a mess! And that is not a block! That is a cat! You are hurting the cat! You are bad!" Mia says.

She runs to the sofa and takes the cat from Tim's tower. She hugs the cat and soothes it. The cat purrs and licks Mia. Mia smiles and kisses the cat.

"Sorry, cat. Tim is not nice. He does not know how to play. You are my friend. You are a good cat." Mia says.

Tim and Mia do not play with each other anymore. They do not talk to each other anymore. They do not seem happy anymore. They only play with their own blocks and their own cat.

Once upon a time there were two jolly friends, Larry and Liz. One day, they decided to mail a letter. They put the letter in an envelope and addressed it to their friend. 

Liz said, "Let's go to the parade while we wait for a response!" 
So they went to the parade and had a great time watching the floats, dancing and laughing. 

After a while, they received a response! Larry said, "Let's go home and check the mail!" 
They ran home, and sure enough, there was a letter. They were so delighted to read a reply from their friend. 

They hugged each other and said, "What a jolly parade!"

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Beth. She liked eating cereal and playing with her friends. One day Beth's mommy and daddy told her they were going to marry each other. Beth was so excited she didn't know what to do!

Beth and her friends decided to play a game of pretend. They pretended that Beth and her mommy were getting married. They pretended to have a big ceremony and that Beth was the bride. 

Beth's mommy made a special breakfast for them. It was a plate of Beth's favorite cereal and a glass of milk. They all ate together and it was so delicious! 

When it was time to say goodbye, Beth's mommy warned her to be careful. She said, "Remember, the world can be a dangerous place. Always stay with your friends and be careful what you do". 

Beth promised that she would be careful and said goodbye to her mommy. She was very excited that her mommy and daddy were going to marry each other. Beth thought it was the most special day ever!

Once upon a time, there was a rabbit named Bun. Bun loved to zoom around the forest. One day he zoomed so far, he stumbled upon a special tree. The tree looked like it had huge, yummy treats! Bun wanted to try one so he hopped up and took a bite. But, he was surprised that the treat was not yummy, but harsh! Bun spat it out and raced away.
