Once there was a ghost. It was very sad because it missed its family. Every time the ghost thought about them it would feel very sad. So it decided to go on an adventure. 

The ghost flew through the sky and landed on a bright beach. It could feel the soft sand between its toes. The ghost looked out at the ocean, and the bright sun shining through the clouds.

The ghost wanted to stay on the beach forever, but it knew it had to do something. So it scooped up some of the sand and put it in a bottle. Now it could take a piece of the sand with it wherever it went, to remind it of its family.

Whenever the ghost felt lonely it would take out the bottle and remember the sand, and how bright the beach was. Although it still missed its family, it felt a bit better.

Once upon a time, there was a man who had an axe. He used it to cut wood for his fire. One day, he saw a bow in the forest. It was very interesting to him. He wanted to take it home, but he didn't know how to use it.

He asked his friend, "What is this interesting thing?" His friend said, "It is a bow. You use it to shoot arrows." The man thought it sounded fun, so he took the bow home with him.

But when he tried to use the bow, he found it was too hard. He couldn't shoot any arrows. He realized that just because something is interesting, doesn't mean it's easy to use. He decided to stick with his trusty axe and not try to do things that were too hard for him. The moral of the story is that it's important to know your own limits and not try to do things that are too difficult.

Anna and Ben were twins who liked to play in the park. One day, they saw a big hill with a lot of flowers and grass. They wanted to climb the hill and see what was on the other side.

"Let's go, Ben!" Anna said. "Maybe we will find something fun!"

"OK, Anna!" Ben said. "But be careful, it is very high!"

They ran up the hill, holding hands. They felt the wind in their hair and the sun on their faces. They laughed and sang as they climbed. They reached the top and looked around. They saw a big lake with ducks and fish. They saw a bridge with cars and bikes. They saw a forest with trees and birds. They saw a lot of wonder.

"Wow, Anna, look at all this!" Ben said. "It is so pretty!"

"Yes, Ben, it is!" Anna said. "Can we go down and play?"

"Sure, Anna, but we have to watch out for the path. It is very steep and slippery. We don't want to fall and hurt ourselves."

They started to go down the hill, but they were too fast. They lost their balance and rolled down the hill. They bumped into rocks and thorns. They screamed and cried as they fell. They lay at the bottom of the hill, bruised and bleeding. They were very frightened.

"Anna, are you OK?" Ben asked.

"Ben, I'm scared!" Anna said.

They hugged each other and sobbed. They wished they had never climbed the hill. They wished they had stayed in the park. They wished their mom and dad were there.

They heard a voice calling their names. It was their mom. She had seen them fall from the bridge. She ran to them and picked them up. She kissed their wounds and hugged them tight.

"Anna, Ben, what happened?" she asked. "Are you hurt?"

"Mom, we're sorry!" they said. "We wanted to see the lake and the forest, but we fell down the hill. It was so scary!"

"Shh, it's OK, my loves," she said. "You're brave and curious, but you have to be careful. The hill is not a safe place to play. You could have been badly hurt. Next time, stay in the park, OK?"

"OK, mom," they said. "We love you."

"I love you too," she said. "Now let's go home and get some ice cream."

name_of_work: Once Upon a Time by Gabriel Okara
content: Once upon a time, son, they used to laugh with their hearts and laugh with their eyes: but now they only laugh with their teeth, while their ice-block-cold eyes search behind my shadow. There was a time indeed they used to shake hands with their hearts: but that's gone, son. Now they shake hands without hearts while their left hands search my empty pockets. 'Feel at home!' 'Come again': they say, and when I come again and feel at home, once, twice, there will be no thrice- for then I find doors shut on me. So I have learned many things, son. I have learned to wear many faces like dresses - homeface, officeface, streetface, hostface, cocktailface, with all their conforming smiles like a fixed portrait smile. And I have learned too to laugh with only my teeth and shake hands without my heart. I have also learned to say,'Goodbye', when I mean 'Good-riddance': to say 'Glad to meet you', without being glad; and to say 'It's been nice talking to you', after being bored. But believe me, son. I want to be what I used to be when I was like you. I want to unlearn all these muting things. Most of all, I want to relearn how to laugh, for my laugh in the mirror shows only my teeth like a snake's bare fangs! So show me, son, how to laugh; show me how I used to laugh and smile once upon a time when I was like you. Gabriel Okara Who is talking in the poem? What assumptions can you make about the kind of life he has lived and his present circumstances? What kind of person do you imagine him to be? What has he learnt to do with his own feelings? Who is the person addressing? What does he hope to learn from him? What does he mean by wanting 'to unlearn all these muting things'? Why do you think the poet has given it the title, 'Once Upon a Time'?

Once upon a time, there was a fairy named Lily. She was a kind fairy and always helped others. One day, Lily saw a little bird that was shivering in the cold. She felt sad for the bird and wanted to help. So, she used her wings to cover the bird and keep it warm.

The bird felt happy and thanked the fairy. Lily smiled and said, "I am compassionate and always want to help others." The bird chirped happily and flew away. From that day on, Lily continued to help others and spread kindness throughout the forest.

One day, John was walking outside when he spotted a big, grey bird flying by. John jumped up and down and said, "Wow!" 

The bird flew really fast up above the trees and into the sky. It zipped and zig-zagged in the air like a zipper. 

John's mom said, "Come on let's follow it!" They walked and ran, trying to keep up with the bird. It was difficult because the bird was going so fast.

But then, the skies grew dark and gloomy. John's mom said, "Oh no, we have to go back now before it rains." 

So, they hurried back home, but John kept looking up at the sky, hoping he would see the bird again. It was exciting to watch it speed through the clouds!

name_of_work: Death of a Young Son by Drowning by Margaret Atwood
content: He, who navigated with success the dangerous river of his own birth once more set forth on a voyage of discovery into the land I floated on but could not touch to claim. His feet slid on the bank, the currents took him; he swirled with ice and trees in the swollen water and plunged into distant regions, his head a bathysphere; through his eyes' thin glass bubbles he looked out, reckless adventurer on a landscape stranger than Uranus we have all been to and some remember. There was an accident; the air locked, he was hung in the river like a heart. They retrieved the swamped body, cairn of my plans and future charts, with poles and hooks from among the nudging logs. It was spring, the sun kept shining, the new grass leapt to solidity; my hands glistened with details. After the long trip I was tired of waves. My foot hit rock. The dreamed sails collapsed, ragged. I planted him in this country like a flag.

Ben is a lawyer. He works in a big building with many books and papers. He helps people with their problems. But he is lonely. He does not have many friends or time to play.

One day, he sees a flyer on the street. It says: "Come to the circus! See the clowns, the animals, and the acrobats!" Ben thinks: "Maybe I can have some fun at the circus. Maybe I can make some friends there."

He buys a ticket and goes to the circus. He sits in a seat and watches the show. He laughs at the clowns, he gasps at the animals, and he claps at the acrobats. He likes the circus very much.

He especially likes the girl who can balance on a rope. She wears a pretty dress and a hat with feathers. She walks on the rope high in the air. She does not fall. She smiles and waves at the people.

Ben thinks: "She is amazing. She is brave. She is beautiful. I want to talk to her. I want to be her friend."

He waits until the show is over. He goes to the back of the tent. He sees the girl who can balance on the rope. She is sitting on a chair. She looks tired and sad.

Ben says: "Hello. I am Ben. I am a lawyer. I saw you on the rope. You were wonderful."

The girl looks at him. She says: "Thank you. I am Lily. I am an acrobat. I have been on the rope since I was three. It is my job."

Ben says: "Do you like your job?"

Lily says: "Sometimes. But it is hard. I have to practice a lot. I have to travel a lot. I do not have many friends or time to play."

Ben says: "I understand. I have the same problem. I work a lot. I do not have many friends or time to play. I am lonely."

Lily says: "You are lonely? But you are a lawyer. You help people. You have a big building. You have many books and papers."

Ben says: "Yes, but that is not enough. I need more. I need fun. I need friends. I need you."

Lily smiles. She says: "You need me? But you are a lawyer. I am an acrobat. We are different. We have different lives."

Ben says: "Maybe. But we also have something in common. We both can balance. You can balance on a rope. I can balance the law. We both have skills. We both have dreams. We both have hearts."

Lily says: "You are right. We do have something in common. We both can balance. We both have skills. We both have dreams. We both have hearts. And we both are lonely."

Ben says: "Maybe we do not have to be lonely anymore. Maybe we can be friends. Maybe we can be more than friends. Maybe we can balance each other."

Lily says: "Maybe we can. Maybe we can balance each other. Maybe we can make each other happy."

They hold hands. They look into each other's eyes. They feel something warm and sweet. They kiss.

The end.

Once upon a time, in a small kitchen, there lived an enthusiastic teaspoon named Timmy. Timmy loved to help his friends, the big spoon and the fork, mix and stir tasty food. They all lived with a nice family who used them every day.

One sunny day, the family wanted to make a yummy cake. Mom called Timmy and his friends to help. She said, "Timmy, please choose which spoon we should use to mix the cake." Timmy thought and thought. He wanted to help, but he was too small to mix the cake all by himself.

So, Timmy said, "Mom, let's use the big spoon to mix the cake. I can help too!" Mom smiled and said, "Good choice, Timmy! Let's all work together." They all mixed the cake, and it was so much fun. The cake turned out to be delicious, and everyone was happy. Timmy felt proud that he could help his family make something so tasty.

Timmy was a little boy who liked to wander. He did not listen to his mommy when she told him to stay close to her. He wanted to see everything in the big park. He saw birds, flowers, swings, and slides. He saw a big pond with ducks and fish. He wanted to feed them, but he had no bread.

He saw a man with a cart. The man had many treats. He had ice cream, candy, popcorn, and soda. Timmy wanted a treat. He forgot about his mommy. He ran to the man and asked for a treat.

"Hello, little boy. Do you want a treat?" the man said.

"Yes, please. I want ice cream," Timmy said.

"OK, here you go. That will be one dollar," the man said.

Timmy did not have a dollar. He had no money at all. He looked sad.

"Sorry, little boy. No money, no treat. Go away," the man said.

Timmy felt upset. He wanted a treat, but he had no money. He wanted his mommy, but he did not know where she was. He looked around, but he did not see her. He was lost.

He started to cry. He cried loud and hard. He hoped his mommy would hear him and find him. But she did not. She was too far away. She was looking for him, but she could not see him. She was worried and scared.

A big dog heard Timmy cry. The dog was hungry and mean. He saw Timmy and ran to him. He barked and growled. He wanted to bite Timmy. Timmy was afraid. He screamed and ran. But the dog was faster. He caught Timmy and bit him. Timmy felt pain. He bled and cried. He wished he had listened to his mommy.

The moral of the story is: Always listen to your mommy and stay close to her. Do not wander away from her. Do not talk to strangers. Do not be greedy for treats. Or you might get hurt.

Late lies the wintry sun a-bed, A frosty, fiery sleepy-head; Blinks but an hour or two; and then, A blood-red orange, sets again. Before the stars have left the skies, At morning in the dark I rise; And shivering in my nakedness, By the cold candle, bathe and dress. Close by the jolly fire I sit To warm my frozen bones a bit; Or with a reindeer-sled, explore The colder countries round the door. When to go out, my nurse doth wrap Me in my comforter and cap; The cold wind burns my face, and blows Its frosty pepper up my nose. Black are my steps on silver sod; Thick blows my frosty breath abroad; And tree and house, and hill and lake, Are frosted like a wedding-cake.

Once there was a three year old child named Jack. He lived in a town that had big open fields. Every day, Jack would jog around the fields. One day, he noticed an old man jogging in the fields too. He ran to the old man and asked what he was doing.

The old man told Jack he was jogging to stay fit and gain wisdom. Jack asked what that meant, and the old man explained wisdom was like a special knowledge that came from experience. Jack thought for a moment, and asked the man if he could teach him how to be wise.

The old man smiled and said learning wisdom was easy. He told Jack he just had to keep his heart and mind open and pay attention to the world around him. Then he said, "Let's keep jogging and when you see something interesting, like a bird in the sky or a butterfly on a flower, let that teach you something - like the importance of being free or watching the world around you".

Jack thought about this and thanked the old man. He said goodbye and went on his way. From that day forward, he started jogging every day and paid attention to the world around him, learning something new every day. In time, little by little, Jack began to gain wisdom.

The mailman smiled and said, "Have a good night, Lily." And with that, he delivered the package and went on his way. Lily went to bed happy, dreaming of all the fun she would have wearing her new dress.

name_of_work: It Is Here by Harold Pinter
content: What sound was that? I turn away, into the shaking room. What was that sound that came in on the dark? What is this maze of light it leaves us in? What is this stance we take, To turn away and then turn back? What did we hear? It was the breath we took when we first met. Listen. It is here.

Once upon a time, there was a bald man who was carrying a mountain of laundry. He was walking down a street, shouting in frustration. Suddenly, he heard a small voice coming from behind him. He turned around and saw a little 3 year old boy. The man scrunched up his face in surprise.

"What are you doing?" he said.
The little boy grinned and shouted, "You can help me carry this laundry, mister!"
The man laughed and said, "Alright, let's get going!" 

The two of them started walking down the street with the mountain of laundry between them. As they went, the little boy kept asking the man questions. He wanted to know why the man was bald, why he was carrying so much laundry, and why he was so grumpy. The bald man answered all of the questions, and soon the two of them were laughing and singing songs. 

When they finally arrived at the bald man's house, the little boy said goodbye and ran away. The man watched him, smiling, before he went inside to put away his laundry.

Once there was a brave fish called Bob. He lived in the deep, blue sea and loved swimming and splashing about. One day, Bob noticed that something was wrong with his fins. They were all bent and crooked, so he couldn't swim in a straight line. 

Bob was worried but he didn't give up. He decided to ask for help to repair his fins. He found a whale called Wally who was very alert and knew all about how to fix things. Wally said he could help Bob, so Bob was very happy. 

Wally gave Bob a hug and then they took a swim together. As they swam, Wally showed Bob how to be still and fix all of the bent fins. Bob was very careful and followed all of Wally's instructions. Finally, the fins were all straight and Bob was ready to swim again! 

With one last wave, Bob said goodbye to Wally and thanked him for helping him. Then he set off happily, swimming in perfect smooth circles and feeling proud of himself for doing such a great job. He was back to being the brave Bob and he loved it!

name_of_work: Hiawatha's Childhood by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
content: By the shores of Gitche Gumee, By yhr shining Big-Sea-Water, Stood the wigwam of Nokomis, Daughter of the Moon, Nokomis. Dark behind it rose the forest, Rose the black and gloomy pine-trees, Rose the firs with cones upon them; Bright before it beat the water, Beat the clear and sunny water, Beat the shingin Big-Set-Water. There the wrinkled old Nokomis Nursed the little Hiawatha, Rocked him in his linden cradle, Bedded soft in moss and rushes, Safely bound with reindeer sinews; Stilled his fretful wail by saying, "Hush, the Naked Bear will hear thee!" Lulled him into slumber, singing, "Ewa-yea! my little owlet! Who is this, that lights the wigwam? With his great eyes lights the wigwam? Ewa-yea! my little owlet!" Many things Nokomis taught him Of the stars that shin in heaven; Showed him Ishkoodah, the comet, Ishkoodah, with fiery tresses, Showed the Death-Dance of the spritits, Warriors with their plumes and war-clubs, Flaring far away to norhtward In the frosty nights ofwinder; Showed the borad white road in heaven, Pathway of the ghosts, the shadows, Running straight across the heavens, Crowded with the ghosts, the shadows. At the door on summer evenings, Sat the little Hiawatha, Heard the whispering of the pine-trees, Heard the lapping of the waters, Sounds of music, words of wonder; "Minne-wawa!" said the pine-trees, "Mudway-aushka!" said the water. Saw the fire-fly Wah-wah-taysee, Flitting through the dusk of evening, With the twinkle of its candle Lighting up the brakes and bushes, And he sang the song of children, Sang the song Nokomis taught him: "Wah-wah-taysee, little fire-fly, Little flitting, white-fire insect, Little, dancing, white-fire creature, Light me with your little candle, Ere upon my bed I lay me, Ere in sleep I close my eyelids!" Saw the moon rise from the water, Rippling, rounding from the water, Saw the flecks and shadows on it, Whispered, "What is that, Nokomis?" And the good Nokomis answered: "Once a warrior, very angry, Seized his grandmother, and threw her Up into the sky at midnight; Right against the moon he threw her; 'Tis her body that you see there." Saw the rainbow in the heaven, In the eastern sky the rainbow, Whispered, "What is that, Nokomis?" And the good Nokomis answered: "'Tis the heaven of flowers you see there; All the wild-flowers of the forest, All the lilies of the prairie, When on earth they fade and perish, Blossom in that heaven above us.', When he heard the owls at midnight, Hooting, laughing in the forest, "What is that?" he cried in terror; "What is that," he said, "Nokomis?" And the good Nokomis answered: "That is but the owl and owlet, Talking in their native language, Talking, scolding at each other." Then the little Hiawatha Learned of every bird its language, Learned their names and all their secrets, How they built their nests in summer, Where they hid themselves in winter, Talked with them whene'er he met them, Called them "Hiawatha's Chickens." Of all beasts he learned the language, Learned their names and all their secrets, How the beavers built their lodges, Where the squirrels hid their acorns, How the reindeer ran so swiftly, Why the rabbit was so timid, Talked with them whene'er he met them, Called them "Hiawatha's Brothers."'

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a special toy, a teddy bear, that she loved very much. One day, she accidentally dropped it and it broke. Lily was very sad and wished her teddy bear could be fixed.

Her mom saw how sad she was and promised to restore the teddy bear. Lily was so happy and felt safe knowing her mom would fix it. She knew her wish had come true and she was so grateful to her mom for making her teddy bear safe again.

name_of_work: Adam's Curse by William Butler Yeats
content: We sat together at one summer's end, That beautiful mild woman, your close friend, And you and I, and talked of poetry. I said, 'A line will take us hours maybe; Yet if it does not seem a moment's thought, Our stitching and unstitching has been naught. Better go down upon your marrow-bones And scrub a kitchen pavement, or break stones Like an old pauper, in all kinds of weather; For to articulate sweet sounds together Is to work harder than all these, and yet Be thought an idler by the noisy set Of bankers, schoolmasters, and clergymen The martyrs call the world.' And thereupon That beautiful mild woman for whose sake There's many a one shall find out all heartache On finding that her voice is sweet and low Replied, 'To be born woman is to know-- Although they do not talk of it at school-- That we must labour to be beautiful.' I said, 'It's certain there is no fine thing Since Adam's fall but needs much labouring. There have been lovers who thought love should be So much compounded of high courtesy That they would sigh and quote with learned looks Precedents out of beautiful old books; Yet now it seems an idle trade enough.' We sat grown quiet at the name of love; We saw the last embers of daylight die, And in the trembling blue-green of the sky A moon, worn as if it had been a shell Washed by time's waters as they rose and fell About the stars and broke in days and years. I had a thought for no one's but your ears: That you were beautiful, and that I strove To love you in the old high way of love; That it had all seemed happy, and yet we'd grown As weary-hearted as that hollow moon.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to do yoga with her mommy. One day, Lily's friend Tommy came over to play. Lily asked Tommy if he wanted to try yoga with them. 

Tommy said, "I don't know how to do yoga. It looks foolish." 

Lily's mommy said, "It's okay, Tommy. We can teach you. Yoga is good for your body and mind." 

Tommy agreed to try, and they all did yoga together. It was fun and they felt happy and relaxed afterwards. Tommy said, "I'm glad I tried yoga. It's not foolish at all!" 

From that day on, Lily, her mommy, and Tommy did yoga together every week. They all felt healthy and happy.

Once upon a time, there was a musician named Mike. He loved to play his guitar and sing songs. One day, he met a little girl named Lily.

Lily asked Mike to play a song for her. Mike was happy to do it. He started to play his guitar and sing. Lily loved the music and started to shake her body.

After the song, Lily said to Mike, "You are a great musician!" Mike smiled and said, "Thank you, Lily. But sometimes I can be selfish and only think about myself."

Lily didn't understand what selfish meant, so she asked Mike. He explained that sometimes he only thinks about what he wants and doesn't think about others. Lily said, "Oh, I don't want to be selfish. I want to be like you and make people happy with my music!"

Tom and Mia liked to play pretend at school. They had a big box of costumes and toys to dress up and act out stories. One day, they found a folder with pictures of animals in it. They decided to pretend they were in the jungle.

Tom put on a brown hat and a green shirt. He said he was a explorer. Mia put on a yellow dress and a flower crown. She said she was a princess. They took the folder and went to the play area. They saw a rug with spots on it. They said it was a leopard. They saw a stuffed toy with stripes on it. They said it was a tiger. They saw a pillow with a mane on it. They said it was a lion.

They opened the folder and looked at the pictures. They saw a picture of a lion. They said it was the king of the jungle. They saw a picture of a tiger. They said it was the queen of the jungle. They saw a picture of a leopard. They said it was the prince of the jungle. They saw a picture of a bear. They said it was the friend of the jungle.

They wanted to make the animals talk. They used their voices to make sounds. Tom made a roar for the lion. Mia made a roar for the tiger. They made a roar for the leopard. They made a growl for the bear. They had fun making noises and telling stories.

But then, they heard a real roar. It was loud and scary. They looked around and saw a big dog. It had a collar and a leash, but it had escaped from its owner. It was barking and running towards them. They were afraid. They dropped the folder and ran to their teacher. The teacher saw the dog and called for help. She hugged Tom and Mia and told them they were safe.

The dog's owner came and caught the dog. He said he was sorry. He said the dog was not mean, but playful. He said the dog liked to chase things. He said the dog's name was Rover. He said he was a modest dog, but sometimes he forgot his manners. He said he would keep him on a leash from now on.

Tom and Mia were still scared, but they were also curious. They asked the teacher if they could pet the dog. The teacher said yes, but only if the owner said it was okay. The owner said it was okay, but only if they were gentle. Tom and Mia went to the dog and touched his fur. It was soft and warm. The dog licked their hands and wagged his tail. It was friendly and happy. Tom and Mia smiled and said hello to Rover. They said he was a good dog, but he should not roar like a lion. They said they liked him better when he was modest. Rover barked and nodded. He agreed.

When I go back to earth And all my joyous body Puts off the red and white That once had been so proud, If men should pass above With false and feeble pity, My dust will find a voice To answer them aloud: "Be still, I am content, Take back your poor compassion-- Joy was a flame in me Too steady to destroy. Lithe as a bending reed Loving the storm that sways her-- I found more joy in sorrow Than you could find in joy."

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily went outside to play in the rain. She didn't have an umbrella, so she got very wet. Then, she saw her friend Timmy coming towards her with an umbrella. Timmy shared his umbrella with Lily and they walked together in the rain. 

As they walked, they heard a noise. It sounded like someone was whispering. They looked around, but they couldn't see anyone. Lily asked Timmy if he heard it too, and he nodded. They walked a little further and heard the whispering again. This time, they saw a little bird hiding under a tree. The bird was harmless and just wanted to say hello. 

Lily and Timmy were happy to have made a new friend. They whispered back to the bird and thanked it for saying hello. Then, they continued to walk in the rain with their umbrella, feeling happy and safe.

Once there was a lively little girl called Sarah. She loved to explore and play every day. One day, Sarah found a tube of glue on the floor in her house and she was so excited. She brought it over to her daddy and said, "look what I found!" 

Her daddy looked at the tube of glue and smiled. "What a great find! What do you want to do with it?"

Sarah said, "I want to put it all over my clothes and my hair!" 

Her daddy was embarrassed but he smiled and said, "I don't think that's a good idea. Let's put it away and find something else to do with it." 

So Sarah and her daddy found lots of fun things to do with the glue. They glued paper to make cards, held a contest to see who could make the tallest glue tower, and created a glue painting where they glued colourful objects to create a unique art piece. 

Sarah and her daddy had a great and lively day with the glue!

Once upon a time, there was a modest little house. It was small, but it was very pretty. The house had a door that was the exit. The door was blue and had a shiny handle. The people who lived in the house loved it very much.

One day, they decided to decorate the house. They wanted to make it even prettier. They got paint, brushes, and paper. They painted the walls with fun colors like red, yellow, and green. They made the house look bright and happy.

When they were done, they looked at the house and smiled. They liked the new colors and the pretty decorations. They were very happy with their little house. From that day on, they loved their home even more. They always remembered to close the exit door and keep their house safe and warm.

Once upon a time, there were two friends named Timmy and Tommy. They both loved to play with toys and eat yummy snacks like lime popsicles. One day, they found a pretty toy car and both wanted to play with it at the same time. They started to quarrel and argue about who should play with it first. 

Suddenly, Timmy accidentally dropped the toy car and it broke into pieces. Tommy got very upset and started to cry. But then, Timmy said sorry and they hugged each other. They realized that it was more important to be friends than to fight over a toy. 

After that, they shared their lime popsicles and played with their other toys together. From then on, they never quarreled again and always remembered to be kind to each other.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sally. Sally liked to explore the world. She was always curious and brave. 

One day, Sally walked deep into the forest. Suddenly, she heard a warning from the trees. "Be careful!" they said.

Sally quickly realised the trees were warning her about the river. She thanked them and left before she got any sicker. She vowed to never forget the warning from the trees.

Once upon a time, there was a penguin named Pip. Pip was a rare penguin because he had a big blue spot on his belly. Pip lived in the cold ice land with his family and friends.

name_of_work: The Spirit is too Blunt an Instrument by Anne Stevenson
content: The spirit is too blunt an instrument to have made this baby. Nothing so unskilful as human passions could have managed the intricate exacting particulars: the tiny blind bones with their manipulating tendons, the knee and the knucklebones, the resilient fine meshings of ganglia and vertebrae, the chain of the difficult spine. Observe the distinct eyelashes and sharp crescent fingernails, the shell-like complexity of the ear, with its firm involutions concentric in miniature to minute ossicles. Imagine the infinitesimal capillaries, the flawless connections of the lungs, the invisible neural filaments through which the completed body already answers to the brain. Then name any passion or sentiment possessed of the simplest accuracy. No, no desire or affection could have done with practice what habit has done perfectly, indifferently, through the body's ignorant precision. It is left to the vagaries of the mind to invent love and despair and anxiety and their pain.

Once upon a time, there was a green frog named Fred. Fred lived in a clean pond with his best friend, a little fish named Sam. They liked to play and swim together all day long.

One day, they found a small box near the pond. "What's that?" asked Sam. "I don't know," said Fred, "let's try to unlock it." They looked around and found a tiny key. Fred used the key to unlock the box. Inside the box, they found a shiny toy car.

"Wow, a toy car!" said Sam. "Let's play with it!" So, Fred and Sam took turns pushing the car around the pond. They had lots of fun and played until the sun went down. Then, they put the car back in the box, locked it, and hid the key. They knew they could unlock the box and play with the car again tomorrow.

One day, Louise wanted to try to sail to a far away island. She got into her boat, but after a few hours she was lost. Then, a strong wind started blowing and the sea became very rough. Louise tried hard to stay afloat, but she was very scared.

Suddenly, Louise noticed a big anchor sticking out of the water. She decided to hold on to it and try to use it to stay safe. She tried her best to keep a hold of it, but it was very difficult. The waves kept pushing her around and every time she tried to keep a tight grip on the anchor she almost fell out of the boat.

After a few hours, Louise finally managed to keep a grip on the anchor and stay in her boat. She was very relieved and felt so proud of herself for succeeding. Louise sailed back home, happy that she had overcome a difficult challenge.

name_of_work: Break of Day in the Trenches by Isaac Rosenberg
content: The darkness crumbles away. It is the same old druid Time as ever, Only a live thing leaps my hand, A queer sardonic rat, As I pull the parapet's poppy To stick behind my ear. Droll rat, they would shoot you if they knew Your cosmopolitan sympathies. Now you have touched this English hand You will do the same to a German Soon, no doubt, if it be your pleasure To cross the sleeping green between. It seems you inwardly grin as you pass Strong eyes, fine limbs, haughty athletes, Less chanced than you for life, Bonds to the whims of murder, Sprawled in the bowels of the earth, The torn fields of France. What do you see in our eyes At the shrieking iron and flame Hurled through still heavens? What quaver--what heart aghast? Poppies whose roots are in man's veins Drop, and are ever dropping; But mine in my ear is safe-- Just a little white with the dust.

name_of_work: The Cool Web by Robert Graves
content: Children are dumb to say how hot the day is, How hot the scent is of the summer rose, How dreadful the black wastes of evening sky, How dreadful the tall soldiers drumming by. But we have speech, to chill the angry day, And speech, to dull the rose's cruel scent. We spell away the overhanging night, We spell away the soldiers and the fright. There's a cool web of language winds us in, Retreat from too much joy or too much fear: We grow sea-green at last and coldly die In brininess and volubility. But if we let our tongues lose self-possession, Throwing off language and its watery clasp Before our death, instead of when death comes, Facing the wide glare of the children's day, Facing the rose, the dark sky and the drums, We shall go mad no doubt and die that way.

name_of_work: To the Rainbow by Thomas Campbell
content: Triumphal arch, that fill'st the sky When storms prepare to part, I ask not proud Philosophy To teach me what thou art; - Still seem; as to my childhood's sight, A midway station given For happy spirits to alight Betwixt the earth and heaven. Can all that Optics teach unfold Thy form to please me so, As when I dreamt of gems and gold Hid in thy radiant bow? When Science from Creation's face Enchantment's veil withdraws, What lovely visions yield their place To cold material laws! And yet, fair bow, no fabling dreams, But words of the Most High, Have told why first thy robe of beams Was woven in the sky. When o'er the green, undeluged earth Heaven's covenant thou didst shine, How came the world's gray fathers forth To watch thy sacred sign! And when its yellow luster smiled O'er mountains yet untrod, Each mother held aloft her child To bless the bow of God. Methinks, thy jubilee to keep, The first-made anthem rang On earth, delivered from the deep, And the first poet sang. Nor ever shall the Muse's eye Unraptured greet thy beam; Theme of primeval prophecy, Be still the prophet's theme! The earth to thee her incense yields, The lark thy welcome sings, When, glittering in the freshened fields, The snowy mushroom springs. How glorious is thy girdle, cast O'er mountain, tower, and town, Or mirrored in the ocean vast, A thousand fathoms down! As fresh in yon horizon dark, As young thy beauties seem, As when the eagle from the ark First sported in thy beam: For, faithful to its sacred page, Heaven still rebuilds thy span; Nor lets the type grow pale with age, That first spoke peace to man.

One day, Tom and Mia went to the park with their mom. They saw a big slide, a swing, and a sandbox. They ran to the slide and took turns going down. "This is fun!" Tom said. "Yes, it is!" Mia agreed.

Then they saw a boy sitting on a bench with a big book. He looked sad. Tom and Mia went to him and asked, "What are you doing?" The boy said, "I am reading about planets. They are big balls in the sky. Some are hot, some are cold, some have rings, some have moons. They are very cool."

Tom and Mia looked at the book. They saw pictures of different planets. They said, "Wow, they are cool. Can we look at your book?" The boy said, "Sure, you can. But be careful. This is my favorite book. My dad gave it to me. He is an astronaut. He goes to space and sees the planets."

Tom and Mia were amazed. They said, "Your dad is an astronaut? That is awesome. Does he use a rocket to go to space?" The boy said, "Yes, he does. He uses a big rocket that makes a loud noise and flies very fast. He wears a special suit and a helmet. He talks to me on the phone sometimes. He tells me stories about the planets. He says they are not like our planet. Our planet is regular. It has water, air, plants, animals, and people. The other planets are different. They have rocks, dust, ice, gas, or fire. They are not good for living."

Tom and Mia listened to the boy. They said, "Your dad is very brave. We want to hear more stories about the planets. Can we be your friends?" The boy smiled. He said, "Yes, you can. I am Ben. What are your names?" Tom and Mia said, "We are Tom and Mia. We like planets too. Can we play with you?" Ben said, "Yes, you can. Let's go to the sandbox. We can use the sand to make our own planets. We can pretend we are astronauts too." Tom, Mia, and Ben went to the sandbox. They had fun making planets and playing together. They became good friends.

name_of_work: I Knew a Woman by Theodore Roethke
content: I knew a woman, lovely in her bones, When small birds sighed, she would sigh back at them; Ah, when she moved, she moved more ways than one: The shapes a bright container can contain! Of her choice virtues only gods should speak, Or English poets who grew up on Greek (I'd have them sing in chorus, cheek to cheek). How well her wishes went! She stroked my chin, She taught me Turn, and Counter-turn, and Stand; She taught me Touch, that undulant white skin; I nibbled meekly from her proffered hand; She was the sickle; I, poor I, the rake, Coming behind her for her pretty sake (But what prodigious mowing we did make). Love likes a gander, and adores a goose: Her full lips pursed, the errant note to seize; She played it quick, she played it light and loose; My eyes, they dazzled at her flowing knees; Her several parts could keep a pure repose, Or one hip quiver with a mobile nose (She moved in circles, and those circles moved). Let seed be grass, and grass turn into hay: I'm martyr to a motion not my own; What's freedom for? To know eternity. I swear she cast a shadow white as stone. But who would count eternity in days? These old bones live to learn her wanton ways: (I measure time by how a body sways).

name_of_work: In the Light of the Moon by Delmira Agustini
content: The moon is pale and sad, the moon is bloodless and lifeless. The crescent moon imagines to me a soft profile of death... I who prefer the distinguished paleness Of all the Arabian pearls, the newly opened rose, In a corner of the land with the color of life, I adore that pale moon, I adore that dead face! And on the altar of the nights, like a flower on fire And drunk with strange perfumes, my soul the rendered incense. I know of lips withered in blasphemy and wine, Who kiss after the orgy their footprints on the road; Fools who die kissing his image in frozen lakes... Because she is the light of innocence, because in that mysterious light White things light up, things turn white, And even the darkest souls take uncertain light!

The cardboard shows me how it was When the two girl cousins went paddling Each one holding one of my mother's hands, And she the big girl - some twelve years or so. All three stood still to smile through their hair At the uncle with the camera, A sweet face My mother's, that was before I was born And the sea, which appears to have changed less Washed their terribly transient feet. Some twenty- thirty- years later She'd laugh at the snapshot. "See Betty And Dolly," she'd say, "and look how they Dressed us for the beach." The sea holiday was her past, mine is her laughter. Both wry With the laboured ease of loss Now she's has been dead nearly as many years As that girl lived. And of this circumstance There is nothing to say at all, Its silence silences.

Once upon a time there was a boy named Mark. Every morning he would wake up happy and ready for the day. He wondered what fun things he would do.

One day when Mark woke up, he noticed something was different. The sun was shining through the window but it was very bright and harsh. He didn't like it. He went to the kitchen and told his mom, "Mom, the sun is too bright and harsh."

Her eyes shine rough as amethysts. She wears a plaid shawl of our clan with the zeal of an Amazon. She is one of those women burnt in her croft rather than moved off the land. She comes from them, her snake's skin. She speaks Gaelic mostly, English only when she has to, then it's blasphemy. My grandmother sits by the fire and swears There'll be no darkie baby in this house My grandmother is a Scottish pine, tall, straight-backed proud and plentiful, her hair tied with pins in a ball of steel wool. Her face is tight as ice and her eyes are amethysts.

name_of_work: O Sleep, My Babe by Sara Coleridge
content: O sleep, my babe, hear not the rippling wave, Nor feel the breeze that round thee ling'ring strays To drink thy balmy breath, And sigh one long farewell. Soon shall it mourn above thy wat'ry bed, And whisper to me, on the wave-beat shore, Deep murm'ring in reproach, Thy sad untimely fate. Ere those dear eyes had open'd on the light, In vain to plead, thy coming life was sold, O waken'd but to sleep, Whence it can wake no more! A thousand and a thousand silken leaves The tufted beech unfolds in early spring, All clad in tenderest green, All of the self-same shape: A thousand infant faces, soft and sweet, Each year sends forth, yet every mother views Her last not least beloved Like its dear self alone. No musing mind hath ever yet foreshaped The face to-morrow's sun shall first reveal, No heart hath e'er conceived What love that face will bring. O sleep, my babe, nor heed how mourns the gale To part with thy soft locks and fragrant breath, As when it deeply sighs O'er autumn's latest bloom.

name_of_work: All But Blind by Walter de la Mare
content: All but blind In his chambered hole, Gropes for worms The four-clawed mole. All but blind In the evening sky, The hooded Bat Twirls softly by. All but blind In the burning day, The barn owl Blunders on her way. And blind as are These three to me, So blind to someone I must be.

name_of_work: The Gods of Copybook Headings by Rudyard Kipling
content: As I pass through my incarnations in every age and race, I make my proper prostrations to the Gods of the Market Place. Peering through reverent fingers I watch them flourish and fall, And the Gods of the Copybook Headings, I notice, outlast them all. We were living in trees when they met us. They showed us each in turn That Water would certainly wet us, as Fire would certainly burn: But we found them lacking in Uplift, Vision and Breadth of Mind, So we left them to teach the Gorillas while we followed the March of Mankind. We moved as the Spirit listed. They never altered their pace, Being neither cloud nor wind-borne like the Gods of the Market Place, But they always caught up with our progress, and presently word would come That a tribe had been wiped off its icefield, or the lights had gone out in Rome. With the Hopes that our World is built on they were utterly out of touch, They denied that the Moon was Stilton; they denied she was even Dutch; They denied that Wishes were Horses; they denied that a Pig had Wings; So we worshipped the Gods of the Market Who promised these beautiful things. When the Cambrian measures were forming, They promised perpetual peace. They swore, if we gave them our weapons, that the wars of the tribes would cease. But when we disarmed They sold us and delivered us bound to our foe, And the Gods of the Copybook Headings said: "Stick to the Devil you know." On the first Feminian Sandstones we were promised the Fuller Life (Which started by loving our neighbour and ended by loving his wife) Till our women had no more children and the men lost reason and faith, And the Gods of the Copybook Headings said: "The Wages of Sin is Death." In the Carboniferous Epoch we were promised abundance for all, By robbing selected Peter to pay for collective Paul; But, though we had plenty of money, there was nothing our money could buy, And the Gods of the Copybook Headings said: "If you don't work you die." Then the Gods of the Market tumbled, and their smooth-tongued wizards withdrew And the hearts of the meanest were humbled and began to believe it was true That All is not Gold that Glitters, and Two and Two make Four And the Gods of the Copybook Headings limped up to explain it once more. As it will be in the future, it was at the birth of Man There are only four things certain since Social Progress began. That the Dog returns to his Vomit and the Sow returns to her Mire, And the burnt Fool's bandaged finger goes wabbling back to the Fire; And that after this is accomplished, and the brave new world begins When all men are paid for existing and no man must pay for his sins, As surely as Water will wet us, as surely as Fire will burn, The Gods of the Copybook Headings with terror and slaughter return!

name_of_work: The Suicide's Soliloquy by Abraham Lincoln
content: Here where the lonely hooting owl Sends forth his midnight moans, Fierce wolves shall o'er my carcase growl Or buzzards pick my bones. No fellow-man shall learn my fate, Or where my ashes lie; Unless by beasts drawn round their bait, Or by the ravens' cry. Yes! I've resolved the deed to do, And this the place to do it: This heart I'll rush a dagger through, Though I in hell should rue it! Hell! What is hell to one like me Who pleasures never knew; By friends consigned to misery By hope deserted too? To ease me of this power to think, That through my bosom raves, I'll headlong leap from hell's high brink, And wallow in its waves. Though devils yell, and burning chains May waken long regret; Their frightful screams, and piercing pains, Will help me to forget. Yes! I'm prepared, through endless night, To take that fiery berth! Think not with tales of hell to fright Me, who am damn'd on earth! Sweet steel! come forth from out your sheath, And glist'ning, speak your powers; Rip up the organs of my breath, And draw my blood in showers! I strike! It quivers in that heart Which drives me to this end; I draw and kiss the bloody dart, My last--my only friend!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the garden and pick flowers. One day, she found a bottle of perfume. It smelled interesting and she wanted to show it to her mommy.

Lily ran inside the house and shouted, "Mommy, mommy, look what I found!" Her mommy turned around and saw the bottle of perfume in Lily's hand. "That's very pretty, Lily. But be careful, it might burn your skin," said her mommy.

Lily was scared and asked, "What does burn mean, mommy?" Her mommy explained that it's when something gets too hot and can hurt you. Lily nodded and promised to be careful. She put the perfume on her dresser and admired it from afar. From that day on, she always made sure to ask her mommy before touching anything that could burn her.

Johnny walked into the modern kitchen. He looked around, seeking something fun to do. His eyes fell on a yellow button on the wall. 

Johnny smiled and ran towards it. He stopped, realizing he couldn't reach it.

"Mommy, can you push this for me," Johnny asked.

His mom smiled and stepped forward. She crouched low and carefully pushed the yellow button. Suddenly, the kitchen table began to move, spinning around at a speed Johnny found thrilling.

"Whee!" Johnny shouted, jumping up and down with excitement.

The table spun around until it stopped. Johnny hugged his mom and thanked her. Then, he ran off to explore the rest of the modern kitchen.

Once upon a time, there was a nosy girl named Pam. Pam went to the store to buy some sugar. But when she got there, she couldn't find it. She looked and looked all around, but there was no sugar to be found.

The store manager said to Pam, "Someone must have lost the sugar." Pam was so sad. She wanted the sugar.

Then, Pam thought of a plan. She asked all the other customers, "Have you seen my sugar?" Everyone said no, until one old man said, "Yes, I saw someone take it." 

Pam soon caught the sneaky thief and got her sugar back. She was so happy that she didn't lose it. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a good king who lived in a small kingdom. The king was very kind, and the people in the kingdom loved him. 

One day, the king heard that his people were suffering. They were very cold and hungry because they didn't have enough food or warm clothes. The king was sad to hear this and he wanted to help them. 

So, the king put on his tightest coat and went to his storehouse. He opened the big door and saw that it was filled with food! He knew that this food was for his people and not just for him, so he took it all out and shared it with his kingdom.

The people were so happy! The king had shared all the food with them, so now there was no more suffering. Everyone thanked the king for his kindness and generosity. 

From that day on, the people in the kingdom always remembered how their king had helped them when they were suffering, and everyone always spoke very highly of him.

name_of_work: On the Death of Anne Bronte by Charlotte Bronte
content: There's little joy in life for me, And little terror in the grave; I 've lived the parting hour to see Of one I would have died to save. Calmly to watch the failing breath, Wishing each sigh might be the last; Longing to see the shade of death O'er those beloved features cast. The cloud, the stillness that must part The darling of my life from me; And then to thank God from my heart, To thank Him well and fervently; Although I knew that we had lost The hope and glory of our life; And now, benighted, tempest-tossed, Must bear alone the weary strife.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to eat candy and cake every day. Her mom told her that she needed to eat fruits and vegetables too so that she can improve her health. 

One day, Lily went to the park and met her friend, Timmy. Timmy said, "Lily, you look different today. Did you lose weight?" Lily replied, "Yes, I did! I ate fruits and vegetables, and now I feel better." 

Timmy said, "That's great! My room is messy. Can you help me clean it?" Lily said, "Sure, I can help you. We can improve your room together!" They cleaned the room and it looked much better. 

After they finished, Timmy said, "Thanks, Lily. You are a good friend." Lily smiled and said, "No problem, Timmy. I'm happy to help." They played together and had fun at the park.

Once upon a time, there was a big box of colors. The colors were all friends and lived happily together. But one day, they became impatient. They wanted to see the world outside the box.

So, the colors decided to split into two groups. One group went to the left, and the other group went to the right. They went out to play and paint the world with their beautiful colors.

The colors painted the sky, the trees, and the flowers. They made everything bright and happy. After a fun day, the colors came back together. They were not impatient anymore. They knew they could always go out and play again. And they lived happily ever after.

name_of_work: The Horse Poisoner by Thomas Lux
content: No one knew why horses were dying -- two from two farms over, one in town, three at the poor farm (not in great shape, anyway, so no concern at first), then the mayor's son's pony, then three stalls in a row at the local sulky track. The vet sent blood to the State Police, who sent it to Boston for "further analysis." Meanwhile, two more died. One so old it was no surprise, and another mistaken for a deer and shot. Some people wanted to make a connection, but the errant hunter was cousin to the sheriff and was known as too dim to pull off a string of horse poisonings. There were no more suspicious deaths in the county for two months. Then three, lying down next to each other, seen first by my cousin Freddy at dawn in the town square. He delivered newspapers. Horses rarely lie down flat unless they're sick, or dead. Test results came back from Boston and, Freddy said, also the Feds. Inconclusive, though each necropsy showed that the poison was delivered with the aid of a carrot or a sugar cube in a carrot.

name_of_work: Silver by Walter de la Mare
content: Slowly, silently, now the moon Walks the night in her silver shoon; This way, and that, she peers, and sees Silver fruit upon silver trees; One by one the casements catch Her beams beneath the silvery thatch; Couched in his kennel, like a log, With paws of silver sleeps the dog; From their shadowy cote the white breasts peep Of doves in a silver-feathered sleep; A harvest mouse goes scampering by, With silver claws and a silver eye; And moveless fish in the water gleam, By silver reeds in a silver stream.

Once upon a time, there was a small car. The small car loved to drive fast and go vroom vroom. One day, the small car was driving on a bumpy road and it hit a big rock. The small car wrecked and it was sad.

But then, a nice person came and helped the small car. The nice person spread a blanket on the ground and put the small car on top of it. The small car felt better and said thank you to the nice person. From that day on, the small car drove more carefully and never wrecked again.

Once there was a little girl named Bella. She was 3 years old. Bella liked to play all day with her friends.

One day some of the grown ups were talking. Bella was curious, so she went closer to listen. Suddenly one of the grown ups said something rude.

Bella was very upset. She didn't like how the grown up was being mean.

Bella's mom saw what was happening and came over. She hugged Bella and said, "Sometimes people are rude. But it's important to remember the most important message: we treat each other with respect."

Bella nodded. She repeated the message to herself. "We must be kind to each other."

Bella smiled. She was thankful for her mom's advice. From that day on, she tried to repeat the message every time she felt angry. She knew it was the best thing to do.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a gifted puppy named Max. Max was very good at fetching balls and sticks.

One day, Lily and Max went for a walk in the park. They met a little boy named Timmy. Timmy had hurt his knee and was crying.

Lily asked, "What happened to your knee?"

"I fell down," Timmy replied.

Max led Lily to a stick and Lily gave it to Timmy. Timmy stopped crying and smiled. "Thank you, Max," said Timmy.

Lily and Timmy became friends and they played together with Max. From that day on, Max became known as the gifted dog who could lead the way to happiness.

Once upon a time, there was a kind penguin who was strolling along the beach. He saw another penguin, and stopped to stare.

The other penguin asked, "Why are you staring at me?"

The kind penguin replied, "I was just wondering why you are so far away from the others."

The other penguin thought for a minute and then said, "I was feeling lonely, so I decided to come here. But now that I'm here, I don't want to leave."

The kind penguin smiled and said, "I am lonely too. Would you like to be friends?"

The other penguin smiled back and said, "Yes, that would be great!"

The two penguins became very good friends, and spent each day together. They laughed and played, and enjoyed being kind to each other.

Once upon a time there was a big puddle in the park. A little girl named Lucy went to explore the puddle. She was excited to see all the tiny creatures swimming around in the water. 

She stooped down to get a closer look. All of a sudden, a tiny fish jumped up and said, "Help me! I'm stuck and can't get out".

Surprised by the fish's words, Lucy quickly asked, "What can I do to help?".

The fish replied, "If you are patient you can hold my fin and I can jump out of the puddle".

Lucy was very patient and she held the fish's fin. After a few tries, the fish finally jumped out of the puddle and back into the pond.

The fish thanked Lucy and then swam away. Lucy was very happy to have helped the fish and she smiled all the way home.

Sometimes from sorrow, for no reason, you sing. For no reason, you accept the way of being lost, cutting loose from all else and electing a world where you go where you want to. Arbitrary, a sound comes, a reminder that a steady center is holding all else. If you listen, that sound will tell you where it is and you can slide your way past trouble. Certain twisted monsters always bar the path -- but that's when you get going best, glad to be lost, learning how real it is here on earth, again and again.

1 I cradled my newborn daughter and felt the heartbeat pull me out of shock. She didn't know what her hands were: she folded them. I asked her was there a place where there was no world. She didn't know what a voice was: her lips were the shape of a nipple. 2 In the park the child says: watch me. It will not count unless you see. And she shows me the cartwheel, the skip, the tumble, the tricks performed at leisure in midair, each unknown until it is finished. At home she orders: see me eat. I watch her curl on herself, sleep; as I try to leave the dark room her dreaming voice commands me: watch. 3 Always we passed the seesaw on the way to the swings but tonight I remember the principle of the lever, I sit the child at one end, I sit near the center, the fulcrum, at once she has power to lift me off the earth and keep me suspended by her tiny weight, she laughing, I stunned at the power of the formula.

Once upon a time, there was an enormous bow. It was huge and sparkled in the sunshine.

Mia was a 3 year old girl and she loved to read. Each day she would take her giant bow and sit beneath a tree. She would open her book and read it till her heart was content.

One day, as she was enjoying her book, a friendly bird landed nearby. "Hello Mia," said the bird. 
"Hi bird," Mia replied. "Do you want to hear a story?"

The bird nodded excitedly. Mia opened her book, and started to read.

The bird was mesmerized. It loved the story and when Mia finished, it gave her a big hug.

Mia was so happy! She took her enormous bow, ran back home and never stopped readying. 
The End.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved going to his classroom because he had lots of friends there. One day, a tough boy named Billy started to tease Timmy. Timmy felt sad and didn't want to go to the classroom anymore.

But Timmy's teacher saw what was happening and talked to Billy. She told him that it's not nice to tease others and that everyone should be kind to each other. Billy felt sorry and apologized to Timmy. Timmy forgave him and they became friends again.

From that day on, Timmy felt happy to go to his classroom again. He knew that his teacher would always be there to help him if someone was being tough or teasing him.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sarah who was only three years old. She lived with her mommy in a big house with many rooms. One day, Sarah's mommy went to work and Sarah was left alone in the house. 

Sarah decided to explore a little bit and walked around the house. She went into a dark, dirty hall and noticed something very interesting in the corner. She forgot to be careful and reached for it. Suddenly, something sharp scratched her hand! 

"Ouch!" Sarah said. She started to cry. Then, she heard her mommy calling her from outside. She went to the door and saw her mommy's relieved face. 

"What happened, Sarah? You forgot to stay safe, didn't you?" her mommy said. 

Sarah shook her head and told her mommy about the hall. 
"Let's go back and take a look," said her mommy. 

When they returned to the hall, they found a big, dirty spider. Sarah's mommy let out a big sigh of relief.

"Sarah, let's go back home now," she said. "You must always be careful and not forget to stay safe!"

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and run around in the park. One day, Lily's mom told her they were going to visit her uncle. Lily was excited to see her uncle, but she didn't know where he lived.

"Mommy, where is uncle's house?" Lily asked.

"I'll explain it to you, sweetie. It's not far from here," her mom replied.

When they arrived at her uncle's house, Lily saw that he looked very sad. "Why are you so miserable, uncle?" she asked.

"I lost my favorite toy," he answered.

Lily knew how it felt to lose something she loved, so she decided to help her uncle find his toy. Together, they looked in every corner of the house until they finally found it. Uncle was so happy and gave Lily a big hug. From that day on, Lily and her uncle played together every time she visited him.

Tim and Lily went to the zoo with Mom and Dad. They saw many animals, like lions, monkeys, and birds. They liked the animals, but they wanted to see the gorilla. The gorilla was big and strong, and he lived in a cage.

They found the gorilla cage, but it was empty. They asked a zoo man, "Where is the gorilla?"

The zoo man said, "The gorilla is sick. He has a hurt leg. We are trying to fix it. He is in the vet room. You can't see him today."

Tim and Lily were sad. They wanted to see the gorilla. They did not listen to the zoo man. They ran away from Mom and Dad. They looked for the vet room. They found a door that said "Vet Room. Do Not Enter."

They opened the door. They saw the gorilla. He was on a table. He had a bandage on his leg. He looked angry. He saw Tim and Lily. He roared.

The gorilla broke the table. He broke the bandage. He ran to Tim and Lily. He grabbed them with his big hands. He squeezed them tight. He hurt them.

Mom and Dad heard the roar. They heard Tim and Lily scream. They ran to the vet room. They saw the gorilla. They saw Tim and Lily. They were scared. They called for help.

But it was too late. The gorilla did not let go of Tim and Lily. He squeezed them too tight. He broke them. They did not move. They did not breathe.

The end.

John was a generous young boy. His parents taught him the importance of being kind, so he tried his best to help others whenever he could.

One day, John went to the park. He saw an old man walking in without an umbrella. John offered the old man his umbrella, but he refused. John was about to leave when he noticed the old man was shivering. He had no coat on!

John gave him his coat. The old man was very thankful and he gave John a small note. He said, "This note will help you. Stay generous." John thanked him and the old man went away.

John opened the note and read it. The note said, "Your generosity will make you happy." From that day on, John tried his best to be generous whenever he could. He knew it made him happy, and it made other people happy too.

name_of_work: Sand Between the Toes by A.A. Milne
content: I went down to the shouting sea, Taking Christopher down with me, For Nurse had given us sixpence each- And down we went to the beach. We had sand in the eyes and the ears and the nose, And sand in the hair, and sand-between-the-toes. Whenever a good nor'wester blows, Christopher is certain of Sand-between-the-toes. The sea was galloping grey and white; Christopher clutched his sixpence tight; We clambered over the humping sand- And Christopher held my hand. We had sand in the eyes and the ears and the nose, And sand in the hair, and sand-between-the-toes. Whenever a good nor'wester blows, Christopher is certain of Sand-between-the-toes. There was a roaring in the sky; The sea-gulls cried as they blew by; We tried to talk, but had to shout- Nobody else was out. When we got home, we had sand in the hair, In the eyes and the ears and everywhere; Whenever a good nor'wester blows, Christopher is found with Sand-between-the-toes.

Once upon a time, there was a special duck who lived in a very beautiful pond. The duck was so popular that other animals wanted to be her friends. Every morning, she would blink her eyes and swim around the pond.

One day, she saw an old turtle swimming near the edge of the pond. She asked him, â€œWhat are you doing here?â€

Once upon a time, there were two friends; Jack and Jill. They were both very independent.

Jack said to Jill, "Let's go for a walk."

Jill agreed and so they set off walking happily.

Suddenly, Jack tripped and fell.

Jill said, "Are you okay?"

Jack said, "Yes, I'm okay but I can't get up!"

Jill came over and said, "Let me help you. I'll carry you."

And so, piece by piece, Jill carried Jack until he was safe.

Jill said, "We need to be careful! We should always stick together so no one has to fall again."

Jack nodded and said, "Yes, that's a good idea".

And so the two friends taught us all a valuable lesson: together we are stronger!

The man with laughing eyes stopped smiling to say, "Until you speak Arabic, you will not understand pain." Something to do with the back of the head, an Arab carries sorrow in the back of the head, that only language cracks, the thrum of stones weeping, grating hinge on an old metal gate. "Once you know," he whispered, "you can enter the room whenever you need to. Music you heard from a distance, the slapped drum of a stranger's wedding, well up inside your skin, inside rain, a thousand pulsing tongues. You are changed." Outside, the snow has finally stopped. In a land where snow rarely falls, we had felt our days grow white and still. I thought pain had no tongue. Or every tongue at once, supreme translator, sieve. I admit my shame. To live on the brink of Arabic, tugging its rich threads without understanding how to weave the rug...I have no gift. The sound, but not the sense. I kept looking over his shoulder for someone else to talk to, recalling my dying friend who only scrawled I can't write. What good would any grammar have been to her then? I touched his arm, held it hard, which sometimes you don't do in the Middle East, and said, I'll work on it, feeling sad for his good strict heart, but later in the slick street hailed a taxi by shouting Pain! and it stopped in every language and opened its doors.

name_of_work: Sorrow by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: Sorrow like a ceaseless rain Beats upon my heart. People twist and scream in pain, -- Dawn will find them still again; This has neither wax nor wane, Neither stop nor start. People dress and go to town; I sit in my chair. All my thoughts are slow and brown: Standing up or sitting down Little matters, or what gown Or what shoes I wear.

name_of_work: Shall earth no more inspire thee by Emily Bronte
content: Shall earth no more inspire thee, Thou lonely dreamer now? Since passion may not fire thee Shall Nature cease to bow? Thy mind is ever moving In regions dark to thee; Recall its useless roving-- Come back and dwell with me. I know my mountain breezes Enchant and soothe thee still-- I know my sunshine pleases Despite thy wayward will. When day with evening blending Sinks from the summer sky, I've seen thy spirit bending In fond idolatry. I've watched thee every hour; I know my mighty sway, I know my magic power To drive thy griefs away. Few hearts to mortals given On earth so wildly pine; Yet none would ask a heaven More like this earth than thine. Then let my winds caress thee; Thy comrade let me be-- Since nought beside can bless thee, Return and dwell with me.

Once upon a time, there was a dog named Mark. Mark had a pretty collar. The collar was wide and blue. Mark liked his collar very much.

One day, Mark went for a walk with his friend, a cat named Tom. They played in the wide, green park. They ran and jumped and had a lot of fun. Mark's collar jingled as he played.

As they walked home, Mark and Tom saw a big tree. They wanted to climb it. Mark tried to climb, but his wide collar got stuck. Tom helped Mark get free. They laughed and went home, happy to have had a fun day.

Sara and Ben like to play with yarn. They have many colors of yarn. They make shapes and animals with yarn. They have fun with yarn.

One day, Sara and Ben find a big ball of yarn in the closet. It is white and soft. They want to play with it. They take it out of the closet and roll it on the floor.

"Look, Sara, the yarn is like snow!" Ben says.

"Yes, Ben, it is very pretty!" Sara says.

They make a snowman with the yarn. They use buttons for eyes and a carrot for a nose. They give the snowman a hat and a scarf. They are happy with their snowman.

But then, they hear a voice from the closet. It is a friendly voice.

"Hello, children, can I have my yarn back?" the voice says.

Sara and Ben are surprised. They look at the closet. They see a cat. The cat is white and fluffy. The yarn is his toy.

"Who are you?" Sara asks.

"I am Fluffy, the cat. I live here with Grandma. She gave me the yarn to play with. It is my favorite toy." the cat says.

"Oh, we are sorry, Fluffy. We did not know. We thought the yarn was for us. We wanted to play with it." Ben says.

"It is okay, children. You can play with the yarn, too. But can you share it with me? I like to chase it and catch it. It is fun." Fluffy says.

"Sure, Fluffy. We can share the yarn with you. You are very friendly. Do you want to play with us?" Sara says.

"Yes, I do. Thank you, children. You are very nice. Let's play together." Fluffy says.

Sara and Ben smile. They make friends with Fluffy. They play with the yarn and the snowman. They have more fun with yarn.

Jenny was a hard worker. Every day she wanted to try to improve and get better.

One day, she asked her mom, "How can I make my work better?"

Her mom smiled and replied, "You just have to keep trying and working hard! If your work is clear and well-thought out it will show that you're improving."

Jenny thought about this for a minute and then got to work. She worked and worked until her work was clear and perfect.

When she showed her mom she was so proud that she gave Jenny a big hug and said, "See, I told you if you keep working hard you can improve!" 

Jenny was happy and felt really proud that her work had improved. She knew she could do it, and with a little hard work, she did!

Once upon a time, three friends were having a lot of fun. They were running around, playing tag, and giggling. One of the friends had a marble and it was very special.

The friends decided to have a race. They dropped the marble on the ground and cheered as it began to roll. The marble rolled very fast and finally reached the finish line! Everyone was very happy and they all applauded.

The owner of the marble was so proud of its speed. He held it up in the air and said, "I have the fastest marble ever!" All his friends agreed that it was really fast and they applauded again.

After the race, everyone went back to playing. They made up new games and continued having fun like they usually did. It was a normal day!

Once upon a time, there was a nice, brown bear. His name was Brown Bear. One day, Brown Bear wanted to go for a walk. He put on his nice, brown suit and went outside.

On his way, he found a hole in the ground. He looked inside and saw something. It was a bone! He wanted to bury it and make it safe.

So, Brown Bear dug a nice, big hole with his hands and carefully put the bone into the hole. Then he used his hands to put the dirt back into the hole until it was full.

When he finished, he looked at the big, brown mound and smiled. The bone was now safe and he was happy. He said goodbye to the mound and went back home to take off his nice, brown suit.

Bob and his mom went to the city. Bob saw lots of interesting things in the city. He saw dogs, cats and lots of people. He saw many big buildings too. 

He also saw an elderly man. The man was walking slowly. Bob started to run around, but he was too fast for the elderly man. The elderly man got angry and he slapped Bob on his arm. 

Bob's mom was very mad. She yelled at the elderly man and then hugged Bob to make him feel better. She said that the elderly man should never do that again. 

They stayed away from the elderly man and continued exploring the city. Bob had fun, despite the incident. He was learning about the city and all the cool things it had to offer.

name_of_work: The Kraken by Alfred Lord Tennyson
content: Below the thunders of the upper deep, Far, far beneath in the abysmal sea, His ancient, dreamless, uninvaded sleep The Kraken sleepeth: faintest sunlights flee About his shadowy sides; above him swell Huge sponges of millennial growth and height; And far away into the sickly light, From many a wondrous grot and secret cell Unnumbered and enormous polypi Winnow with giant arms the slumbering green. There hath he lain for ages, and will lie Battening upon huge sea worms in his sleep, Until the latter fire shall heat the deep; Then once by man and angels to be seen, In roaring he shall rise and on the surface die.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who loved to go to church. Every Sunday morning she put on her best dress and shoes and went to church. She loved to hear the music, see the funny stories and sing all the fun songs.

One day when she was at church, the girl saw something silly. She saw a man wearing a silly hat and blowing bubbles in church! Everyone else in church just laughed and smiled.

The little girl couldn't believe her eyes. She asked her mum, "Mum, why is that man wearing such a silly hat?"

Her mum smiled and said, "Some people believe that wearing silly hats and blowing bubbles shows that you are happy to be in church."

The girl smiled and said, "That's silly, but I like it."

And she kept coming back to church every week, just to see if the man was wearing a silly hat again.

name_of_work: A Rolling Stone by Robert Service
content: There's sunshine in the heart of me, My blood sings in the breeze; The mountains are a part of me, I'm fellow to the trees. My golden youth I'm squandering, Sun-libertine am I; A-wandering, a-wandering, Until the day I die. I was once, I declare, a Stone-Age man, And I roomed in the cool of a cave; I have known, I will swear, in a new life-span, The fret and the sweat of a slave: For far over all that folks hold worth, There lives and there leaps in me A love of the lowly things of earth, And a passion to be free. To pitch my tent with no prosy plan, To range and to change at will; To mock at the mastership of man, To seek Adventure's thrill. Carefree to be, as a bird that sings; To go my own sweet way; To reck not at all what may befall, But to live and to love each day. To make my body a temple pure Wherein I dwell serene; To care for the things that shall endure, The simple, sweet and clean. To oust out envy and hate and rage, To breathe with no alarm; For Nature shall be my anchorage, And none shall do me harm. To shun all lures that debauch the soul, The orgied rites of the rich; To eat my crust as a rover must With the rough-neck down in the ditch. To trudge by his side whate'er betide; To share his fire at night; To call him friend to the long trail-end, And to read his heart aright. To scorn all strife, and to view all life With the curious eyes of a child; From the plangent sea to the prairie, From the slum to the heart of the Wild. From the red-rimmed star to the speck of sand, From the vast to the greatly small; For I know that the whole for good is planned, And I want to see it all. To see it all, the wide world-way, From the fig-leaf belt to the Pole; With never a one to say me nay, And none to cramp my soul. In belly-pinch I will pay the price, But God! let me be free; For once I know in the long ago, They made a slave of me. In a flannel shirt from earth's clean dirt, Here, pal, is my calloused hand! Oh, I love each day as a rover may, Nor seek to understand. To enjoy is good enough for me; The gipsy of God am I; Then here's a hail to each flaring dawn! And here's a cheer to the night that's gone! And may I go a-roaming on Until the day I die! Then every star shall sing to me Its song of liberty; And every morn shall bring to me Its mandate to be free. In every throbbing vein of me I'll feel the vast Earth-call; O body, heart and brain of me Praise Him who made it all!

Once upon a time, there was a smart train named Tom. Tom had a big engine that made him go very fast. He loved to help people and welcome them on his train.

One day, Tom saw a little girl named Lily who was sad. "Why are you sad, Lily?" Tom asked. "I want to go to my friend's house, but I don't know how to get there," Lily said. Tom wanted to help Lily, so he said, "Welcome to my train, Lily! I can take you to your friend's house."

On the way to Lily's friend's house, they met a big, mean train named Max who blocked the tracks. Max said, "You can't go this way, Tom!" Tom was sad, but he was also smart. He said, "If we work together, we can both go on the tracks and help people." Max thought about it and agreed.

Tom and Max became friends and worked together to help people. Lily was happy to reach her friend's house, and everyone loved the smart train Tom and his new friend Max.
