Ben liked to count numbers. He would number stars and clouds, and trees and leaves. Ben liked to be busy counting the things around him.

One day Jill had an idea. She said to Ben, â€œLetâ€™s go outside and count some wild things!â€ Ben and Jill went outside and saw lots of wild animals. They counted butterflies and birds, and cats and dogs.

But then it started to get cold, and Ben and Jill had to go inside. They counted all the items that were inside - chairs and tables, books and toys - but it wasnâ€™t as much fun as counting wild things outside!

Light flows our war of mocking words, and yet, Behold, with tears mine eyes are wet! I feel a nameless sadness o'er me roll. Yes, yes, we know that we can jest, We know, we know that we can smile! But there's a something in this breast, To which thy light words bring no rest, And thy gay smiles no anodyne. Give me thy hand, and hush awhile, And turn those limpid eyes on mine, And let me read there, love! thy inmost soul. Alas! is even love too weak To unlock the heart, and let it speak? Are even lovers powerless to reveal To one another what indeed they feel? I knew the mass of men conceal'd Their thoughts, for fear that if reveal'd They would by other men be met With blank indifference, or with blame reproved; I knew they lived and moved Trick'd in disguises, alien to the rest Of men, and alien to themselves--and yet The same heart beats in every human breast! But we, my love!--doth a like spell benumb Our hearts, our voices?--must we too be dumb? Ah! well for us, if even we, Even for a moment, can get free Our heart, and have our lips unchain'd; For that which seals them hath been deep-ordain'd! Fate, which foresaw How frivolous a baby man would be-- By what distractions he would be possess'd, How he would pour himself in every strife, And well-nigh change his own identity-- That it might keep from his capricious play His genuine self, and force him to obey Even in his own despite his being's law, Bade through the deep recesses of our breast The unregarded river of our life Pursue with indiscernible flow its way; And that we should not see The buried stream, and seem to be Eddying at large in blind uncertainty, Though driving on with it eternally. But often, in the world's most crowded streets, But often, in the din of strife, There rises an unspeakable desire After the knowledge of our buried life; A thirst to spend our fire and restless force In tracking out our true, original course; A longing to inquire Into the mystery of this heart which beats So wild, so deep in us--to know Whence our lives come and where they go. And many a man in his own breast then delves, But deep enough, alas! none ever mines. And we have been on many thousand lines, And we have shown, on each, spirit and power; But hardly have we, for one little hour, Been on our own line, have we been ourselves-- Hardly had skill to utter one of all The nameless feelings that course through our breast, But they course on for ever unexpress'd. And long we try in vain to speak and act Our hidden self, and what we say and do Is eloquent, is well--but 't is not true! And then we will no more be rack'd With inward striving, and demand Of all the thousand nothings of the hour Their stupefying power; Ah yes, and they benumb us at our call! Yet still, from time to time, vague and forlorn, From the soul's subterranean depth upborne As from an infinitely distant land, Come airs, and floating echoes, and convey A melancholy into all our day. Only--but this is rare-- When a beloved hand is laid in ours, When, jaded with the rush and glare Of the interminable hours, Our eyes can in another's eyes read clear, When our world-deafen'd ear Is by the tones of a loved voice caress'd-- A bolt is shot back somewhere in our breast, And a lost pulse of feeling stirs again. The eye sinks inward, and the heart lies plain, And what we mean, we say, and what we would, we know. A man becomes aware of his life's flow, And hears its winding murmur; and he sees The meadows where it glides, the sun, the breeze. And there arrives a lull in the hot race Wherein he doth for ever chase That flying and elusive shadow, rest. An air of coolness plays upon his face, And an unwonted calm pervades his breast. And then he thinks he knows The hills where his life rose, And the sea where it goes.

Once upon a time, there was a stack of wet clothes. The clothes looked very sad because they were so wet. No one liked to wear wet clothes.

One day a clever little girl came along. She had an idea of how to dry the wet clothes. She picked up a few dry sticks and carefully placed them in a neat stack. Then, she put the wet clothes on top of the stack of sticks.

The sun shined brightly that day and, soon enough, the wet clothes were all dry. But, when the little girl went to take them off the stack, they smelled a little bit sour. The little girl frowned, until she remembered something her mom always said: "A little bit of sour is a sign of a good dry!" With a smile, the little girl took the dry clothes off the stack and hugged them tight. The clothes were happy and so was the little girl.

Tom was a little boy who liked to play with his toys. He had a lot of toys, but his favorite was a red truck. He liked to zoom it around the floor and make loud noises. He wanted to be a great truck driver when he grew up.

One day, Tom saw a big chimney on the roof of his house. He wondered what was inside the chimney. He wanted to see it. He asked his mom if he could go up there. His mom said no, it was too high and too dirty. She said he could get hurt or stuck. She said he should play with his toys instead.

But Tom did not listen to his mom. He waited until she was busy in the kitchen. Then he got a chair and climbed on it. He reached for the window that was near the chimney. He opened the window and crawled out. He felt the cold air and the rough tiles. He saw the chimney close by. He wanted to touch it.

He walked carefully on the roof. He got closer and closer to the chimney. He stretched his hand and felt the brick. It was hard and cold. He looked inside the chimney. It was dark and smoky. He wanted to see more. He leaned over the edge and peered down.

Suddenly, he slipped and fell. He screamed as he slid into the chimney. He felt the soot and the ash. He felt the heat and the fire. He was scared and hurt. He wanted his mom. He wanted his red truck. He wanted to get out of the chimney. He cried and cried.

His mom heard his cry. She ran to the window and saw him in the chimney. She was shocked and scared. She called for help. She shouted his name. She told him to stay calm. She said she loved him. She said she would get him out.

Soon, a big fire truck came. It had a ladder and a hose. It had a great fireman. He climbed the ladder and reached the chimney. He used the hose to put out the fire. He used his hands to pull out Tom. He wrapped him in a blanket and gave him to his mom.

Tom was happy to see his mom. He hugged her and said he was sorry. He said he was stupid and naughty. He said he did not want to see the chimney anymore. He said he wanted to play with his toys. He said he wanted to be a great fireman. His mom smiled and kissed him. She said she was glad he was safe. She said he could be anything he wanted. She said he was her great boy.

name_of_work: Concord Hymn by Ralph Waldo Emerson
content: By the rude bridge that arched the flood, Their flag to April's breeze unfurled, Here once the embattled farmers stood And fired the shot heard round the world. The foe long since in silence slept; Alike the conqueror silent sleeps; And Time the ruined bridge has swept Down the dark stream which seaward creeps. On this green bank, by this soft stream, We set today a votive stone; That memory may their deed redeem, When, like our sires, our sons are gone. Spirit, that made those heroes dare To die, and leave their children free, Bid Time and Nature gently spare The shaft we raise to them and thee.

I have done it again. One year in every ten I manage it---- A sort of walking miracle, my skin Bright as a Nazi lampshade, My right foot A paperweight, My face a featureless, fine Jew linen. Peel off the napkin O my enemy. Do I terrify?---- The nose, the eye pits, the full set of teeth? The sour breath Will vanish in a day. Soon, soon the flesh The grave cave ate will be At home on me And I a smiling woman. I am only thirty. And like the cat I have nine times to die. This is Number Three. What a trash To annihilate each decade. What a million filaments. The peanut-crunching crowd Shoves in to see Them unwrap me hand and foot---- The big strip tease. Gentlemen, ladies These are my hands My knees. I may be skin and bone, Nevertheless, I am the same, identical woman. The first time it happened I was ten. It was an accident. The second time I meant To last it out and not come back at all. I rocked shut As a seashell. They had to call and call And pick the worms off me like sticky pearls. Dying Is an art, like everything else. I do it exceptionally well. I do it so it feels like hell. I do it so it feels real. I guess you could say I've a call. It's easy enough to do it in a cell. It's easy enough to do it and stay put. It's the theatrical Comeback in broad day To the same place, the same face, the same brute Amused shout: 'A miracle!' That knocks me out. There is a charge For the eyeing of my scars, there is a charge For the hearing of my heart---- It really goes. And there is a charge, a very large charge For a word or a touch Or a bit of blood Or a piece of my hair or my clothes. So, so, Herr Doktor. So, Herr Enemy. I am your opus, I am your valuable, The pure gold baby That melts to a shriek. I turn and burn. Do not think I underestimate your great concern. Ash, ash-- You poke and stir. Flesh, bone, there is nothing there---- A cake of soap, A wedding ring, A gold filling. Herr God, Herr Lucifer Beware Beware. Out of the ash I rise with my red hair And I eat men like air.

One day, Mama was in the kitchen when Jimmy came over. Jimmy was being very rude, but Mama smiled and asked him what he wanted.

Jimmy lay down on the floor and said "I want an ice cream".
Mama shook her head and said sweetly, "No, Jimmy. We can't have an ice cream now. It's time for bed."

Jimmy didn't like the answer. He crossed his arms and said "I will have an ice cream or else!"
Mama frowned and said, "Jimmy, that is not nice talk. I won't lay an ice cream in front of you if you are going to be so rude. Now let's go to bed."

Jimmy grumbled and said, "Okay, Mama. I'll go to bed." He lay down in bed and, soon enough, was fast asleep.
Mama smiled, happy that her son, despite being a bit rude, listened to her and went to bed. She knew that Jimmy's will power was strong, and she hoped it stayed that way.

name_of_work: George Sand: A Desire by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: Thou large-brained woman and large-hearted man, Self-called George Sand! whose soul, amid the lions Of thy tumultuous senses, moans defiance And answers roar for roar, as spirits can: I would some mild miraculous thunder ran Above the applauded circus, in appliance Of thine own nobler nature's strength and science, Drawing two pinions, white as wings of swan, From thy strong shoulders, to amaze the place With holier light! that thou to woman's claim And man's, mightst join beside the angel's grace Of a pure genius sanctified from blame Till child and maiden pressed to thine embrace To kiss upon thy lips a stainless fame.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Lucy. She was only three years old and loved exploring the garden. One day she was looking around the old shed when she saw a cobweb in the corner. It was filthy and full of dirt.

'What is that?' she said, not understanding what it was.

A voice then echoed from behind her. It was her mum.

'That Lucy is a cobweb. It's made by a spider,' she said.

Lucy wrinkled her nose. 'Why is it so filthy?'

'That's because the spiders catch flies and they are very dirty,' her mum told her.

Lucy nodded and smiled. Now she understood.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Melanie. Melanie was three years old. She had a happy face and loved to explore. 

One day, Melanie was running through the park. She was excited to scatter luggage all around the grass. It was light, so it wasn't too difficult for her to lift it up.

When Melanie's mother saw her, she asked, "What are you doing, Melanie?"

Melanie smiled and said, "I'm scattering the luggage! I want to make the park more fun!"

Melanie's mother smiled and said, "That's so sweet. Let's go home and have some dinner."

The end.

Sara liked to draw with her crayons. She made many images of her family, her friends, and her toys. She was very proud of her images and showed them to everyone. She thought they were very pretty.

One day, she went to play with Lily, her neighbor. Lily also liked to draw, but she used markers instead of crayons. She had many colors and made images of flowers, animals, and stars. She thought they were very pretty too.

Sara and Lily decided to share their images and see what they had drawn. Sara showed Lily her image of her mom and dad. Lily said, "That's nice, but your mom's hair is too yellow and your dad's nose is too big. My mom and dad are more pretty. Look at my image of them."

Lily showed Sara her image of her mom and dad. Sara said, "That's nice, but your mom's eyes are too green and your dad's mouth is too small. My mom and dad are more pretty. Look at my image of them again."

Sara and Lily started to argue about whose images were more pretty. They did not like each other's images and did not want to play anymore. They said, "You are not my friend. Go away."

Sara and Lily were very sad and angry. They did not have fun. They did not welcome each other.

Then, Sara's mom came to pick her up. She saw Sara and Lily crying and asked what happened. Sara and Lily told her about their images and their fight. Sara's mom said, "I'm sorry you had a fight, but you know, everyone can draw in different ways. There is no right or wrong way to make images. You can both make pretty images with your own colors and shapes. You don't have to like the same things, but you can still be friends and welcome each other."

Sara and Lily thought about what Sara's mom said. They realized that she was right. They looked at their images again and saw that they were both pretty in their own ways. They said, "You are right, mom. We are sorry we fought. We can both make pretty images and be friends. Can we play again?"

Sara's mom smiled and said, "Of course you can. I'm glad you made up. You are both very good at drawing. Why don't you make a new image together and welcome each other with a hug?"

Sara and Lily nodded and hugged each other. They said, "We are sorry. We are friends. We welcome each other."

They took their crayons and markers and made a new image together. They drew a big heart with their names inside. They showed it to Sara's mom and said, "Look, mom. This is our image of friendship. It is very pretty."

Sara's mom said, "Yes, it is very pretty. And so are you. I'm proud of you."

Sara and Lily smiled and thanked Sara's mom. They continued to play and draw together. They learned to respect and welcome each other's images and ideas. They had fun.

name_of_work: The Ache of Marriage by Denise Levertov
content: The ache of marriage: thigh and tongue, beloved, are heavy with it, it throbs in the teeth We look for communion and are turned away, beloved, each and each It is leviathan and we in its belly looking for joy, some joy not to be known outside it two by two in the ark of the ache of it.

Lily asked her mum, â€œCan I jump?â€

Her mum smiled at her and said, â€œYes, my love, you can jump. But first you need to put on your shoes.â€

So, Lily put on her shoes and started jumping. She jumped onto the couch, and then onto the bed and then under the table. She jumped everywhere and felt so good.

After a while, Lily asked her mum, â€œCan I jump outside?â€

Her mum smiled and said, â€œYes, you can! But first you need to put on your coat.â€

Once upon a time, in a small town, there lived a famous cat named Kitty. Kitty was very nice and loved to play with her friends. One day, Kitty had an idea. She wanted to invite all her friends to her house for a fun play date.

Kitty went to her friend Doggy's house and said, "Doggy, I invite you to my house to play with me and our friends." Doggy wagged his tail and said, "Yes, Kitty! I would love to come and play." Then, Kitty went to her other friends, Bunny and Birdy, and invited them too. They all were very happy.

On the day of the play date, all the friends came to Kitty's house. They played fun games like hide and seek, and tag. During the games, Doggy hurt his finger. Kitty said, "Oh no, Doggy! Let me help you." She put a band-aid on Doggy's finger and gave him a big hug. They all had a great time at Kitty's play date and couldn't wait for the next one.

name_of_work: Poem in Winter by Elizabeth Jennings
content: Today the children begin to hope for snow and look in the sky for auguries of it. It is not for such omens that we wait. And even if the snow comes down indeed, we shall still stand behind a pane of glass untouched by it, and watch the children press their image on the drifts the snow has laid upon a winter they think they have made. This is a wise illusion. Better to believe the near world is created by a wish, a shaping hand, a certain eye, than hide in the mind's corner as we do, as though there were no world, no fall of snow.

Just as in the horror movies when someone discovers that the phone calls are coming from inside the house so too, I realized that our tender overlapping has been taking place only inside me. All that sweetness, the love and desire-- it's just been me dialing myself then following the ringing to another room to find no one on the line, well, sometimes a little breathing but more often than not, nothing. To think that all this time-- which would include the boat rides, the airport embraces, and all the drinks-- it's been only me and the two telephones, the one on the wall in the kitchen and the extension in the darkened guest room upstairs.

Tim and Sam are friends. They like to play with a ball in the park. One day, it is very cold. Tim and Sam wear hats and coats and gloves. They also wear shoes.

They go to the park with the ball. They kick the ball to each other. They have fun. But then, a big dog comes. The dog is black and furry. The dog likes the ball too. The dog runs to the ball and grabs it with his mouth. He runs away with the ball.

"Hey, that's our ball!" Tim shouts. He runs after the dog. Sam runs after Tim. They want their ball back.

The dog is fast. He runs to a tree. He drops the ball under the tree. He barks at Tim and Sam. He does not want to share the ball.

Tim and Sam are scared of the dog. They stop running. They look at the ball under the tree. They look at the dog. They do not know what to do.

"Maybe we can get another ball," Sam says. He is cold and sad.

"No, we want our ball," Tim says. He is brave and angry. He takes off his shoe. He throws his shoe at the dog. He hopes the dog will go away.

But the dog does not go away. The dog catches the shoe with his mouth. He likes the shoe too. He runs away with the shoe.

"Hey, that's my shoe!" Tim shouts. He runs after the dog again. Sam runs after Tim again. They want their shoe and their ball back.

But the dog is faster. He runs to another tree. He drops the shoe and the ball under the tree. He barks at Tim and Sam again. He does not want to give them back.

Tim and Sam are very scared and very cold and very sad. They have no ball and no shoe. They do not know what to do.

They see a man. The man is walking in the park. The man sees the dog and the ball and the shoe. The man sees Tim and Sam. He knows what to do.

He calls the dog. He says, "Come here, boy. Good dog. Drop it. Drop it." He gives the dog a treat. The dog drops the ball and the shoe. The dog wags his tail. He likes the treat.

The man picks up the ball and the shoe. He gives them to Tim and Sam. He says, "Here you go, kids. Sorry about that. He's my dog. He likes to play, but he doesn't know how to share. He's still learning."

Tim and Sam say, "Thank you, mister. Thank you for our ball and our shoe. Thank you for your dog. He's very cute, but he's very naughty."

The man says, "You're welcome, kids. You're very polite, but you're very cold. You should go home and warm up. And be careful with your ball and your shoe. They might get lost again."

Tim and Sam say, "Okay, mister. We will. Bye bye." They put on their shoe. They take their ball. They wave to the man and the dog. They run to their home. They are happy. They have their ball and their shoe. They have a story to tell.

Lily and Ben were playing in the garden. They liked to pretend they were brave knights and princesses. They had a big stick for a sword and a pot for a helmet.

But then they saw something scary. It was a monster! It was big and green and had sharp teeth and claws. It growled and ran towards them.

Lily and Ben were very afraid. They dropped their stick and pot and ran to the house. They shouted for their mom and dad. They hoped the monster would not catch them.

Mom and dad heard their cries and came out. They saw the monster too. But they did not run away. They laughed and picked it up. It was not a monster. It was their dog, Rex. He had rolled in the grass and mud and looked very green.

Lily and Ben felt silly. They hugged Rex and said sorry. Rex licked their faces and wagged his tail. He was not a mean monster. He was a friendly dog. He had only wanted to play with them. Lily and Ben learned not to judge by looks. They played with Rex and gave him a bath. They did not surrender to their fear. They made a new friend.

name_of_work: The Starlight Night by Gerard Manley Hopkins
content: Look at the stars! look, look up at the skies! O look at all the fire-folk sitting in the air! The bright boroughs, the circle-citadels there! Down in dim woods the diamond delves! the elves'-eyes! The grey lawns cold where gold, where quickgold lies! Wind-beat whitebeam! airy abeles set on a flare! Flake-doves sent floating forth at a farmyard scare! Ah well! it is all a purchase, all is a prize. Buy then! bid then! -- What? -- Prayer, patience, alms, vows. Look, look: a May-mess, like on orchard boughs! Look! March-bloom, like on mealed-with-yellow sallows! These are indeed the barn; withindoors house The shocks. This piece-bright paling shuts the spouse Christ home, Christ and his mother and all his hallows.

name_of_work: A Sad Child by Margaret Atwood
content: You're sad because you're sad. It's psychic. It's the age. It's chemical. Go see a shrink or take a pill, or hug your sadness like an eyeless doll you need to sleep. Well, all children are sad but some get over it. Count your blessings. Better than that, buy a hat. Buy a coat or pet. Take up dancing to forget. Forget what? Your sadness, your shadow, whatever it was that was done to you the day of the lawn party when you came inside flushed with the sun, your mouth sulky with sugar, in your new dress with the ribbon and the ice-cream smear, and said to yourself in the bathroom, I am not the favorite child. My darling, when it comes right down to it and the light fails and the fog rolls in and you're trapped in your overturned body under a blanket or burning car, and the red flame is seeping out of you and igniting the tarmac beside you head or else the floor, or else the pillow, none of us is; or else we all are.

All Greece hates the still eyes in the white face, the lustre as of olives where she stands, and the white hands. All Greece reviles the wan face when she smiles, hating it deeper still when it grows wan and white, remembering past enchantments and past ills. Greece sees unmoved, God's daughter, born of love, the beauty of cool feet and slenderest knees, could love indeed the maid, only if she were laid, white ash amid funereal cypresses.

name_of_work: The Duck and the Kangaroo by Edward Lear
content: I Said the Duck to the Kangaroo, 'Good gracious! how you hop! Over the fields and the water too, As if you never would stop! My life is a bore in this nasty pond, And I long to go out in the world beyond! I wish I could hop like you!' Said the Duck to the Kangaroo. II 'Please give me a ride on your back!' Said the Duck to the Kangaroo. 'I would sit quite still, and say nothing but "Quack," The whole of the long day through! And we'd go to the Dee, and the Jelly Bo Lee, Over the land, and over the sea;-- Please take me a ride! O do!' Said the Duck to the Kangaroo. III Said the Kangaroo to the Duck, 'This requires some little reflection; Perhaps on the whole it might bring me luck, And there seems but one objection, Which is, if you'll let me speak so bold, Your feet are unpleasantly wet and cold, And would probably give me the roo- Matiz!' said the Kangaroo. IV Said the Duck, 'As I sate on the rocks, I have thought over that completely, And I bought four pairs of worsted socks Which fit my web-feet neatly. And to keep out the cold I've bought a cloak, And every day a cigar I'll smoke, All to follow my own dear true Love of a Kangaroo!' V Said the Kangaroo, 'I'm ready! All in the moonlight pale; But to balance me well, dear Duck, sit steady! And quite at the end of my tail!' So away they went with a hop and a bound, And they hopped the whole world three times round; And who so happy,--O who, As the Duck and the Kangaroo?.

Once upon a time, there was a big hero. He was very strong and brave. One day, he saw a little girl who was in trouble. She was trying to push a big box, but it was too heavy for her. The hero came to help her and he pushed the box with all his might. The little girl was very happy and thanked the hero. The hero was happy too because he had helped someone in need. But the hero knew that the world could be harsh sometimes, and he promised to always be there to help those who needed it.

Tom and Lily were playing in the garden. They liked to run and jump and laugh. They saw a big bird in the sky. It was black and white and had a long tail. It was a magpie.

"Look, Lily, a magpie!" Tom said. "It can soar very high. Do you think it can see us?"

Lily nodded. She liked magpies. They were shiny and smart. She wanted to talk to it. She waved her hand and shouted, "Hello, magpie! Do you want to play with us?"

The magpie heard Lily. It was curious and jolly. It flew down and landed on the hedge. It tilted its head and said, "Hello, children! I can play with you. What do you want to do?"

Tom and Lily were happy. They had a new friend. They asked the magpie to show them how it could soar. The magpie agreed. It flapped its wings and soared up and down and around. It made funny noises and tricks. Tom and Lily clapped and cheered. They had a lot of fun with the magpie. They played until the sun set. Then they said goodbye and thanked the magpie for playing with them. The magpie said goodbye and soared away. Tom and Lily went inside and told their mum and dad about their adventure. They hoped to see the magpie again.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toys, but he lost his favorite toy car. He searched and searched for it, but he couldn't find it anywhere.

One day, Timmy's mom told him they were going to visit his grandma in the country. Timmy was excited to go, but he was sad because he thought he could never find his toy car in the big country.

When they arrived at grandma's house, Timmy saw a broken tractor in the yard. He asked his grandpa, "What happened to the tractor?" Grandpa said, "It's broken and we need to fix it." Timmy had an idea, "Maybe we can use the broken tractor to search for my toy car in the country!" They fixed the tractor and went on a search.

After a while, they found Timmy's toy car in the tall grass. Timmy was so happy and thanked his grandpa for helping him. From that day on, Timmy loved going to the country and searching for new things with his grandpa.

Once upon a time, there was a clean little town. In this town, there was a small volcano. The volcano was friendly and never hurt anyone. The people in the town liked their volcano friend.

One day, the volcano wanted to make a cake for the town. It called all its friends to help. They found flour, sugar, and eggs. They started to mix everything together. The volcano was very good at mixing. It mixed and mixed until the cake mix was ready.

The town people were happy to see the cake. They all came to the volcano and said, "Thank you, volcano!" They all ate the cake together. It was a yummy cake. The town and the volcano were happy friends forever.

Once upon a time, there was a big tree. Under the tree, a little ant was playing with a long thread. The thread was red, and it was very pretty. The little ant liked to play with the thread all day.

One day, a sour fruit fell from the tree. It fell right next to the little ant and his thread. The little ant was scared and did not want to play anymore. He did not want the sour fruit to disturb him.

The little ant asked his friends, a bee and a butterfly, for help. The bee and the butterfly helped the little ant move the sour fruit far away. The little ant was very happy and thanked his friends. Now, the little ant could play with his thread without being disturbed.

One night, Billy went outside to see what was happening. In the sky, there were lots of flying reindeer! He could not believe his eyes. He wanted to see them up close, so he walked over to them. He was so excited! He held out his arms and started to pull the reindeer. They moved forward but it was hard work. The reindeer flew slowly and very far. When they got to the clouds, they said goodbye to Billy. He waved and watched them disappear. He pulled harder and harder, and the reindeer flew faster and faster. He was so happy to see them and wished he could fly with them. In the end, he said goodbye and watched until they were out of sight.

name_of_work: A Musical Instrument by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: I. WHAT was he doing, the great god Pan, Down in the reeds by the river ? Spreading ruin and scattering ban, Splashing and paddling with hoofs of a goat, And breaking the golden lilies afloat With the dragon-fly on the river. II. He tore out a reed, the great god Pan, From the deep cool bed of the river : The limpid water turbidly ran, And the broken lilies a-dying lay, And the dragon-fly had fled away, Ere he brought it out of the river. III. High on the shore sate the great god Pan, While turbidly flowed the river ; And hacked and hewed as a great god can, With his hard bleak steel at the patient reed, Till there was not a sign of a leaf indeed To prove it fresh from the river. IV. He cut it short, did the great god Pan, (How tall it stood in the river !) Then drew the pith, like the heart of a man, Steadily from the outside ring, And notched the poor dry empty thing In holes, as he sate by the river. V. This is the way,' laughed the great god Pan, Laughed while he sate by the river,) The only way, since gods began To make sweet music, they could succeed.' Then, dropping his mouth to a hole in the reed, He blew in power by the river. VI. Sweet, sweet, sweet, O Pan ! Piercing sweet by the river ! Blinding sweet, O great god Pan ! The sun on the hill forgot to die, And the lilies revived, and the dragon-fly Came back to dream on the river. VII. Yet half a beast is the great god Pan, To laugh as he sits by the river, Making a poet out of a man : The true gods sigh for the cost and pain, -- For the reed which grows nevermore again As a reed with the reeds in the river.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. Lily loved sausages and ate them every day. One day, Lily was walking in the park when she saw a filthy sausage on the ground. 

"Ew, that sausage is dirty!" said Lily. 

Just then, a squirrel came running up to her. 

"Hello, little girl," said the squirrel. "Can you help me? I can't reach my acorn in the tree. Can you climb up and get it for me?" 

Lily was happy to help. She climbed up the tree and got the acorn for the squirrel. But as she was climbing down, she slipped and fell! 

"Oh no!" cried the squirrel. "Are you okay?" 

Lily got up and dusted herself off. "I'm okay," she said. "But I think I need a clean sausage now!" 

The squirrel laughed and said, "I don't think there's such a thing as a clean sausage, but I can show you where to find some fresh nuts!" 

Lily smiled and followed the squirrel to a tree full of delicious nuts. And they all lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved watching movies on her TV. One day, her mom told her it was time to stop watching and go outside to play. Lily didn't want to quit the movie she was watching. She said, "Mommy, can I please finish the movie?" Her mom said, "No, Lily. You need to go outside and play. You can watch the movie later." 

Lily was sad and didn't want to go outside. She felt clumsy and didn't want to trip and fall. But her mom said, "Don't worry, Lily. You won't be clumsy if you practice." So, Lily went outside and started to play. She ran, jumped, and played with her friends. She forgot all about the movie and had a lot of fun. 

Later that day, Lily came back inside and asked her mom if she could finish watching the movie. But her mom said, "No, Lily. It's time to eat dinner and get ready for bed." Lily was disappointed, but she knew it was time to quit watching the movie and go to sleep. She went to bed happy, knowing she had a fun day outside.

name_of_work: What the Living Do by Marie Howe
content: Johnny, the kitchen sink has been clogged for days, some utensil probably fell down there. And the Drano won't work but smells dangerous, and the crusty dishes have piled up waiting for the plumber I still haven't called. This is the everyday we spoke of. It's winter again: the sky's a deep, headstrong blue, and the sunlight pours through the open living-room windows because the heat's on too high in here and I can't turn it off. For weeks now, driving, or dropping a bag of groceries in the street, the bag breaking, I've been thinking: This is what the living do. And yesterday, hurrying along those wobbly bricks in the Cambridge sidewalk, spilling my coffee down my wrist and sleeve, I thought it again, and again later, when buying a hairbrush: This is it. Parking. Slamming the car door shut in the cold. What you called that yearning. What you finally gave up. We want the spring to come and the winter to pass. We want whoever to call or not call, a letter, a kiss--we want more and more and then more of it. But there are moments, walking, when I catch a glimpse of myself in the window glass, say, the window of the corner video store, and I'm gripped by a cherishing so deep for my own blowing hair, chapped face, and unbuttoned coat that I'm speechless: I am living. I remember you.

Once upon a time there was a wealthy man who loved to whistle. He would whistle all day long as he walked through the town. One day, he decided to take a walk in the country and was surprised to find a deep pit by the lake. He bent down to take a closer look and heard a small voice coming from inside the pit.

"Can you help me please?" the voice said.

"Yes, sure! What can I do to help you?" replied the wealthy man.

"I can't get out of the pit," the voice said.

The wealthy man thought for a moment and then got an idea. He started to whistle as loud as he could and soon, a big bird flew down from the sky and landed next to him.

"Can you help my friend here to get out of the pit?" he asked the bird.

The bird nodded and lifted the man out of the pit, with the wealthy man still whistling all the way. The man thanked the bird and with a wave, the bird flew away and the man continued his walk in the countryside.

Ben and Lily were playing with their blocks in the living room. They liked to build towers and bridges and houses with the blocks. They had many colors and shapes of blocks to choose from.

"Look, Lily, I made a big tower!" Ben said, showing his creation to his sister.

"Wow, Ben, that's very good!" Lily said, admiring his tower. "Can I join you and help you make it bigger?"

"Sure, Lily, you can join me. Here, take some blocks and add them to the tower." Ben said, handing her some blocks.

They worked together to make the tower taller and taller, until it reached the ceiling. They were very happy and proud of their tower.

"Ben, Lily, it's time for a snack!" Mom called from the kitchen.

"Yay, snack time!" Ben and Lily said, leaving their tower and running to the kitchen.

Mom had prepared some juice and cookies for them. She poured some juice into two cups and gave them to Ben and Lily.

"Here you go, kids. Enjoy your snack. But be careful with the juice, don't spill it on the floor or the couch." Mom said, smiling.

"OK, Mom, we will be careful." Ben and Lily said, taking their cups and cookies.

They sat on the couch and sipped their juice and ate their cookies. They were very thirsty and hungry after playing with the blocks.

"Ben, can I tell you a secret?" Lily whispered to Ben.

"Sure, Lily, what is it?" Ben whispered back.

"I think Mom is very serious today. Did you see her face when she gave us the juice?" Lily said, looking at Mom.

"I think that's a good idea, Lily. Let's finish our snack and then give Mom a hug and tell her we love her." Ben agreed, nodding.

They finished their snack and put their cups and plates in the sink. Then they ran to Mom and hugged her tightly.

"Mom, we love you!" Ben and Lily said, smiling.

Mom was surprised and touched by their gesture. She hugged them back and kissed them on their cheeks.

"I love you too, Ben and Lily. You are the best kids in the world. Thank you for being so sweet and thoughtful." Mom said, feeling happy.

They all smiled and cuddled on the couch. They felt warm and cozy and loved. They forgot about the tower and the juice and the serious face. They only remembered the hug and the love.

name_of_work: The Poet's Testament by George Santayana
content: I give back to the earth what the earth gave, All to the furrow, none to the grave, The candle's out, the spirit's vigil spent; Sight may not follow where the vision went. I leave you but the sound of many a word In mocking echoes haply overheard, I sang to heaven. My exile made me free, from world to world, from all worlds carried me. Spared by the furies, for the Fates were kind, I paced the pillared cloisters of the mind; All times my present, everywhere my place, Nor fear, nor hope, nor envy saw my face. Blow what winds would, the ancient truth was mine, And friendship mellowed in the flush of wine, And heavenly laughter, shaking from its wings Atoms of light and tears for mortal things. To trembling harmonies of field and cloud, Of flesh and spirit was my worship vowed. Let form, let music, let all quickening air Fulfil in beauty my imperfect prayer.

You begin this way: this is your hand, this is your eye, that is a fish, blue and flat on the paper, almost the shape of an eye. This is your mouth, this is an O or a moon, whichever you like. This is yellow. Outside the window is the rain, green because it is summer, and beyond that the trees and then the world, which is round and has only the colors of these nine crayons. This is the world, which is fuller and more difficult to learn than I have said. You are right to smudge it that way with the red and then the orange: the world burns. Once you have learned these words you will learn that there are more words than you can ever learn. The word hand floats above your hand like a small cloud over a lake. The word hand anchors your hand to this table, your hand is a warm stone I hold between two words. This is your hand, these are my hands, this is the world, which is round but not flat and has more colors than we can see. It begins, it has an end, this is what you will come back to, this is your hand.

"Help, help!" they shout. "We are stuck!"

name_of_work: Letter in January, with a line from Federico Garcia Lorca by Luisa A. Igloria
content: Every day the light stays a little longer, and night does not fall so hard, so fast. By the upstairs window where the blinds are open, I can read till nearly suppertime: I sought in my heart to give you the ivory letters that say "siempre," "siempre," "siempre:" garden of my agony-- But oh Federico, isn't the exile's heart always a ferment of agony, always in search of the elusive body or the heat of another clime? Here, how quiet it is on our street: the men who clip the grass and trim the hedges will not return until winter is over, and dogs do not roam the streets but howl in the muffled recesses of living rooms behind locked doors. Should I hear chimes from bell towers, their music is mere adornment to the day. Pigeons and gulls inspect the trash bins in the alleyway. Startled, they'll flee-- swath of their wings the color of indeterminacy. Pine needles mark sidewalks with their thin virgules, some strands in puddles left after the last hard rain.

name_of_work: I Am Christ's by Leslie Alexis
content: In Heaven, at the right hand of God I'll sit, I haven't been there, but my eyes can see it. Adorned in righteous robes, I'll stand by the king. name_of_work: At the Fishhouses by Elizabeth Bishop
content: Although it is a cold evening, down by one of the fishhouses an old man sits netting, his net, in the gloaming almost invisible, a dark purple-brown, and his shuttle worn and polished. The air smells so strong of codfish it makes one's nose run and one's eyes water. The five fishhouses have steeply peaked roofs and narrow, cleated gangplanks slant up to storerooms in the gables for the wheelbarrows to be pushed up and down on. All is silver: the heavy surface of the sea, swelling slowly as if considering spilling over, is opaque, but the silver of the benches, the lobster pots, and masts, scattered among the wild jagged rocks, is of an apparent translucence like the small old buildings with an emerald moss growing on their shoreward walls. The big fish tubs are completely lined with layers of beautiful herring scales and the wheelbarrows are similarly plastered with creamy iridescent coats of mail, with small iridescent flies crawling on them. Up on the little slope behind the houses, set in the sparse bright sprinkle of grass, is an ancient wooden capstan, cracked, with two long bleached handles and some melancholy stains, like dried blood, where the ironwork has rusted. The old man accepts a Lucky Strike. He was a friend of my grandfather. We talk of the decline in the population and of codfish and herring while he waits for a herring boat to come in. There are sequins on his vest and on his thumb. He has scraped the scales, the principal beauty, from unnumbered fish with that black old knife, the blade of which is almost worn away. Down at the water's edge, at the place where they haul up the boats, up the long ramp descending into the water, thin silver tree trunks are laid horizontally across the gray stones, down and down at intervals of four or five feet. Cold dark deep and absolutely clear, element bearable to no mortal, to fish and to seals . . . One seal particularly I have seen here evening after evening. He was curious about me. He was interested in music; like me a believer in total immersion, so I used to sing him Baptist hymns. I also sang "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God." He stood up in the water and regarded me steadily, moving his head a little. Then he would disappear, then suddenly emerge almost in the same spot, with a sort of shrug as if it were against his better judgment. Cold dark deep and absolutely clear, the clear gray icy water . . . Back, behind us, the dignified tall firs begin. Bluish, associating with their shadows, a million Christmas trees stand waiting for Christmas. The water seems suspended above the rounded gray and blue-gray stones. I have seen it over and over, the same sea, the same, slightly, indifferently swinging above the stones, icily free above the stones, above the stones and then the world. If you should dip your hand in, your wrist would ache immediately, your bones would begin to ache and your hand would burn as if the water were a transmutation of fire that feeds on stones and burns with a dark gray flame. If you tasted it, it would first taste bitter, then briny, then surely burn your tongue. It is like what we imagine knowledge to be: dark, salt, clear, moving, utterly free, drawn from the cold hard mouth of the world, derived from the rocky breasts forever, flowing and drawn, and since our knowledge is historical, flowing, and flown.

Once upon a time there was a boy named Tom. Tom wanted to go on an adventure. One day Tom decided to go to the forest to explore.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She loved to cook with her mommy. One day, her mommy needed some pepper for their soup, but they didn't have any. So, they went to their neighbor's house to lend some pepper. The neighbor was very fair and gave them some pepper to use. 

Lily and her mommy went back home and added the pepper to their soup. It tasted so good! They were very happy. After they finished eating, Lily's mommy reminded her to always be fair and kind like their neighbor. 

From that day on, Lily always remembered to lend things to her friends and be fair to everyone. She knew that being kind was the best way to make friends and be happy.

Once upon a time, there was a famous cat named Tom. Tom was very good at packing things. One day, Tom decided to go on a trip with his best friend, a dog named Max.

Before they left, Tom packed all the things they would need. He put food, toys, and a small toy pistol in a big bag. Max watched Tom pack and wagged his tail, excited to go on their adventure.

Together, Tom and Max went to the park, played with their toys, and shared their food. They had so much fun, especially when Tom took out the toy pistol and pretended to be a superhero. All the other animals in the park clapped and cheered. Tom and Max were very happy and had the best day ever.

Matilda had a bed with a big, gray mattress. She loved bouncing on it and it felt so soft. Her mom always laughed when she saw Matilda jumping on it and said she was a crazy little girl.

One day, Matilda decided to go even crazier. She went and got a bucket of water and started to soak her mattress with it. She thought it would be even softer if it was wet.

Her mom suddenly saw Matilda and shouted, "What are you doing?!". Matilda smiled and said, "I'm making my mattress softer Mommy. I want to bounce even higher!" 

Her mom smiled. "Oh my Matilda, I'm afraid you won't be able to bounce if your mattress is wet. Come on now, let's dry it up!"

Matilda giggled. She and her mom worked together to dry the mattress and soon it was as good as new, only this time it was much softer. Matilda jumped and laughed, the gray mattress was just perfect for her.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. Lily loved to dance and twirl around in her pink tutu. One day, she fell and hurt her knee. Her mommy took her to the nurse who put a bandage on her knee. 

Lily asked the nurse if she could still dance. The nurse said yes, but to take it easy and not to run around too much. Lily listened and danced slowly. 

Suddenly, Lily's little brother came running and bumped into her. Lily fell again and hurt her knee even more. She had to go to the hospital and get a big bandage. 

Lily was sad because she couldn't dance anymore. Her mommy told her that she would get better soon and be able to dance again. Lily smiled and said, "I will dance again soon."

name_of_work: Flower On the Road by Chitra Padmanabhan
content: Spring has come, said the bougainvillea Crimson, orange, cream and yellow Making a flower wall along the road I bring happiness to all. Wait, said the little flower on the edge of the kerb I, too, blossom though I am small Every now and then a little child walks past, sees me at her height And happily smiles. Doesn't that make us comrades on the road!

I have come to the borders of sleep, The unfathomable deep Forest where all must lose Their way, however straight, Or winding, soon or late; They cannot choose. Many a road and track That, since the dawn's first crack, Up to the forest brink, Deceived the travellers, Suddenly now blurs, And in they sink. Here love ends, Despair, ambition ends; All pleasure and all trouble, Although most sweet or bitter, Here ends in sleep that is sweeter Than tasks most noble. There is not any book Or face of dearest look That I would not turn from now To go into the unknown I must enter, and leave, alone, I know not how. The tall forest towers; Its cloudy foliage lowers Ahead, shelf above shelf; Its silence I hear and obey That I may lose my way And myself.

name_of_work: The Snow Fairy by Claude McKay
content: Throughout the afternoon I watched them there, Snow-fairies falling, falling from the sky, Whirling fantastic in the misty air, Contending fierce for space supremacy. And they flew down a mightier force at night, As though in heaven there was revolt and riot, And they, frail things had taken panic flight Down to the calm earth seeking peace and quiet. I went to bed and rose at early dawn To see them huddled together in a heap, Each merged into the other upon the lawn, Worn out by the sharp struggle, fast asleep. The sun shone brightly on them half the day, By night they stealthily had stol'n away. II And suddenly my thoughts then turned to you Who came to me upon a winter's night, When snow-sprites round my attic window flew, Your hair disheveled, eyes aglow with light. My heart was like the weather when you came, The wanton winds were blowing loud and long; But you, with joy and passion all aflame, You danced and sang a lilting summer song. I made room for you in my little bed, Took covers from the closet fresh and warm, A downful pillow for your scented head, And lay down with you resting in my arm. You went with Dawn. You left me ere the day, The lonely actor of a dreamy play.

Once upon a time, there was a big green field. In the field, there was a big bird called an ostrich. The ostrich had long legs and a long neck. It liked to run very fast.

One day, a little boy came to the field to play. He saw the ostrich and wanted to touch it. But when he got too close, the ostrich got scared and started to run away. The little boy tried to chase after it, but he couldn't keep up.

As the ostrich was running away, it accidentally tore a big hole in its feathers. The little boy felt bad and wanted to help. He picked up the feathers and tried to put them back together. But no matter what he did, the feathers wouldn't stay in place.

In the end, the little boy learned that it's important to be gentle with animals and not scare them. And the ostrich learned that it's okay to be a little bit afraid sometimes.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved animals and had a pet parrot named Polly. Polly was very colorful and could talk just like Timmy. One day, Timmy and Polly were playing outside when they heard a loud noise. It sounded like a bell ringing.

Timmy and Polly went to investigate the noise and found a big box on the ground. Timmy opened the box and found a mild surprise inside. It was a toy phone that could ring! Timmy was so happy and played with the phone all day. Polly even tried to talk on the phone too.

Later that night, Timmy's mom received a call on the real phone. It was the zookeeper calling to say that a parrot had escaped and was flying around the neighborhood. Timmy and Polly knew what they had to do. They rang the toy phone to call for help and soon the zookeeper came to rescue the lost parrot. Timmy and Polly were heroes and felt very proud of themselves.

One day, Gavin was playing outside with his daddy. His daddy had a plan to design something special. Gavin watched as Daddy put all the pieces together. After a while, a shiny, new motorcycle was standing in front of them!

Gavin smiled. Daddy asked him if it looked nice. "Yes, it looks so cool!" he said.

Daddy smiled and told Gavin they would take it for a ride. Gavin was so excited!

But when they tried to start it, there were some problems. Daddy became frustrated. He worked and worked, but the motorcycle wouldn't start. Gavin was worried about Daddy.

Then Daddy said, "Let's take a break and try it again later." Gavin was glad. Daddy gave him a hug and said, "Don't worry, we will get it to work!"

Once upon a time there was a nice girl named Joy. She lived in a small house near the beach. On Saturday morning, Joy took her towel and headed to the beach. 

The sun was shining and the sky was fine. Joy was so excited to go swimming. She said "Welcome beach, I'm ready to swim!"

Joy put on her suit and jumped into the waves. She laughed and splashed around having fun. But then, Joy felt something pull her down. It was so strong and it wouldn't let her go. Joy screamed as monsters started to come close.

The monsters pulled Joy very deep in the ocean. She started to get scared, and she struggled with all her might. Sadly, there was no way Joy could escape. The monsters welcomed her to the deep and she was gone.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who had a magical gift. She could make lightning come out of her hands like a superhero! Every day she practiced, trying to make the lightning bigger and brighter.

One day, some other children saw her lightning and they were very envious. They started to tease her and call her names. This made the little girl very angry.

She shouted, â€œStop it!â€ But they just laughed and kept teasing her.

Then, the little girl got really mad and she lifted her hand into the air. And with one big slap, a huge bolt of lightning flew from her hands and hit the ground. Everyone stopped laughing and looked very surprised.

Tom and Mia were playing in the backyard. They saw a big pile of lumber near the fence. It was from the old shed that Dad had knocked down.

"Let's climb on the lumber!" Tom said. "It looks like fun!"

"No, Tom, we can't!" Mia said. "Dad said it is dangerous. There might be nails or splinters. And he will be grumpy if he sees us."

Tom did not listen to Mia. He ran to the lumber and jumped on it. He felt brave and strong. He laughed and shouted.

"Look at me, Mia! I am the king of the lumber! I dare you to join me!"

Mia was scared and worried. She did not want to climb on the lumber. She did not want to hurt herself or make Dad angry. But she also did not want Tom to think she was a baby.

"OK, Tom, I will come," she said. "But only for a little bit."

She walked slowly to the lumber and stepped on it. She felt wobbly and nervous. She did not like it at all.

Suddenly, they heard a loud voice.

"Tom! Mia! What are you doing on the lumber? Get down from there right now!"

It was Dad. He had come home from work. He looked very grumpy. He had seen them from the window.

Tom and Mia felt sorry and scared. They jumped off the lumber and ran to Dad. They hugged him and said they were sorry.

Dad was not happy. He told them they had been naughty and careless. He said they could have hurt themselves or damaged the lumber. He said they had to go inside and have a time out.

Tom and Mia nodded and said they understood. They followed Dad inside. They wished they had not climbed on the lumber. They learned their lesson. They decided not to dare each other again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sally. Sally loved to play with her red ball. She would throw it up in the air and catch it. One day, Sally saw a boy trying to balance on one foot. She asked him if he wanted to play catch with her. The boy said yes and they started playing together. 

After a while, Sally noticed something strange. The boy's words were not true. He said he had a pet dinosaur, but Sally knew that was impossible. She didn't want to play with someone who told lies. So, Sally told the boy that she didn't want to play anymore. 

Sally went back to playing with her red ball. She bounced it on the ground and tried to balance it on her nose. She was happy because she knew that being true was very important.

name_of_work: Song for the Rainy Season by Elizabeth Bishop
content: Hidden, oh hidden in the high fog the house we live in, beneath the magnetic rock, rain-, rainbow-ridden, where blood-black bromelias, lichens, owls, and the lint of the waterfalls cling, familiar, unbidden. In a dim age of water the brook sings loud from a rib cage of giant fern; vapor climbs up the thick growth effortlessly, turns back, holding them both, house and rock, in a private cloud. At night, on the roof, blind drops crawl and the ordinary brown owl gives us proof he can count: five times--always five-- he stamps and takes off after the fat frogs that, shrilling for love, clamber and mount. House, open house to the white dew and the milk-white sunrise kind to the eyes, to membership of silver fish, mouse, bookworms, big moths; with a wall for the mildew's ignorant map; darkened and tarnished by the warm touch of the warm breath, maculate, cherished; rejoice! For a later era will differ. (O difference that kills or intimidates, much of all our small shadowy life!) Without water the great rock will stare unmagnetized, bare, no longer wearing rainbows or rain, the forgiving air and the high fog gone; the owls will move on and the several waterfalls shrivel in the steady sun.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He lived in a small village with his mommy and daddy. One day, Timmy heard about a giant who lived in the forest. The giant was very scary and everyone was afraid of him. 

But Timmy was a brave boy. He wanted to see the giant and try to be friends with him. So, he packed some cookies and went into the forest. As he walked, he saw a big shadow. It was the giant! Timmy was scared, but he remembered his plan. He walked up to the giant and said, "Hi, I'm Timmy. Do you want some cookies?" 

The giant was surprised. No one had ever been nice to him before. He took a cookie and smiled. From that day on, Timmy and the giant were best friends. They played together and had lots of fun. Timmy was happy that he tried to be friends with the scary giant.

A tiny light You see a tiny light coming down landing on your stomach and lighting you up --A woman stretches out like an ascending flare-- Over there in the corner a shadow is busy reading Her bare unencumbered feet are much much too pretty Short-circuit in the heart-system Engine breakdown What electromagnet is still keeping me running My eyes and my love are both taking the same wrong road A mere nothing A spark they strike only to let it go out again sometime later I've had enough of the wind I've had enough of the sky Essentially everything visible is artificial Even your mouth Despite the fact that I warm up wherever your hand touches me The door is wide open but I refuse to enter I see your face but lack all faith in it You're so pale One night when we were unhappy we sat down together on a trunk Men were laughing somewhere off in the distance Nearly naked children walked by now and then Water flowed by in perfect purity Copper wire conducts the light The sun and your heart are compacted of the same substance

A year ago I fell in love with the functional ward Of a chest hospital: square cubicles in a row Plain concrete, wash basins - an art lover's woe, Not counting how the fellow in the next bed snored. But nothing whatever is by love debarred, The common and banal her heat can know. The corridor led to a stairway and below Was the inexhaustible adventure of a gravelled yard. This is what love does to things: the Rialto Bridge, The main gate that was bent by a heavy lorry, The seat at the back of a shed that was a suntrap.
