Once upon a time, there was a man who had a lot of money. He was very rich. One day, he went outside and it started to rain. He didn't have an umbrella, so he got wet. He didn't like being wet, so he decided to run home. 

As he was running, he saw a little girl who was also getting wet. She didn't have an umbrella either. He stopped and gave her his umbrella. She was very happy and thanked him. 

The man continued to run home in the rain. Even though he was rich, he knew that sometimes it's the little things, like sharing an umbrella, that can make someone else's day better.

John was out in the park with his mum. It was a beautiful day, and they wanted to take a walk. As they walked, John saw a helpful little mosquito. It was buzzing around and he wanted to take it. He asked his mum if he could take it, and she said yes. 

John got his net and carefully tried to take the mosquito, but it was too fast for him. He kept trying, but it would get away. Finally, he decided to ask his mum for help. His mum saw the mosquito and ran to help John take it. Together, they managed to take the mosquito in John's net.

John was so happy to have taken the mosquito. He thanked his mum for her help and took the mosquito home. He kept the mosquito in a jar, and it was his best friend. Every day, John would take the mosquito out of the jar and learn about it.

John and his mosquito had lots of fun together, and he was very happy to have taken it in the park.

Once upon a time, there was a wild boy. He had a shoe that he just loved. Every day he would squeeze his shoe and giggle.

One day, the boy went too far. He squeezed the shoe so tight that it began to cry. The wild boy looked at the shoe and said, "Oh noeee, what have I done?"

The next day the boy was really scared. He knew that something bad was going to happen when he squeezed his shoe. But he put on his brave face and squeezed the shoe again.

To his surprise, nothing bad happened! Instead, the shoe made a special squawking sound. The wild boy was overjoyed - he had created a wild music with his shoe! From that day on, the wild boy enjoyed making wild music with his shoe.

name_of_work: To a Snail by Marianne Moore
content: If "compression is the first grace of style," you have it. Contractility is a virtue as modesty is a virtue. It is not the acquisition of any one thing that is able to adorn, or the incidental quality that occurs as a concomitant of something well said, that we value in style, but the principle that is hid: in the absence of feet, "a method of conclusions"; "a knowledge of principles," in the curious phenomenon of your occipital horn.

Anna likes to play dress-up with her dolls. She has many clothes for them, but her favorite is a pink skirt with flowers. She likes to wrap the skirt around her dolls and pretend they are princesses.

One day, Anna's friend Lily comes to play with her. Lily sees the pink skirt and wants to try it on her doll. She asks Anna, "Can I use your skirt? It is so pretty."

Anna does not want to share her skirt. She likes it too much. She thinks of a lie to tell Lily. She says, "No, you can't. The skirt is broken. It has a big hole in it."

Lily is sad. She does not believe Anna. She says, "Let me see the hole. Where is it?"

Anna feels guilty. She knows she is not honest. She does not want to hurt Lily's feelings. She says, "I'm sorry, Lily. I lied to you. There is no hole. The skirt is fine. You can use it if you want."

Lily smiles. She is happy that Anna tells the truth. She says, "Thank you, Anna. You are a good friend. I will be careful with your skirt. Do you want to play princesses with me?"

Anna nods. She is glad that Lily forgives her. She says, "Yes, I do. Let's play princesses together. And next time, I will be honest with you."

John was playing outside when he saw an old newspaper on the ground. He carried it inside and asked his mom, "What is this?" 

His mom said, "It is a newspaper."

John was so curious and he asked what it was for. His mom said, "It is full of stories and news from all around the world. Sometimes it can even tell us what the weather will be like tomorrow." 

John was excited and he asked, "Can I act silly with it?" His mom said, "Yes, you can!" 

John started to act silly and make funny faces with the newspaper. His mom smiled and laughed, feeling proud of her son.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Today was his birthday and he was very excited! He invited all his friends to come to his party. 

When Timmy's friends arrived, they saw that his house was empty. There were no balloons or decorations. Timmy felt sad because he wanted his party to be fun. 

But then, Timmy's mom surprised him by bringing out a big cake with candles on it. All his friends sang "Happy Birthday" and Timmy blew out the candles. He was so happy that his friends came to his party, even though it was empty.

name_of_work: The People of the Other Village by Thomas Lux
content: hate the people of this village and would nail our hats to our heads for refusing in their presence to remove them or staple our hands to our foreheads for refusing to salute them if we did not hurt them first: mail them packages of rats, mix their flour at night with broken glass. We do this, they do that. They peel the larynx from one of our brothers' throats. We devein one of their sisters. The quicksand pits they built were good. Our amputation teams were better. We trained some birds to steal their wheat. They sent to us exploding ambassadors of peace. They do this, we do that. We canceled our sheep imports. They no longer bought our blankets. We mocked their greatest poet and when that had no effect we parodied the way they dance which did cause pain, so they, in turn, said our God was leprous, hairless. We do this, they do that. Ten thousand (10,000) years, ten thousand (10,000) brutal, beautiful years.

Once upon a time, there was a little bird. The bird was very happy because it had a nice white feather coat. The bird lived in a big tree near a house with a chimney. One day, the bird saw a man walking by the house. The man started to whistle a happy tune. The bird liked the sound of the whistle and decided to try it too. It flew down to the chimney and whistled a little song. The man heard the bird and smiled. From that day on, the bird would often fly down to the chimney and whistle a happy tune with the man. They became good friends and lived happily ever after.

You came out of the sea, skin dappled scales of sunlight; Riding crests, waves of fish in your fists. Washed up, your gills snapped shut. Water whipped the first breath of your lungs, Your lips' bud teased by morning mists. You conquered the shore, its ivory coast. Your legs still rocked with the memory of waves. Sinews of sand ran across your back- Rising runes of your oceanic origins. Your heart thumped- an animal skin drum heralding the coming of a prince. In the jungle, amid rasping branches, trees loosened their shadows to shroud you. The prince beheld you then, a golden sheen. Your eyes, two flickers; emerald blaze You settled back on fluent haunches; The squall of a beast. your roar, your call. In crackling boats, seeds arrived, wind-blown, You summoned their colours to the palm of your hand, folded them snugly into loam, watched saplings swaddled in green, as they sunk roots, spawned shade, and embraced the land that embraced them. Centuries, by the sea's pulmonary, a vein throbbing humming bumboats - your trees rise as skyscrapers. Their ankles lost in swilling water, as they heave themselves higher above the mirrored surface. Remember your self: your raw lion heart, Each beat a stony echo that washes through ribbed vaults of buildings. Remember your keris, iron lightning ripping through tentacles of waves, double-edged, curved to a point- flung high and caught unsheathed, scattering five stars in the red tapestry of your sky.

name_of_work: Mourning Poem for the Queen of Sunday by Robert Hayden
content: Lord's lost Him His mockingbird, His fancy warbler; Satan sweet-talked her, four bullets hushed her. Who would have thought she'd end that way? Four bullets hushed her. And the world a-clang with evil. Who's going to make old hardened sinner men tremble now and the righteous rock? Oh who and oh who will sing Jesus down to help with struggling and doing without and being colored all through blue Monday? Till way next Sunday? All those angels in their cretonne clouds and finery the true believer saw when she rared back her head and sang, all those angels are surely weeping. Who would have thought she'd end that way? Four holes in her heart. The gold works wrecked. But she looks so natural in her big bronze coffin among the Broken Hearts and Gates-Ajar, it's as if any moment she'd lift her head from its pillow of chill gardenias and turn this quiet into shouting Sunday and make folks forget what she did on Monday. Oh, Satan sweet-talked her, and four bullets hushed her. Lord's lost Him His diva, His fancy warbler's gone. Who would have thought, who would have thought she'd end that way?

Cain lifts Crow, that heavy black bird and strikes down Abel. Damn, says Crow, I guess this is just the beginning. The white man, disguised as a falcon, swoops in and yet again steals a salmon from Crow's talons. Damn, says Crow, if I could swim I would have fled this country years ago. The Crow God as depicted in all of the reliable Crow bibles looks exactly like a Crow. Damn, says Crow, this makes it so much easier to worship myself. Among the ashes of Jericho, Crow sacrifices his firstborn son. Damn, says Crow, a million nests are soaked with blood. When Crows fight Crows the sky fills with beaks and talons. Damn, says Crow, it's raining feathers. Crow flies around the reservation and collects empty beer bottles but they are so heavy he can only carry one at a time. So, one by one, he returns them but gets only five cents a bottle. Damn, says Crow, redemption is not easy. Crow rides a pale horse into a crowded powwow but none of the Indian panic. Damn, says Crow, I guess they already live near the end of the world.

One day, two friends played in a garden. They saw a boat that was cheap. The boat looked like it had been left behind and forgotten. One friend said, â€œLetâ€™s play in the boat!â€

The other friend was scared. He shook his head and said, â€œI donâ€™t think so. It looks too old and weak.â€ But the first friend was never scared. He stood near the boat and made a plan. â€œWe can fix it. We donâ€™t need a lot of things. We just need some tape, some glue, and some paint.â€

The two friends worked hard. They held the boat together with tape and glue. Finally, they painted it blue. When the boat was done, it looked like new. Everyone was so happy.

The friends went to the lake and put the boat in the water. But they forgot to check the boat. Suddenly, they heard a loud tear. They looked down and saw a hole in the boat. The friends were sad.

The two friends had to fix the boat again. They used some new tape and glue to patch it up. After some hard work, the boat was back in the water. This time, the boat stayed dry and the friends had a lot of fun.

Once upon a time, there was a mommy who wanted to teach her little boy how to ride the bus. The mommy took her little boy to the bus stop and they waited for the bus to come. When the bus arrived, the mommy and her little boy got on the bus and sat down.

The little boy looked out the window and saw lots of yummy things like candy and ice cream. But the mommy told him that they had to wait until they got home to have a yummy snack. The little boy was sad, but he knew his mommy was right.

As they rode the bus, the mommy taught her little boy about the different stops and how to pay for the ride. The little boy was so happy to learn new things and ride the bus with his mommy. When they got home, they had a yummy snack together and the little boy thanked his mommy for teaching him about the bus.

Once upon a time, there was a brave bunny named Buttons. Buttons was always on an adventure and today he was exploring a nearby forest. As he explored, he stumbled upon a broken kite and noticed it needed some repairs. 

Buttons decided he wanted to repair the kite and he searched high and low for the things he would need. He gathered twigs, leaves, and string. He then closed his eyes and thought about what else he would need. Suddenly, Buttons remembered that he had forgotten something very important: a nose!

Buttons knew he could ask for help. He spotted a very friendly looking fox in the forest. He hopped over and asked him very politely, "Do you have a nose that I can borrow to repair this kite?" 

The fox was crazy! He had a special nose that looked like a star that he was willing to lend to Buttons. Buttons was so excited. He thanked the fox and quickly got to work repairing the kite. After what seemed like forever, Buttons had successfully repaired the kite. He thanked the fox one more time and was off on the next adventure!

name_of_work: Holy Sonnet IX by John Donne
content: If poisonous minerals, and if that tree, Whose fruit threw death on (else immortal) us, If lecherous goats, if serpents envious Cannot be damn'd, alas ! why should I be ? Why should intent or reason, born in me, Make sins, else equal, in me more heinous ? And, mercy being easy, and glorious To God, in His stern wrath why threatens He ? But who am I, that dare dispute with Thee ? O God, O ! of Thine only worthy blood, And my tears, make a heavenly Lethean flood, And drown in it my sin's black memory. That Thou remember them, some claim as debt ; I think it mercy if Thou wilt forget.

I stood still and was a tree amid the wood, Knowing the truth of things unseen before; Of Daphne and the laurel bow And that god-feasting couple old that grew elm-oak amid the wold. 'Twas not until the gods had been Kindly entreated, and been brought within Unto the hearth of their heart's home That they might do this wonder thing; Nathless I have been a tree amid the wood And many a new thing understood That was rank folly to my head before.

Once there was a girl named Jane. She was three years old and loved to play outside. One day she was playing in her garden when she saw a very funny looking thing!

It was small and yellow and made noise when she clapped her hands. Jane was so excited and didn't know what it was. She asked her mom and she said it was a quiz! 

Jane was so happy and excited to play the quiz. She started clapping her hands and sure enough, the quiz made lots of noise and asked her questions. She answered all of them and the quiz started laughing.

At the end of the quiz, the box started to get empty. Jane quickly ran inside and grabbed some coins. She put in the coins and the quiz was full of life again. She clapped her hands and the quiz started up again! 

Jane had so much fun playing the quiz and clapping her hands. She played it every day and always had lots of fun.

Once upon a time there was a lazy kangaroo. He liked to lounge around in the sunshine all day and do nothing else. One day he was napping under a big tree when he heard a noise. It was coming from a nearby bush. The kangaroo slowly got up and hopped towards the sound.

Suddenly the bush started to glow! The kangaroo was so surprised that he bumped into the bush. Out hopped a little fairy!

The fairy spoke in a soft, gentle voice. â€œHello, kangaroo, why were you so lazy? Don't you know there are wonderful things to explore in the world?!â€

The kangaroo felt embarrassed. He had never seen a fairy before and thought that she must be quite magical. He spoke shyly. â€œI'm sorry, fairy. I will try and be more adventurous from now on.â€

The fairy smiled and said, â€œThat's ok. Everyone can be a bit lazy sometimes. Now, let's go explore together!â€

The kangaroo and fairy had a wonderful day together, exploring the world and seeing all the fascinating things it had to offer. They both glowed with happiness.

Once upon a time, there were two friends, Rita and Fred. One day, they decided to go outside after hearing that there was snow outside. When they got out, they were amazed to see how much snow there was. They both began to play in the snow, making snow angels and trying to catch snowflakes on their tongues.

Suddenly, Rita noticed something graceful in the sky. It was an eagle, slowly gliding across the sky. Fred was amazed at the sight and shouted out, "I want to learn to fly like that!" Rita smiled, ears pointed skyward, and replied that it was very hard to learn how to fly like that, but with practice it could be done.

Fred was determined and started practicing every day, throwing himself into the air with all his might, even though he wasn't very graceful yet. Rita cheered him on from the sidelines, helping him learn what he needed to do.

Eventually, two months later, Fred had learned to fly gracefully through the sky just like the eagle. They were both amazed, Rita had helped Fred learn something amazing that day. They shared a high-five and both grinned from ear to ear. The snow had made their day.

That sail which leans on light, tired of islands, a schooner beating up the Caribbean for home, could be Odysseus, home-bound on the Aegean; that father and husband's longing, under gnarled sour grapes, is like the adulterer hearing Nausicaa's name in every gull's outcry. This brings nobody peace. The ancient war between obsession and responsibility will never finish and has been the same for the sea-wanderer or the one on shore now wriggling on his sandals to walk home, since Troy sighed its last flame, and the blind giant's boulder heaved the trough from whose groundswell the great hexameters come to the conclusions of exhausted surf. The classics can console. But not enough.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim loved to play with his blocks. He had red blocks, blue blocks, and yellow blocks. Tim liked to build tall towers with his blocks.

One day, Tim's friend, Sue, came to play with him. "Let's work together and build the tallest tower ever!" said Sue. Tim was very happy. They took turns putting one block on top of the other. The tower grew taller and taller.

When they finished, Tim and Sue looked at their big tower. They were proud of their work. "Now, let's make the room tidy," said Tim. They picked up all the extra blocks and put them away. The room was clean and tidy. Tim and Sue smiled, knowing they had done a great job.

Once upon a time there was a big river. On one side was a big town and on the other side was a small village. It was difficult for people to get from one side to the other side.

The people wanted to build a bridge to help them get across. They asked their king for help. He said yes and he asked the people to help build it.

Everyone worked together to build the bridge and it was ready in no time. It was a very big bridge. Everyone was very happy and they thanked the king.

The king wanted to make sure that no one was foolish and went on the bridge when it wasn't safe. So he said, "Please cross the bridge only when it is safe and you can see the other side". 

The people listened to the king and crossed the bridge only when it was safe. Everyone followed the king's advice and nobody was ever foolish.

Once upon a time, there was a cool fountain. On a hot day, two kids named Jack and Jessie had a great idea. They thought it would be fun to play in the fountain.

When the kids arrived at the fountain, Jack said, "Let's have a race and see who gets to the fountain first!"

Jessie shouted, "I'm going to win, I'm the fastest!"

Jack and Jessie started running as fast as they could. When the kids arrived at the fountain, Jessie was the first to get there. She squealed with delight.

They both had so much fun playing and splashing in the cool fountain. The kids laughed and ran around in the fountain until it was time to go home.

Jack and Jessie said goodbye to the fountain and promised they would be back soon.

Tom and Anna like to play in the park. They see a big slide. They want to go on the slide. But there is a problem. The slide is very high and they are very small.

"How can we go on the slide?" Tom asks Anna.

"Maybe we can balance on the steps," Anna says. "But we have to be careful. We don't want to fall."

They hold hands and start to balance on the steps. They go up and up. They are almost at the top. But then they hear a scary sound.

"Boo!"

They turn around and see a ghost. The ghost is white and smooth. It has big eyes and a big mouth. It smiles at them.

"Hello, little ones," the ghost says. "Do you want to play with me?"

Tom and Anna are very scared. They scream and run down the steps. They forget to balance. They slip and slide. They land on the grass.

The ghost laughs and follows them. It is not a real ghost. It is their big brother, Sam. He has a sheet on his head. He likes to trick them.

"Got you!" Sam says. "That was funny."

Tom and Anna are not happy. They are angry and sad. They don't think it is funny.

"Go away, Sam!" Tom says. "You are mean. You spoiled our fun."

"Yeah, go away!" Anna says. "You are not a ghost. You are a bully."

Sam feels sorry. He takes off the sheet. He hugs them and says sorry.

"I'm sorry, Tom and Anna," Sam says. "I was just joking. I didn't mean to scare you. Can we be friends?"

Tom and Anna look at him. They see his sorry face. They forgive him.

"OK, Sam," Tom says. "We can be friends. But don't do that again."

"OK, Anna," Sam says. "I won't do that again. Can I play with you?"

They nod and smile. They go back to the slide. They help each other balance on the steps. They go on the slide together. They have fun. They are happy.

Once upon a time, there was a friendly potato. The potato liked to walk around the garden and say hello to all the other vegetables. One day, a mean bird came and tried to eat the potato. The potato was scared and didn't know what to do.

But then, the potato had an idea. It started to walk away from the bird as fast as it could. The bird tried to catch the potato, but the potato was too fast. Finally, the potato made it to the other side of the garden, safe and sound. From then on, the potato made sure to always walk with caution and be aware of any mean birds around.

name_of_work: The Lyric in a Time of War by Eloise Klein Healy
content: Let my music be found wanting in comparison to yours (as it must) let me be found loving (as you were) extravagantly the beautiful let me find you and the song (forever) between us in these terrible times

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved planes and always watched them fly in the sky. One day, Timmy's dad took him to the airport to see the planes up close. Timmy was so happy!

As they watched the planes take off, Timmy's dad explained that flying a plane was difficult. Timmy didn't understand why it was so hard. His dad said that the pilots had to pay attention to many things at once, like the weather and the controls.

Suddenly, the loud noise of the planes became too much for Timmy. He asked his dad to pause and take a break. They sat down and watched the planes from a distance. Timmy was happy again, and he knew that one day he would learn how to fly a plane, even if it was difficult.

name_of_work: The New Colossus by Emma Lazarus
content: Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame, With conquering limbs astride from land to land; Here at our sea-washed, sunset gates shall stand A mighty woman with a torch, whose flame Is the imprisoned lightning, and her name Mother of Exiles. From her beacon-hand Glows world-wide welcome; her mild eyes command The air-bridged harbor that twin cities frame. "Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!" cries she With silent lips. "Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, The wretched refuse of your teeming shore. Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me, I lift my lamp beside the golden door!"

name_of_work: Musee des Beaux Arts by W.H. Auden
content: About suffering they were never wrong, The old Masters: how well they understood Its human position: how it takes place While someone else is eating or opening a window or just walking dully along; How, when the aged are reverently, passionately waiting For the miraculous birth, there always must be Children who did not specially want it to happen, skating On a pond at the edge of the wood: They never forgot That even the dreadful martyrdom must run its course Anyhow in a corner, some untidy spot Where the dogs go on with their doggy life and the torturer's horse Scratches its innocent behind on a tree. In Breughel's Icarus, for instance: how everything turns away Quite leisurely from the disaster; the ploughman may Have heard the splash, the forsaken cry, But for him it was not an important failure; the sun shone As it had to on the white legs disappearing into the green Water, and the expensive delicate ship that must have seen Something amazing, a boy falling out of the sky, Had somewhere to get to and sailed calmly on.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to eat peanuts. She would eat them every day and never got tired of them. One day, Lily's mom told her that she couldn't have peanuts anymore because she was allergic to them. Lily was very frustrated and sad because she loved peanuts so much.

Lily went to her friend Timmy's house to play. Timmy saw that Lily was sad and asked her what was wrong. Lily told Timmy that she couldn't eat peanuts anymore and that she hated being allergic to them. Timmy said, "Don't worry, Lily. We can play a game instead. Let's play hide and seek!"

Lily forgot about her peanut allergy for a little while as she played with Timmy. She realized that even though she couldn't eat peanuts anymore, she still had fun playing with her friend. From that day on, Lily didn't hate being allergic to peanuts as much because she had her friend to play with.

Little Kaja was a happy little girl. One day, she saw something moving in the garden. She was curious, so she went closer to take a look.

"What are you?" she asked, cupping her hands around the small creature on the soil.

The creature replied in a gentle voice, "I'm a baby hedgehog".

Kaja was delighted and decided to pick up the creature. She lay it in her doll basket and took it inside the house.

Her mom laughed when she saw the hedgehog and said, "Oh, Kaja! What have you found this time?" But she was very gentle with the creature, and made it a cozy nest in the garden with some soil and leaves.

Kaja smiled. The baby hedgehog seemed happy to be back in its own home. She waved goodbye to the hedgehog and went back inside the house with a big smile on her face.

From the private ease of Mother's womb I fall into the lighted room. Why don't they simply put me back Where it is warm amd wet and black? But one thing follows on another. Things were different inside Mother. Padded and jolly I would ride The perfect comfort of her inside. They tuck me in a rustling bed --I lie there, raging, small, and red. I may sleep soon, I may forget, But I won't forget that I regret. A rain of blood poured round her womb, But all time roars outside this room.

Once upon a time there was a happy cricket named Jim. One day, Jim decided to travel on an adventure across the world. He began to hop across fields, rivers, and mountains. He had so much fun that he couldn't stop smiling!

As Jim was hopping along the way, he saw many other animals traveling too. He saw a fox, a lion, and even an elephant. All of them were going on their own adventures. Jim felt a bit envious; he wanted to have an adventure too.

When Jim was in the middle of his travel, he met another cricket. His name was Bob and he was also traveling. Jim asked Bob where he was going, and Bob said he was visiting a new place.

Jim was so excited to find another cricket traveling just like him! They hopped and jumped together as they completed their journey. Jim was so very happy and he knew it was one of the best trips he ever had.

When their journey was over, Jim and Bob said goodbye. Jim waved and wished Bob the best in his travels. Jim was so glad he decided to travel; it was the best adventure of his life!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to play outside. One day, she went to the creek to play with her friends. They splashed around in the water and had so much fun. But then, Lily's tummy started to rumble.

"I'm hungry," she said.

"Let's go home and eat," her friend replied.

But Lily was impatient. She didn't want to leave yet. She demanded that they stay and play a little longer. But soon, her tummy rumbled again and she realized she was really hungry. So, she said goodbye to her friends and went home to eat some yummy food. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a young girl called Mary. Mary was full of life and loved adventures! She was always willing to explore the new things in life. 

One day, her grandma bought her a small boat and said, "Mary, why don't you sail this boat in the river?" Mary happily agreed and took the boat to the river. 

When she reached the river bank, the sky suddenly became dark and the wind started blowing. Mary was a bit scared so she stepped aside, behind a big curtain.

Just then, a strong voice said, "Mary, don't be scared. Take your boat and sail. You have to be hard and brave in life!"

Mary realized that it was the voice of her grandma. She nodded her head and took her boat out on the river.

The moral of the story is that life is not easy, but we need to be brave and face our challenges with a strong heart and courage. Mary learned this lesson that day and she never gave up her adventures!

Once upon a time there was a small boy who loved to explore. He was very curious and would go to the park every day to find something new and exciting. One day, he found a big blue door with a lock. He wondered what was inside so he tried to open it.

He tried again, but it wouldn't open. He got very frustrated and he wished there was a way to get inside. Then, he had a great idea!

He shouted out, "Hey, can anyone help me get inside this blue door?" Suddenly, he heard a voice. It was an old man who said, "I think I can help you. I'm very competitive and I bet I can open it!"

The old man didn't give up and he tried several times to unlock the door. Finally, the door opened and the little boy was able to see what was inside. It was full of surprise and excitement. He thanked the old man and ran inside to explore. 

The boy had a wonderful time and he thanked the old man for his help. From that day on, the little boy and the old man were friends. They played together every day and explored the wonders of the blue door.

Once upon a time, there was a great king. He wanted to gain something very special. So he searched the entire kingdom for it. He went high into the mountains, low into the valleys and far away in the desert.

But no matter how far and wide the king searched, he still couldn't find what he wanted. Until one day, he was walking through the forest and he came across a magical tree.

The king approached the tree and he noticed something wonderful. Above the tree was a glittering star. When the king touched the star, he gained something beautiful and unforgettable.

The star granted the king one wish. The great king wished for something very special: happiness for his people. And with that, the king and his people lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time there was a small dog called Spot. He was always very adventurous and loved to explore the world around him. One day he decided that he wanted to try the carrot growing in the garden.

Spot walked up to the carrot and insisted that he wanted to try it. His owner, however, was worried that he might not like it and told him that it was dangerous. But Spot just rolled his eyes and said he was sure he wanted it.

The owner sighed and, seeing that Spot was determined, gave in and let him try it. Spot ate the carrot and was thrilled at how delicious it was!

Although Spot was happy with his new food discovery, his owner was still worried. She knew how adventurous Spot was and wanted him to stay away from other areas of the garden that could be more dangerous. She insisted that Spot stay away from the other plants and that he listen to her.

Spot did not like it at first, but soon realised that his owner was right. He had lots of fun exploring the garden but always remembered to listen to his owner.

Once upon a time, there was a chubby little mouse called Tommy. Tommy was walking down a street when he heard a scuttling sound. He wondered what made the noise, so he stopped and looked around the corner. Suddenly he saw a big tabby cat! Tommy was very scared and ran away as fast as he could. 

The cat started chasing Tommy, and they were running round and round in circles. "Please don't catch me!" cried Tommy. But the cat was too fast and soon it caught up with him. It swiped its paw at him and knocked him over.

Tommy knew it was all over. He looked up at the cat and said, "Please don't hurt me." The cat just looked at him and then a wicked idea came into its head. It decided to play a game with Tommy. 

The cat said, "I'm going to let you go, but you have to close your eyes and count to ten. If you can do that, then you can go free. If you don't, I will catch you, again." 

Tommy thought about what to do. Should he close his eyes or should he keep running? In the end, he decided to take a chance and closed his eyes. He started to count, but before he could finish the cat caught up with him. The cat had tricked him, and Tommy was never seen again.

Tom and Lily liked to paint. They had many colors and brushes. They painted flowers, animals, and houses. They had fun.

One day, their teacher said there was a paint contest. The best painting would get a prize. Tom and Lily wanted to win the prize. They worked hard on their paintings.

But Sam was rude. He did not like to paint. He liked to make trouble. He saw Tom and Lily's paintings. He thought they were bad. He took his brush and painted over them. He laughed.

Tom and Lily saw what Sam did. They were sad and angry. They cried. "Why did you do that?" they asked Sam. "You ruined our paintings!"

Sam did not care. He said, "Your paintings are ugly. I made them better. I will win the prize."

The teacher heard the noise. She came and saw what happened. She was not happy. She said, "Sam, that was very rude. You did not respect Tom and Lily's work. You did not follow the rules. You will not win the prize. You will have a time out."

She gave Tom and Lily new papers and colors. She said, "I'm sorry, Tom and Lily. You can paint again. I'm sure your paintings will be beautiful."

Tom and Lily thanked the teacher. They painted again. They made new flowers, animals, and houses. They were proud of their paintings.

The teacher looked at all the paintings. She said, "You all did a great job. But I have to choose one winner. And the winner is... Tom and Lily!"

Tom and Lily were happy. They got the prize. It was a big box of crayons. They shared it with their friends. They said, "Thank you, teacher. We love to paint."

Sam was not happy. He was still in time out. He learned a lesson. He said, "Sorry, Tom and Lily. I was rude. I will not do that again. Can I paint with you?"

Tom and Lily were kind. They said, "Yes, you can. But you have to be nice. And you have to use your own paper and colors."

Sam agreed. He painted with them. He tried to make nice paintings. He had fun. He said, "Painting is fun. I like to paint."

Beloved, men in thick green coats came crunching through the snow, the insignia on their shoulders of uncertain origin, a country I could not be sure of, a salute so terrifying I heard myself lying to avoid arrest, and was arrested along with Jocko, whose tear had snapped off, a tiny icicle he put in his mouth. We were taken to the ice prison, a palace encrusted with hoarfrost, its dome lit from within, Jocko admired the wiring, he kicked the walls to test the strength of his new boots. A television stood in a block of ice, its blue image still moving like a liquid center. You asked for my innermost thoughts. I wonder will I ever see a grape again? When I think of the vineyard where we met in October--when you dropped a cluster custom insisted you be kissed by a stranger--how after the harvest we plunged into a stream so icy our palms turned pink. It seemed our future was sealed. Everyone said so. It is quiet here. Not closing our ranks weakens us hugely. The snowflakes fall in a featureless bath. I am the stranger who kissed you. On sunny days each tree is a glittering chandelier. The power of mindless beauty! Jocko told a joke and has been dead since May. A bullethole in his forehead the officers call a third eye. For a month I milked a barnful of cows. It is a lot like cleansing a chandelier. Wipe and polish, wipe and polish, round and round you go. I have lost my spectacles. Is the book I was reading still open by the side of our bed? Treat it as a bookmark saving my place in our story. (here the letter breaks off)

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Billy. He was very obedient, always doing what his mom asked. One day, Mom told him to go outside and sack some leaves from the front yard. Billy headed outside and grabbed his shirt off the peg by the door. He put it on and began his work. He saked until the front yard was spotless. When he was done, Mom thanked him for being so obedient. She gave him a big hug and said he could have a special treat as a reward. She took out a big bag of candy. Billy was so happy. He had been obedient and now he got a sweet reward.

Once there was a girl who loved to explore. She wanted to see every land she could find. So one day, she set out on an adventure to another land.

The land was beautiful and she loved it! But soon it was time to return home. The girl was a little bit fearful, but she knew she could do it.

So she waved goodbye to the land and began her journey back home. On the way she saw many different things, but none were as wonderful as the land she had left. 

Finally, she reached her home. She was so happy to be back, but also a little bit sad because she knew she couldn't return to the land again.

His loud sharp call seems to come from nowhere. Then, a flash of turquoise in the pipal tree The slender neck arched away from you as he descends, and as he darts away, a glimpse of the very end of his tail. I was told that you have to sit in the veranda And read a book, preferably one of your favourites with great concentration.. The moment you begin to live inside the book A blue shadow will fall over you. The wind will change direction, The steady hum of bees In the bushes nearby will stop. The cat will awaken and stretch. Something has broken your attention; And if you look up in time You might see the peacock turning away as he gathers his tail To shut those dark glowing eyes, Violet fringed with golden amber. It is the tail that has to blink For eyes that are always open.

Once upon a time, there was a giant. The giant was very big and tall. He lived in a big house on a big hill. The giant was very nice and liked to help people.

One day, the giant saw a little girl who was sad. She was hungry and wanted something yummy to eat. The giant wanted to help her, so he went to his big house to get some food.

The giant looked in his big kitchen and found some yummy food. He took the yummy food and gave it to the little girl. The giant supplied her with enough food to make her happy. The little girl was very happy and said thank you to the giant. They became good friends and played together every day.

Once upon a time, in a small town, there was a big box. It was a very organized box, with many small things inside. The people in the town loved the box, and they all took care of it.

One day, a little boy named Tim found the box. He was very excite to see what was inside. He opened the box and found many small things. He played with them and put them back in the box when he was done.

Tim showed the box to his friends. They all played with the things inside and had fun. They made sure to put everything back in the organized box when they were done. The people in the town were happy to see the children play with the box and learn to put things back where they belong.

The moral of the story is that it is important to take care of our things and keep them organized. When we do this, we can all enjoy and share the things we have.

A poem should be palpable and mute As a globed fruit, Dumb As old medallions to the thumb, Silent as the sleeve-worn stone Of casement ledges where the moss has grown-- A poem should be wordless As the flight of birds. * A poem should be motionless in time As the moon climbs, Leaving, as the moon releases Twig by twig the night-entangled trees, Leaving, as the moon behind the winter leaves, Memory by memory the mind-- A poem should be motionless in time As the moon climbs. * A poem should be equal to: Not true. For all the history of grief An empty doorway and a maple leaf. For love The leaning grasses and two lights above the sea-- A poem should not mean But be.

name_of_work: I Loved You by Alexander Pushkin
content: I loved you: yet the love, maybe, Has not extinguished in my heart; But hence may not it trouble thee; I do not want to make you sad. I loved you hopelessly and mutely, Now with shyness, now with jealousy being vexed; I loved you so sincerely, so fondly, Likewise may someone love you next. Translation by Emil Sharafutdinov: I loved you; even now I must confess, Some embers of my love their fire retain; But do not let it cause you more distress, I do not want to sadden you again. Hopeless and tonguetied, yet I loved you dearly With pangs the jealous and the timid know; So tenderly I love you, so sincerely, I pray God grant another love you so.

Lily and Ben are twins. They like to play with their toys and watch TV. But sometimes they get tired and need a nap.

One day, they were watching a show about hairy animals. They saw a lion, a bear, and a monkey. They learned how the animals live and what they eat.

"Wow, look at the lion!" Ben said. "He has a big mane and sharp teeth. He is the king of the animals."

"I like the monkey," Lily said. "He has a long tail and funny face. He can swing from the trees and eat bananas."

They watched the show until it was over. Then their mom came in and said, "Time for a nap, kids. You have been watching TV for a long time. You need to rest your eyes and your brains."

"But mom, we are not sleepy," Ben said. "We want to watch more TV."

"Me too," Lily said. "We want to see more hairy animals."

Mom smiled and said, "I know you like the show, but you also need a nap. Napping is good for you. It helps you grow and learn. And you can watch more TV later, after you wake up."

She took them to their bedroom and tucked them in their beds. She gave them each a kiss and said, "Sweet dreams, my loves. I will be back soon."

Lily and Ben closed their eyes and tried to nap. But they kept thinking about the hairy animals. They imagined they were in the jungle with the monkey, or in the savanna with the lion, or in the forest with the bear. They made noises and pretended to be the animals.

Mom heard them and came back to check on them. She saw them playing and laughing in their beds. She shook her head and said, "You two are not napping at all. You are having too much fun."

She decided to join them and said, "Can I be a hairy animal too? How about a cat? Meow!"

Lily and Ben giggled and said, "Yes, mom, you can be a cat. We love you, our hairy cat mom."

They hugged her and snuggled with her. They felt cozy and warm. They stopped playing and started to nap. They dreamed of hairy animals and happy adventures.

name_of_work: To Any Dead Officer by Siegfried Sassoon
content: Well, how are things in Heaven? I wish you'd say, Because I'd like to know that you're all right. Tell me, have you found everlasting day, Or been sucked in by everlasting night? For when I shut my eyes your face shows plain; I hear you make some cheery old remark-- I can rebuild you in my brain, Though you've gone out patrolling in the dark. You hated tours of trenches; you were proud Of nothing more than having good years to spend; Longed to get home and join the careless crowd Of chaps who work in peace with Time for friend. That's all washed out now. You're beyond the wire: No earthly chance can send you crawling back; You've finished with machine-gun fire-- Knocked over in a hopeless dud-attack. Somehow I always thought you'd get done in, Because you were so desperate keen to live: You were all out to try and save your skin, Well knowing how much the world had got to give. You joked at shells and talked the usual "shop," Stuck to your dirty job and did it fine: With "Jesus Christ! when will it stop? Three years ... It's hell unless we break their line." So when they told me you'd been left for dead I wouldn't believe them, feeling it must be true. Next week the bloody Roll of Honour said "Wounded and missing"--(That's the thing to do When lads are left in shell-holes dying slow, With nothing but blank sky and wounds that ache, Moaning for water till they know It's night, and then it's not worth while to wake!) Good-bye, old lad! Remember me to God, And tell Him that our politicians swear They won't give in till Prussian Rule's been trod Under the Heel of England ... Are you there? ... Yes ... and the war won't end for at least two years; But we've got stacks of men ... I'm blind with tears, Staring into the dark. Cheero! I wish they'd killed you in a decent show.

name_of_work: The Arnolfini Marriage by Paul Durcan
content: We are the Arnolfinis. Do not think you may invade Our privacy because you may not. We are standing to our portrait, The most erotic portrait ever made, Because we have faith in the artist To do justice to the plurality, Fertility, domesticity, barefootedness Of a man and a woman saying "we": To do justice to our bed As being our most necessary furniture; To do justice to our life as a reflection. Our brains spill out upon the floor And the terrier at our feet sniffs The minutiae of our magnitude. The most relaxing word in our vocabulary is "we". Imagine being able to say "we". Most people are in no position to say "we". Are you? Who eat alone? Sleep alone? And at dawn cycle to work With an Alsatian shepherd dog tied to your handlebars? We will pause now for the Angelus. Here you have it: The two halves of the coconut.

I The broken pillar of the wing jags from the clotted shoulder, The wing trails like a banner in defeat, No more to use the sky forever but live with famine And pain a few days: cat nor coyote Will shorten the week of waiting for death, there is game without talons. He stands under the oak-bush and waits The lame feet of salvation; at night he remembers freedom And flies in a dream, the dawns ruin it. He is strong and pain is worse to the strong, incapacity is worse. The curs of the day come and torment him At distance, no one but death the redeemer will humble that head, The intrepid readiness, the terrible eyes. The wild God of the world is sometimes merciful to those That ask mercy, not often to the arrogant. You do not know him, you communal people, or you have forgotten him; Intemperate and savage, the hawk remembers him; Beautiful and wild, the hawks, and men that are dying, remember him. II I'd sooner, except the penalties, kill a man than a hawk; but the great redtail Had nothing left but unable misery From the bones too shattered for mending, the wing that trailed under his talons when he moved. We had fed him for six weeks, I gave him freedom, He wandered over the foreland hill and returned in the evening, asking for death, Not like a beggar, still eyed with the old Implacable arrogance. I gave him the lead gift in the twilight. What fell was relaxed, Owl-downy, soft feminine feathers; but what Soared: the fierce rush: the night-herons by the flooded river cried fear at its rising Before it was quite unsheathed from reality.

name_of_work: I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud by William Wordsworth
content: I wandered lonely as a cloud That floats on high o'er vales and hills, When all at once I saw a crowd, A host, of golden daffodils; Beside the lake, beneath the trees, Fluttering and dancing in the breeze. Continuous as the stars that shine And twinkle on the milky way, They stretched in never-ending line Along the margin of a bay: Ten thousand saw I at a glance, Tossing their heads in sprightly dance. The waves beside them danced; but they Out-did the sparkling waves in glee: A poet could not but be gay, In such a jocund company: I gazed--and gazed--but little thought What wealth the show to me had brought: For oft, when on my couch I lie In vacant or in pensive mood, They flash upon that inward eye Which is the bliss of solitude; And then my heart with pleasure fills, And dances with the daffodils.

Once there was a small mouse, who loved exploring and playing around. One day he came across some big and juicy plums, hanging from a palm tree. He wanted to have them, but he knew that it was not his, so he asked the palm tree:

"Can I take the plums?", he asked.

But the palm tree replied in a funny voice:
"No, it's not nice to steal. It's not right".

The mouse felt sad, but he knew the palm tree was right. He thanked the palm tree, and promised himself that he will never steal again, but find his own food instead.

The small mouse learned that stealing is wrong, even if it looks fun. So be brave and honest, and never take something that doesn't belong to you!

name_of_work: Tavern by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: I'll keep a little tavern Below the high hill's crest, Wherein all grey-eyed people May set them down and rest. There shall be plates a-plenty, And mugs to melt the chill Of all the grey-eyed people Who happen up the hill. There sound will sleep the traveller, And dream his journey's end, But I will rouse at midnight The falling fire to tend. Aye, 'tis a curious fancy-- But all the good I know Was taught me out of two grey eyes A long time ago.

Once there was a girl named Lily. She was three years old. She knew lots of people, but nobody ever seemed too friendly.

But one day, a nice stranger came to talk to her. He smiled and offered her a beautiful flower. He said, "Lily, I want to give you this flower."

Lily was confused. She had never seen such a beautiful flower before. She looked at the stranger, then back at the flower, then back at the stranger.

Finally, Lily said thank you and took the flower. She was so happy to have something so special!

The stranger smiled and said, "You are very welcome! I just wanted to offer you something special." Then he turned and walked away.

Lily was so happy, she ran inside and showed her mom the flower. It was a beautiful white lily, and Lily smiled and hugged it all day.

name_of_work: Our Casuarina Tree by Toru Dutt
content: LIKE a huge Python, winding round and round The rugged trunk, indented deep with scars, Up to its very summit near the stars, A creeper climbs, in whose embraces bound No other tree could live. But gallantly The giant wears the scarf, and flowers are hung In crimson clusters all the boughs among, Whereon all day are gathered bird and bee; And oft at nights the garden overflows With one sweet song that seems to have no close, Sung darkling from our tree, while men repose. When first my casement is wide open thrown At dawn, my eyes delighted on it rest; Sometimes, and most in winter,--on its crest A gray baboon sits statue-like alone Watching the sunrise; while on lower boughs His puny offspring leap about and play; And far and near kokilas hail the day; And to their pastures wend our sleepy cows; And in the shadow, on the broad tank cast By that hoar tree, so beautiful and vast, The water-lilies spring, like snow enmassed. But not because of its magnificence Dear is the Casuarina to my soul: Beneath it we have played; though years may roll, O sweet companions, loved with love intense, For your sakes, shall the tree be ever dear. Blent with your images, it shall arise In memory, till the hot tears blind mine eyes! What is that dirge-like murmur that I hear Like the sea breaking on a shingle-beach? It is the tree's lament, an eerie speech, That haply to the unknown land may reach. Unknown, yet well-known to the eye of faith! Ah, I have heard that wail far, far away In distant lands, by many a sheltered bay, When slumbered in his cave the water-wraith And the waves gently kissed the classic shore Of France or Italy, beneath the moon, When earth lay tranced in a dreamless swoon: And every time the music rose,--before Mine inner vision rose a form sublime, Thy form, O Tree, as in my happy prime I saw thee, in my own loved native clime. Therefore I fain would consecrate a lay Unto thy honor, Tree, beloved of those Who now in blessed sleep for aye repose,-- Dearer than life to me, alas, were they! Mayst thou be numbered when my days are done With deathless trees--like those in Borrowdale, Under whose awful branches lingered pale "Fear, trembling Hope, and Death, the skeleton, And Time the shadow;" and though weak the verse That would thy beauty fain, oh, fain rehearse, May Love defend thee from Oblivion's curse.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who loved math. Every day she would practice matching numbers and shapes. One day she was very excited to do some math but there was something wrong! Her toys were all dirty so she couldn't match them.

The little girl was so sad but then she had an idea. She ran to the garden and picked some pretty flowers. She used the petals of the flowers to make a matching game! She was so happy that she started to sing and dance.

The little girl played her matching game for hours and soon her toys were clean again. She was so proud of herself and couldn't wait to match up some more math. From then on she kept her toys tidy so she could play with them as much as she wanted.

name_of_work: The Widow's Lament in Springtime by William Carlos Williams
content: Sorrow is my own yard where the new grass flames as it has flamed often before but not with the cold fire that closes round me this year. Thirtyfive years I lived with my husband. The plumtree is white today with masses of flowers. Masses of flowers load the cherry branches and color some bushes yellow and some red but the grief in my heart is stronger than they for though they were my joy formerly, today I notice them and turn away forgetting. Today my son told me that in the meadows, at the edge of the heavy woods in the distance, he saw trees of white flowers. I feel that I would like to go there and fall into those flowers and sink into the marsh near them.

name_of_work: Boot and Saddle by Robert Browning
content: Boot, saddle, to horse, and away! Rescue my Castle, before the hot day Brightens the blue from its silvery grey, (Chorus) "Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!" Ride past the suburbs, asleep as you'd say; Many's the friend there, will listen and pray "God's luck to gallants that strike up the lay, (Chorus) "Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!" Forty miles off, like a roebuck at bay, Flouts Castle Brancepeth the Roundheads array: Who laughs, Good fellows ere this, by my fay, (Chorus) "Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!" Who? My wife Gertrude; that, honest and gay, Laughs when you talk of surrendering, "Nay! I've better counsellors; what counsel they?" (Chorus) "Boot, saddle, to horse, and away!"

A gray cat lived in a big house with a girl and a boy. The cat liked to play with the girl and the boy, but they did not know his name. They called him Cat, or Kitty, or Meow. The cat did not like these names. He wanted a real name, like the girl and the boy.

One day, the cat saw a bird on the window. He jumped and tried to catch the bird, but he missed and fell on the floor. The girl and the boy laughed and ran to the cat. They hugged him and said, "Are you OK, Cat? You are so funny and silly!"

The cat was not happy. He did not want to be funny and silly. He wanted to be great and strong. He looked at the girl and the boy and said, "Meow!"

The girl and the boy looked at each other. They thought the cat was trying to tell them something. They asked, "Do you want to say something, Cat? Do you have a name?"

The cat nodded and said, "Meow!"

The girl and the boy tried to guess what the cat's name was. They said, "Is it Max? Is it Sam? Is it Leo?"

The cat shook his head and said, "No, no, no!"

The girl and the boy thought hard. They looked at the cat and saw his gray fur and his green eyes. They said, "Is it Gray? Is it Green? Is it Grrr?"

The cat smiled and said, "Yes, yes, yes!"

The girl and the boy clapped and said, "We found your name, Cat! Your name is Grrr! You are a great gray cat!"

The cat was happy. He liked his name. He liked the girl and the boy. He said, "Thank you, thank you, thank you!"

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a soft cat named Fluffy. Fluffy liked to play with her toys and sleep on her soft bed. One day, Fluffy saw her human draw something on a big paper. It was a design for a new toy.

Fluffy jumped up and said, "Meow! Can I help you design the toy?" Her human smiled and said, "Yes, Fluffy! You can help me pick the colors." Fluffy was very happy to help.

Together, they made a beautiful design for the new toy. It was a soft ball with many colors. Fluffy loved her new toy and played with it every day. She was glad she could help her human with the design.

Once upon a time there was a patient pumpkin. The pumpkin did not like to move and wanted to resist doing anything. But one day, a little girl came and asked the pumpkin if it would join her on an adventure. Though the pumpkin wanted to resist, it saw how kind and happy the little girl was and decided to go with her.

The little girl brought the pumpkin to a big field full of other pumpkins. There were pumpkins of all shapes and sizes, and the little girl asked the pumpkin to run along with them. But the pumpkin still wanted to resist.

The little girl was patient and kept asking the pumpkin to join the other pumpkins. Finally, the patient pumpkin decided to go, and the two raced around happily together. They ran and raced until the little girl's tummy began to growl. She said it was time for a special pumpkin treat.

The little girl and the patient pumpkin went back home and enjoyed a big, warm pumpkin pie. The pumpkin was so happy that it had resisted to try something new because it had the best day ever.

Softly and humbly to the Gulf of Arabs The convoys of dead sailors come; At night they sway and wander in the waters far under, But morning rolls them in the foam. Between the sob and clubbing of the gunfire Someone, it seems, has time for this, To pluck them from the shallows and bury them in burrows And tread the sand upon their nakedness; And each cross, the driven stake of tidewood, Bears the last signature of men, Written with such perplexity, with such bewildered pity, The words choke as they begin - 'Unknown seaman' - the ghostly pencil Wavers and fades, the purple drips, The breath of the wet season has washed their inscriptions As blue as drowned men's lips, Dead seamen, gone in search of the same landfall, Whether as enemies they fought, Or fought with us, or neither; the sand joins them together, Enlisted on the other front.

Ben and Mia like to play with their basketball. They bounce it and throw it and catch it. They have fun with their basketball.

One day, they go to the park with their mom. They see a big hoop and a net. They want to try to put their basketball in the hoop. They take turns to throw the ball.

Ben throws the ball and it goes in the hoop. He is happy. He says, "I did it! I did it!"

Mia throws the ball and it misses the hoop. She is sad. She says, "I can't do it. I can't do it."

Ben says, "It's okay, Mia. You can try again. You can do it."

Mia says, "No, I can't. You are better than me. You always win."

Ben says, "No, I don't. Sometimes you win. Sometimes I win. We are both good."

Mia says, "No, you are not. You are mean. You are grumpy. You make me feel bad."

Ben says, "No, I'm not. I'm not mean. I'm not grumpy. I don't make you feel bad. You are my sister. I love you."

Mia says, "No, you don't. You don't love me. You only love your basketball."

Mia is angry. She grabs the basketball and runs away. She hides behind a tree.

Ben is sad. He looks for Mia. He can't find her. He says, "Mia, where are you? Come back. I'm sorry. I want to play with you."

He hears a noise. He notices a big dog. The dog is barking. The dog is running. The dog has the basketball in its mouth.

Ben is scared. He says, "Mia, help me! The dog has our basketball!"

Mia hears Ben. She sees the dog. She sees the basketball. She feels sorry. She says, "Ben, I'm here! I'm sorry. I want to help you."

She runs to Ben. She hugs him. She says, "Don't worry, Ben. We can get our basketball back. We can work together. We can be brave."

Ben and Mia look at the dog. The dog is not grumpy. The dog is playful. The dog wants to play with the basketball.

Ben and Mia smile. They say, "Hi, dog. Do you want to play with us? Do you want to share our basketball?"

The dog wags its tail. The dog drops the basketball. The dog barks.

Ben and Mia pick up the basketball. They throw it to the dog. The dog catches it. The dog throws it back.

Ben and Mia laugh. They say, "Thank you, dog. You are fun. You are nice. You are our friend."

They play with the dog and the basketball. They have fun with the dog and the basketball.

They forget to be grumpy. They remember to be happy. They remember to love each other.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to pretend that she was a princess and had many treasures. One day, she found a shiny egg in her backyard. She pretended that it was a golden egg and she was now very wealthy.

Lily showed her egg to all her friends and they were amazed. They all wanted to play with the egg too. But one day, Lily accidentally dropped the egg and it cracked open. She was very sad because she lost her treasure and her friends were no longer interested in playing with her.

Lily learned that pretending to be wealthy was not as important as having true friends. She wished she could go back in time and not pretend that the egg was a treasure. But it was too late and now she was alone.

The sleep of this night deepens because I have walked coatless from the house carrying the white envelope. All night it will say one name in its little tin house by the roadside. I have raised the metal flag so its shadow under the roadlamp leaves an imprint on the rain-heavy bushes. Now I will walk back thinking of the few lights still on in the town a mile away. In the yellowed light of a kitchen the millworker has finished his coffee, his wife has laid out the white slices of bread on the counter. Now while the bed they have left is still warm, I will think of you, you who are so far away you have caused me to look up at the stars. Tonight they have not moved from childhood, those games played after dark. Again I walk into the wet grass toward the starry voices. Again, I am the found one, intimate, returned by all I touch on the way.

Once upon a time there was a family. They were an ordinary family, living an ordinary life. Every day, they would get up and get ready for their day. They would have breakfast together and do fun things together.

The family beamed with joy every day. They always acted kind to each other and behaved well. They would do nice things for each other and say kind things. They were always there to help each other.

One day, they decided to do something special. They decided to go to the beach, so they all put on their swimming clothes and drove to the beach. They spent the day having fun together. They laughed and ran and splashed in the sea. That day was the best day ever!

When they got home, they all snuggled up on the sofa and watched a movie. They were all content and happy. That evening they ended with a family cuddle on the sofa - the perfect way to bring the day to an end. 

The family had a wonderful day, and recognised that behaving nicely to each other is the best way to have fun.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl. She loved to draw with her little pen. She drew pictures of little animals and flowers. Her mommy loved her drawings very much.

One day, the little girl lost her pen. She looked everywhere for it, but she couldn't find it. She loved her little pen very much. She was very sad.

The next day, the little girl found her pen. She was very happy. She drew a picture of her mommy and showed it to her. But then, the little girl accidentally dropped her pen and it broke. She was very sad again. Her mommy tried to fix it, but it was impossible. The little girl cried a lot. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved music and he loved to play his trumpet. He would play his trumpet every day and he would feel so happy. One day, Timmy went to the park and he saw a big rock. The rock was very big and Timmy wanted to climb it. He climbed the rock and he played his trumpet on top of it. He was so enthusiastic and he played his trumpet very loud. Everyone in the park could hear Timmy's trumpet and they loved it. Timmy felt so happy on top of the rock playing his trumpet.

I never turned anyone into a pig. Some people are pigs; I make them Look like pigs. I'm sick of your world That lets the outside disguise the inside. Your men weren't bad men; Undisciplined life Did that to them. As pigs, Under the care of Me and my ladies, they Sweetened right up. Then I reversed the spell, showing you my goodness As well as my power. I saw We could be happy here, As men and women are When their needs are simple. In the same breath, I foresaw your departure, Your men with my help braving The crying and pounding sea. You think A few tears upset me? My friend, Every sorceress is A pragmatist at heart; nobody sees essence who can't Face limitation. If I wanted only to hold you I could hold you prisoner.

Mommy was impatient. She kept pointing to the big pretty world. She showed little brother the big buildings, the trees, the sky and the clouds. He liked to watch the cars go by. 

Mommy kept pointing, but he did not understand. He squinted and looked around, but he still could not understand. Was Mommy trying to tell him something? 

Mommy pointed to a bird in a tree. Little brother smiled and laughed; he finally understood what Mommy had been trying to show him. He was excited to discover new things in the world. He smiled at Mommy and hugged her tight. 

Mommy laughed and hugged him back. She was happy that he finally understood. She knew he had a lot to learn about the world, and she would keep pointing things out to him so he could understand.

Anna and Ben were playing with chalk on the sidewalk. They liked to draw shapes and animals and write their names. Anna drew a big heart and wrote "Anna loves Ben" inside it. Ben smiled and drew a star and wrote "Ben loves Anna" next to it.

"Look, we made a love picture!" Anna said, excited.

"Yes, we did! It's very pretty!" Ben said, excited too.

They hugged and kissed each other on the cheek. They were very happy.

But then, a big boy came and saw their picture. He was mean and rude. He stepped on their picture and rubbed it with his shoe. He laughed and said "Ha ha, you are silly! You can't love each other, you are too small!"

Anna and Ben felt very sad and angry. They wanted to cry. They felt uncomfortable.

"Go away, you are bad!" Anna shouted.

"Yeah, go away, you are mean!" Ben shouted.

They picked up their chalk and threw it at the big boy. The chalk hit him on the head and the nose and the arm. He felt pain and surprise. He stopped laughing and started crying.

"Ow, ow, ow! You hurt me! Stop it, stop it!" he cried.

He ran away, scared and sorry.

Anna and Ben looked at each other and smiled. They felt better. They hugged and kissed each other again. They were very brave.

They decided to draw a new picture with their chalk. They drew a rainbow and wrote "Anna and Ben are happy" under it. They were very happy.

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to play outside. One day, they found a hidden motorcycle in the bushes near their house. It was big and shiny and had two wheels.

"Wow, look at this!" Tom said. "Can we ride it?"

"I don't know," Lily said. "It's not ours. Maybe someone is looking for it."

Tom did not care. He wanted to have fun. He climbed on the motorcycle and pushed a button. It made a loud noise and started to move.

"Tom, stop!" Lily shouted. "It's dangerous!"

But Tom did not listen. He drove the motorcycle on the road, where there were many cars and trucks. He felt happy and fast.

Lily ran after him, but she could not catch up. She was scared and sad. She did not want Tom to get hurt.

Then, she saw a police car with a siren and a light. It was following Tom. It wanted him to stop.

"Tom, please stop!" Lily cried. "The police are here!"

Tom heard Lily and the police. He felt scared and sorry. He did not want to get in trouble. He slowed down and stopped the motorcycle. He got off and waited for the police.

The police officer came and talked to Tom. He was not angry, but he was serious. He told Tom that he did something wrong. He took someone else's motorcycle without asking. He drove it on the road without a helmet or a license. He put himself and others in danger.

Tom felt ashamed and sad. He said he was sorry. He did not mean to do anything bad. He just wanted to have fun.

The police officer nodded and smiled. He said he understood. He said he was glad that Tom was safe and that he stopped. He said he would take the motorcycle back to its owner. He said he would not punish Tom, but he would talk to his parents.

Tom thanked the police officer. He hugged Lily and said he was sorry to her too. He said he would not do it again. He said he learned his lesson.

Lily hugged him back and said she forgave him. She said she loved him. She said they would go home and play with their own toys.

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside and explore. One day, he found a cool box in the woods. He picked it up and shook it, but he couldn't figure out what was inside. 

Timmy's friend Billy came over and asked, "What's in the box, Timmy?" 

"I don't know," Timmy replied. "It's a mystery." 

Billy suggested they open the box together. They turned the box over and over, trying to find a way to open it. Finally, they found a latch and the box opened. 

But inside the box was not something cool or fun. It was a big spider! Timmy and Billy were scared and ran away. 

From that day on, Timmy never picked up mysterious boxes again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, her mom asked her what she wanted for breakfast. Lily thought for a moment and then said, "I choose pancakes, please." 

Her mom smiled and got out a pan to make pancakes. While her mom was cooking, Lily had a thoughtful idea. "Mommy, can we make pancakes for our neighbors too?" 

Her mom thought it was a great idea and they made extra pancakes to share with their neighbors. When they brought the pancakes over, their neighbors were very happy and said thank you. Lily felt proud of her choice and her thoughtful idea to share with others.

Lily liked to make hats. She used paper, glue, and things she found in the park. She made hats with leaves, flowers, feathers, and stones. She thought her hats were interesting and pretty.

One day, she wanted to show her hats to her friends. She put on her favorite hat, the one with the big red flower, and went to the playground. She saw Ben, Mia, and Sam playing with a ball. She ran to them and said, "Look at my hat! Do you like it?"

Ben, Mia, and Sam looked at her hat. They did not like it. They thought it was silly and ugly. They laughed at Lily and said mean things. "Your hat is stupid! It looks like a trash can! You are a baby who plays with paper!" They said.

Lily felt sad and angry. She wanted her friends to like her hats and encourage her. She did not want them to be mean and rude. She said, "My hat is not stupid! It is interesting and pretty! You are mean and rude! You are not my friends!" She said.

She turned around and ran away. She wanted to go home and make more hats. But as she ran, she did not see a big rock on the ground. She tripped and fell. Her hat flew off her head and landed on a puddle. The paper got wet and the flower fell off. Her hat was ruined.

Lily cried. She hurt her knee and her hat. She wished she had nice friends who liked her hats and encouraged her. She felt lonely and sad. She did not want to make hats anymore. She had a bad day.

Once upon a time, there lived a selfish soldier. He never thought of anyone but himself, and never bothered to behave. He always got what he wanted and was quite selfish.

Everyone was so scared. The army marched closer and closer, and the soldier was sure they were going to defeat him. But then, seemingly from nowhere, a great and powerful warrior appeared. He had a shield and a sword and was a very brave soldier.

After that, the soldier remembered his duties and started behaving better. He learnt from his mistake that it was so important to be kind to others and to think of others before being selfish.

name_of_work: In the Reading-Room of the British Museum by Louise Imogen Guiney
content: Praised be the moon of books! that doth above A world of men, the fallen Past behold, And fill the spaces else so void and cold To make a very heaven again thereof; As when the sun is set behind a grove, And faintly unto nether ether rolled, All night his whiter image and his mould Grows beautiful with looking on her love. Thou therefore, moon of so divine a ray, Lend to our steps both fortitude and light! Feebly along a venerable way They climb the infinite, or perish quite; Nothing are days and deeds to such as they, While in this liberal house thy face is bright.

Back out of all this now too much for us, Back in a time made simple by the loss Of detail, burned, dissolved, and broken off Like graveyard marble sculpture in the weather, There is a house that is no more a house Upon a farm that is no more a farm And in a town that is no more a town. The road there, if you'll let a guide direct you Who only has at heart your getting lost, May seem as if it should have been a quarry-- Great monolithic knees the former town Long since gave up pretense of keeping covered. And there's a story in a book about it: Besides the wear of iron wagon wheels The ledges show lines ruled southeast northwest, The chisel work of an enormous Glacier That braced his feet against the Arctic Pole. You must not mind a certain coolness from him Still said to haunt this side of Panther Mountain. Nor need you mind the serial ordeal Of being watched from forty cellar holes As if by eye pairs out of forty firkins. As for the woods' excitement over you That sends light rustle rushes to their leaves, Charge that to upstart inexperience. Where were they all not twenty years ago? They think too much of having shaded out A few old pecker-fretted apple trees. Make yourself up a cheering song of how Someone's road home from work this once was, Who may be just ahead of you on foot Or creaking with a buggy load of grain. The height of the adventure is the height Of country where two village cultures faded Into each other. Both of them are lost. And if you're lost enough to find yourself By now, pull in your ladder road behind you And put a sign up CLOSED to all but me. Then make yourself at home. The only field Now left's no bigger than a harness gall. First there's the children's house of make believe, Some shattered dishes underneath a pine, The playthings in the playhouse of the children. Weep for what little things could make them glad. Then for the house that is no more a house, But only a belilaced cellar hole, Now slowly closing like a dent in dough. This was no playhouse but a house in earnest. Your destination and your destiny's A brook that was the water of the house, Cold as a spring as yet so near its source, Too lofty and original to rage. (We know the valley streams that when aroused Will leave their tatters hung on barb and thorn.) I have kept hidden in the instep arch Of an old cedar at the waterside A broken drinking goblet like the Grail Under a spell so the wrong ones can't find it, So can't get saved, as Saint Mark says they mustn't. (I stole the goblet from the children's playhouse.) Here are your waters and your watering place. Drink and be whole again beyond confusion.

name_of_work: Sheltered Garden by H. D. (Hilda Doolittle)
content: have had enough. I gasp for breath. Every way ends, every road, every foot-path leads at last to the hill-crest-- then you retrace your steps, or find the same slope on the other side, precipitate. I have had enough-- border-pinks, clove-pinks, wax-lilies, herbs, sweet-cress. O for some sharp swish of a branch-- there is no scent of resin in this place, no taste of bark, of coarse weeds, aromatic, astringent-- only border on border of scented pinks. Have you seen fruit under cover that wanted light-- pears wadded in cloth, protected from the frost, melons, almost ripe, smothered in straw? Why not let the pears cling to the empty branch? All your coaxing will only make a bitter fruit-- let them cling, ripen of themselves, test their own worth, nipped, shrivelled by the frost, to fall at last but fair with a russet coat. Or the melon-- let it bleach yellow in the winter light, even tart to the taste-- it is better to taste of frost-- the exquisite frost-- than of wadding and of dead grass. For this beauty, beauty without strength, chokes out life. I want wind to break, scatter these pink-stalks, snap off their spiced heads, fling them about with dead leaves-- spread the paths with twigs, limbs broken off, trail great pine branches, hurled from some far wood right across the melon-patch, break pear and quince-- leave half-trees, torn, twisted but showing the fight was valiant. O to blot out this garden to forget, to find a new beauty in some terrible wind-tortured place.
