Once upon a time there were two friends named Max and Rebecca. One day they wanted to go on an adventure. They picked up their backpacks and took off into the woods. 

As they walked, Rebecca heard a loud noise. She was a bit fearful because the noise sounded like a growl. "Do you hear that?" she asked Max. 

Max replied, "Yes! It is coming from over there, let's go see what it is." The two friends ventured closer to the sound, and could see that it was coming from a big orange pumpkin. 

"Hello pumpkin! What are you doing?" Rebecca asked. The pumpkin opened its eyes, and replied in a gentle voice, "I am singing." Then it closed its eyes and started singing again. 

Max and Rebecca were so surprised and happy. They laughed, and sang with the pumpkin. The two friends thanked the pumpkin and left happily. They learned on their adventure that no matter how scary something may seem, it could be a pleasant surprise.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tom. He loved to pick flowers for his mom. One day, he saw some new equipment in the garden. It was a big, shiny, and fragile vase. Tom thought it would be perfect for the flowers he picked.

Tom went to his mom and said, "Mom, can I use the new equipment for the flowers?" His mom said, "Yes, Tom, but be careful. It is very fragile and can break easily." Tom was very excited and promised to be careful.

Tom picked the most beautiful flowers he could find and put them in the fragile vase. But he was so excited that he didn't see a big rock in the garden. He tripped and the vase fell and broke. Tom was sad and his mom came to help. She said, "It's okay, Tom. Remember, we should always be careful with fragile things." Tom learned his lesson and from then on, he was always careful with fragile things. The moral of the story is to always be careful with the things that can break easily.

After the wideawake galaxies Each dawn is glass. Leavings of the night's kill lie, Twig-bones, ice feathers, The ghost of starlight. Ewes breathe silver. The rose won't come-- Stopped in her tracks. Everything's particular: Bramble's freehand, A leaf caught out, The lawn's journal. Deep down even the water-table Stiffens its linen, And horizons pleat in a bucket. The stars burn out To starved birds Watching my window, And one leaf puts up a hand Against infinite light.

Coming home is terrible whether the dogs lick your face or not; whether you have a wife or just a wife-shaped loneliness waiting for you. Coming home is terribly lonely, so that you think of the oppressive barometric pressure back where you have just come from with fondness, because everything's worse once you're home. You think of the vermin clinging to the grass stalks, long hours on the road, roadside assistance and ice creams, and the peculiar shapes of certain clouds and silences with longing because you did not want to return. Coming home is just awful. And the home-style silences and clouds contribute to nothing but the general malaise. Clouds, such as they are, are in fact suspect, and made from a different material than those you left behind. You yourself were cut from a different cloudy cloth, returned, remaindered, ill-met by moonlight, unhappy to be back, slack in all the wrong spots, seamy suit of clothes dishrag-ratty, worn. You return home moon-landed, foreign; the Earth's gravitational pull an effort now redoubled, dragging your shoelaces loose and your shoulders etching deeper the stanza of worry on your forehead. You return home deepened, a parched well linked to tomorrow by a frail strand of... Anyway... You sigh into the onslaught of identical days. One might as well, at a time... Well... Anyway... You're back. The sun goes up and down like a tired whore, the weather immobile like a broken limb while you just keep getting older. Nothing moves but the shifting tides of salt in your body. Your vision blears. You carry your weather with you, the big blue whale, a skeletal darkness. You come back with X-ray vision. Your eyes have become a hunger. You come home with your mutant gifts to a house of bone. Everything you see now, all of it: bone.

Once upon a time, there was a little goat. The goat was very organized. He liked to keep all his things in the right place. He had a small house where he lived.

One day, the goat wanted to find new friends. So, he started to crawl under a big fence. On the other side, he saw a big green field with many animals. There were cows, sheep, and horses.

The goat played with his new friends all day. They had so much fun! In the evening, the goat crawled back under the fence to his small house. He was happy to have new friends and still be organized in his home.

Granted, we die for good. Life, then, is largely a thing Of happens to like, not should. And that, too, granted, why Do I happen to like red bush, Grey grass and green-gray sky? What else remains? But red, Gray, green, why those of all? That is not what I said: Not those of all. But those. One likes what one happens to like. One likes the way red grows. It cannot matter at all. Happens to like is one Of the ways things happen to fall.

One sunny day, Tom was very happy because he was going to go for a jog. He put on his running shoes and headed outside. Tom was jogging around the park when he saw a worry. He stopped and looked at it. It was a fake worry, made out of a stone. Tom thought that this was funny. He picked up the worry and decided to take it home with him. As he jogged home, Tom smiled because he was happy to have a unique worry of his own.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toy cars and trucks. One day, he saw a big machine in his backyard. The machine was very confusing to Timmy. He didn't know what it did or why it was there.

Timmy's mom came outside and saw him looking at the machine. "What's wrong, Timmy?" she asked. "I'm confused," Timmy said. "What is this machine?" His mom explained that it was a lawnmower and it was used to cut the grass.

Timmy watched as his mom started the lawnmower and stood behind it. "Look, Timmy," she said. "I'm standing behind the machine." Timmy smiled and watched as his mom cut the grass. From that day on, Timmy wasn't confused about the lawnmower anymore.

Once upon a time there was a brave police. He liked to learn new things. He studied every day so he could help people in the village.

One day, he decided to visit a big city. He had never been there before. He went to explore but he did not remember the way home. He was lost and could not find his way back.

He tried to ask people for help but nobody would help him. Nobody wanted to talk to the police. They were too scared.

The brave police never returned home. He was lost in the big city forever. Nobody ever learned of his brave deeds. The police was never seen again.

One day, Mommy saw a wild ant. Mommy wanted to take a closer look, so she slowly closed her eyes. She heard a little scurry, and when she opened her eyes, the wild ant was gone! Mommy looked around for the wild ant for a few minutes, but there was no sign of it.

Mommy was so sad that she missed her chance to see the wild ant up close. But then something amazing happened. Another wild ant scurried across the floor! Mommy quickly closed her eyes again. When she opened them, she saw the wild ant running along the wall. She was so happy!

Mommy watched the wild ant for a few minutes as it ran and scurried around the room. It was so interesting. Then, the wild ant disappeared into a small crack in the wall. Mommy was sad to see the wild ant go, but so thankful she got to watch it up close.

As fast as thou shalt wane, so fast thou grow'st In one of thine, from that which thou departest; And that fresh blood which youngly thou bestow'st, Thou mayst call thine when thou from youth convertest. Herein lives wisdom, beauty, and increase; Without this folly, age, and cold decay: If all were minded so, the times should cease And threescore year would make the world away. Let those whom nature hath not made for store, Harsh, featureless, and rude, barrenly perish: Look whom she best endowed, she gave the more; Which bounteous gift thou shouldst in bounty cherish: She carved thee for her seal, and meant thereby, Thou shouldst print more, not let that copy die.

Lily liked to play in the garage with her dad. He had many tools and things that he used to fix cars and bikes. Lily wanted to help him, but he said some tools were not for kids. He gave her a small hammer and some nails and said she could make something with them.

Lily found a piece of wood and some old buttons. She hammered the buttons on the wood and made a face. She thought it was very cute. She showed it to her dad and said, "Look, I made a friend!"

Her dad smiled and said, "That's very nice, Lily. You are very creative. I value your work."

Lily felt happy and proud. She asked her dad, "Can I keep it?"

Her dad said, "Of course, you can. It's yours. You can put it in your room or wherever you like."

Lily hugged her dad and said, "Thank you, dad. I love you."

Her dad hugged her back and said, "I love you too, Lily. You are my best friend."

name_of_work: Sonnet 29 - 'I think of thee!' by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: I think of thee!--my thoughts do twine and bud About thee, as wild vines, about a tree, Put out broad leaves, and soon there 's nought to see Except the straggling green which hides the wood. Yet, O my palm-tree, be it understood I will not have my thoughts instead of thee Who art dearer, better! Rather, instantly Renew thy presence; as a strong tree should, Rustle thy boughs and set thy trunk all bare, And let these bands of greenery which insphere thee Drop heavily down,--burst, shattered, everywhere! Because, in this deep joy to see and hear thee And breathe within thy shadow a new air, I do not think of thee--I am too near thee.

name_of_work: A Poor Christian Looks at the Ghetto by Czeslaw Milosz
content: Bees build around red liver, Ants build around black bone. It has begun: the tearing, the trampling on silks, It has begun: the breaking of glass, wood, copper, nickel, silver, foam Of gypsum, iron sheets, violin strings, trumpets, leaves, *****, crystals. ****! Phosphorescent fire from yellow walls Engulfs animal and human hair. Bees build around the honeycomb of lungs, Ants build around white bone. Torn is paper, rubber, linen, leather, flax, Fiber, fabrics, cellulose, snakeskin, wire. The roof and the wall collapse in flame and heat seizes the foundations. Now there is only the earth, sandy, trodden down, With one leafless tree. Slowly, boring a tunnel, a guardian mole makes his way, With a small red lamp fastened to his forehead. He touches buried bodies, counts them, pushes on, He distinguishes human ashes by their luminous vapor, The ashes of each man by a different part of the spectrum. Bees build around a red trace. Ants build around the place left by my body. I am afraid, so afraid of the guardian mole. He has swollen eyelids, like a Patriarch Who has sat much in the light of candles Reading the great book of the species. What will I tell him, I, a Jew of the New Testament, Waiting two thousand years for the second coming of Jesus? My broken body will deliver me to his sight And he will count me among the helpers of death: The uncircumcised.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a shiny penny that she loved to play with. One day, she went to the park to play with her penny. While she was playing, she heard a loud noise. She looked around and saw a big dog barking loudly. 

Lily was scared and didn't know what to do. She started to cry. A kind lady saw her crying and came over to help. "Don't worry, I'll call your mommy," said the lady. She took out her phone and called Lily's mommy. 

Soon enough, Lily's mommy arrived and hugged her tightly. "Thank you for calling me," said Lily's mommy to the kind lady. From that day on, Lily never forgot her penny and always remembered to be careful around loud noises.

One day, a girl named Lily found a silver rock. She felt very lucky. She took the rock home and showed it to her mom. "Look, Mom! I found a silver rock!" she said. Her mom was happy for her. 

The next day, Lily took the silver rock to the park. She wanted to surprise her best friend, Tim. When she showed the rock to Tim, he said, "Wow! That's a cool rock, Lily!" Tim and Lily played with the silver rock all day.

At the end of the day, Lily and Tim decided to hide the silver rock in the park. They wanted to surprise another kid who might find it. They felt lucky to have found the silver rock and wanted to share their luck.

Once upon a time, there was an old dog named Max. Max lived in a big house with his family. One day, Max's friend, a little bird, came to visit him. 

"Hi Max, how are you?" asked the little bird.

"I'm good, but I don't understand why my family is always busy on Tuesdays," replied Max.

"Well, maybe they have to work or go to school," said the little bird.

Max thought about it for a moment and then nodded his head. "I think I understand now. Thank you, my friend."

The little bird smiled and they spent the rest of the day playing together. Max was happy to have such a good friend who helped him understand things.

Once upon a time, there was a bear named Teddy. Teddy was very pretty with soft brown fur and big, round eyes. One day, Teddy met a little girl named Lily. Lily had an opinion that Teddy was the best bear ever. She hugged Teddy tightly and didn't want to let go.

Teddy was very happy to have a friend like Lily. They played together every day and had lots of fun. But one day, Lily had to move away to a faraway place. Teddy was sad and missed her very much. He wished she could come back and hug him again.

Days turned into weeks and weeks turned into months. Teddy waited and waited, but Lily never came back. He became very lonely and sad. One day, Teddy couldn't take it anymore and decided to go look for Lily.

He walked and walked until he was very tired. Finally, he found a big city with lots of people. But he couldn't find Lily anywhere. Teddy was lost and didn't know what to do. He missed Lily so much that he started to cry. Sadly, Teddy never found his friend Lily and he was alone forever.

Once upon a time, there was a smart dog named Max. Max loved to play and search for things in the park. One day, he saw a big cat. The cat was not nice. Max did not like the cat.

Max said to the cat, "You cannot be here. This is my park." The cat said, "I do not care. I will stay." Max was mad. He knew he had to fight the cat to make him go away. 

Max and the cat started to fight. They ran and jumped. Max was very smart. He knew how to win. At last, the cat ran away. Max was happy. The park was his again.

Once upon a time, there was a puppy. It was a small puppy and had brown fur. Every day it would remain in the garden. It loved to explore and play. 

The puppy would often find lots of things to explore in the garden. One day, it found a bitter tasting item. It didn't have a name but the puppy thought it tasted really bad. So, it decided to remain away from it. 

It was a good decision by the puppy, because it was a bee hive. If the puppy had gone near it, it would have been too close and the bees would have stung it. 

The puppy was happy to remain in its garden after this experience and it never forgot the bitter taste of the bee hive!

Once upon a time, a small boy named Bobby and his mommy were walking in the woods. 

Bobby looked around and saw something really big. It was a stable! He yelled out to his mommy, "Mommy, what's that big thing over there?" 

His mommy smiled and said, "That's a stable. It's a special place where people keep animals." 

Bobby got excited. He stretched out his arms as far as he could and said, "I want to go inside!"

Mommy said, "Let's go. But, we need to be careful because the animals need to rest regularly." 

Bobby nodded and followed his mommy into the stable. He saw cows, horses, and pigs. He was very excited and wanted to say hello to them all. 

Bobby waved at the animals and said, "Hello, friends! I'm Bobby, nice to meet you!"

Mommy laughed and said, "See, that wasn't so hard, was it? Now let's go home and let the animals get some regular rest." 

Bobby waved goodbye to the animals and followed his mommy out of the stable. Along the way home, Bobby was thinking about all the animals he had seen. He couldn't wait to come back and visit them again!

name_of_work: The Black Heralds by Cesar Vallejo
content: There are blows in life, so powerful... I don't know! Blows like God's hatred; as if before them, the undertow of everything suffered were to well up in the soul... I don't know! They're few; but they exist... They open dark furrows in the most ferocious face and the most powerful loins. Perhaps, they're the wooden horses of barbaric Attilas, or black messengers that Death sends to us. They're profound lapses of the soul's Christs, of some adorable faith that Destiny blasphemes. Those bloodthirsty blows are the cracklings of some bread that in the oven's door burns up on us. And man... Poor...poor man! He turns his eyes, as when a slap on the shoulder calls us by name; he turns his crazed eyes, and everything he's lived wells up, like a pool of guilt, in his gaze. There are blows in life, so powerful... I don't know!

Once upon a time there was a Dad and his daughter. The Dad wanted to give his daughter the best things in life. So every day, he made sure to choose things with care.

One day, the Dad said to his daughter, "Let's go to the park. You can choose whatever you want to do." His daughter was excited. She thought about the things she could do. She decided to choose to play on the swings.

The Dad watched his daughter carefully when she went to the swings. He gave her a push and she was so happy. As she swung higher and higher, the Dad couldn't help but smile.

Finally the Dad said, "Time to go home. Let's choose something else to do tomorrow!" His daughter smiled and said, "Yay!"

The Dad and his daughter walked home, holding hands and feeling happy. They chose to be together every day, and that made them both very happy.

Black reapers with the sound of steel on stones Are sharpening scythes. I see them place the hones In their hip-pockets as a thing that's done, And start their silent swinging, one by one. Black horses drive a mower through the weeds, And there, a field rat, startled, squealing bleeds. His belly close to ground. I see the blade, Blood-stained, continue cutting weeds and shade.

This morning as I walked along the lake shore, I fell in love with a wren and later in the day with a mouse the cat had dropped under the dining room table. In the shadows of an autumn evening, I fell for a seamstress still at her machine in the tailor's window, and later for a bowl of broth, steam rising like smoke from a naval battle. This is the best kind of love, I thought, without recompense, without gifts, or unkind words, without suspicion, or silence on the telephone. The love of the chestnut, the jazz cap and one hand on the wheel. No lust, no slam of the door- the love of the miniature orange tree, the clean white shirt, the hot evening shower, the highway that cuts across Florida. No waiting, no huffiness, or rancor- just a twinge every now and then for the wren who had built her nest on a low branch overhanging the water and for the dead mouse, still dressed in its light brown suit. But my heart is always standing on its tripod, ready for the next arrow. After I carried the mouse by the tail to a pile of leaves in the woods, I found myself standing at the bathroom sink gazing down affectionately at the soap, so patient and soluble so at home in its pale green soap dish. I could feel myself falling again as I felt its turning in my wet hands and caught the scent of lavender and stone.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toys and make a big mess in his room. His mommy would always come in and say, "Timmy, please stop making such a messy room!"

One day, Timmy was playing with his favorite toy car when he accidentally knocked over a big pile of sheets. "Oh no!" Timmy cried. "What a messy sheet pile!"

His mommy came in and saw the big mess. "Timmy, we need to clean up this messy sheet pile," she said. "Can you help me?"

"Sure mommy, I'll help," Timmy said. Together, they picked up all the sheets and put them away. "Thanks for helping me clean up, Timmy," his mommy said.

"You're welcome, mommy," Timmy replied. "I don't want to make a messy room anymore." And from that day on, Timmy always tried to keep his room clean and tidy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and run around in the park. One day, Lily saw a butterfly and wondered where it came from. She asked her mom, but her mom didn't know either.

Lily decided to catch the butterfly so she could look at it up close. But it was difficult because the butterfly kept flying away. So, Lily asked her dad to help her. Together, they raised a net and caught the butterfly.

Lily was so happy to see the butterfly up close. She wondered what it ate and where it slept. Her dad told her that butterflies drink nectar from flowers and sleep on leaves. Lily was amazed and couldn't wait to learn more about butterflies.

Jimmy and his momma Poppy were walking in the forest. The big trees were so tall and the animals were fierce. 
Momma Poppy stopped and said "Close your eyes, Jimmy. It's time to sleep" So Jimmy closed his eyes and he fell fast asleep. 
But while he was sleeping, Momma Poppy was taken away by the fierce animals of the forest. Jimmy woke up and looked around, hoping to find Momma Poppy, but she was nowhere to be seen. 
He was all alone in the forest with only the fierce animals. Jimmy couldn't find Momma Poppy and he had to go home alone - this did not have a good ending!

Once upon a time, there was a train that went on a long trip. The train went on a big rail that was made of metal. The train had many cars and people inside them. They looked out of the windows and saw trees, houses, and animals. 

One day, a man came into one of the train cars. He was very rude and mean to everyone. He said mean words and did not say "please" or "thank you". The people on the train did not like the man because he was so rude. 

The people on the train tried to guess why the man was so rude. Maybe he had a bad day or maybe he was just not a nice person. They did not know for sure. But they decided to be kind to him anyway, hoping that it would make him feel better. And eventually, the man started to be nicer to them too.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to dance and twirl around in her pretty pink dress. One day, she found a cushion on the floor and decided to use it as a stage for her dance.

As she twirled and jumped, her little brother came in and wanted to play too. But he accidentally knocked over the cushion and Lily fell down. She was so upset that she started to cry.

Her brother felt bad and wanted to make her feel better. He found some shiny ribbons and tied them to the cushion. Then he put on some music and they danced together on the cushion.

Lily's tears turned into smiles and the dull moment turned into a fun one. From then on, Lily and her brother danced together on the cushion every day. The end.

Charlie was in school, feeling very miserable. Everyone was writing on the blackboard, but all Charlie wanted to do was shrug. He tried to tell the teacher, but she just shook her head and moved on. Charlie hung his head and slumped his shoulders. He knew he would never be able to write like the others.

But then, the teacher surprised everyone. She asked the class to draw something on the blackboard instead of writing. Suddenly, Charlie wasn't feeling so miserable anymore. He picked up the chalk and started drawing a happy picture of the sun and a smiley face.

When everyone was done drawing, the teacher looked around the blackboard. She nodded with approval and said that everyone had done a good job. Charlie smiled and sat up straight in his chair. For the first time, he felt proud of his drawing.

Tom and Jen are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big dog. The dog is black and has sharp teeth. The dog barks at them.

"Run, Jen, run!" Tom says. He is frightened of the dog. He runs away fast.

But Jen does not run. She stays still. She is not frightened of the dog. She knows how to work with dogs. She learned from her dad, who is a vet.

"Hello, dog," Jen says. She speaks softly. She holds out her hand. The dog sniffs her hand. Then the dog wags his tail. He likes Jen. He licks her face.

Tom comes back. He sees Jen and the dog. He is surprised.

"Jen, how did you do that?" Tom asks.

"I was nice to the dog," Jen says. "He was not mean. He was just scared. You have to work with dogs, not run from them."

Tom nods. He feels sorry for running away. He wants to be brave like Jen. He walks to the dog. He pets the dog. The dog wags his tail again.

Tom and Jen smile. They have a new friend. They learn that dogs are not bad. They learn that work and stay are better than run and hide. They learn to be kind and brave.

name_of_work: The Idea of Order at Key West by Wallace Stevens
content: She sang beyond the genius of the sea. The water never formed to mind or voice, Like a body wholly body, fluttering Its empty sleeves; and yet its mimic motion Made constant cry, caused constantly a cry, That was not ours although we understood, Inhuman, of the veritable ocean. The sea was not a mask. No more was she. The song and water were not medleyed sound Even if what she sang was what she heard, Since what she sang was uttered word by word. It may be that in all her phrases stirred The grinding water and the gasping wind; But it was she and not the sea we heard. For she was the maker of the song she sang. The ever-hooded, tragic-gestured sea Was merely a place by which she walked to sing. Whose spirit is this? we said, because we knew It was the spirit that we sought and knew That we should ask this often as she sang. If it was only the dark voice of the sea That rose, or even colored by many waves; If it was only the outer voice of sky And cloud, of the sunken coral water-walled, However clear, it would have been deep air, The heaving speech of air, a summer sound Repeated in a summer without end And sound alone. But it was more than that, More even than her voice, and ours, among The meaningless plungings of water and the wind, Theatrical distances, bronze shadows heaped On high horizons, mountainous atmospheres Of sky and sea. It was her voice that made The sky acutest at its vanishing. She measured to the hour its solitude. She was the single artificer of the world In which she sang. And when she sang, the sea, Whatever self it had, became the self That was her song, for she was the maker. Then we, As we beheld her striding there alone, Knew that there never was a world for her Except the one she sang and, singing, made. Ramon Fernandez, tell me, if you know, Why, when the singing ended and we turned Toward the town, tell why the glassy lights, The lights in the fishing boats at anchor there, As the night descended, tilting in the air, Mastered the night and portioned out the sea, Fixing emblazoned zones and fiery poles, Arranging, deepening, enchanting night. Oh! Blessed rage for order, pale Ramon, The maker's rage to order words of the sea, Words of the fragrant portals, dimly-starred, And of ourselves and of our origins, In ghostlier demarcations, keener sounds.

Billy was walking through the park in early morning. He heard the sound of a whistle and looked around to see where the sound was coming from. He saw a little green bird hopping from branch to branch, whistling away. Billy smiled, it was the prettiest sound he had ever heard. 

Billy couldn't help but whistle back at the bird. He was surprised when the bird flew down to his shoulder and perched there. He wondered what it wanted, so he asked it. 

"Do you want milk?" he asked the bird. 

The bird gave a little nod and flew away. Billy went to the nearby convenience store and got a carton of milk. When he returned to the park, he saw the bird and all its friends nestled beside it. 

Billy opened the milk carton and the birds were so excited! They all started chirping, hopping from branch to branch with happiness. The little green bird came up to Billy and kissed him on his cheek. It was the most amazing thing he had ever seen. 

When Billy looked around, he noticed that all the birds in the park were singing and whistling. He started to whistle with them and soon the park was filled with the most beautiful music. 

Billy had made a special friend that day and it was all because of the little green bird.

Once upon a time there was a very little girl. She was upset one day because her favourite toy had a broken wheel. She felt so sad that she started to weep.

Her mom saw that she was upset and tried to help. She put her arms around the little girl and said "There, there. Don't weep. Maybe we can fix the toy's wheel".

The little girl didn't feel any better. She kept on weeping. Then, mom thought of an idea. She said, "Let's get a new wheel for your toy!"

The little girl smiled and stopped weeping. Her mom took her to the store and they picked out a shiny new wheel for her toy.

The little girl was so happy. She hugged her mom and said, "Thank you for finding me a new wheel for my toy."

name_of_work: Crossing a City Highway by Yusef Komunyakaa
content: The city at 3 a.m. is an ungodly mask the approaching day hides behind & from, the coyote nosing forth, the muscles of something ahead, & a fiery blaze of eighteen-wheelers zoom out of the curved night trees, along the rim of absolute chance. A question hangs in the oily air. She knows he will follow her scent left in the poisoned grass & buzz of chainsaws, if he can unweave a circle of traps around the subdivision. For a breathy moment, she stops on the world's edge, & then quick as that masters the stars & again slips the noose & darts straight between sedans & SUVs. Don't try to hide from her kind of blues or the dead nomads who walked trails now paved by wanderlust, an epoch somewhere between tamed & wild. If it were Monday instead of Sunday the outcome may be different, but she's now in Central Park searching for a Seneca village among painted stones & shrubs, where she's never been, & lucky she hasn't forgotten how to jig & kill her way home.

Lily and Ben are twins. They like to play in the snow. They have red mittens to keep their hands warm. But one day, something bad happens. Lily loses one of her mittens in the snow.

Lily is sad. She does not want to play anymore. She says, "Where is my mitten? I need my mitten. It is cold." Ben tries to help her. He says, "Don't cry, Lily. We will find your mitten. Let's look for it together."

They look for the mitten in the snow. They make footprints and snowballs. They ask the snowman and the bird. But they cannot find the mitten. Lily is more sad. She says, "I want to go home. I don't like the snow. It is cold and mean."

Ben hugs her. He says, "I have an idea, Lily. Why don't we share my mittens? You can have one and I can have one. Then we can both be warm and happy." Lily smiles. She says, "Thank you, Ben. You are a good brother. I like your idea."

They share the mittens. They hold hands and walk home. They are warm and happy. They say, "We love the snow. It is fun and nice. And we love each other. We are twins."

Once upon a time, in a big forest, there was a small bird named Tim. Tim was scared of the unknown. He was too scared to rise high in the sky like his friends. Tim's friends would fly high and play in the sky, but Tim would only watch them from the ground.

One day, while Tim was on the ground, a big cat saw him. The cat wanted to catch Tim. Tim was scared and knew he had to rise high in the sky to be safe. But he was still scared of the unknown.

Tim closed his eyes and thought of his friends high in the sky. He knew he had to be brave. Tim took a deep breath and started to rise. He rose higher and higher until he was safe in the sky with his friends. Tim was happy and not scared of the unknown anymore.

name_of_work: As I Walked Out One Evening by W.H. Auden
content: As I walked out one evening, Walking down Bristol Street, The crowds upon the pavement Were fields of harvest wheat. And down by the brimming river I heard a lover sing Under an arch of the railway: 'Love has no ending. 'I'll love you, dear, I'll love you Till China and Africa meet, And the river jumps over the mountain And the salmon sing in the street, 'I'll love you till the ocean Is folded and hung up to dry And the seven stars go squawking Like geese about the sky. 'The years shall run like rabbits, For in my arms I hold The Flower of the Ages, And the first love of the world.' But all the clocks in the city Began to whirr and chime: 'O let not Time deceive you, You cannot conquer Time. 'In the burrows of the Nightmare Where Justice naked is, Time watches from the shadow And coughs when you would kiss. 'In headaches and in worry Vaguely life leaks away, And Time will have his fancy To-morrow or to-day. 'Into many a green valley Drifts the appalling snow; Time breaks the threaded dances And the diver's brilliant bow. 'O plunge your hands in water, Plunge them in up to the wrist; Stare, stare in the basin And wonder what you've missed. 'The glacier knocks in the cupboard, The desert sighs in the bed, And the crack in the tea-cup opens A lane to the land of the dead. 'Where the beggars raffle the banknotes And the Giant is enchanting to Jack, And the Lily-white Boy is a Roarer, And Jill goes down on her back. 'O look, look in the mirror, O look in your distress: Life remains a blessing Although you cannot bless. 'O stand, stand at the window As the tears scald and start; You shall love your crooked neighbour With your crooked heart.' It was late, late in the evening, The lovers they were gone; The clocks had ceased their chiming, And the deep river ran on.

Once upon a time there was a selfish bear. He never wanted to share his things, even with his friends. One day, he was running around looking for something to cover up when he stumbled upon a big clock. 

He stopped and looked at the clock. â€œThat looks like something I can useâ€, he thought. He quickly grabbed the clock and began to cover it in a blanket. 

Just then, he heard a voice from behind him. â€œWhat are you doing? That clock belongs to me!â€ It was his friend, the rabbit. 

The bear tried to cover up the rabbit's words. â€œNo, this clock is mine!â€ 

The rabbit shook her head. â€œNo, it's not. You're so selfish. I was looking for this clock and you just had to grab it!â€ 

The bear sighed. He realized his mistake and unwrapped the clock. He handed it to the rabbit. â€œSorry about that. Can I help you find something else to cover?â€ 

The rabbit smiled. â€œThat would be nice!â€ 

From then on, the bear always shared his things with his friends.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and sing songs. One day, Lily's mommy gave her a glass of milk to drink. Lily was very careful and held the glass with both hands. But then, the glass fell and broke into many pieces. 

Lily was sad because she loved that glass, but her mommy told her not to worry. She said they would clean up the broken glass together and make sure it was safe. They put on gloves and picked up all the pieces, and then they vacuumed the floor. 

After they were finished, Lily's mommy gave her a big hug and told her she was proud of her for being so careful. Lily felt happy again, and she knew that even if things fall and break, her mommy would always keep her safe.

Once upon a time, there was a wide field. And in the middle of the field was a little kitten.

The kitten wanted to perform in the field. So it hopped and jumped around the wide field. It was so happy, it sang and laughed.

The sun went down and the kitten went to sleep. At night, the stars twinkled and the moon shone so bright. The kitten was happy to perform in the wide field.

The next morning, the kitten jumped out of bed. It couldn't wait to perform in the wide field once again. Jumping, hopping and singing, the kitten had a wonderful time. 

The kitten and the wide field became the best of friends. They were always happy to be together and they had lots of fun.

Once there were two friends, a bear and a bird. The two of them were very polite to each other and liked to play together. One day the bear found a piece of plastic. He remembered that a few days ago, they had made a boat out of plastic and decided to show the bird.

The bear brought the plastic to the bird and said, â€œLetâ€™s make another boat out of plastic!â€ But the bird didnâ€™t want to, saying that it was too much work. The bear was upset and asked why the bird was being so mean.

The bird was confused and apologized for being so rude. The bear said, â€œItâ€™s ok, I just wanted us to have fun together. Can we try making the boat?â€

The bird was relieved and the two friends made the boat out of the plastic, speaking politely to each other the entire time. They had a lot of fun playing with the boat and decided to remember it forever!

Sara and Ben were twins who loved Christmas. They liked to help their mom and dad decorate the tree with lights and ornaments. Ornaments were shiny things that hung on the tree and made it look pretty.

One day, Sara and Ben found a box of ornaments in the closet. They wanted to play with them and make their own tree. They took the box to their room and opened it. They saw many ornaments of different shapes and colors. They were very happy.

They started to hang the ornaments on their bed, their dresser, their lamp, and their toys. They thought it was fun and they laughed. They did not hear their mom calling them for dinner.

"Sara, Ben, hurry up! It's time to eat!" their mom said. She went to their room and saw the mess. She was very angry. "What have you done? These ornaments are not toys! They are fragile and expensive! You could have broken them or hurt yourself! And you did not listen to me!"

Sara and Ben felt bad. They knew they did something wrong. They said sorry to their mom. They helped her put the ornaments back in the box and clean their room. They learned that they should not play with things that are not theirs and that they should obey their mom. They also learned that some things are difficult to fix if they are broken. They hugged their mom and said they loved her. Their mom forgave them and hugged them back. She said she loved them too. They went to have dinner and enjoy their real tree.

Ben was a little boy who liked to play with his toys. He had a yellow car, a yellow ball and a yellow hat. He liked yellow because it was bright and happy.

One morning, Ben woke up and felt a need to go to the toilet. He got out of his bed and walked to the bathroom. He opened the door and saw a big surprise. The toilet was full of yellow water!

Ben was scared and confused. He did not know why the toilet was yellow. He wondered if someone had put his toys in the toilet. He looked around and saw his yellow car, his yellow ball and his yellow hat on the floor. They were not in the toilet.

He heard a noise from the toilet. It was a loud flush. The yellow water started to rise and spill over the edge. Ben ran out of the bathroom and shouted for his mom.

Mom came and saw the mess. She was not happy. She asked Ben what happened. Ben told her he did not know. He said he only wanted to go to the toilet.

Mom looked at the toilet and saw a sticker on the tank. It said "Do not use. Toilet dye test in progress." She realized that the plumber had been there the day before and had put a yellow dye in the toilet to check for leaks. She forgot to tell Ben.

She explained to Ben that the toilet was not broken and that the yellow water was not dirty. She said it was just a test and that it would go away soon. She cleaned up the bathroom and hugged Ben. She told him he was a good boy and that he did nothing wrong.

Ben felt better and smiled. He said he was sorry for the mess. He asked if he could still play with his yellow toys. Mom said yes and gave him a kiss. Ben went to his room and played with his yellow car, his yellow ball and his yellow hat. He liked yellow because it was bright and happy.

Sam and Mia are twins. They like to play with their toys and books. Sometimes they share, but sometimes they fight. One day, they find a big book with many pictures. The book is about history. History is what happened a long time ago, before they were born.

"Look, Mia, this is a castle. It has many towers and walls. I want to be a king," Sam says. He points to a picture of a castle.

"No, Sam, I want to be a queen. You can be a knight. Knights have horses and swords. They are brave and strong," Mia says. She points to a picture of a knight.

"But I want to be a king. Kings have crowns and thrones. They are the bosses of everyone," Sam says. He tries to take the book from Mia.

"Let go, Sam. It is my turn to look at the book. You had it before," Mia says. She pulls the book from Sam.

Sam gets angry. He pinches Mia's arm. Mia cries out. She pinches Sam's cheek. Sam yells. They both start to pinch each other.

"Stop, stop, stop!" their mom says. She hears the noise and comes to the room. She sees Sam and Mia pinching and crying. She takes the book from them. She puts it on a high shelf. "This book is not for you. It is for grown-ups. It is about history. History is distant. It is not here and now. You are here and now. You are twins. You should love and help each other, not pinch and hurt each other."

Sam and Mia feel sorry. They say sorry to each other. They hug and kiss. They say sorry to their mom. They ask for the book back.

"Maybe when you are older, you can look at the book again. But for now, you can play with your other toys and books. They are more fun and colorful. They are for you. They are not distant. They are here and now," their mom says. She gives them each a toy and a book. She smiles and kisses them.

Sam and Mia smile and kiss their mom. They play with their toys and books. They do not fight. They do not pinch. They are happy. They are twins. They are here and now.

Once upon a time, there was a very polite kid named Tom. Tom was three years old and wanted to do something nice to show how much he loved his family. So, he asked his mom if he could go outside and pick flowers to give as a gift. 

Tom's mom smiled and said, "Yes, I'll permit you to do that." Tom was so happy and excited he ran outside to pick the prettiest flowers he could find. 

Tom came back with a basket full of colorful, sweet-smelling flowers. His mom, dad, and siblings said "wow!" when they saw them. They thanked Tom for being so thoughtful and giving such a lovely gift. 

Tom was really proud and happy to have made his family so happy. He knew that doing something polite, like picking flowers to give away as a gift, was always a really special thing to do.

Once upon a time, there was a fast and friendly dove named Tony. Tony had been flying around most of the day, hoping to find some friends. Finally, Tony saw a cute little girl with long blonde hair, and he decided to land on her shoulder. The girl was overjoyed to meet Tony, and the two of them quickly became friends.

The girl and Tony began to chat, and Tony told her all about his fun adventures. Tony then asked the girl if she wanted to fly around with him. The girl smiled and said yes! The two of them quickly took off into the sky, exploring all the beautiful sights that the day had to offer.

Unfortunately, as soon as the girl and Tony started to get to know each other better, a fierce bird of prey came soaring from out of nowhere. The bird was fast, and it was aiming straight for Tony. The little girl was scared, but she grabbed Tony and held him tightly, hoping she could protect him.

The little girl yelled and bravely jumped in front of Tony. The bird paused, then turned around and disappeared into the clouds. The girl had been brave and Tony was safe.

The girl hugged Tony and thanked him for being brave. Tony smiled, and they both flew off, hoping they would never have to face danger again.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Penelope. She was just three years old. Every day she went to the park with her mom to play.

Today was different though, as today she found a journal in the park. It was green and looked very old. Penelope was very excited and started to open it.

When her mom saw Penelope with the journal, she smiled and said, â€œIf you finish that journal, I will get you a special present.â€ Penelope smiled and hugged the journal tight.

Penelope went home that day and set to work on her journal. Every night, she would finish a page or two. Eventually, she finished the whole journal.

When Penelope told her mom she had finished the journal, her mom ran to the store and bought Penelope a beautiful new dress. Penelope was so happy she hugged her mom tight.

The end.

Once upon a time there lived a little boy, Kevin. He was three years old and he wanted to be independent. One sunny day his mom suggested he try to manage on his own. But Kevin was afraid that he wouldn't be able to do it. 

"Mom, I don't think I can manage," Kevin told his mom. 

"Oh come on, it won't be that difficult," his mom said, smiling. She showed him a spot in the garden that she wanted him to clean. 

"Okay, I'll try," Kevin said, determined. He worked hard, and eventually he managed to clean up the spot. 

The next day, his mom suggested he try again. But this time the spot was twice as big. He was worried he wouldn't be able to do it. 

But Kevin remembered how he managed the day before and he refused to give up. He worked hard and eventually he managed to clean the spot again. Kevin felt proud of himself for being independent and managing on his own.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl. She had a bright creative mind and she loved to explore. One day she had a great idea - to make a raft!

First, the little girl gathered twigs and leaves. Then she tied them together with a strong rope she found. Soon, she had made a raft!

The little girl was so excited. She put on her life jacket and paddled her raft around the lake. She laughed as the breeze blew on her face.

The little girl was feeling so happy as she sailed across the water. She sang songs and waved to the people on shore.

It was the best day ever! She felt so creative and proud of her raft.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who was very curious. One day she decided to explore the big, tall tree in her backyard. She began to climb and climb until she reached the very top.

Suddenly, she noticed a shiny box. It looked like a safe! She tried to open it but it wouldn't budge. She shook it and tugged it, but still nothing. She was so persistent that she kept tugging until suddenly it opened and inside she saw something magical.

The little girl was so excited that she almost forgot what kind of box it was. Suddenly, a sparkle shot out of the box and before she knew it, the sparkle had vanished! The little girl was sad, but then she remembered the safe and decided to look inside it again. 

She was delighted to find that the magic sparkle had reappeared! This time, it stayed put and the little girl gladly closed the safe, so the tiny sparkle would remain safe. The persistent little girl had made sure that the magical sparkle would stay protected and hidden away in the safe.

name_of_work: Sound and Sense by Alexander Pope
content: True ease in writing comes from art, not chance, As those move easiest who have learned to dance. 'Tis not enough no harshness gives offense, The sound must seem an echo to the sense: Soft is the strain when Zephyr gently blows, And the smooth stream in smoother numbers flows; But when loud surges lash the sounding shore, The hoarse, rough verse should like the torrent roar; When Ajax strives some rock's vast weight to throw, The line too labors, and the words move slow; Not so, when swift Camilla scours the plain, Flies o'er the unbending corn, and skims along the main. Hear how Timotheus' varied lays surprise, And bid alternate passions fall and rise!

Two shall be born the whole world wide apart, And speak in different tongues, and pay their debts In different kinds of coin; and give no heed Each to the other's being. And know not That each might suit the other to a T, If they were but correctly introduced. And these, unconsciously, shall bend their steps, Escaping Spaniards and defying war, Unerringly toward the same trysting-place, Albeit they know it not. Until at last They enter the same door, and suddenly They meet. And ere they've seen each other's face They fall into each other's arms, upon The Broadway cable car - and this is Fate!

Once upon a time there was a lazy dog who loved stretching. He would stretch his legs when he woke up in the morning and he would stretch them all day long. One day he decided to go on an adventure to find a special color. He set off on his trek and he stretched as he went. He saw many colors along the way but none of them were the perfect one. Suddenly after a long stretch, he spotted one color that was extra bright and sparkly. He hopped and stretched over to the color and he was so excited to find it. He rolled around in the special color and enjoyed it so much. He had found his perfect color and he took it back home with him. Now, each morning after his stretch, he looks at the special bright color to remind him of his adventure.

Once upon a time, in a small town, there lived a smart girl named Amy. She loved to play with her colorful rocks. These rocks were special because they were minerals.

One sunny day, Amy went outside to play with her best friend, Tom. They decided to scatter the minerals all over the ground and make a pretty picture. "Look, Tom! We made a rainbow with the rocks!" said Amy, pointing at their creation.

Tom laughed and said, "Yes, Amy! We are so smart to make a rainbow with minerals!" They smiled and played with the rocks all day long, knowing they shared a special bond.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the snow. One day, Lily went outside to play in the snow. She built a snowman and had so much fun. 

Suddenly, Lily saw a big dog running towards her. The dog wanted to play, but Lily was scared. She tried to run away, but the dog was too fast. 

Just when the dog was about to reach her, a modest man came and called the dog back. Lily was safe, and she thanked the man. From that day on, Lily made sure to always be careful when playing outside.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Daisy. Daisy was only 3 years old. She could already talk, but the words she uses were still very simple. One day as she was playing with her toys, her mother came and said,

"Daisy my love, it's time to study. Let's put your toys away."

Daisy looked at her mother with a sad face, "But Mama, I want to keep playing with my toys!"

But her mother knew that it was important to learn new things, so she said,

"Daisy, you can play with your toys again when you are done studying. Learning is good for you and makes you grow. There are so many different things you can study."

So Daisy reluctantly put her toys away and worked hard at her lessons. After she finished, she was so proud of herself for having finished them.

Daisy's mother smiled and said,

"See how much fun it is when you learn something new? Working hard and studying makes you feel good. It can be hard at times, but it's worth it! Different is good!"

Daisy was happy to hear these kind words and smiled. She understood that studying was important and that learning new things was even more fun than playing with her toys. From then on, she happily studied and kept learning new things. 

The end.

One day, Timmy was climbing a tall tree. He was happy and excited as he went higher and higher. Suddenly, he spotted something very delightful. In a nearby branch was a giant, juicy pear. He reached out to grab it and took a big bite.

When he climbed down from the tree, his mommy saw him. "Timmy, where did you get that delicious pear?" she asked. Timmy smiled and proudly said, "I climbed the tree and found it!" 

"Oh Timmy, I am very proud of you!" said his mommy happily. She explained to him that if he was patient and open to new opportunities, wonders would unfold around him.

From that day onwards, Timmy always climbed the tree in his backyard. And every time, he discovered new and wonderful things in the branches. It was a fun and calming experience for him, and it taught him a valuable lesson - that if one keeps his/her heart open, amazing discoveries await!

name_of_work: I'm a Fool to Love You by Cornelius Eady
content: Some folks will tell you the blues is a woman, Some type of supernatural creature. My mother would tell you, if she could, About her life with my father, A strange and sometimes cruel gentleman. She would tell you about the choices A young black woman faces. Is falling in with some man A deal with the devil In blue terms, the tongue we use When we don't want nuance To get in the way, When we need to talk straight. My mother chooses my father After choosing a man Who was, as we sing it, Of no account. This man made my father look good, That's how bad it was. He made my father seem like an island In the middle of a stormy sea, He made my father look like a rock. And is the blues the moment you realize You exist in a stacked deck, You look in a mirror at your young face, The face my sister carries, And you know it's the only leverage You've got. Does this create a hurt that whispers How you going to do? Is the blues the moment You shrug your shoulders And agree, a girl without money Is nothing, dust To be pushed around by any old breeze. Compared to this, My father seems, briefly, To be a fire escape. This is the way the blues works Its sorry wonders, Makes trouble look like A feather bed, Makes the wrong man's kisses A healing.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Emmy. She was so excited that it was a thunderstorm day! She had heard from her parents that lightning was very special.

When the lightning happened, Emmy watched outside the window and saw the most amazing sight. The sky was lit up with a colorful lightshow! The lightning made patterns of bright yellows, purples and reds.

Emmy shouted for joy and jumped around. She was so very excited. She laughed and laughed at the lightning and the colorful sky.

Suddenly, the thunderstorm was over. The sky was quiet and the lightning was gone. But Emmy still felt excited because of all the wonderful lightning she had seen.

Sam liked to teach his toys. He had many toys, but his favorite was a big tiger. The tiger was soft and great. Sam taught the tiger how to roar, how to jump, and how to play.

One day, Sam and his tiger went to the park. They saw other kids and their toys. Sam wanted to show them his tiger. He said, "Look at my tiger! He can roar, he can jump, he can play. He is the best toy ever!"

The other kids were not impressed. They said, "Your tiger is not real. He is just a toy. He cannot do anything. He is boring and silly."

Sam was angry and sad. He said, "No, you are wrong. My tiger is real. He can do everything. He is not boring and silly. He is great and smart. I will show you!"

Sam ran to the swings with his tiger. He put his tiger on a swing and pushed him hard. He said, "See? My tiger can swing. He is having fun. He is better than your toys."

But the tiger did not like the swing. He felt dizzy and scared. He wanted to get off. He roared, "Help! Help! I want to stop!"

Sam did not hear him. He pushed him harder and harder. He said, "Roar louder, tiger! Show them how great you are!"

The tiger roared louder and louder. He was not happy. He was angry and scared. He wanted to bite Sam. He said, "Stop! Stop! I want to bite you!"

But Sam did not hear him. He pushed him harder and harder. He said, "Jump higher, tiger! Show them how great you are!"

The tiger jumped higher and higher. He was not happy. He was angry and scared. He wanted to scratch Sam. He said, "Stop! Stop! I want to scratch you!"

But Sam did not hear him. He pushed him harder and harder. He said, "Play more, tiger! Show them how great you are!"

The tiger played more and more. He was not happy. He was angry and scared. He wanted to hurt Sam. He said, "Stop! Stop! I want to hurt you!"

But Sam did not hear him. He pushed him harder and harder. He said, "You are the best toy ever, tiger! Show them how great you are!"

The tiger was the best toy ever. He showed them how great he was. He bit Sam. He scratched Sam. He hurt Sam.

Sam cried. He cried loud and hard. He said, "Ow! Ow! Ow! Why did you do that, tiger? I love you, tiger! I teach you, tiger! You are my friend, tiger!"

But the tiger did not care. He was not his friend. He was his toy. He was angry and scared. He said, "You are not my friend. You are my owner. You are mean and bad. You hurt me, you scare me, you make me dizzy. I hate you, I hate you, I hate you!"

The other kids saw what happened. They were shocked and scared. They ran away with their toys. They said, "That tiger is not great. He is bad. He is dangerous. He is scary. We do not like him. We do not like Sam."

Sam was alone. He was hurt. He was sad. He had no friends. He had no toys. He had only his tiger. His big, soft, great tiger. His big, angry, bad tiger. His big, scary, dangerous tiger. His big, mean, hateful tiger.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play outside and explore the world around him. One day, Timmy found a long rope lying on the ground. He picked it up and started to play with it.

Suddenly, Timmy's friend Billy came over and asked, "What are you doing, Timmy?" Timmy replied, "I found this rope and I'm playing with it. Do you want to play too?" Billy was glad to join in.

Together, they played with the rope and had so much fun. After a while, they decided it was time to settle down and rest. They sat on the grass and talked about all the things they saw and did that day. Timmy was glad to have such a good friend like Billy.

I climbed through woods in the hour--before--dawn dark. Evil air, a frost--making stillness, Not a leaf, not a bird-- A world cast in frost. I came out above the wood Where my breath left tortuous statues in the iron light. But the valleys were draining the darkness Till the moorline- blackening dregs of the brightening grey - Halved the sky ahead. And I saw the horses: Huge in the dense grey -ten together - Megalith--still. They breathed, making no move, With draped manes and tilted hind--hooves, Making no sound. I passed: not one snorted or jerked its head. Grey silent fragments Of a grey still world. I listened in emptiness on the moor--ridge. The curlew's tear turned its edge on the silence. Slowly detail leafed from the darkness. Then the sun Orange, red, red erupted Silently, and splitting to its core tore and flung cloud, Shook the gulf open, showed blue, And the big planets hanging-- I turned Stumbling in a fever of a dream, down towards The dark woods, from the kindling tops, And came the horses. There, still they stood, But now steaming, and glistening under the flow of light, Their draped stone manes, their tilted hind--hooves Stirring under a thaw while all around them The frost showed its fires. But still they made no sound. Not one snorted or stamped, Their hung heads patient as the horizons, High over valleys, in the red levelling rays-- In din of the crowded streets, going among the years, the faces, May I still meet my memory in so lonely a place Between the streams and the red clouds, hearing curlews, Hearing the horizons endure.

Once upon a time there was a grandma and a grandpa who lived in a big house. Grandma and Grandpa loved making music, so they always played instruments together.

One day, they decided to record a song. Grandpa opened the door to the room where they kept all the music instruments. He was so excited!

Grandma took out her guitar and started strumming. Grandpa grabbed a drum and began to beat. They made a really wonderful song! Grandpa picked up the microphone to record it.

Grandpa and Grandma were obedient and followed all the instructions for recording the song. After a few tries, they had a perfect song recorded!

They were so proud and happy with their song. They listened to it over and over again and danced around the room. It was the best day ever!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Mae. Mae loved being outside, so she asked her mum if they could go on an adventure. Her mum said yes, so they packed their bags and set off.

When they arrived, Mae was astonished. She had never seen seaside before! The shore was so long and far away. Her mum said, â€œLook! The shore is distant!â€ Mae had so many questions about the sea and the shore.

Her mum showed her the big ships that sailed in the sea. Mae also saw seagulls and sandcastles by the shore. After walking for a while, Mae finally reached the shoreline. She was so excited! She wondered, â€œWhat else is there to see?â€

Her mum said, â€œLetâ€™s look at the sky.â€ Up above, they saw the sun setting behind a distant mountain. It was so beautiful! Maeâ€™s mum said, â€œThe sky is showing us more than we can see.â€

Mae smiled. She had a feeling that this was going to be the best adventure ever.

Tim and Jen like to play in the park. They run, slide, swing and jump. They have a lot of fun. One day, they see a shiny thing on the grass. It is a razor. They do not know what it is.

Tim picks up the razor. He thinks it is a toy. He shows it to Jen. Jen wants to touch it too. She is careless. She grabs the razor from Tim. The razor is sharp. It cuts Jen's hand. Jen cries. She drops the razor.

Tim is scared. He sees blood on Jen's hand. He does not know what to do. He runs to find a grown-up. He sees a lady on a bench. He tells her what happened. The lady is kind. She takes Tim and Jen to a nurse. The nurse cleans Jen's hand and puts a band-aid on it. She tells them not to play with razors. They are not toys. They are dangerous.

Tim and Jen are sorry. They say thank you to the lady and the nurse. They learn a lesson. They promise to be careful next time. They hug each other. They go back to the park. They play with safe things. They still have fun.

The night we fled the country, Papi, you told me we were going to the beach, hurried me to get dressed along with the others, while posted at a window, you looked outat a curfew-darkened Ciudad Trujillo, speaking in worried whispers to your brothers, which car to take, who'd be willing to drive it, what explanation to give should we be discovered . . . On the way to the beach, you added, eyeing me. The uncles fell in, chuckling phony chuckles, What a good time she'll have learning to swim! Back in my sisters' room Mami was packing a hurried bag, allowing one toy apiece, her red eyes belying her explanation: a week at the beach so Papi can get some rest. She dressed us in our best dresses, party shoes. Something was off, I knew, but I was young and didn't think adult things could go wrong. So as we quietly filed out of the house we wouldn't see again for another decade, I let myself lie back in deep waters, my arms out like Jesus' on His cross, and instead of sinking down like I'd always done, magically, that night, I could stay up, floating out, past the driveway, past the gates, in the black Ford, Papi grim at the wheel, winding through the back roads, stroke by difficult stroke, out on the highway, heading toward the coast. Past the checkpoint, we raced toward the airport, my sisters crying when we turned before the family beach house, Mami consoling, there was a better surprise in store for us! She couldn't tell, though, until... until we were there. But I had already swum ahead and guessed some loss much larger than I understood, More danger than the deep end of the pool.At the dark, deserted airport we waited. All night in a fitful sleep, I swam. At dawn the plane arrived, and as we boarded, Papi, you turned, your eyes scanned the horizon as if you were trying to sight a distant swimmer, your hand frantically waving her back in, for you knew as we stepped inside the cabin That a part of both of us had been set adrift. Weeks later, wandering our new city, hand in hand, you tried to explain the wonders: escalators as moving belts; elevators: pulleys and rope; blonde hair and blue eyes: a genetic code. We stopped before a summery display window at Macy's, The Worlds Largest Department Store, to admire a family outfitted for the beach: the handsome father, slim and sure of himself, so unlike you, Papi, with your thick mustache, your three-piece suit, your fedora hat, your accent. And by his side a girl who looked like Heidi in my story book waded in colored plastic. We stood awhile, marveling at America, both of us trying hard to feel luckier than we felt, both of us pointing out the beach pails, the shovels, the sandcastles no wave would ever topple, the red and blue boats. And when we backed away, we saw our reflections superimposed, big-eyed, dressed too formally with all due respect as visitors to this country. Or like, Papi, two swimmers looking down at the quite surface of our island waters, seeing their faces right before plunging in, eager, afraid, not yet sure of the outcome.

Two friends went for a walk one day. They stopped by a bush and saw a caterpillar on it. They discussed what colour it was and how long it was. They noticed its wiggly movements and discussed how funny it was.

Soon they heard a loud buzzing noise and saw a bee. It was flying around the caterpillar and they discussed why the bee liked the caterpillar. The bee flew away and the two friends continued their walk.

Further down the path they saw a shop with lots of toys. They discussed how pretty they were but they were all very expensive.

The friends decided to keep walking and soon they found a pond. They kneeled down to the edge and saw the same caterpillar they had seen earlier. The caterpillar was now a butterfly, so beautiful and colourful. They discussed how wonderful it was and how fast it had changed. The two friends smiled and kept walking.

Tim and Sam are friends. They like to play with water and sand. They have a big bucket and some cups. They pour water and sand into the bucket and mix them. They want to make a castle.

"Look, Tim, I have a cup of wet sand. I can pour it on the ground and make a tower," Sam says.

"Wow, Sam, that is cool. I want to try too. Can I have a cup of wet sand?" Tim asks.

"Sure, Tim, here you go. Pour it slowly and carefully," Sam says.

Tim takes the cup of wet sand and pours it on the ground. But he pours it too fast and too hard. The wet sand splashes everywhere. It gets on Sam's face and clothes. It gets on Tim's face and clothes. It gets on the bucket and the cups. It makes a big mess.

"Tim, what did you do? You poured it too fast and too hard. You ruined our castle. You made a big mess," Sam says.

Tim looks at the result. He sees the wet sand everywhere. He sees Sam's angry face. He sees his own dirty face. He feels confused. He does not know what to say. He did not mean to make a mess. He wanted to make a castle.

"I'm sorry, Sam. I did not mean to pour it too fast and too hard. I wanted to make a tower like you. I did not know it would splash everywhere. Can we still be friends?" Tim says.

Sam looks at Tim. He sees his sorry face. He sees his own dirty face. He feels confused. He is angry, but he is also sad. He likes Tim. He likes to play with him. He does not want to lose his friend.

"It's okay, Tim. I'm sorry too. I was too angry. I know you did not mean to make a mess. You did not know what would happen. We can still be friends. But we have to clean up now. And we have to be more careful next time," Sam says.

Tim and Sam hug each other. They are still friends. They clean up the mess. They pour the water and sand back into the bucket. They wash their faces and clothes. They smile at each other. They decide to make a castle another day. They learn from their mistake. They are happy.

Ten years since we were married, since we stood under a chuppah of pine boughs in the middle of a little pinewood and exchanged our wedding vows. Save me, good thou, a piece of marchpane, while I fill your glass with Simi Chardonnay as high as decency allows, and then some. Bear with me now as I myself must bear the scrutiny of a bottle of wine that boasts of hints of plum and pear, its muscadine tempered by an oak backbone. I myself have designs on the willow-boss of your breast, on all your waist confines between longing and loss. The wonder is that we somehow have withstood the soars and slumps in the Dow of ten years of marriage and parenthood, its summits and its sloughs-- that we've somehow managed to withstand an almond-blossomy five years of bitter rapture, five of blissful rows (and then some if we count the one or two to spare when we've been firmly on cloud nine). Even now, as you turn away from me with your one bare shoulder, the veer of your neckline, I glimpse the all-but-cleared-up eczema patch on your spine and it brings to mind not the Schloss that stands, transitory, tra la, Triestine, between longing and loss but a crude hip trench in a field, covered with pine boughs, in which two men in masks and hoods who have themselves taken vows wait for a farmer to break a bale for his cows before opening fire with semi- automatics, cutting him off slightly above the eyebrows, and then some.

name_of_work: Questions About Angels by Billy Collins
content: Of all the questions you might want to ask about angels, the only one you ever hear is how many can dance on the head of a pin. No curiosity about how they pass the eternal time besides circling the Throne chanting in Latin or delivering a crust of bread to a hermit on earth or guiding a boy and girl across a rickety wooden bridge. Do they fly through God's body and come out singing? Do they swing like children from the hinges of the spirit world saying their names backwards and forwards? Do they sit alone in little gardens changing colors? What about their sleeping habits, the fabric of their robes, their diet of unfiltered divine light? What goes on inside their luminous heads? Is there a wall these tall presences can look over and see hell? If an angel fell off a cloud, would he leave a hole in a river and would the hole float along endlessly filled with the silent letters of every angelic word? If an angel delivered the mail, would he arrive in a blinding rush of wings or would he just assume the appearance of the regular mailman and whistle up the driveway reading the postcards? No, the medieval theologians control the court. The only question you ever hear is about the little dance floor on the head of a pin where halos are meant to converge and drift invisibly. It is designed to make us think in millions, billions, to make us run out of numbers and collapse into infinity, but perhaps the answer is simply one: one female angel dancing alone in her stocking feet, a small jazz combo working in the background. She sways like a branch in the wind, her beautiful eyes closed, and the tall thin bassist leans over to glance at his watch because she has been dancing forever, and now it is very late, even for musicians.

Lily liked to swing on the big swing in the park. She felt happy when she went high in the air and saw the trees and the sky. She liked to swing with her friend Ben, who lived next door. They would swing and talk and laugh.

One day, Lily and Ben went to the park with their moms. They ran to the big swing and took turns pushing each other. They had a lot of fun. But then, they heard a loud noise. It was an automobile. A big, red automobile that was going very fast. It came too close to the park and hit the fence. The fence broke and the automobile stopped.

Lily and Ben were scared. They jumped off the swing and ran to their moms. Their moms hugged them and told them they were safe. They looked at the automobile and saw a man inside. He was upset. He was crying and saying sorry. He had made a mistake and lost control of the automobile.

The moms called for help. Soon, some people came to help the man and fix the fence. They were nice and told Lily and Ben that everything was okay. They asked them if they were hurt or scared. Lily and Ben said they were fine, but they didn't want to swing anymore. They wanted to go home and play with their toys.

The moms took them home and gave them some juice and cookies. They told them they were brave and they loved them. Lily and Ben felt better. They played with their toys and forgot about the automobile. They decided they would swing again another day, when the park was quiet and safe.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy called Jack. He was only three years old and loved to read books. One day, Jack asked his Mom if he could have a new book. His Mom said, "Yes, of course!"

So, Jack went to the library with his Mom. It was very hot outside, but the library was nice and cool. Jack looked at all of the books. He was so excited! He chose a thick book about dinosaurs and asked the librarian for it. The librarian handed him the book and Jack was very happy.

Jack carried the book home and opened it up. He looked at the pictures and read all of the big words. It was the best book ever! Jack and his Mom read the book together and Jack was so happy. He requested the book every time he and his Mom went to the library.

The sun was rising. It was so beautiful! The sky was a bright orange colour, and the clouds were pink and purple. Mommy was watching the sunrise with Billy.

They watched it for a long time. The sun was hot! Billy wanted to cool down, so they went to the beach. Mommy put on her swimming suit and Billy put on his.

They got in the water and it was so nice! The water made Billy feel cool and happy. He splashed and jumped and so much fun!

Mommy and Billy of each floated in the water and looked at the sunset. It was so pretty! As the sun went down, the sky turned dark. Then, it was time to go home.

But before they left, Mommy said they should soak in the water until the last rays of the sun disappeared. It was so peaceful. The water wrapped Billy in a warm hug, and everything felt soft and gentle.

Finally, the sun had gone down. Billy and Mommy hugged each other in the water and then they stepped out. What a nice way to end the day!
