Lily and Tom are hungry. They want to eat something yummy. They walk to the park with Mom and Dad. They see a food truck. It has a big menu on the side. The menu has pictures of food.

"Look, Mom, they have pizza!" Lily says. She points to the menu.

"And they have hot dogs!" Tom says. He points to the menu too.

Mom and Dad smile. They like pizza and hot dogs. They walk to the food truck. A man with a hat and a apron is inside. He is charming. He has a big smile.

"Hello, what can I get for you?" he asks.

"We want pizza and hot dogs, please," Mom says.

"Sure, coming right up. Do you want cheese on your pizza?" he asks.

"Yes, please," Lily says.

"And ketchup on your hot dogs?" he asks.

"Yes, please," Tom says.

The man makes the pizza and the hot dogs. He puts them in boxes. He gives them to Mom and Dad. He also gives them napkins and forks.

"Here you go, enjoy your food," he says.

"Thank you, you are very nice," Mom says.

"You're welcome, have a lovely day," he says.

Lily and Tom are happy. They walk to a bench with Mom and Dad. They sit down and open the boxes. They eat the pizza and the hot dogs. They are yummy. They share with Mom and Dad. They drink water from their bottles. They are full and satisfied.

"That was a good lunch," Dad says.

"Yes, it was. And the food truck man was charming," Mom says.

"He was. Maybe we can come back another day," Dad says.

Lily and Tom nod. They like the food truck. They like the park. They like Mom and Dad. They are a happy family.

Once upon a time there was a tough frog named Joe. He lived in a warm and sunny pond. Every day he would go out to the pond and find something funny to do. 

One day, Joe was feeling extra giggly. He was walking around when he noticed a joke that he had never seen before. He hopped over to it but it was so tough that he couldn't reach it. 

Joe tried and tried but he just couldn't get it. Suddenly, he noticed something near the joke that was glowing in the sun. Joe looked closer and he saw that it was a special kind of flower. 

Joe knew that if he ate the flower, he would get much stronger. So, he ate it and he felt all of his muscles become tough! With his new strength, Joe was able to reach the joke and it was still in one piece, not at all rotted. 

Joe was so happy and he laughed and laughed and laughed. From that day onward, Joe always remembered that flower whenever he needed a little bit of extra strength.

name_of_work: Ode to My Suit by Pablo Neruda
content: Every morning, suit, you are waiting on a chair to be filled by my vanity, my love, my hope, my body. Still only half awake I leave the shower to shrug into your sleeves, my legs seek the hollow of your legs, and thus embraced by your unfailing loyalty I take my morning walk, work my way into my poetry; from my windows I see the things, men, women, events and struggles constantly shaping me, constantly confronting me, setting my hands to the task, opening my eyes, creasing my lips, and in the same way, suit, I am shaping you, poking out your elbows, wearing you threadbare, and so your life grows in the image of my own. In the wind you flap and hum as if you were my soul, in bad moments you cling to my bones, abandoned, at nighttime darkness and dream people with their phantoms your wings and mine. I wonder whether some day an enemy bullet will stain you with my blood, for then you would die with me, but perhaps it will be less dramatic, simple, and you will grow ill, suit, with me, with my body, and together we will be lowered into the earth. That's why every day I greet you with respect and then you embrace me and I forget you, because we are one being and shall be always in the wind, through the night, the streets and the struggle, one body, maybe, maybe, one day, still.

I dreamt a dream! What can it mean? And that I was a maiden Queen Guarded by an Angel mild: Witless woe was ne'er beguiled! And I wept both night and day, And he wiped my tears away; And I wept both day and night, And hid from him my heart's delight. So he took his wings, and fled; Then the morn blushed rosy red. I dried my tears, and armed my fears With ten thousand shields and spears. Soon my Angel came again; I was armed, he came in vain; For the time of youth was fled, And grey hairs were on my head.

Once upon a time there was a special star. She loved to glow. Whenever someone was feeling sad, her bright light would appear in the sky and cheer them up.

One night, there was a storm. The clouds filled the sky and everything got dark. The star felt scared and wished she could go to a safe place. Suddenly, she saw a glowing knot high above the storm. It looked like it was inviting her to come closer. 

She flew higher and higher. Finally, she reached the glowing knot and felt warmth in her heart. She stayed there all night, watching the normal stars twinkle far away. When the sky changed to blue, she noticed the sun starting to rise. 

Her heart was happy again. She waved goodbye to the glowing knot and flew back home to her special star family. She smiled, knowing that her star light would shine again in the sky.

Having been tenant long to a rich lord, Not thriving, I resolved to be bold, And make a suit unto him, to afford A new small-rented lease, and cancel th' old. In heaven at his manor I him sought; They told me there that he was lately gone About some land, which he had dearly bought Long since on earth, to take possession. I straight returned, and knowing his great birth, Sought him accordingly in great resorts; In cities, theaters, gardens, parks, and courts; At length I heard a ragged noise and mirth Of thieves and murderers; there I him espied, Who straight, Your suit is granted, said, and died.

Once upon a time, there was a happy little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and run around outside. One day, Lily's mommy told her they were going to the park. Lily was so excited! She loved to swing and slide and play in the sand.

When they got to the park, Lily saw some other kids playing on the swings. She wanted to join them, but she felt a little shy. Her mommy asked her if she wanted to play with the other kids, and Lily said yes. Her mommy told her not to worry, and that everything would be okay.

Lily ran over to the swings and asked the other kids if she could play too. They said yes, and Lily had so much fun with her new friends. She wasn't worried anymore, and she was even more excited than before. From then on, Lily was never afraid to ask to play with new friends at the park.

Once upon a time, there was a kind boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to draw with his colorful crayons. One day, Timmy went to the park and saw a big dog. The dog stared at Timmy and Timmy stared back. Timmy was a little scared, but the dog was kind too. The dog wagged his tail and Timmy smiled. From that day on, Timmy and the dog were friends and Timmy drew pictures of the dog with his crayons. The end.

Once upon a time there was a family who loved each other very much. They ate dinner together every night and enjoyed delicious food. 

One night Dad had a great idea. Dad suggested that they could all go camping and explore the great outdoors. Everyone thought this was a brilliant suggestion and agreed to go.

The family packed up all their camping gear, loaded up the car, and drove out into the woods. They had the best time exploring nature, climbing hills, and looking for wildlife. 

At night they made a campfire and cooked a delicious dinner. They all sat around the fire, telling stories and snuggling up in blankets. It was a wonderful time. 

Back at home, the family looked back on the wonderful weekend with happiness. Dad suggested that they go camping once a month to enjoy the beauty of life together as a family. 

Everyone agreed wholeheartedly. They all knew that camping together was something delicious and special.

From childhood's hour I have not been As others were--I have not seen As others saw--I could not bring My passions from a common spring-- From the same source I have not taken My sorrow--I could not awaken My heart to joy at the same tone-- And all I lov'd--I lov'd alone-- Then--in my childhood--in the dawn Of a most stormy life--was drawn From ev'ry depth of good and ill The mystery which binds me still-- From the torrent, or the fountain-- From the red cliff of the mountain-- From the sun that 'round me roll'd In its autumn tint of gold-- From the lightning in the sky As it pass'd me flying by-- From the thunder, and the storm-- And the cloud that took the form (When the rest of Heaven was blue) Of a demon in my view--

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim loved to play with his toy car. One day, Tim's toy car got stuck under the couch. He tried to reach it, but he couldn't. So he asked his mom to help him. His mom pulled the toy car out from under the couch and gave it back to Tim. 

Later that day, Tim and his mom went to watch a parade. They saw lots of people marching down the street. Tim was so excited to see all the colorful floats and hear the marching band. He clapped his hands and cheered as the parade went by.

After the parade, Tim and his mom went to the park. Tim wanted to play on the swings, but they were all taken. So they went to the sandbox instead. When they got there, they saw that it was empty. Tim was sad because he wanted to play with the sand. But his mom said they could fill up the sandbox with sand from the big bag they brought. Tim was happy again and he helped his mom pour the sand into the empty sandbox.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the park and swing on the swings. One day, while she was swinging, she got very dizzy and fell off. She hurt her knee and started to cry.

A kind lady saw Lily crying and came over to ask if she was okay. Lily said no and the lady picked her up and carried her to a bench. The lady asked Lily what happened and Lily told her about falling off the swing.

The lady said, "Don't worry, little angel. I care about you and will make sure you feel better." She gave Lily a band-aid for her knee and a hug. Lily felt better and thanked the lady. From that day on, Lily knew that there were kind people who cared about her.

name_of_work: The Staircase of Notre Dame, Paris by Dante Gabriel Rossetti
content: As one who, groping in a narrow stair, Hath a strong sound of bells upon his ears, Which, being at a distance off, appears Quite close to him because of the pent air: So with this France. She stumbles file and square Darkling and without space for breath: each one Who hears the thunder says: "It shall anon Be in among her ranks to scatter her." This may be; and it may be that the storm Is spent in rain upon the unscathed seas, Or wasteth other countries ere it die: Till she,--having climbed always through the swarm Of darkness and of hurtling sound,--from these Shall step forth on the light in a still sky.

One day, Joe asked his mom a question. He asked, "What is today?" His mom laughed and said, "Today is Tuesday." Joe thought for a moment, then asked, "What is Tuesday?" His mom smiled and said, "Tuesday is a day." Joe thought deeper and asked, "What is a day?" Mom explained, "A day is when the sun is up and the moon is down, and it's light outside." Joe took a breath and asked, "What does harsh mean?" His mom smiled again and said, "Harsh means something that is hard or difficult." Joe seemed satisfied with his mom's answer and smiled. He was ready for the day and ready to learn more.

name_of_work: Beale Street Love by Langston Hughes
content: Love Is a brown man's fist With hard knuckles Crushing the lips, Blackening the eyes, -- Hit me again, Says Clorinda.

Here comes the man! He's talking a lot I'm sitting, by myself. I've got A ticket to ride. Outside is, 'Out to lunch.' It's no great pleasure, being on the make. Well, who is? Or, well everyone is, tho. 'I'm laying there, & some guy comes up & hits me with a billyclub!' A fat guy Says. Shut up. & like that we cross a river Into the Afterlife. Everything goes on as before But never does any single experience make total use Of you. You are always slightly ahead, Slightly behind. It merely baffles, it doesn't hurt. It's total pain & it breaks your heart In a less than interesting way. Every day Is payday. Never enough pay. A deja-vu That lasts. It's no big thing, anyway. A lukewarm greasy hamburger, ice-cold pepsi that hurts your teeth.

Tom and Sam are young boys who like to play with cars. They have many cars of different colors and sizes. They like to race them on the floor and make loud noises.

One day, a new boy comes to their school. His name is Ben and he has a big car that looks very shiny and fast. Tom and Sam want to see his car, but Ben does not let them. He says it is his car and he does not share.

Tom and Sam are angry and sad. They think Ben is mean and rude. They want to have his car, but they do not have enough money to buy one. They have a bad idea. They decide to steal his car when he is not looking.

They wait until Ben goes to the bathroom. Then they run to his backpack and open it. They find his car and take it out. They put it in their pocket and run away. They think they are clever and happy.

But Ben sees them. He comes out of the bathroom and sees his backpack is open. He looks inside and sees his car is gone. He knows Tom and Sam took it. He is angry and sad. He runs after them and shouts.

"Hey, you stole my car! Give it back to me! That is not nice!"

Tom and Sam hear him and are scared. They know they did something wrong. They stop and turn around. They see Ben is crying and angry. They feel sorry and ashamed.

They take out his car and give it back to him. They say they are sorry and they will not do it again. They ask him to be their friend and to share his car with them.

Ben is still angry, but he sees they are sorry. He takes his car and looks at it. He sees it is not broken or dirty. He feels a little better. He says he is sorry too and he will share his car with them. He asks them to be his friend and to play with him.

Tom and Sam are happy and relieved. They say yes and they hug him. They go to play with his car and their cars. They race them on the floor and make loud noises. They are friends and they do not steal anymore. They think they are clever and good.

On a clear day, Molly and Jimmy were walking down the beach when they spotted a large reef. It was brightly coloured, with lots of fish swimming around it. Suddenly, they heard a sound coming from it - there was a helpless starfish stuck on a sharp rock. 

Jimmy was determined to help the starfish and so Molly and he decided to bake some cupcakes to help make it feel better. Molly got some of the ingredients together while Jimmy found a suitable spot to build a small fire. 

They lit the fire and started to bake cupcakes. The starfish couldn't move and it looked so helpless. But eventually, after many tries, the cupcakes were cooked and ready to eat. 

Molly broke off a piece of a cupcake and carefully put it on the sharp rock near the starfish's mouth. Suddenly, it came to life and started to eat the cupcake! Once it was finished eating, it slowly made its way out of the reef. 

Molly and Jimmy were both so proud of themselves for their brave and kind efforts. They waved goodbye to the starfish as it slowly left the reef.

name_of_work: Lightenings VIII (The annals say...) by Seamus Heaney
content: The annals say: when the monks of Clonmacnoise Were all at prayers inside the oratory A ship appeared above them in the air. The anchor dragged along behind so deep It hooked itself into the altar rails And then, as the big hull rocked to a standstill, A crewman shinned and grappled down the rope And struggled to release it. But in vain. 'This man can't bear our life here and will drown,' The abbot said, 'unless we help him.' So They did, the freed ship sailed, and the man climbed back Out of the marvellous as he had known it.

Lila and Sam were best friends. They liked to play in the park and look at the sky. One day, they saw something shiny and fast in the sky. It was a rocket!

"Wow, look at that!" Sam said. "It is a rocket. It goes to space."

"I want to see space," Lila said. "Maybe there are stars and planets and aliens."

"Maybe we can meet an alien," Sam said. "That would be fun and rare. Not many people meet aliens."

They ran after the rocket, hoping to get closer. They followed it to a big field, where it landed. They saw a door open and a green creature come out. It had four eyes, two arms and two legs. It looked friendly.

"Hello, little ones," the creature said. "I am Zeebo. I come from Zork. I am here to explore your planet. Do you want to be my friends?"

Lila and Sam were surprised and curious. They nodded and smiled.

"Yes, we want to be your friends," Lila said. "We are Lila and Sam. We come from Earth. This is our planet."

"Nice to meet you, Lila and Sam," Zeebo said. "You are very brave and kind. Do you want to see my rocket? It is very cool and fast."

"Yes, please," Sam said. "We love rockets. They are rare and amazing."

Zeebo took them by the hand and led them to his rocket. He showed them the buttons, the lights and the windows. He told them stories about his home and his travels. Lila and Sam listened and asked questions. They had a lot of fun and learned a lot. They made a new friend from space. They were very happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She was very kind and loved to play with her friends in the park. One day, Lily's mom told her they had to go to a meeting. Lily didn't know what a meeting was, but she knew it sounded boring. 

When they got to the meeting, Lily saw lots of grown-ups talking and not having any fun. She asked her mom if they could leave, but her mom said they had to stay. Lily was sad, but then she saw a little boy who looked even sadder than her. She went over to him and asked him what was wrong. 

The little boy said he was scared because he had a splinter in his finger and didn't want to go to the doctor to have it removed. Lily knew just what to do. She told him that sometimes things might hurt a little bit, but it's important to be brave and get help. She held his hand and together they went to the doctor. The doctor removed the splinter and the little boy was very happy. 

Lily learned that even though meetings might be boring, they can also be a chance to help others. And sometimes, being kind to someone who needs it can make all the difference.

Once upon a time, there lived a wealthy man in a big house. He had a room full of fun toys and games for his 3 year old daughter to enjoy. In the kitchen, he had a big, shiny fridge full of yummy food.

One day, the little girl saw a delicious chocolate cake in the fridge. She asked her dad: "Can I have a piece, please?". The Dad said: "No, that cake isn't for you. Save it for your birthday". The little girl said: "But I want it now!". Her dad replied: "No, you must wait for your birthday".

The little girl did not want to wait. She went to the fridge and took the cake anyway. She enjoyed eating the big piece of cake - but then she felt bad and wondered if her dad would be cross.

Luckily, the dad saw her eat the cake and he was happy to see her enjoying it. He said: "I'm glad you shared that cake. I was saving it for your birthday surprise! But now I know you will appreciate it even more on your special day". The little girl was happy and she smiled at her dad, who gave her a hug.

From then on, the little girl never forgot to appreciate the special things in her life, no matter how wealthy she was. She always remembered to enjoy the little things with gratitude.

name_of_work: 10 Things I Hate About You Poem
content: I hate the way you talk to me, And the way you cut your hair. I hate the way you drive my car, I hate it when you stare. I hate your big dumb combat boots, and the way you read my mind I hate you so much it makes me sick, It even makes me rhyme. I hate the way you're always right, I hate it when you lie I hate it when you make me laugh, Even worse when you make me cry I hate it when you're not around, And the fact that you didn't call But mostly I hate the way I don't hate you, Not even close, Not even a little bit, Not even at all

Once upon a time, there was a brave girl named Laila. One day, Laila wanted to make something special, so she decided to bake a cake.

She got out her bowl and whisk and started to mix all the ingredients together. Suddenly, she heard a funny noise coming from outside.

Laila went to the window and saw something really strange - a big, pink gumball! It was rolling across the park.

Laila was brave, so she decided to go outside and try to catch the gumball. But it was too fast! Just then, Laila had an idea. She ran back inside and got her cake out of the oven.

Maybe the sweet smell of the cake would lure the gumball over to her. Sure enough, it worked! The gumball came rolling up to Laila, and she was able to catch it. 

Laila gave a sigh of relief. She was so happy she was able to catch the gumball. Now that's what you call being brave!

The dead are always looking down on us, they say, while we are putting on our shoes or making a sandwich, they are looking down through the glass-bottom boats of heaven as they row themselves slowly through eternity. They watch the tops of our heads moving below on earth, and when we lie down in a field or on a couch, drugged perhaps by the hum of a warm afternoon, they think we are looking back at them, which makes them lift their oars and fall silent and wait, like parents, for us to close our eyes.

Once upon a time, there was a gifted boy, Benny. One day, Benny saw something appear in front of him. It was a tall judge, wearing a big robe. Benny was afraid and stepped backwards.

The judge said to Benny, "Why are you afraid?". Benny replied, "I don't know, who are you?". The judge replied, "I am a judge and I want to see your special gift". Benny felt excited and smiled. 

Then, Benny displayed his special gift. He juggled three balls in the air and the judge said, "Amazing! Benny danced for joy when the judge praised him. 

Benny felt so happy that he bowed to the judge. The judge smiled and said, "Well done! You are very gifted". Benny was so happy to hear those words.

Benny thanked the judge and waved goodbye. The judge disappeared as suddenly as he had appeared. Benny never forgot his experience with the judge and kept practicing his gift. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a smart girl named Julie. She loved to swim in the river every day. She was very fast and strong.

One day, while Julie was swimming in the river, she saw something glimmering in the water. It was a special gift! She was so excited, she quickly swam to the river shore and opened the package. Inside, she found a shiny red bike. She was so excited, she couldn't believe it.

She quickly thanked the river and waved goodbye. Then, she rode her new bike. She felt so intelligent! She thanked the river many more times, each time she rode her bike. 

Julie was so happy, she called her friend Maria to come over and see her gift. 

"Maria," Julie said. "Look what the river gave me! Isn't it cool?" 

Maria agreed and couldn't believe Julie was so lucky. "That gift was so special," Maria said. "No one else has a shiny red bike like that!"

From then on, Julie and Maria would always go biking together and thank the river for the wonderful gift. Julie was so happy and intelligent for having such a great gift.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to draw and color with his crayons. One day, he went to his mommy and asked, "Mommy, can you help me load my crayons into my backpack? I want to take them to school for show and tell."

"Sure, Timmy," said his mommy. "But first, you have to listen to Daddy's lecture about being creative. He's a very smart man and has lots of good ideas."

Timmy was excited to learn about being creative, so he sat down and listened carefully. After Daddy's lecture, Timmy felt inspired to make a special drawing for show and tell. He loaded his backpack with his crayons and his drawing, and headed off to school.

When he got to school, all of his friends were amazed by his creative drawing. They all clapped and cheered for Timmy, and he felt very proud. From that day on, Timmy knew that being creative was important, and he always remembered Daddy's lecture.

Cold blew the freezing northern blast, And winter sternly frowned; The flaky snow fell thick and fast, And clad the fields around. Forced by the storm's relentless power, Emboldened by despair, A shivering redbreast sought my door, Some friendly warmth to share. 'Welcome, sweet bird!' I fondly cried, 'No danger need'st thou fear, Secure with me thou may'st abide, Till warmer suns appear. 'And when mild spring comes smiling on, And bids the fields look gay, Thou, with thy sweet, thy grateful song, My kindness shalt repay.' Mistaken thought! -- But how shall I The mournful truth display? An envious cat, with jealous eye, Had marked him as her prey. Remorseless wretch! -- her cruel jaws Soon sealed her victim's doom, While I in silence mourn his loss, And weep o'er robin's tomb. So, oft in life's uneven way, Some stroke may intervene; Sweep all our fancied joys away, And change the flattering scene.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Sarah. She liked to play with clay. One day, she was in the backyard playing with her clay and feeling very happy. She made a round clay ball, and then she put the clay ball in the grass.

Suddenly, her brother came running out of the house. He was smiling and his eyes were twinkling. There was something in his hand. It was a toy car. Sarah's brother said, "Look! I got it! I got a toy car!" Sarah gasped and said, "Wow! It's so funny!"

Then, Sarah's brother zoomed the car in circles around the yard. Sarah laughed and said, "That's so cool! Let me try it too!" Her brother said, "Okay," and gave her the toy car. Sarah zoomed the car around and around, and it was so much fun! She was so happy she couldn't help but laugh. 

Sarah and her brother played with the car for hours until it was time for dinner. They put the car away and ate dinner with a big smile. Since then, Sarah looked forward to playing with her clay and the fun toy car.

name_of_work: The Hill We Climb by Amanda Gorman
content: When day comes, we ask ourselves, where can we find light in this never-ending shade? The loss we carry. A sea we must wade. We braved the belly of the beast. We've learned that quiet isn't always peace, and the norms and notions of what "just" is isn't always justice. And yet the dawn is ours before we knew it. Somehow we do it. Somehow we weathered and witnessed a nation that isn't broken, but simply unfinished. We, the successors of a country and a time where a skinny Black girl descended from slaves and raised by a single mother can dream of becoming president, only to find herself reciting for one. And, yes, we are far from polished, far from pristine, but that doesn't mean we are striving to form a union that is perfect. We are striving to forge our union with purpose. To compose a country committed to all cultures, colors, characters and conditions of man. And so we lift our gaze, not to what stands between us, but what stands before us. We close the divide because we know to put our future first, we must first put our differences aside. We lay down our arms so we can reach out our arms to one another. We seek harm to none and harmony for all. Let the globe, if nothing else, say this is true. That even as we grieved, we grew. That even as we hurt, we hoped. That even as we tired, we tried. That we'll forever be tied together, victorious. Not because we will never again know defeat, but because we will never again sow division. Scripture tells us to envision that everyone shall sit under their own vine and fig tree, and no one shall make them afraid. If we're to live up to our own time, then victory won't lie in the blade, but in all the bridges we've made. That is the promise to glade, the hill we climb, if only we dare. It's because being American is more than a pride we inherit. It's the past we step into and how we repair it. We've seen a force that would shatter our nation, rather than share it. Would destroy our country if it meant delaying democracy. And this effort very nearly succeeded. But while democracy can be periodically delayed, it can never be permanently defeated. In this truth, in this faith we trust, for while we have our eyes on the future, history has its eyes on us. This is the era of just redemption. We feared at its inception. We did not feel prepared to be the heirs of such a terrifying hour. But within it we found the power to author a new chapter, to offer hope and laughter to ourselves. So, while once we asked, how could we possibly prevail over catastrophe, now we assert, how could catastrophe possibly prevail over us? We will not march back to what was, but move to what shall be: a country that is bruised but whole, benevolent but bold, fierce and free. We will not be turned around or interrupted by intimidation because we know our inaction and inertia will be the inheritance of the next generation, become the future. Our blunders become their burdens. But one thing is certain. If we merge mercy with might, and might with right, then love becomes our legacy and change our children's birthright. So let us leave behind a country better than the one we were left. Every breath from my bronze-pounded chest, we will raise this wounded world into a wondrous one. We will rise from the golden hills of the West. We will rise from the windswept Northeast where our forefathers first realized revolution. We will rise from the lake-rimmed cities of the Midwestern states. We will rise from the sun-baked South. We will rebuild, reconcile, and recover. And every known nook of our nation and every corner called our country, our people diverse and beautiful, will emerge battered and beautiful. When day comes, we step out of the shade of flame and unafraid. The new dawn balloons as we free it. For there is always light, if only we're brave enough to see it. If only we're brave enough to be it.

Once upon a time, there was a grandma and a grandpa who lived in a big house. They had a puppy, who was very fluffy and playful. The puppy was always having fun, running and jumping around the house. 

One day, the grandpa and the puppy were playing a game and the puppy got a little too excited. Grandpa said it was time to take a break and then, the puppy lay down on the floor. Grandpa thought it was funny, so he laughed and laughed. 

Suddenly, the grandma came out of the kitchen holding a big knife. Grandpa was scared, because he thought grandma was angry. But grandma said she was just making dinner and asked why the puppy was lying on the floor. Grandpa said the puppy was only playing and that he was being funny. 

Everyone laughed and smiled. They all had a nice dinner and the puppy went off to sleep. Grandma put the knife away, and everyone was happy.

I Why should you sweare I am forsworn, Since thine I vow'd to be? Lady it is already Morn, And 'twas last night I swore to thee That fond impossibility. II Have I not lov'd thee much and long, A tedious twelve houres space? I must all other Beauties wrong, And rob thee of a new imbrace; Could I still dote upon thy Face. III Not, but all joy in thy browne haire, By others may be found; But I must search the blank and faire Like skilfull Minerallist's that sound For Treasure in un-plow'd-up ground. IV Then, if when I have lov'd my round, Thou prov'st the pleasant she; With spoyles of meaner Beauties crown'd, I laden will returne to thee, Ev'n sated with Varietie.

name_of_work: On the Day of Judgment by Jonathan Swift
content: With a whirl of thought oppress'd, I sunk from reverie to rest. An horrid vision seized my head; I saw the graves give up their dead! Jove, arm'd with terrors, bursts the skies, And thunder roars and lightning flies! Amaz'd, confus'd, its fate unknown, The world stands trembling at his throne! While each pale sinner hung his head, Jove, nodding, shook the heavens, and said: "Offending race of human kind, By nature, reason, learning, blind; You who, through frailty, stepp'd aside; And you, who never fell - through pride: You who in different sects were shamm'd, And come to see each other damn'd; (So some folk told you, but they knew No more of Jove's designs than you;) - The world's mad business now is o'er, And I resent these pranks no more. - I to such blockheads set my wit! I damn such fools! - Go, go, you're bit."

Tom likes to sail. He has a toy boat that he plays with in the bath. He makes waves with his hand and pretends he is a captain. He likes to sing songs about the sea and the fish.

One day, Tom goes to the gym with his mom. The gym is a big place with many things to do. Tom sees a big pool with water. He wants to sail his boat in the pool. He asks his mom if he can.

Mom says yes, but first he has to put on his swimsuit and his floaties. She helps him get ready and then they go to the pool. Tom is happy. He puts his boat in the water and watches it sail. He pushes it with his hand and makes it go fast. He sings his songs and smiles.

Mom is happy too. She sees that Tom is having fun and learning. She thinks that his boat is very useful. It helps him play and imagine and be brave. She joins him in the pool and they sail together. They have a good time at the gym.

There was a little girl and she wanted something fun. She asked her mom if she could have an expensive toy. Her mom said yes, so they went out to buy it.

When they got there, the little girl saw lots of different toys. She wanted to get them all but her mom said no. So the little girl found an exciting toy that she liked. It was expensive but her mom said she could have it. 

The little girl was happy and started playing with the toy. It was locked and so she asked her mom how to open it. Her mom said she had to unlock it. She found a towel and used it to help her unlock the toy. 

The toy opened and the little girl was very happy. She played with it for a long time until it was time to go home. She held onto the toy tightly as she ran out of the shop.

Once upon a time, there was a little piggy named Peppa. She loved to play outside with her friends. One day, Peppa and her friends decided to build a house out of bricks. It was easy to stack the bricks one on top of the other. 

But then, the wind started to blow and it got very cold. Peppa started to shiver and her friends did too. They realized that their brick house wasn't warm enough. So, they decided to build a fire inside to keep them warm. 

They gathered some sticks and lit a fire. Soon, they were all warm and cozy inside their brick house. Peppa was so happy that they found an easy solution to their problem. From then on, they always made sure to have a fire when it got cold outside. The end.

name_of_work: Lenten Thoughts of a High Anglican by John Betjeman
content: Isn't she lovely, "the Mistress"? With her wide-apart grey-green eyes, The droop of her lips and, when she smiles, Her glance of amused surprise? How nonchalantly she wears her clothes, How expensive they are as well! And the sound of her voice is as soft and deep As the Christ Church tenor bell. But why do I call her "the Mistress" Who know not her way of life? Because she has more of a cared-for air Than many a legal wife. How elegantly she swings along In the vapoury incense veil; The angel choir must pause in song When she kneels at the altar rail. The parson said that we shouldn't stare Around when we come to church, Or the Unknown God we are seeking May forever elude our search. But I hope that the preacher will not think It unorthodox and odd If I add that I glimpse in "the Mistress" A hint of the Unknown God.

Anna liked to crawl under the bookcase in her room. It was her secret place, where she could hide from her big brother Tom and read her favorite books. She had a flashlight and a pillow and some snacks there.

One day, Tom was looking for Anna. He wanted to play with her new doll, but he could not find her anywhere. He searched the whole house, but he did not think of looking under the bookcase. He was angry and bored.

He went to the kitchen and saw a jar of honey on the counter. He loved honey, but he knew he was not allowed to have it without asking. He looked around and saw no one. He decided to take a little bit, just a taste. He opened the jar and dipped his finger in it. He put it in his mouth and waited for the sweet flavor.

But he did not taste honey. He tasted something bitter and spicy and awful. He spat it out and coughed and cried. He looked at the jar and saw a label. It said: "Hot sauce. Do not touch. For Dad's barbecue."

Anna had put the label on the jar as a prank. She knew Tom liked to sneak honey when no one was watching. She had swapped the jars and hid the real honey under the bookcase. She had heard Tom's scream from her secret place and smiled. She crawled out and went to see him.

"Are you okay, Tom?" she asked innocently.

"No, I'm not okay!" Tom shouted. "You tricked me! You put hot sauce in the honey jar!"

Anna giggled. "That's what you get for trying to take my doll. And my honey. Next time, ask first."

Tom glared at her, but he knew she was right. He had learned his lesson. He ran to the sink and washed his mouth. Anna went back to her bookcase and read her books. She was happy. She had her secret place, her doll, and her honey. And she had taught Tom a good joke.

name_of_work: The Picture of Little T.C. In A Prospect of Flowers by Andrew Marvell
content: See with what simplicity This nymph begins her golden days! In the green grass she loves to lie, And there with her fair aspect tames The wilder flowers, and gives them names: But only with the roses plays; And them does tell What colour best becomes them, and what smell. Who can foretell for what high cause This Darling of the Gods was born! Yet this is she whose chaster laws The wanton Love shall one day fear, And, under her command severe, See his bow broke and ensigns torn. Happy, who can Appease this virtuous enemy of man! O, then let me in time compound, And parley with those conquering eyes; Ere they have tried their force to wound, Ere, with their glancing wheels, they drive In triumph over hearts that strive, And them that yield but more despise. Let me be laid, Where I may see thy glories from some shade. Meantime, whilst every verdant thing Itself does at thy beauty charm, Reform the errors of the spring; Make that the tulips may have share Of sweetness, seeing they are fair; And roses of their thorns disarm: But most procure That violets may a longer age endure. But, O young beauty of the woods, Whom Nature courts with fruits and flowers, Gather the flowers, but spare the buds; Lest Flora angry at thy crime, To kill her infants in their prime, Do quickly make the example yours; And, ere we see, Nip in the blossom all our hopes and thee.

Tim is a dog who likes to run and play. He has a red collar with his name on it. He lives with his family in a big house with a yard. He is happy and friendly.

One day, Tim sees a cat on the fence. He barks and runs after the cat. He wants to catch it and make it go away. He does not like cats. The cat is scared and jumps to the other side of the fence. Tim follows the cat and jumps too.

But Tim does not know that the other side of the fence is a busy street. There are many cars and trucks and bikes. They are loud and fast and dangerous. Tim is in trouble. He does not know how to get back to his yard. He is lost and afraid.

He hears a horn and sees a big truck coming. He tries to run away, but his collar gets stuck on a pole. He cannot move. He whines and cries for help. He wishes he did not chase the cat.

Then he sees the cat again. The cat is on the sidewalk. The cat sees Tim and his collar. The cat remembers how Tim barked and ran after him. The cat could run away and leave Tim alone. But the cat does not do that. The cat is brave.

The cat runs to Tim and bites his collar. He pulls and pulls until the collar breaks. He frees Tim from the pole. He saves Tim from the truck. He meows and runs away.

Tim is shocked and grateful. He realizes that the cat is not his enemy. He realizes that the cat is his friend. He realizes that he was wrong to chase and bark at the cat. He realizes that he should be kind and gentle to all animals.

He runs back to his yard and finds his family. He is happy and safe. He tells them what happened. He shows them his broken collar. He says he is sorry for being bad. He says he learned a lesson. He says he will never chase cats again. He says he will be a good dog. His family hugs him and loves him. They are proud of him. They give him a new collar. It is blue with a star on it. He likes it. He is happy and friendly.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to wander in the park with her mommy and daddy. One day, they saw the leaves changing color and falling from the trees. Her mommy told her that it was the season of autumn. 

Lily loved to play games with her friends. They would have races and see who could jump the highest. They were very competitive. One day, they decided to have a race in the park. Lily ran as fast as she could and won the race! 

After the race, Lily and her friends continued to wander in the park. They saw a big tree with lots of leaves on the ground. They decided to jump into the leaves and have fun. Lily had a great day with her friends and she couldn't wait to come back to the park again.

Tom and Sam were playing with their toy guns in the backyard. They liked to pretend they were cowboys and robbers. Tom was the cowboy and Sam was the robber. They ran around the trees and the fence, making loud noises.

"Bang, bang, I shoot you, robber!" Tom shouted.

"No, you miss, cowboy!" Sam shouted back.

They were having fun, until Aunt Jane came to visit. Aunt Jane did not like toy guns. She thought they were bad and scary. She saw Tom and Sam playing and she got angry.

"Stop that, boys! You can't play with toy guns! They are not nice!" Aunt Jane said.

She took the toy guns from Tom and Sam and threw them in the trash. Tom and Sam were sad and mad. They liked their toy guns. They did not understand why Aunt Jane did that.

"Why did you do that, Aunt Jane? We were just playing!" Tom said.

"Playing with toy guns is not playing. It is dangerous and rude. You should play with something else, like blocks or books." Aunt Jane said.

Tom and Sam did not want to play with blocks or books. They wanted to play with their toy guns. They felt uncomfortable with Aunt Jane. They wished she would go away. They looked at each other and had an idea.

They ran to the kitchen and got some spoons. They went back to the backyard and pretended the spoons were toy guns. They continued to play cowboys and robbers, making loud noises.

"Bang, bang, I shoot you, robber!" Tom shouted.

"No, you miss, cowboy!" Sam shouted back.

They smiled and winked at each other. They did not care what Aunt Jane said. They were having fun.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a toy box that was always open, and she loved to play with her toys. One day, Lily went to the park with her mom. While they were there, Lily saw a duck in the pond. She gazed at it for a long time and thought it was so pretty.

Suddenly, Lily saw a boy who had an ugly toy. It was all broken and dirty. Lily felt bad for the boy, so she went over to him and gave him one of her toys. The boy was so happy and thanked her. Lily felt happy too because she made a new friend. 

After a while, it was time to go home. Lily hugged her new friend and said goodbye. She went back to her toy box, closed it, and went to bed. She dreamt about the duck and her new friend, and she felt happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the park. One day, she found a shiny penny on the ground. She picked it up and put it in her pocket. 

As she was walking, she saw a bird high up in a tree. She wanted to say hello, so she knelt down and called out to the bird. But the bird was too high up and didn't hear her. 

Lily kept walking and soon she saw a butterfly. It was so pretty with its colorful wings. She tried to catch it in her pocket, but it flew away too fast. 

Lily had a fun day in the park and when she got home, she took the penny out of her pocket and put it in her piggy bank. She couldn't wait to go back to the park and see what other treasures she could find. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a ranch with a family of four. Mama Bear, Papa Bear, Brother Bear and Sister Bear all lived happily. They had a cozy little house and a barn full of animals.

One day, Brother Bear wanted to go explore outside the ranch. Mama Bear said that it would be okay as long as he was careful. So Brother Bear grabbed his hat and set off, feeling adventurous.

As Brother Bear walked through the desert, he noticed something strange. Across the horizon was a soft, low sound. It almost sounded like someone was crying. He followed the sound until he saw a little kitten, all alone and frightened. Brother Bear knew then that the sound he heard was the kitten weeping. 

He quickly scooped up the kitten and took it back to the ranch. Mama Bear was thrilled to see her new guest. She made a soft bed for the kitten next to the fireplace, so it would be comfortable. 

Ever since that day, the family takes good care of the kitten and everyone at the ranch is happy.

name_of_work: The Frog and the Nightingale by Vikram Seth
content: Once upon a time a frog Croaked away in Bingle Bog Every night from dusk to dawn He croaked awn and awn and awn Other creatures loathed his voice, But, alas, they had no choice, And the crass cacophony Blared out from the sumac tree At whose foot the frog each night Minstrelled on till morning night Neither stones nor prayers nor sticks. Insults or complaints or bricks Stilled the frogs determination To display his heart's elation. But one night a nightingale In the moonlight cold and pale Perched upon the sumac tree Casting forth her melody Dumbstruck sat the gaping frog And the whole admiring bog Stared towards the sumac, rapt, And, when she had ended, clapped, Ducks had swum and herons waded To her as she serenaded And a solitary loon Wept, beneath the summer moon. Toads and teals and tiddlers, captured By her voice, cheered on, enraptured: "Bravo! " "Too divine! " "Encore! " So the nightingale once more, Quite unused to such applause, Sang till dawn without a pause. Next night when the Nightingale Shook her head and twitched her tail, Closed an eye and fluffed a wing And had cleared her throat to sing She was startled by a croak. "Sorry - was that you who spoke? " She enquired when the frog Hopped towards her from the bog. "Yes," the frog replied. "You see, I'm the frog who owns this tree In this bog I've long been known For my splendid baritone And, of course, I wield my pen For Bog Trumpet now and then" "Did you... did you like my song? " "Not too bad - but far too long. The technique was fine of course, But it lacked a certain force". "Oh! " the nightingale confessed. Greatly flattered and impressed That a critic of such note Had discussed her art and throat: "I don't think the song's divine. But - oh, well - at least it's mine". "That's not much to boast about". Said the heartless frog. "Without Proper training such as I - And few others can supply. You'll remain a mere beginner. But with me you'll be a winner" "Dearest frog", the nightingale Breathed: "This is a fairy tale - And you are Mozart in disguise Come to earth before my eyes". "Well I charge a modest fee." "Oh! " "But it won't hurt, you'll see" Now the nightingale inspired, Flushed with confidence, and fired With both art and adoration, Sang - and was a huge sensation. Animals for miles around Flocked towards the magic sound, And the frog with great precision Counted heads and charged admission. Though next morning it was raining, He began her vocal training. "But I can't sing in this weather" "Come my dear - we'll sing together. Just put on your scarf and sash, Koo-oh-ah! ko-ash! ko-ash! " So the frog and nightingale Journeyed up and down the scale For six hours, till she was shivering and her voice was hoarse and quivering. Though subdued and sleep deprived, In the night her throat revived, And the sumac tree was bowed, With a breathless, titled crowd: Owl of Sandwich, Duck of Kent, Mallard and Milady Trent, Martin Cardinal Mephisto, And the Coot of Monte Cristo, Ladies with tiaras glittering In the interval sat twittering - And the frog observed them glitter With a joy both sweet and bitter. Every day the frog who'd sold her Songs for silver tried to scold her: "You must practice even longer Till your voice, like mine grows stronger. In the second song last night You got nervous in mid-flight. And, my dear, lay on more trills: Audiences enjoy such frills. You must make your public happier: Give them something sharper snappier. We must aim for better billings. You still owe me sixty shillings." Day by day the nightingale Grew more sorrowful and pale. Night on night her tired song Zipped and trilled and bounced along, Till the birds and beasts grew tired At a voice so uninspired And the ticket office gross Crashed, and she grew more morose - For her ears were now addicted To applause quite unrestricted, And to sing into the night All alone gave no delight. Now the frog puffed up with rage. "Brainless bird - you're on the stage - Use your wits and follow fashion. Puff your lungs out with your passion." Trembling, terrified to fail, Blind with tears, the nightingale Heard him out in silence, tried, Puffed up, burst a vein, and died. Said the frog: "I tried to teach her, But she was a stupid creature - Far too nervous, far too tense. Far too prone to influence. Well, poor bird - she should have known That your song must be your own. That's why I sing with panache: "Koo-oh-ah! ko-ash! ko-ash! " And the foghorn of the frog Blared unrivalled through the bog.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Lily. She lived with her parents in a big house in the forest. One day, Lily decided to explore the woods. She ran and ran until she came to a maze. The wild maze was filled with winding paths which she wanted to investigate. 

Then, Lily got lost and started to cry. Just then, a little boy appeared out of nowhere. He asked Lily why she was crying and she told him she had gotten lost. The little boy laughed and said, "It's not that hard to get out of the maze. All you have to do is take your time and follow the path!"

So Lily followed his advice and after a few minutes, she found the way back home. When she arrived, her parents welcomed her with open arms and hugs. They were so relieved that she was safe.

The moral of this story is that if you take the time to think about what you're doing, it can help you solve difficult puzzles. It will also help you stay safe in uncertain situations.

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to play with their toys. They had many toys of different colors and shapes. Sometimes they played in their room, sometimes in the living room, and sometimes in the bathroom.

One day, their mom told them to organize their toys and put them in the right boxes. She said she would be back soon and they should not make a mess. Tom and Lily nodded and said yes, mom.

Tom and Lily started to organize their toys. Tom took the red toys and put them in the red box. Lily took the blue toys and put them in the blue box. They were having fun and singing a song.

But then, Lily saw a red toy that she liked very much. It was a fire truck with a ladder and a siren. She wanted to play with it, but it was in Tom's box. She asked Tom if she could have it.

"No, Lily, this is my toy. It is red and it goes in the red box. You have your own toys in the blue box. Go away!" Tom said.

Lily felt sad and angry. She did not like Tom's answer. She thought Tom was mean and selfish. She decided to take the toy anyway. She grabbed the fire truck and ran to the bathroom.

Tom saw what Lily did and he was very mad. He ran after her and shouted, "Give me back my toy, Lily! You are a bad sister! You are a thief!"

Lily locked the door of the bathroom and laughed. She said, "No, Tom, this is my toy now. It is red and I like it. You can't have it!"

Tom banged on the door and cried. He said, "Please, Lily, open the door. Give me back my toy. Mom will be angry if she sees this. Please, Lily, please!"

But Lily did not listen. She played with the fire truck and made loud noises. She pretended to be a firefighter and put out fires. She did not care about Tom or mom.

She did not see the water running from the faucet. She did not see the water filling the sink and the tub. She did not see the water spilling on the floor and the walls. She did not see the water reaching the electric outlet.

She only saw a bright flash and heard a loud boom. Then she saw nothing and heard nothing. She was gone.

Tom heard the boom and saw the smoke. He screamed and ran away. He was scared and alone.

Mom came back and saw the disaster. She saw the fire truck and the red box. She saw the bathroom and the smoke. She saw Lily and the fire. She saw Tom and the tears.

She was shocked and sad. She hugged Tom and cried. She said, "Oh, my babies, what have you done?"

Closed like confessionals, they thread Loud noons of cities, giving back None of the glances they absorb. Light glossy grey, arms on a plaque, They come to rest at any kerb: All streets in time are visited. Then children strewn on steps or road, Or women coming from the shops Past smells of different dinners, see A wild white face that overtops Red stretcher-blankets momently As it is carried in and stowed, And sense the solving emptiness That lies just under all we do, And for a second get it whole, So permanent and blank and true. The fastened doors recede. Poor soul, They whisper at their own distress; For borne away in deadened air May go the sudden shut of loss Round something nearly at an end, And what cohered in it across The years, the unique random blend Of families and fashions, there At last begin to loosen. Far From the exchange of love to lie Unreachable inside a room The trafic parts to let go by Brings closer what is left to come, And dulls to distance all we are.

Once upon a time there was an old man and his wife. Every day they went walking in the woods. One day, the man said to his wife, "I need to find something special today. Let's follow the path until we find it."

Together, the old man and his wife followed the path until it came to a giant tree. The old man said, "I think this is the place." At the base of the tree, the old man found a pot full of gold coins and a key. He put the coins in his pocket and the key in his wife's hand.

The old man and his wife followed a long winding path until they came to a big, strong door with a big lock. His wife put the key in the lock and the door popped open. Inside was a tiny house with a very tight door.

The old man put his arm around his wife and said, "Let's go inside and make this our home." They opened the tiny, tight door and stepped into their special new home. They were very happy living together in their new home and were never separated. The end.

One day, Kiwi the Cat and Mouse the Dog were playing in the garden. They were having a lot of fun. Mouse was running around and shouting with enthusiasm, while Kiwi tried to catch her. Suddenly, Kiwi noticed something in the grass - it was an oat! She shouted excitedly and Mouse came running. They decided to share the oat and together, they ate it all up. They spent the day playing and laughing, and when it was time for bed, they said goodnight to each other and went to sleep, full and happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim liked to play outside, but he did not know how to play with others. He was ignorant about sharing and taking turns. One day, a new girl named Sue came to play with Tim. Sue was very good at playing and had a lot of fun ideas.

"Tim, let's play catch!" said Sue. Tim did not know how to play catch, but he wanted to improve and have fun too. So, Sue showed him how to throw and catch the ball. At first, Tim was not very good, but with Sue's help, he got better and better.

As they played more and more, Tim learned how to share and take turns. He was no longer ignorant and had lots of fun playing with Sue. In the end, Tim and Sue became the best of friends, and they played together every day, having lots of fun and improving their games.

name_of_work: Hearing the Battle.--July 21, 1861 by Sarah Morgan Bryan Piatt
content: One day in the dreamy summer, On the Sabbath hills, from afar We heard the solemn echoes Of the first fierce words of war. Ah, tell me, thou veiled Watcher Of the storm and the calm to come, How long by the sun or shadow Till these noises again are dumb. And soon in a hush and glimmer We thought of the dark, strange fight, Whose close in a ghastly quiet Lay dim in the beautiful night. Then we talk'd of coldness and pallor, And of things with blinded eyes That stared at the golden stillness Of the moon in those lighted skies; And of souls, at morning wrestling In the dust with passion and moan, So far away at evening In the silence of worlds unknown. But a delicate wind beside us Was rustling the dusky hours, As it gather'd the dewy odors Of the snowy jessamine-flowers. And I gave you a spray of the blossoms, And said: "I shall never know How the hearts in the land are breaking, My dearest, unless you go."
One for sorrow, Two for joy, Three for a girl, Four for a boy, Five for silver, Six for gold, Seven for a secret, Never to be told, Eight for a wish, Nine for a kiss Ten for a bird You must not miss.

Once upon a time there was a wise fisherman. He was always polishing his boat, making sure it was shiny and bright.

One day, he noticed a 3 year old child on the shore. The child was very curious and watched the fisherman as he worked. He asked the fisherman why he was always polishing.

The fisherman smiled and said, "Polishing helps keep my boat in good shape. When the weather is nice, I can sail away to explore the sea."

The child said, "Can I help you polish?" The fisherman smiled and gave the child a cloth.

The child was very careful as they polished together. When they were finished the boat was so shiny it sparkled in the sun.

The wise fisherman thanked the child and said, "I'm glad I had your help, thank you!" The child smiled, happy to have helped the wise fisherman.

Jen and her mom were at the park. Jen was so glad to be there. She loved to play with the other kids and to watch the ducks. 

Soon Jen and her mom saw a match on the ground. Jen was curious and wanted to pick it up. 

"No Jen," her mom said. "We must resist playing with fire, so you must not touch the match." 

Jen said she understood and promised not to pick it up. She was glad to listen to her mom and promised to resist the temptation. 

Then a voice sounded from behind them, "Hi there!" 

Jen turned around and saw a new friend named John. She was glad to meet him. John asked Jen if she wanted to play tag. She was very happy to do so, and soon they were having so much fun that she had forgotten all about the match.

Sara and Ben are twins. They share a room and a big mattress. They like to play and read books before bedtime. But sometimes they hear unusual noises at night. They wonder what makes the noises.

One night, they hear a loud thump under the mattress. They are scared and hug each other. They whisper, "What is that?"

They hear another thump and a squeak. They peek under the mattress and see a small mouse. The mouse is looking for food. It has a piece of cheese in its mouth.

"Hello, mouse," Sara says softly. "Are you hungry?"

The mouse stops and looks at Sara and Ben. It nods and squeaks. It seems friendly.

"Can we be your friends?" Ben asks. "We have more cheese in the kitchen."

The mouse smiles and nods again. It follows Sara and Ben to the kitchen. They give it some cheese and crackers. They play with it for a while. They name it Mimi.

Sara and Ben are happy. They have a new friend. They take Mimi back to their room and make a cozy bed for it under the mattress. They say good night and fall asleep. They do not hear any more unusual noises. They dream of cheese and crackers and Mimi.

Once upon a time, there was a daddy lion and a baby lion. The daddy was very strong, but the baby wasn't. Every day, Daddy and Baby would go for a walk and look for food.

One day, they saw a big bowl of soup. Daddy said to Baby, â€œYou can have the soup if you can reach it.â€ Baby tried and tried, but she couldn't reach it. Daddy wanted Baby to be strong, so he said. â€œIf you really want to get the soup, you have to rise.â€

So Baby tried once more. She rose and rose until she could get the soup. Daddy was so proud that Baby was strong enough to rise and get the soup!

The moral of the story is that even if you think you can't do something, you should always try and rise up -- reach higher and you can achieve anything you set your mind to!

Anna liked to play with puzzles. She had many puzzles with animals, cars, and flowers. She could make the puzzles by herself. She was independent.

One day, Anna wanted to make a new puzzle. It was a big puzzle with a castle and a dragon. She opened the box and took out the pieces. She put them on the floor and started to look for the edges.

"Can I help you, Anna?" her mom asked.

"No, thank you, mom. I can do it by myself," Anna said. She wanted to show her mom how independent she was.

Anna worked hard on the puzzle. She found the corners and the sides. She filled in the sky and the grass. She made the castle and the dragon. She was almost done. She only needed one more piece.

She looked for the last piece. She looked in the box. She looked on the floor. She looked under the sofa. She could not find it.

"Mom, I can't find the last piece. Where is it?" Anna asked.

Her mom came to see the puzzle. She smiled and pointed to Anna's pocket.

"Look, Anna. You have the last piece in your pocket. You must have put it there by mistake," her mom said.

Anna felt her pocket. She found the piece. She was happy. She put the piece in the puzzle. The puzzle was complete.

"Wow, Anna. You did a great job. You made the puzzle by yourself. You are very independent," her mom said.

"Thank you, mom. I like puzzles. They are fun. Can we make another one?" Anna asked.

name_of_work: Milton by Firelight by Gary Snyder
content: 'O Hell, what do mine eyes with grief behold?' Working with an old Singlejack miner, who can sense The vein and cleavage In the very guts of rock, can Blast granite, build Switchbacks that last for years Under the beat of snow, thaw, mule-hooves. What use, Milton, a silly story Of our lost general parents, eaters of fruit? The Indian, the chainsaw boy, And a string of six mules Came riding down to camp Hungry for tomatoes and green apples. Sleeping in saddle-blankets Under a bright night-sky Han River slantwise by morning. Jays squall Coffee boils In ten thousand years the Sierras Will be dry and dead, home of the scorpion. Ice-scratched slabs and bent trees. No paradise, no fall, Only the weathering land The wheeling sky, Man, with his Satan Scouring the chaos of the mind. Oh Hell! Fire down Too dark to read, miles from a road The bell-mare clangs in the meadow That packed dirt for a fill-in Scrambling through loose rocks On an old trail All of a summer's day.

Daybreak: the household slept. I rose, blessed by the sun. A horny fiend, I crept out with my father's gun. Let him dream of a child obedient, angel-mind- old no-sayer, robbed of power by sleep. I knew my prize who swooped home at this hour with day-light riddled eyes to his place on a high beam in our old stables, to dream light's useless time away. I stood, holding my breath, in urine-scented hay, master of life and death, a wisp-haired judge whose law would punish beak and claw. My first shot struck. He swayed, ruined, beating his only wing, as I watched, afraid by the fallen gun, a lonely child who believed death clean and final, not this obscene bundle of stuff that dropped, and dribbled through the loose straw tangling in bowels, and hopped blindly closer. I saw those eyes that did not see mirror my cruelty while the wrecked thing that could not bear the light nor hide hobbled in its own blood. My father reached my side, gave me the fallen gun. 'End what you have begun.' I fired. The blank eyes shone once into mine, and slept. I leaned my head upon my father's arm, and wept, owl blind in early sun for what I had begun

The wind was a torrent of darkness among the gusty trees, The moon was a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas, The road was a ribbon of moonlight over the purple moor, And the highwayman came riding-- Riding--riding-- The highwayman came riding, up to the old inn-door. He'd a French cocked-hat on his forehead, a bunch of lace at his chin, A coat of the claret velvet, and breeches of brown doe-skin; They fitted with never a wrinkle: his boots were up to the thigh! And he rode with a jewelled twinkle, His pistol butts a-twinkle, His rapier hilt a-twinkle, under the jewelled sky. Over the cobbles he clattered and clashed in the dark inn-yard, And he tapped with his whip on the shutters, but all was locked and barred; He whistled a tune to the window, and who should be waiting there But the landlord's black-eyed daughter, Bess, the landlord's daughter, Plaiting a dark red love-knot into her long black hair. And dark in the dark old inn-yard a stable-wicket creaked Where Tim the ostler listened; his face was white and peaked; His eyes were hollows of madness, his hair like mouldy hay, But he loved the landlord's daughter, The landlord's red-lipped daughter, Dumb as a dog he listened, and he heard the robber say "One kiss, my bonny sweetheart, I'm after a prize to-night, But I shall be back with the yellow gold before the morning light; Yet, if they press me sharply, and harry me through the day, Then look for me by moonlight, Watch for me by moonlight, I'll come to thee by moonlight, though hell should bar the way." He rose upright in the stirrups; he scarce could reach her hand, But she loosened her hair i' the casement! His face burnt like a brand As the black cascade of perfume came tumbling over his breast; And he kissed its waves in the moonlight, (Oh, sweet black waves in the moonlight!) Then he tugged at his rein in the moonlight, and galloped away to the West. He did not come in the dawning; he did not come at noon; And out o' the tawny sunset, before the rise o' the moon, When the road was a gipsy's ribbon, looping the purple moor, A red-coat troop came marching-- Marching--marching-- King George's men came marching, up to the old inn-door. They said no word to the landlord, they drank his ale instead, But they gagged his daughter and bound her to the foot of her narrow bed; Two of them knelt at her casement, with muskets at their side! There was death at every window; And hell at one dark window; For Bess could see, through her casement, the road that he would ride. They had tied her up to attention, with many a sniggering jest; They had bound a musket beside her, with the barrel beneath her breast! "Now keep good watch!" and they kissed her. She heard the dead man say-- Look for me by moonlight; Watch for me by moonlight; I'll come to thee by moonlight, though hell should bar the way! She twisted her hands behind her; but all the knots held good! She writhed her hands till her fingers were wet with sweat or blood! They stretched and strained in the darkness, and the hours crawled by like years, Till, now, on the stroke of midnight, Cold, on the stroke of midnight, The tip of one finger touched it! The trigger at least was hers! The tip of one finger touched it; she strove no more for the rest! Up, she stood up to attention, with the barrel beneath her breast, She would not risk their hearing; she would not strive again; For the road lay bare in the moonlight; Blank and bare in the moonlight; And the blood of her veins in the moonlight throbbed to her love's refrain. Tlot-tlot; tlot-tlot! Had they heard it? The horse-hoofs ringing clear; Tlot-tlot, tlot-tlot, in the distance? Were they deaf that they did not hear? Down the ribbon of moonlight, over the brow of the hill, The highwayman came riding, Riding, riding! The red-coats looked to their priming! She stood up, straight and still! Tlot-tlot, in the frosty silence! Tlot-tlot, in the echoing night! Nearer he came and nearer! Her face was like a light! Her eyes grew wide for a moment; she drew one last deep breath, Then her finger moved in the moonlight, Her musket shattered the moonlight, Shattered her breast in the moonlight and warned him--with her death. He turned; he spurred to the West; he did not know who stood Bowed, with her head o'er the musket, drenched with her own red blood! Not till the dawn he heard it, his face grew grey to hear How Bess, the landlord's daughter, The landlord's black-eyed daughter, Had watched for her love in the moonlight, and died in the darkness there. Back, he spurred like a madman, shrieking a curse to the sky, With the white road smoking behind him and his rapier brandished high! Blood-red were his spurs i' the golden noon; wine-red was his velvet coat, When they shot him down on the highway, Down like a dog on the highway, And he lay in his blood on the highway, with the bunch of lace at his throat. And still of a winter's night, they say, when the wind is in the trees, When the moon is a ghostly galleon tossed upon cloudy seas, When the road is a ribbon of moonlight over the purple moor, A highwayman comes riding-- Riding--riding-- A highwayman comes riding, up to the old inn-door. Over the cobbles he clatters and clangs in the dark inn-yard; He taps with his whip on the shutters, but all is locked and barred; He whistles a tune to the window, and who should be waiting there But the landlord's black-eyed daughter, Bess, the landlord's daughter, Plaiting a dark red love-knot into her long black hair.

My black hills have never seen the sun rising, Eternally they look north towards Armagh. Lot's wife would not be salt if she had been Incurious as my black hills that are happy When dawn whitens Glassdrummond chapel. My hills hoard the bright shillings of March While the sun searches in every pocket. They are my Alps and I have climbed the Matterhorn With a sheaf of hay for three perishing calves In the field under the Big Forth of Rocksavage. The sleety winds fondle the rushy beards of Shancoduff While the cattle-drovers sheltering in the Featherna Bush Look up and say: "Who owns them hungry hills That the water-hen and snipe must have forsaken? A poet? Then by heavens he must be poor." I hear, and is my heart not badly shaken?

Anna liked to play with her toy piano. She had many songs in her head that she wanted to make. She pressed the keys and made sounds. Sometimes she sang along. She felt happy when she played.

One day, her mom came to her room and said, "Anna, it's time to go to the park. Do you want to come?"

Anna nodded. She liked the park. There were swings and slides and flowers. She put on her shoes and coat and followed her mom.

On the way to the park, they passed by a street musician. He had a guitar and a hat. He played and sang songs that Anna did not know. But they sounded nice. Anna stopped and listened.

"Mom, can we stay and hear him?" she asked.

"Sure, honey. He's very good, isn't he?" her mom said.

Anna smiled. She liked the musician. He reminded her of her toy piano. He made music with his fingers and voice. She wanted to make music like him.

She took a coin from her pocket and put it in his hat. The musician saw her and smiled. He said, "Thank you, little girl. You are very kind. Do you like music?"

Anna nodded. She said, "Yes, I do. I have a toy piano. I play and sing songs."

The musician said, "That's wonderful. You are a musician too. Keep playing and singing. You will make many people happy."

Anna felt glad. She said, "Thank you, sir. You make me happy too."

She waved goodbye and went to the park with her mom. She had a fun day. But she also thought of the musician. She wanted to see him again. She wanted to hear more songs. She wanted to learn from him. She wanted to be a musician too.

name_of_work: Reflections Irregular by John Rollin Ridge
content: I cast a backward look--how changed The scenes of other days! I walk, a wearied man, estranged From youth's delightful ways. There in the distance rolleth yet That stream whose waves my Boyish bosom oft has met, When pleasure lit mine eye. It rolleth yet, as clear, as bold, As pure as it did then; But I have grown in youth-time old, And, mixing now with men, My sobered eye must not attend To that sweet stream, my early friend! The music of its waters clear Must now but seldom reach my ear, But murmur still now carelessly To every heedless passer-by. How often o'er its rugged cliffs I've strayed, And gaily listened, as its billows played Such deep, low music at their base-- And then such brightening thoughts would trace Upon the tablet of my mind! Alas, those days have run their race, Their joys I nowhere now can find. I have no time to think Of climbing Glory's sunny mount I have no time to drink At Learning's bubbling fount! Now corn and potatoes call me From scenes were wont to enthrall me-- A weary wight, Both day and night My brain is full of business matters, Reality has snatched the light, From fancy's head, that shone so bright, And tore the dreams she wove, to tatters!

Once there was a little boy who had to clean his room. He was very calm as he moved around and made sure that everything was cleared up. Then he saw it, a gigantic chunk of beef hidden under his bed. 

He asked his mom: "Mom, why is this beef in my room?". His mom took a deep breath and replied, "we were planning to have beef for dinner tonight but it looks like it has been here since last week". 

The little boy did not understand what was happening and started to scream,"I want to keep the beef! I want to eat it!".

His mom sighed and said, "No, we can't keep it, it is not clean anymore. We need to throw it away. Promise me that you will clean up the room after and I'll cook something else for dinner". 

The little boy crossed his arms and grumbled but he understood that he was not going to get to enjoy the beef anymore. Sullenly, he grabbed his cleaning supplies and started tidying up his room. 

At the end of the day, his room was back in perfect shape and the family had a calm meal of vegetables and pasta. The little boy was content with his day, even if there was no beef for dinner.

name_of_work: A Different History by Sujata Bhatt
content: Great Pan is not dead; he simply emigrated to India. Here, the gods roam freely, disguised as snakes or monkeys; every tree is sacred and it is a sin to be rude to a book. It is a sin to shove a book aside with your foot, a sin to slam books down hard on a table, a sin to toss one carelessly across a room. You must learn how to turn the pages gently without disturbing Sarasvati, without offending the tree from whose wood the paper was made. Which language has not been the oppressor's tongue? Which language truly meant to murder someone? And how does it happen that after the torture, after the soul has been cropped with a long scythe swooping out of the conqueror's face - the unborn grandchildren grow to love that strange language.
