name_of_work: Love & Fame & Death by Charles Bukowski
content: it sits outside my window now like and old woman going to market; it sits and watches me, it sweats nevously through wire and fog and dog-bark until suddenly I slam the screen with a newspaper like slapping at a fly and you could hear the scream over this plain city, and then it left. the way to end a poem like this is to become suddenly quiet.

name_of_work: Ring Out Wild Bells by Alfred Tennyson
content: Ring out, wild bells, to the wild sky, The flying cloud, the frosty light: The year is dying in the night; Ring out, wild bells, and let him die. Ring out the old, ring in the new, Ring, happy bells, across the snow: The year is going, let him go; Ring out the false, ring in the true. Ring out the grief that saps the mind For those that here we see no more; Ring out the feud of rich and poor, Ring in redress to all mankind. Ring out a slowly dying cause, And ancient forms of party strife; Ring in the nobler modes of life, With sweeter manners, purer laws. Ring out the want, the care, the sin, The faithless coldness of the times; Ring out, ring out my mournful rhymes But ring the fuller minstrel in. Ring out false pride in place and blood, The civic slander and the spite; Ring in the love of truth and right, Ring in the common love of good. Ring out old shapes of foul disease; Ring out the narrowing lust of gold; Ring out the thousand wars of old, Ring in the thousand years of peace. Ring in the valiant man and free, The larger heart, the kindlier hand; Ring out the darkness of the land, Ring in the Christ that is to be.

Ben and Lily are friends. They like to play with toys. Ben has a big truck. Lily has a doll. They share their toys sometimes.

One day, Lily wants to play with Ben's truck. She asks him, "Can I lend your truck, please?"

Ben says, "No, you can't. It is my truck. You have your doll."

Lily feels sad. She says, "But I like your truck. It is big and red. My doll is small and pink. Can we trade?"

Ben says, "No, we can't. I don't like dolls. They are boring. Go away."

Lily gets angry. She says, "You are mean. You are not a good friend. I don't want to play with you anymore."

She tries to grab the truck from Ben. Ben pulls it back. They fight over the truck. The truck falls on the ground. It breaks. One of its legs comes off.

Ben and Lily stop fighting. They look at the broken truck. They feel sorry. They say, "Oh no. What have we done?"

They look at each other. They say, "I'm sorry. I was wrong. Can we be friends again?"

They hug. They say, "Yes, we can. We are friends. We can share our toys."

They pick up the broken truck and the doll. They go to Ben's mom. They say, "Mom, can you fix the truck, please? It has a broken leg."

Ben's mom says, "Of course, I can. But first, you have to clean your hands. They are dirty from fighting."

Ben and Lily say, "OK, mom. We will clean our hands. We will not fight again. We will be nice to each other."

They go to the sink. They wash their hands. They smile. They are happy. They are friends.

Once upon a time, there was a little duck who lived in a pond. The duck was very happy because all his friends lived in the pond too. They played together every day and had lots of fun.

One day, it rained a lot and the pond became very muddy. The little duck got very dirty and didn't like it. He wished the mud would go away. He said, "Please make the mud go away. I don't like it!"

The next day, the little duck woke up and all his friends were gone. He was very lonely and sad. He looked around and saw that the pond was now completely covered in mud. The little duck realized that his friends had left because they didn't like the muddy pond. The little duck was now all alone and very sad.

Lily and Ben were making cookies with Mom. They had a big ball of dough and some shapes to cut out. Lily wanted to make stars and Ben wanted to make circles.

"Look, Mom, I made a star!" Lily said, holding up her cookie. "It is pretty!"

"Good job, Lily!" Mom said. "Now put it on the tray."

Ben tried to cut out a circle, but his shape was too big. He pushed hard on the dough, but it did not fit. He got angry and threw his shape on the floor.

"Ben, what are you doing?" Mom asked. "Don't throw things!"

"I can't make a circle!" Ben said. "It is too hard!"

Mom picked up the shape and showed Ben how to make it smaller. She rolled the dough and cut out a smaller circle. She gave it to Ben and smiled.

"See, Ben, you can make a circle!" Mom said. "It is easy!"

Ben looked at his circle and felt happy. He said sorry to Mom and put his cookie on the tray.

"Thank you, Mom!" Ben said. "You are nice!"

Mom hugged Lily and Ben and put the tray in the oven. She said they had to wait for the cookies to bake. They cleaned up the table and washed their hands.

Soon, the cookies were ready. They smelled yummy and looked yummy. Mom took them out of the oven and let them cool. She gave Lily and Ben each a cookie and a glass of milk.

"Here you go, Lily and Ben!" Mom said. "You made yummy cookies!"

Lily and Ben bit into their cookies and smiled. They liked their cookies. They liked their shapes. They liked their Mom.

"Mom, you are the best!" Lily and Ben said. "We love you!"

Mom kissed Lily and Ben and said she loved them too. They ate their cookies and drank their milk. They were happy.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Lucy who loved playing outside. One day she saw a big gray bird in the sky. Lucy wanted to catch the bird so she began to chase it. But when she jumped too high to reach it, she fell and spoiled her new shoes. 

Lucy was very sad because she knew her mom wouldn't be happy. That night, Lucy promised not to waste any more of her things. 

A few weeks later, a gray cloud appeared in the sky. While Lucy watched the cloud rain came down and filled the bucket that she'd left outside. It felt so good to save the water and not waste it. Lucy was so proud of herself for not spoiling any more of her things!

Once upon a time, there was a small boy named Tommy. He was three years old and loved to explore the forest with his parents. One day, Tommy and his parents were walking through the woods and Tommy decided to rush ahead of them.

Suddenly, he heard a rustling sound and looked up. There, perched upon a branch, was an owl. The owl looked very majestic with its big eyes and smooth feathers. Tommy was amazed and ran over to get a closer look.

The owl spoke suddenly, â€œHello little one! What is your name?â€

Tommy smiled and said, â€œMy name is Tommy.â€

â€œWell, it is very nice to meet you Tommy!â€ said the owl.

Tommy and the owl talked for a little while and then Tommyâ€™s parents caught up to him.

â€œTommy, there you are!â€ said his mom. â€œWe were worried that you had gotten lost.â€

Tommy told his mom about the owl and then the three of them said goodbye to the owl and rushed home together.

name_of_work: The Instruction Manual by John Ashbery
content: As I sit looking out of a window of the building I wish I did not have to write the instruction manual on the uses of a new metal. I look down into the street and see people, each walking with an inner peace, And envy them--they are so far away from me! Not one of them has to worry about getting out this manual on schedule. And, as my way is, I begin to dream, resting my elbows on the desk and leaning out of the window a little, Of dim Guadalajara! City of rose-colored flowers! City I wanted most to see, and most did not see, in Mexico! But I fancy I see, under the press of having to write the instruction manual, Your public square, city, with its elaborate little bandstand! The band is playing Scheherazade by Rimsky-Korsakov. Around stand the flower girls, handing out rose- and lemon-colored flowers, Each attractive in her rose-and-blue striped dress (Oh! such shades of rose and blue), And nearby is the little white booth where women in green serve you green and yellow fruit. The couples are parading; everyone is in a holiday mood. First, leading the parade, is a dapper fellow Clothed in deep blue. On his head sits a white hat And he wears a mustache, which has been trimmed for the occasion. His dear one, his wife, is young and pretty; her shawl is rose, pink, and white. Her slippers are patent leather, in the American fashion, And she carries a fan, for she is modest, and does not want the crowd to see her face too often. But everybody is so busy with his wife or loved one I doubt they would notice the mustachioed man's wife. Here come the boys! They are skipping and throwing little things on the sidewalk Which is made of gray tile. One of them, a little older, has a toothpick in his teeth. He is silenter than the rest, and affects not to notice the pretty young girls in white. But his friends notice them, and shout their jeers at the laughing girls. Yet soon all this will cease, with the deepening of their years, And love bring each to the parade grounds for another reason. But I have lost sight of the young fellow with the toothpick. Wait--there he is--on the other side of the bandstand, Secluded from his friends, in earnest talk with a young girl Of fourteen or fifteen. I try to hear what they are saying But it seems they are just mumbling something--shy words of love, probably. She is slightly taller than he, and looks quietly down into his sincere eyes. She is wearing white. The breeze ruffles her long fine black hair against her olive cheek. Obviously she is in love. The boy, the young boy with the toothpick, he is in love too; His eyes show it. Turning from this couple, I see there is an intermission in the concert. The paraders are resting and sipping drinks through straws (The drinks are dispensed from a large glass crock by a lady in dark blue), And the musicians mingle among them, in their creamy white uniforms, and talk About the weather, perhaps, or how their kids are doing at school. Let us take this opportunity to tiptoe into one of the side streets. Here you may see one of those white houses with green trim That are so popular here. Look--I told you! It is cool and dim inside, but the patio is sunny. An old woman in gray sits there, fanning herself with a palm leaf fan. She welcomes us to her patio, and offers us a cooling drink. "My son is in Mexico City," she says. "He would welcome you too If he were here. But his job is with a bank there. Look, here is a photograph of him." And a dark-skinned lad with pearly teeth grins out at us from the worn leather frame. We thank her for her hospitality, for it is getting late And we must catch a view of the city, before we leave, from a good high place. That church tower will do--the faded pink one, there against the fierce blue of the sky. Slowly we enter. The caretaker, an old man dressed in brown and gray, asks us how long we have been in the city, and how we like it here. His daughter is scrubbing the steps--she nods to us as we pass into the tower. Soon we have reached the top, and the whole network of the city extends before us. There is the rich quarter, with its houses of pink and white, and its crumbling, leafy terraces. There is the poorer quarter, its homes a deep blue. There is the market, where men are selling hats and swatting flies And there is the public library, painted several shades of pale green and beige. Look! There is the square we just came from, with the promenaders. There are fewer of them, now that the heat of the day has increased, But the young boy and girl still lurk in the shadows of the bandstand. And there is the home of the little old lady-- She is still sitting in the patio, fanning herself. How limited, but how complete withal, has been our experience of Guadalajara! We have seen young love, married love, and the love of an aged mother for her son. We have heard the music, tasted the drinks, and looked at colored houses. What more is there to do, except stay? And that we cannot do. And as a last breeze freshens the top of the weathered old tower, I turn my gaze Back to the instruction manual which has made me dream of Guadalajara.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily's mom brought home a newspaper. The newspaper was very old and had lots of words and pictures inside. 

Lily was very curious and wanted to see the newspaper. Her mom held the newspaper and showed it to her. Lily looked at the pictures and tried to read the words, but they were too hard for her. 

Lily's mom told her that the newspaper was from a long time ago and had important news in it. Lily thought it was cool to hold something that was so old and important. From that day on, Lily loved looking at the old newspaper and imagining what life was like a long time ago.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy had a pair of boots that he loved to wear. They were his favorite boots because they were the original ones that his grandma gave him.

One day, Timmy went outside to play in the snow. He was having fun until he noticed that his boots were starting to freeze. "Oh no!" Timmy said, "My boots are frozen! What should I do?"

Just then, Timmy's friend Billy came over. "Hey Timmy, what's wrong?" Billy asked. "My boots are frozen and I can't move," Timmy replied. Billy had an idea. He went inside and got a hairdryer to warm up Timmy's boots. After a few minutes, Timmy's boots were no longer frozen and he was able to play again. Timmy was so happy and grateful to have such a good friend like Billy.

What am I? I am Earth the mother, With all her nebulous memories; And the young Day, and Night her brother, And every god that was and is. As Eve I walked in paradise, Dreaming of nations, braving death For knowledge; nor begrudged the price When the first baby first drew breath. I sang Deborah's triumph song; I struck the foe with Judith's sword; 'Twas I who to the angel said, "Behold the handmaid of the Lord!" I was fair Helen, she for whom A nation was content to die; And Cleopatra, in whose doom The world went down with Antony. I am the harlot in the street, And the veiled nun all undefiled; In me must queen and beggar meet, Wise age hark to the little child. I am the life that ever is, And the new glory that shall be; The pain that dies, and the brave bliss That mounts to immortality.

Lily and Ben were playing in their room. They liked to pretend they were in different places. Sometimes they were pirates, sometimes they were astronauts, sometimes they were fairies.

Today they wanted to be kings and queens. They looked for some clothes to wear in their wardrobe. They found a big red cloak, a shiny crown, a long blue dress and a furry cape. They put them on and felt very royal.

"Let's go to our castle," said Lily. "We can have a tea party with our friends."

"OK," said Ben. "But who will we include in our tea party?"

Lily thought for a moment. She looked around the room and saw her teddy bear, her doll, her robot and her book. She smiled and said, "We can include all of them. They are our loyal subjects."

Ben nodded and said, "That sounds fun. Let's go."

They picked up their toys and carried them to their castle. Their castle was a big cardboard box that their dad had brought home. It had windows and a door and a flag on top. They put their toys inside and sat down on some pillows.

They pretended to pour tea from a plastic pot and eat cookies from a paper plate. They talked to their toys and asked them how they were. They had a lot of fun.

But then they heard their mom calling them. "Lily, Ben, it's time for lunch. Come downstairs, please."

They looked at each other and sighed. They didn't want to leave their castle. They wanted to play more.

"Can we come back later?" asked Lily.

"Of course," said Ben. "Our castle will be here. And our toys will be dry and warm in the wardrobe."

They took off their clothes and put them back in the wardrobe. They hugged their toys and said goodbye. They left their castle and went downstairs.

They hoped they could play again soon. They loved being kings and queens.

name_of_work: Full Moon and Little Frieda by Ted Hughes
content: A cool small evening shrunk to a dog bark and the clank of a bucket - And you listening. A spider's web, tense for the dew's touch. A pail lifted, still and brimming - mirror To tempt a first star to a tremor. Cows are going home in the lane there, looping the hedges with their warm wreaths of breath - A dark river of blood, many boulders, Balancing unspilled milk. 'Moon!' you cry suddenly, 'Moon! Moon!' The moon has stepped back like an artist gazing amazed at a work That points at him amazed.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a house with her mommy and daddy. Lily loved to play outside and see her neighbors. One day, Lily's mommy told her to be quiet because the neighbor was sleeping. Lily didn't know what that meant, but she learned that being quiet means not making any noise. From that day on, Lily always tried to be quiet when she saw her neighbor sleeping. The end.

Lily likes to dress up in her mom's clothes. She finds a big hat, a long dress, and some shiny shoes. She looks in the mirror and smiles. She feels like a princess.

She wants to show her mom how pretty she is. She runs to the kitchen, where her mom is making lunch. She says, "Mom, look at me! I am a princess!"

Her mom turns around and sees Lily. She laughs and hugs her. She says, "You are a beautiful princess, Lily. I love your outfit. Did you make it yourself?"

Lily nods. She says, "Yes, I did. I also made a poem for you. Do you want to hear it?"

Her mom says, "Of course, I do. Let me hear your poem, Lily."

Lily clears her throat and says, "Mom, you are the best. You make me happy and fed. You are always kind and sweet. You are my favorite treat."

Her mom claps and kisses her. She says, "That is a wonderful poem, Lily. You are very clever and creative. I am so proud of you."

Lily beams and says, "Thank you, mom. I love you."

They hug and smile. They are happy.

Some people would deny that I'm Jamaican British. Anglo nose. Hair straight. No way I can be Jamaican British. They think I say I'm black when I say Jamaican British but the English boys at school made me choose Jamaican, British? Half-caste, half mule, house slave - Jamaican British. Light skin, straight male, privileged - Jamaican British. Eat callaloo, plantain, jerk chicken - I'm Jamaican British don't know how to serve our dishes, they enslaved us. In school I fought a boy in the lunch hall - Jamaican. At home, told Dad I hate dem, all dem Jamaicans - I'm British. He laughed, said you cannot love sugar and hate your sweetness, took me straight to Jamaica - passport, British. Cousins in Kingston called me Jah-English, proud to have someone in their family - British. Plantation lineage, World War service, how do I serve Jamaican British? When knowing how to war is Jamaican British. Give I want to climb towards him, the one who is not in the ground. He is sat somewhere with his brother scooping jelly from the inside of a coconut. White afro comb, vaseline and blue ironed shirts, looking sharp as the grief that drapes my body. If he saw his shirts on my back and his afro comb in my hair, he would stroke his white beard and call me revivalist. Away It's the grief talking, asking the dead why they aren't here. That's all it wants to know. I have his shirt, I even kept the ones he never wore, the green one that shrunk and smells of mothballs in closed cupboards. His Clothes Give away his clothes all things of his will still fit in this jumbled world. When He Died I told no one how old he was, in case his death seemed too inevitable. When asked his age, I made him years younger, needing their understanding - he was taken from me too soon.

name_of_work: A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning by John Donne
content: As virtuous men pass mildly away, And whisper to their souls to go, Whilst some of their sad friends do say The breath goes now, and some say, No: So let us melt, and make no noise, No tear-floods, nor sigh-tempests move; 'Twere profanation of our joys To tell the laity our love. Moving of th' earth brings harms and fears, Men reckon what it did, and meant; But trepidation of the spheres, Though greater far, is innocent. Dull sublunary lovers' love (Whose soul is sense) cannot admit Absence, because it doth remove Those things which elemented it. But we by a love so much refined, That our selves know not what it is, Inter-assured of the mind, Care less, eyes, lips, and hands to miss. Our two souls therefore, which are one, Though I must go, endure not yet A breach, but an expansion, Like gold to airy thinness beat. If they be two, they are two so As stiff twin compasses are two; Thy soul, the fixed foot, makes no show To move, but doth, if the other do. And though it in the center sit, Yet when the other far doth roam, It leans and hearkens after it, And grows erect, as that comes home. Such wilt thou be to me, who must, Like th' other foot, obliquely run; Thy firmness makes my circle just, And makes me end where I begun.

Lily and Ben were playing in the park with their ball. They liked to kick the ball to each other and run after it. Sometimes they missed the ball and it rolled away. They always ran to get it back.

One time, the ball rolled too far and went into the street. Lily and Ben saw a big car coming fast. They stopped and waited for the car to pass. But the car did not pass. It stopped next to the ball and a man got out. He picked up the ball and looked at it.

"Hey, this is a nice ball," the man said. "I think I'll keep it."

Lily and Ben were angry and scared. They wanted their ball back. They ran to the man and said, "No, that's our ball. Give it back!"

The man laughed and said, "No, it's mine now. Go away, you little brats."

He got back in his car and tried to drive away. But he could not. Another car was behind him. It was a police car. A police officer got out and walked to the man's car. He had a badge and a hat.

"Sir, what are you doing?" the police officer asked. "Why did you take that ball from those kids?"

The man lied and said, "It's my ball. I bought it yesterday."

The police officer did not believe him. He said, "No, you didn't. I saw you take it from them. That's not nice. That's stealing. You have to give it back."

The man refused. He said, "No, I won't. It's mine. Go away."

The police officer was not happy. He said, "Sir, you have to give it back or I will arrest you. You have to follow the rules."

The man still refused. He said, "No, I don't. You can't make me."

The police officer said, "Yes, I can. You are under arrest. Get out of the car."

He opened the door and pulled the man out. He put handcuffs on him and put him in the back of the police car. He took the ball and gave it back to Lily and Ben.

"Here you go, kids. I'm sorry this man took your ball. He was very bad. You did the right thing by telling me. You are very brave and smart."

Lily and Ben thanked the police officer. They were very happy to have their ball back. They hugged the ball and each other. They thought the police officer was very nice and cool. They thought the man was very mean and silly. They thought the whole thing was very interesting. They went back to the park and played with their ball. They had a lot of fun.

Lily loves books. She likes to look at the pictures and hear the stories. Sometimes she tries to read the words by herself. She wants to learn more books.

Today is Lily's birthday. She is very happy. She has a cake with candles and a big balloon. She also has some presents. She opens them with her mom and dad.

One of the presents is a book. It is a brilliant book. It has many colors and shapes and animals. It also has a surprise. When Lily opens the book, it makes a sound. It says "Hello, Lily! Happy birthday!"

Lily is amazed. She laughs and claps her hands. She says "Thank you, thank you!" She hugs the book and her mom and dad. She wants to hear the book again and again. She receives a brilliant book and a lot of love.

Once upon a time, there was a squirrel named Sam. He was very curious and loved to explore his surroundings. One day, Sam saw something interesting on the ground. It was an acorn! 

Sam said to himself, "This looks interesting. I'm going to pick it up and take it home!" So he grabbed the acorn and held it tightly in his front paws.

Sam started to walk back to his tree house but then he stopped. He had completely forgotten what he was doing. He thought it over for a minute and then he remembered, "Oh yeah! I was going to take the acorn home with me!" 

So Sam kept on walking until he reached his tree house. When he got there, he placed the acorn on his bed and he said, "I'm not going to quit until I figure out what it is." 

The next day, Sam did some research and learned that the acorn was a type of nut. He was so excited to learn something new, that he couldn't quit smiling. 

And so, Sam decided to save the acorn as a reminder of his new discovery. From then on, every time he passed by the same spot, he would always take a moment to take a look at the interesting acorn and remember the day he learned something new.

Once upon a time, there was a purple bird named Polly. Polly loved to cook. One day, she found a big grape in her garden. She was very happy.

Polly had a friend named Timmy. Timmy was a small green frog. Polly said to Timmy, "Look at the big grape I found! Let's cook something yummy with it." Timmy was excited and said, "Yes, let's do it!"

Together, Polly and Timmy cooked a yummy grape pie. They shared the pie with their friends. Everyone loved the pie and they all had a fun day.

Ben loves his scooter. He rides it every day in the park. He likes to go fast and make turns. He is very good at it.

One day, he sees a big ramp in the park. He wants to try it. He thinks it will be fun to jump with his scooter. He is very enthusiastic.

He rides his scooter to the ramp. He sees some older kids there. They are also jumping with their scooters. They are doing tricks and flips. They are very cool.

Ben waits for his turn. He is a little nervous, but also excited. He says to himself, "I can do this. I can jump with my scooter."

He pushes his scooter hard. He goes up the ramp. He feels the wind in his face. He lifts his scooter in the air. He jumps with his scooter. He is very happy.

He lands on the other side of the ramp. He hears some clapping. He looks around. He sees the older kids. They are smiling at him. They say, "Wow, that was awesome. You are very brave. You can jump with your scooter."

Ben feels proud. He says, "Thank you. You are very nice. You can jump with your scooters too."

He makes some new friends. They jump with their scooters together. They have a lot of fun. Ben loves his scooter.

Once upon a time there was a modern bush. It was green and fluffy and it was the most beautiful bush in the world. Every day, a little boy came to the bush and he would rock it very carefully. He would rock it back and forth and the bush would shake and sway. The little boy would laugh and smile as he rocked the bush and the bush would sway back and forth with the wind.

The little boy rocked the bush every day, and soon the bush was very happy. It was so happy that it began to dance! The little boy and the bush would dance and sway together in the sunshine. They would dance until they were very tired and then the little boy would rest and the bush would go back to sleep.

The little boy and the modern bush were very happy together. Every day, the little boy would come back and rock the bush and the bush would dance and sway with joy. Those were very special days for the little boy and the modern bush.

O generation of the thoroughly smug and thoroughly uncomfortable, I have seen fishermen picnicking in the sun, I have seen them with untidy families, I have seen their smiles full of teeth and heard ungainly laughter. And I am happier than you are, And they were happier than I am; And the fish swim in the lake and do not even own clothing.

One day, Sam was playing in the garden when he heard a noise. He went to investigate and saw a little bird stuck in a bush. Sam jumped to try and help the bird, but it only flapped its wings in fear.

"Don't be scared! What can I do to help you?" asked Sam.

The bird replied,"I am stuck in the ash bush and can't get out!" 

"Let me try!" said Sam and he began to move the bush from side to side. After a few tries, the bird was set free!

Sam and the bird were both relieved and looked at each other with a calm smile. 

"Thank you for helping me!" said the bird, before flying away.

Sam was very happy and watched the bird as it flew up towards the sky. He waved goodbye and then went back to play in the garden.

Once there was a pepper. It was red, round, and smelled very nice. The pepper was lonely, so it decided to go on an adventure. First, it rolled out of the garden and onto the street. It rolled and rolled until it felt dizzy. The pepper was so dizzy it couldn't see right. Then, it felt someone pick it up. It was a little boy! He smiled and put the pepper in his pocket. The pepper was happy to have someone to keep it company. Together, they explored the park and even flew a kite. The pepper and the little boy were fast friends and had lots of fun. The pepper never felt so happy and never wanted the day to end.

name_of_work: Living in Sin by Adrienne Rich
content: She had thought the studio would keep itself; no dust upon the furniture of love. Half heresy, to wish the taps less vocal, the panes relieved of grime. A plate of pears, a piano with a Persian shawl, a cat stalking the picturesque amusing mouse had risen at his urging. Not that at five each separate stair would writhe under the milkman's tramp; that morning light so coldly would delineate the scraps of last night's cheese and three sepulchral bottles; that on the kitchen shelf amoong the saucers a pair of beetle-eyes would fix her own-- envoy from some village in the moldings... Meanwhile, he, with a yawn, sounded a dozen notes upon the keyboard, declared it out of tune, shrugged at the mirror, rubbed at his beard, went out for cigarettes; while she, jeered by the minor demons, pulled back the sheets and made the bed and found a towel to dust the table-top, and let the coffee-pot boil over on the stove. By evening she was back in love again, though not so wholly but throughout the night she woke sometimes to feel the daylight coming like a relentless milkman up the stairs.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. He had a new toy car that he loved to play with every day. One day, Timmy accidentally spilled some juice on his toy car and it got all sticky. 

Timmy's mom saw what happened and told him they needed to wash the car. They went to the lab where his mom worked and used soap and water to clean the car. Timmy was happy to see his toy car looking new again. 

After they finished washing the car, Timmy's mom showed him some new toys in the lab. Timmy was excited to play with them and thanked his mom for taking him to the lab. From that day on, Timmy made sure to be careful with his toys so he wouldn't have to wash them again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lucy. She was three years old and loved to travel. One day, Lucy decided to go on a fancy journey. She packed her bag with some clothes and some tasty peanuts. She was so excited! 

On her journey, Lucy stumbled across a tall, old tree in the middle of the forest. She was so curious, so she ventured closer to explore. As she got closer, Lucy heard someone talking to her! 

"Hello! Where are you going?" asked the voice. Lucy was surprised, she had never seen a talking tree before. 

"I'm going on a fancy journey," said Lucy. "Would you like to come with me?"

The tree was delighted and said, "Yes! I would love to join you on your travels." So off they went, Lucy and the talking tree, on a fancy journey together!

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily who loved to collect pebbles. She had a big jar filled with all kinds of pebbles she found at the park. One day, she found a very special pebble that was shiny and had a heart shape. She was so happy and showed it to her mom.

"Mommy, look at this pretty pebble I found! Do you think it's famous?" asked Lily.

"Well, it could be famous if you make it famous," replied her mom.

Lily had an idea. She decided to marry the pebble and make it famous. She put the pebble in a small box and decorated it with flowers. She invited all her friends and family to the wedding.

During the wedding, Lily said, "I now pronounce you pebble and wife. You may kiss the bride!" Everyone laughed and had a good time. From that day on, Lily's pebble became famous and she was known as the girl who married a pebble.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Abbie. She loved to go outside and ride her bike. She always remembered to wear her helmet to keep her safe. 

Today was a very special day because Abbie was given a unique helmet. It was purple and sparkly, it had a picture of a puppy on the front. Abbie was so excited she wanted to try it right away.

She put it on and hopped on her bike. She rode around the street, up the hill and down the driveway. It was so much fun with her new helmet.

When she got back inside, Abbie thanked her parents for her new helmet. She was so grateful and couldn't imagine ever having a cooler helmet. Abbie was so happy she could ride around with her shiny, special and unique helmet.

Once upon a time there was a small, eager boy named Charlie. Charlie's parents took him on safari, and he was so excited. He followed the guide who was leading the group through the thick jungle. 

As they journeyed along, Charlie spotted a lion in the distance. He eagerly ran up to his father and said, "Daddy, look! A lion!" His dad smiled, and they halted to watch the magnificent animal as it walked across the savannah.

The guide laughed and said to Charlie, "Do you want to follow him, Charlie? We could watch him up close if you like." 
Charlie's eyes lit up, and he nodded his head eagerly. His parents and the guide followed Charlie as he cautiously tiptoed towards the mighty lion. The lion roared and jumped away, but Charlie kept his eyes closed the entire time. 

The safari ended shortly after, and Charlie was still full of excitement from his encounter with the lion. He couldn't wait to tell all of his friends about his amazing adventure.

name_of_work: The Machinist, Teaching His Daughter to Play the Piano by B.H. Fairchild
content: The brown wrist and hand with its raw knuckles and blue nails packed with dirt and oil, pause in mid-air, the fingers arched delicately, and she mimics him, hand held just so, the wrist loose, then swooping down to the wrong chord. She lifts her hand and tries again. Drill collars rumble, hammering the nubbin-posts. The helper lifts one, turning it slowly, then lugs it into the lathe's chuck. The bit shears the dull iron into new metal, falling into the steady chant of lathe work, and the machinist lights a cigarette, holding in his upturned palms the polonaise he learned at ten, then later the easiest waltzes, etudes, impossible counterpoint like the voice of his daughter he overhears one night standing in the backyard. She is speaking to herself but not herself, as in prayer, the listener is some version of herself, and the names are pronounced carefully, self-consciously: Chopin, Mozart, Scarlatti., . . . these gestures of voice and hands suspended over the keyboard that move like the lathe in its turning toward music, the wind dragging the hoist chain, the ring of iron on iron in the holding rack. His daughter speaks to him one night, but not to him, rather someone created between them, a listener, there and not there, a master of lathes, a student of music.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Rita. Rita was three years old. She was trying to figure out what to do when she saw an old man walking by.

"Hello!" Rita said cheerfully.

"Hello, little one," the old man replied. "Where are you headed?"

Rita hesitated, unsure how to answer.

The old man smiled. "I can provide you with something special," he said.

Rita was curious. "What is it?" she asked.

The old man produced a small box from his pocket. Inside was a tiny heart made of glass.

"This is a heart," the old man explained. "It will be useful for you to have."

Rita was excited. "Thank you," she said gratefully.

The old man patted her head. "Always remember," he said. "This heart is full of love. Keep it safe and it will provide you with much joy."

Rita hugged the heart tightly and ran off, full of joy and excitement.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to play outside. One day, she saw a big, scary dog and her leg started to tremble. 

Her mom asked, "What's wrong, Lily?" 

"I'm scared of the dog," Lily said. 

"Don't worry, I'll be with you," her mom said. 

But Lily wanted to be independent and face her fear. So she took a deep breath and walked slowly towards the dog. 

The dog barked, but Lily didn't tremble anymore. She stood tall and said, "Hello, doggy. Do you want to play?" 

The dog wagged its tail and Lily played with it all afternoon. From that day on, Lily felt brave and independent, and she wasn't scared of anything anymore.

Tim and Mia like to play with their bikes. They have red bikes with big wheels. They ride their bikes on the road near their house. The road is long and smooth. Sometimes they race each other to see who is faster.

One day, they see a big hill on the road. They have never seen it before. It looks fun and scary. Tim says, "Let's go down the hill on our bikes. It will be fast and fun." Mia says, "OK, but be careful. The hill is very steep. We have to brake hard at the bottom."

They pedal hard and go up the hill. They feel the wind in their hair. They reach the top and look down. The hill is very high and long. They see a sharp turn at the bottom. They feel excited and nervous.

They say, "Ready, set, go!" and start to go down the hill. They go faster and faster. They feel like they are flying. They laugh and shout. They slide on their bikes. They are having fun.

But they are going too fast. They can't brake hard enough. They can't turn in time. They slide off the road and into the grass. They fall off their bikes and roll on the ground. They are not hurt, but they are dirty and scared.

They look at each other and say, "Wow, that was fast and fun. But also scary and dangerous. Maybe we should not go down the hill again. Maybe we should play somewhere else." They pick up their bikes and walk back to their house. They hug each other and say, "We are glad we are OK. We are good friends." They are happy.

Jimmy and his mommy were walking in the subway. Jimmy saw some old, disgusting posters up on the walls. "Mommy, can we decorate the walls?" he asked. His mommy smiled and said, "Sure, what do you want to do?" 

Jimmy thought carefully and finally said, "Let's make colourful pictures!" His mommy smiled and said, "Okay, let's go shopping for some paint and markers." But when they got to the shops, the shopkeeper said he didn't sell those things. 

Jimmy got sad. He wanted to make the subway pretty. His mommy noticed, and said, "Don't worry, we can find something else." They looked around and eventually found some paper, scissors and glitter. 

Jimmy and his mommy got to work. With the glitter, they drew sparkly stars on the walls. Jimmy was so happy to see his work and the subway become more beautiful. Meanwhile, the shopkeeper watched in shock as the two decorated. He muttered to himself, "Who would ever think of decorating a disgusting subway like this?"

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a pet bird named Tweety. One day, Lily took Tweety out of his cage to play with him. Tweety flew away and Lily got sad. 

Lily's mom said, "Don't worry, we will find Tweety." They looked for Tweety everywhere but couldn't find him. 

Suddenly, they heard a bird chirping. It was Tweety! He was stuck in a tree. Lily's dad climbed up the tree and released Tweety from the branches. 

Tweety flew back to Lily and stayed with her. Lily was happy again. She said, "Thank you, dad. Tweety is not deaf. He can hear me when I call him."

It was a bright and cheerful day. Sally, who was three years old, was playing with her friends in the park. She was running around and having lots of fun.

Suddenly, a loud noise made Sally jump in shock. Everyone looked around to see what had caused the loud noise. It was the sound of a big balloon popping! All the children were scared and ran away.

Sally felt a wave of fear come over her. She wanted to gain courage and fight this fear, but it seemed too hard for her. She closed her eyes, took a deep breath and opened them again.

With a burst of determination, Sally stepped forward. All her friends looked at her with admiration. She took another step forward and popped the big balloon with her foot.

Everyone cheered for Sally! She had gained courage and stopped the fear with her determination. From then on, Sally was known to be brave and courageous!

name_of_work: Macavity: The Mystery Cat by T. S. Eliot
content: Macavity's a Mystery Cat: he's called the Hidden Paw-- For he's the master criminal who can defy the Law. He's the bafflement of Scotland Yard, the Flying Squad's despair: For when they reach the scene of crime--Macavity's not there! Macavity, Macavity, there's no one like Macavity, He's broken every human law, he breaks the law of gravity. His powers of levitation would make a fakir stare, And when you reach the scene of crime--Macavity's not there! You may seek him in the basement, you may look up in the air-- But I tell you once and once again, Macavity's not there! Macavity's a ginger cat, he's very tall and thin; You would know him if you saw him, for his eyes are sunken in. His brow is deeply lined with thought, his head is highly domed; His coat is dusty from neglect, his whiskers are uncombed. He sways his head from side to side, with movements like a snake; And when you think he's half asleep, he's always wide awake. Macavity, Macavity, there's no one like Macavity, For he's a fiend in feline shape, a monster of depravity. You may meet him in a by-street, you may see him in the square-- But when a crime's discovered, then Macavity's not there! He's outwardly respectable. (They say he cheats at cards.) And his footprints are not found in any file of Scotland Yard's And when the larder's looted, or the jewel-case is rifled, Or when the milk is missing, or another Peke's been stifled, Or the greenhouse glass is broken, and the trellis past repair Ay, there's the wonder of the thing! Macavity's not there! And when the Foreign Office find a Treaty's gone astray, Or the Admiralty lose some plans and drawings by the way, There may be a scrap of paper in the hall or on the stair-- But it's useless to investigate--Macavity's not there! And when the loss has been disclosed, the Secret Service say: It must have been Macavity!'--but he's a mile away. You'll be sure to find him resting, or a-licking of his thumb; Or engaged in doing complicated long division sums. Macavity, Macavity, there's no one like Macavity, There never was a Cat of such deceitfulness and suavity. He always has an alibi, and one or two to spare: At whatever time the deed took place--MACAVITY WASN'T THERE ! And they say that all the Cats whose wicked deeds are widely known (I might mention Mungojerrie, I might mention Griddlebone) Are nothing more than agents for the Cat who all the time Just controls their operations: the Napoleon of Crime!

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to dance and sing to the rhythm of the music. One day, he went outside to play and it started to rain. Timmy got all wet and his clothes became very wet too. He went inside and asked his mom to dry his clothes. 

"Mommy, can you please dry my clothes?" Timmy requested. 

His mom put his clothes in the dryer and turned it on. Timmy heard the rhythm of the dryer and started to dance to it. Suddenly, the dryer caught on fire! Timmy's mom tried to put it out but it was too late. The house burned down and Timmy and his family lost everything. 

Timmy was very sad and didn't understand what had happened. He wished he could dance and sing again, but now he had nowhere to do it.

name_of_work: The Heavy Bear Who Goes With Me by Delmore Schwartz
content: The heavy bear who goes with me, A manifold honey to smear his face, Clumsy and lumbering here and there, The central ton of every place, The hungry beating brutish one In love with candy, anger, and sleep, Crazy factotum, dishevelling all, Climbs the building, kicks the football, Boxes his brother in the hate-ridden city. Breathing at my side, that heavy animal, That heavy bear who sleeps with me, Howls in his sleep for a world of sugar, A sweetness intimate as the water's clasp, Howls in his sleep because the tight-rope Trembles and shows the darkness beneath. --The strutting show-off is terrified, Dressed in his dress-suit, bulging his pants, Trembles to think that his quivering meat Must finally wince to nothing at all. That inescapable animal walks with me, Has followed me since the black womb held, Moves where I move, distorting my gesture, A caricature, a swollen shadow, A stupid clown of the spirit's motive, Perplexes and affronts with his own darkness, The secret life of belly and bone, Opaque, too near, my private, yet unknown, Stretches to embrace the very dear With whom I would walk without him near, Touches her grossly, although a word Would bare my heart and make me clear, Stumbles, flounders, and strives to be fed Dragging me with him in his mouthing care, Amid the hundred million of his kind, The scrimmage of appetite everywhere.

Once upon a time there was a bear who lived in a wood. He was a happy bear who never needed anything. But one day, he got a big surprise.

He found a delicate chain lying on the ground. He took it and was so excited. He thought it was so pretty.

The bear wanted to show off his new chain, so he decided to borrow a friend's tricycle. He put the chain on the tricycle and cycled around the wood.

The bear was so happy and everyone wanted to see the delicate chain on the tricycle.

Then, the bear gave the chain back to its owner, thanked them and went home. He was still very happy and excited about the chain.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Jack. He was very sick and his mommy wanted to help him feel better. She got some medicine from the store and made him take it.

Jack did not like the medicine. "Yuck!" he said. But his mommy said he had to take it if he wanted to feel better. So, Jack took the medicine.

Then his mommy said it was time to get washed up. She filled up the bathtub with water. The water was warm and soft. Jack spent a long time playing in the tub.

When Jack was finished, his mommy said he was all better. She hugged and kissed him and said, "I love you, Jack!" Jack said, "I love you too, mommy!"

There are some days the happy ocean lies Like an unfingered harp, below the land. Afternoon guilds all the silent wires Into a burning music for the eyes On mirrors flashing between fine-strung fires The shore, heaped up with roses, horses, spires Wanders on water tall above ribbed sand. The motionlessness of the hot sky tires And a sigh, like a woman's from inland, Brushes the instrument with shadowy hand Drawing across those wires some gull's sharp cry Or bell, or shout, from distant, hedged-in, shires; These, deep as anchors, the hushing wave buries. Then from the shore, two zig-zag butterflies Like errant dog-roses cross the bright strand Spiralling over waves in dizzy gyres Until the fall in wet reflected skies. They drown. Fishermen understand Such wings sunk in such ritual sacrifice. Remembering legends of undersea, drowned cities. What voyagers, oh what heroes, flamed like pyres With helmets plumed have set forth from some island And them the seas engulfed. Their eyes Distorted to the cruel waves desires, Glitter with coins through the tide scarcely scanned, While, far above, that harp assumes their sighs.

Once upon a time, there was a jolly little girl called Jenny. She was only three years old and was very excited for her first day at the doctors.

At the doctor's, Jenny was a bit scared but the doctors were very kind. They gave her a special needle. Seeing as she was so brave they allowed her to take it home.

Jenny was so excited that she immediately played with the needle. She tried to change it into different shapes. First she tried to make a star, then a heart and finally a circle. It was so much fun!

At the end of the day, Jenny realised that the needle could not change shape, no matter how much she tried. But Jenny wasn't mad - she was happy to have a needle that didn't change. After all, it was always there when she needed it.

name_of_work: Swallows Travel To and Fro by Robert Louis Stevenson
content: Swallows travel to and fro, And the great winds come and go, And the steady breezes blow, Bearing perfume, bearing love. Breezes hasten, swallows fly, Towered clouds forever ply, And at noonday, you and I See the same sunshine above. Dew and rain fall everywhere, Harvests ripen, flowers are fair, And the whole round earth is bare To the moonshine and the sun; And the live air, fanned with wings, Bright with breeze and sunshine, brings Into contact distant things, And makes all the countries one. Let us wander where we will, Something kindred greets us still; Something seen on vale or hill Falls familiar on the heart; So, at scent or sound or sight, Severed souls by day and night Tremble with the same delight - Tremble, half the world apart.

name_of_work: An Introduction to Some Poems by William Stafford
content: Look: no one ever promised for sure that we would sing. We have decided to moan. In a strange dance that we don't understand till we do it, we have to carry on. Just as in sleep you have to dream the exact dream to round out your life, so we have to live that dream into stories and hold them close at you, close at the edge we share, to be right. name_of_work: The Passing of the Year by Robert Service
content: My glass is filled, my pipe is lit, My den is all a cosy glow; And snug before the fire I sit, And wait to feel the old year go. I dedicate to solemn thought Amid my too-unthinking days, This sober moment, sadly fraught With much of blame, with little praise. Old Year! upon the Stage of Time You stand to bow your last adieu; A moment, and the prompter's chime Will ring the curtain down on you. Your mien is sad, your step is slow; You falter as a Sage in pain; Yet turn, Old Year, before you go, And face your audience again. That sphinx-like face, remote, austere, Let us all read, whate'er the cost: O Maiden! why that bitter tear? Is it for dear one you have lost? Is it for fond illusion gone? For trusted lover proved untrue? O sweet girl-face, so sad, so wan What hath the Old Year meant to you? And you, O neighbour on my right So sleek, so prosperously clad! What see you in that aged wight That makes your smile so gay and glad? What opportunity unmissed? What golden gain, what pride of place? What splendid hope? O Optimist! What read you in that withered face? And You, deep shrinking in the gloom, What find you in that filmy gaze? What menace of a tragic doom? What dark, condemning yesterdays? What urge to crime, what evil done? What cold, confronting shape of fear? O haggard, haunted, hidden One What see you in the dying year? And so from face to face I flit, The countless eyes that stare and stare; Some are with approbation lit, And some are shadowed with despair. Some show a smile and some a frown; Some joy and hope, some pain and woe: Enough! Oh, ring the curtain down! Old weary year! it's time to go. My pipe is out, my glass is dry; My fire is almost ashes too; But once again, before you go, And I prepare to meet the New: Old Year! a parting word that's true, For we've been comrades, you and I-- I thank God for each day of you; There! bless you now! Old Year, good-bye!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to draw with chalk on the sidewalk. One day, she found a filthy piece of chalk and decided to use it anyway. 

As she was drawing, a boy came up to her and said, "Can I draw with you?" Lily said yes and they started to draw together. 

But soon, the boy started to get rough and push Lily. She told him to stop, but he wouldn't yield. Suddenly, he grabbed the filthy chalk and threw it at Lily. 

Lily was hurt and cried all the way home. Her mom asked her what happened and Lily told her everything. Her mom said, "Always remember, if someone is being mean to you, it's okay to say no and walk away. And never use something that's dirty or filthy." 

From that day on, Lily never used a filthy piece of chalk again and always stood up for herself when someone was being mean.

An old-fashioned word, coined in a bygone world. It is a taking hold and a letting go, girlhood left behind like a favourite toy, irreversible step over invisible brink. A new frock will be made, which is a country hemmed with the white lace of its shores, and here is a vast garden of weald and wold, mountain and fell, lake, loch, cwm. It is constancy and it is change: the age of clockwork morphs into digital days, but the song of the blackbird remains the same. Queenhood: a long winding procession from the abbey door to the abbey door. Queenhood: vows taken among bibles and blades, beneath braided banners and heralding horns; the anointment of hand, breast, head, with oil of cinnamon, orange, musk and rose; promises sworn in secret under tented gold so daylight won't frighten the magic away, too sacred by far for the camera to see. It is an undressing first then a dressing up, a shedding of plain white cloth then the putting on of a linen gown and the supertunica - dazzling gold foil lined with crimson silk. Man will walk on the moon, great elms will fail and fall. But a knife's still a knife. A fork's still a fork. So the emblems and signs of royalty are produced: the gilded spurs; the blued steel sword - like a sliver of deep space drawn from the scabbard of night - to punish and protect; bracelets to each wrist, sincerity and wisdom - both armour and bond. Love is still love is still love, and war is war. And indestructible towers will atomise in a blink. The God particle will be flushed from its hiding place. The sound barrier will twang with passenger planes. Civilisation will graft its collected thoughts onto silicon wafers, laureates will pass through court . . . But Taurus, the bull, on its heavenly tour, will breach the same horizon at the given hour. Queenhood: it is the skies, it is also the soil of the land. It is life behind glass walls and fortified stones. Robe and stole are lifted onto your shoulders - both shield and yoke. Motherhood and womanhood will be taken as read. 'Multitasking' will be canonised as a new word. It is an honouring, but also an honour. In the flare and blur of an old film ghostly knights and chess-piece bishops deliver the unearthly orb, with its pearled equator and polished realms, into your open palm; and pass you the sceptre and rod of mercy and justice, one bearing the cross, one plumed with a white dove; and load your fourth finger with a ring that makes you the nation's bride; and offer the white kid glove with its scrollwork tattoo of thistles and shamrocks, oak leaves and acorns; then finally furnish your head with the crown - jewelled with history, dense with glory - both owned and loaned at the same time. Do those burnished relics still hold the fingerprints of a twenty-seven-year-old? A priceless freight for a young woman to bear, but, draped and adorned, a monarch walks forward into the sideways weather of oncoming years. And the heavy cargoes of church and state lighten with each step, syrupy old gold transmuted to platinum, alchemy redefined. Queenhood: it is law and lore, the dream life and the documentary, a truthful fantasy. For generations we will not know such majesty.

name_of_work: The ribs and terrors in the whale by Herman Melville
content: "The ribs and terrors in the whale, Arched over me a dismal gloom, While all God's sun-lit waves rolled by, And lift me deepening down to doom. "I saw the opening maw of hell, With endless pains and sorrows there; Which none but they that feel can tell-- Oh, I was plunging to despair. "In black distress, I called my God, When I could scarce believe him mine, He bowed his ear to my complaints-- No more the whale did me confine. "With speed he flew to my relief, As on a radiant dolphin borne; Awful, yet bright, as lightning shone The face of my Deliverer God. "My song for ever shall record That terrible, that joyful hour; I give the glory to my God, His all the mercy and the power."

Once upon a time, there was an elderly lady. She lived in a small house with her cat. The lady loved to make dough to bake yummy bread.

name_of_work: Being Brave at Night by Edgar Albert Guest
content: The other night 'bout two o'clock, or maybe it was three, An elephant with shining tusks came chasing after me. His trunk was wavin' in the air an' spoutin' jets of steam An' he was out to eat me up, but still I didn't scream Or let him see that I was scared - a better thought I had, I just escaped from where I was and crawled in bed with Dad. One time there was a giant who was horrible to see, He had three heads and twenty arms, an' he came after me And red hot fire came from his mouths and every hand was red And he declared he'd grind my bones and make them into bread. But I was just too smart for him, I fooled him mighty bad, Before his hands could collar me I crawled in bed with Dad. I ain't scared of nothin' that comes pesterin' me at night. Once I was chased by forty ghosts all shimmery an' white. An' I just raced 'em round the room an' let 'em think maybe I'd have to stop an' rest awhile, when they could capture me. Then when they leapt onto my bed, Oh Gee! But they were mad To find that I had slipped away an' crawled in bed with Dad. No giants, ghosts or elephants have dared to come in there 'Coz if they did he'd beat 'em up and chase 'em to their lair. They just hang 'round the children's rooms an' snap an' snarl an' bite An' laugh if they can make 'em yell for help with all their might. But I don't ever yell out loud. I'm not that sort of lad, I slip from out the covers and I crawl in bed with Dad.

Once there was a girl named Sarah who loved to play with her stuffed animals. Every day she would take them to the park and play. One day, Sarah was so happy playing in the park that she didn't notice a huge storm rolling in. A tight wind blew and Sarah was scared. She grabbed her stuffed animals and ran home.

When she got home, her Mommy looked at the sky. Mommy saw how dark the clouds were and knew Sarah needed to stay inside. Mommy said, "It's time to go inside and play, Sarah." 

Sarah was sad, but then Mommy had a great idea. She said, "I think I'll recommend a new game for us. Let's play 'Cuddle Bear Race'. We can pretend to race with the stuffed animals and see who wins!"

Sarah was so excited. She got her stuffed animals ready and they started the race. She had so much fun! Afterwards, they hugged the stuffed animals tight to give them a hug of love. 

When the storm was finally over, Sarah and Mommy went back to the park. Sarah was so happy that she could play in the park and that Mommy had recommended such a fun game.

Lily and Tom are twins. They like to play with their toys and books. One day, they see a big bus outside their house. The bus is yellow and has many windows. They want to go inside the bus and see what is there.

"Can we go, Mom?" Lily asks. "Please, please, please?"

Mom looks at the bus. She does not know who drives the bus or where it goes. She thinks the bus is unknown and maybe not safe. She shakes her head. "No, Lily. We don't go inside unknown buses. We stay here."

"But Mom, it looks fun!" Tom says. "Maybe there are more toys and books inside. Maybe there are other kids to play with."

Mom sighs. She knows Lily and Tom are curious and bored. She wants them to be happy and learn new things. But she also wants them to be careful and listen to her. She thinks of a way to make them happy and safe. She has an idea.

"Okay, Lily and Tom. You can go inside the bus, but only for a little while. And only if I go with you. And only if the bus driver says yes. And only if we don't go far. Do you understand?"

Lily and Tom nod. They are very excited. They grab their coats and hats and run to the door. Mom follows them. She hopes the bus driver is nice and the bus is not too strange.

They go outside and walk to the bus. The bus driver sees them and smiles. He opens the door and says hello.

"Hello, sir. We are Lily and Tom. We live in this house. We want to see your bus. Can we go inside?" Lily asks.

The bus driver laughs. He likes Lily and Tom. They are polite and cute. He nods. "Sure, you can go inside. But only for a little while. And only if your mom goes with you. And only if you don't touch anything. Do you understand?"

Lily and Tom nod. They say thank you and go inside. Mom goes with them. She holds their hands and looks around.

The bus is big and bright. There are many seats and windows. There are also some pictures and words on the walls. Lily and Tom see some things they know and some things they don't know. They point and ask questions. The bus driver answers them. He tells them the bus is a school bus. He drives the bus to take kids to school and back. He says the bus is fun and safe. He says he likes his job.

Lily and Tom like the bus driver. They like the bus. They learn new things. They have fun. They manage to see the bus and be happy and safe. Mom is happy and safe too. She smiles and says thank you to the bus driver. She says it is time to go back home. Lily and Tom say goodbye to the bus driver. They say they like his bus. They say they want to go to school someday. The bus driver says he hopes to see them again. He says he is glad they came. He closes the door and waves. Lily and Tom wave back. They go back to their house. They tell their dad what they saw and learned. They play with their toys and books. They are happy. They are safe. They are Lily and Tom.

Tom and Mia go home after school. They have their books and pictures of animals. They want to study for the quiz. But Tom sees his bike. He likes his bike. He wants to ride his bike. He says to Mia, "Let's go to the park. We can ride our bikes. The quiz is easy. We know all the animals."

Tom makes a face. He says, "No, Mia. I do not want to study. I want to have fun. Studying is boring. Riding bikes is fun. Come on, let's go to the park."

Mia and Tom are not happy. They are angry at each other. They do not know what to do. They want to be friends, but they have different ideas. They look at each other. They do not say anything. They are quiet.

Once upon a time there lived a deaf boy named Jack. He was always curious and loved to go out and explore. One day, he wandered far away from home and soon he was feeling very hungry! He looked around and saw a big house far away, so he decided to try his luck and went to the house.

When he reached the house, he knocked on the door. The door opened and a kind old lady appeared. She asked Jack what he wanted. Jack said he was hungry, so the old lady brought him into her kitchen and made some yummy soup for him.

Jack ate up the soup and felt much better. After he finished the soup, he thanked the old lady. Then the old lady asked Jack to help her with her chickens, so he agreed and settled the chickens into their coop.

The old lady was so thankful and she thanked Jack for his help. She told him he could stay at her house until it was time to go back home.

Jack thanked the old lady kindly and spent the night in her house. By the next morning, he had settled in nicely and was very happy to have found such a lovely place to stay.

name_of_work: The Freaks at Spurgin Road Field by Richard Hugo
content: The dim boy claps because the others clap. The polite word, handicapped, is muttered in the stands. Isn't it wrong, the way the mind moves back. One whole day I sit, contrite, dirt, L.A. Union Station, '46, sweating through last night. The dim boy claps because the others clap. Score, 5 to 3. Pitcher fading badly in the heat. Isn't it wrong to be or not be spastic? Isn't it wrong, the way the mind moves back. I'm laughing at a neighbor girl beaten to scream by a savage father and I'm ashamed to look. The dim boy claps because the others clap. The score is always close, the rally always short. I've left more wreckage than a quake. Isn't it wrong, the way the mind moves back. The afflicted never cheer in unison. Isn't it wrong, the way the mind moves back to stammering pastures where the picnic should have worked. The dim boy claps because the others clap.

Sara and Ben were twins who liked to play in their room. They had many toys and books and pictures on the wall. But they did not like to clean up after themselves. Their room was always messy and their mom was always angry.

One day, mom told them to tidy up their room before dinner. She said, "If you don't clean up, you will not get any dessert." Sara and Ben nodded, but they did not listen. They wanted to play more. They took out more toys and books and made more mess.

Then, they saw a picture on the wall that they had never seen before. It was a picture of a big forest with many animals and flowers. It looked very pretty and fun. Sara and Ben wanted to go there. They touched the picture and suddenly, they felt a strange wind. The picture became a door and they walked through it. They were in the forest.

Sara and Ben were amazed. They saw rabbits and birds and butterflies. They smelled the flowers and picked the berries. They wandered around the forest and forgot about their room and their mom and their dinner. They did not see that the sun was going down and the forest was getting dark.

Soon, they were lost. They could not find the picture door. They could not see any animals or flowers. They only saw shadows and heard noises. They were scared and cold and hungry. They cried and called for their mom, but no one answered. They wished they had cleaned up their room and listened to their mom. They learned that being messy and disobedient can lead to trouble. But it was too late. They were stuck in the forest.

Once upon a time, there was a thin object in the middle of a field. Joe, a little boy, had been wandering around and found it. He knelt down and picked it up.

"What could it be?" he asked himself.

He took it home and lay it on the table. He asked his parents, "What is this?"

His parents said, "It looks like a box. Open it and find out."

Joe pulled and tugged, but it wouldn't open. He tried with all his might, but he could not open the box.

He felt so angry that he screamed and shouted. Alas, the box remained closed. Joe decided that the only thing he could do was lay it in the field again and forget all about it.

Sadly, Joe never discovered the surprise that was inside the box. He never found out what was in it, and it remained a mystery to him.

Mommy and Baby Bear were preparing for a picnic. Baby Bear was very excited and wanted to take his blanket. Mommy was happy to let him take the blanket, since it would be useful during their picnic. 

Mommy said, "You can take your blanket but remember that you'll have to carry it." 

Baby Bear replied, "Yes, Mommy. I will take it with me!"

So, Mommy and Baby Bear took the blanket and went off to the park. Once they arrived, they spread the blanket on the grass and started eating all the yummy food that Mommy had prepared.

Mommy smiled and said, "You are very welcome, my dear. The blanket was definitely useful!"

One day, Ben and Lily were playing in the park. They liked to run, slide and swing. They saw a big black dog with a red collar. The dog looked friendly, so they went to say hello.

"Hi, doggy! What is your name?" Lily asked. She reached out to pet the dog's head. The dog wagged its tail and licked her hand.

"Can I rub your belly?" Ben asked. He knelt down and rubbed the dog's soft fur. The dog rolled over and made a happy sound.

Suddenly, they heard a loud noise. It was an ambulance with blue lights and a siren. It was driving very fast on the road. The dog got scared and jumped up. It barked and ran away.

"Come back, doggy!" Ben and Lily shouted. They tried to follow the dog, but it was too fast. They lost sight of it.

They felt sad and worried. They hoped the dog was okay. They hoped the ambulance was going to help someone who was hurt.

They walked back to the park bench, where their mom was waiting. She saw their faces and hugged them.

"What's wrong, my loves?" she asked.

"We met a nice black dog, but it ran away because of the ambulance," Lily said.

"We wanted to be its friends, but we don't know where it went," Ben said.

Mom smiled and kissed their cheeks.

"Don't worry, sweeties. Maybe the dog will come back another day. Maybe it has a home and a family who love it. Maybe the ambulance was just passing by and no one was hurt. You did a good thing by being kind to the dog. I'm proud of you both."

Ben and Lily felt a little better. They still missed the dog, but they were glad they had each other and their mom. They decided to play some more and have fun. Maybe they would see the dog again someday.

Once upon a time, there was a pretty diamond. It was shiny and sparkly. Everyone liked it because it was popular. 

One day, a little boy saw the diamond and wanted it. He tried to grab it but it was too high up. So, he climbed a tree to get it. 

When the boy finally got the diamond, he was so happy. But then, he accidentally snapped it in half! He felt very sad and didn't know what to do. 

Luckily, a kind lady saw what happened and helped the boy. She glued the diamond back together and gave it to him. The boy was grateful and promised to take better care of the diamond. And from that day on, he always remembered to be careful and not let anything snap again. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a kind bear named Benny. Benny lived in a big forest with his animal friends. One day, Benny saw a little bird who was very sad. 

"What's wrong?" asked Benny in a compassionate voice. 

"I lost my way home," the bird said with a sad chirp. 

"Don't worry," said Benny. "I can help you find your way. Let's weigh your options." 

Benny picked up the little bird and held him gently in his big paws. He looked up at the sun in the sky and used his keen sense of direction to lead the bird back to his home. 

"Thank you, Benny!" chirped the little bird happily as he flew into his nest. Benny smiled and waved goodbye, happy to have helped his friend find his way home.

All thoughts, all passions, all delights, Whatever stirs this mortal frame, All are but ministers of Love, And feed his sacred flame. Oft in my waking dreams do I Live o'er again that happy hour, When midway on the mount I lay, Beside the ruined tower. The moonshine, stealing o'er the scene Had blended with the lights of eve; And she was there, my hope, my joy, My own dear Genevieve! She leant against the arm{'e}d man, The statue of the arm{'e}d knight; She stood and listened to my lay, Amid the lingering light. Few sorrows hath she of her own, My hope! my joy! my Genevieve! She loves me best, whene'er I sing The songs that make her grieve. I played a soft and doleful air, I sang an old and moving story-- An old rude song, that suited well That ruin wild and hoary. She listened with a flitting blush, With downcast eyes and modest grace; For well she knew, I could not choose But gaze upon her face. I told her of the Knight that wore Upon his shield a burning brand; And that for ten long years he wooed The Lady of the Land. I told her how he pined: and ah! The deep, the low, the pleading tone With which I sang another's love, Interpreted my own. She listened with a flitting blush, With downcast eyes, and modest grace; And she forgave me, that I gazed Too fondly on her face! But when I told the cruel scorn That crazed that bold and lovely Knight, And that he crossed the mountain-woods, Nor rested day nor night; That sometimes from the savage den, And sometimes from the darksome shade, And sometimes starting up at once In green and sunny glade,-- There came and looked him in the face An angel beautiful and bright; And that he knew it was a Fiend, This miserable Knight! And that unknowing what he did, He leaped amid a murderous band, And saved from outrage worse than death The Lady of the Land! And how she wept, and clasped his knees; And how she tended him in vain-- And ever strove to expiate The scorn that crazed his brain;-- And that she nursed him in a cave; And how his madness went away, When on the yellow forest-leaves A dying man he lay;-- His dying words--but when I reached That tenderest strain of all the ditty, My faltering voice and pausing harp Disturbed her soul with pity! All impulses of soul and sense Had thrilled my guileless Genevieve; The music and the doleful tale, The rich and balmy eve; And hopes, and fears that kindle hope, An undistinguishable throng, And gentle wishes long subdued, Subdued and cherished long! She wept with pity and delight, She blushed with love, and virgin-shame; And like the murmur of a dream, I heard her breathe my name. Her bosom heaved--she stepped aside, As conscious of my look she stepped-- Then suddenly, with timorous eye She fled to me and wept. She half enclosed me with her arms, She pressed me with a meek embrace; And bending back her head, looked up, And gazed upon my face. 'Twas partly love, and partly fear, And partly 'twas a bashful art, That I might rather feel, than see, The swelling of her heart. I calmed her fears, and she was calm, And told her love with virgin pride; And so I won my Genevieve, My bright and beauteous Bride.

name_of_work: Holy Sonnet VI: This is my play's last scene by John Donne
content: This is my play's last scene; here heavens appoint My pilgrimage's last mile; and my race, Idly, yet quickly run, hath this last pace, My span's last inch, my minute's latest point; And gluttonous death will instantly unjoint My body and my soul, and I shall sleep a space; But my'ever-waking part shall see that face Whose fear already shakes my every joint. Then, as my soul to'heaven, her first seat, takes flight, And earth-born body in the earth shall dwell, So fall my sins, that all may have their right, To where they'are bred, and would press me, to hell. Impute me righteous, thus purg'd of evil, For thus I leave the world, the flesh, the devil.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lettie. She was three years old and loved to explore. One day, Lettie decided to go for a walk in the forest near her house. 

"I'll be back soon," she called to her mom as she headed out. She brought her best friend, her blue stuffed bear, for company.

As Lettie walked, she noticed a strange zigzag pattern on the ground. Curious, she approached it and saw that it made a shapeâ€”a shape that she'd never seen before. Lettie decided to stand in the shape, just to explore the feeling.

Suddenly, her bear spoke: "I don't think this is a good idea, Lettie. That pattern is cursed. I think it's best to stay away." But Lettie had already stepped into the pattern. Instantly, the ground started shaking and Lettie could feel a strange power.

Time seemed to stand still as Lettie felt the dead power in the air. After a few moments, though, the power faded and the shaking stoppedâ€”only to be replaced by a bright, happy light. From the light came a voice, the voice of the forest. 

"Thank you, little one, for answering my call," the voice said. "The darkness has been banished and now you have saved the forest. You have my deepest gratitude."

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. He loved to play outside in the park with his friends. One day, they decided to gather some flowers and make a pretty bouquet for Timmy's mom. They ran around the park, picking colorful flowers and laughing.

Suddenly, they heard a loud noise. It was Timmy's big brother playing with his toy gun. Timmy's friends didn't like guns, but his brother said it was popular to play with them. Timmy didn't know what to do. He wanted to keep playing with his friends, but he didn't want to upset his brother.

In the end, Timmy decided to tell his brother how he felt. He said, "I don't like guns. They scare me and my friends. Can we play something else?" His brother listened and agreed. They all played together and had fun without any guns. Timmy was happy he spoke up and his friends were happy too.

Lily liked to study fish. She had a big tank in her room with many fish of different colors and shapes. She liked to watch them swim and play and eat. She learned their names and how to take care of them.

One day, she saw a new fish in the tank. It was small and shiny and had a long tail. It was very beautiful. Lily wanted to be friends with it. She said hello to the fish and asked what its name was.

The fish did not answer. It was shy and scared. It hid behind a rock and did not come out. Lily felt sad. She wanted the fish to like her and be happy.

She thought of a way to make the fish feel better. She got some food from the jar and sprinkled it in the tank. She said, "This is for you, little fish. I hope you like it. I want to be your friend. You are very beautiful."

The fish smelled the food and felt hungry. It peeked out from behind the rock and saw Lily smiling at it. It saw the other fish eating and having fun. It felt curious and brave. It swam out and took a bite of the food. It liked it. It said, "Thank you, Lily. You are very nice. My name is Sparkle. I want to be your friend too."

Lily was happy. She clapped her hands and said, "Yay, Sparkle! I'm glad you came out. You are very welcome. Let's study together and learn more about fish. You are very smart and beautiful."

Sparkle was happy too. He nodded and said, "Yes, Lily. Let's study together and learn more about fish. You are very smart and beautiful too."

They smiled and swam and played and ate. They became good friends and studied fish every day. They had a lot of fun in the tank.

Once upon a time, there were two twins named Tim and Tom. They were very funny and loved to play together. One day, they went to the park to play.

At the park, they saw a big rock. Tim and Tom decided to climb it. As they climbed, Tim said, "Be careful, Tom!" But Tom didn't listen and he stumbled. Tim quickly caught him and they both laughed.

After playing at the park, they went home. Their mom asked, "Did you have fun?" Tim and Tom said, "Yes, we had lots of fun! But we learned to be careful when we play."

The moral of the story is to always be careful and listen to others when they give advice.
