John Brown went off to war to fight on a foreign shore His mama sure was proud of him He stood straight and tall in his uniform and all His mama's face broke out all in a grin "Oh son, you look so fine, I'm glad you're a son of mine You make me proud to know you hold a gun Do what the captain says, lots of medals you will get And we'll put them on the wall when you come home" As that old train pulled out, John's ma began to shout Tellin' ev'ryone in the neighborhood "That's my son that's about to go, he's a soldier now, you know" She made well sure her neighbors understood She got a letter once in a while and her face broke into a smile As she showed them to the people from next door And she bragged about her son with his uniform and gun And these things you called a good old-fashioned war Oh, good old-fashioned war! Then the letters ceased to come, for a long time they did not come They ceased to come for about ten months or more Then a letter finally came saying, "Go down and meet the train Your son's a-coming home from the war" She smiled and went right down, she looked everywhere around But she could not see her soldier son in sight But as all the people passed, she saw her son at last When she did she could hardly believe her eyes Oh his face was all shot up and his hand was all blown off And he wore a metal brace around his waist He whispered kind of slow, in a voice she did not know While she couldn't even recognize his face! Oh, lord, not even recognize his face! "Oh tell me, my darling son, pray tell me what they done How is it you come to be this way?" He tried his best to talk but his mouth could hardly move And the mother had to turn her face away "Don't you remember, ma, when I went off to war You thought it was the best thing I could do? I was on the battleground, you were home acting proud You wasn't there standing in my shoes" "Oh, and I thought when I was there, God, what am I doing here? I'm a-tryin' to kill somebody or die tryin' But the thing that scared me most was when my enemy came close And I saw that his face looked just like mine" Oh, lord, just like mine! "And I couldn't help but think, through the thunder rolling and stink That I was just a puppet in a play And through the roar and smoke, this string is finally broke And a cannonball blew my eyes away" As he turned away to walk, his ma was still in shock At seein' the metal brace that helped him stand But as he turned to go, he called his mother close And he dropped his medals down into her hand

Once there was a girl. She was always very quiet and she liked to listen. 
One day, she was walking outside and she heard a sweet sound. It was a strawberry! She walked over and picked the strawberry off the bush. It was so juicy and delicious - it made her smile. 

The girl listened some more, and this time she heard a dull sound. She looked around and saw a bee buzzing nearby. She watched it carefully and then listened again. She heard more buzzing coming from a nearby flower. She got closer and saw lots of bees working hard to help the flower grow. 

The girl smiled. She learned that listening can be a lot of fun too!

name_of_work: The Cold Within by James Patrick Kinney
content: Six humans trapped by happenstance In bleak and bitter cold. Each one possessed a stick of wood Or so the story's told. Their dying fire in need of logs The first man held his back For of the faces round the fire He noticed one was black. The next man looking 'cross the way Saw one not of his church And couldn't bring himself to give The fire his stick of birch. The third one sat in tattered clothes. He gave his coat a hitch. Why should his log be put to use To warm the idle rich? The rich man just sat back and thought Of the wealth he had in store And how to keep what he had earned From the lazy shiftless poor. The black man's face bespoke revenge As the fire passed from his sight. For all he saw in his stick of wood Was a chance to spite the white. The last man of this forlorn group Did nought except for gain. Giving only to those who gave Was how he played the game. Their logs held tight in death's still hands Was proof of human sin. They didn't die from the cold without They died from the cold within.

John and Jane were playing in their room. John said, "What's that thing over there?" Jane said, "It's a cabinet. It's ordinary. We can put things in it."

John said, "Can I open it?" Jane said, "Yes, but be careful. Don't pull too hard." John opened the cabinet and saw there were lots of books inside. He said, "Wow!"

John and Jane had lots of fun exploring the cabinet. They opened it and closed it, and it made a fun noise. They found lots of fun things inside it. After a while, John and Jane decided to close the cabinet and find something else to do.

They said goodbye to the cabinet, and then they went off to have more fun.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. Lily loved to ride her bike. One day, she saw a boy who was sad. The boy had a toy sword, but it was broken. Lily wanted to help him.

Lily took the broken sword and fixed it with some tape. The boy was very happy and grateful. They played together all day, using the toy sword to fight pretend dragons.

The moral of the story is: when we help others, we make new friends and make the world a better place.

Once upon a time there was a girl who was very sad. She was sad because she had no friends. One day, she picked up a telephone, and dialed a number. She talked to someone on the phone and when she hung up, she was no longer sad.

The girl was happy now, and she decided to show her happiness. She put on her cap and she clapped and cheered. She called out "Yippee" and all her neighbours joined in, applauding her.

The girl was so happy that she bought something for her telephone; a shiny new bell! Now every time she finished a phone call, everyone around applauded. They were all so happy for her.

The girl was no longer sad and had many new friends. She smiled and enjoyed spending time with everyone around.

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her pastel crayons. One day, she drew a big, open sky with many pretty colors.

Later, Lily's mom called her, "Lily, it's time to bathe!" Lily went to the bathroom and found a fun surprise. Her mom had put pastel-colored bath bombs in the water. The water looked like her drawing!

Lily played and splashed in the colorful water. She felt like she was in her own open sky. When she was done, she said, "Thank you, Mom! That was the best bath ever!"

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy liked to play outside in the garden with his hose. He would water the flowers and the grass. One day, Timmy's hose suddenly stopped working. It was empty and no water would come out.

Timmy went to his dad and said, "Daddy, my hose is empty. Can you fix it?" His dad said, "Let me take a look." But when his dad tried to fix it, the hose started to tremble and shake. Suddenly, the hose burst and water went everywhere.

Timmy was sad because he couldn't play with his hose anymore. His dad said, "It's okay, we can buy a new one." But Timmy didn't want a new one. He wanted his old hose. He cried and cried until his dad hugged him and said, "It's okay to be sad. We can try to fix it again tomorrow."

name_of_work: Renascence by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: All I could see from where I stood Was three long mountains and a wood; I turned and looked another way, And saw three islands in a bay. So with my eyes I traced the line Of the horizon, thin and fine, Straight around till I was come Back to where I'd started from; And all I saw from where I stood Was three long mountains and a wood. Over these things I could not see; These were the things that bounded me; And I could touch them with my hand, Almost, I thought, from where I stand. And all at once things seemed so small My breath came short, and scarce at all. But, sure, the sky is big, I said; Miles and miles above my head; So here upon my back I'll lie And look my fill into the sky. And so I looked, and, after all, The sky was not so very tall. The sky, I said, must somewhere stop, And--sure enough!--I see the top! The sky, I thought, is not so grand; I 'most could touch it with my hand! And reaching up my hand to try, I screamed to feel it touch the sky. I screamed, and--lo!--Infinity Came down and settled over me; Forced back my scream into my chest, Bent back my arm upon my breast, And, pressing of the Undefined The definition on my mind, Held up before my eyes a glass Through which my shrinking sight did pass Until it seemed I must behold Immensity made manifold; Whispered to me a word whose sound Deafened the air for worlds around, And brought unmuffled to my ears The gossiping of friendly spheres, The creaking of the tented sky, The ticking of Eternity. I saw and heard, and knew at last The How and Why of all things, past, And present, and forevermore. The Universe, cleft to the core, Lay open to my probing sense That, sick'ning, I would fain pluck thence But could not,--nay! But needs must suck At the great wound, and could not pluck My lips away till I had drawn All venom out.--Ah, fearful pawn! For my omniscience paid I toll In infinite remorse of soul. All sin was of my sinning, all Atoning mine, and mine the gall Of all regret. Mine was the weight Of every brooded wrong, the hate That stood behind each envious thrust, Mine every greed, mine every lust. And all the while for every grief, Each suffering, I craved relief With individual desire,-- Craved all in vain! And felt fierce fire About a thousand people crawl; Perished with each,--then mourned for all! A man was starving in Capri; He moved his eyes and looked at me; I felt his gaze, I heard his moan, And knew his hunger as my own. I saw at sea a great fog bank Between two ships that struck and sank; A thousand screams the heavens smote; And every scream tore through my throat. No hurt I did not feel, no death That was not mine; mine each last breath That, crying, met an answering cry From the compassion that was I. All suffering mine, and mine its rod; Mine, pity like the pity of God. Ah, awful weight! Infinity Pressed down upon the finite Me! My anguished spirit, like a bird, Beating against my lips I heard; Yet lay the weight so close about There was no room for it without. And so beneath the weight lay I And suffered death, but could not die. Long had I lain thus, craving death, When quietly the earth beneath Gave way, and inch by inch, so great At last had grown the crushing weight, Into the earth I sank till I Full six feet under ground did lie, And sank no more,--there is no weight Can follow here, however great. From off my breast I felt it roll, And as it went my tortured soul Burst forth and fled in such a gust That all about me swirled the dust. Deep in the earth I rested now; Cool is its hand upon the brow And soft its breast beneath the head Of one who is so gladly dead. And all at once, and over all The pitying rain began to fall; I lay and heard each pattering hoof Upon my lowly, thatched roof, And seemed to love the sound far more Than ever I had done before. For rain it hath a friendly sound To one who's six feet underground; And scarce the friendly voice or face: A grave is such a quiet place. The rain, I said, is kind to come And speak to me in my new home. I would I were alive again To kiss the fingers of the rain, To drink into my eyes the shine Of every slanting silver line, To catch the freshened, fragrant breeze From drenched and dripping apple-trees. For soon the shower will be done, And then the broad face of the sun Will laugh above the rain-soaked earth Until the world with answering mirth Shakes joyously, and each round drop Rolls, twinkling, from its grass-blade top. How can I bear it; buried here, While overhead the sky grows clear And blue again after the storm? O, multi-colored, multiform, Beloved beauty over me, That I shall never, never see Again! Spring-silver, autumn-gold, That I shall never more behold! Sleeping your myriad magics through, Close-sepulchred away from you! O God, I cried, give me new birth, And put me back upon the earth! Upset each cloud's gigantic gourd And let the heavy rain, down-poured In one big torrent, set me free, Washing my grave away from me! I ceased; and through the breathless hush That answered me, the far-off rush Of herald wings came whispering Like music down the vibrant string Of my ascending prayer, and--crash! Before the wild wind's whistling lash The startled storm-clouds reared on high And plunged in terror down the sky, And the big rain in one black wave Fell from the sky and struck my grave. I know not how such things can be; I only know there came to me A fragrance such as never clings To aught save happy living things; A sound as of some joyous elf Singing sweet songs to please himself, And, through and over everything, A sense of glad awakening. The grass, a-tiptoe at my ear, Whispering to me I could hear; I felt the rain's cool finger-tips Brushed tenderly across my lips, Laid gently on my sealed sight, And all at once the heavy night Fell from my eyes and I could see,-- A drenched and dripping apple-tree, A last long line of silver rain, A sky grown clear and blue again. And as I looked a quickening gust Of wind blew up to me and thrust Into my face a miracle Of orchard-breath, and with the smell,-- I know not how such things can be!-- I breathed my soul back into me. Ah! Up then from the ground sprang I And hailed the earth with such a cry As is not heard save from a man Who has been dead, and lives again. About the trees my arms I wound; Like one gone mad I hugged the ground; I raised my quivering arms on high; I laughed and laughed into the sky, Till at my throat a strangling sob Caught fiercely, and a great heart-throb Sent instant tears into my eyes; O God, I cried, no dark disguise Can e'er hereafter hide from me Thy radiant identity! Thou canst not move across the grass But my quick eyes will see Thee pass, Nor speak, however silently, But my hushed voice will answer Thee. I know the path that tells Thy way Through the cool eve of every day; God, I can push the grass apart And lay my finger on Thy heart! The world stands out on either side No wider than the heart is wide; Above the world is stretched the sky,-- No higher than the soul is high. The heart can push the sea and land Farther away on either hand; The soul can split the sky in two, And let the face of God shine through. But East and West will pinch the heart That can not keep them pushed apart; And he whose soul is flat--the sky Will cave in on him by and by.

One day, a wise cat named Mia was walking in the hall of her home. She liked to explore and find new things. She saw a door that was open a little bit. She pushed it with her paw and went inside.

The room was dark and full of big things. Mia saw a seat that was soft and red. She jumped on it and felt cozy. She curled up and closed her eyes. She was happy.

But then, she heard a loud noise. It was a dog that lived in the home too. He was big and noisy and liked to chase Mia. He saw the open door and ran inside. He saw Mia on the seat and barked.

Mia was scared and angry. She hissed and scratched the dog's nose. The dog yelped and ran away. Mia jumped off the seat and ran after him. She wanted to teach him a lesson.

She chased him out of the room and into the hall. She saw her human, who was holding a bowl of food. She ran to him and rubbed her head on his leg. He smiled and put the bowl on the floor. Mia ate the food and felt better. She was a wise cat.

content: When I get to be a colored composer I'm gonna write me some music about Daybreak in Alabama And I'm gonna put the purtiest songs in it Rising out of the ground like a swamp mist And falling out of heaven like soft dew I'm gonna put some tall tall trees in it And the scent of pine needles And the smell of red clay after rain And long red necks And poppy colored faces And big brown arms And the field daisy eyes Of black and white black white black people And I'm gonna put white hands And black hands and brown and yellow hands And red clay earth hands in it Touching everybody with kind fingers Touching each other natural as dew In that dawn of music when I Get to be a colored composer And write about daybreak In Alabama.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved her grandma very much. Her grandma had a big heart and was very thoughtful. She always baked cookies and cakes for Lily and hugged her tight when she felt sad.

One day, Lily's grandma went away on a long trip. Lily missed her grandma so much and felt very sad. She wanted to see her grandma again and give her a big hug.

But then, Lily had a thoughtful idea. She decided to draw a picture of her and her grandma together and send it to her. When her grandma received the picture, she felt so happy and knew that Lily loved her very much.

The moral of the story is that even when we miss someone, we can show them that we love them by doing something thoughtful.

Mia loves animals. She wants to be a veterinarian when she grows up. A veterinarian is a person who helps animals when they are sick or hurt. Mia has a dog named Spot and a cat named Fluffy. She likes to play with them and give them hugs.

One day, Mia and her mom go to the veterinarian's office. They want to check if Spot and Fluffy are healthy and happy. Mia is excited to see the veterinarian. She hopes he will let her see the other animals too.

"Hello, Mia," the veterinarian says. "Welcome to my office. You have two very cute pets. Do you take good care of them?"

"Yes, I do," Mia says. "I feed them and brush them and cuddle them. They are my best friends."

"That's wonderful," the veterinarian says. "You are a very good pet owner. Let me examine them and give them some treats."

The veterinarian checks Spot and Fluffy's ears, eyes, teeth, and fur. He says they are both very healthy and strong. He gives them some treats and stickers. Mia is happy to see them wag their tails and purr.

"Thank you, veterinarian," Mia says. "You are very nice and helpful. Can I see the other animals too?"

"Sure, you can," the veterinarian says. "But you have to be careful. Some of them are scared or hurt. You have to be gentle and quiet."

The veterinarian shows Mia the other animals in his office. He has a rabbit, a hamster, a bird, and a turtle. He also has a penguin. The penguin is very special. He came from a faraway place where it is very cold and icy. The penguin was injured by a seal and the veterinarian is helping him heal.

"Wow, a penguin!" Mia says. "He is so cute and funny. Can I touch him?"

"Yes, you can," the veterinarian says. "But be careful. He is very icy. He likes the cold. He doesn't like the heat."

Mia gently strokes the penguin's feathers. They are soft and smooth. The penguin makes a funny noise and winks at Mia. Mia giggles and smiles.

"I like you, penguin," Mia says. "You are very brave and cool. I hope you get better soon."

The penguin nods and flaps his wings. He likes Mia too. He thinks she is very kind and sweet. He hopes she will come back to visit him.

Once upon a time, there was a round ball named Bally. Bally loved to race with his friends. They would race all day long. Bally was very fast and always won the races. His friends were frustrated because they wanted to win too.

One day, Bally and his friends went to a big hill. They all wanted to race down the hill. Bally was excited because he knew he would win again. His friends were frustrated but they still wanted to try.

The race began and they all rolled down the hill. Bally was in the lead, but then something happened. Bally got stuck in a hole! His friends rolled past him and finished the race. Bally was frustrated, but he learned that winning isn't everything. From then on, Bally and his friends had more fun racing together.

name_of_work: Still I Rise by Maya Angelou
content: You may write me down in history With your bitter, twisted lies, You may trod me in the very dirt But still, like dust, I'll rise. Does my sassiness upset you? Why are you beset with gloom? 'Cause I walk like I've got oil wells Pumping in my living room. Just like moons and like suns, With the certainty of tides, Just like hopes springing high, Still I'll rise. Did you want to see me broken? Bowed head and lowered eyes? Shoulders falling down like teardrops, Weakened by my soulful cries? Does my haughtiness offend you? Don't you take it awful hard 'Cause I laugh like I've got gold mines Diggin' in my own backyard. You may shoot me with your words, You may cut me with your eyes, You may kill me with your hatefulness, But still, like air, I'll rise. Does my sexiness upset you? Does it come as a surprise That I dance like I've got diamonds At the meeting of my thighs? Out of the huts of history's shame I rise Up from a past that's rooted in pain I rise I'm a black ocean, leaping and wide, Welling and swelling I bear in the tide. Leaving behind nights of terror and fear I rise Into a daybreak that's wondrously clear I rise Bringing the gifts that my ancestors gave, I am the dream and the hope of the slave. I rise I rise I rise.

name_of_work: The Field of Waterloo by Thomas Hardy
content: Yea, the coneys are scared by the thud of hoofs, And their white scuts flash at their vanishing heels, And swallows abandon the hamlet-roofs.The mole's tunnelled chambers are crushed by wheels, The lark's eggs scattered, their owners fled; And the hedgehog's household the sapper unseals.The snail draws in at the terrible tread, But in vain; he is crushed by the felloe-rim. The worm asks what can be overhead,And wriggles deep from a scene so grim, And guesses him safe; for he does not know What a foul red flood will be soaking him!Beaten about by the heel and toe Are butterflies, sick of the day's long rheum, To die of a worse than the weather-foe.Trodden and bruised to a miry tomb Are ears that have greened but will never be gold, And flowers in the bud that will never bloom.

A lively dog named Max liked to play. One day, Max saw a big tree. The tree had lots of fruit. Max wanted to play with the fruit. He jumped and tried to catch the fruit.

A little boy named Tom saw Max. Tom said, "Max, do not play with the fruit! It can fall and make a mess." But Max did not listen. Max ignored Tom and kept jumping.

Tom was sad. He thought of an idea. Tom got a ball and threw it. Max saw the ball and stopped jumping. Max ran to get the ball. Now, Max and Tom played with the ball and left the fruit alone.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. She was very stubborn and loved to go to camp. One day, Sue was playing hide and seek at camp with her friends. She hid behind a huge tree, but she got so distracted watching the birds flying in the sky that she completely forgot to move. 

When her friends returned to find Sue they couldn't find her. They looked everywhere but they couldn't find her.

Finally, one of Sue's friends shouted, "Where are you Sue?"

Sue replied, "I'm still here! I'm sorry I was so stubborn and lost track of time!" 

Everyone was so happy that Sue was found. They all laughed and gave Sue a big hug. 

From then on, Sue always remembered to stay with her friends, so she wouldn't get lost again.

That spring was late. We watched the sky and studied charts for shouldering isobars. Birds were late to pair. Crows drank from the lamb's eye. Over Finland small birds fell: song-thrushes steering north, smudged signatures on light, migrating warblers, nightingales. Wing-beats failed over fjords, each lung a sip of gall. Children were warned of their dangerous beauty. Milk was spilt in Poland. Each quarrel the blowback from some old story, a mouthful of bitter air from the Ukraine brought by the wind out of its box of sorrows. This spring a lamb sips caesium on a Welsh hill. A child, lifting her head to drink the rain, takes into her blood the poisoned arrow. Now we are all neighbourly, each little town in Europe twinned to Chernobyl, each heart with the burnt firemen, the child on the Moscow train. In the democracy of the virus and the toxin we wait. We watch for spring migrations, one bird returning with green in its voice. Glasnost. Golau glas. A first break of blue.

Lily and Ben were playing in the snow. They made a big snowman with a hat and a scarf. They gave him a carrot nose and two rocks for eyes. They were very happy with their snowman.

"Can we give him a name?" Lily asked Ben.

"Sure, let's call him Frosty," Ben said.

They hugged Frosty and said hello to him. They pretended he was their friend.

"Hello, Frosty. Do you like the snow?" Lily questioned.

"Yes, I do. It is cold and white and fun," Ben answered in a funny voice.

They laughed and played with Frosty for a long time. They rolled snowballs and threw them at each other. They made snow angels and snow forts. They had a lot of fun.

But soon they started to feel cold and tired. Their fingers and toes were numb. Their noses were red. They decided to go back home.

"Bye, Frosty. We will come back tomorrow," Lily said.

"Bye, Lily and Ben. Have a nice day," Ben said in a funny voice again.

They waved to Frosty and ran to their house. Their mom was waiting for them with a big smile. She had made them hot cocoa with marshmallows. She helped them take off their wet clothes and gave them warm blankets.

"Did you have fun in the snow?" Mom asked.

"Yes, we did. We made a snowman and named him Frosty. He is our friend," Lily said.

"That sounds wonderful. You are very creative," Mom said.

She gave them their mugs of cocoa and kissed their cheeks. They sipped their cocoa and felt the warmth in their bellies. They told Mom about their snow adventure. They smiled and cuddled with Mom. They felt very happy and cozy.

A dependable desk stood in the corner of a bedroom. It was a very trusty desk, one that could be relied on no matter what.

One morning, a small girl entered the room. She walked over to the desk and ran her hands over the smooth wood. Her eyes twinkled with delight as she noticed something special. It was a special note that had been placed on the desk.

The note said that the desk would remain there, no matter what. That made the little girl very happy, because she could always depend on the desk to stay.

Each day she would come to the desk and open the drawers. Inside, she would find things to do and new adventures were always waiting! The dependable desk became her favorite place to play.  

And so the desk remained in the corner, a dependable friend for the small girl.

Once there was a boy named Billy. He wanted to be successful so he tried climbing every day.

He would climb hills and trees and even big rocks. He was getting better and better every day.

One day he went to a big mountain and decided to try climbing it. It was hard but he kept going and kept trying.

Finally he made it to the top! He had succeeded! He was so proud and excited that he couldn't help but yell a big "Yee-Haw!"

From then on, he didn't find climbing to be boring at all. He kept climbing and getting better and better each time.

Billy never gave up, and that's how he became a successful climber!

Evening will come, however determined the late afternoon, Limes and oaks in their last green flush, pearled in September mist. I have conjured a lily to light these hours, a token of thanks, Zones and auras of soft glare framing the brilliant globes. A promise made and kept for life - that was your gift - Because of which, here is a gift in return, glovewort to some, Each shining bonnet guarded by stern lance-like leaves. The country loaded its whole self into your slender hands, Hands that can rest, now, relieved of a century's weight. Evening has come. Rain on the black lochs and dark Munros. Lily of the Valley, a namesake almost, a favourite flower Interlaced with your famous bouquets, the restrained Zeal and forceful grace of its lanterns, each inflorescence A silent bell disguising a singular voice. A blurred new day Breaks uncrowned on remote peaks and public parks, and Everything turns on these luminous petals and deep roots, This lily that thrives between spire and tree, whose brightness Holds and glows beyond the life and border of its bloom.

When I looked into your eyes, I saw a garden With peonies, and tinkling pagodas, And round-arched bridges Over still lakes. A woman sat beside the water In a rain-blue, silken garment. She reached through the water To pluck the crimson peonies Beneath the surface, But as she grasped the stems, They jarred and broke into white-green ripples, And as she drew out her hand, The water-drops dripping from it Stained her rain-blue dress like tears.

Once there was a lonely bear. He wanted to act wild but he had no one to play with. One day he heard a noise in the woods. When he got there he saw a rabbit hopping around. The bear and the rabbit started to act wild, jumping and running around the woods. They jumped and chased each other around, until they both got tired. The bear and the rabbit were no longer lonely, and they played together every day in the woods.

Tommy was walking through the woods when he saw something sparkling in the sunlight. He ran to it and there was an axe! It was so shiny and long. He picked it up and started to play with it.

Suddenly, he heard a strange noise. He looked up and saw a small creature on a tree branch. It was laughing and it teased, "Why don't you chop the tree down with that axe?" 

Tommy thought that was a great idea. He held the axe tightly and tried to chop the tree. But it was too long and he was too little. He just couldn't get the axe high enough to chop the trunk. 

The creature stopped laughing and said with a smile, "Why don't you ask for help? I bet somebody would chop the tree for you."

Tommy thanked the creature and ran home to find his big brother. His brother held the axe and chopped the tree down easily.

Tommy was so happy. He thanked his brother and they both went home with a smile.

name_of_work: The New Bride by Catherine Smith
content: Dying, darling, is the easy bit. Fifty paracetamol, bride-white and sticking in the throat, ten shots of Johnny Walker, and the deed is done. A twilight day of drowsing, then the breathing slows to a whisper, like a sinner in Confession. Death is dead easy. No, what happens next is the difficulty. You bastard, howlng in public, snivelling over photos, ringing round for consolation. And you have me burnt, like a dinner gone wrong, you keep the charred remains of me on show at the Wake, inviting everyone I hate. Oh God, they come in packs, sleek as rats with platitudes and an eye on my half of the bed, hoping to find leftover skin, a hint of fetid breath. I leave them no hairs on the pillow. There are none to leave. And a year to the day since I shrug off the yoke of life, you meet the new bride. In group therapy. You head straight for a weeper and wailer, telling strangers all her little tragedies. You love the way she languishes, her tears sliming your neck, you give in to her on vile pink Austrian blinds. The Wedding is a riot of white nylon. Everybody drinks your health and hers, the simpering bitch. She and Della Smith keep you fat and happy as a pig in shit. I want her cells to go berserk. Some nights I slip between you. The new bride sleeps buttoned up, slug-smug in polyester. You, my faithless husband, turn over in your dreams, and I'm there, ice-cold and seeking out your eyes and for a moment you brush my lips, and freeze.

Once upon a time, there was a squirrel. She was looking for something to eat. She scurried around looking for acorns. Suddenly, she found a big acorn laying on the ground. It was dirty.

The squirrel was very happy and she raced over to grab it. But, before she could eat it, she heard a voice.

"Hey! That's mine!" said the voice.

The squirrel saw a little bird. He was looking up at her with his beady eyes.

"No, I found it first," said the squirrel.

"No. I attached it to a tree. That means it belongs to me." said the little bird.

The squirrel thought for a moment.

"Okay fine, you can have it back," said the squirrel.

The bird was so excited. He flew over and hugged the acorn.

"Thank you!" he said with a smile.

The squirrel waved goodbye and scampered off in search of a new acorn.

name_of_work: A Country Life by Randall Jarrell
content: A bird that I don't know, Hunched on his light-pole like a scarecrow, Looks sideways out into the wheat The wind waves under the waves of heat. The field is yellow as egg-bread dough Except where (just as though they'd let It live for looks) a locust billows In leaf-green and shade-violet, A standing mercy. The bird calls twice, "Red clay, red clay"; Or else he's saying, "Directly, directly." If someone came by I could ask, Around here all of them must know -- And why they live so and die so -- Or why, for once, the lagging heron Flaps from the little creek's parched cresses Across the harsh-grassed, gullied meadow To the black, rowed evergreens below. They know and they don't know. To ask, a man must be a stranger -- And asking, much more answering, is dangerous; Asked about it, who would not repent Of all he ever did and never meant, And think a life and its distresses, Its random, clutched-for, homefelt blisses, The circumstances of an accident? The farthest farmer in a field, A gaunt plant grown, for seed, by farmers, Has felt a longing, lorn urbanity Jailed in his breast; and, just as I, Has grunted, in his old perplexity, A standing plea. From the tar of the blazing square The eyes shift, in their taciturn And unavowing, unavailable sorrow. Yet the intonation of a name confesses Some secrets that they never meant To let out to a soul; and what words would not dim The bowed and weathered heads above the denim Or the once-too-often washed wash dresses? They are subdued to their own element. One day The red, clay face Is lowered to the naked clay; After some words, the body is forsaken The shadows lengthen, and a dreaming hope Breathes, from the vague mound, Life; From the grove under the spire Stars shine, and a wandering light Is kindled for the mourner, man. The angel kneeling with the wreath Sees, in the moonlight, graves.

name_of_work: And Day Brought Back My Night by Geoffrey Brock
content: It was so simple: you came back to me And I was happy. Nothing seemed to matter But that. That you had gone away from me And lived for days with him--it didn't matter. That I had been left to care for our old dog And house alone--couldn't have mattered less! On all this, you and I and our happy dog Agreed. We slept. The world was worriless. I woke in the morning, brimming with old joys Till the fact-checker showed up, late, for work And started in: Item: it's years, not days. Item: you had no dog. Item: she isn't back, In fact, she just remarried. And oh yes, item: you Left her, remember? I did? I did. (I do.)

name_of_work: La Figlia Che Piange by T.S. Eliot
content: O quam te memorem virgo ... Stand on the highest pavement of the stair-- Lean on a garden urn-- Weave, weave the sunlight in your hair-- Clasp your flowers to you with a pained surprise-- Fling them to the ground and turn With a fugitive resentment in your eyes: But weave, weave the sunlight in your hair. So I would have had him leave, So I would have had her stand and grieve, So he would have left As the soul leaves the body torn and bruised, As the mind deserts the body it has used. I should find Some way incomparably light and deft, Some way we both should understand, Simple and faithless as a smile and shake of the hand. She turned away, but with the autumn weather Compelled my imagination many days, Many days and many hours: Her hair over her arms and her arms full of flowers. And I wonder how they should have been together! I should have lost a gesture and a pose. Sometimes these cogitations still amaze The troubled midnight and the noon's repose.

Once upon a time, there lived a kid. He was a nice and friendly kid and kept looking for his friend.

One day, while the kid was playing in the park, something white appeared in the sky. The kid was very curious and looked up to see what it was.

It was a huge white bird, flying high. The kid was amazed to see such a beautiful thing in the sky.

The bird kept flying closer and closer until it stopped right above the kid. The kid gasped in excitement as the bird circled around him.

The white bird had made the kid so happy and the kid waved goodbye to the bird as it flew away.

The kid was smiling from ear to ear and ran off to tell everyone about his wonderful adventure.

name_of_work: The Forsaken Wife by Elizabeth Thomas
content: Methinks, 'tis strange you can't afford One pitying look, one parting word; Humanity claims this as due, But what's humanity to you? Cruel man! I am not blind, Your infidelity I find; Your want of love my ruin shows, My broken heart, your broken vows. Yet maugre all your rigid hate, I will be true in spite of fate; And one preeminence I'll claim, To be for ever still the same. Show me a man that dare be true, That dares to suffer what I do; That can for ever sigh unheard, And ever love without regard: I then will own your prior claim To love, to honour, and to fame; But till that time, my dear, adieu, I yet superior am to you.

name_of_work: Where I'm From by George Ella Lyon
content: I am from clothespins, from Clorox and carbon-tetrachloride. I am from the dirt under the back porch. (Black, glistening, it tasted like beets.) I am from the forsythia bush the Dutch elm whose long-gone limbs I remember as if they were my own. I'm from fudge and eyeglasses, from Imogene and Alafair. I'm from the know-it-alls and the pass-it-ons, from Perk up! and Pipe down! I'm from He restoreth my soul with a cottonball lamb and ten verses I can say myself. I'm from Artemus and Billie's Branch, fried corn and strong coffee. From the finger my grandfather lost to the auger, the eye my father shut to keep his sight. Under my bed was a dress box spilling old pictures, a sift of lost faces to drift beneath my dreams. I am from those moments-- snapped before I budded -- leaf-fall from the family tree.

Once upon a time, there was a little bunny named Benny. Benny was very curious and loved to explore the forest. One day, he saw a big, scary wolf with sharp teeth. Benny was scared and ran away as fast as he could.

As he was running, he saw a squirrel with a soft, fluffy fur. Benny thought it was so pretty and wanted to touch it. But when he got close, the squirrel disappeared. Benny was confused and didn't understand where it went.

He kept running until he found a big rock that was very hard. Benny tried to move it, but it was too heavy. He thought about giving up, but then he remembered the squirrel that disappeared. He realized that sometimes things can appear or disappear, and that's okay. He learned that it's important to keep trying, even if things seem hard at first. From that day on, Benny was brave and never gave up.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to eat yummy candy and play with his toys. But at night, Timmy would have scary nightmares. 

One night, Timmy woke up crying from a nightmare. His mommy came to his room and asked him what was wrong. Timmy told her about the scary monster in his dream. 

Mommy hugged Timmy and told him that the monster wasn't real, it was just a bad dream. She asked Timmy to close his eyes and imagine a happy place. Timmy closed his eyes and imagined himself eating yummy candy with his friends. 

Soon, Timmy fell back asleep and didn't have any more nightmares. From then on, whenever Timmy had a bad dream, he would answer his mommy's question about what was wrong and imagine happy thoughts.

Once there was a girl named Sarah who liked to write. She wanted to write something wild, so she wrote a letter to the mailbox. But when she went to put it in the mailbox, there was a big, wild rabbit standing in front of it.

Sarah was very scared, and the rabbit didn't seem like it was going to move. Sarah was scared to try to take the letter to the mailbox, so she just stood there and watched the rabbit.

But then, Sarah got brave. She decided to march up to the mailbox, stepping closer to the wild rabbit. The rabbit hopped away, and Sarah was finally able to write the letter and put it in the mailbox.

Sarah was proud of herself. She was happy she didn't give up and she finally was able to write something wild!

Ben did not like cauliflower. He thought it was white and yucky and smelled bad. He always tried to hide it under his plate or give it to his dog. But his mom knew his tricks and always made him eat it.

One day, mom made a big pot of cauliflower soup for dinner. Ben looked at it and felt sick. He did not want to eat it at all. He wished he could make it disappear.

"Ben, come and eat your soup. It is good for you," mom said.

"No, thank you, mom. I am not hungry," Ben said.

"Yes, you are. You have to eat your soup or you will not get any dessert," mom said.

Ben sighed and went to the table. He looked at his bowl of soup and saw something shiny in it. It was a spoon. He picked it up and saw that it had a button on it. He pressed the button and the spoon made a beep.

"What is that, Ben?" mom asked.

"It is a magic spoon, mom. It can make things disappear," Ben said.

"Really? How does it work?" mom asked.

Ben pointed the spoon at his soup and pressed the button again. The soup vanished from his bowl. Ben smiled.

"See, mom? It works. The soup is gone," Ben said.

Mom looked at his empty bowl and gasped. She did not believe it. She thought Ben was playing a trick on her.

"Ben, where did you get that spoon? And where did the soup go?" mom asked.

"I found it in the soup, mom. And the soup went away. Far, far away," Ben said.

Mom was very confused and worried. She did not know what to do. She wondered if the spoon was dangerous or if Ben was crazy.

"Ben, give me that spoon. It is not a toy. It might be dangerous," mom said.

But Ben did not want to give up his spoon. He liked it. He thought it was fun. He wanted to make more things disappear.

"No, mom. It is mine. I like it. It is fun," Ben said.

He ran away from the table and into his room. He closed the door and locked it. He looked around and saw his toys, his books, his clothes. He pointed the spoon at them and pressed the button. One by one, they all disappeared. Ben laughed and laughed. He thought he was having the best time ever.

But soon, he realized that he had nothing left in his room. He had made everything disappear. He felt lonely and bored. He wished he had his toys, his books, his clothes back. He wished he had not made his soup disappear. He wished he had listened to his mom.

He tried to press the button again, but nothing happened. The spoon was out of power. It could not make things appear. It could only make things disappear.

Ben started to cry. He wanted his mom. He wanted to say sorry. He wanted to hug her. He wanted to eat his soup.

He opened the door and ran to the kitchen. He hoped his mom was still there. He hoped she was not mad at him. He hoped she still loved him.

But when he got to the kitchen, he saw that it was empty. There was no mom. There was no pot. There was no soup. There was nothing.

Ben had made his mom disappear.

name_of_work: Always Marry an April Girl by Ogden Nash
content: Praise the spells and bless the charms, I found April in my arms. April golden, April cloudy, Gracious, cruel, tender, rowdy; April soft in flowered languor, April cold with sudden anger, Ever changing, ever true -- I love April, I love you

Once upon a time, there was a young boy named Jack. Jack was always nice to other people. One day he saw an old man walking with a cane. The man was walking very slowly and seemed a bit sad.

Jack ran up to the old man and said hello. The old man looked very happy to see him. The old man asked Jack if he wanted to come with him on his walk. Jack said yes and they started walking together.

Jack noticed that the road was very rough. He asked the old man why he was walking on the rough road. The old man said that sometimes life is rough too and we have to keep walking. 

Jack thought about this. He decided that no matter what happens, he should keep walking and always be nice to others.

At the end of the walk, the old man gave Jack a big hug. He thanked Jack for being so kind and for coming with him on his rough walk. Jack learned an important lesson from the old man and he promised himself he would always be kind and remember that life can be tough sometimes.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who was very impatient. She had a toy that she loved, but it was looking very dull. She said, "I want to polish it up so it looks nice again!"

So, she fetched a cloth and a bottle of polish and spread it carefully over her toy. As she finished polishing, the toy looked much brighter and shinier.

Later that day, the girl's Mom brought home an avocado from the market. "What a fantastic avocado!" said the girl, as she looked at the green and shiny fruit.

She picked up her polishing cloth and began polishing the avocado. With a few strokes, the skin of the avocado shone.

Suddenly, her Mom walked in and saw what she was doing. "What a clever girl!" she said. "You have used your polishing skill to make this avocado look really nice!"

The little girl smiled proudly and continued to polish everything in sight until her impatience finally subsided!

One day, a big cat and a little dog were playing in the yard. The big cat was very impatient. He wanted to play with the cable that was spread on the ground. The little dog wanted to play with it too.

The big cat said, "I want to play with the cable first!" The little dog said, "No, I want to play with it first!" They both tried to grab the cable at the same time. The cable was pulled and pulled by the big cat and the little dog.

Then, a wise bird saw them and said, "Stop! You can both play with the cable. One of you can hold one end, and the other can hold the other end. Then you can both have fun!" The big cat and the little dog listened to the wise bird. They played with the cable together and had a great time.

Once upon a time there was a mama, papa, and their two kids. Every holiday, mama and papa always did something special to spoil their kids.

One holiday, mama and papa decided to take their kids to the beach. The water was warm and the beach was filled with so many fun things to do.

The two kids laughed and ran around in little circles and giggle as they built sandcastles and raced to see who could get furthest into the ocean. Mama and papa laughed and smiled as they saw how happy their children were.

But then, one of the kids noticed some poor, hungry seagulls. They were sad and looking for food. So the kids ran back to mama and papa, asked for some food and quickly brought it back to the seagulls.

Mama and papa were so proud of their kids for being so kind and generous. They had learned what it meant to be truly great; to be generous and kind on a holiday. 

Mama and papa smiled as they hugged their kids. They knew they had been true examples of spoiling the day in the best way possible.

name_of_work: In the Western Lands by J.R.R. Tolkien
content: In western lands beneath the Sun the flowers may rise in Spring, the trees may bud, the waters run, the merry finches sing. Or there maybe 'tis cloudless night and swaying beeches bear the Elven-stars as jewels white amid their branching hair. Though here at journey's end I lie in darkness buried deep, beyond all towers strong and high, beyond all mountains steep, above all shadows rides the Sun and Stars for ever dwell: I will not say the Day is done, nor bid the Stars farewell.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named John. John was very smart and often wore a nice tie.

One day his mom gave him an old tie to wear. But John didn't like it, he said it was too boring.

So his mom went to the store and bought him a brand new tie. The old one she put away and replaced it with the nice new one.

John was so happy, he put it on and ran to show his dad. His dad smiled and said John looked so smart in it.

John felt very proud of his new tie. He knew he could look smart whenever he wore it.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a big shelf in her room where she kept all her toys. One day, Lily found a little bird outside and she wanted to keep it as a pet. She gently picked up the bird and brought it to her room. 

Lily put the bird on the shelf with her other toys. She made sure to be gentle and not scare the bird. The bird felt safe and happy on the shelf with Lily's toys. 

Every day, Lily would visit the bird on the shelf and they would play together. The bird was happy to be kept as a pet by Lily. And Lily was happy to have a new friend on her shelf. The end.

The little white clouds are racing over the sky, And the fields are strewn with the gold of the flower of March, The daffodil breaks under foot, and the tasselled larch Sways and swings as the thrush goes hurrying by. A delicate odour is borne on the wings of the morning breeze, The odour of leaves, and of grass, and of newly upturned earth, The birds are singing for joy of the Spring's glad birth, Hopping from branch to branch on the rocking trees. And all the woods are alive with the murmur and sound of Spring, And the rose-bud breaks into pink on the climbing briar, And the crocus-bed is a quivering moon of fire Girdled round with the belt of an amethyst ring. And the plane to the pine-tree is whispering some tale of love Till it rustles with laughter and tosses its mantle of green, And the gloom of the wych-elm's hollow is lit with the iris sheen Of the burnished rainbow throat and the silver breast of a dove. See! the lark starts up from his bed in the meadow there, Breaking the gossamer threads and the nets of dew, And flashing adown the river, a flame of blue! The kingfisher flies like an arrow, and wounds the air.

Once upon time, there was a poor aunt. She had been feeling sad for many days. One day, the aunt decided to take a walk to try and restore her happiness. As she walked, she noticed the birds singing and the sun shining. She smiled and started to feel better. Then, she heard someone calling her name. It was her niece! The poor aunt smiled as she hugged her niece and felt her sadness restoring. The niece asked the aunt to come and play with her. Together they played in the park, running and chasing each other. For one moment, everything seemed perfect and the aunt was happy again. The sea breezes made the aunt feel peaceful and restored. The aunt thanked her niece for helping her feel better. Together, they walked home with the aunt's happiness completely restored.

Today, two special friends were going on an adventure. John was a bear and Alice was a rabbit. Firstly, they ran hand in hand through the fields and jumped over the tall grass. Then, they came upon a unique tree. The tree had a special secret. If you joined hands and circled around the tree three times, a magical doorway would open. 

Alice and John looked at each other excitedly and joined their hands together. With anticipation, they ran but they needed to be careful because they only had three turns. They each counted out loud as they whirled around the tree. 

"One, two, three!" they shouted at the same time. 

The moment they finished, a magical doorway appeared and the two friends ran through it and discovered a secret garden. They laughed and gasped in astonishment at the enchanting sights before them.

"This is amazing!" said Alice.

"Yes, it's so unique," smiled John. 

They spent the day together running around the beautiful garden, hand in hand, exploring the wonders of this magical place. 

At the end of the day, John and Alice hugged each other tightly and parted ways. They both knew that this special day was one that they would treasure forever.

Sara and Ben are twins. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big slide. Sara wants to try it, but Ben is scared.

"Come on, Ben. It is fun. You can do it," Sara says. She encourages Ben to go with her.

Ben shakes his head. He feels weak in his legs. He does not want to start the slide. He thinks it is too high and too fast.

Sara sees that Ben is afraid. She does not laugh at him. She holds his hand and says, "It is okay, Ben. I am here with you. We can go together. I will help you."

Ben looks at Sara. He trusts her. He nods his head. He starts to walk with her to the slide. He still feels weak, but he also feels brave.

Sara and Ben climb the steps. They sit on the slide. Sara wraps her arms around Ben. She says, "Ready, set, go!" They slide down together. They feel the wind in their hair. They laugh and scream.

They reach the bottom. They are happy. They hug each other. They did it. They are not weak. They are strong. They thank each other. They want to go again.
Me We

is a river you wade in until you get to the other side. But I am here, stuck in the middle, water parting around my ankles, moving downstream over the flat rocks. I'm not able to lift a foot, move on. Instead, I'm going to stay here in the shallows with my sorrow, nurture it like a cranky baby, rock it in my arms. I don't want it to grow up, go to school, get married. It's mine. Yes, the October sunlight wraps me in its yellow shawl, and the air is sweet as a golden Tokay. On the other side, there are apples, grapes, walnuts, and the rocks are warm from the sun. But I'm going to stand here, growing colder, until every inch of my skin is numb. I can't cross over. Then you really will be gone.

It is not the moon, I tell you. It is these flowers lighting the yard. I hate them. I hate them as I hate sex, the man's mouth sealing my mouth, the man's paralyzing body- and the cry that always escapes, the low, humiliating premise of union- In my mind tonight I hear the question and pursuing answer fused in one sound that mounts and mounts and then is split into the old selves, the tired antagonisms. So you see? We were made fools of. And the scent of mock orange drifts through the window. How can I rest? How can I be content when there is still that odor in the world?

name_of_work: To an army wife, in Sardis by Sappho
content: To an army wife, in Sardis: Some say a cavalry corps, some infantry, some, again, will maintain that the swift oars of our fleet are the finest sight on dark earth; but I say that whatever one loves, is. This is easily proved: did not Helen--she who had scanned the flower of the world's manhood-- choose as first among men one who laid Troy's honor in ruin? warped to his will, forgetting love due her own blood, her own child, she wandered far with him. So Anactoria, although you being far away forget us, the dear sound of your footstep and light glancing in your eyes would move me more than glitter of Lydian horse or armored tread of mainland infantry

Once upon a time there was a famous superhero named Captain Fantastic. He was always helping people and saving the world with his special powers.

One day, Captain Fantastic saw something very scary in the sky. It was a missile! Captain Fantastic was scared and he didn't know what to do.

He asked his super friends to help him stop the missile from destroying the town. One of them said, "I know how to help! We can use our super powers to stop the missile."

The superhero friends used their super powers and worked together to stop the missile. When the missile was finally stopped, everyone in the town cheered for Captain Fantastic and his friends.

From then on, Captain Fantastic was known as even more famous for his brave actions!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the garden. One day, she was digging in the soil with her hands, making a big hole. Her mom asked her, "What are you doing, Lily?"

"I'm making a special surprise for you, Mommy," Lily replied with a smile.

Her mom didn't know what to expect, but she trusted her daughter. Later that day, Lily showed her mom the surprise - a beautiful flower had grown in the hole she had dug. It was so graceful and colorful.

"Wow, Lily, you did such a great job! This flower is amazing," her mom said, giving her a big hug.

Lily was so happy that her surprise had worked out. From that day on, she loved playing in the garden even more, knowing that she could do something special with the soil.

Tom and Anna are friends. They like to play in the sand. They have a bucket and a shovel. They dig a big hole. They find something shiny in the hole.

"Look, Anna, I found a coin!" Tom says.

"Wow, Tom, it is shiny and round. Can I see?" Anna says.

Tom gives Anna the coin. She rubs it with her hand. It feels smooth and cold. She likes the coin.

"Can we keep it, Tom?" Anna says.

"Yes, we can. But we have to hide it. Someone might take it," Tom says.

They think of a good place to hide the coin. They see a jar of salt on the picnic table. Salt is white and tasty. They like to put salt on their food.

"I have an idea, Anna. We can bury the coin in the salt. Then no one will find it," Tom says.

"That is a good idea, Tom. Let's do it," Anna says.

They take the jar of salt and pour some of it in the hole. They put the coin in the salt. They pour more salt on top of the coin. They pat the salt with their hands. They make it flat and smooth.

They put the jar of salt back on the picnic table. They smile at each other. They are happy. They have a secret. They have a shiny coin. They will come back later and dig it out. They hug and run to play some more.

Once there was a little girl named Mia. She loved to go on adventures; fantastical places filled with new people and things to explore. One day, Mia decided to explore the big city.

As Mia explored, she noticed a big building and heard music coming from it. She asked her Mom what it was and her Mom said, "That's a music club. Musicians go there to play for people."

Mia wanted to go in and see the musicians, but her Mom said, "Honey, it's very expensive to go in there."

So Mia began to look for a way inside. She noticed one of the musicians had left the door open and she quickly ran in. Inside, Mia met many musicians and they sang and danced. She decided it was the best place on her adventures!

Once upon a time there was a three year old named Ru. Ru liked to skip everywhere he went. One day Ru was skipping to the park and noticed a storm drain. It had bars on it so no one could fall in. Ru stopped and put his hand against the bars.

Suddenly, a crab walked up to Ru and said, "What are you doing here?" Ru smiled and said, "I'm skipping and I found this cool storm drain." The crab then said, "Well, I don't think you should stay here. The crab was being a little rude.

Ru said, "I'm just having fun." But the crab said, "No, you should leave." So Ru skipped away and waved goodbye to the crab. He was still a little sad that the crab had been so rude.

Ru arrived safely at the park and played for the rest of the day. He never forgot the storm drain or the rude crab. But he sure had fun skipping all the way there.

Once there was a fox. He was a very purple fox. He had purple fur and purple eyes. 

The fox wanted to explain something to a special friend. He said to the 3 year old child, "I can do something special." 

The 3 year old was excited to hear this. He asked what it was. 

The fox explained, "I can turn things into purple. I can make purple trees, purple rocks, and purple flowers. It's so cool!" 

The 3 year old laughed with joy. He thought the fox was so special and so cool. He thanked the fox for explaining it to him.

Once upon a time, there was a little bird named Tweetie. Tweetie was very graceful and loved to fly in the sky. One day, Tweetie saw some seeds on the ground and wanted to gather them for her family. But, as she was gathering the seeds, she saw a big cat coming towards her. 

"Hey, Tweetie, what are you doing?" asked the cat.

"I'm gathering seeds for my family," replied Tweetie.

"Well, those seeds are mine. Give them to me," said the cat, trying to take the seeds away.

"No, they are mine. I gathered them fair and square," said Tweetie, flapping her wings.

The cat tried to grab the seeds again, but he accidentally tripped and fell. Tweetie quickly flew away with the seeds and brought them back to her family. They were very happy and grateful for the delicious seeds. From that day on, Tweetie knew that even though she was small, she could still be brave and stand up for herself.

Once upon a time there was a little girl. Her name was Lucy. She was only three years old and she loved to explore the world around her.

One day Lucy wanted to explore the ocean. She found a boat and asked her Dad if she could take it out. He said yes and off she went!

As soon as Lucy was out in the ocean, she saw a large and beautiful reef. She wanted to explore it, so she got closer to the reef.

Suddenly, Lucy noticed something frightening. It was a large fish! She was scared and scared to go any closer. She turned her boat around and bumped back home.

Lucy had a great adventure at the ocean, but she learned that there can be some frightening things out there! She will always remember to include being careful in her adventures.

name_of_work: Upon the Table the Tea Turning Cold by Riyas Qurana
content: When the Past and the Future met, I created anew a tea-shop there. Placing a table there and two chairs too facing each other I waited for ages. They didn't come. I say it just for the sake of telling. For, none had promised to come. It is here that the complication comes to be. How to continue the poem Recounting the poem from an angle unthought of by you No possibility is seen. Hence, forced to act, I grab at two persons going that way and make them sit in the chairs. One of the, a male The other, female. This simple knot Caused a spark in me. Hurriedly I place a lone cup of tea Upon the table. Now, see there _ a situation has come to be where they can be conceived as lovers. After that I did nothing. But, even if proved that they are no lovers making it impossible to believe it, things took shape on their own Each one suggesting that the other should drink the tea, with none drinking the tea turning cold upon the table is indeed an embarrassing situation between two Strangers. Oh, We know very well. But, doesn't this very situation help many to guess it to be the magical game of love? Both rising leave for their respective work in their different ways. In fact this is how the poem was about to conclude Yet, keeping our Tamil viewers in mind I had changed the verdict as follows: The vapour coming out of the tea-cup upon he table constructed a boundary-line between them. After remaining silent for too long they parted ways - She heading towards Future and he heading toward Past. Here I have also set a melancholic tune only a few can hear it. As I may have to write it twice I have given the climax as the title.

name_of_work: The Chalk Pit by Edward Thomas
content: Is this the road that climbs above and bends Round what was one a chalk pit: now it is By accident an amphitheatre. Some ash trees standing ankle-deep in brier And bramble act the parts, and neither speak Nor stir.' 'But see: they have fallen, every one, And briar and bramble have grown over them.' 'That is the place. As usual no one is here. Hardly can I imagine the drop of the axe, And the smack that is like an echo, sounding here.' 'I do not understand.' 'Why, what I mean is That I have seen the place two or three times At most, and that its emptiness and silence And stillness haunt me, as if just before It was not empty, silent, still, but full Of life of some kind, perhaps tragical. Has anything unusual happened here?' 'Not that I know of. It is called the Dell. They have not dug chalk here for a century. That was the ash trees' age. But I will ask.' 'No. Do not. I prefer to make a tale, Or better leave it like the end of a play, Actors and audience and lights all gone; For so it looks now. In my memory Again and again I see it, strangely dark, And vacant of a life but just withdrawn. We have not seen the woodman with the axe. Some ghost has left it now as we two came.' 'And yet you doubted if this were the road?' 'Well, sometimes I have thought of it and failed To place it. No. And I am not quite sure, Even now, this is it. For another place, Real or painted, may have combined with it. Or I myself a long way back in time...' 'Why, as to that, I used to meet a man--- I had forgotten,---searching for birds' nests Along the road and in the chalk pit too. The wren's hole was an eye that looked at him For recognition. Every nest he knew. He got a stiff neck, by looking this side or that, Spring after spring, he told me, with his laugh,--- A sort of laugh. He was a visitor, A man of forty,---smoked and strolled about. At orts and crosses Pleasure and Pain had played On his brown features;---I think both had lost;--- Mild and yet wild too. You may know the kind. And once or twice a woman shared his walks, A girl of twenty with a brown boy's face, And hair brown as a thrush or as a nut, Thick eyebrows, glinting eyes---' 'You have said enough. A pair,---free thought, free love,---I know the breed: I shall not mix my fancies up with them.' 'You please yourself. I should prefer the truth Or nothing. Here, in fact, is nothing at all Except a silent place that once rang loud, And trees and us---imperfect friends, we men And trees since time began; and nevertheless Between us still we breed a mystery.'

name_of_work: Before The Cask of Wine by Li Bai
content: The spring wind comes from the east and quickly passes, Leaving faint ripples in the wine of the golden bowl. The flowers fall, flake after flake, myriads together. You, pretty girl, wine-flushed, Your rosy face is rosier still. How long may the peach and plum trees flower By the green-painted house? The fleeting light deceives man, Brings soon the stumbling age. Rise and dance In the westering sun While the urge of youthful years is yet unsubdued! What avails to lament after one's hair has turned white like silken threads?

One day there was a yellow dog. His name was Rudy. Rudy was walking around the house looking for something to do. Suddenly he heard a loud noise. It scared him. He ran quickly to the table. It was bigger than him, so he felt safe underneath it.

The noise continued. Rudy was very scared. He wanted to know what it was. He called out for his owner, "Mommy, what is that noise?".

Mommy came over and put her hand on Rudy's head. She thought for a moment and then said, "It's just the washing machine, Rudy. It's nothing to be scared of. Can you hear it?"

Rudy listened carefully and heard the washing machine spinning and humming. He wasn't scared anymore. He felt so happy that he gave Mommy a big kiss and a big hug. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to explore the forest. One day, she saw a mushroom and got very enthusiastic. "Look, Mommy! A mushroom!" she said, pointing at it. "Can we pick it?"

Her mother replied, "No, Lily. We can't pick mushrooms in the forest. They belong here."

Lily leaned down to get a closer look at the mushroom. "It's so pretty," she said.

Suddenly, they heard a rustling in the bushes. "What was that?" Lily asked, feeling a bit scared.

"It's probably just a squirrel," her mother reassured her. "Let's keep walking and see what else we can find." And with that, they continued their exploration of the forest.

name_of_work: A Lake and a Fairy Boat by Thomas Hood
content: A lake and a fairy boat To sail in the moonlight clear, - And merrily we would float From the dragons that watch us here! Thy gown should be snow-white silk And strings of oriental pearls, Like gossamers dipped in milk, Should twine with thy raven curls! Red rubies should deck thy hands, And diamonds should be thy dower - But fairies have broke their wands, And wishing has lost its power!

Once there was a poor boy named Martin. He lived alone in a small shack beside an old oak tree. He never had much money, but he managed to get by. 

One day, Martin decided to see if he could climb the old oak tree. He could see branches high above him and he thought it might be fun. He tried to get close to the trunk, but it was too tall for him. He felt really disappointed, but then he spotted a large branch sticking out from the tree.
 
He decided to try and grab it and see if he could manage to climb up. As he grabbed the branch, it suddenly snapped and Martin went tumbling down to the ground. He lay there for a few minutes, feeling really sore and embarrassed.

Suddenly, he heard a voice. An old man with a white beard was standing nearby. He said, â€œYoung man, you must always know your limits, so you donâ€™t risk injuring yourselfâ€.

Martin looked up and thanked the old man. He knew the old man was right, so instead of trying to climb the tree, he decided to just enjoy the view from the ground. He looked up and smiled as the sun shone through the leaves of the old oak.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a big head with curly hair. One day, Lily went to the park and saw her friend, Timmy.

Timmy said, "Lily, let's play a game!"

Lily nodded her head and said, "What game?"

Timmy said, "We will lay down and close our eyes. Then, we will see who can stay quiet the longest."

Lily agreed and they both laid down on the grass. But, after a few minutes, Lily got frustrated because she couldn't stay quiet. She opened her eyes and said, "I can't do it anymore, Timmy!"

Timmy laughed and said, "That's okay, Lily. You tried your best!"

Once upon a time, there was a little blue bird. The blue bird lived in a tree with all of its friends. One day, the blue bird heard a loud noise. It was coming from a big building called a factory. 

The blue bird decided to fly to the factory to see what was happening. When the blue bird arrived, it saw that the factory was making lots of smoke and it smelled bad. The blue bird didn't like it and wanted it to stop. 

The blue bird talked to the workers at the factory and asked them to stop making the smoke. The workers didn't listen and kept making the smoke. The blue bird was sad and flew back to its tree. The blue bird's friends saw that it was sad and asked what happened. The blue bird told them about the factory and how it was making lots of smoke. The friends decided to help the blue bird and together they went to the factory to ask the workers to stop. This time, the workers listened and the factory stopped making the smoke. The blue bird and its friends were happy again.

Tom and Lily are brother and sister. They like to play together in the garden. One day, they find a pair of scissors in the shed. Tom has an idea.

"Let's play haircut!" he says to Lily. "I can cut your hair and make you look pretty."

Lily nods and sits on a chair. Tom picks up the scissors and starts to snip snip snip. He cuts off a lot of Lily's hair. He puts it on the ground. He thinks it looks funny.

"Look, Lily, you have a new haircut!" he says. "Do you like it?"

Lily looks in the mirror. She sees her hair is very short and uneven. She feels sad and angry. She does not like her haircut at all.

"Tom, you are a bad brother!" she cries. "You ruined my hair! I don't want to play with you anymore!"

She runs to the house and tells their mom. Mom sees Lily's haircut and gasps. She is shocked and upset. She scolds Tom and takes him to his room. She says he can't play outside for a week.

Tom feels sorry and ashamed. He wishes he did not cut Lily's hair. He wants to say sorry to her and make her happy again.

He thinks of a way to cheer her up. He remembers that Lily loves cookies. He sneaks out of his room and goes to the kitchen. He finds some cookies in the jar. He puts them on a plate. He writes a note that says "I'm sorry, Lily. I love you. From Tom." He takes the plate and the note and goes to Lily's room.

He knocks on the door and says "Lily, can I come in? I have something for you."

Lily opens the door and sees Tom. She sees the plate of cookies and the note. She reads the note and smiles. She feels a little better.

"Thank you, Tom," she says. "That's very nice of you. I love you too."

She takes a cookie and bites it. It is tasty and sweet. She gives Tom a cookie too. They hug and make up.

Mom sees them and smiles. She is glad they are friends again. She says they can go to the salon tomorrow and get a new haircut for Lily. She says she loves them both very much.

Anna and Ben were twins who liked to play outside. They had a big dog named Rex who was very obedient. Rex always listened to Anna and Ben and did what they said. He was a good dog.

One day, Anna and Ben saw a wild rabbit in the garden. They wanted to catch it and admire it. They ran after the rabbit, but it was too fast. Rex ran after them, but he did not want to hurt the rabbit. He barked to warn them to stop.

"Come back, Anna and Ben!" Rex barked. "The rabbit is wild. It might bite you or scratch you. It is not a toy."

But Anna and Ben did not listen to Rex. They wanted the rabbit. They chased it into the woods, where they saw a big hole. They thought the rabbit was hiding there. They went inside the hole, but it was dark and scary. They heard a loud growl.

"Help, Rex!" Anna and Ben cried. "There is something in here!"

Rex heard their cries and ran to the hole. He saw a big bear coming out of the hole. The bear was angry and hungry. It saw Anna and Ben and Rex. It roared and attacked them.

Rex tried to protect Anna and Ben, but he was no match for the bear. The bear bit Rex and hurt him badly. Rex whimpered and fell down. Anna and Ben screamed and ran away, but the bear was faster. It caught them and ate them.

The bear was full and happy. It went back to the hole and slept. Rex was sad and hurt. He crawled out of the hole and looked for help. But no one came. He died alone in the woods.

The end.

Tom and Lily were playing in the woods. They liked to look for bugs and sticks and flowers. They saw a big tree with a hole in it. They wanted to see what was inside.

"Maybe there is a bird or a mouse or a fairy," Lily said.

"Let's go and look," Tom said.

They ran to the tree and peeked inside. They saw something shiny and sharp. It was an axe. Someone had left it there.

"Wow, look at that!" Tom said. "It is a big knife. I want to touch it."

"No, Tom, don't touch it!" Lily said. "It is dangerous. It can hurt you. Mama said we should not touch things that are not ours."

But Tom did not listen. He reached his hand inside the hole and grabbed the axe. He pulled it out and swung it in the air.

"Look, Lily, I am strong. I can cut the tree," he said.

He hit the tree with the axe. The axe made a loud noise and a big mark on the bark. Tom smiled. He hit the tree again and again.

"Stop, Tom, stop!" Lily said. "You are hurting the tree. The tree is alive. It is not nice to hurt things that are alive. You should be gentle with them."

But Tom did not stop. He liked the noise and the mark. He hit the tree harder and harder.

Suddenly, the axe slipped from his hand. It flew in the air and landed on the ground. It hit a rock and broke in half. The blade was bent and the handle was cracked.

Tom and Lily gasped. They looked at the broken axe. They looked at each other. They felt scared and sorry.

"What have we done?" Tom said.

"We have to go home," Lily said. "We have to tell Mama and Papa. Maybe they can fix it. Maybe they can say sorry to the person who owns it."

They picked up the broken axe and ran back to their house. They hoped they would not get in trouble. They hoped they would learn to be gentle and careful. They hoped the tree would forgive them.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. He loved to play with his toys, but he also loved to climb on the furniture. His favorite was the gray couch. He would jump on it and bounce up and down.

One day, Timmy's mom told him to stop jumping on the couch. But Timmy didn't listen. He kept jumping and jumping until he accidentally squeezed the cushion too hard. Suddenly, the stuffing started to come out!

Timmy's mom was very upset. She told him he had to be careful with the furniture. But it was too late. The gray couch was ruined and Timmy was very sad. From that day on, he never jumped on the furniture again.

name_of_work: The Old Maid by Sara Teasdale
content: I saw her in a Broadway car, The woman I might grow to be; I felt my lover look at her And then turn suddenly to me. Her hair was dull and drew no light And yet its color was as mine; Her eyes were strangely like my eyes Tho' love had never made them shine. Her body was a thing grown thin, Hungry for love that never came; Her soul was frozen in the dark Unwarmed forever by love's flame. I felt my lover look at her And then turn suddenly to me, -- His eyes were magic to defy The woman I shall never be.

Once there was a mommy who wanted to teach little Jenny how to make a cake. So she got out all the ingredients like flour, eggs, and sugar. 

But the mommy soon found out that it was not so easy. Jenny was so little, it was hard for her to understand what her mommy wanted her to do. 

This made the mommy feel frustrated. She tried to think of a way to help Jenny. Then, she came up with an idea. 

The mommy asked Jenny to help her find the spoons and other kitchen tools. Jenny was so happy to be a part of it. 

Soon, they had mixed all the ingredients together and voila! A delicious cake was ready. Jenny was so excited to have helped make this special treat.

One day, a little girl named Ella was playing in the park. She was 3 years old and had beautiful, curly, blonde hair.

Ella loved to explore new things and this day was no different. She saw a violin, and she had never seen anything like it before.

Ella walked over to it, wanting to discover what it was. With one finger she pointed at the violin.

Before long, a man and his daughter walked up to her. The girl was a bit older than Ella, and she could tell that she was spoiled. She had a dress on that Ella thought was so pretty.

"What is it?" Ella asked, pointing to the violin again.

The girl smiled and said, "It's a violin. It makes music."

Ella was fascinated. She wanted to try it, so she asked the girl if she could touch it. The girl nodded yes, and Ella had a wonderful time making music.

Though she was smart for her age, Ella still hadn't fully figured out what the violin was. But that didn't matter, because she already knew she loved it.

name_of_work: A Prayer for my Daughter by William Butler Yeats
content: Once more the storm is howling, and half hid Under this cradle-hood and coverlid My child sleeps on. There is no obstacle But Gregory's wood and one bare hill Whereby the haystack- and roof-levelling wind, Bred on the Atlantic, can be stayed; And for an hour I have walked and prayed Because of the great gloom that is in my mind. I have walked and prayed for this young child an hour And heard the sea-wind scream upon the tower, And under the arches of the bridge, and scream In the elms above the flooded stream; Imagining in excited reverie That the future years had come, Dancing to a frenzied drum, Out of the murderous innocence of the sea.
