May she be granted beauty and yet not Beauty to make a stranger's eye distraught, Or hers before a looking-glass, for such, Being made beautiful overmuch, Consider beauty a sufficient end, Lose natural kindness and maybe The heart-revealing intimacy That chooses right, and never find a friend. Helen being chosen found life flat and dull And later had much trouble from a fool, While that great Queen, that rose out of the spray, Being fatherless could have her way Yet chose a bandy-legged smith for man. It's certain that fine women eat A crazy salad with their meat Whereby the Horn of Plenty is undone. In courtesy I'd have her chiefly learned; Hearts are not had as a gift but hearts are earned By those that are not entirely beautiful; Yet many, that have played the fool For beauty's very self, has charm made wise, And many a poor man that has roved, Loved and thought himself beloved, From a glad kindness cannot take his eyes. May she become a flourishing hidden tree That all her thoughts may like the linnet be, And have no business but dispensing round Their magnanimities of sound, Nor but in merriment begin a chase, Nor but in merriment a quarrel. O may she live like some green laurel Rooted in one dear perpetual place. My mind, because the minds that I have loved, The sort of beauty that I have approved, Prosper but little, has dried up of late, Yet knows that to be choked with hate May well be of all evil chances chief. If there's no hatred in a mind Assault and battery of the wind Can never tear the linnet from the leaf. An intellectual hatred is the worst, So let her think opinions are accursed. Have I not seen the loveliest woman born Out of the mouth of Plenty's horn, Because of her opinionated mind Barter that horn and every good By quiet natures understood For an old bellows full of angry wind? Considering that, all hatred driven hence, The soul recovers radical innocence And learns at last that it is self-delighting, Self-appeasing, self-affrighting, And that its own sweet will is Heaven's will; She can, though every face should scowl And every windy quarter howl Or every bellows burst, be happy still. And may her bridegroom bring her to a house Where all's accustomed, ceremonious; For arrogance and hatred are the wares Peddled in the thoroughfares. How but in custom and in ceremony Are innocence and beauty born? Ceremony's a name for the rich horn, And custom for the spreading laurel tree.

Mummy was frustrated. Every day she was trying to fit the round lemon in the square box, but it just wouldn't fit. She tried harder and harder, squashing the lemon but nothing she did worked.

Mummy said to her little boy, "I just don't understand, why won't it fit!" But the little boy didn't have an answer. 

After trying for a really long time, Mummy decided that the lemon just wasn't ever going to fit in the square box. She was so angry and frustrated she threw the box on the ground and screamed in frustration.

Mummy took a deep breath and said, "It's no good, the lemon won't fit, we'll just have to forget about it." 

The little boy was very sad. He had been hoping the lemon would fit in the box so he and Mummy could share the lemon together. But now it seemed like this was never going to happen.

Fortunately for the little boy, his Mummy was a wise woman and she said, "It's alright, I will get us some other lemons so we can still have some to share together." 

The little boy was very happy and hugged Mummy, but he still felt a little frustrated that the lemon hadn't fit in the square box.

Once upon a time, there was a kind lady named Mary. She had a big house and lots of toys. She was very wealthy. One day, Mary went to the store to buy some food. She put the food on a scale to weigh it. 

While she was at the store, a mean man came into her house and stole all of her toys. When Mary got home, she saw that her toys were gone. She was very sad and started to cry. 

Her neighbor, Timmy, heard her crying and came over to ask what was wrong. Mary told Timmy what happened and asked him to help her find her toys. Timmy said, "I will help you find your toys, please don't cry." 

They looked everywhere, but they couldn't find the toys. Mary was still very sad. Timmy said, "I'm sorry we couldn't find your toys." Mary said, "It's okay, thank you for trying to help." And so, Mary was left without her toys, and she felt very sad.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Sarah. One day, Sarah asked her mom for a lollipop. She was so excited and could feel the sweetness on her tongue already. But her mom said, "No, sweetheart. That candy is not allowed." 

Sarah was so upset. She started to cry and feel very sad. Then, her mom said, "There is something else I can give you." She reached into a drawer and pulled out another sweet treat. It was a big, round lollipop. Sarah was happy when she saw it, but when she tasted it, it was so bitter! 

Her mom said, "That one is allowed. But only for a special occasion." Sarah was still sad but she said, "Thank you." She decided to save the lollipop for a special day so she could enjoy it even more. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a kind lady named Mrs. Smith. She loved to share her lollipops with everyone. She was very generous. One day, a little girl named Emily came to her house. Emily loved lollipops too. Mrs. Smith gave her a big red lollipop. Emily was very happy and said, "Thank you, Mrs. Smith!" Mrs. Smith smiled and said, "I will teach you how to share your lollipops with others too." Emily nodded and said, "Okay, I will share my lollipop with my brother." From that day on, Emily learned to be generous and share her lollipops with others, just like Mrs. Smith.

name_of_work: In the Prison Pen by Herman Melville
content: Listless he eyes the palisades And sentries in the glare; 'Tis barren as a pelican-beach-- But his world is ended there. Nothing to do; and vacant hands Bring on the idiot-pain; He tries to think--to recollect, But the blur is on his brain. Around him swarm the plaining ghosts Like those on Virgil's shore-- A wilderness of faces dim, And pale ones gashed and hoar. A smiting sun. No shed, no tree; He totters to his lair-- A den that sick hands dug in earth Ere famine wasted there, Or, dropping in his place, he swoons, Walled in by throngs that press, Till forth from the throngs they bear him dead-- Dead in his meagerness.

name_of_work: To a Little Invisible Being Who is Expected Soon to Become Visible by Anna Laetitia Barbauld
content: Germ of new life, whose powers expanding slow For many a moon their full perfection wait,-- Haste, precious pledge of happy love, to go Auspicious borne through life's mysterious gate. What powers lie folded in thy curious frame,-- Senses from objects locked, and mind from thought! How little canst thou guess thy lofty claim To grasp at all the worlds the Almighty wrought! And see, the genial season's warmth to share, Fresh younglings shoot, and opening roses glow! Swarms of new life exulting fill the air,-- Haste, infant bud of being, haste to blow! For thee the nurse prepares her lulling songs, The eager matrons count the lingering day; But far the most thy anxious parent longs On thy soft cheek a mother's kiss to lay. She only asks to lay her burden down, That her glad arms that burden may resume; And nature's sharpest pangs her wishes crown, That free thee living from thy living tomb. She longs to fold to her maternal breast Part of herself, yet to herself unknown; To see and to salute the stranger guest, Fed with her life through many a tedious moon. Come, reap thy rich inheritance of love! Bask in the fondness of a Mother's eye! Nor wit nor eloquence her heart shall move Like the first accents of thy feeble cry. Haste, little captive, burst thy prison doors! Launch on the living world, and spring to light! Nature for thee displays her various stores, Opens her thousand inlets of delight. If charmed verse or muttered prayers had power, With favouring spells to speed thee on thy way, Anxious I'd bid my beads each passing hour, Till thy wished smile thy mother's pangs o'erpay.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to skip around her garden and play with her toys. One day, while she was skipping, she saw a hedge. It was tall and green, and she wondered what was on the other side.

Lily walked up to the hedge and looked through the leaves, but she couldn't see anything. She asked the hedge, "What's on the other side?" But the hedge didn't answer, because it was unknown to her.

Lily decided to climb over the hedge to see what was on the other side. When she got to the top, she saw a beautiful meadow with flowers and butterflies. She skipped down into the meadow and played with the butterflies. When she was done, she climbed back over the hedge and went home, happy to have discovered something new.

name_of_work: The Parable of the Old Man and the Young by Wilfred Owen
content: So Abram rose, and clave the wood, and went, And took the fire with him, and a knife. And as they sojourned both of them together, Isaac the first-born spake and said, My Father, Behold the preparations, fire and iron, But where the lamb for this burnt-offering? Then Abram bound the youth with belts and straps, And builded parapets and trenches there, And stretched forth the knife to slay his son. When lo! an Angel called him out of heaven, Saying, Lay not thy hand upon the lad, Neither do anything to him, thy son. Behold! Caught in a thicket by its horns, A Ram. Offer the Ram of Pride instead. But the old man would not so, but slew his son, And half the seed of Europe, one by one.

I had walked since dawn and lay down to rest on a bare hillside Above the ocean. I saw through half-shut eyelids a vulture wheeling high up in heaven, And presently it passed again, but lower and nearer, its orbit narrowing, I understood then That I was under inspection. I lay death-still and heard the flight- feathers Whistle above me and make their circle and come nearer. I could see the naked red head between the great wings Bear downward staring. I said, 'My dear bird, we are wasting time here. These old bones will still work; they are not for you.' But how beautiful he looked, gliding down On those great sails; how beautiful he looked, veering away in the sea-light over the precipice. I tell you solemnly That I was sorry to have disappointed him. To be eaten by that beak and become part of him, to share those wings and those eyes-- What a sublime end of one's body, what an enskyment; what a life after death.

Once upon a time there was a boy. His name was Tommy. Tommy was happy. He loved to play outside.

One day he saw a tower. It was tall and long. Tommy liked it. He wanted to try and touch it. So he ran over to it.

He tried to touch it, but it was too tall. He jumped and jumped, but couldn't reach the top. He was sad.

But then Tommy had an idea. He clapped his hands. When he did, the tower started to get smaller and smaller. Soon, Tommy could touch the top of the tower. He was so excited! He clapped and clapped with joy. 

He had made the tower small enough for him to reach. Tommy was happy and so were his friends. Everyone clapped and clapped for Tommy.

Once upon a time, there was a man who wanted to go on an adventurous trip. He went to the store to buy an axe to help him cut through the forest. He was very excited to go on his trip.

He walked and walked and finally found a big forest. He started to chop down trees with his new axe. But then, he accidentally chopped his leg with the axe! He was hurt very badly and could not walk anymore.

He cried and cried and wished he had never bought the axe. He was stuck in the forest and could not get help. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Yesterday, Timmy went to the park with his mommy. He loved going to the park because he could play on the swings and slide down the slide. 

But yesterday, there was a problem. Another little boy was on the swings and wouldn't let Timmy have a turn. Timmy got impatient and started to cry. His mommy tried to talk to the other boy, but he didn't listen. 

Then, Timmy had an idea. He went to the slide and started to play. The other boy saw how much fun Timmy was having and wanted to play too. They ended up playing together and having a great time. Timmy learned that sometimes it's better to be patient and wait for your turn, and that sharing is important. He went home happy and loved his day at the park.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in the field behind her house. One day, her mom said, "Lily, if you behave today, we can go play in the field later." Lily was very excited and promised to be good.

They went to the store and Lily saw a toy she really wanted. She asked her mom if she could have it, but her mom said no. Lily started to cry and throw a tantrum. Her mom said, "Lily, if you don't behave, we won't be able to play in the field later."

Lily knew she had to stop crying and be good if she wanted to play in the field. She took a deep breath and calmed down. Later that day, they went to the field and had so much fun playing together. They ran around and played hide and seek. Lily was happy she behaved and got to play in the field with her mom.

From that day on, Lily remembered that if she behaved, she could have fun in the field with her mom. She knew it was important to be good and not throw tantrums, or else she might not get to play in the field again.

name_of_work: Part II: The Rime of The Ancient Mariner By S.T. Coleridge
content: The Sun now rose upon the right: Out of the sea came he, Still hid in mist, and on the left Went down into the sea. And the good south wind still blew behind, But no sweet bird did follow, Nor any day for food or play Came to the mariner's hollo! And I had done a hellish thing, And it would work 'em woe: For all averred, I had killed the bird That made the breeze to blow. Ah wretch! said they, the bird to slay, That made the breeze to blow! Nor dim nor red, like God's own head, The glorious Sun uprist: Then all averred, I had killed the bird That brought the fog and mist. 'Twas right, said they, such birds to slay, That bring the fog and mist. The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew, The furrow followed free; We were the first that ever burst Into that silent sea. Down dropt the breeze, the sails dropt down, 'Twas sad as sad could be; And we did speak only to break The silence of the sea! All in a hot and copper sky, The bloody Sun, at noon, Right up above the mast did stand, No bigger than the Moon. Day after day, day after day, We stuck, nor breath nor motion; As idle as a painted ship Upon a painted ocean. Water, water, every where, And all the boards did shrink; Water, water, every where, Nor any drop to drink. The very deep did rot: O Christ! That ever this should be! Yea, slimy things did crawl with legs Upon the slimy sea. About, about, in reel and rout The death-fires danced at night; The water, like a witch's oils, Burnt green, and blue and white. And some in dreams assured were Of the Spirit that plagued us so; Nine fathom deep he had followed us From the land of mist and snow. And every tongue, through utter drought, Was withered at the root; We could not speak, no more than if We had been choked with soot. Ah! well a-day! what evil looks Had I from old and young! Instead of the cross, the Albatross About my neck was hung.

Once there was a happy bird, chirping in the meadow all day. One day, he heard a beautiful sound coming from around the hill. It was the sound of a girl singing!

The bird decided to fly towards the sound. He was surprised to see a girl sitting under the tree, singing softly.

The bird said to the girl, "Why are you singing?"

The girl smiled and said, "Because it makes me feel happy!"

The bird thought for a moment, then said, "It's nice to be happy and sing! Just remember, it's not just about singing, it's about sharing your happiness with others as well. When you sing, make it wide, so everyone can hear and be happy together!"

The girl smiled and nodded in agreement. From then on, whenever the girl sang, she made sure to sing to the wide open valley, so everyone could hear her beautiful voice. 

The bird flew away happy, knowing he'd been able to share his own happiness with another.

Once upon a time, there lived a nosy old sheep. Every day, she liked to go on a long walk to explore her land.

One day, on her walk, the sheep heard something. It sounded like a voice repeating the same words over and over. Intrigued, the nosy sheep kept following the sound.

Finally, she came to a clearing. In the middle of the clearing, there was a small girl dancing and repeating the same words. 

The nosy old sheep stepped closer, trying to understand the words the girl was saying. Suddenly, the girl saw the sheep and looked up in surprise.

"Oh! I've been having so much fun with my sheep game," the girl said. She giggled as she held out her hands. And with that, the three of them began to play.

Once upon a time, there was a small boat. It sailed on the sea, with no one guiding it. The boat felt scared and alone. Then, there was a rumbling sound coming closer and closer. It was the sound of a drum. The boat felt safe and peaceful. As the rumbling sound got louder, the boat began to sail faster. It was so happy!

Soon, the boat reached an island. It was a magical place full of new sights and sounds. There were colorful trees and bright flowers everywhere. The boat was so excited!

As the boat sailed around the island, the beautiful sound of the drum still echoed in the air. The boat was no longer scared. It was filled with calmness and joy as it sailed around the island.

At the end of the day, the boat was happy and content. It had made a new friend â€“ the drum! Together, they shared a wonderful day. The boat had learned that it can always be brave and make new friends.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys, but one day she noticed that her favorite toy was broken. She went to her mom and said, "Mommy, my toy is broken, can you fix it?"

Mommy said, "Let me test it first." So, mommy took the toy and tested it. She found out that the toy was missing a part. "Don't worry, Lily," mommy said. "I will supply the missing part and fix your toy."

Lily was so happy and said, "Thank you, mommy! You are so quiet when you work." Mommy smiled and said, "I don't want to disturb you while you play." From that day on, Lily made sure to take good care of her toys so they wouldn't break.

Once upon a time there were two friends, Jack and Jill, who were very intelligent. They liked to play together every day.

One day Jack had an itch, so he asked Jill to help him feel better. Jill had an idea and said, â€œLetâ€™s clap together! That'll help your itch go away.â€

Jack tried and when he was done he felt better. He was so happy that he clapped even harder!

Jill said, â€œThank you for giving it a try. That was very smart.â€

The moral of this story is to try things that you don't think will work out and you might be surprised by how well it works out. Being intelligent means being willing to go outside your comfort zone and try something different.

name_of_work: Going Home (Burlington Route) by Willa Cather
content: How smoothly the trains run beyond the Missouri; Even in my sleep I know when I have crossed the river. The wheels turn as if they were glad to go; The sharp curves and windings left behind, The roadway wide open, (The crooked straight And the rough places plain.) They run smoothly, they run softly, too. There is not noise enough to trouble the lightest sleeper. Nor jolting to wake the weary-hearted. I open my window and let the air blow in, The air of morning, That smells of grass and earth - Earth, the grain-giver. How smoothly the trains run beyond the Missouri; Even in my sleep I know when I have crossed the river. The wheels turn as if they were glad to go; They run like running water, Like Youth, running away... They spin bright along the bright rails, Singing and humming, Singing and humming, They run remembering, They run rejoicing, As if they, too, were going home.

I am a man now. Pass your hand over my brow. You can feel the place where the brains grow. I am like a tree, From my top boughs I can see The footprints that led up to me. There is blood in my veins That has run clear of the stain Contracted in so many loins. Why, then, are my hands red With the blood of so many dead? Is this where I was misled? Why are my hands this way That they will not do as I say? Does no God hear when I pray? I have no where to go The swift satellites show The clock of my whole being is slow, It is too late to start For destinations not of the heart. I must stay here with my hurt.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to draw pictures and show them to his mom. One day, Timmy drew a picture of a big red apple. He wanted to make a copy of his picture so he could share it with his friends. 

Timmy asked his mom to help him make a copy. His mom said, "Let's test the printer first to make sure it works." They put a piece of paper in the printer and pressed the button. The printer made a loud noise and then printed a copy of Timmy's apple picture. 

Timmy was so happy to have a copy of his picture. He said, "Look mom, it's just like the original!" His mom smiled and said, "Yes, it's a perfect copy. Now you can share your picture with all your friends." Timmy ran outside to show his friends his apple picture and they all thought it was great.

There is a train inside this iris: You think I'm crazy, & like to say boyish & outrageous things. No, there is A train inside this iris. It's a child's finger bearded in black banners. A single window like a child's nail, A darkened porthole lit by the white, angular face Of an old woman, or perhaps the boy beside her in the stuffy, Hot compartment. Her hair is silver, & sweeps Back off her forehead, onto her cold and bruised shoulders. The prairies fail along Chicago. Past the five Lakes. Into the black woods of her New York; & as I bend Close above the iris, I see the train Drive deep into the damp heart of its stem, & the gravel Of the garden path Cracks under my feet as I walk this long corridor Of elms, arched Like the ceiling of a French railway pier where a boy With pale curls holding A fresh iris is waving goodbye to a grandmother, gazing A long time Into the flower, as if he were looking some great Distance, or down an empty garden path & he believes a man Is walking toward him, working Dull shears in one hand; & now believe me: The train Is gone. The old woman is dead, & the boy. The iris curls, On its stalk, in the shade Of those elms: Where something like the icy & bitter fragrance In the wake of a woman who's just swept past you on her way Home & you remain.

Once there was a cabin in the woods. Inside was a family with a 3 year old child. The child was very upset. Everyday the child would look outside to watch the sun rise. It was the most beauty thing the child had ever seen. Each morning the sun rose higher and higher, making the sky brighter and brighter. When the sun was highest in the sky, the child would go outside to feel the warmth. It made the child feel better. 

One day the sun rose higher than usual and the sky was brighter than ever. The child was so excited to go outside and enjoy the warmth. But it was very windy and the cabin shook. This made the child very scared and upset. He started to cry. But then something amazing happened. The wind stopped and the cabin stopped shaking. The sun kept rising and the sky continued to get brighter and brighter. 

The child's fear and sadness were gone. He looked outside and saw how beautiful the sun was. So, with a smile, the child watched the sun rise higher and higher in the sky.

Once upon a time, there were two friends named Timmy and Tommy. They loved playing together, but one day they got into a fight over a toy car. They both wanted to play with it, but there was only one.

Timmy said, "I want the car. It's mine!" 

Tommy replied, "No, it's mine. I had it first." 

They argued and fought, but eventually, they both got hurt and the car got broken. 

Their mom came in and saw what had happened. She said, "Boys, fighting is not good. You should share and play together. And remember, even if you are famous, you still need to be kind to others." 

Timmy and Tommy felt bad and apologized to each other. From that day on, they learned to share and play nicely together.

name_of_work: The Autumn day its course has run by Charlotte Bronte
content: The Autumn day its course has run--the Autumn evening falls Already risen the Autumn moon gleams quiet on these walls And Twilight to my lonely house a silent guest is come In mask of gloom through every room she passes dusk and dumb Her veil is spread, her shadow shed o'er stair and chamber void And now I feel her presence steal even to my lone fireside Sit silent Nun--sit there and be Comrade and Confidant to me.

Once upon a time, there was a little bunny. His name was Hop. Every day, he liked to go exploring. 

One day, he hopped and hopped until he saw a distant apple tree. He had never seen one so far away before! He was excited, so he hopped even faster.

When he arrived, there were the most delicious apples. Hop grabbed one and bit into it. It was very sweet! He ate a few more, and then went back home.

Hop was very tired from his long hop, but it was worth it. He had found the best apples ever!

Once upon a time there was a sweet little bear. One day, he got an invitation in the mail and was so excited! He couldn't believe his luck. He was going to the best party and invited all his friends!

When the day of the party came, the little bear was so happy. He put on his cutest outfit and raced to the party.

At the party, there were lots of delicious treats. The little bear ate so much that he couldn't eat any more.

The next morning, the little bear found that some of the treats had rotted overnight. He was so sad and disappointed but he still had a fun time at the party.

Once upon a time, there was a distant castle full of yet undecorated walls. But one day, a kind fairy arrived and decided to help.

She sprinkled sparkly dust all around the walls, turning them into rainbow colours. Then, she carefully used her magic wand to hang sparkly stars and shining suns. Finally, she picked colourful flowers to create a dazzling pattern all around the castle.

When the fairy finished decorating, the castle glowed and shone brighter than ever before! The villagers who lived nearby were delighted and gathered around the walls to admire the delightful decorations. The castle was now more beautiful than anyone could ever have imagined! The fairy smiled with pride, satisfied with her work.

name_of_work: Let Me Not Forget by Rabindranath Tagore
content: If it is not my portion to meet thee in this life then let me ever feel that I have missed thy sight ---let me not forget for a moment, let me carry the pangs of this sorrow in my dreams and in my wakeful hours. As my days pass in the crowded market of this world and my hands grow full with the daily profits, let me ever feel that I have gained nothing ---let me not forget for a moment, let me carry the pangs of this sorrow in my dreams and in my wakeful hours. When I sit by the roadside, tired and panting, when I spread my bed low in the dust, let me ever feel that the long journey is still before me ---let me not forget a moment, let me carry the pangs of this sorrow in my dreams and in my wakeful hours. When my rooms have been decked out and the flutes sound and the laughter there is loud, let me ever feel that I have not invited thee to my house ---let me not forget for a moment, let me carry the pangs of this sorrow in my dreams and in my wakeful hours

Once upon a time, there was a bear named Brownie. Brownie was very hungry and he wanted to find some honey. He asked his friend, a bird named Tweetie, if she knew where to find some honey.

"Tweetie, do you know where I can find some honey?" asked Brownie.

"Yes, I do!" replied Tweetie. "I saw some honey in a thin tree over there. But be careful, the tree is very high and you might fall."

Brownie thanked Tweetie and decided to climb the tree. He climbed and climbed until he reached the top. He saw the honey and he was so happy that he started to soar down to the ground. When he reached the ground, he shared the honey with Tweetie and they both had a delicious snack.
Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall, Humpty Dumpty had a great fall; All the king's horses and all the king's men Couldn't put Humpty together again.

Once upon a time, a little boy named Tim went for a walk. He loved to step on the crunchy leaves. Tim saw a bandage on the ground. "Yuck!" he said. He thought it was disgusting.

Tim kept walking and found a small cat. The cat had a hurt paw. Tim wanted to help the cat. He remembered the bandage he saw earlier. Tim went back and picked up the bandage.

He put the bandage on the cat's paw. The cat felt better and walked with Tim. They stepped on crunchy leaves together. Tim and the cat became good friends. They played every day, and the cat's paw got better.

Am I a stone, and not a sheep, That I can stand, O Christ, beneath Thy cross, To number drop by drop Thy blood's slow loss, And yet not weep? Not so those women loved Who with exceeding grief lamented Thee; Not so fallen Peter, weeping bitterly; Not so the thief was moved; Not so the Sun and Moon Which hid their faces in a starless sky, A horror of great darkness at broad noon - I, only I. Yet give not o'er, But seek Thy sheep, true Shepherd of the flock; Greater than Moses, turn and look once more And smite a rock.

name_of_work: The Ivy Green by Charles Dickens
content: Oh, a dainty plant is the Ivy green, That creepeth o'er ruins old! Of right choice food are his meals, I ween, In his cell so lone and cold. The wall must be crumbled, the stone decayed, To pleasure his dainty whim: And the mouldering dust that years have made Is a merry meal for him. Creeping where no life is seen, A rare old plant is the Ivy green. Fast he stealeth on, though he wears no wings, And a staunch old heart has he. How closely he twineth, how tight he clings, To his friend the huge Oak Tree! And slily he traileth along the ground, And his leaves he gently waves, As he joyously hugs and crawleth round The rich mould of dead men's graves. Creeping where grim death has been, A rare old plant is the Ivy green. Whole ages have fled and their works decayed, And nations have scattered been; But the stout old Ivy shall never fade, From its hale and hearty green. The brave old plant, in its lonely days, Shall fatten upon the past: For the stateliest building man can raise, Is the Ivy's food at last. Creeping on, where time has been, A rare old plant is the Ivy green.

Beside a humble stone, a tree Floats in the cemetery's air, Not planted in memoriam there, But growing wild, uncultured, free. A bird comes perching there to sing, Winter and summer, proffering Its faithful song--sad, bittersweet. That tree, that bird are you and I: You, memory; absence, me, that tide And time record. Ah, by your side To live again, undying! Aye, To live again! But ma petite, Now nothingness, cold, owns my flesh. . . Will your love keep my memory fresh?

Once upon a time, there was a little boy who liked to use his imagination. He liked to imagine all sorts of things. One day, he was imagining he was in a swamp. The swamp was big and brown. The ground was made of soft, squishy mud and the trees were tall and skinny. 

The little boy thought it was so fun to explore the swamp. He spotted a sea turtle in the water. He jumped in and the water felt cold and slimy. He swam around and found a lot of interesting creatures like frogs and crawly bugs. 

Before long it was time to go home. The little boy was sad to leave the swamp, but he was also excited to tell his family about his adventure. He said goodbye and waved to all the animals he had met in the swamp. He promised to come back and explore again soon.

One morning, a bright sun was shining. Mommy and Baby Bear were in the kitchen. Baby Bear saw a big pot of yogurt on the table and said, â€œYum! Yogurt!â€ Mommy said, â€œYes, Baby Bear. I made it just for you.â€ 

Baby Bear was so happy. He grabbed a spoon and ate the yogurt. He said, â€œMmmm! Letâ€™s have more yogurt!â€ 

Mommy smiled. She took the pot of yogurt and let Baby Bear have some more. Baby Bear giggled and ate more yogurt. 

Mommy said, â€œYou must be full! That was lots of yogurt!â€ Baby Bear smiled and nodded his head. He had had so much fun eating the bright and creamy yogurt!

name_of_work: In The Bazaars of Hyderabad by Sarojini Naidu
content: What do you sell O ye merchants ? Richly your wares are displayed. Turbans of crimson and silver, Tunics of purple brocade, Mirrors with panels of amber, Daggers with handles of jade. What do you weigh, O ye vendors? Saffron and lentil and rice. What do you grind, O ye maidens? Sandalwood, henna, and spice. What do you call , O ye pedlars? Chessmen and ivory dice. What do you make,O ye goldsmiths? Wristlet and anklet and ring, Bells for the feet of blue pigeons Frail as a dragon-fly's wing, Girdles of gold for dancers, Scabbards of gold for the king. What do you cry,O ye fruitmen? Citron, pomegranate, and plum. What do you play ,O musicians? Cithar, sarangi and drum. what do you chant, O magicians? Spells for aeons to come. What do you weave, O ye flower-girls With tassels of azure and red? Crowns for the brow of a bridegroom, Chaplets to garland his bed. Sheets of white blossoms new-garnered To perfume the sleep of the dead.

name_of_work: This Is a Photograph of Me by Margaret Atwood
content: It was taken some time ago. At first it seems to be a smeared print: blurred lines and grey flecks blended with the paper; then, as you scan it, you see in the left-hand corner a thing that is like a branch: part of a tree (balsam or spruce) emerging and, to the right, halfway up what ought to be a gentle slope, a small frame house. In the background there is a lake, and beyond that, some low hills. (The photograph was taken the day after I drowned. I am in the lake, in the center of the picture, just under the surface. It is difficult to say where precisely, or to say how large or small I am: the effect of water on light is a distortion but if you look long enough, eventually you will be able to see me.)

One day, Mommy and Daddy sent Mikey to the park. He was very happy! He had a big smile.

When they got to the park, they saw a tent. It was red and green and it looked very nice.

Mommy said, "Mikey, do you want to practice putting up the tent?"

Mikey was excited. He said, "Yes!"

Mommy and Daddy showed Mikey how to put the pieces of the tent together. It was a little hard, but Mikey kept trying. Finally, he had put it together just like Mommy and Daddy taught him.

Then, Daddy said, "Let's make sure the tent is tight. We don't want it to blow away!"

Mommy and Daddy helped Mikey pull the tent tight. Mikey felt very proud.

He could not wait to show his friends the tent he put up!

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy had some money in his pocket, and he wanted to buy a toy. He went to the toy store and saw a rough-looking toy truck. He liked it very much and decided to buy it with his money. 

Timmy spent all his money on the toy truck, and he was very happy. He played with it all day long, driving it over rocks and bumps. But then, he accidentally broke it! Timmy was sad because he spent all his money on the toy truck, and now it was broken. 

Timmy's mom saw how sad he was and decided to take him back to the toy store. They exchanged the broken toy truck for a new one, and Timmy was happy again. He learned that sometimes things can be rough, but it's okay to spend money on things that make us happy.

Why should I let the toad work Squat on my life? Can't I use my wit as a pitchfork And drive the brute off? Six days of the week it soils With its sickening poison - Just for paying a few bills! That's out of proportion. Lots of folk live on their wits: Lecturers, lispers, Losers, loblolly-men, louts- They don't end as paupers; Lots of folk live up lanes With fires in a bucket, Eat windfalls and tinned sardines- They seem to like it. Their nippers have got bare feet, Their unspeakable wives Are skinny as whippets - and yet No one actually _starves_. Ah, were I courageous enough To shout, Stuff your pension! But I know, all too well, that's the stuff That dreams are made on: For something sufficiently toad-like Squats in me, too; Its hunkers are heavy as hard luck, And cold as snow, And will never allow me to blarney My way of getting The fame and the girl and the money All at one sitting. I don't say, one bodies the other One's spiritual truth; But I do say it's hard to lose either, When you have both.

name_of_work: After Making Love We Hear Footsteps by Galway Kinnell
content: For I can snore like a bullhorn or play loud music or sit up talking with any reasonably sober Irishman and Fergus will only sink deeper into his dreamless sleep, which goes by all in one flash, but let there be that heavy breathing or a stifled come-cry anywhere in the house and he will wrench himself awake and make for it on the run--as now, we lie together, after making love, quiet, touching along the length of our bodies, familiar touch of the long-married, and he appears--in his baseball pajamas, it happens, the neck opening so small he has to screw them on-- and flops down between us and hugs us and snuggles himself to sleep, his face gleaming with satisfaction at being this very child. In the half darkness we look at each other and smile and touch arms across this little, startlingly muscled body-- this one whom habit of memory propels to the ground of his making, sleeper only the mortal sounds can sing awake, this blessing love gives again into our arms.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily who loved to play with her toys. She had a special toy, a microscope, that helped her see tiny things up close. One day, Lily decided to be creative and draw pictures of the tiny things she saw under her microscope. She drew a picture of a bow she saw on a bug's antenna and another picture of a tiny flower. Her mommy was so proud of her creative drawings and hung them up on the fridge for everyone to see. From that day on, Lily loved using her microscope to find new things to draw and share with her family.

Sara and Ben were twins who liked to play with their toys. But they were also selfish. They did not like to share their toys with each other or with their friends. They always wanted to have the best and the most toys.

One day, their mom gave them a big puzzle. It had many pieces and a picture of a farm. Sara and Ben both wanted to do the puzzle by themselves. They grabbed the pieces and tried to fit them together. But they could not. The puzzle was too hard for one person to do.

They started to get angry and frustrated. They blamed each other for taking the wrong pieces. They shouted and cried. Their mom heard them and came to see what was wrong. She saw the mess and the tears. She asked them a question.

"Why are you fighting over the puzzle? Don't you know that puzzles are more fun when you do them together? You need to unite and work as a team. Then you can see the whole picture and be proud of what you made."

Sara and Ben looked at each other. They felt sorry for being selfish. They decided to listen to their mom and unite. They said sorry and hugged. They put the pieces back in the box and started again. They helped each other find the right pieces and places. They talked and laughed. They enjoyed the puzzle.

Soon, they finished the puzzle. They saw the beautiful farm with the animals and the trees. They were happy and proud. They thanked their mom for the puzzle and for the lesson. They learned that being selfish is not good and that being united is better. They promised to share their toys and play nicely from then on.

name_of_work: Still will I harvest beauty where it grows by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: Still will I harvest beauty where it grows: In coloured fungus and the spotted fog Surprised on foods forgotten; in ditch and bog Filmed brilliant with irregular rainbows Of rust and oil, where half a city throws Its empty tins; and in some spongy log Whence headlong leaps the oozy emerald frog. . . . And a black pupil in the green scum shows. Her the inhabiter of divers places Surmising at all doors, I push them all. Oh, you that fearful of a creaking hinge Turn back forevermore with craven faces, I tell you Beauty bears an ultra fringe Unguessed of you upon her gossamer shawl!

Once upon a time, there was a car. It was a big car and it was bright blue. One day, the car felt very gloomy. It was very sad. Then, something strange happened! The car started to shrink. It got smaller and smaller until it was the size of a toy car. It was a very funny sight!

The car was happy now. It drove around in circles and had lots of fun. But it was still very small. It couldn't do many things that bigger cars could do.

Then one day, something wonderful happened! The car started to get bigger again. It became bigger and bigger, until it was the same size as before. The car was so excited! It could do all the things a bigger car could do.

The car was happy again. It drove around in circles, enjoying the sunshine and the fresh air. And it was never gloomy again!

name_of_work: You should appear less often in my dreams by Anna Akhmatova
content: You should appear less often in my dreams, Since we meet so frequently; Yet only in night's sanctuary Are you sad, troubled, and tender. And sweeter than seraphic praise Is your lips' dear flattery... Ah, in dreams you won't mistake my name, Or gently sigh, as you do here.

Once upon a time there was a big, important crocodile. The crocodile wanted to go to a special place so that he could rest. He swam and swam until he came to a beautiful lake. The lake was calm and peaceful, so the crocodile knew that this was the perfect spot to rest.

The crocodile lay down in the lake and shut his eyes. He felt relaxed and soon he was snoring softly. He spent the whole day by the lake resting and feeling happy.

But then, just as the sun was setting, the crocodile woke up. He was rested and ready to go! He thanked the lake for the special place it had given him to rest and then he swam away.

And from that day on, the crocodile always remembered how important it was to take time to rest.

Color floods to the spot, dull purple. The rest of the body is all washed out, The color of pearl. In a pit of rock The sea sucks obsessively, One hollow the whole sea's pivot. The size of a fly, The doom mark Crawls down the wall. The heart shuts, The sea slides back, The mirrors are sheeted.

Once upon a time there lived a young fair girl named Jane. One day, Jane went out with her mum to search for something special. They searched in the garden, up the tree and in the flower beds, but couldn't find anything. Jane was beginning to get very frustrated when she noticed a tall plant standing in a corner of the garden. She was curious, so she went to take a closer look.

"Mum, what's this plant?" Jane asked, pointing to the tall plant.

"Why don't you have a look under the leaves and see," her mum answered.

So, Jane eagerly bent down and covered the leaves to take a closer look. She gasped when she uncovered something dazzlingly fair and gold beneath the leaves!

"Mum! Look what I found! What is it?" Jane asked, full of joy and anticipation.

Her mum smiled and replied, "Why don't you pick it up and see what it is?" 

Jane carefully reached under the leaves and lifted the mysterious object. When she saw that it was a shiny golden star, she couldn't contain her joy! She hugged her mum and thanked her for helping her search.

Jane and her mum went inside, to proudly display the fair golden star in the home. Jane learned a valuable lesson that day, that good things often come to those who search!

Once upon a time, in a big sea, there was an oyster named Ollie. Ollie had a long shell that he could open and close. He lived with his friends, the fish, in the water.

One day, a little fish named Finny swam up to Ollie and asked, "Can I hide in your shell, Ollie? I am scared of the big fish." Ollie said, "I permit you to hide inside my shell, Finny. You will be safe here."

Finny stayed inside Ollie's shell for a while. They talked and became good friends. Soon, Finny felt brave and was ready to leave the shell. Ollie opened his long shell and let Finny out. Finny said, "Thank you, Ollie, for letting me hide in your shell."

The other fish saw how Ollie helped Finny and they learned that it is good to help friends when they need it. Ollie and Finny played together in the sea every day, and they were always there to help each other.

name_of_work: Refugee Mother and Child by Chinua Achebe
content: No Madonna and Child could touch that picture of a mother's tenderness for a son she soon would have to forget. The air was heavy with odours of diarrhoea of unwashed children with washed-out ribs and dried-up bottoms struggling in laboured steps behind blown empty bellies. Most mothers there had long ceased to care but not this one; she held a ghost smile between her teeth and in her eyes the ghost of a mother's pride as she combed the rust-coloured hair left on his skull and then - singing in her eyes - began carefully to part it... In another life this would have been a little daily act of no consequence before his breakfast and school; now she did it like putting flowers on a tiny grave.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play outside in the sun. But today it is very hot. Anna and Ben feel sweaty and thirsty.

"Let's go under the big tree," Anna says. "It is cool there."

"OK," Ben says. They run to the tree and sit under the shade. They drink some water from their bottles.

"Look, a bird!" Ben says. He points to a brown bird on a branch. The bird sings a pretty song.

"Hello, bird!" Anna says. She waves to the bird. The bird looks at them and tilts its head.

"Can you stay with us, bird?" Ben asks. He smiles at the bird. The bird flaps its wings and flies away.

"Bye, bird!" Anna and Ben say. They watch the bird fly to another tree. They are happy. They stay under the big tree and play with their toys. They are cool and not hot.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She was very hungry, so she asked her mommy if they could go to a restaurant. Her mommy said yes, and they went to a big restaurant with lots of people.

When they sat down at their table, Lily saw a big bell on the wall. She asked her mommy what it was, and her mommy said it was a bell that rang when food was ready. Lily thought that was cool.

After they ate, Lily felt proud of herself for being such a good girl at the restaurant. She said to her mommy, "I'm proud of me!" Her mommy smiled and said, "I'm proud of you too, Lily." Then they went home and had a nap. The end.

One day, a boy named Tom went to the park with his mom. He saw a big hill with many holes. He wanted to see what was inside the holes. He ran to the hill and put his hand in one hole.

"Ouch!" he cried. He pulled out his hand and saw a small brown animal with a long nose and tiny eyes. It was a mole. The mole bit his finger and ran away.

"Tom, are you okay?" his mom asked. She came to him and looked at his finger. It had a red mark.

"I'm okay, mom. But the mole was not nice. He bit me," Tom said.

"I'm sorry, Tom. The mole was scared. He thought you wanted to hurt him. He lives in the hole and he does not like strangers," his mom said.

"Really? But I just wanted to say hello. I like animals," Tom said.

"I know, Tom. But some animals are shy and need their space. You have to be careful and respectful when you meet them. Maybe you can gain their trust if you are gentle and quiet," his mom said.

"Okay, mom. I will try that. Can we go to the zoo next time? I want to see more animals. Maybe some great ones, like lions and elephants," Tom said.

"Sure, Tom. We can go to the zoo next time. I'm sure you will love it. But for now, let's go home and put some ice on your finger. It will make it feel better," his mom said.

Tom nodded and hugged his mom. He learned something new today. He learned that moles are small and shy, and that he has to be careful and respectful when he meets new animals. He also learned that there are many great animals in the world, and he wanted to see them all. He was happy and curious. He loved his mom and the park. He had a good day.

One day, two friends John and Kate were playing in their garden. The sun was shining and it was a beautiful day.

John saw something on the ground and he went to touch it. It was a small welcome card. He opened it and inside it said "Welcome".

His friend Kate asked "What is it?".

John said "It's a welcome card".

Kate said "Where did it come from?"

John said "I don't know, but it looks kind of fake."

Kate touched it and said "It feels fake too". They looked around but they couldn't find who left the card. Then they decided to take it home and figure out where it came from.

Nothing marks the car quarry now, just raised earth like the hummock of a grave, a headstone of trees, wind-written epitaphs running in their leaves. Filled in years ago, but still I can't help standing at its edge, where the ground once gave to an elephant's graveyard of cars, a motorway pile-up in the corner of the field. One of the places we came when we had tired of catching the commas and apostrophes of minnows and bullheads; or shooting at pumpkins in the field, shouldering the kick of your father's shotgun; or playing at war in the barn, dying again and again under its gap-toothed roof and broken beams. A place where we tested our voices, young as the buzzards above us striking their cries against a flint sky, smashed black holes in the windows, sat in the drivers' seats, going nowhere, operated on engines, dock-leaves and nettles running in their pistons or just walked among them, reading aloud from the names of the dead: Volvo, Ford, Vauxhall, Their primary colours rusting to red. Where we lost ourselves in the hours before dark, year on year, until that day when life put on the brakes and pitched you, without notice, through the windscreen of your youth. Your father found at dawn -- a poppy sown in the unripe corn. I came back once, to find the cars smaller or the undergrowth grown, whichever, the whole diminished to steel and stone. Just cars in a quarry, their dashboards undone and the needles of the speedos settled at zero. As I climbed back out I disturbed a buzzard that flew from its branch like a rag shaken out in the wind, before spiralling upwards above the shuffling trees and on over the fields -- the spittle sheep, the ink-dot cows, a tractor writing with its wheels, and on over the lanes, where a boy meandered between the hedges, trailing a stick, kicking a stone, trying once more to find his way home.

Once there was a boy called Dave who had a very special coat. It was his original coat and it always kept him warm. One day Dave went out to play and he forgot to take his coat with him. He was sad and worried, feeling the chill of the wind without it.

Dave asked his mum, "What should I do? I can't find my coat!" His mum looked around the house and said, "I know! First, let's go back to where you were playing. Maybe you left your coat there."

So they went back to the park and Dave was so excited when he saw his coat! He ran toward it and hugged it tightly, feeling a wave of relief. "Thank you mum", said Dave, "I'm never going to forget my coat again." His mum gave him a big smile and said, "That's my boy. Always remember your coat!"

Once upon a time there was a happy girl named Jane. Jane loved to play with her toys and her friends. One day she was playing with her friends when she saw something on the ground. It was a piece of gum. She quickly picked it up and stuck it in her mouth. Her friends said, â€œYuck! Thatâ€™s gross!â€ 

Jane didnâ€™t like the gum anymore. She wanted to remove it from her mouth. She tried to grab it with her fingers, but it was too sticky. She asked her friends for help, but none of them knew what to do. 

Eventually, she found a piece of straw. She put the straw in her mouth and slowly pulled out the gum. She was so happy when it finally came out!  Jane promised herself that she would never put gum in her mouth again.

Once upon a time, there was a big mountain. On the mountain, there lived a little boy named Tim and a little girl named Sue. They were friends and liked to play together.

One day, while they were playing, Tim pinched Sue's arm. Sue said, "Ouch! That hurt!" Tim said, "I'm sorry, I didn't know it would hurt you." Sue said, "It's okay, but please don't do it again." Tim was ignorant about pinching, but now he knew better.

From that day on, Tim and Sue played on the mountain without any pinching. They had lots of fun together and learned many new things. And they lived happily ever after.

Riding against the east, A veering, steady shadow Purrs the motor-call Of the man-bird Ready with the death-laughter In his throat And in his heart always The love of the big blue beyond. Only a man, A far fleck of shadow on the east Sitting at ease With his hands on a wheel And around him the large gray wings. Hold him, great soft wings, Keep and deal kindly, O wings, With the cool, calm shadow at the wheel.

utside the green velvet sitting room white roses bloom after rain. They hold water and sunlight like cups of fine white china. Within the boy who sleeps in my care in the big chair the cold bloom opens at terrible speed and the splinter of ice moves in his blood as he stirs in the chair. Remembering me he smiles politely, gritting his teeth in silence on pain's red blaze. A stick man in the ashes, his fires die back. He is spars and springs. He can talk again, gather his cat to his bones. She springs with a small cry in her throat, kneading with diamond paws his dry as tinder flesh. The least spark of pain will burn him like straw. The sun carelessly shines after rain. The cat tracks thrushes in sweet dark soil. And without concern the rose outlives the child.

Once upon a time, there was a helpful boy named Tim. He liked to help his mom and dad with their work. One day, Tim's mom asked him to record a song for his baby sister. Tim was very happy to help.

Tim put on his favorite pants and went to his room. He picked up his toy guitar and started to play. He sang a fun song about a big red ball. Tim's baby sister clapped her hands and laughed. Tim's mom used her phone to record the song.

When the song was over, Tim's mom said, "Thank you, Tim, for being so helpful." Tim felt proud and happy. His baby sister liked the song, and he had helped his mom. From that day, Tim always wore his favorite pants when he played his guitar and sang songs for his family.

Once upon a time there was a cool fox called Joe. Joe was very dependable and was always looking to help. Every day he went out and looked for something delicious to eat. 

One day while Joe was out, he saw a big piece of meat. It was sitting in the middle of the road and Joe was very hungry. So he decided to take the meat home. When he got back to his den, he shared the meat with all of his friends. 

Joe's friends were very happy, but one of them said, "Joe, why didnâ€™t you keep this meat for yourself? You need to be a little selfish sometimes". But Joe replied, "It's important to think about others and help them out. If we all help each other, we will all be happier". 

Joe was right. By helping his friends, he made them feel special and important. Helping others is always a good thing and can bring a lot of joy to all. Joe showed us that being dependable and looking to help those in need are important values to have.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved playing with her pony named Sparky. One day, Lily and Sparky went to the park to play. While they were playing, Sparky did a big poop on the grass. Lily felt embarrassed because other kids were watching. 

A kind lady saw what happened and came to help. She gave Lily a bag to pick up the poop and showed her how to do it. Lily was grateful for the lady's help. The lady explained to Lily that it's important to clean up after our pets, so we don't make a mess for others to step in. 

Lily learned a valuable lesson that day. She promised to always clean up after Sparky and to not feel embarrassed about it. From that day on, Lily and Sparky had even more fun playing together in the park, and Lily felt proud to be a responsible pet owner.

Tom and Sam are brothers. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big slide. Tom wants to go first. He runs to the slide and climbs up the ladder. He sits on the top and looks down. He is ready to slide.

Sam wants to go too. He runs after Tom and climbs up the ladder. He sits behind Tom and pushes him. Tom slides down very fast. He is scared. He tries to stop, but he can't. He reaches the end of the slide and falls off. He lands on the hard ground. He hurts his head and his arm. He cries.

Sam slides down after Tom. He is not scared. He thinks it is fun. He reaches the end of the slide and jumps off. He lands on his feet. He laughs. He does not see Tom crying. He does not care. He runs to the other side of the park. He wants to play more.

Tom is alone. He is hurt. He is sad. He wants his mom. He calls for her, but she does not hear him. She is on the other side of the park. She is talking to a friend. She does not see Tom crying. She does not know what happened. She is not ready to help him.

One day, a little girl named Lucy wanted to have a picnic. She asked her mom, "Can we please have a picnic today?" Her mom said, "Yes, we can have a picnic today."

They went to the park and found a nice spot under a tree. Lucy and her mom put a blanket on the ground and took out their food. They had sandwiches, fruits, and juice. Lucy was very happy.

But then, it started to rain. Lucy and her mom looked up at the sky and saw dark clouds. They felt sad because their picnic was ruined. Lucy said, "I regret not bringing an umbrella." Her mom replied, "It's okay, we can have another picnic another day."

The rain made their sandwiches wet and the fruits were all muddy. They were poor little sandwiches and fruits. Lucy and her mom packed up their things and went home.

Even though their picnic was ruined, Lucy and her mom still had a fun day together. They promised to have another picnic soon, and next time, they would bring an umbrella just in case it rained again.

Anna and Ben were playing in the garden. They liked to look for bugs and flowers. They saw a big green salad on the table. It had many colors and shapes.

"Can we eat some salad?" Anna asked.

"OK, but we have to wash our hands first," Ben said.

They ran to the sink and washed their hands. Then they took some salad and put it on their plates. They sat on the grass and ate.

"Yum, this salad is good," Anna said. "I like the red ones and the yellow ones."

"Me too," Ben said. "And the green ones and the orange ones."

They ate and talked. They saw a bird fly by. It was blue and shiny. It made a loud noise.

"Wow, look at that bird!" Ben said. "It glows in the sun."

"It's so pretty," Anna said. "But it sounds wild. Do you think it's friendly?"

"I don't know," Ben said. "Maybe it's looking for some salad too."

They watched the bird land on the table. It pecked at the salad. It liked the red ones and the yellow ones too.

"Hey, that's our salad!" Anna said. "Shoo, bird, shoo!"

They waved their arms and shouted. The bird flew away. It left some feathers on the table.

"Look, it gave us a gift," Ben said. He picked up a feather and gave it to Anna.

"Thank you, bird," Anna said. She smiled and put the feather in her hair.

They finished their salad and played some more. They had a fun day in the garden.

Lila and Tom were playing with their blocks in the living room. They liked to build towers and bridges and castles. Lila was gifted at making shapes and colors match. Tom was gifted at making things strong and tall.

Suddenly, they heard a loud boom outside. They looked out the window and saw dark clouds and flashes of lightning. They felt scared and ran to their mom.

"Mom, mom, what is that?" Lila asked, pointing at the sky.

"That is a storm, sweetie. It is when the rain and the wind and the lightning come together. Sometimes it makes noise and light, but it is not dangerous if we remain inside the house," mom explained, hugging them.

"Can we play with our blocks again?" Tom asked.

"Of course, you can. But let's move them away from the window, just in case. And maybe we can make a cozy fort with some pillows and blankets. How does that sound?" mom suggested.

Lila and Tom nodded and smiled. They liked the idea of a fort. They followed mom to the couch and helped her make a soft and warm shelter. They brought their blocks and some books and toys. They crawled inside the fort and played happily. They forgot about the storm and felt safe and loved.

One day, a charming little boy named Tim went outside to play. The sun was shining, and the birds were singing. Tim saw a big puddle from the rain last night. He thought it would be fun to jump and splash in the puddle.

"Hey, friend!" Tim called to his friend, Sam, who was nearby. "Come play with me in this puddle!" Sam ran over to Tim, and they both jumped into the puddle. They laughed and splashed each other, having so much fun.

But then, as they played, the puddle began to grow bigger and deeper. Tim and Sam got scared. They tried to get out of the puddle, but they couldn't. The puddle was too deep and slippery. They called for help, but no one could hear them.

"Help, help!" Tim and Sam cried, but no one came to save them. They were stuck in the big, deep puddle. It was not a happy day for Tim and Sam. They wished they had never played in the puddle.

I wish we could live as the flowers live, To breathe and to bloom in the summer and sun; To slumber and sway in the heart of the night, And to die when our glory had done. I wish we could love as the bees love, To rest or to roam without sorrow or sigh; With laughter, when, after the wooer had won, Love flew with a whispered goodbye. I wish we could die as the birds die, To fly and to fall when our beauty was best No trammels of time on the years of our face; And to leave but an empty nest.

name_of_work: Windfall, 8 Parnell Hill, Cork by Paul Durcan
content: But, then, at the end of day I could always say - Well, now, I am going home. I felt elected, steeped, sovereign to be able to say - I am going home. When I was at home I liked to stay at home; At home I stayed at home for weeks; At home I used sit in a winged chair by the window Overlooking the river and the factory chimneys, The electricity power station and the car assembly works, The fleets of trawlers and the pilot tugs, Dreaming that life is a dream which is real, The river a reflection of itself in its own waters, Goya sketching Goya among the smokey mirrors. The industrial vista was my Mont Sainte-Victoire. While my children sat on my knees watching TV Their mother, my wife, reclined on the couch Knitting a bright-coloured scarf, drinking a cup of black coffee, Smoking a cigarette - one of her own roll-ups. I closed my eyes and breathed in and breathed out. It is ecstacy to breathe if you are at home in the world. What a windfall! A home of our own! Our neighbours' houses had names like 'Con Amore', 'Sans Souci', 'Pacelli', 'Montini', 'Homesville'. But we called our home 'Windfall'. 'Windfall', 8 Parnell Hill, Cork. In the gut of my head coursed the leaf of tranquility Which I dreamed was known only to Buddhist Monks In lotus monasteries high up in the Hindu Kush. Down here in the dark depths of Ireland, Below sea level in the city of Cork, In a city as intimate and homicidal as Little Marseilles, In a country where all children of the nation Are not cherished equally And where the best go homeless, while the worst Erect block-house palaces - self-regardingly ugly - Having a home of your own can give to a family A chance in a lifetime to transcend death. At the high window, shipping from all over the world Being borne up and down the busy, yet contemplative, river; Skylines drifting in and out of skylines in the cloudy valley; Firelight at dusk, and city lights; Beyond them the control tower of the airport on the hill - A lighthouse in the sky flashing green to white to green; Our black-and-white cat snoozing in the corner of a chair; Pastels and etchings on the four walls, and over the mantelpiece 'Van Gogh's Grave' and 'Lovers in Water'; A room wallpapered in books and family photograph albums Chronicling the adventures and metamorphoses of family life: In swaddling clothes in Mammy's arms on baptism day; Being a baby of nine months and not remembering it; Face-down in a pram, incarcerated in a high chair; Everybody, including strangers, wearing shop-window smiles; With Granny in Felixstowe, with Granny in Ballymaloe; In a group photo in First Infants, on a bike at thirteen; In the back garden in London, in the back garden in Cork; Performing a headstand after First Holy Communion; Getting a kiss from the Bishop on Confirmation Day; Straw hats in the Bois de Boulougne, wearing wings at the seaside; Mammy and Daddy holding hands on the Normandy Beaches; Mammy and Daddy at the wedding of Jeremiah and Margot; Mammy and Daddy queueing up for Last Tango in Paris; Boating on the Shannon, climbing mountains in Kerry; Building sandcastles in Killala, camping in Barley Cove; Picknicking in Moone, hide-and-go-seek in Clonmacnoise; Riding horses, cantering, jumping fences; Pushing out toy yachts in the pond in the Tuileries; The Irish College revisited in the Rue des Irlandais; Sipping on an orange presse through a straw on the roof of the Beaubourg; Dancing in Pere Lachaise, weeping at Auvers. Year in, year out, I pored over these albums accumulating, My children looking over my shoulder, exhilarated as I was, Their mother presiding at out ritual from a distance - The far side of the hearthrug, diffidently, proudly. Schoolbooks on the floor and pyjamas on the couch - Whose turn is it tonight to put the children to bed? Our children swam about our home As if it were their private sea, Their own unique, symbiotic fluid Of which their parents also partook. Such is home - a sea of your own - In which you hang upside down from the ceiling With equanimity, while postcards from Thailand on the mantelpiece Are raising their eyebrow markings benignly: Your hands dangling their prayers to the floorboards of your home, Sifting the sands underneath the surfaces of conversations. The marine insect life of the family psyche. A home of your own - or a sea of your own - In which climbing the walls is as natural As making love on the stairs; In which when the telephone rings Husband and wife are metamorphosed into smiling accomplices, Both declining to answer it; Initiating, instead, a yet more subversive kiss - A kiss they have perhaps never attempted before - And might never have dreamed of attempting Were it not for the telephone belling. Through the bannisters or along the bannister rails The pyjama-clad children solemnly watching Their parents at play, jumping up and down in support, Race back to bed, gesticulating wordlessly: The most subversive unit in society is the human family. We're almost home, pet, almost home... Our home is at... I'll be home... I have to go home now... I want to go home now... Are you feeling homesick? Are you anxious to get home?... I can't wait to get home... Let's stay at home to tonight and... What time will you be coming home at?... If I'm not home by six at the latest, I'll phone... We're nearly home, don't worry, we're nearly home... But then with good reason I was put out of my home: By a keen wind felled. I find myself now without a home Having to live homeless in the alien, foreign city of Dublin. It is an eerie enough feeling to be homesick Yet knowing you will be going home next week; It is an eerie feeling beyond all ornithological analysis To be homesick knowing that there is no home to go to: Day by day, creeping, crawling, Moonlighting, escaping, Bed-and-breakfast to bed-and-breakfast; Hostels, centres, one-night hotels. Homeless in Dublin, Blown about the suburban streets at evening, Peering in the windows of other people's homes, Wondering what it must feel like To be sitting around a fire - Apache or Cherokee or Bourgeoisie - Beholding the firelit faces of your family, Beholding their starry or their TV gaze: Windfall to Windfall - can you hear me? Windfall to Windfall... We're almost home, pet, don't worry anymore, we're almost home.

Jill was a very independent girl. She was only three but she liked to do things on her own. So when her mom gave her a flashlight to take outside to play, she was very excited.

Jill went outside and explored with her flashlight. She was admiring the backyard when she saw something sparkle in the corner. She walked over and saw it was a bee. She smiled and stuck out her hand, trying to make friends.

The bee wasn't expecting this, and it flew up in the air and scared her. Jill started to laugh but then she heard her mom and dad come outside. She was embarrassed. She turned off the flashlight and ran back inside.

Later, her mom asked her why she came back in so quickly. Jill had to tell the truth - she was embarrassed. Her parents smiled and said that was ok, then they hugged her and told her they were proud of her for trying to be independent.

Jill smiled, feeling much less embarrassed. They went outside again, arm-in-arm, this time with two flashlights.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She loved to play with her dolls and teddy bears. One day, Lily went to the park and met a boy named Max. Max was a fireman and he wore a heavy hat on his head. Lily thought Max was very brave.

Lily and Max played together every day. They played hide-and-seek and tag. One day, Max said to Lily, "I want to marry you when we grow up." Lily didn't know what "marry" meant, so Max explained that it meant they would always be together and love each other forever.

Lily thought about it and decided that she wanted to marry Max too. They hugged and went back to playing. From that day on, Lily knew that Max would always be her special friend, even when they grew up to be adults.

Tom and Mia are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big bunch of grapes on a table. They are hungry and want to eat some.

"Look, grapes!" Tom says. "Let's get some."

"OK, but be careful. They are not ours." Mia says.

They run to the table and each take a grape. They are sweet and juicy. They want more. They take another grape and another.

"Stop, Tom! That's enough!" Mia says. "Someone will see us."

But Tom does not listen. He takes a big handful of grapes and puts them in his mouth. He looks happy.

Suddenly, a man comes out of the house. He sees Tom and Mia. He is angry. He shouts at them.

"Hey, you! What are you doing? Those are my grapes! Get away from there!"

Tom and Mia are scared. They drop the grapes and run. But Tom has too many grapes in his mouth. He cannot run fast. He trips and falls. The grapes fly out of his mouth. They hit the man in the face.

"Ow! Ow! Ow!" The man says. "You crazy kids! You hurt me!"

Mia stops and looks back. She sees Tom on the ground and the man with grapes on his face. She laughs. She thinks it is funny.

"Come on, Tom! Get up!" She says. "Let's go!"

Tom gets up. He spits out the last grape. He is sorry. He did not mean to hurt the man. He says sorry.

"Sorry, mister. Sorry for the grapes."

The man is still angry. He does not accept Tom's sorry. He pushes Tom. Tom falls again.

"Hey, don't push him!" Mia says. "That's not nice!"

She runs to Tom and helps him up. She pushes the man back. The man is surprised. He does not expect Mia to push him. He loses his balance and falls on the table. The table breaks. The rest of the grapes fall on him.

"Ow! Ow! Ow!" The man says again. "You crazy kids! You broke my table!"

Tom and Mia are shocked. They did not mean to break the table. They say sorry again.

"Sorry, mister. Sorry for the table."

But the man does not hear them. He is too busy getting the grapes off him. He is very mad. He wants to catch them.

"Come here, you! I'll teach you a lesson!"

Tom and Mia are afraid. They run away as fast as they can. They do not look back. They do not want to see the man again. They do not want to eat grapes again. They learned their lesson. They will not take things that are not theirs. They will not be crazy. They will be good.

Once upon a time, there was a humble boy. He had a brother. They loved to play together. The humble boy liked to include his brother in all his games.

One day, they went to the park. They saw a big tree. The humble boy said, "Let's climb the tree!" He helped his brother climb up. They had so much fun.

Soon, it was time to go home. The humble boy and his brother walked home together. They were happy to include each other in their fun day. They loved being together.

Once upon a time, there was a brave girl called Lucy. Everyday Lucy would go to the park and bow to all the animals she saw. One day, Lucy found a beautiful key on the floor of the park. She had never seen a key like this before and got very excited. She wanted to try the key in the park gate, as she thought it might open it!

But when she tried to open the gate, the key did not fit. It wasn't the right key for that gate. Lucy was very upset. She wanted to get inside the park, but she couldn't find the right key.

Just then, Lucy remembered how brave she was. She decided to try a different key in the gate. She looked around the park and found a small key lying on a bench. She quickly tried the key in the gate and was overjoyed when it opened! Lucy was so happy and proud of herself for being so brave.

From then on, whenever Lucy went to the park, she would bow to all the animals and use the special key to open the gate.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved going to the park with his mommy. They would play on the swings and slide down the slide. One day, they went to the park and it was very busy. There were lots of people and lots of noise. Timmy and his mommy tried to find a spot to play, but everywhere was taken.

Suddenly, a big boy came over and pushed Timmy off the swing. Timmy was very sad and started to cry. His mommy saw what happened and got very angry. She went over to the big boy and told him to say sorry. The big boy said sorry and went away.

Timmy's mommy hugged him and they decided to go jog around the park instead. They had lots of fun jogging and looking at all the pretty flowers. Timmy forgot all about the mean big boy and was happy again. The end.

Once upon a time there was a big, red dragon. The dragon was scared of the night and would cry out in fear. His best friend was a little firefly called Buzzy. Buzzy wanted to help the dragon, so he asked what the dragon needed.

The dragon replied,â€I need someone to show me that the night isn't so scary. I have a nightmare every time it gets dark.â€

Buzzy thought about it for a moment before he said, â€œI think I know what you need! We can have a party! You can invite all your friends and we can laugh and play together. That way the night won't be so scary anymore!â€ 

The dragon was so excited and he followed Buzzy's advice. That night they lit up the sky with their laughter and friendship. From that night on, the dragon never had a nightmare again. 

The moral of the story is that friendship and shared joy can help get rid of our fears.

name_of_work: Fra Lippo Lippi by Robert Browning
content: I am poor brother Lippo, by your leave! You need not clap your torches to my face. Zooks, what's to blame? you think you see a monk! What, 'tis past midnight, and you go the rounds, And here you catch me at an alley's end Where sportive ladies leave their doors ajar? The Carmine's my cloister: hunt it up, Do,--harry out, if you must show your zeal, Whatever rat, there, haps on his wrong hole, And nip each softling of a wee white mouse, Weke, weke, that's crept to keep him company! Aha, you know your betters! Then, you'll take Your hand away that's fiddling on my throat, And please to know me likewise. Who am I? Why, one, sir, who is lodging with a friend Three streets off--he's a certain . . . how d'ye call? Master--a ...Cosimo of the Medici, I' the house that caps the corner. Boh! you were best! Remember and tell me, the day you're hanged, How you affected such a gullet's-gripe! But you, sir, it concerns you that your knaves Pick up a manner nor discredit you: Zooks, are we pilchards, that they sweep the streets And count fair price what comes into their net? He's Judas to a tittle, that man is! Just such a face! Why, sir, you make amends. Lord, I'm not angry! Bid your hang-dogs go Drink out this quarter-florin to the health Of the munificent House that harbours me (And many more beside, lads! more beside!) And all's come square again. I'd like his face-- His, elbowing on his comrade in the door With the pike and lantern,--for the slave that holds John Baptist's head a-dangle by the hair With one hand ("Look you, now," as who should say) And his weapon in the other, yet unwiped! It's not your chance to have a bit of chalk, A wood-coal or the like? or you should see! Yes, I'm the painter, since you style me so. What, brother Lippo's doings, up and down, You know them and they take you? like enough! I saw the proper twinkle in your eye-- 'Tell you, I liked your looks at very first. Let's sit and set things straight now, hip to haunch. Here's spring come, and the nights one makes up bands To roam the town and sing out carnival, And I've been three weeks shut within my mew, A-painting for the great man, saints and saints And saints again. I could not paint all night-- Ouf! I leaned out of window for fresh air. There came a hurry of feet and little feet, A sweep of lute strings, laughs, and whifts of song, -- Flower o' the broom, Take away love, and our earth is a tomb! Flower o' the quince, I let Lisa go, and what good in life since? Flower o' the thyme--and so on. Round they went. Scarce had they turned the corner when a titter Like the skipping of rabbits by moonlight,--three slim shapes, And a face that looked up . . . zooks, sir, flesh and blood, That's all I'm made of! Into shreds it went, Curtain and counterpane and coverlet, All the bed-furniture--a dozen knots, There was a ladder! Down I let myself, Hands and feet, scrambling somehow, and so dropped, And after them. I came up with the fun Hard by Saint Laurence, hail fellow, well met,-- Flower o' the rose, If I've been merry, what matter who knows? And so as I was stealing back again To get to bed and have a bit of sleep Ere I rise up to-morrow and go work On Jerome knocking at his poor old breast With his great round stone to subdue the flesh, You snap me of the sudden. Ah, I see! Though your eye twinkles still, you shake your head-- Mine's shaved--a monk, you say--the sting 's in that! If Master Cosimo announced himself, Mum's the word naturally; but a monk!
