From that day on, the bird would visit the boat every day and nod its head on the anchor. The people on the boat would always give the bird some food and they all became good friends. The end.

name_of_work: The Housewife by Charlotte Anna Perkins Gilman
content: Here is the House to hold me -- cradle of all the race; Here is my lord and my love, here are my children dear -- Here is the House enclosing, the dear-loved dwelling place; Why should I ever weary for aught that I find not here? Here for the hours of the day and the hours of the night; Bound with the bands of Duty, rivetted tight; Duty older than Adam -- Duty that saw Acceptance utter and hopeless in the eyes of the serving squaw. Food and the serving of food -- that is my daylong care; What and when we shall eat, what and how we shall wear; Soiling and cleaning of things -- that is my task in the main -- Soil them and clean them and soil them -- soil them and clean them again. To work at my trade by the dozen and never a trade to know; To plan like a Chinese puzzle -- fitting and changing so; To think of a thousand details, each in a thousand ways; For my own immediate people and a possible love and praise. My mind is trodden in circles, tiresome, narrow and hard, Useful, commonplace, private -- simply a small back-yard; And I the Mother of Nations! -- Blind their struggle and vain! -- I cover the earth with my children -- each with a housewife's brain.

His books are all jammed in the closet, His vest has been left in the hall. A lizard named Ed is asleep in his bed, And his smelly old sock has been stuck to the wall. Groping along the tunnel, step by step, He winked his prying torch with patching glare From side to side, and sniffed the unwholesome air. Tins, boxes, bottles, shapes and too vague to know; A mirror smashed, the mattress from a bed; And he, exploring fifty feet below The rosy gloom of battle overhead. Tripping, he grabbed the wall; saw someone lie Humped at his feet, half-hidden by a rug. And stooped to give the sleeper's arm a tug. "I'm looking for headquarters." No reply. "God blast your neck!" (For days he'd had no sleep.) "Get up and guide me through this stinking place." Savage, he kicked a soft, unanswering heap, And flashed his beam across the livid face Terribly glaring up, whose eyes yet wore Agony dying hard of ten days before; And fists of fingers clutched a blackening wound. Alone he staggered on until he found Dawn's ghost that filtered down a shafted stair To the dazed, muttering creatures underground Who hear the boom of shells in muffled sound. At last, with sweat and horror in his hair, He climbed through darkness to the twilight air, Unloading hell behind him step by step.

Wow! The boy smiled. Inside the bushes there was a secret box! The boy felt so excited. He opened the box, but he was a bit scared.

Inside the box, he heard a tiny whisper coming from a little mouse. She said, "Welcome brave explorer! The secret you seek is mine alone to keep." The boy was so surprised but he was also relieved.

The mouse shared her secret with the boy and made him promise not to tell anyone else. The boy smiled and said, "Thank you! I won't tell a soul." He was very happy! 

The brave explorer ran off to share his exciting news with his friends. He never forgot his adventure and the secret that he heard.

content: Two households, both alike in dignity, In fair Verona where we lay our scene, From ancient grudge break to new mutiny, Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean. From forth the fatal loins of these two foes, A pair of star-crossed lovers take their life, Whose misadventured piteous overthrows Doth, with their death, bury their parents' strife. The fearful passage of their death-marked love And the continuance of their parents' rage -- Which, but their children's end, nought could remove -- Is now the two hours' traffic of our stage; The which, if you with patient ears attend, What here shall miss, our toil shall strive to mend.

Lily and Tom were playing in the park. They saw a big kangaroo jumping near the trees. They wanted to pet the kangaroo, but it was too fast and too far.

"Let's try to catch the kangaroo!" Tom said. He ran after the kangaroo, but he tripped on a rock and fell down.

"Ouch!" Tom cried. "That hurt!"

Lily ran to help Tom. She saw the kangaroo stop and look at them. The kangaroo had a jolly face and a long tail.

"Hello, kangaroo!" Lily said. "We want to be your friends. Can we pet you?"

The kangaroo nodded and hopped closer to Lily and Tom. It let them touch its soft fur and its big ears. It made a funny noise that sounded like a laugh.

Lily and Tom were happy. They had made a new friend. They thanked the kangaroo and gave it a hug.

"Bye, kangaroo!" they said. "We hope to see you again!"

The kangaroo waved its tail and jumped away. Lily and Tom smiled and went back to their mom. They told her about their adventure with the kangaroo. Mom was proud of them for trying something new and being kind to animals.

name_of_work: My Love is like to ice, and I to fire by Edmund Spenser
content: My Love is like to ice, and I to fire: How comes it then that this her cold so great Is not dissolved through my so hot desire, But harder grows the more I her entreat? Or how comes it that my exceeding heat Is not allayed by her heart-frozen cold, But that I burn much more in boiling sweat, And feel my flames augmented manifold? What more miraculous thing may be told, That fire, which all things melts, should harden ice, And ice, which is congeal'd with senseless cold, Should kindle fire by wonderful device? Such is the power of love in gentle mind, That it can alter all the course of kind.

Sam and Lily were two little mice who lived in a shelter under a big tree. They liked to play and explore, but they were always careful not to disturb the big cat who slept on the porch of the house nearby. The cat was mean and scary, and he liked to chase and catch mice.

One day, Sam and Lily were very hungry, and they decided to look for some food in the house. They waited until the cat was snoring, and then they sneaked across the yard. They found a hole in the wall and crawled inside. They smelled something yummy in the kitchen, and followed their noses.

They saw a big bowl of cheese on the table, and their eyes sparkled. They climbed up a chair and jumped on the table. They nibbled and nibbled, and felt very happy. They did not notice that the cat had woken up and smelled them too. He crept into the kitchen, and saw them on the table. He grinned and pounced.

Sam and Lily heard a loud roar, and turned around. They saw the cat's big teeth and claws, and felt very scared. They ran and ran, but the cat was faster. He caught Lily by the tail, and lifted her up. He opened his mouth to eat her.

Sam did not want to lose his sister. He saw a fork on the table, and had an idea. He grabbed the fork and threw it at the cat's eye. The cat yowled and dropped Lily. He ran away, rubbing his eye. Sam and Lily hugged each other, and ran back to the hole. They escaped from the house, and ran back to their shelter. They were safe and sound.

They learned a lesson that day. They never tried to steal cheese from the house again. They did not want to disturb the cat, or get caught by him. They found other food in the fields and the woods, and they were happy. They thanked the fork for saving them, and kept it as a souvenir. They lived happily ever after.

The cows were so happy to drink their cold and delicious water. One day, a strange thing happened. The water in the buckets stopped tasting sweet. The farmer was so puzzled and couldn't understand why the water stopped tasting so good.

The farmer put his hand into the water and found out that a bee had been drinking the sweet water and had made it yucky. The farmer quickly scooped the bee out of the water and the cows were once again able to drink sweet water. 

The cows were so grateful and they thanked the farmer for ensuring that they still had their sweet water. From that day on, the farmer always checked the water to make sure that no bees were spoiling the water.

Lily and Tom are twins. They like to play in their room. They have many toys and books. They also have a big bookshelf. The bookshelf is tall and heavy.

One day, Lily and Tom want to read a book. They look at the bookshelf. They see a book they like. It is on the top shelf. It has a picture of a dragon on the cover.

"I want that book!" Lily says.

"Me too!" Tom says.

They try to reach the book. They stand on their toes. They stretch their arms. But the book is too high. They cannot get it.

They have an idea. They get a chair. They put the chair near the bookshelf. Tom climbs on the chair. He tries to grab the book. But the chair is wobbly. It shakes and tilts. Tom loses his balance. They hug Mom. They are scared but safe.

Once upon a time, there were two twins, Jim and Tim. They loved to go to the beach and play in the sand. One day, Jim and Tim decided to explore the ocean near their beach.
 
Jim and Tim were having so much fun looking at all the colorful fish and coral when they saw something unusual. It was a large reef just a few feet away. Jim and Tim decided they should see what was inside the reef so they swam closer.

When they got to the reef, they noticed something was scared. They turned around to see a giant sea turtle. Jim and Tim were scared too, so they started to swim away quickly. 

The sea turtle saw that Jim and Tim were scared and said, "It's okay kids, I just wanted to show you the beauty of the reef." 

Jim and Tim smiled and decided to return, this time a little bit more brave. As they looked around the reef, they found it filled with wonders. Colorful fish, plants, and sea creatures. They had never seen a more beautiful sight.

Once upon a time, there lived a little chipmunk named Lily. She lived in a small and cozy burrow, tucked away in a peaceful forest.

One day, Lily was looking for food when she heard a loud noise. Seeing a furry bear, she quickly ran into her burrow and closed the entrance, hoping it was quiet enough there.

The bear shouted, "Don't worry dwarf, I won't hurt you! I've just been searching for some food."

Lily poked her head out from the entrance and asked, "What kind of food?"

"Delicious berries! I'm sure you'd like them too," answered the bear.

Lily thought for a moment, then jumped out of the burrow. She found the delicious berries and shared them with the bear.

After they both ate, the bear said, "It would be fun if you came with me. We can explore this forest together!"

Lily smiled and nodded. They started walking when suddenly everything froze. Lily wondered what had happened and why the forest around them had gone so quiet.

The bear explained to her, "This is called hibernation. In winter, the animals in this forest go to sleep so they can survive the cold weather. They freeze until spring comes again."

Lily smiled, happy to know so much about her furry new friend and the forest they lived in.

One day, a zebra was walking in the jungle. He came to a deep, unknown pool of water. The zebra thought the pool looked fun and he decided to dive in. As he dove deep into the water, he noticed something really exciting - he could see hundreds of colorful fish swimming around him! He quickly swam back up to the surface and looked around, but there was nobody around. He had discovered a secret underwater paradise, all for himself. The zebra was so happy that he splashed and jumped in the water, feeling free and joyous. He dove back down to the bottom one more time and looked around, smiling and laughing, before heading back up to the surface.

name_of_work: The One Girl at the Boys Party by Sharon Olds
content: When I take my girl to the swimming party I set her down among the boys. They tower and bristle, she stands there smooth and sleek, her math scores unfolding in the air around her. They will strip to their suits, her body hard and indivisible as a prime number, they'll plunge into the deep end, she'll subtract her height from ten feet, divide it into hundreds of gallons of water, the numbers bouncing in her mind like molecules of chlorine in the bright blue pool. When they climb out, her ponytail will hang its pencil lead down her back, her narrow silk suit with hamburgers and french fries printed on it will glisten in the brilliant air, and they will see her sweet face, solemn and sealed, a factor of one, and she will see their eyes, two each, their legs, two each, and the curves of their sexes, one each, and in her head she'll be doing her wild multiplying, as the drops sparkle and fall to the power of a thousand from her body.

We're writing as the daughter of a / dying world / as its new-faced alert. / In math, the slash / also called the solidus / means division, divided by. / We were divided / from each other, person / person. / Some griefs, like rivers, are uncross / able. They are not to be waded across / but walked beside. Our loss / colossal & blossomed / is never lost on us. Love the earth / like we've failed it. To put it plain / we have shipwrecked the earth / soiled the soil / & run the ground aground. / Listen. We are the loud toll / on this planet. / Our future needs us / alarmed. Man is a myth / in the making. / What is now dust will not return, / not the beloveds / nor their breath, / nor the sugar-crumbling glaciers, / nor the crows chewing / on their own soured song, / nor all the species / slashed / down / in one smogged swoop. / Extinction is a chorus / of quiet punching / that same note. What can never be brought back / can still be brought forth / in memory / in mouth / in mind. To say it plain is to tell / only half / of the story.

Sara and Ben were twins who liked to play pretend. They had many toys and costumes, but their favorite thing was to own masks. They had masks of animals, heroes, and monsters. They liked to wear them and act like different characters.

One day, they found a new mask in their toy box. It was a mask of an old man with a long beard and a hat. Sara and Ben wondered who it belonged to. They decided to try it on and see how it looked.

Sara put on the mask first and said, "Hello, I am a wise old man. I know many things and I can tell you stories. Do you want to hear one?"

Ben laughed and said, "No, thank you. You are not a wise old man. You are my sister Sara. You are silly and you don't know many things. Give me the mask. I want to try it on."

Sara took off the mask and gave it to Ben. Ben put on the mask and said, "Hello, I am a wise old man. I know many things and I can tell you jokes. Do you want to hear one?"

Sara smiled and said, "Yes, please. You are a wise old man. You are my brother Ben. You are funny and you know many things. Tell me a joke."

Ben thought for a moment and said, "Why did the chicken cross the road?"

Sara said, "I don't know. Why?"

Ben said, "To get to the other side."

Sara and Ben laughed and laughed. They liked the mask of the wise old man. They decided to keep it and share it. They played with it and had fun. They learned that they could be wise and silly at the same time.

One day, Mary and her Dad were playing in the park. Mary had a brilliant pink bow in her hair and she was very excited to show it off. She spun around in circles and grinned at her Dad.

"Look Dad! Isn't my bow brilliant?" she said, twirling around again.

"Yes, it is," Dad nodded.

Suddenly, the wind blew hard and separated Mary from her bow. Mary gasped and ran after it, smiling as she saw the bow flying away from her. She chased it all around the park but couldn't catch it. 

Dad saw Mary running and quickly ran after her. He chased the bow while Mary ran after him, clapping her hands with excitement. Then, Dad managed to catch the bow and presented it to Mary with a big smile. 

"Here you go," he said, and Mary smiled brightly at him. She hugged the bow tightly, and thanked her Dad for catching it. 

"You're brilliant, Dad," she said.

"And you are too," he said, ruffling her hair.

Mary smiled, happy that she was reunited with her bow.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to wander in the forest and pick flowers. One day, she found a bottle of perfume and sprayed it on herself. She smelled so good!

As she walked deeper into the forest, she saw a shy deer. The deer was scared of Lily, but Lily just wanted to be friends. She tried to approach the deer, but it ran away.

Lily kept wandering and soon got lost. She couldn't find her way back home. She cried and cried, but no one came to help her. Night fell and it got very dark. Suddenly, she heard a scary noise and ran away, but she tripped and fell. She hurt herself badly and couldn't get up. She was all alone and scared. The end.

Once upon a time, there lived a bunny named Lucy. She was very cute and adorable. She loved wearing her soft and fuzzy fur coat. It was so fluffy and cuddly that every time she wore it, she felt warm and happy. 

One day, Lucy went for a walk in the forest and found a pond. Near the pond, there were many big and beautiful trees. Lucy decided to explore them. She touched the bark and felt the bumpy texture.

As the sun began to set, Lucy spotted some colorful flowers. She picked one and placed it in her fur coat. The flower looked so pretty and amazing! She smiled and kept walking.

As the night came, Lucy safely went back home. She said goodnight to the stars and the moon, then went to bed while wearing her furry and cozy coat. The night was as lovely as she was - adorable!

Once upon a time there was a mom and a baby. The baby was a little boy. He was so excited, so he decided to go for a walk. He went outside, and he saw lots of things. He saw a bird and a tree, and a ladybug too. 

But then the baby got very tired. His eyes drooped, and he felt so weary. The mom saw how tired the baby was and she said, "Let's go inside now".

So they went inside, and the baby curled up in a chair and he gave a big sigh. He was so tired, and his mom couldn't help but smile. The baby lay down on the floor, and tucked himself under the blanket. He snuggled in, and he closed his eyes for a nap. 

The mom watched her baby, feeling so glad he was safe and resting. She gave a big sigh of her own, because her baby was so tired. But soon he was feeling much better, and both of them were happy again.

Once there was a brave little girl. She had bright clothes and loved to explore. One day, she went to the park by herself.

At the park, she saw many new things. She saw tall trees and small bugs. She saw green grass and blue skies. She pointed to everything, excitedly.

Then, she saw something shining in the distance. It looked like something special. She was very brave and walked closer to it.

When she got there, she saw it was a small pond. It was sparkly in the sunlight and had ducks swimming happily. She pointed to them, excitedly. 

The brave little girl made some new friends that day. She gave them pieces of her bright clothes, so they could always remember her. 

The brave little girl was excited to come back to the park soon. She will always remember the special pond she found, and how brave she was to explore.

This darksome burn, horseback brown, His rollrock highroad roaring down, In coop and in comb the fleece of his foam Flutes and low to the lake falls home. A windpuff-bonnet of faawn-froth Turns and twindles over the broth Of a pool so pitchblack, fell-frowning, It rounds and rounds Despair to drowning. Degged with dew, dappled with dew, Are the groins of the braes that the brook treads through, Wiry heathpacks, flitches of fern, And the beadbonny ash that sits over the burn. What would the world be, once bereft Of wet and of wildness? Let them be left, O let them be left, wildness and wet; Long live the weeds and the wilderness yet.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Jane. She was three years old and very curious.

One day, a big truck pulled up to Jane's house. She was a bit fearful, but then the truck driver smiled and called for her. "Good morning, Jane! I have a special delivery for you," he said.

Jane was excited. She ran out to the truck and opened the back. Inside, she found a big box filled with jars of jelly. She was so excited that she immediately asked if she could eat one.

The driver chuckled. "You can eat one, but you have to wait until your mom and dad say it's okay," he said. Jane nodded and said thank you before taking the box inside.

When her mom and dad saw the box, they were so excited. They opened the jars and spread the jelly on their morning toast. They all laughed and enjoyed a tasty breakfast.

When Jane was done, she waved goodbye to the driver. He smiled back, then left with his truck. Jane was happy that the driver had delivered her delicious jelly!

Think, two things on their own and both at once The first, that exercise in trust, where those in front stand with their arms spread wide and free-fall backwards, blind, and those behind take all the weight. The second, one canary-yellow cotton jacket on a cloakroom floor, uncoupled from its hook becoming scuffed and blackened underfoot. Back home the very model of a model of a mother, yours, puts two and two together, makes a proper fist of it and points the finger. Temper, temper. Questions in the house. You seeing red. Blue murder. Bed. Then midnight when you slip the latch and sneak no further than the call-box at the corner of the street; I'm waiting by the phone, although it doesn't ring because it's sixteen years or so before we'll meet. Retrace that walk towards the garden gate; in silhouette a father figures waits there, wants to set things straight. These ribs are pleats or seams. These arms are sleeves. These fingertips are buttons, or these hands can fold into a clasp, or else these fingers make a zip or buckle, you say which. Step backwards into it and try the same canary-yellow cotton jacket, there, like this, for size again. It still fits.

One day, Sammy was flying his kite high in the sky. The wind was gentle and the kite sailed up and up until it seemed like it would never come down. All of a sudden, there was a loud noise and the ground started shaking! Sammy was scared. It was an earthquake!

The ground continued to shake and Sammy got down low. He held onto his kite tightly. When the shaking stopped, Sammy looked up. His kite was still in the sky, gently floating. He was so relieved.

Sammy slowly flew his kite back down to him. He was so glad that he was safe and his kite wasn't lost in the sky. He knew never to fly his kite during an earthquake again. Instead, he'd find somewhere safe where he could watch his kite fly in the gentle wind.

name_of_work: Wynken, Blynken, and Nod by Eugene Field
content: Wynken, Blynken, and Nod one night Sailed off in a wooden shoe,-- Sailed on a river of crystal light Into a sea of dew. "Where are you going, and what do you wish?" The old moon asked the three. "We have come to fish for the herring-fish That live in this beautiful sea; Nets of silver and gold have we," Said Wynken, Blynken, And Nod. The old moon laughed and sang a song, As they rocked in the wooden shoe; And the wind that sped them all night long Ruffled the waves of dew; The little stars were the herring-fish That lived in the beautiful sea. "Now cast your nets wherever you wish,-- Never afraid are we!" So cried the stars to the fishermen three, Wynken, Blynken, And Nod. All night long their nets they threw To the stars in the twinkling foam,-- Then down from the skies came the wooden shoe, Bringing the fishermen home: 'Twas all so pretty a sail, it seemed As if it could not be; And some folk thought 'twas a dream they'd dreamed Of sailing that beautiful sea; But I shall name you the fishermen three: Wynken, Blynken, And Nod. Wynken and Blynken are two little eyes, And Nod is a little head, And the wooden shoe that sailed the skies Is a wee one's trundle-bed; So shut your eyes while Mother sings Of wonderful sights that be, And you shall see the beautiful things As you rock in the misty sea Where the old shoe rocked the fishermen three:-- Wynken, Blynken, And Nod.

Once upon a time, there was a bear named Benny. Benny was feeling grumpy because he didn't have anyone to play with. One day, Benny decided to go on a picnic all by himself. He packed some yummy food in a basket and went to the park. 

As he was eating his sandwich, he heard a loud snap! He looked around and saw a squirrel trying to crack open a nut. Benny asked the squirrel if he wanted to have a picnic with him. The squirrel was happy to join Benny and they shared the food together. 

After the picnic, Benny was no longer feeling grumpy. He realized that he didn't need to be alone to have fun. From that day on, Benny and the squirrel became best friends and had many more picnics together.

Once there was a human who wanted to remove something from a cupboard. The human opened the cupboard and was surprised to see a tiny animal inside! The animal was very scared, but the human wanted to help it.

The human gently lowered her hand and slowly started to remove the animal from the cupboard. When the animal was safely out, the human gave him a hug and made sure he was alright. The animal was so happy and grateful to the human for saving him!

The human opened the door and carefully released the animal back into the wild. Goodbye, little animal! The human smiled, satisfied with the good deed they had done.

The woods decay, the woods decay and fall, The vapours weep their burthen to the ground, Man comes and tills the field and lies beneath, And after many a summer dies the swan. Me only cruel immortality Consumes: I wither slowly in thine arms, Here at the quiet limit of the world, A white-hair'd shadow roaming like a dream The ever-silent spaces of the East, Far-folded mists, and gleaming halls of morn. Alas! for this gray shadow, once a man-- So glorious in his beauty and thy choice, Who madest him thy chosen, that he seem'd To his great heart none other than a God! I ask'd thee, 'Give me immortality.' Then didst thou grant mine asking with a smile, Like wealthy men, who care not how they give. But thy strong Hours indignant work'd their wills, And beat me down and marr'd and wasted me, And tho' they could not end me, left me maim'd To dwell in presence of immortal youth, Immortal age beside immortal youth, And all I was, in ashes. Can thy love, Thy beauty, make amends, tho' even now, Close over us, the silver star, thy guide, Shines in those tremulous eyes that fill with tears To hear me? Let me go: take back thy gift: Why should a man desire in any way To vary from the kindly race of men Or pass beyond the goal of ordinance Where all should pause, as is most meet for all? A soft air fans the cloud apart; there comes A glimpse of that dark world where I was born. Once more the old mysterious glimmer steals From thy pure brows, and from thy shoulders pure, And bosom beating with a heart renew'd. Thy cheek begins to redden thro' the gloom, Thy sweet eyes brighten slowly close to mine, Ere yet they blind the stars, and the wild team Which love thee, yearning for thy yoke, arise, And shake the darkness from their loosen'd manes, And beat the twilight into flakes of fire. Lo! ever thus thou growest beautiful In silence, then before thine answer given Departest, and thy tears are on my cheek. Why wilt thou ever scare me with thy tears, And make me tremble lest a saying learnt, In days far-off, on that dark earth, be true? 'The Gods themselves cannot recall their gifts.' Ay me! ay me! with what another heart In days far-off, and with what other eyes I used to watch--if I be he that watch'd-- The lucid outline forming round thee; saw The dim curls kindle into sunny rings; Changed with thy mystic change, and felt my blood Glow with the glow that slowly crimson'd all Thy presence and thy portals, while I lay, Mouth, forehead, eyelids, growing dewy-warm With kisses balmier than half-opening buds Of April, and could hear the lips that kiss'd Whispering I knew not what of wild and sweet, Like that strange song I heard Apollo sing, While Ilion like a mist rose into towers. Yet hold me not for ever in thine East: How can my nature longer mix with thine? Coldly thy rosy shadows bathe me, cold Are all thy lights, and cold my wrinkled feet Upon thy glimmering thresholds, when the steam Floats up from those dim fields about the homes Of happy men that have the power to die, And grassy barrows of the happier dead. Release me, and restore me to the ground; Thou seest all things, thou wilt see my grave: Thou wilt renew thy beauty morn by morn; I earth in earth forget these empty courts, And thee returning on thy silver wheels.

Yesterday, Mama went to the store. She found an original toy and pulled it off the shelf. Mama was so excited! She couldn't wait to show it to Baby. 

Mama brought the toy home and showed it to Baby. It was a big, shiny truck. Baby's eyes lit up and he grabbed it right away. He pulled the truck around the living room, making lots of noise.

Mama and Baby were so happy with the original toy they found. They laughed and played with it all day long.

Mama said, "I'm so glad I found this toy yesterday."

Baby nodded and said, "Me too!"

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to go on adventures with his family. One day, they went on a camping trip. Timmy was so excited to sleep in a tent and roast marshmallows over the fire.

As they were setting up camp, Timmy's dad said, "Let's go for a walk and peek at the animals in the woods." Timmy's eyes got big and he said, "Yes, please!"

They walked through the woods and saw birds, squirrels, and even a deer. Timmy was so happy, he said, "This is hard to believe! I love camping!" His dad smiled and said, "I'm glad you're having fun, Timmy."

Lily and Tom liked to collect rocks. They had a big box full of rocks of different colors and shapes. They liked to look at them and sort them and play with them.

One day, they went to the park with their mom. They saw a lot of rocks under the trees and on the grass. They ran to pick them up and put them in their pockets.

"Look, Lily, I found a red rock!" Tom said.

"Wow, that's a charming rock, Tom!" Lily said. "Can I see it?"

Tom showed her the rock. It was shiny and smooth. Lily wanted to have it.

"Can I have it, Tom? Please?" Lily asked.

"No, Lily, it's mine. I found it first. You can have another rock." Tom said.

"But I like this rock. It's the most charming rock I ever saw. Please, Tom, give it to me." Lily said.

They started to argue and pull the rock. They both wanted it very much.

Their mom heard them and came over. She saw them fighting over the rock.

"What's going on, Lily and Tom?" she asked.

They both told her their side of the story. They both said they deserved the rock.

Their mom looked at them and shook her head.

"Lily and Tom, you are both being selfish. You have so many rocks already. Why do you need to have this one? Can't you share it or trade it or find another one? You are hurting each other and your friendship over a rock. That's not nice." she said.

Lily and Tom felt ashamed. They realized their mom was right. They were being selfish and mean. They didn't want to lose their friend over a rock.

They looked at each other and said sorry.

"Sorry, Tom. You can have the rock. I don't need it." Lily said.

"Sorry, Lily. You can have the rock. I don't need it." Tom said.

They hugged and smiled. They gave the rock to their mom.

"Mom, you can have the rock. It's a gift for you. You are the most charming mom ever." they said.

Their mom smiled and thanked them. She put the rock in her purse.

They went back to playing and collecting rocks. They found more rocks and shared them and traded them and had fun. They learned to be generous and kind. They were happy.

Once upon a time, there was a clumsy little boy named Ben. Every day he would try to lean against the tree outside his house, but he was too short and would tumble back over. He told himself he was only one little wish away from being tall.

One evening, Ben made a very special wish. Closing his eyes tight, he wished to be tall enough to lean against the tree. Suddenly, Ben grew until he was almost touching the sky. His magic wish had been granted.

Gently, he leaned against the tree, smiling as it felt solid and strong. From the front garden, Ben could see the stars in the sky. He told himself that he could make it to the stars if he leant from the tree.

But it was too hard â€“ Ben was too clumsy and kept slipping back down. Even with his special wish, slowly he tumbled back to the ground. His magic had been just enough to give him a lovely wish and it was enough to make him happy.

name_of_work: My Heart and I by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: I. ENOUGH ! we're tired, my heart and I. We sit beside the headstone thus, And wish that name were carved for us. The moss reprints more tenderly The hard types of the mason's knife, As heaven's sweet life renews earth's life With which we're tired, my heart and I. II. You see we're tired, my heart and I. We dealt with books, we trusted men, And in our own blood drenched the pen, As if such colours could not fly. We walked too straight for fortune's end, We loved too true to keep a friend ; At last we're tired, my heart and I. III. How tired we feel, my heart and I ! We seem of no use in the world ; Our fancies hang grey and uncurled About men's eyes indifferently ; Our voice which thrilled you so, will let You sleep; our tears are only wet : What do we here, my heart and I ? IV. So tired, so tired, my heart and I ! It was not thus in that old time When Ralph sat with me 'neath the lime To watch the sunset from the sky. Dear love, you're looking tired,' he said; I, smiling at him, shook my head : 'Tis now we're tired, my heart and I. V. So tired, so tired, my heart and I ! Though now none takes me on his arm To fold me close and kiss me warm Till each quick breath end in a sigh Of happy languor. Now, alone, We lean upon this graveyard stone, Uncheered, unkissed, my heart and I. VI. Tired out we are, my heart and I. Suppose the world brought diadems To tempt us, crusted with loose gems Of powers and pleasures ? Let it try. We scarcely care to look at even A pretty child, or God's blue heaven, We feel so tired, my heart and I. VII. Yet who complains ? My heart and I ? In this abundant earth no doubt Is little room for things worn out : Disdain them, break them, throw them by And if before the days grew rough We once were loved, used, -- well enough, I think, we've fared, my heart and I.

Once upon a time, there were two brothers named Bob and Bill. Bob was three and Bill was five. They were very close and liked to do fun things together. 

One day, their mom told them they could not go outside to play because it was raining. Bob was worried and wanted to go out anyway. He asked his brother Bill, but he refused. 

Bob's mom then asked if they wanted something to eat. Bob immediately said "yes!" and asked if they could have cookies. Bill refused again and suggested that they eat something from the refrigerator instead. He said it would be healthier. 

Bob was worried about not getting to eat the cookies. He thought that Bill was not being nice and getting mad at him. But then, to his surprise, Bill opened the refrigerator and brought out a plate with some homemade cookies inside. 

He said, "Mom said we could have these cookies, but only if we eat something healthy from the refrigerator too." Bob was very happy and quickly accepted Bill's offer. 

The two brothers enjoyed their snacks and played together for a long time afterwards.

One beautiful day, Anna was running around in the meadow. She loved to feel the wind on her face and the long, lush grass tickling her toes.

Suddenly, she stumbled upon a large cliff with a magnificent view. She was so excited to explore the area, calling out to her family, "Look at this huge cliff!"

Her family ran over to join her. Her dad said, "Let's see what is over the edge. Maybe we can find something exciting!"

Anna was very curious. She quickly gathered some stones and pebbles from the ground and started to scatter them at the top of the cliff.

The stones rolled down the side of the huge cliff - occasionally bouncing down to the ground - as Anna watched in delight. She ran after each one of them, collecting them from the bottom again. 

After a while, Anna's family joined in the fun as well. They too began to scatter the stones down the cliff one by one, laughing as the stones rolled down to the ground. 

It was a truly wonderful time - full of laughter and joy.

Once upon a time, there was a little rabbit named Benny. Benny was very smart and always knew how to find the best carrots to eat. One day, Benny saw a big, shiny trophy in the forest. He wanted it so badly, but he knew it wasn't his. 

Benny thought about it and realized that taking the trophy would be stealing. He knew that stealing was not a good thing to do. Instead, Benny decided to go find his friends and tell them about the trophy. 

When they found the trophy, they all talked about what they should do with it. They decided to give it to the bunny who had been the kindest and most helpful to others. Benny was so happy that he didn't take the trophy, and he felt proud of himself for doing the right thing. 

The moral of the story is that it's always better to do the right thing, even if it means giving up something you really want. Benny was a smart bunny who knew that stealing was wrong, and he made the right choice.

Once while walking through the city, a little girl saw a large parade that had just settled down. She ran to get a closer look and saw many people with bright colors and smiles on their faces. The girl started to get excited and take off her shoes. She began to dance and skip along with the parade; everyone laughed and cheered her on!

Suddenly, the parade stopped. The girl felt a bit hurt and confused. The people around her started to whisper in low voices and the girl heard someone say "an accident". She became frightened and started to cry.

Then the little girl's mom stepped in and gently took her hand. She said, "We can wait and see what happens here. Things will settle down soon."

Sure enough, soon after the parade began to move again and the girl was able to stay and watch it continue with a smile on her face. She felt relieved and happy, and as the parade went on she got to take part in many fun things like twirling ribbons, waving flags and singing songs. Eventually, it was time for the parade to end and the girl went home with wonderful memories of the day!

Once upon a time, there were two friends who liked to decorate. One day, they decided to decorate the nearby meadow. 

The first friend said: "Let's make the meadow beautiful!" 

The second friend replied: "Let's put up some decorations!"

The first friend said: "We can hang up some ribbons!" 

The second friend said: "Yes, and we can make it sparkly!"

The two friends worked together to make the meadow beautiful. They hung ribbons, glitter, and flowers. Suddenly, they saw a grumpy sheep watching them. 

The grumpy sheep said: "What are you two doing?" 

The first friend said: "We are decorating the meadow!"

The sheep seemed to like their work and the two friends were happy. In the end, the meadow was decorated and everyone was happy!

name_of_work: My Boy the Hero by James Khan
content: My boy, the hero played his part, Upon his sleeve; his stripes, his heart And when they marched out on parade My boy, the hero played, A patriot like Churchill's own, He fought the fight and bought it home And in the band to serenade My boy, the hero played, But now the anchor left its mark, Marooned, my son, his outlook dark And plucked like fiddles, strings all frayed- My boy, the hero played, The hauntings of a ghost within The shell that holds his mortal sin The game of life, a live grenade- My boy, the hero played.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who dreamed of flying. She wanted to go on a rocket ship, but she was scared. One day she asked her mom if she could go on one. Her mom said yes, but told her she must be brave.

The little girl was so excited. She got on the rocket and flew higher and higher into the sky. When she reached the highest point, she looked down and saw the world below. She felt so happy.

But then something happened. The rocket started to shake and smoke started to come out of the engine. The little girl was scared and started to cry. Then the rocket began to spin and she felt like she was going to be sick.

Finally, the rocket started to slow down and the little girl stopped suffering. When they were on the ground again, the little girl hugged her mom and thanked her for making her brave enough to go on the rocket. From then on, she never stopped dreaming of flying.

Once upon a time, there was a little chick who really loved to race. She could never find anyone else who could keep up with her, so she raced all by herself.

One day, she found a filthy old nest on the ground. She thought it was perfect for her to race around and around. She started running around the nest and having a great time.

Suddenly, she stopped and heard a voice. "What are you doing?"

She looked up and saw a hummingbird hovering above her. The hummingbird continued, "You were racing around that old, filthy nest. That doesn't seem very safe. Why don't we race around this tree branch instead?"

The little chick was so excited! She figured the branch would make a much better racetrack. The chick and the hummingbird raced around the branch together. They had a wonderful time, and from then on, they raced together every day.

name_of_work: The White Man's Burden by Rudyard Kipling
content: Take up the White Man's burden - Send forth the best ye breed - Go bind your sons to exile To serve your captives' need; To wait in heavy harness On fluttered folk and wild - Your new-caught sullen peoples, Half devil and half child. Take up the White Man's burden - In patience to abide To veil the threat of terror And check the show of pride; By open speech and simple, An hundred times made plain, To seek another's profit, And work another's gain. Take up the White Man's burden - The savage wars of peace - Fill full the mouth of famine And bid the sickness cease; And when your goal is nearest The end for others sought, Watch Sloth and heathen Folly Bring all your hopes to nought. Take up the White Man's burden - No tawdry rule of kings, But toil of serf and sweeper - The tale of common things. The ports ye shall not enter, The roads ye shall not tread, Go make them with your living, And mark them with your dead ! Take up the White Man's burden - And reap his old reward, The blame of those ye better, The hate of those ye guard - The cry of hosts ye humour (Ah slowly !) towards the light:- "Why brought ye us from bondage, "Our loved Egyptian night ?" Take up the White Man's burden - Ye dare not stoop to less - Nor call too loud on Freedom To cloak your weariness; By all ye cry or whisper, By all ye leave or do, The silent sullen peoples Shall weigh your Gods and you. Take up the White Man's burden - Have done with childish days - The lightly proffered laurel, The easy, ungrudged praise. Comes now, to search your manhood Through all the thankless years, Cold-edged with dear-bought wisdom, The judgement of your peers.

name_of_work: For Whom the Bell Tolls/No Man is an Island by John Donne
content: No man is an island, Entire of itself. Each is a piece of the continent, A part of the main. If a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is the less. As well as if a promontory were. As well as if a manor of thine own Or of thine friend's were. Each man's death diminishes me, For I am involved in mankind. Therefore, send not to know For whom the bell tolls, It tolls for thee.

Once upon a time there was a green player. He was very brave and loved to roar! Everywhere he went, he roared loudly. Everyone enjoyed the player's roars and it made them laugh.

One day, the player was walking in the forest when he heard a big, loud roar. It was much deeper than his and came from deep in the trees. The player was scared and curious. He wanted to find out what was roaring.

The player looked around and saw a big, green monster! It was roaring and seemed to be angry. The player was scared and ran away, but he didn't forget the monster's roar.

From that day onwards, the player gave everyone big roars of his own whenever he wanted to show them he was brave and strong. And, even though he was still scared of the big green monster, the player never forgot his roar.

Mummy took Jack to the shop. He had a very big smile on his face. He could feel his hair getting longer and longer.

"Let get you a haircut, Jack," said Mummy.

Jack was so excited! He liked getting his hair cut and he liked going to the shop too. 

At the shop, Mummy bought Jack a nice haircut. The barber was very friendly and made Jack's hair look so good!

"Wow!" said Jack, when the barber finished. His hair felt nice and smooth.

"Was that easy?" asked Mummy.

Jack nodded. "Yes, easy," he said. 

Mummy gave Jack a big hug. "Good job!" she said. 

Jack smiled as they headed home. He liked his new haircut and he knew he looked handsome.

name_of_work: The White Horse by D.H. Lawrence
content: The youth walks up to the white horse, to put its halter on and the horse looks at him in silence. They are so silent, they are in another world.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to bake yummy cookies with her mom. One day, she wanted to surprise her mom by baking cookies all by herself. She went to the kitchen and started to mix flour, sugar, and butter. After that, she put the cookies in the oven to bake.

While waiting for the cookies to bake, Lily turned on the radio to listen to some lovely music. She danced around the kitchen, waiting for the cookies to be done. Suddenly, she smelled something burning. She ran to the oven and saw that the cookies were burnt!

Lily was sad, but her mom told her that it's okay to make mistakes and that she should try again. Lily learned that even if things don't turn out perfectly, it's important to keep trying and never give up.

Ben and Sam liked to play with cars. They had many cars of different colors and sizes. They liked to make them go fast and make loud noises. Sometimes they pretended they were drivers and raced each other.

One day, they found a big car in the garage. It was red and shiny and had a big motor. They wanted to play with it, but they knew it was Dad's car and they were not allowed to touch it. Dad was not home, he was at work. Mom was in the kitchen, making lunch.

"Let's play with the big car, just for a little bit," Ben said. "It will be fun. We can pretend we are going to the park."

"No, we can't," Sam said. "Dad will be angry. He said the big car is dangerous. We can get hurt."

Ben did not listen. He opened the door and climbed into the driver's seat. He put on the seat belt and turned the key. The motor made a loud noise and the car started to move.

"Ben, stop!" Sam shouted. He ran after the car, but it was too fast. He saw Ben lean out of the window and wave at him. He looked scared and happy at the same time.

The car went out of the garage and onto the street. There were other cars and people and bikes and dogs. Ben did not know how to steer or brake. He tried to push the pedals, but he did not know which one was which. The car went faster and faster and bumped into things.

Sam watched in horror as the car hit a big truck. There was a loud bang and a flash of fire. The car and the truck were smashed and burned. Sam saw Ben's body fly out of the car and land on the pavement. He was not moving. He was covered in blood and smoke.

Sam screamed and cried. He ran to Ben and tried to wake him up, but he did not. He was gone. Sam felt warm tears on his face and warm blood on his hands. He wished he had stopped Ben. He wished he had listened to Dad. He wished he had never played with the big car.

Once there was a girl named Sally. Every day Sally would go to the kitchen and get a yummy treat. Today she got some cookies so she could measure them for baking.

Sally found a big spoon and scooped some of her cookies onto it. She put the spoon on the table and wiped her hands clean. 

Then she grabbed a big measuring cup and filled it up with cookies. When she was done, she wiped her hands again and put the measuring cup on the counter.

Sally was ready to bake her treats. With the measuring cup full of yummy cookies, she smiled from ear to ear. She knew that once she finished baking, she would get to enjoy a delicious snack!

The little boy was so excited! Today he was taking his very first bike ride. His father was helping him get the bike ready. He watched as his dad put the bike together and attached the pedals. Then he reached for the handlebar and grabbed on tight.

"Let's go!" said the little boy.

The little boy had a broad smile on his face. He was so proud of himself. His father looked on with a beaming smile, happy his son was enjoying his first ride. 

The little boy pulled the pedals until he reached the end of the street. He looked up at his dad and said, "Can I do it again?"

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a gray cat named Mittens. Mittens liked to play with Lily's toys. One day, Lily's mommy asked her to help her with her nails. Lily smiled and said, "Okay, Mommy!" 

As they were painting their nails, Mittens jumped onto the table and knocked over the nail polish. "Oh no!" said Lily's mommy. "Don't worry, Mommy," said Lily. "I'll clean it up." She got a paper towel and wiped up the spilled nail polish. 

Lily's mommy smiled and said, "Thank you, Lily. You're such a big helper!" Lily smiled back and said, "I love helping you, Mommy." Mittens meowed and rubbed against Lily's leg. "Mittens likes to help too," said Lily. "But he's not very good at it." They all laughed and finished painting their nails.

Sam and Lily were friends who liked to play together. One day, they saw a big jar of cookies on the kitchen table. The cookies looked yummy and sweet.

"Let's take some cookies," Sam said. "Mommy won't mind."

"I don't know," Lily said. "Mommy said we have to wait for snack time."

Sam saw a black cookie in the jar. It looked different from the other cookies. He had an idea.

"Look, Lily, a black cookie!" he said. "Maybe it is a special cookie. Maybe it has chocolate inside. Do you want to try it?"

Lily was curious. She liked chocolate. She nodded.

"Okay, let's try it," she said.

Sam took the black cookie and broke it in half. He gave one half to Lily and kept the other half for himself. They bit into the cookie.

But the cookie was not sweet. It was bitter and spicy. It burned their mouths and made them cough. They spit out the cookie and cried.

Mommy heard them and came to the kitchen. She saw the cookie jar and the black cookie on the floor. She was angry.

"Sam, Lily, what did you do?" she said. "That was not a cookie. That was a pepper. A very hot pepper. You could have hurt yourself. You are in big trouble. No cookies for you today. Go to your rooms and think about what you did."

Sam and Lily felt sorry and sad. They wished they had listened to Mommy. They wished they had not taken the black cookie. They learned a hard lesson.

Once upon a time, there was a little boat. The boat was very happy to sail on the big blue sea. One day, the boat saw a big iron ship. The boat was fearful of the iron ship because it was so big. But the iron ship was friendly and waved to the little boat. The little boat felt happy and not so fearful anymore. They sailed together and had a great adventure on the sea. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily went to her grandma's house. When she got there, she saw a big cobweb in the corner. "What is that, grandma?" asked Lily.

"That's a cobweb, dear," said grandma. "It means a spider has been busy making a home."

"I don't like it," said Lily. "Can we solve the problem?"

"Of course, we can," said grandma. "Let's get the broom and sweep it away." 

Lily and her grandma worked together to sweep away the cobweb. "Wow, that was easy!" said Lily. "Now the room looks fit for a princess."

Once upon a time there was a girl named Jane. She was three years old and loved to play with her dolls. One day while she was playing, she had an idea. She wanted to make a new dress for one of her dolls.

So Jane found some pretty cloth and began to measure it. But then something awful happened! She accidentally cut it too short.

Jane was so sorry. She tried her best to fix it, but she couldn't. She started to cry.

But then her mom came over and said, "Don't worry, Jane. We can just measure some more cloth and try again."

And so Jane measured some new cloth and made a beautiful dress for her doll. She was so happy!

The end.

Nothing is lonelier than what's human: a group of them at work or play is enough to send a quiver through my differences. Especially up North where windows ignite early hanging the dark with inner lives like tiny drive-in screens showing underrated grade B stars, and bingo-playing ladies hover, intent as air controllers, above their cards in social halls. At tables long as football fields, they acquire a taste for the metallic: coins, flat Coke; and Bic lighters puff like the souls of exclamation points as winners collect their macrame plant cradles. I attended once and know that by the end a gray funk plaques the air, dense enough to choke a poet Or a pit pony. But for the cold life you can't do better than a 6 X 6 mobile hut defined against snow only by its black trim, like felt- tip on bond, or lacking trim, perishing into a blank square suspended from transmission wires. Where inside, anglers ease lines through floor- holes and the river underneath is gauntleted with hooks to snag tom cod. By day's end, window ledges bubble with gleanings: bagged in plastic, the catch curves like primitive spoons brimful with a light blurry as the light through tears. And let me add the certain loneliness of looking at the snow- shoe maker: a plump woman in brogues, dark socks, bifocals, who fixes herself on a frame of ash, weaving cowhide through its tear-shape. Who sits, hemmed by maritime light shed from a window view of moonish pasture and fishing boats in their complicated ice-bound ropes. It takes shoes like blow-ups of lace, of butterfly veins, to suspend hunters and lovers above the delicacies of snow. I admire her staid aviation but think she'd have no use for me. I can tell a snowshoe from a crosse only because I once saw one all-women's match: the Maliotenam Indian Reserve versus Ursula's Body Shop. High colors tussled with the white. Knowing nothing of the sport, I was surprised at how important it seemed: a ball going win or lose from net to net, flimsy webs against the shifty air.

Mary was very scared. She was all alone, and she didn't know what to do.

Suddenly, she heard a voice in her mind that said, "Mary, pray." She had never prayed before, but she wanted to be brave. So she closed her eyes and said a prayer.

As soon as she said the prayer, something strange happened. An exit appeared! It was a door she had never noticed before. She knew she was meant to go through it.

Mary took a deep breath and stepped through the exit. She was still a bit scared, but she felt safer too. She had prayed and something wonderful had happened.
