name_of_work: A Prayer For My Son by William Butler Yeats
content: BID a strong ghost stand at the head That my Michael may sleep sound, Nor cry, nor turn in the bed Till his morning meal come round; And may departing twilight keep All dread afar till morning's back. That his mother may not lack Her fill of sleep. Bid the ghost have sword in fist: Some there are, for I avow Such devilish things exist, Who have planned his murder, for they know Of some most haughty deed or thought That waits upon his future days, And would through hatred of the bays Bring that to nought. Though You can fashion everything From nothing every day, and teach The morning stats to sing, You have lacked articulate speech To tell Your simplest want, and known, Wailing upon a woman's knee, All of that worst ignominy Of flesh and bone; And when through all the town there ran The servants of Your enemy, A woman and a man, Unless the Holy Writings lie, Hurried through the smooth and rough And through the fertile and waste, protecting, till the danger past, With human love.

name_of_work: The Charge of the Light Brigade by Alfred Lord Tennyson
content: Half a league, half a league, Half a league onward, All in the valley of Death Rode the six hundred. "Forward, the Light Brigade! Charge for the guns!" he said. Into the valley of Death Rode the six hundred. "Forward, the Light Brigade!" Was there a man dismayed? Not though the soldier knew Someone had blundered. Theirs not to make reply, Theirs not to reason why, Theirs but to do and die. Into the valley of Death Rode the six hundred. Cannon to right of them, Cannon to left of them, Cannon in front of them Volleyed and thundered; Stormed at with shot and shell, Boldly they rode and well, Into the jaws of Death, Into the mouth of hell Rode the six hundred. Flashed all their sabres bare, Flashed as they turned in air Sabring the gunners there, Charging an army, while All the world wondered. Plunged in the battery-smoke Right through the line they broke; Cossack and Russian Reeled from the sabre stroke Shattered and sundered. Then they rode back, but not Not the six hundred. Cannon to right of them, Cannon to left of them, Cannon behind them Volleyed and thundered; Stormed at with shot and shell, While horse and hero fell. They that had fought so well Came through the jaws of Death, Back from the mouth of hell, All that was left of them, Left of six hundred. When can their glory fade? O the wild charge they made! All the world wondered. Honour the charge they made! Honour the Light Brigade, Noble six hundred!

Paula was very anxious as she took her daughter to the mall. She had always adored going to the mall and was excited to take her daughter shopping. As they passed through the large doors, her daughter Sarah saw a fountain in the center. She was excited and ran to it, but Paula stopped her.

"Honey, you can't play here," Paula said. "It's too deep, and you could get soaked."

Sarah started to pout, but Paula could tell that she was still anxious to get her feet wet. She tried to distract her with a few shops, but Sarah stayed focused on the fountain. After a few minutes, Paula began to worry, so she decided to move closer to the water.

As soon as Paula got closer, Sarah jumped in and started splashing around. Paula was frozen with fear as she saw her daughter soak in the water. She quickly ran to Sarah to get her out of the fountain, but it was too late. Sarah had already had an accident and the mall was now full of people watching in shock.

Paula had been so anxious to get Sarah to the mall and had been so careless. She regretted not stopping Sarah sooner. She scooped up Sarah and took her home, knowing this would be her last time at the mall.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Jessica. She was three and always loved to play. One day Jessica decided to perform a special show. She put on her dress and some shoes and announced to her mom she was ready. 

"I'm going to put on a show, mommy," Jessica said proudly.

"That sounds wonderful," her mom replied.

Jessica started to do some silly things. She hopped around, made funny faces and spun in circles. Then she did something really cool. She flipped around and around in a turn. 

"Wow, that was awesome! How did you do that?" her mom asked, clapping.

Jessica grinned. "I practiced and practiced until I could do it," she said.

But then things went wrong. Jessica tried to do the same turn again, but she fell and bumped her head. Her mom rushed to her side. 

"Are you okay?" her mom asked, feeling worried.

Jessica started to cry, "I'm so stupid. I can't do it!"

Her mom hugged her tight. "It's okay, Jessica. You tried your best and that's what matters. You'll get it right soon!" 

Jessica smiled and wiped away her tears. No matter how hard things seemed, she knew she could do it with some practice.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lucy. She went with her mom and dad to a restaurant. The restaurant was big and had many tables.

Lucy and her parents sat down and ordered food. Lucy's mom got a salad and her dad got a big burger. Lucy got a small plate of spaghetti. When the food came, Lucy took a bite of her spaghetti and made a face. It was bitter and she didn't like it.

Lucy started to panic because she didn't want to eat the bitter spaghetti. Her mom and dad saw her worry and told her it was okay. They asked the nice waiter for a new plate of food. This time, Lucy got some yummy chicken nuggets and was very happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside and explore the world around her. One day, she saw a gray cloud in the sky. It looked like it might rain soon.

Lily decided to go for a walk before it started to pour. As she walked, she saw a man performing tricks with a light-up yo-yo. The yo-yo glowed brightly as he spun it around and around. Lily was amazed by the light and the tricks.

Later that day, Lily went back inside her house just as the rain started to fall. She curled up with a book and a warm blanket. As she read, she thought about the man and his light-up yo-yo. She wondered if she could perform tricks like that someday.

Sara and Ben are twins. They like to play and laugh. They are jolly children. But they do not like to share. They want everything for themselves.

One morning, Mom makes toast for breakfast. She puts butter and jam on the toast. She cuts the toast into four pieces. She gives two pieces to Sara and two pieces to Ben.

"Thank you, Mom," Sara and Ben say. They start to eat their toast. They like the toast. It is yummy and warm.

But then, Sara sees that Ben has more jam on his toast. She wants more jam too. She thinks that Ben's toast is better than hers.

"Sara, can I have some of your butter?" Ben asks. He likes butter too.

"No, Ben. This is my butter. You have more jam. You are greedy," Sara says. She is angry.

"Please, Sara. Just a little bit. I will give you some of my jam," Ben says. He is sad.

"No, Ben. Go away. This is my toast. You cannot have it," Sara says. She pushes Ben away.

Ben cries. He does not like to be pushed. He does not like to be called greedy. He does not like to be sad.

Mom hears Ben crying. She comes to the table. She sees Sara and Ben fighting over the toast.

"What is going on here?" Mom asks. She is not happy.

"Sara is mean. She will not share her butter. She has more toast than me," Ben says.

"Ben is greedy. He wants my butter. He has more jam than me," Sara says.

Mom shakes her head. She is disappointed.

"Sara, Ben, you are both wrong. You have the same amount of toast. You have enough butter and jam. You should be grateful and kind. You should share and be jolly. That is what good children do," Mom says.

She takes one piece of toast from Sara and one piece of toast from Ben. She swaps them. She gives Sara a piece of toast with more jam and Ben a piece of toast with more butter.

"There. Now you both have what you want. Can you say sorry to each other and eat your toast nicely?" Mom says.

Sara and Ben look at their toast. They look at each other. They feel sorry. They do not want to fight. They want to be jolly.

"Sorry, Sara. I was greedy. You can have some of my butter," Ben says.

"Sorry, Ben. I was mean. You can have some of my jam," Sara says.

They hug each other. They smile. They eat their toast. They are jolly again.

Mom smiles too. She is proud of Sara and Ben. She is happy. She hugs them too.

"Good children. I love you both. Enjoy your toast," Mom says.

The end.

Anna and Ben are twins. They like to play with their toys in the living room. One day, they see a big bottle on the table. It is red and shiny. They want to know what it is.

"Look, Ben, what is that?" Anna asks, pointing at the bottle.

"I don't know, Anna. Maybe it is juice?" Ben says.

They climb on the chairs and reach for the bottle. They open it and smell it. It does not smell like juice. It smells funny.

"Yuck, this is not juice. This is wine," Anna says.

"Wine? What is wine?" Ben asks.

"Wine is a drink for grown-ups. Mommy and Daddy drink wine sometimes. They say it makes them happy. But we are not allowed to drink wine. It is bad for us," Anna says.

"Oh, I see. Then we should not drink wine. We should put it back," Ben says.

They try to put the bottle back on the table, but it is too heavy. They drop it on the floor. It breaks and spills everywhere. The wine makes a big mess.

"Oh no, we are in trouble!" Anna says.

"Quick, let's hide!" Ben says.

They run to their room and hide under the bed. They hear Mommy and Daddy come home. They hear them gasp and shout.

"Who did this? Who broke the wine bottle?" Mommy asks.

"Look, there are footprints on the carpet. They lead to the twins' room," Daddy says.

They follow the footprints and find Anna and Ben under the bed. They look scared and sorry.

"Anna, Ben, did you do this?" Mommy asks.

"Yes, Mommy, we did. We are sorry. We were curious. We thought it was juice. We did not drink it. We tried to put it back, but it fell," Anna says.

"We are very sorry, Mommy, Daddy. We did not mean to make a mess. We did not know it was wine," Ben says.

Mommy and Daddy sigh. They are angry, but they are also glad that the twins did not drink the wine. They hug them and tell them they love them.

"Anna, Ben, we are not happy with what you did. You should not touch things that are not yours. You should not climb on the chairs. You should not open bottles that are not for you. You could have hurt yourselves or made yourselves sick. Do you understand?" Mommy says.

"Yes, Mommy, we understand. We are sorry. We will not do it again," Anna and Ben say.

"Good. Now, let's go and clean up the mess. And then we will have some juice and cookies. You are lucky that we are not too mad at you. You are lucky that we have another bottle of wine for later," Daddy says.

Anna and Ben smile. They are happy that Mommy and Daddy are not too mad at them. They are happy that they have juice and cookies. They are happy that they have each other. They are lucky twins.

Once upon a time, there was a furry eraser. She was round, pink and sparkly. She was different than the other erasers.

One day, she decided to go explore the world. She stumbled upon a hill filled with flowers. The flowers were all different colors and sizes.

Suddenly, the furry eraser started to glow. It was so beautiful! The colors were so bright and vibrant. The eraser started to dance and twirl around in the flowers. She was so happy. The glowing light filled everything around her.

When the sun set, the eraser stopped glowing. She was sad but at least she knew she could always glow again. She thanked the flowers for being so wonderful to her, and she gently went to sleep.

name_of_work: Ode on Melancholy by John Keats
content: No, no, go not to Lethe, neither twist Wolf's-bane, tight-rooted, for its poisonous wine; Nor suffer thy pale forehead to be kiss'd By nightshade, ruby grape of Proserpine; Make not your rosary of yew-berries, Nor let the beetle, nor the death-moth be Your mournful Psyche, nor the downy owl A partner in your sorrow's mysteries; For shade to shade will come too drowsily, And drown the wakeful anguish of the soul. But when the melancholy fit shall fall Sudden from heaven like a weeping cloud, That fosters the droop-headed flowers all, And hides the green hill in an April shroud; Then glut thy sorrow on a morning rose, Or on the rainbow of the salt sand-wave, Or on the wealth of globed peonies; Or if thy mistress some rich anger shows, Emprison her soft hand, and let her rave, And feed deep, deep upon her peerless eyes. She dwells with Beauty--Beauty that must die; And Joy, whose hand is ever at his lips Bidding adieu; and aching Pleasure nigh, Turning to poison while the bee-mouth sips: Ay, in the very temple of Delight Veil'd Melancholy has her sovran shrine, Though seen of none save him whose strenuous tongue Can burst Joy's grape against his palate fine; His soul shalt taste the sadness of her might, And be among her cloudy trophies hung.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Sally. Sally loved exploring and she was always looking for something new to find. One day, Sally was examining her closet when she spotted something fair. It was an old box that she had never seen before. She opened the box and found a magical toy inside. It was a stuffed monkey that could move and talk! Sally was so excited she couldn't believe it. She took the stuffed monkey out and hugged it. Then she heard a voice say, "I'm so glad you found me." Sally was so happy to have a new friend! The two of them played together all day long. From that day on, Sally and her new friend had lots of fun adventures.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl. She wanted to do something special. She wanted to succeed. Every day, she tried her hardest. She worked hard to do her best.

The little girl went outside and saw a bird. She wanted to fly just like the bird. She jumped, twirled and hopped all around. She jumped higher, twirled better and hopped further until she felt she could fly.

Suddenly, she took off like the bird. She flew and flew, feeling like she could keep flying forever. Finally, she was flying higher and higher. She had succeeded!

The little girl was so happy and proud. She had succeeded in flying like a bird. It was a magical moment. She flew around until it was time to go home. As she flew back to the ground, she smiled and knew she had done her best.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue loved the color orange. She had an orange ball, an orange dress, and even an orange cat. Sue's cat was named Hug because he gave the best hugs.

One sunny day, Sue and Hug went to the park. They saw a man selling orange ice cream. Sue wanted some, but she needed to pay the man first. She looked in her pocket and found some coins.

Sue gave the coins to the man and he gave her the orange ice cream. She was so happy! Sue shared the ice cream with Hug. After they finished, Hug gave Sue a big hug to say thank you. Sue and Hug had a great day at the park, and they went home with big smiles on their faces.

Once upon a time there was a little bunny who wanted to find a playmate. He looked everywhere, but nobody wanted to play with him. He was so sad that he plopped down and started to cry.

Suddenly, a big wind started to blow. The wind carried a beautiful hat to him. The bunny immediately felt excited and put it on. The hat looked so good on him he decided to wear it all the time.

The bunny was so stubborn about wearing his hat that he refused to take it off or even get it wet. He even bathed with it still on! But he soon found out the hard way that water and hats don't mix. After swimming, the bunny realized his hat was all wet and he had to dry it.

The bunny learned a valuable lesson: never be too stubborn to follow the rules. Even if the hat looked great on him, he should have taken it off so it wouldn't get wet and be ruined.

Once upon a time there was a big mop. The mop was so large and it was special. Every day it would talk to the little boy, who would mention all sorts of adventures he would like to go on. He liked to imagine going far away, like to the moon.

One day, the little boy looked around and noticed the mop was missing. He began to look all around, asking his mom and dad if they knew where it was. But they didn't know. So the little boy went to the back yard and found his mop. It had gotten so big! He was so happy to see it there. 

The little boy thought of a plan. He ran to the kitchen and filled up the mop with water. Then he ran back out to the mop and sprayed it all over. He wisely used the mop to scrub off dirt and mud on the grass and it worked very well. The mop was so big that it could even clean the garden.

The little boy danced happily as he mopped around. He was sure glad he had such a large mop!

We do not speak like Petrarch or wear a hat like Spenser and it is not fourteen lines like furrows in a small, carefully plowed field but the picture postcard, a poem on vacation, that forces us to sing our songs in little rooms or pour our sentiments into measuring cups. We write on the back of a waterfall or lake, adding to the view a caption as conventional as an Elizabethan woman's heliocentric eyes. We locate an adjective for the weather. We announce that we are having a wonderful time. We express the wish that you were here and hide the wish that we were where you are, walking back from the mailbox, your head lowered as you read and turn the thin message in your hands. A slice of this place, a length of white beach, a piazza or carved spires of a cathedral will pierce the familiar place where you remain, and you will toss on the table this reversible display: a few square inches of where we have strayed and a compression of what we feel.

name_of_work: A Supermarket in California by Allen Ginsberg
content: What thoughts I have of you tonight, Walt Whitman, for I walked down the sidestreets under the trees with a headache self-conscious looking at the full moon. In my hungry fatigue, and shopping for images, I went into the neon fruit supermarket, dreaming of your enumerations! What peaches and what penumbras! Whole families shopping at night! Aisles full of husbands! Wives in the avocados, babies in the tomatoes!--and you, Garcia Lorca, what were you doing down by the watermelons? I saw you, Walt Whitman, childless, lonely old grubber, poking among the meats in the refrigerator and eyeing the grocery boys. I heard you asking questions of each: Who killed the pork chops? What price bananas? Are you my Angel? I wandered in and out of the brilliant stacks of cans following you, and followed in my imagination by the store detective. We strode down the open corridors together in our solitary fancy tasting artichokes, possessing every frozen delicacy, and never passing the cashier. Where are we going, Walt Whitman? The doors close in an hour. Which way does your beard point tonight? (I touch your book and dream of our odyssey in the supermarket and feel absurd.) Will we walk all night through solitary streets? The trees add shade to shade, lights out in the houses, we'll both be lonely. Will we stroll dreaming of the lost America of love past blue automobiles in driveways, home to our silent cottage? Ah, dear father, graybeard, lonely old courage-teacher, what America did you have when Charon quit poling his ferry and you got out on a smoking bank and stood watching the boat disappear on the black waters of Lethe?

Once upon a time, there was a small boy named Peter. He liked to play in the garden. Every day, Peter would point to something new in the garden and say, "Good!" 

One morning, Peter was pointing to a big tree, when he spotted a large bush. He said, "Good!" and ran to it. "What is this?" he asked. 

A big bird was perched on the bush. It flew away when Peter came close. But it left behind a shiny yellow egg! 

Peter pointed at the egg and said, "Good!" He carefully picked it up and took it back to the tree. Then he called for his mommy and showed her the egg. 

His mommy looked surprised. Then she smiled and said, "Very good, Peter! We will take care of it together until it hatches. Can you do that?" 

Peter nodded and pointed at the egg. He knew he was going to look after something very special. And soon, he found out what it was - a little baby bird!

Lily and Tom were friends who liked to play in the park. One day, they saw a big cake on a table near the swings. It looked tasty and had pink icing and sprinkles. Lily and Tom wanted to eat some of the cake, but they did not know who it belonged to.

"Maybe it is for a party," Lily said. "But no one is here. Can we have a bite?"

"I don't know," Tom said. "It is not nice to take things that are not ours. Maybe someone will be angry."

But Lily was hungry and curious. She reached for the cake and broke off a piece. She put it in her mouth and smiled. "Mmm, it is so good! You should try some, Tom."

Tom was tempted, but he was also scared. He looked around and saw no one. He thought maybe it was okay to have a little bit of the cake. He took a piece and ate it. It was tasty, too. He and Lily ate more and more of the cake, until they felt full and happy.

But then, they heard a loud voice behind them. "Hey, what are you doing? That is my cake! You are very naughty!"

Lily and Tom turned around and saw a big man with a red face. He was holding a bag of balloons and a hat. He looked very angry and scary. Lily and Tom felt bad and scared. They had eaten his cake without asking. They had been greedy and rude.

They ran away from the man, but their stomachs hurt. They had eaten too much cake and it made them sick. They felt sorry and sad. They wished they had not eaten the cake. They wished they had been good and polite.

They learned a lesson that day. They learned that it is not good to take things that are not yours. They learned that it is better to share and be kind. They learned that being greedy can make you sick and scare you. They decided to say sorry to the man and to be more careful next time.

Sara loves to play with her toy cars. She has many cars of different colors and sizes. She likes to zoom them on the floor, on the table, and on the couch. She makes noises like vroom, beep, and honk.

One day, Sara's mom says she has a surprise for her. She takes Sara to a big building with many cars. Sara is very excited. She sees cars that are shiny, fast, and big. She wants to zoom them all.

Sara's mom says they are here for a massage. Sara does not know what that is. She thinks it is something to do with cars. She follows her mom to a room with a big bed. There is a lady who smiles and says hello. She tells Sara to lie down on the bed. She says she will give Sara a massage. She says it will make Sara feel good and relaxed.

Sara is curious. She lies down on the bed. The lady puts some oil on her hands. She rubs Sara's back, arms, legs, and feet. She makes gentle movements and presses on some spots. Sara feels warm and ticklish. She giggles and says it feels nice. She closes her eyes and enjoys the massage.

Sara's mom watches and smiles. She is happy that Sara likes the massage. She thinks it is a good way to treat Sara after a busy week. She also thinks it is a good way to teach Sara new words. She tells Sara that massage is a word that means to rub and squeeze someone's body to make them feel good. She also tells Sara that available is a word that means to be free and ready for something. She says that today they are lucky because the massage lady was available for them. She says that sometimes people have to wait or make an appointment for a massage.

Sara listens and learns. She repeats the words massage and available. She thinks they are fun words. She thanks the massage lady and gives her a hug. She tells her mom that she loves her and the massage. She asks her mom if they can zoom some cars now. Her mom laughs and says yes. They go to the car park and zoom some cars. Sara has a great day.

John and his mom were on a road trip. It was a hot summer day and their car was boiling!

"John, can you do something for me?" his mom asked.

"Yes, mommy," he said.

"Can you open the window and let some fresh air in the car? It's too hot in here," she said.

John was excited. He quickly rolled the window down and felt the breeze.

"Ahhh," they both said in relief.

John was having lots of fun and looked outside the window. He noticed a sign.

"Mommy, what does that sign say?" John asked pointing at the sign.

"It says we have reached the end of the road," she said smiling.

John was amazed and clapped his hands.
"We did it! We drove all the way across the country in one year!" he said cheerfully.
His mom smiled, "Yes, honey, we did!"

Once upon a time there was a Mommy and Daddy who loved each other very much. But one day they had an argument and they said mean things to each other. They felt so sad and sorry.

Then Daddy had a great idea. He went to the store and bought Mommy her favorite pink pastry. He said, â€œIâ€™m sorryâ€ and gave it to Mommy.

Mommy smiled and said, â€œI forgive youâ€ and they hugged. Suddenly, they were happy again! The pink pastry was a symbol of their love and showed them that they could forgive each other and be happy again.

Lila and Tom were playing in the garden. They liked to run and jump and chase each other. They saw a big green thing with spikes. It was a cactus.

"What is that?" Lila asked.

"It is a cactus. It is a plant that lives in the hot and dry places. It has spikes to protect itself from animals that want to eat it," Tom said.

"Why does it have spikes? That is weird. It must hurt to touch it," Lila said.

Tom was curious. He wanted to touch the cactus. He reached out his hand slowly. He touched one of the spikes. It pricked his finger. He cried out in pain.

"Ow! Ow! Ow! That hurts!" Tom said.

Lila ran to him. She saw his finger was bleeding. She hugged him and said, "I'm sorry, Tom. Are you okay?"

Tom nodded. He was brave. He said, "I'm okay. It was a silly thing to do. I should have listened to you. The cactus is weird and spiky. I don't want to touch it again."

Lila and Tom went back to their house. They washed Tom's finger and put a band-aid on it. They decided to play with their toys instead. They liked their toys. They were soft and cuddly. They did not have spikes. They remained friends. They learned a lesson. They did not touch the cactus again.

Once upon a time, there lived a little girl called Ella. She was three years old and had long blond hair. Every day, she would tidy her bedroom and make her bed nice and neat. She liked when it was tidy.

One day, Ella was in the garden and she found something strange. She looked carefully and saw it was a sack! Ella touched it and felt something inside. She found a button inside. It was shiny and round, and she liked it.

Ella took the sack and button inside. She held the bag close, like it was her treasure. She put the button in her room and kept it safe.

The next day, Ella showed her best friend the button. She showed it to all of her friends, and they said it was so pretty. Ella then put the button back in the sack, and together they played a game of hide and seek. 

Ella loved the tidy room and her special button in the sack. From then on, she kept it safe and it stayed a special treasure to her.

The End.

name_of_work: Lift Every Voice and Sing by James Weldon Johnson
content: Lift every voice and sing Till earth and heaven ring, Ring with the harmonies of Liberty; Let our rejoicing rise High as the listening skies, Let it resound loud as the rolling sea. Sing a song full of the faith that the dark past has taught us, Sing a song full of the hope that the present has brought us. Facing the rising sun of our new day begun, Let us march on till victory is won. Stony the road we trod, Bitter the chastening rod, Felt in the days when hope unborn had died; Yet with a steady beat, Have not our weary feet Come to the place for which our fathers sighed? We have come over a way that with tears has been watered, We have come, treading our path through the blood of the slaughtered, Out from the gloomy past, Till now we stand at last Where the white gleam of our bright star is cast. God of our weary years, God of our silent tears, Thou who hast brought us thus far on the way; Thou who hast by Thy might Led us into the light, Keep us forever in the path, we pray. Lest our feet stray from the places, our God, where we met Thee, Lest, our hearts drunk with the wine of the world, we forget Thee; Shadowed beneath Thy hand, May we forever stand. True to our God, True to our native land.

Lily and Ben are friends. They live next to each other. They like to play together. Sometimes they pretend to be animals. Lily likes to be a cat. Ben likes to be a dog.

One day, they find a big box in Lily's yard. They think it is a good place to play. They open the box and go inside. They pretend the box is a house. Lily is the cat who lives in the house. Ben is the dog who guards the house.

They have fun in the box. They make noises and act like animals. They do not hear Lily's mom calling them. She wants them to come inside for lunch. She looks for them in the yard. She does not see them in the box.

She gets worried. She asks Ben's mom if she knows where they are. Ben's mom does not know either. They look around the neighborhood. They ask other people if they have seen Lily and Ben. No one has seen them.

They are about to call the police. Then they hear some noises from the box. They go to the box and open it. They see Lily and Ben inside. They are surprised and relieved. They hug them and scold them.

They tell them they should not hide in the box. They should always tell their moms where they are. They should listen when their moms call them. They should not make their moms worry.

Lily and Ben are sorry. They say they are sorry. They did not mean to scare their moms. They just wanted to play. They promise to be more careful next time.

They learn a lesson. They learn to be safe and responsible. They learn to respect their moms. They still like to play and pretend. But they always tell their moms where they are. And they always come when their moms call them.

Happy are men who yet before they are killed Can let their veins run cold. Whom no compassion fleers Or makes their feet Sore on the alleys cobbled with their brothers. The front line withers. But they are troops who fade, not flowers, For poets' tearful fooling: Men, gaps for filling: Losses, who might have fought Longer; but no one bothers. And some cease feeling Even themselves or for themselves. Dullness best solves The tease and doubt of shelling, And Chance's strange arithmetic Comes simpler than the reckoning of their shilling. They keep no check on armies' decimation. Happy are these who lose imagination: They have enough to carry with ammunition. Their spirit drags no pack. Their old wounds, save with cold, can not more ache. Having seen all things red, Their eyes are rid Of the hurt of the colour of blood for ever. And terror's first constriction over, Their hearts remain small-drawn. Their senses in some scorching cautery of battle Now long since ironed, Can laugh among the dying, unconcerned. Happy the soldier home, with not a notion How somewhere, every dawn, some men attack, And many sighs are drained. Happy the lad whose mind was never trained: His days are worth forgetting more than not. He sings along the march Which we march taciturn, because of dusk, The long, forlorn, relentless trend From larger day to huger night. We wise, who with a thought besmirch Blood over all our soul, How should we see our task But through his blunt and lashless eyes? Alive, he is not vital overmuch; Dying, not mortal overmuch; Nor sad, nor proud, Nor curious at all. He cannot tell Old men's placidity from his. But cursed are dullards whom no cannon stuns, That they should be as stones. Wretched are they, and mean With paucity that never was simplicity. By choice they made themselves immune To pity and whatever moans in man Before the last sea and the hapless stars; Whatever mourns when many leave these shores; Whatever shares The eternal reciprocity of tears.

Lila and Ben went to the park with Mom. They saw many birds by the pond. Lila liked the ducks. Ben liked the swans. He wanted to touch a swan.

"Can I touch a swan, Mom?" Ben asked.

"No, Ben. Swans are not pets. They can bite. They are wild birds. You can look at them, but not touch them," Mom said.

Ben did not listen. He ran to a swan. He reached out his hand. The swan did not like that. It hissed and snapped at Ben. Ben was scared. He ran back to Mom. He wept.

"Ow, ow, ow! The swan bit me! It hurt!" Ben cried.

Mom hugged Ben. She checked his hand. It was not bleeding. It was just red.

"I'm sorry, Ben. The swan was scared too. It thought you were a threat. You have to be careful with wild animals. They are not like toys. They have feelings and instincts. They need space and respect," Mom said.

Lila came over. She saw Ben weeping. She felt sorry for him.

"Ben, don't weep. I have something for you. Look!" Lila said.

She showed Ben a feather. It was white and soft. It was from a swan.

"Wow, Lila. Where did you get that?" Ben asked.

"I found it on the ground. It fell from a swan. It is amazing. You can have it. It is a gift," Lila said.

Ben smiled. He took the feather. He thanked Lila. He felt better.

"Thank you, Lila. You are a good sister. This is an amazing feather. It is from a swan. It is beautiful," Ben said.

Mom smiled too. She was proud of Lila. She was glad that Ben learned a lesson.

"Let's go home, kids. We had a fun day at the park. We saw many birds. We learned about swans. We shared a feather. We are a happy family," Mom said.

Leo was a little lion who loved to learn. He liked to listen to his grandpa tell him stories about the history of their pride. Grandpa was very wise and knew many things. He told Leo how they used to live in a big forest, how they hunted and played, and how they roared to scare away bad animals.

One day, Leo wanted to try roaring like his grandpa. He went to a hill and opened his mouth wide. But instead of a loud roar, he made a tiny squeak. He tried again and again, but he could not roar. He felt sad and ran back to his grandpa.

Grandpa saw Leo and hugged him. He asked him what was wrong. Leo told him he could not roar. He said he wanted to be like grandpa and make history. Grandpa smiled and said, "Leo, you are still very young. You have time to grow and learn. You do not need to roar to make history. You can make history by being kind, brave, and smart. You can make history by helping others and following your dreams. You are my little lion, and I am proud of you."

Leo felt better and thanked his grandpa. He said he loved him and his stories. He said he wanted to be wise like him. Grandpa said, "You are already wise, Leo. You have a big heart and a curious mind. And one day, you will roar like a king." He tickled Leo and made him laugh. They cuddled and watched the sun set. They were happy.

name_of_work: One Perfect Rose by Dorothy Parker
content: A single flow'r he sent me, since we met. All tenderly his messenger he chose; Deep-hearted, pure, with scented dew still wet-- One perfect rose. I knew the language of the floweret; "My fragile leaves," it said, "his heart enclose." Love long has taken for his amulet One perfect rose. Why is it no one ever sent me yet One perfect limousine, do you suppose? Ah no, it's always just my luck to get One perfect rose.

Things concentrate at the edges; the pond-surface Is bourne to fish and man and it is spread In textile scum and damask light, on which The lily-pads are set; and there are also Inlaid ruddy twigs, becalmed pine-leaves, Air-baubles, and the chain mail of froth. Descending into sleep (as when the night-lift Falls past a brilliant floor), we glimpse a sublime Decor and hear, perhaps, a complete music, But this evades us, as in the night meadows The crickets' million roundsong dies away From all advances, rising in every distance. Our riches are centrifugal; men compose Daily, unwittingly, their final dreams, And those are our own voices whose remote Consummate chorus rides on the whirlpool's rim, Past which we flog our sails, toward which we drift, Plying our trades, in hopes of a good drowning

Once upon a time there was a little boy called Peter. Peter loved to make things, especially with stones. 

One day, Peter found a very big stone and decided to make something with it. He worked hard and whistled while he was building. 

Peter's mother heard the noisy whistling and came out of the house. She asked him what he was doing with the stone and Peter said that he wanted to make something. 

"No," said his mother sternly, "you mustn't make anything with that stone. It is too noisy and could disturb the neighbours."

Peter was sad. He wanted to make something with the stone and now he couldn't. He put the stone down and hung his head. 

Then an idea came to him! He picked up the stone and ran to the garden. He built a beautiful little house with the stone. It was a wonderful creation and it didn't make any noise! 

Peter smiled and felt very proud of his work. His mother was happy too, and the neighbours were not disturbed. 

The End

name_of_work: Into My Own by Robert Frost
content: One of my wishes is that those dark trees, So old and firm they scarcely show the breeze, Were not, as 'twere, the merest mask of gloom, But stretched away unto the edge of doom. I should not be withheld but that some day Into their vastness I should steal away, Fearless of ever finding open land, Or highway where the slow wheel pours the sand. I do not see why I should e'er turn back, Or those should not set forth upon my track To overtake me, who should miss me here And long to know if still I held them dear. They would not find me changed from him they knew-- Only more sure of all I thought was true.

yourself and the laughter crackles like hellfire The sparks gild the ground and background of your life Your life is a painting in a dark museum And sometimes you examine it closely You are walking in sorrowful and giddy travels Ignorant still of dishonesty and old age Love afflicted you at twenty and again at thirty I've lived like a fool and I've wasted my time You dare not look at your hands I want to weep all the time On you on the one I love on everything that frightened you And now you are crying at the sight of refugees Who believe in God who pray whose women nurse babies The hall of the train station is filled with the refugee-smell Like the Magi refugees believe in their star They expect to find silver mines in the Argentine And to return like kings to their abandoned countries One family carries a red eiderdown you carry your heart Eiderdown and dreams are equally fantastic Some of the refugees stay on in Paris settling Into slums on the rue des Rosiers or the rue des Ecouffes I have seen them often at dusk they breathe at their doorways They budge from home as reluctantly as chessmen They are chiefly Jewish the women wear wigs And haunt backrooms of little shops in little chairs You're standing at the metal counter of some dive Drinking wretched coffee where the wretched live You are in a cavernous restaurant at night These women are not evil they are used-up regretful Each has tormented someone even the ugliest She is the daughter of a police sergeant from Jersey Her hands I'd never noticed are hard and cracked My pity aches along the seams of her belly I you drink an alcohol as caustic as your life Your life you drink as alcohol You walk to Auteuil you want to go on foot to sleep At home among your South Sea and Guinean fetishes Christs of another Mia was excited. She was going to Grandma and Grandpa's house. On the way, she asked, "What are we going there for?"

Dad answered, "To eat something yummy of course!"

When they arrived, Mia found out something even more exciting; Grandma had brought something special for her.

Dad said, "It's a surprise for you."

Mia smiled and asked, "Can I see it?"

Grandpa said, "Yes, you can!"

He opened the box and revealed a pencil and a paper. Grandpa said, "See Mia? This pencil is really sharp." Mia touched it, amazed. Grandpa then said, "Now you can use it to write a word."

Mia was so happy. She picked up the pencil and began writing the word. When she was finished, Grandma said, "Now that we all wrote a word, let's have something yummy!"

Mia ran off to the kitchen, excited. When she got back, there was a yummy meal waiting for them. As they ate, Grandma said, "Remember Mia, always listen carefully to the words of your elders."

Mia beamed with joy as she remembered the surprise. She realized that all the words that were spoken were meant to lead her to the special surprise.

Tim and Mia are friends. They like to play on the shore. The shore is where the water and the sand meet. They can make castles with the sand and splash in the water.

One day, Tim and Mia see a big boat on the water. The boat has many flags and people. The people are happy and loud. They are celebrating something.

Tim and Mia are curious. They want to know what the people are celebrating. They wave at the boat and shout, "Hello! Hello! What are you celebrating?"

A man on the boat sees them and smiles. He waves back and shouts, "Hello, children! We are celebrating our journey. We have been on the water for a long time. We have seen many things. But now we are happy to see the shore. The shore is our home."

Tim and Mia are amazed. They think the boat is very heavy and the journey is very long. They wonder what the people have seen on the water. They say, "Wow! That is amazing! We are happy for you. Welcome home!"

The man on the boat thanks them and throws them a candy. Tim and Mia catch the candy and say, "Thank you! Thank you! Enjoy your celebration!"

They eat the candy and watch the boat get closer to the shore. They think the people are very brave and lucky. They hope to see them again. They smile and hug. They are happy to be friends on the shore.

Once upon a time, there was a nosy dog named Spot. Spot liked to take walks with his best friend, Tom. One day, they saw a big motorcycle on their walk. Spot and Tom had never seen a motorcycle before, so they wanted to look closer.

Tom said, "Spot, let's take a look at the motorcycle!" Spot wagged his tail and barked, "Yes, let's go!" They walked up to the motorcycle and saw it was red and shiny. Spot sniffed it and Tom touched it. They both thought it was very cool.

Just then, a nice man came out of a house. He said, "Hi, I see you like my motorcycle!" Tom and Spot looked at the man and smiled. The man let Tom sit on the motorcycle and Spot sat in the sidecar. They had so much fun pretending to ride the motorcycle. The nosy dog and his friend had a great day exploring and making a new friend.

name_of_work: The Poem Unwritten by Denise Levertov
content: The Poem Unwritten For weeks the poem of your body, of my hands upon your body stroking, sweeping, in the rite of worship, going their way of wonder down from neck-pulse to breast-hair to level belly to cock - for weeks that poem, that prayer unwritten. That poem unwritten, the act left to the mind, undone. The years a forest of giant stones, of fossil stumps, blocking the altar.

Once there was a mouse who was being very bad. He was running up and down the walls and making a mess. His mum was very cross and decided to punish him.

The mouse was scared and tried to hide. He slipped away into the corner, but his mum found him. She said "You have been very bad and you must be punished!"

The mouse was so scared that he started to cry. His mum knew she needed to think of a special punishment that the mouse could understand. So she made a fake mouse out of wood and put it into the corner.

Then she said to the mouse "If you're naughty again, this fake mouse will punish you!"

The mouse was so scared of the fake mouse, he promised to be good. From that day on, he was the best behaved mouse ever!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sarah. She was three years old and loved to play in the garden with her pet mule. 

One bright sunny day, Sarah and her mule decided to go skipping in the meadow. The meadow was full of tall, green grass and brightly coloured wildflowers. Sarah was so excited, she skipped as fast as she could, while her mule followed slowly behind.

When they reached the middle of the meadow, Sarah saw a fragile little bird perched on a tree branch. She stopped skipping and pointed the bird out to her mule. "Look!" she said, "How pretty!" The mule looked up and noticed the bird too.

The bird was so tiny and quiet that Sarah thought it must be sleeping. She slowly and quietly crept towards it, but suddenly the bird jumped up and flew away. Sarah gasped in surprise and laughed. That was too much fun!

She turned to her mule and said, â€œLetâ€™s keep skipping!â€. The mule agreed and together they skipped back to the garden.

Once upon a time, in a land far away, there lived a famous wizard. He was very powerful and wise, and every day he was worked hard doing his magic. One day, he felt very tired and decided to nap.

Just then, he had a dream. In the dream, he saw a card that he was meant to find. He knew that the card was important, but he didnâ€™t know why. When he woke up, he felt calmer, but also excited to find the card.

The wizard decided to search the land for the card. He searched high and low, but he couldnâ€™t find it. He was about to give up, when finally he found the card in the last place he thought to look - his pocket! When he looked at the card, he realized that the card was a ticket to a famous festival. 

The wizard was so happy, and the next day he set off for the festival. With the card, he was able to attend the festival and it was pure joy! He was never so glad to have taken a nap!
