Lily liked to design things. She used paper, crayons, scissors and glue to make different shapes and colors. She made a fan with yellow and green paper. She cut out a circle and some triangles. She glued the triangles around the circle. She made a handle with a stick. She was very proud of her fan.

She showed her fan to her friend Max. Max liked to play with cars and trucks. He did not like to design things. He said, "What is that? It looks silly."

Lily felt sad. She said, "It is a fan. It can make wind. See?" She waved her fan in front of Max's face. Max felt the wind. He said, "It tickles. Stop it."

Lily did not stop. She said, "My fan is not silly. It is mysterious. It can make magic. Watch." She waved her fan in the air. She said some words that she made up. She said, "Fan, fan, make a plan. Change Max into a can."

Nothing happened. Max laughed. He said, "That is not magic. That is nonsense. You cannot change me into a can."

Lily felt angry. She said, "Yes, I can. You are mean. You do not like my fan. You do not like me. Go away."

Max felt sorry. He said, "I am sorry. I do like you. You are my friend. I was just joking. Your fan is nice. Can I try it?"

Lily smiled. She said, "Okay. You can try it. But be careful. It is mysterious. You never know what it can do."

They took turns to wave the fan and say funny words. They pretended to make magic. They had fun. They forgot to be mad. They were happy. They liked to design things. They liked to play with cars and trucks. They liked each other. They were friends.

John was a tidy boy who lived in a small house. He had a strange day one morning. He decided to go exploring and found a dark cave. He stepped inside and started to twist his way through the darkness. Suddenly, he saw something scary and twisted in fear. He tried to back away but there was no way out. He was so scared and felt lonely in the dark cave. Sadly, he didn't make it out alive. The next day, his family found him in the dark cave and they cried when they saw him. He was still twisted in fear and ran away to a better place.

Once there was a clumsy girl named Maria. She decided to cook for the first time. Her mom said it would take a few minutes. First, Maria found the big kitchen. She saw pots, pans, and all the other things she needed. She was very excited.

Next, Maria grabbed her ingredients and started cooking. She used her clumsy hands to stir and mix. Sometimes, she even made a mess on the floor. But Maria kept going. She was determined to make something special.

Finally, after a few minutes, Maria was done. She had made a yummy dinner. All her hard work was worth it! And best of all, her mom was very proud of her. From that day on, Maria found a love for cooking.

name_of_work: Comes the Dawn by Jorge Luis Borges
content: After a while you learn the subtle difference between holding a hand and chaining a soul. And you learn that love doesn't mean leaning, and company doesn't mean security. And you begin to learn that kisses aren't contracts and presents aren't promises. And you begin to accept defeats with your head up and your eyes open with the grace of a woman, not the grief of a child. And you learn to build all your roads on today because tomorrow's ground is too uncertain for plans and futures have a way of falling down in mid-flight. After a while you learn that even sunshine burns if you get too much. So you plant your own garden and decorate your own soul, instead of waiting for someone to bring you flowers. And you learn that you really can endure... that you really are strong, and you really do have worth. And you learn and learn... with every goodbye you learn.

Anger, as black as a hook, overtakes me. Each day, each Nazi took, at 8:00 A.M., a baby and sauteed him for breakfast in his frying pan. And death looks on with a casual eye and picks at the dirt under his fingernail. Man is evil, I say aloud. Man is a flower that should be burnt, I say aloud. Man is a bird full of mud, I say aloud. And death looks on with a casual eye and scratches his anus. Man with his small pink toes, with his miraculous fingers is not a temple but an outhouse, I say aloud. Let man never again raise his teacup. Let man never again write a book. Let man never again put on his shoe. Let man never again raise his eyes, on a soft July night. Never. Never. Never. Never. Never. I say those things aloud.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to draw pictures with her crayons. One day, she found an empty book with no pictures in it. Lily wanted to fill the book with her own pictures.

Lily started to draw in the empty book. She drew a big sun, green trees, and a blue river. She even drew a little house with a red door. Lily was very happy with her pictures. She showed them to her mommy and daddy, who were very proud of her.

Lily decided to name her book "Lily's World." She kept drawing more and more pictures in her book. Every day, she would show her new pictures to her family and friends. And they all loved her beautiful, colorful world.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy. He was a curious 3 year old and enjoyed exploring his surroundings. One morning, he decided to take a walk in the woods. He walked along until he saw a broken wolf.

The little boy was astounded, and he wanted to help the wolf. He ran back to his home and took some food with him. He then went back and hand-fed the wolf until it had finished eating. 

The little boy told the wolf, "I hope you feel better soon," and smiled. The wolf replied, "Thank you for helping me. I feel better already." The little boy was very happy.

He said goodbye to the wolf, ran back home, and told his parents the story of the broken wolf. They were so proud of their son for helping the wolf. The little boy finished with a smile on his face, knowing that he had done something good that day.

name_of_work: The Last Hero by G.K. Chesterton
content: The wind blew out from Bergen from the dawning to the day, There was a wreck of trees and fall of towers a score of miles away, And drifted like a livid leaf I go before its tide, Spewed out of house and stable, beggared of flag and bride. The heavens are bowed about my head, shouting like seraph wars, With rains that might put out the sun and clean the sky of stars, Rains like the fall of ruined seas from secret worlds above, The roaring of the rains of God none but the lonely love. Feast in my hall, O foemen, and eat and drink and drain, You never loved the sun in heaven as I have loved the rain. The chance of battle changes --so may all battle be; I stole my lady bride from them, they stole her back from me. I rent her from her red-roofed hall, I rode and saw arise, More lovely than the living flowers the hatred in her eyes. She never loved me, never bent, never was less divine; The sunset never loved me, the wind was never mine. Was it all nothing that she stood imperial in duresse? Silence itself made softer with the sweeping of her dress. O you who drain the cup of life, O you who wear the crown, You never loved a woman's smile as I have loved her frown. The wind blew out from Bergen to the dawning of the day, They ride and run with fifty spears to break and bar my way, I shall not die alone, alone, but kin to all the powers, As merry as the ancient sun and fighting like the flowers. How white their steel, how bright their eyes! I love each laughing knave, Cry high and bid him welcome to the banquet of the brave. Yea, I will bless them as they bend and love them where they lie, When on their skulls the sword I swing falls shattering from the sky. The hour when death is like a light and blood is like a rose, -- You never loved your friends, my friends, as I shall love my foes. Know you what earth shall lose to-night, what rich uncounted loans, What heavy gold of tales untold you bury with my bones? My loves in deep dim meadows, my ships that rode at ease, Ruffling the purple plumage of strange and secret seas. To see this fair earth as it is to me alone was given, The blow that breaks my brow to-night shall break the dome of heaven. The skies I saw, the trees I saw after no eyes shall see, To-night I die the death of God; the stars shall die with me; One sound shall sunder all the spears and break the trumpet's breath: You never laughed in all your life as I shall laugh in death.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to bake cakes with her mom. One day, they decided to make a special cake for Lily's dad's birthday. They gathered all the ingredients they needed, including flour, sugar, and eggs. Lily's mom asked her to stir the batter until it was smooth.

As they were baking the cake, Lily noticed a wide bowl on the counter. She asked her mom what it was for, but her mom said it was for something special later. Lily was curious, but she didn't ask any more questions.

After the cake was done, they took it out of the oven and let it cool. Then, Lily's mom brought out the wide bowl and poured something on top of the cake. It was a thing called frosting! Lily was so excited that she helped her mom spread it all over the cake. When they were done, they put candles on top and sang "Happy Birthday" to Lily's dad. He loved the cake and said it was the best one he ever had. Lily was proud of herself for helping make such a special thing for her dad.

Once upon a time, there were two friends, Fred and Jane, who liked to play together.

One day, they were both playing together in Fred's bedroom. Jane was jumping on his bed, while Fred was playing with his toy cars.

Suddenly, Fred looked up and said, "What's that nosy noise?". Jane answered, "It's my pillow. It's talking to me!"

Fred laughed, "That's silly. Pillows don't talk!"

But Jane disagreed. "Yes they do! My pillow talks to me all the time."

Fred said, "I don't believe it. Let's hear it then!"

So Jane hugged her pillow and said, "Hello pillow. What do you have to say?"

At first, there was no answer. But then, her pillow said, "Hello Jane. It's nice to meet you!"

Fred was so surprised, he had to believe it was true! From that day on, Fred and Jane's pillow became their best friend.

Once upon a time there was a friendly store. The store sold lots of fun things. One day the store had a surprise - a bouncy ball! The little ball was so excited that it decided to bounce around the store. It bounced up and down the shelves, under the counters and over the toys. It was so much fun! Everyone in the store loved watching the bouncy ball. The store keeper laughed and cheered as the little ball continued to bounce around. Even the customers had a great time watching it. After a while, the ball got tired and decided to rest. Everyone in the store said goodbye and the ball went to sleep. It was a very happy day at the friendly store.

name_of_work: Ode on Solitude by Alexander Pope
content: Happy the man, whose wish and care A few paternal acres bound, Content to breathe his native air, In his own ground. Whose herds with milk, whose fields with bread, Whose flocks supply him with attire, Whose trees in summer yield him shade, In winter fire. Blest, who can unconcernedly find Hours, days, and years slide soft away, In health of body, peace of mind, Quiet by day, Sound sleep by night; study and ease, Together mixed; sweet recreation; And innocence, which most does please, With meditation. Thus let me live, unseen, unknown; Thus unlamented let me die; Steal from the world, and not a stone Tell where I lie.

Once upon a time there was a young girl named Julie. She loved wearing pink, especially her favourite pink dress with a zip in the back. She always felt great in it and it made her smile.

One day Julie wanted to play outside, but her mom wasn't able to support her. Julie was so sad that she started to cry. She put on her pink dress and started walking in the forest on her own.

Julie felt hopeful in her pink dress and it gave her the courage to go further and further into the forest. Suddenly, she noticed that her zip was coming undone. She panicked and started running home, but it was too late. The zip broke, splitting the dress in half and leaving Julie feeling disappointed.

She never wore it again and never felt supported to explore the world on her own.

Anna and Ben were twins who loved to go outside and play. They liked to run, jump, climb and explore. One day, their mom said they could go to the big park with the mountain. Anna and Ben were very enthusiastic. They put on their hats, shoes and backpacks and got in the car.

At the park, they saw the mountain. It was very tall and green. They wanted to climb to the top and see what was there. They asked their mom if they could go. She said yes, but they had to stay together and be careful. Anna and Ben nodded and started to walk up the hill.

As they climbed, they saw many things. They saw flowers, birds, rocks and bugs. They also saw other people who were climbing or biking or having picnics. They said hello to them and kept going. They felt happy and curious.

They reached the top of the mountain and looked around. They saw the park, the city, the sky and the clouds. They also saw something else. It was a big, round, shiny thing. It looked like a ball, but it was not a ball. It was a balloon. It was red and blue and yellow and had a string. It was floating in the air.

"Wow, look at that!" Anna said.

"Where did it come from?" Ben asked.

"Maybe someone let it go by mistake," Anna said.

"Can we have it?" Ben asked.

They both wanted the balloon. They thought it was pretty and fun. They reached for the string, but it was too high. They jumped, but they could not catch it. They felt sad and frustrated.

Then, they had an idea. They could change something. They could use their backpacks. They took off their backpacks and emptied them. They had some snacks, some water, some books and some toys. They put them on the ground. Then, they tied the backpacks together with the straps. They made a long rope. They threw one end of the rope at the balloon. They missed. They tried again. They missed again. They tried one more time. They got it! They pulled the rope and the balloon came down. They caught the balloon. They felt proud and excited.

"Yay, we did it!" Anna said.

"We changed our backpacks into a rope!" Ben said.

They hugged each other and the balloon. They thanked their backpacks and put their things back inside. They decided to share the balloon and take turns holding it. They walked down the mountain with their mom. They felt happy and grateful. They had a great day at the park.
Razors pain you; Rivers are damp; Acids stain you; And drugs cause cramp. Guns aren't lawful; Nooses give; Gas smells awful; You might as well live.

You are beautiful and faded, Like an old opera tune Played upon a harpsichord; Or like the sun-flooded silks Of an eighteenth-century boudoir. In your eyes Smoulder the fallen roses of outlived minutes, And the perfume of your soul Is vague and suffusing, With the pungence of sealed spice-jars. Your half-tones delight me, And I grow mad with gazing At your blent colors. My vigor is a new-minted penny, Which I cast at your feet. Gather it up from the dust That its sparkle may amuse you.

name_of_work: The Word by Ella Wheeler Wilcox
content: Oh, a word is a gem, or a stone, or a song, Or a flame, or a two-edged sword; Or a rose in bloom, or a sweet perfume, Or a drop of gall is a word. You may choose your word like a connoisseur, And polish it up with art, But the word that sways, and stirs, and stays, Is the word that comes from the heart. You may work on your word a thousand weeks, But it will not glow like one That all unsought, leaps forth white hot, When the fountains of feeling run.

In May my heart was breaking- Oh, wide the wound, and deep! And bitter it beat at waking, And sore it split in sleep. And when it came November, I sought my heart, and sighed, "Poor thing, do you remember?" "What heart was that?" it cried.

Smile a little, smile a little, As you go along, Not alone when life is pleasant, But when things go wrong. Care delights to see you frowning, Loves to hear you sigh; Turn a smiling face upon her, Quick the dame will fly. Smile a little, smile a little, All along the road; Every life must have its burden, Every heart its load. Why sit down in gloom and darkness, With your grief to sup? As you drink Fate's bitter tonic Smile across the cup. Smile upon the troubled pilgrims Whom you pass and meet; Frowns are thorns, and smiles are blossoms Oft for weary feet. Do not make the way seem harder By a sullen face, Smile a little, smile a little, Brighten up the place. Smile upon your undone labor; Not for one who grieves O'er his task, waits wealth or glory; He who smiles achieves. Though you meet with loss and sorrow In the passing years, Smile a little, smile a little, Even through your tears.

Gold! Gold! Gold! Gold! Bright and yellow, hard and cold Molten, graven, hammered and rolled, Heavy to get and light to hold, Hoarded, bartered, bought and sold, Stolen, borrowed, squandered, doled, Spurned by young, but hung by old To the verge of a church yard mold; Price of many a crime untold. Gold! Gold! Gold! Gold! Good or bad a thousand fold! How widely it agencies vary, To save - to ruin - to curse - to bless - As even its minted coins express : Now stamped with the image of Queen Bess, And now of a bloody Mary.

name_of_work: How Poetry Comes to Me by Gary Snyder
content: It comes blundering over the Boulders at night, it stays Frightened outside the Range of my campfire I go to meet it at the Edge of the light

Lovely tree, Yesterday wild winds of winter combed your black and twining hair. When dawn blinked You emerged softly capped in ermine, star-kissed with diamonds. Wind's sharp breath caught in his throat and sun, stricken sun, can't turn his eye from you

So much rain, so much life like the swollen sky of this black August. My sister, the sun, broods in her yellow room and won't come out. Everything goes to hell; the mountains fume like a kettle, rivers overrun; still, she will not rise and turn off the rain. She is in her room, fondling old things, my poems, turning her album. Even if thunder falls like a crash of plates from the sky, she does not come out. Don't you know I love you but am hopeless at fixing the rain ? But I am learning slowly to love the dark days, the steaming hills, the air with gossiping mosquitoes, and to sip the medicine of bitterness, so that when you emerge, my sister, parting the beads of the rain, with your forehead of flowers and eyes of forgiveness, all with not be as it was, but it will be true (you see they will not let me love as I want), because, my sister, then I would have learnt to love black days like bright ones, The black rain, the white hills, when once I loved only my happiness and you.

name_of_work: Teach me your mood, O patient stars! by Ralph Waldo Emerson
content: Teach me your mood, O patient stars! Who climb each night the ancient sky, Leaving on space no shade, no scars, No trace of age, no fear to die.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she saw a mysterious rat in her room. She was scared and didn't know what to do. 

She went to her mom and said, "Mommy, help! There's a rat in my room!" 

Her mom came to her room and saw the rat too. She said, "Don't worry, Lily. I'll help you get rid of the rat." 

Together, they caught the rat and took it outside. Lily felt happy and safe again. She hugged her mom and said, "Thank you for helping me, Mommy."

Let not my love be called idolatry, Nor my beloved as an idol show, Since all alike my songs and praises be To one, of one, still such, and ever so. Kind is my love to-day, to-morrow kind, Still constant in a wondrous excellence; Therefore my verse to constancy confined, One thing expressing, leaves out difference. Fair, kind, and true, is all my argument, Fair, kind, and true, varying to other words; And in this change is my invention spent, Three themes in one, which wondrous scope affords. Fair, kind, and true, have often lived alone, Which three till now, never kept seat in one.

Lily and Ben were playing in the living room. They liked to pretend they were animals and make noises. Lily was a cat and Ben was a dog. They ran around the furniture and chased each other.

"Meow, meow, I am a cat!" Lily said.

"Woof, woof, I am a dog!" Ben said.

They had fun, but they also made a lot of noise. Mom was in the kitchen, making dinner. She heard them and came to the living room.

"Kids, please be quiet. I need some peaceful time. Can you play something else?" Mom said.

Lily and Ben looked at each other. They did not want to make Mom angry. They thought of a new game.

"OK, Mom. We will play statues. We will stand very still and not make any noise. You can guess what we are," Lily said.

"That sounds like a good game. Thank you, kids. I will come and see you soon," Mom said.

Lily and Ben nodded. They started to play statues. They stood very still and made funny poses. They tried to look like different things, like a tree, a star, a bird, or a flower. They did not make any noise. They smiled at each other.

Mom finished making dinner. She came to the living room and saw Lily and Ben. They were still playing statues. They looked very cute and funny. Mom smiled too.

"Wow, you are very good at playing statues. You are very quiet and peaceful. I am proud of you, kids. Can I join you?" Mom said.

Lily and Ben nodded again. They were happy that Mom liked their game. They made room for Mom. Mom stood next to them and made a pose too. She looked like a heart. They all laughed.

They played statues for a while. Then they had dinner together. They talked about their game and their day. They were a happy family.

Once upon a time there was a very intelligent pear. It could move around on its own. It especially loved to move around in big circles. One day, it saw something fascinating on the other side of the room. It was a bouncing ball. The pear was so excited, it immediately moved closer to see it. It moved around so quickly that it almost bumped into the wall. But it was able to make a turn just in time and kept moving. It was so fun that it just couldn't stop. The pear kept moving around the room, never getting tired of the bouncing ball. Finally, when it felt like it had gone around the room enough times, the pear stopped and happily moved back to its original spot. It had so much fun that day, it couldn't wait to move around the room again someday soon.

Life is a stream On which we strew Petal by petal the flower of our heart; The end lost in dream, They float past our view, We only watch their glad, early start. Freighted with hope, Crimsoned with joy, We scatter the leaves of our opening rose; Their widening scope, Their distant employ, We never shall know. And the stream as it flows Sweeps them away, Each one is gone Ever beyond into infinite ways. We alone stay While years hurry on, The flower fared forth, though its fragrance still stays.

Once upon a time, there was a very cute pigeon. He had big eyes and pretty feathers. The pigeon loved to explore outside.

One day, the pigeon was out for a walk when he saw something that made him very excited. It was a park full of trees and grass! He hopped around exploring the park.

Soon, the pigeon started to feel sleepy. He did a big yawn, closed his eyes and lay down in the grass. He was so happy that he even started to hum a soft tune.

The pigeon stayed in the park until it was time to go home. Home was a cozy little nest up in a tree. When he arrived, the pigeon waved goodnight to all his friends before turning in for the night.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl. She wanted to win a prize.

So, the girl and her mum went to a special weighing machine. The girl put some coins in the machine and the mum put in some furry objects.

Then, the girl and her mum waited for the machine to weigh their things.

Finally, after what felt like a long wait, the machine made a sound.

The girl and her mum looked up in excitement. Out of the machine, came a big prize!

The girl was so happy and thanked her mum for taking her to the machine.

The prize was so exciting, that the little girl decided to weigh all her favorite things: dolls, stuffed animals and more. After that, she was always sure to have a furry prize!

name_of_work: First Love: A Quiz by A.E. Stallings
content: He came up to me: a. in his souped-up Camaro b. to talk to my skinny best friend c. and bumped my glass of wine so I wore the ferrous stain on my sleeve d. from the ground, in a lead chariot drawn by a team of stallions black as crude oil and breathing sulfur: at his heart, he sported a tiny golden arrow. He offered me: a. a ride b. dinner and a movie, with a wink at the cliche c. an excuse not to go back alone to the apartment with its sink of dirty knives d. a narcissus with a hundred dazzling petals that breathed a sweetness as cloying as decay. I went with him because: a. even his friends told me to beware b. I had nothing to lose except my virginity c. he placed his hand in the small of my back and I felt the tread of honeybees d. he was my uncle, the one who lived in the half-finished basement, and he took me by the hair The place he took me to: a. was dark as my shut eyes b. and where I ate biter seed and became ripe c. and from which my mother would never take me wholly back, though she wept and walked the earth and made the bearded ears of barley wither on their stalks and the blasted flowers drop from their sepals d. is called by some men hell and others love e. all of the above

name_of_work: The Stick-Together Families by Edgar Guest
content: The stick-together families are happier by far Than the brothers and the sisters who take separate highways are. The gladdest people living are the wholesome folks who make A circle at the fireside that no power but death can break. And the finest of conventions ever held beneath the sun Are the little family gatherings when the busy day is done. There are rich folk, there are poor folk, who imagine they are wise, And they're very quick to shatter all the little family ties. Each goes searching after pleasure in his own selected way, Each with strangers likes to wander, and with strangers likes to play. But it's bitterness they harvest, and it's empty joy they find, For the children that are wisest are the stick-together kind. There are some who seem to fancy that for gladness they must roam, That for smiles that are the brightest they must wander far from home. That the strange friend is the true friend, and they travel far astray they waste their lives in striving for a joy that's far away, But the gladdest sort of people, when the busy day is done, Are the brothers and the sisters who together share their fun. It's the stick-together family that wins the joys of earth, That hears the sweetest music and that finds the finest mirth; It's the old home roof that shelters all the charm that life can give; There you find the gladdest play-ground, there the happiest spot to live. And, O weary, wandering brother, if contentment you would win, Come you back unto the fireside and be comrade with your kin.

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play and joke with each other. One day, they have spaghetti for lunch. Lily thinks spaghetti is interesting. She likes to make funny shapes with it on her plate.

"Look, Ben, I made a snake!" Lily says, holding up a long strand of spaghetti.

"That's not a snake, that's a worm!" Ben jokes, poking it with his fork.

Lily laughs. She thinks Ben is funny. She makes another shape with her spaghetti.

"Look, Ben, I made a hat!" Lily says, putting a loop of spaghetti on her head.

"That's not a hat, that's a ring!" Ben jokes, pulling it off her head.

Lily giggles. She likes to joke with Ben. She makes one more shape with her spaghetti.

"Look, Ben, I made a heart!" Lily says, twisting two strands of spaghetti together.

"That's not a heart, that's a..." Ben starts to joke, but then he stops. He looks at Lily and smiles. He thinks Lily is nice. He takes the spaghetti heart and puts it on his plate.

"That's a heart, Lily. And you are my friend." Ben says, softly.

Lily smiles back. She thinks Ben is sweet. She takes his hand and squeezes it.

"You are my friend, too, Ben. And this is the best spaghetti ever." Lily says, happily.

I am come into my garden, my sister, my spouse: I have gathered my myrrh with my spice; I have eaten my honeycomb with my honey; I have drunk my wine with my milk: eat, O friends; drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved. I sleep, but my heart waketh: it is the voice of my beloved that knocketh, saying, Open to me, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled: for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of the night. I have put off my coat; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? My beloved put in his hand by the hole of the door, and my bowels were moved for him. I rose up to open to my beloved; and my hands dropped with myrrh, and my fingers with sweet smelling myrrh, upon the handles of the lock. I opened to my beloved; but my beloved had withdrawn himself, and was gone: my soul failed when he spake: I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer. The watchmen that went about the city found me, they smote me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took away my veil from me. I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love. What is thy beloved more than another beloved, O thou fairest among women? what is thy beloved more than another beloved, that thou dost so charge us? My beloved is white and ruddy, the chiefest among ten thousand. His head is as the most fine gold, his locks are bushy, and black as a raven. His eyes are as the eyes of doves by the rivers of waters, washed with milk, and fitly set. His cheeks are as a bed of spices, as sweet flowers: his lips like lilies, dropping sweet smelling myrrh. His hands are as gold rings set with the beryl: his belly is as bright ivory overlaid with sapphires. His legs are as pillars of marble, set upon sockets of fine gold: his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars. His mouth is most sweet: yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.

name_of_work: Telling the Bees by Lizette Woodworth Reese
content: A Colonial Custom Bathsheba came out to the sun, Out to our walled cherry-trees; The tears adown her cheek did run, Bathsheba standing in the sun, Telling the bees. My mother had that moment died; Unknowing, sped I to the trees, And plucked Bathsheba's hand aside; Then caught the name that there she cried Telling the bees. Her look I never can forget, I that held sobbing to her knees; The cherry-boughs above us met; I think I see Bathsheba yet Telling the bees.

I'm your guide here. In the evening-dark morning streets, I point and name. Look, the sycamores, their mottled, paint-by-number bark. Look, the leaves rusting and crisping at the edges. I walk through Schiller Park with you on my chest. Stars smolder well into daylight. Look, the pond, the ducks, the dogs paddling after their prized sticks. Fall is when the only things you know because I've named them begin to end. Soon I'll have another season to offer you: frost soft on the window and a porthole sighed there, ice sleeving the bare gray branches. The first time you see something die, you won't know it might come back. I'm desperate for you to love the world because I brought you here.

1. The Cane Fields There is a parrot imitating spring in the palace, its feathers parsley green. Out of the swamp the cane appears to haunt us, and we cut it down. El General searches for a word; he is all the world there is. Like a parrot imitating spring, we lie down screaming as rain punches through and we come up green. We cannot speak an R-- out of the swamp, the cane appears and then the mountain we call in whispers Katalina. The children gnaw their teeth to arrowheads. There is a parrot imitating spring. El General has found his word: perejil. Who says it, lives. He laughs, teeth shining out of the swamp. The cane appears in our dreams, lashed by wind and streaming. And we lie down. For every drop of blood there is a parrot imitating spring. Out of the swamp the cane appears. 2. The Palace The word the general's chosen is parsley. It is fall, when thoughts turn to love and death; the general thinks of his mother, how she died in the fall and he planted her walking cane at the grave and it flowered, each spring stolidly forming four-star blossoms. The general pulls on his boots, he stomps to her room in the palace, the one without curtains, the one with a parrot in a brass ring. As he paces he wonders Who can I kill today. And for a moment the little knot of screams is still. The parrot, who has traveled all the way from Australia in an ivory cage, is, coy as a widow, practising spring. Ever since the morning his mother collapsed in the kitchen while baking skull-shaped candies for the Day of the Dead, the general has hated sweets. He orders pastries brought up for the bird; they arrive dusted with sugar on a bed of lace. The knot in his throat starts to twitch; he sees his boots the first day in battle splashed with mud and urine as a soldier falls at his feet amazed-- how stupid he looked!-- at the sound of artillery. I never thought it would sing the soldier said, and died. Now the general sees the fields of sugar cane, lashed by rain and streaming. He sees his mother's smile, the teeth gnawed to arrowheads. He hears the Haitians sing without R's as they swing the great machetes: Katalina, they sing, Katalina, mi madle, mi amol en muelte. God knows his mother was no stupid woman; she could roll an R like a queen. Even a parrot can roll an R! In the bare room the bright feathers arch in a parody of greenery, as the last pale crumbs disappear under the blackened tongue. Someone calls out his name in a voice so like his mother's, a startled tear splashes the tip of his right boot. My mother, my love in death. The general remembers the tiny green sprigs men of his village wore in their capes to honor the birth of a son. He will order many, this time, to be killed for a single, beautiful word.

Nina was a curious 3 year old. She watched her mom step off the bus and walked over to the post office. Nina followed her. Her mom smiled and said, "Let's see if we have any letters today." Inside the post office, the lady at the counter smiled and handed her mom an envelope. She said her mom had a reliable letter. Nina wanted to see the letter too. 

Her mom said, "I'm sorry sweetheart, this letter is for me." She gave Nina a hug and stepped outside the post office. Even though Nina couldn't see the letter, she was happy that her mom had a reliable one. Together, they stepped back on the bus and went home. 

From then on, any time Nina and her mom went to the post office, Nina hoped for a reliable letter. Sometimes they had one, other times they didn't. But each time, Nina learned to be patient and reliable like the letters they sometimes got.

Once upon a time, there was a cute little girl named Grace. Grace lived in a cozy cottage in the forest. She loved going for walks in the fresh air. One day, Grace decided to go for a longer walk than usual.

As she walked, the sky suddenly got very dark, and the wind started to blow. The air was cold, and Grace began to shiver. She didn't have a hat, so she wrapped her arms around her head to keep warm.

Suddenly, grace heard a noise nearby. She looked around, and saw a graceful swan swimming in the lake next to her. Grace's heart filled with joy as he watched the swan. The swan then flew over to Grace, and gave her a big, warm hat that it had been wearing. Grace put the beautiful hat on, and she stopped shivering right away.

Grace thanked the graceful swan, and it flew away. Grace continued on her walk, wearing the warm hat, and feeling cozy and happy.

Once upon a time, there was a wise old owl. He lived in a big tree in the forest. The owl loved to blink his big eyes and watch the little animals play.

One day, he saw a small bunny hopping near the tree. The bunny had a shiny buckle on his collar. The wise owl blinked and looked closer. He saw that the buckle was stuck on a branch.

The owl wanted to help the bunny. He blinked his eyes, flew down from the tree, and used his beak to free the buckle. The bunny was very happy and thanked the wise owl.

From that day on, the wise owl and the bunny became good friends. They played together in the forest, and the owl always blinked his eyes to watch over his little friend.
Things that go 'bump' in the night Should not really give one a fright. It's the hole in each ear That lets in the fear, That, and the absence of light!

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy had a blue jacket that he loved to wear. One day, Timmy and his friend Billy were playing outside when it started to rain. 

Billy said, "Timmy, let's go inside before we get wet." 

But Timmy didn't want to go inside. He said, "I don't want to leave my jacket out here in the rain." 

Billy said, "Don't worry, Timmy. We can pause our game and come back to it later." 

Timmy thought about it and decided that was a good idea. They went inside and took off their wet jackets. 

Timmy's mom asked him, "Why did you come inside so early?" 

Timmy said, "We paused our game because we didn't want our jackets to get wet." 

His mom smiled and said, "That was an honest decision, Timmy. Good job."

Once upon a time, in a small garden, there was a magic herb. This herb would only appear when the sun was shining bright. It was a very slow-growing plant, but all the animals loved it.

One day, a little rabbit named Remy came to the garden. He saw the magic herb and wanted to take a bite. The herb was so slow to grow that Remy had to wait for a long time. He sat down and watched the herb grow, little by little.

Finally, the magic herb was big enough for Remy to eat. He took a small bite and something amazing happened. Remy could now hop faster than any other rabbit in the forest! He was so happy and thanked the magic herb. From that day on, Remy was the fastest rabbit and always remembered the slow-growing magic herb that helped him.

name_of_work: On the Sale By Auction of Keats' Love Letters by Oscar Wilde
content: These are the letters which Endymion wrote To one he loved in secret, and apart. And now the brawlers of the auction mart Bargain and bid for each poor blotted note, Ay! for each separate pulse of passion quote The merchant's price. I think they love not art Who break the crystal of a poet's heart That small and sickly eyes may glare and gloat. Is it not said that many years ago, In a far Eastern town, some soldiers ran With torches through the midnight, and began To wrangel for mean raiment, and to throw Dice for the garments of a wretched man, Not knowing the God's wonder, or His woe?

name_of_work: A Martian Sends a Postcard Home by Craig Raine
content: Caxtons are mechanical birds with many wings and some are treasured for their markings - they cause the eyes to melt or the body to shriek without pain. I have never seen one fly, but sometimes they perch on the hand. Mist is when the sky is tired of flight and rests its soft machine on ground: then the world is dim and bookish like engravings under tissue paper. Rain is when the earth is television. It has the property of making colours darker. Model T is a room with the lock inside - a key is turned to free the world for movement, so quick there is a film to watch for anything missed. But time is tied to the wrist or kept in a box, ticking with impatience. In homes, a haunted apparatus sleeps, that snores when you pick it up. If the ghost cries, they carry it to their lips and soothe it to sleep with sounds. And yet, they wake it up deliberately, by tickling with a finger. Only the young are allowed to suffer openly. Adults go to a punishment room with water but nothing to eat. They lock the door and suffer the noises alone. No one is exempt and everyone's pain has a different smell. At night, when all the colours die, they hide in pairs and read about themselves - in colour, with their eyelids shut.

name_of_work: Love's Philosophy by Percy Bysshe Shelley
content: The fountains mingle with the river And the rivers with the ocean, The winds of heaven mix for ever With a sweet emotion; Nothing in the world is single; All things by a law divine In one spirit meet and mingle. Why not I with thine?-- See the mountains kiss high heaven And the waves clasp one another; No sister-flower would be forgiven If it disdained its brother; And the sunlight clasps the earth And the moonbeams kiss the sea: What is all this sweet work worth If thou kiss not me?

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Maria. She was very excited because she was going on her first adventure. 

Maria looked around and saw a big brown tree. She wanted to climb it, but it was too high and so she asked her friend James to help. 

James said, "I can help you Maria. I will give you a boost!" So he lifted Maria to the top of the tree and said, "Do you see anything up there?" 

And Maria saw a big brown box. She said, "What is that?" 

James replied, "I don't know, but I think it's something special. We can try and solve it" 

So Maria and James opened the box and inside there was a toy nurse. Maria was so excited and she shouted with joy. She ran over to her mum and showed her the toy nurse. 

And that's how Maria solved the mystery of the brown box!

Collecting refracted light, we probe the far beyond Telescopes peer the infinite distances beyond our orb Polishing reflective mirrors, focusing faceted prisms Apprehension and excitement, mysteries revealed in time Knowledge is the first step on the path of enlightenment Gathering the light, we must gaze into our speckled past Distance spans epochs of space and time in reverse Triumphant success and tragic error, beauty with pain The further we look, the marching eons merely reveal History only, unable to unveil what our future holds Focusing the light, we are invited to look deep within Microscopes expose clearly what our cloudy eyes obscure Atoms, electrons, photons, bosons, and particle beams Invisible with naked eye, following hidden rules and laws Our quest for the elusive unified theory of everything Magnifying the light, we behold our humble place Sapient ancestors bravely struck matches in the dark Seek the sage voices in humanity's hallowed halls Take up the torch, carrying the flame boldly forward Stepping stones illumine, follow only those spiraling up Discerning the light, we are making essential choices Refracting both aspects, single particles and flowing waves Ignorance falls away as dark matter slips from sight Super massive black holes, spectral light cannot escape The event horizon always brims with blinding brilliance Inviting the light, we endeavor to reflect radiant virtues All things wise have already been written and recorded Summoning sacred scrolls, striving to make them our own Truth, compassion, forgiveness, redemption, and service Forever the enlightened path, the eternal echo from the void

Once there was a girl called Jessie. She was 3 years old.

Every day she helped her mum with the laundry. She loved to take the clothes out of the washing machine and put them in the basket.

One day when she was taking out the laundry, something strange happened. The red shirt had changed! It was green! She was so surprised and shouted to her mum.

Her mum came and saw the shirt. She wasn't mad. She just smiled and said that sometimes clothes change in the washing machine.

The next day Jessie put the same shirt in the machine again, but this time it stayed red. Jessie was happy that the original colour had come back.

She enjoyed doing laundry with her mum every day.

Once upon a time, there was a big forest. In the forest, there lived many animals. There were deer, rabbits, and squirrels. They all played together and had fun.

One day, a group of humans came to the forest. They brought with them big machines that made a lot of noise. The animals were scared and didn't know what to do. The humans started cutting down the trees with their machines. The animals tried to stop them, but they couldn't.

The humans didn't allow the animals to stay in the forest anymore. They took away their homes and food. The animals had to leave the forest and find a new place to live. They were sad and scared. The forest was no longer lively and full of joy. It was now just a pile of lumber.

THERE'S no use in weeping, Though we are condemned to part: There's such a thing as keeping A remembrance in one's heart: There's such a thing as dwelling On the thought ourselves have nurs'd, And with scorn and courage telling The world to do its worst. We'll not let its follies grieve us, We'll just take them as they come; And then every day will leave us A merry laugh for home. When we've left each friend and brother, When we're parted wide and far, We will think of one another, As even better than we are. Every glorious sight above us, Every pleasant sight beneath, We'll connect with those that love us, Whom we truly love till death ! In the evening, when we're sitting By the fire perchance alone, Then shall heart with warm heart meeting, Give responsive tone for tone. We can burst the bonds which chain us, Which cold human hands have wrought, And where none shall dare restrain us We can meet again, in thought. So there's no use in weeping, Bear a cheerful spirit still; Never doubt that Fate is keeping Future good for present ill !

name_of_work: To an Athlete Dying Young by A. E. Housman
content: The time you won your town the race We chaired you through the market-place; Man and boy stood cheering by, And home we brought you shoulder-high. Today, the road all runners come, Shoulder-high we bring you home, And set you at your threshold down, Townsman of a stiller town. Smart lad, to slip betimes away From fields where glory does not stay, And early though the laurel grows It withers quicker than the rose. Eyes the shady night has shut Cannot see the record cut, And silence sounds no worse than cheers After earth has stopped the ears. Now you will not swell the rout Of lads that wore their honours out, Runners whom renown outran And the name died before the man. So set, before its echoes fade, The fleet foot on the sill of shade, And hold to the low lintel up The still-defended challenge-cup. And round that early-laurelled head Will flock to gaze the strengthless dead, And find unwithered on its curls The garland briefer than a girl's.

Once upon a time there was a lively astronaut. He wanted to go to space and explore. One day, he went to the spaceship and shot off into space. In space, he found many new and exciting things. He saw stars, comets and planets. He also saw creatures and aliens, colourful and joyful to look at. He shot around space, visiting different places and having lots of fun. Finally, after visiting many wonderful places, the astronaut flew back to Earth. He shared his adventures with everyone and was very happy. The End.

Once upon a time, there was a little birdie. The birdie was restless and wanted to fly high in the sky. It flapped its wings and flew up, up, up. Suddenly, it saw an arrow fall from the sky. The arrow fell down, down, down and landed on the ground with a thud. The little birdie was scared and flew away to rest on a tree branch. From then on, whenever the birdie felt restless, it remembered the arrow that fell and stayed safe on the branch.

Once upon a time, there was a boat. It was a very special boat, because it was flexible. That meant that the boat could stretch in different shapes and sizes. 

One day, the boat went to the beach. It had so much fun in the sand and the water. Then, it decided to go a little bit further and stretch out. It stretched and stretched until it got to the other side of the beach. 

On the other side, the boat saw a dock with lots and lots of boats. All these boats had different colors, sizes, and shapes. But the flexible boat knew it was different, because it could stretch much further than all the other boats. 

The boat then decided to stretch out even further and eventually it went out to sea. It stretched and stretched until it could not see the land. It was having the best time exploring the big ocean. 

Suddenly, the flexible boat had to come back to the beach because it was time to go home. It quickly stretched back to the beach and thanked all the other boats for being its friends. Then it went home, content and happy.

What is it to grow old? Is it to lose the glory of the form, The luster of the eye? Is it for beauty to forego her wreath? --Yes, but not this alone. Is it to feel our strength-- Not our bloom only, but our strength--decay? Is it to feel each limb Grow stiffer, every function less exact, Each nerve more loosely strung? Yes, this, and more; but not Ah, 'tis not what in youth we dreamed 'twould be! 'Tis not to have our life Mellowed and softened as with sunset glow, A golden day's decline. 'Tis not to see the world As from a height, with rapt prophetic eyes, And heart profoundly stirred; And weep, and feel the fullness of the past, The years that are no more. It is to spend long days And not once feel that we were ever young; It is to add, immured In the hot prison of the present, month To month with weary pain. It is to suffer this, And feel but half, and feebly, what we feel. Deep in our hidden heart Festers the dull remembrance of a change, But no emotion--none. It is--last stage of all-- When we are frozen up within, and quite The phantom of ourselves, To hear the world applaud the hollow ghost Which blamed the living man.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to eat yogurt, especially the fancy kind with sprinkles on top. One day, Lily was walking in the park when she saw a tiny bird with a broken wing. The bird was sad and scared, so Lily decided to protect it.

Lily picked up the bird and brought it home. She gave the bird some water and some of her fancy yogurt with sprinkles. The bird was very happy and ate all the yogurt. Lily was happy too because she had made a new friend.

Lily took care of the bird every day. She protected it from the rain and the wind. She gave it more fancy yogurt with sprinkles. And after a few weeks, the bird's wing was all better. The bird was so happy that it flew away, but Lily knew that she had protected it and made it strong again.

Through every nook and every cranny The wind blew in on poor old Granny Around her knees, into each ear (And up her nose as well, I fear) All through the night the wind grew worse It nearly made the vicar curse The top had fallen off the steeple Just missing him (and other people) It blew on man, it blew on beast It blew on nun, it blew on priest It blew the wig off Auntie Fanny- But most of all, it blew on Granny!

Once upon a time, there was a slow butterfly. Everywhere it flew, it made everyone feel excited. One day, the butterfly was fluttering around in a meadow, looking for something to nibble on. Suddenly, it spotted a yummy bowl of butter. Without a care in the world, it slowly flew down, landed on the butter and started to eat it. As the butterfly savored the butter, it felt a wonderful feeling of excitement. Later, when the butterfly had finished eating the butter, it slowly flapped its wings and flew away, full of excitement.  The end.

Once upon a time, there were two friends called John and Jane. They were walking through a park when they came across a little lonesome bow. It looked like it was kinda sad and they felt sorry for it.

John said to Jane, "Let's take the lonesome bow home and give it some company". 

Jane smiled and said, "Yes, let's do it!"

So they took the bow and gave it a big warm hug and carried it home. They put the bow in their room and opened the menu of snacks. Jane said, "Oh, look! Let's get the bow something delicious to eat!". 

John smiled and said, "Yes, let's do it!"

So John and Jane filled the bow's bowl with all kinds of delicious treats. The bow was so happy and had so much fun with its new friends.

John and Jane also had a lot of fun with their new lonesome bow!

Billy was outside in the park with his mom. He was watching the birds and playing in the sand when he spotted something in the tall grass. He couldn't recognize what it was. Billy's mom took him over to take a closer look and they saw a small bird with a white eye. The bird was hopping around and looked very restless. Billy was amazed by the bird and smiled at the little creature. Mom told him the bird was a sparrow and it was looking for its family. She told him that the white eye was a special mark so the bird's family could recognize it. Billy liked that idea and started to look around for the bird's family. After a few minutes, the bird hopped up on Billy's leg and sat there quietly. Billy gave the bird a gentle pat and they watched as a mom and dad sparrow flew down to recognize the little bird. All of a sudden the bird hopped off Billy's leg and flew up to the mom and dad sparrow. The family all flew away to their nest. Billy smiled and waved goodbye to the family. He was happy he and his mom were able to help the little bird find his family.

Once upon a time there was a sunflower who lived in a meadow. The sunflower was very sad because all of the other flowers laughed at her. The sunflower was much bigger than the rest of the flowers, so it was very difficult for her to play.

One day, the sunflower was very surprised when a little ladybug came to visit her. The ladybug said, "I want you to help me with something! I need you to weigh something for me." The sunflower didn't know how to weigh things, but the ladybug was very nice and showed her how to do it.

When the sunflower finished weighing, the ladybug said, "Thank you for your help! You're a good sunflower." That made the sunflower feel much better.

The other flowers saw this and stopped laughing at the sunflower. They even started helping her weigh things and do other bad things.

The sunflower learned something very important that day - it doesn't matter what size you are, because kindness can make even the bad things better.

name_of_work: There May Be Chaos Still Around The World by George Santayana
content: There may be chaos still around the world, This little world that in my thinking lies; For mine own bosom is the paradise Where all my life's fair visions are unfurled. Within my nature's shell I slumber curled, Unmindful of the changing outer skies, Where now, perchance, some new-born Eros flies, Or some old Cronos from his throne is hurled. I heed them not; or if the subtle night Haunt me with deities I never saw, I soon mine eyelid's drowsy curtain draw To hide their myriad faces from my sight. They threat in vain; the whirlwind cannot awe A happy snow-flake dancing in the flaw.

One day, Emily was walking in the park. She stopped to watch some birds eating in a tree.
Suddenly, a bright, shiny bracelet fell from the tree. Emily picked it up, but then she heard a big call. It came from high up in the tree.

"Help! I'm stuck up here. Can someone help me?" Emily looked up and saw a baby bird with fluffy feathers. It must have dropped the bracelet.

Emily found a ladder and propped it up against the tree. She carefully climbed up the ladder to help the bird.

"Thank you," said the bird. "Can you please feed me?" Emily smiled and gave the bird some food she had in her pocket. After the bird had eaten, Emily carefully carried it down the ladder and released it.

The bird flew away and waved goodbye with its wing. As a thank you, it left Emily the bracelet. Emily smiled and couldn't believe how lucky she was. She put the bracelet on and admired the glimmering jewels in the sun.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Raya. Raya was gifted. She was brave and strong and could always manage to do things other children could not. 

One day Raya wanted to go into the forest. She asked for permission from her parents and they said she could. So Raya set off into the woods. 

As she walked, Raya noticed something shiny in the bushes. She moved closer to see what it was and saw a little rub. At first Raya was scared of the rub, but then realized it was friendly. 

So Raya managed to overcome her fear and pet the rub gently. The rub was very gentle and nuzzled against Raya. They became fast friends and the rub followed her the rest of her journey through the woods. 

When it was time to leave the woods, Raya said goodbye to her new friend and went home with a smile. She would never forget how she managed to overcome her fear and make a new friend.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in her backyard. One day, she found a small bird with a broken wing. She felt sad for the bird and wanted to help it.

Lily had an idea. She decided to make a little bed for the bird out of some soft grass. She carefully picked up the bird and held it gently in her hands. The bird looked up at her with its big, round eyes.

Lily knew the bird needed some help, so she took it inside to her mommy. Her mommy helped her take care of the bird and nurse it back to health. After a few days, the bird was ready to fly again. Lily was so happy that she could help the bird and make it feel better. From that day on, she always kept an eye out for animals in need of help.

Once upon a time, there was a person walking in a field. Suddenly, the person saw something that made him stop in his tracks. He looked closely and recognized that it was a little animal.

The person moved closer and saw that the animal was a small puppy. It was lying on the ground, frightened and alone. The person quickly picked up the puppy and made sure it was safe.

The person asked the puppy "What is your name?" The puppy did not answer but the person thought he heard the sound of a cry.

The person took the puppy home and named it Rocky. Rocky quickly felt safe and happy in his new home. He began to show the person that he was thankful. Every day he licked his hand to say thank you.

The person quickly recognized that Rocky had become part of their family. He was so glad that he brought the scared puppy home and made him feel safe.

name_of_work: Lady Weeping at the Crossroads by W.H. Auden
content: Lady, weeping at the crossroads, Would you meet your love In the twilight with his greyhounds, And the hawk on his glove? Bribe the birds then on the branches, Bribe them to be dumb, Stare the hot sun out of heaven That the night may come. Starless are the nights of travel, Bleak the winter wind; Run with terror all before you And regret behind. Run until you hear the ocean's Everlasting cry; Deep though it may be and bitter You must drink it dry, Wear out patience in the lowest Dungeons of the sea, Searching through the stranded shipwrecks For the golden key, Push on to the world's end, pay the Dread guard with a kiss, Cross the rotten bridge that totters Over the abyss. There stands the deserted castle Ready to explore; Enter, climb the marble staircase, Open the locked door. Cross the silent ballroom, Doubt and danger past; Blow the cobwebs from the mirror See yourself at last. Put your hand behind the wainscot, You have done your part; Find the penknife there and plunge it Into your false heart.

I know two women, and one is chaste And cold as the snows on a winter waste. Stainless ever in act and thought (As a man, born dumb, in speech errs not.) But she has malice toward her kind, A cruel tongue and a jealous mind. Void of pity and full of greed, She judges the world by her narrow creed: A brewer of quarrels, a breeder of hate, Yet she holds the key to "Society's" Gate. The other woman, with heart of flame, Went mad for a love that marred her name: And out of the grave of her murdered faith She rose like a soul that has passed through death. Her aims are noble, her pity so broad, It covers the world like the mercy of God. A soother of discord, a healer of woes, Peace follows her footsteps wherever she goes The worthier life of the two no doubt, And yet "Society" locks her out.

name_of_work: The Falling Leaves by Margaret Postgate Cole
content: Today, as I rode by, I saw the brown leaves dropping from their tree In a still afternoon, When no wind whirled them whistling to the sky, But thickly, silently, They fell, like snowflakes wiping out the noon; And wandered slowly thence For thinking of a gallant multitude Which now all withering lay, Slain by no wind of age or pestilence, But in their beauty strewed Like snowflakes falling on the Flemish clay.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim loved to play with his toy hammer. He would bang it on everything he could find. One day, Tim saw his friend Billy with a new toy hammer. Tim felt envious and wanted one too.

Tim's mom saw how sad he was and decided to take him to the toy store. They found a toy hammer that Tim liked and bought it. Tim was so happy that he started to wave his new toy hammer in the air.

From that day on, Tim and Billy played together with their toy hammers. They would wave them in the air and pretend to build things. Tim was no longer envious of Billy's toy hammer because he had his own.

One day, Johnny walked outside to play. It was a beautiful day, the sun was shining and the birds in the trees were singing. 

Johnny spotted a rabbit in the grass and he started to walk closer. As soon as he was close enough, the rabbit stood up and looked at him. Johnny smiled, and the rabbit smiled back. 

Johnny continued to walk around the yard, looking at the birds and other animals. He noticed his dog sleeping under a tree, and he started to walk over to her. As soon as Johnny came close, his dog's ears perked up and she looked at him with alert eyes. Johnny smiled, and his dog wagged her tail. 

Johnny decided to walk back home. He was happy to have enjoyed such a nice day outside with all of his animal friends.

Once there was a girl named Tina. Tina was a very creative girl and she loved to use her fingers to make things. One day, Tina wanted to draw a picture, but she couldn't find her crayons.

Tina asked her mom if she could lend her some crayons. So, Tina's mom gave Tina some of her crayons. She showed Tina how to hold the crayons in her fingers to color the page.

name_of_work: Lines Composed a Few Miles above Tintern Abbey by William Wordsworth
content: Five years have past; five summers, with the length Of five long winters! and again I hear These waters, rolling from their mountain-springs With a soft inland murmur.--Once again Do I behold these steep and lofty cliffs, That on a wild secluded scene impress Thoughts of more deep seclusion; and connect The landscape with the quiet of the sky. The day is come when I again repose Here, under this dark sycamore, and view These plots of cottage-ground, these orchard-tufts, Which at this season, with their unripe fruits, Are clad in one green hue, and lose themselves 'Mid groves and copses. Once again I see These hedge-rows, hardly hedge-rows, little lines Of sportive wood run wild: these pastoral farms, Green to the very door; and wreaths of smoke Sent up, in silence, from among the trees! With some uncertain notice, as might seem Of vagrant dwellers in the houseless woods, Or of some Hermit's cave, where by his fire The Hermit sits alone. These beauteous forms, Through a long absence, have not been to me As is a landscape to a blind man's eye: But oft, in lonely rooms, and 'mid the din Of towns and cities, I have owed to them, In hours of weariness, sensations sweet, Felt in the blood, and felt along the heart; And passing even into my purer mind With tranquil restoration:--feelings too Of unremembered pleasure: such, perhaps, As have no slight or trivial influence On that best portion of a good man's life, His little, nameless, unremembered, acts Of kindness and of love. Nor less, I trust, To them I may have owed another gift, Of aspect more sublime; that blessed mood, In which the burthen of the mystery, In which the heavy and the weary weight Of all this unintelligible world, Is lightened:--that serene and blessed mood, In which the affections gently lead us on,-- Until, the breath of this corporeal frame And even the motion of our human blood Almost suspended, we are laid asleep In body, and become a living soul: While with an eye made quiet by the power Of harmony, and the deep power of joy, We see into the life of things. If this Be but a vain belief, yet, oh! how oft-- In darkness and amid the many shapes Of joyless daylight; when the fretful stir Unprofitable, and the fever of the world, Have hung upon the beatings of my heart-- How oft, in spirit, have I turned to thee, O sylvan Wye! thou wanderer thro' the woods, How often has my spirit turned to thee! And now, with gleams of half-extinguished thought, With many recognitions dim and faint, And somewhat of a sad perplexity, The picture of the mind revives again: While here I stand, not only with the sense Of present pleasure, but with pleasing thoughts That in this moment there is life and food For future years. And so I dare to hope, Though changed, no doubt, from what I was when first I came among these hills; when like a roe I bounded o'er the mountains, by the sides Of the deep rivers, and the lonely streams, Wherever nature led: more like a man Flying from something that he dreads, than one Who sought the thing he loved. For nature then (The coarser pleasures of my boyish days And their glad animal movements all gone by) To me was all in all.--I cannot paint What then I was. The sounding cataract Haunted me like a passion: the tall rock, The mountain, and the deep and gloomy wood, Their colours and their forms, were then to me An appetite; a feeling and a love, That had no need of a remoter charm, By thought supplied, nor any interest Unborrowed from the eye.--That time is past, And all its aching joys are now no more, And all its dizzy raptures. Not for this Faint I, nor mourn nor murmur; other gifts Have followed; for such loss, I would believe, Abundant recompense. For I have learned To look on nature, not as in the hour Of thoughtless youth; but hearing oftentimes The still sad music of humanity, Nor harsh nor grating, though of ample power To chasten and subdue.--And I have felt A presence that disturbs me with the joy Of elevated thoughts; a sense sublime Of something far more deeply interfused, Whose dwelling is the light of setting suns, And the round ocean and the living air, And the blue sky, and in the mind of man: A motion and a spirit, that impels All thinking things, all objects of all thought, And rolls through all things. Therefore am I still A lover of the meadows and the woods And mountains; and of all that we behold From this green earth; of all the mighty world Of eye, and ear,--both what they half create, And what perceive; well pleased to recognise In nature and the language of the sense The anchor of my purest thoughts, the nurse, The guide, the guardian of my heart, and soul Of all my moral being. Nor perchance, If I were not thus taught, should I the more Suffer my genial spirits to decay: For thou art with me here upon the banks Of this fair river; thou my dearest Friend, My dear, dear Friend; and in thy voice I catch The language of my former heart, and read My former pleasures in the shooting lights Of thy wild eyes. Oh! yet a little while May I behold in thee what I was once, My dear, dear Sister! and this prayer I make, Knowing that Nature never did betray The heart that loved her; 'tis her privilege, Through all the years of this our life, to lead From joy to joy: for she can so inform The mind that is within us, so impress With quietness and beauty, and so feed With lofty thoughts, that neither evil tongues, Rash judgments, nor the sneers of selfish men, Nor greetings where no kindness is, nor all The dreary intercourse of daily life, Shall e'er prevail against us, or disturb Our cheerful faith, that all which we behold Is full of blessings. Therefore let the moon Shine on thee in thy solitary walk; And let the misty mountain-winds be free To blow against thee: and, in after years, When these wild ecstasies shall be matured Into a sober pleasure; when thy mind Shall be a mansion for all lovely forms, Thy memory be as a dwelling-place For all sweet sounds and harmonies; oh! then, If solitude, or fear, or pain, or grief, Should be thy portion, with what healing thoughts Of tender joy wilt thou remember me, And these my exhortations! Nor, perchance-- If I should be where I no more can hear Thy voice, nor catch from thy wild eyes these gleams Of past existence--wilt thou then forget That on the banks of this delightful stream We stood together; and that I, so long A worshipper of Nature, hither came Unwearied in that service: rather say With warmer love--oh! with far deeper zeal Of holier love. Nor wilt thou then forget, That after many wanderings, many years Of absence, these steep woods and lofty cliffs, And this green pastoral landscape, were to me More dear, both for themselves and for thy sake!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to drink juice from a jug. Every day, she would pour herself a glass of juice from the jug and enjoy it very much. One day, her mom had to go to the store and Lily became anxious because she thought there would be no more juice left in the jug.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in nature. One day, she found a pretty flower and picked it. But then she saw a bee frown at her. 

Lily said, "Oh no, Mr. Bee, I'm sorry. I didn't mean to take your flower." 

The bee said, "It's okay, Lily. But remember to be humble and ask nature before taking things." 

Lily felt bad and put the flower back where she found it. From then on, she always asked nature before taking anything. And the bee smiled at her every time she did.

Once there was an ugly pillow. He was all by himself, so he was very sad. Every day he said to himself, "I wish someone would come and wash me." 
Then one day, a little girl named Daisy heard him say this, and she stopped and said, "I will wash you!" She brought him to the sink and started rubbing him with soapy bubbles. She was very gentle and it felt so nice. 

When she finished washing the pillow, he looked so much cleaner, brighter, shinier. He felt so happy! Daisy brought him back to his spot and hugged him tight. 
 
From that day forward, Daisy always made sure to wash the pillow twice a week. She liked having a clean and happy pillow around. He never felt so lucky!

Leo was having a great time playing in the park. He loved to explore and was having a blast running from one end to the other.

Suddenly, he noticed something off to the side. It was a big stack of boxes, covered in filthy paint. He ran over to investigate.

As he got closer, Leo noticed that the paint was chipping off the boxes. "Ew!" he exclaimed. He used his hands to start picking off the paint, but it was too tough. 

At that moment, Leo heard a strange voice. "What do you think you're doing?" 

Leo looked up and saw an old man. He must have been the owner of the boxes. 

"I'm sorry," Leo said. "I was just trying to clean up this paint." 

The old man laughed. "That's a tough job, little one. Why don't you just quit? It's not worth the trouble." 

Leo stopped trying to pick off the paint and instead ran away laughing. He knew the old man was right.

name_of_work: An Acrostic by Edgar Allan Poe
content: Elizabeth it is in vain you say "Love not" -- thou sayest it in so sweet a way: In vain those words from thee or L.E.L. Zantippe's talents had enforced so well: Ah! if that language from thy heart arise, Breath it less gently forth -- and veil thine eyes. Endymion, recollect, when Luna tried To cure his love -- was cured of all beside -- His follie -- pride -- and passion -- for he died.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Joe who loved to catch things. He caught butterflies, frogs, and even fireflies! One day, Joe saw a jet flying in the sky. He wanted to catch it, so he started running and jumping to try and reach it. But the jet was too high up, and Joe just couldn't catch it.

Joe was getting frustrated. A stupid idea popped into his head. He ran to get a big net from his house. He knew it was a silly idea, but he thought he could use the net to catch the jet. He rushed back to the sky, but the jet was gone! Joe sighed, feeling silly for trying to catch it. But he smiled when he noticed a rainbow in the sky. He loved rainbows and all the colors they made, so he couldn't help but smile. 

The next day, Joe was outside again. All of the sudden, he saw the jet again! He grinned when he saw it and grabbed his net. He raced to the sky and slowly raised the net up in the air. At first, the jet didn't notice. But then, to Joe's surprise, the jet flew right into his net and he had caught it! Joe was so proud of himself and he ran home so excited to show everyone what he had done.

name_of_work: The House of Ghosts by Margaret Widdemer
content: The House of Ghosts was bright within, Aglow and warm and gay, A place my own once loved me in, That is not there by day: My hound lay drowsing on the floor: From sunken graves returned My folk that I was lonely for Sat where the hearth-fire burned. There was no lightest echo lost When I undid the door, There was no shadow where I crossed The well-remembered floor. I bent to whisper to my hound (So long he had been dead!) He slept no lighter nor more sound, He did not lift his head. I brushed my father as I came; He did not move or see-- I cried upon my mother's name; She did not look at me. Their faces in the firelight bent, They smiled in speaking slow Of some old gracious merriment Forgotten years ago. I was so changed since they had died! How could they know or guess A voice that plead for love, and cried Of grief and loneliness? Out from the House of Ghosts I fled Lest I should turn and see The child I had been lift her head And stare aghast at me!

Once upon a time there was a little girl who had a favourite toy. She loved to hug and cuddle it, and it always made her laugh. One day her mother decided it was time for her to go outside and play. The little girl sighed; she didn't want to leave the toy behind.

So, the little girl went outside with the toy in her hands and, as she was looking around, she noticed a little boy playing with a toy of his own. She went over to him, and they quickly became friends.

The little girl offered him her toy so they can play together. The little boy was happy and put his toy around her neck. He started to pull and tug on her neck, and the little girl got scared. She started to cry, and the little boy quickly realized what he had done. He let go and ran inside.

The little girl stood there, too scared to move, until her mother arrived and hugged her. She reassured her that everything will be ok and told her "sometimes little things can cause big problems; but always remember to be kind to others".

Once upon a time there was a bear named Joe. Joe was very envious of his neighbour, Mr Rabbit. Mr Rabbit had a red car that went really fast. Joe wanted a car too but he was too poor to get one. 

One day Joe decided to pinch some gas from Mr Rabbit's car. He waited until Mr Rabbit was away and then he quickly opened the car's tank and pinched just a little bit of gas. 

When Mr Rabbit came back he noticed something strange. His car was not running properly! He opened the tank and saw that the gas was missing. That's when he realised that Joe had pinched some gas! 

Mr Rabbit was very angry and he confronted Joe. Joe hung his head and said he was sorry. He promised Mr Rabbit that he would never pinch the gas ever again and that he would find another way to get a car of his own. 

Mr Rabbit was still angry, but he saw that Joe was sorry and he said he would forgive him if Joe kept his promise. Joe said he would and gave Mr Rabbit a big hug. From that day onwards, Joe worked hard and saved up until one day he could buy a car of his own!

John went to the park almost every day after that. He and his slide had become best friends. Whenever he slide, it was like he was soaring through the sky. His creative spirit was happy and alive.

name_of_work: The Sea and the Hills by Rudyard Kipling
content: Who hath desired the Sea? - the sight of salt water unbounded - The heave and the halt and the hurl and the crash of the comber wind-hounded? The sleek-barrelled swell before storm, grey, foamless, enormous, and growing Stark calm on the lap of the Line or the crazy-eyed hurricane blowing - His Sea in no showing the same - his Sea and the same 'neath each showing: His Sea as she slackens or thrills? So and no otherwise - so and no otherwise - hillmen desire their Hills! Who hath desired the Sea ? - the immense and contemptuous surges? The shudder, the stumble, the swerve, as the star-stabbing bowsprit emerges? The orderly clouds of the Trades, the ridged, roaring sapphire thereunder - Unheralded cliff-haunting flaws and the headsail's low-volleying thunder - His Sea in no wonder the same - his Sea and the same through each wonder: His Sea as she rages or stills? So and no otherwise - so and no otherwise - hillmen desire their Hills. Who hath desired the Sea? Her menaces swift as her mercies? The in-rolling walls of the fog and the silver-winged breeze that disperses? The unstable mined berg going South and the calvings and groans that declare it - White water half-guessed overside and the moon breaking timely to bare it - His Sea as his fathers have dared - his Sea as his children shall dare it: His Sea as she serves him or kills? So and no otherwise - so and no otherwise - hillmen desire their Hills. Who hath desired the Sea? Her excellent loneliness rather Than forecourts of kings, and her outermost pits than the streets where men gather Inland, among dust, under trees - inland where the slayer may slay him - Inland, out of reach of her arms, and the bosom whereon he must lay him - His Sea from the first that betrayed - at the last that shall never betray him: His Sea that his being fulfils? So and no otherwise - so and no otherwise - hillmen desire their Hills.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sarah. Every day, she would play outside and have lots of fun. Today, while Sarah was playing outside, she found a crazy snack. Sarah was so excited and couldn't wait to show her friends.

Suddenly, Sarah heard a loud sound. She looked around and saw two boys shooting their toy guns at each other. Sarah was very scared. "No, don't do that!" she shouted.

The boys stopped and looked at Sarah. "Why shouldn't we play with guns?" they asked.

Sarah said, "Because guns can hurt people and make them sad. Let's all play with something else that is fun, like our snacks!" The boys agreed and soon all of them were playing with the crazy snack.

The moral of the story is that it's always better to play with toys and snacks than with guns. Guns can be very dangerous and can make people sad. Let's all choose to have fun in a safe way.
