Once upon a time, there was a young boy named Jack. He liked going to the park and playing with his friends.

One day while Jack was at the park he saw a big tree with lots of fruit hanging from it. He was excited - it looked like it had lots of delicious fruit! He wanted to take some with him for a snack.
 
Jack grabbed as many fruits as he could, but he lifted too hard and some of them fell on the ground. He felt embarrassed so he quickly put the fruit back on the tree and ran away.

Jack felt ashamed. He knew he shouldn't have taken the fruit without asking the tree first. He was sad that he made a mistake and he knew he had to make things right. 

So the next day, Jack brought a basket of fruit to the park and gave it to the tree. He apologized to the tree and thanked it for the fruit. The tree was happy and smiled at Jack.

Jack felt better now. He realized that he had to take responsibility for what he had done and that apologizing was the right thing to do. He vowed to never take anything from the tree again without asking first.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside with her friends, but every day she would delay going back home. Her mom would always tell her to come home before it got dark, but she never listened.

One day, Lily got lost while playing with her friends. She didn't know how to get back home and it was getting dark. She felt scared and wished she had listened to her mom. Suddenly, she saw an amazing light in the distance. It was her mom with a flashlight looking for her.

Lily realized that she should always listen to her mom and come home on time. She learned that home is a safe and happy place and it's important to be responsible. From that day on, Lily never delayed going back home again.

Once upon a time, there were two little bears, one called Big and one called Small. Big had an amazing idea - to create a barrel so that it could be filled with fun and games. After much hard work, Big finally finished creating the barrel.

The two little bears were so excited to see what was inside it. As Small opened the barrel with trembling hands, he and Big were filled with amazement. Inside the barrel were all sorts of breathtaking toys, colors, and drawings.

Small and Big were so thrilled that they decided to play together. Small asked Big, "Do you think we should play catch or hide and seek first?"

Big thought for a minute and then smiled excitedly and said, "Let's play catch! That looks like the most fun!"

And so the two little bears spent the day playing together, having the most amazing time ever.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who wanted to do yoga. She went to find her yoga mat, which was hidden in a big box in her room. She found it and laid it out on the floor. She was very excited to begin.

She got down on the ground and started to move her body. She tried to do all the different positions, but it was so hard. She kept getting stuck and having to start over.

She was getting really frustrated, so she decided to take a break. She sat down and started to stir a big bowl of soup. As she was stirring, she kept thinking about all the yoga poses she was trying to do.

Then, she remembered all the times her teacher had told her to keep trying. She felt sorry for giving up so easily, so she decided to keep practicing. Eventually, she was able to do all the poses!

The little girl was happy and proud of herself that she stuck with it and didn't give up. She knew she could do anything if she didn't give up.

name_of_work: I wake and feel the fell of dark, not day by Gerard Manley Hopkins
content: I wake and feel the fell of dark, not day. What hours, O what black hours we have spent This night! what sights you, heart, saw; ways you went! And more must, in yet longer light's delay. With witness I speak this. But where I say Hours I mean years, mean life. And my lament Is cries countless, cries like dead letters sent To dearest him that lives alas! away. I am gall, I am heartburn. God's most deep decree Bitter would have me taste: my taste was me; Bones built in me, flesh filled, blood brimmed the curse. Selfyeast of spirit a dull dough sours. I see The lost are like this, and their scourge to be As I am mine, their sweating selves; but worse.

Anna and Ben are twins. They like to help their mom in the kitchen. Today, mom is making wraps for lunch. She gives Anna and Ben a job. They have to put cheese and ham on the tortillas.

"Can I have more cheese, please?" Anna asks mom.

"Sure, here you go. But don't put too much, or the wrap will be too big," mom says.

"I like cheese. It is tasty," Anna says.

Ben likes ham. He puts a lot of ham on his tortilla. He thinks ham is tasty, too.

"Can I have more ham, please?" Ben asks mom.

"OK, but leave some for me and dad. And don't forget the lettuce and tomato," mom says.

"I like lettuce and tomato. They are crunchy and juicy," Ben says.

When Anna and Ben are done, they roll up their tortillas. They make two wraps each. They are proud of their job.

"Look, mom, we made wraps!" they say.

"Wow, you did a great job! They look delicious. Let's go to the table and eat them," mom says.

Anna and Ben follow mom to the table. They sit down and take a bite of their wraps. They are tasty and filling. They smile and say, "Thank you, mom!"

The sun shone in the sky and little Katya enjoyed the peaceful day. She ran out of the house and into the lawn with glee. Everywhere she looked there were beautiful flowers and green grass. She launched herself into an exciting game of tag with her teddy bear.

Katya laughed as she chased the bear faster and faster. When she finally caught him, she hugged him tight. Then she noticed some ladybugs flying about the lawn. She watched them for a while with wonder and joy.

The day came to an end but Katya felt content. She gave the teddy bear one last hug before going inside. She was happy that she'd spent the day playing in the peaceful lawn.

Anna liked to play with her dolls. She had many dolls, but her favorite was Lily. Lily had long hair, a pink dress and a smile. Anna took Lily everywhere with her.

One day, Anna and Lily went to the park with Mommy. They saw a big slide, a swing and a sandbox. Anna wanted to try the slide. She put Lily on her lap and slid down. But the slide was too fast and Anna and Lily fell off at the end. Lily hit a rock and her dress tore. Anna saw a big cut on Lily's arm. She cried and hugged Lily.

"Mommy, Mommy, Lily is hurt!" Anna shouted.

Mommy came running and saw Lily's arm. She said, "Oh, poor Lily. Don't worry, Anna, we can heal her. Let's go home and get some bandages and glue."

Anna nodded and followed Mommy. She held Lily close to her chest.

At home, Mommy took out a pot from the kitchen. She filled it with water and put it on the stove. She said, "We need to boil some water to clean Lily's arm. It will kill the germs and make it better."

Anna watched as the water bubbled and steamed. She thought it was unusual. She had never seen water do that before. She asked, "Mommy, why does the water do that?"

Mommy said, "That's what happens when water gets very hot. It turns into steam. Steam is like a cloud, but hotter. We have to be careful not to touch it, because it can burn us."

Anna said, "Oh, I see. Can I help you heal Lily?"

Mommy said, "Of course, you can. You are a good helper. Here, take this cloth and dip it in the water. Then, gently wipe Lily's arm with it. That will clean the cut."

Anna did as Mommy said. She was careful not to touch the steam or the pot. She wiped Lily's arm with the cloth. She saw the dirt and blood come off. She said, "Look, Mommy, Lily's arm is cleaner now."

Mommy said, "Good job, Anna. Now, we need to put some glue on the cut. That will stick the skin together and stop the bleeding. Then, we need to wrap a bandage around it. That will protect the cut and make it heal faster."

Mommy took out a tube of glue and a roll of bandage. She squeezed some glue on Lily's arm and pressed the edges of the cut together. She said, "This glue is special. It is safe for dolls and people. It will dry quickly and make a thin layer of skin. It will not hurt Lily."

Anna said, "Wow, that's amazing. Lily is lucky to have you, Mommy."

Mommy said, "Thank you, Anna. You are very sweet. Now, let's put the bandage on. Can you hold Lily's arm still for me?"

Anna held Lily's arm still while Mommy wrapped the bandage around it. She made sure it was not too tight or too loose. She said, "There, we are done. Lily is all healed. How do you feel, Lily?"

Anna made Lily say, "I feel much better, Mommy. Thank you for healing me. And thank you, Anna, for being my friend. I love you both."

Mommy said, "You are very welcome, Lily. We love you too. Now, why don't you and Anna go play in your room? I'll make some cookies for you."

Anna said, "Yay, cookies! Come on, Lily, let's go play. We can have a tea party with your new bandage. You look very pretty."

Anna and Lily went to Anna's room and played happily. They forgot about the slide and the rock. They were glad they had each other and Mommy. They knew Mommy could heal anything.

Lila and Ben were twins who liked to help their mom in the kitchen. One day, mom asked them to peel some onions for the soup. Lila and Ben took the onions and a knife and went to the table.

"Be careful with the knife," mom said. "And don't touch your eyes after you peel the onions. They can make you cry."

Lila and Ben nodded and started to peel the onions. They wanted to be helpful and make mom happy. But soon, they felt a sting in their eyes and tears came out. They rubbed their eyes with their hands, but it only made it worse.

"Ow, ow, ow!" Lila and Ben cried. "The onions hurt our eyes!"

Mom heard them and came to the table. She saw the twins crying and the onions on the floor. She took a wet cloth and wiped their eyes gently.

"I'm sorry, my loves," mom said. "The onions have a strong smell that makes your eyes water. You have to peel them under water or with a fan on. Here, let me show you."

Mom took the knife and the onions and put them in a bowl of water. She peeled the onions under the water and the smell did not bother her eyes. She showed Lila and Ben how to do it and gave them each an onion to try.

"Wow, mom, you are so smart!" Lila and Ben said. "The onions don't hurt our eyes anymore!"

They peeled the onions under water and put them in a pot for the soup. Mom smiled and hugged them.

"Thank you, Lila and Ben, for being so helpful and brave," mom said. "You learned something new today. Sometimes, things that seem hard or scary can be easier or funnier if you try a different way. And if you need help, you can always ask me or someone else who knows. I'm proud of you, my loves."

Lila and Ben smiled and hugged mom back. They felt happy and proud too. They helped mom make the soup and enjoyed it with the whole family. They liked the onions in the soup. They did not make them cry. They made them yummy.

Once there was a little girl. She was only three years old. One day, she went outside to play in her garden. The garden was very big and there were many things to explore. She found a pumpkin in the garden. It was a big, round pumpkin and it was sitting in the deep grass. She was very excited. She reached for the pumpkin and said "please" in a sweet voice. Her mom smiled and said "of course, honey". Together, they made a sweet and delicious pumpkin pie. The little girl was so happy!

When they got back home, Max was so proud he had been able to carry the table. Mummy laughed and said, "You did a great job, Max!" They placed the table in the room and Max smiled with joy. He had never felt so proud before.

Bulkeley, Hunt, Willard, Hosmer, Meriam, Flint, Possessed the land which rendered to their toil Hay, corn, roots, hemp, flax, apples, wool, and wood. Each of these landlords walked amidst his farm, Saying, "'Tis mine, my children's and my name's. How sweet the west wind sounds in my own trees! How graceful climb those shadows on my hill! I fancy these pure waters and the flags Know me, as does my dog: we sympathize; And, I affirm, my actions smack of the soil." Where are these men? Asleep beneath their grounds: And strangers, fond as they, their furrows plough. Earth laughs in flowers, to see her boastful boys Earth-proud, proud of the earth which is not theirs; Who steer the plough, but cannot steer their feet Clear of the grave. They added ridge to valley, brook to pond, And sighed for all that bounded their domain; "This suits me for a pasture; that's my park; We must have clay, lime, gravel, granite-ledge, And misty lowland, where to go for peat. The land is well,--lies fairly to the south. 'Tis good, when you have crossed the sea and back, To find the sitfast acres where you left them." Ah! the hot owner sees not Death, who adds Him to his land, a lump of mould the more. Hear what the Earth say:-- EARTH-SONG "Mine and yours; Mine, not yours. Earth endures; Stars abide-- Shine down in the old sea; Old are the shores; But where are old men? I who have seen much, Such have I never seen. "The lawyer's deed Ran sure, In tail, To them and to their heirs Who shall succeed, Without fail, Forevermore. "Here is the land, Shaggy with wood, With its old valley, Mound and flood. But the heritors?-- Fled like the flood's foam. The lawyer and the laws, And the kingdom, Clean swept herefrom. "They called me theirs, Who so controlled me; Yet every one Wished to stay, and is gone, How am I theirs, If they cannot hold me, But I hold them?" When I heard the Earth-song I was no longer brave; My avarice cooled Like lust in the chill of the grave.

name_of_work: The History of Red by Linda Hogan
content: First there was some other order of things never spoken but in dreams of darkest creation. Then there was black earth, lake, the face of light on water. Then the thick forest all around that light, and then the human clay whose blood we still carry rose up in us who remember caves with red bison painted in their own blood, after their kind. A wildness swam inside our mothers, desire through closed eyes, a new child wearing the red, wet mask of birth, delivered into this land already wounded, stolen and burned beyond reckoning. Red is this yielding land turned inside out by a country of hunters with iron, flint and fire. Red is the fear that turns a knife back against men, holds it at their throats, and they cannot see the claw on the handle, the animal hand that haunts them from some place inside their blood. So that is hunting, birth, and one kind of death. Then there was medicine, the healing of wounds. Red was the infinite fruit of stolen bodies. The doctors wanted to know what invented disease how wounds healed from inside themselves how life stands up in skin, if not by magic. They divined the red shadows of leeches that swam in white bowls of water: they believed stars in the cup of sky. They cut the wall of skin to let what was bad escape but they were reading the story of fire gone out and that was a science. As for the animal hand on death's knife, knives have as many sides as the red father of war who signs his name in the blood of other men. And red was the soldier who crawled through a ditch of human blood in order to live. It was the canal of his deliverance. It is his son who lives near me. Red is the thunder in our ears when we meet. Love, like creation, is some other order of things. Red is the share of fire I have stolen from root, hoof, fallen fruit. And this was hunger. Red is the human house I come back to at night swimming inside the cave of skin that remembers bison. In that round nation of blood we are all burning, red, inseparable fires the living have crawled and climbed through in order to live so nothing will be left for death at the end. This life in the fire, I love it. I want it, this life.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue loved to bake with her mom. They baked yummy cookies and cakes. One day, Sue wanted to bake something new.

Sue and her mom went outside to the garden. They saw a big, pretty sunflower. The sunflower was wet from the rain. Sue had an idea. She wanted to bake sunflower seeds.

name_of_work: Chrysalis by LJ Bovey - A Poem about Coronavirus/Covid-19 and Lockdown
content: Corona used to be just the name of a beer I'd have a few Twice a year On the odd occasion I'd go out I wish I could go outCovid is not a word we'd be familiar with Before all this Before queues outside Tesco's, two metres between us Before we stocked up on toilet rolls Before pasta became platinum Before the lower class got hooked on quinoa But they knew what baked beans were They assumed it was pronounced Quinn Noah And I know a social commentary And pedantry Seems unpleasant of me But I have to confess to you I pronounced it that way too. Every lunch time packets soups 4 nights of stew Britons doing, what Britons do When reduced to our core Whether rich or poor We are better with, Our backs t'wall Our leader has this plague And our future heir too So we respond with funny memes After all, it's just a flu We point to facts and figures That help support our claims We rationalise, our social lives Our going to our mates We need to come together And join in staying apart And though we can't link arms We can carry love in hearts So, Facebook take the stage Your time is now, as social distance grows From reaching out to, Bev from work Or chatting to our folks In the past you have been divisive Your popularity divided us And now quarantine divides us In social media we trust? If we must So we quell our party spirit And dust off that guitar Download the Duolingo Doesn't matter where we are We are here now for weeks It could be far more This virus knows no class divide Between the rich, The poor Don't view this isolation As being in a cell It's a chrysalis and we're out of hell We will be better We will appreciate more All we had and couldn't see before.

One day, Mommy and Johnny were walking in the park. Johnny stopped suddenly and pointed. "Look, Mommy!" he said. Mommy saw a small bird on the ground. "Oh, how sweet!" She said. 

Mommy and Johnny walked over to the bird. "Can I pick it up, Mommy?" Johnny asked. Mommy nodded her head. Johnny carefully held the bird. It was so soft, and clean. 

Suddenly, a dog ran up to Mommy and Johnny. It was huge, with sharp teeth. "Let go of the bird, Johnny!" Mommy said. Johnny quickly put the bird back on the ground. Then Johnny and Mommy ran away. 

The bird flew away. It was safe again. Johnny was so proud that he had saved the little bird. He had done something brave and courageous. Mommy hugged him tight. "You did a very good job, Johnny," She said. 

Mommy and Johnny continued their walk, feeling proud and happy.

name_of_work: The Witch by Mary Elizabeth Coleridge
content: I have walked a great while over the snow, And I am not tall nor strong. My clothes are wet, and my teeth are set, And the way was hard and long. I have wandered over the fruitful earth, But I never came here before. Oh, lift me over the threshold, and let me in at the door! The cutting wind is a cruel foe. I dare not stand in the blast. My hands are stone, and my voice a groan, And the worst of death is past. I am but a little maiden still, My little white feet are sore. Oh, lift me over the threshold, and let me in at the door! Her voice was the voice that women have, Who plead for their heart's desire. She came--she came--and the quivering flame Sunk and died in the fire. It never was lit again on my hearth Since I hurried across the floor, To lift her over the threshold, and let her in at the door.

We were characters in a story the writer couldn't bring himself to finish. When he left us it was late, a child was crying, newsprint smudged on our fingertips as if to make of us a mechanism by which the world would repeat itself, its story: this happened -- did you hear? -- then that. So many disparate versions. The terror risen into words, shrouded there, hanging, so cold. And the tenderness -- how the words barely touched it, as if to speak it were a further hurt. It was night when he left us, and the child who could not yet remember her dreams woke saying, where are the toys of the moon, are we the moon's toys? Outside, lines of stiff trees stood like hieroglyphs, the configuration of the one for dagger so close to the one that stands for shrub, so hard to understand the difference; or the one for fear that also could mean reverence, the one for medicine so similar to entreaty and to prayer. And in the distance the red tremor of the radio tower, and the planes that passed above us as we held to the earth and didn't understand the earth.

Once upon a time, there was a hero. He was a brave knight and he always helped people in need. One day, he had to go hang his bright armour in a tree. He was so proud of his shiny armour. It was beautiful! 

That night, a big storm came. He was too scared to go back and get it, so it stayed in the tree, high in the sky.

The next morning, the hero had a surprise. Everyone in the village was waiting to see him. They wanted to thank him for being so brave. The hero was so proud! They had taken his armour and hung it proudly on the outside of the town hall. Everyone smiled and cheered.

The hero smiled and waved at the crowd. From that day on, the hero was a hero to everyone in the village. And they would hang his armour in the town hall forever as a token of their love and respect.

name_of_work: The Nightingale by Sir Philip Sidney
content: The nightingale, as soon as April bringeth Unto her rested sense a perfect waking, While late bare earth, proud of new clothing, springeth, Sings out her woes, a thorn her song-book making, And mournfully bewailing, Her throat in tunes expresseth What grief her breast oppresseth For Tereus' force on her chaste will prevailing. O Philomela fair, O take some gladness, That here is juster cause of plaintful sadness: Thine earth now springs, mine fadeth; Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth. Alas, she hath no other cause of anguish But Tereus' love, on her by strong hand wroken, Wherein she suffering, all her spirits languish; Full womanlike complains her will was broken. But I, who daily craving, Cannot have to content me, Have more cause to lament me, Since wanting is more woe than too much having. O Philomela fair, O take some gladness, That here is juster cause of plaintful sadness: Thine earth now springs, mine fadeth; Thy thorn without, my thorn my heart invadeth.

name_of_work: The Hope of My Heart by John McCrae
content: "Delicta juventutis et ignorantius ejus, quoesumus ne memineris, Domine." I left, to earth, a little maiden fair, With locks of gold, and eyes that shamed the light; I prayed that God might have her in His care And sight. Earth's love was false; her voice, a siren's song; (Sweet mother-earth was but a lying name) The path she showed was but the path of wrong And shame. "Cast her not out!" I cry. God's kind words come -- "Her future is with Me, as was her past; It shall be My good will to bring her home At last."

name_of_work: A River by A. K. Ramanujan
content: In Madurai, city of temples and poets, who sang of cities and temples, every summer a river dries to a trickle in the sand, baring the sand ribs, straw and women's hair clogging the watergates at the rusty bars under the bridges with patches of repair all over them the wet stones glistening like sleepy crocodiles, the dry ones shaven water-buffaloes lounging in the sun The poets only sang of the floods. He was there for a day when they had the floods. People everywhere talked of the inches rising, of the precise number of cobbled steps run over by the water, rising on the bathing places, and the way it carried off three village houses, one pregnant woman and a couple of cows named Gopi and Brinda as usual. The new poets still quoted the old poets, but no one spoke in verse of the pregnant woman drowned, with perhaps twins in her, kicking at blank walls even before birth. He said: the river has water enough to be poetic about only once a year and then it carries away in the first half-hour three village houses, a couple of cows named Gopi and Brinda and one pregnant woman expecting identical twins with no moles on their bodies, with different coloured diapers to tell them apart.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She went on a trip with her family and had to pack her luggage. She put her clothes, toys, and snacks in her bag. Her mom said they needed to bring extra snacks to supply everyone on the trip.

name_of_work: A Hymn to God the Father by John Donne
content: Wilt thou forgive that sin where I begun, Which was my sin, though it were done before? Wilt thou forgive that sin, through which I run, And do run still, though still I do deplore? When thou hast done, thou hast not done, For I have more. Wilt thou forgive that sin which I have won Others to sin, and made my sin their door? Wilt thou forgive that sin which I did shun A year or two, but wallow'd in, a score? When thou hast done, thou hast not done, For I have more. I have a sin of fear, that when I have spun My last thread, I shall perish on the shore; But swear by thyself, that at my death thy Son Shall shine as he shines now, and heretofore; And, having done that, thou hast done; I fear no more.

Once upon a time, there was a cute little bear named Teddy. Teddy loved to take showers in the rain. One day, Teddy met a bird named Bluey. Bluey said, "Hi Teddy! What are you doing?" Teddy replied, "I'm taking a shower in the rain. It's so much fun!" Bluey said, "That sounds like fun. Can I join you?" Teddy said, "Of course!"

After their shower, Bluey said, "Teddy, I have a letter to mail. Do you want to come with me?" Teddy said, "Yes, I love going on adventures with my friends!" So, they went to the post office to mail Bluey's letter. They met a friendly postman who said, "Hello there! What can I help you with?" Bluey said, "I need to mail this letter." The postman said, "No problem, let me take care of that for you." Teddy and Bluey were happy to have made a new friend and to have completed their mission.

name_of_work: If I Were King by A.A. Milne
content: I often wish I were a King, And then I could do anything. If only I were King of Spain, I'd take my hat off in the rain. If only I were King of France, I wouldn't brush my hair for aunts. I think, if I were King of Greece, I'd push things off the mantelpiece. If I were King of Norroway, I'd ask an elephant to stay. If I were King of Babylon, I'd leave my button gloves undone. If I were King of Timbuctoo, I'd think of lovely things to do. If I were King of anything, I'd tell the soldiers, "I'm the King!"

name_of_work: Inniskeen Road: July Evening by Patrick Kavanagh
content: The bicycles go by in twos and threes - There's a dance in Billy Brennan's barn tonight, And there's the half-talk code of mysteries And the wink-and-elbow language of delight. Half-past eight and there is not a spot Upon a mile of road, no shadow thrown That might turn out a man or woman, not A footfall tapping secrecies of stone. I have what every poet hates in spite Of all the solemn talk of contemplation. Oh, Alexander Selkirk knew the plight Of being king and government and nation. A road, a mile of kingdom. I am king Of banks and stones and every blooming thing.

name_of_work: Sorrow by Aubrey Thomas de Vere
content: COUNT each affliction, whether light or grave, God's messenger sent down to thee; do thou With courtesy receive him; rise and bow; And, ere his shadow pass thy threshold, crave Permission first his heavenly feet to lave; Then lay before him all thou hast; allow No cloud of passion to usurp thy brow, Or mar thy hospitality; no wave Of mortal tumult to obliterate The soul's marmoreal calmness: Grief should be, Like joy, majestic, equable, sedate; Confirming, cleansing, raising, making free; Strong to consume small troubles; to commend Great thoughts, grave thoughts, thoughts lasting to the end.

I saw Eternity the other night, Like a great ring of pure and endless light, All calm, as it was bright; And round beneath it, Time in hours, days, years, Driv'n by the spheres Like a vast shadow mov'd; in which the world And all her train were hurl'd. The doting lover in his quaintest strain Did there complain; Near him, his lute, his fancy, and his flights, Wit's sour delights, With gloves, and knots, the silly snares of pleasure, Yet his dear treasure All scatter'd lay, while he his eyes did pour Upon a flow'r. The darksome statesman hung with weights and woe, Like a thick midnight-fog mov'd there so slow, He did not stay, nor go; Condemning thoughts (like sad eclipses) scowl Upon his soul, And clouds of crying witnesses without Pursued him with one shout. Yet digg'd the mole, and lest his ways be found, Work'd under ground, Where he did clutch his prey; but one did see That policy; Churches and altars fed him; perjuries Were gnats and flies; It rain'd about him blood and tears, but he Drank them as free. The fearful miser on a heap of rust Sate pining all his life there, did scarce trust His own hands with the dust, Yet would not place one piece above, but lives In fear of thieves; Thousands there were as frantic as himself, And hugg'd each one his pelf; The downright epicure plac'd heav'n in sense, And scorn'd pretence, While others, slipp'd into a wide excess, Said little less; The weaker sort slight, trivial wares enslave, Who think them brave; And poor despised Truth sate counting by Their victory. Yet some, who all this while did weep and sing, And sing, and weep, soar'd up into the ring; But most would use no wing. O fools (said I) thus to prefer dark night Before true light, To live in grots and caves, and hate the day Because it shews the way, The way, which from this dead and dark abode Leads up to God, A way where you might tread the sun, and be More bright than he. But as I did their madness so discuss One whisper'd thus, "This ring the Bridegroom did for none provide, But for his bride."

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play in the garden with his spade. He would dig and dig until he found something special, like a shiny rock or a big worm.

One day, Timmy's friend Billy came over to play. Billy saw Timmy's spade and said he wanted to play too. Timmy let Billy use his spade, but Billy was not honest. He accidentally broke Timmy's spade and didn't tell him.

When Timmy saw his broken spade, he felt sad. Billy felt bad too and finally told Timmy the truth. Timmy forgave him and they played together with Timmy's other toys. From then on, Billy promised to always be honest with his friend Timmy.

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to play with their toys. They had many toys, but their favorite was a big red wheel that they could roll and chase. They took turns to push the wheel and run after it, laughing and shouting.

One day, they went to the park with their mom and dad. They brought their wheel with them and ran to the grass. They saw another boy playing with a ball. He was alone and looked lonely. Tom and Lily wanted to be his friend.

"Hi, what is your name?" Tom asked the boy.

"Sam," the boy said.

"Do you want to play with us?" Lily asked.

"OK," Sam said.

They showed him their wheel and how to roll it. Sam liked the wheel and pushed it hard. He ran after it and caught it. He smiled and said, "This is fun!"

Tom and Lily smiled too. They took turns to push the wheel with Sam. They had a good time.

But then, Sam did not want to share the wheel anymore. He held it tight and said, "This is my wheel now. You can't have it."

Tom and Lily were shocked and sad. They said, "No, this is our wheel. We let you play with it. You have to share."

Sam shook his head and said, "No, I don't. Go away."

He tried to run away with the wheel, but Tom and Lily ran after him. They tried to grab the wheel from him, but he resisted. He pulled and pushed and shouted, "Mine, mine, mine!"

They fought over the wheel and made a lot of noise. Their mom and dad heard them and came to see what was wrong. They saw them fighting and said, "Stop, stop, stop!"

They separated them and asked them what happened. Tom and Lily told them how Sam took their wheel and did not want to share. Sam said he was lonely and wanted the wheel for himself.

Their mom and dad said, "That is not nice, Sam. You can't take things that are not yours. You have to ask and share. Tom and Lily were kind to you and wanted to be your friend. You should say sorry to them and give them back their wheel."

Sam felt ashamed and sorry. He said, "I'm sorry, Tom and Lily. I was wrong. Can I give you back your wheel and play with you again?"

Tom and Lily forgave him and said, "OK, Sam. We can be friends. But you have to share."

They hugged and made up. They played with the wheel and the ball together. They had more fun when they shared. They were not lonely anymore.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play with dolls and cars. One day, Anna has a new doll. It has long hair and a pretty dress. Ben likes the doll too. He wants to play with it.

"Can I have your doll?" Ben asks Anna.

"No, it is mine. You have your car," Anna says.

But Ben does not listen. He takes the doll from Anna. He runs away with it. Anna is sad and angry. She cries.

"Give me back my doll!" Anna shouts.

Ben does not stop. He runs to his room. He plays with the doll. He pulls the doll's hair. He makes a knot. He cuts the hair with scissors. He makes the hair short and ugly.

Anna follows Ben. She sees what he did. She is very sad and angry. She screams.

"You are bad! You ruined my doll! I hate you!" Anna says.

Ben is scared. He sees that he did a bad thing. He is sorry. He wants to make Anna happy again.

"I am sorry, Anna. I was wrong. I should not take your doll. I should not cut her hair. I am sorry," Ben says.

He gives the doll back to Anna. He gives her a hug. He gives her a thread. The thread is long and colorful.

"Maybe you can fix your doll's hair with this thread. Maybe you can make her pretty again. I hope you forgive me," Ben says.

Anna is still sad and angry. But she sees that Ben is sorry. She sees that he tries to help. She remembers that he is her friend. She thinks for a while. She takes the thread. She takes the doll. She takes the hug.

"Thank you, Ben. I am still sad, but I forgive you. You are my friend. Maybe we can fix my doll together," Anna says.

They go to Anna's room. They use the thread to make new hair for the doll. They make the hair long and colorful. They make the doll pretty again. They play with the doll and the car. They are happy. They are friends.

Mama and Papa took their little girl to the park. She was so excited. But when they got there she refused to go. She didn't like the park because there weren't any other children to play with her.

Mama said, "Let's try something else." So they went to the zoo. The little girl was so happy and ran around looking at all of the animals. But soon she became bored.

Mama suggested that they go to the beach. The little girl scoffed and said, "No way! That's even more boring than the park."

Papa laughed and said, "Come on. It'll be fun. Let's go as a family."

The little girl thought about it and decided it was worth a try. When they got to the beach, she loved it! She spent the whole day playing in the sand and seeing all the different sea creatures. It was definitely the perfect family day!

Once upon a time there was a girl who really wanted a pony. She asked her parents for one every day, but their answer was always the same.

â€œSorry, you canâ€™t have a pony,â€ they said.

The girl was sad and she didnâ€™t know what to do. One day, her Mom suggested an idea.

â€œWhy donâ€™t you make a light out of paper,â€ Mom said.

The girl was excited and she couldnâ€™t wait to start her project. She got to work right away and the next day, she had a beautiful paper light.

At twilight, the girl held up her light and wished for a pony. Miraculously, a light pony appeared in the sky. The girl was so happy and she shouted with joy.

â€œMom, look! My wish came true!â€

The girl took her new pony for a ride every day and she was so proud. Her parents were proud of her too and they never forgot the magical light.

Once upon a time, in a small house, there lived a nosy little mouse named Mimi. Mimi loved to fill her cheeks with all kinds of food. One day, Mimi found a big, shiny tooth under a pillow. She thought it was a treasure and wanted to keep it.

Mimi went to her friend, a wise old owl, and said, "Look at this tooth I found! I want to keep it." The wise old owl looked at the tooth and said, "Oh Mimi, be careful with that tooth. It belongs to the big, scary cat who lives next door. If the cat finds out you have it, he will be very angry."

But Mimi didn't listen to the wise old owl. She took the tooth home and hid it under her bed. The next day, the big, scary cat came to Mimi's house. He had heard from the nosy little birds that Mimi had his tooth. The cat said, "Give me my tooth back, or else!"

Mimi was scared, but she didn't want to give the tooth back. She tried to run away, but the big, scary cat caught her. He took his tooth back and said, "You should have listened to the wise old owl." And from that day on, Mimi learned not to be so nosy and to listen to her wise old friend.

name_of_work: We Were Simply Talking by Andrew Hudgins
content: We were simply talking, probably work, or relatives or even Christmas presents, when the car slid and I corrected, fishtailed and I corrected, then we were gone, sliding sideways, sliding backward on black ice and staring into the grill of a diesel tractor, also sliding, and in that instant I was ready to die. I saw my wife and was overjoyed that I had married her, though our marriage was already falling apart, and I loved the car, a brown Toyota, loved being warm in the car while it was white, cold, bitter out in the world we'd lost control of. I loved every molecule of breath I wasn't taking, and for the moment I forgave myself every sin and failure of my life, including this ridiculous and undignified early death. The car snapped backward into a frozen ditch. I sat speechless, shaking, my wife speechless also, and a man pulled up, a salesman: You folks okay? Suddenly the car radio roared, and by the car a dog barked wildly and, yes, we were fine. Fine. We were fine. But what was "fine," I wondered, and why do we always, always have to speak?

Once there was a little girl called Mary. She was three years old and loved to run around outside. Today, she decided to run faster than ever.

She started running at full speed, pushing herself to go as fast as she could. Everything happened so quickly and soon she was running too fast.

â€œWhoa!â€ she shouted, but her feet didnâ€™t stop. 

Mary was worried and started to slow down. But then, from a distance, she heard her mum's voice.

â€œMary,â€ her mum shouted. â€œBe careful, you could get hurt if you run too fast.â€

Mary stopped, remembering how worried her mum had been when she said it. She realised it was probably her way of telling Mary to slow down.

Mary smiled to herself and walked the rest of the way, thinking her mum was always looking out for her.

Once upon a time there was a small bunny. He had two soft ears and a little white nose. His name was Timmy.

One day, Timmy was hopping in the garden when he saw something that looked tasty. It was a small, juicy carrot! He hopped over to it, and started chewing. He chewed and chewed and it was delicious!

He hopped away to find some more carrots, but instead he found a tasty, green leaf. He started chewing it too and it was just as good.

He kept hopping and looking for something yummy to chew. He found some juicy apples and chewy berries, so he munched away.

Finally, he was full! He dug a little burrow and curled up in it and took a nap.

The end.

Once upon a time there lived a family of five with an enormous wardrobe. It was bigger than anyone in the family had ever seen. Everyday everyone in the family would put their clothes in the wardrobe and enjoy looking at how nicely it was all stored away. But one night something strange happened. During the night, the wardrobe started trembling and shaking, and then the doors opened. Everyone was so surprised but the wardrobe was no longer enormous. It had become much smaller. The family was sad and didn't know what to do when a magical fairy appeared. She said she could help them and she waved her wand. Suddenly the wardrobe was back to normal and the family was so happy. They thanked the fairy for restoring the wardrobe to its enormous size. The family rejoiced and they all lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time there was a little boy. His name was Jack and he was three years old. Jack wanted to solve a tricky puzzle!

He asked his parent to help him. His parent sat down with him and showed him the puzzle. It was a dull puzzle, with lots of different pieces that were hard to fit together. Jack knew it would be difficult to solve, but he was determined.

He was very shy, so at first he stayed quiet, watching his parent put together the pieces. But then he said, "I can do it, too!" His parent smiled and took a step back.

Jack carefully started to put the pieces together. It was slow and quiet work, but Jack didn't get too frustrated. He tried one piece, then another and soon he had solved the puzzle!

Jack was so happy that he solved it! He gave his parent a big hug, and they clapped and cheered. Jackâ€™s parent was so proud of him!

Once upon a time, there was a pig named Wilbur. Wilbur was very dirty because he loved rolling in the mud. One day, Wilbur was walking through the forest when he met a little girl named Lily.

"Hello, Wilbur! You are a dirty pig!" said Lily.

Wilbur replied, "Yes, I love rolling in the mud. It's so much fun!"

Lily said, "But Wilbur, if you pause and take a bath, you will be clean and smell nice. Then, everyone will want to be your friend."

Wilbur thought about what Lily said and decided to take a bath. After he was clean, all the other animals in the forest wanted to be his friend. Wilbur learned that sometimes it's important to pause and do things that might not be fun at first, but will make you happy in the end.

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play outside. One day, it rains a lot. The water goes up and up. It is a flood.

"Oh no, the flood is coming!" Lily says. "We have to go home!"

They run to their bikes. But Ben's bike is stuck in the mud. He tries to pull it out, but he can't. He is scared.

"Lily, help me!" Ben cries. "The water is too high!"

Lily is strong. She picks up Ben's bike and puts it on her bike. She tells Ben to sit behind her.

"Hold on tight, Ben!" Lily says. "I will take you home!"

They ride fast. The water splashes on their legs. They see their moms and dads waiting for them. They are happy and proud.

"Lily, you are so brave and strong!" Ben says. "Thank you for saving me and my bike!"

Lily smiles. She gives Ben a hug.

"You are welcome, Ben!" Lily says. "You are my best friend!"

Suzie was feeling very lonely and sad. She was sitting in her room all by herself, with no one to talk to. Suddenly, she noticed a card lying on the floor. She was curious, so she picked it up and opened it. Inside the card, there was something written: "Relax and enjoy!"

Suzie smiled. She knew what to do now. She decided to get some fresh air, so she took a blanket to the backyard and lay down. She stared at the clouds, listening to the birds and feeling the sun's warmth. She felt relaxed and happy.

Suddenly, she heard a voice asking, "What's going on here, Suzie?" She turned around and saw it was her friend, Lucy. Lucy had come to her backyard to see her.

"I'm trying to relax," Suzie said.

"That sounds like fun," Lucy replied. "Want me to join you?"

Suzie smiled and said, "Yes, I would love that!" So they lay down side by side, and relaxed in the sunshine together. Suzie was no longer lonely. She had a friend to enjoy the day with.

One day, a little girl named Sue was playing in her room. She had a small toy gun that she liked to play with. She would pretend to shoot at things, like her toys and the pictures on the wall. She was not frightened of her toy gun because she knew it was just for fun.

Sue's mom called her from the kitchen, "Sue, it's time for tea!" Sue loved tea time with her mom. She put her toy gun down and went to the kitchen. They sat at the table and had tea together. Sue felt happy and warm inside.

After tea, Sue went back to her room to play. She picked up her toy gun and started to play again. This time, she pretended to shoot at her tea cup. She said, "Bang! Bang!" Suddenly, the tea cup fell off the table and broke. Sue was frightened. She did not know her toy gun could do that. Sue's mom came in and saw the broken tea cup. She was not mad, but she told Sue to be more careful next time.

Mia was a little girl who loved to measure. She had a box of special tools and measured everything she could.

One day, Mia wanted to measure how high a mountain was. She asked her mom, â€œCan I measure the mountain?â€

Her mom smiled and said, â€œYes, but you have to stay in the safe place.â€ Mia nodded and ran off with her box of special tools.

When Mia got to the top of the mountain, she was so excited. She measured every inch of the mountain. It was very high. 

Mia smiled to herself and said, â€œSee mommy, I measured it!â€ She couldn't wait to show her mom all she had accomplished.

name_of_work: Smile, Smile, Smile by Wilfred Owen
content: Head to limp head, the sunk-eyed wounded scanned Yesterday's Mail; the casualties (typed small) And (large) Vast Booty from our Latest Haul. Also, they read of Cheap Homes, not yet planned; "For," said the paper, "when this war is done The men's first instinct will be making homes. Meanwhile their foremost need is aerodromes, It being certain war has just begun. Peace would do wrong to our undying dead,-- The sons we offered might regret they died If we got nothing lasting in their stead. We must be solidly indemnified. Though all be worthy Victory which all bought. We rulers sitting in this ancient spot Would wrong our very selves if we forgot The greatest glory will be theirs who fought, Who kept this nation in integrity." Nation?--The half-limbed readers did not chafe But smiled at one another curiously Like secret men who know their secret safe. (This is the thing they know and never speak, That England one by one had fled to France Not many elsewhere now save under France). Pictures of these broad smiles appear each week, And people in whose voice real feeling rings Say: How they smile! They're happy now, poor things.

Once upon a time, there was a chubby white cat named Snowball. Snowball loved to sit on the windowsill and watch the birds outside. One day, Snowball saw a little girl walking by outside. "Meow!" said Snowball. "Hello, little girl. Do you want to come sit with me?"

The little girl came inside and sat next to Snowball on the windowsill. They watched the birds together and Snowball purred happily. "You're a very pretty cat," said the little girl. "Thank you," said Snowball. "You're a very nice girl."

After a while, the little girl had to go home. "Goodbye, Snowball," she said. "Goodbye, little girl," said Snowball. "Come back and sit with me anytime." And from that day on, the little girl would come visit Snowball every day and they would sit together on the windowsill, watching the birds and chatting happily.

name_of_work: You, Andrew Marvell by Archibald MacLeish
content: And here face down beneath the sun And here upon earth's noonward height To feel the always coming on The always rising of the night: To feel creep up the curving east The earthy chill of dusk and slow Upon those under lands the vast And ever climbing shadow grow And strange at Ecbatan the trees Take leaf by leaf the evening strange The flooding dark about their knees The mountains over Persia change And now at Kermanshah the gate Dark empty and the withered grass And through the twilight now the late Few travelers in the westward pass And Baghdad darken and the bridge Across the silent river gone And through Arabia the edge Of evening widen and steal on And deepen on Palmyra's street The wheel rut in the ruined stone And Lebanon fade out and Crete High through the clouds and overblown And over Sicily the air Still flashing with the landward gulls And loom and slowly disappear The sails above the shadowy hulls And Spain go under and the shore Of Africa the gilded sand And evening vanish and no more The low pale light across that land Nor now the long light on the sea: And here face downward in the sun To feel how swift how secretly The shadow of the night comes on ...

Jill and John were very excited. After running very fast, they had won gold medals. They smiled at each other and started to laugh.

John put his gold medal around his neck. It was round and shiny. Then Jill put hers around hers.

Suddenly, the medal split in two! John and Jill were very surprised.

"What happened?" asked John.

Jill laughed, "I think it was too loud when we cheered!"

John smiled and said, "Let's get new medals and cheer again, but not as loud this time!"

And so, that is exactly what they did; they replaced their medals, cheered a little quieter, and still had a great time!

Once upon a time, there was a big pool. It was outside and had lots of water in it. The pool was so wet that you could jump in and splash around. 

One day, a big storm came and the pool got all dirty. The water was no longer clear and it was hard to see the bottom. The people who owned the pool were sad and didn't know what to do. 

But then, a kind man came and said he could restore the pool. He worked hard and cleaned the water until it was crystal clear again. The people were so happy and jumped back into the pool, splashing around and having fun.

Once upon a time, there was a slow pilot. One day, he wanted to spend some time in the sky. 
So, he hopped into his plane and flew away. 
He went up high and then he flew slowly over the cities and towns. 
He loved to spend time in the air and admired the beautiful scenery below. 
He flew for a long time until he had to go back home. 
He was happy with his time in the sky and couldn't wait to spend more.

name_of_work: Some One by Walter de la Mare
content: Some one came knocking At my wee, small door; Someone came knocking; I'm sure-sure-sure; I listened, I opened, I looked to left and right, But nought there was a stirring In the still dark night; Only the busy beetle Tap-tapping in the wall, Only from the forest The screech-owl's call, Only the cricket whistling While the dewdrops fall, So I know not who came knocking, At all, at all, at all.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys, especially her doll. One day, her mom asked her to serve dinner. Lily didn't want to stop playing, but her mom urged her to come to the table.

Lily sat down and started to eat, but the food was dull and tasted bad. She didn't like it at all. She wanted to go back to playing with her doll, but her mom said she had to finish her dinner first.

Lily didn't want to eat anymore, so she tried to sneak away. But she accidentally knocked over her plate, and the food spilled all over the floor. Her mom was very upset and Lily felt bad. She knew she should have listened and finished her dinner. The end.

Once upon a time, in a big wood, there lived a rare bird. This bird was very special because it had many colors on its wings. All the other birds in the wood liked to look at the rare bird's pretty wings.

One day, a big, loud man came to the wood. The man wanted to catch the rare bird because he liked its pretty wings too. The big, loud man tried to get the rare bird, but the other birds did not want the man to disturb their friend.

The other birds made a plan to help the rare bird. They all flew around the big, loud man, and made a lot of noise. The man got scared and ran away from the wood. The rare bird was safe, and all the birds were happy.

The moral of the story is that we should help our friends when they are in trouble, and not disturb others who are different from us.

And another regrettable thing about death is the ceasing of your own brand of magic, which took a whole life to develop and market -- the quips, the witticisms, the slant adjusted to a few, those loved ones nearest the lip of the stage, their soft faces blanched in the footlight glow, their laughter close to tears, their tears confused with their diamond earrings, their warm pooled breath in and out with your heartbeat, their response and your performance twinned. The jokes over the phone. The memories packed in the rapid-access file. The whole act. Who will do it again? That's it: no one; imitators and descendants aren't the same.

Alice looked at the onion, frustrated. It was too hard to separate the layers of the onion. She knew that if she wanted to make the perfect soup, then she needed to separate them.

Her mum saw her struggling and asked, "Would you like help?"

Alice shook her head. She wanted to do it all by herself. She started to pull on the layers of the onion again.

Her mum watched her and said, "It often makes us cry when we separate onions."

Alice didn't understand what her mum meant by that. She kept trying and trying but she couldn't separate them.

Suddenly, her eyes started to fill with tears. She was surprised! She looked back at her mum, surprised and she said, "Mum, why am I crying?"

Her mum smiled and said, "It happens to all of us. The oils in the onions make us cry when we try and separate them - but you can do it!"

Alice wiped her tears away and tried again with renewed determination. She managed to separate the layers of the onion and was proud of herself. She smiled and shouted, "I did it!"

Once upon a time, there was a hairy monster. It was the size of the universe and it was very scared and lonely. 

One day, the monster looked in the mirror and saw that it wasn't as hairy as it wanted to be. So it went off on a journey to find something to make it even more hairy. 

First, it passed a pond full of fish. But the fish didn't have anything to help the monster's fur. Next, it passed a park full of trees. But the trees didn't have anything to help its fur either. 

Finally, it passed a shop with all sorts of shiny things. One shiny thing caught the monster's eye. It was a polish brush. The monster took it and began to polish its fur. It was amazed to see how shiny and hairy it had become. 

The monster was no longer scared or lonely. It was proud of its shiny, hairy fur and it was happy. The end.

Once upon a time there was a harmless patient. He needed some help to move around. So, the patient had to crawl to get from one place to another. He slowly and carefully crawled from room to room. Every day he practiced and he got better and better at crawling.

One day, the patient was crawling in the garden. There he saw a butterfly! He was so happy and he carefully crawled towards it. The butterfly flew away but he kept crawling until he found a pretty flower. With a big smile on his face, he carefully picked it up and crawled back inside.

He showed the flower to his friends and they all smiled. For the first time in a long time, the patient felt happy and content. From then on the patient felt strong and independent again and kept crawling around, with a smile on his face.

It is time to be old, To take in sail:-- The god of bounds, Who sets to seas a shore, Came to me in his fatal rounds, And said: "No more! No farther shoot Thy broad ambitious branches, and thy root. Fancy departs: no more invent; Contract thy firmament To compass of a tent. There's not enough for this and that, Make thy option which of two; Economize the failing river, Not the less revere the Giver, Leave the many and hold the few. Timely wise accept the terms, Soften the fall with wary foot; A little while Still plan and smile, And,--fault of novel germs,-- Mature the unfallen fruit. Curse, if thou wilt, thy sires, Bad husbands of their fires, Who, when they gave thee breath, Failed to bequeath The needful sinew stark as once, The Baresark marrow to thy bones, But left a legacy of ebbing veins, Inconstant heat and nerveless reins,-- Amid the Muses, left thee deaf and dumb, Amid the gladiators, halt and numb." As the bird trims her to the gale, I trim myself to the storm of time, I man the rudder, reef the sail, Obey the voice at eve obeyed at prime: "Lowly faithful, banish fear, Right onward drive unharmed; The port, well worth the cruise, is near, And every wave is charmed."

I have lived in important places, times When great events were decided; who owned That half a rood of rock, a no-man's land Surrounded by our pitchfork-armed claims. I heard the Duffys shouting 'Damn your soul!' And old McCabe stripped to the waist, seen Step the plot defying blue cast-steel - 'Here is the march along these iron stones' That was the year of the Munich bother. Which Was more important? I inclined To lose my faith in Ballyrush and Gortin Till Homer's ghost came whispering to my mind. He said: I made the Iliad from such A local row. Gods make their own importance.

Once upon a time, there was a little bear named Teddy. Teddy loved to play with his friends in the forest. One day, he was feeling very tired and wanted to take a nap. But he couldn't find his pillow anywhere.

Teddy asked his friend, a bunny, "Have you seen my pillow?" The bunny replied, "No, I haven't seen your pillow. But I have an available carrot you can use as a pillow."

Teddy tried to use the carrot as a pillow, but it was too hard. He said, "This doesn't work. I need my soft pillow to sleep." The bunny said, "Don't worry, I can help you find it." They both started to look for the pillow.

After searching for a while, they finally found Teddy's pillow. It was stretched out under a tree. Teddy was so happy and said, "Thank you for helping me find my pillow. Now I can take a nap." Teddy stretched out on his pillow and fell asleep with a smile on his face.

Once upon a time, there was a dog named Max. Max was a useful dog who lived in a lab. He liked to help the people who worked there. The people in the lab were always busy doing different things.

One day, Max saw two friends, Tom and Sue, who were trying to separate some toys. They wanted to put the big toys in one box and the small toys in another box. Max wanted to help, so he went to them and said, "Can I help you separate the toys?"

Tom and Sue were happy for Max's help. They said, "Yes, Max! You can help us separate the toys." So, Max helped them by picking up the big toys with his mouth and putting them in one box. Then, he picked up the small toys and put them in the other box.

Max was very good at separating the toys. Tom and Sue were so happy that they gave Max a big hug. They said, "Thank you, Max! You are a very useful dog!" Max wagged his tail and felt proud of his work. From that day on, Max continued to help his friends in the lab with their tasks, and everyone loved him very much.

When men were all asleep the snow came flying, In large white flakes falling on the city brown, Stealthily and perpetually settling and loosely lying, Hushing the latest traffic of the drowsy town; Deadening, muffling, stifling its murmurs failing; Lazily and incessantly floating down and down: Silently sifting and veiling road, roof and railing; Hiding difference, making unevenness even, Into angles and crevices softly drifting and sailing. All night it fell, and when full inches seven It lay in the depth of its uncompacted lightness, The clouds blew off from a high and frosty heaven; And all woke earlier for the unaccustomed brightness Of the winter dawning, the strange unheavenly glare: The eye marvelled--marvelled at the dazzling whiteness; The ear hearkened to the stillness of the solemn air; No sound of wheel rumbling nor of foot falling, And the busy morning cries came thin and spare. Then boys I heard, as they went to school, calling, They gathered up the crystal manna to freeze Their tongues with tasting, their hands with snowballing; Or rioted in a drift, plunging up to the knees; Or peering up from under the white-mossed wonder, 'O look at the trees!' they cried, 'O look at the trees!' With lessened load a few carts creak and blunder, Following along the white deserted way, A country company long dispersed asunder: When now already the sun, in pale display Standing by Paul's high dome, spread forth below His sparkling beams, and awoke the stir of the day. For now doors open, and war is waged with the snow; And trains of sombre men, past tale of number, Tread long brown paths, as toward their toil they go: But even for them awhile no cares encumber Their minds diverted; the daily word is unspoken, The daily thoughts of labour and sorrow slumber At the sight of the beauty that greets them, for the charm they have broken.

One day, Sophie and her mommy went to camp. Mommy was going to teach Sophie some new activities. When they arrived, Sophie was amazed by how incredible camp was. She couldn't believe that she would get to play fun games and make new friends.

As they approached the camp, Mommy said, "I am so excited to teach you all the fun things you can do at camp!"

Sophie asked, "Do I get to play in the sand?"

Mommy answered, "Yes, and you can try lots of other things like rope climbing and painting. It's going to be so much fun!"

Sophie was so excited to start learning new things and making new friends that she could hardly wait. With a big smile, she said "Let's go!" 

Mommy and Sophie had an incredible time at camp. She made new friends, played fun games and learned lots of new things. Sophie couldn't wait to come back the next day.

Once upon a time there was a mouse who wanted to go on an adventure. He hopped into a tube and suddenly he began to move. The tube went fast and threw him around, but he kept holding on tight.

The mouse shouted, "This is fun!" 

When the tube stopped, he was suddenly in a new place. It looked different and smelled strange. But then he noticed something familiar. It was smooth and dark. 

It was chocolate! 

The mouse laughed and said, "Time for a snack!" 

He quickly ate all the chocolate and burped loudly. Then he hopped out of the tube, feeling happy and content. 

His adventure had come to an end.

Tom and Jen are friends. They like to play with toys and eat snacks. One day, they find a can of tuna in the kitchen. Tom says, "Let's open it and see what's inside." Jen says, "OK, but be careful. It might be yucky."

Tom uses a can opener to open the can. He sees a lot of fish inside. He says, "Wow, look at all the fish. They look tasty." Jen says, "I don't like fish. They smell bad." Tom says, "Don't be silly. Fish are good for you. Here, try some." He picks up a piece of tuna and puts it in Jen's mouth.

Jen spits out the tuna. She says, "Blech! That's gross. Why did you do that?" Tom laughs. He says, "I was joking. I wanted to see your face. It was funny." Jen feels angry. She says, "That's not a joke. That's mean. You hurt my feelings. I don't want to play with you anymore." She runs away, crying.

Tom feels troubled. He says, "I'm sorry, Jen. I didn't mean to make you cry. I thought you would laugh too. Please come back. I want to be your friend." He follows Jen and tries to hug her.

Jen pushes him away. She says, "No, go away. You're not my friend. You're a bully. You don't care about me. You only care about yourself." She runs to her room and slams the door.

Tom sits on the floor. He says, "I'm sorry, Jen. I'm sorry, I'm sorry, I'm sorry." He wishes he could take back his joke. He wonders if Jen will ever forgive him. He feels sad and lonely. He wishes he had never opened the can of tuna.

Once upon a time there was a nice girl called Beth. Beth was friendly and always helped others. 

One day, Beth needed to lay her clothes out to dry. She went to the garden and lay them all out in the sun. 

Beth heard a little noise in the garden. She saw a small cat had come over. The cat was very friendly and was rubbing against Beth's legs.

Beth said: "Oh hello little cat, I'm Beth! What's your name?" 
But the cat didn't answer. 

Beth bent down and said: "Would you like to help me? I need to lay out my clothes."

The cat meowed and then lay down on the clothes. Beth laughed and said: "Okay, thank you for helping me!"

After a few minutes, all the clothes had been laid out. Beth thanked the friendly cat, who then went on its way. 

Beth smiled and said to herself: "I'm so lucky to have such a friendly helper!"

name_of_work: The Vast Hour by Genevieve Taggard
content: All essences of sweetness from the white Warm day go up in vapor, when the dark Comes down. Ascends the tune of meadow-lark, Ascends the noon-time smell of grass, when night Takes sunlight from the world, and gives it ease. Mysterious wings have brushed the air; and light Float all the ghosts of sense and sound and sight; The silent hive is echoing the bees. So stir my thoughts at this slow, solemn time. Now only is there certainty for me When all the day's distilled and understood. Now light meets darkness: now my tendrils climb In this vast hour, up the living tree, Where gloom foregathers, and the stern winds brood.

name_of_work: On a Drop of Dew by Andrew Marvell
content: See how the orient dew, Shed from the bosom of the morn Into the blowing roses, Yet careless of its mansion new, For the clear region where 'twas born Round in itself incloses: And in its little globe's extent, Frames as it can its native element. How it the purple flow'r does slight, Scarce touching where it lies, But gazing back upon the skies, Shines with a mournful light, Like its own tear, Because so long divided from the sphere. Restless it rolls and unsecure, Trembling lest it grow impure, Till the warm sun pity its pain, And to the skies exhale it back again. So the soul, that drop, that ray Of the clear fountain of eternal day, Could it within the human flow'r be seen, Remembering still its former height, Shuns the sweet leaves and blossoms green, And recollecting its own light, Does, in its pure and circling thoughts, express The greater heaven in an heaven less. In how coy a figure wound, Every way it turns away: So the world excluding round, Yet receiving in the day, Dark beneath, but bright above, Here disdaining, there in love. How loose and easy hence to go, How girt and ready to ascend, Moving but on a point below, It all about does upwards bend. Such did the manna's sacred dew distill, White and entire, though congealed and chill, Congealed on earth : but does, dissolving, run Into the glories of th' almighty sun.

The little girl was walking down the street. She felt scared, her arms and legs started to shiver. She looked up and saw a big brown building. She had never seen it before.

The girl walked closer and she noticed a sign on the building. It said 'Theater'. She didn't understand what it meant. She stood there, shivering and feeling very scared.

Then a nice lady noticed the girl. She told her it was okay and explained that the building was a theater. The nice lady said that in a theater, people can watch movies or plays.

The little girl felt less scared and her shivering stopped. She said thank you to the nice lady and felt happy that the theater was a safe place.

name_of_work: O Were My Love Yon Lilac Fair by Robert Burns
content: O were my love yon Lilac fair, Wi' purple blossoms to the Spring, And I, a bird to shelter there, When wearied on my little wing! How I wad mourn when it was torn By Autumn wild, and Winter rude! But I wad sing on wanton wing, When youthfu' May its bloom renew'd. O gin my love were yon red rose, That grows upon the castle wa'; And I myself a drap o' dew, Into her bonie breast to fa'! O there, beyond expression blest, I'd feast on beauty a' the night; Seal'd on her silk-saft faulds to rest, Till fley'd awa by Phoebus' light!

I'm all alone in this world, she said, Ain't got nobody to share my bed, Ain't got nobody to hold my hand-- The truth of the matter's I ain't got no man. Once upon a time there was a big, huge bear. His name was Tom. Tom loved to spend his days snuggling and playing in the cosy forest. 

One day Tom was feeling hungry. He decided to go on an adventure to find something to munch on. As he was walking, he noticed something on the ground - it was a napkin! 

Tom picked up the napkin and saw that it had a sandwich inside. He took a big bite and it was yummy! But then he realized that it was his friend, Joe's sandwich. Joe was a rabbit and he had dropped the sandwich while he was hopping around the forest.

Tom missed Joe so he decided to take the napkin and find him. He followed the breadcrumbs that Joe had left, but he couldn't find him. 

"Oh no! Where can Joe be?", asked Tom. Then he heard a little familiar voice.

"I'm right here Tom!", said Joe. He had been hiding behind a huge tree the whole time.

Tom was so happy to see Joe that he offered him the napkin with the sandwich inside.

"Thank you Tom!", said Joe.

They hugged, and from then on Tom and Joe became the best of friends. They even shared their lunch every day.

Once upon a time, there was a furry animal named Avocado. Every day Avocado invited his friends and neighbours over for lunch. One day, Avocado invited a rabbit, a fox, and a squirrel to come eat the yummy food he had cooked.

The rabbit was so excited! He brought a carrot as a surprise. The fox had some delicious berries. The squirrel brought an extra nut that he had found.

Avocado made a big salad with all the food they brought. Everyone had a wonderful time eating it and they said it was the best salad they had ever had!

After lunch, Avocado invited his friends to come back and visit again soon. Everyone said they would, and they all said bye and went home with smiles on their faces. Avocado waved goodbye and went back inside, very happy that his friends had enjoyed the meal he had cooked for them.

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to play outside. One day, they found a creek near their house. It had clear water and many fish and frogs. They wanted to catch some and put them in a bucket.

"Look, Lily, a big frog!" Tom said, pointing to a green and brown animal on a rock. "I want to get it!"

He ran to the creek and tried to grab the frog. But the frog was not sleepy. It jumped away and splashed Tom with water. Tom slipped and fell into the creek. He got wet and cold and cried.

"Tom, are you okay?" Lily asked, running to him. She helped him stand up and hugged him. "Don't cry, Tom. It was just a frog. It did not want to be caught. It wanted to be free."

Tom sniffed and nodded. He was sorry for scaring the frog. He looked at the bucket and saw that it was empty. All the fish and frogs had escaped when he fell. He felt bad for taking them from their home.

"Let's go back, Lily," he said. "We should not bother the animals in the creek. They are happy there. We can watch them from far away, but not touch them."

Lily agreed. She took Tom's hand and they walked back to their house. They told their mom what happened and she gave them warm towels and cookies. She was glad that they learned to respect the creek and its creatures. She hugged them and said, "I'm proud of you, Tom and Lily. You are kind and smart."

I must go down to the seas again, to the lonely sea and the sky, And all I ask is a tall ship and a star to steer her by; And the wheel's kick and the wind's song and the white sail's shaking, And a grey mist on the sea's face, and a grey dawn breaking. I must go down to the seas again, for the call of the running tide Is a wild call and a clear call that may not be denied; And all I ask is a windy day with the white clouds flying, And the flung spray and the blown spume, and the sea-gulls crying. Meanwhile her mum was thrilled to see her little girl so happy.

Once upon a time, there was a naughty woman. She liked to do things that weren't allowed. One day, she decided to climb up a very tall tree. As she climbed, the branches began to tremble. She was so scared that she started to tremble too. 

Finally she reached the top of the tree. She looked around and saw the whole world from high above. She was so excited she clapped and shouted.

Once upon a time, there was a little red fish. He was going for a swim in the ocean, when he saw something strange! It was a jellyfish. At first it looked very nice, but when he got closer he saw it was scary!

Once upon a time, there were two friends named Jane and John. They wanted to go sailing. John was excited but Jane was scared. She thought the boat looked heavy. But John told her not to worry.

One day, Bella was playing in the kitchen. She found a special fork. It was shiny and new, so she decided to keep it.

name_of_work: Ode on a Grecian Urn by John Keats
content: Thou still unravish'd bride of quietness, Thou foster-child of silence and slow time, Sylvan historian, who canst thus express A flowery tale more sweetly than our rhyme: What leaf-fring'd legend haunts about thy shape Of deities or mortals, or of both, In Tempe or the dales of Arcady? What men or gods are these? What maidens loth? What mad pursuit? What struggle to escape? What pipes and timbrels? What wild ecstasy? Heard melodies are sweet, but those unheard Are sweeter; therefore, ye soft pipes, play on; Not to the sensual ear, but, more endear'd, Pipe to the spirit ditties of no tone: Fair youth, beneath the trees, thou canst not leave Thy song, nor ever can those trees be bare; Bold Lover, never, never canst thou kiss, Though winning near the goal yet, do not grieve; She cannot fade, though thou hast not thy bliss, For ever wilt thou love, and she be fair! Ah, happy, happy boughs! that cannot shed Your leaves, nor ever bid the Spring adieu; And, happy melodist, unwearied, For ever piping songs for ever new; More happy love! more happy, happy love! For ever warm and still to be enjoy'd, For ever panting, and for ever young; All breathing human passion far above, That leaves a heart high-sorrowful and cloy'd, A burning forehead, and a parching tongue. Who are these coming to the sacrifice? To what green altar, O mysterious priest, Lead'st thou that heifer lowing at the skies, And all her silken flanks with garlands drest? What little town by river or sea shore, Or mountain-built with peaceful citadel, Is emptied of this folk, this pious morn? And, little town, thy streets for evermore Will silent be; and not a soul to tell Why thou art desolate, can e'er return. O Attic shape! Fair attitude! with brede Of marble men and maidens overwrought, With forest branches and the trodden weed; Thou, silent form, dost tease us out of thought As doth eternity: Cold Pastoral! When old age shall this generation waste, Thou shalt remain, in midst of other woe Than ours, a friend to man, to whom thou say'st, "Beauty is truth, truth beauty,--that is all Ye know on earth, and all ye need to know."

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and draw pictures with her crayons. One day, she was drawing a square when her big brother came in.

"Hey Lily, be careful with those crayons. They can make a big mess," warned her brother.

Lily didn't like when her brother was bossy, but she knew he was trying to help. She continued to draw her square and then showed it to her brother.

"Look, I drew a square! Do you like it?" Lily asked.

Her brother smiled and said, "Wow, that's really good! You're getting better at drawing."

Lily was happy that her brother liked her drawing. From that day on, she made sure to be careful with her crayons and listen when her brother warned her about things.

Once upon a time, there was a big jungle. In the jungle, there were many animals like monkeys, lions, and elephants. One day, a little boy named Timmy went to the jungle to meet the animals. He saw the monkeys swinging from tree to tree and the lions sleeping in the sun. 

Timmy wanted to make friends with the animals, so he decided to tidy up the jungle. He picked up all the leaves and branches on the ground and put them in a pile. The animals saw Timmy working hard and were impressed. They decided to help him tidy up the jungle too. 

Together, Timmy and the animals made the jungle look very tidy. They all became friends and played together in the jungle every day. Timmy was very happy to have met such wonderful new friends in the jungle.

name_of_work: The Wind by Robert Louis Stevenson
content: I saw you toss the kites on high And blow the birds about the sky; And all around I heard you pass, Like ladies' skirts across the grass- O wind, a-blowing all day long! 5 O wind, that sings so loud a song! I saw the different things you did, But always you yourself you hid. I felt you push, I heard you call, I could not see yourself at all- 10 O wind, a-blowing all day long, O wind, that sings so loud a song! O you that are so strong and cold, O blower, are you young or old? Are you a beast of field and tree, 15 Or just a stronger child than me?
