Tom was a lazy cat. He liked to sleep all day on the sofa. He did not like to play with his toys or run after mice. He only woke up when he was hungry or thirsty.

One day, Tom saw a string on the floor. It was red and shiny and long. Tom felt curious. He wanted to touch the string. He got off the sofa and walked slowly to the string.

But when he got close, the string moved. It went under the table and then out again. Tom was surprised. He followed the string with his eyes. He wanted to catch it.

The string moved again. It went up the stairs and then down again. Tom was excited. He ran after the string. He tried to jump on it and bite it.

But the string was too fast. It went into a room and then out again. Tom was tired. He stopped and panted.

Then he saw who was holding the string. It was Lily, his little human friend. She was laughing and smiling. She had been playing with Tom all along.

Tom felt happy. He liked Lily. He ran to her and rubbed his head on her leg. Lily hugged him and said, "Good boy, Tom. You are not so lazy after all. You are a fun cat. Do you want to play some more?"

Tom nodded and purred. He liked to play with Lily and the string. He forgot about the sofa and the sleep. He had a new game and a new friend.

Once there was a little bird who was feeling very lonely in the evening. He looked around and he could not find a single friend to play with. He felt so alone and sad, that he had to find something to do. All of a sudden he saw a star twinkling in the night sky! He was so very surprised, that his sadness had been replaced with a sense of joy.

He flew closer to the star and something unexpected happened. He saw he wasn't alone there! There were other birds that were playing together in the night sky. He felt so excited, that he did not hesistate to join them in a game of tag.

He spent the evening playing with his new friends and the loneliness had been replaced with joy. He was not alone anymore!

The little bird learned an important lesson that night. Even when you feel like you have no one to turn to, you should always look to the sky and remember there are always new friends near.

Alice was very excited when she arrived at the park. She could hear the birds singing and see the flowers blooming. She ran to the playground and began to play.

Suddenly, Alice noticed a cool image painted on the wall of the playground. She stopped in awe and asked her mother, "What is it mama?" Her mother smiled and said, "It's an image of a big, strong fish jumping out of the sea."
 
Alice nodded and asked her mother, "Can I be like the fish and jump?" Her mother nodded and said, "Yes. But first, you need to practice. Do you want to practice now?" Alice nodded and began to practice.

At first, Alice struggled to jump. But then she saw the cool image again and she was inspired. She mustered her courage and jumped. She was so happy when she landed that she jumped again and again. Finally, she leapt as high as the cool image of the fish on the wall.

Alice's mother watched in delight and said, "Now you can jump like the strong fish." Alice nodded proudly as she looked at the image on the wall and smiled.

Ollie was having a picnic in the garden with his aunt. They were laughing and having a great time until Ollie accidentally dropped the delicate glass his aunt had brought out. It shattered into a thousand pieces. His aunt was not happy.

"Ollie, why did you do that?" Aunt asked. 

Ollie looked sadly at the broken glass and said he was sorry.

Aunt sighed and said, "Things can be so delicate. We need to be more careful."

The picnic was over. Aunt said it was time for Ollie to go home. Ollie said goodbye and went home feeling sad. He had ruined the day and disappointed his aunt.

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. They run, jump, slide and swing. They have fun.

One day, Lily and Ben see a new boy in the park. He has a big red ball. He looks sad. Lily and Ben want to play with him.

They go to the new boy and say hello. They ask him his name. He says his name is Sam. He says he is new in town. He says he has no friends.

Lily and Ben say they can be his friends. They ask him if he wants to play with them. He says yes. He smiles.

They share the big red ball. They play catch, kick and roll. They laugh. They have more fun.

Lily, Ben and Sam become good friends. They play in the park every day. They are happy.

But one day, Sam says he has to go. He says his dad has a new job in another town. He says he has to part with Lily and Ben.

Lily and Ben are sad. They hug Sam. They say they will miss him. They say they will always be his friends.

Sam hugs Lily and Ben. He says he will miss them too. He says he will always remember them. He says they are the best part of his youth.

They say goodbye. Sam leaves with his dad. Lily and Ben watch him go. They cry.

They hope they will see Sam again. They hope he will find new friends. They hope he will be happy. They hope they will be happy too.

name_of_work: Nine Gold Medals by David Roth
content: The athletes had come from all over the country To run for the gold, for the silver and bronze Many weeks and months of training All coming down to these games. The spectators gathered around the old field To cheer on all the young women and men The final event of the day was approaching Excitement grew high to begin. The blocks were all lined up for those who would use them The hundred-yard dash and the race to be run These were nine resolved athletes in back of the starting line Poised for the sound of the gun. The signal was given, the pistol exploded And so did the runners all charging ahead But the smallest among them, he stumbled and staggered And fell to the asphalt instead. He gave out a cry in frustration and anguish His dreams and his efforts all dashed in the dirt But as sure as I'm standing here telling this story The same goes for what next occurred. The eight other runners pulled up on their heels The ones who had trained for so long to compete One by one they all turned around and went back to help him And brought the young boy to his feet. Then all the nine runners joined hands and continued The hundred-yard dash now reduced to a walk And a banner above that said (Special Olympics) Could not have been more on the mark. That's how the race ended, with nine gold medals They came to the finish line holding hands still And a standing ovation and nine beaming faces Said more than these words ever will.

Lila and Ben were twins who liked to play in the forest. They saw many trees, birds and animals. One day, they found a big pine tree with many cones. Lila wanted to eat the cones, but Ben said no.

"Why not?" Lila asked. "They look yummy and crunchy."

"Because they are not food for us," Ben said. "They are food for the squirrels and the birds. If we eat them, we take away their food. That is not fair."

Lila did not listen. She picked a cone and bit it. It was hard and bitter. She spat it out and made a face. "Blech! This is not yummy at all!"

Ben laughed. "I told you so. Now you know why we should not eat the cones. They are not good for us, and they are good for the animals. We should share the forest with them and be fair."

Lila nodded. She felt sorry for being greedy. She put the cone back on the ground. "You are right, Ben. I am sorry. I will not eat the cones again. I will share the forest with the animals and be fair."

They hugged and went to look for other things to play with. They saw a berry bush and picked some berries. They were sweet and juicy. They ate some and left some for the birds. They were happy and fair.

Ben liked to surf. He had a big board that his dad gave him. He went to the beach every day with his dad and his dog. They had a lot of fun in the water.

One day, Ben saw a big boat on the water. It was shiny and white. It had a lot of people on it. They looked wealthy. They had nice clothes and hats and glasses. They had a lot of things on the boat. Ben wondered what they were doing.

Ben's dad told him that they were supplying things to the island. The island was far away and had no shops. The people on the island needed food and water and clothes and toys. The boat was helping them. Ben thought that was nice.

Ben wanted to see the island. He asked his dad if they could go there. His dad said maybe one day. He said it was too far and too dangerous for them. He said they had to stay close to the shore. Ben was sad. He wanted to go on an adventure.

The next day, Ben had an idea. He took his board and his dog and went to the beach. He did not tell his dad. He waited for the boat to come. He saw it on the horizon. He paddled towards it. He wanted to see what they were supplying. He wanted to see the island. He did not think of the waves or the wind or the sharks. He did not think of his dad or his home. He only thought of the boat and the island.

He did not know that he was making a big mistake. He did not know that the boat was not nice. He did not know that the people on the boat were not wealthy. He did not know that they were not supplying things to the island. He did not know that they were stealing things from the island. He did not know that they had guns and knives and ropes. He did not know that they would see him and his dog. He did not know that they would catch him and his dog. He did not know that they would take him and his dog to the island. He did not know that he would never see his dad again. He did not know that he would regret his idea. He did not know that he would cry and scream and beg. He did not know that he would wish he had listened to his dad. He did not know that he would miss his home. He did not know that he would hate the boat and the island. He did not know that he would be sorry. He did not know. He did not know. He did not know.

In the midnight heavens burning Thro' ethereal deeps afar, Once I watch'd with restless yearning An alluring, aureate star; Ev'ry eye aloft returning, Gleaming nigh the Arctic car. Mystic waves of beauty blended With the gorgeous golden rays; Phantasies of bliss descended In a myrrh'd Elysian haze; And in lyre-born chords extended Harmonies of Lydian lays. There (thought I) lies scenes of pleasure, Where the free and blessed dwell, And each moment bears a treasure Freighted with a lotus-spell, And there floats a liquid measure From the lute of Israfel. There (I told myself) were shining Worlds of happiness unknown, Peace and Innocence entwining By the Crowned Virtue's throne; Men of light, their thoughts refining Purer, fairer, than our own. Thus I mus'd, when o'er the vision Crept a red delirious change; Hope dissolving to derision, Beauty to distortion strange; Hymnic chords in weird collision, Spectral sights in endless range. Crimson burn'd the star of sadness As behind the beams I peer'd; All was woe that seem'd but gladness Ere my gaze with truth was sear'd; Cacodaemons, mir'd with madness, Thro' the fever'd flick'ring leer'd. Now I know the fiendish fable That the golden glitter bore; Now I shun the spangled sable That I watch'd and lov'd before; But the horror, set and stable, Haunts my soul for evermore.

Once there was a brave knight who had a big, shiny shield. He was a fierce protector to the town he lived in. One day he was riding off to battle when an old woman stopped him.

The woman said, "Please, kind knight. I am so hungry. Could you please help me?"

The knight felt bad for the old woman and he wanted to help. He took out a piece of bread from his bag.

The knight said, "Here, take this and feed yourself." 

The old woman was overjoyed and thanked the knight for his kindness. She said, "Thank you for feeding me and for protecting our town with your fierce shield!" 

The knight smiled and rode away, content that he had helped the old woman. He felt sure that his fierce shield would always protect the town and its people.

Lily was sleeping in her bed. She had a dream about flying with her friends. She felt happy and free in the air. But then she heard a loud noise. It was a pigeon. The pigeon was tapping on her window. Lily opened her eyes and saw the pigeon. It was gray and white, with a red ring on its leg.

"Hello, pigeon," Lily said. "Why are you here?"

The pigeon cooed and tilted its head. It looked at Lily with its black eyes. It seemed to want something from her.

"Are you hungry, pigeon?" Lily asked. "Do you want some bread?"

Lily got out of her bed and went to the kitchen. She found some bread and broke it into small pieces. She took the bread and went back to her window. She opened the window and threw some bread to the pigeon. The pigeon ate the bread and thanked Lily with a coo.

"Where do you come from, pigeon?" Lily asked. "Do you have a home?"

The pigeon cooed again and pointed with its wing. It showed Lily a tall building with many windows. It was far away from Lily's house. It was an unknown place to Lily.

"That's where you live, pigeon?" Lily asked. "It looks very big and busy. Do you have friends there?"

The pigeon nodded and flapped its wings. It seemed to be happy in its home. But it also liked Lily and her bread.

"Can you come back and visit me, pigeon?" Lily asked. "I like you. You are a nice pigeon."

The pigeon smiled and nodded. It agreed to come back and visit Lily. It flew away and waved with its wing. Lily waved back and closed the window. She felt happy and warm. She had made a new friend. She went back to her bed and fell asleep. She dreamed about flying with the pigeon.

One day, a big rhinoceros went for a walk. He had a hard, strong body. He walked and walked until he saw a little bird. The bird was singing a nice song. The rhinoceros liked the song and wanted to speak to the bird.

"Hi, bird!" said the rhinoceros. "I like your song. Can you teach me to sing like you?" The bird looked at the rhinoceros and said, "Sure, I can help you. But your voice is very big and loud. Let's try to make it soft and nice like mine."

The rhinoceros and the bird tried to sing together. The rhinoceros tried very hard to make his voice soft and nice. But it was still big and loud. The bird did not give up. They tried and tried until the rhinoceros' voice became softer and nicer.

In the end, the rhinoceros and the bird sang a beautiful song together. They were very happy and became good friends. They spent their days singing and playing together, and everyone loved to listen to their songs.

name_of_work: In My Craft Or Sullen Art by Dylan Thomas
content: In my craft or sullen art Exercised in the still night When only the moon rages And the lovers lie abed With all their griefs in their arms, I labour by singing light Not for ambition or bread Or the strut and trade of charms On the ivory stages But for the common wages Of their most secret heart. Not for the proud man apart From the raging moon I write On these spindrift pages Nor for the towering dead With their nightingales and psalms But for the lovers, their arms Round the griefs of the ages, Who pay no praise or wages Nor heed my craft or art.

Once upon a time there was a mixer. It was big and yellow, and lovely. The mixer was in a big rush. It whizzed and spun around and around. 

One day the mixer was hurrying about in the kitchen, making a big mess. Then, it heard a happy voice. It was a little girl who was standing in the kitchen. She said, "Hi Mixer. Can you make me something yummy and lovely?"

The mixer was so excited. It started to move faster than ever before. It hurried to mix all of the ingredients until they were just right. The little girl was delighted. She had a big smile on her face.

The mixer was super happy that it could help the little girl. It was even more happy when it saw how much she enjoyed the lovely treat that it had made for her. The little girl thanked the mixer and said, "You're the best!"

The mixer smiled. It knew that it had done a good job, and that it had made someone very happy. It was certainly glad that it had hurried to help the little girl.

name_of_work: Sonnet--To Science by Edgar Allen Poe
content: Science! true daughter of Old Time thou art! Who alterest all things with thy peering eyes. Why preyest thou thus upon the poet's heart, Vulture, whose wings are dull realities? How should he love thee? or how deem thee wise, Who wouldst not leave him in his wandering To seek for treasure in the jewelled skies, Albeit he soared with an undaunted wing? Hast thou not dragged Diana from her car, And driven the Hamadryad from the wood To seek a shelter in some happier star? Hast thou not torn the Naiad from her flood, The Elfin from the green grass, and from me The summer dream beneath the tamarind tree?

The sun was shining and the birds were singing. Max wanted to get outside and have some fun. His mom said, "Let's go to the ranch!" Max couldn't wait.

When they arrived to the ranch, Max was so excited. He ran around, looking at all the animals. He petted a sweet little horse and saw a few cows.

Max's mom said, "Let's go get an ice cream!" Max was so excited he jumped up and down. They got two scoops of ice cream and walked back to the ranch.

Max ate his ice cream and smiled. It was so sweet and delicious. He couldn't wait to come back the next day and do it all over again!

Once, a little girl named Lily was going to school. She was very happy. She saw her friend Tom. Tom had a big red ball. Lily wanted to play with the ball too. But Tom did not want to share. Tom seemed mean.

Lily felt sad and walked away. She found a teacher and told her about Tom. The teacher talked to Tom. Tom felt ashamed. He knew he should share with his friends. Sharing is good.

Tom went to Lily and said sorry. He gave her the ball to play with. They both played with the ball and had fun. Lily and Tom became best friends. They learned that sharing makes everyone happy.

To cure myself of wanting Cuban songs, I wrote a Cuban song about the need For people to suppress their fantasies, Especially unhealthy ones. The song Began by making reference to the sea, Because the sea is like a need so great And deep it never can be swallowed. Then The song explores some common myths But the Cuban people and their folklore: The story of a little Carib boy Mistakenly abandoned to the sea; The legend of a bird who wanted song So desperately he gave up flight; a queen Whose strength was greater than a rival king's. The song goes on about morality, And then there is a line about the sea, How deep it is, how many creatures need Its nourishment, how beautiful it is To need. The song is ending now, because I cannot bear to hear it any longer. I call this song of needful love my voice.

Nothing is so beautiful as Spring - When weeds, in wheels, shoot long and lovely and lush; Thrush's eggs look little low heavens, and thrush Through the echoing timber does so rinse and wring The ear, it strikes like lightnings to hear him sing; The glassy peartree leaves and blooms, they brush The descending blue; that blue is all in a rush With richness; the racing lambs too have fair their fling. What is all this juice and all this joy? A strain of the earth's sweet being in the beginning In Eden garden. - Have, get, before it cloy, Before it cloud, Christ, lord, and sour with sinning, Innocent mind and Mayday in girl and boy, Most, O maid's child, thy choice and worthy the winning.

Tyger Tyger, burning bright, In the forests of the night; What immortal hand or eye, Could frame thy fearful symmetry? In what distant deeps or skies. Burnt the fire of thine eyes? On what wings dare he aspire? What the hand, dare seize the fire? And what shoulder, & what art, Could twist the sinews of thy heart? And when thy heart began to beat, What dread hand? & what dread feet? What the hammer? what the chain, In what furnace was thy brain? What the anvil? what dread grasp, Dare its deadly terrors clasp! When the stars threw down their spears And water'd heaven with their tears: Did he smile his work to see? Did he who made the Lamb make thee? Tyger Tyger burning bright, In the forests of the night: What immortal hand or eye, Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

name_of_work: The Night of the Scorpion by Nissim Ezekiel
content: I remember the night my mother was stung by a scorpion. Ten hours of steady rain had driven him to crawl beneath a sack of rice. Parting with his poison - flash of diabolic tail in the dark room - he risked the rain again. The peasants came like swarms of flies and buzzed the name of God a hundred times to paralyse the Evil One. With candles and with lanterns throwing giant scorpion shadows on the mud-baked walls they searched for him: he was not found. They clicked their tongues. With every movement that the scorpion made his poison moved in Mother's blood, they said. May he sit still, they said May the sins of your previous birth be burned away tonight, they said. May your suffering decrease the misfortunes of your next birth, they said. May the sum of all evil balanced in this unreal world against the sum of good become diminished by your pain. May the poison purify your flesh of desire, and your spirit of ambition, they said, and they sat around on the floor with my mother in the centre, the peace of understanding on each face. More candles, more lanterns, more neighbours, more insects, and the endless rain. My mother twisted through and through, groaning on a mat. My father, sceptic, rationalist, trying every curse and blessing, powder, mixture, herb and hybrid. He even poured a little paraffin upon the bitten toe and put a match to it. I watched the flame feeding on my mother. I watched the holy man perform his rites to tame the poison with an incantation. After twenty hours it lost its sting. My mother only said Thank God the scorpion picked on me And spared my children.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She loved to play on her swing in the park. One day, she saw a boy playing on a board. She went over to him and asked, "Can I play too?" The boy said, "Yes, you can."

Lily was happy and started to play on the board. She swung back and forth, feeling the wind in her hair. The boy said, "You're very good at this. You should come and play with us more often."

Lily was so excited to have new friends. She went home and told her mom about her fun day. Her mom said, "That sounds great, Lily. But remember to keep your room tidy before you go out to play."

The next day, Lily went back to the park to play with her new friends. But when she got there, she saw that the boy had broken the board. She was sad and said, "Oh no! What happened?" The boy said, "I don't know. It just broke."

Lily knew she couldn't play on the broken board. She went home and cried, telling her mom what happened. Her mom said, "I'm sorry, Lily. But sometimes things break and we can't fix them." Lily learned that sometimes things don't go the way we want them to, but that's okay.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a small hut in the forest with her mommy and daddy. The hut was cozy and had a warm light inside.

One day, Lily went for a walk in the forest. She saw a pretty flower and wanted to pick it. But then a big, scary man came and stole her flower! Lily was very sad and ran back to her hut to tell her mommy and daddy what happened.

Lily's mommy and daddy were very upset. They told her that stealing is bad and that the man did a very mean thing. Lily was still sad and wished she could get her flower back. But sadly, she never saw the man or her flower again. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a man and a woman who were married. They were arguing with each other and soon they were quarrel ing. The man had an old axe and he was holding it in his hand.

The woman saw this and she started to get scared. She said, "Why do you have the axe?"
The man said, "I am going to use it to chop the wood."
The woman said, "Be careful with the axe. It looks old and broken."

The man nodded and said, "Don't worry, I will be careful." He took the axe and went outside to chop the wood. He carefully used the axe and was able to chop a lot of wood. 

The man and woman were now happy and the argument was forgotten. They hugged each other and were friends again.

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play with toys and talk to each other. One day, they find a big box with many labels on it. The labels have words and pictures of different things.

"What is this?" Lily asks.

"Let's open it and see," Ben says.

They open the box and see many colorful blocks. Some blocks have letters, some have numbers, and some have shapes. They are happy and start to build with the blocks.

"I can make a house," Lily says.

"I can make a car," Ben says.

They talk and share the blocks. They have fun.

But then, Tom comes. Tom is bigger and older than Lily and Ben. He sees the box and the blocks.

"Hey, these are mine!" Tom says.

He takes the box and the blocks from Lily and Ben. He does not ask or say please. He is rude and mean.

"Give them back!" Lily and Ben say.

"No, they are mine. I am powerful. You are small and weak. Go away!" Tom says.

He pushes Lily and Ben. He laughs and starts to build with the blocks. He does not share or talk. He is selfish and lonely.

Lily and Ben are sad and angry. They want to play with the blocks. They do not like Tom.

But then, they see a big label on the box. The label has words and a picture of a man. The words say: "To Lily and Ben, from Grandpa. I hope you enjoy these blocks. They are for you to learn and have fun. Remember to be kind and generous to others. Love, Grandpa."

Lily and Ben smile. They know Grandpa loves them. They know the blocks are theirs. They know Tom is wrong.

They go to Tom and show him the label.

"Look, Tom. This is our box. Our Grandpa gave it to us. He wants us to be kind and generous to others. You are not kind or generous. You are rude and mean. You should not take things that are not yours. You should say sorry and give them back," Lily says.

"Yeah, Tom. You are not powerful. You are selfish and lonely. You do not have friends. You do not have fun. You should be nice and share. You should talk and play with us," Ben says.

Tom looks at the label. He feels ashamed and sorry. He knows Lily and Ben are right. He knows he was wrong.

He gives the box and the blocks back to Lily and Ben. He says sorry and please. He is polite and humble.

"Can I play with you?" Tom asks.

"Sure, Tom. You can play with us. But you have to be kind and generous. You have to share and talk. You have to be a good friend," Lily and Ben say.

They teach Tom how to play with the blocks. They talk and share. They have fun.

They are happy and friendly. They are powerful.

name_of_work: Touched By An Angel by Maya Angelou
content: We, unaccustomed to courage exiles from delight live coiled in shells of loneliness until love leaves its high holy temple and comes into our sight to liberate us into life. Love arrives and in its train come ecstasies old memories of pleasure ancient histories of pain. Yet if we are bold, love strikes away the chains of fear from our souls. We are weaned from our timidity In the flush of love's light we dare be brave And suddenly we see that love costs all we are and will ever be. Yet it is only love which sets us free

name_of_work: How the Grinch stole Christmas by Dr. Seuss
content: Every Who down in Whoville liked Christmas a lot. But the Grinch who lived just North of Whoville did not! The Grinch hated Christmas! The whole Christmas season! Now, please don't ask why. No one quite knows the reason. It could be, perhaps, that his shoes were too tight. It could be his head wasn't screwed on just right. But I think that the most likely reason of all May have been that his heart was two sizes too small. But, whatever the reason, his heart or his shoes, He stood there on Christmas Eve hating the Whos, Staring down from his cave with a sour, Grinchy frown At the warm lighted windows below in their town, For he knew every Who down in Whoville beneath Was busy now hanging a hollywho wreath. "And they're hanging their stockings," he snarled with a sneer. "Tomorrow is Christmas! It's practically here!" Then he growled, with his Grinch fingers nervously drumming, "I must find some way to keep Christmas from coming! For, tomorrow, I know all the Who girls and boys Will wake bright and early. They'll rush for their toys! And then! Oh, the noise! Oh, the noise! Noise! Noise! Noise! There's one thing I hate! All the NOISE! NOISE! NOISE! NOISE! [...] They'll stand close together, with Christmas bells ringing. They'll stand hand-in-hand, and those Whos will start singing!" Fahoo forays, dahoo dorays Welcome Christmas! Come this way Fahoo forays, dahoo dorays Welcome Christmas, Christmas Day Welcome, welcome, fahoo ramus Welcome, welcome, dahoo damus Christmas Day is in our grasp So long as we have hands to clasp Fahoo forays, dahoo dorays... "And they'll sing! And they'll sing! And they'll SING! SING! SING! SING!" And the more the Grinch thought of this Who Christmas Sing, The more the Grinch thought, "I must stop this whole thing! Why for fifty-three years I've put up with it now! I must stop Christmas from coming! But how?" Then he got an idea! An awful idea! The Grinch got a wonderful, awful idea! "I know just what to do!" The Grinch laughed in his throat. "I'll make a quick Santy Claus hat and a coat." [...] "This is stop number one," the old Grinchy Claus hissed, As he climbed to the roof, empty bags in his fist. Then he slid down the chimney, a rather tight pinch. But if Santa could do it, then so could the Grinch. He got stuck only once, for a minute or two. Then he stuck his head out of the fireplace flue Where the little Who stockings hung all in a row. "These stockings," he grinched, "are the first things to go!" Then he slithered and slunk, with a smile most unpleasant, Around the whole room, and he took every present! [...] It was quarter of dawn. All the Whos still a-bed, All the Whos still a-snooze, when he packed up his sled, Packed it up with their presents, their ribbons, their wrappings, Their snoof and their fuzzles, their tringlers and trappings! Ten thousand feet up, up the side of Mount Crumpet, He rode with his load to the tiptop to dump it! "Pooh-pooh to the Whos!" he was grinchily humming. "They're finding out now that no Christmas is coming! They're just waking up! I know just what they'll do! Their mouths will hang open a minute or two Then the Whos down in Whoville will all cry boo-hoo! That's a noise," grinned the Grinch, "that I simply must hear!" He paused, and the Grinch put a hand to his ear. And he did hear a sound rising over the snow. It started in low, then it started to grow. But this sound wasn't sad! Why, this sound sounded glad! Every Who down in Whoville, the tall and the small, Was singing without any presents at all! He hadn't stopped Christmas from coming! It came! Somehow or other, it came just the same! And the Grinch, with his grinch feet ice-cold in the snow, Stood puzzling and puzzling. "How could it be so? It came without ribbons! It came without tags! It came without packages, boxes, or bags!" He puzzled and puzzed till his puzzler was sore. Then the Grinch thought of something he hadn't before. Maybe Christmas, he thought, doesn't come from a store. Maybe Christmas, perhaps, means a little bit more! And what happened then? Well, in Whoville they say That the Grinch's small heart grew three sizes that day! And then the true meaning of Christmas came through, And the Grinch found the strength of ten Grinches, plus two! And now that his heart didn't feel quite so tight, He whizzed with his load through the bright morning light With a smile to his soul, he descended Mount Crumpet Cheerily blowing "Who! Who!" on his trumpet. He rode into Whoville. He brought back their toys. He brought back their floof to the Who girls and boys. He brought back their snoof and their tringlers and fuzzles, Brought back their pantookas, their dafflers and wuzzles. He brought everything back, all the food for the feast! And he, he himself, the Grinch carved the roast beast! Welcome Christmas. Bring your cheer, Cheer to all Whos, far and near. Christmas Day is in our grasp So long as we have hands to grasp. Christmas Day will always be Just as long as we have we. Welcome Christmas while we stand Heart to heart and hand in hand.

name_of_work: A Woman's Last Word by Robert Browning
content: I. Let's contend no more, Love, Strive nor weep: All be as before, Love, ---Only sleep! II. What so wild as words are? I and thou In debate, as birds are, Hawk on bough! III. See the creature stalking While we speak! Hush and hide the talking, Cheek on cheek! IV. What so false as truth is, False to thee? Where the serpent's tooth is Shun the tree--- V. Where the apple reddens Never pry--- Lest we lose our Edens, Eve and I. VI. Be a god and hold me With a charm! Be a man and fold me With thine arm! VII. Teach me, only teach, Love As I ought I will speak thy speech, Love, Think thy thought--- VIII. Meet, if thou require it, Both demands, Laying flesh and spirit In thy hands. IX. That shall be to-morrow Not to-night: I must bury sorrow Out of sight: X ---Must a little weep, Love, (Foolish me!) And so fall asleep, Love, Loved by thee.

Bare-handed, I hand the combs. The man in white smiles, bare-handed, Our cheesecloth gauntlets neat and sweet, The throats of our wrists brave lilies. He and I Have a thousand clean cells between us, Eight combs of yellow cups, And the hive itself a teacup, White with pink flowers on it, With excessive love I enameled it Thinking "Sweetness, sweetness." Brood cells gray as the fossils of shells Terrify me, they seem so old. What am I buying, wormy mahogany? Is there any queen at all in it? If there is, she is old, Her wings torn shawls, her long body Rubbed of its plush-- Poor and bare and unqueenly and even shameful. I stand in a column Of winged, unmiraculous women, Honey-drudgers. I am no drudge Though for years I have eaten dust And dried plates with my dense hair. And seen my strangeness evaporate, Blue dew from dangerous skin. Will they hate me, These women who only scurry, Whose news is the open cherry, the open clover? It is almost over. I am in control. Here is my honey-machine, It will work without thinking, Opening, in spring, like an industrious virgin To scour the creaming crests As the moon, for its ivory powders, scours the sea. A third person is watching. He has nothing to do with the bee-seller or with me. Now he is gone In eight great bounds, a great scapegoat. Here is his slipper, here is another, And here the square of white linen He wore instead of a hat. He was sweet, The sweat of his efforts a rain Tugging the world to fruit. The bees found him out, Molding onto his lips like lies, Complicating his features. They thought death was worth it, but I Have a self to recover, a queen. Is she dead, is she sleeping? Where has she been, With her lion-red body, her wings of glass? Now she is flying More terrible than she ever was, red Scar in the sky, red comet Over the engine that killed her-- The mausoleum, the wax house

Once upon a time, there lived two friends in a small village. Their names were Paul and Matt. They were very good friends and they loved to play football together. One day they got into a quarrel and decided to play a game of football to decide who was right. 

Paul kicked the ball really hard and it flew really high in the air. But Matt was too slow and the ball went over his head. The ball flew so high, it landed in a deep river. 

The two friends were not able to get the ball out. They tried and tried but the river was too deep. They were both very sad and promised each other to never quarrel again.

My black face fades, hiding inside the black granite. I said I wouldn't dammit: No tears. I'm stone. I'm flesh. My clouded reflection eyes me like a bird of prey, the profile of night slanted against morning. I turn this way--the stone lets me go. I turn that way--I'm inside the Vietnam Veterans Memorial again, depending on the light to make a difference. I go down the 58,022 names, half-expecting to find my own in letters like smoke. I touch the name Andrew Johnson; I see the booby trap's white flash. Names shimmer on a woman's blouse but when she walks away the names stay on the wall. Brushstrokes flash, a red bird's wings cutting across my stare. The sky. A plane in the sky. A white vet's image floats closer to me, then his pale eyes look through mine. I'm a window. He's lost his right arm inside the stone. In the black mirror a woman's trying to erase names: No, she's brushing a boy's hair.

Oliver was having a mighty difficult time. His parents disagreed about painting their house. His mom wanted to paint it blue, but his dad only wanted to paint it green. Oliver had an idea - to paint the chimney both blue and green!

He ran to his mom and dad and suggested it. His dad disagreed and wanted to keep painting it green. But his mom thought it was a great idea. With a little bit of negotiation they decided that they would paint the chimney blue green!

They went to the shop to buy the paint. Very soon the mighty chimney was looking like a rainbow with blue and green stripes. It became a special part of the house.

Oliver was so happy he had solved the problem. His parents were both happy too and hugged him. From now on, whenever Oliver saw the chimney he knew that he had solved the disagreement!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Suzy. She lived with her daddy in a big house in the city.

One day, Suzy was playing in her room. Suddenly, she heard her father crying. She was scared and went to see what was wrong.

When she found her daddy, he had a sad look on his face. He told Suzy, "I decided I don't want to stay here anymore." Suzy was really hurt. She asked, "Why, Daddy?" 

Her father replied, "Because living here makes me too sad. I need to find a new place to live."

Suzy gave her daddy a big hug and said, "I love you even if you decide to move away. Please come visit me often." Daddy was happy to hear this, and he smiled at Suzy. 

The next day, Suzy's daddy moved away and Suzy was very sad. But she was happy that he had decided to do something that would make him feel better.

Once there was a mommy and a baby. Mommy was very tired, so she decided to take a seat in the park. She sat down on the bench and closed her eyes. 

Suddenly the baby heard a noise. He opened his eyes and saw a beautiful rose. The rose was so pretty, it made the baby smile! He showed it to his mommy, who opened her eyes and smiled too. 

Mommy took the rose and smelled it. She said it smelt sweet and lovely. The baby was so excited he sat down next to mommy and showed her how pretty the rose was. 

Mommy was so tired she decided to take a nap, so she lay down on the bench and fell asleep. The baby was still so excited about the rose that he stayed seated next to mommy and talked to the rose until it was time to go home.

name_of_work: At an Inn by Thomas Hardy
content: WHEN we as strangers sought Their catering care, Veiled smiles bespoke their thought Of what we were. They warmed as they opined Us more than friends-- That we had all resigned For love's dear ends. And that swift sympathy With living love Which quicks the world--maybe The spheres above, Made them our ministers, Moved them to say, "Ah, God, that bliss like theirs Would flush our day!" And we were left alone As Love's own pair; Yet never the love-light shone Between us there! But that which chilled the breath Of afternoon, And palsied unto death The pane-fly's tune. The kiss their zeal foretold, And now deemed come, Came not: within his hold Love lingered numb. Why cast he on our port A bloom not ours? Why shaped us for his sport In after-hours? As we seemed we were not That day afar, And now we seem not what We aching are. O severing sea and land, O laws of men, Ere death, once let us stand As we stood then!

name_of_work: Absent from thee by John Wilmot
content: Absent from thee I languish still; Then ask me not, when I return? The straying fool 'twill plainly kill To wish all day, all night to mourn. Dear! from thine arms then let me fly, That my fantastic mind may prove The torments it deserves to try That tears my fixed heart from my love. When, wearied with a world of woe, To thy safe bosom I retire where love and peace and truth does flow, May I contented there expire,Lest, once more wandering from that heaven, I fall on some base heart unblest, Faithless to thee, false, unforgiven, And lose my everlasting rest.

1. Is it winter again, is it cold again, didn't Frank just slip on the ice, didn't he heal, weren't the spring seeds planted didn't the night end, didn't the melting ice flood the narrow gutters wasn't my body rescued, wasn't it safe didn't the scar form, invisible above the injury terror and cold, didn't they just end, wasn't the back garden harrowed and planted-- I remember how the earth felt, red and dense, in stiff rows, weren't the seeds planted, didn't vines climb the south wall I can't hear your voice for the wind's cries, whistling over the bare ground I no longer care what sound it makes when was I silenced, when did it first seem pointless to describe that sound what it sounds like can't change what it is-- didn't the night end, wasn't the earth safe when it was planted didn't we plant the seeds, weren't we necessary to the earth, the vines, were they harvested? 2. Summer after summer has ended, balm after violence: it does me no good to be good to me now; violence has changed me. Daybreak. The low hills shine ochre and fire, even the fields shine. I know what I see; sun that could be the August sun, returning everything that was taken away-- You hear this voice? This is my mind's voice; you can't touch my body now. It has changed once, it has hardened, don't ask it to respond again. A day like a day in summer. Exceptionally still. The long shadows of the maples nearly mauve on the gravel paths. And in the evening, warmth. Night like a night in summer. It does me no good; violence has changed me. My body has grown cold like the stripped fields; now there is only my mind, cautious and wary, with the sense it is being tested. Once more, the sun rises as it rose in summer; bounty, balm after violence. Balm after the leaves have changed, after the fields have been harvested and turned. Tell me this is the future, I won't believe you. Tell me I'm living, I won't believe you. 3. Snow had fallen. I remember music from an open window. Come to me, said the world. This is not to say it spoke in exact sentences but that I perceived beauty in this manner. Sunrise. A film of moisture on each living thing. Pools of cold light formed in the gutters. I stood at the doorway, ridiculous as it now seems. What others found in art, I found in nature. What others found in human love, I found in nature. Very simple. But there was no voice there. Winter was over. In the thawed dirt, bits of green were showing. Come to me, said the world. I was standing in my wool coat at a kind of bright portal-- I can finally say long ago; it gives me considerable pleasure. Beauty the healer, the teacher-- death cannot harm me more than you have harmed me, my beloved life. 4. The light has changed; middle C is tuned darker now. And the songs of morning sound over-rehearsed. This is the light of autumn, not the light of spring. The light of autumn: you will not be spared. The songs have changed; the unspeakable has entered them. This is the light of autumn, not the light that says I am reborn. Not the spring dawn: I strained, I suffered, I was delivered. This is the present, an allegory of waste. So much has changed. And still, you are fortunate: the ideal burns in you like a fever. Or not like a fever, like a second heart. The songs have changed, but really they are still quite beautiful. They have been concentrated in a smaller space, the space of the mind. They are dark, now, with desolation and anguish. And yet the notes recur. They hover oddly in anticipation of silence. The ear gets used to them. The eye gets used to disappearances. You will not be spared, nor will what you love be spared. A wind has come and gone, taking apart the mind; it has left in its wake a strange lucidity. How privileged you are, to be passionately clinging to what you love; the forfeit of hope has not destroyed you. Maestoso, doloroso: This is the light of autumn; it has turned on us. Surely it is a privilege to approach the end still believing in something. 5. It is true there is not enough beauty in the world. It is also true that I am not competent to restore it. Neither is there candor, and here I may be of some use. I am at work, though I am silent. The bland misery of the world bounds us on either side, an alley lined with trees; we are companions here, not speaking, each with his own thoughts; behind the trees, iron gates of the private houses, the shuttered rooms somehow deserted, abandoned, as though it were the artist's duty to create hope, but out of what? what? the word itself false, a device to refute perception-- At the intersection, ornamental lights of the season. I was young here. Riding the subway with my small book as though to defend myself against the same world: you are not alone, the poem said, in the dark tunnel. 6. The brightness of the day becomes the brightness of the night; the fire becomes the mirror. My friend the earth is bitter; I think sunlight has failed her. Bitter or weary, it is hard to say. Between herself and the sun, something has ended. She wants, now, to be left alone; I think we must give up turning to her for affirmation. Above the fields, above the roofs of the village houses, the brilliance that made all life possible becomes the cold stars. Lie still and watch: they give nothing but ask nothing. From within the earth's bitter disgrace, coldness and barrenness my friend the moon rises: she is beautiful tonight, but when is she not beautiful?

name_of_work: The Undertaker's Horse by Rudyard Kipling
content: The eldest son bestrides him, And the pretty daughter rides him, And I meet him oft o' mornings on the Course; And there kindles in my bosom An emotion chill and gruesome As I canter past the Undertaker's Horse. Neither shies he nor is restive, But a hideously suggestive Trot, professional and placid, he affects; And the cadence of his hoof-beats To my mind this grim reproof beats: -- "Mend your pace, my friend, I'm coming. Who's the next?" Ah! stud-bred of ill-omen, I have watched the strongest go -- men Of pith and might and muscle -- at your heels, Down the plantain-bordered highway, (Heaven send it ne'er be my way!) In a lacquered box and jetty upon wheels. Answer, sombre beast and dreary, Where is Brown, the young, the cheery, Smith, the pride of all his friends and half the Force? You were at that last dread dak We must cover at a walk, Bring them back to me, O Undertaker's Horse! With your mane unhogged and flowing, And your curious way of going, And that businesslike black crimping of your tail, E'en with Beauty on your back, Sir, Pacing as a lady's hack, Sir, What wonder when I meet you I turn pale? It may be you wait your time, Beast, Till I write my last bad rhyme, Beast -- Quit the sunlight, cut the rhyming, drop the glass -- Follow after with the others, Where some dusky heathen smothers Us with marigolds in lieu of English grass. Or, perchance, in years to follow, I shall watch your plump sides hollow, See Carnifex (gone lame) become a corse -- See old age at last o'erpower you, And the Station Pack devour you, I shall chuckle then, O Undertaker's Horse! But to insult, jibe, and quest, I've Still the hideously suggestive Trot that hammers out the unrelenting text, And I hear it hard behind me In what place soe'er I find me: -- "'Sure to catch you sooner or later. Who's the next?"

Lily liked to draw with her pencil. She had many colors of pencils, but her favorite was the red one. She drew flowers and hearts and stars with her red pencil.

One day, she went to play with her friend Ben. Ben had a big box of pencils, too. He showed Lily his pencils and said, "Look, I have a different pencil. It is yellow and it can write by itself. Do you want to try it?"

Lily was curious. She wanted to see the yellow pencil that could write by itself. She took it from Ben and tried to draw a flower. But the yellow pencil did not make a line. It made a beep.

Lily was scared. She dropped the yellow pencil and ran to Ben. "What is this? This is not a pencil. This is a scary thing. I don't like it."

Ben laughed. He picked up the yellow pencil and said, "This is not a scary thing. This is a fun thing. This is a magic pencil. It can talk to you. You have to press this button and then say what you want to draw. Then it will draw it for you. Watch."

He pressed the button and said, "Draw a car." The yellow pencil made a beep and then drew a car on the paper. Ben smiled and said, "See? It is easy and fun. You should try it again. I urge you to try it again."

Lily looked at the car. It was nice, but it was not her drawing. She did not want to draw with the yellow pencil. She wanted to draw with her red pencil. She said, "No, thank you. I don't want to try it again. I like my red pencil. It is not magic, but it is mine. I can draw what I want with my red pencil. Can I have my red pencil back, please?"

Ben shrugged. He gave Lily her red pencil back and said, "OK, fine. You can have your red pencil back. But I think you are missing out. The yellow pencil is different and cool. I like it better."

Lily did not care. She took her red pencil and drew a big heart on the paper. She said, "I like my red pencil better. It is not different, but it is special. It is my friend."

name_of_work: Peter Quince at the Clavier by Wallace Stevens
content: Just as my fingers on these keys Make music, so the selfsame sounds On my spirit make a music, too. Music is feeling, then, not sound; And thus it is that what I feel, Here in this room, desiring you, Thinking of your blue-shadowed silk, Is music. It is like the strain Waked in the elders by Susanna: Of a green evening, clear and warm, She bathed in her still garden, while The red-eyed elders, watching, felt The basses of their beings throb In witching chords, and their thin blood Pulse pizzicati of Hosanna. In the green water, clear and warm, Susanna lay. She searched The touch of springs, And found Concealed imaginings. She sighed, For so much melody. Upon the bank, she stood In the cool Of spent emotions. She felt, among the leaves, The dew Of old devotions. She walked upon the grass, Still quavering. The winds were like her maids, On timid feet, Fetching her woven scarves, Yet wavering. A breath upon her hand Muted the night. She turned-- A cymbal crashed, And roaring horns. Soon, with a noise like tambourines, Came her attendant Byzantines. They wondered why Susanna cried Against the elders by her side; And as they whispered, the refrain Was like a willow swept by rain. Anon, their lamps' uplifted flame Revealed Susanna and her shame. And then, the simpering Byzantines Fled, with a noise like tambourines. Beauty is momentary in the mind-- The fitful tracing of a portal; But in the flesh it is immortal. The body dies; the body's beauty lives. So evenings die, in their green going, A wave, interminably flowing. So gardens die, their meek breath scenting The cowl of winter, done repenting. So maidens die, to the auroral Celebration of a maiden's choral. Susanna's music touched the bawdy strings Of those white elders; but, escaping, Left only Death's ironic scraping. Now, in its immortality, it plays On the clear viol of her memory, And makes a constant sacrament of praise.

The woman is perfected. Her dead Body wears the smile of accomplishment, The illusion of a Greek necessity Flows in the scrolls of her toga, Her bare Feet seem to be saying: We have come so far, it is over. Each dead child coiled, a white serpent, One at each little Pitcher of milk, now empty. She has folded Them back into her body as petals Of a rose close when the garden Stiffens and odors bleed From the sweet, deep throats of the night flower. The moon has nothing to be sad about, Staring from her hood of bone. She is used to this sort of thing. Her blacks crackle and drag.

Once upon a time, there was a bird with big wings. The bird liked to fly high in the sky and spread its wings wide. One day, the bird found a smelly cheese on the ground. The bird didn't like the smelly cheese, but it knew that some animals did. So, the bird spread its wings and flew to find some animals who wanted to eat the smelly cheese. The bird found some mice who were happy to eat the smelly cheese. The bird was happy it could help the mice find something to eat.

When the food came, it smelled so good. Bob was happy. He ate slowly and asked lots of questions about the restaurant. His mom answered all his questions. When they finished, Bob said good-bye to the restaurant and thanked his mom for taking him. They were both glad they went to the restaurant.

Tom and Lily are playing in the park with their ball. They like to kick the ball to each other and run after it. Sometimes the ball goes too far and they have to look for it in the grass or behind the trees.

One day, the ball goes over the fence and into the road. Tom and Lily are scared. They know the road is not for playing. There are big cars and buses that go fast and make loud noises. They can hurt them if they are not careful.

They see a man in a blue suit and a hat. He has a whistle and a sign. He is a crossing guard. He helps people cross the road safely. He sees the ball and blows his whistle. He holds up his sign and stops the cars and buses. He picks up the ball and walks to the fence.

"Is this your ball?" he asks Tom and Lily. They nod and say yes. He smiles and gives them the ball. "Be careful, kids. Don't let your ball go into the road again. It's an emergency. Someone could get hurt."

Tom and Lily say thank you and sorry. They gather their ball and run back to the park. They find a nice spot with a lot of open space. They kick the ball to each other and have fun. They are happy and safe.

Once upon a time there were two good friends called Tim and Tom. They were playing in the park with their toy cars when they heard a sound. It was a loud spray coming from a nearby mill. Tim wanted to explore the mill but Tom was scared. 

Tim said "let's go! We can be independent and explore the mill together. Nothing bad will happen to us." But Tom stayed still. 

Tim said "Come on Tom, it's safe. Look, I'm not scared. So you can't be scared either."

With that, Tim waived at Tom and walked to the mill. Reluctantly, Tom followed him. When they arrived, they saw that the mill was spraying water. Tim and Tom watched the mill for a little while until Tim said: "See Tom, I told you nothing bad would happen. We were brave and independent and had a great time together".

Tom agreed and they both smiled with joy. The moral of the story is that it's important to be brave and independent, but it's always safer to explore with a friend.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy who loved vegetables. His mom always sent him to the grocery store to buy some. One day, Timmy went to the store, but he forgot his list. He didn't know what to buy, so he just grabbed everything he saw.

When Timmy got home, his mom asked him what he bought. Timmy said he got everything, but his mom saw that his bag was empty. She asked him where the vegetables were, but Timmy didn't know. His mom was sad because they didn't have anything to eat for dinner.

Timmy's mom decided to send him back to the store to get some vegetables. Timmy was excited to go back and get some more. But when he got to the store, he couldn't find any vegetables. He asked the store worker, but they didn't have any. Timmy was sad because he couldn't bring any vegetables home.

When Timmy got home, his mom was even more sad. They didn't have anything to eat for dinner. Timmy felt bad that he couldn't bring any vegetables home. He promised he would do better next time.

Lily and Tom were playing in the kitchen. They saw a big jug of juice on the table. They wanted some juice, but they did not know how to pour it.

"Let me do it," said Tom. He grabbed the jug and tried to lift it. But it was too heavy for him. He dropped the jug on the floor. The juice spilled everywhere.

"Oh no!" said Lily. "You made a big mess. Mom will be angry."

Tom started to cry. He was frightened. He did not want to get in trouble.

"Stop crying," said Lily. "We have to clean it up. Get a towel."

Tom did not want to clean it up. He wanted to complain. He said, "It's not fair. You wanted juice too. Why do I have to clean it up?"

"Because you dropped it," said Lily. "And you have to say sorry."

Tom did not want to say sorry. He said, "No. You say sorry. You made me drop it. You were pushing me."

Lily was angry. She said, "I did not push you. You were clumsy. You always break things."

They started to argue. They did not hear Mom coming. Mom saw the mess and the jug. She was not happy. She said, "What happened here? Who did this?"

Lily and Tom stopped arguing. They looked at Mom. They were both frightened. They did not know what to say.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily's mommy said they were going to the mall. Lily was excited to go because she loved to look at all the toys and clothes. 

When they got to the mall, Lily's mommy said they needed to load up on groceries. Lily didn't like grocery shopping, but she helped her mommy pick out some yummy fruits and vegetables. 

As they were walking around the mall, Lily saw a toy she really wanted. She tugged on her mommy's shirt and said, "Mommy, can we get that toy?" Her mommy replied, "Not today, Lily. Maybe next time." Lily felt anxious because she really wanted the toy, but she knew her mommy couldn't buy everything she wanted. 

After they finished shopping, they went home and Lily helped her mommy put away the groceries. She felt proud of herself for being a good helper. And even though she didn't get the toy she wanted, she was happy to have spent time with her mommy at the mall. The end.

Overnight, very Whitely, discreetly, Very quietly Our toes, our noses Take hold on the loam, Acquire the air. Nobody sees us, Stops us, betrays us; The small grains make room. Soft fists insist on Heaving the needles, The leafy bedding, Even the paving. Our hammers, our rams, Earless and eyeless, Perfectly voiceless, Widen the crannies, Shoulder through holes. We Diet on water, On crumbs of shadow, Bland-mannered, asking Little or nothing. So many of us! So many of us! We are shelves, we are Tables, we are meek, We are edible, Nudgers and shovers In spite of ourselves. Our kind multiplies: We shall by morning Inherit the earth. Our foot's in the door.

name_of_work: Romeo and Juliet Act II Prologue by William Shakespeare
content: Enter Chorus Chorus Now old desire doth in his death-bed lie, And young affection gapes to be his heir; That fair for which love groan'd for and would die, With tender Juliet match'd, is now not fair. Now Romeo is beloved and loves again, Alike betwitched by the charm of looks, But to his foe supposed he must complain, And she steal love's sweet bait from fearful hooks: Being held a foe, he may not have access To breathe such vows as lovers use to swear; And she as much in love, her means much less To meet her new-beloved any where: But passion lends them power, time means, to meet Tempering extremities with extreme sweet. Exit

name_of_work: Epitaph on a Hare by William Cowper
content: Here lies, whom hound did ne'er pursue, Nor swifter greyhound follow, Whose foot ne'er tainted morning dew, Nor ear heard huntsman's hallo', Old Tiney, surliest of his kind, Who, nursed with tender care, And to domesticate bounds confined, Was still a wild jack-hare. Though duly from my hand he took His pittance every night, He did it with a jealous look, And, when he could, would bite. His diet was of wheaten bread, And milk, and oats, and straw, Thistles, or lettuces instead, With sand to scour his maw. On twigs of hawthorn he regaled, On pippins' russet peel; And, when his juicy salads failed, Sliced carrot pleased him well. A Turkey carpet was his lawn, Whereon he loved to bound, To skip and gambol like a fawn, And swing his rump around. His frisking was at evening hours, For then he lost his fear; But most before approaching showers, Or when a storm drew near. Eight years and five round-rolling moons He thus saw steal away, Dozing out all his idle noons, And every night at play. I kept him for his humor's sake, For he would oft beguile My heart of thoughts that made it ache, And force me to a smile. But now, beneath this walnut-shade He finds his long, last home, And waits in snug concealment laid, Till gentler Puss shall come. He, still more aged, feels the shocks From which no care can save, And, partner once of Tiney's box, Must soon partake his grave.

name_of_work: Can Someone Bring Me My Entire Self by Noshi Gillani
content: Can someone bring me my entire being? My arms, my eyes, my face? I am a river flowing into the wrong sea If only someone could restore me to the desert Life goes on but I want no more from it Than my childhood, my firefly, my doll My vision does not admit this new season Take me back to my old dream Of finding one face among the many in my city Whose eyes can read deep into me My life has been a boat in a whirlpool for so long O god, please let it sink or drift back to the desert.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. One day, he went to the park to play with his friends. It was a rainy day, so he took his umbrella with him. But while playing, he forgot his umbrella under a big tree.

A rude girl named Lily saw Tim's umbrella under the tree. She took it and started playing with it. Tim saw her and felt sad. He wanted his umbrella back, but Lily wouldn't give it back to him.

Tim asked his friends for help. They all went to Lily and said, "Please give Tim his umbrella back. It is not nice to take things that are not yours." Lily felt bad for being rude. She gave the umbrella back to Tim and said sorry. Tim and his friends were happy, and they all played together in the park.

Tim and Mia are friends. They like to play outside. They have bikes with pedals. They can ride fast and have fun.

One day, Tim and Mia go to the park. They see a big hill. Tim says, "Let's go up the hill. It will be fun." Mia says, "OK, let's go."

They step on their pedals and start to go up the hill. It is hard. They have to push hard. They get tired. Mia says, "I want to stop. It is too hard." Tim says, "No, don't stop. We can do it. Come on."

They keep going. They reach the top of the hill. They are happy. They see a lot of things. They see trees and flowers and birds and clouds. They see the pond and the swings and the slide. They see other kids playing.

Tim says, "Wow, look at all the things we can see. It is beautiful." Mia says, "Yes, it is. I'm glad we came up here. It was worth it." Tim says, "Me too. I'm glad you are my friend. You are brave and strong." Mia says, "Thank you. You are my friend too. You are kind and helpful."

They smile at each other. They step on their pedals and start to go down the hill. They go fast and have fun. They laugh and shout. They are happy. They are friends.

It was like watching a wave approach from a great distance, so great that at first it is not a wave at all, but a mere horizon, static and singular, so that one, it being possible, presumably, to avail oneself of the diversions of the beach, might turn one's back on the ocean altogether, might turn instead to the sand, heaped and tunnelled, the sunscreened hand that fumbles for a book, indeed, the book, the sentence, the syntax, the sun blanching the page, stained, perhaps, with sweat, the creamy pleasure of not-laboring, when one would otherwise labor, the pleasure of wasting oneself, of decadent uselessness, though one might, of course, always alarm to some emergency, a child caught in the undertow, say, who must be dragged to shore and breathed into like an empty balloon, an empty balloon on which everything depends, might, bent over the small body, waiting for it to rise, to float, casting a shadow the size of oneself, not even see, though one was, of course, warned it would come, and soon, the shadow of that wave, like a new sky, already overhead and even now descending.

Once upon a time there was an ugly pot. Every day it would bounce around the room. It was so excited to be alive and loved to jump and move.

One day, a little girl named Mia saw the pot bouncing and decided to join in. She laughed and bounced with it, and the pot was even happier now.

They both bounced around the room, laughing all the while. They were having so much fun that they didn't even notice the sun setting outside!

Eventually, Mia got tired and had to go to bed. But before she left, she gave the pot a big hug and said goodnight.

The pot was all alone in the room again, but it was still smiling. It knew it had made a new friend for life.

Lily and Tom like to play in the kitchen. They find a big jar of jam on the shelf. They want to eat some jam on bread. But the jar is too high for them to reach.

They look for a chair to stand on. But all the chairs are in the living room. They see a stool by the sink. They drag the stool to the shelf. Tom climbs on the stool. He tries to grab the jar of jam. But the jar is too heavy for him. He drops the jar on the floor.

The jar breaks. Jam spills everywhere. Lily and Tom are scared. They hear Mom coming. They kneel on the floor. They try to hide behind the stool. But Mom sees them. She sees the broken jar and the jam.

Mom is not happy. She says, "What have you done? You made a big mess. You could have hurt yourself. You should not play with jam. Jam is for eating, not for spilling."

Lily and Tom are sorry. They say, "We are sorry, Mom. We wanted some jam on bread. But the jar was too high and too heavy. We did not mean to break it."

Mom sighs. She says, "I know you did not mean to break it. But you should have asked me for help. I would have given you some jam on bread. Now we have to clean up this mess. And we have no more jam."

She takes a cloth and a mop. She starts to clean up the jam. She tells Lily and Tom to help her. They pick up the pieces of the jar. They wipe the jam from the floor. They are careful not to cut themselves.

When they are done, Mom hugs them. She says, "I love you, Lily and Tom. But next time, please do not play with jam. Jam is sticky and sweet. It makes a lot of trouble."

Lily and Tom nod. They say, "We love you, Mom. We will not play with jam again. We will ask you for help. Can we have some jam on bread now?"

Mom smiles. She says, "Yes, you can have some jam on bread. But only a little bit. We have to save some jam for later. And we have to close the jar. We do not want to leave it open. Open jars can attract bugs and ants. And we do not want bugs and ants in our kitchen."

She takes another jar of jam from the cupboard. She opens it. She spreads some jam on bread. She gives a slice to Lily and a slice to Tom. They eat their jam on bread. They say, "Thank you, Mom. This jam is yummy."

Mom says, "You are welcome, Lily and Tom. This jam is yummy. But you know what is yummier? You are yummier. You are my sweet and sticky jam." She kisses them on their cheeks. They giggle. They hug her. They are happy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to look at tiny things. One day, her friend Tim had a cool toy called a microscope. A microscope helps you see very small things up close. Lily wanted to play with it too, so she asked Tim if she could borrow his microscope. Tim said yes, because he was a good friend.

Lily was very patient as she waited for her turn to use the microscope. When it was her turn, she looked at a small bug. The bug had many legs and tiny eyes. Lily was so happy to see the bug up close. She thanked Tim for letting her borrow his microscope.

After playing with the microscope, Lily and Tim went outside to find more tiny things to look at. They found a small flower, a tiny rock, and a little feather. They had so much fun looking at all the small things with the microscope. At the end of the day, Lily gave the microscope back to Tim and they both went home with big smiles on their faces.

Once upon a time, there were two friends. One was a clown and the other was a bee. One day, the bee wanted to know how heavy the clown was. So he asked his friend to stand on the scales so he could weigh him. 

The bee was very careful as he placed his friend on the scales. He slowly took out the weights and put them on the other side. Then he watched and waited as the scales balanced out.

When the scales finished, the bee was surprised by how heavy the clown was. He said, "Wow! You must be really strong and hard if you weighed that much!" 

The clown just smiled and said, "That's what all clowns do."

The bee was very impressed and thought, "One day I will be as strong and hard as this clown is!" 

And from that day forward, the bee set out to be the best and strongest bee he could be. The end.

Anna likes to learn new things. She likes to read books, draw pictures, and play games. But she does not like math. Math is hard and boring. She does not understand the numbers and the shapes.

One day, her mom tells her that she has a tutor. A tutor is someone who helps you learn. Anna is scared. She does not want a tutor. She thinks the tutor will be mean and make her do math all the time.

The next day, the tutor comes to Anna's house. She is an elderly lady. She has white hair and glasses. She smiles at Anna and says, "Hello, I'm Mrs. Lee. I'm here to help you with math. But first, let's get to know each other. What do you like to do?"

Anna is shy. She does not answer. She looks at her mom, who nods and says, "Go on, Anna. Mrs. Lee is very nice. She will make math fun for you."

Anna decides to give Mrs. Lee a chance. She tells her that she likes to read books, draw pictures, and play games. Mrs. Lee says, "That's wonderful. I like those things too. Do you know that math can help you with them? Math is not just numbers and shapes. It is also patterns, colors, and logic. Let me show you."

Mrs. Lee takes out a book, a paper, and some crayons. She reads Anna a story about a cat and a mouse. She asks Anna to draw the cat and the mouse. She shows Anna how to count the cat's whiskers, the mouse's ears, and the cheese slices. She teaches Anna how to make circles, triangles, and squares. She plays a game with Anna where they have to match the shapes and the colors.

Anna is surprised. She starts to like math. She thinks math is fun and interesting. She likes Mrs. Lee. She is not mean. She is kind and patient. She makes Anna laugh and think.

Anna says, "Thank you, Mrs. Lee. You are a good tutor. You make math easy and fun. Can you come again tomorrow?"

Mrs. Lee says, "You're welcome, Anna. You are a smart and curious girl. You make me happy and proud. Of course I can come again tomorrow. I look forward to it."

Anna hugs Mrs. Lee. She is not scared of math anymore. She is excited to learn more. She thinks math is a good thing.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big truck go by. The truck makes a lot of noise and smoke.

"Look, Anna, smoke!" Ben says. He points to the truck.

"Smoke is bad," Anna says. She covers her nose. "It makes me cough."

"Me too," Ben says. "Let's go away from the smoke."

They run to the other side of the park. There, they see a man with a cart. The cart has many colorful things on it. The man smiles at them.

"Hello, kids," the man says. "Do you want some candy? It is very sweet."

Anna and Ben love candy. They nod and go to the cart. The man gives them each a lollipop. They lick the lollipops and smile.

"Mmm, this is good," Anna says. "Thank you, mister."

"You're welcome," the man says. "But be careful, kids. Too much candy is not good for you. It can make your teeth hurt."

Anna and Ben look at each other. They remember what their mommies told them. They should not eat too much candy. They should brush their teeth every day.

"OK, mister," Ben says. "We will not eat too much candy. We will brush our teeth."

"Good," the man says. "Now, go and have fun. But stay away from the smoke."

Anna and Ben wave goodbye to the man. They go back to the park. They play with their lollipops. They are happy. They stay away from the smoke.

Jenny was walking in the park. She saw a white cone on the ground and she thought it was interesting. She walked over to it and picked it up. She felt the bumps and curves on the cone and smiled. 

Jenny then started playing with it. She pretended that the cone was a telephone and talked into it. She was having so much fun! After a while, she put the cone down gently. 

Jenny looked around and saw that the sky was getting dark. She thought it was time to go home and picked up the white cone to take it with her. She put the cone in her pocket and skipped away happily.

Tom and Anna are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a bright rainbow in the sky. They run to the rainbow and try to touch it.

"Wow, look at the colors!" Tom says. "Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple!"

"I like purple best," Anna says. "It is pretty."

They enjoy the rainbow for a long time. They make up stories about what is at the end of the rainbow. They pretend they are fairies and unicorns.

But then, the sky gets dark and it starts to rain. The rainbow fades away.

"Oh no, where did the rainbow go?" Tom asks. "I want to see it again."

Anna hugs Tom. "Don't be sad," she says. "The rainbow will come back another day. It is the truth. My mom told me."

Tom smiles. "OK, I believe you. You are a good friend."

They hold hands and run to the shelter. They wait for the rain to stop. They hope to see the rainbow again soon.

Jill and Tom were twins who liked to play in the garden. One day, they saw a big purple pot on the porch. They wondered what was inside.

"Let's look!" Jill said.

"No, it's Mom's pot. She said not to touch it." Tom said.

But Jill did not listen. She ran to the pot and gazed inside. She saw something shiny and round. She reached out to grab it.

"Jill, stop!" Tom shouted.

But it was too late. The shiny thing was a ball of fire. It burned Jill's hand and made a loud noise. The pot broke into pieces. Mom came out and saw the mess.

"Jill, Tom, what have you done?" Mom said. She was very angry and sad. She took Jill to the doctor and Tom to his room. She said they were in big trouble.

Jill and Tom felt sorry and scared. They wished they had listened to Mom and left the pot alone. They learned a hard lesson. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a man who had a wife. The wife was very ignorant and always made mistakes. One day, the man asked his wife to make him a sandwich. But the wife didn't know how to make a sandwich. The man got upset and said, "Why are you so ignorant? Making a sandwich is easy!" 

The wife didn't know what to do, so she went to her friend's house to ask for help. Her friend told her to twist the bread and put some cheese and meat inside. The wife was very happy that she learned something new. 

When the wife came back home, she made a sandwich for her husband. The husband was surprised and asked, "Wow, this sandwich is delicious! How did you make it?" The wife replied, "I twisted the bread and put some cheese and meat inside, just like my friend told me." 

The husband was happy that his wife learned something new and they both enjoyed the sandwich together. From that day on, the wife learned many new things and was no longer ignorant.

name_of_work: Patience Taught By Nature by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: "O Dreary life!" we cry, "O dreary life!" And still the generations of the birds Sing through our sighing, and the flocks and herds Serenely live while we are keeping strife With Heaven's true purpose in us, as a knife Against which we may struggle. Ocean girds Unslackened the dry land: savannah-swards Unweary sweep: hills watch, unworn; and rife Meek leaves drop yearly from the forest-trees, To show, above, the unwasted stars that pass In their old glory. O thou God of old! Grant me some smaller grace than comes to these;-- But so much patience, as a blade of grass Grows by contented through the heat and cold.

Once upon a time, there was a cat named Sam. Sam was a dirty cat. He liked to play in the mud all day. One day, Sam found a big book. The book had a spell in it. Sam wanted to fix the spell.

Sam asked his friend, a dog named Max, to help him. Max was very good at fixing things. They tried to fix the spell together. But they did not know what the spell would do. They were a little scared.

Finally, they fixed the spell. The spell made Sam clean! Sam was so happy. He was not dirty anymore. Sam and Max played together, but now Sam stayed clean. They were the best of friends.

Once upon a time, there was a wise old man. He liked to eat yummy food and use his hammer to fix broken things.

One day, he was sitting down to eat his lunch when a 3 year old child wandered up to him. "Excuse me, sir!" she said. "Will you teach me how to use the hammer?"

The man smiled. "Of course, I can show you how to use a hammer," he said.

The girl nodded and watched carefully as the man showed her how to swing the hammer and how to hit the nail without hurting herself. After a few tries, she managed to hammer the nail into the wall. She smiled proudly.

"Thank you! You are very wise," the girl said.

The man smiled. "You're welcome," he said. "Now, let's eat our lunch." 
The girl and the man happily ate their lunch together.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She had a lovely red dress that she liked to wear. One day, she went to the park with her mom and dad. They found a seat on a big bench and sat down to rest. 

Lily saw a butterfly and tried to catch it, but it flew away. She felt sad because she wanted to keep it. Suddenly, a kind lady came and gave Lily a toy butterfly. Lily was happy and gained a new toy. 

She played with the toy butterfly on the bench and felt very happy. She looked at her mom and dad and saw that they were happy too. They all enjoyed a lovely day at the park together. The end.

Once upon a time there was a jolly world. All of the animals and birds got along so everyone was happy. One day, an sneaky fox decided to lie to the other animals. He told them that the world wasn't jolly anymore. The animals believed the fox and so they all started to cry. 

But then, a sweet little bunny hopped up and showed everybody it was still a jolly world. She did a jig and showed them a big smile. It reminded them that being jolly was still important. 

The fox was embarrassed and scurried away. Everyone cheered for the bunny and the world went back to being jolly again. They all became friends once more and lived happily ever after.
