name_of_work: Willow Poem by William Carlos Williams
content: It is a willow when summer is over, a willow by the river from which no leaf has fallen nor bitten by the sun turned orange or crimson. The leaves cling and grow paler, swing and grow paler over the swirling waters of the river as if loath to let go, they are so cool, so drunk with the swirl of the wind and of the river-- oblivious to winter, the last to let go and fall into the water and on the ground.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue loved to play games with her friends. One day, they decided to play a game with a ball and a basket.

Sue wanted to win the game. She knew it was important to try her best. She threw the ball into the basket many times. Her friends were happy and clapped for her.

At the end of the game, Sue and her friends counted the balls in the basket. Sue had the most balls in the basket, so she won. She felt very proud and knew that trying her best was important. Sue and her friends had a lot of fun playing the game, and they all went home with big smiles on their faces.

At low tide like this how sheer the water is. White, crumbling ribs of marl protrude and glare and the boats are dry, the pilings dry as matches. Absorbing, rather than being absorbed, the water in the bight doesn't wet anything, the color of the gas flame turned as low as possible. One can smell it turning to gas; if one were Baudelaire one could probably hear it turning to marimba music. The little ochre dredge at work off the end of the dock already plays the dry perfectly off-beat claves. The birds are outsize. Pelicans crash into this peculiar gas unnecessarily hard, it seems to me, like pickaxes, rarely coming up with anything to show for it, and going off with humorous elbowings. Black-and-white man-of-war birds soar on impalpable drafts and open their tails like scissors on the curves or tense them like wishbones, till they tremble. The frowsy sponge boats keep coming in with the obliging air of retrievers, bristling with jackstraw gaffs and hooks and decorated with bobbles of sponges. There is a fence of chicken wire along the dock where, glinting like little plowshares, the blue-gray shark tails are hung up to dry for the Chinese-restaurant trade. Some of the little white boats are still piled up against each other, or lie on their sides, stove in, and not yet salvaged, if they ever will be, from the last bad storm, like torn-open, unanswered letters. The bight is littered with old correspondences. Click. Click. Goes the dredge, and brings up a dripping jawful of marl. All the untidy activity continues, awful but cheerful.

name_of_work: Hurrahing in Harvest by Gerard Manley Hopkins
content: Summer ends now; now, barbarous in beauty, the stooks rise Around; up above, what wind-walks! what lovely behaviour Of silk-sack clouds! has wilder, wilful-wavier Meal-drift moulded ever and melted across skies? I walk, I lift up, I lift up heart, eyes, Down all that glory in the heavens to glean our Saviour; And, eyes, heart, what looks, what lips yet gave you a Rapturous love's greeting of realer, of rounder replies? And the azurous hung hills are his world-wielding shoulder Majestic--as a stallion stalwart, very-violet-sweet!-- These things, these things were here and but the beholder Wanting; which two when they once meet, The heart rears wings bold and bolder And hurls for him, O half hurls earth for him off under his feet.

name_of_work: Letter to My Great, Great, Grandchild by J.P. Grasser
content: Oh button, don't go thinking we loved pianos more than elephants, air conditioning more than air. We loved honey, just loved it, and went into stores to smell the sweet perfume of unworn leather shoes. Did you know, on the coast of Africa, the Sea Rose and Carpenter Bee used to depend on each other? The petals only opened for the Middle C their wings beat, so in the end, we protested with tuning forks. You must think we hated the stars, the empty ladles, because they conjured thirst. We didn't. We thanked them and called them lucky, we even bought the rights to name them for our sweethearts. Believe it or not, most people kept plants like pets and hired kids like you to water them, whenever they went away. And ice! Can you imagine? We put it in our coffee and dumped it out at traffic lights, when it plugged up our drinking straws. I had a dog once, a real dog, who ate venison and golden yams from a plastic dish. He was stubborn, but I taught him to dance and play dead with a bucket full of chicken livers. And we danced too, you know, at weddings and wakes, in basements and churches, even when the war was on. Our cars we mostly named for animals, and sometimes we drove just to drive, to clear our heads of everything but wind.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl. She was three years old. Her mommy had an ordinary rope that she wanted to sell. So the girl went to the market with her mommy.

At the market, the little girl saw lots of things that people were selling. But she saw nothing as special as the rope her mommy was selling.

The rope was long and wide, and of very ordinary colour. But people still wanted to buy it. So her mommy sold it to three people at the market.

The little girl was very excited. She was so glad that her mommy had been able to sell the rope. It made her very happy. And the girl and her mummy lived happily ever after!

name_of_work: I am very bothered by Simon Armitage
content: I am very bothered when I think of the bad things I have done in my life. Not least that time in the chemistry lab when I held a pair of scissors by the blades and played the handles in the naked lilac flame of the Bunsen burner; then called your name, and handed them over. O the unrivalled stench of branded skin as you slipped your thumb and middle finger in, then couldn't shake off the two burning rings. Marked, the doctor said, for eternity. Don't believe me, please, if I say that was just my butterfingered way, at thirteen, of asking you if you would marry me.

One day, John was in his kitchen counting his five apples. He had three green ones and two pink ones. They looked so healthy, he could not wait to eat them.

Suddenly, a big monster appeared in front of him! The monster said in a deep voice, "give me the pink apples!". John was so scared. He picked up the two pink apples and slowly handed them over to the monster. 

John asked, "please don't take them, they are so healthy and I still haven't eaten them". But the monster didn't care. It just snatched the apples away and said, "these apples belong to me now!"

Unfortunately, there was nothing John could do. The monster was too big and strong. He sadly watched as the monster disappeared with his two pink apples.

Ben is a bald boy. He likes to play with his toys. He has a big red car that can go fast. He has a small blue plane that can fly high. He has a yellow button that can make sounds.

One day, Ben is playing with his toys in his room. He puts the button on the floor. He makes the car go fast on the floor. He makes the plane fly high in the air. He is having fun.

But then, he hears his mom call him. She says, "Ben, it is time for lunch. Come to the kitchen." Ben does not want to stop playing. He says, "One more minute, mom."

He makes the car go faster and faster. He makes the plane fly higher and higher. He does not see the button on the floor. He steps on the button. The button makes a loud sound. It sounds like a siren.

Ben is scared. He thinks there is a fire. He drops his toys. He rushes to the door. He opens the door. He runs to the kitchen.

He sees his mom. She is not scared. She is smiling. She says, "Ben, what is that noise? Did you press the button?"

Ben is confused. He says, "Yes, mom. I pressed the button. I thought there was a fire. I rushed to the kitchen."

Mom says, "No, Ben. There is no fire. The button is just a toy. It makes funny sounds. You do not have to rush. You can play with it later. Now, it is time for lunch. Come and sit down."

Ben says, "Oh, mom. I am sorry. I did not know. The button is a funny toy. Can I play with it after lunch?"

Mom says, "Yes, Ben. You can play with it after lunch. But first, you have to eat your sandwich and your apple. They are good for you. They will make you grow strong and healthy. Maybe, they will even make your hair grow."

Ben says, "OK, mom. I will eat my sandwich and my apple. But I do not want hair. I like being bald. I think it is cool."

Mom says, "I think you are cool, too, Ben. I love you, bald or not. Now, let's eat our lunch and enjoy the day."

Once upon a time, in a big forest, there was a tall tree. The tree was very rich with many green leaves. It was friends with a small bird. The bird would sit on the tree's branches and sing.

One day, a strong wind blew. The tree told the bird, "Trust me, I will keep you safe." The bird was scared, but it trusted the tree. The wind blew harder, but the tree held the bird tight with its leaves.

The wind stopped, and the sun came out. The bird was so happy that it sang a happy song. The tree smiled and knew that it had kept its promise. From that day on, the bird and the tree were best friends.

name_of_work: The House Was Quiet and The World Was Calm by Wallace Stevens
content: The house was quiet and the world was calm. The reader became the book; and summer night Was like the conscious being of the book. The house was quiet and the world was calm. The words were spoken as if there was no book, Except that the reader leaned above the page, Wanted to lean, wanted much most to be The scholar to whom his book is true, to whom The summer night is like a perfection of thought. The house was quiet because it had to be. The quiet was part of the meaning, part of the mind: The access of perfection to the page. And the world was calm. The truth in a calm world, In which there is no other meaning, itself Is calm, itself is summer and night, itself Is the reader leaning late and reading there.

There is that moment when the young human child stares at the young monkey child who stares back - Innocence facing innocence in a space where the young monkey child is not in captivity. There is purity clarity there is a transparence in this stare which lasts a long time... eyes of water eyes of sky the soul can still fall through because the monkey has yet to learn fear and the human has yet to learn fear - let alone arrogance. Witnessing it all one can count eyelashes one can count the snails in the grass while waiting for eyes to blink waiting to see who will look away first. Still the monkey looks at the human not in the same way he would look at leaves or at his own siblings. And the human looks at the monkey knowing this is some totally other being. And yet, there is such good will such curiosity brightening their faces. I would like to slip inside that stare, to know what the human child thinks what the monkey child thinks at that very moment. Remember, the human child is at that age when he begins to use words with power but without the distance of alphabets, of abstractions. Mention bread and he wants a slice, buttered and with honey - immediately. Mention the cat and he runs over to awaken her. The word is the thing itself. Language is simply a necessary music suddenly connected to the child's own heartbeat. While the young monkey child grows at a different rate, looks at a tree, a bush, at the human child and thinks... Who knows what? What remains burning is that moment of staring: the two newly formed heads balanced on fragile necks tilting towards each other, the monkey face and the human face absorbing each other with intense gentleness....

Once upon a time there was a gifted girl called Daisy. She wanted to be like the other children and play with them on the playground. She saw a pole and thought it would be fun to swing.

Daisy happily jumped up to swing and took a hold of the pole. Suddenly the pole snapped in half, Daisy gasped and exploded into tears.

A kind stranger came to comfort Daisy and asked, "What's wrong?".

Daisy sniffled and said, "The pole broke and I can't swing anymore".

The kind stranger said, "Don't worry, I can fix it. I can make a new pole with special glue, so you can keep swinging!"

Daisy smiled and said, "Really?"

The kind stranger nodded and made a new pole for Daisy to swing on. Daisy was so happy that she thanked the kind stranger and kept on swinging until the sun went down. She was the happiest and most gifted girl in the playground that day.

One day, a girl named Jenny decided to shout. She shouted and shouted until she was out of breath. Then she saw an onion. It looked ordinary, but she wanted to inspect it. She shouted again as she got closer to the onion. Suddenly, the onion began to move. Jenny was so surprised that she shouted even louder. The onion shook and rolled right out of its spot. Jenny chased it until it stopped. She picked it up and shouted with excitement. She had found a very special onion.

Once upon a time, there was a big and strong man. He was called a mighty hero. He loved to play a fun game where he had to match different colors. One day, he saw a beautiful statue in the park. The statue was very pretty and he wanted to take a picture with it. He tried to match his shirt with the statue's color, but he didn't have the right color. He felt sad, but then he remembered that he could still take a picture with the statue even if he didn't match. And so, he took a picture with the statue and it made him very happy. The end.

name_of_work: Tonight No Poetry Will Serve by Adrienne Rich
content: Saw you walking barefoot taking a long look at the new moon's eyelid later spread sleep-fallen, naked in your dark hair asleep but not oblivious of the unslept unsleeping elsewhere Tonight I think no poetry will serve

Sara and Ben are twins. They like to play with yarn. They make hats and scarves and dolls with yarn. They have many colors of yarn.

Today is their birthday. They are three years old. They are happy. They want to celebrate. They ask their mom and dad for a cake and candles.

"Can we have a cake and candles, please?" they say.

"Of course, my loves," mom says. "But first, we have a surprise for you."

Mom and dad take them to the park. The park is big and green. There are swings and slides and a sandbox. There are also many animals. There are ducks and geese and squirrels and rabbits.

Sara and Ben love animals. They run and laugh and feed the animals. They have fun. The animals are friendly and mild. They do not bite or scratch.

"Look, mom, dad, a duck!" Sara says.

"Look, mom, dad, a rabbit!" Ben says.

Mom and dad smile and take pictures. They are proud of their twins.

After a while, they go back home. Mom and dad have made a cake and candles. The cake is chocolate and vanilla. The candles are red and blue. There are also balloons and streamers and gifts.

Sara and Ben are surprised and excited. They clap and cheer. They blow the candles and make a wish. They cut the cake and share it. They open the gifts and thank mom and dad.

One of the gifts is a big box of yarn. There are many colors and types of yarn. There are soft and fluffy and shiny and sparkly yarn.

Sara and Ben are very happy. They hug mom and dad. They hug each other. They say, "This is the best birthday ever!"

They celebrate with yarn. They make more hats and scarves and dolls with yarn. They give some to mom and dad. They keep some for themselves. They play with yarn until bedtime.

They are tired and sleepy. They brush their teeth and put on their pajamas. They go to bed. They cuddle with their yarn dolls. They say goodnight to mom and dad. They say goodnight to each other.

They dream of yarn and animals and cake and candles. They are happy. They are twins. They are three years old.

name_of_work: Love of My Flesh, Living Death by Lorna Dee Cervantes
content: Once I wasn't always so plain. I was strewn feathers on a cross of dune, an expanse of ocean at my feet, garlands of gulls. Sirens and gulls. They couldn't tame you. You know as well as they: to be a dove is to bear the falcon at your breast, your nights, your seas. My fear is simple, heart-faced above a flare of etchings, a lineage in letters, my sudden stare. It's you. It's you! sang the heart upon its mantel pelvis. Blush of my breath, catch of my see--beautiful bird--It's you.

name_of_work: In Memory of W.B. Yeats by W. H. Auden
content: I He disappeared in the dead of winter: The brooks were frozen, the airports almost deserted, And snow disfigured the public statues; The mercury sank in the mouth of the dying day. What instruments we have agree The day of his death was a dark cold day. Far from his illness The wolves ran on through the evergreen forests, The peasant river was untempted by the fashionable quays; By mourning tongues The death of the poet was kept from his poems. But for him it was his last afternoon as himself, An afternoon of nurses and rumours; The provinces of his body revolted, The squares of his mind were empty, Silence invaded the suburbs, The current of his feeling failed; he became his admirers. Now he is scattered among a hundred cities And wholly given over to unfamiliar affections, To find his happiness in another kind of wood And be punished under a foreign code of conscience. The words of a dead man Are modified in the guts of the living. But in the importance and noise of to-morrow When the brokers are roaring like beasts on the floor of the bourse, And the poor have the sufferings to which they are fairly accustomed And each in the cell of himself is almost convinced of his freedom A few thousand will think of this day As one thinks of a day when one did something slightly unusual. What instruments we have agree The day of his death was a dark cold day. II You were silly like us; your gift survived it all: The parish of rich women, physical decay, Yourself. Mad Ireland hurt you into poetry. Now Ireland has her madness and her weather still, For poetry makes nothing happen: it survives In the valley of its making where executives Would never want to tamper, flows on south From ranches of isolation and the busy griefs, Raw towns that we believe and die in; it survives, A way of happening, a mouth. III Earth, receive an honoured guest: William Yeats is laid to rest. Let the Irish vessel lie Emptied of its poetry. In the nightmare of the dark All the dogs of Europe bark, And the living nations wait, Each sequestered in its hate; Intellectual disgrace Stares from every human face, And the seas of pity lie Locked and frozen in each eye. Follow, poet, follow right To the bottom of the night, With your unconstraining voice Still persuade us to rejoice; With the farming of a verse Make a vineyard of the curse, Sing of human unsuccess In a rapture of distress; In the deserts of the heart Let the healing fountain start, In the prison of his days Teach the free man how to praise.

Once upon a time, there was a loyal pigeon. Every day it would fly high in the sky, looking for something interesting. One day, it found something amazing. The pigeon saw a small boy, playing in the garden. He was looking for a friend, with no one to talk to.

The pigeon saw how sad the little boy was and decided to say hello. He fluttered down and landed on the little boyâ€™s shoulder. The boy was so surprised that he replied â€œHello!â€. The pigeon was so happy to have made a new friend.

From that day onwards, the pigeon and the little boy were best friends. Every day, the pigeon would fly down from the sky, just to show the little boy how much he cared. He would always reply to the little boy, showing his loyalty and friendship. 

Years passed and the little boy grew older, but the pigeon was still there, loyal to his friend. No matter what happened, the pigeon always replied to the boy, forever loyal and faithful.

Charlie the fox was walking around the forest looking for adventure. He watched a squirrel moving fast and laughed. Suddenly he had an idea! He decided to measure the style of the squirrel's running. 

Charlie asked the squirrel if he want to play a game. The squirrel said yes. Charlie then explained the rules of the game to him. He said, â€œI will measure how fast you can go. Go as fast as you can!â€ 

The squirrel was very excited and said, â€œThis will be so much fun! I will go very fast and you can measure me.â€ 

Charlie laughed and said, â€œLet's go!â€ 

So the squirrel raced across the forest and Charlie measured him. The squirrel went faster and faster and it was a close race. Finally, Charlie declared the squirrel the winner and gave him a big hug. 

Charlie was very happy with his new game. From that day on he would measure animals' running styles whenever he wanted an adventure. 

The end.

name_of_work: All You Have is a Country by Ha Jin
content: You are so poor that all you have is a country. Whenever you open your mouth you talk about the country to which you can no longer return. China is a giant shield that you use to conceal your cowardice and to preempt the onslaught of duties and hardships. You dare not take these as your rights: the warm sunlight, clean water, fresh air, a happy mood for an ordinary day. As long as you live, you want to grieve for the fairy tale of patriotism. You dare not take a country as a watchdog-- a good dog wags its tail to please its master, becomes fierce in deterring burglars; a bad dog ignores invaders and only bites and barks at its master. You dare not clasp the dog's ear, telling it, "You won't have food if you continue to misbehave like this." Actually, you are merely a grain of rice that fell through China's teeth, but you treat it as your god, your universe, and the source of your suffering and happiness.

name_of_work: The Circuit Judge by Edgar Lee Masters
content: Take note, passers-by, of the sharp erosions Eaten in my head-stone by the wind and rain i Almost as if an intangible Nemesis or hatred Were marking scores against me, But to destroy, and not preserve, my memory. I in life was the Circuit Judge, a maker of notches, Deciding cases on the points the lawyers scored, Not on the right of the matter. O wind and rain, leave my head-stone alone! For worse than the anger of the wronged, The curses of the poor, Was to lie speechless, yet with vision clear, Seeing that even Hod Putt, the murderer, Hanged by my sentence, Was innocent in soul compared with me.

One day, Lucy and her mommy were walking in the dessert. As they walked, the sand was very hot and the sun was high in the sky.

"Mommy, when will we get to the oasis?" Lucy asked.

"It won't be long now," her mommy said.

Soon, Lucy heard something far away. "Is that the water from the oasis?" she asked.

"No," her mommy replied. "It's just the wind."

The two kept walking until they finally arrived at the oasis. It was lush and green and the sound of the water was so relaxing!

"Wow!" Lucy said. "Let's take a swim!"

They both jumped in the water and started to swim. It was cool and refreshing. Then, all of a sudden, Lucy heard something.

"Help! Help!"

It was a stranded animal! Lucy swam fast towards it. With one big push, she pushed the animal to shore.

"Good job, Lucy," her mommy said. "You saved the day!"

Lucy was proud that she had arrived just in time to save the animal!

name_of_work: Richard Cory by Edwin Arlington Robinson
content: Whenever Richard Cory went down town, We people on the pavement looked at him: He was a gentleman from sole to crown, Clean favored and imperially slim. And he was always quietly arrayed, And he was always human when he talked, But still he fluttered pulses when he said, "Good-morning," and he glittered when he walked. And he was rich--yes, richer than a king-- And admirably schooled in every grace: In fine, we thought that he was everything To make us wish that we were in his place. So on we worked, and waited for the light, And went without the meat and cursed the bread; And Richard Cory, one calm summer night, Went home and put a bullet through his head. This poem is in the public domain.

Age saw two quiet children Go loving by at twilight, He knew not whether homeward, Or outward from the village, Or (chimes were ringing) churchward, He waited, (they were strangers) Till they were out of hearing To bid them both be happy. "Be happy, happy, happy, And seize the day of pleasure." The age-long theme is Age's. 'Twas Age imposed on poems Their gather-roses burden To warn against the danger That overtaken lovers From being overflooded With happiness should have it. And yet not know they have it. But bid life seize the present? It lives less in the present Than in the future always, And less in both together Than in the past. The present Is too much for the senses, Too crowding, too confusing- Too present to imagine.

Once there was a great aeroplane. It was so big that it could fly all around the world! It was even bigger than a mountain.

The aeroplane flew very high in the sky. But one day, it had to make an emergency landing because of a broken wing. Everyone on the aeroplane was very afraid.

Fortunately, there was a friendly man who had the power to heal things. He waved his hands in the air, and the broken wing healed with a big puff of magical smoke! Everyone was very happy and the aeroplane flew higher and higher with its great wings.

The friendly man had saved the day and everyone on the aeroplane cheered. They all waved goodbye as the aeroplane flew off into the sky and they thanked the man for his magical healing powers.

Once upon a time, there were two twin sisters who loved collecting blue flowers. They lived in a small house near a big field where lots of flowers grew. Every day, they would go outside and collect as many blue flowers as they could find. They would put them in a big basket and bring them back to their house.

One day, while they were collecting flowers, they saw a blue bird flying above them. The bird was so pretty and they wanted to collect it too! But they knew that they couldn't collect a bird, so they just watched it fly away. They continued collecting blue flowers until their basket was full.

When they got back to their house, they put the blue flowers in a vase and put it on the table. They were so happy with their collection and admired it all day long. From that day on, they made it their mission to collect as many blue flowers as they could find.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to travel with her family. One day, they decided to go on a big adventure to a faraway land. But when they got to the airport, Lily realized she forgot her passport. She was sad and scared that she couldn't go on the trip. 

Her mom saw how sad she was and encouraged her to not give up. They went to the passport office and got a new passport just in time for their flight. Lily was so happy and felt light as a feather. She couldn't wait to explore the new place with her family. And from that day on, she always made sure to double-check that she had her passport before going on any trip.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a new watch that she loved very much. One day, she went to the park to play with her friends. While she was playing, a boy came and asked her if he could play with her watch. Lily was very polite and said yes.

The boy played with the watch for a long time, and Lily started to worry that he wouldn't return it. But she didn't want to be rude and ask for it back. Finally, it was time for the boy to go home, and Lily was sad because she thought she would never see her watch again.

But the next day, the boy returned the watch to Lily. She was so happy and grateful that she gave him a big hug. Lily learned that it's important to be polite and share, but also to trust that people will return what they borrow.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to go on adventures in the forest behind her house. One day, she was walking through the forest and saw a big bush full of blueberries. 

Lily was so excited that she started picking the blueberries. Suddenly, she heard a lively voice behind her. "Hi there, little girl! What are you doing?" It was a friendly squirrel who had been watching her. 

"I'm picking blueberries," said Lily. "Do you want some?" 

"Yes, please!" said the squirrel. "I love blueberries!" So, Lily shared her blueberries with the squirrel and they became good friends. From that day on, they went on many lively adventures together in the forest.

Once upon a time there was a big barber. He loved to cut peoples' hair. One day he had a strange feeling. He began to shrink until he was very small. He couldn't believe it.

He started to look for help and he found a big dog. "Please help me," said the barber. The big dog understood and he licked the barber. Suddenly, the barber started to get bigger and bigger again.

The barber was so happy and he thanked the big dog. Then he went back to his barber shop and started cutting peoples' hair. He was glad that he was not small anymore.

One day, a small bunny named Hoppy went to find food. The sky was gloomy with big gray clouds. Hoppy was a little scared, but he needed to find food for his family.

Hoppy hopped and hopped until he found a big pile of hay. He was so happy! He lay down on the hay and started to eat. It was so yummy and soft. Hoppy knew his family would love it too.

Hoppy carried the hay back to his home. The clouds went away and the sun came out. His family was so happy to see the hay. They all lay down together on the soft hay and ate. They were not hungry anymore and they all felt safe and warm.

Jill and Daisy were sisters. They were so happy to be together each and every day. One day, they decided to go on an adventure together. They grabbed hands and held tight. They smiled at each other as they went.

Suddenly, a terrible monster appeared! He was huge and scary. Daisy screamed and grabbed Jill's hand tightly. She held Jill close, so the monster couldn't get her. Jill held her sister's hand and didn't let it go.

The monster was so terrible that the girls started to cry. But when he saw their tears, he started to cry, too. The monster hugged them and said he was sorry. He just wanted to be friends.

The girls held a tight hug and then it was time for them to go home. They smiled and waved goodbye to the monster and he waved back.

The girls held hands and ran home, happy that they had faced the terrible monster together. They had each other and that was enough.

Once upon a time there were two friends, Jane and Fred. They lived far away from each other so they only wrote letters. One day Fred wrote to Jane with a special pen. The pen had ink inside of it that changed colour. Jane was so excited!

She opened the letter to see the beautiful ink inside. It was very slow to move and it made the most beautiful patterns. When the ink finally finished moving Jane said, "Wow! That's so cool!"

Jane wrote to Fred with the same kind of pen. She sent it off in the post and waited and waited. Finally the letter arrived and sure enough inside was the special ink again. Fred opened the letter and smiled when he saw the pattern the ink had made.

He said, "That looks so beautiful! Jane is so clever!â€ 
They kept writing back and forth with their special ink pen, each one amazed by the different patterns it created. 

The two friends had so much fun making things with the ink pen that their letters became very long!

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to collect cards. He had a big box full of them. One day, Timmy went to the park to show his cards to his friend, Johnny.

Johnny looked at the cards and said, "I want to buy one of your cards, Timmy."

Timmy thought about it and said, "Okay, I will sell you one of my cards, but you have to promise to take good care of it."

Johnny promised and bought one of Timmy's cards.

The moral of the story is that it's important to be compassionate and care about the things you buy and the people you sell to.

Once upon a time, there was a quick fox. He was always very busy because he wanted to keep busy. He wanted to show everyone how fast he could go.

One day, the quick fox heard something he had never heard before. It was loud and high, but the fox couldn't make out what it was. He kept looking around to try and figure out the sound.

Then, he saw a small deer on the path. The deer was deaf, so he couldn't hear the sound the fox was hearing. But the fox kept watching the deer to see what it would do.

The deer hopped around, looking for something to eat. The fox watched the deer for a long time, but he still couldn't figure out what the sound was. Finally, the deer hopped away and the fox was alone again.

The fox kept searching for the sound, and soon he found it - the sound was coming from the river! All of a sudden the fox knew what the sound was - it was the river, turning and bubbling and giving life to everything nearby.

The fox kept watching the river, amazed by its sound and beauty. He thought to himself how lucky he was to have found such an amazing sound.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. One night, Timmy was playing with his toys in his room. He was having so much fun that he didn't notice he knocked over a lamp. The lamp fell and broke into many pieces. Timmy was sad because he was careless and destroyed the lamp.

Timmy's mom heard the noise and came to see what happened. When she saw the broken lamp, she was not angry with Timmy. She knew it was an accident. She hugged Timmy and said, "It's okay, accidents happen. Let's clean up the mess together."

Timmy learned that it's important to be careful with things and to always clean up after himself. He also learned that his mom loves him no matter what. From that night on, Timmy was more careful with his toys and never destroyed anything again.

One day there was a cat. The cat was very charming. Everywhere she went people said how beautiful she was. She was so happy.

The cat went to the store to buy something special. As she was looking around she saw something shiny! It was a printer. She thought it looked so cool.

So the cat bought the printer and took it home. She was so excited to try it out. She put in some paper and started printing. She was so proud with what she made!

The cat made pictures for all her friends. They all said how charming the pictures were. The cat was so happy that she had bought a printer. It made her days so much more fun!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a brown teddy bear that she loved very much. One day, Lily's mom asked her to help with the dishes. Lily was happy to help and picked up a brown dish to wash. 

Suddenly, a big, scary dog appeared outside. Lily was scared and hugged her teddy bear tight. Her mom quickly ran outside and stood in front of the dog to protect Lily. The dog barked and growled, but Lily's mom didn't move. 

Finally, the dog ran away and Lily's mom came back inside. Lily hugged her mom and thanked her for protecting her. She finished washing the dishes and went to bed with her brown teddy bear by her side, feeling safe and loved.

I love you as a sheriff searches for a walnut That will solve a murder case unsolved for years Because the murderer left it in the snow beside a window Through which he saw her head, connecting with Her shoulders by a neck, and laid a red Roof in her heart. For this we live a thousand years; For this we love, and we live because we love, we are not Inside a bottle, thank goodness! I love you as a Kid searches for a goat; I am crazier than shirttails In the wind, when you're near, a wind that blows from The big blue sea, so shiny so deep and so unlike us; I think I am bicycling across an Africa of green and white fields Always, to be near you, even in my heart When I'm awake, which swims, and also I believe that you Are trustworthy as the sidewalk which leads me to The place where I again think of you, a new Harmony of thoughts! I love you as the sunlight leads the prow Of a ship which sails From Hartford to Miami, and I love you Best at dawn, when even before I am awake the sun Receives me in the questions which you always pose.

Once upon a time, there were two little dogs, Max and Millie. Max was brave and grew big and strong. Millie was quiet and liked to curl up tight. Every night, they would bark hello to each other and say goodnight before they went to bed.

One day, Millie said to Max, "Today we should try something new. Let's bark a different style."

Max thought that sounded fun so they tried making different 'woofs' and 'arfs'. Soon, they were making loud and silly noises and they both had a great time.

Max and Millie continued to practice their new style of barking, day after day. Soon, they were experts at barking in a new and exciting way.

Max and Millie's style of barking was so loud that it could be heard all over the neighbourhood. Everyone loved their loud bark and the two little dogs were happy with their new skill.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved muffins more than anything in the world. One day, she went to the bakery to buy a muffin, but they were all sold out.

Lily was very upset and demanded that the baker make more muffins. But the baker told her that he couldn't because he was out of ingredients.

Lily was stubborn and didn't want to leave without a muffin. But the baker suggested that she try a cupcake instead. Lily tried it and loved it even more than muffins! From that day on, Lily always asked for a cupcake instead of a muffin.

name_of_work: Song at the Beginning of Autumn by Elizabeth Jennings
content: Now watch this Autumn that arrives In smells. All looks like Summer still; Colours are quite unchanged, the air On green and white serenely thrives. Heavy the trees with growth and full The fields. Flowers flourish everywhere. Proust who collected time within A child's cake would understand The ambiguity of this - Summer still raging while a thin Column of smoke stirs from the land Proving that Autumn gropes for us. But every season is a kind Of rich nostalgia. We give names - Autumn and Summer, Winter, Spring - As though to unfasten from the mind Our moods and give them outward forms. We want the certain, solid thing. But I am carried back against My will into a childhood where Autumn is bonfires, marbles, smoke; I lean against my window fenced From evocations in the air. When I said Autumn, Autumn broke.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to explore the world and look at maps. She had a map of the whole world in her room and she would admire it every day.

One day, Lily went on an adventure to find a treasure. She followed the map and found a big cave. Inside the cave, she saw a shiny treasure chest. She was so excited and opened it quickly. But when she looked inside, she saw that the treasure was fake! She felt sad and disappointed.

But then, Lily remembered something her mom had told her. Sometimes, things are not what they seem. She looked closer at the fake treasure and saw that it was actually a puzzle. She put the puzzle together and it revealed a secret message. The message led her to a real treasure! Lily was so happy and proud of herself for not giving up.

name_of_work: What is Poetry? by John Ashbery
content: The medieval town, with frieze Of boy scouts from Nagoya? The snow That came when we wanted it to snow? Beautiful images? Trying to avoid Ideas, as in this poem? But we Go back to them as to a wife, leaving The mistress we desire? Now they Will have to believe it As we believed it. In school All the thought got combed out: What was left was like a field. Shut your eyes, and you can feel it for miles around. Now open them on a thin vertical path. It might give us--what?--some flowers soon?

Once upon a time, there was an amazing princess. She liked to ride around the kingdom on her special horse. Every day, she would grab the reins and take a ride around the castle.

The princess loved the wind in her hair and the smell of the grass. She would make beautiful patterns with her horse. Everywhere they went, people would admire their amazing moves.

One day, the princess got so excited, she forgot to hold on to the reins. She flew off her horse and landed right in a pond. She laughed and splashed around, having so much fun. The princess said that riding was the best thing ever.

The people cheering for the princess made the ride even more amazing. Everyone was so proud of her and gave her lots of hugs.

The princess enjoyed her ride so much, she decided to do it every day. She and her horse became the best of friends and would ride around the kingdom together, making amazing memories.

Once upon a time there were two best friends, Maisie and Sue. They loved playing together everyday but today was special as Sue had brought a prune for them to share.

Maisie was very jealous when Sue took a bite of the prune. She wanted her own bite too! So she said, "Sue wait! delay a little, I want some too."

Sue replied, "No delay! I want it all for me."

Maisie insisted, "Please delay! Share with me too."

Sue agreed, and the two friends happily shared the prune and had lots of fun together.

Lily and Sam were twins. They liked to play together in the park. One day, their mom said they could have ice-cream if they were good. Lily and Sam were very happy.

They ran to the ice-cream truck and waited in line. Lily wanted a pink ice-cream and Sam wanted a blue one. They held their mom's hand and said please and thank you to the ice-cream man.

Mom gave them a napkin and said, "Be careful, don't drop your ice-cream. It will melt in the sun. Stay close to me and don't run away."

Lily and Sam nodded and licked their ice-creams. They were very yummy. They saw some birds and flowers and swings. They wanted to see them more.

"Mom, can we go there?" Lily asked, pointing to the swings.

"Not now, sweetie. We have to finish our ice-creams first. They will make a mess if we move too much." Mom said.

"But I want to swing!" Sam said, pouting.

"Me too!" Lily said.

They looked at their ice-creams. They were still big and cold. They looked at the swings. They were empty and fun.

They had an idea. They put their ice-creams on the ground and ran to the swings. They forgot what mom said. They thought they would be back soon.

Mom saw them and called, "Lily! Sam! Come back! Where are you going? Don't leave your ice-creams!"

But Lily and Sam did not hear her. They were too busy swinging. They laughed and shouted and pushed each other. They had a lot of fun.

But they did not see what happened to their ice-creams. The sun was hot and the ice-creams were not. They melted and dripped and made a puddle. Some ants and flies came and ate them. Some dogs and cats came and licked them. Some kids and adults came and stepped on them.

When Lily and Sam were tired of swinging, they remembered their ice-creams. They ran back to where they left them. But they did not find them. They only found a mess.

They looked at each other and felt sad. They had no ice-creams. They had no napkins. They had no mom.

They started to cry. They wanted their ice-creams. They wanted their mom.

Mom heard them and came to them. She saw the mess and felt angry. She said, "Lily! Sam! What did you do? I told you to stay with me and not to drop your ice-creams. Look what happened. They are gone. You wasted them. You disobeyed me. You made me worry. I am not proud of you."

Lily and Sam felt sorry. They said, "We are sorry, mom. We wanted to swing. We forgot our ice-creams. We did not mean to make you angry. We love you, mom."

Mom hugged them and said, "I love you too, Lily and Sam. But you have to listen to me and do what I say. I know what is best for you. I want you to be safe and happy and good. Next time, stay with me and finish your ice-creams. Then we can go to the swings. OK?"

Lily and Sam nodded and said, "OK, mom. We will do that. We will be good. We will make you proud."

Mom smiled and said, "That's my twins. Come on, let's go home and clean up. Maybe we can have some more ice-cream later. But only if you are good."

Lily and Sam smiled and said, "Yes, mom. We will be good. We love ice-cream. We love you more."

Once upon a time, there were twin sisters named Lily and Lucy. They looked the same and had the same birthday. They loved to play together and always had fun.

One day, they went to the park to play. They saw a sign that said "Do not climb the tree". But they wanted to climb the tree because it looked fun. They climbed the tree and had a great time.

Suddenly, Lily slipped and fell down from the tree. She hurt her head and couldn't wake up. Lucy was so sad and cried a lot. She missed her sister so much. She knew that Lily was unique and special to her.

Once upon a time there were two friends, a fox and a bear. The fox and the bear would often go to the beach to talk and play. But one day the tide came in very quickly and soon the beach was covered in water.

The fox and the bear began to talk and discuss. The bear said "The tide has come and we must leave!". The fox argued, "no, let's stay and have fun!".

The bear thought for a moment. "I have an idea. Let's leave now and come back tomorrow when the tide is lower. We can make sure the beach is tidy so when we come back we can still have fun."

The fox agreed and the two friends left. The next day the bear and fox returned. The beach was still and the sand was tidy. They had lots of fun that day.

The moral of the story is to always be thoughtful and to think before you act. Cleaning up after yourself and being tidy is important and helps the environment around you.

Once upon a time, there was a great duck. This duck was very kind and liked to help others. One day, the duck saw a little bird with a hurt wing.

The duck wanted to help the bird, so it used its special power to heal. It touched the bird's wing gently, and the wing started to feel better. The little bird was very happy.

The great duck and the little bird became best friends. They played and swam together every day. And from that day on, the great duck helped many more animals with its healing power.

name_of_work: Home they Brought her Warrior Dead by Alfred Lord Tennyson
content: Home they brought her warrior dead: She nor swoon'd nor utter'd cry: All her maidens, watching, said, "She must weep or she will die." Then they praised him, soft and low, Call'd him worthy to be loved, Truest friend and noblest foe; Yet she neither spoke nor moved. Stole a maiden from her place, Lightly to the warrior stepped, Took the face-cloth from the face; Yet she neither moved nor wept. Rose a nurse of ninety years, Set his child upon her knee-- Like summer tempest came her tears-- "Sweet my child, I live for thee."

Sara and Tom are camping with their mom and dad. They have a big tent that is flexible and can bend in the wind. Sara and Tom like to play inside the tent and pretend they are on an adventure.

One day, they see a big truck coming to their campsite. The truck has a loud horn and a big sign that says "Park Ranger". Sara and Tom are curious and want to see what the truck is doing. They run out of the tent and wave to the driver.

"Hello, kids!" the driver says. "I'm here to check on the campsite and make sure everything is safe. Do you like camping?"

"Yes, we do!" Sara and Tom say. "We have a flexible tent and a lot of fun!"

"That's good to hear," the driver says. "But you have to be careful, too. There are some rules you have to follow when you camp. Do you know the rules?"

Sara and Tom shake their heads. They don't know the rules.

"Well, one of the rules is that you have to keep your food in a special box, not in your tent. Do you know why?" the driver asks.

Sara and Tom shake their heads again. They don't know why.

"Because there are some animals that like to eat your food, like bears and raccoons. If they smell your food in your tent, they might come and try to get it. And that can be dangerous for you and for them. Do you understand?" the driver explains.

Sara and Tom nod. They understand.

"But we have some food in our tent," Sara says. "We have some cookies and some juice and some cheese."

"Oh, no," the driver says. "That's not good. You have to take your food out of your tent and put it in the box. I'll show you where the box is. Come with me."

Sara and Tom follow the driver to the box. They take their food out of their tent and put it in the box. They lock the box with a key.

"There, that's better," the driver says. "Now your food is safe and so are you. And so are the animals. You did a good job, kids. Thank you for listening to me."

"You're welcome," Sara and Tom say. "Thank you for telling us the rules."

The driver smiles and waves to them. He gets back in his truck and drives away. Sara and Tom wave back. They go back to their tent and continue their adventure. They are happy and safe.

Lily and Ben are playing in the living room. They have many toys and books, but they want to do something new and interesting. They see a big box in the corner. It is empty and has a lid.

"Let's make a fort with the box!" Lily says. "We can hide inside and pretend we are in a castle or a spaceship."

"OK!" Ben says. "But how do we make the fort?"

Lily thinks for a moment. She has an idea. She gets a chair and puts it next to the box. She climbs on the chair and lifts the lid of the box. She pushes it up until it touches the ceiling. She asks Ben to support the lid with his hands.

"Look, Ben!" Lily says. "Now we have a roof for our fort. We can go inside and close the lid. It will be dark and cozy."

Ben likes the idea. He supports the lid with his hands and climbs on the chair. He joins Lily inside the box. They close the lid and sit down. They can hear each other's breathing and giggling. They feel happy and safe.

They start to imagine that they are in a different place. They tell each other stories about what they see and hear and feel. They have a lot of fun in their fort. They forget about the toys and books. They only need the box, the lid, the ceiling, and each other.

Tim and Lily were playing in the bathroom. They liked to splash water in the tub and make bubbles with the soap. They also liked to put toys in the water and pretend they were boats or fish.

One day, Tim had a new toy. It was a red car that could go very fast. He wanted to show Lily how fast it could go in the water. He said, "Look, Lily, this is my new car. It can go faster than any of your toys. Watch this!"

He put the car in the water and pushed a button. The car zoomed across the tub and hit the drain. The drain was open and the car went inside. Tim and Lily heard a clunk and then nothing.

Tim was very sad. He cried, "My car! My car! It went in the drain! I want it back!"

Lily was scared. She said, "I'm sorry, Tim. I didn't know the drain was open. Maybe we can get it back. Let's ask Mommy."

They ran out of the bathroom and looked for Mommy. They found her in the kitchen. She was busy making dinner. She saw them and said, "What's wrong, kids? Why are you wet and crying?"

Tim and Lily told her what happened. They said, "Mommy, Mommy, we were playing in the tub and Tim's new car went in the drain. Can you get it back for us? Please, please, please!"

Mommy was angry. She said, "You were playing in the tub without me? That's very dangerous. You could have drowned or slipped or hurt yourself. And you wasted water and soap and made a mess. And you lost Tim's new car in the drain. That's very ignorant. You should know better. You are both in big trouble. Go to your rooms right now. No dinner for you. And no more toys for a week."

Tim and Lily felt very bad. They said, "We're sorry, Mommy. We didn't mean to. We just wanted to have fun. Please don't be mad at us. Please don't send us to our rooms. Please don't take away our toys."

But Mommy didn't listen. She said, "Go now. And don't come out until I say so. And don't expect me to get your car back. It's gone forever. Maybe that will teach you a lesson."

Tim and Lily went to their rooms. They cried and cried. They wished they had never played in the tub. They wished they had never seen the car. They wished Mommy would forgive them. But she didn't. She was too busy and too angry. She forgot about them and their car. She was ignorant too.

Once upon a time there was a cat named Spot. He liked to climb up tall trees. One day he saw a tall tree with a branch that looked perfect for him to sit on. Spot climbed up and reached the branch.

It was wet and slippery. Spot slipped and started to fall, but then he saw a bird on a nearby branch. "Help me," said Spot.

The bird replied, "I will provide." She flew down and caught Spot before he could fall. "Thank you," said Spot.

The bird smiled and said, "Glad I could help. Take care now."

Spot thanked the bird again and climbed back up the wet branch. It was a bit tricky, but Spot made it safely to the top. From then on, Spot never forgot to be careful when on a wet branch!

name_of_work: Beyond the Years by Paul Laurence Dunbar
content: I Beyond the years the answer lies, Beyond where brood the grieving skies And Night drops tears. Where Faith rod-chastened smiles to rise And doff its fears, And carping Sorrow pines and dies-- Beyond the years. II Beyond the years the prayer for rest Shall beat no more within the breast; The darkness clears, And Morn perched on the mountain's crest Her form uprears-- The day that is to come is best, Beyond the years. III Beyond the years the soul shall find That endless peace for which it pined, For light appears, And to the eyes that still were blind With blood and tears, Their sight shall come all unconfined Beyond the years.

Once upon a time, there was a grumpy bear. He was always warm and cozy in his home. But one day he decided to go out and explore. So he left his home and joined the rail.

The rail was long and it crossed through many different places. As the bear journeyed along, he noticed the animals running gracefully through the fields by the rail. He waved hello to them, but they didn't wave back. 

The little bear was starting to get lonely, and he wished he had some friends to ride the rail with him. Then he saw two rabbits hopping along together, and he asked if he could join them.

The rabbits were happy to have some company, so they welcomed the bear. Soon they were all travelling on the rail together, laughing and having fun. 

The bear got to explore all kinds of wonderful places, thanks to their graceful journey on the rail. And from then on, the bear never travelled alone again.

Go inside a stone That would be my way. Let somebody else become a dove Or gnash with a tiger's tooth. I am happy to be a stone. From the outside the stone is a riddle: No one knows how to answer it. Yet within, it must be cool and quiet Even though a cow steps on it full weight, Even though a child throws it in a river; The stone sinks, slow, unperturbed To the river bottom Where the fishes come to knock on it And listen. I have seen sparks fly out When two stones are rubbed, So perhaps it is not dark inside after all; Perhaps there is a moon shining From somewhere, as though behind a hill-- Just enough light to make out The strange writings, the star-charts On the inner walls.

Once there was an elderly beetle who wanted to bake something. He looked around his house for something tasty to make. After much searching, he found some ingredients and made a delicious pastry. He washed the dishes and proudly took the pastry outside to show his friends.

The other beetles were so excited to see what he had made. They all gathered around and cheered as the elderly beetle cut the pastry into slices. Everyone took a slice and declared it was delicious. They asked him what it was called and the elderly beetle replied that it was an "Elderly Beetle's Special"! Everyone laughed and they all shared the pastry until it was gone. So, the elderly beetle had successfully baked his very first treat!

name_of_work: Why Some Girls Love Horses by Paisley Rekdal
content: And then I thought, Can I have more of this, would it be possible for every day to be a greater awakening: more light, more light, your face on the pillow with the sleep creases rudely fragmenting it, hair so stiff from paint and sheet rock it feels like the dirty short hank of mane I used to grab on Dandy's neck before he hauled me up and forward, white flanks flecked green with shit and the satin of his dander, the livingness, the warmth of all that blood just under the skin and in the long, thick muscle of the neck-- He was smarter than most of the children I went to school with. He knew how to stand with just the crescent of his hoof along a boot toe and press, incrementally, his whole weight down. The pain so surprising when it came, its iron intention sheathed in stealth, the decisive sudden twisting of his leg until the hoof pinned one's foot completely to the ground, we'd have to beat and beat him with a brush to push him off, that hot insistence with its large horse eye trained deliberately on us, to watch-- Like us, he knew how to announce through violence how he didn't hunger, didn't want despite our practiced ministrations: too young not to try to empathize with this cunning: this thing that was and was not human we must respect for itself and not our imagination of it: I loved him because I could not love him anymore in the ways I'd taught myself, watching the slim bodies of teenagers guide their geldings in figure eights around the ring as if they were one body, one fluid motion of electric understanding I would never feel working its way through fingers to the bit: this thing had a name, a need, a personality; it possessed an indifference that gave me logic and a measure: I too might stop wanting the hand placed on back or shoulder and never feel the desired response. I loved the horse for the pain it could imagine and inflict on me, the sudden jerking of head away from halter, the tentative nose inspecting first before it might decide to relent and eat. I loved what was not slave or instinct, that when you turn to me it is a choice, it is always a choice to imagine pleasure might be blended, one warmth bleeding into another as the future bleeds into the past, more light, more light, your hand against my shoulder, the image of the one who taught me disobedience is the first right of being alive.

One day, a cool cat named Tom went to the park. He saw his friend, a dog named Max. They wanted to have some fun together.

"Let's play a game," Tom said to Max. "I suggest we play hide and seek."

"Great idea!" Max agreed. They started to play. Tom closed his eyes and counted to ten. Max ran and hid behind a big tree.

Tom looked around the park to find Max. He saw him hiding and said, "I found you, Max! Now it's your turn to count."

Max counted to ten while Tom hid behind a slide. Max found Tom quickly, and they laughed together. They had a lot of fun playing hide and seek at the park.

name_of_work: Sadie and Maud by Gwendolyn Brooks
content: Maud went to college. Sadie stayed at home. Sadie scraped life With a fine-tooth comb. She didn't leave a tangle in. Her comb found every strand. Sadie was one of the livingest chits In all the land. Sadie bore two babies Under her maiden name. Maud and Ma and Papa Nearly died of shame. When Sadie said her last so-long Her girls struck out from home. (Sadie had left as heritage Her fine-tooth comb.) Maud, who went to college, Is a thin brown mouse. She is living all alone In this old house.

Anna and Ben are playing with their toys in the living room. They have a lot of fun making noises and pretending to be animals. Anna is a graceful cat and Ben is a loud lion. They chase each other around the sofa and the table.

"Roar!" Ben says, jumping on Anna. "I am the king of the jungle!"

"Meow!" Anna says, scratching Ben's nose. "I am the queen of the cats!"

They laugh and roll on the floor. They are very happy.

But then they hear a loud snap from the kitchen. They stop playing and look at each other. What was that?

They run to the kitchen and see their mom holding a broken plate. She looks sad and angry. She was making dinner for them, but she dropped the plate and it snapped in half.

"Oh no!" Anna says. "Mom, are you okay?"

"I'm fine, sweetie, but I'm sorry. I ruined your dinner. It was your favorite, spaghetti and meatballs." Mom says.

Ben and Anna feel sorry for their mom. They don't care about the dinner. They care about her.

"It's okay, mom. We love you. We can have something else for dinner. Maybe some soup and bread." Ben says.

"Yes, mom. We can help you clean up the mess. And we can give you a big hug." Anna says.

They hug their mom and help her pick up the pieces of the plate. They are very kind and helpful.

Mom smiles and thanks them. She is very proud of them. She says they are the best kids in the world.

They have soup and bread for dinner, and they are still happy. They tell their mom about their game and their toys. They make her laugh and smile.

They are a happy family.

Once there was a bald man. He was walking down the street until he noticed a jar on the ground. He was curious and so he bent down to open it. He twisted the top and opened the jar. Inside the jar, he found a small toy car and a big bag of candy. The man was so happy. He put the candy in his pocket and held the toy car in his hand. He smiled and walked away, enjoying the candy and playing with the toy car. The end.

Lily was a very intelligent girl. She liked to read books and learn new things. She had many books in her room, and she often gazed at them with curiosity and wonder.

One day, her brother Tom came into her room. He was bored and wanted to play. He saw Lily's books and said, "Books are boring. Let's play with my cars and trucks. They are fun and noisy."

Lily did not want to play with Tom's cars and trucks. She wanted to read her books and learn new things. She said, "No, thank you. I like books. They are interesting and quiet."

Tom did not like Lily's answer. He got angry and said, "Books are stupid. You are stupid. You don't know how to have fun." He grabbed one of Lily's books and threw it on the floor.

Lily was very sad and mad. She loved her books and did not like Tom to be mean to them. She said, "Stop it, Tom. Books are not stupid. You are rude. You don't know how to be nice."

Tom and Lily started to yell and fight. They made a big mess in Lily's room. They did not hear their mom coming upstairs. She opened the door and saw them. She was very disappointed and said, "What are you doing, Tom and Lily? Why are you fighting and making a mess? You should be kind and respectful to each other and to your things."

Tom and Lily felt ashamed and sorry. They realized they were wrong and said, "We are sorry, mom. We were not kind and respectful. We will clean up the mess and apologize to each other."

Mom smiled and said, "That's good, Tom and Lily. I'm glad you learned your lesson. Books are not boring or stupid. They are valuable and enriching. Cars and trucks are not fun or noisy. They are playful and exciting. You can both enjoy different things and still get along. You can also share and learn from each other. That's what intelligent and loving siblings do."

Tom and Lily hugged and said, "Thank you, mom. We love you. We love each other. We love books and cars and trucks. We will be intelligent and loving siblings from now on."

name_of_work: Sleeping in the Forest by Mary Oliver
content: I thought the earth remembered me, she took me back so tenderly, arranging her dark skirts, her pockets full of lichens and seeds. I slept as never before, a stone on the riverbed, nothing between me and the white fire of the stars but my thoughts, and they floated light as moths among the branches of the perfect trees. All night I heard the small kingdoms breathing around me, the insects, and the birds who do their work in the darkness. All night I rose and fell, as if in water, grappling with a luminous doom. By morning I had vanished at least a dozen times into something better.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Ruby. She was very smart and liked to explore the world. 

One day, Ruby went to explore a new place. She discovered a very shiny knife. She thought it looked very pretty, so she turned it around and around in her hands. 

Ruby decided she was going to take the knife home and show her family. She was clever, so she found a safe way to hold it. She carefully turned the knife so that the sharp part faced away from her. 

Ruby went back home and proudly showed her family her shiny new knife. They were very impressed and said that she was very smart! 

From that day on, Ruby was even more curious and kept turning things around to explore the world.

Tom was a boy who liked to play outside. He liked to run, jump, and climb trees. He also liked to look for bugs and animals. He had a jar where he kept some of his finds, like ants, worms, and beetles.

One day, he saw a big spider on a web. It had eight legs and many eyes. It was black and shiny. Tom thought it was cool and wanted to catch it. He took his jar and went closer to the web. He reached out his hand to grab the spider.

But the spider did not want to be caught. It was scared of Tom and his jar. It refused to let go of its web. It bit Tom's hand with its fangs. Tom felt a sharp pain and dropped his jar. He cried out loud and ran away.

Tom's mom heard him and came to see what was wrong. She saw his hand was red and swollen. She took him inside and put some ice on it. She told him he was brave, but he should not touch spiders. They can be dangerous and hurt him.

Tom learned his lesson. He still liked to play outside, but he did not try to catch spiders anymore. He was more careful with bugs and animals. He also made sure to close his jar tightly, so his other finds would not escape. He was happy and safe.

Once upon a time, there was a dark farmer. One day, the farmer had an idea - he wanted to send his little dog far away. When he told his dog, the pup was confused. "Where am I going, Farmer?" asked the pup.

The farmer smiled. "You're going to a nice, green field. You'll be able to run around and chase rabbits all day long!"

The pup was excited! She started to run around the farm, barking and jumping. "I'm ready to go, Farmer!" she said. 

The farmer opened the barn door, and waved goodbye.  "Bye, little pup! Be good, and don't worry - I'll come and visit soon!" The pup barked with joy, and set off for the dark field. The farmer watched until his pup was out of sight. 

And that's how the farmer sent his pup off to a dark field filled with green grass and plenty of room to run. The pup lived happily ever after.

Once upon a time, there was a little rabbit named Benny. Benny loved to eat celery. One day, Benny's friend, a squirrel named Sammy, came to visit him. 

Sammy said, "Benny, I brought you a carrot to eat!" 

Benny replied, "No thank you, Sammy. I only want to eat celery today." 

Sammy said, "But Benny, I don't like celery. Can't we eat carrots together?" 

Benny thought for a moment and said, "I'm sorry, Sammy. I can't resist the taste of celery. Maybe next time we can eat something else together." 

Sammy understood and said, "That's okay, Benny. I don't want you to be careless with your food choices. Enjoy your celery!" 

Benny happily munched on his celery while Sammy nibbled on his carrot. They both enjoyed their snacks and had a fun day playing together. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily's mom brought home a new newspaper. Lily thought it looked amazing with all the pictures and colors.

Lily's mom said, "Be careful, Lily. The edges of the newspaper are sharp." 

Lily replied, "Okay, Mommy. I will be careful." 

Later that day, Lily's friend came over to play. Lily showed her the amazing newspaper. Her friend said, "Wow! That is so cool!" 

Lily said, "Just be careful, the edges are sharp." 

Lily and her friend had a fun time looking at the pictures and reading the newspaper together. They were happy and excited to learn new things.

One day, a little boy named Tim wanted to sing. He went to gather his toy microphone. But he could not find it. Tim felt frustrated.

Tim asked his sister, Lily, "Have you seen my microphone?" Lily thought for a moment and said, "I saw it near your toys, but I don't know where it is now." Tim looked near his toys but still could not find it.

Later, Tim found the microphone in a box. He was so happy! He remembered that he put it there a few days ago. Tim sang his favorite song and felt much better.

name_of_work: Farewell to Kurdistan by Rosemary Tonks
content: As my new life begins, I start smiling at the people around me, You would think I'd just been given a substantial meal, I see all their good points. The railroad sheds are full of greenish-yellow electricity, It's the great mad-day hour in London...that suddenly goes brown. ...My stupefying efforts make money And to have a life! Well, I'm leaving; nothing can hold me. The platforms are dense to the foot, Rich, strong-willed travellers pace about in the dark daylight, And how they stink of green fatty soaps, the rich. More dirty weather...you can hardly see the newspaper stand With its abominable, ludicrous papers...which are so touching I ought to laugh and cry, instead of gritting my teeth. Let me inhale the filthy air for the last time Good heavens, how vile it is...I could take you step by step Back among the twilight buildings, into my old life... The trains come in, boiling, caked ! The station half tames them, there's the sound of blows; the uproar! And I -- I behave as though I've been starved of noise, My intestinr eats up this big music And my new bourgeois soul promptly bursts into flames, in mid-air. No use pouring me a few last minutes of the old life From your tank of shadow, filled with lost and rotten people, I admit: the same flow of gutter-sugar to the brain... No one to see me off -- Ah! I would like to be seen off; it must be the same agonizing woman Who does not want to understand me, and who exposes me in public, So that I can turn away, choked with the cold bile, And feel myself loved absoltely; the bitch. These carriages, that have heavy brown and black bread Up their sides! But look out for the moment of cowardice, It's Charon's rowing-boat that lurches and fouls my hand As I climb on -- exile, Limboist. ...The way these people get on with thir lives; I bow down With my few deeds and my lotus scars. Last minutes...last greenish-yellow minutes Of the lost and rotten hours...faro, and old winters dimmed, On which the dark -- Yes, the black sugar-crust is forming, London. I'm leaving! Nothing can hold me! The trains, watered and greased, scream to be off. Hullo -- I'm already sticking out my elbows for a piece of territory, I occupy my place as though I can't get enough of it -- And with what casual, haughty, and specific gestures, incidentally. Tradesmen, Pigs, regenerative trains -- I shall be saved! I shall go to the centre of Europe; gliding, As children skate on the diamond lid of the lake Never touching gound -- Xenophile, on the blue-plated meadows. Oh I shall live off myself, rainclothes, documents, The great train simmers....Life is large, large! ...I shall live off your loaf of shadows, London; I admit it, at the last.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She liked to play with her toys and sing songs. One day, her mom took her to church. Lily saw a lot of people there and she felt happy.

During the church service, Lily saw a boy who was being naughty. He was running around and making noise. Lily's mom whispered to her, "Don't be like that boy, Lily. He's not being good."

After the service, Lily's mom asked her if she wanted to request a song to sing at church next week. Lily thought about it and said yes. She wanted to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star". Her mom smiled and said, "That's a great idea, Lily."

These times strike monied worldlings with dismay: Even rich men, brave by nature, taint the air With words of apprehension and despair: While tens of thousands, thinking on the affray, Men unto whom sufficient for the day And minds not stinted or untilled are given, Sound, healthy, children of the God of heaven, Are cheerful as the rising sun in May. What do we gather hence but firmer faith That every gift of noble origin Is breathed upon by Hope's perpetual breath; That virtue and the faculties within Are vital,--and that riches are akin To fear, to change, to cowardice, and death?

One day, Mary was looking for something to do. She thought and thought, then she had an idea. She decided to go and watch the waffle in the park.

Mary ran to the park, but when she arrived the waffle was nowhere to be seen. Mary started to look everywhere she could. She looked behind some bushes and up trees.

Finally, she spotted something hidden in the long grass. To get a better look, Mary stepped a little closer. Suddenly, the hidden thing moved! It was a small dog, and it started to bark at Mary.

Mary was very scared, but she knew not to move. The small dog watched her very closely. After a few moments, the dog stopped barking and ran away.

Mary waited until the coast was clear, then she continued her hunt for the waffle. After a while, she finally found it. Mary watched the waffle as it hopped from one place to the next. She was very happy and knew that she would never forget this special day.

name_of_work: No Coward Soul Is Mine by Emily Bronte
content: No coward soul is mine No trembler in the world's storm-troubled sphere I see Heaven's glories shine And Faith shines equal arming me from Fear O God within my breast Almighty ever-present Deity Life, that in me hast rest, As I Undying Life, have power in Thee Vain are the thousand creeds That move men's hearts, unutterably vain, Worthless as withered weeds Or idlest froth amid the boundless main To waken doubt in one Holding so fast by thy infinity, So surely anchored on The steadfast rock of Immortality. With wide-embracing love Thy spirit animates eternal years Pervades and broods above, Changes, sustains, dissolves, creates and rears Though earth and moon were gone And suns and universes ceased to be And Thou wert left alone Every Existence would exist in thee There is not room for Death Nor atom that his might could render void Since thou art Being and Breath And what thou art may never be destroyed.

Once upon a time, there was a dead park. No one went there anymore. The grass was brown and the flowers had dried up.

One day, a little boy and his dad saw the dead park and the dad said it was time to help. 

They started to pick up all the waste that was laying around. Little by little, it got tidier. 

Finally, when all the waste was gone, the dad went to the town hall to ask for permission. The people at the town hall said yes. 

The dad and the little boy went back to the dead park and started to plant flowers, new grass and trees. After a few weeks, the dead park was alive again. 

The dad and the little boy were so proud of their hard work. They could now see birds flying around and butterflies drinking the nectar of the flowers.
