Once there was a little girl named Emily. She was very happy and felt spoiled because she had lots of special toys. 

One day, she went out to play with her toys when something strange appeared. It was a magical castle! Emily was so excited and she didn't know what to do. 

She went up to the castle and saw lots of work to do. There was cleaning, painting and planting. Emily decided that it must be her special work and she wanted to do it all by herself. 

She worked very hard and when she was done, the castle looked beautiful. Emily was so proud of her work. 

Suddenly, the castle disappeared but Emily was happy because she knew she had done a good job and felt spoiled for the chance to do it.

Once upon a time there was an old Parrot who lived in a big tree in the forest. He liked to lean from the branch and listen to the other animals. One day, the Parrot leaned over too far and fell out of his tree. 

He flapped his wings and flew away until he spotted a small girl in the garden. She had bright yellow hair and a big smile. As she saw the Parrot, she clapped her hands and said "Hello, Parrot!"

The Parrot was so happy he said "Hello! How old are you?" 

The girl smiled and said "I am three years old. Do you want to be my friend?". 

The Parrot smiled and said "Yes, I would love to be your friend". 

From that day onwards, the Parrot and the girl were the best of friends. They played together, laughed together and took long naps together in the sun. They shared many wonderful and happy days together.

Once upon a time there was a driver. Every day he would leave his house with a big smile. He was a very graceful driver.

One day, when he was driving, he spotted a little girl. She was standing on the side of the road, looking very sad. The driver pulled over and asked, "What's wrong?"

The little girl said, "I want to drive." She was only three years old and she wanted to be a driver like the man in the car.

The driver laughed and said, "You're too little! Come back when you are bigger, and I will help you."

The little girl was very happy. She thanked the driver and ran off.

The driver watched her, smiling. She was very graceful as she ran. He knew, one day, she would be a great driver.

name_of_work: The Arrow and the Song by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
content: I shot an arrow into the air, It fell to earth, I knew not where; For, so swiftly it flew, the sight Could not follow it in its flight. I breathed a song into the air, It fell to earth, I knew not where; For who has sight so keen and strong, That it can follow the flight of song? Long, long afterward, in an oak I found the arrow, still unbroke; And the song, from beginning to end, I found again in the heart of a friend.

One day, a green frog was hopping around near the pond. A curious butterfly flew over to say hello and asked the frog, "What are you doing?". The frog paused and thought for a moment before he replied, "I am looking for a place to call my own. I want to be independent!"

The butterfly smiled. She thought it was adorable that the frog was so independent. "I know a perfect place for you," the butterfly said.

The butterfly and the frog hopped over to a nearby tree. The frog was very excited when he saw it! There were lots of interesting things to explore.

"This is perfect," the frog replied. He thanked the butterfly for her help and hopped inside the tree.

The green frog was so happy in his new home. He felt safe and independent. Every day he explored the tree and learned something new about the world.

Once upon a time there was a little boy named Ben. He wanted to make a cake for his friend's birthday, so he asked his mom for help. His mom told him that if he was careful and did not smash the ingredients he could make the cake. Ben was excited and agreed to be careful. 

He mixed the ingredients and placed the cake in the the oven to bake. Then, Ben waited and waited. Finally, after some time, it was time to take out the cake. 

When Ben opened the oven, he found the cake was flipped upside down. Ben was so disappointed and started to cry. He asked his mom, "Why did the cake flip over? I was careful and I minded what you said!" 

His mom hugged him and said, "I know you were careful and minded what I said, but Ben, sometimes things don't go as planned. What's important is that you tried your best and remain flexible. As long as you have a flexible attitude and try your best, even when things don't go as planned, you can still be proud of yourself." 

Ben smiled, thanked his mom and agreed to remain flexible.

The moral of the story is that even when things don't turn out the way you had hoped, being flexible and trying your best is whatâ€™s most important.

name_of_work: The Truth the Dead Know by Anne Sexton
content: Gone, I say and walk from church, refusing the stiff procession to the grave, letting the dead ride alone in the hearse. It is June. I am tired of being brave. We drive to the Cape. I cultivate myself where the sun gutters from the sky, where the sea swings in like an iron gate and we touch. In another country people die. My darling, the wind falls in like stones from the whitehearted water and when we touch we enter touch entirely. No one's alone. Men kill for this, or for as much. And what of the dead? They lie without shoes in their stone boats. They are more like stone than the sea would be if it stopped. They refuse to be blessed, throat, eye and knucklebone.

name_of_work: The Ballad of the Landlord by Langston Hughes
content: Landlord, landlord, My roof has sprung a leak. Don't you 'member I told you about it Way last week? Landlord, landlord, These steps is broken down. When you come up yourself It's a wonder you don't fall down. Ten Bucks you say I owe you? Ten Bucks you say is due? Well, that's Ten Bucks more'n I'l pay you Till you fix this house up new. What? You gonna get eviction orders? You gonna cut off my heat? You gonna take my furniture and Throw it in the street? Um-huh! You talking high and mighty. Talk on-till you get through. You ain't gonna be able to say a word If I land my fist on you. Police! Police! Come and get this man! He's trying to ruin the government And overturn the land! Copper's whistle! Patrol bell! Arrest. Precinct Station. Iron cell. Headlines in press: MAN THREATENS LANDLORD TENANT HELD NO BAIL JUDGE GIVES NEGRO 90 DAYS IN COUNTY JAIL!

Once upon a time, there was a king who loved to wear a shiny crown on his head. One day, while playing in the garden, the crown fell off his head and got lost in the grass. The king searched for it but couldn't find it. He asked his helpers to find it but it was difficult for them too.

Suddenly, a little boy came running and said, "I can find your crown!" The king was surprised and asked, "How can you find it?" The little boy replied, "I have sharp eyes and can see things that are difficult to find." The king was impressed and asked the boy to help him.

The little boy looked carefully and found the crown in no time. The king was very happy and gave the little boy a reward. From that day on, the king always kept the little boy with him as his helper. And the little boy was very happy to help the king with his sharp eyes.

Once upon a time, there were two friends. They were good friends and liked to play together. One day, they decided to do something special to make their house cleaner. They went to the closet and got a big mask. They wore it and began to clean the house.

They scrubbed the floor and washed the windows. They picked up all the toys and swept the cobwebs away. They even dust the walls and vacuumed the stairs. Everything looked so clean and good.

When they were done, they felt so pleased with themselves. They hugged each other and high fived. They had done a great job of cleaning. Then they removed their masks and went outside to play together.

name_of_work: Breaking the Surface by Jean Bleakney
content: I have gone beyond the childish delight of plumping the heaviest stone into the shallows, and yet, distance throwing has defeated me. Head bowed, I clamber the scree of the shore filling my pockets with its loose change - each cool button of basalt tentatively flipped before selection. This is my talent - a whiplash from the hip, the skite, innumerable tangents, then a glide until, as if remembering the laws of gravity, it stops and languidly slews before anchoring. One facet of the art of skimming, I say is that, by overriding the big splash, sound release is reduced to a whispering skiff thus reinforcing the attenuated decay of energy... I take it, from your broadening grin, that no amount of gilding with applied physics can disguise pure panache or my primitive desire to rearrange the shoreline - in a minimalist sort of way

Once upon a time, there was a baby bear who wanted to peek outside. It was cold outside, but the bear was so eager to look. He peeked through the window but all he saw was snow. He got so impatient and ran back to his cozy bed.

The bear took a nap and when he woke up he decided to try again. He put on his warm coat and went back to the window. He peeked outside and saw something so wonderful! He saw white trees and sparkling snowflakes. The bear was so excited, he wanted to go out and explore.

The bear ran as fast as he could to the front door. He opened it and peeked out. The cold was so strong that it made him shiver, but he was too curious. He stepped tentatively out into the snow and looked around. He saw ice and snow, and the most beautiful sights he had ever seen. The bear was so happy he could hardly contain it.

The bear stayed out in the snow, playing and exploring all day. When he finally went back inside, he was so content. He was glad that he had peeked outside, even though it was cold. He knew that he had made a great adventure.

Once upon a time, there was a big hippo. He lived by a river. The hippo liked to play with his friends, the birds and the fish. The hippo was very happy.

One day, the hippo found a bright stone. It was very pretty. He wanted to keep it safe. So, the hippo decided to bury it in the mud near his home. He dug a hole and put the stone in it. Then, he covered it up with mud.

The next day, the hippo wanted to show his friends the bright stone. He went to the spot where he buried it and dug it up. The birds and the fish were very excited to see it. They all played with the bright stone and had a fun day together.

name_of_work: A Toccata of Galuppi's by Robert Browning
content: I Oh Galuppi, Baldassaro, this is very sad to find! I can hardly misconceive you; it would prove me deaf and blind; But although I take your meaning, 'tis with such a heavy mind! II Here you come with your old music, and here's all the good it brings. What, they lived once thus at Venice where the merchants were the kings, Where Saint Mark's is, where the Doges used to wed the sea with rings? III Ay, because the sea's the street there; and 'tis arched by . . . what you call . . . Shylock's bridge with houses on it, where they kept the carnival: I was never out of England--it's as if I saw it all. IV Did young people take their pleasure when the sea was warm in May? Balls and masks begun at midnight, burning ever to mid-day, When they made up fresh adventures for the morrow, do you say? V Was a lady such a lady, cheeks so round and lips so red,-- On her neck the small face buoyant, like a bell-flower on its bed, O'er the breast's superb abundance where a man might base his head? VI Well, and it was graceful of them--they'd break talk off and afford --She, to bite her mask's black velvet--he, to finger on his sword, While you sat and played Toccatas, stately at the clavichord? VII What? Those lesser thirds so plaintive, sixths diminished, sigh on sigh, Told them something? Those suspensions, those solutions--"Must we die?" Those commiserating sevenths--"Life might last! we can but try! VIII "Were you happy?" --"Yes."--"And are you still as happy?"--"Yes. And you?" --"Then, more kisses!"--"Did I stop them, when a million seemed so few?" Hark, the dominant's persistence till it must be answered to! IX So, an octave struck the answer. Oh, they praised you, I dare say! "Brave Galuppi! that was music! good alike at grave and gay! "I can always leave off talking when I hear a master play!" X Then they left you for their pleasure: till in due time, one by one, Some with lives that came to nothing, some with deeds as well undone, Death stepped tacitly and took them where they never see the sun. XI But when I sit down to reason, think to take my stand nor swerve, While I triumph o'er a secret wrung from nature's close reserve, In you come with your cold music till I creep thro' every nerve. XII Yes, you, like a ghostly cricket, creaking where a house was burned: "Dust and ashes, dead and done with, Venice spent what Venice earned. "The soul, doubtless, is immortal--where a soul can be discerned. XIII "Yours for instance: you know physics, something of geology, "Mathematics are your pastime; souls shall rise in their degree; "Butterflies may dread extinction,--you'll not die, it cannot be! XIV "As for Venice and her people, merely born to bloom and drop, "Here on earth they bore their fruitage, mirth and folly were the crop: "What of soul was left, I wonder, when the kissing had to stop? XV "Dust and ashes!" So you creak it, and I want the heart to scold. Dear dead women, with such hair, too--what's become of all the gold Used to hang and brush their bosoms? I feel chilly and grown old.

Of all the public places, dear to make a scene, I've chosen here. Of all the doorways in the world to choose to sleep, I've chosen yours. I'm on the street, under the stars. For coppers I can dance or sing. For silver-swallow swords, eat fire. For gold-escape from locks and chains. It's not as if I'm holding out for frankincense or myrrh, just change. You give me tea. That's big of you. I'm on my knees. I beg of you.

Once there was a little girl called Sarah. She was three years old and loved to dance. She wanted her movements to have a rhythm but she had never done it before.

One day she put on some music and started to move. She felt kind of tough at first but then something amazing happened. She started to slip into a rhythm. Her moves were smooth and her feet kept time with the beat.

Sarah laughed as she continued to dance. She felt full of joy and didn't want to stop. She moved around the room with a smile on her face. She felt alive and free.

The music faded away and then stopped and Sarah stopped too. She was smiling and her mum came to hug her. She whispered, "That was incredible! I'm so proud of you."

Sarah felt really happy and knew she could do this again. She couldn't wait to slip into that rhythm again soon.

Once upon a time, there was a horse named Brownie. Brownie was a normal horse who loved to run and play in the fields. One day, Brownie saw a little girl who was sad. Brownie asked, "Why are you sad?" The little girl said, "I don't have a pretty dress to wear to the party."

Brownie had an idea. He said, "I can help you! I know where to find the prettiest dress." So, Brownie took the little girl to a nearby meadow where there were lots of flowers. Brownie found a beautiful flower and said, "This flower will make a pretty dress for you."

The little girl was so happy and thanked Brownie. She picked the flower and made a dress. At the party, everyone loved the little girl's dress and asked where she got it. The little girl said, "My friend Brownie helped me find it."

The moral of the story is that even if you are just a normal horse, you can still help someone in need.

Once upon a time there was a soft insect. It was small and fluffy and living in a garden. The insect was all alone, but it was happy. Every day it enjoyed going outside and exploring the world.

One day, the insect saw something big on the ground. It was a colourful flower! The insect hopped over and touched the soft petals with its antennae. As it stayed there, a gentle breeze blew by. The insect was so surprised it remained very still.

The breeze began to pick up and the insect was carried away! It floated through the sky and eventually landed in a tree. The insect was so high up but it was not scared. Instead, it happily remained in the tree and watched the world below. 

The insect stayed in the tree for many days, then one day the wind blew again and the insect flew away. It was happy to have seen so much and the insect went back to his garden to remain there for a long time.

A story, a story! (Let it go. Let it come.) I was stamped out like a Plymouth fender into this world. First came the crib with its glacial bars. Then dolls and the devotion to their plactic mouths. Then there was school, the little straight rows of chairs, blotting my name over and over, but undersea all the time, a stranger whose elbows wouldn't work. Then there was life with its cruel houses and people who seldom touched- though touch is all- but I grew, like a pig in a trenchcoat I grew, and then there were many strange apparitions, the nagging rain, the sun turning into poison and all of that, saws working through my heart, but I grew, I grew, and God was there like an island I had not rowed to, still ignorant of Him, my arms, and my legs worked, and I grew, I grew, I wore rubies and bought tomatoes and now, in my middle age, about nineteen in the head I'd say, I am rowing, I am rowing though the oarlocks stick and are rusty and the sea blinks and rolls like a worried eyebal, but I am rowing, I am rowing, though the wind pushes me back and I know that that island will not be perfect, it will have the flaws of life, the absurdities of the dinner table, but there will be a door and I will open it and I will get rid of the rat insdie me, the gnawing pestilential rat. God will take it with his two hands and embrace it. As the African says: This is my tale which I have told, if it be sweet, if it be not sweet, take somewhere else and let some return to me. This story ends with me still rowing.

name_of_work: Memories of West Street and Lepke by Robert Lowell
content: Only teaching on Tuesdays, book-worming in pajamas fresh from the washer each morning, I hog a whole house on Boston's "hardly passionate Marlborough Street," where even the man scavenging filth in the back alley trash cans, has two children, a beach wagon, a helpmate, and is "a young Republican." I have a nine months' daughter, young enough to be my granddaughter. Like the sun she rises in her flame-flamingo infants' wear. These are the tranquilized Fifties, and I am forty. Ought I to regret my seedtime? I was a fire-breathing Catholic C.O., and made my manic statement, telling off the state and president, and then sat waiting sentence in the bull pen beside a negro boy with curlicues of marijuana in his hair. Given a year, I walked on the roof of the West Street Jail, a short enclosure like my school soccer court, and saw the Hudson River once a day through sooty clothesline entanglements and bleaching khaki tenements. Strolling, I yammered metaphysics with Abramowitz, a jaundice-yellow ("it's really tan") and fly-weight pacifist, so vegetarian, he wore rope shoes and preferred fallen fruit. He tried to convert Bioff and Brown, the Hollywood pimps, to his diet. Hairy, muscular, suburban, wearing chocolate double-breasted suits, they blew their tops and beat him black and blue. I was so out of things, I'd never heard of the Jehovah's Witnesses. "Are you a C.O.?" I asked a fellow jailbird. "No," he answered, "I'm a J.W." He taught me the "hospital tuck," and pointed out the T-shirted back of Murder Incorporated's Czar Lepke, there piling towels on a rack, or dawdling off to his little segregated cell full of things forbidden to the common man: a portable radio, a dresser, two toy American flags tied together with a ribbon of Easter palm. Flabby, bald, lobotomized, he drifted in a sheepish calm, where no agonizing reappraisal jarred his concentration on the electric chair hanging like an oasis in his air of lost connections....

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Clara. She was playing in the park when she found an enormous suit. She picked it up and was so happy because the suit was so special and beautiful. She put it on and twirled around in it.

When suddenly something very strange happened, the suit began to grow and grow. Clara soon realized that she was getting much bigger too. She became an enormous giant! She was very scared.

Clara thanked the fairy and ran off to show her mom the enormous suit. Her mom smiled and said, "Itâ€™s so beautiful! Where did you get it?" Clara replied, "From a fairy who asked me to please stop growing!â€

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy who loved to play chess. He had a shiny chess set that he played with every day. One day, Timmy's friend, Billy, came over to play. But Billy didn't have any chess pieces to play with, so Timmy decided to supply him with some of his own.

But then, Timmy's little sister, Sally, came in and accidentally knocked over the chess set. All the pieces fell onto the harsh floor and broke into tiny pieces. Timmy was very sad and didn't know what to do. But then, Billy had an idea. He said they could use some of his own chess pieces to play with instead.

Timmy was very happy that his friend had helped him out, and they continued to play chess together with Billy's pieces. From that day on, Timmy learned that sometimes it's important to supply help to others, but it's also important to accept help when you need it.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Sarah. She was only three and loved watching cartoons on TV.

One day, Sarah was in her living room watching her favourite cartoon when her mom told her to turn it off. "But I don't want to," said Sarah with a pout.

Her mom shook her head and said, "Sorry, Sarah. It's bedtime now. You can watch the cartoon tomorrow."

Sarah reluctantly turned off the TV but she was feeling very restless. She wanted to keep watching it.

The next day at school, Sarah found herself missing her cartoon. She regretted not watching it the night before. All of her classmates were talking about the cartoon and she felt left out. 

One of her classmates noticed she was feeling down and said, "Don't worry Sarah, it's ok. We can watch the cartoon together after school."

Sarah smiled and said, "That sounds great! I can't wait!"

The moral of the story is to never regret missed opportunities because there's always a chance to have fun and make new memories with your friends.

Once upon a time, there was a kitty named Fluffy. Fluffy loved to play with yarn. She would chase it around the house and make a big mess. One day, Fluffy's owner took her to the park. Fluffy was very excited to play in the bright sun. 

At the park, Fluffy saw a big ball of yarn on the ground. She ran over to it and started to play. She batted it with her paws and rolled around in it. Fluffy was having so much fun! 

After a while, Fluffy's owner called her to go home. Fluffy was sad to leave the park and the yarn behind. But she knew she could always come back and play again another day. And that made her very happy. The end.

WHAT YOU HAVE HEARD is true. I was in his house. His wife carried a tray of coffee and sugar. His daughter filed her nails, his son went out for the night. There were daily papers, pet dogs, a pistol on the cushion beside him. The moon swung bare on its black cord over the house. On the television was a cop show. It was in English. Broken bottles were embedded in the walls around the house to scoop the kneecaps from a man's legs or cut his hands to lace. On the windows there were gratings like those in liquor stores. We had dinner, rack of lamb, good wine, a gold bell was on the table for calling the maid. The maid brought green mangoes, salt, a type of bread. I was asked how I enjoyed the country. There was a brief commercial in Spanish. His wife took everything away. There was some talk then of how difficult it had become to govern. The parrot said hello on the terrace. The colonel told it to shut up, and pushed himself from the table. My friend said to me with his eyes: say nothing. The colonel returned with a sack used to bring groceries home. He spilled many human ears on the table. They were like dried peach halves. There is no other way to say this. He took one of them in his hands, shook it in our faces, dropped it into a water glass. It came alive there. I am tired of fooling around he said. As for the rights of anyone, tell your people they can go fuck them- selves. He swept the ears to the floor with his arm and held the last of his wine in the air. Something for your poetry, no? he said. Some of the ears on the floor caught this scrap of his voice. Some of the ears on the floor were pressed to the ground. May 1978

My mother was a hanky queen when hanky meant a thing of cloth, not paper tissues bought in packs from late-night garages and shops, but things for waving out of trains and mopping the corners of your grief: when hankies were material she'd have one, always, up her sleeve. Tucked in the wrists of every cardi, a mum's embarrassment of lace embroidered with a V for Viv, spittled and scrubbed against my face. And sometimes more than one fell out as is she had a farm up there where dried-up hankies fell in love and mated, raising little squares. She bought her own; I never did. Hankies were presents from distant aunts in boxed sets, with transparent covers and script initials spelling ponce, the naffest Christmas gift you'd get - my brothers too, more often than not, got male ones: serious, and grey, and larger, like they had more snot. It was hankie that closed department stores, with headscarves, girdles, knitting wool and trouser presses; homely props you'd never find today in malls. Hankies, which demanded irons, and boiling to be purified shuttered the doors of family stores when those who used to buy them died. And somehow, with the hanky's loss, greengrocer George with his dodgy foot delivering veg from a Comma van is history, and the friendly butcher who'd slip and extra sausage in, the fishmonger whose marble slab of haddock smoked the colour of yolks and parcelled rows of local crab lay opposite the dancing school where Mrs White, with painted talons, taught us When You're Smiling from a stumbling, out of tune piano: step-together, step-together, step-together, point! The Annual Talent Show when every mother, fencing tears, would whip a hanky from their sleeve and smudge the rouge from little dears. Nostalgia only makes me old. The innocence I want my brood to cling on to like ten-bob notes was killed in TV's lassitude. And it was me that turned it on and eat bought biscuits I would bake if I'd commit to being home. There's never a hanky up my sleeve. I raised neglected-looking kids, the kind whose noses strangers clean. What awkwardness in me forbids me to keep tissues in my bag when handy packs are 50p? I miss material handkerchiefs, their soft and hidden history. But it isn't mine. I'll let it go. My mother too, eventually, who died not leaving handkerchiefs but tissues and uncertainty: and she would say, should I complain of the scratchy and disposable, that this is your material to do with, daughter, what you will.
