Sara and Tom are playing with their toys in the living room. Sara has a big doll with long hair and a pink dress. Tom has a small car with four wheels and a horn. Sara likes her doll very much and does not want anyone to touch it. Tom likes his car very much and does not want anyone to touch it.

"Can I see your doll?" Tom asks Sara. He wants to touch the doll's hair and dress.

"No, you can't!" Sara says. "This is my doll and she is very clean. You have dirty hands and you will make her dirty too."

"Can I see your car?" Sara asks Tom. She wants to touch the car's wheels and horn.

"No, you can't!" Tom says. "This is my car and he is very fast. You have slow hands and you will make him slow too."

Sara and Tom are not happy. They do not want to share their toys. They turn away from each other and play alone.

But then they hear a loud noise from the kitchen. It is their mom. She is making cookies for them. They smell the cookies and they feel hungry.

"Come here, Sara and Tom!" their mom calls. "I have a surprise for you!"

Sara and Tom run to the kitchen. They see a big plate of cookies on the table. They look yummy and sweet.

"Wow, cookies!" Sara and Tom say. "Can we have some, mom?"

"Yes, you can, but first you have to do something for me," their mom says. "You have to wash your hands and be nice to each other. Can you do that?"

Sara and Tom look at each other. They remember their toys and their words. They feel sorry and ashamed.

"Yes, mom, we can do that," they say. "We are sorry for being mean. We will share our toys and be friends."

They hug each other and say sorry. Then they wash their hands and sit at the table. Their mom gives them each a cookie and a glass of milk. They smile and thank their mom. They eat their cookies and drink their milk. They are happy and full.

They learn a lesson. They learn that sharing is caring and that cookies are better than toys.

Where sunless rivers weep Their waves into the deep, She sleeps a charmed sleep: Awake her not. Led by a single star, She came from very far To seek where shadows are Her pleasant lot. She left the rosy morn, She left the fields of corn, For twilight cold and lorn And water springs. Through sleep, as through a veil, She sees the sky look pale, And hears the nightingale That sadly sings. Rest, rest, a perfect rest Shed over brow and breast; Her face is toward the west, The purple land. She cannot see the grain Ripening on hill and plain; She cannot feel the rain Upon her hand. Rest, rest, for evermore Upon a mossy shore; Rest, rest at the heart's core Till time shall cease: Sleep that no pain shall wake; Night that no morn shall break Till joy shall overtake Her perfect peace.

Molly was a 3 year old who loved playing in the snow. One day she put on her warm coat and hat and went outside with her parents. She found some big mittens and slipped them onto her hands. Inside the mitten was something unusual. She reached her hand in and pulled out a toy dog.

Molly was excited and ran over to her parents. She showed them the toy and showed them how it barked. But Molly's parents weren't as excited about the toy. They said to Molly that she should put the mitten back where she found it. Molly didn't like this and started to complain.

Her mom and dad reminded Molly that she was lucky to have found the toy in the first place. Molly wasn't sure, but she decided to put the mitten back where she found it.

As Molly walked away, she wished the mitten had something a little more unusual inside instead of just a toy. But playing in the snow was still a lot of fun!

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Tom. Tom was three years old and he liked to play outside in the sun. One day, he went outside to play in the wind. 

Tom loved the feeling of the wind in his hair and laughed. Suddenly, he heard a voice. It said, "Hey, Tom. I'm the wind!" 
Tom was surprised! He asked, "You can talk?!" The wind laughed and said, "Yes! I wanted to show you something." 

Tom followed the wind. The wind showed him some birds and said, "Look, these birds are so stupid!" Tom laughed and said, "Yes, they are so stupid!" 

The wind was happy that Tom agreed and said, "Come back another day and I will show you more!" Tom was very excited and said goodbye to the wind. 

When Tom got home, he told his mom about the wind and the stupid birds. She laughed and said, "That sounds like fun!" 

Tom smiled from ear to ear and knew he would have to come back and show the wind again soon!

Once, there was a lion who was feeling very foolish. He thought he could climb up a very tall tree. The lion tried and tried, but he could not reach the top. He was getting very discouraged, when all of a sudden, he heard a voice say, "Let me help you!" 

The lion looked up and saw a monkey. The monkey was very small and was already halfway to the top of the tree. The monkey said, "I will help you climb up the tree." 

The lion was very grateful and he followed the monkey. Together they climbed higher and higher until they reached the top. The lion was so happy, and he thanked the monkey for helping him. The monkey giggled and said, "It was no problem at all!"

name_of_work: Non sum qualis eram bonae sub regno Cynarae by Ernest Dowson
content: Last night, ah, yesternight, betwixt her lips and mine There fell thy shadow, Cynara! thy breath was shed Upon my soul between the kisses and the wine; And I was desolate and sick of an old passion, Yea, I was desolate and bowed my head: I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion. All night upon mine heart I felt her warm heart beat, Night-long within mine arms in love and sleep she lay; Surely the kisses of her bought red mouth were sweet; But I was desolate and sick of an old passion, When I awoke and found the dawn was grey: I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion. I have forgot much, Cynara! gone with the wind, Flung roses, roses riotously with the throng, Dancing, to put thy pale, lost lilies out of mind, But I was desolate and sick of an old passion, Yea, all the time, because the dance was long: I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion. I cried for madder music and for stronger wine, But when the feast is finished and the lamps expire, Then falls thy shadow, Cynara! the night is thine; And I am desolate and sick of an old passion, Yea, hungry for the lips of my desire: I have been faithful to thee, Cynara! in my fashion.

Lily and Ben were playing with clay in the garden. They made shapes of animals and people with their hands. Lily made a cat and Ben made a dog.

"Look at my cat, it is so pretty and tidy," Lily said, showing her clay cat to Ben.

"My dog is better, it is big and strong," Ben said, holding his clay dog.

"No, my cat is better, it can climb and scratch," Lily said.

"No, my dog is better, it can run and bite," Ben said.

They started to fight over whose clay animal was better. They pushed and pulled each other's clay shapes. The clay cat and the dog broke into pieces.

"Stop, stop, you are ruining our clay!" a voice said. It was Mom, who came to see what they were doing.

"Look at this mess, you have to clean it up right now," Mom said, pointing at the clay bits on the ground.

Lily and Ben felt sorry for fighting and breaking their clay. They said sorry to each other and to Mom. They helped each other to pick up the clay and put it back in the box.

"Next time, you can share and play nicely with your clay," Mom said, smiling.

Lily and Ben nodded and hugged each other. They decided to make a new clay animal together, a bird that could fly and sing.

name_of_work: Hush little baby, don't say a word by Mother Goose
content: Hush little baby, don't say a word, Papa's gonna buy you a mockingbird. And if that mockingbird won't sing, Papa's gonna buy you a diamond ring. And if that diamond ring turns to brass, Papa's gonna buy you a looking glass. And if that looking glass gets broke, Papa's gonna buy you a billy goat. And if that billy goat won't pull, Papa's gonna buy you a cart and bull. And if that cart and bull turn over, Papa's gonna buy you a dog named Rover. And if that dog named Rover won't bark, Papa's gonna buy you a horse and cart. And if that horse and cart fall down, You'll still be the sweetest little baby in town!

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Sarah. She was three years old. One day, Sarah discovered a phone in the garden. It was a charming phone with many different buttons.

Sarah was so happy, she decided to keep it. She wanted to find out who the phone belonged too.

Sarah asked all the people she knew but none of them said it was their phone. She had to figure it out on her own.

So one day, Sarah decided to go to the park to ask people she saw there. After talking to lots of people, Sarah found out the phone belonged to a charming little boy called Bob. She was so happy that she gave him back his phone and they both hugged each other.

The end!

Once upon a time there was a dog who lived in a big house. His name was Fido. Every day Fido would go outside to play. Fido had an ugly collar with a big bell on it. 

One day Fido went outside and he got very muddy. He rolled around in the dirt and had so much fun!

When it was time to go in, Fido had a problem. His ugly collar was stuck in the mud and he couldn't finish his fun. Fido's owner had to help him to get it off and finish his play.

Once the collar was off, Fido was very relieved. He ran back inside the big house and enjoyed a nice bath. 

The end.

Once upon a time there was a clumsy bear. The clumsy bear was very clumsy. No matter what he did he always seemed to trip and be clumsy. On his birthday, he was feeling especially clumsy. He tried to be careful, but he still kept making mistakes. 

One day as he was walking, he saw a pond with a beautiful rainbow in it. He stopped and stared in awe at the beauty of the rainbow. He felt inspired and vowed to be more graceful and smooth with his movements. 

From this day forward, he was more aware of his movements and was less clumsy. He learned the importance of being mindful of what he was doing and the rewards this would bring. This was his birthday present - a new, more graceful version of himself.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big car on the road. The car is shiny and has four doors. It looks very rich.

"Wow, look at that car!" Ben says. "It is so big and nice. I wish I had a car like that."

Anna looks at the car too. She does not think it is nice. She thinks it is loud and dirty. She likes her bike better. It is small and quiet. She can ride it fast and have fun.

"I don't like that car," Anna says. "It makes too much noise and smoke. It hurts the air and the trees. I like my bike more. It is good for me and the park."

Ben and Anna have different ideas. They talk to each other. They try to understand why they like different things. They are still friends. They agree to play with both the car and the bike. They share and take turns. They have fun in the park.

name_of_work: Clown in the Moon by Dylan Thomas
content: My tears are like the quiet drift Of petals from some magic rose; And all my grief flows from the rift Of unremembered skies and snows. I think, that if I touched the earth, It would crumble; It is so sad and beautiful, So tremulously like a dream.

Once there was a little boy called David. He was three years old and he was very lonely. One day, he decided he needed a new haircut. So he asked his mum if he could get one.

His mum said yes and took him to the hairdresser. At the hairdresser, David had to sit in a big chair and he was very scared. He started to suffer.

The hairdresser cut David's hair very carefully. When the haircut was done, David looked in the mirror. He couldn't believe it - he had a brand new haircut!

David felt much happier now that he had a new haircut. He wasn't lonely anymore. From that day onwards, he always remembered to keep his hair well brushed and tidy.

Bald Bill was taking his usual morning walk along the beach. He liked to observe the waves crashing onto the shore, and the people enjoying the sunny day. All of a sudden, he noticed something strange. Something was moving in the water! It was a bright red strip with a long tail. Bill was very curious and so he decided to take a closer look.

When he got to the edge of the sea, he realised what the red strip was - an aggressive shark! He had never seen one before, and was afraid that it might attack him. He was about to turn back and quickly leave, when he noticed that the shark was chasing a little fish. She seemed helpless and scared, with nowhere left to go.

That's when Bill realised what he had to do. He must help the helpless fish! He took a deep breath and jumped into the ocean. Despite his bravery, he was no match for the huge shark. Bill disappeared under the waves, and the shark easily took the little fish away.

The moral of this story is that we sometimes have to take risks to help others in need. Even though Bald Bill didn't make it out alive, his courage should be admired. We can all learn from his example.

Sam was very happy. He had a brilliant idea. He wanted to invite his friends to his house for a tea party. He had a big box of labels. He wrote the names of his friends on the labels. He stuck the labels on some paper. He made some cards.

He went to his mom. He showed her the cards. He said, "Mom, can I invite my friends for a tea party? I made these cards for them. Look, this is for Lily, this is for Ben, this is for Mia, and this is for Tom."

Mom smiled. She said, "That is very nice of you, Sam. You are very thoughtful. Yes, you can invite your friends for a tea party. I will help you make some sandwiches and cookies. When do you want to have the tea party?"

Sam said, "I want to have it tomorrow. Can I go and give the cards to my friends now?"

Mom said, "Sure, you can. But first, put on your coat and hat. It is cold outside. And be careful when you cross the street. I will wait for you here."

Sam said, "Okay, mom. Thank you. I love you." He gave mom a hug and a kiss. He put on his coat and hat. He took the cards and ran outside. He was very excited. He hoped his friends would come to his tea party. He thought it would be a lot of fun.

Once upon a time, there was a vet with lots of colorful animals! He was a very nice veterinarian who always took good care of the animals.

One day, the vet was in the vet's office and he saw a small animal hiding in the corner. He realized it was a scared little kitten. He spoke softly, "It's ok little kitty, I'm here to help you."

The vet carefully reached out his hand and the kitty slowly came out from behind the chair. The vet could see that the kitten was very sick and needed help.

The vet took the kitten to the vet room where he could care for it. He took out his colorful tools and examined the kitten. Then, he started to give the kitten medicine to help it get better.

The vet was very careful, and soon the kitten started to feel better. The vet was so happy and he thanked the kitten for letting him help it.

The vet then found the kitten a nice home where it could live and be happy. The vet will always remember that scared little kitty hiding in the corner and all the colorful animals he helps everyday.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play in her backyard, but one day, she saw a big, scary spider. It made her so scared that she ran inside and hid.

Lily's mom noticed that Lily seemed scared and asked her what was wrong. Lily told her about the spider, and her mom went outside to check. She found the spider sitting on an ashtray that had been left outside.

Lily's mom picked up the ashtray and brought it inside. She showed Lily that the spider was gone and the ashtray was empty. Lily felt much better and hugged her mom, saying, "You're perfect, Mommy!" From then on, Lily remembered to always check for spiders before playing outside.

name_of_work: Stormcock in Elder by Ruth Pitter
content: In my dark hermitage, aloof From the world's sight and the world's sound, By the small door where the old roof Hangs but five feet above the ground, I groped along the shelf for bread But found celestial food instead: For suddenly close at my ear, Loud, loud and wild, with wintry glee, The old unfailing chorister Burst out in pride of poetry; And through the broken roof I spied Him by his singing glorified. Scarcely an arm's-length from the eye, Myself unseen, I saw him there; The throbbing throat that made the cry, The breast dewed from the misty air, The polished bill that opened wide And showed the pointed tongue inside; The large eye, ringed with many a ray Of minion feathers, finely laid, The feet that grasped the elder-spray; How strongly used, how subtly made The scale, the sinew, and the claw, Plain through the broken roof I saw; The flight-feathers in tail and wing, The shorter coverts, and the white Merged into russet, marrying The bright breast to the pinions bright, Gold sequins, spots of chestnut, shower Of silver, like a brindled flower. Soldier of fortune, northwest Jack, Old hard-times' braggart, there you blow But tell me ere your bagpipes crack How you can make so brave a show, Full-fed in February, and dressed Like a rich merchant at a feast. One-half the world, or so they say, Knows not how half the world may live; So sing your song and go your way, And still in February contrive As bright as Gabriel to smile On elder-spray by broken tile.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. Lily loved to play outside in the sunshine and pick flowers. One day, Lily went for a walk in the forest and saw a sad bunny. The bunny was crying because it was lost and didn't know how to get home. 

Lily felt sorry for the bunny and wanted to help. She picked up the bunny and held it close to her chest. She whispered kind words to the bunny and tried to comfort it. 

Lily knew the way back to her house, so she carried the bunny all the way home. When they arrived, Lily gave the bunny some carrots to eat and made a cozy bed for it to sleep in. 

The bunny was so grateful to Lily for her honest kindness. From that day on, the bunny and Lily became best friends and they would often play together in the pine forest.

Once upon a time, there was a mummy and a daddy who had a baby. They loved the baby very much, and wanted to show her the world. So, one day the mummy and the daddy got in the car. The car was going very fast.

But then something bad happened. A tyre on the car twisted, and it started to make a funny noise. The mummy and the daddy tried their best to stop but they couldn't. The car kept going at a high speed.

The baby started to cry. "Mummy, daddy, I'm so sad," she said.

The mummy and the daddy were sad too. They hugged the baby tightly, and said "Don't worry, we will make it better soon."

They stopped the car, and fixed the tyre. And soon, they were all back in the car and going at a safe speed. They were all so glad. 

And the baby learned an important lesson that day: it's always best to be careful and drive with care, even when you're in a hurry.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to run and play outside. One day, Timmy was running so fast that he stumbled and fell. He hurt his knee and started to cry.

Timmy's mom came outside and saw that he had fallen. She picked him up and carried him inside. Timmy's mom looked at his knee and saw that it was red and hard. She knew she needed to put a frame on it to help it heal.

Timmy didn't like the frame because it made it hard for him to move around. He wanted to run and play outside again. But his mom said he needed to rest and let his knee heal. Timmy was sad, but he knew his mom was right. He waited patiently until his knee was better and he could run and play again.

Anna liked to help her mom with the dishes. She wanted to be a big girl and do things by herself. Sometimes, mom let her put the cups and plates in the dishwasher. Anna felt very proud when she did that.

One day, mom was busy with the baby and asked Anna to load the dishwasher. Anna was happy to help. She took the dishes from the table and carried them to the kitchen. She opened the dishwasher and saw that it was empty. She smiled and started to put the dishes inside.

She put the cups on the top rack and the plates on the bottom rack. She tried to fit as many as she could. She wanted to show mom how good she was. She saw a big pot on the stove. It was shiny and attractive. Anna wanted to put it in the dishwasher too. She reached for the pot handle and pulled it.

But the pot was heavy and hot. Anna did not know that mom had just cooked soup in it. The pot slipped from her hand and fell on the floor. The soup splashed everywhere. Anna screamed and dropped the pot. She felt the soup burn her skin. She started to cry.

Mom heard the noise and ran to the kitchen. She saw Anna on the floor, covered in soup. She saw the pot and the mess. She felt scared and angry. She picked up Anna and hugged her. She checked her for injuries. She said, "Anna, what did you do? Why did you touch the pot? It was hot and dangerous. You could have hurt yourself badly. You should have asked me for help. You are not ready to load the dishwasher by yourself. You are still a little girl."

Anna sobbed and said, "I'm sorry, mom. I wanted to help. I wanted to be a big girl. I wanted to put the pot in the dishwasher. It was pretty."

Mom sighed and said, "I know, Anna. I know you meant well. But you have to be careful. You have to listen to me. You have to learn from your mistakes. You are a big girl in some ways, but you still need my guidance. I love you, Anna. But please, don't touch the pot again."

Once upon a time, there was a fox who wanted to hide. He looked all around for a good place to hide. The fox saw a big, flexible tree.

He said to himself, "That's a perfect hiding spot!"

The fox scampered over to the tree, brushed off the dirt, and wriggled through the flexible branches. He closed his eyes and wiggled until he felt cozy and safe.

All of a sudden, a rabbit hopped by, saying, "Boo! Where's the fox?"

The fox shivered and tried to be quiet. He thought to himself, "Nobody can find me here." But the flexible branches moved, and he knew the rabbit had spotted him.

"There you are!" the rabbit said. "You're such a sneaky fox!"

The fox smiled and wriggled out of the tree. He said goodbye to the rabbit, and they both continued on their way.

One day, a boy named Tim found a dead bug. He felt sad for the bug. Tim went to the park to forget about the bug. He saw kids playing baseball. Tim wanted to play too.

"Can I play with you?" Tim asked. The kids said yes. Tim was happy. But his friend Ben was not. Ben wanted to be the best. Ben did not want Tim to play.

Tim and Ben played baseball. Tim tried to hit the ball. But he missed. Ben laughed at Tim. "You can't play," Ben said. Tim felt sad again. He wanted to be good at baseball too.

Tim's mom came to the park. She saw Tim was sad. She had an idea. She gave Tim a special zip-up shirt. Tim put on the shirt and felt strong. Tim hit the ball very far. Ben was surprised. Tim was happy. Now, Tim and Ben were both good at baseball. They played together and had fun.

Once upon a time, there was a small girl who was very curious. She was playing outside when she saw something shiny in the sky. The girl reached up and plucked away at the shiny thing, until it fell from the sky.

The girl was so excited to see what it was! She reached down and found it was a harmless coin, which had fallen into the sand. The girl smiled and scooped it up, running off to show her mom.

When she arrived home, her mom asked, "What do you have there?"

The little girl showed her mom the harmless coin that had fallen from the sky. The little girl was so proud that she had found it in the sand. Her mom was even more proud of her daughter and gave her a big hug.

"I'm so proud of you! You found something special falling from the sky."

The little girl felt so happy. She realized that wonderful things can often fall from the sky, you just have to be brave and curious to find them.

name_of_work: On Killing a Tree by Gieve Patel
content: It takes much time to kill a tree, Not a simple jab of the knife Will do it. It has grown Slowly consuming the earth, Rising out of it, feeding Upon its crust, absorbing Years of sunlight, air, water, And out of its leperous hide Sprouting leaves. So hack and chop But this alone wont do it. Not so much pain will do it. The bleeding bark will heal And from close to the ground Will rise curled green twigs, Miniature boughs Which if unchecked will expand again To former size. No, The root is to be pulled out - Out of the anchoring earth; It is to be roped, tied, And pulled out - snapped out Or pulled out entirely, Out from the earth-cave, And the strength of the tree exposed, The source, white and wet, The most sensitive, hidden For years inside the earth. Then the matter Of scorching and choking In sun and air, Browning, hardening, Twisting, withering, And then it is done.

Once there was a little girl named Grace. She had two big ears and was always very curious.

One day she was sitting in a park with her mom when she saw a man folding paper into funny shapes. He was folding it really tight and it was so cool to watch!

Grace asked her mom if she could try it. Her mom said yes, and showed her how to fold the paper. She tried it and she was delighted when she was able to make something with her own hands!

Grace kept folding and folding, making lots of different things out of paper. She got so good at it that she started folding things into tiny shapes, so small they fit in her ear!

Grace had so much fun playing with paper and folding it tight. She couldn't believe how much she had learned and how good she had gotten. She was so proud of herself.

Mia and Leo were twins who liked to play outside. They had a big yard with a swing, a slide and a sandbox. They also had a dog named Spot who liked to run and bark.

One night, their mom said, "It's time for bed, my loves. You played a lot today and you must be sleepy."

"But mom, we want to see the moon!" Mia said. "It's so bright and pretty!"

"Yeah, mom, can we stay up a little longer?" Leo said. "We hope to see a star too!"

Mom smiled and said, "Okay, you can stay up for a little while, but only if you put on your pajamas and brush your teeth first. Then we can go outside and look at the sky together."

Mia and Leo did what mom said and then ran outside with Spot. They looked up and saw the moon shining like a big silver ball. They also saw some stars twinkling like little diamonds.

"Wow, the moon is so big!" Mia said.

"And the stars are so many!" Leo said.

"Can we make a wish, mom?" Mia asked.

"Sure, you can make a wish, but you have to keep it a secret," mom said.

Mia and Leo closed their eyes and made their wishes. They hoped for something good and happy.

Then mom said, "It's time to go inside now, my loves. The moon and the stars will be here tomorrow night too. Let's say good night to them and go to bed."

"Good night, moon!" Mia said.

"Good night, stars!" Leo said.

"Good night, Spot!" they both said.

They hugged mom and went inside. They were sleepy and happy. They dreamed of their wishes and the moon and the stars.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved animals and wanted to see them up close. So, he asked his dad to take him to the zoo. His dad said yes and they went to the zoo.

At the zoo, Timmy saw many animals like lions, tigers, and elephants. He was happy, but he wanted to see more. Then, he saw a sign that said "Coming Soon: Penguin Exhibit". Timmy was excited and asked his dad when it would be ready.

His dad said, "It will take some time to build the penguin exhibit, but we can come back when it's done." Timmy was frustrated because he wanted to see the penguins now. But his dad promised they would come back and see them soon. 

Months later, Timmy and his dad went back to the zoo. The penguin exhibit was ready! Timmy was overjoyed and ran to see the penguins. He was so happy that he forgot all about being frustrated.

Once there was a little girl who wanted to understand more. She wanted to fill her jug up with understanding so she could learn. 

So she went to the store and saw a cheap understanding jug. She asked the store keeper for it and he said yes. 

The little girl went back home and opened the jug. She was so excited to learn and understand more. She put her hands into it and pulled out a sparkling understanding. 

She sipped from the understanding and tasted the sweet wisdom it gave her. She now understood more than ever before!

The little girl was so happy she had found her understanding in the cheap jug. From then on, she learned and understood a lot more.

Once upon a time, Jack's mommy bought him a new belt. It was bright and shiny, with a big buckle. Jack was very excited and wanted to wear it right away.

He put the belt on, but the buckle was too big. His mommy said he had to put the belt around his waist. Jack put the belt on, but he worried it might be too tight.

So he pulled the belt tighter and tighter. Suddenly, it snapped and made Jack jump. His mommy said he had been too silly. She told him to take the belt off, and put it away.

But it was too late, the belt was very dry from being pulled so tight. It couldn't be fixed. Jack was so sad. His mommy had a stern look and said: "When we worry about something, things can turn out bad."

The moral of this story is to never worry because it can lead to bad outcomes.

Once there was a little girl called Anna. She was three years old and very excited.

One day, Anna and her mum went for a walk in the park. As they walked along, Anna saw something moving in the grass. She looked closer and saw a rat!

Anna was very excited and ran over to get a better look. The rat was very small and grey, with a long pointed nose. It was sniffing around the ground, looking for food.

Anna wanted to get a closer look, so she moved in slowly. As she got closer, the rat scurried away!

Anna was a bit disappointed, but excited at the same time. She had never seen a rat before and it was a very exciting experience!

name_of_work: Wind by Subramania Bharati, translated by A. K. Ramanujan
content: The wind blows strongly and causes a lot of destruction. How can we make friends with it? Wind, come softly. Don't break the shutters of the windows. Don't scatter the papers. Don't throw down the books on the shelf. There, look what you did -- you threw them all down. You tore the pages of the books. You brought rain again. You're very clever at poking fun at weaklings. Frail crumbling houses, crumbling doors, crumbling rafters, crumbling wood, crumbling bodies, crumbling lives, crumbling hearts -- the wind god winnows and crushes them all. He won't do what you tell him. So, come, let's build strong homes, Let's joint the doors firmly. Practise to firm the body. Make the heart steadfast. Do this, and the wind will be friends with us. The wind blows out weak fires. He makes strong fires roar and flourish. His friendship is good. We praise him every day.

name_of_work: Epistle to a Young Friend by Robert Burns
content: I Lang hae thought, my youthfu' friend, A something to have sent you, Tho' it should serve nae ither end Than just a kind memento: But how the subject-theme may gang, Let time and chance determine; Perhaps it may turn out a sang: Perhaps turn out a sermon. Ye'll try the world soon, my lad; And, Andrew dear, believe me, Ye'll find mankind an unco squad, And muckle they may grieve ye: For care and trouble set your thought, Ev'n when your end's attained; And a' your views may come to nought, Where ev'ry nerve is strained. I'll no say, men are villains a'; The real, harden'd wicked, Wha hae nae check but human law, Are to a few restricked; But, Och! mankind are unco weak, An' little to be trusted; If self the wavering balance shake, It's rarely right adjusted! Yet they wha fa' in fortune's strife, Their fate we shouldna censure; For still, th' important end of life They equally may answer; A man may hae an honest heart, Tho' poortith hourly stare him; A man may tak a neibor's part, Yet hae nae cash to spare him. Aye free, aff-han', your story tell, When wi' a bosom crony; But still keep something to yoursel', Ye scarcely tell to ony: Conceal yoursel' as weel's ye can Frae critical dissection; But keek thro' ev'ry other man, Wi' sharpen'd, sly inspection. The sacred lowe o' weel-plac'd love, Luxuriantly indulge it; But never tempt th' illicit rove, Tho' naething should divulge it: I waive the quantum o' the sin, The hazard of concealing; But, Och! it hardens a' within, And petrifies the feeling! To catch dame Fortune's golden smile, Assiduous wait upon her; And gather gear by ev'ry wile That's justified by honour; Not for to hide it in a hedge, Nor for a train attendant; But for the glorious privilege Of being independent. The fear o' hell's a hangman's whip, To haud the wretch in order; But where ye feel your honour grip, Let that aye be your border; Its slightest touches, instant pause- Debar a' side-pretences; And resolutely keep its laws, Uncaring consequences. The great Creator to revere, Must sure become the creature; But still the preaching cant forbear, And ev'n the rigid feature: Yet ne'er with wits profane to range, Be complaisance extended; An atheist-laugh's a poor exchange For Deity offended! When ranting round in pleasure's ring, Religion may be blinded; Or if she gie a random sting, It may be little minded; But when on life we're tempest driv'n- A conscience but a canker- A correspondence fix'd wi' Heav'n, Is sure a noble anchor! Adieu, dear, amiable youth! Your heart can ne'er be wanting! May prudence, fortitude, and truth, Erect your brow undaunting! In ploughman phrase, "God send you speed," Still daily to grow wiser; And may ye better reck the rede, Then ever did th' adviser!
"A planet doesn't explode of itself," said drily The Martian astronomer, gazing off into the air. "That they were able to do it is proof that highly Intelligent beings must have been living there."

Once upon a time there was a guard who walked in the dark. He had a secret that was very special. 

The guard reached into his pocket and took out a key. He used it to open a big door. 

When he opened the door, he saw a magical box with a bright light. He was sure that it held a wonderful surprise. 

The guard grabbed the box and ran away with it. But then he heard a loud noise coming from behind. 

He looked back and saw a big monster trying to reach him. He quickly put the box somewhere safe and ran away. 

The guard was safe, but the monster was still in the dark. He had protected the special secret and was thankful for his luck.

Lily was going to start school soon. She was happy and scared. She wanted to make new friends and learn new things. But she did not like the uniform. It was black and boring. She liked to wear pink and purple and yellow.

"Mom, do I have to wear this?" she asked, holding the black dress and the black shoes.

"Yes, you do, sweetie. It is the rule of the school. Everyone wears the same uniform. It makes you look smart and neat." Mom said, smiling.

"But I don't want to look like everyone else. I want to look like me." Lily said, frowning.

Mom hugged her and said, "I know, honey. But sometimes we have to accept things that we don't like. It is part of growing up. And you can still be yourself, even if you wear the same clothes as others. You can show your personality with your hair, your backpack, your lunch box, and your smile."

Lily thought about it. She liked her hair, her backpack, her lunch box, and her smile. Maybe she could wear the uniform and still be Lily. She nodded and said, "Okay, Mom. I will try."

The next day, Lily went to school. She saw many kids wearing the same black uniform. She felt a little shy and nervous. But then she saw a girl with a pink bow in her hair, a boy with a dinosaur backpack, a girl with a rainbow lunch box, and a boy with a big smile. They looked happy and friendly. They waved at her and said, "Hi, Lily. Welcome to our class. We like your unicorn hair clip. It is very pretty."

Lily smiled and said, "Thank you. I like your things too. They are very cool."

She felt happy and excited. She realized that Mom was right. She could accept the uniform and still be herself. She made new friends and learned new things. She liked school. She liked the uniform. It was black and beautiful.

name_of_work: The Old Pond by Matsuo Basho
content: Old pond... a frog jumps in water's sound

This is the gay cliff of the nineteenth century, Drenched in the hopeful ozone of a new day, Erect and brown, like retired sea-captains, The houses gaze vigorously at the ocean. With the hospitable eyes of the retired captains They preside over the meeting of the sea and river. On Sunday mornings the citizens revisit their beginnings, Whole families walk in the fresh air of the past. Their children tricycle down the nineteenth century: America comes smiling towards them like a neighbour. While the past on three wheels rolls beneath them, They hammer in the blazing forge of the future. Brooklyn Bridge flies through the air on feathers. The children do not know the weight of its girders. It is the citizens carry the bridge on their shoulders: Its overhead lights crackle in their blood-vessals. But now it is Sunday morning, and a sky swept clean. The citizens put down the bridge and stroll at ease. They jingle hopeful change in their pockets. They forget the tripping dance of the profit motive. The big ships glide in under the high statue, The towers cluster like spear-grass on the famous island. And citizens dream themselves back in a sparkle of morning. They ride with their children under a sky swept clearn. Dream on, citizens! Dream the true America, the healer, Drawing the hot blood from throbbing Europe! Dream the dark-eyed immigrants from the narrow cities: Dream the iron steamers loaded with prayers and bundles: Breathe the ozone older than the name of commerce: Be the citizens of true survival!

Sara and Tom were playing with their toys in the living room. Sara had a doll and Tom had a car. They liked to make up stories with their toys and act them out.

"Look, my doll is a princess and she lives in a castle," Sara said, holding her doll high.

"My car is a dragon and he can fly and breathe fire," Tom said, zooming his car around.

They were having fun, but then they heard a cry from the other room. It was their infant brother, Ben, who had woken up from his nap. Their mom went to check on him and told Sara and Tom to keep playing quietly.

Sara and Tom nodded, but they were curious about Ben. They wanted to see him and play with him too. They decided to sneak into his room and surprise him.

They tiptoed to his room and opened the door. They saw Ben lying in his crib, kicking his legs and making noises. He looked happy to see them.

"Hi, Ben!" Sara and Tom said together, smiling.

Ben smiled back and reached out his arms. Sara and Tom climbed into his crib and hugged him. They gave him some of their toys to play with.

"Look, Ben, this is a princess and this is a dragon," Sara said, showing him her doll and Tom's car.

"Wow, you are so creative, Sara," Tom said, admiring her story.

"Thank you, Tom. You are creative too," Sara said, complimenting his car.

They played with Ben for a while, making him laugh and giggle. They forgot about their mom and the time.

Suddenly, they heard their mom's voice from the living room.

"Sara, Tom, where are you? It's time for lunch!"

Sara and Tom gasped. They had vanished from the living room and their mom did not know where they were. They quickly got out of Ben's crib and ran to the living room.

"Sorry, mom, we were playing with Ben," Sara said, holding her doll.

"We wanted to surprise him and make him happy," Tom said, holding his car.

Their mom looked at them and smiled. She was not angry, but amused.

"Well, you certainly surprised me too. You are very creative, but next time, please tell me where you are going," she said, hugging them.

"OK, mom, we will," Sara and Tom said, nodding.

They followed their mom to the kitchen, where a delicious lunch was waiting for them. They ate and talked about their toys and their stories. They were happy and loved.

Moist, bright, and green, the landscape laughs around. Full swell the woods; their every music wakes, Mix'd in wild concert, with the warbling brooks Increased, the distant bleatings of the hills, And hollow lows responsive from the vales, Whence, blending all, the sweeten'd zephyr springs. Meantime, refracted from yon eastern cloud, Bestriding earth, the grand ethereal bow Shoots up immense; and every hue unfolds, In fair proportion running from the red To where the violet fades into the sky. Here, awful Newton, the dissolving clouds Form, fronting on the sun, thy showery prism; And to the sage-instructed eye unfold The various twine of light, by thee disclosed From the white mingling maze. Not so the boy; He wondering views the bright enchantment bend, Delightful, o'er the radiant fields, and runs To catch the falling glory; but amazed Beholds th' amusive arch before him fly, Then vanish quite away.

Lily and Max were playing in their room when they heard a loud noise outside. It was a hurricane, a big wind that can break things and make people scared. Mommy and Daddy told them to stay inside and be quiet.

But Lily and Max were curious. They wanted to see the hurricane. They waited until Mommy and Daddy were busy and then they sneaked to the window. They peeked through the curtains and saw the trees bending and the rain falling.

"Wow, look at that!" Max said. "The hurricane is so strong!"

"Shh, don't talk so loud!" Lily said. "Mommy and Daddy will hear us!"

But it was too late. Mommy and Daddy came into the room and saw them peeking. They were not happy.

"What are you doing?" Mommy asked. "You know you are not supposed to look at the hurricane. It is dangerous!"

"Sorry, Mommy," Lily and Max said. "We just wanted to see it."

Mommy and Daddy hugged them and explained that the hurricane was not a game. It was a real thing that could hurt people and animals. They said they had to stay inside until the hurricane was over.

"But how do we know when it is over?" Max asked.

Mommy and Daddy smiled and showed them a fake hurricane. It was a toy that made wind and rain sounds when you turned it on. They said they would turn it on and off to let them know when the hurricane was over.

Lily and Max liked the fake hurricane. They played with it and pretended they were in a boat or a plane. They forgot about the real hurricane and had fun. They were glad Mommy and Daddy were with them. They felt safe and happy.

Once upon a time, there was a blue bird. The bird had soft feathers with a bumpy texture. It liked to sit on a branch and sing songs. One day, a little girl saw the bird and wanted to be friends. She sat under the tree and the bird hopped down to say hello. The girl petted the bird and felt its bumpy texture. They became the best of friends and would sit together every day, watching the world go by.

Every day Daisy liked to practice playing her flute. It was a special red flute which she loved. Her mummy had urged her to play it, and so she did.

One day the flute behaved differently. It felt very tight in her hands. Daisy tried to make a sound, but the flute would not play. No matter how much she urged it, nothing happened.

Mummy tried to help. She urged Daisy to be careful and to think about what the problem could be. They looked and saw the flute was broken. Daisy was sad.

Mummy hugged Daisy tight and told her it was ok. Everything can be fixed. Daisy was happy again. They got a new flute so Daisy could play again.

One day, Jack was walking down the street to play. Everything was so interesting in town. He saw a man sitting on a bench. Jack thought it would be nice to say hello and he went over to talk to him. 

"Good morning," said Jack. The man gave a warm welcome to Jack and smiled. He said he had a present for Jack and handed him a box. It was wrapped in shiny paper and had a big bow on top. 

Jack thought it looked really fun and he began to open it. Inside was a toy robot. Jack loved robots, so he trusted the man and thanked him for the toy. 

But as soon as he thanked him, the man grabbed Jack and ran away. Jack was scared and tried to escape, but it was too late. 

Jack had trusted the man too easily and he never should have taken the present. It was a mistake that Jack would regret forever.

Once upon a time, there was a cat and a dog. They lived in a big house with a smooth floor. The cat liked to slide on the floor and the dog liked to chase the cat.

One day, the cat and the dog had a quarrel. The cat said, "I am faster than you!" The dog said, "No, I am faster!" They decided to have a race to see who was the fastest.

The race began and the cat and the dog ran as fast as they could. The cat slipped on the smooth floor and the dog laughed. The dog said, "I have a joke! Why did the cat slide on the floor? Because it's too smooth!" The cat laughed too. They stopped quarreling and became friends again. They played together and had fun in their big house with the smooth floor.

Tom and Mary were best friends. One day, Tom was frustrated because his toy was broken and he didn't know how to save it. Mary grabbed an orange from her bag and said to Tom, "Let's try this!" Tom tried to use the orange to fix his toy, but nothing worked.

Tom got even more frustrated and started to cry. Mary tried to calm him down, but she didn't know what to do. She tried to think of another way to save Tom's toy, but nothing worked.

Suddenly, Tom came up with an idea. "How about using magic? It could save my toy!" he exclaimed. Mary was hesitant but eventually agreed.

They grabbed a wand from her bag and waved it around the toy. But unfortunately, the toy still did not work. Tom was so frustrated that he started to cry again.

Mary gave Tom a hug and said, "It's okay, Tom. I'm sorry, but we couldn't save your toy."

Anna is a pupil at the big school. She likes to learn new things and play with her friends. But today, she is not happy. She has a long cut on her knee from falling down on the playground. It hurts and it is dirty.

"Anna, you need to bathe your knee," says her teacher, Miss Lee. "It will help it heal and stop the germs."

Anna does not want to bathe her knee. She is afraid of the water and the soap. She thinks they will sting and make her cry. She shakes her head and holds her knee.

"No, no, no," she says. "I don't want to bathe. I want to go home."

Miss Lee is kind and gentle. She takes Anna to the nurse's office. There, she shows her a big tub of warm water and a soft cloth. She also has a band-aid with a picture of a bunny on it.

"Look, Anna," she says. "This is not scary. The water is warm and the cloth is soft. They will not hurt you. They will make your knee feel better. And then you can have this band-aid with a bunny on it. Don't you like bunnies?"

Anna likes bunnies. She thinks they are cute and fluffy. She looks at the band-aid and then at Miss Lee. She sees that Miss Lee is smiling and caring. She decides to trust her.

"Okay," she says. "I will bathe my knee. But you have to help me."

"Of course, I will help you," says Miss Lee. "You are a brave and good pupil, Anna."

Miss Lee helps Anna bathe her knee. She gently washes the dirt and the blood away. She dries it with a towel and puts the band-aid on it. Anna feels a little pain, but she does not cry. She feels proud of herself.

"Thank you, Miss Lee," she says. "You are a nice teacher. And I like the bunny band-aid. It makes me happy."

"You are very welcome, Anna," says Miss Lee. "I am glad you are happy. And I am proud of you for bathing your knee. You did a great job."

Anna smiles and hugs Miss Lee. She feels better and ready to go back to class. She has learned a new thing today. She has learned that bathing can help her heal and that Miss Lee is a good friend.

Once upon a time, there was a baby. The baby was very small and cute. One day, the baby went for a walk with its mommy. They walked through the park and saw many things. The baby liked to observe the flowers and the trees. Suddenly, they saw something mysterious in the bushes. It was a little kitten! The baby and its mommy were very happy to see the kitten. They picked it up and brought it home. Now, the baby had a new friend to play with. They named the kitten Mimi. The end.

One day, Old Tom was walking along a trail in the woods. He came across a big pile of coal. He said to himself, "What should I do with this coal?"

Suddenly, a little mouse popped up from behind the pile. "Please accept this coal, kind Tom," said the mouse. "It would make me very happy if you did."

Old Tom thought for a moment. "You know what, little mouse? I'll accept your coal," he replied.

The mouse looked so pleased! He thanked Old Tom and thanked him, again and again. Old Tom smiled and carried the coal back home.

The end.

Spades take up leaves No better than spoons, And bags full of leaves Are light as balloons. I make a great noise Of rustling all day Like rabbit and deer Running away. But the mountains I raise Elude my embrace, Flowing over my arms And into my face. I may load and unload Again and again Till I fill the whole shed, And what have I then? Next to nothing for weight, And since they grew duller From contact with earth, Next to nothing for color. Next to nothing for use, But a crop is a crop, And who's to say where The harvest shall stop?

In the morning, Jack's mom said, "Let's go outside!" Jack was very excited to go outside. So he went with his mom and as soon as he stepped outside, he heard a lot of birds singing. He was so happy to hear the birds! He said, "Mom, I can hear the birds singing! They sound so nice!" 

Jack's Mom smiled and said, "Yes, the birds are singing. That's how they communicate with each other." Jack started to explore the garden and soon he saw a light. He asked his mom what it was. She said, "That is the sun. It brings us sunshine." 

Jack frowned. He was a bit scared of the sun. He asked his mom why it was so serious and why it had to be so bright. His mom said, "Just like the birds, the sun is communicating with us. It gives us warmth and light which is very important to keep things growing." She then said, "As long as we respect and care for nature, it will always take care of us." 

Jack understood this lesson well. He happily went back home and promised himself to always take care of nature.

Once upon a time, there was a happy bird named Blue. Blue loved to fly high in the sky and see all the pretty things down below. One day, Blue saw a big, old mill in the distance. Blue wanted to fly over and see it up close.

But Blue wasn't ready for the big adventure yet. Blue needed to eat and rest first. So, Blue flew to a nearby tree and ate some yummy berries. Then, Blue took a nap in the warm sun.

After eating and resting, Blue felt ready to fly to the mill. But as Blue got closer, a big storm came. The wind was strong and the rain was heavy. Blue tried to fly through the storm, but it was too hard. Blue had to turn back and go home.

The moral of the story is that sometimes we need to be patient and wait until we are ready for big adventures. And sometimes, even when we are ready, things out of our control can happen. But that's okay, because we can always try again another day.

Once upon a time, there was a very adorable ghost. He liked to jump around. He would jump and hop through the day. 
When night time came, the ghost liked to fly around the moon and sing songs while he jumped in the sky. His happy little singing could be heard.
Every night, the ghost would take a break and sit on the clouds to watch the stars twinkle. He thought they were so pretty! 
One night, a big storm came. The wind was blowing and the rain was pouring down. But, the ghost was brave and he still wanted to jump. He bravely jumped through the storm and it was fun!
When the storm was over, the ghost was happy. He had enjoyed his jumping adventure. 
The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play and act like a doctor. Lily wanted to help people feel healthy and strong.

One day, Lily found a toy needle in her room. She thought, "I can use this to help my toys feel better!" She took the toy needle and went to find her teddy bear, Mr. Snuggles.

"Mr. Snuggles, do you want to play doctor with me?" Lily asked. Mr. Snuggles nodded his head. Lily pretended to give Mr. Snuggles a shot with the toy needle. "There you go, Mr. Snuggles. Now you will be healthy and strong!"

Lily and Mr. Snuggles played doctor all day long. They had so much fun acting and helping their toy friends feel better. And they all lived happily ever after.

Jill was so excited to go to the park with her mommy. She loved playing on the swings and climbing up the jungle gym. Today she was most excited to play a very special game with her mommy.

When they arrived, Mommy took out a box with brightly coloured shapes inside. Her mommy called them a â€˜memory matchâ€™ game and explained how it worked. Jill began picking up pieces, looking at the pictures which were very yummy looking foods. She loved playing and within no time she had matched all the pieces. 

Mommy was so proud of Jill for her memory and with a hug, said â€˜you are a true champion of this game!â€™ Jill was very happy and excited for the next game that Mommy would bring.

Once there was a little boy called Jack. He was 3 years old and loved to explore the beach near his house. On this day, Jack looked very excited. He picked up a bucket, shovel and his toy surfboard, and ran towards the beach.

When he reached the beach, he put his gear down and ran towards the shore. He was so excited to go in the water. As his feet touched the sea, he could feel the cold surf against them.

Suddenly, he saw something shiny at the bottom of the sea. He shouted with excitement and put on his goggles. He quickly opened his bucket and started collecting the shiny objects. 

Jack's mom approached him. "What do you have there, Jack?" she asked. Jack was suddenly filled with guilt, for he had found a box of jewels. But his mom smiled, and said, "It's ok Jack. You can keep them if you close the box and put it in the bucket." 

Jack nodded and quickly closed the box and put it in the bucket. He ran towards the beach to continue surfing and have fun with the waves. His guilt was gone and the sun was shining more brightly than ever. 

The end.

Tim and Lily like to play with their toy tank. It is big and green and has a lid that can open and close. They pretend that the tank is going on a mission to find treasure.

One day, they find a big box in the garage. It has a picture of a tank on it. Tim and Lily are very excited. They think it is a new toy tank for them.

"Can we open it, please?" they ask their mom.

"Okay, but be careful. It is not a toy. It is a real tank that your dad used to have when he was in the army. He gave it to me as a gift. It is very old and fragile," mom says.

Tim and Lily open the box carefully. Inside, they see a shiny metal tank. It looks like their toy tank, but much smaller and more detailed. It has wheels and tracks and a cannon and a hatch.

"Wow, it is so cool!" Tim says.

"Can we play with it?" Lily asks.

Mom nods. "Yes, but only on the table. And don't break anything. This tank is very special to me and your dad."

Tim and Lily put the tank on the table. They take turns to open and close the hatch and move the cannon. They make noises like "boom" and "vroom".

They pretend that the tank is going on a mission to find treasure. They use their toy soldiers and animals and blocks as enemies and allies and obstacles.

They have a lot of fun with the tank. They are very clever and creative. They make up stories and jokes and songs.

Mom watches them and smiles. She is happy that they like the tank. She thinks they are very sweet and smart. She loves them very much.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she wanted to help her mommy cook some yummy food. Her mommy told her to stay away from the stove because it was very hot and could burn her. 

But Lily didn't listen and got too close to the stove. She accidentally touched it and it was so hot that it made her hand hurt. She cried and her hand turned pale. 

Her mommy quickly put her hand in some cold water to make it feel better. She told Lily that the stove was very sharp and dangerous, and that she needed to be careful around it. From that day on, Lily always listened to her mommy and stayed far away from the stove.

Lily liked to write in her diary every day. She had a pink diary with a lock and a key. She wrote about her friends, her toys, her dreams and her feelings. She kept her diary under her pillow, so no one could find it.

One day, Lily's brother Jake was looking for his ball in her room. He saw the diary under the pillow and took it. He opened it and started to read it. He saw Lily's drawings and words. He thought they were funny and silly. He laughed out loud.

Lily heard Jake's laugh and ran to her room. She saw him with her diary in his hands. She was angry and sad. She shouted, "Jake, give me back my diary! That's mine! You are not nice!"

Jake looked at Lily and said, "Sorry, Lily, I was just curious. I didn't mean to hurt you. Your diary is very cute. Can I see more?"

Lily snatched her diary from Jake and hugged it. She said, "No, you can't. This is my diary, not yours. It's private and quiet. You have to ask me before you touch it. And you have to say sorry again."

Jake felt sorry for Lily. He said, "I'm sorry, Lily, I won't do it again. Can we still be friends?"

Lily looked at Jake and saw that he was sincere. She said, "OK, Jake, we can still be friends. But you have to promise me to never touch my diary again. And you have to play with me sometimes."

Jake nodded and said, "I promise, Lily. And I will play with you sometimes. What do you want to play?"

Lily smiled and said, "Let's play hide and seek. You count to ten and I will hide. And don't peek!"

Jake agreed and said, "OK, Lily, let's play hide and seek. One, two, three..."

Lily ran to find a good hiding spot. She put her diary in her backpack and zipped it. She hoped Jake would not find her. She also hoped he would not laugh at her diary again. She liked her diary. It was her special friend.

Once upon a time, there was a frog named Freddy. Freddy was very sad because he didn't have any friends to play with. One day, he saw a little girl named Lily walking by the pond. 

"Hi there, little froggy!" said Lily. "You look so smooth and green. Do you want to play with me?"

"Yes, please!" said Freddy, hopping up and down with excitement. 

Lily picked up Freddy and brought him to her sandbox. "Let's add some water to make some mud pies!" said Lily. 

Freddy was so happy to have a new friend and they played together all day. From that day on, Lily would come visit Freddy at the pond and they would play together, adding different things to their games to make them even more fun.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys in the garden. One day, she found a ladybug on a flower. She picked it up and watched it crawl on her hand.

Suddenly, the sun began to rise in the sky. Lily looked up and saw the tip of the sun peeking over the trees. She knew it was time to go inside for breakfast.

Later that day, Lily's mom told her that there were cookies available in the kitchen. Lily was so happy and ran to the kitchen to get a cookie. She ate it all up and smiled. It was a great day!

Once upon a time there was a brave bear. He wanted to have a party and so he set off to find a special invitation.

The bear marched through the woods, looking at everything that he could find. He saw birds, butterflies and even a spider! After a while he found a beautiful invitation tucked away in a tree trunk.

The bear was excited and he quickly took the invitation back to his own home. He set up decorations and put the invitation on the table. He wanted everyone to see it and to come and join the party.

The bear sent out the invitations and all of his friends arrived at the party on time. They ate yummy treats, laughed and danced together. It was the best day ever!

Once there was a little girl called Lucy. She was very sad because her friends were teasing her. They laughed at her and pointed their fingers at her.

One day, Lucy went to the park. She saw a little boy with his thumb in his mouth and he was also very sad. She walked over to him and asked why he was sad. The boy said his friends had been teasing him too.

Lucy smiled and said, "That's not nice. Why don't we play together? I'll help you feel better." They played together and soon they were both giggling and smiling again.

Lucy and the boy were now friends and they decided to never tease each other. Whenever one was feeling sad, they would just play and soon they would be laughing and smiling again.

Once upon a time, there was an ancient man. He was happy and he always danced whenever he heard a song. He would listen for a song, jump up and dance. He would spin around and around as if he had no care in the world.

One day, he heard a very special song. It sounded so old and special! He started to dance like he had never danced before. He jumped up, spun around, and even clapped his hands to the beat.

The man danced and danced until the sun went down. Everyone who watched him was amazed and they all started to clap and cheer.

The man smiled and bowed. He said goodbye and he kept on dancing into the night. 

The people said goodbye as they watched him go. They smiled and waved as the man danced far away.  The ancient man would forever dance in the wind, forever to the sound of a special song.

Excitedly, she ran inside to get her mum. She said to her, â€œMummy, look, look! A pretty mint in my garden!â€ 

Her mum smiled and said, â€œThatâ€™s wonderful, Sam. Letâ€™s pick some mint and make a fresh lemonade.â€

So they went outside and picked some mint. They washed it, put it in a jug and added some lemons. Soon, the lemonade was ready and it tasted so delicious. 

Sam and her mum enjoyed the minty lemonade in the garden, which was now all the more special to her. She was so grateful to have the mint in her garden.

name_of_work: The Yellowhammer's Nest by John Clare
content: Just by the wooden brig a bird flew up, Frit by the cowboy as he scrambled down To reach the misty dewberry--let us stoop And seek its nest--the brook we need not dread, 'Tis scarcely deep enough a bee to drown, So it sings harmless o'er its pebbly bed --Ay here it is, stuck close beside the bank Beneath the bunch of grass that spindles rank Its husk seeds tall and high--'tis rudely planned Of bleached stubbles and the withered fare That last year's harvest left upon the land, Lined thinly with the horse's sable hair. Five eggs, pen-scribbled o'er with ink their shells Resembling writing scrawls which fancy reads As nature's poesy and pastoral spells-- They are the yellowhammer's and she dwells Most poet-like where brooks and flowery weeds As sweet as Castaly to fancy seems And that old molehill like as Parnass' hill On which her partner haply sits and dreams O'er all her joys of song--so leave it still A happy home of sunshine, flowers and streams. Yet in the sweetest places cometh ill, A noisome weed that burthens every soil; For snakes are known with chill and deadly coil To watch such nests and seize the helpless young, And like as though the plague became a guest, Leaving a houseless home, a ruined nest-- And mournful hath the little warblers sung When such like woes hath rent its little breast.

name_of_work: Soliloquy of the Spanish Cloister by Robert Browning
content: Gr-r-r--there go, my heart's abhorrence! Water your damned flower-pots, do! If hate killed men, Brother Lawrence, God's blood, would not mine kill you! What? your myrtle-bush wants trimming? Oh, that rose has prior claims-- Needs its leaden vase filled brimming? Hell dry you up with its flames! At the meal we sit together; Salve tibi! I must hear Wise talk of the kind of weather, Sort of season, time of year: Not a plenteous cork crop: scarcely Dare we hope oak-galls, I doubt; What's the Latin name for "parsley"? What's the Greek name for "swine's snout"? Whew! We'll have our platter burnished, Laid with care on our own shelf! With a fire-new spoon we're furnished, And a goblet for ourself, Rinsed like something sacrificial Ere 'tis fit to touch our chaps-- Marked with L. for our initial! (He-he! There his lily snaps!) Saint, forsooth! While Brown Dolores Squats outside the Convent bank With Sanchicha, telling stories, Steeping tresses in the tank, Blue-black, lustrous, thick like horsehairs, --Can't I see his dead eye glow, Bright as 'twere a Barbary corsair's? (That is, if he'd let it show!) When he finishes refection, Knife and fork he never lays Cross-wise, to my recollection, As do I, in Jesu's praise. I the Trinity illustrate, Drinking watered orange pulp-- In three sips the Arian frustrate; While he drains his at one gulp! Oh, those melons! if he's able We're to have a feast; so nice! One goes to the Abbot's table, All of us get each a slice. How go on your flowers? None double? Not one fruit-sort can you spy? Strange!--And I, too, at such trouble, Keep them close-nipped on the sly! There's a great text in Galatians, Once you trip on it, entails Twenty-nine district damnations, One sure, if another fails; If I trip him just a-dying, Sure of heaven as sure can be, Spin him round and send him flying Off to hell, a Manichee? Or, my scrofulous French novel On grey paper with blunt type! Simply glance at it, you grovel Hand and foot in Belial's gripe; If I double down its pages At the woeful sixteenth print, When he gathers his greengages, Ope a sieve and slip it in't? Or, there's Satan!--one might venture Pledge one's soul to him, yet leave Such a flaw in the indenture As he'd miss till, past retrieve, Blasted lay that rose-acacia We're so proud of! Hy, Zy, Hine... 'St, there's Vespers! Plena gratia Ave, Virgo! Gr-r-r--you swine!
