There is an evening coming in Across the fields, one never seen before, That lights no lamps. Silken it seems at a distance, yet When it is drawn up over the knees and breast It brings no comfort. Where has the tree gone, that locked Earth to the sky? What is under my hands, That I cannot feel? What loads my hands down?

name_of_work: Crossing the Loch by Kathleen Jamie
content: Remember how we rowed toward the cottage on the sickle-shaped bay, that one night after the pub loosed us through its swinging doors and we pushed across the shingle till water lipped the sides as though the loch mouthed 'boat'? I forget who rowed. Our jokes hushed. The oars' splash, creak, and the spill of the loch reached long into the night. Out in the race I was scared: the cold shawl of breeze, and hunched hills; what the water held of deadheads, ticking nuclear hulls. Who rowed, and who kept their peace? Who hauled salt-air and stars deep into their lungs, were not reassured; and who first noticed the loch's phosphorescence, so, like a twittering nest washed from the rushes, an astonished small boat of saints, we watched water shine on our fingers and oars, the magic dart of our bow wave? It was surely foolhardy, such a broad loch, a tide, but we live -- and even have children to women and men we had yet to meet that night we set out, calling our own the sky and salt-water, wounded hills dark-starred by blaeberries, the glimmering anklets we wore in the shallows as we shipped oars and jumped, to draw the boat safe, high at the cottage shore.

name_of_work: O sweet spontaneous by E.E. Cummings
content: O sweet spontaneous earth how often have the doting fingers of prurient philosophers pinched and poked thee ,has the naughty thumb of science prodded thy beauty how often have religions taken thee upon their scraggy knees squeezing and buffeting thee that thou mightest conceive gods (but true to the incomparable couch of death thy rhythmic lover thou answerest them only with spring)

In sixth grade Mrs. Walker slapped the back of my head and made me stand in the corner for not knowing the difference between persimmon and precision. How to choose persimmons. This is precision. Ripe ones are soft and brown-spotted. Sniff the bottoms. The sweet one will be fragrant. How to eat: put the knife away, lay down newspaper. Peel the skin tenderly, not to tear the meat. Chew the skin, suck it, and swallow. Now, eat the meat of the fruit, so sweet, all of it, to the heart. Donna undresses, her stomach is white. In the yard, dewy and shivering with crickets, we lie naked, face-up, face-down. I teach her Chinese. Crickets: chiu chiu. Dew: I've forgotten. Naked: I've forgotten. Ni, wo: you and me. I part her legs, remember to tell her she is beautiful as the moon. Other words that got me into trouble were fight and fright, wren and yarn. Fight was what I did when I was frightened, Fright was what I felt when I was fighting. Wrens are small, plain birds, yarn is what one knits with. Wrens are soft as yarn. My mother made birds out of yarn. I loved to watch her tie the stuff; a bird, a rabbit, a wee man. Mrs. Walker brought a persimmon to class and cut it up so everyone could taste a Chinese apple. Knowing it wasn't ripe or sweet, I didn't eat but watched the other faces. My mother said every persimmon has a sun inside, something golden, glowing, warm as my face. Once, in the cellar, I found two wrapped in newspaper, forgotten and not yet ripe. I took them and set both on my bedroom windowsill, where each morning a cardinal sang, The sun, the sun. Finally understanding he was going blind, my father sat up all one night waiting for a song, a ghost. I gave him the persimmons, swelled, heavy as sadness, and sweet as love. This year, in the muddy lighting of my parents' cellar, I rummage, looking for something I lost. My father sits on the tired, wooden stairs, black cane between his knees, hand over hand, gripping the handle. He's so happy that I've come home. I ask how his eyes are, a stupid question. All gone, he answers. Under some blankets, I find a box. Inside the box I find three scrolls. I sit beside him and untie three paintings by my father: Hibiscus leaf and a white flower. Two cats preening. Two persimmons, so full they want to drop from the cloth. He raises both hands to touch the cloth, asks, Which is this? This is persimmons, Father. Oh, the feel of the wolftail on the silk, the strength, the tense precision in the wrist. I painted them hundreds of times eyes closed. These I painted blind. Some things never leave a person: scent of the hair of one you love, the texture of persimmons, in your palm, the ripe weight.

name_of_work: Then I Saw What the Calling Was by Muriel Rukeyser
content: All the voices of the wood called "Muriel!" but it was soon solved; it was nothing, it was not for me. The words were a little like Mortal and More and Endure And a world like Real , a sound like Health or Hell. Then I saw what the calling was : it was the road I traveled, the clear time and these colors of orchards, gold behind gold and the full shadow begin each tree and behind each slope. Not to me the calling, but to anyone and at last I saw : where the road lay through sunlight and many voices and the marvel orchards, not for me, not for me, not for me. I cam into my clear being; uncalled, alive, and sure. Nothing was speaking to me, but I offered and all was well. And I arrived at the powerful green hill.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys in her room. One day, she saw her toy car and wanted to play with it. She picked it up and started to zoom it around her room.

Suddenly, her little brother, Max, came into the room. He wanted to play too. "Can I play with you, Lily?" Max asked. "Sure!" said Lily. "But first, let's build a castle for our cars to drive through."

They started to build a castle out of blocks. Max accidentally knocked it over and it became dirty. "Uh oh, our castle is dirty now," said Lily. "Let's clean it up!" They cleaned the castle and started to zoom their cars through it. They had so much fun playing together.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to dance. She had a delicate body and her muscles were not very strong. One day, Lily's mom took her to a ballet class. Lily was excited to stretch her body and learn new moves.

At the ballet class, Lily met a mean girl named Sarah. Sarah had strong muscles and could stretch her body very far. Sarah laughed at Lily and said, "You can't dance, your muscles are too weak!" Lily felt sad and wanted to go home.

During the class, Lily tried her best to stretch her muscles and dance. But her body was not strong enough to do the moves. She felt embarrassed and started to cry. The teacher tried to help her, but it was too late. Lily's muscles were too delicate and she hurt herself badly.

Lily had to go to the hospital and couldn't dance anymore. She learned that it's not nice to make fun of others and that everyone has different strengths. From then on, Lily decided to be kind to others and to love herself just the way she is.

name_of_work: A Western Ballad by Allen Ginsberg
content: When I died, love, when I died my heart was broken in your care; I never suffered love so fair as now I suffer and abide when I died, love, when I died. When I died, love, when I died I wearied in an endless maze that men have walked for centuries, as endless as the gate was wide when I died, love, when I died. When I died, love, when I died there was a war in the upper air: all that happens, happens there; there was an angel by my side when I died, love, when I died.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved going to the theater with her mommy and daddy. They would watch plays and sing songs together.

One day, Lily saw a man who looked foolish. He was wearing big shoes and a funny hat. He was juggling balls and making silly faces. Lily thought he was very funny.

Later that day, Lily and her family went to pick some apples at the orchard. As they were walking, they saw the same man from the theater. He was picking apples too! He smiled at Lily and showed her a trick with the apples.

Lily was so happy to see the man again. She realized that he wasn't foolish after all, he was just different. From that day on, Lily learned that everyone is unique and special in their own way.

One day, a little girl named Lily wanted to play with her toy blocks. She got out her blocks and started to build a tower. But then, the tower fell down! Lily was sad. 

Her mommy came over and said, "Don't worry, Lily. I will support you." She helped Lily build a new tower, and this time it didn't fall down! 

Later, Lily wanted to play outside, but it was raining. She asked her mommy if they could still go outside. "Not yet, sweetie," said her mommy. "But we can play inside instead." 

Lily was happy to hear that there were still fun things available to do, even if they couldn't go outside.

John was a curious three-year-old boy. One day, he decided to examine his mother's purse. He opened it up carefully and looked inside. Inside, he found a few coins and some colorful beads. He was so fascinated by these new findings that he decided to pick them up.

Suddenly, he heard his mother's voice: "John! What are you doing?" She had come in to ask what John was up to.

John replied, "I'm examining your purse and the things inside." He showed the coins and beads he was holding.

His mother smiled and said, "You can examine it, just don't take any of the things out."

John put the coins and beads back inside the purse and said, "Gotcha, mom." He zipped up the purse carefully and smiled as he watched her leave his room.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved playing basketball with his friends. He had a fierce passion for the game and always wanted to win.

One day, Timmy and his friends were playing a game when a stranger came up and asked to join. Timmy's friends said no, but Timmy felt bad and said yes. The stranger was very good and soon they were winning.

But then, the stranger started to cheat. Timmy knew it was wrong, but he didn't know what to do. Finally, he asked his friends for help. They told him to talk to the stranger and ask him to stop cheating.

Timmy went over to the stranger and asked him to stop cheating. The stranger got angry and pushed Timmy down. Timmy hit his head and had to go to the hospital. The moral of the story is that it's important to stand up for what's right, even if it's hard to do.

Once upon a time, there was a little birdie who lived in a big tree. The birdie loved to sing and fly around in the blue sky. One day, the birdie felt an urge to explore the world beyond the tree. It wanted to see the nature and all the beautiful things.

But the birdie's mother told it that it was foolish to leave the tree. She said that there were many dangers outside and the birdie should stay safe in the tree. But the birdie could not resist the urge to see the world outside.

So, one day, the birdie flew out of the tree and saw the most amazing things. It saw the green grass, the blue ocean, and the big mountains. The birdie was so happy that it had followed its urge to explore the nature.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Jenny. She was only three years old. One day, Jenny was playing in the garden when an old grandmother appeared.

"Would you like a cup of coffee?" the grandmother asked kindly.

Jenny's eyes sparkled. "Yes please!" she said.

So, off they went to the kitchen. The grandmother put the coffee into an old cup and handed it to Jenny. "This is my original cup!" Jenny said happily.

Jenny took small sips of the coffee, enjoying the warm liquid. Then she asked the grandmother, "How long can I stay?"

"As long as you want," the grandmother smiled.

So, Jenny stayed with the grandmother for the rest of the day, sipping her original cup of coffee.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big display of fruit in a shop. There are apples, bananas, oranges, and more.

"Wow, look at all the fruit!" Anna says. "I want to try some."

"Me too," Ben says. "But we have no money."

They go closer to the display. They see a sign that says "Free Samples". They are happy.

"Free means we can have some," Anna says. "Let's take one each."

They reach for the fruit. But a man stops them. He is the shop owner. He is angry.

"Hey, what are you doing?" he says. "You can't take the fruit. The sign is for customers only. You have to buy something first."

"But we have no money," Ben says. "We are sorry."

The man looks at them. He sees they are weak and hungry. He feels sorry for them too.

"OK, OK," he says. "You can have one fruit each. But only one. And don't come back again."

"Thank you, sir," Anna and Ben say. They take an apple and a banana. They run away.

They eat the fruit in the park. They are happy. They share their fruit with a bird and a squirrel. They are kind.

The end.
The year's at the spring, And day's at the morn; Morning's at seven; The hill-side's dew-pearl'd; The lark's on the wing; The snail's on the thorn; God's in His heaven, All's right with the world!

Once upon a time there was a dog. He was looking for something to do. He saw a bone on the ground and thought it would be fun to have. But the bone was stuck in the ground. The dog tried to use his paw to get it out, but it was no use!

Then he saw a mouse. The mouse said that he could help. He asked the dog to step aside and he started to dig. He dug and dug until he solved the problem. The mouse had dug the bone out of the ground!

The dog was so happy. He said thank you and took the bone. But then he saw that the bone was ugly. He didn't want to keep it. So, he decided to share the bone and give it back to the mouse.

The mouse was so happy. He thanked the dog and ran off with the bone. The dog smiled and went off to look for something else to do. He had solved a problem and made a new friend!

Once there was a big, hot summer and it made everyone very miserable. Everyone wanted to relax, but it was too hot.

One day, a little girl asked her dad if he could help her be comfortable again. So her dad made her a little pool with water in it. They both put their feet in the pool and it felt so nice.

They both stayed in the pool all day and it was so much fun. Soon, the little girl and her dad were feeling much better and relaxed.

The summer was still miserable, but at least the little girl and her dad had their pool to help them relax.

Tom and Sue are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big tent. They hear music from inside. They want to see what is in the tent.

They go inside the tent. It is dark. They see many people. They see pots and pans. They smell food. They see a man with a hat. He is cooking. He sees Tom and Sue.

"Hello, little ones," he says. "Do you like music? Do you like food? I am cooking for the people. They are here for a party. Do you want to join the party?"

Tom and Sue nod. They like music. They like food. They want to join the party.

"Come, then," the man says. "I will give you some food. You can sit and listen to the music. You can have fun. But don't touch the pots and pans. They are hot. And don't go outside the tent. It is dark. You might get lost."

Tom and Sue follow the man. He gives them some food. They sit and listen to the music. They have fun. They are happy. They thank the man. They make new friends. They enjoy the party.

Once upon a time, there was a happy cat named Mittens. Mittens liked to play with yarn and chase mice. One day, Mittens saw a big knife on the kitchen counter. Mittens knew knives were sharp and dangerous, so she stayed away. 

Later that day, Mittens went to the park to play with her friends. They ran around and played games. Mittens was the most lively of all her friends. She could run and jump very fast. 

When Mittens got home, her owner wanted to weigh her. Mittens didn't know what that meant, but she sat still while her owner put her on a big scale. Mittens was happy to see that she had gained some weight. She purred and rubbed her head against her owner's hand.

Lily and Ben were excited to go to camp with Mom and Dad. They packed their bags, their toys and their snacks. They got in the car and drove for a long time. They saw trees, cows and birds on the way.

When they got to camp, they helped Mom and Dad set up the tent. They put the poles, the fabric and the pegs together. They made a cozy bed with blankets and pillows. They were happy to have their own little house.

But then, a big wind came and blew hard. The tent shook and flapped. One of the poles broke and the tent fell down. Lily and Ben were scared and sad. They ran to Mom and Dad.

"Mom, Dad, our tent is broken!" they cried.

"Don't worry, sweeties, we can fix it," Mom said. She hugged them and gave them a kiss. "Let's go and find a new pole. Maybe we can ask the other campers for help."

They walked around the camp and saw many people. They saw some kids playing, some adults cooking and some dogs barking. They asked them if they had a spare pole. Some said no, some said yes, but they were too big or too small. They kept looking until they found a nice lady who had a pole that was just right.

"Here you go, you can have this pole," she said. "I have an extra one. I hope you enjoy your camp."

"Thank you, thank you!" Lily and Ben said. They took the pole and ran back to their tent. They helped Mom and Dad fix it. They put the new pole in place and lifted the tent up. They checked if it was sturdy and secure. It was.

They were proud and happy. They had fixed their tent. They thanked Mom and Dad for their help. They went inside and played with their toys. They were excited to sleep in their tent and have more fun at camp. They had a great day.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Daisy. Daisy was three years old and loved to go on adventures.

Suddenly, Daisy had an idea. "Let's go on a holiday!" she said.

But her mum said no. "I refuse to go on holiday," said her mum. "It's too expensive."

Daisy was not happy. She wanted to go on a holiday so badly.

A few weeks later, Daisy's aunt came to visit. "How about we all go on a holiday together?" she said.

Daisy's mum couldn't refuse the offer. "Ok, let's go!" she said.

So they all packed their suitcases and flew off on their holiday. When they arrived, the sun was shining and the beach was lively. Daisy had a great time swimming and building sandcastles.

It was the best holiday ever!

One day, a brown bear went for a walk in the forest. He saw a big event up ahead. As he got closer, he called out to his friends to join him.

Bear: "Hello everyone! Come join me! There's a big event up ahead."

Together, the bear and his friends walked to see what the event was. Finally, they reached the event. It was a big, brown bird's nest! The bear put his paw up to the nest and pulled out an egg.

Bear: "Look, everyone! It's a big, brown egg!"

The bear smiled. He knew what he was going to do! He carefully put the egg back into the nest, and they all waited to see what would come next. Soon enough, they heard chirping noises. The egg had hatched, and a little brown bird hopped out.

The bear smiled, knowing he had helped a new life enter the world. From then on, the bear and his friends kept a close eye on the nest and all its events that were taking place.

One day, Jenny and her Mommy were in the park. Jenny was so excited to be there, because she loved to play on the swings and the slide. She was running around chasing butterflies, when she suddenly heard a loud and scary voice.

"Stop!" shouted the voice.

Jenny and her Mommy stopped in their tracks. Looking up, they saw a tall man wearing a policeman's uniform. He had a large mustasche and spoke in a very serious tone.

"I'm ordering you to stop," he said.

Jenny's Mommy smiled and asked, "Is there something wrong, Officer?"

The policeman pointed to a large calendar that he was holding in his hands. He said, "We're planning an important event on this day, and it is against the law to be in the park at this time."

Jenny thought the policeman was scary and she wanted to go home. Her Mommy quickly agreed, and thanked the officer for his help before heading back to the car.

In the end, Jenny was safe, and she learned an important lesson about following the law.

One day, it was raining outside. A young boy named Joe wanted to go out and play. He grabbed his red eraser and ran out the door, smiling as the rain tickled his face. Joe loved the rain and ran around in the raindrops until he was tired. 

He sat down under a tree and watched the rain, the eraser in his hand. After a while, he started using his eraser to draw pictures in the mud. Soon he was drawing all sorts of things.

The young boy was so absorbed in his drawing that he didn't realize the rain had stopped. The sun was shining brightly, and his drawings were starting to dry up. Joe sighed, disappointed that his creations were gone. 

He got up and looked around, smiling as he realized all the new puddles around him. With his eraser in hand, he jumped into the puddles, laughing as the water splashed on his legs. Before long he was running around, splashing and laughing, feeling much better after enjoying a rainy day.

Once upon a time, there was a happy dog named Max. Max was always loyal to his owner, Sarah. One day, Sarah was doing her laundry and Max wanted to help. He grabbed a sock in his mouth and ran around the house. Sarah smiled and laughed as Max played with the sock. 

Max loved to make Sarah smile. He was her loyal companion and always wanted to make her happy. After Sarah finished her laundry, Max snuggled up next to her on the couch. Sarah smiled as Max rested his head on her lap. They were both very happy together.

Once upon a time there was a fat cat. It liked to dream. One day it saw a lime and had a big dream. It dreamed it could fly to the moon and back. Everywhere it looked in its dream, it could see limes. In the sky and on the ground, there were limes everywhere. The fat cat was so happy in its dream.

Then suddenly the cat's dream was gone and it woke up. But the lime was still there! It was real and not a dream. The fat cat ate the lime and felt energized. It decided to try and fly to the moon.

It jumped and jumped but it never made it. The cat was too fat. Even with the help of the lime, it just couldn't get close to the moon.

The fat cat was sad but then it had an idea. It closed its eyes and imagined again. It dreamed it was flying and that it could touch the moon. The fat cat was so happy, it was finally flying! And this time, it was no dream.

name_of_work: Chorus of the Captains by Amanda Gorman
content: Today we honor our three captains For their actions and impact in A time of uncertainty and need. They've taken the lead, Exceeding all expectations and limitations Uplifting their communities and neighbors As leaders, healers, and educators. James has felt the wounds of warfare, But this warrior still shares His home with at-risk kids. During Covid, he's event lent a hand, Live-streaming football for family and fans. Trimaine is an educator who works nonstop, Providing his community with hotspots, Laptops, and tech workshops, So his students have all the tools They need to succeed in life and school. Suzie is the ICU nurse manager at a Tampa Hospital. Her chronicles prove that even in tragedy, hope is possible. She lost her grandmothers to the pandemic, And fights to save other lives in the ICU battle zone, Defining the frontline heroes risking their lives for our own. Let us walk with these warriors, Charge on with these champions, And carry forth the call of our captains! We celebrate them by acting With courage and compassion, By doing what is right and just. For while we honor them today, It is them who every day honor us

Once upon a time, there was an elderly woman who loved her skirt very much. She wore it every day and took good care of it. One day, she went for a walk and saw a little bird with a broken wing. The woman felt sad for the bird and decided to help it.

She gently picked up the bird and held it close to her chest. The bird felt warm and safe in her arms. The woman knew she had to take the bird to the vet, but she didn't want to let go of her skirt. She was afraid it would get dirty or ruined.

But then she remembered something her mother had told her when she was young. She said, "Sometimes you have to squeeze a little to help others." So, the woman took a deep breath and squeezed the bird tightly against her chest. She knew it was the right thing to do.

In the end, the bird got better and the woman's skirt was just fine. She learned that helping others is more important than worrying about material things. And the bird became her friend, flying by her side whenever she went for a walk.

My old man's a white old man And my old mother's black. If ever I cursed my white old man I take my curses back. If ever I cursed my black old mother And wished she were in hell, I'm sorry for that evil wish And now I wish her well. My old man died in a fine big house. My ma died in a shack. I wonder where I'm gonna die, Being neither white nor black?

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play with blocks and cars. They have a network of roads and buildings with their blocks. They make sounds for the cars and the people.

One day, Lily has an idea. She wants to make a bridge with blocks. She tells Ben her idea.

"Let's make a bridge with blocks. We can put it over the road. Then the cars can go under the bridge or over the bridge. It will be fun!" Lily says.

Ben thinks for a moment. He likes the idea, but he sees a problem.

"But how will we make the bridge? We need a lot of blocks. And we need to make it tight. If the bridge is not tight, it will fall down. And the cars will crash. That will be bad." Ben says.

Lily and Ben discuss how to make the bridge. They look at their blocks and their network. They count how many blocks they have. They try different ways to stack the blocks. They test the bridge with their cars.

After a while, they find a way to make the bridge. They use long blocks and short blocks. They make a pattern with the blocks. They make the bridge tight and strong. They are happy with their bridge.

They put the bridge over the road. They play with their cars and their network. They make the cars go under the bridge and over the bridge. They have fun with their bridge. They are proud of their bridge. They smile at each other. They are good friends.

One day, there was a little boy playing in the garden. He was feeling brave and adventurous and he wanted to try something new. So he walked up to a big, deep well and looked down inside. It was so deep, he couldn't even see the bottom! He felt a bit fearful but he was determined. He took a deep breath and closed his eyes. Then he jumped in, diving deep into the water!

As he was swimming, he felt the water all around him. It was dark and cold, but he kept swimming. Finally, he reached the bottom! He was so excited to see what was down there. He looked around and saw some rocks and a shell. He picked them up and swam back to the surface. When he reached the top, he felt relieved and proud of himself!

He called his mom to come see what he had found at the bottom of the well. She was amazed and gave him a big hug. From then on, the boy was no longer fearful of the well. He knew it was full of surprises and wonders, and he would explore it every chance he got.

Once upon a time there was a cute little girl. She was walking along the street one day and saw a blueberry stand. "Mmm I would like some blueberries," said the little girl.

The shopkeeper smiled at the little girl and said, "Ok sweetie, I'll sell you some blueberries. They are really yummy!"

The little girl smiled and nodded. She took some of the blueberries and thanked the shopkeeper. 

The little girl was so excited and happy. She couldn't stop eating her blueberries! Everyone she passed said how cute she looked with a big smile on her face and blueberry juice on her cheeks. 

The little girl finished all of her blueberries and thanked the shopkeeper once again. The shopkeeper smiled at the little girl and said, "Come again, sweetie! I will have more blueberries to sell next time!" 

The little girl waved goodbye to the shopkeeper and walked away with a happy skip in her step.

A movie of Robert Bresson's showed a yacht, at evening on the Seine, all its lights on, watched by two young, seemingly poor people, on the bridge adjacent the classic boy and girl, of the story, any one cares to tell. So years pass, of course, but I identified with the young, embittered Frenchman, knew his only almost complacent anguish and the distance he felt from his girl. Yet another film of Bresson's has the aging Lancelot with his awkward armor standing in a woods, of small trees dazed, bleeding, both he and his horse are, trying to get back to the castle, itself of no great size. It moved me, that life was afterall like that. You are in love. You stand in the woods, with a horse, bleeding. The story is true.

Tommy was a three-year-old little boy. He loved to run and play. One afternoon, Tommy had a bright idea. He took his blanket and threw it on the ground. Then, he put it over his head and started to race around his room. He thought it was so much fun!

Suddenly, Tommy tripped over a toy and fell. His blanket was all wrinkled. Tommy started to get mad, then his mom appeared. She laughed and said, "It was so silly of you to try to race with a blanket on your head!"

Tommy said he was sorry and put the blanket back in its place. He learned that it was a stupid thing to do, but he had a lot of fun!

Anna and Ben were friends who liked to play together. One day, they decided to mail a letter to their grandma, who lived far away. They wrote "We love you, Grandma" on a piece of paper and drew some pictures of flowers and hearts. Then they put the letter in an envelope and went to the mailbox.

On the way, they saw a rabbit nibbling on a carrot in a garden. Anna and Ben loved animals, so they stopped to watch the rabbit. The rabbit was brown and fluffy, and had long ears and a twitchy nose. It looked very happy with its carrot.

"Can we pet the rabbit?" Anna asked Ben.

"Maybe, but we have to be very quiet and patient," Ben said. "Rabbits are shy and run away if they hear loud noises or see strangers."

Anna and Ben nodded and crept closer to the rabbit, holding out their hands gently. The rabbit saw them and stopped eating. It looked at them with curious eyes, but did not run away. Anna and Ben smiled and waited for the rabbit to come to them.

After a while, the rabbit hopped closer and sniffed their hands. It felt their fingers with its whiskers and licked them softly. Anna and Ben giggled and stroked the rabbit's fur. The rabbit seemed to like them and let them pet it for a long time.

Anna and Ben were so happy that they forgot about their letter. They played with the rabbit until it was time to go home. Then they said goodbye to the rabbit and thanked it for being their friend. They remembered their letter and ran to the mailbox. They put the letter in the slot and waved to their grandma in their minds.

They learned that if they are patient and kind, they can make new friends and have fun. They also learned that they should not forget their promises and duties, even when they are having fun. They hoped that their grandma would like their letter and be proud of them.

Once there was a girl named Lila, and she had a very fancy dress that she was so proud of. She would often let her mom know all about it, but what made her happiest was when she could wear that dress. She would twirl and spin and feel so fancy. 

On this particular day, Lila was playing in the garden and she saw some petals on the ground. She loved the way they looked and she decided to use them in her dress. She picked up a handful of petals and let them fall over her dress. When she twirled, she could feel the pretty petals flutter around her.

Lila's mom came out to the garden and saw her. Lila was so proud to show off her fancy dress, but her mom said: "Oh no! Come on let's tidy up. We can't let these pretty petals fall onto the ground!"

name_of_work: The Eolian Harp by Samuel Taylor Coleridge
content: My pensive Sara! thy soft cheek reclined Thus on mine arm, most soothing sweet it is To sit beside our Cot, our Cot o'ergrown With white-flowered Jasmin, and the broad-leaved Myrtle, (Meet emblems they of Innocence and Love!) And watch the clouds, that late were rich with light, Slow saddening round, and mark the star of eve Serenely brilliant (such would Wisdom be) Shine opposite! How exquisite the scents Snatched from yon bean-field! and the world so hushed! The stilly murmur of the distant Sea Tells us of silence. And that simplest Lute, Placed length-ways in the clasping casement, hark! How by the desultory breeze caressed, Like some coy maid half yielding to her lover, It pours such sweet upbraiding, as must needs Tempt to repeat the wrong! And now, its strings Boldlier swept, the long sequacious notes Over delicious surges sink and rise, Such a soft floating witchery of sound As twilight Elfins make, when they at eve Voyage on gentle gales from Fairy-Land, Where Melodies round honey-dropping flowers, Footless and wild, like birds of Paradise, Nor pause, nor perch, hovering on untamed wing! O! the one Life within us and abroad, Which meets all motion and becomes its soul, A light in sound, a sound-like power in light, Rhythm in all thought, and joyance everywhere-- Methinks, it should have been impossible Not to love all things in a world so filled; Where the breeze warbles, and the mute still air Is Music slumbering on her instrument. And thus, my Love! as on the midway slope Of yonder hill I stretch my limbs at noon, Whilst through my half-closed eyelids I behold The sunbeams dance, like diamonds, on the main, And tranquil muse upon tranquility: Full many a thought uncalled and undetained, And many idle flitting phantasies, Traverse my indolent and passive brain, As wild and various as the random gales That swell and flutter on this subject Lute! And what if all of animated nature Be but organic Harps diversely framed, That tremble into thought, as o'er them sweeps Plastic and vast, one intellectual breeze, At once the Soul of each, and God of all? But thy more serious eye a mild reproof Darts, O beloved Woman! nor such thoughts Dim and unhallowed dost thou not reject, And biddest me walk humbly with my God. Meek Daughter in the family of Christ! Well hast thou said and holily dispraised These shapings of the unregenerate mind; Bubbles that glitter as they rise and break On vain Philosophy's aye-babbling spring. For never guiltless may I speak of him, The Incomprehensible! save when with awe I praise him, and with Faith that inly feels; Who with his saving mercies healed me, A sinful and most miserable man, Wildered and dark, and gave me to possess Peace, and this Cot, and thee, heart-honored Maid!

name_of_work: Casey at the Bat by Ernest Lawrence Thayer
content: The outlook wasn't brilliant for the Mudville nine that day: The score stood four to two, with but one inning more to play, And then when Cooney died at first, and Barrows did the same, A pall-like silence fell upon the patrons of the game. A straggling few got up to go in deep despair. The rest Clung to the hope which springs eternal in the human breast; They thought, "If only Casey could but get a whack at that-- We'd put up even money now, with Casey at the bat." But Flynn preceded Casey, as did also Jimmy Blake, And the former was a hoodoo, while the latter was a cake; So upon that stricken multitude grim melancholy sat, For there seemed but little chance of Casey getting to the bat. But Flynn let drive a single, to the wonderment of all, And Blake, the much despised, tore the cover off the ball; And when the dust had lifted, and men saw what had occurred, There was Jimmy safe at second and Flynn a-hugging third. Then from five thousand throats and more there rose a lusty yell; It rumbled through the valley, it rattled in the dell; It pounded on the mountain and recoiled upon the flat, For Casey, mighty Casey, was advancing to the bat. There was ease in Casey's manner as he stepped into his place; There was pride in Casey's bearing and a smile lit Casey's face. And when, responding to the cheers, he lightly doffed his hat, No stranger in the crowd could doubt 'twas Casey at the bat. Ten thousand eyes were on him as he rubbed his hands with dirt; Five thousand tongues applauded when he wiped them on his shirt; Then while the writhing pitcher ground the ball into his hip, Defiance flashed in Casey's eye, a sneer curled Casey's lip. And now the leather-covered sphere came hurtling through the air, And Casey stood a-watching it in haughty grandeur there. Close by the sturdy batsman the ball unheeded sped-- "That ain't my style," said Casey. "Strike one!" the umpire said. From the benches, black with people, there went up a muffled roar, Like the beating of the storm-waves on a stern and distant shore; "Kill him! Kill the umpire!" shouted someone on the stand; And it's likely they'd have killed him had not Casey raised his hand. With a smile of Christian charity great Casey's visage shone; He stilled the rising tumult; he bade the game go on; He signaled to the pitcher, and once more the dun sphere flew; But Casey still ignored it and the umpire said, "Strike two!" "Fraud!" cried the maddened thousands, and echo answered "Fraud!" But one scornful look from Casey and the audience was awed. They saw his face grow stern and cold, they saw his muscles strain, And they knew that Casey wouldn't let that ball go by again. The sneer is gone from Casey's lip, his teeth are clenched in hate, He pounds with cruel violence his bat upon the plate; And now the pitcher holds the ball, and now he lets it go, And now the air is shattered by the force of Casey's blow. Oh, somewhere in this favoured land the sun is shining bright, The band is playing somewhere, and somewhere hearts are light; And somewhere men are laughing, and somewhere children shout, But there is no joy in Mudville--mighty Casey has struck out.

Once upon a time, in a small house, there lived a little cat named Kitty. Kitty loved to play with her toys and eat tasty food. One day, Kitty went outside to play in the sun.

While she was playing, she saw a big tree. Kitty thought, "I want to find something fun to play with!" So, she looked around the tree and found a jar of cream. Kitty was very happy and said, "Wow! I love cream!"

Kitty took the jar of cream back to her house. She opened it and tasted the cream. It was very tasty! Kitty shared the cream with her friends, and they all loved it too. They played and ate the tasty cream all day long. And they lived happily ever after.

Once there was a little boy who wanted to explore the world. One day he decided to walk up a hill. When the boy reached the top, he saw how attractive it was. The hill was covered in blooming flowers and he could see the sun and the moon. The boy thought that was very special!

The boy decided to sit on the hill and close his eyes and enjoy the view. He could feel the wind brushing against his cheeks and he breathed in the fresh air. He felt happy and content.

After a while, the boy opened his eyes and looked around. He saw a little door on the hill and felt curious. He opened the door and discovered a lovely garden. He saw tall trees and colorful butterflies. But then he heard somebody say, "Please shut the door!" He realized he had to leave the garden and started to walk away from the hill.

The boy felt sad but he looked back at the hill one last time. He waved goodbye and smiled, because he knew the hill would always be there for him to explore again.

Once upon a time there was a girl named Emma. She was out in the garden playing with her rake. She loved to rake the leaves and it made her very happy. 

One day, Emma was pretending to be a princess. She said, "I am brilliant Princess Emma, and I need something to drink." She looked around and saw a big cup filled with water. 

Emma took the cup and started to drink. Then she looked around and saw a big rake. She said, "That's brilliant. I can use that rake to make my garden even more beautiful!" 

So Emma took the rake and used it to tidy up the garden. In no time, the garden was clean and neat. Emma was very pleased with her work. 

"See," she said. "Being a brilliant Princess isn't so hard when you have the right tools!"

Once upon a time, there was a messy boy named Tim. Tim liked to eat toast every morning. He loved to put butter and jam on his toast. But sometimes, he made a big mess. His mom would always have to clean up after him.

One day, Tim's mom decided to teach him how to make toast without making a mess. She showed him how to put the bread in the toaster and how to spread the butter and jam carefully. Tim watched and listened to his mom. He wanted to learn how to do it right.

The next morning, Tim tried to make his toast all by himself. He remembered what his mom taught him. He was very careful when he spread the butter and jam. Tim was so happy when he made his toast without making a mess. His mom was proud of him too. They both enjoyed their toast together.

name_of_work: Mother, Any Distance by Simon Armitage
content: Mother, any distance greater than a single span requires a second pair of hands. You come to help me measure windows, pelmets, doors, the acres of the walls, the prairies of the floors. You at the zero-end, me with the spool of tape, recording length, reporting metres, centimetres back to base, then leaving up the stairs, the line still feeding out, unreeling years between us. Anchor. Kite. I space-walk through the empty bedrooms, climb the ladder to the loft, to breaking point, where something has to give; two floors below your fingertips still pinch the last one-hundredth of an inch...I reach towards a hatch that opens on an endless sky to fall or fly.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to sit on her cushion and read books. One day, her little brother Jack came into her room and wanted to play. But Lily was feeling bossy and didn't want to play with him.

Jack asked, "Why won't you play with me, Lily?"

Lily replied, "I don't want to play with you. I want to read my book."

Jack said, "Can we discuss it? Maybe we can find something fun to do together."

Lily thought about it and said, "Okay, let's think of something fun we can do together."

They talked and decided to build a fort out of cushions. They had so much fun building it and playing inside. Lily realized that it was much more fun to play with her brother than to be bossy. From then on, they played together all the time.

Lila and Tom were playing in the garden. They liked to create things with dirt, rocks, and leaves. They made a house, a car, and a cake.

"Look at my cake!" Lila said. "It has thick icing and herb sprinkles. Do you want a slice?"

"Yes, please!" Tom said. "It looks yummy. Can I have some of this herb? It smells good."

Lila gave him some of the herb. It was mint. They both tasted it and made a funny face.

"Ew, it's spicy!" Lila said.

"It's not spicy, it's minty!" Tom said. "I like it. It makes my mouth feel cool."

They laughed and ate their dirt cake with mint. They pretended it was chocolate and vanilla. They had fun creating and sharing.

Once upon a time, there was a big tree in a forest. The tree was very humble and always gave shade to the animals who passed by. One day, a big storm came and the wind blew very hard. The tree was scared and held on tight to the ground. But the wind was too strong and the branches started to separate from the tree. 

The animals who lived in the forest saw what was happening and tried to help the tree. The birds flew to the top of the tree and held on to the branches. The squirrels climbed up the trunk and tried to hold on too. But the wind was too strong and the tree couldn't hold on anymore. 

Finally, the tree fell down with a big thud. The animals were sad and didn't know what to do. But then they remembered all the good things the tree had done for them. They decided to plant a new tree in the same spot and take care of it just like the old tree. And so, the animals worked together to plant a new tree and the forest was happy once again.

Once upon a time, there was a thick chicken. It liked to dance around the farm and talk to the other animals. One day, the chicken was walking around the barn when it noticed a small mouse.

The chicken stopped and asked, "Are you ok?" 
The mouse replied, "Yes, I am ok, but I need to find someone to teach me the dance steps." 

The chicken smiled, "I can help. I'm the best dancer on the farm and I know all the steps. Let's practice together!"

The mouse was very happy and followed the chicken around the barn. The chicken talked and taught the mouse each step of the dance. After a few hours, the mouse was a pro and danced as well as the chicken! 

The mouse and the chicken were now great friends and danced together every day.

name_of_work: At Last We Killed The Roaches by Lucille Clifton
content: at last we killed the roaches. mama and me. she sprayed, i swept the ceiling and they fell dying onto our shoulders, in our hair covering us with red. the tribe was broken, the cooking pots were ours again and we were glad, such cleanliness was grace when i was twelve. only for a few nights, and then not much, my dreams were blood my hands were blades and it was murder murder all over the place.

We are the music makers, And we are the dreamers of dreams, Wandering by lone sea-breakers, And sitting by desolate streams; -- World-losers and world-forsakers, On whom the pale moon gleams: Yet we are the movers and shakers Of the world for ever, it seems. With wonderful deathless ditties We build up the world's great cities, And out of a fabulous story We fashion an empire's glory: One man with a dream, at pleasure, Shall go forth and conquer a crown; And three with a new song's measure Can trample a kingdom down. We, in the ages lying, In the buried past of the earth, Built Nineveh with our sighing, And Babel itself in our mirth; And o'erthrew them with prophesying To the old of the new world's worth; For each age is a dream that is dying, Or one that is coming to birth. A breath of our inspiration Is the life of each generation; A wondrous thing of our dreaming Unearthly, impossible seeming -- The soldier, the king, and the peasant Are working together in one, Till our dream shall become their present, And their work in the world be done. They had no vision amazing Of the goodly house they are raising; They had no divine foreshowing Of the land to which they are going: But on one man's soul it hath broken, A light that doth not depart; And his look, or a word he hath spoken, Wrought flame in another man's heart. And therefore to-day is thrilling With a past day's late fulfilling; And the multitudes are enlisted In the faith that their fathers resisted, And, scorning the dream of to-morrow, Are bringing to pass, as they may, In the world, for its joy or its sorrow, The dream that was scorned yesterday. But we, with our dreaming and singing, Ceaseless and sorrowless we! The glory about us clinging Of the glorious futures we see, Our souls with high music ringing: O men! it must ever be That we dwell, in our dreaming and singing, A little apart from ye. For we are afar with the dawning And the suns that are not yet high, And out of the infinite morning Intrepid you hear us cry -- How, spite of your human scorning, Once more God's future draws nigh, And already goes forth the warning That ye of the past must die. Great hail! we cry to the comers From the dazzling unknown shore; Bring us hither your sun and your summers; And renew our world as of yore; You shall teach us your song's new numbers, And things that we dreamed not before: Yea, in spite of a dreamer who slumbers, And a singer who sings no more.

One cold, icy day, a little boy zoomed out of his house in search of an adventure. He walked down the street and soon came across a big tree with a trunk so thick that it was like a wall. He decided to climb it, and when he was at the top, he was so high that he could see forever!

The little boy kept looking around and the farther he looked, the more the landscape changed. The trees seemed to go on forever, and he could see all the way to the horizon. Suddenly, he noticed something in the distance, a glittering lake that looked like a big mirror! The lake was frozen and so icy.

The little boy thought it was the most amazing sight he had ever seen. He wanted to explore it, so he got down from the tree and started to zoom towards the lake. When he got closer, the little boy saw a path leading to the other side. He couldn't believe his eyes: the path was icy, and it seemed like the only way to get across! So he carefully stepped onto it, and soon he was back at home, but with a new story to tell.

Ben and Sam were brothers who liked to play with boats. They had many boats of different colors and sizes. They liked to pretend that they were sailors and explorers. They made a big port with blocks and sand, where they parked their boats.

One day, a new boy came to the park. His name was Tom. He had a big boat that was ugly and dirty. It had holes and stains and broken parts. He put his boat in the port and said, "This is my boat. It is the best boat in the world. Your boats are small and silly. You can't play with me."

Ben and Sam were sad and angry. They did not like Tom or his boat. They said, "Your boat is ugly and bad. It does not belong in our port. Go away and leave us alone."

Tom did not go away. He laughed and said, "You can't make me go away. I can do what I want. I will take your boats and break them. Then you will have no boats to play with."

Ben and Sam were scared and worried. They did not want to lose their boats. They did not know what to do. They looked at each other and had an idea. They said, "We have to unite. We have to work together and stop Tom. We have to show him that our boats are better and stronger. We have to protect our port."

Ben and Sam united. They took their boats and made a big fleet. They used ropes and sticks and stones to make weapons and shields. They sailed their boats towards Tom and his boat. They shouted, "This is our port. You can't take our boats. You can't break our boats. Go away or we will fight you."

Tom was surprised and scared. He saw that Ben and Sam had united and had many boats and weapons. He saw that his boat was ugly and weak. He said, "No, no, don't fight me. Don't hurt me. Don't hurt my boat. I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I was wrong. I was mean. Please, let me play with you."

Ben and Sam stopped. They looked at Tom and his boat. They felt sorry for him. They said, "OK, we will let you play with us. But you have to be nice and share. You have to respect our boats and our port. You have to help us fix your boat and make it better."

Tom nodded and smiled. He said, "Thank you, thank you. I will be nice and share. I will respect your boats and your port. I will help you fix my boat and make it better."

Ben and Sam smiled and nodded. They said, "You're welcome, you're welcome. Come on, let's play together. Let's unite and have fun."

They united and played together. They fixed Tom's boat and made it nicer. They shared their boats and their port. They pretended that they were sailors and explorers. They had a lot of fun.

name_of_work: Daylight and Moonlight by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
content: In broad daylight, and at noon, Yesterday I saw the moon Sailing high, but faint and white, As a school-boy's paper kite. In broad daylight, yesterday, I read a Poet's mystic lay; And it seemed to me at most As a phantom, or a ghost. But at length the feverish day Like a passion died away, And the night, serene and still, Fell on village, vale, and hill. Then the moon, in all her pride, Like a spirit glorified, Filled and overflowed the night With revelations of her light. And the Poet's song again Passed like music through my brain; Night interpreted to me All its grace and mystery.

Once upon a time, there was a bad bunny named Benny. Benny loved to eat sweets and never ate his vegetables, especially prunes. One day, Benny's mommy gave him a prune and said, "Eat this, Benny. It will make you strong and healthy." But Benny said, "No, mommy. Prunes are bad." 

Later that day, Benny went to play with his friend, Bobby. Bobby had a yummy snack, but Benny didn't have anything to eat. Bobby said, "Here, Benny. Pass this apple to me and I'll share my snack with you." Benny passed the apple to Bobby and Bobby shared his snack with Benny. Benny realized that sharing was good and that prunes weren't so bad after all. From that day on, Benny started eating his vegetables and became a healthy bunny.

Lily and Ben were best friends. They liked to play with blocks, draw with crayons and sing songs. They always joined each other at school and at home. They shared their toys and their snacks. They had big hearts and were kind to everyone.

One day, Lily and Ben had a fight. Lily wanted to play with the red car, but Ben wanted it too. They both pulled and tugged, but neither would let go. They shouted and cried, and said mean words. They did not join each other anymore. They played by themselves, but they were not happy. They missed their friend and their fun.

The next day, Lily and Ben saw each other at school. They looked away and pretended not to care. But inside, they felt sorry and sad. They wanted to say sorry and hug, but they did not know how. They wished they had not fought over the red car. It was not worth losing their friend.

Then, their teacher had an idea. She gave them a big piece of paper and some crayons. She told them to draw something together. Lily and Ben looked at each other and nodded. They took the paper and the crayons and sat down. They started to draw a big heart, with their names inside. They smiled and said sorry. They hugged and joined hands. They were best friends again. They learned that sharing and forgiving are better than fighting and hurting. They had big hearts and were kind to everyone.

Once upon a time, there was a furry bunny named Benny. He lived on a hill with his friends, the squirrels and the birds. One day, Benny wanted to decorate his home with pretty flowers, but he did not know how to do it.

Benny asked his friends for help, but they were too busy playing. Feeling sad, Benny decided to do it alone. He went to the forest and picked up some flowers. However, he accidentally stepped on a nest of baby birds and they started chirping loudly.

Benny felt bad and realized that he should have asked for help. He went back to his friends and apologized for not asking nicely. They forgave him and helped him decorate his home with beautiful flowers. Benny learned that it is always better to work together and ask for help when needed.

Lily and Tom were playing in the garden. They liked to dig and make mud pies. They did not see Mom enter the kitchen. Mom was making a cake. She wore a nice apron with flowers on it.

"Let's go and see what Mom is doing," Lily said to Tom. "Maybe she has a treat for us."

They ran to the kitchen door. They did not wipe their feet. They did not take off their shoes. They entered the kitchen with mud on their feet and hands.

"Oh no!" Mom said. "Look at the mess you made! You are very foolish. You have to go back outside and clean up. And you have to say sorry to me and to my apron."

Lily and Tom felt bad. They did not mean to make Mom angry. They said sorry to Mom and to her apron. They went back outside and washed their feet and hands. They hoped Mom would still give them a slice of cake.

Once upon a time, there was a kind lady named Mary. She loved to help people and always had a smile on her face. One day, Mary decided to serve food to the homeless people in her city. She packed sandwiches, fruits, and water in a big basket and went to the park where many homeless people lived.

When she arrived, the homeless people were happy to see her. They thanked Mary for her compassionate heart and started eating the food she brought. Mary was happy to see them smile and eat the food she had prepared. 

After some time, Mary realized she had left her favorite sheet at the park. She went back to look for it, but it was already dark and she couldn't see well. Suddenly, she fell and hurt herself badly. Nobody was around to help her, and she couldn't get up. She cried for help, but nobody heard her. 

The next morning, some people found Mary lying on the ground. They took her to the hospital, but it was too late. Mary had passed away. The homeless people were very sad when they heard the news. They remembered her compassionate heart and how she had served them with love. They missed her very much.

Once upon a time there was a girl who wanted to watch TV. But her mom didn't allow it. This made the girl very frustrated.

She started to cry.

"Mommy," she cried, "please let me watch!"

But her mom said no, explaining she was too young to watch television.

This made the girl even more frustrated. She started to stomp her feet and cry even harder.

Finally, her mom said, "Okay, you can watch a little bit, but then you have to do something else."

The girl was so happy! She ran to the TV and began to watch. Her mom smiled at her daughter's joy.

The girl watched her show, and when it was done she thanked her mom. Her mom gave her a hug and said, "You better get ready for bed now."

The girl hugged her mom back and went to get ready for bed. She was much less frustrated now that she was allowed to watch TV.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She loved to jog in the park with her dog. One day, she saw a bird that looked very interesting. She wanted to learn more about it, so she asked her mom to send her a book about birds. 

When the book arrived, Lily was so happy! She sat down with her dog and read all about different kinds of birds. She thought it was very interesting that some birds could fly very high and some could swim in the water. 

After reading the book, Lily went for a jog in the park with her dog. She saw the same bird that she had seen before and now she knew what kind of bird it was! She felt very happy and excited to have learned something new.

name_of_work: The Butterfly and the Bee by William Lisle Bowles
content: Methought I heard a butterfly Say to a labouring bee: 'Thou hast no colours of the sky On painted wings like me.' 'Poor child of vanity! those dyes, And colours bright and rare,' With mild reproof, the bee replies, 'Are all beneath my care. 'Content I toil from morn to eve, And scorning idleness, To tribes of gaudy sloth I leave The vanity of dress.'

Once upon a time, there were two best friends - a fox and a rabbit. The rabbit loved to jump and bounce around in the sunshine. One day, he noticed an acorn bouncing in the meadow. He asked the fox, "Shall we bounce the acorn together?"

The fox was excited, so he said, "Yes! Let's bounce the acorn fair and square." The rabbit smiled, grabbed the acorn and bounded across the meadow. The fox raced after him and together, they bounced the acorn from one side of the meadow to the other. They laughed and giggled as the acorn flew higher and higher with each bounce.

After an hour of bouncing, they were exhausted. The fox declared, "That was so much fun! Let's do it again tomorrow." The rabbit agreed and they said goodbye before going off to their homes.

From that day on, the fox and the rabbit were inseparable - always bouncing acorns together in the meadow. They had lots of fun and lived happily ever after.

It is blue-butterfly day here in spring, And with these sky-flakes down in flurry on flurry There is more unmixed color on the wing Than flowers will show for days unless they hurry. But these are flowers that fly and all but sing: And now from having ridden out desire They lie closed over in the wind and cling Where wheels have freshly sliced the April mire.

name_of_work: The Windhover by Gerard Manley Hopkins
content: I caught this morning morning's minion, king- dom of daylight's dauphin, dapple-dawn-drawn Falcon, in his riding Of the rolling level underneath him steady air, and striding High there, how he rung upon the rein of a wimpling wing In his ecstasy! then off, off forth on swing, As a skate's heel sweeps smooth on a bow-bend: the hurl and gliding Rebuffed the big wind. My heart in hiding Stirred for a bird, - the achieve of, the mastery of the thing! Brute beauty and valour and act, oh, air, pride, plume, here Buckle! AND the fire that breaks from thee then, a billion Times told lovelier, more dangerous, O my chevalier! No wonder of it: sheer plod makes plough down sillion Shine, and blue-bleak embers, ah my dear, Fall, gall themselves, and gash gold-vermilion.

Once there was a thoughtful boy. He liked to drink his juice in a special style. He would take each sip in a slow and careful way. Every day, he would enjoy his juice with a big smile.

One day, his mommy noticed how he liked to drink his juice. She thought it was so cute! She decided to surprise him with a special cup. She put lots of colourful polka-dots on it and she filled it with his favourite juice.

When the boy saw the cup, he was so excited. He hugged his mommy and thanked her. Then he quickly started drinking in his special style. He looked so happy!

The mommy also looked happy. She had done something thoughtful for her son. It was a delicious surprise!

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Millie. One day Millie was playing in the garden when she suddenly saw steam coming out of the ground! Millie was not sure what it was so she asked her mum, "Mummy, what is this?" Her mum replied, "It's just steam, sweetheart. Everything is ok." Millie was excited and wanted to stay to explore a bit more but her mum said it was time for them to go home. 

As Millie and her mum were walking home, Millie felt ashamed as she realized she had forgotten to turn off the tap after she had been watering the garden. She knew that she had made a mistake and she was worried that her mum would be angry. She quickly turned to her mum and said, "Mummy, I'm sorry I forgot to turn off the tap." Her mum just smiled and said, "It's ok sweetheart. Let's stay here a bit longer and enjoy the sunshine." 

Millie felt very relieved and happily stayed outside with her mum until it was time to go home.

I've tinkered at my bits of rhymes In weary, woeful, waiting times; In doleful hours of battle-din, Ere yet they brought the wounded in; Through vigils of the fateful night, In lousy barns by candle-light; In dug-outs, sagging and aflood, On stretchers stiff and bleared with blood; By ragged grove, by ruined road, By hearths accurst where Love abode; By broken altars, blackened shrines I've tinkered at my bits of rhymes. I've solaced me with scraps of song The desolated ways along: Through sickly fields all shrapnel-sown, And meadows reaped by death alone; By blazing cross and splintered spire, By headless Virgin in the mire; By gardens gashed amid their bloom, By gutted grave, by shattered tomb; Beside the dying and the dead, Where rocket green and rocket red, In trembling pools of poising light, With flowers of flame festoon the night. Ah me! by what dark ways of wrong I've cheered my heart with scraps of song. So here's my sheaf of war-won verse, And some is bad, and some is worse. And if at times I curse a bit, You needn't read that part of it; For through it all like horror runs The red resentment of the guns. And you yourself would mutter when You took the things that once were men, And sped them through that zone of hate To where the dripping surgeons wait; And wonder too if in God's sight War ever, ever can be right. Yet may it not be, crime and war But effort misdirected are? And if there's good in war and crime, There may be in my bits of rhyme, My songs from out the slaughter mill: So take or leave them as you will.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went to the kitchen and saw a yellow banana on the table. She was so happy and grabbed it quickly. 

Her mother noticed her excitement and asked, "What are you going to do with that banana, Lily?" 

"I'm going to eat it! I'm so grateful for this yummy banana," Lily replied with a big smile. 

Her mother smiled back and said, "I'm glad you're grateful for the banana. It's important to be thankful for the little things in life." 

Lily nodded and enjoyed her delicious banana. From that day on, she always noticed and appreciated the little things in life.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her dolls and toys. One day, she went to the park with her mom. At the park, she saw a boy playing with a ball. She went to him and said, "Hi, can I play with you?"

The boy said, "Sure, let's play catch!" They played catch for a while, but then Lily saw some rocks on the ground. She picked them up and started to stack them in a pattern. The boy was curious and asked, "What are you doing?"

"I'm making a tower with these rocks. Look, it's a pattern!" Lily said proudly. But then, the tower fell down and some of the rocks hit the boy's foot. He started to cry.

Lily felt sorry and said, "I'm sorry, I didn't mean to hurt you. Let me help you feel better." She gave him a hug and they continued to play together. From that day on, they became good friends and played at the park every week.

Jim was a powerful boy. One day, he was walking in the park. He saw a nail on the ground. Jim looked around and nobody was there. He bent down and picked it up. It was shiny. 

He decided to try something fun. He squeezed the nail in one of his hands until it was no longer shiny. Then he did the same with the other hand. Jim felt strong and powerful squeezing the nail like that. 

Suddenly, a bird landed on his shoulder. "WOW!" Jim said. His breath was heavy from squeezing the nail. He sat down to rest and looked at the nail. It was no longer shiny, but he still liked it. It was a special nail. 

The bird flew away, but Jim still held the nail. He put it in his pocket to keep it safe. He stood up and went back home, feeling powerful and strong.

To fling my arms wide In some place of the sun, To whirl and to dance Till the white day is done. Then rest at cool evening Beneath a tall tree While night comes on gently, Dark like me-- That is my dream! To fling my arms wide In the face of the sun, Dance! Whirl! Whirl! Till the quick day is done. Rest at pale evening . . . A tall, slim tree . . . Night coming tenderly Black like me.

Once upon a time, there was a girl who went on a great adventure. She stepped out of her front door into the bright sunshine and headed off on her travels. Firstly, she spotted a field full of amazing sheep. They were white and fluffy and lovely to look at. The girl stepped right up to them and couldn't believe how friendly they were! She patted the sheep and they softly bleated back in response. The girl stepped away and waved goodbye, feeling very happy to have met them. 

Soon, she saw a magical hill, with a strange arrangement of stones at the top. She stepped up to the hill and saw a magnificent view of the countryside spread out before her. It was so amazing, she knew she had to share it with her friends. She stepped back down the hill and decided it was time for her to go home. 

The girl went back to her front door, full of wonderful memories. She stepped inside and called out to her family that she had had an amazing day full of new, exciting experiences - and she even made a new friend, a friendly sheep!

Once upon a time there were two friends, Sam and Jane. Sam had a pupil that was very dull, but Jane could see the beauty in her. She knew that together, they could find a way to release the pupil's light.

Every day Sam and Jane would practice, by playing games and drawing pictures. They worked hard and watched their pupil slowly brighten.

One day, the fantastic result was clear. Sam's pupil was no longer dull - it glowed as bright as the sun!

The friends had done it - they had released the pupil's amazing light! They were so proud of themselves, and everyone could see the difference.

From then on, anytime anyone seemed dull, Sam and Jane would help them release their special light. They were the best of friends!

Once upon a time, there was a young girl named Sari and she had a dream. She wanted to paint the world in lots of cool colors.

One day, Sari went to the park with her paint and brush in her hand. She was so excited and she skipped all the way to the park. 

When she got there, she saw that there were lots of other kids playing in the park. Sari started painting the park, but the other kids didn't like it. They took away her paint and threw it away.

Sari felt so sad but she knew that it was wrong to paint other people's property. She learned an important lesson - if you want to be creative, make sure to do it in the right way. 
 
So Sari went home with a bad ending feeling. She knew she had made a mistake, and she wanted to make it right. But it was too late. She learned that sometimes being creative can have bad outcomes if it is not done in the right way.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a big sister who had a sweet pig named Rosie. Lily loved Rosie very much and always wanted to play with her. name_of_work: The Tiger in the Menagerie by Emma Jones
content: No one could say how the tiger got into the menagerie. It was too flash, too blue, too much like the painting of a tiger. At night the bars of the cage and the stripes of the tiger looked into each other so long that when it was time for those eyes to rock shut the bars were the lashes of the stripes the stripes were the lashes of the bars and they walked together in their dreams so long through the long colonnade that shed its fretwork to the Indian main that when the sun rose they'd gone and the tiger was one clear orange eye that walked into the menagerie. No one could say how the tiger got out in the menagerie. It was too bright, too bare. If the menagerie could, it would say 'tiger.' If the aviary could, it would lock its door. Its heart began to beat in rows of rising birds when the tiger came inside to wait.

It seemed that out of battle I escaped Down some profound dull tunnel, long since scooped Through granites which titanic wars had groined. Yet also there encumbered sleepers groaned, Too fast in thought or death to be bestirred. Then, as I probed them, one sprang up, and stared With piteous recognition in fixed eyes, Lifting distressful hands, as if to bless. And by his smile, I knew that sullen hall,-- By his dead smile I knew we stood in Hell. With a thousand fears that vision's face was grained; Yet no blood reached there from the upper ground, And no guns thumped, or down the flues made moan. "Strange friend," I said, "here is no cause to mourn." "None," said that other, "save the undone years, The hopelessness. Whatever hope is yours, Was my life also; I went hunting wild After the wildest beauty in the world, Which lies not calm in eyes, or braided hair, But mocks the steady running of the hour, And if it grieves, grieves richlier than here. For by my glee might many men have laughed, And of my weeping something had been left, Which must die now. I mean the truth untold, The pity of war, the pity war distilled. Now men will go content with what we spoiled. Or, discontent, boil bloody, and be spilled. They will be swift with swiftness of the tigress. None will break ranks, though nations trek from progress. Courage was mine, and I had mystery; Wisdom was mine, and I had mastery: To miss the march of this retreating world Into vain citadels that are not walled. Then, when much blood had clogged their chariot-wheels, I would go up and wash them from sweet wells, Even with truths that lie too deep for taint. I would have poured my spirit without stint But not through wounds; not on the cess of war. Foreheads of men have bled where no wounds were. "I am the enemy you killed, my friend. I knew you in this dark: for so you frowned Yesterday through me as you jabbed and killed. I parried; but my hands were loath and cold. Let us sleep now. . . ."

name_of_work: The Way Through the Woods by Rudyard Kipling
content: They shut the road through the woods Seventy years ago. Weather and rain have undone it again, And now you would never know There was once a road through the woods Before they planted the trees. It is underneath the coppice and heath, And the thin anemones. Only the keeper sees That, where the ring-dove broods, And the badgers roll at ease, There was once a road through the woods. Yet, if you enter the woods Of a summer evening late, When the night-air cools on the trout-ringed pools Where the otter whistles his mate, (They fear not men in the woods, Because they see so few.) You will hear the beat of a horse's feet, And the swish of a skirt in the dew, Steadily cantering through The misty solitudes, As though they perfectly knew The old lost road through the woods. But there is no road through the woods.

name_of_work: A Far Cry from Africa by Derek Walcott
content: A wind is ruffling the tawny pelt Of Africa. Kikuyu, quick as flies, Batten upon the bloodstreams of the veldt. Corpses are scattered through a paradise. Only the worm, colonel of carrion, cries: "Waste no compassion on these separate dead!" Statistics justify and scholars seize The salients of colonial policy. What is that to the white child hacked in bed? To savages, expendable as Jews? Threshed out by beaters, the long rushes break In a white dust of ibises whose cries Have wheeled since civilization's dawn From the parched river or beast-teeming plain. The violence of beast on beast is read As natural law, but upright man Seeks his divinity by inflicting pain. Delirious as these worried beasts, his wars Dance to the tightened carcass of a drum, While he calls courage still that native dread Of the white peace contracted by the dead. Again brutish necessity wipes its hands Upon the napkin of a dirty cause, again A waste of our compassion, as with Spain, The gorilla wrestles with the superman. I who am poisoned with the blood of both, Where shall I turn, divided to the vein? I who have cursed The drunken officer of British rule, how choose Between this Africa and the English tongue I love? Betray them both, or give back what they give? How can I face such slaughter and be cool? How can I turn from Africa and live?

Ben was a tall boy who liked to eat spaghetti. He liked to make long strings with his fork and slurp them up. He liked to have cheese and sauce on his spaghetti. He liked to eat spaghetti every day.

One day, his mom said, "Ben, we have a new neighbor. Her name is Lily and she is three years old, like you. She is coming over for dinner. Do you want to play with her?"

Ben nodded. He liked to play with other kids. He hoped Lily liked spaghetti too.

Lily came over with her dad. She was a short girl who had curly hair and a pink dress. She smiled at Ben and said, "Hi, I'm Lily. Do you want to play with me?"

Ben smiled back and said, "Hi, I'm Ben. Yes, I want to play with you. What do you like to play?"

Lily said, "I like to play with dolls and tea sets. Do you have any?"

Ben shook his head. He did not have any dolls or tea sets. He had cars and trucks and blocks. He said, "I don't have any dolls or tea sets. I have cars and trucks and blocks. Do you want to play with them?"

Lily shook her head. She did not like cars and trucks and blocks. She said, "I don't like cars and trucks and blocks. They are boring. I want to play with dolls and tea sets."

Ben and Lily did not know what to do. They did not like the same things. They sat on the floor and looked at each other.

Then, Ben's mom called them for dinner. She said, "Come on, kids. It's time to eat. We have spaghetti."

Ben jumped up and ran to the table. He loved spaghetti. He said, "Yay, spaghetti!"

Lily followed him slowly. She did not like spaghetti. She said, "Ew, spaghetti."

Ben looked at Lily and said, "You don't like spaghetti? Why not? It's yummy."

Lily said, "I don't like spaghetti. It's messy and sticky and icky. I like rice and beans and salad."

Ben and Lily looked at their plates. They had different food. They did not like the same food.

Ben's mom said, "Ben, why don't you try some of Lily's rice and beans and salad? Maybe you will like them. And Lily, why don't you try some of Ben's spaghetti? Maybe you will like it."

Ben and Lily looked at each other. They did not want to try the other's food. They did not think they would like it.

But then, they remembered that they wanted to be friends. They wanted to play with each other. They wanted to have fun.

So, they decided to accept the other's food. They decided to try something new. They decided to be brave.

They took a bite of the other's food. They chewed and swallowed. They made a face.

Then, they smiled. They liked the other's food. It was not so bad. It was actually good.

They said, "Thank you for sharing your food. It's tasty."

They ate their food and talked. They found out that they had some things in common. They both liked to draw and sing and read. They both liked to laugh and joke and hug.

They finished their food and asked for more. They ate more of the other's food. They liked it more and more.

They said, "Thank you for being my friend. You're nice."

They hugged and smiled. They were happy.

They learned that they could like different things and still be friends. They learned that they could accept each other and try new things. They learned that they could have fun together.

They played with dolls and tea sets and cars and trucks and blocks. They had a lot of fun.

They said, "We like spaghetti and rice and beans and salad. We like everything."

They ate spaghetti every day.
