Ben and Lily were playing in the yard. They saw a big pile of leaves that their dad had raked. They wanted to jump in the leaves and have fun.

"Let's go, Lily!" Ben said. "The leaves are dry and soft. We can make a big mess!"

"No, Ben," Lily said. "Dad worked hard to rake the leaves. He told us to help him fold the bags and put the leaves inside. If we jump in the leaves, we will make more work for him."

"But it's boring to fold bags," Ben said. "It's fun to jump in leaves. Come on, Lily, don't be a baby."

Ben ran to the pile and jumped in. He laughed and threw leaves in the air. Lily watched him and felt sad. She knew dad would be angry when he saw the mess.

She went to the garage and got a rake. She started to rake the leaves back into the pile. She worked hard and did not stop.

Soon, dad came back from the store. He saw Ben in the leaves and Lily with the rake. He was not happy.

"Ben, what are you doing?" he asked. "You made a big mess of the leaves. You did not listen to me or help me. You were selfish and lazy."

He saw Lily and smiled. "Lily, thank you for raking the leaves. You listened to me and helped me. You were kind and helpful."

He gave Lily a hug and a cookie. He told Ben to get out of the leaves and fold the bags. Ben felt sorry and ashamed. He wished he had listened to Lily and dad.

The moral of the story is: It is better to be helpful and kind than selfish and lazy.

One day, a little girl named Sue found an interesting wagon in her yard. She was very happy and wanted to play with it. Sue decided to put her toys in the wagon and skip around the yard.

As she was skipping, Sue saw her friend Tom. Tom saw the interesting wagon and said, "Wow! That's a fun wagon! Can I play too?" Sue smiled and said, "Yes, let's play together!"

Tom and Sue took turns pulling the interesting wagon and skipping around the yard. They had so much fun playing with the wagon all day. In the end, they were tired but happy. They knew they would have more fun days with the interesting wagon.

Tom and Sue live on a big farm with their dad and mom. They like to help with the animals and the plants. One day, dad tells them they will change the wheat into bread. Tom and Sue are jolly. They want to see how wheat becomes bread.

They go with dad to the field where the wheat grows. The wheat is tall and yellow. Dad cuts some wheat with a big knife. He puts the wheat in a big basket. He tells Tom and Sue to carry the basket to the barn. They are strong and careful. They do not drop the basket.

In the barn, dad has a big machine. He puts the wheat in the machine. The machine makes a loud noise. It shakes and spins. It breaks the wheat into small pieces. Dad calls the pieces flour. He tells Tom and Sue to take some flour to the kitchen. They are curious and happy. They do not spill the flour.

In the kitchen, mom has a big bowl. She puts the flour in the bowl. She adds some water, some salt, some sugar, and some yeast. She mixes everything with a big spoon. She tells Tom and Sue to knead the dough. They use their hands and fingers. They have fun and make a mess. They do not mind.

Mom puts the dough in a big pan. She puts the pan in the oven. She tells Tom and Sue to wait for a while. They smell something good. They are hungry and excited. They do not get bored.

Mom takes the pan out of the oven. She shows Tom and Sue the bread. The bread is brown and soft. It is hot and steamy. She cuts some slices and gives them to Tom and Sue. They put some butter and jam on the bread. They taste the bread. It is delicious and sweet. They are proud and thankful. They do not want to stop.

Tom and Sue change the wheat into bread. They have a jolly day. They love their dad and mom. They love their farm. They love their bread.

Once there was a little girl named Lucy who wanted to play but she bumped into a mirror and it hurt. She started to cry and felt very sad.

Mummy came in and said, "What's wrong, my darling?"

Lucy showed her the broken mirror and said, "I destroyed it."

Mummy smiled and gave her a hug, "It's only a mirror, it can be fixed. There is nothing here that can't be fixed."

Lucy stopped crying and realised mummy was right. She promised herself she would never destroy anything again. 

Mummy kissed Lucy on the forehead and said, "Let's make the mirror better."

They worked together, cleaning the broken pieces and putting them back. After a few minutes, the mirror was back to normal. Lucy was very happy and hugged mummy tightly.

Mummy said, "See, when something is broken it can still be fixed. We just need to be a little more careful." 

Lucy nodded and said, "I understand." From then on, when Lucy played around the house she was always very careful. She never wanted to destroy anything ever again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to visit her grandma's house. Her grandma always had grapes for her to eat, and Lily was very enthusiastic about it. 

One day, Lily's little brother Jack came along on the visit. Jack was not happy because he wanted to play with his toys at home. He did not like grapes either. 

Lily tried to convince Jack to try the grapes, but he refused. They started to argue, and Lily got upset. 

But then, their grandma came in with a surprise. She had made grape juice for them to try. Jack was hesitant at first, but he finally agreed to try it. To their surprise, Jack loved the grape juice! They all had a great time visiting and drinking grape juice together.

name_of_work: Come, Walk With Me by Emily Bronte
content: Come, walk with me, There's only thee To bless my spirit now - We used to love on winter nights To wander through the snow; Can we not woo back old delights? The clouds rush dark and wild They fleck with shade our mountain heights The same as long ago And on the horizon rest at last In looming masses piled; While moonbeams flash and fly so fast We scarce can say they smiled - Come walk with me, come walk with me; We were not once so few But Death has stolen our company As sunshine steals the dew - He took them one by one and we Are left the only two; So closer would my feelings twine Because they have no stay but thine - 'Nay call me not - it may not be Is human love so true? Can Friendship's flower droop on for years And then revive anew? No, though the soil be wet with tears, How fair soe'er it grew The vital sap once perished Will never flow again And surer than that dwelling dread, The narrow dungeon of the dead Time parts the hearts of men -'

One day, there was a curious boy. He was playing outside with his golf ball. He took a swing and hit the ball. It traveled so far, it went into a garden. 

The boy was excited and he ran to the garden to get his golf ball. He looked around but he couldn't find it. The boy looked very high and very low but still couldn't find the golf ball. 

Then he heard a voice, â€œWhy are you here?â€ Startled, he looked around and saw a lady.

The boy said, â€œI hit the golf ball very far, but now I can't find it.â€ The lady smiled and said, â€œFollow me, I know where it is.â€

The boy was happy and followed the lady to a tree, and there was his lost golf ball! 

The lady gave the boy the golf ball and said, â€œThat was a very good strike!â€ The boy beamed and thanked the lady for finding his golf ball.

One day, the sun was shining brightly outside. Little Ben wanted to go outside and play. He asked his mom if he could play.

"Yes, sweetheart. You can go outside and play. But don't forget to stay in the garden," said his mom.

Ben was very excited. He ran outside and saw a net hanging in the tree. He wanted to swing on it. But then he remembered his mom's warning to stay in the garden. He thought to himself, so he decided to ask if it was okay.

He went back to his mom and said, "Mom, can I swing on the net?"

She smiled and said, "Yes, I will allow you to swing on the net. Just make sure not to leave the garden."

So Ben went outside and used the net to swing. It was so much fun! He kept swinging until he got tired and sweaty. By this time, the net was no longer empty, as Ben had filled it up with lots of joy. He was very happy.

The squall sweeps gray-winged across the obliterated hills, And the startled lake seems to run before it; From the wood comes a clamor of leaves, Tugging at the twigs, Pouring from the branches, And suddenly the birds are still. Thunder crumples the sky, Lightning tears at it. And now the rain! The rain--thudding--implacable-- The wind, reveling in the confusion of great pines! And a silver sifting of light, A coolness; A sense of summer anger passing, Of summer gentleness creeping nearer-- Penitent, tearful, Forgiven!

George was a happy little boy. He wanted to win a prize, so he decided to go on a jog. He put on his shoes and ran far away. George was feeling strong and he ran for a long time.

Eventually, George saw a distant sign that said PRIZE. He felt excited and ran even faster. The prize was in a big room with lots of other prizes. George saw a big, blue bike and he knew he had to have it.

He picked up the bike and took it with him. He jogged all the way home and was very proud. When he arrived, his Mom was so happy for Georgeâ€™s prize. She gave him a big hug and said that he had earned it. George was very happy and never forgot the day he jogged for his prize.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to ride his bike, but he never wore his helmet. His mom always told him to wear it, but Timmy thought it was too tight and uncomfortable. 

One day, Timmy was riding his bike really fast. He loved to speed down the hill near his house. But then, he hit a bump and fell off his bike. He hurt his head really badly and had to go to the hospital. 

The doctors said that if Timmy had been wearing his helmet, he wouldn't have gotten hurt. Timmy felt really bad and wished he had listened to his mom. From that day on, Timmy always wore his helmet when he rode his bike. It was an incredible feeling to know he was safe.

Once upon a time, there was a rhinoceros who wanted to be popular. He wanted to make friends and play. So, he went off to find other animals and ask them to join him in some fun.

At first, no one wanted to be his friend. He got very sad and he realized that he was different from other animals. He had a big horn on his nose and was so much bigger than the others.

But then one day, something special happened. He found a giraffe who wanted to be his friend. She thought his horn was cool and funny. Soon, other animals started to notice the rhinoceros and his new friend. They started to like him too and wanted to be his pals.

The rhinoceros was so happy. He realized that different wasn't so bad. Suddenly he was popular and everyone wanted to be his friend. He was so excited and ran around, playing and laughing with his new pals.

The rhinoceros was very happy. He had made lots of new friends and was very popular. From then on, he played with his new friends whenever he could.

name_of_work: The Traveling Onion by Naomi Shihab Nye
content: When I think how far the onion has traveled just to enter my stew today, I could kneel and praise all small forgotten miracles, crackly paper peeling on the drainboard, pearly layers in smooth agreement, the way the knife enters onion and onion falls apart on the chopping block, a history revealed. And I would never scold the onion for causing tears. It is right that tears fall for something small and forgotten. How at meal, we sit to eat, commenting on texture of meat or herbal aroma but never on the translucence of onion, now limp, now divided, or its traditionally honorable career: For the sake of others, disappear.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. He loved to imagine big things. Tim had a box with many symbols. He liked to play with them. They were very fine symbols.

One day, Tim found a new symbol in his box. It was a small cat. He imagined that the cat symbol could become a real cat. He put the cat symbol under his pillow and went to sleep.

The next morning, Tim woke up and looked under his pillow. He found a fine, real cat! Tim was so happy that his imagine came true. They played together all day and became best friends. The cat was a gift from his mom, but Tim always thought it was his imagine that made it real.

I went out at night alone; The young blood flowing beyond the sea Seemed to have drenched my spirit's wings-- I bore my sorrow heavily. But when I lifted up my head From shadows shaken on the snow, I saw Orion in the east Burn steadily as long ago. From windows in my father's house, Dreaming my dreams on winter nights, I watched Orion as a girl Above another city's lights. Years go, dreams go, and youth goes too, The world's heart breaks beneath its wars, All things are changed, save in the east The faithful beauty of the stars.

name_of_work: My Papa's Waltz by Theodore Roethke
content: The whiskey on your breath Could make a small boy dizzy; But I hung on like death: Such waltzing was not easy. We romped until the pans Slid from the kitchen shelf; My mother's countenance Could not unfrown itself. The hand that held my wrist Was battered on one knuckle; At every step you missed My right ear scraped a buckle. You beat time on my head With a palm caked hard by dirt, Then waltzed me off to bed Still clinging to your shirt.

Maggie was three years old and she loved to play with her cards. One day, Maggie was playing a card game with her daddy. She put the cards in a pile and then held one in each hand. She was about to put the cards in the pile when she heard her daddy say "Wait, let me show you something much easier". 

Maggie looked at her daddy and asked "What can I do?". Her daddy leaned over and said "It's easy. Just put one card on top of the other card like this". He demonstrated by slowly leaning one card over the other card until they were touching. 

Maggie smiled, eager to try it herself. She picked up two cards and leaned one over the other. "I did it!" she exclaimed. 

Maggie's daddy smiled. "That was easy, wasn't it?" he said. Maggie nodded enthusiastically, and they continued to play the card game.

name_of_work: Inexorable Deities by Edgar Lee Masters
content: Deities! Inexorable revealers, Give me strength to endure The gifts of the Muses, Daughters of Memory. When the sky is blue as Minerva's eyes Let me stand unshaken; When the sea sings to the rising sun Let me be unafraid; When the meadow lark falls like a meteor Through the light of afternoon, An unloosened fountain of rapture, Keep my heart from spilling Its vital power; When at the dawn The dim souls of crocuses hear the calls Of waking birds, Give me to live but master the loveliness. Keep my eyes unharmed from splendors Unveiled by you, And my ears at peace Filled no less with the music Of Passion and Pain, growth and change. But O ye sacred and terrible powers, Reckless of my mortality, Strengthen me to behold a face, To know the spirit of a beloved one Yet to endure, yet to dare!

Once upon a time there was a little girl who loved to play with shapes. Every day she would take out lots of different shapes and send them flying all around the room. She especially loved sending the little shapes the highest and watching them slowly drift back down to the floor.

One day, the little girl took out a special shape and sent it up as high as she could. But no matter how hard she tried, she just couldn't make it reach the same height as the other little shapes.

The little girl looked up and smiled. She then shouted, "Hello? Can you help me send the shape higher?"

Suddenly, a mysterious voice replied from the sky. "Of course! I can help you send it higher!"

The little girl was so excited and thanked the voice for helping her. With a wave of its hand, the voice sent the shape higher than the little girl had ever seen before!

The little girl was so happy and exclaimed, "Thank you so much! I will always remember your kind deed!" 

The voice replied, "It's my pleasure. I'm glad I could help you send the shape higher!" 

And from that day on, the little girl always thought of the voice whenever she played with her shapes.

name_of_work: A Jet Ring Sent by John Donne
content: THOU art not so black as my heart, Nor half so brittle as her heart, thou art ; What would'st thou say ? shall both our properties by thee be spoke, --Nothing more endless, nothing sooner broke? Marriage rings are not of this stuff ; Oh, why should ought less precious, or less tough Figure our loves ? except in thy name thou have bid it say, "--I'm cheap, and nought but fashion ; fling me away." Yet stay with me since thou art come, Circle this finger's top, which didst her thumb ; Be justly proud, and gladly safe, that thou dost dwell with me ; She that, O ! broke her faith, would soon break thee.

There was once a popular dinner. It was so popular that everyone wanted to try it. But when they all sat down to eat the dinner, it started to shrink! Everyone was surprised, but they all still wanted a taste.

They looked around to find the cause and they noticed a little mouse shrinking the dinner! They all shouted in surprise and the mouse ran away quickly. 

The dinner was too small now for everyone to eat, so they all laughed and decided to have a dinner party another night. They all waved goodbye to the mouse and had a lot of fun that night. 
 
The end.

Once upon a time, there was a mommy who liked to cook. She wore an apron to keep her clothes clean. One day, she was making pancakes for breakfast when she accidentally spilled some batter on the floor. Her little girl saw what happened and wanted to help. She got a towel to support her mommy and clean up the terrible mess. Mommy was so happy and gave her a big hug. From that day on, the little girl always helped her mommy in the kitchen, wearing her own tiny apron.

Once upon a time there was a little bug. He was a very hungry bug and looking for something tasty to eat. He looked around and saw a trail that was leading to something far away. He decided to crawl along the trail and see where it went.

The trail was long and winding. The bug crawled up the hill and down the valley. He was getting very tired, but he was determined to find something tasty. After a long time of crawling, he finally made it to the end of the trail.

At the end of the trail was a big tree. There was a hole in the tree, and the bug peered inside. To his surprise, there were lots of tasty insects inside the hole. He quickly crawled inside and grabbed one. It was the best tasting thing he had ever eaten!

He quickly finished the insect and crawled outside of the tree. The bug was so full and happy that he skipped all the way back along the trail.

This is to the motherland, Where I am born. This is to the teacher, Who taught me nothing. This is to my lover, Who turned away from me. Many are there to address, Very few to notice. What have you taught me? Why the hell you came in? Why did I even open my eyes mother! Hybridity, Modernization, Temporary. Yes, You all have lost me, Lost your identity in my life.

Once there was a fierce tiger called Tippy. One day, Tippy was looking for food in the jungle. He saw Nana, a parrot, perched on a branch.

"Nana!" called Tippy. "Can you show me where I can find food?".

Nana paused and thought hard. Then, she flapped her wings and flew off. After a few minutes, Nana returned and showed Tippy to a beehive. When Tippy saw all the honey, he was so happy that he roared out of joy.

When Tippy was about to tuck in, Nana stopped him. She said, "Before you eat, I have a message for you."

Tippy listened intently. Nana said, "You are fierce and strong. You should always be kind!"

Tippy nodded his head in approval, then happily tucked in to the feast of honey!

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Ellie. She was very organized and liked to stay in her room and play. One day, while she was playing, she had a wonder. She wondered what it would be like to stay in a different place.

So, she asked her mom and dad if she could stay in a different place. They said yes, so Ellie got all of her things organized and they drove to a campground. She was so excited!

At the campground, Ellie got to play outside. She made friends and had so much fun. Every night she looked up at the sky and saw the stars. She was so happy to stay at the campground.

The week went by so quickly, and soon Ellie had to go home. She said goodbye to her new friends and was sad to leave. But she remembered the wonderful time she had staying at the campground and smiled.

Max was a cute little mouse. He loved the outdoors. Today, he decided to gather fur.
Max found a patch of fur in the woods. He was so excited! He began to gather it under his tiny arms.

Suddenly, he heard a voice. It was a kind old fox! "That looks difficult - here, let me help you," said the fox.

Max was so grateful for the help. Together, they gathered the fur into a big pile. Max smiled with delight.

"Thanks for your help," said Max.

The fox smiled. "You're welcome, little one," the fox said.

Since I haven't danced among my fellow initiates, following a looped processions from woods at the edge of a village, Tata's people would think me unfinished - a child who never sloughed off the childish estate to cross the river boys of our tribe must cross in order to die and come back grown. I was raised in a strange land, by small increments: when I bathed my mother the days she was too weak, when auntie broke the news and I chose a yellow suit and white shoes to dress my mother's body, at the grave-side when the man I almost grew to call dad, though we both needed a hug, shook my hand. If my alternate self, who never left, could see me what would he make of these literary pretensions, this need to speak with a tongue that isn't mine? Would he be strange to me as I to him, frowning as he greets me in the language of my father and my father's father and my father's father's father?

name_of_work: Love on the Farm by D.H. Lawrence
content: What large, dark hands are those at the window Lifted, grasping the golden light Which weaves its way through the creeper leaves To my heart's delight? Ah, only the leaves! But in the west, In the west I see a redness come Over the evening's burning breast-- --'Tis the wound of love goes home! The woodbine creeps abroad Calling low to her lover: The sun-lit flirt who all the day Has poised above her lips in play And stolen kisses, shallow and gay Of pollen, now has gone away --She woos the moth with her sweet, low word, And when above her his broad wings hover Then her bright breast she will uncover And yield her honey-drop to her lover. Into the yellow, evening glow Saunters a man from the farm below, Leans, and looks in at the low-built shed Where hangs the swallow's marriage bed. The bird lies warm against the wall. She glances quick her startled eyes Towards him, then she turns away Her small head, making warm display Of red upon the throat. His terrors sway Her out of the nest's warm, busy ball, Whose plaintive cry is heard as she flies In one blue stoop from out the sties Into the evening's empty hall. Oh, water-hen, beside the rushes Hide your quaint, unfading blushes, Still your quick tail, and lie as dead, Till the distance folds over his ominous tread. The rabbit presses back her ears, Turns back her liquid, anguished eyes And crouches low: then with wild spring Spurts from the terror of _his_ oncoming To be choked back, the wire ring Her frantic effort throttling: Piteous brown ball of quivering fears! Ah soon in his large, hard hands she dies, And swings all loose to the swing of his walk. Yet calm and kindly are his eyes And ready to open in brown surprise Should I not answer to his talk Or should he my tears surmise. I hear his hand on the latch, and rise from my chair Watching the door open: he flashes bare His strong teeth in a smile, and flashes his eyes In a smile like triumph upon me; then careless-wise He flings the rabbit soft on the table board And comes towards me: ah, the uplifted sword Of his hand against my bosom, and oh, the broad Blade of his hand that raise my face to applaud His coming: he raises up my face to him And caresses my mouth with his fingers, which still smell grim Of the rabbit's fur! God, I am caught in a snare! I know not what fine wire is round my throat, I only know I let him finger there My pulse of life, letting him nose like a stoat Who sniffs with joy before he drinks the blood: And down his mouth comes to my mouth, and down His dark bright eyes descend like a fiery hood Upon my mind: his mouth meets mine, and a flood Of sweet fire sweeps across me, so I drown Within him, die, and find death good.

name_of_work: If I Could Tell You by W.H. Auden
content: Time will say nothing but I told you so, Time only knows the price we have to pay; If I could tell you I would let you know. If we should weep when clowns put on their show, If we should stumble when musicians play, Time will say nothing but I told you so. There are no fortunes to be told, although, Because I love you more than I can say, If I could tell you I would let you know. The winds must come from somewhere when they blow, There must be reasons why the leaves decay; Time will say nothing but I told you so. Perhaps the roses really want to grow, The vision seriously intends to stay; If I could tell you I would let you know. Suppose all the lions get up and go, And all the brooks and soldiers run away; Will Time say nothing but I told you so? If I could tell you I would let you know.

name_of_work: Sonnet 20 (Beloved, my Beloved, when I think) by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: Beloved, my Beloved, when I think That thou wast in the world a year ago, What time I sate alone here in the snow And saw no footprint, heard the silence sink No moment at thy voice ... but, link by link, Went counting all my chains, as if that so They never could fall off at any blow Struck by thy possible hand ... why, thus I drink Of life's great cup of wonder! Wonderful, Never to feel thee thrill the day or night With personal act or speech,--nor ever cull Some prescience of thee with the blossoms white Thou sawest growing! Atheists are as dull, Who cannot guess God's presence out of sight.

Once upon a time there was a smart little girl who loved to help her mom. One day her mom asked her to fetch a pan from the kitchen. She ran to the kitchen and picked up the pan. She was so happy that she was able to help so quickly.

But when she brought the pan back, she noticed that it was rot. Her mom saw it too and said that she now needed to go outside and find a new pan. The little girl was disappointed, but she was still so smart and set off to find a new pan.

She looked around the garden but couldn't find one. After a few minutes, she remembered the neighbor's garden! She ran to the neighbor's garden and saw a new, shiny pan. She was so excited and quickly grabbed the pan and brought it back to her mom.

When her mom saw the pan she was so proud of her daughter and said, "You are so smart to think of looking in the neighbor's garden!"

The little girl was happy to have helped her mom. With the new pan, they were able to make a delicious dinner for the family to share.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. She had a big, red ball that she loved to play with. One day, Sue was playing with her ball near an expensive store. She did not want to break anything, but she was having fun.

Suddenly, the ball went into the store through the exit. Sue ran after it, but she bumped into a tall shelf. Many things fell and broke. Sue felt regret because she knew she should not have played near the store.

Sue's mom came and saw the mess. She was not happy, but she understood it was an accident. They helped clean up and said sorry to the store owner. From that day on, Sue never played near the expensive store again.

Once upon a time, there was a pretty girl named Lily. One day, Lily wanted to watch a movie but she didn't have one. She went to her friend Tommy's house and asked him if she could borrow a movie. Tommy said yes and lent her a movie.

However, when Lily got home, she realized that the movie was broken. She went back to Tommy's house and told him what happened. Tommy got upset and said that he didn't want to lend her anything anymore.

Lily felt sad and apologized to Tommy. She promised to be more careful next time. Tommy forgave her and they became friends again. From that day on, Lily made sure to take good care of things that she borrowed from others.

Once upon a time there was a sad little girl. She was so sad that she wouldn't eat. No matter what her mom tried to make, the girl just shook her head and said no. 

One day, her mom thought of a plan. She went to the library and found a tiny book. It was a story about a brave little girl who's sad face changed when she found a special surprise. 

The little girl opened the book and started reading. Before she even finished the first page, she felt the corners of her mouth turn up. She couldn't help but smile! 

When the girl was done reading, she had a new found happiness. She said to her mom, "I'm ready to eat now". 

From that day on, the girl and her mom read stories every day. And soon enough, the girl was no longer sad, because stories filled her heart with joy.

Ted and his mom were in need of a raft. They had to cross a big river to get to the other side. Ted was very worried because the river seemed so wide. But his mom told him not to worry and have a little bit of faith.

They went to the store to find a raft. It was difficult to pick just one. Finally Ted found a humble-looking one that he liked. His mom paid for it and they took it home.

When they got home, Ted and his mom put the raft in the river. Ted held his mom's hand tightly as the raft wobbled and drifted along. The water was spinning and splashing all around them. Luckily, the humble raft stayed steady and soon they reached the other side of the river. Ted was so relieved. Now they had done what they needed. 

At the end of the day Ted was happy that he had helped get them across the river. He felt proud of himself and had learned an important lesson - having faith can help you accomplish anything.

When they arrived, they saw the smooth sand and blue, sparkling water. â€œCan I swim?â€ Jane asked Mark.

â€œYes, of course you can,â€ Mark replied. He watched as Jane ran into the water. She was having so much fun! 

When Jane was done swimming, she came back onto the beach with a big smile. She had a smooth stone in her hand that sheâ€™d found underwater.

name_of_work: All Legendary Obstacles by John Montague
content: All legendary obstacles lay between Us, the long imaginary plain, The monstrous ruck of mountains And, swinging across the night, Flooding the Sacramento, San Joaquin, The hissing drift of winter rain. All day I waited, shifting Nervously from station to bar As I saw another train sail By, the San Francisco Chief or Golden Gate, water dripping From great flanged wheels. At midnight you came, pale Above the negro porter's lamp. I was too blind with rain And doubt to speak, but Reached from the platform Until our chilled hands met. You had been traveling for days With an old lady, who marked A neat circle on the glass With her glove, to watch us Move into the wet darkness Kissing, still unable to speak.

Once upon a time, there was a big, brown cow named Bessie. Bessie lived on a farm with lots of other animals like chickens and pigs. One day, Bessie was feeling crazy and decided to run around the farm. She ran so fast that she accidentally knocked over a bucket of milk!

Later that day, the farmer came to feed the animals. He brought some meat for the pigs to eat. But as he was walking by Bessie's pen, he accidentally struck his foot on a rock and fell down. Bessie saw this and felt bad, so she mooed loudly to get the farmer's attention. The farmer looked up and saw that Bessie was trying to help him. He smiled and patted her head, and they both felt happy. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a big lion who lived in the jungle. He loved to roar and scare his animal friends. One day, he went for a walk in the bush and met a little rabbit. The rabbit was scared of the lion's roar and asked him why he was so loud. The lion said, "I roar because it's fun and it makes me feel strong."

The rabbit asked the lion if he could play with him, but the lion said he was too busy. The rabbit was sad, but then he saw a bunch of carrots in the bush. He picked them and offered them to the lion. The lion was happy and thanked the rabbit. He realized that it's important to make time for friends and that sometimes, the best things are available in the simplest places. From that day on, the lion and the rabbit played together in the bush and the lion roared only when they were playing a game.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Lucy. She was only three-years-old and she was very obedient. One day, Lucy went out to play in the snow. She loved it when it snowed and would go out as often as she could.

The snow was cold, so Lucy started to shiver. She felt so cold that she couldn't stand it any longer, so she went to find some help. Eventually, she found a candy shop. She went in and the shop owner gave her a mint. It was sweet and warm, and she felt so much better afterwards.

Lucy thanked the shopkeeper and went back outside. She was all warm and cozy, and so she enjoyed playing in the snow even more. She was very brave and was so happy, she even shook the snow off a tree so she could see all the glittery flakes as they fell down.

It was a beautiful day, and Lucy was so glad that she had listened to her parents and been obedient. It was the perfect day to play in the snow!

Once, there was a funny man who loved to joke. He lived in a small house with his dog, Spot. The man liked to drink something called coffee. It was a drink that made him feel awake and happy.

One day, the man found a shop that sold very cheap coffee. He was very happy and bought a lot of it. He took the coffee home and made a big cup to drink. Spot watched him and wagged his tail.

The man took a sip of the cheap coffee and made a funny face. It did not taste good, but he laughed and joked about it. Spot barked and they both laughed together. Even though the coffee was not good, the man and Spot had fun joking and laughing.

Once there was a wise man who wanted to introduce a circle to the world. He had been thinking about it for a long time and he was very excited to do something new and special.

The man called all of his friends together and told them his idea. He explained that the circle could be used to play together, and that it could help to keep them safe. Everyone was interested in what the man had to say.

The man began to draw a circle in the sand. Everyone watched as he worked. Once it was finished, the man stood back and said, â€œNow, we can have fun together.â€

Everyone was so excited that they began to jump around and sing. They ran around the circle, playing a game. They laughed and hugged each other.

The man was so happy that he had introduced the circle to his friends. He knew that it would help them to stay safe and have fun together. Everyone thanked the man for his wise idea.

Once there was a little girl named Jane. She loved to draw with her pencil. One day, she was happily drawing a picture and having lots of fun. 

All of a sudden she noticed that her pencil was gone. She looked everywhere but could not find it. She started to cry and search frantically.

Jane's mum heard her crying and came to the rescue. She handed Jane a new pencil and said, "Don't worry, darling. This one is good for drawing and I'm sure you'll find your old pencil soon."

Jane stopped crying. She smiled and hugged her mum. With her new pencil in hand, she got back to drawing her picture and was happy again.

name_of_work: A Dream of Death by William Butler Yeats
content: I DREAMED that one had died in a strange place Near no accustomed hand, And they had nailed the boards above her face, The peasants of that land, Wondering to lay her in that solitude, And raised above her mound A cross they had made out of two bits of wood, And planted cypress round; And left her to the indifferent stars above Until I carved these words: She was more beautiful than thy first love, But now lies under boards.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a smart cat named Max. One day, Lily was playing with her toys when she smelled something funny. She looked around and saw that her toy house was on fire! She quickly called out to Max, "Max, help! The house is burning!" Max ran to Lily and meowed loudly. 

Lily's mom came running and saw the fire. She called the firemen and they came with a big truck. They put out the fire with water. After the fire was out, the firemen took an x-ray of the house to make sure there were no more fires hiding inside. 

Lily was sad that her toy house burned down, but she was happy that Max was there to help her. She hugged Max and said, "Thank you for being so smart, Max. You helped me when the house was burning." Max purred and licked Lily's hand. From that day on, Lily knew that Max was not just a cute cat, but a helpful friend too.

Tom and Anna are brother and sister. They live with Mom and Dad in a small house. They like to play with their toys, read books, and watch cartoons. They are happy and normal.

One day, Mom and Dad tell them that they have to go to the hospital. They say that Mom is sick and needs a big operation. They say that they love them very much and will be back soon. They give them a big hug and a kiss.

Tom and Anna are scared and sad. They don't want Mom and Dad to go. They don't want Mom to be sick. They don't understand what a big operation is. They cry and hold each other.

Grandma comes to stay with them. She says that she will take care of them and that everything will be okay. She says that they can pray for Mom and Dad and that God will hear them. She says that praying is talking to God and asking him for help and thank him for his love.

Tom and Anna try to pray. They close their eyes and fold their hands. They say, "Dear God, please help Mom and Dad. Please make Mom better and bring them back soon. Please don't let them be hurt or scared. Please let them know that we love them and miss them. Thank you for Grandma and for our toys and books and cartoons. Thank you for your love. Amen."

They feel a little better after praying. They still miss Mom and Dad, but they trust that God will take care of them. They hug Grandma and each other. They hope that Mom and Dad will come back soon and that everything will be normal again.

Lily and Ben were best friends. They liked to play in the forest near their home. One day, they found a big log that looked like a horse. Lily and Ben decided to ride the log-horse together.

"Can I be the head?" Lily asked.

"OK, I will be the tail," Ben said.

They climbed on the log and pretended to gallop through the trees. They made sounds like a horse and laughed. They felt the wind in their hair and the sun on their skin. The forest was beautiful.

Suddenly, they saw a real horse. It was brown and shiny, with a long mane and tail. It was eating grass in a clearing. Lily and Ben stopped their log-horse and got off.

"Wow, look at that horse!" Lily said.

"It is so pretty!" Ben said.

They walked slowly towards the horse, hoping to pet it. The horse saw them and lifted its head. It snorted and neighed, then trotted away.

"Bye, horse!" Lily and Ben said.

They waved at the horse, then went back to their log-horse. They rode it again, happy and free. They loved their log-horse and their forest. They were best friends.

As you set out for Ithaka hope your road is a long one, full of adventure, full of discovery. Laistrygonians, Cyclops, angry Poseidon--don't be afraid of them: you'll never find things like that on your way as long as you keep your thoughts raised high, as long as a rare excitement stirs your spirit and your body. Laistrygonians, Cyclops, wild Poseidon--you won't encounter them unless you bring them along inside your soul, unless your soul sets them up in front of you. Hope your road is a long one. May there be many summer mornings when, with what pleasure, what joy, you enter harbors you're seeing for the first time; may you stop at Phoenician trading stations to buy fine things, mother of pearl and coral, amber and ebony, sensual perfume of every kind-- as many sensual perfumes as you can; and may you visit many Egyptian cities to learn and go on learning from their scholars. Keep Ithaka always in your mind. Arriving there is what you're destined for. But don't hurry the journey at all. Better if it lasts for years, so you're old by the time you reach the island, wealthy with all you've gained on the way, not expecting Ithaka to make you rich. Ithaka gave you the marvelous journey. Without her you wouldn't have set out. She has nothing left to give you now. And if you find her poor, Ithaka won't have fooled you. Wise as you will have become, so full of experience, you'll have understood by then what these Ithakas mean.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who was feeling very miserable. She looked out the window, and saw a little stream with a rod floating in it. She had a good idea. 

The little girl opened the window and reached for the rod, but it was too far away. She was almost in tears, when suddenly the rod started to drift closer! She was so happy, she reached out and grabbed it!

The little girl was thrilled - she had the rod! She spent the day running around, swinging the rod and pretending it was a magic wand. She cast magical spells and felt like the happiest girl in the world.

When nightfall arrived, she put the rod back into the stream. She wished it a good journey and went back to bed dreaming of all the magical adventures she could have with her rod.

Once there was a boy called Tom. He loved to paint pictures and he was very fair. One day, Tom found a microscope in his back garden which he had never seen before. He was very excited and decided to paint a picture of it.

Tom quickly got some paper and paints and started to work. As he painted, a big, old lady walked up to him. She said in a cross voice, "What are you doing? That is my microscope!"

Tom didn't know what to say. He was too scared to ask the lady why it was hers and he felt sad that he couldn't finish his painting. He put the paints away and politely said sorry to the lady. 

She just glared and moved closer to him. Tom was too scared to move and he didnâ€™t know what to do. Suddenly, the lady grabbed the microscope and returned home. Tom was very disappointed, he had wanted to finish his painting. 

The lady never came back and Tomâ€™s painting of the microscope was never finished.

Once upon a time, there was an ugly little girl who loved pasta. She would eat it every day and never say no to it. One day, the girl's mom asked her how she liked it. 

The girl said, "I really like the pasta, Mommy."

Her mom smiled and said, "I'm glad you understand how to enjoy it! But remember to always eat it with some veggies and not just the pasta, okay?"

The girl said, "Yes, Mommy. I understand."

The girl kept eating her pasta and every day she would remind herself to eat some vegetables with it. She was happy that she could understand what her mom said and always ate her pasta the right way.

name_of_work: Simple Song Blues Villanelle by Tim Seibles

Today I'll take one off, sip the dew, and sift the breeze I wish the time could last. It won't last All these TV talking Teds can give a man a rash I squint my ears and listen like I must be going deef Time has passed me--I think older--night comes slowly fast You see the worry on your face, then think about your stash The hours cast and reel you in: the worm between your teeth All you have to hold onto is a simple song at last Drowse along the riverside and dream into the grass Let the baby blue jays jitterbug from branch to leaf They think all this will last. It might last Whip those sweet potatoes, baby, quick into a mash Only thing can fill me up is just this late belief-- Time is passing, I grow older, things are happening fast All you get to hold onto is a simple song at last

Once upon a time, there was a baby named Lily. She was very popular because she was always smiling and laughing. One day, Lily's mom asked her to tie her shoes so they could go for a walk. Lily tried her best, but she couldn't do it.

Suddenly, a big dog came running towards them. Lily's mom picked her up and tried to run away, but she tripped on her untied shoelaces and fell. The dog came closer and closer until it was too late.

Lily's mom was very sad and cried a lot. She wished she had tied her shoelaces before they left the house. From that day on, she always double-checked her shoelaces before going outside with Lily.

One day, a little girl named Peter was playing in the park with her friends. She was so happy! Suddenly, there was a loud buzzing in the sky. It was a hurricane! The wind was blowing harder and harder and the sky was getting darker. Peter and her friends were scared. 

But then, Peter's mommy came to the park. She brought an umbrella to protect Peter and her friends from the rain. She also brought jackets for them to keep warm. The kids were so happy to see her! 

Then, Peter's mommy suggested that they all go home. She held Peter's hand and they ran home as fast as they could. Once they got home, they felt safe. The hurricane was over!

Once upon a time, there was a parent who had three children. The parent knew that in order to get things done, the children had to be organized. One day, the parent tried to explain this to the children.

"I need you all to be organized," said the parent in an orderly tone.

The oldest child nodded and said, "We can do that!"

The other two children were more hesitant. One of them asked, "What does that mean?"

The parent took a deep breath and smiled. "It means I need you to clean up after yourselves and put your things away. Can you do that?"

The children nodded and the parent said, "Great! Let's try it out. Who can remove their shoes the fastest?" 

The children all cheered and quickly removed their shoes. The parent sighed in relief as the children were getting organized.

The moral of the story is that with a little guidance, young children can learn how to be organized.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy was playing in the park when he saw a little bird with a broken wing. The bird was very sad and couldn't fly.

Timmy was a very patient boy. He sat down next to the bird and waited for it to feel better. He knew the bird was tough and would get better soon.

After a while, the bird started to feel better. It looked at Timmy and said, "Please, can you help me fly again?" Timmy smiled and gently picked up the bird. He held it in his hands and ran around the park until the bird was strong enough to fly again.

From then on, Timmy and the bird were the best of friends. The bird would fly around the park and Timmy would watch, happy to have helped his new friend.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue had a big, round head. One day, Sue felt troubled. She did not know what to do.

Sue went to her mom and said, "Mom, I am troubled. Can you help me?" Her mom said, "Let's sit down and talk." So, they sat down and talked about what was troubling Sue. Sue told her mom that she was sad because her head was big and round.

Her mom hugged her and said, "Sue, your big, round head is what makes you special. It is a part of who you are. Let's be happy and love our big, round heads." Sue smiled and felt better. From that day on, Sue was not troubled about her big, round head. She was happy and loved herself just the way she was.

One day, a little boy named Tim wanted to go on a fun adventure. He had a smooth, round rock that he liked to play with. Tim decided to go to the park to find more smooth rocks like his.

When Tim got to the park, he saw a big group of kids playing together. They were all making a network of friends. Tim wanted to join them, but he was a little shy.

Tim took a deep breath and walked up to the kids. He showed them his smooth rock and asked if they wanted to help him find more. The kids smiled and said yes. They all went to look for smooth rocks together. Tim was happy to be part of the network of friends.

Sara was very happy. Today was her birthday and she was having a party. She invited her friends from school and they came with gifts and balloons. Sara's mom made a big cake with candles and sprinkles. Sara's dad played music and games.

"Let's play pin the tail on the donkey!" Sara's dad said. He gave each child a paper tail with tape and a blindfold. He spun them around and pointed them to the wall where a picture of a donkey was. The children tried to stick the tail on the right spot, but they missed and made funny shapes. Sara and her friends laughed and laughed. They thought it was very fun.

Then it was time to open the gifts. Sara sat on the floor and her friends gave her their presents. She opened them one by one and said thank you. She got a doll, a book, a puzzle, a hat, and a teddy bear. She liked them all, but her favorite was the teddy bear. It was brown and soft and had a red bow. Sara hugged it and said, "You are so cute! I love you, teddy!"

Sara's mom brought the cake and everyone sang happy birthday. Sara blew out the candles and made a wish. She wished for more fun and laughter with her friends and family. She cut the cake and shared it with everyone. It was yummy and sweet. Sara and her friends ate and talked and smiled. They had a great time at the party. Sara was very happy.

name_of_work: The Broken Heart by William Barnesa
content: News o' grief had overteaken Dark-eyed Fanny, now vorseaken; There she zot, wi' breast a-heaven, While vrom zide to zide, wi' grieven, Vell her head, wi' tears a-creepen Down her cheaks, in bitter weepen. There wer still the ribbon-bow She tied avore her hour ov woe, An' there wer still the hans that tied it Hangen white, Or wringen tight, In ceare that drowned all ceare bezide it. When a man, wi' heartless slighten, Mid become a maiden's blighten, He mid cearelessly vorseake her, But must answer to her Meaker; He mid slight, wi' selfish blindness, All her deeds o' loven-kindness, God wull waigh 'em wi' the slighten That mid be her love's requiten; He do look on each deceiver, He do know What weight o' woe Do break the heart ov ev'ry griever.

ME imperturbe, standing at ease in Nature, Master of all, or mistress of all--aplomb in the midst of irrational things, Imbued as they--passive, receptive, silent as they, Finding my occupation, poverty, notoriety, foibles, crimes, less important than I thought; Me private, or public, or menial, or solitary--all these subordinate, (I am eternally equal with the best--I am not subordinate;) Me toward the Mexican Sea, or in the Mannahatta, or the Tennessee, or far north, or inland, A river-man, or a man of the woods, or of any farm- life of These States, or of the coast, or the lakes, or Kanada, Me, wherever my life is lived, O to be self-balanced for contingencies! O to confront night, storms, hunger, ridicule, acci- dents, rebuffs, as the trees and animals do.

name_of_work: Still Falls the Rain by Edith Sitwell
content: Still falls the Rain-- Dark as the world of man, black as our loss-- Blind as the nineteen hundred and forty nails Upon the Cross. Still falls the Rain With a sound like the pulse of the heart that is changed to the hammer-beat In the Potter's Field, and the sound of the impious feet On the Tomb: Still falls the Rain In the Field of Blood where the small hopes breed and the human brain Nurtures its greed, that worm with the brow of Cain. Still falls the Rain At the feet of the Starved Man hung upon the Cross. Christ that each day, each night, nails there, have mercy on us-- On Dives and on Lazarus: Under the Rain the sore and the gold are as one. Still falls the Rain-- Still falls the Blood from the Starved Man's wounded Side: He bears in His Heart all wounds,--those of the light that died, The last faint spark In the self-murdered heart, the wounds of the sad uncomprehending dark, The wounds of the baited bear-- The blind and weeping bear whom the keepers beat On his helpless flesh... the tears of the hunted hare. Still falls the Rain-- Then-- O Ile leape up to my God: who pulles me doune-- See, see where Christ's blood streames in the firmament: It flows from the Brow we nailed upon the tree Deep to the dying, to the thirsting heart That holds the fires of the world,--dark-smirched with pain As Caesar's laurel crown. Then sounds the voice of One who like the heart of man Was once a child who among beasts has lain-- "Still do I love, still shed my innocent light, my Blood, for thee."

Once upon a time, a little girl called Sally wanted to mail a stick to her friend. She wanted to show her friend how big the stick was so Sally decided that sending it by post will work best.

Sally went to the post office with the stick in her hand. She saw a friendly-looking postman and said, "Hello! I want to mail this stick!"

The postman chuckled and said, "Oh, I'm sorry, I'm afraid that this stick is too big to mail. It won't fit into the postbox, Sally.'

Sally felt sad and uncomfortable but she was determined to send the stick. "Is there any way for me to send it?" She asked.

The postman said, "Yes, there is! You can use a special box that's just the right size for your stick." 

Sally was so excited and she quickly paid for the box. Soon enough, Sally mailed the stick to her friend. They were both so happy when they received the stick!

One day, there was a boy. He was very restless. He wanted to do something fun. He was looking around for something to do. He then saw a pail filled with water. He thought it could be fun to lift it. So, he grabbed the handle of the pail and started to lift it up. It was heavy, but he was strong and managed to lift it. After lifting the pail, the boy was very happy. He moved around with the pail, enjoying his new game. He was having so much fun! After a few minutes, he was getting tired. So, he decided to put the pail down. Even though it was hard work, it was a fun game. The boy was no longer restless and was very pleased with himself.
