Lily liked to repeat what her big sister said. She thought it was funny to copy her words and make fun of her. But her big sister did not like it. She felt angry and sad when Lily repeated her.

One day, Lily's big sister was doing her homework. She had to write a story for school. She worked hard and thought of many good words. She was proud of her story. She read it out loud to check it.

Lily was hiding behind the door. She heard her big sister's story. She decided to repeat it. She waited for her big sister to finish. Then she jumped out and said the same words in a silly voice. She laughed and laughed.

Her big sister was shocked and hurt. She saw that Lily had a paper in her hand. It was her story. Lily had taken it when she was not looking. She had torn it into pieces. She had wasted her work.

Her big sister cried and cried. She felt miserable. She had no story to show her teacher. She had to start again. She did not want to talk to Lily. She did not want to play with her.

Lily felt sorry. She saw that she had done a bad thing. She had hurt her big sister's feelings. She had ruined her story. She had been mean and rude. She wished she had not repeated her.

She went to her big sister and said sorry. She hugged her and helped her pick up the pieces. She asked her to tell her the story again. She listened and said nice things. She did not repeat her.

Her big sister smiled and forgave her. She thanked her for helping her. She told her the story again. She asked her to help her write it. They worked together and made a new story. They were happy and friendly.

The moral of the story is: Do not repeat what others say to make fun of them. It is not funny. It is hurtful. It can waste their work. It can make them miserable. It can make you lose their love. Be kind and respectful. Listen and learn. Help and share. It can make them happy. It can make you happy.

Sam and Mia were playing in the garden. They liked to run and jump and laugh. They saw a big tree with many fruits. They were peaches. Sam and Mia loved peaches. They were sweet and juicy.

"Look, Mia, a peach!" Sam said. He pointed to a peach that was low on the tree. He ran to the tree and tried to reach the peach. But he was too short. He jumped and stretched his arms, but he could not touch the peach.

"Let me help you, Sam," Mia said. She was taller than Sam. She ran to the tree and lifted Sam up. Sam grabbed the peach and pulled it off the tree. He was happy. He smiled and said, "Thank you, Mia. You are a good friend."

Sam and Mia sat on the grass and shared the peach. They bit into the peach and felt the juice run down their chins. They licked their lips and said, "Mmm, this is a good peach."

But then they heard a loud noise. It was thunder. They looked at the sky and saw dark clouds. They felt raindrops on their heads. They were wet. They did not like to be wet.

"Let's go inside, Sam," Mia said. She took Sam's hand and they ran to the house. They lay their peach on the porch and went inside. They dried themselves with towels and put on dry clothes. They were warm and cozy.

They looked out the window and saw the rain. They saw their peach on the porch. It was wet too. They felt sorry for the peach.

"Maybe we can eat the peach later, Mia," Sam said.

"Maybe, Sam," Mia said. "But I think we should share it with Mom and Dad. They would like a peach too."

Sam and Mia nodded. They hugged each other and said, "We are good friends."

Sara and Tom were playing in the garden. They had a big iron pot and some cups and spoons. They pretended to make tea and cake for their dolls and teddies.

"Would you like some tea, Mr. Bear?" Sara asked, pouring some water from the pot into a cup.

"Yes, please, Sara. You are very kind," Tom said, making his teddy talk.

They drank their tea and ate their cake. They had a lot of fun.

But then, Sara noticed that the pot was empty. There was no more water to make tea.

"Oh no, Tom. We have no more tea. What can we do?" Sara said, looking sad.

Tom thought for a moment. He had an idea.

"Don't worry, Sara. I know where we can get more water. Come with me," Tom said, taking Sara's hand.

They ran to the house. Tom knew that there was a tap in the kitchen. He had seen his mom use it to fill the kettle.

"Look, Sara. There is water here. We can use it to make more tea," Tom said, pointing to the tap.

He climbed on a chair and reached for the tap. He turned it on and water came out.

"Wow, Tom. You are very smart," Sara said, admiring Tom.

Tom smiled. He took the iron pot and held it under the tap. He filled it with water.

"Let's go back to the garden and make more tea," Tom said, lifting the pot.

But the pot was very heavy. Tom was not strong enough to carry it. He lost his balance and fell off the chair. The pot fell too and water spilled everywhere.

"Tom, are you okay?" Sara asked, worried.

Tom was not hurt, but he was wet and sad. He had made a big mess.

"I'm sorry, Sara. I wanted to make more tea, but I dropped the pot. Now we have no water and no pot," Tom said, crying.

Sara hugged Tom. She was not angry. She was kind.

"It's okay, Tom. It was an accident. You tried to help. We can still play with our dolls and teddies. We don't need tea. We have each other," Sara said, comforting Tom.

Tom smiled. He hugged Sara back. He was happy.

They cleaned up the mess and went back to the garden. They played with their dolls and teddies. They had a lot of fun.

Once upon a time, there was a charming hero named Timmy. He was very kind and always helped his friends. One day, Timmy saw a little bird that was hurt. The bird said, "Help me, please!" Timmy knew he had to help the bird. He picked it up gently and took it to his house.

At his house, Timmy took care of the bird. He gave it food and water and made a cozy bed for it to rest. The bird said, "Thank you, Timmy. You are my hero." Timmy felt happy to help the bird.

The moral of the story is that we should always help others when they need it. Even if it's a small thing like helping a little bird, it can make a big difference. Timmy was a hero because he listened to the bird and helped it.

Once upon a time there was a humble little boy who loved to explore. Every day he would go for a walk in the park and find something exciting to do. But one night, the boy had a bad nightmare. He woke up feeling sad and scared, and started to weep. 

He didn't know what to do, until he remembered that his favourite park was always just around the corner. He decided to go there, and when he arrived he saw lots of flowers, birds, and trees. It was a lovely, peaceful place and soon he felt calm again. 

The boy looked up at the sky and made a wish: to never have a bad nightmare ever again. He dried his eyes and said goodbye to the park before heading off home. 

From then on, the boy never had a bad nightmare again and was thankful to the park for always being there to help him feel better.

Once upon a time, there was a happy boy who wanted to explore the world. So one day, he walked out into the sun and he saw a gun. He picked it up and began to play with it. Suddenly, a voice called out to him, "Put the gun down, it's too dangerous for you!"

The boy listened and put the gun down. He looked around and saw a warm, cozy spot beneath a tree. So he took off his shoes and lay down, resting beneath the tree. He closed his eyes and fell asleep, dreaming of all the places he wanted to explore.

When he woke up, the sun was setting and he was feeling very sleepy again. He put his shoes back on and made his way back home. He felt so happy, having had a wonderful day of resting and exploring.

The eye can hardly pick them out From the cold shade they shelter in, Till wind distresses tail and mane; Then one crops grass, and moves about - The other seeming to look on - And stands anonymous again Yet fifteen years ago, perhaps Two dozen distances sufficed To fable them : faint afternoons Of Cups and Stakes and Handicaps, Whereby their names were artificed To inlay faded, classic Junes - Silks at the start : against the sky Numbers and parasols : outside, Squadrons of empty cars, and heat, And littered grass : then the long cry Hanging unhushed till it subside To stop-press columns on the street. Do memories plague their ears like flies? They shake their heads. Dusk brims the shadows. Summer by summer all stole away, The starting-gates, the crowd and cries - All but the unmolesting meadows. Almanacked, their names live; they Have slipped their names, and stand at ease, Or gallop for what must be joy, And not a fieldglass sees them home, Or curious stop-watch prophesies : Only the grooms, and the grooms boy, With bridles in the evening come.

Ah, did you once see Shelley plain, And did he stop and speak to you? And did you speak to him again? How strange it seems, and new! But you were living before that, And you are living after, And the memory I started at-- My starting moves your laughter! I crossed a moor, with a name of its own And a certain use in the world no doubt, Yet a hand's-breadth of it shines alone 'Mid the blank miles round about: For there I picked up on the heather And there I put inside my breast A moulted feather, an eagle-feather-- Well, I forget the rest.

name_of_work: He Is More Than A Hero by Sappho
content: He is more than a hero he is a god in my eyes-- the man who is allowed to sit beside you -- he who listens intimately to the sweet murmur of your voice, the enticing laughter that makes my own heart beat fast. If I meet you suddenly, I can't speak -- my tongue is broken; a thin flame runs under my skin; seeing nothing, hearing only my own ears drumming, I drip with sweat; trembling shakes my body and I turn paler than dry grass. At such times death isn't far from me.

My soul looked down from a vague height with Death, As unremembering how I rose or why, And saw a sad land, weak with sweats of dearth, Gray, cratered like the moon with hollow woe, And fitted with great pocks and scabs of plaques. Across its beard, that horror of harsh wire, There moved thin caterpillars, slowly uncoiled. It seemed they pushed themselves to be as plugs Of ditches, where they writhed and shriveled, killed. By them had slimy paths been trailed and scraped Round myriad warts that might be little hills. From gloom's last dregs these long-strung creatures crept, And vanished out of dawn down hidden holes. (And smell came up from those foul openings As out of mouths, or deep wounds deepening.) On dithering feet upgathered, more and more, Brown strings towards strings of gray, with bristling spines, All migrants from green fields, intent on mire. Those that were gray, of more abundant spawns, Ramped on the rest and ate them and were eaten. I saw their bitten backs curve, loop, and straighten, I watched those agonies curl, lift, and flatten. Whereat, in terror what that sight might mean, I reeled and shivered earthward like a feather. And Death fell with me, like a deepening moan. And He, picking a manner of worm, which half had hid Its bruises in the earth, but crawled no further, Showed me its feet, the feet of many men, And the fresh-severed head of it, my head.

O truant muse, what shall be thy amends For thy neglect of truth in beauty dyed? Both truth and beauty on my love depends; So dost thou too, and therein dignified. Make answer, muse. Wilt thou not haply say "Truth needs no color with his color fixed, Beauty no pencil beauty's truth to lay; But best is best if never intermixed"? Because he needs no praise, wilt thou be dumb? Excuse not silence so, for 't lies in thee To make him much outlive a gilded tomb And to be praised of ages yet to be. Then do thy office, muse; I teach thee how To make him seem long hence as he shows now.

Once upon a time, there was a mommy and a daddy. They both wanted to raise something special. So they went to the store and got a sausage.

The mommy and daddy were so proud of their sausage. They cooked it together and made it all yummy. Everyone in the family said it was the best sausage they ever had.

Then something magical happened. After the mommy and daddy fed the sausage to the family, something began to grow in the garden. It was huge!

The mommy and daddy were very proud when they saw what the sausage had done. It had grown into a big vegetable garden! The mommy and daddy could now feed their whole family fresh vegetables. They were so glad they had raised the sausage.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Ava. She was three years old and always had lots of fun. Ava had a best friend called Jenny.

One day, it had just stopped raining and the sun came out, so Jenny and Ava decided to go for a walk outside. As they were walking, they noticed a big orange on the ground.

"Let's see how far we can split it!" said Ava.

Jenny agreed and the two of them took it home.

At home, they found a knife and cut the orange into two halves. They each took a half and then proceeded to split it into smaller pieces. It was so funny to see all the different-sized wedges they managed to create! 

Ava tried to make the smallest piece to rule them all - it was only an inch big!

Jenny and Ava laughed until their stomachs hurt, it was the most fun afternoon ever.

The End.

Ben and Lily went to the park with Mom. They liked to play on the swings and slide. Ben wanted to swing high and fast. Lily wanted to swing slow and low.

"Push me, Mom!" Ben said. "I want to touch the sky!"

"Okay, Ben. Hold on tight!" Mom said. She pushed Ben hard and he laughed.

Lily got off her swing and walked to the sandbox. She had a bucket and a shovel. She wanted to search for treasure. She dug and dug in the sand. She found a shiny rock, a feather, and a button. She put them in her bucket.

"Look, Mom! Look what I found!" Lily said. She ran to Mom with her bucket.

"Wow, Lily! You found some nice things!" Mom said. She looked at Lily's bucket. "But it looks heavy. Do you need help?"

"No, Mom. I can carry it. It's my treasure!" Lily said. She smiled and hugged her bucket.

Ben saw Lily and her bucket. He wanted to see what she found. He stopped swinging and jumped off. He ran to Lily and Mom.

"Can I see your treasure, Lily?" Ben asked.

"Sure, Ben. But be careful. It's heavy." Lily said. She showed Ben her bucket.

"Wow, Lily! You found a rock, a feather, and a button!" Ben said. He touched them gently.

"Can I have the button, Lily? It's pretty." Ben asked.

"Okay, Ben. You can have the button. It's a gift." Lily said. She gave Ben the button.

"Thank you, Lily. You're a good sister." Ben said. He put the button in his pocket.

"You're welcome, Ben. You're a good brother." Lily said. She hugged Ben.

Mom smiled and hugged them both. She was happy to see them share and be kind. She said, "I love you, Ben and Lily. You're my treasures."

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved playing outside in the sunshine. But one day, the clouds came and covered the sunshine. Lily became worried that the sunshine would never come back.

She asked her mommy, "Where did the sunshine go?" Her mommy said, "Don't worry, it will come back soon." Lily waited and waited, but the sunshine didn't come back.

Then, suddenly, the clouds went away and the sunshine became bright again! Lily was so happy and she ran outside to play. She knew that even if the sunshine goes away, it will always come back.

name_of_work: In Flanders Fields by John McCrae
content: In Flanders fields the poppies blow Between the crosses, row on row, That mark our place; and in the sky The larks, still bravely singing, fly Scarce heard amid the guns below. We are the Dead. Short days ago We lived, felt dawn, saw sunset glow, Loved and were loved, and now we lie, In Flanders fields. Take up our quarrel with the foe: To you from failing hands we throw The torch; be yours to hold it high. If ye break faith with us who die We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders fields.

Once there was a little girl named Ruth. She was three years old and loved to peek. One morning she took a peek outside her window and saw something very pretty. It was a broccoli plant!

Ruth was so excited that she ran outside to take a closer look. It was so pretty. The broccoli was bright green with lots of little buds. Ruth wanted to pick a broccoli so she carefully picked one. It was so crunchy and yummy!

Ruth took the broccoli back inside to show her mom. She was so happy! Ruth's mom was so proud to have such a smart girl who knew how to pick vegetables. From that day on, Ruth was excited to peek outside her window and see the prettiest broccoli in the world.

Once upon a time, there was a furry root. One day, he decided to speak. He said, "Hello, world!" Everyone was amazed--a root that could speak! All the animals gathered around to listen to the root's stories. He told stories about wonderful adventures he had gone on, and all the different places he had seen. 

The root was very popular, and all the animals wanted to be his friend. The root enjoyed speaking to the animals so much that he decided to never stop. Every day he would tell a new story and his friends would always be eager to listen. 

The furry root's stories were so funny, creative, and exciting that everyone wanted to listen to him. He remained the center of attention until the day he stopped speaking. Everyone was so sad, but they all knew that they would never forget the furry root's wonderful stories.

Once there was a apple tree in a large field and it was the home of two friends - Bob and Lisa. Bob was a bee and Lisa was a butterfly. One day they decided to explore the field. 

As they walked through the tall grass, Lisa shouted, "Let's play a game!" Bob agreed and they played tag. Lisa ran around trying to catch Bob. 

 Suddenly, Bob stopped and said, "Look! What is that?" Lisa looked ahead and saw a large laser pointing at them. "Let's go closer," said Bob. 

The two friends approached the laser and Bob said, "What do you think it is?" Lisa thought for a moment and then said, "I don't know, but it looks funny." 

Then Bob realized it was a toy and the two friends started having fun with the laser. They used it to draw shapes in the sky and made funny noises. 

Suddenly, Lisa said, "Let's explore more," and the two friends continued through the field. What other fun things would they find?

Once there was an elephant, Who tried to use the telephant-- No! No! I mean an elephone Who tried to use the telephone-- (Dear me! I am not certain quite That even now I've got it right.) Howe'er it was, he got his trunk Entangled in the telephunk; The more he tried to get it free, The louder buzzed the telephee-- (I fear I'd better drop the song Of elephop and telephong!)

Once upon a time, there was a cute little bunny named Bun Bun. Bun Bun loved to play in the park with his friends. One day, Bun Bun and his friend, a little birdie named Tweet, were playing on the swings.

Suddenly, a big gust of wind blew Bun Bun's hat off his head and it landed on the ground. Bun Bun tried to reach for it, but he couldn't. "Can you help me, Tweet?" Bun Bun asked. "Sure, I can push you!" Tweet replied.

So, Tweet pushed Bun Bun on the swing and he was able to reach his hat. "Yay, thank you, Tweet!" Bun Bun said happily. They played until noon and then went home. Bun Bun wore his hat proudly, feeling happy and grateful for his friend's help.

Molly and Jake were at a party. Molly saw a big brown cake that was full of colorful sprinkles. She wanted some of the cake, so she asked Jake if she could have a piece. Jake said yes and cut a slice of the cake for Molly.

While Molly ate the cake, a song came on that she liked. She started to dance. Molly moved and twirled around the room. Everyone else at the party started to dance too. They all had so much fun dancing and laughing together.

Soon the time had come for them to leave the party. Molly was sad. She didn't want the fun to end. Jake said goodbye to all the other guests. Then Molly and Jake headed out.

But they didn't leave empty handed! Jake had brought a big brown box full of pieces of cake for them to eat at home. That way, they could remember the good times they had at the party.

Tom and Jen are friends. They like to play with toys. Tom has a toy car. Jen has a toy unicorn. The unicorn has a horn on its head. The horn is shiny and pink.

One day, Tom and Jen go to the park. They bring their toys with them. They play on the swings, the slide and the seesaw. They have fun. But then, Tom sees a big dog. The dog is black and furry. It barks loud. Tom is scared. He runs away. He forgets his toy car.

Jen sees Tom run away. She is worried. She follows him. She forgets her toy unicorn.

The dog sees the toys. It is curious. It sniffs the car and the unicorn. It likes the unicorn. It bites the horn. The horn breaks. It is not shiny and pink anymore. It is dull and white.

Tom and Jen find each other. They hug. They are not scared anymore. They go back to the park. They look for their toys. They see the dog. The dog has the unicorn in its mouth. The horn is broken. Jen is sad. She cries.

"Bad dog! Give me back my unicorn!" Jen shouts.

The dog drops the unicorn. It runs away. Tom picks up the unicorn. He gives it to Jen.

"I'm sorry, Jen. Your unicorn is broken. The horn is dull." Tom says.

"It's okay, Tom. It's not your fault. You forgot your car. I forgot my unicorn. We were scared." Jen says.

"Can we still be friends?" Tom asks.

"Of course we can. You are my friend. I don't care about the horn. I care about you." Jen says.

They hug again. They smile. They play with their toys. They are happy.

Eric and Susie were best friends. They were very adventurous. One day Susie said, "Let's play with my new mixer!"

Eric asked, "What can we do with it?"

Susie said, "We can push the buttons and see what happens!"

So they began pushing the buttons. When they pushed the red one, the mixer sang songs. When they pushed the blue one, it spun around. Every time they pushed a button, something new and exciting happened.

Eric laughed and said, "This is so much fun!"

Susie agreed and they kept pushing the buttons, discovering all the different things the mixer could do. They had an adventurous and exciting day together!

When their time comes they fall without wind, without rain. They seep through the trees' muslin in a slow fermentation. Daily the low sun warms them in a late love that is sweeter than summer. In bed at night we hear heartbeat of fruitfall. The secretive slugs crawl home to the burst honeys, are found in the morning mouth on mouth, inseparable. We spread patchwork counterpanes for a clean catch. Baskets fill, never before such harvest, such a hunters' moon burning the hawthorns, drunk on syrups that are richer by night when spiders pitch tents in the wet grass. This morning the red sun is opening like a rose on our white wall, prints there the fishbone shadow of a fern. The early blackbirds fly guilty from a dawn haul of fallen fruit. We too breakfast on sweetnesses. Soon plum trees will be bone, grown delicate with frost's formalities. Their black angles will tear the snow.

Under a splintered mast, torn from ship and cast near her hull, a stumbling shepherd found embedded in the ground, a sea-gull of lapis lazuli, a scarab of the sea, with wings spread-- curling its coral feet, parting its beak to greet men long dead.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy. He was three years old and always liked to explore. He decided to go for a walk in the park.

As he walked, he stopped to observe the soil. It was so dark and dirty. He found it so interesting that he wanted to touch it. He reached out with his hand and touched the soil. It felt very yucky!

The little boy quickly pulled his hand away. He scrunched his nose up, it was most disgusting! He decided that the soil was not a good place to explore so he walked away.

The little boy continued to walk around the park, only stopping to observe the things he found. Soon, he found a beautiful flower and decided to look at it. It was so much better than the soil! He enjoyed watching the flower and forgot all about the bad soil. 

The End.

Sam and Tom are friends. They like to play outside. One day, they see a big dog. The dog is friendly and has a collar. Sam wants to pet the dog. Tom wants to lead the dog.

"Can I lead the dog?" Tom asks Sam.

"OK, but be careful," Sam says.

Tom takes the leash from the collar. He is enthusiastic. He wants to go for a walk with the dog. He pulls the leash and runs. The dog follows him.

"Wait for me!" Sam shouts.

But Tom does not listen. He is too excited. He does not see the street. He does not see the car. He does not hear the horn.

BEEP! BEEP!

The car stops. The driver is angry. He yells at Tom.

"Are you crazy? You could have been hurt! And the dog too! Where is the owner of this dog?"

Tom is scared. He does not know what to say. He looks at the dog. The dog looks sad.

Sam runs to Tom. He is worried. He hugs Tom.

"Are you OK?" Sam asks.

"I'm sorry," Tom says. "I was not careful. I was not a good leader. I did not think about the dog. I did not think about you."

Sam nods. He understands. He is still Tom's friend.

The owner of the dog comes. He is relieved. He thanks the driver. He takes the leash from Tom. He pets the dog.

"I'm glad you are both OK," he says. "But you should not lead a dog you do not know. It is dangerous. You should always ask for permission first. And you should always look both ways before crossing the street. Do you understand?"

Tom and Sam nod. They say sorry. They learn their lesson. They promise to be more careful. They promise to be better leaders. They promise to be better friends.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy had a big green lawn in front of his house. He loved playing on the lawn with his toys. One day, Timmy's friend came over to play. His friend had a silly hat on his head. Timmy thought it looked funny. 

Timmy's friend wanted to play with Timmy's toys, but Timmy didn't want to share. Timmy's mom saw what was happening and said, "Timmy, sharing is important. Your toys belong to both of you." Timmy thought about it and decided to share his toys with his friend. 

They played together on the lawn, making silly faces and laughing. Timmy realized that it was more fun to play with his friend than to play alone. From that day on, Timmy and his friend shared their toys and played together on the lawn every day.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue had a pink mitten. She loved her pink mitten very much. She wore it all the time.

One day, Sue went to visit her friend, Tom. Tom lived in a small house with a big tree. They played and had fun. But when it was time to go home, Sue could not find her pink mitten.

Sue was sad. She looked everywhere for her pink mitten. Then, Tom saw something in the big tree. It was Sue's pink mitten! Sue was very happy. She put on her pink mitten and went home with a big smile.

name_of_work: My Dog Practices Geometry by Cathryn Essinger
content: I do not understand the poets who tell me that I should not personify. Every morning the willow auditions for a new role outside my bedroom window--today she is Clytemnestra; yesterday a Southern Belle, lost in her own melodrama, sinking on her skirts. Nor do I like the mathematicians who tell me I cannot say, "The zinnias are counting on their fingers," or "The dog is practicing her geometry," even though every day I watch her using the yard's big maple as the apex of a triangle from which she bisects the circumference of the lawn until she finds the place where the rabbit has escaped, or the squirrel upped the ante by climbing into a new Euclidian plane. She stumbles across the lawn, eyes pulling her feet along, gaze fixed on a rodent working the maze of the oak as if it were his own invention, her feet tangling in the roots of trees, and tripping, yes, even over themselves, until I go out to assist, by pointing at the squirrel, and repeating, "There! There!" But instead of following my outstretched arm to the crown of the tree, where the animal is now lounging under a canopy of leaves, catching its breath, charting its next escape, she looks to my mouth, eager to read my lips, confident that I--who can bring her home from across the field with a word, who can speak for the willow and the zinnia-- can surely charm a squirrel down from a tree.

name_of_work: 'The Trial by Existence' by Robert Frost
content: Even the bravest that are slain Shall not dissemble their surprise On waking to find valor reign, Even as on earth, in paradise; And where they sought without the sword Wide field of asphodel fore'er, To find that the utmost reward Of daring should be still to dare. The light of heaven falls whole and white And is not shattered into dyes, The light for ever is morning light; The hills are verdured pasture-wise; The angel hosts with freshness go, And seek with laughter what to brave;-- And binding all is the hushed snow Of the far-distant breaking wave. And from a cliff-top is proclaimed The gathering of the souls for birth, The trial by existence named, The obscuration upon earth. And the slant spirits trooping by In streams and cross- and counter-streams Can but give ear to that sweet cry For its suggestion of what dreams! And the more loitering are turned To view once more the sacrifice Of those who for some good discerned Will gladly give up paradise. And a white shimmering concourse rolls Toward the throne to witness there The speeding of devoted souls Which God makes his especial care. And none are taken but who will, Having first heard the life read out That opens earthward, good and ill, Beyond the shadow of a doubt; And very beautifully God limns, And tenderly, life's little dream, But naught extenuates or dims, Setting the thing that is supreme. Nor is there wanting in the press Some spirit to stand simply forth, Heroic in its nakedness, Against the uttermost of earth. The tale of earth's unhonored things Sounds nobler there than 'neath the sun; And the mind whirls and the heart sings, And a shout greets the daring one. But always God speaks at the end: 'One thought in agony of strife The bravest would have by for friend, The memory that he chose the life; But the pure fate to which you go Admits no memory of choice, Or the woe were not earthly woe To which you give the assenting voice.' And so the choice must be again, But the last choice is still the same; And the awe passes wonder then, And a hush falls for all acclaim. And God has taken a flower of gold And broken it, and used therefrom The mystic link to bind and hold Spirit to matter till death come. 'Tis of the essence of life here, Though we choose greatly, still to lack The lasting memory at all clear, That life has for us on the wrack Nothing but what we somehow chose; Thus are we wholly stripped of pride In the pain that has but one close, Bearing it crushed and mystified.

Once there was a mighty goose that liked to write. He wrote stories, songs and letters. Everywhere he went, he wrote something. He wrote in the fields, he wrote in the mountains, he wrote in the forests. 

One day, he decided to write a letter in the pond. But when he dropped his paper into the water, a big wave came and it washed it away. 

The mighty goose was very sad - he had lost his letter. He realised though, that it was his own fault - if he had written it in the ground or on a rock, it would not have been lost. 

The moral of the story was that sometimes it's important to choose the right place for things, otherwise it may get lost!

Ben was an adventurous boy who liked to explore nature. He always had many questions about the animals, the plants and the rocks he saw. He wanted to learn everything he could.

One day, he went to the park with his mom and saw a big pond. He saw ducks, fish and frogs in the water. He ran to the edge of the pond and asked his mom, "Can I touch them? Can I feed them? Can I catch them?"

His mom said, "No, Ben. You have to be careful. The water is deep and you might fall in. The animals might bite you or get scared. You have to respect nature and leave them alone."

But Ben did not listen. He was too curious and excited. He took a stick and tried to poke a frog. The frog jumped away and splashed water on Ben. Ben got wet and cold. He tried to grab a fish, but the fish was too fast and slippery. Ben slipped and fell into the pond. He got soaked and muddy. He cried for help.

His mom heard him and ran to him. She pulled him out of the pond and hugged him. She said, "Ben, are you okay? You were very naughty and foolish. You did not listen to me. You could have hurt yourself or the animals. You have to be more careful and respectful of nature. Nature is beautiful and wonderful, but also dangerous and wild. You have to ask questions, but also follow the rules."

Ben felt sorry and ashamed. He said, "I'm sorry, mom. I was wrong. I won't do it again. I love nature, but I also love you. You are right. I have to be more careful and respectful of nature. And I have to listen to you. You know more than me. You are smart and kind."

His mom smiled and said, "I love you too, Ben. You are a good boy and a good learner. You are adventurous and curious, but you also have to be safe and responsible. Come on, let's go home and change your clothes. And maybe we can read a book about nature and learn more about it."

Ben nodded and said, "Okay, mom. Thank you. You are the best mom ever."

The end.

name_of_work: The Kingfisher by William Henry Davies
content: It was the Rainbow gave thee birth, And left thee all her lovely hues; And, as her mother's name was Tears, So runs it in my blood to choose For haunts the lonely pools, and keep In company with trees that weep. Go you and, with such glorious hues, Live with proud peacocks in green parks; On lawns as smooth as shining glass, Let every feather show its marks; Get thee on boughs and clap thy wings Before the windows of proud kings. Nay, lovely Bird, thou art not vain; Thou hast no proud, ambitious mind; I also love a quiet place That's green, away from all mankind; A lonely pool, and let a tree Sigh with her bosom over me.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to bake with her mommy. One day, they decided to make brownies.

Lily's mommy said, "Can you measure the flour for me, Lily?" Lily nodded and got the measuring cup. She filled it up and poured it in the bowl.

After they mixed all the ingredients, Lily's mommy said, "Let's wipe the counter clean." Lily grabbed a cloth and wiped the crumbs away.

When the brownies were done, they smelled so good! Lily's daddy came in and said, "Wow, those brownies look delicious!" Lily's mommy said, "We made them together. Lily measured the flour and wiped the counter clean." Lily felt proud of herself and smiled.

Once upon a time, there was a boy called Jack. Jack was three years old and loved playing with toys. One day, Jack was in his bedroom playing with his favourite toy car when he heard a noise from the kitchen. Jack decided to go and explore. 

In the kitchen, he saw his mom. His mom was putting items onto a tray. She was very busy and looked a bit upset. Jack asked her why she was upset.

Jack's mom replied, "I'm upset because I have a lot to do. I'm making lunch for your brother and I still have to grab some snacks for the picnic."

Jack asked if he could help. His mom smiled and said she had an idea. She grabbed the tray and told Jack to go and get a snack from the cupboard.

Jack rushed off excitedly to the cupboard. He opened the doors and saw a wide range of snacks. He grabbed a packet of crisps and close the cupboard doors.

He rushed back to his mom and handed her the packet of crisps. His mom was so happy that Jack was being helpful. She smiled and gave him a big hug.

Mark was walking through the park when he noticed a dependable tree. He decided to mark the tree by scratching the bark with a rock. But the tree was not happy with Mark. It shook and sent Mark jumping back to avoid being hit. Filled with anger, the tree uprooted itself and it started to move towards Mark. He quickly ran as fast as he could, but the tree was fast and strong. The tree chased after Mark until it eventually caught and crushed him underneath it. The last thing Mark saw was the dependable tree that he had marked.

name_of_work: My Grandmother's Houses by Jackie Kay
content: 1 She is on the second floor of a tenement. From her front room window you see the cemetery. Her bedroom is my favourite: newspapers dating back to the War covering every present she's ever got since the War. What's the point in buying her anything my mother moans. Does she use it. Does she even look at it. I spend hours unwrapping and wrapping endless tablecloths, napkins, perfume, bath salts, stories of things I can't understand, words like conscientious objector. At night I climb over all the newspaper parcels to get to bed, harder than the school's obstacle course. High up in her bed all the print merges together. When she gets the letter she is hopping mad. What does she want with anything modern, a shiny new pin? Here is home. The sideboard solid as a coffin. The newsagents next door which sells hazelnut toffees and her Daily Record. Chewing for ages over the front page, her toffees sticking to her false teeth. 2 The new house is called a high rise. I play in the lift all the way up to 24. Once I get stuck for a whole hour. From her window you see noisy kids playing hopscotch or home. She makes endless pots of vegetable soup, a bit bit of hoch floating inside like a fish. Till finally she gets to like the hot running water in her own bathroom, the wall-to-wall foam-backed carpet, the parcels locked in her air-raid shelter. But she still doesn't settle down; even at 70 she cleans people's houses for ten bob and goes to church on Sundays, dragging me along to the strange place where the air is trapped and ghosts sit at the altar. My parents do not believe. It is down to her. A couple of prayers. A hymn or two. Threepenny bit in the collection hat. A flock of women in coats and fussy hats flapping over me like missionaires, and that is that, until the next time God grabs me in Glasgow with Gran. 3 By the time I am seven we are almost the same height. She still walks faster, rushing me down the High Street till we get to her cleaning house. The hall is huge. Rooms lead off like an octopus's arms. I sit in a room with a grand piano, top open - a one-winged creature, whilst my gran polishes for hours. Finally bored I start to pick some notes, oh can you wash a sailor's shirt oh can you wash and clean till my gran comes running, duster in hand. I told you don't touch anything. The woman comes too; the posh one all smiles that make goosepimples run up my arms. Would you like to sing me a song? Someone's crying my Lord Kumbaya. Lovely, she says, beautiful child, skin the colour of cafe au lait. 'Cafe oh what? Hope she's not being any bother.' Not at all. Not at all. You just get back to your work. On the way to her high rise I see her like the hunchback of Notre Dame. Everytime I crouch over a comic she slaps me. Sit up straight. She is on the ground floor of a high rise. From her living-room you see ambulances, screaming their way to the Royal Infirmary.

name_of_work: Slow, Slow, Fresh Fount by Ben Jonson
content: Slow, slow, fresh fount, keep time with my salt tears; Yet slower, yet, O faintly, gentle springs! List to the heavy part the music bears, Woe weeps out her division, when she sings. Droop herbs and flowers; Fall grief in showers; Our beauties are not ours. O, I could still, Like melting snow upon some craggy hill, Drop, drop, drop, drop, Since nature's pride is now a withered daffodil.

name_of_work: Joining the Colours by Katharine Tynan
content: There they go marching all in step so gay! Smooth-cheeked and golden, food for shells and guns. Blithely they go as to a wedding day, The mothers' sons. The drab street stares to see them row on row On the high tram-tops, singing like the lark. Too careless-gay for courage, singing they go Into the dark. With tin whistles, mouth-organs, any noise, They pipe the way to glory and the grave; Foolish and young, the gay and golden boys Love cannot save. High heart! High courage! The poor girls they kissed Run with them : they shall kiss no more, alas! Out of the mist they stepped-into the mist Singing they pass.

Once upon a time there was an old bag. It was locked tight, and nothing could get in or out. 

One day a boy found the bag. He was only three years old, but he was determined to unlock the bag and see what was inside. He tried and tried, but he couldn't find the key. 

Then, the boy had an idea. He had seen his Dad using a paperclip to unlock doors, so he decided to try using a paperclip on the bag. He bent the clip until it looked like a key, and he put it into the lock. 

The old bag unlocked with a click! The boy was so excited. He pulled open the bag, and inside he found a bunch of treasures - toys, candy, and even a tiny bike. He was so happy that he had unlocked the bag. 

The end.

Once upon a time there was a little boy who was very scared. He did not know why he was scared, but he was. Everywhere he looked, he saw things that scared him. One day, he saw a huge bookshelf. It was so tall that it almost reached the ceiling! He was so scared that he wanted to run away, but then he noticed something. The bookshelf was moving! It was slowly reversing to the other side of the room!

The little boy watched in amazement as the bookshelf slowly moved backwards. It was so strange! He stared in wonder until the bookshelf finally came to a stop. He breathed a sigh of relief and began to look at all the books on the shelves. He started to feel better and his fear began to fade away.

The little boy thanked the bookshelf for helping him to not be so scared. He knew now that the bookshelf was not something to be afraid of. He looked around the room and realized that nothing else scared him anymore.

He waved goodbye to the bookshelf, happy that he had figured out that there was nothing to be scared of. He was so pleased that he had reversed his fear!

name_of_work: Something Told the Wild Geese by Rachel Field
content: Something told the wild geese It was time to go. Though the fields lay golden Something whispered,--'Snow.' Leaves were green and stirring, Berries, luster-glossed, But beneath warm feathers Something cautioned,--'Frost.' All the sagging orchards Steamed with amber spice, But each wild breast stiffened At remembered ice. Something told the wild geese It was time to fly,-- Summer sun was on their wings, Winter in their cry.

name_of_work: In The Park by Gwen Harwood
content: She sits in the park. Her clothes are out of date. Two children whine and bicker, tug her skirt. A third draws aimless patterns in the dirt Someone she loved once passed by - too late to feign indifference to that casual nod. "How nice" et cetera. "Time holds great surprises." From his neat head unquestionably rises a small balloon..."but for the grace of God..." They stand a while in flickering light, rehearsing the children's names and birthdays. "It's so sweet to hear their chatter, watch them grow and thrive, " she says to his departing smile. Then, nursing the youngest child, sits staring at her feet. To the wind she says, "They have eaten me alive."

One day, a little crab named Timmy went for a walk by the sea. He saw a big, pretty shell on the sand. Timmy wanted to enter the shell and make it his new home. He walked closer and looked inside.

Inside the shell, Timmy met a tiny fish named Finny. Finny was hiding from a big, scary bird. Timmy said, "Hi, can I come in?" Finny said, "Yes, please enter and help me hide from the bird."

Together, they hid inside the shell until the bird flew away. Then, they went out to find some yummy food to eat. They found a tasty seaweed and shared it. Timmy and Finny became best friends and lived in the shell together, always sharing yummy food and having fun.

John and his new neighbor, Sarah, were walking down the street together. John saw a tall fence and he wondered what was behind it. He asked Sarah, "Do you dare to go through the fence?"

Sarah smiled. "Why not? Let's go!" she said.

They went through the fence and came to a playground. John was so excited! He'd never seen one before and wanted to explore. Sarah showed him so many fun things to do. He was laughing and jumping around the whole time.

John thought Sarah was so brave for coming with him and he was feeling a bit envious. But then Sarah said, "I dare you to try the swings!" 

John was a bit scared but he decided to bravely take the challenge. He jumped on the swing and started swinging. Back and forth, higher and higher. As he swung, the envious feeling disappeared because he was now brave and adventurous like his new neighbor. 

John and Sarah had so much fun! They ran and laughed, played and explored the playground until the sun started to set. John was so glad he'd come on this adventure - he'd even grown brave enough to go through a fence!  He had a feeling that he and Sarah were going to be the best of friends.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Abby. She was 3 years old and loved lollipops very much. One day, she was playing in her living room when she noticed something on the wall - it was a big clean sheet of paper!

Abby was so excited that she did not know what to do. She asked her mom if she could print something on it. Her mom said yes, and so Abby began printing with some crayons.

She drew a lollipop on the paper and it looked so colorful and yummy! Then, she took a real lollipop out of its wrapper and placed it next to her drawing - it was the perfect addition!

Abby was so happy with the results! She showed it to her mom and dad, who both said it looked great. Everybody was very pleased with her work.

The end.

Once upon a time, in a small house, there lived a little girl named Mia. Mia had a big toy bear named Bobo. Bobo was a selfish bear. He did not like to share his toys with Mia. One day, Mia's mom told her that they were going on a trip. Mia was very happy and excited.

Mia started to pack her luggage for the trip. She put her clothes and toys inside the luggage. But Bobo did not want to go. He did not want to share the luggage with Mia's toys. So, he tried to squeeze himself inside the luggage and push out Mia's toys. Mia saw what Bobo was doing and felt sad.

On the trip, Mia met a new friend named Lily. Lily had a toy bunny named BunBun. BunBun was a nice bunny and liked to share. Mia and Lily played together, and they shared their toys. Bobo saw how happy Mia was with her new friend and her nice bunny. He realized that being selfish was not good. So, Bobo decided to share his toys with Mia and her new friend. From that day on, Bobo was not selfish anymore, and they all played happily together.

Ben and Mia are friends. They like to play in the park. One day, they see a big tree with red apples. They want to eat some apples.

"Look, Ben, apples!" Mia says. "They look yummy. Can we get some?"

Ben nods. He is strong. He can move a big rock. He puts the rock under the tree. He climbs on the rock. He reaches for an apple.

"Ouch!" Ben says. He falls off the rock. He hurts his arm. He drops the apple.

Mia runs to Ben. She hugs him. She is sorry. She picks up the apple. She gives it to Ben.

"Here, Ben, this is for you. You are brave. You tried to get an apple for us. Are you okay?"

Ben smiles. He is not too hurt. He is happy. He has a good friend. He has an apple. He shares it with Mia.

They eat the apple. It is sweet and juicy. They thank the tree. They thank each other. They are happy. They play some more.

Once there was a little boy. His name was Bob. He was very helpful. He spent his days helping his mom, dad and sisters around the house. One day, he was playing in the garden when he saw something glinting in the sun. He went over and saw a pair of sunglasses. Bob nodded in amazement as he carefully picked them up.

Suddenly, he heard a voice. He turned around and saw a very old man. 

"Those sunglasses were mine," the old man said.

Bob explained that he found the sunglasses and asked if he could keep them.

The old man nodded. "Yes, you can keep them. In exchange, I need a favour."

Bob agreed. The old man explained he needed help around his house. Bob nodded eagerly.

Afterwards, Bob felt so happy. He had helped the old man, and in exchange, he got sunglasses as a reward.

Bob learned a valuable lesson that day: no matter how big or small, being helpful is always worth it.

Once upon a time, there was a little dog named Max. Max loved to run and play all day long. One day, Max started feeling very dizzy and couldn't run anymore. Max's owner, Lily, noticed that Max wasn't feeling well and decided to call the veterinarian. 

"Hello, veterinarian! Max is feeling dizzy and can't run anymore. Can you help him?" asked Lily. 

The veterinarian said, "Yes, I can help Max. Bring him to my clinic so I can take a look at him." 

Lily took Max to the veterinarian's clinic. The veterinarian examined Max and found out that he had eaten something bad. After giving Max some medicine, Max started feeling better and could run and play again. Max was very happy and licked the veterinarian's face to say thank you.
