name_of_work: A Poem For My Librarian, Mrs. Long by Nikki Giovanni
content: A Poem for My Librarian, Mrs. Long (You never know what troubled little girl needs a book) At a time when there was not tv before 3:00 P.M. And on Sunday none until 5:00 We sat on the front porches watching The jfg sign go on and off greeting The neighbors, discussion the political Situation congratulating the preacher On his sermon There was always the radio which brought us Songs from wlac in nashville and what we would now call Easy listening or smooth jazz but when I listened Late at night with my portable (that I was so proud of) Tucked under my pillow I heard nat king cole and matt dennis, june christy and ella fitzgerald And sometimes sarah vaughan sing black coffee Which I now drink It was just called music There was a bookstore uptown on gay street Which I visited and inhaled that wonderful odor Of new books Even today I read hardcover as a preference paperback only As a last resort And up the hill on vine street (The main black corridor) sat our carnegie library Mrs. Long always glad to see you The stereoscope always ready to show you faraway Places to dream about Mrs. Long asking what are you looking for today When I wanted Leaves of Grass or alfred north whitehead She would go to the big library uptown and I now know Hat in hand to ask to borrow so that I might borrow Probably they said something humiliating since southern Whites like to humiliate southern blacks But she nonetheless brought the books Back and I held them to my chest Close to my heart And happily skipped back to grandmother's house Where I would sit on the front porch In a gray glider and dream of a world Far away I love the world where I was I was safe and warm and grandmother gave me neck kissed When I was on my way to bed But there was a world Somewhere Out there And Mrs. Long opened that wardrobe But no lions or witches scared me I went through Knowing there would be Spring

Once upon a time, there was a dog named Spot. Spot loved to eat sausages. One day, he found a sausage on the floor. He looked around and saw no one. He felt a little guilty, but he ate the sausage anyway.

Later, Spot saw his friend, the cat named Fluffy. Fluffy was sad because she lost her sausage. Spot knew the sausage did not belong to him. He felt very guilty for eating Fluffy's sausage.

Spot wanted to make Fluffy happy again. He went to find another sausage for her. When he found one, he gave it to Fluffy. Fluffy was happy, and Spot felt good. From that day on, Spot learned to only eat sausages that belong to him.

name_of_work: The Listeners by Walter de la Mare
content: 'Is there anybody there?' said the Traveller, Knocking on the moonlit door; And his horse in the silence champed the grasses Of the forest's ferny floor: And a bird flew up out of the turret, Above the Traveller's head: And he smote upon the door again a second time; 'Is there anybody there?' he said. But no one descended to the Traveller; No head from the leaf-fringed sill Leaned over and looked into his grey eyes, Where he stood perplexed and still. But only a host of phantom listeners That dwelt in the lone house then Stood listening in the quiet of the moonlight To that voice from the world of men: Stood thronging the faint moonbeams on the dark stair, That goes down to the empty hall, Hearkening in an air stirred and shaken By the lonely Traveller's call. And he felt in his heart their strangeness, Their stillness answering his cry, While his horse moved, cropping the dark turf, 'Neath the starred and leafy sky; For he suddenly smote on the door, even Louder, and lifted his head:-- 'Tell them I came, and no one answered, That I kept my word,' he said. Never the least stir made the listeners, Though every word he spake Fell echoing through the shadowiness of the still house From the one man left awake: Ay, they heard his foot upon the stirrup, And the sound of iron on stone, And how the silence surged softly backward, When the plunging hoofs were gone.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she found a bright letter in her mailbox. She was so happy and ran to her mom to show her the letter.

"Mommy, look at this!" Lily said, holding up the letter.

"What is it, sweetie?" her mom asked.

"It's a letter! It's so bright and pretty!" Lily said.

Her mom smiled and said, "Who is it from?"

"I don't know, but I promise to read it carefully and write back!" Lily said excitedly.

And so, Lily sat down with her mom and read the letter. It was from her grandma, who lived far away. Lily wrote back and promised to visit her grandma soon.

Once upon a time, there was a cheerful bird. The bird loved to fly in the lovely landscape. The landscape was full of pretty colors and the bird flapped its wings with joy.

The bird flew across the landscape, singing its happy songs. Whenever it flew, it felt so free. It flew high, it flew low and it flew through the trees.

But then one day, something very special happened. The bird spotted another bird that was also flying! The two birds began to fly together, making figure eights and dipping in and out of the clouds. They were so happy.

The two birds kept flying together and the landscape seemed to become even more cheerful. The sun was brighter and the sky was bluer. They soared and twirled until they finally reached the shore.

The two birds waved goodbye to each other and then flew away. They promised they would come back and fly together again soon. It was a day full of cheerful flying and a beautiful landscape that neither bird would ever forget.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with marbles, and he had a big collection of them. He liked to roll them around and make them go "clack clack" on the floor.

One day, Timmy's friend Billy came over to play. Billy was very alert and always looking for a joke to play on Timmy. Timmy didn't know it, but Billy had a plan. He wanted to take one of Timmy's marbles and hide it, just to see if Timmy would notice.

So, while Timmy was distracted, Billy took one of Timmy's marbles and hid it in his pocket. Timmy didn't notice, and they kept playing. But later, when Timmy went to put his marbles away, he realized one was missing. He looked and looked, but he couldn't find it.

Timmy was very sad that he had lost one of his marbles. He didn't know that Billy had taken it as a joke. From that day on, Timmy never trusted Billy again.

Once upon a time there was a little boy who was very busy. He built a lot of things with his toy blocks, and he was very proud of all his creations.

One day he decided to build something special. He used all the blocks he had and with a lot of hard work he built a tall tower. It was beautiful! He was so excited and amazed by what he had built. 

Suddenly, a big, bright butterfly fluttered by. The boy was in wonder and he watched the butterfly fly around in the sky. He had never seen anything so amazing and beautiful. 

The boy waved goodbye to the butterfly and then he went back to playing with his blocks. He was very busy making new, beautiful creations. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her blocks and make a big stack. One day, while she was playing, she felt a tickle in her nose. She knew what was coming - a sneeze! 

Lily tried to hold it in, but it was too strong. She sneezed and her big stack of blocks fell down. She felt sad, but then she heard a noise. It was her dog, Max. He was barking and jumping up and down. He was alert because he heard the sneeze and wanted to make sure Lily was okay. 

Lily smiled and hugged Max. She knew that even though her blocks fell down, she still had her best friend to make her feel better. From that day on, Lily made sure to cover her nose when she felt a sneeze coming, so her blocks wouldn't fall down again.

Once upon a time, there was an intelligent girl. She was walking in the fog one morning when she saw an owl. The owl asked her a big question.

The girl didn't know what to do! She thought and thought, trying to find an answer. Suddenly, an idea came to her.

She smiled and gave her answer. The owl clapped its wings in delight and flew away. The fog cleared and the sun came out. The girl was happy. She had found the right answer!

There's just no accounting for happiness, or the way it turns up like a prodigal who comes back to the dust at your feet having squandered a fortune far away. And how can you not forgive? You make a feast in honor of what was lost, and take from its place the finest garment, which you saved for an occasion you could not imagine, and you weep night and day to know that you were not abandoned, that happiness saved its most extreme form for you alone. No, happiness is the uncle you never knew about, who flies a single-engine plane onto the grassy landing strip, hitchhikes into town, and inquires at every door until he finds you asleep midafternoon as you so often are during the unmerciful hours of your despair. It comes to the monk in his cell. It comes to the woman sweeping the street with a birch broom, to the child whose mother has passed out from drink. It comes to the lover, to the dog chewing a sock, to the pusher, to the basketmaker, and to the clerk stacking cans of carrots in the night. It even comes to the boulder in the perpetual shade of pine barrens, to rain falling on the open sea, to the wineglass, weary of holding wine.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a patient puppy named Max. Max was always safe with Lily. Lily knew that Max liked to play with his ball. 

One day, Lily and Max went for a walk in the park. They saw a big tree with a bird's nest. Lily wanted to see the baby birds, but Max knew it was not safe to climb the tree. Lily listened to Max and they walked away. 

Later, they met a nice lady who gave them some treats. Lily shared her treats with Max because she knew he liked them too. Max was a happy puppy and Lily was a happy girl. They went back home and took a nap together.

name_of_work: The Witch's Life by Anne Sexton
content: When I was a child there was an old woman in our neighborhood whom we called The Witch. All day she peered from her second story window from behind the wrinkled curtains and sometimes she would open the window and yell: Get out of my life! She had hair like kelp and a voice like a boulder. I think of her sometimes now and wonder if I am becoming her. My shoes turn up like a jester's. Clumps of my hair, as I write this, curl up individually like toes. I am shoveling the children out, scoop after scoop. Only my books anoint me, and a few friends, those who reach into my veins. Maybe I am becoming a hermit, opening the door for only a few special animals? Maybe my skull is too crowded and it has no opening through which to feed it soup? Maybe I have plugged up my sockets to keep the gods in? Maybe, although my heart is a kitten of butter, I am blowing it up like a zeppelin. Yes. It is the witch's life, climbing the primordial climb, a dream within a dream, then sitting here holding a basket of fire.

When fishes flew and forests walked And figs grew upon thorn, Some moment when the moon was blood Then surely I was born. With monstrous head and sickening cry And ears like errant wings, The devil's walking parody On all four-footed things. The tattered outlaw of the earth, Of ancient crooked will; Starve, scourge, deride me: I am dumb, I keep my secret still. Fools! For I also had my hour; One far fierce hour and sweet: There was a shout about my ears, And palms before my feet.

name_of_work: July in Washington by Robert Lowell
content: The stiff spokes of this wheel touch the sore spots of the earth. On the Potomac, swan-white power launches keep breasting the sulphurous wave. Otters slide and dive and slick back their hair, raccoons clean their meat in the creek. On the circles, green statues ride like South American liberators above the breeding vegetation-- prongs and spearheads of some equatorial backland that will inherit the globe. The elect, the elected . . . they come here bright as dimes, and die dishevelled and soft. We cannot name their names, or number their dates-- circle on circle, like rings on a tree-- but we wish the river had another shore, some further range of delectable mountains, distant hills powdered blue as a girl's eyelid. It seems the least little shove would land us there, that only the slightest repugnance of our bodies we no longer control could drag us back.

Is it thy will that I should wax and wane, Barter my cloth of gold for hodden grey, And at thy pleasure weave that web of pain Whose brightest threads are each a wasted day? Is it thy will That my Soul's House should be a tortured spot Wherein, like evil paramours, must dwell Nay, if it be thy will I shall endure, And sell ambition at the common mart, And let dull failure be my vestiture, And sorrow dig its grave within my heart. Perchance it may be better so I have not made my heart a heart of stone, Nor starved my boyhood of its goodly feast, Nor walked where Beauty is a thing unknown. Many a man hath done so; sought to fence In straitened bonds the soul that should be free, Trodden the dusty road of common sense, While all the forest sang of liberty, Passed on wide pinion through the lofty air, To where the steep untrodden mountain height Caught the last tresses of the Sun God1s hair. The daisy, that white-feathered shield of gold, Followed with wistful eyes the wandering sun Content if once its leaves were aureoled. But surely it is something to have been The best beloved for a little while, To have walked hand in hand with Love, and seen Ay! though the gorged asp of passion feed On my boy's heart, yet have I burstG the bars, Stood face to face with Beauty, known indeed The Love which moves the Sun and all the stars!

name_of_work: Air and Angels by John Donne
content: Twice or thrice had I lov'd thee, Before I knew thy face or name; So in a voice, so in a shapeless flame Angels affect us oft, and worshipp'd be; Still when, to where thou wert, I came, Some lovely glorious nothing I did see. But since my soul, whose child love is, Takes limbs of flesh, and else could nothing do, More subtle than the parent is Love must not be, but take a body too; And therefore what thou wert, and who, I bid Love ask, and now That it assume thy body, I allow, And fix itself in thy lip, eye, and brow. Whilst thus to ballast love I thought, And so more steadily to have gone, With wares which would sink admiration, I saw I had love's pinnace overfraught; Ev'ry thy hair for love to work upon Is much too much, some fitter must be sought; For, nor in nothing, nor in things Extreme, and scatt'ring bright, can love inhere; Then, as an angel, face, and wings Of air, not pure as it, yet pure, doth wear, So thy love may be my love's sphere; Just such disparity As is 'twixt air and angels' purity, 'Twixt women's love, and men's, will ever be.

I love all films that start with rain: rain, braiding a windowpane or darkening a hung-out dress or streaming down her upturned face; one big thundering downpour right through the empty script and score before the act, before the blame, before the lens pulls through the frame to where the woman sits alone beside a silent telephone or the dress lies ruined on the grass or the girl walks off the overpass, and all things flow out from that source along their fatal watercourse. However bad or overlong such a film can do no wrong, so when his native twang shows through or when the boom dips into view or when her speech starts to betray its adaptation from the play, I think to when we opened cold on a starlit gutter, running gold with the neon drugstore sign and I'd read into its blazing line: forget the ink, the milk, the blood-- all was washed clean with the flood we rose up from the falling waters the fallen rain's own sons and daughters and none of this, none of this matters.

Once upon a time, there was a mitten that could fly. The mitten was very playful. Every day it would fly around the sky and have fun. The mitten liked to race the clouds and even try to catch the birds.

The mitten had lots of friends. Some of them were other mittens, but some were birds and clouds. The mitten would make funny shapes with them in the air and sometimes, it would even make a little nest out of twigs that it had found down on the ground. 

The mitten's playful spirit made everyone happy. Whenever someone felt sad, all they had to do was look up at the sky and the mitten would be there, soaring and showing off.

The mitten flew until one day it didn't. Some big bad people caught it and kept it in a cage. But the mitten was too playful to stay inside a cage. So, with one big flap of its wings, it escaped out the window and flew away. 

The mitten was free again and it flew around the sky, making the world happy and playing with the friends it had made before.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play in the park. They see a big round thing that can spin. They want to try it.

"Can we go on the spinny thing?" Anna asks Ben.

"Yes, let's go!" Ben says. They run to the spinny thing and climb on. They hold on tight and push with their feet. The spinny thing goes faster and faster. They feel the wind on their faces and laugh.

"Wow, this is fun!" Anna says.

"I like it too!" Ben says.

They spin for a long time. Then they feel dizzy and stop. They get off the spinny thing and sit on the grass. They close their eyes and wait for the dizziness to go away.

"Are you okay?" Anna asks Ben.

"I'm okay, just a little dizzy," Ben says.

"Me too," Anna says.

They open their eyes and look at each other. They smile.

"That was a good spin," Ben says.

"Yes, it was," Anna says.

They lie down on the grass and relax. They feel the sun on their skin and the breeze on their hair. They feel happy and safe.

"Can I give you a massage?" Anna asks Ben.

"A massage? What is that?" Ben asks.

"It's when you rub someone's back or shoulders or head to make them feel good," Anna says.

"Okay, you can try," Ben says.

Anna moves closer to Ben and puts her hands on his back. She rubs gently and makes circles with her fingers. She moves up to his shoulders and then to his head. She massages his hair and ears.

"How does that feel?" Anna asks Ben.

"It feels nice," Ben says. "You are a good friend, Anna."

"Thank you, Ben. You are a good friend too," Anna says.

They hug each other and smile. They feel happy and safe. They like to play in the park. They like to spin and massage. They are friends.

Once upon a time there was a boy called Pete. He liked to build things. But one day he found a knife. It looked very shiny and he wanted to play with it. 

Pete's mum saw him with the knife and said, "Hey Pete, you must not play with that! Knives can be dangerous!" Pete did not want to listen.

Later on, Pete used the knife to build a small tower from blocks. It looked really cool and he was proud of what he had made. 

His mum came over to look at the tower and said, "Well done Pete. Building is really important, but it is much more important to stay safe. Now you know why it is so important not to play with knives." 

Pete nodded and said, "Yes, mum, I understand." Ever since that day he had been very careful with knives and made sure he knew how to stay safe. 

The end

Lily and Ben are friends. They like to play on the farm. They see many animals and plants. They see cows, pigs, chickens, sheep, corn, wheat and oats.

One day, they want to feed the sheep. They ask the farmer for some oats. The farmer gives them a big bucket. He says, "Be careful. The oats are heavy. Don't spill them."

Lily and Ben carry the bucket together. They walk to the sheep pen. They see many sheep. The sheep are hungry. They make loud noises. "Baa, baa, baa!"

Lily and Ben want to give the oats to the sheep. But the bucket is too high. They cannot reach the trough. They try to lift the bucket. But it is too heavy. They almost spill the oats.

Lily has an idea. She says, "Ben, let's lean the bucket on the fence. Then we can pour the oats into the trough."

Ben likes the idea. He says, "OK, Lily, let's do that."

They lean the bucket on the fence. They tilt the bucket slowly. The oats fall into the trough. The sheep see the oats. They run to the trough. They eat the oats happily. "Baa, baa, baa!"

Lily and Ben smile. They are happy. They are successful. They fed the sheep. They say, "Good job, sheep. Enjoy your oats."

The farmer sees Lily and Ben. He is proud of them. He says, "Well done, Lily and Ben. You are very smart and helpful. You are good friends to the sheep."

Lily and Ben say, "Thank you, farmer. We love the sheep. We love the farm. We love to play here."

In this blue light I can take you there, snow having made me a world of bone seen through to. This is my house, my section of Etruscan wall, my neighbor's lemontrees, and, just below the lower church, the airplane factory. A rooster crows all day from mist outside the walls. There's milk on the air, ice on the oily lemonskins. How clean the mind is, holy grave. It is this girl by Piero della Francesca, unbuttoning her blue dress, her mantle of weather, to go into labor. Come, we can go in. It is before the birth of god. No one has risen yet to the museums, to the assembly line--bodies and wings--to the open air market. This is what the living do: go in. It's a long way. And the dress keeps opening from eternity to privacy, quickening. Inside, at the heart, is tragedy, the present moment forever stillborn, but going in, each breath is a button coming undone, something terribly nimble-fingered finding all of the stops.

Once upon a time, there was a lively dog named Spot. He loved to run and play all day. Spot had a big yard to play in, and he would imagine he was a superhero.

One day, Spot saw a little boy named Tim. Tim was sad because he lost his ball. Spot wanted to help, so he said, "Tim, imagine we are superheroes, and we can find your ball together!" Tim smiled and they started to look for the ball.

As they searched, Spot saw a big street. He forgot what his mom told him about not going to the street alone. Spot ran across the street to get the ball. But, a car came and hit Spot. Tim cried and learned that he should always listen to his mom. The moral of the story is to always be careful and listen to your parents.

Jenny was very happy. She was going to the palace with her mom and dad. They were going to meet the queen. Jenny loved the queen. She had seen her on TV and in books. She wanted to say hello and give her a hug.

They got to the palace and waited in a big room. There were many other people there. They all wore nice clothes and smiled. Jenny wore a pink dress and a bow in her hair. She felt like a princess. She held her mom's hand and looked around.

Soon, a man came and said it was time to meet the queen. He led them to another room. There was a red carpet and a big chair. The queen was sitting on the chair. She wore a long dress and a shiny crown. She looked very pretty and kind. Jenny was excited.

The man said their names and they walked up to the queen. Jenny's mom and dad bowed and said hello. The queen smiled and nodded. Then she looked at Jenny. Jenny smiled and said, "Hi, queen. I'm Jenny. I'm very happy to meet you. You are very pretty and nice. Can I give you a hug?"

The queen was surprised. She was not used to children talking to her like that. She did not like hugs. She thought they were messy and rude. She frowned and said, "No, you can't. You are a very naughty girl. You should not talk to me like that. You should be quiet and respectful. Go away. You are not welcome here."

Jenny was shocked. She did not understand. She had only wanted to be friendly. She felt sad and scared. She started to cry. Her mom and dad were also shocked. They tried to apologize and comfort Jenny. They said they were sorry and they loved her. They wanted to leave.

But the queen was angry. She did not accept their apology. She said they had offended her. She said they had to be punished. She called her guards and told them to take them away. She said they had to go to the dungeon. She said they would never see the sun again.

The guards grabbed Jenny and her mom and dad. They dragged them out of the room. They did not listen to their pleas and cries. They took them to a dark and cold place. They locked them in a cell. They left them alone.

Jenny and her mom and dad hugged each other. They were very sad and afraid. They did not know what would happen to them. They wished they had never come to the palace. They wished they had never met the queen. They wished they had stayed home and had a delicious cake.

name_of_work: A Line-storm Song by Robert Frost
content: The line-storm clouds fly tattered and swift, The road is forlorn all day, Where a myriad snowy quartz stones lift, And the hoof-prints vanish away. The roadside flowers, too wet for the bee, Expend their bloom in vain. Come over the hills and far with me, And be my love in the rain. The birds have less to say for themselves In the wood-world's torn despair Than now these numberless years the elves, Although they are no less there: All song of the woods is crushed like some Wild, easily shattered rose. Come, be my love in the wet woods; come, Where the boughs rain when it blows. There is the gale to urge behind And bruit our singing down, And the shallow waters aflutter with wind From which to gather your gown. What matter if we go clear to the west, And come not through dry-shod? For wilding brooch shall wet your breast The rain-fresh goldenrod. Oh, never this whelming east wind swells But it seems like the sea's return To the ancient lands where it left the shells Before the age of the fern; And it seems like the time when after doubt Our love came back amain. Oh, come forth into the storm and rout And be my love in the rain.

One day, a blue little girl was walking through the woods. She saw a huge pile of lumber and said, "Wow!" Suddenly, the girl sneezed. The surprise made all of the lumber stack topple down! 

She began to cry, when exactly then a magical creature appeared. He had a magical wand and with the wave of his wand, the lumber stacked back up. The girl was so happy that all of her tears turned into giggles.

The magical creature asked, "What is your name?" She replied, "My name is Liz." The creature smiled and said, "Liz, every time you sneeze, something magical will happen." 

Liz smiled, thanked the creature and ran off, calling back, "I'll remember!" Whenever she sneezed, something magical and wonderful happened. Liz and her blue dress were very happy.

Once upon a time, there was a silly monkey named Max. Max lived in a big jungle with his friends. One day, Max went to the zoo and saw a lion. The lion was very big and Max was scared. 

Max learned that lions are not silly and can be dangerous. He decided to stay away from the lion's cage. But then, Max did something very silly. He stole a banana from the zookeeper and got caught. The zookeeper called the police and Max was taken to jail. 

Max was very sad and missed his friends. He learned his lesson and promised to never do anything silly again. The next day, Max was released from jail and went back to his jungle. He apologized to his friends and they forgave him. Max was happy to be back home and grateful for the lesson he learned.

Tim and Jen are friends. They like to play with cars and trucks. They have a big box of cars and trucks in their room. One day, they find a new toy in the box. It is a rocket. It is red and shiny. It has a button on the side.

"Wow, look at this!" Tim says. "It is a rocket. Maybe it can fly."

"Let me see!" Jen says. She takes the rocket from Tim. She pushes the button. Nothing happens.

"It does not work," Jen says. "It is broken."

"Maybe it needs fuel," Tim says. He remembers that his dad puts fuel in his car. He thinks fuel is a kind of water. He sees a bottle of water on the table. He takes the bottle and pours some water into the rocket.

"Stop!" Jen says. "That is not fuel. That is water. Water is not good for rockets. You will make it worse."

Tim does not listen. He pours more water into the rocket. He thinks he is helping. He pushes the button again. The rocket makes a loud noise. Smoke comes out of the rocket. The rocket flies out of Jen's hand. It hits the wall. It breaks into pieces.

"Look what you did!" Jen says. She is angry and sad. She liked the rocket. She wanted to play with it. Now it is gone.

"I am sorry," Tim says. He is scared and sorry. He did not mean to break the rocket. He wanted to make it fly.

"You should have trusted me," Jen says. "I told you water is not fuel. You should have listened. Now we have no rocket."

Tim and Jen are friends. But they are not happy. They learned a serious lesson. They learned to trust each other. They learned to be careful with toys. They learned that water is not fuel.

name_of_work: The Indian Serenade by Percy Bysshe Shelley
content: I arise from dreams of thee In the first sweet sleep of night, When the winds are breathing low, And the stars are shining bright: I arise from dreams of thee, And a spirit in my feet Hath led me--who knows how? To thy chamber window, Sweet! The wandering airs they faint On the dark, the silent stream-- The Champak odours fail Like sweet thoughts in a dream; The Nightingale's complaint, It dies upon her heart;-- As I must on thine, Oh, beloved as thou art! Oh lift me from the grass! I die! I faint! I fail! Let thy love in kisses rain On my lips and eyelids pale. My cheek is cold and white, alas! My heart beats loud and fast;-- Oh! press it to thine own again, Where it will break at last.

Once upon a time, there was an old lady. She had a plan to eat lunch with her friend. But then, something unexpected happened. Her friend had to delay their lunch for a little bit.

The old lady was very sad. She waited and waited for her friend. She just wanted to start eating lunch. Finally, the old lady saw her friend coming. They were so happy to see each other.

The old lady and her friend had a lot of fun at lunch. They talked, laughed, and ate lots of delicious food. It was the best lunch they ever had!

The old lady was glad that she didn't have to delay lunch anymore. They had a wonderful time together!

Once upon a time there was a girl who loved to smile. Every day she would wake up and smile at the sun before playing with her friends.

One day, the girl's family went to the stadium to watch a special show. Everyone was happy and they smiled when they saw all the big people. 

When they got to the stadium, they saw that some seats were still available. They quickly chose the best seats and sat down to enjoy the show. They could hardly contain their happiness when they saw the stage and the people in their costumes. 

The girl was so excited and couldn't stop smiling. She laughed and giggled with her friends throughout the show. Even when it was over, she still had a big smile on her face. 

It was a fantastic day and the girl was so happy she couldn't help but keep smiling. She had a smile on her face all the way home from the stadium.

name_of_work: I've Got an Apple Ready by John Walsh
content: My hair's tightly plaited; I've a bright blue bow; I don't want my breakfast, And now I must go. My satchel's on my shoulder; Nothing's out of place; And I've got an apple ready, Just in case. So it's 'Goodbye, Mother!' And off down the street! Briskly at first On pit-a-pat feet, But slow and more slow As I reach the tarred Trackway that runs By Hodson's Yard; For it's there sometimes Bill Craddock waits for me To snatch off my beret And throw it in a tree. Bill Craddock is leaning On Hodson's rails; Bill with thin hands And dirty nails; Bill with a front tooth Broken and bad; His dark eyes cruel, And somewhat sad. Often there are workmen, And then he doesn't dare; But this morning I feel He'll be there. At the corner he will pounce ... But quickly I'll say 'Hallo, Bill, have an apple!' - In an ordinary way. I'll push it in his hand And walk right on; And when I'm round the corner I'll run.

There was a family that went on an adventure together. Mom and Dad and their three year old son named Jake. As they drove along, Jake wondered what they would find.

Mom and Dad said, "We are going to a special walk today. We will meet some special animals!"

The family arrived at the park, and Jake was so excited. He couldn't wait to see all the animals. 

Mom and Dad said, "Look over there! Look at all the weird animals. Can you guess what they are?"

Jake looked around, but he didn't know what the animals were. He had never seen anything like them before. 

Father smiled and said, "They are called camels. And they are here to surprise us."

Jake was so excited to meet the camels. He couldn't wait to get closer and find out what they were like.
 
The family had a great time with the weird camels. Jake even got to ride on one of them! 

It was an adventure Jake never forgot, and he couldn't wait for the next time they would come together.
Whirl up, sea-- whirl your pointed pines, splash your great pines on our rocks, hurl your green over us, cover us with your pools of fir.

name_of_work: The Hour is Come by Louisa Lawson
content: How did she fight? She fought well. How did she light? Ah, she fell. Why did she fall? God, who knows all, Only can tell. Those she was fighting for -- they Surely would go to her? Nay! What of her pain! Their's is the gain. Ever the way. Will they not help her to rise If there is death in her eyes? Can you not see? She made them free. What if she dies ? Can we not help her? Oh, no! In her good fight it is so That all who work never must shirk Suff'ring and woe. But she'll not ever lie down - On her head, in the dust, is a crown Jewelled and bright, under whose light She'll rise alone.

Mia likes to draw with her crayons. She makes many images on the paper. She draws a sun, a flower, a cat and a house. She is very happy with her images.

But then, her baby brother Leo comes. He grabs a crayon and scribbles on Mia's paper. He makes a big mess. He does not care about Mia's images. He just laughs.

Mia is very angry. She shouts at Leo. "No, Leo, no! That is my paper! You ruined my images! Go away!"

Leo does not listen. He keeps scribbling. He thinks it is fun.

Mia runs to Mom. She cries and shows her paper. "Mom, look what Leo did! He wiped my images with his crayon! He is bad!"

Mom hugs Mia and wipes her tears. She says, "I'm sorry, Mia. Leo is just a little baby. He does not know how to draw. He does not understand that you worked hard on your images. He just wanted to play with you."

Mom takes another paper and gives it to Mia. She says, "Here, Mia. You can draw again. Make new images. And I will talk to Leo. I will teach him how to draw nicely. And how to share and be kind."

Mia smiles and says, "Thank you, Mom. I love you."

She takes the paper and the crayons. She goes back to her table. She draws new images. She is happy again.

Once upon a time, there lived a tall man. His name was Dad. Dad wanted to make some music. He suggested to his little boy that they could make a band. 

The little boy was very excited. He clapped his hands and jumped around. Dad said they would need instruments, so they went to the store to pick some up. They bought a drum, a guitar and a tambourine.

Back at home, Dad and the little boy started playing their music. Dad taught the little boy to use the drum and the guitar. The little boy also liked to jiggle the tambourine. Dad said it sounded really nice.

At the end of the day, the little boy was so happy. He thought making music with his Dad was lots of fun.

name_of_work: November by Elizabeth Drew Barstow Stoddard
content: Much have I spoken of the faded leaf; Long have I listened to the wailing wind, And watched it ploughing through the heavy clouds, For autumn charms my melancholy mind. When autumn comes, the poets sing a dirge: The year must perish; all the flowers are dead; The sheaves are gathered; and the mottled quail Runs in the stubble, but the lark has fled! Still, autumn ushers in the Christmas cheer, The holly-berries and the ivy-tree: They weave a chaplet for the Old Year's bier, These waiting mourners do not sing for me! I find sweet peace in depths of autumn woods, Where grow the ragged ferns and roughened moss; The naked, silent trees have taught me this,-- The loss of beauty is not always loss!

Once upon a time there were two friends, Chris and Jane. They lived together in a big house that had two rooms. 

One day, Chris asked Jane if he could open the door to the other room. Jane said yes, and Chris demanded that she open the door. Jane opened the door, and they both saw a big box inside. 

Chris demanded to open the box, but it was locked. Jane said that only a successful person could open the box. Chris was sad, but then Jane had an idea. 

She said, "I know a special code to open the box!" She whispered the secret code to Chris. Then he knew the number and he typed it in the lock on the box. 

The box opened, and the room was full of colorful toys! Chris and Jane were so excited that they jumped with joy.

The End.

Tom and Lily were twins who liked to explore. One day, they found a big hole in the fence of their backyard. They crawled through the hole and saw a jungle. The jungle had many trees, flowers, and animals. Tom and Lily were curious and wanted to see more.

"Let's go in the jungle!" Tom said.

"OK, but we have to be careful," Lily said.

They walked into the jungle, holding hands. They saw a monkey, a parrot, and a snake. They also saw a big cave. It was dark and gloomy inside.

"Let's go in the cave!" Tom said.

"No, it looks scary," Lily said.

"Don't be a baby, it will be fun," Tom said.

He let go of Lily's hand and ran into the cave. Lily was scared and sad. She waited for Tom to come back, but he did not. She heard a loud roar from the cave. She was very scared and ran back to the hole in the fence. She cried and cried.

Soon, Mom and Dad came home. They saw Lily crying and asked her what happened. Lily told them everything. They were very worried and angry. They ran to the jungle and looked for Tom. They heard the roar again and followed the sound. They found the cave and saw a big lion. The lion had Tom in his mouth. He was hurt and bleeding.

Mom and Dad shouted and threw rocks at the lion. The lion dropped Tom and ran away. Mom and Dad picked up Tom and hugged him. They carried him back to the house and called a doctor. The doctor came and fixed Tom's wounds. He said Tom would be OK, but he had to rest and take medicine.

Tom was sorry and ashamed. He said sorry to Lily, Mom, and Dad. He said he was wrong to go in the cave and not listen to Lily. He said he learned his lesson and would never do it again.

Lily forgave Tom and hugged him. She said she was glad he was OK. She said she loved him and would always be his sister.

Mom and Dad were happy and proud. They said they loved Tom and Lily and would always be their parents. They said they were glad Tom learned his lesson and hoped he would be more careful and respectful. They said they would fix the hole in the fence and keep the jungle away.

The end.

Moral value: The story teaches the value of listening to others, being careful, and respecting nature. It also shows the importance of family and forgiveness.

Lily and Tom were playing in the garden. They liked to imagine they were explorers in a jungle. They had a big stick for a sword and a hat for a helmet.

"Look, Tom, a spike!" Lily said, pointing to a rose bush. "Maybe it is a dragon's tail. We have to be careful."

Tom nodded. He wanted to be brave. He held his stick and approached the bush. He pretended to fight the dragon. He swung his stick and hit the spike.

"Ow!" Tom cried. He dropped his stick and held his hand. He saw blood on his finger. He felt pain and fear.

Lily ran to him. She saw his wound. She felt sorry and scared. She hugged him and said, "Don't cry, Tom. It's okay. You are not careless. You are a hero. Let's go to mom. She will make it better."

Once upon a time, there were two friends named Timmy and Sally. They loved to play together every day. One day, Timmy came to Sally's house wearing a mask. Sally asked, "Why are you wearing a mask, Timmy?" Timmy replied, "I'm pretending to be a superhero!"

Sally thought it was a friendly game and said, "I want to be a superhero too!" They played together for a while, but then they started to fight over who was the better superhero. Timmy said, "I'm stronger than you!" Sally replied, "No, I'm faster than you!"

Their fight got louder and louder until Sally's mom came in and said, "What's going on here?" They explained the game and how they were fighting over who was the better superhero. Sally's mom suggested they work together as a team instead of fighting.

Timmy and Sally agreed and decided to be friendly superheroes who work together to save the world. They went outside to play and save the day, side by side, wearing their masks and feeling like the best of friends. The end.

Once upon a time, in a small house, there was a little boy named Tom. Tom loved to play with his toy cars. One day, Tom found a box with matches in it. He knew that playing with matches was not safe. So, he asked his mom, "Mom, can I please play with these matches?"

His mom said, "No, Tom. Matches are not for playing. They can be very dangerous. Let's put them away where they belong." Tom listened to his mom and put the matches away.

That night, it was very dark outside. Tom was a little scared, but he remembered that matches could make a little light. He asked his mom, "Mom, can we please use a match to make a little light?" His mom smiled and said, "Yes, Tom. We can light a candle with a match, but I will do it for you." Tom felt safe and happy with the candle's light, and he went to sleep.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Rosa. Rosa was a bit nervous, but she was also curious. One day, she wanted to explore outside her house. She followed a path that led to a big house.

Suddenly, Rosa heard a sound that made her very jumpy. She saw a bathtub and something was moving inside! She was scared, but she also wanted to find out what it was. She stepped closer, and as she did so, a small creature appeared! It was a tiny mouse!

The mouse was so surprised to see Rosa. The mouse was a bit nervous too, but it was happy to have a new friend. The mouse revealed its name to Rosa - it was called Jane.

Rosa and Jane talked for a while and Rosa asked Jane what she liked to do. Jane said she liked to go swimming in the bathtub! Rosa was happy to hear it and she laughed and smiled with Jane. 

Rosa soon said goodbye to Jane and returned home. She was not as nervous as before and she felt excited to go back to the big house and explore again with her new friend.

name_of_work: The British (serves 60 Million) by Benjamin Zephaniah
content: Take some Picts, Celts and Silures And let them settle, Then overrun them with Roman conquerors. Remove the Romans after approximately 400 years Add lots of Norman French to some Angles, Saxons, Jutes and Vikings, then stir vigorously. Mix some hot Chileans, cool Jamaicans, Dominicans, Trinidadians and Bajans with some Ethiopians, Chinese, Vietnamese and Sudanese. Then take a blend of Somalians, Sri Lankans, Nigerians And Pakistanis, Combine with some Guyanese And turn up the heat. Sprinkle some fresh Indians, Malaysians, Bosnians, Iraqis and Bangladeshis together with some Afghans, Spanish, Turkish, Kurdish, Japanese And Palestinians Then add to the melting pot. Leave the ingredients to simmer. As they mix and blend allow their languages to flourish Binding them together with English. Allow time to be cool. Add some unity, understanding, and respect for the future, Serve with justice And enjoy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the sun. One day, she found a patch of flowers in her backyard. The flowers were so pretty and smelled so nice. Lily picked some and put them in a vase in her room. 

Later that day, Lily's mom came home from work. She saw the pretty flowers and asked Lily where she got them. Lily told her about the patch in the backyard. Her mom smiled and said, "You have such a good eye for pretty things, Lily." 

Lily was happy that her mom liked the flowers. She wanted to share them with her deaf neighbor, Mr. Brown. She knocked on his door and showed him the flowers. He couldn't hear her, but he smiled and nodded. Lily knew he liked them too.

Once upon a time, there was a little bird named Tweety. Tweety loved to whistle and sing all day long. One day, Tweety saw a worm moving with a lot of motion on the ground. Tweety felt uncomfortable because he thought the worm might get hurt.

Tweety flew down to the worm and said, "Hello, little worm. Are you okay?" The worm replied, "Yes, I am moving to find some food." Tweety felt happy and said, "That's great! I love to whistle while I fly. Would you like to sing with me?"

The worm replied, "I can't sing, but I can listen." Tweety whistled and sang, and the worm listened happily. Suddenly, a big cat appeared and chased Tweety. Tweety flew away quickly, but the cat caught him and ate him.

The moral of the story is that sometimes, even if we try to help others, we can still get hurt. It's important to be careful and stay safe.

Once upon a time, there was a happy little girl named Sally. Sally loved chocolate and enjoyed eating it every day.

One day, Sally found a chocolate bar in a box under her bed. She smiled and said, "Yay! Chocolate!"

She excitedly opened the wrapper and took a big bite. But, the chocolate was old and had started to rot.

Sally made a face and said, "Yuck! This chocolate tastes bad!"

Sally was not happy, but then she had an idea. She quickly found some marshmallows and a bowl. She mixed the marshmallows with the rotten chocolate and said, "Now it's yummy!"

Sally smiled as she ate her special treat. She was happy again!

name_of_work: His Return to London by Robert Herrick
content: From the dull confines of the drooping west To see the day spring from the pregnant east, Ravish'd in spirit, I come, nay more, I fly To thee, blest place of my nativity! Thus, thus with hallow'd foot I touch the ground, With thousand blessings by thy fortune crown'd. O fruitful genius! that bestowest here An everlasting plenty, year by year. O place! O people! Manners! fram'd to please All nations, customs, kindreds, languages! I am a free-born Roman; suffer then That I amongst you live a citizen. London my home is, though by hard fate sent Into a long and irksome banishment; Yet since call'd back, henceforward let me be, O native country, repossess'd by thee! For, rather than I'll to the west return, I'll beg of thee first here to have mine urn. Weak I am grown, and must in short time fall; Give thou my sacred relics burial.

Once upon a time, a little bunny hopped around in the meadow. He was looking for something to do, but there wasn't much to find. He kept hopping along until he came across a hammer. It was lying forgotten in the grass.

He was excited, but a tiny bit scared too. All of a sudden, it felt like something was watching him. He froze and looked around, but he couldn't see anything.

With a quivering voice, he said, "Hello? Is anyone there?"

But there was no answer. After a few moments of silence, he gathered up the courage to pick up the hammer. He hopped around, swinging the hammer into the air, learning all its secrets.

After a while, he got brave enough to use it to smash rocks into tiny pieces. He was so proud of himself. He carried the hammer home, knowing that he'd have lots of fun with it!

name_of_work: Abraham Lincoln Walks at Midnight by Vachel Lindsay
content: It is portentous, and a thing of state That here at midnight, in our little town A mourning figure walks, and will not rest, Near the old court-house pacing up and down. Or by his homestead, or in shadowed yards He lingers where his children used to play, Or through the market, on the well-worn stones He stalks until the dawn-stars burn away. A bronzed, lank man! His suit of ancient black, A famous high top-hat and plain worn shawl Make him the quaint great figure that men love, The prairie-lawyer, master of us all. He cannot sleep upon his hillside now. He is among us:--as in times before! And we who toss and lie awake for long Breathe deep, and start, to see him pass the door. His head is bowed. He thinks on men and kings. Yea, when the sick world cries, how can he sleep? Too many peasants fight, they know not why, Too many homesteads in black terror weep. The sins of all the war-lords burn his heart. He sees the dreadnaughts scouring every main. He carries on his shawl-wrapped shoulders now The bitterness, the folly and the pain. He cannot rest until a spirit-dawn Shall come;--the shining hope of Europe free; The league of sober folk, the Workers' Earth, Bringing long peace to Cornland, Alp and Sea. It breaks his heart that kings must murder still, That all his hours of travail here for men Seem yet in vain. And who will bring white peace That he may sleep upon his hill again?

Once upon a time, there was a smart cat who lived with a family of three. His name was Pat. Every day, Pat would go out to play. One day, he wanted to jump in the river, but he was scared of getting wet.

"Don't worry Pat," said Mommy, "I will help you stay dry." Mommy got a big towel and carefully put it around Pat. Pat was very happy and used his paws to help keep the towel shut around him.

After running and playing in the river, Pat was happy and dry! He thanked Mommy for her help. 

"You are so smart, Pat," said Mommy. Pat purred with pride and thanked her again. From that day on, Pat was never afraid to play in the river.

name_of_work: Dust If You Must by Rose Milligan
content: Dust if you must, but wouldn't it be better To paint a picture, or write a letter, Bake a cake, or plant a seed; Ponder the difference between want and need? Dust if you must, but there's not much time, With rivers to swim, and mountains to climb; Music to hear, and books to read; Friends to cherish, and life to lead. Dust if you must, but the world's out there With the sun in your eyes, and the wind in your hair; A flutter of snow, a shower of rain, This day will not come around again. Dust if you must, but bear in mind, Old age will come and it's not kind. And when you go (and go you must) You, yourself, will make more dust.

Once upon a time, there was a little dog named Max. Max liked to do many things like run, play, and bark. One day, Max was playing with his ball when he accidentally broke his tail. Max's tail hurt a lot and he couldn't do many of the things he loved anymore. Max's owner took him to the vet who fixed his broken tail. Max was very happy because he could do all the things he loved again.

In Singapore, in the airport, A darkness was ripped from my eyes. In the women's restroom, one compartment stood open. A woman knelt there, washing something in the white bowl. Disgust argued in my stomach and I felt, in my pocket, for my ticket. A poem should always have birds in it. Kingfishers, say, with their bold eyes and gaudy wings. Rivers are pleasant, and of course trees. A waterfall, or if that's not possible, a fountain rising and falling. A person wants to stand in a happy place, in a poem. When the woman turned I could not answer her face. Her beauty and her embarrassment struggled together, and neither could win. She smiled and I smiled. What kind of nonsense is this? Everybody needs a job. Yes, a person wants to stand in a happy place, in a poem. But first we must watch her as she stares down at her labor, which is dull enough. She is washing the tops of the airport ashtrays, as big as hubcaps, with a blue rag. Her small hands turn the metal, scrubbing and rinsing. She does not work slowly, nor quickly, like a river. Her dark hair is like the wing of a bird. I don't doubt for a moment that she loves her life. And I want her to rise up from the crust and the slop and fly down to the river. This probably won't happen. But maybe it will. If the world were only pain and logic, who would want it? Of course, it isn't. Neither do I mean anything miraculous, but only the light that can shine out of a life. I mean the way she unfolded and refolded the blue cloth, The way her smile was only for my sake; I mean the way this poem is filled with trees, and birds.

Jimmy was in the park with his mum. There were lots of things to do and see. He saw some children playing on a swing and wanted to join them. 

Mum said Jimmy could play but he had to be careful. Jimmy sat on the swing and started to swing. He felt happy and enjoyed it very much. 

Suddenly, He heard a shooting sound. It made him scared because he didn't know what it was. He quickly looked around the park to check where it came from. 

The sound had come from a big gun that an older boy was playing with. The gun was shooting small, mild plastic balls at a colourful target. 

Jimmy was still scared, but his mum told him that it was nothing to worry about. She said the gun only shot mild, harmless balls that can't hurt anyone. 

Jimmy was relieved and he felt much better. He went back to the swing and kept enjoying himself until it was time to go.

Sara was a jolly girl who liked to play outside. She had a big yard with many flowers and trees. She also had a toy house where she kept her dolls and books.

One day, Sara saw a rainbow in the sky. It was very bright and had many colors. Sara wanted to see it closer. She thought maybe there was a pot of gold at the end of the rainbow. She put on her boots and coat and ran outside.

She followed the rainbow across the yard, but it seemed to move away from her. She ran faster and faster, but she could not catch it. She did not see where she was going. She tripped over a rock and fell down. She scraped her knee and elbow and started to cry.

She heard a voice behind her. It was her dog, Spot. Spot was a good friend who always stayed with her. Spot licked her face and wagged his tail. He wanted to make her feel better. He also saw the rainbow and wanted to play with it.

Spot showed Sara how to crawl on the ground. He said it was fun and easy. He said they could pretend they were lions or bears or worms. Sara stopped crying and smiled. She crawled with Spot and made funny noises. They had a lot of fun.

Sara learned that the rainbow was not something she could touch or have. It was only a pretty thing to look at. She also learned that she should be careful where she ran and not chase things that were too far. She was happy that she had Spot, who was always there for her. She gave him a big hug and said thank you. They went back to the toy house and played with the dolls and books. They were jolly again.

Once upon a time there was a wide festival. All the people there were so happy and excited to be together. They played games and sang songs. 
At the end of the festival all the children got to watch a special show. It had bright lights and loud music and it was so much fun.
When the show finished all the children cheered with excitement. They ran around, hugged their friends and said goodbye. 
Finally it was time to go home. Everyone left with smiles on their faces and joy in their hearts. It had been the best day ever!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Emily. She was three years old and loved to learn about the world around her.

One day, Emily asked her mom to explain what a head was. Her mom smiled and thought for a moment. Then she said, "A head is the top part of your body. It has two eyes, a nose, and a mouth."

Emily smiled and ran off to play. A few minutes later, she wanted to know how to run fast. Again, her mom smiled and explained how to run. She said, "To run fast, you have to push your feet off the ground hard and pump your arms back and forth."

Emily listened carefully and practiced running with her arms and legs until she was running fast. She had so much fun running around. She thanked her mom for explaining these things to her and they shared a big hug. 

The end.

Once upon a time there was a mighty bear. He was a brave bear who loved to explore the world. But one day, disaster struck! He saw a little bird that had gotten stuck in a tree and he tried to rescue it. He climbed the tree and finally got to the bird. But, he was too big to fit in the tree and he couldn't get the bird out.

Suddenly, a giant sneaked up behind him! The giant was very hungry and wanted to eat the bear. He was about to grab the bear when the bear had a brainwave! He remembered he had a salad in his pocket. He quickly grabbed the salad and threw it to the giant. 

The giant was so happy he got his dinner that he quickly picked up the salad and ran away. But sadly, the bear could not rescue the little bird. And the bear had to go home all alone, sad that he could not save the little bird.

name_of_work: Anything Can Happen by Seamus Heaney
content: Anything can happen. You know how Jupiter Will mostly wait for clouds to gather head Before he hurls the lightning? Well, just now He galloped his thunder cart and his horses Across a clear blue sky. It shook the earth And the clogged underearth, the River Styx, The winding streams, the Atlantic shore itself. Anything can happen, the tallest towers Be overturned, those in high places daunted, Those overlooked regarded. Stropped-beak Fortune Swoops, making the air gasp, tearing the crest off one, Setting it down bleeding on the next. Ground gives. The heaven's weight Lifts up off Atlas like a kettle-lid. Capstones shift, nothing resettles right. Telluric ash and fire-spores boil away.

Tom is a hunter. He likes to take animals from the forest. He has a big gun and a big bag. He is not kind to the animals.

One day, he sees a rabbit. The rabbit is white and soft. Tom wants to take the rabbit. He points his gun at the rabbit. But the rabbit is creative. He has a plan.

The rabbit says to Tom, "Please do not take me. I have a friend who is bigger and better than me. He is in that hole. You can take him instead."

Tom is greedy. He thinks he can take two rabbits. He puts down his gun and his bag. He goes to the hole. He puts his head inside.

But there is no rabbit in the hole. There is a skunk. The skunk is angry. He sprays Tom with a bad smell. Tom screams and runs away.

The rabbit is happy. He takes Tom's bag and his gun. He gives them to the other animals in the forest. They are happy too. They thank the rabbit for being creative. They say, "You are a hero, rabbit. You saved us from the hunter."

Once upon a time there was a big gold box. It was heavy. Inside the box was something very special - a gold key. The key was so shiny that it sparkled in the sun. It was so pretty!

One day a little girl picked up the key and was surprised by how heavy it was. She took it outside where it shone even brighter. The sun made the gold sparkle in the light.

The little girl was so excited. She thought it was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen. She wanted to keep it forever. 

So she held the key tight in her hand and ran back inside to show it to her mommy. 

Mommy was so excited to see the shiny gold key. She said, "This treasure will make us very happy." Then she gave the little girl lots of hugs and kisses.

The little girl and her mommy kept the gold key safe forever. It shone and sparkled in the sun, making them both very happy.

I expected a quiet wedding high above a lost city a marriage to balance on my head like a forest of sticks, a pot of water. The ceremony tasted of nothing had little colour - guests arrived stealthy as sandalwood smugglers. When they opened their suitcases England spilled out. They scratched at my veil like beggars on a car window. I insisted my dowry was simple - a smile, a shadow, a whisper, my house an incredible structure of stiffened rags and bamboo. We travelled along roads with English names, my bridegroom and I. Our eyes changed colour like traffic-lights, so they said. The time was not ripe for us to view each other. We stared straight ahead as if we could see through mountains breathe life into new cities. I wanted to marry a country take up a river for a veil sing in the Jinnah Gardens hold up my dream, tricky as a snake-charmer's snake. Our thoughts half-submerged like buffaloes under dark water we turned and faced each other with turbulence and imprints like maps on our hands.

Once upon a time, there was a big party in the park. Everyone was happy and excited to see the fireworks. Suddenly, someone saw a firework that didn't look right. They shouted "alert" to warn everyone. People looked up and saw that the firework was going in the wrong direction. 

The firework went higher and higher until it reached the sky. Then, it exploded with a loud sound and bright lights. Everyone was amazed and happy to see the pretty colors. But soon, the fireworks ended and it was time to go home. The people said goodbye and left the park, feeling happy and tired from the fun night. The end.

name_of_work: Moments of Vision by Thomas Hardy
content: That mirror Which makes of men a transparency, Who holds that mirror And bids us such a breast-bared spectacle to see Of you and me? That mirror Whose magic penetrates like a dart, Who lifts that mirror And throws our mind back on us, and our heart, Until we start? That mirror Works well in these night hours of ache; Why in that mirror Are tincts we never see ourselves once take When the world is awake? That mirror Can test each mortal when unaware; Yea, that strange mirror May catch his last thoughts, whole life foul or fair, Reflecting it--where?

name_of_work: The Bean Eaters by Gwendolyn Brooks
content: They eat beans mostly, this old yellow pair. Dinner is a casual affair. Plain chipware on a plain and creaking wood, Tin flatware. Two who are Mostly Good. Two who have lived their day, But keep on putting on their clothes And putting things away. And remembering ... Remembering, with twinklings and twinges, As they lean over the beans in their rented back room that is full of beads and receipts and dolls and cloths, tobacco crumbs, vases and fringes.

I did not promise to stay with you till death do us part, or anything like that, so part I must, and quickly. There are things I cannot suffer any longer: Mother, you never, ever said a kind word or a thank-you for all the tedious chores I have done; Father, your breath smells like a camel's and gives me the hump; all you ever say is: 'Are you off in the cream puff, Lady Muck?' In this day and age? I would be better off in an orphanage. I want a divorce. There are parents in the world whose faces turn up to the light who speak in the soft murmur of rivers and never shout. There are parents who stroke their children's cheeks in the dead of night and sing in the colourful voices of rainbows, red to blue. These parents are not you. I never chose you. You are rough and wild, I don't want to be your child. All you do is shout and that's not right. I will file for divorce in the morning at first light.

Once upon a time, there was a happy girl named Lily. She loved to dance and did it every day. One day, Lily and her mommy went on a subway ride. Lily was so excited to see all the people and the big train.

As they were riding, Lily saw a man who looked sad. She smiled at him, but he didn't smile back. Lily's mommy told her that sometimes people have bad days and it's important to be kind and grateful for what we have.

Suddenly, the subway train stopped and everyone had to get off. Lily's mommy realized they were on the wrong train and they were lost. The man who looked sad before came to help them, but they couldn't find their way back home. Lily was sad because she missed her daddy and her bed. 

In the end, they had to stay on the subway all night long. Lily was grateful to have her mommy with her, but she was too tired to dance. She fell asleep and dreamed of finding her way back home.

name_of_work: How Soon Hath Time by John Milton
content: How soon hath Time, the subtle thief of youth, Stol'n on his wing my three-and-twentieth year! My hasting days fly on with full career, But my late spring no bud or blossom shew'th. Perhaps my semblance might deceive the truth That I to manhood am arriv'd so near; And inward ripeness doth much less appear, That some more timely-happy spirits endu'th. Yet be it less or more, or soon or slow, It shall be still in strictest measure ev'n To that same lot, however mean or high, Toward which Time leads me, and the will of Heav'n: All is, if I have grace to use it so As ever in my great Task-Master's eye.

name_of_work: I, Too, Sing America by Langston Hughes
content: I, too, sing America. I am the darker brother. They send me to eat in the kitchen When company comes, But I laugh, And eat well, And grow strong. Tomorrow, I'll be at the table When company comes. Nobody'll dare Say to me, "Eat in the kitchen," Then. Besides, They'll see how beautiful I am And be ashamed-- I, too, am America.

Once upon a time, there was an elderly man named Grandpa. He loved to play sport with his grandkids. One day, after playing, he said to his grandkids, "Let's go wash up before dinner." 

The grandkids agreed and they all went to the bathroom to wash their hands and faces. Grandpa reminded them to use soap and warm water to get rid of all the dirt.

After washing up, they all sat down for dinner. Grandpa told them stories about when he was young and played sport with his friends. The grandkids were amazed and asked lots of questions.

As they finished dinner, Grandpa said, "I had so much fun playing sport with you today. Let's do it again soon!" The grandkids cheered and hugged their grandpa, grateful for the fun day they had together.

name_of_work: The Clown's Wife by John Agard
content: About my husband, the clown, what could I say? On stage, he's a different person. Up there he's a king on a throne, but at home you should hear him moan. The moment he walks through that door without that red nose and them funny clothes, he seems to have the world on his shoulder. I do me best to cheer him up, poor soul. I juggle with eggs, I turn cartwheels, I tell jokes, I do me latest card trick, I even have a borrow of his red nose. But he doesn't say exactly how he feels, doesn't say what's bothering him inside. Just sits there saying almost to himself: 'O life, ah life, what would I do without this clown of a wife?'

Once upon a time, there was a little flower. It was very small and green, but it wanted to bloom. One day, the sun came out and shone on the flower. It felt warm and happy, and it started to bloom! The flower turned into a beautiful red and yellow flower.

One day, a friendly cow named Betsy came to visit the flower. Betsy loved to eat beef, but she was also very friendly. She saw the flower and said, "Oh, what a pretty flower! I won't eat you, because you are too pretty to eat." The flower was happy that Betsy was so friendly.

From that day on, Betsy came to visit the flower every day. They became good friends, and the flower was always happy to see Betsy. And every day, the flower continued to bloom and grow bigger and bigger.

Once upon a time there was a young girl named Sarah. One day Sarah went to the store to buy a present for her mom. She looked around to see what she wanted to buy. As Sarah looked around, she saw a box with a price on it. She looked at the price and thought she could afford it. 

"Oh, this is perfect!", she said to herself.

Sarah asked the store clerk for help. The clerk was very helpful and showed her how to pack the present. She followed the clerk's instructions and packed the box. 

Once Sarah had the box all packed up, she said goodbye to the clerk and went home with her present. When she got home, her mom was so happy with her present - it was just what she wanted! Sarah was glad she had found such a helpful clerk at the store.

Once upon a time, there was a lonely man who liked to sell things. One day, he had a big, pretty umbrella to sell. He went to the park to find someone who would like to buy it.

In the park, he saw a little girl playing with her ball. The man went to her and said, "Hi, little girl! Do you want to buy my big, pretty umbrella?" The little girl looked at the umbrella and said, "Yes, I want it! But I don't have any money." The lonely man felt sad for the girl and gave her the umbrella for free.

Soon, dark clouds came, and it started to rain. The little girl was happy to have the big, pretty umbrella. She shared it with the lonely man, and they both stayed dry. The man was not lonely anymore because he made a new friend. The moral of the story is that being kind and helping others can make us happy and not feel lonely.

name_of_work: A Thousand Martyrs by Aphra Behn
content: A thousand martyrs I have made, All sacrificed to my desire; A thousand beauties have betrayed, That languish in resistless fire. The untamed heart to hand I brought, And fixed the wild and wandering thought. I never vowed nor sighed in vain But both, though false, were well received. The fair are pleased to give us pain, And what they wish is soon believed. And though I talked of wounds and smart, Love's pleasures only touched my heart. Alone the glory and the spoil I always laughing bore away; The triumphs, without pain or toil, Without the hell, the heav'n of joy. And while I thus at random rove Despise the fools that whine for love.

Once there was a young pirate called Jack. He was determined to succeed and become the best pirate ever. He set sail with his crew and went on all kinds of exciting adventures.

Jack found a big treasure chest. But it was locked up tight. He used all his strength to try and open it, but he could not succeed. Suddenly he had an idea. He got his crew and they all pulled the chest together. With their combined strength they managed to open the chest and they uncovered a lot of treasure!

Jack was very excited. He took the treasure and shared it with his crew. He and his crew were so happy. Jack proved that even a young pirate like him could succeed in his mission.

Once upon a time, there was a family of three, a mom, dad and little girl. They were so excited when they moved into their new home. Dad said, "Let's explore!"

First, they went to the kitchen and saw a shiny new dishwasher. Dad said, "What's this?" Mom smiled and said, "It's a dishwasher! It's going to make washing dishes much easier!"
 
Little Girl looked at her parents and asked, "What does it include?" Mom said, "It includes buttons to press, soap and water! Let's try it." 

Dad pressed the buttons, and then they heard a loud whirring noise. Little Girl smiled. She liked the dishwasher already! She knew it was going to be a great part of their new home.
