name_of_work: A Psalm of Life by Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
content: What The Heart Of The Young Man Said To The Psalmist. Tell me not, in mournful numbers, Life is but an empty dream! For the soul is dead that slumbers, And things are not what they seem. Life is real! Life is earnest! And the grave is not its goal; Dust thou art, to dust returnest, Was not spoken of the soul. Not enjoyment, and not sorrow, Is our destined end or way; But to act, that each to-morrow Find us farther than to-day. Art is long, and Time is fleeting, And our hearts, though stout and brave, Still, like muffled drums, are beating Funeral marches to the grave. In the world's broad field of battle, In the bivouac of Life, Be not like dumb, driven cattle! Be a hero in the strife! Trust no Future, howe'er pleasant! Let the dead Past bury its dead! Act,-- act in the living Present! Heart within, and God o'erhead! Lives of great men all remind us We can make our lives sublime, And, departing, leave behind us Footprints on the sands of time; Footprints, that perhaps another, Sailing o'er life's solemn main, A forlorn and shipwrecked brother, Seeing, shall take heart again. Let us, then, be up and doing, With a heart for any fate; Still achieving, still pursuing, Learn to labor and to wait.

Anna and Ben are playing with blocks. They like to build towers and houses and bridges. Anna is very independent. She does not like to share or follow rules. Ben is more careful. He likes to make his blocks strong and balanced.

"Look at my tower!" Anna says. "It is the biggest and the best!"

Ben looks at Anna's tower. It is very tall, but it is also very wobbly. He thinks it will fall down soon.

"Your tower is too heavy," Ben says. "It will destroy itself."

Anna does not listen to Ben. She thinks he is jealous. She adds more blocks to her tower. She wants to make it even bigger and better.

"Stop!" Ben says. "You are making it worse!"

Anna ignores Ben. She puts one more block on top of her tower. But that is too much. The tower cannot hold the weight. It starts to shake and tilt. Then it crashes down. Blocks fly everywhere. Some hit Anna and Ben. They both cry.

"Ow! Ow! Ow!" Anna and Ben say.

Mom hears the noise and comes to see what happened. She sees the mess and the tears. She hugs Anna and Ben and helps them clean up.

"I'm sorry, Mom," Anna says. "I was trying to make a big tower, but I destroyed it."

"I'm sorry, too, Mom," Ben says. "I was trying to warn Anna, but she did not listen."

Mom smiles and kisses them. "It's okay, my loves," she says. "You can try again. But next time, remember to share and cooperate. Building together is more fun and more safe."

name_of_work: Say over again... (Sonnet 21) by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: Say over again, and yet once over again, That thou dost love me. Though the word repeated Should seem "a cuckoo-song," as thou dost treat it, Remember, never to the hill or plain, Valley and wood, without her cuckoo-strain Comes the fresh Spring in all her green completed. Beloved, I, amid the darkness greeted By a doubtful spirit-voice, in that doubt's pain Cry, "Speak once more--thou lovest!" Who can fear Too many stars, though each in heaven shall roll, Too many flowers, though each shall crown the year? Say thou dost love me, love me, love me--toll The silver iterance!--only minding, Dear, To love me also in silence with thy soul.

Sara and Ben were playing with their toy cars in the garden. They liked to make them go fast and make loud noises. Sara had a red car and Ben had a blue car. They pretended they were racing each other.

"Vroom, vroom, I'm faster than you!" Sara said.

"No, you're not, I'm faster than you!" Ben said.

They zoomed their cars around the grass and the flowers. They had fun, but they did not see the big dog that was watching them from the fence. The dog was hungry and angry. It wanted to play with the toy cars too.

The dog jumped over the fence and ran towards Sara and Ben. It barked and growled. Sara and Ben were scared. They dropped their cars and ran away. The dog picked up the red car in its mouth and shook it. It broke the car and spit it out. Then it saw the blue car and chased it.

"Help, help, the dog has my car!" Ben cried.

Sara ran to the house and knocked on the door. She hoped her mom or dad would hear her and come out. But they did not. They were busy inside. Sara did not know what to do. She wanted to help Ben, but she was afraid of the dog.

She saw a stick on the ground. She thought maybe she could use it to make the dog go away. She was brave and wise. She picked up the stick and ran back to the garden. She saw the dog biting the blue car and Ben lying on the ground. He was hurt. The dog had bitten his leg.

"Go away, bad dog, go away!" Sara shouted. She waved the stick at the dog. The dog saw her and dropped the blue car. It growled and ran towards her. It was bigger and stronger than her. It knocked her down and bit her arm.

Sara screamed and dropped the stick. She felt pain and fear. She wished her mom or dad would come and save her. But they did not. They did not hear her. They did not know what was happening. The dog kept biting her and Ben. They cried and cried. No one came to help them. The dog did not stop. The end.

name_of_work: A Minor Poet by Stephen Vincent Benet
content: I am a shell. From me you shall not hear The splendid tramplings of insistent drums, The orbed gold of the viol's voice that comes, Heavy with radiance, languorous and clear. Yet, if you hold me close against the ear, A dim, far whisper rises clamorously, The thunderous beat and passion of the sea, The slow surge of the tides that drown the mere. Others with subtle hands may pluck the strings, Making even Love in music audible, And earth one glory. I am but a shell That moves, not of itself, and moving sings; Leaving a fragrance, faint as wine new-shed, A tremulous murmur from great days long dead.

Once upon a time, there was a big surprise for Timmy. His mom said, "Tomorrow, we will go to the zoo." Timmy was very excited because he loved animals, especially elephants. He had a toy elephant that he played with every day.

The next day, Timmy and his mom went to the zoo. They walked around and saw many animals, but Timmy was waiting for the elephants. Finally, they arrived at the elephant exhibit. Timmy saw a big elephant with a long trunk. It was adorable! 

Suddenly, the elephant moved and something fell out of its mouth. Timmy's mom picked it up and said, "It's a key!" They looked around and saw a locked door. Timmy's mom said, "Let's see if the key can open the door." They tried the key and it worked! They opened the door and found a secret room with more adorable animals inside. Timmy was so happy and thanked the elephant for the surprise.

In summer when the Christmas beetles filled each day with thin brass shrilling, heat would wake you, lapping at the sheet, and drive you up and out into the glare to find the mulberry's sweet shade or watch ants marching underneath the guava tree. And in the house Mommy would start the daily ritual, whipping curtains closed, then shutters latched against the sun and when you crept in, thirsty, from the garden, the house would be a cool, dark cave, an enclave barricaded against light and carpeted with shadow, still except the kitchen where the door was open to nasturtiums flaming at the steps while on the stove the pressure cooker chugged in tandem with the steamy day. And in the evenings when the sun had settled and crickets started silvering the night, just home from school, smelling of chalk and sweat, Daddy would do his part of it, the checking, on the front verandah, of the scientific facts. Then if the temperature had dropped enough the stays were loosened and the house undressed for night. Even the front door wide now for the slightest breeze, a welcoming of all the season's scents, the jasmine, someone else's supper, and a neighbour's voice - out walking labradors, the only time of day for it, this time of year. How well the world was ordered then. These chill machines don't do it half as true, the loving regulation of the burning days. Somehow my judgment isn't quite as sure when faced with weather-signs. Let me come home to where you watch the skies and keep things right.

The gray path glided before me Through cool, green shadows; Little leaves hung in the soft air Like drowsy moths; A group of dark trees, gravely conferring, Made me conscious of the gaucherie of sound; Farther on, a slim lilac Drew me down to her on the warm grass. "How sweet is peace!" My serene heart said. Then, suddenly, in a curve of the road, Red tulips! A bright battalion, swaying, They marched with fluttering flags, And gay fifes playing! A swift flame leapt in my heart; I burned with passion; I was tainted with cruelty; I wanted to march in the wind, To tear the silence with gay music, And to slash the sober green Until it sobbed and bled. The tulips have found me out.

Once upon a time, there was a loud lion. Everywhere she went she liked to roar. One day she wanted to see what a church looked like, so she decided to visit one.

When she got there, the church was so quiet. All she could hear was the whistling of the wind. But the lion couldn't help herself. She opened her mouth and let out a big roar that echoed through the church.

The people in the church were surprised when they heard the lion's roar. They had never heard a roar in a church before! Everyone ran out of the church as fast as they could.

The lion was happy she had made such a loud noise in the church. From then on, she visited the church every day, just so she could roar.

Once upon a time, there was a dirty horse. The horse had many duties, such as carrying people and things from one place to another. He had to work hard all day long, but he barely ever got a rest. The horse was always tired, so he started to complain.

He complained to the people who used him. He said, "I'm hot and tired, can I please have a rest?" But the people just ignored him and kept walking.

He complained to the sun, asking why it shone so brightly. But the sun just kept shining. He complained to the rain, asking why it wouldn't come, but the rain still didn't come.

The horse was so tired and so hot, but no one seemed to care. He kept on asking, but no one ever listened. So the poor, tired, dirty horse had to keep on working until he finally got a rest.

Once upon a time, there was a deaf white dog who lived in a house with a family. His name was Fuzzy and he was very happy living with them. 

One day, Fuzzy went for a walk outside the house and got lost. He didn't know how to get back.

Fuzzy started to worry. He felt so far from where he belonged.

Suddenly, he saw an old lady. He barked at her and she asked: "Are you lost?"

Fuzzy nodded his head. The old lady smiled and said, "Don't worry. Just follow me and I'll help you find your way home."

Fuzzy followed the old lady and soon she took him back to his family. They were delighted to see Fuzzy safe again.

Fuzzy was glad to be back home where he belonged.

name_of_work: Farewell to Barn and Stack and Tree by A. E. Housman
content: "Farewell to barn and stack and tree, Farewell to Severn shore. Terence, look your last at me, For I come home no more. "The sun burns on the half-mown hill, By now the blood is dried; And Maurice amongst the hay lies still And my knife is in his side." "My mother thinks us long away; 'Tis time the field were mown. She had two sons at rising day, To-night she'll be alone." "And here's a bloody hand to shake, And oh, man, here's good-bye; We'll sweat no more on scythe and rake, My bloody hands and I." "I wish you strength to bring you pride, And a love to keep you clean, And I wish you luck, come Lammastide, At racing on the green." "Long for me the rick will wait, And long will wait the fold, And long will stand the empty plate, And dinner will be cold."

name_of_work: Glory of Women by Siegfried Sassoon
content: You love us when we're heroes, home on leave, Or wounded in a mentionable place. You worship decorations; you believe That chivalry redeems the war's disgrace. You make us shells. You listen with delight, By tales of dirt and danger fondly thrilled. You crown our distant ardours while we fight, And mourn our laurelled memories when we're killed. You can't believe that British troops "retire" When hell's last horror breaks them, and they run, Trampling the terrible corpses--blind with blood. O German mother dreaming by the fire, While you are knitting socks to send your son His face is trodden deeper in the mud.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved going to the beach with her family. She would run around and play in the sand and surf. 

One day, Lily found a shiny seashell that was different from all the others she had collected before. It had sharp edges and was very pretty. She showed it to her mommy and daddy and they were very proud of her. 

Lily decided to keep the seashell safe and put it in a special place in her room. Whenever she looked at it, she felt happy and remembered the fun day she spent at the beach with her family.

Once upon a time, there was a bunny named Hop. He lived in a big thick forest, and he loved to jump around and explore. But when winter came, the forest got cold and dark. All of the leaves on the trees turned black and blew away.

But still, Hop loved to hop around, even when it was cold and dark. He hopped up and down the hills, looking for something new to explore. He hopped through the trees, over logs, and around the streams.

Suddenly, one cold and dark winter day, Hop spotted something new. He hopped over to find a big, black bird. The bird was singing so quietly, it almost seemed like winter didn't exist. Hop hopped closer and watched the bird for a moment, before moving on.

He hopped around for the rest of the day, exploring all the new places the winter brought. He saw some foxes and rabbits, and the stars came out in the night. Hop had a wonderful time, despite the cold and darkness of winter.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her puzzles all day long. One day, Lily was playing with her puzzle when her friend Tom came to visit her. Tom said, "Can I play with you, Lily?"

Lily said, "Yes, you can play with me. But this puzzle is very hard, Tom. Are you sure you can do it?"

Tom said, "Yes, I can do it. I am very good at puzzles."

So, Lily and Tom started to play with the puzzle. They were having so much fun, but suddenly Lily noticed something strange. She said, "Tom, why did you freeze? Are you okay?"

Tom said, "Yes, I am okay. I just can't find the last piece of the puzzle. Can you help me?"

Lily said, "Sure, I can help you. Let's find it together." They looked for the last piece and finally found it. Tom was so happy and said, "Thank you, Lily. You are very modest." 

Lily smiled and said, "You're welcome, Tom. Let's play again soon." And they continued to play with their puzzle happily ever after.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Sue. Sue had a pretty skirt. She loved her skirt very much. Sue wore her skirt every day.

One day, Sue played in her room. She played with her toys. It was a boring day. Sue wanted to have more fun. She heard her mom talking on the phone in the next room. Sue thought, "I will go and talk to mom."

Sue walked to her mom. She said, "Mom, I am bored. Can we play?" Her mom said, "Not now, Sue. I am on the phone. Please do not disturb me." Sue felt sad. She went back to her room.

Sue put on her pretty skirt. She danced and twirled in her room. Sue felt happy again. She played with her toys and forgot about being bored. Sue learned that she could have fun all by herself.

One day Beatrice was playing in the park when she saw something very exciting. It was a microphone! She had always wanted to try singing into one.

Beatrice picked up the microphone and put it close to her lips. She sung a song and it was so loud it echoed in the park. She felt so proud of how she sounded.

Just then, she heard a voice on the other end of the microphone. It was a friendly voice asking Beatrice if the microphone fit in her hand. She said it did and she was very happy that the microphone felt just the right size.

The voice on the microphone thanked Beatrice for trying it out. She was so glad she got to have a go on the microphone. Beatrice held the microphone tight in her hands as she left the park feeling a great sense of accomplishment.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved ice-cream, it was his favorite treat. One day, Timmy's mom took him to the park and they saw an ice-cream truck. Timmy asked his mom if he could have some ice-cream, but his mom said he had to wait until after lunch.

Later that day, Timmy's mom surprised him with a big scoop of impressive ice-cream. Timmy was so happy and thanked his mom for the delicious treat. 

As Timmy was enjoying his ice-cream, he saw his friend Billy who looked sad. Timmy asked Billy what was wrong and Billy said he didn't have any money to buy ice-cream. Timmy remembered how happy he felt when he received his ice-cream and wanted to share that feeling with his friend. Timmy gave Billy some of his ice-cream and they both enjoyed it together.

The moral of the story is that it feels good to receive things, but it feels even better to share with others.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She lived in a house with a big roof. One day, Lily was playing outside when she saw a bird on her roof. She said, "Hello birdie, what are you doing up there?"

The bird replied, "I am looking for my friend. He is rude and he always flies away when I try to talk to him."

Lily asked, "Why is he rude?"

The bird said, "He thinks he is too important to talk to me. But I want to be his friend."

Lily thought for a moment and said, "Maybe he is just scared. You should try to be kind to him and maybe he will be your friend. And if he is too heavy, he might weigh down your wings."

The bird thanked Lily for her advice and flew away. From that day on, Lily always looked up at her roof, hoping to see the bird and his friend flying together.

name_of_work: The Secret Heart by Robert Coffin
content: Across the years he could recall His father one way best of all. In the stillest hour of night The boy awakened to a light. Half in dreams, he saw his sire With his great hands full of fire. The man had struck a match to see If his son slept peacefully. He held his palms each side the spark His love had kindled in the dark. His two hands were curved apart In the semblance of a heart. He wore, it seemed to his small son, A bare heart on his hidden one, A heart that gave out such a glow No son awake could bear to know. It showed a look upon a face Too tender for the day to trace. One instant, it lit all about, And then the secret heart went out. But it shone long enough for one To know that hands held up the sun.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Billy. He was very unhappy because he had a lot of worry. Billy had a tough time and he was very sad.

One day, Billy went to the park. He saw some kids playing games and he wanted to join them. He asked them to let him play, but they said no.

Billy was so sad that he started to cry. But then a nice lady came to him and gave him a hug. She said, "Don't worry. I have something special for you."

The lady took out a small pinch from her pocket. She said it was a magical pinch. Billy was excited and said, "What does it do?"

The lady smiled and said, "If you pinch someone with it, all your worries will go away. That's why I gave it to you!"

Billy smiled, thanked the lady and went off to play with the kids. Every time he felt scared or sad, he pinched himself with the magical pinch. Finally, he wasn't scared anymore and had lots of fun playing with his new friends.

Billy never had to worry again. With the magical pinch, he could make difficult times much easier.

O soft embalmer of the still midnight, Shutting, with careful fingers and benign, Our gloom-pleas'd eyes, embower'd from the light, Enshaded in forgetfulness divine: O soothest Sleep! if so it please thee, close In midst of this thine hymn my willing eyes, Or wait the "Amen," ere thy poppy throws Around my bed its lulling charities. Then save me, or the passed day will shine Upon my pillow, breeding many woes,-- Save me from curious Conscience, that still lords Its strength for darkness, burrowing like a mole; Turn the key deftly in the oiled wards, And seal the hushed Casket of my Soul.

Once upon a time there was a king who lived in a castle on top of a hill. He was very sad because he was worried.

He didn't have any friends because he was very rude. He shouted and yelled when anyone tried to talk to him.

One day a friendly princess came to visit him. Immediately, the king felt happier and less worried.

The princess and the king talked and talked and had lots of fun. The princess told him stories and they laughed together.

The king stopped being so rude and learned how to be polite. Everyone in the kingdom was glad to be friends with the king.

He was no longer worried and he lived happily with the princess in his castle on the hill. The end.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Emma who wanted to build a castle. She looked around for things that she could use and found some cords. She was so excited! She spent the morning gathering cords and building the castle.

Suddenly, the castle started to give way and the cords came undone. Emma started to feel sad, but then she remembered she was very persistent. She knew she could get it to work.

So, Emma started over again, more determined than ever. She worked hard and spent the whole day trying to build the castle. She put the cords in different places, tried out different things, and kept at it until she found a way to make it work.

Finally, after a lot of trying, Emma completed her castle! She was beaming with pride. She knew that if she kept being persistent, she could do anything.

Emma shouted, "I did it!" 

â€œYes, you did," said her mom, who was watching proudly. "You should always remember that if you keep trying, you can do anything!" 

Emma smiled and nodded, feeling very proud of herself. From then on, she never stopped being persistent.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved flowers and had a pretty garden. One day, she planted a seed and waited for it to bloom. She was so happy when it finally did!

But one day, Lily woke up to find that her flowers were gone. She was so sad and didn't know what to do. She went to the police station to tell them what happened.

The police listened to Lily and promised to help her find out who took her flowers. After a few days, they found the person who did it and made sure they never did it again. Lily was happy again and her flowers started to bloom once more.

name_of_work: The River-Merchant's Wife: A Letter by Ezra Pound
content: While my hair was still cut straight across my forehead I played about the front gate, pulling flowers. You came by on bamboo stilts, playing horse, You walked about my seat, playing with blue plums. And we went on living in the village of Chokan: Two small people, without dislike or suspicion. At fourteen I married My Lord you. I never laughed, being bashful. Lowering my head, I looked at the wall. Called to, a thousand times, I never looked back. At fifteen I stopped scowling, I desired my dust to be mingled with yours Forever and forever, and forever. Why should I climb the look out? At sixteen you departed You went into far Ku-to-en, by the river of swirling eddies, And you have been gone five months. The monkeys make sorrowful noise overhead. You dragged your feet when you went out. By the gate now, the moss is grown, the different mosses, Too deep to clear them away! The leaves fall early this autumn, in wind. The paired butterflies are already yellow with August Over the grass in the West garden; They hurt me. I grow older. If you are coming down through the narrows of the river Kiang, Please let me know beforehand, And I will come out to meet you As far as Cho-fu-Sa.

Once there was a little girl named Susie who loved butterflies. One day she was walking in the garden and she saw a broken butterfly. She gently picked it up and started to cry, because memories of her own broken wings came flooding back. She remembered how it felt when she was younger and didn't know how to fly.

Her mom saw her crying and came to hug her. She said, "Susie, why are you crying?"

"Mom, I don't know how to help this hurt butterfly," Susie said.

"Sometimes, even if we have broken wings, we still have the power to help others fly," her mom said.

So Susie tried her best to fix the broken wings of the butterfly and, with patience and love, she succeeded. That day Susie learned that even if we have been broken, we can still be a light for others and help them.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who lived in a small town. Every day she would hang around the town with her friends. One day, they went to the park to play. The little girl was so excited to be outside in the sunshine that she spun around and around until she was dizzy. 

The little girl and her friends laughed and laughed as she spun around and around. Suddenly, she got so dizzy that she couldn't stand. She hung onto a nearby tree so she wouldn't fall down. 

When the girl's spinning had stopped, her friends hugged her and helped her to walk home. The little girl felt like she was still spinning but she was happy to be back in her own town. From that day on, she never forgot the fun she had that day in the park and she was careful not to spin for too long - just in case she got dizzy again!

name_of_work: Waking Early Sunday Morning by Robert Lowell
content: O to break loose, like the chinook salmon jumping and falling back, nosing up to the impossible stone and bone-crushing waterfall - raw-jawed, weak-fleshed there, stopped by ten steps of the roaring ladder, and then to clear the top on the last try, alive enough to spawn and die. Stop, back off. The salmon breaks water, and now my body wakes to feel the unpolluted joy and criminal leisure of a boy - no rainbow smashing a dry fly in the white run is free as I, here squatting like a dragon on time's hoard before the day's begun! Fierce, fireless mind, running downhill. Look up and see the harbor fill: business as usual in eclipse goes down to the sea in ships - wake of refuse, dacron rope, bound for Bermuda or Good Hope, all bright before the morning watch the wine-dark hulls of yawl and ketch. I watch a glass of water wet with a fine fuzz of icy sweat, silvery colors touched with sky, serene in their neutrality - yet if I shift, or change my mood, I see some object made of wood, background behind it of brown grain, to darken it, but not to stain. O that the spirit could remain tinged but untarnished by its strain! Better dressed and stacking birch, or lost with the Faithful at Church - anywhere, but somewhere else! And now the new electric bells, clearly chiming, "Faith of our fathers," and now the congregation gathers. O Bible chopped and crucified in hymns we hear but do not read, none of the milder subtleties of grace or art will sweeten these stiff quatrains shoveled out four-square - they sing of peace, and preach despair; yet they gave darkness some control, and left a loophole for the soul. When will we see Him face to face? Each day, He shines through darker glass. In this small town where everything is known, I see His vanishing emblems, His white spire and flag- pole sticking out above the fog, like old white china doorknobs, sad, slight, useless things to calm the mad. Hammering military splendor, top-heavy Goliath in full armor - little redemption in the mass liquidations of their brass, elephant and phalanx moving with the times and still improving, when that kingdom hit the crash: a million foreskins stacked like trash ... Sing softer! But what if a new diminuendo brings no true tenderness, only restlessness, excess, the hunger for success, sanity or self-deception fixed and kicked by reckless caution, while we listen to the bells - anywhere, but somewhere else! O to break loose. All life's grandeur is something with a girl in summer ... elated as the President girdled by his establishment this Sunday morning, free to chaff his own thoughts with his bear-cuffed staff, swimming nude, unbuttoned, sick of his ghost-written rhetoric! No weekends for the gods now. Wars flicker, earth licks its open sores, fresh breakage, fresh promotions, chance assassinations, no advance. Only man thinning out his kind sounds through the Sabbath noon, the blind swipe of the pruner and his knife busy about the tree of life ... Pity the planet, all joy gone from this sweet volcanic cone; peace to our children when they fall in small war on the heels of small war - until the end of time to police the earth, a ghost orbiting forever lost in our monotonous sublime.

John was walking along the path by the river and suddenly came across an attractive bridge. He thought it was pretty and so he decided to mark it. He put his hands on the bridge and closed his eyes.

John focused all his energy and been to the bridge. Then, he opened his eyes and noticed a bright yellow mark on the bridge. It was so beautiful! He couldn't believe it.

John continued walking and kept thinking about how attractive the bridge was. The mark was still there and he felt so proud that he made it look even better.

John smiled as he thought about the bridge and kept walking. He wasn't sure what he had done but it was very special. And it was even more special to him because he had marked it.

Lila and Ben are friends. They like to play with toys. Lila has a doll and Ben has a car. They want to trade toys for a while.

"Can I have your car, Ben?" Lila asks.

"OK, but be careful. It is my favorite car," Ben says.

"Can I have your doll, Lila?" Ben asks.

"OK, but be gentle. She is my best friend," Lila says.

They trade toys and play happily. But then, Lila pushes the car too hard and it hits the wall. The car breaks. The wheel falls off.

"Oh no! I broke your car, Ben! I'm sorry!" Lila cries.

Ben runs to see his car. He is sad and angry.

"You broke my car, Lila! You are a bad friend!" Ben shouts.

Lila feels bad. She wants to fix the car. She looks for glue or tape. She finds some stickers.

"Maybe I can use these stickers to fix the car," Lila thinks.

She puts a sticker on the wheel and tries to stick it back to the car. But it does not work. The wheel falls off again.

"This is not working. The car is still broken," Lila says.

She gives the car back to Ben.

"Here, Ben. I'm sorry I broke your car. Can we trade back?" Lila asks.

Ben takes his car and looks at it. He sees the sticker on the wheel. He thinks it is funny.

"Hey, this sticker is cute. It has a star on it," Ben says.

He smiles a little.

"Maybe I can use another sticker to fix the car," Ben says.

He finds another sticker with a heart on it. He puts it on the other wheel.

"Look, Lila. Now my car has two stickers. It is a special car," Ben says.

He shows the car to Lila. Lila smiles too.

"That is a special car, Ben. It is a nice car," Lila says.

She gives the doll back to Ben.

"Here, Ben. Thank you for letting me play with your doll. She is a nice doll," Lila says.

Ben takes the doll and hugs it.

"Thank you for playing with my doll, Lila. She is a happy doll," Ben says.

They hug each other.

"We are still friends, right?" Lila asks.

"Of course we are. We are good friends," Ben says.

They play with their toys again. They are careful and gentle. They are happy and safe.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who wanted to remember to eat her vegetables. She had to choose between broccoli, carrots and radishes every day. The little girl had a favorite; radishes!

She loved the bright red color of the radishes and the crunchy taste. Every day, her mom made sure radishes were available for her. 

Every day, when the girl had her radishes, she would remember to be thankful. She was thankful for the radishes, the crunchiness and the color.

The little girl would remember to eat all her radishes so she would grow up to be strong and healthy. She would also always be thankful for the radishes that were available to her every day.

Once upon a time, there was a man who was bald. He lived in a house next to the sun, which was bright and yellow.

One day, the man decided he wanted to go out into the sun and enjoy the warmth. He grabbed a towel and wiped the sweat from his head.

Suddenly, something magical happened. As the man was wiping, his bald head began to sprout hair! The man was so surprised; his bald head had turned into a real head of hair. 

"Wow!" exclaimed the man. "What kind of magic is this?"

The sun, who had been watching the whole time, spoke loudly from up above.

"It's the magic of the sun, my friend. And it's in all of us. When we need a little help, all we have to do is wipe the sweat away and allow the sun to warm us up."

Once upon a time there was a wide green field. In this field there lived a very happy family. Every day the family would play games and have lots of fun.

One day the family decided to have a picnic in the wide green field. As they unpacked the rug to spread out the food, they noticed that one of the things they had brought was a big bowl of broccoli.

The Daddy said "Let's play a game. Whenever I say 'repeat', I want you to say 'broccoli'". So the family started to play the game - every time the Daddy said "repeat", they all shouted "broccoli". The game made them laugh and everyone had a lot of fun.

The children repeated the word so many times, they started to drool. The Daddy said "Just look at you all. You're like a bunch of little rabbits!" They all laughed and had a great time playing the game, again and again.

Once there was a little girl named Jane who loved to go outside and jog. One day as she was jogging, she saw a fly resting on a tree. Jane stopped and watched the fly. She thought it was so cool to see a fly sitting still.

Jane thoughtfully watched the fly for a while before she decided to take some time to play. She started to jog in a circle around the tree, with the fly flying around in circles too!

As she circled around the tree, Jane exclaimed: "Look at me fly!" She laughed as the fly flew around with her, it was like they were playing tag!

Jane joked and laughed as she continued to jog around the tree. She even took off her shoes and ran faster and faster, making the fly fly faster too! When she tired of the game, Jane thanked the fly for being such a thoughtful playmate, before she put her shoes on and jogged off.

When George's Grandmamma was told That George had been as good as gold, She promised in the afternoon To buy him an Immense BALLOON. And so she did; but when it came, It got into the candle flame, And being of a dangerous sort Exploded with a loud report! The lights went out! The windows broke! The room was filled with reeking smoke. And in the darkness shrieks and yells Were mingled with electric bells, And falling masonry and groans, And crunching, as of broken bones, And dreadful shrieks, when, worst of all, The house itself began to fall! It tottered, shuddering to and fro, Then crashed into the street below- Which happened to be Savile Row. When help arrived, among the dead Were Cousin Mary, Little Fred, The Footmen (both of them), the Groom, The man that cleaned the Billiard-Room, The Chaplain, and the Still-Room Maid. And I am dreadfully afraid That Monsieur Champignon, the Chef, Will now be permanently deaf- And both his aides are much the same; While George, who was in part to blame, Received, you will regret to hear, A nasty lump behind the ear. The moral is that little boys Should not be given dangerous toys.

name_of_work: Facing West From California's Shores by Walt Whitman
content: Facing west, from California's shores, Inquiring, tireless, seeking what is yet unfound, I, a child, very old, over waves, towards the house of maternity, the land of migrations, look afar, Look off the shores of my Western Sea--the circle almost circled; For, starting westward from Hindustan, from the vales of Kashmere, From Asia--from the north--from the God, the sage, and the hero, From the south--from the flowery peninsulas, and the spice islands; Long having wander'd since--round the earth having wander'd, Now I face home again--very pleas'd and joyous; (But where is what I started for, so long ago? And why is it yet unfound?)

Tom and Mia were friends who liked to play outside. They liked to run, jump, and climb on the grass and trees. One day, they saw a big bird with red and yellow feathers. It was flying in the sky, making loud noises.

"Wow, look at that bird!" Tom said. "It is so pretty and fast. I wish I could fly like that."

"Me too," Mia said. "Maybe we can fly if we try hard. Let's find something to help us fly."

They looked around and saw a big hill with a ramp at the top. There were some old bikes and boards lying on the ground. Tom and Mia ran to the hill and picked up a bike and a board. They put on some helmets and gloves that they found.

"Are you ready, Mia?" Tom asked.

"Yes, Tom. Let's fly!" Mia said.

They pushed the bike and the board up the hill. They reached the top and saw the bird flying over them. They smiled and got on the bike and the board. They pushed off the ramp and felt the wind in their hair.

"We are flying, Tom! We are flying!" Mia shouted.

"Yes, Mia! We are flying!" Tom shouted.

They felt happy and free. They looked down and saw the green grass and the flowers. They saw the other kids playing and waving at them. They saw the sun shining and the clouds moving. They saw the spring.

But they did not see the big tree in front of them. They did not see the branches and the leaves. They did not see the danger. They flew too fast and too high. They crashed into the tree and fell to the ground. They heard a loud bang and felt a lot of pain. They cried and screamed. They were hurt and scared.

The bird flew away and did not care. The other kids ran to help them and called for help. Tom and Mia wished they did not fly. They wished they stayed on the ground. They learned a hard lesson. Flying was not fun. Flying was bad.

One day, a raven saw a farmer work in his field. The raven was hungry and wanted to eat some of the farmer's corn. He flew down and landed on a scarecrow. He thought the scarecrow was a real person and said, "Hello, friend. Can I have some of your corn?"

The scarecrow did not answer, because it was not alive. The raven thought the scarecrow was rude and said, "Fine, then I will take some anyway." He pecked at the corn and filled his beak. He was about to fly away when he heard a loud noise. It was the farmer, who had seen the raven and shouted, "Hey, you! Stop stealing my corn!"

The raven was scared and tried to fly away, but his beak was too full. He dropped some of the corn and flew faster. The farmer ran after him and threw a stick at him. The stick hit the raven's wing and made him fall to the ground. The farmer caught the raven and said, "You are a bad bird. You should not take what is not yours. You should work for your food, like I do."

The raven felt sorry and said, "Please, let me go. I will not do it again. I will work for my food, like you do." The farmer looked at the raven and said, "How will you work for your food? You are a bird, not a farmer."

The raven thought for a moment and said, "I can sing for you. I have a beautiful voice. I can make you happy with my songs." The farmer smiled and said, "That is a good idea. You can sing for me and I will give you some corn. But you must promise to never steal from me again." The raven nodded and said, "I promise. Thank you for being kind to me." The farmer let the raven go and gave him some corn. The raven sang a happy song and flew away.

The moral of the story is: It is better to work for what you want than to steal from others. Stealing can get you into trouble and make you lose friends. Working can make you proud and earn you respect.

One day, two best friends were walking together. They were so happy to be together; they had so much fun. They were walking along a long road, when suddenly an urge to separate came to them. They stopped and looked at each other.

"Do you want to stay together?", one of them asked.

The other one nodded. "Yes, I do. I don't want to separate."

But the urge was so strong that the two friends had to part. They hugged and said goodbye. One of them started walking away. It felt like it was going to be a long time until they would see each other again. 

The two friends finally separated, but even though they had to go separate ways, their friendship stayed strong. They knew that one day, they would be together again.

What's that fluttering in the breeze? It's just a piece of cloth that brings a nation to its knees. What's that unfurling from a pole? It's just a piece of cloth That makes the guts of men grow bold. What's that rising over the tent? It's just a piece of cloth that dares the coward to relent. What's that flying across a field? It's just a piece of cloth that will outlive the blood you bleed. How can I possess such a cloth? Just ask for a flag my friend. Then blind your conscience to the end.

name_of_work: what if a much of a which of a wind by E.E. cummings
content: what if a much of a which of a wind gives truth to the summer's lie; bloodies with dizzying leaves the sun and yanks immortal stars awry? Blow king to beggar and queen to seem (blow friend to fiend:blow space to time) --when skies are hanged and oceans drowned, the single secret will still be man what if a keen of a lean wind flays screaming hills with sleet and snow: strangles valleys by ropes of thing and stifles forests in white ago? Blow hope to terror;blow seeing to blind (blow pity to envy and soul to mind) --whose hearts are mountains, roots are trees, it's they shall cry hello to the spring what if a dawn of a doom of a dream bites this universe in two, peels forever out of his grave and sprinkles nowhere with me and you? Blow soon to never and never to twice (blow life to isn't: blow death to was) --all nothing's only our hugest home; the most who die,the more we live

name_of_work: Monologue for an Onion by Suji Kwock Kim
content: I don't mean to make you cry. I mean nothing, but this has not kept you From peeling away my body, layer by layer, The tears clouding your eyes as the table fills With husks, cut flesh, all the debris of pursuit. Poor deluded human: you seek my heart. Hunt all you want. Beneath each skin of mine Lies another skin: I am pure onion--pure union Of outside and in, surface and secret core. Look at you, chopping and weeping. Idiot. Is this the way you go through life, your mind A stopless knife, driven by your fantasy of truth, Of lasting union--slashing away skin after skin From things, ruin and tears your only signs Of progress? Enough is enough. You must not grieve that the world is glimpsed Through veils. How else can it be seen? How will you rip away the veil of the eye, the veil That you are, you who want to grasp the heart Of things, hungry to know where meaning Lies. Taste what you hold in your hands: onion-juice, Yellow peels, my stinging shreds. You are the one In pieces. Whatever you meant to love, in meaning to You changed yourself: you are not who you are, Your soul cut moment to moment by a blade Of fresh desire, the ground sown with abandoned skins. And at your inmost circle, what? A core that is Not one. Poor fool, you are divided at the heart, Lost in its maze of chambers, blood, and love, A heart that will one day beat you to death.

name_of_work: I wish I could remember that first day by Christina Rossetti
content: I wish I could remember that first day, First hour, first moment of your meeting me, If bright or dim the season, it might be Summer or Winter for aught I can say; So unrecorded did it slip away, So blind was I to see and to foresee, So dull to mark the budding of my tree That would not blossom yet for many a May. If only I could recollect it, such A day of days! I let it come and go As traceless as a thaw of bygone snow; It seemed to mean so little, meant so much; If only now I could recall that touch, First touch of hand in hand - Did one but know!

name_of_work: We Should Make a Documentary About Spades by Terrance Hayes
content: And here is all we'll need: a card deck, quartets of sun people Of the sort found in black college dormitories, some vintage Music, indiscriminate spirits, fried chicken, some paper, A writing utensil, and a bottomless Saturday. We should explore The origins of a derogatory word like spade as well as the word For feeling alone in polite company. And also the implications Of calling someone who is not your brother or sister, Brother or Sister. So little is known of our past, we can imagine Damn near anything. When I say maybe slaves held Spades Tournaments on the anti-cruise ships bound for the Colonies, You say when our ancestors were cooped on those ships They were not yet slaves. Our groundbreaking film should begin With a low-lit den in the Deep South and the deep fried voice Of somebody's grandmother holding smoke in her mouth As she says, "The two of Diamonds trumps the two of Spades In my house." And at some point someone should tell the story Where Jesus and the devil are Spades partners traveling The juke joints of the 1930s. We could interview my uncle Junior And definitely your skinny cousin Mary and any black man Sitting at a card table wearing shades. Who do you suppose Would win if Booker T and MLK were matched against Du Bois And Malcolm X in a game of Spades? You say don't talk Across the table. Pay attention to the suits being played. The object of the game is to communicate invisibly With your teammate. I should concentrate. Do you suppose We are here because we are lonely in some acute diasporafied Way? This should be explored in our film about Spades. Because it is one of the ways I am still learning what it is To be black, tonight I am ready to master Spades. Four players Bid a number of books. Each team adds the bids Of the two partners, and the total is the number of books That team must try to win. Is that not right? This is a game That tests the boundary between mathematics and magic, If you ask me. A bid must be intuitive like the itchiness Of the your upper lip before you sip strange whiskey. My mother did not drink, which is how I knew something Was wrong with her, but she held a dry spot at the table When couples came to play. It's a scene from my history, But this probably should not be mentioned in our documentary About Spades. Renege is akin to the word for the shame You feel watching someone else's humiliation. Slapping A card down must be as dramatic as hitting the face of a drum With your palm, not hitting the face of a drum with a drumstick. You say there may be the sort of outrage induced By liquor, trash talk, and poor strategy, but it will fade The way a watermark left on a table by a cold glass fades. I suspect winning this sort of game makes you feel godly. I'm good and ready for who ever we're playing Against tonight. I am trying to imagine our enemy. I know you are not my enemy. You say there are no enemies In Spades. Spades is a game our enemies do not play.

name_of_work: Halfway Down by A. A. Milne
content: Halfway down the stairs is a stair where i sit. there isn't any other stair quite like it. i'm not at the bottom, i'm not at the top; so this is the stair where I always stop. Halfway up the stairs Isn't up And it isn't down. It isn't in the nursery, It isn't in town. And all sorts of funny thoughts Run round my head. It isn't really Anywhere! It's somewhere else Instead!

name_of_work: Autumn Begins in Martins Ferry, Ohio by James Wright
content: In the Shreve High football stadium, I think of Polacks nursing long beers in Tiltonsville, And gray faces of Negroes in the blast furnace at Benwood, And the ruptured night watchman of Wheeling Steel, Dreaming of heroes. All the proud fathers are ashamed to go home. Their women cluck like starved pullets, Dying for love. Therefore, Their sons grow suicidally beautiful At the beginning of October, And gallop terribly against each other's bodies.

Once upon a time there was a little girl called Mary. She had a small, blue purse. She was very proud of her purse and would take it everywhere.

One day she took her purse to the park. She went to the park with her mom. While running around and playing, Mary accidentally dropped her purse on the ground. It was so blue and easy to miss.

Mary's mom said, "Oh no! I think you dropped your purse, Mary!"

Mary felt upset and started to cry. She said, "My purse! It's gone forever!"

But then her mom said, "Look! I can see it over there. I can mark it with this blue stick."

So Mary's mom marked the purse with the blue stick. Then Mary was very happy.

"Is that my purse? Is it really my purse?" she said with a smile.

Her mom smiled and said, "Yes, that's your purse. You found it!"

Mary hugged her purse tight and never let it go. She was so glad that she had found it. She was no longer upset.

Once upon a time there was a girl named Jenny. She loved to dive off the rocks in a big lake by her house. She was so delighted when she had learnt how to do it. 

One day, Jenny took a big dive into the lake. But this time, she fell and hurt her foot. She cried out in pain and reached for help. Her dad heard and ran towards her. 

He picked her up and took her to the hospital. Jenny was scared, but the nurses and doctors were so nice to her. They patched up her foot and soon she was feeling better. 

When she got home, Jenny was so grateful for all the help that she received. She promised herself that she would dive more carefully next time. 

The end.

Just then, a voice called out, "I can help you with that note!" It was his friend, Sam.

"Can you help me put it back together? I want to know what it says," said Jack.

Sam said, "Sure, I will try! Let's see if we can put the pieces together."

They had to fit all the pieces back together. Finally, they did it! They had fixed the note. 
It said, â€œHave fun at the park today.â€

Jack was very happy. He hugged Sam and said, "Thank you, you're the best!" 

The two of them went and had lots of fun in the park.

Once upon a time there was a big walk. It was full of things that a little girl wanted to do. 

One day, the girl's friend, a little boy, came to join the walk. The little girl was so excited to have a friend to join her in the big walk.

The friend asked, "What shall we do?"

The little girl said, "Let's fill up our buckets with water and have a race!"

The friend was a bit hesitant. He said, "But your bucket is much bigger than mine!"

The little girl laughed and said, "It's okay, just fill it up as much as you can. I will fill up my bucket slowly so you can catch up."

The little boy smiled and did as the little girl said. The two friends filled up their buckets and had a great race. After that, they continued their big walk, filled with games and lots of laughs.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily who loved to play games. She had a special game called chess that she really liked to play. It was a game with lots of pieces and rules, but Lily was very smart and organized, so she always won.

One day, Lily's friend Timmy came over to play. He saw the chess game and wanted to play too. Lily was happy to share her game, but she knew that Timmy didn't know how to play chess. So, she decided to teach him.

Lily showed Timmy how to move the pieces and explained the rules. At first, Timmy was confused, but Lily was patient and helped him understand. Soon, they were playing a real game of chess together. Lily was happy that she could share her favorite game with her friend.

name_of_work: Who Said It Was Simple by Audre Lorde
content: There are so many roots to the tree of anger that sometimes the branches shatter before they bear. Sitting in Nedicks the women rally before they march discussing the problematic girls they hire to make them free. An almost white counterman passes a waiting brother to serve them first and the ladies neither notice nor reject the slighter pleasures of their slavery. But I who am bound by my mirror as well as my bed see causes in colour as well as sex and sit here wondering which me will survive all these liberations.

name_of_work: The Willing Mistress by Aphra Behn
content: Amyntas led me to a Grove, Where all the Trees did shade us; The Sun it self, though it had Strove, It could not have betray'd us: The place secur'd from humane Eyes, No other fear allows. But when the Winds that gently rise, Doe Kiss the yielding Boughs. Down there we satt upon the Moss, And id begin to play A Thousand Amorous Tricks, to pass The heat of all the day. A many Kisses he did give: And I return'd the same Which made me willing to receive That which I dare not name. His Charming Eyes no Aid requir'd To tell their softning Tale; On her that was already fir'd 'Twas easy to prevaile. He did but Kiss and Clasp me round, Whilst those his thoughts Exprest: And lay'd me gently on the Ground; Ah who can guess the rest?

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Tilly. She liked to bathe in the river and pretend she could swim. One day, when she was bathing, she found a broken triangle in the water. She couldn't understand why anyone would throw such a strange thing in the river.

Tilly decided to take the triangle home with her so she could have a closer look. When she got back, she looked at the triangle closely, but it was so broken, she still couldn't figure out what it was. 

Tilly wanted to keep the triangle safe, so she put it up high. But a few days later when she went to look for it, it was gone! Instead, she found the broken triangle pieces scattered all over the ground!

Tilly was sad and disappointed, she had so wanted to find out what the triangle was. Now, it was completely ruined and she could never figure out what it was. 

Tilly had lost her broken triangle.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She loved her pretty skirt that twirled around when she spun. One day, she went to the park with her mom and saw a butterfly. She was so excited and started to run after it. 

Suddenly, the wind blew and her skirt flew up! Lily was embarrassed and wanted to shut her eyes. But her mom said it was okay and helped her fix her skirt. Lily felt better and continued to chase the butterfly. 

When it was time to go home, Lily was sad to leave the park but happy to have had a fun day. She went to bed that night dreaming of twirling in her skirt and chasing butterflies again.

Once there was a girl called Susie. She was very brave and loved to play. One day her parents said she was going to play a game. The game was called Operation. 

They all sat down at the table and Susie looked at the game. It looked tricky but Susie was excited to try. She tried to use the special tool that came with the game, but she was clumsy and it didn't work. 

But Susie wouldn't give up. After a few tries she got better. She was careful and patient and soon enough she was doing really well. 

At the end of the game, Susie won! Everyone cheered and clapped. Susie was delighted and so proud to have won. 

From then on, Susie wanted to play Operation every day. With a bit of practice, Susie eventually became an Operation expert!

One day, Betty and her Dad decided to go on a special trip. They took a car to a unique factory. When they got there, Betty and her Dad saw so many things that were interesting. 

"What do you think, Betty?" asked the Dad.

"It's so cool," said Betty. 

They walked to a special place in the factory, and Dad said, "Let's all pray!"

Betty, Dad and all the other people in the factory joined together in prayer. Dad was smiling, and Betty felt happy.

When the prayer finished, Dad hugged Betty and said, "That was a special prayer. We are so lucky to share it together. Now let's explore the factory!"

Betty agreed and they set out to explore the unique factory.

Once upon a time there was a clever fox. He was playing in a meadow when he suddenly saw a log. He wondered what he could do with it. He wanted to play and have fun.

He decided to bite the log. He sank his teeth into the log and bit and bit. He was surprised that it was so hard and solid. He kept biting and eventually he got through it.

He saw something inside. It was a shiny coin! The fox was so excited that he had found it.

He went to a friend and shows the coin. His friend said, "That's clever! Where did you find it?"

The fox said, "I found it inside a log. I bit the log until I got through and there it was!" 

His friend said, "Wow, you're really clever. That coin could buy us lots of treats. Think of all the fun we can have with it!" 

The two friends decided to use the coin to buy food and they enjoyed a feast together. The clever fox was happy that he had bitten the log!

Once upon a time, there was a little boy. He was walking in the park and everyone he met said hello to him.

One day he saw a big dog in the park. The boy wanted to play with the dog, but it was barking very loudly. The boy thought it was too noisy and his opinion was to pass on playing with the dog.

But then the dog's owner called out to the boy, "Come over and give my dog some love!" The little boy was very scared, but the owner talked very kindly so in the end the boy decided to come over.

The little boy started to pet the dog and it stopped barking. He was very happy and thought, "My opinion was wrong, this dog is not so noisy after all."

But then the dog bit the boy. Everyone was very scared and the little boy had to go to the hospital.

The moral of the story is that sometimes others know better than you. We should always listen to what others say and not be too quick to ignore their opinion.

Once upon a time, there was a cherry tree in Grandma and Grandpa's garden. Every day, Grandma would pick the cherries and cover them in a big bowl. 

One day, it was very hot. The cherries were so dry that Grandma was worried about them. She wanted to find a way to keep them cool. 

Grandma got a big piece of cloth and covered the cherries with it. It was big enough to make a nice shade over the cherries and keep them cool. 

Grandpa was so happy with Grandma's idea. He said that the cherries were much better now that they were covered and shaded. 

From then on, every day when it was hot, Grandma and Grandpa would cover the cherries with the cloth. They kept the cherries cool, and soon they were as juicy and sweet as ever.

name_of_work: Don't Go Far Off by Pablo Neruda
content: Don't go far off, not even for a day, because -- because -- I don't know how to say it: a day is long and I will be waiting for you, as in an empty station when the trains are parked off somewhere else, asleep. Don't leave me, even for an hour, because then the little drops of anguish will all run together, the smoke that roams looking for a home will drift into me, choking my lost heart. Oh, may your silhouette never dissolve on the beach; may your eyelids never flutter into the empty distance. Don't leave me for a second, my dearest, because in that moment you'll have gone so far I'll wander mazily over all the earth, asking, Will you come back? Will you leave me here, dying?

There was a pale squirrel named Tim. Tim loved to eat nuts. One day, Tim saw a big nut high in a tree. Tim wanted to get the nut, but it was too high.

Tim thought, "I can stretch to get the nut!" Tim climbed the tree and stretched his arm out. He reached for the nut, but he still could not get it.

Then, Tim's friend, a bird, saw Tim. The bird flew up and got the nut for Tim. Tim was happy and said, "Thank you, bird!" They both ate the nut and played together.

name_of_work: Everywhere Is Out of Town by Kevin Young
content: Beanville. Tea party. Five black cats & a white boy. Chitlin circuit. Gravy-colored suits, preacher stripes. Didn't know you could buy muttonchops these days. Afros. Horns slung round necks like giant ladles. Dressing. Uptempo blessing: Good God everywhere! We bow our heads before the band lets loose. Drummer unknown as a hymn's third verse. Older woman pushes toward the front, catching the spirit like the crazy lady at church six scotches later. Communion breath. Hands waving. Sweaty face rags, post-sermon mop, suicidal white girls crying like the newly baptized. All that water. Play it. Swing it. Be suggestive. Request "Chicken" & "Pass the Peas" like we used to say. Have mercy! Thanksgiving's back in town & we're all crammed in the club white as the walls of a church basement. Feet impatient as forks. Only ten bucks a plate for this leftover band. Thigh, drumsticks, neck. Dark meat.

name_of_work: The Dying Child by John Clare
content: He could not die when trees were green, For he loved the time too well. His little hands, when flowers were seen, Were held for the bluebell, As he was carried o'er the green. His eye glanced at the white-nosed bee; He knew those children of the spring: When he was well and on the lea He held one in his hands to sing, Which filled his heart with glee. Infants, the children of the spring! How can an infant die When butterflies are on the wing, Green grass, and such a sky? How can they die at spring? He held his hands for daisies white, And then for violets blue, And took them all to bed at night That in the green fields grew, As childhood's sweet delight. And then he shut his little eyes, And flowers would notice not; Birds' nests and eggs caused no surprise, He now no blossoms got; They met with plaintive sighs. When winter came and blasts did sigh, And bare were plain and tree, As he for ease in bed did lie His soul seemed with the free, He died so quietly.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and her dog, Max. One day, her mom gave her a candle to hold. It was hard to hold because it was hot. 

Lily's mom said, "Lily, you can hold the candle, but you cannot light it. It's not safe for you." Lily nodded her head and understood. She was happy to be allowed to hold the candle, even though she couldn't light it. 

Later that night, Lily's mom lit the candle and put it on the table. Lily watched the flame dance and flicker. She was happy that her mom allowed her to hold the candle earlier, even though it was hard to hold. She went to bed with a smile on her face, dreaming of all the fun toys she would play with tomorrow. The end.

Once there was a boy named Jack. Jack loved pictures and always carried one in his pocket. Jack also had a very selfish nature. He was always thinking of himself first and no one else.

One day Jack saw a very special picture that he wanted to have. It was an amazing picture of a tree in a field. Jack knew he had to have it so he asked the owner to sell it to him. The owner refused and said it was too special to sell. This made Jack very angry.

Jack remembered a plan to get what he wanted so he snuck up to the window of the owner. He peeked inside and saw that the owner had put down the picture. Jack grabbed it quickly and ran away quickly.

The owner followed and called out for help. Soon, a lot of people were chasing Jack. He ran away and hid in a dark alley. But he was so selfish that he wouldn't give back the picture. Once upon a time there was a jolly girl named Jane. Jane did not believe in magic but one day that changed! The magic happened when she stepped on a print on the ground. Jane was so excited she spun in a circle and smiled.

Once upon a time, there was a mule. The mule was very strong and could carry heavy things. One day, the mule wanted to go for a walk by himself. He did not want anyone to come with him. He was very independent.

As the mule was walking, he met a little girl. The little girl wanted to talk to the mule, but the mule did not speak. The little girl kept talking to the mule, and finally, the mule spoke! The little girl was very happy and they became friends.

From that day on, the mule was not so independent anymore. He liked having friends to talk to. The little girl would visit him every day and they would talk about the things they saw on their walks. The mule was very happy to have a friend.

Father, when he passed on, left dust on a table of papers, left debts and daughters, a bedwetting grandson named by the toss of a coin after him, a house that leaned slowly through our growing years on a bent coconut tree in the yard. Being the burning type, he burned properly at the cremation as before, easily and at both ends, left his eye coins in the ashes that didn't look one bit different, several spinal discs, rough, some burned to coal, for sons to pick gingerly and throw as the priest said, facing east where three rivers met near the railway station; no longstanding headstone with his full name and two dates to holdin their parentheses everything he didn't quite manage to do himself, like his caesarian birth in a brahmin ghetto and his death by heartfailure in the fruit market. But someone told me he got two lines in an inside column of a Madras newspaper sold by the kilo exactly four weeks later to streethawkers who sell it in turn to the small groceries where I buy salt, coriander, and jaggery in newspaper cones that I usually read for fun, and lately in the hope of finding these obituary lines. And he left us a changed mother and more than one annual ritual.

Once upon a time there was an oyster who lived in the sea. She was an independent oyster who liked to do things her own way.

One day, the oyster left her home and ventured to a new place. She was excited to try something new and see what happened. She explored the new reef and encountered several other sea creatures.

The oyster got to know the creatures, and soon she found that the reef was full of tasty treats. She wanted to try them all, so she worked hard to search the reef for more.

The oyster was persistent and soon her efforts began to yield results! She found lots of delicious things that she hadn't seen before. She gathered them all in her shell and returned home, happy and full.

The oyster had discovered a treasure trove of goodies and was proud of her independence and all her hard work. She would come back to the reef every day, yielding something new each time!

name_of_work: The War Horse by Eavan Boland
content: This dry night, nothing unusual About the clip, clop, casual Iron of his shoes as he stamps death Like a mint on the innocent coinage of earth. I lift the window, watch the ambling feather Of hock and fetlock, loosed from its daily tether In the tinker camp on the Enniskerry Road, Pass, his breath hissing, his snuffling head Down. He is gone. No great harm is done. Only a leaf of our laurel hedge is torn-- Of distant interest like a maimed limb, Only a rose which now will never climb The stone of our house, expendable, a mere Line of defence against him, a volunteer You might say, only a crocus, its bulbous head Blown from growth, one of the screamless dead. But we, we are safe, our unformed fear Of fierce commitment gone; why should we care If a rose, a hedge, a crocus are uprooted Like corpses, remote, crushed, mutilated? He stumbles on like a rumour of war, huge Threatening. Neighbours use the subterfuge Of curtains. He stumbles down our short street Thankfully passing us. I pause, wait, Then to breathe relief lean on the sill And for a second only my blood is still With atavism. That rose he smashed frays Ribboned across our hedge, recalling days Of burned countryside, illicit braid: A cause ruined before, a world betrayed.

name_of_work: Childhood in Heidelberg by Andries Walter Oliphant
content: I was born in a house where ancestors were suspended from the walls. On hot afternoons they would descend and walk silently through the cool passages of the dark house, slowly as if strolling through a womb. The roof is a vantage point for birds and pigeons. On the stoep in an ancient folding chair my name-sake sits. there is a giant gumtree at the gate in which the sun sets. The stars are candles which my grandmother has lit. Every morning father wakes to find a man with a hole in his head sleeping in the drift sand of the furrow which runs along the creosoted split-pole fence. I go in search of the orchestra of crickets. In the kitchen mother cries as she turns the toast on the black plates of the Welcome Dover. When father packed my pigeons into boxes, I ended up with Rover and the cats on the back of a truck with all the household goods. I thought, if this is part of life, it's fun. At the end of the truck's journey through the sky, we arrived in a toy town of match-box houses lined up like tombstones in a graveyard. At once, I understood why mother cried.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to run around the house and play with his toys. One day, Timmy's mom asked him to clean up his toys in the kitchen. Timmy didn't want to clean up his toys, he wanted to keep playing.

"Timmy, I need you to clean up your toys now," said Timmy's mom.

"But Mom, I want to keep playing!" whined Timmy.

"You can play after you clean up your toys. Now go to the kitchen and get started," replied Timmy's mom.

Timmy reluctantly went to the kitchen, which was painted a dull gray color. He grumpily picked up his toys and put them away. But as he was cleaning, he found a toy he had forgotten about and started playing with it again. Suddenly, he heard his mom's footsteps coming towards the kitchen.

"Timmy, I thought I told you to clean up your toys. Why are you still playing?" asked Timmy's mom.

Timmy knew he was in trouble, so he quickly put away his toy and finished cleaning up. From then on, Timmy learned that it was important to listen to his mom and do what she asked, even if he didn't want to.

name_of_work: A Mental Hospital Sitting-Room by Elizabeth Jennings
content: Utrillo on the wall. A nun is climbing Steps in Montmartre. We patients sit below. It is as if a scream were opened wide, A mouth demanding everyone to listen. Too many people cry, too many hide And stare into themselves. I am afraid. There are no life-belts here on which to fasten. The only hope is visitors will come And talk of other things than our disease ... So much is stagnant and yet nothing dies.

Once upon a time, there was a boy called John. He was 3 years old and had never been to a church before. One Sunday, his parents took him for a visit. When John saw the church, he shivered. It looked so big and it was kind of scary! 

Inside the church, John saw fake things. He saw fake candles, fake statues and fake windows. John didn't like it. He kept shivering, but his parents said he had to stay a little while.

John didn't like staying in the church at all. He just wanted to go back home. Then, his parents took him outside and he felt much better. When he looked back at the church, he shivered one last time. He was sure glad that he didn't have to stay there!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved playing with her toys, especially her stuffed bunny named Floppy. One day, Lily was playing with Floppy when she heard an alarm go off in the distance. She asked her mommy what the noise was, and her mommy told her that it was a fire alarm.

Lily got scared and asked her mommy what they should do. Her mommy told her to stay calm and listen to her instructions. She told Lily to grab Floppy and follow her outside. As they were leaving the house, Lily noticed that her favorite toy car had vanished. She started to cry and told her mommy that she couldn't find it.

Her mommy hugged her and told her that it's okay to lose things sometimes, but what's important is that they are safe. Lily learned that it's better to focus on what's really important, like her family and her safety, rather than her toys. From that day on, whenever she heard an alarm in the distance, she remembered the lesson she learned and knew that her mommy would keep her safe.

Once there was a father and his daughter. He was a very loving father and always played with his daughter. Every morning they would go for a walk and hold hands. The father felt like his daughter was so special and he would tell her how much he loved her every day.

He felt like he was the luckiest father on earth to have such a special daughter. Every day he would hold her a little tighter and remind her how much he loved her.

name_of_work: I, Being born a Woman and Distressed by Edna St. Vincent Millay
content: vI, being born a woman and distressed By all the needs and notions of my kind, Am urged by your propinquity to find Your person fair, and feel a certain zest To bear your body's weight upon my breast: So subtly is the fume of life designed, To clarify the pulse and cloud the mind, And leave me once again undone, possessed. Think not for this, however, the poor treason Of my stout blood against my staggering brain, I shall remember you with love, or season My scorn with pity,--let me make it plain: I find this frenzy insufficient reason For conversation when we meet again.

name_of_work: On Mother's Day by Bruce Lansky
content: On Mother's Day it isn't smart To give your mom a broken heart. So here are thing you shouldn't say To dear old mom on Mother's Day: Don't tell her that you'll never eat A carrot, celery, bean, or beet. Don't tell her you think smoking's cool. Don't tell her you've dropped out of school. Don't tell her that you've drowned the cat. Don't tell her that she looks too fat. Dont't tell her when you're grown you'll be A starving poet--just like me.

name_of_work: To The Stone-Cutters by Robinson Jeffers
content: Stone-cutters fighting time with marble, you foredefeated Challengers of oblivion Eat cynical earnings, knowing rock splits, records fall down, The square-limbed Roman letters Scale in the thaws, wear in the rain. The poet as well Builds his monument mockingly; For man will be blotted out, the blithe earth die, the brave sun Die blind and blacken to the heart: Yet stones have stood for a thousand years, and pained thoughts found The honey of peace in old poems.

I am the Lost Classmate being hunted down the superhighways and byways of infinite cyber-space. How long can I evade the class committee searching for my lost self? I watch the list of Found Classmates grow by the month Corralled into a hotel ballroom festooned with 70s paraphernalia, bombarded with atmospheric hit tunes, the Captured Classmates from Sullivan High School will celebrate thirty years of freedom from each other. I peek at the message board: my locker partner, out in California, looks forward to being reunited with her old school chums. Wearing a disguise, I calculate the number of months left for me to do what I do best, what I've always done: slip through the net.

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily who loved to listen to jazz music. She would dance and sing along to the music every day. One day, Lily's mom asked her to pour some juice into a cup. Lily poured the juice, but she poured too much and the cup became empty.

Lily's mom got angry and scolded her. Lily didn't like being scolded and she felt sad. She went to her room and turned on her jazz music to make herself feel better. But her mom came into her room and turned off the music, saying that Lily needed to learn her lesson.

Lily got angry and had a fight with her mom. She didn't want to talk to her mom anymore and ran away from home. She walked and walked until it became dark outside. Lily was scared and didn't know where to go. She wished she had listened to her mom and poured the juice more carefully.

Once upon a time there was a little girl named Millie. Millie loved animals and the outdoors. She wanted to be independent and have her own farm. 

One day, she saw a sign at the store that said 'Happy Farm'. Millie excitedly grabbed the sign and pulled it out of the store. 

Millie's mom saw what Millie was doing and said, "Where are you going with that sign, Millie?"

Millie replied, "Mommy, I'm going to find my very own farm! I'm going to be independent and take care of the animals." 

Excited, Millie set off on her adventure. She walked for long hours and eventually she found the perfect farm. 

Millie tugged on the gate to the farm and said, "I'm ready to be independent. I'm going to take care of this farm!" 

And that's how Millie started her very own farm and became an independent young girl.

Anna and Ben are playing in the park. They see a big track on the ground. It looks like a big snake.

"Wow, look at this track!" Anna says. "Do you think it is a snake?"

Ben shakes his head. "No, it is too big for a snake. Maybe it is a dragon!"

Anna and Ben follow the track. They want to find the dragon. They walk and walk, but they do not see the dragon.

They come to a big hill. The track goes up the hill. Anna and Ben climb the hill. They are very brave.

At the top of the hill, they see a big slide. The track ends at the slide.

"Look, there is the dragon!" Ben says. He points to the slide.

Anna laughs. "That is not a dragon, silly. That is a slide. The track is from the slide. Someone was sliding down the slide and made the track."

Ben feels silly. He did not know that. He smiles.

"Can we slide down the slide?" he asks.

"Sure, let's go!" Anna says.

Anna and Ben run to the slide. They take turns sliding down the slide. They have a lot of fun. They forget about the dragon. They are happy.

Jimmy was a popular little boy. One day, he wanted to do something special with his friends. He ran to his room and found a big jug. He took it to his friends, who were all in the garden.

Jimmy kneeled down and said "let's play!" He slowly filled the jug with water from the hosepipe. Then, everyone started to splash each other with the water. They laughed and ran around in circles.

When the jug was empty, Jimmy kneeled down again. He said goodbye to his friends and took the empty jug back to his room. He smiled to himself, happy that he had a special day with his friends.

name_of_work: Us Two by A. A. Milne
content: Wherever I am, there's always Pooh, There's always Pooh and Me. Whatever I do, he wants to do, "Where are you going today?" says Pooh: "Well, that's very odd 'cos I was too. Let's go together," says Pooh, says he. "Let's go together," says Pooh. "What's twice eleven?" I said to Pooh. ("Twice what?" said Pooh to Me.) "I think it ought to be twenty-two." "Just what I think myself," said Pooh. "It wasn't an easy sum to do, But that's what it is," said Pooh, said he. "That's what it is," said Pooh. "Let's look for dragons," I said to Pooh. "Yes, let's," said Pooh to Me. We crossed the river and found a few- "Yes, those are dragons all right," said Pooh. "As soon as I saw their beaks I knew. That's what they are," said Pooh, said he. "That's what they are," said Pooh. "Let's frighten the dragons," I said to Pooh. "That's right," said Pooh to Me. "I'm not afraid," I said to Pooh, And I held his paw and I shouted "Shoo! Silly old dragons!"- and off they flew. "I wasn't afraid," said Pooh, said he, "I'm never afraid with you." So wherever I am, there's always Pooh, There's always Pooh and Me. "What would I do?" I said to Pooh, "If it wasn't for you," and Pooh said: "True, It isn't much fun for One, but Two, Can stick together, says Pooh, says he. "That's how it is," says Pooh.
