Once upon a time, there was a very wealthy family. They had a daughter who was always excited to go to school. Every day she hopped in her family's car and they drove her to her classroom. 

When she arrived, she said hello to all of her friends, and they smiled back. They all gathered in the classroom and their teacher began their lesson. 

One day, their teacher decided to split them up into two groups. The wealthy kids went to one side of the room and the other kids went to the other side. The wealthy kids cheered and clapped their hands. 

The poorer kids were sad. They looked sadly at their teacher. But, the teacher made sure that everyone had fun in the classroom. And, no matter what, the wealthy kids and the other kids remained friends. 

The end.

Tom and Lily are twins. They like to eat waffles for breakfast. Mom makes waffles with honey and butter. They smell good and taste sweet.

One morning, Tom and Lily are very hungry. They run to the kitchen and see a big plate of waffles on the table. They each grab a waffle and sit down.

"Yum, yum, yum!" Tom says. He bites his waffle and smiles.

"Yum, yum, yum!" Lily says. She bites her waffle and frowns.

"Tom, your waffle is heavy!" Lily says. She holds her waffle with both hands. It is too big and thick for her.

"Ha, ha, ha!" Tom laughs. He holds his waffle with one hand. It is small and thin for him.

"Mom, why is Lily's waffle heavy and mine is not?" Tom asks.

Mom looks at the plate and sees the problem. She mixed up the waffles. She gave Tom the waffle for Lily and Lily the waffle for Tom.

"Oops, I'm sorry, Tom and Lily. I made a mistake. Here, switch your waffles. Lily, you have the small and thin waffle. Tom, you have the big and thick waffle. They are both yummy. Enjoy!" Mom says.

Tom and Lily switch their waffles and thank Mom. They bite their waffles and smile.

"Yum, yum, yum!" Tom and Lily say. They eat their waffles and are happy.

Sara was a rich girl. She had many toys and clothes and books. She liked to play with her toys and dress up in her clothes and look at her books. But she did not like to share. She wanted to keep everything for herself.

One day, her cousin Ben came to visit. Ben was not rich. He had few toys and clothes and books. He liked to play with Sara's toys and dress up in her clothes and look at her books. But Sara did not let him. She said, "No, these are mine! Go away!"

Ben was sad. He wanted to have fun with Sara. He saw a big teddy bear on Sara's bed. He liked the teddy bear. He wanted to hug it and rub it. He reached for the teddy bear. But Sara saw him. She ran to the bed and grabbed the teddy bear. She said, "No, this is mine! Go away!"

Ben was angry. He wanted the teddy bear. He pulled the teddy bear. Sara pulled the teddy bear. They both pulled the teddy bear. The teddy bear ripped. The stuffing came out. Sara and Ben both screamed.

Sara's mom and Ben's mom heard the scream. They came to the room. They saw the ripped teddy bear and the stuffing and the crying Sara and Ben. They were not happy. They said, "What did you do? Why did you scream? Why did you rip the teddy bear?"

Sara and Ben felt bad. They said, "We are sorry. We wanted the teddy bear. We did not share. We did not play nice."

Sara's mom and Ben's mom said, "You need to learn to share. Sharing is good. Sharing is fun. Sharing makes friends. You need to say sorry to each other and to the teddy bear."

Sara and Ben said sorry to each other and to the teddy bear. They hugged and kissed. They helped to fix the teddy bear. They played with the teddy bear and the other toys and clothes and books. They shared. They had fun. They made friends.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to eat sausages for breakfast. One day, Timmy's mom made him a delicious sausage for breakfast. Timmy admired the sausage and said, "Mom, this sausage is really yummy!"

After breakfast, Timmy went to play with his toys. He was playing with his favorite toy car when his little sister came into the room crying. Timmy asked, "What's wrong, sis?" His sister said, "I lost my teddy bear and I can't find it anywhere!" Timmy remained calm and said, "Don't worry, I'll help you find it." 

Timmy and his sister searched the whole house and finally found the teddy bear under the bed. Timmy's sister was so happy and said, "Thank you, Timmy! You're the best brother ever!" Timmy smiled and said, "I just wanted to help. That's what big brothers do."

name_of_work: Poem at Thirty by Sonia Sanchez
content: it is midnight no magical bewitching hour for me i know only that i am here waiting remembering that once as a child i walked two miles in my sleep. did i know then where i was going? traveling. i'm always traveling. i want to tell you about me about nights on a brown couch when i wrapped my bones in lint and refused to move. no one touches me anymore. father do not send me out among strangers. you you black man stretching scraping the mold from your body. here is my hand. i am not afraid of the night.

One day, there were two friends, Jack and Joe. They both wanted to eat a pie. But Jack had no money to pay for it. Joe was very helpful and said he could pay for it. Jack was so happy. They went to the store and Joe paid for the pie. When they brought the pie back home they each had a big slice. It was so delicious! They were so happy they were able to eat the pie. They were even happier because Joe was so helpful. They were the best of friends.

Lily and Anna were best friends. They liked to play with dolls and dress up. One day, they found a box of jewelry in Anna's mom's closet. It had shiny rings, necklaces, and earrings.

"Wow, look at these!" Lily said. "Can we try them on?"

Anna nodded. "Yes, but we have to be careful. Mom said they are very old and special. We can't break them or lose them."

They put on the jewelry and pretended to be princesses. They danced and sang and had fun. But then, Lily tripped on a rug and fell down. She heard a snap.

"Oh no!" she cried. "I broke your mom's necklace! I'm so sorry, Anna!"

Anna ran to her and helped her up. She saw the broken necklace on the floor. She felt sad, but she also saw that Lily was hurt. She had a scratch on her knee.

"It's okay, Lily," Anna said. "You didn't mean to break it. Are you okay? Does your knee hurt?"

Lily nodded. "Yes, it hurts a little. But I'm more sorry about the necklace. Your mom will be mad at me."

Anna hugged her. "No, she won't. She is very friendly and nice. She will understand that it was an accident. We can tell her the truth and say sorry. Maybe she can fix it."

Lily smiled. "Thank you, Anna. You are a good friend. I'm sorry I broke your mom's jewelry."

Anna smiled back. "You're welcome, Lily. You are a good friend too. I'm glad you're okay. Come on, let's go find my mom and tell her what happened."

They held hands and walked to the living room. They hoped that Anna's mom would not be too upset. They learned that playing with jewelry was fun, but also risky. They decided to be more careful next time.

John was a little boy. He was 3 years old and loved swimming. Every day, he asked his mum if he could go to the pool.

Today, she said yes! So they drove to the pool together.

John was so excited. He rushed to the pool and was amazed by its enormous size. He looked up at the ceiling and said to his mum, "Wow, it's so high!" 

His mum said, "Yes, it is. Now, are you ready to swim?"

John smiled and nodded. He put on his special swimming hat and stepped into the pool. He was thrilled to be swimming and splashing around with his new friends.

John was having so much fun. He was glad that his mum had let him come swimming!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, Lily's mom made her a yummy sandwich with olives on it. Lily loved olives!

As she was about to take a bite, her little brother Max reached over and grabbed the sandwich from her. "No, Max! That's mine!" Lily yelled.

Max just giggled and took a big bite of the sandwich. Lily was so upset that she started to cry. "Mom, Max took my sandwich!" she said, tears streaming down her face.

Mom came over and asked Max to give the sandwich back to Lily. Max handed it over and said, "Sorry, Lily." Lily wiped away her tears and took a big bite of the olive sandwich. It was still yummy!

The unpurged images of day recede; The Emperor's drunken soldiery are abed; Night resonance recedes, night-walkers' song After great cathedral gong; A starlit or a moonlit dome disdains All that man is, All mere complexities, The fury and the mire of human veins. Before me floats an image, man or shade, Shade more than man, more image than a shade; For Hades' bobbin bound in mummy-cloth May unwind the winding path; A mouth that has no moisture and no breath Breathless mouths may summon; I hail the superhuman; I call it death-in-life and life-in-death. Miracle, bird or golden handiwork, More miracle than bird or handiwork, Planted on the starlit golden bough, Can like the cocks of Hades crow, Or, by the moon embittered, scorn aloud In glory of changeless metal Common bird or petal And all complexities of mire or blood. At midnight on the Emperor's pavement flit Flames that no faggot feeds, nor steel has lit, Nor storm disturbs, flames begotten of flame, Where blood-begotten spirits come And all complexities of fury leave, Dying into a dance, An agony of trance, An agony of flame that cannot singe a sleeve. Astraddle on the dolphin's mire and blood, Spirit after spirit! The smithies break the flood, The golden smithies of the Emperor! Marbles of the dancing floor Break bitter furies of complexity, Those images that yet Fresh images beget, That dolphin-torn, that gong-tormented sea.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside on her porch. One day, she saw a new boy in the neighborhood. His name was Max. Lily wanted to be friends with Max, so she went over to introduce herself.

"Hi, I'm Lily. What's your name?" she asked.

"I'm Max," he replied.

Lily noticed that Max's bike was broken. "That's too bad," she said. "Do you want to play on my porch instead?"

Max smiled and said, "Sure, that sounds like fun!"

From that day on, Lily and Max played together on her porch every day. They became the best of friends and had lots of fun together.

name_of_work: The Bright Lights of Sarajevo by Tony Harrison
content: After the hours that Sarajevans pass Queuing with empty canisters of gas to get the refills they wheel home in prams, or queuing for the precious meagre grams of bread they're rationed to each day, and often dodging snipers on the way, or struggling up sometimes eleven flights of stairs with water, then you'd think the nights of Sarajevo would be totally devoid of people walking streets Serb shells destroyed, but tonight in Sarajevo that's just not the case- The young go walking at a strollers pace, black shapes impossible to mark as Muslim, Serb or Croat in such dark, in unlit streets you can't distinguish who calls bread hjleb or hleb or calls it kruh, All takes the evening air with a strollers stride, no torches guide them, but they don't collide except as one of the flirtatious ploys when a girl's dark shape is fancied by a boy's. Then the tender radar of the tone of voice shows by its signals she approves his choice. Then mach or lighter to a cigarette to check in her eyes if he's made progress yet. And I see a pair who've certainly progressed beyond the tone of voice and match-lit flare test and he's about, I think, to take her hand and lead her away from where they stand on two shells scars, where, in 1992 Serb mortars massacred the breadshop queue and blood-dunked crusts of shredded bread lay on this pavement with the broken dead. And at their feet in holes made by the mortar that caused the massacre, now full of water from the rain that's poured down half the day, though now even the smallest clouds have cleared away, leaving the Sarajevo star-filled evening sky ideally bright and clear for the bombers eye, in those two rain-full shell-holes the boy sees fragments of the splintered Pleiades, sprinkled on those death-deep, death-dark wells splashed on the pavement by Serb mortar shells. The dark boy-shape leads dark-girl shape away to share one coffee in a candlelit cafe until the curfew, and he holds her hand behind AID flour-sacks refilled with sand.

Once upon a time, in a humble little garden, there lived a tiny bug named Bob. Bob was a happy bug who loved to play with his friends. One day, while playing, Bob saw a big bug named Billy. Billy was not very nice and liked to quarrel with other bugs.

One day, Bob and Billy were playing near the flowers. "I bet I can jump higher than you," said Billy. Bob didn't like to quarrel, but he didn't want to seem scared. "Okay," said Bob, "let's see who can jump the highest." They both knew that the winner would get a sweet treat from the flowers.

Bob and Billy started to jump. At first, they jumped the same height. But then, Bob jumped a little bit higher. Billy was mad and started to quarrel with Bob. "You cheated!" he yelled. But Bob knew he didn't cheat. He just tried his best and jumped high.

In the end, Bob got the sweet treat from the flowers, and Billy went away still mad. Bob felt happy, not because he won, but because he didn't let the quarrel get to him. He knew that being humble and kind was more important than winning.

From that day on, Bob and his friends played happily in the garden, and they learned that it was better to be humble and kind than to quarrel with others. And sometimes, when they saw Billy, they would invite him to play too, hoping that one day he would learn the same lesson.

Once upon a time, there were two little birds. They lived in a big tree with lots of leaves. One day, they both wanted to see the view from the top of the tree. But they couldn't agree on who would go first.

The first bird said, "I want to go first and see the view from up high." The second bird said, "No, I want to go first and see the view too." They argued and argued, but they couldn't decide who would go first.

Then, the first bird had an idea. "Let's mark the tree with a special sign, so we know who goes first." The second bird agreed, and they marked the tree with a big X. Now they could take turns and see the view from up high. They both saw the view, and it was different from what they had seen before. They were both happy and flew back to their nest in the big tree.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved playing with her doll, but sometimes she got impatient when her mom asked her to do things like eat or take a nap. 

One day, Lily was playing with her doll when she felt a tickle in her nose. She tried to hold it in, but she couldn't help it - she sneezed! 

Her doll fell over, but Lily picked her up and said, "Sorry, dolly. I sneezed and knocked you over." 

Lily's mom heard her sneeze and came in to check on her. "Bless you, Lily," she said. "Are you feeling okay?" 

Lily nodded and went back to playing with her doll, feeling happy that she had said sorry and that her mom cared about her.

Once upon a time there lived a young girl. She was very excited as she was invited by her grandparents to visit them. She had a seat on the train to take her there.

The girl was very happy about her invitation and she couldn't wait to begin her journey. On the journey, she saw her friend who wasn't as lucky. He looked very envious and he told the girl that he wished he could go too.

The girl shared her invitation with her friend, telling him he could come along. He was so pleased that he soon had a seat on the train next to her.

Now they they were both going, they had so much fun during the journey.

The moral of the story is that it's always better to share than not to. That way, everyone can be happy and nobody has to feel envious!

Once upon a time, there was a musician. He loved to play music on his guitar. One day, he saw a light in the sky. It was very bright and shiny. He said, "Wow, that's beautiful!" He decided to play his guitar under the light. The music was so lovely that all the animals in the forest came to listen. They danced and sang along with the musician. From that day on, the musician played his guitar under the light every night. And the animals always came to listen and dance.

Tom and Anna are friends. They like to play with dolls and cars. One day, they find a big cake in the kitchen. It looks sweet and yummy. They want to eat some.

But Mom says, "No, this cake is for Grandma's birthday. You can have a slice later. Now go and play outside."

Tom and Anna are sad. They really want some cake. They have an idea. They lie to Mom. They say, "We are going to the park. We will be back soon."

But they do not go to the park. They sneak back to the kitchen. They take a big knife. They cut a piece of cake. They eat it. It is sweet and soft. They are happy.

But Mom sees them. She is angry. She says, "You lied to me! You did a bad thing! You ruined Grandma's cake! You are naughty! Go to your rooms. No cake for you. No toys for you. No TV for you."

Tom and Anna are sorry. They cry. They say, "We are sorry, Mom. We love you. We love Grandma. We will not lie again."

But Mom does not listen. She is still angry. She sends them to their rooms. They have no success. They have no fun. They have a bad ending.

name_of_work: Shine, Perishing Republic by Robinson Jeffers
content: While this America settles in the mould of its vulgarity, heavily thickening to empire, And protest, only a bubble in the molten mass, pops and sighs out, and the mass hardens, I sadly smiling remember that the flower fades to make fruit, the fruit rots to make earth. Out of the mother; and through the spring exultances, ripeness and decadence; and home to the mother. You making haste haste on decay: not blameworthy; life is good, be it stubbornly long or suddenly A mortal splendor: meteors are not needed less than mountains: shine, perishing republic. But for my children, I would have them keep their distance from the thickening center; corruption Never has been compulsory, when the cities lie at the monster's feet there are left the mountains. And boys, be in nothing so moderate as in love of man, a clever servant, insufferable master. There is the trap that catches noblest spirits, that caught-they say-God, when he walked on earth.

Once upon a time, there was a clean teaspoon. The teaspoon was so special that it never got tired. Every day, the teaspoon went off on an adventure.

On this day, the teaspoon went to the beach. The sun was shining and the birds were singing. The teaspoon was very happy.

The teaspoon played in the sand and splashed in the water. But after a while it was time to rest. So the teaspoon lay down on a soft blanket of sand and fell asleep.

The teaspoon didn't wake up for a long time. When it did, it felt very refreshed. With a smile on its face, the teaspoon continued exploring. It was ready for more adventures!

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily. She had a purple backpack that she brought to school every day. One day, Lily was playing with her pencil on her desk. She accidentally snapped her pencil in half. 

Lily felt sad because she loved that pencil. But then she remembered her mom telling her that accidents happen and it's okay to make mistakes. So, she didn't cry and instead, she decided to ask her teacher for a new pencil. 

Her teacher was happy to give her a new pencil and told Lily that it's important to ask for help when we need it. Lily learned that it's okay to make mistakes and ask for help. She went back to her desk, ready to learn and play.

Once upon a time there was an ordinary elephant. He did lots of things every day. He liked to take walks around the forest and roll in the mud.

One day the elephant went to the pond to do some fishing. He was so excited when he caught a big fish!

He was so proud of himself he decided to do some dancing. He put on some music and began to sway and move his trunk. He was having such a wonderful time.

The other animals watched from afar in awe. They had never seen an elephant do so much in one day. It was extraordinary!

The ordinary elephant had done something extraordinary- but only to prove that ordinary things can be very special.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to build things with his blocks. He would build tall towers and houses with big doors. One day, Timmy's mommy told him that if he built a big tower, he would get a prize. 

Timmy was very excited and started building right away. He built and built until he had the biggest tower he had ever made. He was so proud of himself! But then, the tower fell down. It was too rough and not strong enough to stand up. Timmy was very sad because he didn't get the prize. 

Timmy's mommy hugged him and told him that it was okay. She said that building things takes practice and that he would get better. Timmy felt a little better, but he still wished he had gotten the prize. From then on, Timmy practiced building every day so that one day he could build the biggest tower ever and win the prize.

There was a dog named Max. Max was brave. He liked to go for adventures. One sunny day, Max decided to go for a walk.

He walked and walked until he saw something very interesting. It was an armchair at the end of the road. Max wanted to try it out. He walked right up to it and hopped on.

It was very comfortable. Just then, a man walked out of a house. He was very angry. 

"Who stole my armchair?!" exclaimed the man.

Max just looked at the man. He wasn't sure what to do.

"Are you brave enough to admit that you stole my armchair?" asked the man.

Max knew he was brave enough to admit it. So he did. 

The man was very surprised. He didn't expect Max to be so honest. He patted him on the head and said, "You are a brave dog, Max. I'm glad you owned up to it!" Then, he went back in the house.

Max was happy he was brave enough to admit he stole the armchair. He hopped off it and went back home, feeling proud.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Mia. Mia liked to play outside with her friends. They would run, jump and laugh. Mia was a regular girl who liked to have fun.

One day, Mia and her friends found a well near their play area. They were curious and looked inside. They saw water and thought it would be fun to stir the water with a stick. Mia picked up a long stick and started to stir the water. She made big circles in the water.

Mia's friend, Tom, said, "Mia, let's make a wish while you stir the water!" All the friends agreed and closed their eyes to make a wish. They wished for more sunny days to play outside together. After making their wishes, they continued to play and have fun. They knew the well was a special place and promised to visit it again soon.

Tom and Sue like to play in the park. They have a big box of toys. They have cars, dolls, balls and flags. They like to make races with the cars and the flags.

One day, they find a new flag in the box. It is black. It has a white skull and bones on it. Tom says, "This is a pirate flag. Pirates are bad. They take things from other people."

Sue says, "I want to be a pirate. Pirates are fun. They have ships and treasure."

Tom says, "No, you can't be a pirate. Pirates are not nice. They are mean and scary."

Sue says, "Yes, I can. Watch me. I will mark the park with the pirate flag. Then it will be mine."

Sue runs to the slide. She puts the pirate flag on top of it. She says, "This is my slide. No one can use it."

Tom runs to the swing. He puts another flag on it. It is red. It has a white cross on it. He says, "This is my swing. I am a knight. Knights are good. They fight pirates."

Sue runs to the sandbox. She puts the pirate flag on it. She says, "This is my sandbox. I have buried treasure here."

Tom runs to the bench. He puts the red flag on it. He says, "This is my bench. I have a castle here."

Sue and Tom look at each other. They both want to play with the toys. But they have different flags. They do not want to share.

They start to yell. They say, "Go away. This is mine. You can't have it."

A lady sees them. She is their mom. She comes to them. She says, "What are you doing? Why are you fighting? You have to share. Sharing is nice. Fighting is not."

Sue and Tom look at their mom. They feel bad. They say, "Sorry, mom. We were playing pirates and knights. But we forgot to share."

Mom says, "It's okay. Pirates and knights can be friends. You can play together. You can take turns. You can use both flags. But remember, they are just toys. They are not real. The park is for everyone."

Sue and Tom nod. They say, "Okay, mom. We will share. We will play together. We will use both flags."

Mom smiles. She says, "Good. I'm glad. Now, have fun. But be careful. Don't hurt anyone. And don't mark the park with the flags. They might get lost or dirty."

Sue and Tom say, "Okay, mom. We won't mark the park. We will just play."

They hug their mom. They take their flags and their toys. They go to the slide and the swing and the sandbox and the bench. They play pirates and knights. They share. They have fun. They are happy.

Pam and her mommy were at the airport. It was the first time Pam had been to the airport and she was very excited. 

When they reached the aeroplane, Pam's mommy requested the porter to take their luggage to the cabin. The porter smiled and said, "Sure!"

When they got on the aeroplane, Pam noticed that it was cold. "Mommy, why is it so cold?" she asked.

Her mommy replied, "That's because the aeroplane has air conditioning. It keeps the air inside the cabin cool so that you don't feel too hot."

Pam nodded her head in understanding. She wished the aeroplane journey would hurry up, so she could get off the plane and take a look around at the new place. 

The flight was fun and soon they landed. Pam had requested her mommy to bring her to the airport and they had a wonderful time.

Once upon a time, there was a thoughtful little girl named Lucy. She loved to help her mom in the kitchen. One day, her mom was making a pie for dinner. Lucy wanted to help, so she asked her mom if she could.

Her mom said yes, and Lucy helped to make the pie. They put apples and sugar inside the pie. Lucy even got to put the top on the pie. Then, they put the pie in the oven to cook.

While they waited for the pie to cook, Lucy's little brother Sam came into the kitchen. He smelled the pie and wanted some right away. Sam said, "I want pie now!" But Lucy told him that they had to wait for the pie to cook. Sam was not happy, but he knew that Lucy was right. When the pie was ready, they all sat down and had a yummy dinner with the pie they made together.

Once upon a time, there was a happy train named Tom. Tom loved to go on the track. He would go fast and slow. He liked to make his friends smile.

One day, Tom met a pretty butterfly. The butterfly said, "Hi, I am Betty." Tom said, "Hi, I am Tom. Do you want to play with me?" Betty said, "Yes, let's play together!"

So, Tom and Betty played on the track. They laughed and had fun. Then, Betty gave Tom a kiss on his nose. Tom blushed and smiled. They became best friends and played together every day.

Tom and Lily were playing with their toys in the living room. Tom had a red car and Lily had a yellow top. They liked to make the car zoom and the top spin on the floor.

But then Tom saw Lily's top and wanted to play with it. He said, "Give me your top, Lily. It is shiny and fun."

Lily said, "No, Tom. It is my top. You have your car. Go away."

Tom did not listen. He grabbed Lily's top and ran away. Lily was angry. She chased Tom and shouted, "Give it back, Tom. Give it back!"

Tom ran to the sofa and hid behind it. He thought he was safe. But he did not see the hairy cat sleeping on the sofa. The cat did not like Tom. He did not like loud noises. He did not like his tail being pulled.

The cat woke up and saw Tom. He hissed and scratched Tom's face. Tom cried out and dropped the top. Lily picked it up and hugged it. She said, "Bad Tom. Bad cat. You are both mean."

Tom ran to his mom and showed her his face. He said, "Mom, the cat hurt me. He is a bad cat. He slapped me with his paw."

Mom looked at Tom's face and saw the scratch. She said, "Oh, Tom. I'm sorry. The cat was scared. He did not mean to hurt you. But you should not take Lily's top. That was not nice. You should say sorry to Lily and the cat."

Tom felt sorry. He said, "Sorry, Lily. Sorry, cat. Can I play with your top, Lily? Please?"

Lily smiled and said, "OK, Tom. You can play with my top. But you have to share. And you have to be gentle with the cat. He is hairy and soft."

Tom and Lily played with the top and the car. They took turns and made them spin and zoom. The cat watched them and purred. He was happy and calm. He liked Tom and Lily. He liked his sofa. He liked his tail.

Sandy was a curious three year old girl. One day, she was playing with her toy car when her mom came out of the house with a box. When Sandy opened the box, she found a very special model inside. 

She had never seen anything like it before. It was bright and colourful, and it had small wings that twinkled when she moved them. Sandy wanted to try it out right away, but her mom said she needed to be careful. 

Sandy went into the garden and started to play with her new model. She picked it up and flew it around, but it kept slipping out of her hands. Eventually, Sandy gave up and tried to resist the urge to keep playing. 

Suddenly, something amazing happened. The model flew around Sandy in perfect circles and then flew back into her hands. Sandy was so surprised, she jumped up and down with joy. 

Sandy had found a way to make the model fly. She was a curious and determined girl, and she had managed to make the model do what she wanted it to. The model belonged to Sandy forever.

I am--yet what I am none cares or knows; My friends forsake me like a memory lost: I am the self-consumer of my woes-- They rise and vanish in oblivious host, Like shadows in love's frenzied stifled throes And yet I am, and live--like vapours tossed Into the nothingness of scorn and noise, Into the living sea of waking dreams, Where there is neither sense of life or joys, But the vast shipwreck of my life's esteems; Even the dearest that I loved the best Are strange--nay, rather, stranger than the rest. I long for scenes where man hath never trod A place where woman never smiled or wept There to abide with my Creator, God, And sleep as I in childhood sweetly slept, Untroubling and untroubled where I lie The grass below--above the vaulted sky.
All the while they were talking the new morality Her eyes explored me. And when I rose to go Her fingers were like the tissue Of a Japanese paper napkin.

name_of_work: Spring Morning by A. A. Milne
content: Where am I going? I don't quite know. Down to the stream where the king-cups grow- Up on the hill where the pine-trees blow- Anywhere, anywhere. I don't know. Where am I going? The clouds sail by, Little ones, baby ones, over the sky. Where am I going? The shadows pass, Little ones, baby ones, over the grass. If you were a cloud, and sailed up there, You'd sail on water as blue as air, And you'd see me here in the fields and say: "Doesn't the sky look green today?" Where am I going? The high rooks call: "It's awful fun to be born at all." Where am I going? The ring-doves coo: "We do have beautiful things to do." If you were a bird, and lived on high, You'd lean on the wind when the wind came by, You'd say to the wind when it took you away: "That's where I wanted to go today!" Where am I going? I don't quite know. What does it matter where people go? Down to the wood where the blue-bells grow- Anywhere, anywhere. I don't know.

Tom and Ben were best friends. They liked to play golf together. One day when they went to the golf course, Tom was so surprised when he saw Ben! He was dressed in an amazing, bright red golf outfit. Ben saw the surprise in Tom's eyes and said, "Look, I brought this amazing outfit to wear today!" Tom was so surprised. He gave Ben a big hug. They went out and had an amazing time playing golf. All the other players couldn't help but keep looking at Ben's amazing outfit. Tom and Ben couldn't stop laughing and had the best time!

One day, Tom and Lily were playing with their blocks in the living room. They liked to build tall towers and bridges with their blocks. They were very proud of their creations.

"Look at my tower, Lily! It is so high and strong!" Tom said.

"That is impressive, Tom. But my bridge is longer and prettier!" Lily said.

They were having fun, but they also wanted to show off their skills. They started to argue about whose blocks were better.

"My blocks are better than yours! They are more colorful and shiny!" Tom said.

"No, my blocks are better than yours! They are more smooth and round!" Lily said.

They did not listen to each other. They did not share their blocks. They did not say nice words.

Suddenly, they felt the floor shake. They heard a loud noise. They saw their blocks fall down. It was an earthquake!

They were scared. They hugged each other. They cried for their mom and dad.

Mom and dad came running. They saw the mess in the living room. They saw Tom and Lily crying.

"What happened here?" Mom asked.

"It was an earthquake, Mom! It broke our blocks!" Tom said.

"We were playing with our blocks, but we were also fighting. We were not nice to each other. We are sorry, Mom!" Lily said.

Mom and dad hugged them. They said, "We are glad you are safe. We are sorry your blocks are broken. But you know what? Blocks can be fixed. But friendship is more important. You should always be kind and respectful to each other. You should always serve each other with love. That is what makes a good team."

Tom and Lily nodded. They said, "You are right, Mom and Dad. We are sorry. We love each other. We love you. Can we play with our blocks again?"

Mom and dad smiled. They said, "Of course you can. But first, let's clean up this mess together. And then, let's make some new and better blocks. And then, let's have some cookies and milk. How does that sound?"

Tom and Lily smiled. They said, "That sounds great! Thank you, Mom and Dad!"

They learned their lesson. They helped each other. They enjoyed their blocks. They had a happy day.

Lila saw a little kitten on the street. It was black and white and very cute. She wanted to play with it and take it home. She ran to the kitten and tried to pick it up.

"Meow!" the kitten said. It was scared of Lila and scratched her hand. Lila cried and let go of the kitten. It ran away and hid under a car.

Lila's mom came and saw what happened. She hugged Lila and said, "I'm sorry, honey. You hurt the kitten and it hurt you back. You should not grab animals you don't know. They might be afraid or sick or have a home. You should be gentle and kind to them."

Lila nodded and said, "I'm sorry, mom. I just wanted a friend. I love kittens."

Mom smiled and said, "I know, sweetie. But you can't take any kitten you see. Maybe we can go to the shelter and find a kitten that needs a home and a friend. Would you like that?"

Lila smiled and said, "Yes, mom. That would be nice. Can we go now?"

Mom said, "Sure. Let's go. But first, let's wash your hand and put a band-aid on it. And maybe have a snack. I made some delicious cookies for you."

Lila said, "Yay! Cookies! Thank you, mom. You are the best."

Mom said, "You're welcome, honey. I love you."

They held hands and walked to the car. Lila learned to be careful and respectful with animals. And she hoped to find a kitten that would love her too.

name_of_work: On the Circuit by W.H. Auden
content: Among pelagian travelers, Lost on their lewd conceited way To Massachusetts, Michigan, Miami or L.A., An airborne instrument I sit, Predestined nightly to fulfill Columbia-Giesen-Management's Unfathomable will, By whose election justified, I bring my gospel of the Muse To fundamentalists, to nuns, to Gentiles and to Jews, And daily, seven days a week, Before a local sense has jelled, From talking-site to talking-site Am jet-or-prop-propelled. Though warm my welcome everywhere, I shift so frequently, so fast, I cannot now say where I was The evening before last, Unless some singular event Should intervene to save the place, A truly asinine remark, A soul-bewitching face, Or blessed encounter, full of joy, Unscheduled on the Giesen Plan, With, here, an addict of Tolkien, There, a Charles Williams fan. Since Merit but a dunghill is, I mount the rostrum unafraid: Indeed, 'twere damnable to ask If I am overpaid. Spirit is willing to repeat Without a qualm the same old talk, But Flesh is homesick for our snug Apartment in New York. A sulky fifty-six, he finds A change of mealtime utter hell, Grown far too crotchety to like A luxury hotel. The Bible is a goodly book I always can peruse with zest, But really cannot say the same For Hilton's Be My Guest. Nor bear with equanimity The radio in students' cars, Muzak at breakfast, or--dear God!-- Girl-organists in bars. Then, worst of all, the anxious thought, Each time my plane begins to sink And the No Smoking sign comes on: What will there be to drink? Is this a milieu where I must How grahamgreeneish! How infra dig! Snatch from the bottle in my bag An analeptic swig? Another morning comes: I see, Dwindling below me on the plane, The roofs of one more audience I shall not see again. God bless the lot of them, although I don't remember which was which: God bless the U.S.A., so large, So friendly, and so rich.

name_of_work: Ode to My Socks by Pablo Neruda
content: Maru Mori brought me a pair of socks which she knitted herself with her sheepherder's hands, two socks as soft as rabbits. I slipped my feet into them as though into two cases knitted with threads of twilight and goatskin. Violent socks, my feet were two fish made of wool, two long sharks sea-blue, shot through by one golden thread, two immense blackbirds, two cannons: my feet were honored in this way by these heavenly socks. They were so handsome for the first time my feet seemed to me unacceptable like two decrepit firemen, firemen unworthy of that woven fire, of those glowing socks. Nevertheless I resisted the sharp temptation to save them somewhere as schoolboys keep fireflies, as learned men collect sacred texts, I resisted the mad impulse to put them into a golden cage and each day give them birdseed and pieces of pink melon. Like explorers in the jungle who hand over the very rare green deer to the spit and eat it with remorse, I stretched out my feet and pulled on the magnificent socks and then my shoes. The moral of my ode is this: beauty is twice beauty and what is good is doubly good when it is a matter of two socks made of wool in winter.

name_of_work: To a Friend in Love with the Wrong Man Again by Stephen Dunn
content: It was never meant to be sensible, fully understandable. The digger wasp, for example, goes up to the tarantula like a friend and the tarantula freezes, allows itself to be inspected. Then it digs the tarantula's grave while the tarantula watches. You, I bet, would have guessed with a name like tarantula, the tarantula would've been the villain. But it is we who named the tarantula and made the digger wasp sound honest, hard-working. And, of course, there is no villain, only the scheme of things, only horror, and occasionally the strange birth of a butterfly and its short, gorgeous, utterly careless season. I should have mentioned the digger wasp doesn't kill its victim, but stuns it, drags it to the grave, lays one egg on its stomach, and closes up. You see, the instinct is maternal. The newborn wasp feeds off the tarantula for weeks, digs itself out at the right time and enters the odd, wonderful world. I've no advice for you, my friend. You, who would take it-- as all of us would--and offer it up to the heart, like a sacrifice.

ln the arid sun, over the field where the corn has rotted and then dried up, you flock and squabble. Now I must confront the angel who says Win, who tells me to wave any banner that you will follow for you ignore me, my baffled people, you have been through too many theories too many stray bullets your eyes are gravel, skeptical, in this hard field you pay attention only to the rhetoric of seed fruit stomach elbow. name_of_work: Acrostic: Georgiana Augusta Keats by John Keats
content: Give me your patience, sister, while I frame Exact in capitals your golden name; Or sue the fair Apollo and he will Rouse from his heavy slumber and instill Great love in me for thee and Poesy. Imagine not that greatest mastery And kingdom over all the Realms of verse, Nears more to heaven in aught, than when we nurse And surety give to love and Brotherhood. Anthropophagi in Othello's mood; Ulysses storm'd and his enchanted belt Glow with the Muse, but they are never felt Unbosom'd so and so eternal made, Such tender incense in their laurel shade To all the regent sisters of the Nine As this poor offering to you, sister mine. Kind sister! aye, this third name says you are; Enchanted has it been the Lord knows where; And may it taste to you like good old wine, Take you to real happiness and give Sons, daughters and a home like honied hive.

name_of_work: Hay for the Horses by Gary Snyder
content: He had driven half the night From far down San Joaquin Through Mariposa, up the Dangerous Mountain roads, And pulled in at eight a.m. With his big truckload of hay behind the barn. With winch and ropes and hooks We stacked the bales up clean To splintery redwood rafters High in the dark, flecks of alfalfa Whirling through shingle-cracks of light, Itch of haydust in the sweaty shirt and shoes. At lunchtime under Black oak Out in the hot corral, ---The old mare nosing lunchpails, Grasshoppers crackling in the weeds--- "I'm sixty-eight" he said, "I first bucked hay when I was seventeen. I thought, that day I started, I sure would hate to do this all my life. And dammit, that's just what I've gone and done."

name_of_work: The Harlem Dancer by Claude McKay
content: Applauding youths laughed with young prostitutes And watched her perfect, half-clothed body sway; Her voice was like the sound of blended flutes Blown by black players upon a picnic day. She sang and danced on gracefully and calm, The light gauze hanging loose about her form; To me she seemed a proudly-swaying palm Grown lovelier for passing through a storm. Upon her swarthy neck black shiny curls Luxuriant fell; and tossing coins in praise, The wine-flushed, bold-eyed boys, and even the girls, Devoured her shape with eager, passionate gaze; But looking at her falsely-smiling face, I knew her self was not in that strange place.

They shall not return to us, the resolute, the young, The eager and whole-hearted whom we gave: But the men who left them thriftily to die in their own dung, Shall they come with years and honour to the grave? They shall not return to us, the strong men coldly slain In sight of help denied from day to day: But the men who edged their agonies and chid them in their pain, Are they too strong and wise to put away? Our dead shall not return to us while Day and Night divide-- Never while the bars of sunset hold. But the idle-minded overlings who quibbled while they died, Shall they thrust for high employments as of old? Shall we only threaten and be angry for an hour? When the storm is ended shall we find How softly but how swiftly they have sidled back to power By the favour and contrivance of their kind? Even while they soothe us, while they promise large amends, Even while they make a show of fear, Do they call upon their debtors, and take counsel with their friends, To conform and re-establish each career? Their lives cannot repay us--their death could not undo-- The shame that they have laid upon our race. But the slothfulness that wasted and the arrogance that slew, Shall we leave it unabated in its place?

content: She is all there. She was melted carefully down for you and cast up from your childhood, cast up from your one hundred favorite aggies. She has always been there, my darling. She is, in fact, exquisite. Fireworks in the dull middle of February and as real as a cast-iron pot. Let's face it, I have been momentary. A luxury. A bright red sloop in the harbor. My hair rising like smoke from the car window. Littleneck clams out of season. She is more than that. She is your have to have, has grown you your practical your tropical growth. This is not an experiment. She is all harmony. She sees to oars and oarlocks for the dinghy, has placed wild flowers at the window at breakfast, sat by the potter's wheel at midday, set forth three children under the moon, three cherubs drawn by Michelangelo, done this with her legs spread out in the terrible months in the chapel. If you glance up, the children are there like delicate balloons resting on the ceiling. She has also carried each one down the hall after supper, their heads privately bent, two legs protesting, person to person, her face flushed with a song and their little sleep. I give you back your heart. I give you permission - for the fuse inside her, throbbing angrily in the dirt, for the bitch in her and the burying of her wound - for the burying of her small red wound alive - for the pale flickering flare under her ribs, for the drunken sailor who waits in her left pulse, for the mother's knee, for the stocking, for the garter belt, for the call - the curious call when you will burrow in arms and breasts and tug at the orange ribbon in her hair and answer the call, the curious call. She is so naked and singular She is the sum of yourself and your dream. Climb her like a monument, step after step. She is solid. As for me, I am a watercolor. I wash off.

Once upon a time, there was a tall mommy. The tall mommy wanted to take her two little kids to the theater. So she put on her shoes and off they went. The theater was very big and the kids were excited. After they found their seats, the mommy poured a bag of popcorn for the kids to eat. They munched on the popcorn as they watched the show. After the show, the mommy poured a bottle of juice into two cups for them to drink. The kids felt so happy after their day at the theater. They hugged the mommy and thanked her for the fun day.

Once upon a time, there was a little tiger named Tom. Tom lived in a big jungle with his mom and dad. They had a perfect home under a big tree.

One day, Tom met a monkey named Max. Max liked to tease Tom. "You can't catch me!" Max said as he jumped from tree to tree. Tom wanted to show Max that he could catch him, so he ran and jumped too.

Tom and Max played together all day. They laughed and had fun. In the end, Tom caught Max and they became best friends. From that day on, they played together every day in their perfect jungle home.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the sun. One day, she saw a big yellow flower in the grass. She ran over to it and stared at it for a long time. She had never seen a flower like this before. It was unknown to her. 

Lily picked the flower and brought it inside to show her mommy. Her mommy was surprised to see such a pretty flower. Lily told her mommy that it was yellow and unknown to her. Her mommy smiled and said, "It's always fun to discover new things." 

From that day on, Lily loved to explore and find new things that were unknown to her. She never forgot about the big yellow flower that she found in the grass. It was her favorite discovery.

Once upon a time, there was a young girl named Lizzy. She lived in a small town and everyday she liked to go to the well. 

One day, Lizzy went to the well with her bucket and said, â€œLet's gather some water from the well today.â€ She looked around and saw that the well was available for use. 

Lizzy began to scoop up some water with her bucket, when suddenly she heard a voice coming from the well. "You're a very nice girl, Lizzy," said the voice. 

Lizzy was surprised and asked, "Who are you?"

The voice said, "I am an old friend that lives in the well. Would you like to come in and see me?" 

Lizzy was excited and quickly put her bucket down. She stepped into the well and looked around. There, she saw a big, friendly frog. 

The frog said, "Welcome, Lizzy! Let's play a game with the water I gathered. Are you ready?"

Lizzy smiled and nodded in agreement. She was very happy and gathered with her old friend from the well.

Mama and Jack went to the store. Mama said, "Let's look around and find something we want to buy." Jack found a nice picture and said, "Mama, I like this one!" Mama said, "That's a nice picture, but it's too pricey." Jack said, "Is there a cheaper one?" Mama said, "Yes, look over there!"

Once upon a time, there was a girl named Lily who loved to help her mom with the dishwasher. One day, Lily's friend came over to play. Her friend was very popular and always got what she wanted. When it was time to put the dishes in the dishwasher, Lily's friend wanted to do it all by herself.

Once upon a time there was a little girl who loved to study. She liked to learn new things, especially when the sun was shining!

On a sunny day, the little girl went outside with her books and a pencil. She sat in the grass and studied hard. She was so happy and lively!

The sun was warm and bright, making everything around her look cheerful. She read her books and worked on math problems, learning lots of new things.

As the day turned to night, the little girl was happy with all she had learned. She packed up her books and pencil, and went back inside with a wide smile.

Every sunny day she would go outside and study hard. And the little girl was always joyful, learning lots of amazing things!

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play outside in the park. One day, she found a big box. She wanted to know what was inside, so she opened it. 

Inside the box, there was a balloon. She blew it up and held it tight. Suddenly, the balloon popped and she couldn't breathe. She needed oxygen! 

Luckily, her mommy was nearby and she quickly revealed a small bottle of oxygen. She put the mask on Lily's face and she could breathe again. From that day on, Lily knew to be careful with balloons and always ask for help when she needs it.

Once there was a zebra who loved to explore the jungle. One day, he came across some unknown trees and wanted to see what was beyond them. He scattered around them, but could not get through. But then he heard a voice from beyond the trees.

"Hello!" It called out.

The zebra stopped and replied, "Hello! Who are you?"

The voice said, "I'm a little animal and I can help you get through these trees."

The zebra was very excited. He asked the animal, "How can you help me?"

The animal explained, "Take a deep breath, then scatter around these trees as fast as you can. That will get you through them."

The zebra did as the animal said and scattered around the trees as fast as he could. Sure enough, the trees moved apart, revealing a big unknown cave beyond them. The zebra was amazed, and he thanked the animal for helping him.

The animal smiled and said, "You're welcome! Now you can explore the unknown cave."

The zebra was so excited. He was sure that he would find lots of new and exciting things in there. He thanked the animal again and ran off into the cave to explore.

Like Bunyan's pilgrim with his pack, Forth went the dreaming youth To seek, to find, and make his own Wisdom, virtue, and truth. Life was his book, and patiently He studied each hard page; By turns reformer, outcast, priest, Philosopher and sage. Christ was his Master, and he made His life a gospel sweet; Plato and Pythagoras in him Found a disciple meet. The noblest and best his friends, Faithful and fond, though few; Eager to listen, learn, and pay The love and honor due. Power and place, silver and gold, He neither asked nor sought; Only to serve his fellowmen, With heart and word and thought. A pilgrim still, but in his pack No sins to frighten or oppress; But wisdom, morals, piety, To teach, to warn and bless. The world passed by, nor cared to take The treasure he could give; Apart he sat, content to wait And beautifully live; Unsaddened by long, lonely years Of want, neglect, and wrong, His soul to him a kingdom was, Steadfast, serene, and strong. Magnanimous and pure his life, Tranquil its happy end; Patience and peace his handmaids were, Death an immortal friend. For him no monuments need rise, No laurels make his pall; The mem'ry of the good and wise Outshines, outlives them all.

name_of_work: To a Dark Girl by Gwendolyn Bennett
content: I love you for your brownness, And the rounded darkness of your breast, I love you for the breaking sadness in your voice And shadows where your wayward eyelids rest. Something of old forgotten queens Lurks in the lithe abandon of your walk And something of the shackled slave Sobs in the rhythm of your talk. Oh, little brown girl, born for sorrow's mate, Keep all you have of queenliness, Forgetting that you once were slave, And let your full lips laugh at Fate!

Once upon a time, in a small town, there was a purple cat named Mimi. Mimi loved to play outside and chase birds. One day, Mimi saw a big bag of mail. She wanted to help the mailman deliver the mail.

Mimi went to the mailman and said, "Can I help you?" The mailman smiled and said, "Yes, Mimi. You can carry the small letters for me." Mimi was very happy and started to carry the small letters in her mouth.

Mimi and the mailman went from house to house. They put the mail in the mailboxes. Mimi was very good at helping. She did not drop any letters. At the end of the day, the mailman said, "Thank you, Mimi. You did a great job!" Mimi was proud that she could succeed in helping the mailman.

name_of_work: Life is but a Dream by Lewis Carroll
content: A boat, beneath a sunny sky Lingering onward dreamily In an evening of July Children three that nestle near, Eager eye and willing ear, Pleased a simple tale to hear Long has paled that sunny sky; Echoes fade and memories die; Autumn frosts have slain July. Still she haunts me, phantomwise, Alice moving under skies Never seen by waking eyes. Children yet, the tale to hear, Eager eye and willing ear, Lovingly shall nestle near. In a Wonderland they lie, Dreaming as the days go by, Dreaming as the summers die; Ever drifting down the stream Lingering in the golden gleam Life, what is it but a dream?

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toys and talk with his friends. One day, Timmy's mom told him they were going on a trip to visit his grandma.

Timmy was excited to see his grandma, but he didn't want to be late. "Hurry, Mommy!" he said. "We don't want to be late!"

When they arrived at his grandma's house, Timmy noticed something different about her. "Grandma, your language is different," he said. "What happened?"

"Oh, Timmy," his grandma said. "I learned a new language. It's called modern language. It's a way to talk that's easier for everyone to understand."

Timmy was amazed. He had never heard of modern language before. "Can you teach me, Grandma?" he asked. And so, his grandma taught him how to speak in modern language, and they all had a wonderful visit together.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy was a youth, which means he was still very young. One day, Timmy's mom said, "Timmy, it's time to dress for school." Timmy didn't like to dress up, but he knew he had to. 

As Timmy was getting dressed, he accidentally tore his shirt. It was a terrible tear! Timmy started to cry because he didn't want to go to school with a terrible shirt. His mom saw him crying and asked, "What's wrong, Timmy?" Timmy replied, "I tore my shirt and it looks terrible." 

His mom smiled and said, "Don't worry, Timmy. I'll fix your shirt and make it look nice again." Timmy felt better knowing his mom could help him. He put on his shoes and backpack and said, "Thank you, Mom. You're the best!" And off he went to school, feeling happy and ready to learn.

name_of_work: How It Is by Maxine Kumin
content: Shall I say how it is in your clothes? A month after your death I wear your blue jacket. The dog at the center of my life recognizes you've come to visit, he's ecstatic. In the left pocket, a hole. In the right, a parking ticket delivered up last August on Bay State Road. In my heart, a scatter like milkweed, a flinging from the pods of the soul. My skin presses your old outline. It is hot and dry inside. I think of the last day of your life, old friend, how I would unwind it, paste it together in a different collage, back from the death car idling in the garage, back up the stairs, your praying hands unlaced, reassembling the bits of bread and tuna fish into a ceremony of sandwich, running the home movie backward to a space we could be easy in, a kitchen place with vodka and ice, our words like living meat. Dear friend, you have excited crowds with your example. They swell like wine bags, straining at your seams. I will be years gathering up our words, fishing out letters, snapshots, stains, leaning my ribs against this durable cloth to put on the dumb blue blazer of your death.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to dance and twirl around in her pretty pink dress. One morning, Lily woke up early and felt so excited to go to dance class. She quickly got dressed and ran to the car with her mommy.

At dance class, Lily learned a new dance that required her to move her waist back and forth. She tried her best to follow the teacher's instructions and move her waist just right. It was a little tricky, but she kept trying until she got it.

One day, a little boy named Jack was walking with his mom and dad. Jack was feeling uncomfortable because he argued with his parents earlier. He wasn't even sure why, but he knew he was in the wrong.

Jack saw a cable laying across the sidewalk. He was curious and wanted to pick it up. He asked his mom and dad if he could take it home. His parents said he could, so Jack scooped it up and started walking along again.

The cable felt so cool in his hands, Jack thought it was the best thing ever! But then he stumbled over a bump in the sidewalk, and the cable went flying far away. Jack looked and was sad because the cable was gone.

Jack's dad saw the cable too and he told Jack to go fetch it. Jack was nervous because he knew he had been disobedient earlier. He walked slowly and picked it up, then offered it to his dad meekly. His dad knew Jack was sorry and he said "I forgive you."

Jack was relieved and felt much better. He smiled and hugged his mom and dad. He was so happy his parents had forgiven him. From that day forward, Jack remembered to be obedient and always asked before doing something. Forgiveness is a precious gift!

Once upon a time, there was a strong boy called Joe. Joe loved playing in the sand on the beach. He would turn it over and over with his hands, making sandcastles and sculptures that he thought were the best.

One day, Joe heard a voice coming from the sand. "Help me, please," it said. Joe stopped what he was doing and looked around. He saw no one, only sand. He took a step closer and said," Who's there?"

"I'm stuck in the sand and can't get out by myself. Please turn the sand and help me out," the voice said again.

So Joe turned the sand and soon he saw a little crab. He picked it up and showed it to the people on the beach. Everyone was so surprised. Joe had been so kind and strong to help the crab.

From then on, Joe was known as the strong helper who didn't give up until the crab had been freed from the sand.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she was playing outside when she saw a needle on the ground. She picked it up and got a little poke on her finger. It hurt a lot and she started to cry.

Her mom heard her crying and asked, "What happened, Lily?"

"I got a poke from a needle and it hurts," Lily said.

Her mom looked at her finger and saw a little red dot. "Let's clean it up and put a band-aid on it," her mom said.

Lily nodded and her mom cleaned up her finger. "Does it still hurt?" her mom asked.

"No, it feels better now," Lily said with a smile. "But I don't want to be deaf like the needle." 

"Deaf?" her mom asked, confused.

"Yeah, it doesn't listen to anyone and just pokes people," Lily explained. 

Her mom laughed and hugged her. "You're right, but don't worry, you won't be deaf like the needle."

name_of_work: In Memory of Major Robert Gregory by William Butler Yeats
content: Now that we're almost settled in our house I'll name the friends that cannot sup with us Beside a fire of turf in th' ancient tower, And having talked to some late hour Climb up the narrow winding stair to bed: Discoverers of forgotten truth Or mere companions of my youth, All, all are in my thoughts to-night being dead. Always we'd have the new friend meet the old And we are hurt if either friend seem cold, And there is salt to lengthen out the smart In the affections of our heart, And quatrels are blown up upon that head; But not a friend that I would bring This night can set us quarrelling, For all that come into my mind are dead. Lionel Johnson comes the first to mind, That loved his learning better than mankind. Though courteous to the worst; much falling he Brooded upon sanctity Till all his Greek and Latin learning seemed A long blast upon the horn that brought A little nearer to his thought A measureless consummation that he dreamed. And that enquiring man John Synge comes next, That dying chose the living world for text And never could have rested in the tomb But that, long travelling, he had come Towards nightfall upon certain set apart In a most desolate stony place, Towards nightfall upon a race passionate and simple like his heart. And then I think of old George Pollexfen, In muscular youth well known to Mayo men For horsemanship at meets or at racecourses, That could have shown how pure-bred horses And solid men, for all their passion, live But as the outrageous stars incline By opposition, square and trine; Having grown sluggish and contemplative. They were my close companions many a year. A portion of my mind and life, as it were, And now their breathless faces seem to look Out of some old picture-book; I am accustomed to their lack of breath, But not that my dear friend's dear son, Our Sidney and our perfect man, Could share in that discourtesy of death For all things the delighted eye now sees Were loved by him: the old storm-broken trees That cast their shadows upon road and bridge; The tower set on the stream's edge; The ford where drinking cattle make a stir Nightly, and startled by that sound The water-hen must change her ground; He might have been your heartiest welcomer. When with the Galway foxhounds he would ride From Castle Taylor to the Roxborough side Or Esserkelly plain, few kept his pace; At Mooneen he had leaped a place So perilous that half the astonished meet Had shut their eyes; and where was it He rode a race without a bit? And yet his mind outran the horses' feet. We dreamed that a great painter had been born To cold Clare rock and Galway rock and thorn, To that stern colour and that delicate line That are our secret discipline Wherein the gazing heart doubles her might. Soldier, scholar, horseman, he, And yet he had the intensity To have published all to be a world's delight. What other could so well have counselled us In all lovely intricacies of a house As he that practised or that understood All work in metal or in wood, In moulded plaster or in carven stone? Soldier, scholar, horseman, he, And all he did done perfectly As though he had but that one trade alone. Some burn dam faggots, others may consume The entire combustible world in one small room As though dried straw, and if we turn about The bare chimney is gone black out Because the work had finished in that flare. Soldier, scholar, horseman, he, As 'twere all life's epitome. What made us dream that he could comb grey hair? I had thought, seeing how bitter is that wind That shakes the shutter, to have brought to mind All those that manhood tried, or childhood loved Or boyish intellect approved, With some appropriatc commentaty on each; Until imagination brought A fitter welcome; but a thought Of that late death took all my heart for speech.

Once there was a little girl who wanted a pair of sunglasses. She asked her mom to give her a pair, so her mom went and picked out the most beautiful pair of sunglasses she could find. The little girl put them on, and they felt so good on her face. She jumped up and down with joy.

On a sunny day, the little girl put on her sunglasses and went outside. She was so happy and felt so grown up. Everywhere she went, people smiled and gave her compliments.

One day the sun got too strong and it made the little girl feel a bit restless. She decided to take off her sunglasses and take a break. When she took off her sunglasses and laid them down, a gust of wind blew them away. 

The little girl was so sad, but her mom came to the rescue. She got some new sunglasses for the little girl and gave them to her. Now the little girl is never without her sunglasses, and she always feels safe and happy when she wears them.

Struck with grief you were, though only four, The day your mother cut her mermaid hair And stood, a stranger, smiling at the door. They frowned, tsk-tsked your willful, cruel despair, When you slunk beneath the long piano strings And sobbed until your lungs hiccupped for air, Unbribable with curses, cake, playthings. You mourned a mother now herself no more, But brave and fashionable. The golden rings That fringed her naked neck, whom were they for? Not you, but for the world, now in your place, A full eclipse. Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved playing with her favorite red button. One day, she went to the park to play with her friends. While playing, she accidentally dropped her button and couldn't find it.

Once upon a time, there was a charming little girl named Lily. Lily loved to play outside in the big park with her friends. They would run, jump, and laugh all day long.

Every morning the world is created. Under the orange sticks of the sun the heaped ashes of the night turn into leaves again and fasten themselves to the high branches- and the ponds appear like black cloth on which are painted islands of summer lilies. If it is your nature to be happy you will swim away along the soft trails for hours, your imagination alighting everywhere. And if your spirit carries within it the thorn that is heavier than lead- if it's all you can do to keep on trudging- there is still somewhere deep within you a beast shouting that the earth is exactly what it wanted- each pond with its blazing lilies is a prayer heard and answered lavishly, every morning, whether or not you have ever dared to be happy, whether or not you have ever dared to pray.

Once there was a boy named John. One day, he was walking down the street and he stepped on a pit in the ground. He fell down and started to frown. He was feeling uncomfortable and sad.

A friendly cat saw John and saw that he was feeling down. That's why it asked him what was wrong. John told the cat about the pit and it walked up to the pit. It looked down and said "I have an idea." 

The cat moved away from the pit and got some dirt from the ground. It brought the dirt to the pit and started to carefully fill the pit with dirt. Soon, the pit was no more.

John was very happy. He thanked the cat for helping. Now he could walk down the street and feel comfortable. He smiled and continued his walk with the cat by his side.
