Anna and Ben like to play with their toy cars. They have a big rug with roads and buildings on it. They make sounds like vroom and beep as they drive their cars around. Sometimes they have races or pretend to go to the shop or the park.

One day, Anna and Ben have a problem. They both want to play with the same car. It is a red car with a shiny sticker on it. They think it is the coolest car ever. They both reach for it at the same time and pull on it.

"Let go, it's mine!" Anna says.

"No, it's mine!" Ben says.

They tug and tug until the car breaks in half. They both gasp and drop the pieces. They feel sad and angry.

"Look what you did!" Anna says.

"You did it!" Ben says.

They start to cry and yell at each other. Their mom hears them and comes to see what is wrong. She sees the broken car and the upset children.

"What happened here?" she asks.

They both point at each other and say, "He/she did it!"

Mom sighs and picks up the pieces of the car. She looks at them and says, "I think I can fix this. But first, you two need to calm down and say sorry to each other. How about you do some exercise to get rid of your bad feelings?"

Anna and Ben nod. They don't like to fight. Mom shows them how to do some jumping jacks, some squats, and some stretches. They follow her and start to feel better. They breathe deeply and smile.

"Are you ready to say sorry now?" Mom asks.

Anna and Ben look at each other and say, "Sorry."

They hug and say, "I love you."

Mom smiles and says, "I love you too. And I have good news. I fixed your car. See, it can still drive and reverse. And the sticker is still cool. But you have to share it and be gentle with it, okay?"

Anna and Ben nod and say, "Okay."

They take the car and thank Mom. They go back to their rug and play nicely. They take turns driving and reversing the car. They make sounds like vroom and beep. They are happy again.

"A true Arab knows how to catch a fly in his hands," my father would say. And he'd prove it, cupping the buzzer instantly while the host with the swatter stared. In the spring our palms peeled like snakes. True Arabs believed watermelon could heal fifty ways. I changed these to fit the occasion. Years before, a girl knocked, wanted to see the Arab. I said we didn't have one. After that, my father told me who he was, "Shihab"--"shooting star"-- a good name, borrowed from the sky. Once I said, "When we die, we give it back?" He said that's what a true Arab would say. Today the headlines clot in my blood. A little Palestinian dangles a truck on the front page. Homeless fig, this tragedy with a terrible root is too big for us. What flag can we wave? I wave the flag of stone and seed, table mat stitched in blue. I call my father, we talk around the news. It is too much for him, neither of his two languages can reach it. I drive into the country to find sheep, cows, to plead with the air: Who calls anyone civilized? Where can the crying heart graze? What does a true Arab do now?

Like a joy on the heart of a sorrow, The sunset hangs on a cloud; A golden storm of glittering sheaves, Of fair and frail and fluttering leaves, The wild wind blows in a cloud. Hark to a voice that is calling To my heart in the voice of the wind: My heart is weary and sad and alone, For its dreams like the fluttering leaves have gone, And why should I stay behind?

Alice was very miserable. Her little brother was at a friend's house and she was home alone. She had been inside all day and was not allowed to go outside. The house was too quiet.

Suddenly, the phone rang. Alice jumped up and ran to answer it. It was her brother on the other end. He said he was having so much fun, he wanted to stay another night.

Alice felt even more miserable. She said goodbye to her brother, hung up the phone, and sat on the couch.

Just then, the doorbell rang. Alice was surprised. She looked through the window and saw a friendly face. She cracked the door open and he said, "I heard you were alone, so I made you something special." 

Alice opened the box and found her favorite treats. She was so happy! She said to the man, "Thank you!" 

The man said, "I'm glad I can help. Have a good night and sweet wake!" 

Alice hugged the box of treats and said, "Good night!"

The man smiled and waved goodbye. Alice closed the door, happy and not so miserable anymore.

name_of_work: Edgar Allan Poe by Timothy Thomas Fortune
content: I know not why, but it is true--it may, In some way, be because he was a child Of the fierce sun where I first wept and smiled-- I love the dark-browed Poe. His feverish day Was spent in dreams inspired, that him beguiled, When not along his path shone forth one ray Of light, of hope, to guide him on the way, That to earth's cares he might be reconciled. Not one of all Columbia's tuneful choir Has pitched his notes to such a matchless key As Poe--the wizard of the Orphic lyre! Not one has dreamed, has sung, such songs as he, Who, like an echo came, an echo went, Singing, back to his mother element.

name_of_work: A Leave-Taking by Algernon Charles Swinburne
content: Let us go hence, my songs; she will not hear. Let us go hence together without fear; Keep silence now, for singing-time is over, And over all old things and all things dear. She loves not you nor me as all we love her. Yea, though we sang as angels in her ear, She would not hear. Let us rise up and part; she will not know. Let us go seaward as the great winds go, Full of blown sand and foam; what help is here? There is no help, for all these things are so, And all the world is bitter as a tear. And how these things are, though ye strove to show, She would not know. Let us go home and hence; she will not weep. We gave love many dreams and days to keep, Flowers without scent, and fruits that would not grow, Saying 'If thou wilt, thrust in thy sickle and reap.' All is reaped now; no grass is left to mow; And we that sowed, though all we fell on sleep, She would not weep. Let us go hence and rest; she will not love. She shall not hear us if we sing hereof, Nor see love's ways, how sore they are and steep. Come hence, let be, lie still; it is enough. Love is a barren sea, bitter and deep; And though she saw all heaven in flower above, She would not love. Let us give up, go down; she will not care. Though all the stars made gold of all the air, And the sea moving saw before it move One moon-flower making all the foam-flowers fair; Though all those waves went over us, and drove Deep down the stifling lips and drowning hair, She would not care. Let us go hence, go hence; she will not see. Sing all once more together; surely she, She too, remembering days and words that were, Will turn a little toward us, sighing; but we, We are hence, we are gone, as though we had not been there. Nay, and though all men seeing had pity on me, She would not see.

name_of_work: To one who has been long in city pent by John Keats
content: To one who has been long in city pent, 'Tis very sweet to look into the fair And open face of heaven,--to breathe a prayer Full in the smile of the blue firmament. Who is more happy, when, with heart's content, Fatigued he sinks into some pleasant lair Of wavy grass, and reads a debonair And gentle tale of love and languishment? Returning home at evening, with an ear Catching the notes of Philomel,--an eye Watching the sailing cloudlet's bright career, He mourns that day so soon has glided by: E'en like the passage of an angel's tear That falls through the clear ether silently.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim loved to run and play outside. One day, Tim's mom gave him a cushion to sit on while he played. Tim thought the cushion was very soft and comfy.

Tim's friend came over to play and Tim showed him the cushion. His friend said, "That cushion is very modest." Tim didn't know what modest meant, but he thought it sounded nice.

After playing for a while, Tim and his friend decided to have a race. They ran as fast as they could, but Tim won because he was very good at running. Tim's friend was happy for him and they both sat on the cushion to rest. Tim was happy to have such a good friend to play with. The end.

Hush-a-bye, don't you cry, Go to sleep my little baby. When you wake you shall have All the pretty little horses. Black and bays, dapples, grays, All the pretty little horses. Hush-a-bye, don't you cry, Go to sleep my little baby. Hush-a-bye, don't you cry, Go to sleep my little baby. When you wake you shall have All the pretty little horses.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to eat butter on her toast every morning. One day, Lily's mom went to the store to buy more butter, but she forgot her phone at home. Lily's dad was at work, so there was no one to call Lily's mom and remind her to buy butter. 

Lily was worried that her mom would forget to buy butter, so she decided to wait by the window and watch for her mom's car. After a while, Lily saw her mom's car coming down the street. She was so happy that she shouted, "Mommy, mommy, you're back!" 

Lily's mom was surprised to see Lily waiting by the window, but she was happy to see her too. Lily told her mom that she was worried she would forget to buy butter, but her mom told her not to worry because she is reliable and always remembers what she needs to buy at the store. From that day on, Lily knew that she could always rely on her mom to buy butter.

Once upon a time there was a hairy bear called Joe. Joe wasn't like other bears: he loved to start things! One day, Joe wanted to start something special, so he started digging a big hole in the forest. 

Every day he was out digging, and it was hard work. One day Joe's friend, Kevin the rabbit, saw him digging and asked what he was doing. 

Joe stopped digging and said, "I'm digging this big hole so that maybe I can find something special. I want to see what's at the bottom!" 

Kevin said, "That sounds like a great idea! I'll help you!" 

So the two friends worked together, digging and digging. Finally, they reached the bottom of the hole, and sure enough there was something very special at the bottom. It was sparkly, and Joe knew it was a treasure! 

Joe and Kevin were so happy, they hugged each other and cheered. Joe said, "We did it! We started something special, and we found a treasure!" 

The two of them went home with the treasure, and they were very pleased with what they had achieved.

Sleep little baby, clean as a nut, Your fingers uncurl and your eyes are shut. Your life was ours, which is with you. Go on your journey. We go too. The bat is flying round the house Like an umbrella turned into a mouse. The moon is astonished and so are the sheep: Their bells have come to send you to sleep. Oh be our rest, our hopeful start. Turn your head to my beating heart. Sleep little baby, clean as a nut, Your fingers uncurl and your eyes are shut.

The sun was up and the happy little boy was ready for the day. He jumped out of bed and ran out to the beach. The tide was coming in and the water was bright and sparkly. He welcomed the smell of the salty air and the sound of the waves.

He walked down the beach, skipping and singing. He stopped for a moment to dig in the sand with his plastic shovel and then he ran back to the tide. He laughed as the cold water splashed around him. He saw some crabs scurrying by and began to chase them.

Just as the tide was starting to get too deep, his mom called. She took him to a nearby food stand and they had a spicy lunch. He loved the spicy food and gobbled it down, delighted.

He waved goodbye to the waves as he bid farewell to the beach. He said thank you to the welcome tide and smiled as the sun shone down on him. With one last look at the beach, he ran off home, looking forward to coming back again soon.

Once upon a time, there was a fisherman named Jack. He loved to go out on his boat and catch fish. But one day, he got bored of catching the same kind of fish over and over again. 

So, he decided to reverse his usual route and go to a new spot. He hoped to catch some new and exciting fish. 

As he was sailing, he saw a school of colorful fish swimming in the water. He quickly cast his net and caught some of the most beautiful fish he had ever seen. From that day on, he always reversed his route and found new and exciting fish to catch.

name_of_work: The Three Little Pigs by Roald Dahl
content: The animal I really dig, Above all others is the pig. Pigs are noble. Pigs are clever, Pigs are courteous. However, Now and then, to break this rule, One meets a pig who is a fool. What, for example, would you say, If strolling through the woods one day, Right there in front of you you saw A pig who'd built his house of STRAW? The Wolf who saw it licked his lips, And said, "That pig has had his chips." "Little pig, little pig, let me come in!" "No, no, by the hairs on my chinny-chin-chin!" "Then I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house in!" The little pig began to pray, But Wolfie blew his house away. He shouted, "Bacon, pork and ham! Oh, what a lucky Wolf I am!" And though he ate the pig quite fast, He carefully kept the tail till last. Wolf wandered on, a trifle bloated. Surprise, surprise, for soon he noted Another little house for pigs, And this one had been built of TWIGS! "Little pig, little pig, let me come in!" "No, no, by the hairs on my chinny-chin-chin!" "Then I'll huff and I'll puff and I'll blow your house in!" The Wolf said, "Okay, here we go!" He then began to blow and blow. The little pig began to squeal. He cried, "Oh Wolf, you've had one meal! Why can't we talk and make a deal? The Wolf replied, "Not on your nelly!" And soon the pig was in his belly. "Two juicy little pigs!" Wolf cried, "But still I'm not quite satisfied! I know how full my tummy's bulging, But oh, how I adore indulging." So creeping quietly as a mouse, The Wolf approached another house, A house which also had inside A little piggy trying to hide. "You'll not get me!" the Piggy cried. "I'll blow you down!" the Wolf replied. "You'll need," Pig said, "a lot of puff, And I don't think you've got enough." Wolf huffed and puffed and blew and blew. The house stayed up as good as new. "If I can't blow it down," Wolf said, I'll have to blow it up instead. I'll come back in the dead of night And blow it up with dynamite!" Pig cried, "You brute! I might have known!" Then, picking up the telephone, He dialed as quickly as he could The number of red Riding Hood. "Hello," she said. "Who's speaking? Who? Oh, hello, Piggy, how d'you do?" Pig cried, "I need your help, Miss Hood! Oh help me, please! D'you think you could?" "I'll try of course," Miss Hood replied. "What's on your mind...?" "A Wolf!" Pig cried. "I know you've dealt with wolves before, And now I've got one at my door!" "My darling Pig," she said, "my sweet, That's something really up my street. I've just begun to wash my hair. But when it's dry, I'll be right there." A short while later, through the wood, Came striding brave Miss Riding Hood. The Wolf stood there, his eyes ablaze, And yellowish, like mayonnaise. His teeth were sharp, his gums were raw, And spit was dripping from his jaw. Once more the maiden's eyelid flickers. She draws the pistol from her knickers. Once more she hits the vital spot, And kills him with a single shot. Pig, peeping through the window, stood And yelled, "Well done, Miss Riding Hood!" Ah, Piglet, you must never trust Young ladies from the upper crust. For now, Miss Riding Hood, one notes, Not only has two wolfskin coats, But when she goes from place to place, She has a PIGSKIN TRAVELING CASE.

name_of_work: Fire and Sleet and Candlelight by Elinor Wylie
content: For this you've striven Daring, to fail: Your sky is riven Like a tearing veil. For this, you've wasted Wings of your youth; Divined, and tasted Bitter springs of truth. From sand unslaked Twisted strong cords, And wandered naked Among trysted swords. There's a word unspoken, A knot untied. Whatever is broken The earth may hide. The road was jagged Over sharp stones: Your body's too ragged To cover your bones. The wind scatters Tears upon dust; Your soul's in tatters Where the spears thrust. Your race is ended-- See, it is run: Nothing is mended Under the sun. Straight as an arrow You fall to a sleep Not too narrow And not too deep.

Once there was a ship that sailed across the sea. But it was in danger when a big, scary monster came out of the deep water. The monster roared and its eyes glowed red. The brave sailors on the ship were scared. 

They knew they had to do something to get away from the monster. They thought about running away but it was too late. They had to fight the monster. 

They got their weapons and bravely went to fight. But the monster was too strong. It laughed at them and they had to retreat. The monster was too powerful and the stupid ship crew had no chance of stopping it. 

The monster left soon after, and the ship was safe again. The brave sailors on the ship were happy. They had survived!

One day, there was an important mission to work on. It was a mission to launch a missile. Everyone was very excited. Volunteers worked hard to make sure everything was perfect. They wanted to make sure the mission was successful. On the big day, they all watched as the missile flew off in the sky. Everyone cheered and clapped in delight. The mission was a success! Everyone hugged and celebrated together. It was a wonderful feeling to know that all the hard work had paid off!

I Jesus, Estrella, Esperanza, Mercy: Sails flashing to the wind like weapons, sharks following the moans the fever and the dying; horror the corposant and compass rose. Middle Passage: voyage through death to life upon these shores. "10 April 1800-- Blacks rebellious. Crew uneasy. Our linguist says their moaning is a prayer for death, ours and their own. Some try to starve themselves. Lost three this morning leaped with crazy laughter to the waiting sharks, sang as they went under." Desire, Adventure, Tartar, Ann: Standing to America, bringing home black gold, black ivory, black seed. Deep in the festering hold thy father lies, of his bones New England pews are made, those are altar lights that were his eyes. Jesus Saviour Pilot Me Over Life's Tempestuous Sea We pray that Thou wilt grant, O Lord, safe passage to our vessels bringing heathen souls unto Thy chastening. Jesus Saviour "8 bells. I cannot sleep, for I am sick with fear, but writing eases fear a little since still my eyes can see these words take shape upon the page & so I write, as one would turn to exorcism. 4 days scudding, but now the sea is calm again. Misfortune follows in our wake like sharks (our grinning tutelary gods). Which one of us has killed an albatross? A plague among our blacks--Ophthalmia: blindness--& we have jettisoned the blind to no avail. It spreads, the terrifying sickness spreads. Its claws have scratched sight from the Capt.'s eyes & there is blindness in the fo'c'sle & we must sail 3 weeks before we come to port." What port awaits us, Davy Jones' or home? I've heard of slavers drifting, drifting, playthings of wind and storm and chance, their crews gone blind, the jungle hatred crawling up on deck. Thou Who Walked On Galilee "Deponent further sayeth The Bella J left the Guinea Coast with cargo of five hundred blacks and odd for the barracoons of Florida: "That there was hardly room 'tween-decks for half the sweltering cattle stowed spoon-fashion there; that some went mad of thirst and tore their flesh and sucked the blood: "That Crew and Captain lusted with the comeliest of the savage girls kept naked in the cabins; that there was one they called The Guinea Rose and they cast lots and fought to lie with her: "That when the Bo's'n piped all hands, the flames spreading from starboard already were beyond control, the negroes howling and their chains entangled with the flames: "That the burning blacks could not be reached, that the Crew abandoned ship, leaving their shrieking negresses behind, that the Captain perished drunken with the wenches: "Further Deponent sayeth not." Pilot Oh Pilot Me II Aye, lad, and I have seen those factories, Gambia, Rio Pongo, Calabar; have watched the artful mongos baiting traps of war wherein the victor and the vanquished Were caught as prizes for our barracoons. Have seen the nigger kings whose vanity and greed turned wild black hides of Fellatah, Mandingo, Ibo, Kru to gold for us. And there was one--King Anthracite we named him-- fetish face beneath French parasols of brass and orange velvet, impudent mouth whose cups were carven skulls of enemies: He'd honor us with drum and feast and conjo and palm-oil-glistening wenches deft in love, and for tin crowns that shone with paste, red calico and German-silver trinkets Would have the drums talk war and send his warriors to burn the sleeping villages and kill the sick and old and lead the young in coffles to our factories. Twenty years a trader, twenty years, for there was wealth aplenty to be harvested from those black fields, and I'd be trading still but for the fevers melting down my bones. III Shuttles in the rocking loom of history, the dark ships move, the dark ships move, their bright ironical names like jests of kindness on a murderer's mouth; plough through thrashing glister toward fata morgana's lucent melting shore, weave toward New World littorals that are mirage and myth and actual shore. Voyage through death, voyage whose chartings are unlove. A charnel stench, effluvium of living death spreads outward from the hold, where the living and the dead, the horribly dying, lie interlocked, lie foul with blood and excrement. Deep in the festering hold thy father lies, the corpse of mercy rots with him, rats eat love's rotten gelid eyes. But, oh, the living look at you with human eyes whose suffering accuses you, whose hatred reaches through the swill of dark to strike you like a leper's claw. You cannot stare that hatred down or chain the fear that stalks the watches and breathes on you its fetid scorching breath; cannot kill the deep immortal human wish, the timeless will. "But for the storm that flung up barriers of wind and wave, The Amistad, senores, would have reached the port of Principe in two, three days at most; but for the storm we should have been prepared for what befell. Swift as the puma's leap it came. There was that interval of moonless calm filled only with the water's and the rigging's usual sounds, then sudden movement, blows and snarling cries and they had fallen on us with machete and marlinspike. It was as though the very air, the night itself were striking us. Exhausted by the rigors of the storm, we were no match for them. Our men went down before the murderous Africans. Our loyal Celestino ran from below with gun and lantern and I saw, before the cane- knife's wounding flash, Cinquez, that surly brute who calls himself a prince, directing, urging on the ghastly work. He hacked the poor mulatto down, and then he turned on me. The decks were slippery when daylight finally came. It sickens me to think of what I saw, of how these apes threw overboard the butchered bodies of our men, true Christians all, like so much jetsam. Enough, enough. The rest is quickly told: Cinquez was forced to spare the two of us you see to steer the ship to Africa, and we like phantoms doomed to rove the sea voyaged east by day and west by night, deceiving them, hoping for rescue, prisoners on our own vessel, till at length we drifted to the shores of this your land, America, where we were freed from our unspeakable misery. Now we demand, good sirs, the extradition of Cinquez and his accomplices to La Havana. And it distresses us to know there are so many here who seem inclined to justify the mutiny of these blacks. We find it paradoxical indeed that you whose wealth, whose tree of liberty are rooted in the labor of your slaves should suffer the august John Quincy Adams to speak with so much passion of the right of chattel slaves to kill their lawful masters and with his Roman rhetoric weave a hero's garland for Cinquez. I tell you that we are determined to return to Cuba with our slaves and there see justice done. Cinquez-- or let us say 'the Prince'--Cinquez shall die." The deep immortal human wish, the timeless will: Cinquez its deathless primaveral image, life that transfigures many lives. Voyage through death to life upon these shores.

Once upon a time, there was an enormous angel. He had the most encouraging words for everyone. Everywhere he flew, people felt his love. One day, he was flying around a small village and he saw a little girl crying. He went over to her and asked why she was crying.

The little girl said she was afraid of the dark and that she couldn't go to sleep. The angel was so kind and encouraging. He told her, â€œThere is nothing to be afraid of. When it is dark, just look around, you can see the stars in the sky, and you will feel better.â€

The little girl was so happy and thanked the angel for his encouraging words. She looked up and saw the twinkling stars and she knew she would be okay.

The angel was pleased that he had given the little girl such an important lesson â€“ that even in the dark, there can be light, if we just look for it.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Timmy. Timmy loved animals, especially lions and monkeys. One day, Timmy's mommy took him to the zoo. Timmy was so excited to see all the animals! They saw zebras, giraffes, and even a big elephant.

As they walked through the zoo, they came across a tight rope walker. He was walking across a thin rope high above them. Timmy watched in amazement as the tight rope walker made his way across. Suddenly, the tight rope walker slipped and fell! Timmy gasped as the man hit the ground hard.

Timmy's mommy quickly grabbed him and rushed him away from the scene. Timmy couldn't stop thinking about what had happened. He asked his mommy, "Why did the man fall?" His mommy replied, "Sometimes things appear safe, but they're really not. It's important to be careful." Timmy learned a valuable lesson that day, but he couldn't help feeling sad for the tight rope walker.

Once upon a time there was a boy who was in trouble. His family didn't have enough food to eat, and he was feeling very sad. He went to a quiet spot and kneeled down. He closed his eyes and began to pray. He asked God to help his family and to make something good happen for them. 

Suddenly, he heard something strange. It was the sound of a voice. It was coming from nearby.  He opened his eyes and looked around. There, on the ground, was an old book. He picked it up and opened it. Inside was a magical spell. 

The boy read the spell aloud, and a bright light filled the sky. Soon after, a basket of food appeared before him. It was full of yummy treats and fresh fruit. He couldn't believe his eyes.

The boy thanked God for the wonderful gift. He offered some of the food to the poor people in his town. He spread the magic spell around.  Even in the filthiest places, joyful smiles began to appear. 

The boy and his family were now happy and healthy. They were grateful for the magical spell, and would never forget to pray.

Love in my bosom like a bee Doth suck his sweet; Now with his wings he plays with me, Now with his feet. Within mine eyes he makes his nest, His bed amidst my tender breast; My kisses are his daily feast, And yet he robs me of my rest. Ah, wanton, will ye? And if I sleep, then percheth he With pretty flight, And makes his pillow of my knee The livelong night. Strike I my lute, he tunes the string; He music plays if so I sing; He lends me every lovely thing; Yet cruel he my heart doth sting. Whist, wanton, still ye! Else I with roses every day Will whip you hence, And bind you, when you long to play, For your offense. I'll shut mine eyes to keep you in, I'll make you fast it for your sin, I'll count your power not worth a pin. Alas! what hereby shall I win If he gainsay me? What if I beat the wanton boy With many a rod? He will repay me with annoy, Because a god. Then sit thou safely on my knee, And let thy bower my bosom be; Lurk in mine eyes, I like of thee. O Cupid, so thou pity me, Spare not, but play thee!

Once upon a time there were two friends, Tim and Jake. They were always together and enjoyed doing the same things. One day, Tim said to Jake, "let's go explore the big building near our house!" 

Jake thought it was a wonderful idea and he agreed to go. When they arrived at the building, Tim said "Let's take the elevator and go to the top!" Jake was a bit scared but he urged himself to try. In the elevator, they felt different! 

At the top, the friends looked out of the window and saw a beautiful view. They felt so lucky that they were brave enough to take the elevator. As the friends looked out of the window with excitement, they learned an important lesson: by taking risks and trying different things, you can find all sorts of wonderful things. 

The friends smiled to each other and knew they would always remember this day.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She had a piggy bank where she kept all her money. One day, she went to the store with her mom to buy some candy. When they got to the store, Lily realized she forgot her piggy bank at home. She felt sad because she couldn't buy any candy.

Her mom saw how sad she was and asked her what was wrong. Lily told her she forgot her piggy bank and couldn't buy candy. Her mom felt compassionate and gave her some money to buy candy. Lily was so happy and thanked her mom.

As they were leaving the store, Lily saw a homeless man sitting on the sidewalk. She asked her mom why he was there. Her mom explained that some people don't have homes or money to buy food. Lily felt sad for the homeless man and asked her mom if they could give him some money. Her mom agreed and they gave the man some money. Lily felt happy that they could help someone who needed it.

John and his mom were in the park. John saw a slide and ran towards it. He stopped in front of it and said to his mom, "Look Mom!"

His mom said, "That looks like fun!" Then she added, "If you want to go on it you must clap three times first." John clapped and clapped and clapped.

John went to the top of the slide and sat down. He slid down the slide and said, "Again!"

John and his mom spent the day playing on the slide and other things in the park. The day was mild and sunny.

At the end of the day, John's mom said, "That was great! Let's clap for the top of the slide!"

John clapped and clapped, with a big smile on his face. He said, "Let's do it again tomorrow!"

Once there were two best friends, John and Mary. They went for a picnic in the park. They had a big basket full of yummy food.

John said to Mary, "Let's play a game. I'll give you a basket and you have to record how fast you can put it down."

Mary was excited, so she agreed. She put the basket down with a big smile.

But then something happened. Mary noticed the basket was empty. She was very upset.

John said, "I'm sorry, Mary. I didn't mean to make you upset. I thought you wanted to play a game."

Mary was still upset, but then she smiled.

"It's okay, John. Let's just have fun and enjoy our picnic today."

And they did!

One day, a little girl named Lily went for a walk. She saw a big, fierce dog. The dog had sharp teeth and a loud bark. Lily was scared, but she wanted to look at the dog.

Lily said, "Hi, dog. You look fierce. Are you nice?" The dog stopped barking and wagged its tail. Lily knew the dog was nice, even though it looked fierce.

Just then, an alarm went off. The loud noise scared the dog. Lily said, "Don't worry, dog. It's just an alarm." The dog felt better and they became friends. They played together all day and had lots of fun.

Once, there was a girl who wanted to learn how to swim. She was very patient and decided to start by practising in the pool. She grabbed her swim rod, and put one arm on the rod and the other behind it, just like her teacher had taught her.

Slowly, she began to move through the water. She liked feeling the cool liquid as she moved her arms. She kept practising, until she was able to move through the water with her rod and without it. She was so proud of herself!

Every day, she went swimming for a little bit longer. She was so patient, and didn't give up even when she felt tired. After a month, she was an expert swimmer! She even started swimming competitions with her friends.

She could now swim like a fish in the water. She loved it so much that she kept practising for years and became the best swimmer in her city. All her hard work had paid off.

name_of_work: I look into my glass by Thomas Hardy
content: I look into my glass, And view my wasting skin, And say, "Would God it came to pass My heart had shrunk as thin!" For then, I, undistrest By hearts grown cold to me, Could lonely wait my endless rest With equanimity. But Time, to make me grieve, Part steals, lets part abide; And shakes this fragile frame at eve With throbbings of noontide.

Once upon a time, there was a big van. The van was red and shiny. It liked to drive down the road and go beep-beep.

One day, the van met a gentle cat. The cat was soft and fluffy. The cat said, "Hello, van! Can I ride with you?" The van said, "Yes! Hop in, gentle cat!"

The cat jumped into the van and they went for a ride. They saw a big tree with a lot of fruit. The cat jumped out and picked up a fruit. The cat gave the fruit a squeeze. Juice came out! The gentle cat and the big van had a fun day together.

Once upon a time there was a good little boy called Timmy. He loved to play and have fun with his friends.

One day, Timmy and his friends were playing near a lake. They saw a big rock near the water and decided to stand on it. 

"Let's jump in the lake!" said Timmy. His friends cheered and shouted, "Yeah!"

They jumped into the lake and the water splashed everywhere. They had so much fun!

They played in the water and watched the fish swim by. They also saw a cartoon on the lake - it was swimming too!

Timmy and his friends laughed and cheered. It was a really good day!

He talks, turning a sun-stained Cheek to me, his mouth, a dark Cavern, where stalactites of Uneven teeth gleam, his right Hand on my knee, while our minds Are willed to race towards love; But, they only wander, tripping Idly over puddles of Desire. .... .Can this man with Nimble finger-tips unleash Nothing more alive than the Skin's lazy hungers? Who can Help us who have lived so long And have failed in love? The heart, An empty cistern, waiting Through long hours, fills itself With coiling snakes of silence. ..... I am a freak. It's only To save my face, I flaunt, at Times, a grand, flamboyant lust.

Lily was a little girl who liked to play in the woods. She had a big flashlight that she used to see in the dark. One night, she saw a bright light moving among the trees. She was curious and followed it.

She came to a clearing and saw a fox. The fox had a shiny collar around its neck that made it glow. Lily thought it was pretty and wanted to touch it. She said, "Hello, fox. Can I be your friend?"

The fox was scared and ran away. It did not like the flashlight or the noise. It wanted to be free and quiet. It said, "No, no, go away. You are too loud and bright. You hurt my eyes and ears."

Lily was sad and confused. She did not mean to scare the fox. She turned off her flashlight and said, "I'm sorry, fox. I just wanted to play with you. You have a nice collar. Where did you get it?"

The fox stopped and looked back. It felt sorry for Lily. It said, "I got it from a bad man. He put it on me and tried to catch me. He wanted to sell me to a zoo. But I escaped and ran away. The collar is dull and heavy. It makes me sick and tired. I wish I could take it off."

Lily felt sorry for the fox. She said, "That's awful, fox. Maybe I can help you. I have a tool in my backpack that can cut the collar. Do you want me to try?"

The fox nodded and came closer. Lily took out her tool and carefully cut the collar. It fell off and stopped glowing. The fox felt lighter and happier. It said, "Thank you, Lily. You are very kind and brave. You are my friend."

Lily smiled and hugged the fox. She said, "You're welcome, fox. You are very smart and fast. You are my friend too."

They played together for a while and then said goodbye. Lily went back to her home and the fox went back to its den. They both slept well and dreamed of each other.

Once upon a time, there was a happy dog named Max. Max loved to run and play in the park with his owner, Sarah. One day, Max saw a little flea jumping around on his fur. 

Max barked, "Hey, little flea! What are you doing on me?!"

The cheerful flea replied, "I'm just looking for a new home to live in. Can I stay with you?"

Max thought about it and said, "Sure, you can follow me around wherever I go!"

So, the flea hopped onto Max's back and they went on an adventure together. Max ran and played, and the flea enjoyed the ride. They had so much fun together that they became best friends. From that day on, Max and the flea were inseparable, and they lived happily ever after.

Sam and Mia were playing with their toy rockets in the garden. They liked to pretend they were astronauts and explore the stars. They made loud noises as they launched their rockets into the air.

"Look, my rocket is faster than yours!" Sam said to Mia.

"No, mine is cleverer than yours!" Mia said to Sam. "It can do tricks and turn around."

They both laughed as they watched their rockets fly and spin. They did not see the big bird that was flying above them. The bird saw the rockets and thought they were tasty worms. It swooped down and grabbed Sam's rocket in its beak.

"Hey, that's my rocket!" Sam shouted. "Give it back, bird!"

The bird did not listen. It flew away with the rocket, happy with its snack. Sam was sad and angry. He wanted his rocket back.

Mia felt sorry for Sam. She had an idea. She took her rocket and aimed it at the bird. She pressed the button and the rocket zoomed after the bird. The rocket was clever and followed the bird wherever it went. The bird was scared and tried to shake off the rocket. It dropped Sam's rocket and flew away.

"Wow, you did it!" Sam said to Mia. "You saved my rocket!"

Mia smiled and gave Sam his rocket. They hugged and laughed. They were happy to have their rockets and each other. They decided to share their rockets and play together. They had more fun that way.

name_of_work: The Weary Blues by Langston Hughes
content: Droning a drowsy syncopated tune, Rocking back and forth to a mellow croon, I heard a Negro play. Down on Lenox Avenue the other night By the pale dull pallor of an old gas light He did a lazy sway. . . . He did a lazy sway. . . . To the tune o' those Weary Blues. With his ebony hands on each ivory key He made that poor piano moan with melody. O Blues! Swaying to and fro on his rickety stool He played that sad raggy tune like a musical fool. Sweet Blues! Coming from a black man's soul. O Blues! In a deep song voice with a melancholy tone I heard that Negro sing, that old piano moan-- "Ain't got nobody in all this world, Ain't got nobody but ma self. I's gwine to quit ma frownin' And put ma troubles on the shelf." Thump, thump, thump, went his foot on the floor. He played a few chords then he sang some more-- "I got the Weary Blues And I can't be satisfied. Got the Weary Blues And can't be satisfied-- I ain't happy no mo' And I wish that I had died." And far into the night he crooned that tune. The stars went out and so did the moon. The singer stopped playing and went to bed While the Weary Blues echoed through his head. He slept like a rock or a man that's dead.

Snow falling and night falling fast, oh, fast In a field I looked into going past, And the ground almost covered smooth in snow, But a few weeds and stubble showing last. The woods around it have it - it is theirs. All animals are smothered in their lairs. I am too absent-spirited to count; The loneliness includes me unawares. And lonely as it is, that loneliness Will be more lonely ere it will be less - A blanker whiteness of benighted snow WIth no expression, nothing to express. They cannot scare me with their empty spaces Between stars - on stars where no human race is. I have it in me so much nearer home To scare myself with my own desert places.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. One day, she went to the zoo with her mom and dad. They saw lots of animals, like lions and monkeys, but Lily was most excited to see the gorillas.

As they walked closer to the gorilla exhibit, Lily's dad said, "Be careful, Lily. Gorillas are very big and strong." Lily nodded, but she was too excited to be frightened.

Suddenly, they heard a loud noise. It was the sound of the gorilla pounding on its chest. Lily stopped in her tracks and looked up. The gorilla was staring right at her! Lily was frightened and wanted to leave, but her dad said, "Don't worry, Lily. The gorilla is just saying hello."

But then, the gorilla started to run towards them! Lily's dad quickly picked her up and they ran away. "Stop, gorilla, stop!" Lily yelled. Finally, they made it to safety. From then on, Lily was always a little bit frightened of gorillas, but she still loved going to the zoo with her family.

One day a little girl named Abigail went for a walk with her father to a special place. On the way, Abigail saw a hive with lots of bees buzzing around. She found it very interesting. 

Her father told Abigail that the hive was storing some very special honey, so they had to be careful not to disturb the bees. Abigail was so excited to find out what the honey would be used for! 

When they arrived at the special place, Abigail saw that lots of people were there. Her father explained that they were all beekeepers and they were going to make honey cookies. Abigail couldn't believe it! 

The beekeepers opened the hive and carefully scooped out the honey. They put it into the cookie batter and baked it in the oven. 

Abigail was amazed. She couldn't believe that the interesting hive she had seen on her walk had stored the honey that went into her delicious cookies.

Once upon a time there was a boy. He was very happy. He went to the store and saw lots of tasty things. He wanted to buy them all so he could have a healthy snack. He had some money, but it wasn't enough for all the snacks he wanted.

The boy started to cry. He wanted to get all the snacks so badly. Then, an idea came to him. He grabbed all of his money and threw it in the air. He watched as the coins flew up high and then rained back down everywhere. 

The boy clapped his hands excitedly. He ran around the store and scooped up as many healthy snacks as he could. He was so happy. Now he had enough snacks to eat every day. He thanked the store and was on his way. 

The boy looked back one more time before he left. He knew he had made the right decision. He smiled and waved goodbye to the store. He was happy with his healthy snacks!

Tim and Mia like to play with rockets. They have many rockets of different colors and sizes. They pretend to fly to the moon and the stars with their rockets.

One day, they find a big black rocket in the garage. It looks old and dusty, but they think it is cool. They want to play with it, but they don't know how it works.

"Let's try to make it fly!" Tim says. He pushes some buttons and pulls some levers on the rocket.

"Wait, Tim, I don't think that's a good idea!" Mia says. She is scared of the rocket. She thinks it might be dangerous.

But Tim does not listen to Mia. He keeps pushing and pulling. Suddenly, the rocket makes a loud noise and starts to shake. Smoke comes out of the back of the rocket.

"Tim, stop, stop, stop!" Mia shouts. She runs to Tim and tries to pull him away from the rocket.

But it is too late. The rocket blasts off and flies out of the garage. It zooms into the sky, leaving a trail of fire behind it.

Tim and Mia watch the rocket disappear. They are shocked and scared. They don't know what to do.

"Mom, Dad, help!" they cry. They hope their parents can hear them and come to save them. They hope the rocket does not hurt anyone or anything. They wish they had not played with the rocket. They wish they had listened to Mia.

Once upon a time, there was a baby named Timmy. Timmy loved to play with his toys and crawl around the house. One day, Timmy's big sister came over to play with him. She wanted to hold Timmy, but he was angry and didn't want to be picked up.

Timmy's sister tried to make him happy by showing him her favorite toy. It was a paper airplane that she had folded herself. Timmy was interested and wanted to play with it too. But when he tried to fold the paper, he couldn't do it right and got even more angry.

His sister saw that Timmy was struggling and helped him fold the paper airplane. Timmy was so happy and forgot all about being angry. They played with the paper airplane together and had lots of fun. From that day on, Timmy's sister helped him with his toys whenever he needed it.

name_of_work: I Am Lonely by George Eliot
content: The world is great: the birds all fly from me, The stars are golden fruit upon a tree All out of reach: my little sister went, And I am lonely. The world is great: I tried to mount the hill Above the pines, where the light lies so still, But it rose higher: little Lisa went And I am lonely. The world is great: the wind comes rushing by. I wonder where it comes from; sea birds cry And hurt my heart: my little sister went, And I am lonely. The world is great: the people laugh and talk, And make loud holiday: how fast they walk! I'm lame, they push me: little Lisa went, And I am lonely.

name_of_work: Bredon Hill by A. E. Housman
content: In summertime on Bredon The bells they sound so clear; Round both the shires they ring them In steeples far and near, A happy noise to hear. Here of a Sunday morning My love and I would lie, And see the coloured counties, And hear the larks so high About us in the sky. The bells would ring to call her In valleys miles away: 'Come all to church, good people; Good people, come and pray. But here my love would stay. And I would turn and answer Among the springing thyme, 'Oh, peal upon our wedding, And we will hear the chime, And come to church in time. But when the snows at Christmas On Bredon top were strewn, My love rose up so early And stole out unbeknown And went to church alone. They tolled the one bell only, Groom there was none to see, The mourners followed after, And so to church went she, And would not wait for me. The bells they sound on Bredon, And still the steeples hum. 'Come all to church, good people,' - Oh, noisy bells, be dumb; I hear you, I will come.

Lily and Sam were twins who loved to play on the beach. They liked to build sand castles, dig holes, and collect shells. One day, they found a shiny starfish on the sand. It was red and orange and had five arms.

"Wow, look at this!" Lily said. "It's so pretty. Can we keep it?"

Sam shook his head. "No, we can't. It belongs to the ocean. It needs water and friends. If we take it home, it will die."

"But I want it!" Lily said. "It's mine. I found it first."

She grabbed the starfish and ran away. Sam followed her, trying to make her stop. He was worried about the starfish.

Lily ran to their car, where their mom was waiting. She showed her the starfish and said, "Look, mom, I found a treasure. Can I have it?"

Mom looked at the starfish and frowned. She saw that it was dry and limp. She said, "Lily, this is not a treasure. This is a living thing. It belongs to the ocean, not to you. You have to put it back, or it will die."

Lily felt sad and guilty. She realized that she had been selfish and cruel. She said, "I'm sorry, mom. I'm sorry, starfish. I didn't know. I thought it was just a toy."

Mom hugged her and said, "It's okay, Lily. You made a mistake, but you can fix it. Let's go back to the beach and return the starfish to the water. Maybe it will survive and be happy again."

Lily and Sam ran back to the beach and gently placed the starfish in the water. They watched as it slowly moved its arms and sank into the waves. They hoped that it would find its family and be safe.

They learned a lesson that day. They learned that some things are not meant to be owned. They learned to respect the wild and the ocean. They learned to be kind and careful with all living things.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys in her room. One day, she threw her ball up high and it hit the ceiling. The ceiling was white and very tall. 

Lily wanted to get her ball back, but she couldn't reach it. So, she asked her mom for help. Her mom got a chair and stood on it. She reached up and grabbed the ball. She released the ball and it bounced on the floor. 

Lily noticed that the ball looked different now. It had a small dent on it from hitting the ceiling. But she didn't mind, she was just happy to have her ball back. From then on, she made sure to be careful when playing with her toys near the ceiling. The end.

name_of_work: I Shall Not Pass This Way Again by Eva Rose York
content: I shall not pass this way again-- Although it bordered be with flowers, Although I rest in fragrant bowers, And hear the singing Of song-birds winging To highest heaven their gladsome flight; Though moons are full and stars are bright, And winds and waves are softly sighing, While leafy trees make low replying; Though voices clear in joyous strain Repeat a jubilant refrain; Though rising suns their radiance throw On summer's green and winter's snow, In such rare splendor that my heart Would ache from scenes like these to part; Though beauties heighten, And life-lights brighten, And joys proceed from every pain,-- I shall not pass this way again. Then let me pluck the flowers that blow, And let me listen as I go To music rare That fills the air; And let hereafter Songs and laughter Fill every pause along the way; And to my spirit let me say: "O soul, be happy; soon 'tis trod, The path made thus for thee by God. Be happy, thou, and bless His name By whom such marvellous beauty came." And let no chance by me be lost To kindness show at any cost. I shall not pass this way again. Then let me now relieve some pain, Remove some barrier from the road, Or brighten someone's heavy load; A helping hand to this one lend, Then turn some other to befriend. O God, forgive That I now live As if I might, sometime, return To bless the weary ones that yearn For help and comfort every day,-- For there be such along the way. O God, forgive that I have seen The beauty only, have not been Awake to sorrow such as this; That I have drunk the cup of bliss Remembering not that those there be Who drink the dregs of misery. I love the beauty of the scene, Would roam again o'er fields so green; But since I may not, let me spend My strength for others to the end,-- For those who tread on rock and stone, And bear their burdens all alone, Who loiter not in leafy bowers, Nor hear the birds nor pluck the flowers. A larger kindness give to me, A deeper love and sympathy; Then, O, one day May someone say-- Remembering a lessened pain-- "Would she could pass this way again."

Once upon a time, there were two friends, Jack and Jill. Jack was very strong and Jill was very fragile. One day, they came across an onion. Jack wanted to show off his strength, so he decided to try and destroy the onion. 

Jill was against the idea and asked Jack not to do it. But Jack was too proud to listen. He thought that by destroying the onion, everyone would be impressed. So, he stretched his arms, yelled and destroyed the onion. 

Jill was disappointed. She said, "it's no use being so strong if you cannot control yourself. Being strong doesn't mean you should destroy something that is fragile". 

Jack then realized that his arrogance had prevented him from thinking sensibly. He apologized to Jill and promised to be careful in the future. 

Moral of the story: Being strong doesn't mean you should destroy something that is fragile.

Once upon a time, there was a little orange cat named Tim. Tim lived in a big house with a long stair. He loved to play with his ball and run up and down the stair all day.

One sunny day, Tim saw a little bird trapped in a cage. The bird was sad and wanted to go back to its family. Tim wanted to help and save the bird. So, he thought of a plan.

Tim used his ball to hit the cage door. With a loud "bang", the door opened. The bird was free and happy. Tim and the bird became best friends, and they played on the stair together every day. And they lived happily ever after.

Lily and Tom were playing in the bathroom. They saw a shiny thing on the sink. It was a razor. Lily wanted to touch it.

"Look, Tom, a shiny thing!" Lily said.

"No, Lily, don't touch it! It can hurt you!" Tom said.

But Lily did not listen. She reached for the razor. She cut her finger. She cried out loud.

"Ow, ow, ow! It hurts, Tom, it hurts!" Lily said.

Tom felt helpless. He did not know what to do. He saw some paper on the floor. He wrapped it around Lily's finger.

"Shh, Lily, shh. It's okay. I'll help you. Let's go find Mommy," Tom said.

He took Lily's hand and they ran out of the bathroom. They saw Mommy in the kitchen. She was making cookies.

"Mommy, Mommy, Lily cut her finger with the shiny thing!" Tom said.

Mommy looked at Lily's finger. She saw the blood and the paper. She was worried.

"Oh, no, Lily, what did you do? Come here, sweetie, let me see," Mommy said.

She took Lily in her arms and kissed her. She took off the paper and cleaned the cut. She put a band-aid on it.

"There, there, Lily, it's all better now. You're a brave girl. But you should never touch the shiny thing. It's a razor. It's for Daddy to shave his beard. It's very sharp and dangerous. Do you understand?" Mommy said.

Lily nodded. She felt sorry. She hugged Mommy.

"I'm sorry, Mommy. I won't touch it again. I love you, Mommy," Lily said.

Mommy smiled. She hugged Lily and Tom.

"I love you too, Lily. And I love you, Tom. You're a good brother. You tried to help Lily. But next time, if something like this happens, call me right away, okay?" Mommy said.

Tom nodded. He felt relieved. He hugged Mommy.

"Okay, Mommy. I'm sorry, too. I love you, Mommy," Tom said.

Mommy kissed them both.

"It's okay, my darlings. Now, let's go have some cookies. And then we'll settle down for a nap. How does that sound?" Mommy said.

Lily and Tom smiled. They liked cookies. And they were tired. They followed Mommy to the living room. They settled down on the couch with Mommy. They ate some cookies and drank some milk. They felt warm and cozy. They closed their eyes and fell asleep. Mommy watched them and smiled. She loved them very much.

Once upon a time, it was night. The moon was big and round, and it made everything outside look pale.

Amy was 3 years old and she was sleeping in her bed. Her parents were downstairs and it felt nice to be quiet and still. 

Suddenly, a loud noise came from outside her window! Amy was scared and she began to cry. 

"Don't worry, sweetie," her mom said, coming into her bedroom. "That's just the rain. It's heavy tonight, but it won't hurt you." 

Amy was relieved and she smiled. Her mom hugged her tight and said, "Now get some rest and soon the rain will be gone."

Amy drifted to sleep, feeling safe and happy in her mom's arms. When she woke in the morning, the sun was shining and the birds were singing. The rain had gone and the day was bright.

Tim and Lily were playing in the kitchen. They liked to pretend they were chefs and make yummy food. They used pots and pans and spoons and bowls. They also used water from the faucet to fill the pots and wash the dishes.

"Look, Lily, I made soup!" Tim said, holding a pot full of water and some carrots. "Do you want some?"

"Yes, please!" Lily said, grabbing a spoon. She tasted the soup and made a funny face. "Blech! This soup is bad! It has no salt or pepper or anything!"

Tim felt embarrassed. He wanted to make good soup for Lily. He thought maybe he could fix it. He saw a bottle of ketchup on the counter. He thought ketchup was red and tasty, so he poured some into the pot. He stirred the soup and said, "Here, try it now. It's better!"

Lily took another spoonful of the soup. She spat it out and cried, "Ew! This soup is worse! It's too sweet and sour and gross!"

Tim felt more embarrassed. He wanted to make Lily happy, not sad. He thought maybe he could make something else. He saw a box of cereal on the shelf. He thought cereal was crunchy and yummy, so he dumped some into the pot. He stirred the soup and said, "Here, try it now. It's the best!"

Lily looked at the soup. She saw water and carrots and ketchup and cereal. She shook her head and said, "No, thank you. This soup is not soup. It's a mess!"

Tim felt very embarrassed. He wanted to hide. He turned the faucet on and tried to wash the soup away. But the faucet was too powerful. It sprayed water everywhere. It splashed on the floor and the counter and the walls. It soaked Tim and Lily and the pots and pans and the spoons and bowls.

Tim and Lily screamed. They ran out of the kitchen. They saw Mom and Dad coming in. They saw their angry faces. They knew they were in trouble. They wished they had never played in the kitchen. They wished they had never made soup.

Tom and Lily are playing in the park. They have new toys. Tom has a weapon. It is a big gun that makes noise. Lily has a doll. It is a pretty doll with a dress.

"Look at my weapon!" Tom says. "It is so cool. I can shoot bad guys with it."

"Look at my doll!" Lily says. "It is so nice. I can hug her and dress her."

Tom and Lily show each other their toys. They are happy.

She looks around. She sees a stick. It is a big stick. She picks it up.

She runs to the big boy. She hits him with the stick. He drops Tom's weapon. He cries.

Lily stops. She gives Tom his weapon. He hugs her.

"Thank you, Lily!" he says. "You are brave. You are my friend."

Lily smiles. She hugs him back.

"You are welcome, Tom!" she says. "You are strong. You are my friend."

Tom and Lily play with their toys. They are happy. The big boy runs away. He is sad.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl who really wanted to go to the museum. But she was a bit nervous because she thought it might be a bit scary.

So her mom said, "Why don't you take your big brother with you? He won't let anything scare you."

The little girl nodded and held her brother's hand. They entered the museum and felt excited as they explored every corner. They looked at all the funny and cool things, but then they heard a loud sound.

The little girl got scared and asked her brother, "What was that?" He answered, "It's alright, don't be nervous. It was just a strange machine."

So the little girl smiled and they continued exploring the museum. She knew that her brother was there to protect her, so nothing could scare her anymore!

name_of_work: Is it Still the Same by Eavan Boland
content: young woman who climbs the stairs, who closes a child's door, who goes to her table in a room at the back of a house? The same unlighted corridor? The same night air over the wheelbarrows and rain-tanks? The same inky sky and pin-bright stars? You can see nothing of her, but her head bent over the page, her hand moving, moving again, and her hair. I wrote like that once. But this is different: This time, when she looks up, I will be there.

With how sad steps, O Moon, thou climb'st the skies! How silently, and with how wan a face! What, may it be that even in heavenly place That busy archer his sharp arrows tries? Sure, if that long-with-love-acquainted eyes Can judge of love, thou feel'st a lover's case, I read it in thy looks; thy languished grace, To me that feel the like, thy state descries. Then, even of fellowship, O Moon, tell me, Is constant love deemed there but want of wit? Are beauties there as proud as here they be? Do they above love to be loved, and yet Those lovers scorn whom that love doth possess? Do they call virtue there ungratefulness?

Once upon a time, there was a little girl called Sarah. She was playing in her garden one day when she found a dead bird. She was very sad and asked her Mom what she should do.

Mom said, "Let's rescue it! See that red button on the ground beside it? That's the rescue button. Press it and it will help the bird."

So Sarah pressed the button, but nothing happened. She looked closely at the button and noticed that it was dead.

"Oh no," said Mom. "It mustn't work anymore. The poor little bird can't be rescued now."

Sarah was very sad and she couldn't stop thinking about the bird all day. She was sad that the rescue button was dead, and that the poor little bird hadn't been rescued.

Once upon a time, there was a helpful boy named Tim. Tim loved to feed his pet cat, Fluffy. Every day, Tim would give Fluffy food and water. Fluffy was happy and grew big and strong.

One day, Tim and Fluffy went to the park. They saw a big muscle man lifting heavy things. "Wow," said Tim, "I want to be strong like him!" The muscle man heard Tim and said, "If you want to be strong, you must be helpful and feed your muscles with good food."

Tim listened to the muscle man and started to eat good food. He also helped his mom and dad with chores. As days went by, Tim grew stronger and stronger. One day, he saw the muscle man again. "Look at me now!" said Tim. The muscle man smiled and said, "You did it! You are strong and helpful, just like me." Tim and Fluffy were very happy.

Once upon a time, there was a big dog named Spot. Spot was very impatient. He wanted to play all day.

One day, Spot went to the park with his friend, a little boy named Tim. Tim said, "Let's play ball!" Spot was very happy. They set the ball on the ground and kicked it back and forth.

As they played, a little girl named Sue came to the park. Sue said, "Can I play too?" Tim and Spot said, "Yes!" They all played together and had a fun day at the park.

Lily liked to organize her toys. She had a box for her dolls, a box for her cars, and a box for her books. She liked to make everything neat and tidy. She did not like it when her brother Max messed up her toys. He liked to throw them around and mix them up.

One day, Lily and Max had steak for dinner. Lily loved steak. She ate it all up and said thank you to Mom. Max did not like steak. He said it was terrible and made a face. He did not eat it and said he wanted candy instead. Mom said no, he had to eat his steak first. Max got angry and threw his steak on the floor. Lily was shocked. She thought that was very rude and wasteful.

Mom was upset too. She said Max had to go to his room and think about what he did. She said he could not have any candy or dessert until he apologized and cleaned up his mess. Max stomped to his room and slammed the door. He did not say sorry or pick up his steak.

Lily felt sorry for Mom. She wanted to help her. She asked Mom if she could organize the kitchen. Mom smiled and said yes, that would be very nice of her. Lily got a cloth and a bucket and started to wipe the table and the chairs. She put the dishes in the sink and the leftovers in the fridge. She even found Max's steak on the floor and threw it in the trash. She did a good job and made the kitchen look clean and cozy.

Mom hugged Lily and thanked her for being such a good helper. She said she was very proud of her. She said she could have a piece of cake and some milk for dessert. Lily was happy. She enjoyed her cake and milk and felt warm and cozy. She learned that it was better to be organized and polite than to be messy and rude. She hoped that Max would learn that too.

Mum and Dad were walking in the park one day.  All of a sudden, Dad said, "Look over there!" Sure enough, there was a gray deer walking in the bushes. Mum was excited, and she said, "Let's give that deer some food!"

Dad smiled and nodded. He bent down and picked up a handful of nuts. Then he walked up to the deer and reached out his hand. The deer trusted Dad and took the nuts from him. It seemed so gentle and happy!

Mum and Dad smiled as they watched the deer eating the nuts. They couldn't believe how lucky they were to have seen such a beautiful sight. Suddenly, the deer tilted its head and looked up at Dad and brushed its head against his hand!

Dad smiled back at the deer, and he said, "It's nice to meet you, little one." He looked at Mum and said, "I think we should give the deer some more food."

Mum nodded, and the couple went back home to get some more food for the deer. As they left, Mum said, "I'm so glad we were able to give the deer some food!"
