Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and talk on her phone. One day, Lily's mom told her they were going to visit her grandma's house. Lily was very excited to see her grandma, but she didn't know what was waiting for her.

When they arrived at grandma's house, Lily saw a big tree in the backyard. Her mom told her they were going to hang a swing from the tree. Lily was so happy! She loved to swing and play outside.

After they hung the swing, Lily's mom told her to be quiet because grandma was taking a nap. Lily tried to be quiet, but she was so excited to play on the swing that she couldn't help but scream with joy. Suddenly, her phone rang. Lily answered it, but it was just a beep sound. She realized she forgot to charge her phone and it died. 

Lily was sad that her phone didn't work, but she didn't need it anymore because she was having so much fun on the swing. She swung back and forth, feeling the wind in her hair, and she knew she would always remember this fun day with her grandma.

Sleepless in the cold dark, I look through the closed dim door be- fore me, which be- comes an abyss into which my memories have fallen past laughter or horror, passion or hard work--my memories of our past laughter, horror, passion, hard work. An ache of be- ing. An ache of being, over love. An ache of being over love. Like projections on the screen of the heavy window curtains, flashing lights of a slow-scraping after- midnight snowplow for a moment pulse in this room.

Lily and Max were twins who liked to go on adventures. They always wanted to see new things and have fun. One day, they asked their mom if they could go to the zoo. Mom said yes, but they had to be good and listen to her.

They got in the car and drove to the zoo. But on the way, they saw a lot of cars and trucks on the road. They were stuck in traffic. Lily and Max did not like traffic. They wanted to get to the zoo fast. They started to whine and cry.

"Mom, why are there so many cars?" Lily asked.

"Mom, when will we get to the zoo?" Max asked.

Mom tried to calm them down. She said, "I know you are excited, but we have to be patient. There is a lot of traffic today. Maybe there was an accident or something. We will get to the zoo soon, I promise."

But Lily and Max did not listen. They kept whining and crying. They kicked the seats and threw their toys. They made a lot of noise. Mom was very angry. She said, "Stop it, you two! You are spoiling our trip to the zoo. If you don't behave, we will go back home and you will not see any animals."

Lily and Max did not want that. They liked animals. They wanted to see the lions and the monkeys and the elephants. They realized they were being naughty. They said, "Sorry, mom. We will be good. We will wait for the traffic to go away."

Mom smiled and said, "Thank you, Lily and Max. I love you. You are my adventurous twins. But sometimes you have to be calm and quiet. The zoo will be more fun if you are happy and polite."

Lily and Max nodded and hugged their mom. They said, "We love you, mom. You are the best. We will be calm and quiet. We will enjoy the zoo."

Mom hugged them back and said, "That's my good twins. I'm proud of you. Now let's see if the traffic moves. Maybe we will get to the zoo soon."

Once upon a time, there was a little girl. She was very lonely and wanted to find a friend. One day, when she was walking in the park, she saw a notebook lying on the ground. She thought it looked lonely, so she picked it up and took it home with her.

When she got home, she opened the notebook and found lots of pictures and stories inside. She was so happy! She sat down on her bed and read every page in the notebook. She couldn't believe her luck; she had found a new friend!

The little girl kept the notebook with her everywhere she went. People started to notice that she had the notebook and they got jealous. So one day, when the girl wasn't looking, one of the boys in her class tried to steal the notebook.

The little girl was very angry. She ran after the boy and grabbed the notebook back. She held it close to her heart and never let it go. After that, she was always very careful. She never let anyone steal her notebook again.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and draw pictures. One day, her mom brought home a beautiful vase. It was so pretty, Lily wanted to touch it. But her mom said, "Be careful, Lily. It's fragile."

Lily promised to be careful, but she forgot. She accidentally knocked the vase over and it broke into many pieces. She was scared her mom would be mad at her. When her mom saw the broken vase, she sighed and said, "Lily, I'm not mad. But you need to be more careful. Accidents happen, but you need to learn from them."

Lily felt bad and promised to be more careful. Her mom said, "Repeat after me, Lily. I will be careful with fragile things." Lily repeated the words and felt better. From then on, she was more careful with fragile things and never broke anything again.

Once upon a time there was a little deer named Lucky who lived in the forest. Lucky was always hopping around, looking for something to do.

One day Lucky was walking. He noticed a patch of soft grass in a sunny spot, and he thought it would be the perfect place for a nap. After laying down, Lucky quickly fell asleep in the warm sunshine.

Suddenly, Lucky heard a voice. "Wake up, Lucky!," it said. Lucky looked up, and saw a little rabbit sitting next to him. "Why don't we go explore the forest together?" the rabbit said.

Lucky hopped up and smiled. He was very excited. "Let's go!," he said.

So Lucky and the rabbit hopped off to explore the forest. With every step, Lucky felt even luckier to have such a good friend. The two animals had a wonderful time, and before they knew it, it was time to go home.

But Lucky knew he'd be back soon. After all, the forest was his favorite place to nap.

Once upon a time, there was a yummy pastry. It was sweet, soft and full of creamy goodness. 

Big Johnny was very hungry and he wanted to eat the pastry. He reached out to take it, but was careful not to touch the icy cool surface. 

Suddenly, the pastry started to move. Johnny suffered a shock and screamed! But it was just a mouse nibbling away at the pastry. 

Johnny wanted the pastry, so he chased the mouse away. He grabbed the pastry and ran home to eat it. 

Johnny was happy that he could eat the pastry. He soon forgot about the mouse and the icy cold pastry.

Once upon a time there was a girl who was almost three. One day she was walking and she met a muffin. The muffin was very nice and mild. She said hello to the muffin and the muffin said hello back.

The muffin asked the girl if she wanted to play. The girl said yes and they played hide-and-seek. After a while the girl had to go home, but she asked the muffin if she wanted to visit.

The muffin said yes and they made plans to meet again soon. The girl was very happy and skipped all the way home, thinking about how much fun they would have when they met again.

Once upon a time, there was a perfect cow. She was having a great day, grazing in a pretty meadow. Suddenly, she heard a noise coming from the forest near by. It was a wolf! He was struggling to get out of a deep hole he had fallen in. 
"Help me!" he cried.
The cow thought for a moment, and then decided that she had to rescue the wolf. She started searching for something to help her. Then, she found some leaves and grass, and started piling them up to the edge of the hole. 
The wolf quickly climbed onto the pile and was soon out of the hole. He was so grateful to the cow for rescuing him, and thanked her before slipping back into the forest. The cow was happy that she had been able to help the perfect wolf. 
She watched him go, happy to have been part of his perfect rescue.

name_of_work: Part VII: The Rime of The Ancient Mariner by S.T. Coleridge
content: This Hermit good lives in that wood Which slopes down to the sea. How loudly his sweet voice he rears! He loves to talk with marineres That come from a far countree. He kneels at morn, and noon, and eve-- He hath a cushion plump: It is the moss that wholly hides The rotted old oak-stump. The skiff-boat neared: I heard them talk, 'Why, this is strange, I trow! Where are those lights so many and fair, That signal made but now?' 'Strange, by my faith!' the Hermit said-- 'And they answered not our cheer! The planks looked warped! and see those sails, How thin they are and sere! I never saw aught like to them, Unless perchance it were Brown skeletons of leaves that lag My forest-brook along; When the ivy-tod is heavy with snow, And the owlet whoops to the wolf below, That eats the she-wolf's young.' 'Dear Lord! it hath a fiendish look-- (The Pilot made reply) I am a-feared'--'Push on, push on!' Said the Hermit cheerily. The boat came closer to the ship, But I nor spake nor stirred; The boat came close beneath the ship, And straight a sound was heard. Under the water it rumbled on, Still louder and more dread: It reached the ship, it split the bay; The ship went down like lead. Stunned by that loud and dreadful sound, Which sky and ocean smote, Like one that hath been seven days drowned My body lay afloat; But swift as dreams, myself I found Within the Pilot's boat. Upon the whirl, where sank the ship, The boat spun round and round; And all was still, save that the hill Was telling of the sound. I moved my lips--the Pilot shrieked And fell down in a fit; The holy Hermit raised his eyes, And prayed where he did sit. I took the oars: the Pilot's boy, Who now doth crazy go, Laughed loud and long, and all the while His eyes went to and fro. 'Ha! ha!' quoth he, 'full plain I see, The Devil knows how to row.' And now, all in my own countree, I stood on the firm land! The Hermit stepped forth from the boat, And scarcely he could stand. 'O shrieve me, shrieve me, holy man!' The Hermit crossed his brow. 'Say quick,' quoth he, 'I bid thee say-- What manner of man art thou?' Forthwith this frame of mine was wrenched With a woful agony, Which forced me to begin my tale; And then it left me free. Since then, at an uncertain hour, That agony returns: And till my ghastly tale is told, This heart within me burns. I pass, like night, from land to land; I have strange power of speech; That moment that his face I see, I know the man that must hear me: To him my tale I teach. What loud uproar bursts from that door! The wedding-guests are there: But in the garden-bower the bride And bride-maids singing are: And hark the little vesper bell, Which biddeth me to prayer! O Wedding-Guest! this soul hath been Alone on a wide wide sea: So lonely 'twas, that God himself Scarce seemed there to be. O sweeter than the marriage-feast, 'Tis sweeter far to me, To walk together to the kirk With a goodly company!-- To walk together to the kirk, And all together pray, While each to his great Father bends, Old men, and babes, and loving friends And youths and maidens gay! Farewell, farewell! but this I tell To thee, thou Wedding-Guest! He prayeth well, who loveth well Both man and bird and beast. He prayeth best, who loveth best All things both great and small; For the dear God who loveth us, He made and loveth all. The Mariner, whose eye is bright, Whose beard with age is hoar, Is gone: and now the Wedding-Guest Turned from the bridegroom's door. He went like one that hath been stunned, And is of sense forlorn: A sadder and a wiser man, He rose the morrow morn.

One day, the sun was shining brightly. Little Sue was in her garden, playing with her toys. She noticed a plant growing in the garden that she had never seen before. She went closer to take a better look.

"Look at that plant, mommy!" She said.

"Yes, Sue," replied Mommy. "It looks very organized. I'm sure it will shine brightly."

Little Sue looked at the plant with admiration. She wanted to reach out and touch it. But before she could do so, a gust of wind blew it away.

Little Sue was so sad. She had been so excited to see the plant growing in their garden. She cried and asked Mommy why the plant had been taken away.

Mommy looked around and said, "Sometimes, things just don't work out the way we want them to."

One day, John and his mom went to the store. John loved going shopping and this time, he saw something extra special. It was a big, red lollipop. John wanted it desperately and asked his mom to buy it for him.

His mom shook her head. "No, John," she said. "It would be bad for your teeth. Besides, it has too much sugar."

John was unhappy and he asked again. He said, "Please, Mom. I really want the lollipop!" His mom frowned and said, "No, John. The answer is still no."

John was upset, but his mom had made her decision. Then, from behind some shelves, John spotted a shiny bald man. The man smiled and said, "Greetings, young sir! Would you like to measure how long this lollipop is?"

John was thrilled! He grabbed the lollipop and held it up. Then, using the man's ruler, he carefully measured it. When he was finished, the man thanked him and gave him the lollipop.

John was elated! He ran back to his mom and proudly showed her the lollipop. His mom smiled and said, "That was clever of you, John. You found a nice way to get your lollipop after all."

John smiled and thanked the bald man. He was so excited to have his lollipop

name_of_work: In the Waiting Room by Elizabeth Bishop
content: In Worcester, Massachusetts, I went with Aunt Consuelo to keep her dentist's appointment and sat and waited for her in the dentist's waiting room. It was winter. It got dark early. The waiting room was full of grown-up people, arctics and overcoats, lamps and magazines. My aunt was inside what seemed like a long time and while I waited I read the National Geographic (I could read) and carefully studied the photographs: the inside of a volcano, black, and full of ashes; then it was spilling over in rivulets of fire. Osa and Martin Johnson dressed in riding breeches, laced boots, and pith helmets. A dead man slung on a pole --"Long Pig," the caption said. Babies with pointed heads wound round and round with string; black, naked women with necks wound round and round with wire like the necks of light bulbs. Their breasts were horrifying. I read it right straight through. I was too shy to stop. And then I looked at the cover: the yellow margins, the date. Suddenly, from inside, came an oh! of pain --Aunt Consuelo's voice-- not very loud or long. I wasn't at all surprised; even then I knew she was a foolish, timid woman. I might have been embarrassed, but wasn't. What took me completely by surprise was that it was me: my voice, in my mouth. Without thinking at all I was my foolish aunt, I--we--were falling, falling, our eyes glued to the cover of the National Geographic, February, 1918. I said to myself: three days and you'll be seven years old. I was saying it to stop the sensation of falling off the round, turning world. into cold, blue-black space. But I felt: you are an I, you are an Elizabeth, you are one of them. Why should you be one, too? I scarcely dared to look to see what it was I was. I gave a sidelong glance --I couldn't look any higher-- at shadowy gray knees, trousers and skirts and boots and different pairs of hands lying under the lamps. I knew that nothing stranger had ever happened, that nothing stranger could ever happen. Why should I be my aunt, or me, or anyone? What similarities-- boots, hands, the family voice I felt in my throat, or even the National Geographic and those awful hanging breasts-- held us all together or made us all just one? How--I didn't know any word for it--how "unlikely". . . How had I come to be here, like them, and overhear a cry of pain that could have got loud and worse but hadn't? The waiting room was bright and too hot. It was sliding beneath a big black wave, another, and another. Then I was back in it. The War was on. Outside, in Worcester, Massachusetts, were night and slush and cold, and it was still the fifth of February, 1918.

Once upon a time, there was a beautiful black bird who lived in the forest. His wings were very fragile and he loved to soar through the air. 

One day, the bird decided he wanted to build himself a nest. He gathered twigs and set the nest up in a nearby tree.

He was very proud of himself, but the tree was very close to a big river. When a storm came, it started to rain heavily and the river started to swell.

The bird became scared, but he didn't want to leave his beautiful nest. His friend, the wise fox, warned him that it wasn't wise. She said, "Your nest is delicate and will not protect you from the rain and the rising waters. You must set off now and find a new place to stay.

The bird was very sad, but he understood the fox's advice and set off to search for a new home. After a long time, he found a cave with a dry, safe shelter. He was happy and forever grateful to his wise friend for saving him.

The moral of the story is: listen to wise advice, even if it is difficult.

name_of_work: Venus of the Louvre by Emma Lazarus
content: Down the long hall she glistens like a star, The foam-born mother of Love, transfixed to stone, Yet none the less immortal, breathing on. Time's brutal hand hath maimed but could not mar. When first the enthralled enchantress from afar Dazzled mine eyes, I saw not her alone, Serenely poised on her world-worshipped throne, As when she guided once her dove-drawn car,-- But at her feet a pale, death-stricken Jew, Her life adorer, sobbed farewell to love. Here Heine wept! Here still he weeps anew, Nor ever shall his shadow lift or move, While mourns one ardent heart, one poet-brain, For vanished Hellas and Hebraic pain.

Once upon a time there was a popular pine. Everyone in the forest loved it and would often stop to admire it.

One day, a little 3-year old girl was visiting the pine. As soon as she spotted it, she wanted to go and explore it. Her mother warned her to stay back, but the little girl just wanted to see it up close. She didn't listen.

The little girl reached the popular pine and was so excited to see the bark. She reached out to touch it and suddenly she heard a voice behind her.

"You must never touch the popular pine!" it said.

The little girl quickly turned around. She saw a large owl standing before her. 

"Why?" the little girl asked.

"Because this pine is very special," the owl said. "It is part of the magical forest and if you touch it, bad things might happen." 

The little girl quickly stepped away from the pine. She thanked the owl for warning her and learned to never try and touch it again. 

The little girl and her mother enjoyed the rest of their time in the magical forest and the little girl was always sure to stay away from the popular pine.

Once upon a time, there was a little boy named Tim. Tim had a club that he loved to play with. One day, Tim's friend Jake came over to play with him. Tim was happy to see Jake, but he didn't trust him with his club. 

Jake wanted to play with the club too, but Tim was afraid that Jake might break it. Tim told Jake that he couldn't play with his club. Jake was sad, but he understood that Tim didn't want anything bad to happen to his club.

After a while, Tim's mom brought them some sour candy to share. Tim and Jake both loved the candy and they laughed and played together. Tim realized that he could trust Jake with his candy, just like he trusted his mom to give him good things to eat. Tim decided to let Jake play with his club too, and they had a great time playing together. From that day on, Tim knew that he could trust Jake with his toys and his candy.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys and always made a big mess in her room. One day, her mom came in and noticed how messy her room was. She asked Lily to clean up her toys and make her room tidy. 

Lily didn't want to clean up because she wanted to play more. But her mom told her that it was important to keep her room tidy so she wouldn't lose her toys and could find them easily. 

Lily realized that her mom was telling the True and decided to clean up her room. She put all her toys away and made her bed. When she was finished, she noticed how much better her room looked and how happy it made her feel. From that day on, Lily made sure to keep her room tidy so she could always find her toys and feel happy.

Once upon a time there lived a little girl named April. April was only three years old, but she was very smart. Every day she would play with her friends at the park. 

One day April went to the park and found a funny looking bug. She had never seen a bug like it before, so she picked it up. April thought it was the most colorful bug she had ever seen. 

But then her friend Susie screamed, "Put it down! Don't trust that bug." April was scared, so she dropped the bug quickly and ran to Susie. 

Susie hugged April and said, "It's ok. You don't ever have to trust something you are unsure about. Next time, just ask me first." April understood and hugged Susie back. 

From then on, whenever April felt unsure about anything, she knew she could trust Susie and ask her questions.

Once upon a time, there was a silly monkey named Max. Max liked to play all day in the jungle with his friends. One day, Max found a stick and started to rub it against a rock. Suddenly, fire came out of the stick!

Max was very surprised and ran to tell his friends. They all gathered around the fire and watched it dance and flicker. They roasted some bananas and had a nice snack.

After playing for a while, Max realized that he had rubbed his hand too hard against the rock and it hurt a little. His friends helped him rub some leaves on it to make it better. Max was happy again and they all went back to playing in the jungle. The end.

Lily and Sam were playing with blocks. Lily liked to build tall towers with many colors. Sam liked to knock them down with his car. Lily was not happy when Sam did that. She said, "Stop, Sam! You are mean! You break my towers!"

Sam laughed and said, "It is fun, Lily! You can build them again. Look, I can make a bridge with my blocks. It is better than your towers."

Lily looked at Sam's bridge. It was long and strong. She was envious of Sam. She wanted to make a bridge too. But she did not know how. She tried to copy Sam, but her blocks fell down. She felt sad and angry.

She said, "Sam, you are not fair! You have more blocks than me. You do not share. You make a bridge and I cannot. You are a bad friend!"

Sam looked at Lily. He saw that she was crying. He felt sorry for her. He said, "Lily, I am sorry. I did not mean to hurt you. I have an idea. Why don't we make a bridge together? We can use both our blocks. We can help each other. It will be fun."

Lily wiped her tears. She liked Sam's idea. She said, "Okay, Sam. Let us make a bridge together. But you have to be nice. You cannot break it."

Sam nodded. He said, "Okay, Lily. I will be nice. I will not break it."

They started to work on the bridge. They used their fingers to connect the blocks. They managed to make a big bridge. It was bigger than Sam's bridge. It was bigger than Lily's towers. They were both happy. They said, "Wow, look at our bridge! It is amazing! We are good friends!"

Once upon a time, there was a world full of fun and adventure. One day, a little girl named Lucy asked her mom, "Can I go play in the forest?" Her mom replied, "Be careful, there are thieves out there!"

Lucy was not scared. She thought thieves were just a crazy story. She quickly ran off into the woods.

The little girl was walking through the forest when she heard a rustling in the trees. Suddenly, a strange creature appeared! Lucy was scared at first, but then she saw a tiny twinkle in its eyes. She believed that it was a friendly creature, so she went close to it.

The creature started to tell her a story. It said, "You should believe in the things you can't see. A thief might come and steal away your fun, but if you keep believing, you'll get your happy back soon."

Lucy thanked the creature for its wise advice and continued her journey into the forest. She knew that no matter what, she should always believe.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play with her toys all day long. One day, Lily's mom told her it was time to go to the park. Lily was so excited, she put on her shoes and ran outside.

At the park, Lily saw a big cross on the ground. She asked her mom what it was for. Her mom explained that it was a special symbol for some people. Lily thought it was pretty.

After playing for a while, Lily started to feel tired. She told her mom that she wanted to go home. Her mom said, "Okay, let's go." They walked back home together.

When they got home, Lily's mom asked her to put away her toys. Lily groaned and said, "I'm so tired!" Her mom smiled and said, "I know, but let's put them away so they don't get lost." Lily nodded and put her toys in their box.

Nothing would sleep in that cellar, dank as a ditch, Bulbs broke out of boxes hunting for chinks in the dark, Shoots dangled and drooped, Lolling obscenely from mildewed crates, Hung down long yellow evil necks, like tropical snakes. And what a congress of stinks! Roots ripe as old bait, Pulpy stems, rank, silo-rich, Leaf-mold, manure, lime, piled against slippery planks. Nothing would give up life: Even the dirt kept breathing a small breath.

name_of_work: Metrical Feet by Samuel Taylor Coleridge
content: Trochee trips from long to short; From long to long in solemn sort Slow Spondee stalks, strong foot!, yet ill able Ever to come up with Dactyl's trisyllable. Iambics march from short to long. With a leap and a bound the swift Anapests throng. One syllable long, with one short at each side, Amphibrachys hastes with a stately stride -- First and last being long, middle short, Amphimacer Strikes his thundering hoofs like a proud high-bred Racer. If Derwent be innocent, steady, and wise, And delight in the things of earth, water, and skies; Tender warmth at his heart, with these meters to show it, With sound sense in his brains, may make Derwent a poet -- May crown him with fame, and must win him the love Of his father on earth and his father above. My dear, dear child! Could you stand upon Skiddaw, you would not from its whole ridge See a man who so loves you as your fond S.T. Colerige.

name_of_work: Good-Bye, Little Cabin by Robert Service
content: O dear little cabin, I've loved you so long, And now I must bid you good-bye! I've filled you with laughter, I've thrilled you with song, And sometimes I've wished I could cry. Your walls they have witnessed a weariful fight, And rung to a won Waterloo: But oh, in my triumph I'm dreary to-night -- Good-bye, little cabin, to you! Your roof is bewhiskered, your floor is a-slant, Your walls seem to sag and to swing; I'm trying to find just your faults, but I can't -- You poor, tired, heart-broken old thing! I've seen when you've been the best friend that I had, Your light like a gem on the snow; You're sort of a part of me -- Gee! but I'm sad; I hate, little cabin, to go. Below your cracked window red raspberries climb; A hornet's nest hangs from a beam; Your rafters are scribbled with adage and rhyme, And dimmed with tobacco and dream. "Each day has its laugh", and "Don't worry, just work". Such mottoes reproachfully shine. Old calendars dangle -- what memories lurk About you, dear cabin of mine! I hear the world-call and the clang of the fight; I hear the hoarse cry of my kind; Yet well do I know, as I quit you to-night, It's Youth that I'm leaving behind. And often I'll think of you, empty and black, Moose antlers nailed over your door: Oh, if I should perish my ghost will come back To dwell in you, cabin, once more! How cold, still and lonely, how weary you seem! A last wistful look and I'll go. Oh, will you remember the lad with his dream! The lad that you comforted so. The shadows enfold you, it's drawing to-night; The evening star needles the sky: And huh! but it's stinging and stabbing my sight -- God bless you, old cabin, good-bye!

But the bracelet was fragile and easily broke. One day, as Lily was playing, the bracelet fell off her hand and broke into many pieces. She was very sad and cried a lot. Her mommy tried to fix the bracelet, but it was too fragile to be fixed.

Lily learned an important lesson that day. She realized that sometimes pretty things can be fragile and easily broken. She promised herself that she would be more careful with her things from now on. Even though she was sad about the broken bracelet, she knew that it was important to be responsible and take care of her belongings.

name_of_work: Loveliest of Trees by A. E. Housman
content: Loveliest of trees, the cherry now Is hung with bloom along the bough, And stands about the woodland ride Wearing white for Eastertide. Now, of my threescore years and ten, Twenty will not come again, And take from seventy springs a score, It only leaves me fifty more. And since to look at things in bloom Fifty springs are little room, About the woodlands I will go To see the cherry hung with snow

name_of_work: The Circus Animals' Desertion by W.B. Yeats
content: I sought a theme and sought for it in vain, I sought it daily for six weeks or so. Maybe at last being but a broken man I must be satisfied with my heart, although Winter and summer till old age began My circus animals were all on show, Those stilted boys, that burnished chariot, Lion and woman and the Lord knows what. What can I but enumerate old themes, First that sea-rider Oisin led by the nose Through three enchanted islands, allegorical dreams, Vain gaiety, vain battle, vain repose, Themes of the embittered heart, or so it seems, That might adorn old songs or courtly shows; But what cared I that set him on to ride, I, starved for the bosom of his fairy bride. And then a counter-truth filled out its play, `The Countess Cathleen' was the name I gave it, She, pity-crazed, had given her soul away But masterful Heaven had intervened to save it. I thought my dear must her own soul destroy So did fanaticism and hate enslave it, And this brought forth a dream and soon enough This dream itself had all my thought and love. And when the Fool and Blind Man stole the bread Cuchulain fought the ungovernable sea; Heart mysteries there, and yet when all is said It was the dream itself enchanted me: Character isolated by a deed To engross the present and dominate memory. Players and painted stage took all my love And not those things that they were emblems of. Those masterful images because complete Grew in pure mind but out of what began? A mound of refuse or the sweepings of a street, Old kettles, old bottles, and a broken can, Old iron, old bones, old rags, that raving slut Who keeps the till. Now that my ladder's gone I must lie down where all the ladders start In the foul rag and bone shop of the heart.

name_of_work: The Inward Morning by Henry David Thoreau
content: Packed in my mind lie all the clothes Which outward nature wears, And in its fashion's hourly change It all things else repairs. In vain I look for change abroad, And can no difference find, Till some new ray of peace uncalled Illumes my inmost mind. What is it gilds the trees and clouds, And paints the heavens so gay, But yonder fast-abiding light With its unchanging ray? Lo, when the sun streams through the wood, Upon a winter's morn, Where'er his silent beams intrude, The murky night is gone. How could the patient pine have known The morning breeze would come, Or humble flowers anticipate The insect's noonday hum-- Till the new light with morning cheer From far streamed through the aisles, And nimbly told the forest trees For many stretching miles? I've heard within my inmost soul Such cheerful morning news, In the horizon of my mind Have seen such orient hues, As in the twilight of the dawn, When the first birds awake, Are heard within some silent wood, Where they the small twigs break, Or in the eastern skies are seen, Before the sun appears, The harbingers of summer heats Which from afar he bears.

name_of_work: Sonnet 43: How do I love thee? by Elizabeth Barrett Browning
content: How do I love thee? Let me count the ways. I love thee to the depth and breadth and height My soul can reach, when feeling out of sight For the ends of being and ideal grace. I love thee to the level of every day's Most quiet need, by sun and candle-light. I love thee freely, as men strive for right. I love thee purely, as they turn from praise. I love thee with the passion put to use In my old griefs, and with my childhood's faith. I love thee with a love I seemed to lose With my lost saints. I love thee with the breath, Smiles, tears, of all my life; and, if God choose, I shall but love thee better after death.

Once upon a time, two little friends were playing together in the forest. As they looked around, they saw a dirty acorn appear from the ground. 

"What is that?" one of the little friends asked.
The other one said, "I think it's an acorn. It looks very dirty." 

The two friends walked over to the acorn and saw that it was even dirtier up close. One of them said, "Let's get it cleaned up!" 

The other little friend agreed, so they grabbed the acorn, found a puddle nearby, and put it in the water. 

After they had washed the acorn, they took it out again, and it was now all clean. 

The two friends were very proud of what they had done. Then, all of a sudden, a little bird appeared. It was looking for food, so the two friends fed it the acorn. 

The bird was so happy that it flew away, and the little friends were happy too. Once the bird had gone, they looked at each other and smiled. 

And they all lived happily ever after!

name_of_work: Double, Double Toil and Trouble from Macbeth
content: Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn and caldron bubble. Fillet of a fenny snake, In the caldron boil and bake; Eye of newt and toe of frog, Wool of bat and tongue of dog, Adder's fork and blind-worm's sting, Lizard's leg and howlet's wing, For a charm of powerful trouble, Like a hell-broth boil and bubble. Double, double toil and trouble; Fire burn and caldron bubble. Cool it with a baboon's blood, Then the charm is firm and good.

Anna and Ben are friends. They like to play games together. One day, they play a game with a medal. The medal is shiny and pretty. Anna and Ben both want the medal.

They start to quarrel. They pull the medal from each other. They say, "It is mine!" They do not share. They do not have fun.

Mom sees them quarrel. She is not happy. She says, "Stop! The medal is not yours. It is a prize for the successful person who wins the game. You have to play fair and nice. Then you can have a chance to get the medal."

Anna and Ben listen to Mom. They say sorry to each other. They play the game again. They take turns. They help each other. They have fun.

At the end, Mom gives the medal to the successful person who wins the game. It is Anna. She is happy. She says, "Thank you, Mom. Thank you, Ben. You are a good friend. Do you want to share the medal with me?"

Ben smiles. He says, "Yes, thank you, Anna. You are a good friend too. We can share the medal. We can play more games together."

Anna and Ben hug. They are happy. They are friends.

Once upon a time, there was a careless deer in the woods. The deer loved to search the woods, but it got really cold in the winter. So when the snow started falling, the deer put on its warmest fur to keep itself safe and warm.

The deer still wanted to search the woods, and with its warm fur on, it ran and jumped around finding all sorts of things. It found a bunch of yummy apples, some crunchy leaves to munch on, and even some acorns.

Then it started raining. The deer had to go back to his den to keep dry and safe. But before it went back, it spotted something shiny on the ground. It was a shiny new pocket knife!

The careless deer picked it up, thinking it would make a great present for his mother. So the deer went back to his den, excited to give his mother the pocket knife. His mother was so happy and thanked her little deer for being so thoughtful and kind.

No matter what the weather, the deer still loves to search the woods!

One day, Jane was playing in the backyard of her house when she noticed something in her neighbor's tree. It was something delicious-looking. She wanted to take a look, but she was too small to reach the tree. She was about to give up when she heard someone talking.

"Hi there," said a friendly voice. Jane looked up and saw her neighbor's face peeking out from the window. "What are you looking at?"

Jane explained that she had spotted something delicious in the tree. The neighbor smiled and said, "I know - it's a bowl of cherries! They must have been left there by the birds. Would you like to have some?"

Jane got excited. The neighbor offered to help her. He tied a rope to the top of the tree and hung it down so Jane could climb up to the cherries. Jane was happy to get her delicious treat in the end, but it had been a difficult adventure getting to them.

Once upon a time, there was a mommy and a baby. The mommy was very thirsty and said, "I need to drink some water." The baby saw the mommy and said, "Drink! Drink!" The mommy got some water and drank it all up. The baby was happy and said, "Good job!"

The mommy then looked at the baby and said, "You are such a cute infant." The baby smiled and said, "Thank you!" The mommy then said, "I need to go to the store and get some regular milk for you." The baby clapped and said, "Yay! Milk!"

The mommy went to the store and got some regular milk for the baby. When she got back, she gave the baby the milk and said, "Here you go, sweetie." The baby drank the milk and said, "Yummy!" The mommy and the baby were both happy and smiled at each other. The end.

From weariness I looked out on the stars And there beheld them, fixed in throbbing joy, Nor racked by such mad dance of moods as mars For us each moment's grace with swift alloy. And as they pierced the heavens' serene deep An envy of that one consummate part Swept me, who mock. Whether I laugh or weep, Some inner silences are at my heart. Cold shame is mine for all the masks I wear, Belying that in me which shines and sings Before Him, to face down man's alien stare-- A graceless puppet on unmeaning strings, I that looked out, and saw, and was at rest, Stars, and faint wings, rose-etched along the west.

name_of_work: Miracle on St. David's Day by Gillian Clarke
content: 'They flash upon that inward eye which is the bliss of solitude' (from 'The Daffodils' by William Wordsworth) An afternoon yellow and open-mouthed with daffodils. The sun treads the path among cedars and enormous oaks. It might be a country house, guests strolling, the rumps of gardeners between nursery shrubs. I am reading poetry to the insane. An old woman, interrupting, offers as many buckets of coal as I need. A beautiful chestnut-haired boy listens entirely absorbed. A schizophrenic on a good day, they tell me later. In a cage of first March sun a woman sits not listening, not feeling. In her neat clothes the woman is absent. A big, mild man is tenderly led to his chair. He has never spoken. His labourer's hands on his knees, he rocks gently to the rhythms of the poems. I read to their presences, absences, to the big, dumb labouring man as he rocks. He is suddenly standing, silently, huge and mild, but I feel afraid. Like slow movement of spring water or the first bird of the year in the breaking darkness, the labourer's voice recites 'The Daffodils'. The nurses are frozen, alert; the patients seem to listen. He is hoarse but word-perfect. Outside the daffodils are still as wax, a thousand, ten thousand, their syllables unspoken, their creams and yellows still. Forty years ago, in a Valleys school, the class recited poetry by rote. Since the dumbness of misery fell he has remembered there was a music of speech and that once he had something to say. When he's done, before the applause, we observe the flowers' silence. A thrush sings and the daffodils are flame.

name_of_work: The Definition of Love by Andrew Marvell
content: My love is of a birth as rare As 'tis for object strange and high; It was begotten by Despair Upon Impossibility. Magnanimous Despair alone Could show me so divine a thing Where feeble Hope could ne'er have flown, But vainly flapp'd its tinsel wing. And yet I quickly might arrive Where my extended soul is fixt, But Fate does iron wedges drive, And always crowds itself betwixt. For Fate with jealous eye does see Two perfect loves, nor lets them close; Their union would her ruin be, And her tyrannic pow'r depose. And therefore her decrees of steel Us as the distant poles have plac'd, (Though love's whole world on us doth wheel) Not by themselves to be embrac'd; Unless the giddy heaven fall, And earth some new convulsion tear; And, us to join, the world should all Be cramp'd into a planisphere. As lines, so loves oblique may well Themselves in every angle greet; But ours so truly parallel, Though infinite, can never meet. Therefore the love which us doth bind, But Fate so enviously debars, Is the conjunction of the mind, And opposition of the stars.

Once upon a time, there was a hunter. He liked to go into the forest to find animals. One day, he found a unique bird with colorful feathers. He wanted to catch it and show it to his friends. But the bird was too fast and flew away. 

The hunter was sad and angry. He went deeper into the forest to find the bird. He searched and searched, but he couldn't find it. He was lost and didn't know how to go back home. 

As the sun went down, it became dark and scary. The hunter was scared and cold. He tried to find a way out, but he couldn't. He was stuck in the forest forever.

I work all day, and get half-drunk at night. Waking at four to soundless dark, I stare. In time the curtain-edges will grow light. Till then I see what's really always there: Unresting death, a whole day nearer now, Making all thought impossible but how And where and when I shall myself die. Arid interrogation: yet the dread Of dying, and being dead, Flashes afresh to hold and horrify. The mind blanks at the glare. Not in remorse --The good not done, the love not given, time Torn off unused--nor wretchedly because An only life can take so long to climb Clear of its wrong beginnings, and may never; But at the total emptiness for ever, The sure extinction that we travel to And shall be lost in always. Not to be here, Not to be anywhere, And soon; nothing more terrible, nothing more true. This is a special way of being afraid No trick dispels. Religion used to try, That vast moth-eaten musical brocade Created to pretend we never die, And specious stuff that says No rational being Can fear a thing it will not feel, not seeing That this is what we fear--no sight, no sound, No touch or taste or smell, nothing to think with, Nothing to love or link with, The anaesthetic from which none come round. And so it stays just on the edge of vision, A small unfocused blur, a standing chill That slows each impulse down to indecision. Most things may never happen: this one will, And realisation of it rages out In furnace-fear when we are caught without People or drink. Courage is no good: It means not scaring others. Being brave Lets no one off the grave. Death is no different whined at than withstood. Slowly light strengthens, and the room takes shape. It stands plain as a wardrobe, what we know, Have always known, know that we can't escape, Yet can't accept. One side will have to go. Meanwhile telephones crouch, getting ready to ring In locked-up offices, and all the uncaring Intricate rented world begins to rouse. The sky is white as clay, with no sun. Work has to be done. Postmen like doctors go from house to house.

Pure? What does it mean? The tongues of hell Are dull, dull as the triple Tongues of dull, fat Cerberus Who wheezes at the gate. Incapable Of licking clean The aguey tendon, the sin, the sin. The tinder cries. The indelible smell Of a snuffed candle! Love, love, the low smokes roll From me like Isadora's scarves, I'm in a fright One scarf will catch and anchor in the wheel, Such yellow sullen smokes Make their own element. They will not rise, But trundle round the globe Choking the aged and the meek, The weak Hothouse baby in its crib, The ghastly orchid Hanging its hanging garden in the air, Devilish leopard! Radiation turned it white And killed it in an hour. Greasing the bodies of adulterers Like Hiroshima ash and eating in. The sin. The sin. Darling, all night I have been flickering, off, on, off, on. The sheets grow heavy as a lecher's kiss. Three days. Three nights. Lemon water, chicken Water, water make me retch. I am too pure for you or anyone. Your body Hurts me as the world hurts God. I am a lantern---- My head a moon Of Japanese paper, my gold beaten skin Infinitely delicate and infinitely expensive. Does not my heat astound you! And my light! All by myself I am a huge camellia Glowing and coming and going, flush on flush. I think I am going up, I think I may rise---- The beads of hot metal fly, and I love, I Am a pure acetylene Virgin Attended by roses, By kisses, by cherubim, By whatever these pink things mean! Not you, nor him Nor him, nor him (My selves dissolving, old whore petticoats)---- To Paradise.

My father was four years in the war, and afterward, according to my mother, had nothing to say. She says he trembled in his sleep the next four years. My father was twice the father of sons miscarried, and afterward said nothing. My mother keeps this silence also. Four times my father was on strike, and according to my mother; had nothing to say. She says the company didn't understand, nor can her son, the meaning of an extra fifteen cents an hour in 1956 to a man tending a glass furnace in August. I have always remembered him a tired man. I have respected him like a guest and expected nothing. It is April now. My life lies before me, enticing as the woman at my side. Now, in April, I want him to speak. I want to stand against the worn body of his pain. I want to try it on like a coat that does not fit.

Jessica and her mom were in the kitchen. Jessica was watching intently as her mom prepared a special cake.

"What are you making, Mommy?" Jessica asked. 

Her mom smiled. "I'm making a beautiful birthday cake, sweetheart," she answered.

Jessica watched as her mom carefully added the flour, sugar, and milk. She always loved watching her mom make things in the kitchen.

When the cake was finished, Jessica saw that it had a point on the top.

"What's the point for?" Jessica asked.

"The point is for a special candle," her mom said.

Jessica couldn't wait for the cake to be done! She knew that when it was ready it would look beautiful.

Once upon a time there was a brave little bear who loved to go on adventures. One day, he decided to explore the forest near his home. He was feeling quite adventurous, and he started to run! He ran and ran until he tripped and fell down.

The little bear was a bit sad and scared, but then he noticed a beautiful butterfly and decided to follow it. The butterfly flew away, and the brave little bear ran after it.

As he chased the butterfly, he ended up far away from home. He started to feel tired, and the sun was setting. He was getting very scared and sad, but then he heard a voice. 

The voice said, "Don't worry, little bear. Follow the stars, and you'll find your way home!"

The brave little bear followed the stars, and he eventually found his way home. He was so happy and thankful that he found his way back. 

The end.

Once there was a body that was very smooth. Everywhere the body went, it made people smile. One day, the body decided to provide a present. It brought lots of flowers in a big basket. Everyone was so happy when they saw the flowers. Everyone thanked the body for providing them with a special present. 

The body felt happy and smiled. It was so happy to provide the people with something special. From then on, the body always looked for new ways to provide fun things for the people. It always tried to make the people happy. 

The body continued to provide the people with different goodies. Everyone was so thankful to have a body that was so kind. The body was always happy that it could provide something special to the people. 

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a lively duck who lived in a pond. He admired the pond's beauty, but he was missing something. One day he spotted a pile of ash across the pond. He wondered what it was so he paddled over to take a closer look.

The ash had a sparkle in it, and the duck was amazed! He carefully used his beak to pick up some of the ash, and he admired its color and texture. He then flew back to his pond and sprinkled some of the ash around.

Suddenly, the water lit up! Sparkles of light were everywhere. The duck was so happy! He admired the mostly pond's beauty and knew that the ash gave it a special touch. He swam around in the lively water, feeling grateful to have found the ash. The end.

name_of_work: The Fisherman Mourned by His Wife by Patrick Fernando
content: When you were not quite thirty and the sun Had not yet tanned you into old-boat brown, When you were not quite thirty and had not begun To be embittered like the rest, nor grown obsessed with death, then would you come Hot with continence upon the sea Chaste as a gull flying pointed home, In haste to be with me! Now that, being dead, you are beyond detection. And I need not be discreet, let us confess. It was not love that married us no affection, But elders' persuasion, not even loneliness, Recall how first you were so impatient and afraid, My eyes were open in the dark unlike in love, Trembling, lest in fear, you'll let me go a maid, Trembling on the other hand for my virginity. Three months the monsoon thrashed the sea, and you Remained at home; the sky cracked like a shell In thunder, the rain broke through, At last when the pouring ceased the storm winds fell, When gulls returned new plumed and wild, When in our wind torn flamboyant New buds broke, I was with child. My face was wan while telling you and voice fell low And you seemed full of guilt and not to know Whether to repent or rejoice over the situation You nodded at the ground and went to sea. But soon I was to you more than God or temptation. And so were you to me. Men come and go, some say they understand. Our children weep, the youngest thinks you're fast asleep. There is fear and wonderment. You had grown so familiar as my hand, That I cannot with simple grief Assuage dismemberment. Outside the wind despoils of leaf Tree that it used to nurse; Once more the flamboyant is torn, The sky cracks like a shell again. So someone practical has gone To make them bring the hearse Before the rain.

name_of_work: Long, too long America by Walt Whitman
content: Long, too long America, Traveling roads all even and peaceful you learn'd from joys and prosperity only, But now, ah now, to learn from crises of anguish, advancing, grappling with direst fate and recoiling not, And now to conceive and show to the world what your children en-masse really are, (For who except myself has yet conceiv'd what your children en-masse really are?)

Once upon a time, there was a bear who was very excited. She wanted to look for something special but she did not know what it was.

One day, she saw a strange looking tree in the middle of the forest. As she walked closer to it, she heard a voice crying.

The bear was very curious, she crept closer to see who was weeping. It was an old, small bird who was very sad. The bear asked the bird why he was crying. The bird told her that he had lost all his feathers and couldn't fly anymore.

The bear heard this and felt very sorry for the bird. She sang a beautiful song and brushed the bird with her paws. The old bird smiled and his beautiful feathers started to grow back!

The bear was so happy and excited for her new friend. After that, they were always together. The bear and the bird brought joy to the forest and all the animals around them.

Once upon a time there was a big pillow. It was so big it filled the whole room! But one day, Hanna had a plan. She wanted to push the pillow outside. So she started pushing. She pushed and pushed until the pillow was outside the house.

Hanna was so happy to see the pillow outside. But then, she found something strange. A big pill was stuck in the middle of the pillow! Hanna was very curious and wanted to know what it was. She looked around, but she couldn't find the answer!

Finally, Hanna decided to see what would happen if she pushed the pill. She grabbed the pill and gave it a push.

Suddenly, the pill started to roll down the street! Hanna followed the pill, pushing it with all her might. After a while the pill came to a stop in the park.

Hanna was so excited to see what the pill had done. She looked around and saw that the pill had made a big hole in the ground! Hanna couldn't believe it.

The big pill had made a big surprise for Hanna that day! From then on, every time she saw a big pillow she would always think of how she pushed the pill and made a big surprise!

Once there was a little boy called Jack. He was a very modest boy who loved to have lots of adventures. One day Jack put on his cape and decided to zoom around his garden. He zoomed around the trees, the flowers and the grass. He even zoomed around his garden fence!

But then, Jack heard a loud voice coming from one of the plants. It was a judge! He was a strict old judge who wanted to give Jack an important message. The judge said "Jack, be sure to stay modest. Zoom around if you need to, but always remember to be modest."

Jack was surprised, but he did as the judge said. He thanked the judge and promised to be a modest boy from now on. He zoomed off back to his house, and from that day on, Jack remembered to be modest and have lots of adventures. He was the happiest little boy around.

One day, Spike was feeling very sleepy. He was so tired he just wanted to keep still. He had been running and playing all day.

Spike decided he should take a nap. He stretched and lay down on the floor. He snuggled up and kept really still. His eyes were getting heavier, and before long he had fallen asleep.

As he was sleeping, Spike dreamt of far-off places. He kept dreaming and dreaming until he was awoken by a loud noise. It was his mom, calling him for dinner. Spike rubbed his eyes and got up. He was so sleepy, but he knew he had to keep going!

Once upon a time, a silly old man called Grampy was very curious about beans. He wanted to observe the beans to find out why they were so crazy.

So he decided to go to the bean shop. Grampy stood in front of the place and stared at the beans for a long time.

The shopkeeper said, "Hello! Can I help you?".

Grampy replied, "Yes please! I want to observe these beans and find out why they're so crazy!".

The shopkeeper smiled, "Ah, very well. I think you'll be surprised when you see what happens with the beans."

Grampy quickly bought the beans, thanked the shopkeeper and went home. 

When he got back home, he poured out the beans. Then to his surprise, the beans started to jump around the room! They were dancing, singing and doing crazy things. Grampy couldn't believe it! It was the craziest thing he had ever seen. 

Grampy had finally discovered why the beans were so crazy. They weren't just beans, they were magical beans!

With the frenzy of an old snake shedding its skin, the speckled road, scored with ruts, smelling of mold, twisted on itself and reentered the forest where the dasheen leaves thicken and folk stories begin. Sunset would threaten us as we climbed closer to her house up the asphalt hill road, whose yam vines wrangled over gutters with the dark reek of moss, the shutters closing like the eyelids of that mimosa called Ti-Marie; then -- lucent as paper lanterns, lamplight glowed through the ribs, house after house -- there was her own lamp at the black twist of the path. There's childhood, and there's childhood's aftermath. She began to remember at the minute of the fireflies, to the sound of pipe water banging in kerosene tins, stories she told to my brother and myself. Her leaves were the libraries of the Caribbean. The luck that was ours, those fragrant origins! Her head was magnificent, Sidone. In the gully of her voice shadows stood up and walked, her voice travels my shelves. She was the lamplight in the stare of two mesmerized boys still joined in one shadow, indivisible twins.

Once upon a time, there was a little girl named Lily. She loved to play pretend with her dolls and teddy bears. One day, she pretended to be a princess who lived in a big castle.

For dinner, the princess had broccoli. She didn't like it at first, but then she pretended that the broccoli was a magical tree that gave her powers. She ate it all up and felt strong and brave.

After dinner, the princess went to her delicate bed made of soft pillows and blankets. She cuddled with her teddy bear and fell asleep, dreaming of more magical adventures. The end.

Tom and Lily are playing in the park. They see a big kangaroo with a baby in her pouch. They want to pet the kangaroo, but she is scared of them.

"Hello, kangaroo," Tom says. "We are nice. Can we touch you?"

The kangaroo shakes her head. She hops away from Tom and Lily. She looks for a safe place to hide.

Tom and Lily run after the kangaroo. They think it is a game. They do not see the big fence with a sign that says "Do not enter".

The kangaroo sees the fence. She jumps over it. She lands in a big cage with a lock. She is trapped.

Tom and Lily reach the fence. They see the kangaroo in the cage. They see the sign that says "Do not enter". They feel bad.

"Sorry, kangaroo," Lily says. "We did not mean to scare you. We just wanted to be your friends."

The kangaroo looks at Tom and Lily. She sees that they are sorry. She nods her head.

Tom and Lily look for a way to help the kangaroo. They see a big key on a hook. They take the key and put it in the lock. They turn the key and open the cage.

The kangaroo is free. She hops out of the cage. She thanks Tom and Lily with a smile. She takes her baby and hops away.

Tom and Lily wave goodbye to the kangaroo. They are happy that they helped her. They go back to the park.

It starts to rain. Tom and Lily are wet. They do not mind. They laugh and splash in the puddles. They have fun.

Once upon a time, there was a girl who loved to play at the park. One day, she went to the park to have some fun. 

Suddenly, she noticed a big lock on the gate. She asked the park keeper, "What is the lock for?"

The park keeper said, "This lock keeps people from taking something that doesn't belong to them."

The girl asked, "What is there to take?" 

The park keeper said, "There is a ball hidden inside and if someone takes it, they will feel very guilty." 

The girl was surprised. She said, "I will never take something that doesn't belong to me!"

The park keeper was very happy. He said, "You are a good girl. Please don't take anything that doesn't belong to you." 

The girl was glad and felt proud. She had a wonderful time at the park that day without taking anything that didn't belong to her.

Tom and Lily went to the park with their mom. They saw a big pond with many fish. Tom and Lily liked the fish. They wanted to feed them.

"Mom, can we give the fish some bread?" Tom asked.

"Sure, but be careful. Don't throw too much bread or you will make the water dirty. And don't touch the fish or you will hurt them." Mom said.

Tom and Lily nodded. They broke some bread into small pieces and threw them into the pond. The fish came to eat the bread. They were happy.

But then, a rude boy came to the pond. He had a big stick. He started to poke the fish with the stick. He laughed when the fish jumped and splashed.

"Hey, stop that! You are being rude and mean to the fish!" Lily shouted.

"Yeah, leave the fish alone! They are not toys!" Tom added.

The rude boy ignored them. He kept poking the fish with the stick. He made the fish scared and sad.

Tom and Lily ran to their mom. They told her what the rude boy was doing.

"Mom, there is a rude boy who is hurting the fish with a stick. He won't stop. He is making the fish cry." Lily said.

"That's not nice at all. Let's go and tell him to stop." Mom said.

Mom, Tom and Lily went to the pond. They saw the rude boy still poking the fish with the stick.

"Excuse me, young man. What are you doing?" Mom asked.

"I'm having fun. The fish are funny. They jump and splash." The rude boy said.

"That's not fun. That's cruel. You are hurting the fish and making them unhappy. You need to behave and respect the animals. How would you like it if someone poked you with a stick?" Mom said.

The rude boy looked at Mom. He looked at the stick. He looked at the fish. He realized he was wrong. He felt sorry.

"I'm sorry. I didn't think. I won't do it again. I'm sorry, fish." The rude boy said.

He dropped the stick and walked away. He learned his lesson.

Tom and Lily smiled. They thanked their mom. They said sorry to the fish. They gave them some more bread. The fish forgave them. They were happy again.

The end.

Once upon a time, there was a prince who lived in a big castle. He was very happy because he had many friends and a big garden to play in. One day, the prince saw a modern car driving by and he clapped his hands in excitement. He had never seen anything like it before.

The next day, the prince's father, the king, came to him and said, "I have a surprise for you, my son. I have bought you a modern car!" The prince was so happy and he clapped his hands again. He couldn't wait to drive it around the castle.

The prince was very grateful to his father for the wonderful gift. From that day on, the prince loved all things modern and would always clap his hands in excitement whenever he saw something new and exciting.

name_of_work: You Will Know When You Get There by Allen Curnow
content: Nobody comes up from the sea as late as this in the day and the season, and nobody else goes down the last steep kilometre, wet-metalled where a shower passed shredding the light which keeps pouring out of its tank in the sky, through summits, trees, vapours thickening and thinning. Too credibly by half celestial, the dammed reservoir up there keeps emptying while the light lasts over the sea where 'it gathers the gold against it'. The light is bits of crushed rock randomly glinting underfoot, wetted by the short shower, and down you go and so in its way does the sun which gets there first. Boys, two of them, turn campfirelit faces, a hesitancy to speak is a hesitancy of the earth rolling back and away behind this man going down to the sea with a bag to pick mussels, having an arrangement with the tide, the ocean to be shallowed three point seven meters, one hour's light to be left, and there's the excrescent moon sponging off the last of it. A door slams, a heavy wave, a door, the sea-floor shudders. Down you go alone, so late, into the surge-black fissure.

Once upon a time there lived a little girl, named Jane. Jane was very shy. She had a secret wish to help her family, but she was too afraid to ask for help.

One day, she wanted to surprise her family. She had the plan to wash the family's laundry! She took all their clothes and brought them down to the river. She was so excited to surprise her family, she didn't notice the rain clouds in the sky.

When the rain started pouring down, Jane panicked. She tried to get all the clothes back to the house, but it was too late. Everything was so wet and heavy. 

Jane felt embarrassed and ashamed and ran away. 

The bad ending of her story taught her a lesson. Being brave and not being too shy can help in situations like this. It's important to trust yourself, and to communicate and ask for help when you need it.

Once upon a time, there was a girl who loved Spring. She loved to see the blossoms on the trees, the song of the birds, and the pretty flowers.

One day, she went outside and saw a white cloth flying in the wind. It was so beautiful! She ran over and picked it up. She knew it was a special cloth and she wanted to do something special with it.

So that night, she tiptoed out of her bedroom and went outside. She spread the white cloth on the grass and waited.

Suddenly, the air was filled with a spritely music. And the cloth began to move. It was as if it was dancing in the wind! The girl stood and watched until the sun came up and the wind stilled. 

The girl gathered the white cloth, held it close and went inside. She was so very happy, for she now had a magical memory of a special Spring night.

Once upon a time, there was a boy named Tim. Tim loved to travel. One day, he went on a walk with his dog, Spot. They walked and walked until they found a big hill. Tim and Spot climbed the hill and saw a pretty rainbow.

Tim and Spot walked to the end of the rainbow. There, they found a big box. Tim opened the box and saw something shiny. It was gold! Tim and Spot were very happy. They knew they found something special.

Tim and Spot took the gold back to their house. They showed it to their mom and dad. Now, Tim and his family were rich. They used the gold to buy a big new house and lots of toys. Tim, Spot, and their family lived happily ever after.

name_of_work: There was an Indian by J.C. Squire
content: There was an Indian, who had known no change, Who strayed content along a sunlit beach Gathering shells. He heard a sudden strange Commingled noise: looked up; and gasped for speech. For in the bay, where nothing was before, Moved on the sea, by magic, huge canoes With bellying cloths on poles, and not one oar, And fluttering coloured signs and clambering crews. And he, in fear, this naked man alone, His fallen hands forgetting all their shells, His lips gone pale, knelt low behind a stone, And stared, and saw, and did not understand, Columbus's doom-burdened caravels Slant to the shore, and all their seaman land.

name_of_work: The Self Banished by Edmund Waller
content: It is not that I love you less Than when before your feet I lay, But to prevent the sad increase Of hopeless love, I keep away. In vain (alas!) for everything Which I have known belong to you, Your form does to my fancy bring, And makes my old wounds bleed anew. Who in the spring from the new sun Already has a fever got, Too late begins those shafts to shun, Which Phoebus through his veins has shot. Too late he would the pain assuage, And to thick shadows does retire; About with him he bears the rage, And in his tainted blood the fire. But vow'd I have, and never must Your banish'd servant trouble you; For if I break, you may distrust The vow I made to love you, too.

Sara loves animals. She wants to be a veterinarian when she grows up. A veterinarian is a person who helps animals when they are sick or hurt. Sara likes to play with her stuffed animals and pretend they are her patients.

One day, Sara finds a small bird in her backyard. The bird has a broken wing and cannot fly. Sara feels sorry for the bird and wants to help it. She carefully picks up the bird and brings it inside her house. She puts the bird in a shoebox with some soft towels and some water.

Sara tells her mom about the bird. Her mom is proud of Sara for being kind and brave. She says, "You are a good veterinarian, Sara. But we need to take the bird to a real veterinarian. They have special tools and medicine to fix the bird's wing."

Sara nods and agrees. She says, "Can I come with you, mom? I want to see how they help the bird."

"Of course, Sara. But you have to be calm and quiet when we are there. The bird is scared and needs to rest. And we have to clean our hands before and after we touch the bird. We don't want to make it sick or dirty."

Sara and her mom go to the veterinarian's office. They meet a nice lady who wears a white coat and a name tag. She says, "Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I'm a veterinarian. What do you have in the box?"

Sara shows her the bird and tells her what happened. Dr. Lee smiles and says, "You are a very good veterinarian, Sara. You did the right thing to bring the bird here. Let me take a look at it and see what I can do."

Sara watches as Dr. Lee gently examines the bird. She uses a small scissors to cut the feathers around the wing. She uses a small stick and some tape to make a splint for the wing. She uses a small syringe to give the bird some medicine. She says, "The bird has a fracture in its wing. It will take some time to heal, but it should be able to fly again. I will keep the bird here for a few days and then release it back to the wild. Do you want to name the bird, Sara?"

Sara thinks for a moment and says, "I want to name it Sunny. Because it has yellow feathers and it makes me happy."

Dr. Lee says, "That's a lovely name, Sara. Sunny is lucky to have you as a friend. You are a very good veterinarian, Sara. Thank you for caring for Sunny."

Sara smiles and says, "Thank you, Dr. Lee. You are a very good veterinarian, too. Can I come back and visit Sunny before you let him go?"

Dr. Lee says, "Of course, Sara. You are always welcome here. Just remember to be calm and clean when you see Sunny. He needs your love and support."

Sara hugs her mom and says, "I love you, mom. And I love Sunny. And I love being a veterinarian."

name_of_work: Portrait in Georgia by Jean Toomer
content: Hair-braided chestnut, coiled like a lyncher's rope, Eye-fagots, Lips-old scars, or the first red blisters, Breath-the last sweet scent of cane, And her slim body, white as the ash of black flesh after flame.

name_of_work: No More Boomerang by Oodgeroo Noonuccal
content: No more boomerang No more spear; Now alll civilized- Colour bar and beer. No more corroboree, Gay dance and din. Now we got movies, And pay to go in. No more sharing What the hunter brings. Now we work for money, Then pay it back for things. Now we track bosses To catch a few bob, Now we go walkabout On bus to the job. One time naked, Who never knew shame; Now we put clothes on To hide whatsaname. No more gunya, Now bungalow, Paid by hire purchase In twenty year or so. Lay down the stone axe, Take up the steel, And work like a nigger For a white man meal. No more firesticks That made the whites scoff. Now all electric, And no better off. Bunyip he finish, Now got instead White fella Bunyip, Call him Red. Abstract picture now- What they coming at? Cripes, in our caves we Did better than that. Black hunted wallaby, White hunt dollar; White fella witch-doctor Wear dog-collar. No more message-stick; Lubras and lads Got television now. Mostly ads. Lay down the woomera, Lay down the waddy. Now we got atom-bomb, End everybody.

name_of_work: The Book of Questions, III by Pablo Neruda
content: Tell me, is the rose naked or is that her only dress? Why do trees conceal the splendor of their roots? Who hears the regrets of the thieving automobile? Is there anything in the world sadder than a train standing in the rain?

name_of_work: One Life by Paul Laurence Dunbar
content: Oh, I am hurt to death, my Love; The shafts of Fate have pierced my striving heart, And I am sick and weary of The endless pain and smart. My soul is weary of the strife, And chafes at life, and chafes at life. Time mocks me with fair promises; A blooming future grows a barren past, Like rain my fair full-blossomed trees Unburden in the blast. The harvest fails on grain and tree, Nor comes to me, nor comes to me. The stream that bears my hopes abreast Turns ever from my way its pregnant tide. My laden boat, torn from its rest, Drifts to the other side. So all my hopes are set astray, And drift away, and drift away. The lark sings to me at the morn, And near me wings her skyward-soaring flight; But pleasure dies as soon as born, The owl takes up the night, And night seems long and doubly dark; I miss the lark, I miss the lark. Let others labor as they may, I'll sing and sigh alone, and write my line. Their fate is theirs, or grave or gay, And mine shall still be mine. I know the world holds joy and glee, But not for me,--'t is not for me.

name_of_work: The Lily of the Valley by Paul Laurence Dunbar
content: Sweetest of the flowers a-blooming In the fragrant vernal days Is the Lily of the Valley With its soft, retiring ways. Well, you chose this humble blossom As the nurse's emblem flower, Who grows more like her ideal Every day and every hour. Like the Lily of the Valley In her honesty and worth, Ah, she blooms in truth and virtue In the quiet nooks of earth. Tho' she stands erect in honor When the heart of mankind bleeds, Still she hides her own deserving In the beauty of her deeds. In the silence of the darkness Where no eye may see and know, There her footsteps shod with mercy, And fleet kindness come and go. Not amid the sounds of plaudits, Nor before the garish day, Does she shed her soul's sweet perfume, Does she take her gentle way. But alike her ideal flower, With its honey-laden breath, Still her heart blooms forth its beauty In the valley shades of death.

Tommy was having a gloomy day. He was walking along in the park, feeling itchy and wondering just why he was feeling so itchy and gloomy. He heard a voice behind him and turned around, but he only saw a patch of grass.

"Hey, little guy," said the voice.

Tommy peered into the grass. To his surprise, a funny little bug was talking to him.

"Why you itchin' so much?" asked the bug.

"I don' know," said Tommy, scratching his itchy arms.

The bug smiled. He pointed to a tall tree with an old, hollowed-out trunk. "Have you considered climbin' up there to get away from those itches?"

Tommy thought about it for a moment. He was scared he might fall, but he was also feeling a little bit brave. He decided to give it a try.

He waved goodbye to the bug and started climbing the tree. He was slow and careful, but he made it all the way to the top. Suddenly, his itches were gone! He smiled in joy and let out a little laugh.

The bug cheered from below. "You did it! You got away from your itches!" Tommy was so relieved and happy. He waved to the bug, thanking him for his help. From then on, Tommy never felt gloomy again.

name_of_work: Death In Leamington by John Betjeman
content: She died in the upstairs bedroom By the light of the ev'ning star That shone through the plate glass window From over Leamington Spa Beside her the lonely crochet Lay patiently and unstirred, But the fingers that would have work'd it Were dead as the spoken word. And Nurse came in with the tea-things Breast high 'mid the stands and chairs- But Nurse was alone with her own little soul, And the things were alone with theirs. She bolted the big round window, She let the blinds unroll, She set a match to the mantle, She covered the fire with coal. And "Tea!" she said in a tiny voice "Wake up! It's nearly five" Oh! Chintzy, chintzy cheeriness, Half dead and half alive. Do you know that the stucco is peeling? Do you know that the heart will stop? From those yellow Italianate arches Do you hear the plaster drop? Nurse looked at the silent bedstead, At the gray, decaying face, As the calm of a Leamington ev'ning Drifted into the place. She moved the table of bottles Away from the bed to the wall; And tiptoeing gently over the stairs Turned down the gas in the hall.

name_of_work: Lines Written in Kensington Gardens by Matthew Arnold
content: In this lone, open glade I lie, Screen'd by deep boughs on either hand; And at its end, to stay the eye, Those black-crown'd, red-boled pine-trees stand! Birds here make song, each bird has his, Across the girdling city's hum. How green under the boughs it is! How thick the tremulous sheep-cries come! Sometimes a child will cross the glade To take his nurse his broken toy; Sometimes a thrush flit overhead Deep in her unknown day's employ. Here at my feet what wonders pass, What endless, active life is here! What blowing daisies, fragrant grass! An air-stirr'd forest, fresh and clear. Scarce fresher is the mountain-sod Where the tired angler lies, stretch'd out, And, eased of basket and of rod, Counts his day's spoil, the spotted trout. In the huge world, which roars hard by, Be others happy if they can! But in my helpless cradle I Was breathed on by the rural Pan. I, on men's impious uproar hurl'd, Think often, as I hear them rave, That peace has left the upper world And now keeps only in the grave. Yet here is peace for ever new! When I who watch them am away, Still all things in this glade go through The changes of their quiet day. Then to their happy rest they pass! The flowers upclose, the birds are fed, The night comes down upon the grass, The child sleeps warmly in his bed. Calm soul of all things! make it mine To feel, amid the city's jar, That there abides a peace of thine, Man did not make, and cannot mar. The will to neither strive nor cry, The power to feel with others give! Calm, calm me more! nor let me die Before I have begun to live.

Once upon a time, there was a little bear who loved to play. One day, he wanted to explore the world, so he jumped into a big forest. He made his way through the thick trees and soon found an old mask. He thought it looked so cool and put it on his face. It was so thick, it almost covered his whole head.

Suddenly, the little bear heard a noise. He looked around and saw a big, brown spider crawling near him. He was scared and quickly jumped behind a tree. He peeked his head around the tree and saw the spider was getting closer. He quickly grabbed a stick and started to mark a circle around himself.

The spider stopped at the marks on the ground. It was curious, but it was too scared to cross the line. The little bear smiled and patted the mask on his face. Thanks to the thick mask, he'd been able to make the spider stay away. He felt brave and he felt safe.

From that day on, the little bear kept the mask with him to remind him of his bravery. He would never forget the day he decided to mark a circle around himself.

Once upon a time there was a little boy who loved to relax. Every day he would take a nap and dream of wonderful things. 

One day, his mom cooked some soup and tried to get him to eat it. But the soup smelled weird and the little boy didn't want to eat it. He tried to relax and ignore the soup.

The moral of this story is that it's important to be open minded and try new things.

Once upon a time, there was poor Sarah. She lived in a small house with just her four-legged buddy, Max.

One afternoon, Sarah and Max decided to venture outside and explore the world. They came upon a strange chest and Max barked with excitement. Sarah bent down and twisted the golden latch, and opened the chest. 

Inside, there was a map and some jewels. But Sarah was not interested in these things as she had nothing to store them in. 

Then a voice came from the sky. "If you can solve my riddle, you can have the chest," it said.

"If an apple is red, what color is a grape?" the voice asked.

Max looked up and barked, "Purple!" 

The voice laughed and said, "Yes you are right! Here is the chest. It is now yours!" 

Sarah was so excited. She thanked the voice and then carried the chest home. It was the perfect size for her and Max to store all of their treasures. 

The End.
